The four objects that support and sustain the faculties serve as their bases.
If the four objects, such as visible form and so forth, are not separated from the faculties,
then although they are not the [primary] supports themselves, they may still be said to be "bases."
This [body] is that which is closely attached to, supported by, and serves as the support for the mind and its associates;
it is called the "basis" (āśraya) and is termed "appropriated" (upātta).
The mind and mental factors [in turn] depend upon that basis.
Because loss and gain follow one another in turn:
that is to say, when the mind and mental factors give rise to sorrow and suffering, there is loss;
and when they give rise to joy and pleasure, there is gain. Furthermore, the basis upon which these arise is likewise subject to loss or gain.
The basis is also benefited;
if the basis receives the benefit of excellent food and so forth,
the mind and other factors are likewise benefited.
When there is damage from poor food and so forth,
the mind and its associates are likewise damaged;
for this reason, these nine elements are termed "appropriated," which refers to all worldly beings.

Regarding the five physical sense faculties and the four objects that support them, it is said that there is "contact with awareness" within their coexistence; for when these nine groups of conditions come into contact and encounter one another, they are able to perceive suffering, pleasure, and so forth.
That which is contrary to this is called "non-appropriated" (*anupātta*). The *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya-nyāyānusāra* states that the *Vibhāṣā* says:
"If various material phenomena (*rūpadharma*) are subject to oppression, severance, or destruction, they are able to produce suffering."
That which is contrary to this can produce pleasure.
That which is comprised within one's own body is called "appropriated" (upātta). Other masters say:
If sentient beings grasp [these things] as their own self,
they protect them at all times and in all places through various means from conditions such as grass, ash, fire, thorns, frost, and hail.
That which is encompassed by one's own body is called "appropriated" (upātta).
Thus has been explained that which reaches both [categories] and that which is neither;
hereafter begins the ninth section: the gate of the primary elements (mahābhūta) and their derivatives (bhautika).
The tenth section, the gate of accumulation and non-accumulation, may be understood.
As for the passage from "Venerable Buddhadeva" up to "only the nature of the great elements," this records his doctrinal position.
This can be understood.
Furthermore, the *Nyāyabindu* (Treatise on Right Reasoning), chapter five, states:
"The Dārṣṭāntika masters speak as follows."
Regarding the claim that "derived matter is not distinct from the primary elements," that statement is incorrect; it is certainly not the ultimate truth.
The Master [Vasubandhu] refutes this, stating that solidity, moisture, and so forth are not what is apprehended by the eye and other sense faculties.
Therefore, one knows that solidity and so forth are not form, sound, and so forth.
One knows this because they are not perceived by the body-faculty in the same way as form, sound, and so forth are.
Form and so forth are not solidity, moisture, and so on.
Furthermore, the scriptural authority is the Sūtra which states that "all [derived matter] are not primary elements.
This is the proof from scripture.
This can be understood.
If so, why [is it said] "up to and including the full explanation"?
[It was said by] Buddhadeva.
Citing scripture as an objection: If the eye and other faculties are not derived from the primary elements (*mahābhūta*), why does the Sūtra say: "What is called the internal earth element?
It is that which exists within the mass of flesh of the eye"?
"If there were internal, individual solidity and solid-like qualities," and so forth,
as extensively explained;
that sutra speaks of solidity and other such qualities in relation to the eye.
Therefore, it is known that the eye-faculty is itself solidity and so forth;
in that sutra, the eye is designated as the "fleshly mass."
The "fleshly lump" is the general;
"solidity" and so forth are the particulars.
The particulars depend upon the general.
Therefore, it is said that "among them" is used to exclude non-sentient things;
and "if internal," it is said that "sentient beings are distinct" means they are called individual because their names differ, or they are called individual because their sizes differ.
The exclusion of moisture and other qualities is termed "solidity. That which is solid and not of a single [identical] nature is called a "type of solidity" (*khakkhaṭatvajāti*).
Alternatively, this very nature of solidity that exists within other types of solidity is what is called a "type of solidity."
...up to the detailed explanation of the nature of moisture, warmth, and motion.

Regarding their claim that there is no contradiction in [the sense-faculties] not being separate from [their respective elements], the Master [Vasubandhu], in order to harmonize with the Sūtra, explains that the eye-faculty is indeed a distinct category of derived matter (*upādāya-rūpa*).
The lump of flesh is precisely the four objects that support the sense organs;
their natures are each distinct.
The world does not understand the true substance of the eye faculty.
The name "eye" is established upon this mass of flesh;
this mass of flesh, in its entirety,
is said to be composed of the primary elements (mahābhūta) derived from the eye-faculty (cakṣur-indriya), none of which are separate from it.
Therefore, that sutra states that within the fleshy mass of the eye-faculty (*cakṣur-indriya*),
there exists the essential nature of solidity and so forth which serves as its support;
it does not mean that the actual eye is itself solidity and so forth.
Regarding the passage in the *Garbha-avakrānti-sūtra* where the meaning of differentiation is established,
the author of the treatise further provides a specific explanation for why the sūtra speaks only of the six elements as constituting the person (*pudgala*).
This is intended to demonstrate that these six [elements] are present at the very moment of initial conception.
Their substance and function are powerful and superior,
for they are able to accomplish the fundamental tasks of a person;
this is because the four great elements are the basis upon which derived matter depends.
Space is the basis for motion;
the mind is the basis for mental factors.
Because these bases are preeminent, they are mentioned separately, and not merely those [other phenomena] alone.
This is explained in detail in the fifty-sixth fascicle of the *Yogācārabhūmi*.
Although the Sūtra speaks of the six types of contact (*sparśa*),
there are nevertheless other mental factors (*caitasika-dharma*).
Although the Sūtra speaks of six elements,
what prevents there being other derived matter?
If you argue that because it mentions six elements, there can be no other derived matter, [that is not so].
The Sūtra also speaks of the six types of contact; thus,
there should be no other mental factors (caitta),
nor should one maintain that mental factors are identical to the mind (citta).
The Sūtra states that perception and so forth depend upon the mind;
how could the very essence of the mind itself depend upon itself?
Furthermore, the Sūtra also speaks of a "mind with attachment" and so forth.
Regarding the term "sphere of tangibility" (*spraṣṭavyāyatana*): it is called the sphere of tangibility because it is the basis upon which contact (*sparśa*) depends;
that is, the six faculties, such as the eye and so forth.
Therefore, the *Vibhāṣā* (74) states:

"Furthermore, the six bases, such as the eye and so forth, which function as the basis for contact, are termed the 'six bases of contact' (*ṣaṭ-spraṣṭavyāyatana*). This is the intended meaning cited from the treatise herein.
It grasps the contact that serves as the dependent, not the locus that serves as the support.
Thus, it should be understood that what has already been explained applies because [the object] does not extend to the ultimate atom (*paramāṇu*).
Thus has been explained that which can burn and that which is weighed in dispute.
Below this follows the eleventh gate, concerning that which can cut and that which is cut, and the twelfth gate, concerning that which can burn and that which is burned.
Thirteen: The Gate of the Cutter and the Cuttable.
This concludes the summary verse and its response.
The treatise says, up to the point of "the cutter and the cuttable."
According to the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 143:
"Some say that these four bases are capable of cutting and the four bases are what is cut.
Other masters say that the nature of solidity is what is capable of cutting."
The four bases (*āyatana*) are that which is cut;
however, there is no commentary on this point.
This treatise agrees with the former master. Furthermore, it is explained as follows:
The statement that the four [elements] are capable of cutting refers to them as inseparable; when discussing their essential natures, it is said that solidity is what cuts.
Each is based on a single meaning, and thus there is no contradiction between the two principles.
Although the nature of solidity pervades both the agent and the object equally,
in terms of their functional efficacy, that which excels is designated as the "cutter," while that which is deficient in such efficacy is designated as the "cut."

"What dharma is called the 'cutter'? [The opponent] asks. "Is it not the case that conditioned phenomena perish spontaneously in each moment, such that there can be neither a cutter nor something to be cut?
For instance, when a mass of matter such as firewood reaches a state like the radiance of a jewel, [it perishes on its own]."
Answer: In reality, conditioned phenomena perish spontaneously in each moment;
they are neither the agent nor the object of cutting.
Rather, it is simply that prior aggregates of matter, such as fuel, arise in extreme proximity to one another in continuous succession.
When axes and other distinct conditions separate firewood and the like,
causing them to arise as successive continuations in distinct portions,
this phenomenon is called "cutting."
It does not cause the extinction of the Dharma; therefore, there is no contradiction.
The factors are separated from the body.
Because the sense faculties do not exist [as substantial entities], they cannot be cut;
because they consist of pure and sublime dharmas, they also cannot be that which cuts. Question: Regarding the dismemberment of the body in the hells—
Or, they may sever snakes and the like,
causing them to become many parts,
each part moving separately.
This refers to those who possess sense organs but are separated from their bodies by limbs.
The commentary explains:
in hell, the manifestation of signs is seen for the most part.
In reality, all parts [of such a body] possess the body-faculty (*kāyendriya*).
Because the severed bodies of snakes and the like continue to move due to residual momentum, the *Vibhāṣā* (vol. 19) states:
Other masters say that although one's limbs and joints may be severed into hundreds or thousands of pieces within the various hells, [the sensation of pain does not cease].
Furthermore, within each of its parts there exists the body-faculty (*kāyendriya*),
because there is continuity between the parts,
just as in a crushed piece of *dūrvā* grass or in the roots and stalks of a lotus.
It is also like the seeds of a split melon, which are not separate from one another;
if they were separate, the body-faculty would simply not exist.
Since it is not the case that a single sentient being possesses two bodies, this is what is observed in the world.
Regarding the fact that even when the bodies of various worms have been mostly severed, they still move about:

this is due to the influence of the wind-element (*vāyu-dhātu*), and not because they possess a body-faculty (*kāya-indriya*). Question: Are there cases where snakes and other such creatures regenerate their individual bodies after being severed?
How is this explained? The explanation says: because other sentient beings rely upon it for their birth.
It is like the relationship between that which cuts and that which is cut, or as it applies to what is weighed, where only the weight itself is considered.
The material sense-faculties, such as the body, are likewise not two distinct things;
that is to say, they are neither the burner nor the burned,
nor the weigher nor the weighed.
Because it is pure and subtle,
when the body is consumed by fire and comes to an end, the sense faculties also come to an end;
this is because the four objects that support the faculties are absent, and thus the faculties likewise cease to exist.
The faculty of hearing (*śrotra-indriya*) and the sound-element (*śabda-dhātu*) are not the burner;
all six meanings [of fire] are collectively excluded because they do not form a continuous series. [This applies to] that which burns and that which is weighed.
There are two points of contention.
The former is stated as "the four elements" because it speaks from the perspective of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) regarding their inseparability;
the latter is discussed from the perspective of ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) by defining their essential nature, asserting that only fire is capable of burning.
What is being discussed here emphasizes only the weight [of the argument]; each is based on a single principle, and thus there is no contradiction.
Furthermore, although both nature and fire are omnipresent as subject and object, [the distinction remains].
Based on their functional predominance, they are described as the "burner";
if their function is subordinate, they are described as the "burned.
Thus it has been explained that, down to the momentary level, only the final three [elements] possess these functions.
Below this is the fourteenth section, the Gate of the Five Categories.
Within it, there are two parts: first, a general explanation of the five categories;
second, a specific elucidation of the capacity of the verses.
Regarding the explanation of the five categories:
first, those born of maturation (*vipākaja*), which consist of a portion of seventeen elements excluding the sound element (*śabdadhātu*); second, those that are nurtured (*aupacayika*).
Generally speaking, there are two types of nurtured [phenomena].
First, regarding the predominance of the function of nourishment (*aupacayika*),
it pervades all eighteen realms (*dhātu*).
Second, regarding the increase of the substance of nourishment, it consists of the five sense faculties (*indriya*) and a small portion of the five sense objects (*viṣaya*).

Herein, this is explained according to the nature of the *aupacayika* (nutritive). Regarding the three types of *naiṣyandika* (outflowing), it is generally stated that there are two kinds of *naiṣyandika*:
first, those produced from homogeneous (*sabhāga*) and pervasive (*sarvatraga*) causes are termed *naiṣyandika*.
According to this principle, fifteen elements in their entirety and a portion of the final three are not of the nature of maturation (*vipāka*),
but are comprised within the category of growth (*aupacayika*).
However, those among them that arise from homogeneous (*sabhāga*) and omnipresent (*sarvatraga*) causes are [also] of the nature of maturation.
Regarding the term "outflow" (*niṣyanda*), according to this specific sense, it refers to the thirteen elements—
excluding the five material sense-faculties— as well as a portion of the remaining [eighteen] elements;
for although these may also be results of maturation (*vipāka*) or growth (*aupacayika*), they likewise possess the nature of outflow.
To distinguish between different categories, the general discussion is set aside to treat the particular.
Here, based on the second type of *niṣyanda* (outflow), four moments are explained.
Generally speaking, there are two kinds of moments: first, because [all conditioned things] perish in a moment (*kṣaṇika*).
Therefore, they are called "momentary" (*kṣaṇika*).
Seventeen elements in their entirety and a small portion of one element do not arise from homogeneous or universal causes (*sabhāga-hetu* and *sarvatraga-hetu*).
Because it is not a result of uniform outflow (*niṣyanda*), it is called "momentary" (*kṣaṇika*).
This refers to a small portion of the first untainted (*anāsrava*) mental consciousness, the dharma-consciousness, and the mental consciousness.
Here, based on the second moment, five real entities (*dravya*) are described.
Generally speaking, there are two types of real entities (*vastu*).
First, those called "real" because they possess substantial reality (*dravya*);
these comprise the eighteen elements (*dhātu*) in their entirety.
Because its substance is firm and solid, it is called "real" (*satya*).
It is exclusively a small portion of the unconditioned *dharmadhātu*.
Here, one should understand that this is explained according to the second sense of "real."
The five categories subsume the eighteen elements (*dhātu*), yet their essential natures are each distinct and do not mutually subsume one another.

Among these five categories, the latter four do not include that which is called "maturation" (*vipāka*); among the latter four, the final three do not include that which is called "nourishment" (*aupacayika*).
Regarding the latter three [categories], the last two do not include those termed "outflow" (niṣyanda).
Regarding the latter two, the last one does not include those termed "momentary" (kṣaṇika).
The remainder are termed "real" (dravya).
This is an explanation in accordance with the sequence.
Furthermore, it is explained that among the five categories, those not included within the first four are designated as "real" (dravya).
Within those first four, those not included within the first three are designated as "momentary" (kṣaṇika).
Among the first three [categories], the first two do not include those termed "outflow" (*niṣyanda*);
among the first two of those, the first does not include those termed "nourishment" (*puṣṭi*).
The remainder are termed "maturation" (*vipāka*).

This is an inverse explanation. Among the five categories, for the time being, based on the sequence of the characteristics of conditioned and unconditioned phenomena, it is said that the fourth is the momentary and the fifth is the substantial entity.
If one follows the sequence of the text,
there is no contradiction in explaining it through both the direct and reverse orders. Furthermore,
another explanation is that among the five categories, that which is not subsumed by the other four is called "maturation" (vipāka).
In this manner, up to the point where the other four categories of inclusion are not termed "momentary" (kṣaṇika).

This indicates that these are mutually related in a sequential manner rather than being mutually inclusive; it demonstrates how the eighteen elements (dhātus) correspond to and include the five categories.
This refers to the five internal material faculties (indriya),
which possess both maturation (vipāka) and nourishment (aupacayika);
it is not said that they possess outflow (naiṣyandika).
Thus, one should know that they are not outflows;
in reality, they are only the dharma-dhātu and do not extend to the other seventeen [bases]. Momentarily, they exist only in the final three [moments].
The remaining fifteen [bases] do not apply; this is determined by the same principle.
Among these three, the five internal [bases] do not exist as having arisen from maturation (*vipākaja*); sound does not arise from maturation.
Since it does not explicitly state that there are no *aupacayika* (nourished) or *naiṣyandika* (outflowing) [dharmas],
their existence is known by implication;
the preceding [passage] has thus metaphorically included the *aupacayika*.
The "lower" [category] refers to the outflow (*niṣyanda*) such as images and so forth;
it lacks substantial momentary existence, as previously stated.

Since it is said among the eighteen elements that eight are non-obstructive (*apratigha*), it is clearly understood that these are the seven mental elements and the dharma-element; these eight possess outflows.
There is also maturation (vipāka);
since it is not stated to be nurtured (aupacayika),
it is clearly understood that [nurturing] does not exist [therein].
The five consciousnesses are without substantial reality and are momentary.
The mind-element and the mental-consciousness-element are also without substantial reality;
all are as previously explained. "The rest" refers to those elements remaining after the fourteen elements previously mentioned.
These are form, odor, taste, and tangibility.
Each of these four is threefold—
namely, resultant (*vipāka*), nurtured (*aupacayika*), and outflowing (*naiṣyandika*)— and they are likewise unreal and momentary, as previously explained.
In reality, it is solely the dharma-dhātu.
The word "solely" excludes the other seventeen dhātus.
The dharma-dhātu was previously included among the eight unimpeded [dharmas].
Having already established two categories,
we now add the "real" (dravya) to complete the preceding set as three.
The latter three are precisely the mind-base (manāyatana), the dharma-base (dharmāyatana), and the mental-consciousness-element (manovijñānadhātu).
The momentary [nature] exists only within these latter three;
the word "only" indicates that the momentary does not extend to the other fifteen.
Furthermore, when reaching the dharma-realm (dharmadhātu), one additional type is added.
The four types of mental attention (*manasikāra*) mentioned previously, together with the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*),
each obtain two kinds within the preceding state of non-obstruction;
now, by adding one more, they become three.
The Commentary says: "Up to 'because there is no distinct nature,' the five elements beginning with the eye possess both maturation (*vipāka*) and nourishment (*aupacayika*)."
These five, such as the eye and so forth, which arise from similar causes (sabhāga-hetu), are also outflows (niṣyanda). Now,
to clarify a different perspective,
the general category is set aside to discuss the specific.
Because there is no distinct nature apart from the matured (vipāka) and the nurtured (aupacayika),
they are not mentioned.
[The term] "that which has arisen from the ripening cause" refers to that which was previously performed as karma.
There are four general interpretations of "born of maturation" (*vipākaja*). Regarding the first interpretation, it states:
"Maturation" (*vipāka*) means that "difference" (*vi*) pertains to the cause, while "ripening" (*pāka*) pertains to the fruit; or alternatively, "difference" pertains to the fruit.

Vipāka (ripening) occurs either in the cause or it extends to both cause and fruit; vipāka-phala (the fruit of ripening) occurs either in the fruit or in the cause, or ripening extends to both cause and fruit.
Vipāka-viśeṣa (distinctive ripening) occurs either in the cause or in the fruit, or it is simply vipāka.
In the cause, there is either difference or maturation;
in the fruit, there is either difference or maturation.
Regarding both cause and fruit, if one says that "difference" itself is called "maturation," [it is so].
If one says "the ripening of that which is different," it is a *tatpuruṣa* (dependent determinative) compound;
thus it is called "ripening of difference" (*vipāka*). Alternatively, regarding the term "ripening" (*vipāka*) itself:
This is a general explanation;

it has not yet been specifically assigned [to individual categories]. Regarding the term "ripening cause" (*vipāka-hetu*): if one says that the ripening itself is the cause, this is a *karmadhāraya* (appositional) compound.
If it is said that [the term] "ripening cause" (*vipāka-hetu*) is a *tatpuruṣa* compound, then the fruit produced by the ripening cause is called "born of ripening" (*vipākaja*).
This is also an *tatpuruṣa* (dependent) compound, omitting the two characters "yin-suo" (cause-of).
It is like saying "ox-cart," which omits the two characters "suo-jia" (that which is drawn). Second, [it explains] how past karma previously created reaches the time when its fruit is obtained.
It is called "different" (*visama*) because its arising and its causal function differ from those of the preceding [moment].
It is called "ripening" (*pāka*) because it is capable of maturing [the result].
Since this "difference" itself is termed "ripening," it is called "maturation" (*vipāka*).
The third interpretation: it is a *karmadhāraya* (descriptive compound) because that which arises from the fruit is called "born of maturation" (*vipākaja*).
It is a *tatpuruṣa* (dependent compound) because maturation belongs to the cause, and what is born belongs to the fruit.
The cause is wholesome or unwholesome,
while the fruit is indeterminate.
That fruit which is obtained differs in category from its cause and is thus termed "distinct."
That which is ripened is called "ripening" (*vipāka*).
Because it is a ripening that is distinct [from its cause], it is called "distinct ripening" (*vipāka*).
That which is a distinct ripening and is also an arising is called "arising from distinct ripening" (*vipākaja*).
This is a *karmadhāraya* (appositional) compound.
Both "maturation" (*vipāka*) and "arising" (*jāti*) belong to the category of results. Regarding the fourth explanation:
the result is maturation, as explained previously.
Regarding the statement "the cause is not the maturation" and "the cause is the maturation," this applies the name of the effect to the cause;
the cause receives its name from the effect.
This is a *bahuvrīhi* (possessive) compound.
Because it possesses maturation (*vipāka*), it is called "maturation.
Because the fruit arises from that [maturation], it is called "born of maturation" (*vipākaja*).
This is an *ṣaṣṭhī-tatpuruṣa* compound. Generally speaking, there are various ways in which names are derived.
There are also instances where the name of the cause is applied to the effect, as the Sūtra says:
"The present six bases of contact are the effects."
It should be understood that these are the causes of karma created in the past.
The bases upon which contact relies are called the six bases of contact (*ṣaḍ-āyatana*).
These are the six faculties, such as the eye; herein, "basis" refers specifically to the six bases of support.
It does not grasp the six types of contact that serve as its support;
it is nourished by food and drink until it reaches the inner city of protection.
This explains what is nurtured: that which was small is made large.
Nourishing the emaciated to make them plump.
All obstructive phenomena that are designated as "atoms" (paramāṇu) are called "nourished by name" (aupacayika).
There is one [cause]: food and drink.
Second, assistance,
which refers to such things as applying oil; third, sleep.
The four types of meditative concentration (samādhi) refer to meditative absorption (dhyāna).
These four superior conditions are capable of nourishing;
through these conditions, the substance of the eyes and other faculties increases as they are benefited.

When the eyes and so forth increase, they are said to be "nourished" (*aupacayika*). A teacher of the *Miśraka* school asserts that observing the precepts and practicing the holy life (*brahmacarya*) can also bring about such nourishment.
The Master of the Treatise refutes this, saying:
This is merely non-detrimental;
it does not constitute a distinct entity of nourishment that provides benefit.
The matter resulting from maturation (*vipākaja-rūpa*) is inferior.
Since it is not produced by maturation (*vipākaja*) and is free from being nurtured (*aupacayika*),
it is constantly nurtured and maintained; thus,
the matter that is nurtured is superior.
There are cases where [the faculties] arise apart from maturation (vipāka).
For example, one who lacks eyes or ears may acquire them through cultivation (bhāvanā).
Thus, the *Vibhāṣā* states:
The eye born of maturation is distinct from the eye produced by nourishment,
just as a person is distinct from another person,
or as a kiln is distinct from another kiln.
The nourishment and protection of the matured (*vipāka*) is likewise.

However, there is nourishment of the eye that arises apart from the arising of the matured eye, such as when one who previously lacked eyes attains the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*). Question: Does nourishment extend to non-sentient things as well?
The commentary says: It is not universally applicable. The objection is like that of grains such as rice and wheat;
although they lack the benefit derived from food, drink, sleep, and meditative concentration (*samādhi*), they do possess the benefit provided by assistance such as manure.
How is it that "nourishment" (puṣṭi) does not apply to insentient things?
The explanation says:
if one speaks of nourishment in a general sense, it also applies to insentient things.
Because conditions such as excrement and water are able to nourish and develop it.
In this context, what is called "nourishment" (puṣṭi) refers exclusively to that which is benefited by the superior conditions of sentient beings.
External phenomena that are insentient and do not provide benefit through superior conditions are not called "nourished" (*aupacayika*).
Regarding the statement that sound has an "outflow" (*naiṣyandika*) up to its "arising according to desire" (*icchā-pravartana*):
there are two categories of sound.
There is no sound produced by maturation (*vipākaja*). For while material form produced by maturation arises spontaneously, sound arises according to one's will; therefore, it is not maturation-born.
If that were so, it would follow that [the Buddha] could not possess the mark of the Brahma-voice.
To address this, the treatise raises an objection: "If sound were not a result of maturation (*vipāka*), then it would be incorrect to say that [the Buddha] is free from harsh speech."
One attains the mark of Brahma-like voice among the thirty-two marks of a Great Being.
Regarding this, some say that sound belongs to the striking of conditions when they meet.
Answer: There are two explanations.
This refers to the first master.
Some say that because sound belongs to the third transmission,
although it is produced through a remote succession, it nonetheless arises from that karma.
It cannot be directly experienced, yet it is not a result of maturation (vipāka).
That is to say, karma is the first transmission; from karma, the primary elements (mahābhūta) arise as the second transmission.
The production of sound from the primary elements constitutes the third transmission.
Logically, there should also be a fourth and a fifth transmission;
yet they are not mentioned.
Sound produced from the great elements of maturation (*vipāka*) is not even [itself] maturation;
sound produced from those of growth (*aupacayika*) and outflow (*naiṣyandika*) is likewise [not maturation].
Since the principle is beyond doubt, it is not explained separately. Furthermore, one should formulate a formal inference (*pramāṇa*) as follows:
Sound is not a maturation (*vipāka*), because it belongs to the third transmission.
As with the experience of pleasant and unpleasant sensations: Question:

If sound arises from karma and the primary elements (*mahābhūta*), and these four primary elements are themselves maturation (*vipāka*), then what kind of maturing primary elements give rise to this sound?
The commentary explains:
First, there are matured primary elements (vipāka-mahābhūta) existing independently;
when they strike one another, sound is immediately produced.
When they do not strike one another, there are only the primary elements (*mahābhūta*). Question:
If that is so, there should be present primary elements without any derived matter (*upādāyarūpa*).
Explanation: [This is as follows.]
This is also permissible and incurs no fault.
Therefore, the *Nyāyānusāra* (Treatise on Right Reasoning), volume twenty,
in explaining that the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) are not simultaneous causes (*sahabhū-hetu*) with respect to derived matter (*upādāya-rūpa*), states:

That is to say, there are those who possess derived matter but not the four great elements, or those who possess the great elements that produce [matter] but not derived matter. The commentary explains:
this refers to noble ones born in the formless realm.
One who has attained the lower grade of untainted precepts does not accomplish the great primary elements that constitute them;
likewise, one abiding in the desire or form realms who accomplishes past, future, or fixed present precepts does not accomplish the great primary elements that constitute them.
In the desire realm, from the second moment onward, present and past precepts are established;
however, the past [precepts] do not constitute the capacity to perform great deeds.
This applies if one has initially received the prātimokṣa vows.
In the first moment, there are co-emergent (niṣyanda) four great elements that project future non-manifest karma (avijñapti) which is yet to arise;
those great elements are currently possessed.
The unmanifest (avijñapti) produced therein still abides in the future;
because there is no prior acquisition (prāpti), it is not yet accomplished.
Such are the categories of this kind.
This is called "accomplishing the primary elements (mahābhūta) but not the derived matter (upādāyarūpa).

According to that treatise, one should know that there is also the case of "accomplishing the primary elements that are capable of producing [matter], but not the derived matter. Question: If that is so, then...
This directly contradicts the *Mahāvibhāṣā*.
Thus, the *Mahāvibhāṣā*, fascicle 132, states:
"If one possesses the present primary elements (*mahābhūta*)."
Does he possess derived matter of the present?
Answer: Yes. If he possesses derived matter of the present, [does he necessarily possess it]?
Are those present primary elements? Answer: Yes.
Because there are no present primary elements that lack a fruit.

Nor is it the case that the derived matter (*upādāya-rūpa*) produced in the present is without a cause; for the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* already states: "Because there are no great elements (*mahābhūta*) in the present that lack a fruit.
From this it is clearly known that all great elements in the present possess the fruit of derived matter, and there are no great elements that exist in isolation.
The commentary explains:
The intentions of the treatises are each distinct, so there is no need for laborious reconciliation;
alternatively, they may not be mutually contradictory.
The *Mahāvibhāṣā* speaks from the perspective of the majority.
Were it not so, it would be as when one receives the precepts: at the very first moment, one would already be creating future-world precepts in advance.
How could that constitute the future precept? [Objection: Regarding the primary elements (mahābhūta) as the outflow (niṣyanda), one might create the future precept in advance;
however, can there be primary elements existing alone in the present?
The great elements of maturation (*vipāka*) do not arise as something remote;
otherwise, there would be no great elements existing independently in the present.
The commentary explains:
Although their specific meanings differ,
because they belong to the same general category,
it is permissible for the outflow (*niṣyanda*) to exist as something present and solitary.
It is possible for there to be maturation;
what reasoning could prevent this?
Furthermore, it is explained that there are no great elements (mahābhūta) of maturation in the present.
There is no derived matter (*upādāya-rūpa*).
This is because the previously cited *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* is extremely clear on this point;
it states that there is no fruit because the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) are not present.
Therefore, it is known that there is no present great [element] existing in isolation;
for it has already been stated that non-present derived matter (upādāya-rūpa) lacks a cause.
Therefore, one should know that there is no manifestly produced matter (*rūpa*) that exists independently; thus,
it should be understood that the subsequent moment of non-informative matter (*avijñapti*) is dependent upon the present primary elements (*mahābhūta*).
"Although there is no cause of arising, there is a cause of dependence. Question: "If that is so, it contradicts the *Nyāya* (Correct Principle).
For that treatise states:"
It is clearly known that there are cases where the primary elements (mahābhūta) that act as creators exist, yet no derived matter (upādāyarūpa) is produced; furthermore,
there are also cases where the primary elements that act as creators exist, but no derived matter is produced.
The commentary states:
The author of the *Nyāyānusāra* (*Zhenglilun*) recounts the views of dissenting masters;
one must examine the treatises of the *Mahāvibhāṣā* (*Poshasha*) from beginning to end.
There is no such statement at all.
That there is a "productive" great element (*mahābhūta*) which is not a derived form (*upādāyarūpa*) is the specific intent of the treatise;
there is no need for laborious reconciliation. Or perhaps it may be so.
Nor is there any contradiction;
for example, at the moment of receiving the precepts, the primary elements (mahābhūta) of the first moment produce the precepts of that first moment,
and these are precisely those same primary elements.
Furthermore, it is also able to project the non-informative matter (*avijñapti*) for the duration of one lifetime within a future body;
in principle, the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) of this first moment actually constitute both that [future] non-informative matter and the present non-informative matter produced by them.
Furthermore, because it is intended to establish the discourse on the elements (dhātu) in anticipation of what follows,
the *Nyāyānusāra* states that there can be primary elements (*mahābhūta*) capable of producing [something] that are not themselves derived matter (*upādāyarūpa*).
If one adopts this interpretation:

This does not contradict correct reasoning. Question: If it is said that this sound has no prior independent existence as a maturation derived from the primary elements (*mahābhūta*), then what are these primary elements?
If one were to say that these primary elements exist whenever the sound exists, [then...]
If sound were non-existent when absent,
then resultant form would have to be interrupted and then resume;
this would entail the fault of contradicting your own tenets.
If it is claimed that the very same ripened great elements (*mahābhūta*) that produce the body-faculty (*kāyendriya*) and so forth produce two types of resistant form (*sapratigha-rūpa*),
this would still contradict your own tenet.

If it is argued that sound is produced by the striking of the matured great elements (mahābhūta) of the body and sense organs as its conditions, then from the perspective of the nature of those conditions,
the great elements are said to be the second [cause].
Next, the sound that arises is called the third sound.
In reality, this sound is produced by great elements (mahābhūta) that are either nourished (aupacayika) or outflowing (naiṣyandika), according to the case.
If one were to interpret it in this way,
although there would be no error,
how would it differ from the fourth and fifth lineages of transmission?
Since it is not produced by those ripened (*vipāka*) great elements (*mahābhūta*), why is it necessary to speak separately of a third transmission? The explanation says:
although the ripened great elements are not directly capable of producing that sound-element (*śabda-dhātu*).
According to the perspective of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*), there is no fault in stating that sound is the third [factor].
Some say that sound belongs to that which has reached [the sense organ], and only then does the sound arise.
This is the response of the second master. Some say that because sound belongs to the fifth transmission,
although it arises through a distant succession, it is nonetheless produced by that karma.
It is induced by what is neither an enemy nor a relative,
yet it is not a maturation (vipāka);
that is to say, karma is the primary transmission.
The great elements (mahābhūta) that constitute the maturation (vipāka) of the body-faculty and so forth, produced by karma, constitute the second transmission.
From these maturation-side elements, there further arise the great elements of nourishment (aupacayika) that constitute the body-faculty and so forth; these constitute the third transmission.
From this, the nurtured matter (*aupacayika-rūpa*) further gives rise to the outflowing primary elements (*nisyanda-mahābhūta*), which constitutes the fourth transmission.
From these outflowing elements, sound is then produced, constituting the fifth transmission. It is also logically necessary to admit the existence of this fourth transmission.
As for what is not mentioned:
it may be that it was omitted and not stated.
Or perhaps it is acceptable.

Regarding the manifestation of shadows or the nourishment of sound: although these may be interrupted at a single location, if one considers them within the various limbs and joints of a single body, they circulate without interruption;
thus, they are said not to be *vipāka* (maturation).
The principle of this is somewhat obscure;
therefore, it is not discussed here.
If the sound of an outflow were to be entirely interrupted, [it would follow that there is no continuity].
It is said that [sound] is not a result of maturation (*vipāka*).
This is somewhat evident in principle; this master’s intention is to explain it by focusing primarily on this point:
the nourishing primary elements (*aupacayika-mahābhūta*) produce nourished sound (*aupacayika-śabda*).
Because the sound produced by the outflowing (*naiṣyandika*) great elements is itself an outflowing sound,
it is accepted that there is a fourth and fifth transmission of sound which is not maturation (*vipāka*).
Since it is not produced by maturation great elements, a third transmission is not admitted.
Therefore, the Nyāyānusāra, recounting the explanation of the second master, states:
"Other masters say that sound is not a result of maturation (vipāka)."
How could it be produced by the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) that are themselves maturation (*vipāka*)?
Therefore, one must admit that sound belongs to the fourth or fifth transmission; because it is thus removed from the original cause, it is not maturation.
That is to say: from karma arises the maturation primary elements.
From these, the nurtured primary elements (*aupacayika-mahābhūta*) arise; from these, in turn, the outflowing primary elements (*naiṣyandika-mahābhūta*) arise.

The nurtured primary elements produce nurtured sound, while the outflowing primary elements produce outflowing sound. Furthermore, this interpretation may be understood as a distinct explanation by another master.
The *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 118,
also has the third and fifth traditions identical to this treatise.
Furthermore, the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 127, states:
Question: Regarding the sounds produced by various classes of sentient beings, where should they be said to be derived from? Some say:
It is produced by the primary elements at the throat;
some say it is produced by the primary elements at the heart.
Some say it is produced by the primary elements (mahābhūta) located at the navel.
The critique says:
In general,
this sound is produced by the primary elements (mahābhūta) of all parts of the body.
To speak of it specifically:
Subtle and small sounds of speech should be said to be produced by the primary elements (mahābhūta) at the throat;
this includes sounds such as hissing, shouting, roaring, and wailing.
It should be said that they are produced by the primary elements (mahābhūta) pervading the entire body;
for it is observed that these [factors] cause the whole body to be agitated.
If it is argued that [the claim] "bodily sensation reaches [the object]" contradicts correct reasoning,
although this treatise contains two positions, the author’s intention lies with the latter master.
He refutes the former master as follows:
If it is argued that this sound is not a maturation because it arises from the primary elements produced by karma and thus belongs to a third transmission,
then the feeling associated with body-consciousness would also not be a maturation, as it likewise arises from the primary elements produced by karma.
This means that karma is the first transmission;
the primary elements of maturation (*vipāka-mahābhūta*) are the second transmission;
and the bodily sensation produced by these primary elements is the third transmission.
The body and sensation arise simultaneously with the voice during the third transmission;
they should therefore not be considered maturation (*vipāka*).
If it were admitted that feeling, like sound, is not a maturation,
it would contradict correct reasoning.
Because, according to our school’s doctrine, sensation is understood to include both the resultant (vipāka) and the non-resultant. The *Nyāyānusāra* offers this defense:
"This objection is not valid;
it is not the case that all bodily sensations have the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) as their cause."
Furthermore, those produced by the primary elements (mahābhūta) arising from karma are not all exclusively maturation (vipāka).
This is because bodily sensations are also produced by primary elements that arise neither from karma nor from [other] primary elements.
This refers to the arising of bodily sensation,
which necessarily depends on conditions such as the body, contact, and body-consciousness;
for this reason, it also arises depending on external primary elements (mahābhūta).
It is not necessary to wait for a great birth induced by karma;
this does not contradict reason, and therefore it is consistent with being a maturation (*vipāka*). This is the intended meaning of the *Nyāyānusāra*’s defense.
This means that the arising of bodily sensation is not entirely caused by the primary elements;

it also depends on conditions such as the body—which is conventionally designated though not itself composed of the primary elements—as well as tangibles and body-consciousness. Even if there were instances where it is caused by the primary elements, [it would still depend on these other factors].
Furthermore, it is not only because of karma that the primary elements (mahābhūta) arise;
they also arise from primary elements that are neither karmic, nor are they outflows (naiṣyandika), nor are they nurtured (aupacayika).
Even if the primary elements were to arise because of karma, [the same principle would apply].
Furthermore, its essence is not exclusively maturation (*vipāka*);
it also extends to the wholesome, the unwholesome, and so forth.
Because these three meanings are indeterminate, it is categorized as maturation.
To rescue the third position, if a teacher of the *Abhidharmakośa* were to object:
"If you say that bodily sensation arises from the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) and not from what is not a primary element, then it follows that it must be a result of maturation (*vipāka*)."
If it is argued that sound arises solely from the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) and does not extend to being a result of maturation (*vipāka*),
then visible form (*rūpa*) likewise arises solely from the primary elements.

It should not be restricted to being exclusively maturation-born (*vipāka*). If you say that bodily sensation arises from the great elements (*mahābhūta*) that are maturation-born, nourishment-born (*aupacayika*), and outflow-born (*naiṣyandika*),
and thus it is common to all three types of birth,
then you must also admit that sound likewise arises from these three.

It should be understood as including both [the maturation of sensation and the great elements]. If you say that the great elements produced by the maturation of bodily sensation are also not all exclusively maturations—
since some are associated with the wholesome or the unwholesome— [then the same applies here].
I also do not say that all bodily sensations produced from the great elements of maturation are themselves maturations.
It also applies to both the wholesome and the unwholesome;
however, it is refuted here in this context.
For now, we rely on the fact that bodily sensation is a result of maturation (*vipāka*).
It is difficult to maintain that the great elements produced from karma give rise [to sound].
If you claim that sound belongs to a third transmission and is not a result of maturation (*vipāka*),
this third transmission does not constitute a definitive proof.
It is as with the experience of maturation (vipāka) in the body;
because it belongs to the third transmission,
sound is a maturation.
It is as with the experience of pleasant and unpleasant bodily sensations;
because it belongs to the third transmission,
sound is not a result of maturation (vipāka).
I have pointed out your error by means of what is not fixed.
You claim that because bodily sensation is not fixed, it is categorized as "maturation" (vipāka);
is this not merely empty talk?
Since he ultimately failed to rescue [the doctrine] from its difficulties,
the sound [of the teaching] does not belong to the third transmission. Thus,
the first master having been refuted, [the second is likewise dismissed].
Later, the Master [Śaṅkarasvāmin] returned to establish [the position]. Furthermore, the *Nyāyabindu* (Treatise on Correct Reasoning) offers a defense for the third tradition, stating:
"Is it not the case that, just as wholesome or unwholesome sounds are produced from neutral primary elements (*mahābhūta*), and non-appropriated [sounds] are produced from appropriated [elements]?"
If an auditory object arises from a tactile object,
what contradiction is there in this— that which arises from non-retributive primary elements (*mahābhūta*) is itself non-retributive?
This is how one might refute [the opponent] as an Abhidharmakośa master.
In principle, there is no fixed rule regarding the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) and their derived matter (*upādāyarūpa*).
Since this sound produced by the maturation primary elements is not itself a result of maturation (*vipāka*),
[it does not share the same nature].
What is this? If it were something nurtured,
it would logically consist of those great elements that are themselves nurtured.
If these were outflows (*niṣyanda*),
then logically they should be composed of the great elements that are outflows;
for what reason would they instead be composed of the great elements of maturation (*vipāka*)?
Regarding the eight unimpeded [knowledges] up to "that which is not nourished":
this explains the third and fourth lines. That which is equal before and after is called "equal" (*sama*).
That which is similar in its continuous flow is called "flow" (*srotas*).

Alternatively, because the fruit continues the cause, it is called a "stream" (*pravāha*). Although all that is born of maturation (*vipākaja*) also arises from similar types (*sabhāga-hetu*), in order to manifest its specific characteristic, the general category is set aside to discuss the particular; thus, it is designated specifically as "maturation."
Only that which is not subsumed under maturation (*vipāka*) is termed "outflow" (*niṣyanda*).
In terms of its function, it also extends to the formless realm (*ārūpya-dhātu*),
where there is no "nourishment" (*puṣṭi*) because this [classification] is stated according to the essential nature (*svabhāva*) of the phenomena.
Regarding the phrase "the rest," this refers to the remaining four [factors] up to those that possess a nature of outflow (*niṣyanda*).
This explains the three remaining [categories], which can be understood accordingly.

Regarding the phrase "in reality, only dharmas," up to the point where it says "only these are called 'possessing substance' (*dravyavat*)," this explains that in reality, only dharmas [are substantial]. By applying this principle [to the other categories], they should be understood in the same way.
"Reality is exclusively unconditioned (asaṃskṛta).
Regarding the statement "the mind, dharmas, and mental consciousness, up to what is called the dharma-element":
this explains the sixth phrase. Mind, dharmas, and mental consciousness exist for only a single moment.
This refers to the first category of untainted *duḥkha-dharma-jñāna-kṣānti* (receptivity to the knowledge of the dharma of suffering).
It is called "one moment" because it is not a result of outflow (*naiṣyandika*).

This explains that what is ultimately not produced from a cause of similar type is termed "one moment. All other conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) are none other than results of outflow. The mind associated with this receptivity to suffering is termed the "mind-element" (*manodhātu*) and the "mental-consciousness-element" (*manovijñānadhātu*).
That which follows the moment of expectation is called *manas* (mind); that which precedes it is called *mano-vijñāna* (mental consciousness).

Other factors that arise simultaneously—namely, the associated mental states and so forth—are termed the *dharma-dhātu* (dharma-realm). The initial mention of "patience regarding suffering" (*duḥkha-dharma-jñāna-kṣānti*) indicates the apprehension of present patience.
Therefore, the *Nyāyānusāra* states: "This teaching holds that even when [the path] is currently active, it is not an outflow (*niṣyanda*).
Question: Why is only the present forbearance (*kṣānti*) taken up, and not the future?
Explanation:
It is certain that the present active patience toward suffering (*duḥkha-kṣānti*) is not a result of outflow (*niṣyanda*).
Although the future patience toward suffering exists while one is still at the stage of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*), it is not a result of outflow;
however, when one reaches the stage of an Arya, it abides as non-arising.
Because it is the outflow-result (*niṣyanda-phala*) of present patience (*kṣānti*), it is not momentary;
thus, its meaning is not yet determined. Question: As described above, when patience is manifest, future inferior patience abides in the state of non-arising.
If it were not included within the category of outflow (*niṣyanda*), it would have to be momentary (*kṣaṇika*).
Why, then, is only the present forbearance (*kṣānti*) taken?
The explanation says:
The patience of suffering is called a single moment because it possesses two meanings:
first, its actual manifestation.
Second, there are those that are not outflows (*niṣyanda*); for example, when one does not give rise to the lower degree of patience (*mṛdu-kṣānti*),
although it is not an outflow, there is an absence of its active manifestation (*samudācāra*).
Just as with the dharma-knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-dharmajñāna*) and so forth,
although there may be instances where the manifestation lacks its natural outflow (*nisyanda*),
this is not the case when one does not give rise to higher patience (*adhimātra-ksānti*).
Both meanings are absent [in that case].
The remaining cases should be explained accordingly based on this principle. According to the *Nyāyānusāra*, there are two interpretations regarding the five categories.
One interpretation is the same as this treatise.
Furthermore, another interpretation states: there are other masters who say...
Regarding this, there is another explanation:
because all phenomena possess substantial entities and possess real characteristics, with the exception of unconditioned phenomena, they are all of a single moment, for they perish rapidly.
Furthermore, with the exception of the first untainted mind and its concomitants, all other conditioned phenomena [are likewise of a single moment].

All of these are outflows; a small portion of the ten material elements are nurtured; and a small portion of seventeen are born of maturation. By means of this, the five internal material faculties, such as the eye, [are established].
Each has two types: namely,
those produced by nourishment (*aupacayika*) and those born of maturation (*vipākaja*).
Although the other three exist,
they lack a distinct nature;
because their meanings would become confused, they are not mentioned.

All others are to be understood accordingly. The sound-element has two types, and the same applies to the five sensory consciousnesses. The mind-element and mental-consciousness-element have three types; the same is true for the objects such as visible form. The dharma-element has four types, excluding that which is produced by nourishment (*aupacayika*).
Thus has been explained [the section on] "attaining individually, together, or neither.
Below this is the fifteenth gate: the Gate of Attainment and Accomplishment (*prāpti-samanvāgama*). "Attaining individually" refers to the two simple (single) propositions.
Both are obtained;
this refers to the third phrase, not the fourth phrase.
The term "etc. refers to the inclusion of accomplishment and so forth.
Herein, the attainment, accomplishment, relinquishment, and non-accomplishment are explained in general.
As explained in detail in the *Abhidharmamahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, I shall not describe it here for fear of prolixity.
To summarize, it is further said: "and so forth. Question: What is the difference between *prāpti* (attainment) and *samanvāgama* (possession)?
What is the difference between relinquishment (*tyāga*) and non-acquisition (*aprāpti*)?
The explanation states that they are each distinct and different.
If a dharma has newly arrived at its characteristic of arising (*jāti-lakṣaṇa*), it is then termed "attained" (*prāpti*).
If the flux reaches the present, it is then called "attainment" (*samanvāgama*);
at the moment of acquisition, it is not called attainment, and at the moment of attainment, it is not called acquisition. Therefore, the *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra*, fascicle 12, states:
Is it not the case that even at the time of attaining Buddhahood, the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) is not yet called "attained"?

How much more so for the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*)? For it is only when Bodhisattvas abide in the diamond-like samādhi (*vajropamasamādhi*) that they are said to have attained the knowledge of exhaustion.

Since it is stated that "the arising of the entity itself is called 'acquisition' (prāpti)," and the *Nyāyānusāra* further says, "The arising of the entity itself is named acquisition," we know that when a dharma reaches its characteristic of arising (*jāti-lakṣaṇa*), it is termed "acquisition."

It is only when [a dharma] flows into the present that it is called "accomplished" (*siddha*). Even if there were a scriptural passage stating that a dharma is called "accomplished" upon reaching the characteristic of arising (*utpāda-lakṣaṇa*), the designation "accomplished" would be established here with respect to its acquisition (*prāpti*).
Even if there were a scriptural passage stating that a dharma is called "attained" (*prāpta*) upon reaching the present, [the term "accomplished"] would still refer to its acquisition.
Because it receives its name based on its establishment within the state of accomplishment: if a dharma previously arose in a continuous succession,
but now suddenly encounters conditions such that it does not reach the stage of arising,
yet remains established in the present, at that time it is called "abandoned."

Upon reaching the second moment, when the present dharma has already ceased, it is then designated as "not accomplished" (*asiddha*). At the time of relinquishing, it is not yet called "not accomplished";
at the time of non-accomplishment, it is not termed "relinquishing."

For example, from the moment the patience regarding the dharma of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-kṣānti*) reaches the state of arising, at that time one is said to have "attained" (*prāpta*) the noble nature (*āryatva*), but not yet "accomplished" (*samanvāgata*) it.

If [the patience] flows into the present, one is said to have "accomplished" the noble dharmas, but not yet "attained" them. Similarly, when the supreme mundane dharmas (*laukikāgra-dharma*) are in the present, one is said to have "abandoned" the nature of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva*).
It is not called "non-accomplishment.
Only when it has fallen away into the past is it termed "non-accomplishment," but not "abandoned.
At the very moment one correctly attains the nature of an ārya, one abandons the nature of an ordinary person (pṛthagjanatva).
This is the simultaneous attainment and relinquishment:
at the very moment one achieves the noble dharmas,
one simultaneously ceases to possess the nature of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva*).

This constitutes the simultaneous occurrence of accomplishment and non-accomplishment; other phenomena should be understood accordingly. Furthermore, the moment of accomplishment should be termed "attainment" (*prāpti*), and the moment of non-accomplishment should be termed "relinquishment" (*tyāga*).
Therefore, the Nyāyānusāra (Treatise on Correct Reasoning), fascicle 56,
states: "As for the terms 'acquisition' and 'relinquishment,' these are stated in anticipation of what is to follow."
Furthermore, the *Abhidharmamahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 155, states:
"This refers to the stage of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*),
up to and including the stage of supreme patience (*adhimātra-kṣānti*)."
Regarding the untainted faculties (anāsrava-indriya), there is neither relinquishment nor acquisition;
they are neither extinguished nor arisen while one abides in the state of the Supreme Mundane Dharma (laukikāgra-dharma).
Regarding the untainted faculties (anāsravendriya), they are neither abandoned nor acquired,
and they do not arise through cessation.
This is the case when noble ones (ārya) abide in the receptivity to the knowledge of the dharma regarding suffering (duḥkha-dharma-jñāna-kṣānti).
Up until the time of the knowledge of the dharma regarding the path (*mārga-dharmajñāna*),
one does not abandon but rather acquires the untainted faculties (*anāsrava-indriya*);
they both cease and arise.

At the time of the patience of the subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārgānvayajñānakṣānti*), one both abandons and acquires, and both ceases and arises, with respect to the untainted faculties (*anāsravendriya*).
There are many further passages in the *Abhidharmamahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* and the *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra* that cannot be fully recounted here. Question: If they are acquired...
Regarding the fact that the attainments do not occur simultaneously: why does the *Vibhāṣā*, fascicle 162,
state that attainment occurs only at the very beginning?
Regarding the phrase "accomplishing the first and the last," the commentary explains:
this refers to distinguishing the first and the last within the context of accomplishment itself.
It is not based on having already attained the first [dhyāna], because at the time of its attainment, it has not yet been perfected.
An ancient master said:
Establishing [the argument] by means of both the new and the old treatises, one can rely on the new treatise to establish that it does not apply to both the new and the old.
Abandoning [the argument] by means of the new treatise.
To claim that "attaining [the state] is called accomplishment, while relinquishing it is called non-accomplishment" is a mistaken interpretation. The Treatise states:
"As for 'reaching,' this refers to the exclusion of the aforementioned characteristics."
This clarifies "attainment" (prāpti). It refers to those born in the desire realm through womb-birth, egg-birth, or moisture-birth who gradually acquire the eye-faculty (*cakṣur-indriya*).
This distinguishes it from "simultaneous attainment.
Since the material faculties (*rūpīndriya*) are neutral (*avyākṛta*), they do not constitute [the acquisition of] the past or the future.
The moment it arises is called "attainment" (prāpti).
Consciousness permeates all three natures and also possesses both prior and subsequent attainments.
Because consciousness has already been established previously, it is not now termed "attainment" (*prāpti*).
This remains true even for those born blind, for those who gradually lose their eyesight,
or for those who die in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and are reborn again in the desire realm.
It is said that one attains the eye but does not attain consciousness. If,
from the second dhyāna or above, one is born into the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and so forth, at the initial moment of mind,
one is said to attain consciousness but not the eye.
If one dies in the formless realm and is reborn in the desire realm and so forth, one simultaneously acquires both the eye and consciousness.
This is because being reborn in the desire realm and so forth is not fixed;
it is explained with reference to the gradual acquisition of the eye. Furthermore, another interpretation states:
This is stated briefly and not exhaustively;

furthermore, it is explained that the phrase "gradually attaining the eye" also includes these cases, as well as the initial moment of the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) when one passes away from the formless realm and is reborn in any of the three higher meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*).
The first phrase means that one necessarily acquires the eye-faculty (cakṣur-indriya), which is called "attaining the eye";

however, because visual consciousness has not yet arisen, it is not called "attaining [consciousness]. The second phrase refers to cases such as being born into the second dhyāna or higher, where visual consciousness is currently manifest.
It is called "attainment" (prāpti) because consciousness manifests;
the word "manifest" (pratyutpanna) means "present," and the word "arise" (udbhava) means "to be born."
When consciousness is in the state of arising, it is called "manifestation" (*samudācāra*).
At that time, it is said to be "attained.

Because the eye has already been established previously, it is not said to be attained [at that moment]. Furthermore, when one passes away from the two meditative attainments (*dhyāna*) and so forth and is born into the desire realm or the first dhyāna, there is the initial mind of the intermediate existence (*antarābhava*).
Because one necessarily acquires consciousness, it is called "attaining consciousness.
"Passing away from that" indicates that one is currently abiding in the state of death-existence (cyuti-bhava).
Among these, when it reaches the moment of the characteristic of arising, it is said to be "born" in the lower stage;
at that time, it is said to be "attained.
Because the eye has already been established [prior to this], it is not called "attained."
The third and fourth phrases may be understood accordingly.

It should be known that when one is born in the three higher realms, the arising of eye-consciousness belonging to a lower realm is exclusively indeterminate (*avyākṛta*). Thus, the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* (Vibhāṣā), fascicle 73, states: [text follows].
In this context, when eye-consciousness relies on an eye of its own level and takes an object that is of a lower level,
it may be of two types— excluding the defiled.
When it takes an object of its own level, it may be of three types.
If one relies on the eye of a higher stage, it is exclusively non-obscured and indeterminate (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*).
Eye-consciousness that is wholesome (*kuśala*) or defiled (*kliṣṭa*) can only arise when belonging to its own stage and is capable of manifesting.

This is because such consciousness is necessarily bound to the stage of birth. Question: When one is born in the three higher dhyānas and gives rise to the three lower consciousnesses, [how does this occur]?
What is this "unspecified" (avyākṛta)? The explanation says:

Generally speaking, that which arises [as such] refers to the unspecified mind of deportment (airyāpathika) or the mind born of maturation (vipākaja); it does not arise from a different stage (bhūmi).

The *śailpasthānika* (artistic) consciousness does not exist in the higher realms; furthermore, since one merely borrows the consciousness of a lower realm, it cannot be a result of supernormal power (*abhijñā-phala*).

Therefore, it is known that [the remaining] is *airyāpathika* (postural). Question: When one born in the three higher meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*) gives rise to the two supernormal powers of the eye and ear belonging to a lower realm, [how is this explained]?
What is this "indeterminate" (avyākṛta)?
The commentary explains that the master of the *Saṃyuktābhidharmahṛdaya-śāstra*, Dharmatrāta, states in the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya*:
"The divine eye..."
The supernormal power of the ear is ethically neutral in terms of deportment;
the skillful arts belong only to the desire realm and do not extend to the higher realms.
Retribution does not arise in a different stage;
transformation is produced solely by the mental consciousness, as it is not produced by the other three.
The interpretation that "the two supernormal knowledges (abhijñā) are necessarily associated with meditative absorption (samādhi) and deportment (īryāpatha)" is incorrect,
as it contradicts both reason and scripture.
As the treatise states below:
The deportment mind (*airyāpathika-citta*) of the form realm arises from five minds among the twenty minds;
namely, from the five minds of its own realm— excluding the fruition-of-superknowledge mind— it can produce seven minds.
That is to say: four from one's own realm—excluding the preparatory and the supernormal fruit;
two defiled from the desire realm;
and one defiled from the formless realm. If one says there are two supernormal powers:
Regarding the mind of deportment,
one should give rise to a wholesome mind of application,
just as a mind of transformation is induced by meditative concentration.
They arise together with meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and do not arise together with other states of mind;
the two types of supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) are likewise.

Since they are induced by meditative concentration, they should also arise together with meditative concentration and not with other states of mind. If it is argued that the modes of deportment (*īryāpatha*) can induce meditative concentration, [the same principle would apply].
This is not the case, for it contradicts the treatise.

One in a state of deportment (īryāpatha-samādhi) cannot produce an application-mind (prayoga-citta). If you say that one produces the two lower supernormal knowledges (abhijñā) while arising from the three higher dhyānas, [that too is incorrect].
It is not that one enters meditative absorption;

rather, according to what is appropriate, one enters the minds acquired at birth (*upapatti-labdha*) and so forth belonging to the three higher absorptions. This too is not the case, for one who is born in a higher realm gives rise to [minds] of a lower realm.
Even if this interpretation were granted:
When those of the three vehicles who are beyond training (aśaikṣa) born in the desire realm give rise to the two higher supernormal knowledges (abhijñā),
from what state of mind do they emerge?
Since they possess no afflictions, they cannot emerge from a defiled state.
One born in a lower stage cannot give rise to a wholesome mind acquired at birth (*upapattipratilambhika*) belonging to a higher stage;
nor can one give rise to a wholesome mind acquired at birth belonging to a different stage.
This is stated in the *Nyāyānusāra*.
As will be cited below,
it is also unable to give rise to the wisdom of hearing (śrutamayī-prajñā) belonging to another stage;
this wisdom is induced by that which is acquired through birth (upapatti-labdha).
Since one cannot give rise to the wholesome mind acquired at birth (*upapatti-lābhika-kuśala-citta*),
one likewise cannot give rise to the wholesome mind of wisdom derived from hearing (*śruta-mayī-prajñā-citta*).
One does not give rise to the wholesome mind of wisdom derived from hearing belonging to a different level (*bhūmi*).
There is a textual passage in the *Vibhāṣā*, as cited below;
even assuming that [the attainment] could arise.
Even the wisdom born of hearing cannot arise,
because a mind of deportment cannot give rise to a mind of applied virtue;
since the wisdom born of cultivation is itself an application of effort.
The principle of majestic deportment (*airyāpathika*) likewise does not arise [from other states].
A mind born of maturation (*vipākaja*) does not give rise to a mind of a different level.
Transformation (*nairmāṇika*) arises only from a mind of meditative concentration (*samāhita*).
Furthermore, the aforementioned sublime deportment cannot give rise to wholesome states associated with desire or to the unobscured-neutral;
this is as explained in detail regarding the "vast mind.
It is on account of this that the objection is raised.
Thus, it is known that their position— that the supernormal powers of the divine eye and divine ear are states of mind belonging to the deportment category—
is logically untenable. Furthermore, the master Guṇaprabha of the West [holds as follows].

The *Satyasiddhi-śāstra* states that the two supernormal powers of the eye and ear are neutral by nature (*svabhāva-avyākṛta*) and are not among the four types of neutral states; this, however, is also incorrect.
The various treatises extensively explain that there are only twenty minds;
if it were said that there is additionally an intrinsic indeterminate (svabhāva-avyākṛta),
one should say there are twenty-one minds.
Therefore, that [previous position] is also unreasonable.
Now, according to the correct interpretation:
both the eye and ear [faculties] are included within the four types of neutral (avyākṛta) states, specifically among the neutral states that are "resultant" (vipāka).
It should be understood that the term "resultant of supernormal power" (abhijñā-phala) is broad in scope,
whereas "transformation" (nirmāṇa) and so forth are narrow.
Just as the designation "non-learner" (aśaikṣa) is broad while the "nature of an ordinary person" (pṛthagjanatva) and so forth are narrow,
it has already been stated that both are subsumed under the fruit of liberation (vimukti-phala).

If it arises together with the characteristics of meditative concentration (*samādhi*), then there is no contradiction. Question: If these two supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) are subsumed under the mind that is the fruit of supernormal power (*abhijñā-phala-citta*), they would be identical to the transformative mind (*nirmāṇa-citta*).
All treatises state that the two types of supernormal powers (abhijñā) and the mind of transformation (nirmāṇacitta) are accomplished throughout the three periods of time.
It remains unknown, however, how one born in the higher three dhyānas accomplishes the transformative mind of a lower level.
The two [types of knowledge] both serve to establish that [the eye-consciousness] does not exist in the lower realms. If one were to say it is established as existing in the lower realms,
then one should not say that eye-consciousness arises manifestly only when one is born in the three higher meditative absorptions (dhyānas) to then obtain that consciousness.
If it does not achieve a lower [level],
then since that transformative mind (*nirmāṇa-citta*) is identical to it in being a fruit of supernormal power (*abhijñā-phala*) and identical in being neutral (*avyākṛta*),
why is it that while one achieves a lower transformative mind, one does not achieve the two types of supernormal powers?
The commentary explains:
One born in the three higher meditative absorptions (dhyānas) accomplishes the two lower supernormal powers (abhijñās),
because these are the fruits of those supernormal powers.
As with the accomplishment of the mind of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*), the treatise does not mention its accomplishment here; this is stated by way of general analogy.
Furthermore, it is explained that one born in the three higher dhyānas does not accomplish the two lower supernormal powers (*abhijñā*).
There are two types of fruition-attainment (nairmāṇika-samādhi).
The first occurs within the mental consciousness;
its power is so intense that it can produce lower states while one is born in a higher realm.
Just as with the mind of transformation,
two [types] exist within the five consciousnesses;
their power is somewhat inferior and thus they cannot produce lower [states].
If it is bound to its own level and arises based on its own level,
then there is acquisition [of it] across the three time periods.

Just as one who is well-practiced in the postures (*īryāpatha*) of their own stage [attains mastery], so too regarding the three types of craftsmanship (*śilpa*) and the two supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) mentioned in the various treatises, there is attainment across the three periods of time.
Regarding "attainment across the three periods of time":
According to the explanation based on the first dhyāna and the two supernormal knowledges (*abhijñā*):

if one born in the three higher dhyānas gives rise to the two supernormal knowledges of a lower level or a different stage, they possess only those that are co-existent with the mental factors (*dharmasahaja*).
Just as when one temporarily borrows the three lower consciousnesses,
or when the mind of deportment (*airyāpathika*) is not a wholesome habituation,
they are acquired only together with the dharma itself.

This treatise states that [the lower stage] is not established; based on this, it is explained as follows. Question: If one born in a higher realm does not achieve the two types of supernormal knowledge (abhijñā) belonging to a different level in the lower realm, then when one’s body is in the desire realm and has become detached from the defilements of the desire realm—
It should also follow that there is no accomplishment of the two higher knowledges (*abhijñā*) belonging to other stages;

yet, the treatise states that the five knowledges are "attained through the separation from defilements" (*vairāgya-pratilambhika*) when previously cultivated. Since they are attained through the separation from defilements, [they must exist].
It is clearly known that there are also cases where [a dhyāna] can be accomplished in a different stage.
For what reason is it that one born in a higher stage does not accomplish a lower one,
while one born in a lower stage can accomplish a higher one?
The commentary explains:
It is easy for the lower to produce the upper and for the upper to accomplish the lower; however, it is difficult for the upper to accomplish the lower and for the lower to produce the upper.
It is not established. Furthermore, according to another interpretation:
for one born in the three higher dhyānas, the two supernormal knowledges (*abhijñā*) of the lower stages may or may not be established.
If one has practiced it habitually, it is accomplished;
if one has not practiced it habitually, it is not accomplished.
Because it is not certain, its accomplishment is not definitively stated.
"‘Etc. means that if there is ‘arrival,’ it refers to excluding the aforementioned characteristics.
This clarifies the accomplishment of the four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*). The first proposition is:
being born in the three higher meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*).
The first phrase means that although the eye is manifested as being accomplished, visual consciousness does not arise.
