The second phrase means that although the consciousness is not manifested as being accomplished—
referring to one born in the desire realm.
The first phrase indicates that although concentration is established as consciousness, it has not yet been attained or has already been lost.
The second phrase indicates that the eye is not established; this refers to the third phrase, namely, those born in the desire realm.
It is shown that the eye is established as consciousness; having acquired it and not lost it,
it is further shown to be established as the eye for one born in the Brahma-world.
The eye and consciousness are necessarily accomplished when one is born in the three higher meditative absorptions (dhyānas).
It is established that the eye is present in those states; this is known from the statement regarding the "correct seeing of forms."
Furthermore, this further clarifies and establishes consciousness. Since it is stated that "when one correctly sees forms," it is clearly known that the manifestation of dharmas is established.
Thus, from the eye-element up to the totality, it is further stated that they are "equal."
The following is a classification by way of analogy: If one considers the eye in relation to visible forms, there are two possible cases:
that if one acquires a visible form, one necessarily acquires the eye.
Because the aggregates of the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) necessarily possess the sense faculties (*indriya*).
There is the case of attaining the eye-faculty but not the objects of sight (*rūpa*);
this refers to one born in the desire realm who gradually acquires the eye-faculty. There are likewise two phrases regarding its accomplishment (*samanvāgama*).
If one possesses the eye faculty, one necessarily possesses the object-form (rūpa).

However, there are cases where one possesses form but does not possess the eye faculty—namely, those born in the desire realm who have not yet acquired the eye faculty, or who have acquired it but subsequently lost it. If one considers consciousness in relation to form, four permutations (catuṣkoṭi) are possible.
There are cases where one acquires consciousness but does not acquire form:
namely, when one is born into the three higher meditative absorptions (dhyānas) and visual consciousness manifests;
and when one dies from those three higher absorptions and is reborn in the desire realm or the Brahma-world.
There is the case where one acquires matter but does not acquire consciousness:
namely, when one dies in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) and is reborn in the three higher meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*). There is the case where both are acquired:
namely, when one dies in the formless realm and is reborn in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) or the Brahma-world (*brahmaloka*). There is the case where neither is acquired.
That is to say, excluding the aforementioned characteristics,
there are two propositions regarding accomplishment:
if one accomplishes consciousness, one necessarily accomplishes form.
There are cases where one achieves form but does not achieve consciousness;
that is to say, when one is born in the [upper] three dhyānas and visual consciousness does not arise.

Therefore, it is said that "achieving" and so forth should be considered according to reason. Regarding the six [realms] and the three [groups], I shall first distinguish how the first three are achieved in relation to one another.
Regarding the latter five types of the three [categories],
there is both acquisition (*prāpti*) and possession (*samanvāgama*), as well as their mutual relationship.
Furthermore, matters such as relinquishment and non-attainment should all be investigated;
they are explained in detail in the *Vibhāṣā*.
It would be impossible to describe them in detail.
Therefore, the verse again uses the term "and so forth" (*ādi*).
Thus, it has already been explained that "reaching the external" refers to whatever remains beyond this.
Below this is the sixteenth section, the "Gate of Internal and External. Generally speaking, there are three types of internal and external phenomena.
Thus, the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 148, states:
"However, there are three distinctions regarding internal and external phenomena."

First, internal and external in terms of the single continuum: that which resides within one's own body is called "internal," while that which resides in another's body or among insentient things is called "external.
Second, internal and external in terms of location.
That which serves as the basis for the mind and mental factors is called "internal";
that which is their object is called "external.
Regarding the three types—sentient, insentient, and both—these are categorized as internal or external accordingly.

That is to say, phenomena belonging to the category of sentient beings are called "internal," while phenomena belonging to the category of non-sentient things are called "external. Now, in this treatise, regarding the internal and external in terms of the sense bases (*āyatana*),
the mind is designated as the "self."
That which is based upon the sense faculties is called "internal";
thus, there are twelve.
"External" refers to the remaining six objects, such as visible forms and so forth.
Because they are not the basis for the self.
Although the sense faculties and consciousnesses also function as objects of cognition,
they are explained here in terms of the bases (āyatana).
That which serves as the basis [of cognition] is always fixed and is designated only as "internal";
it is not designated as "external" based on its being an object.
Since the essence of a self does not exist, how could there be internal or external?
Question:
Why is it said that because they are the basis for the grasping at a self, they are called "external"?
Answer: [It is] the grasping at a self.
That which is called the basis for the view of self is the mind;
this is because the mind is associated with the view of self.
It is called the basis for the grasping at a self (*ātmagrāha*).
The mind is the basis for the self, and is thus conventionally designated as "self.
Although other moments of mind are not associated with the view of a self (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), [they are still the basis for it].

Because it belongs to the same category as that mind, it is also designated by the name "self. Furthermore, another interpretation holds that because the mind is the object of the grasping for a self (*ātmagrāha*), it is called the "basis of the grasping for a self" (*ātmagrāhāśraya*).
Although all contaminated phenomena (*sāsrava*) are objects of the view of a self (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), [the mind is specifically so designated].
Because the mind is preeminent, it is predominantly clung to as the self;

although other untainted minds are not taken as an object of the notion of "I," they are also designated by the name "self" because they belong to the same category of that mind. Furthermore, another interpretation states:
There are two types of self-grasping.
The first is deluded grasping,
which refers to the view of a self.
It takes only that which is tainted (*sāsrava*) as its object.
Second is grasping (*parāmarśa*),
which refers to all states of mind.
The grasping at objects with sovereign power— namely, the apprehension of all preceding objects— is termed *ātma-grāha* (self-clinging).
Although the focal objects (*ālambana*) of these two types of clinging pertain to all phenomena (*dharma*),
it is specifically designated as the "basis" because the mind is preeminent and powerful.
Therefore, the designation "self" is applied metaphorically to this mind;
this interpretation, which relies upon the mind as its basis, can be accepted without contradiction as it applies universally to all states of mind. Furthermore, he cites a sutra as proof.
The preceding sutra disciplines the "self," while the subsequent sutra subdues the mind;
thus we know that the term "self" is used as a mere designation for the mind. The twelve bases, such as the eye and so forth, serve as the basis for this conventional designation of a self.
Because they are closely associated, they are called "internal.
The six objects, such as form and so forth,
are called "external" because they are distant from this provisional self that serves as their objective referent.
Although the various mental factors share the same arising and other characteristics as that mind-king upon which they depend,
they are not designated as "internal."
Because things of different categories do not serve as mutual bases for one another, they are not termed "intimate";
however, all bases and the mind,
though of different categories, mutually serve as bases for one another.
Therefore, it is called "intimate" (*pratyāsanna*) and may be termed "internal. Furthermore, the *Nyāyabhāṣya*, chapter six, explains the mind as the self, stating:
"Because it always functions with mastery over its own internal objects. If one were to refute this as a teacher of the *Abhidharmakośa*:
This is no different from my third interpretation above.
If it is argued that "if so, the six consciousnesses would not have a mental basis," this is a challenge. If so...
The six consciousnesses of the present and future have not yet reached the past stage of the mental faculty (*manas*);
because they do not serve as the support for the mind (*citta*), they should not be designated as "internal."
Regarding the statement "because when it reaches the stage of the mind (manas), it remains without alteration":
this refers to the six consciousnesses reaching the past stage of the mind; even then, they do not lose their status as the six consciousness-elements (vijñāna-dhātu).
The present, future, and not-yet-arrived [states] are the past mental states;

nor do they transcend the characteristic of mind. If it were otherwise, the following section presents a counter-objection against the opponent to demonstrate the fault of contradicting their own tenets.
Furthermore, if the mental element (*manodhātu*) were not established when the six consciousnesses have not yet arisen in the present,
then the past mental element would likewise not be established.
This school maintains that the characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) of the three time periods do not undergo alteration.
Having already explained the internal and external [bases] regarding what is produced and what is not produced as one’s own karma,
hereafter, the seventeenth [topic] clarifies the *sabhāga* (homogeneous) and *tatsabhāga* (non-homogeneous) [factors] within the dharma-element (*dharmadhātu*).
That which is invariably taken as an object by the mental consciousness is always termed *sabhāga*.
The remaining seventeen are each twofold:
when they perform their own function, they are called "homogeneous" (sabhāga);
when they do not perform their own function, they are called "counter-homogeneous" (tatsabhāga).
The Commentary states: "That which extends to the *dhruva* [constituent] is called the *sabhāga*.
This explains the *dharmasabhāga*.
Before explaining the *dharmasabhāga*, the characteristics of the *viṣayasabhāga* are first clarified.
Now, as for what is called "having a common objective sphere" (*sabhāga-viṣaya*):
if an object is definitely the focal object (*ālambana*) of consciousness,
being definitely the focal object constitutes the meaning of "not shared" (*asādhāraṇa*).

The six objects are each termed "fixed objects" (*niyata-ālambana*) because they serve as the objects of their respective consciousnesses. Question: It may be said that the object of mental phenomena (*dharmāyatana*) is "fixed," since it is the object of only one consciousness.
However, the five [sensory] objects are the objects of two consciousnesses; how can they be called "fixed"?
How can one expect certainty for oneself?
The commentary explains:
there are two types of objective certainty.
Either the object is fixed upon the mind,
as phenomena correspond to the intellect;
or the mind is fixed upon the object.
Just as the five consciousnesses take objects,
if a phenomenon faces the mind,
it is necessarily an object of cognition (ālambana).
If the five objects confront the five consciousnesses,
they immediately become the objects of meditative concentration;
thus, there is a state of concentration regarding those very objects.
One distinguishes the homogeneous class (*sabhāga*) based on its fixed location;
consciousness arises— past, present, or future— with respect to its objective referent (*ālambana*).
Future dharmas that are destined to arise—
by specifying those dharmas that will arise as distinct from those that will not arise—
this objective referent is called "homogeneity" (sabhāgatā).

This is a general explanation of the common characteristics of objects and their respective spheres (*sabhāga*). Question: Since the six sense organs (*indriya*) are also capable of apprehending their respective objects, why does this text state that consciousness (*vijñāna*) is not an organ? Answer: *Note: The original Chinese text contains a lacuna regarding the specific answer provided by the commentator. The translation above reflects the structure of the question and the introductory phrase of the response.*
The mental faculty (manas) of the past cannot apprehend objects;
the five faculties are present.
Alternatively, it is neither grasped nor not grasped;
because it is indeterminate, it is omitted and not mentioned. Another interpretation states that consciousness can be used to subsume the sense faculties.
When consciousness perceives an object, the sense faculty also perceives it;
therefore, it is said that consciousness can represent the faculty as its reflection.
Thus, there is no limit to mental consciousness.
This contemplation of non-self takes all phenomena as its object;
within the dharma-realm,
there is not a single phenomenon that is not included therein.
The infinite mental consciousnesses that have arisen, are arising,
and will arise are always termed "homogeneous" (sabhāga) because they arise from meditative concentration. From this point downward,
the various noble ones specifically demonstrate the contemplation of non-self.
It should be understood that when the mental consciousness takes the dharma-realm as its object,
it is termed "homogeneous" (*sabhāga*).
The remaining seventeen realms are also objects of the mental consciousness.
"Why are they not of the same class (*sabhāga*)?
The explanation says:
"Regarding the eighteen elements (*dhātu*), those termed 'of the same class' (*sabhāga*) and 'of the same class in another way' (*tatsabhāga*)."
The six sense faculties and the six consciousnesses are termed "homogeneous" (sabhāga) based on their capacity to apprehend objects;
however, only those that actually apprehend an object are called homogeneous.
This is because the designation "homogeneous" does not apply merely by virtue of being an object.
Although the mental consciousness has them as its objects, they are not "homogeneous" (sabhāga).

If the six external objects are designated as "homogeneous" by virtue of being objects, then even though they are established as homogeneous by virtue of being objects, [they are still not so for the mental consciousness].
However, according to the definitive teaching,
the six objects and two concentrations have already been explained as before;
the dharma-element is designated as "definitive."
Its essence is concentration (*samādhi*).
It is perceived solely by the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) and does not extend to the other five [sensory] consciousnesses.
When the mental consciousness takes concentration as its object, it is termed "homogeneous" (*sabhāga*).
If the five sense objects are called "concentrated" (*samāhita*), it is because they serve as the objects of concentration; thus they are called "concentrated.
Furthermore, each of the five perceives only its own respective object and does not perceive other phenomena; therefore, they are called "concentrated."
Therefore, it is only when the five consciousnesses take an object that they are designated as "homogeneous" (sabhāga);
for the mental consciousness (manovijñāna), this is not fixed.
Although it takes the five objects as its conditions, it is not called "homogeneous" (sabhāga).
Alternatively, among the six objects,
the object of phenomena (dharmāyatana) is precisely the objective condition for the mental consciousness.
The intended meaning is that "homogeneity" (sabhāgatā) refers to the five objects serving as the direct objective conditions (ālambana) for the five consciousnesses. This is why.
The fifth is called "homogeneity" (sabhāgatā).
Although it also involves mental objects (ālambana), because it is not primary, it is not considered homogeneity. Another explanation is as follows:
Among the six objects,
five dharmas are fixed while one is indeterminate;
this is stated in terms of their general categories for fear of confusion.
Regarding the six sense faculties and the six consciousnesses,
five are fixed and one is indeterminate;
they do not become confused or disordered.
Therefore, it is explained in terms of its function. Furthermore, another interpretation holds that the intention behind the classification of dharmas lies in their differentiation;
if they merely serve as objects of mental attention, they are termed "homogeneous" (sabhāga).
There is not a single dharma that is not of the same class (sabhāga), for there would otherwise be no distinction.
This is explained either by way of its function or by way of its essential nature.
Alternatively, it is distinguished by way of its primary [object].
Thus, the *Abhidharmamahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 71, states:
"Question: The remaining seventeen elements (*dhātu*) are also objects cognized by the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*)."
If all were necessarily *sabhāga*, there would be no *tatsabhāga*.
How then can it be said that *tatsabhāga* exists? Answer:
The remaining seventeen elements are not established as "homogeneous" (sabhāga) or "partially homogeneous" (tatsabhāga) based on the mental consciousness element; rather,
they are so established solely in relation to their respective faculties and objects.
The eye encounters forms; forms encounter the eye, and so on,
up to the body encountering tangibles.

Contacting the body. Question: If that is so, then the mind-element (*manodhātu*) and the mind-consciousness-element (*manovijñānadhātu*) should only be established as "homogeneous" (*sabhāga*) and "partially homogeneous" (*tatsabhāga*) with respect to the dharma-element (*dharmadhātu*);
they would thus only have the remaining seventeen elements as their objects.
It should not be of the same class (*sabhāga*).
The answer is: it should indeed be so;
however, by means of the mind-element (*manodhātu*).

And the mental consciousness element (manovijñānadhātu) are established as having the same function (sabhāga) based on their own activity, because they are collectively capable of cognizing all phenomena (dharmas).
Just as the sense organs such as the eye possess functions such as seeing and are never established as being "of that same class" (tatsabhāga), so too for the other two [objects and consciousness],
that which is designated as "reached" (prāpta) is called "of that same class."
The following explains the remaining seventeen [bases].
This is a general heading followed by a brief explanation.
Regarding the passage from "Herein, the eye-element" up to "it should be said that it functions for its own sake":
Below this, there is a detailed explanation of the seventeen elements (*dhātu*).
This specifically explains eleven of those elements.
Within this [section]:
First, the direct explanation;
second, the differentiation of distinctions.
This is the direct explanation: the six sense organs each individually confront their respective six objects, which are termed "their own objects. Furthermore, there is another interpretation.
If the five faculties apprehend their respective objects, they are called "their own objects" (*svaviṣaya*).

The mental faculty (*manas*) universally apprehends all things, and these are all called its "own objects. Question: Why are those [faculties] that have passed, those not yet arisen, and those currently functioning all said to be "homogeneous" (*sabhāga*)?
The past, the future, and the present—all should be termed "appropriated" (*upātta*).
The commentary explains:
there exists the sense of being appropriated, which is distinct from the characteristics of the entity itself.
The meaning of existence is established only by depending on mutual reliance;
therefore, it exists solely in the present.
The homogeneous character (*sabhāgatā*) is based upon the possession of functional activity.
Because it does not function apart from its substance,
it is termed "homogeneity" (sabhāgatā) with respect to both the past and the future. Furthermore, another interpretation holds that "part" (bhāga) signifies "category" (jāti),
by which all similar types can be universally subsumed.
The appropriated [mind] is of a different category;
therefore, it is restricted solely to the present. The questioner’s intention is that the mind capable of producing consciousness may be termed "homogeneous" (sabhāga);
however, since the final mind of one beyond training (aśaikṣa) does not produce further consciousness, [it cannot be so termed].
It should not be the same as "homogeneity" (sabhāgatā).
The commentary explains:
there are two ways in which the name "homogeneity" is applied.
First, the consciousness of a single lifetime;
second, the apprehension of objects.
Although the final mind of one beyond training (aśaikṣa) does not give rise to further consciousness, [it still possesses these two functions].
Because it can apprehend its object, it is called "sabhāga" (homogeneous). In Kaśmīra,
"ka" means "bad" (akuśala) and "śmīra" means "name" (nāman).

The old term "Jibin" (罽賓) is a corruption. Furthermore, when the old *Abhidharmakośa* states that [the author] was a Western Master (*paścātīya-ācārya*), this is an error on the part of the translator.
The various Western Masters referred to here are those from Gandhāra, which lies to the west of Kaśmīra.

There are also many masters of the Sarvāstivāda school who explain that which is non-arisen as being twofold; however, this interpretation is incorrect, for if there were faculties in the state of non-arising, yet no consciousness, [it would contradict the nature of the sense bases].
It also exists within birth;
why then would it alone not arise? Since birth is not opened [as a distinct category], [it cannot be established].
How can that which is non-arising be established as distinct?
This would contradict reason.
Furthermore, the *Vibhāṣā* states:
The former masters of this country taught that there are five types;
the masters of the Western regions taught that there are four types;
now this current master of the country teaches that there are four types.
The masters of the West maintain that there are five types;
however, since the *Vibhāṣā* was composed taking four types as correct,
it is clear that the claim of five is irrational.
This is the scriptural proof: as it is with the eye, so it should be understood for the body element as well, up to that point.
Regarding the mind element (*manodhātu*), those that have arisen, are arising, or will arise, are all of the same class (*sabhāga*).
Therefore, those of the same class (*sabhāga*) are exclusively dharmas that do not arise;
since the arising of consciousness in the past and present must necessarily have an object as its condition,
they are all [considered] of the same class.
The five faculties, such as the eye, in past, present, and future births, possess their "homogeneous portion" (sabhāga) because they exist even when not functioning in dependence on conditions;
this is not the case for those belonging to a different realm of existence (*dhātu*). The rest of the text may be understood accordingly.

Regarding the statement "it should be known that the same applies up to the 'spheres of knowability' (vijñeya-sabhāgatā)," the following section distinguishes the differences: the sense faculties (indriya) are not shared;
for example, the eye of one person [is not common to others].
It is certain that many people do not simultaneously use this same eye to perceive visible forms;
therefore, the faculties are non-common (*asādhāraṇa*). The five objects, however, can be experienced by many people;
therefore, they are called common (*sādhāraṇa*).
Because it is unique [to each individual], when it performs its function, it is called "homogeneous" (sabhāga).
All other [eyes] that do not perform their function are also homogeneous in relation to this eye;
the same applies to the "non-homogeneous" (tatsabhāga) as well.
Because form is common [to all],
those who give rise to views and so forth toward this form and the like are called "homogeneous" (sabhāga);
those who do not give rise to views and so forth are called "counterpart-homogeneous" (tat-sabhāga).
If it is argued that sound may be like visible form in its reaching [the sense organ], yet unlike visible form in its description,
then this is refuted by the fact that among the three— odor, taste, and tangible objects—
only one is apprehended at a time, not all others.
It should be like the eye and so forth,
and not like form; although this principle holds, because [the object] reaches [the sense organ], it is explained as being like form.
Answer: The two objects of form and sound are called "common" because many sentient beings see and hear them together.
The three—odor, taste, and tangibility—are likewise [common].
Although when the sense faculty is correctly joined with one person, it cannot apprehend others;
yet if it were in the future, before being joined with the faculty,
it would [apprehend] both that one and the others.
In all cases, there is the possibility of generating consciousnesses such as that of the nose;
thus, there can be a common apprehension [of an object].
This is not the case for the eye and the other [faculties].
Therefore, it is as explained regarding form. Furthermore,
another interpretation is that it is like two people whose three faculties— the nose, tongue, and body—
each touch one another.
They smell the intermediate fragrance together;
they taste the intermediate flavor together;
they perceive the intermediate touch together.
Therefore, they are called "common.
The sense faculties (*indriya*) are not like this;
there are no two people who share a single faculty. However, a single type of odor, taste, or tangible object can give rise to multiple consciousnesses; for this reason, they are called "common."
The sense faculties (*indriya*) are not like that;
there is no single type of faculty that two people can share to produce consciousness, because the faculties are distinct for each individual.
Question: As stated in the *Nyāyānusāra* (Treatise on Right Reasoning), fascicle 6:
Sound is explained as being like visible form because it is a common object;
whereas odor, taste, and tangibility are explained as being like the internal sense bases because they are not common objects.
Nevertheless, worldly people rely upon conventional designations and conceptual notions.
Some say: "We all smell this fragrance together;
we all taste this flavor together;
we all perceive this touch together."
The various mental factors (caitta) are explained according to the *Nyāya* [system].

Odor, taste, and touch are explained in the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*) as in the case of the eye; in conventional enumeration (*saṃvṛti-saṃkhyā*), they are explained as in the case of visible form (*rūpa*).
Does this treatise not contradict that [other position]?
The explanation is as follows: This treatise refers to external odors, tastes, and tangibles at the time they have not yet been apprehended, when they exist in the future;
in such a state, there is the possibility that many people may experience them together.
Therefore, as it is said regarding form: according to the *Saṃyuktābhidharmahṛdaya* and the *Nyāyānusāra*,
at the time of correctly apprehending [an object], other [faculties] cannot apprehend it.
Because it is taught that they are not common objects, like the internal elements;
thus, each [explanation] is based on a distinct meaning and is not contradictory. Furthermore, another interpretation holds that the intent of the treatise in each case is different.
In the *Abhidharmahṛdaya* and the *Nyāyānusāra*,
it is held that one perceives only the internal odors, tastes, and tangibles within the body, and cannot perceive external ones;
external objects merely serve as conditions to trigger those internal perceptions.
The intent of this treatise is to state that not only does [the nose] apprehend internal odors, tastes, and tangibles, it can also apprehend external ones; thus,
the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 71, also records two views, saying:
Some wish to have only the odors, tastes, and tangibles within one's own body smelled, tasted, and felt;
others wish to also smell, taste, and feel the odors, tastes, and tangibles belonging to others as well as to insentient things.
If one follows the previous interpretation, it should be stated as follows:
the realms of odor, taste, and tangibility are explained according to conventional reasoning in the same manner as the realm of form.
According to the ultimate meaning,
it is as explained regarding the eye-element;
however, if one relies on the latter sense:
It should be stated as follows:
when the elements of odor, flavor, and tangibility have already been experienced,
or are being experienced.
According to conventional truth, it is as explained in the case of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*);
according to ultimate truth, it is as explained in the case of the eye element (*cakṣurdhātu*).
If it has not yet been experienced, even according to ultimate truth, it may also be said to be as explained in the case of the form realm.
Therefore, all treatises state this.

As it is with the element of visible form, so it is with the elements of sound, odor, taste, and tangible objects, because these—odor, taste, and tangible objects—are obtainable by more than one [sense-faculty]. (Above from the *Abhidharmahṛdaya* and the *Nyāyānusāra*).
The former masters of the *Mahāvibhāṣā* [hold this view];
this treatise agrees with the later masters of the *Mahāvibhāṣā*.
If one relies on the former interpretation...
The *Saṃyuktābhidharmahṛdaya* and the *Nyāyānusāra* are likewise in agreement with the later masters of the *Mahāvibhāṣā*.
Although the *Mahāvibhāṣā* contains two positions, it lacks a formal adjudication;
for now, we shall take the position of the later masters as correct.
Because the categories of phenomena (dharmas) are thus exhausted:
if external odors, tastes, and tangibles were not apprehended by the three [other] faculties, they would have to be subsumed under the sphere of phenomena (dharmāyatana).
Since the three [objects] beginning with odor do not exist within the sphere of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*),
it is clear that the latter master’s position is correct.
Regarding the six consciousnesses, such as the visual consciousness, up to the explanation of the mental faculty (*manodhātu*):
This explains the six consciousnesses;
by analogy, the same applies to the mental faculty (*manas*).
What is the meaning of "homogeneous" (*sabhāga*) and "partially homogeneous" (*tatsabhāga*)?
Question: Regarding the two types of meaning, why are the triad of sense-faculties, objects, and consciousnesses termed "homogeneous" (*sabhāga*)?
Answer: Because each of the three—the sense-faculty, the object, and the consciousness—performs its respective function.
Because they mutually accord with one another and further interact, it is called "part" (*bhāga*).
Because they equally possess this part of interaction, it is called "homogeneity" (*sabhāgatā*). Alternatively:
"Sharing" (sabhāga) refers to that which has already performed its function;
therefore, it was previously stated:
"If it performs its own activity, it is called sabhāga."
The triad of faculty, object, and consciousness share this same functional portion;
therefore, they are called "homogeneous" (sabhāga). Alternatively:
"Part" refers to the fruit of contact that has arisen;
the sense faculty, the object, and consciousness all share this resultant part.
Therefore, it is called "homogeneous" (sabhāga). That which is the opposite of this is called "non-homogeneous" (tatsabhāga).
For example, an eye that does not see visible forms is called non-homogeneous;
an eye that sees visible forms is called homogeneous.
The eye that does not see visible forms because it is non-homogeneous (asabhāga) is of the same category as the eye that sees visible forms,
being identical in its essential nature.
Regarding the term "sabhāga" (homogeneous), it is said that its "part" (*bhāga*) is the same as the "kind" (*jāti*).
The *Nyāyānusāra* asks:
"In what way is its part the same as that kind?"
This means that this and that share identical characteristics such as views and so forth,
and because they occupy the same location and the same realm,
they act as causes for one another.
Because they are mutually connected and mutually induce one another,
their categories and divisions are identical. The commentary explains:
The useless [eye] and that which is useful are identical in their category and share the same function of seeing; thus,
they are equally the eye-base (*cakṣur-āyatana*).
The visual faculties serve as mutual homogeneous causes for one another and are mutual outflow fruits;
they are interconnected and mutually induce one another.
Such a category is called a "portion" (*bhāga*).

When that which is functional and that which is non-functional both possess this same portion, the latter is designated as "homogeneous with that" (*tatsabhāga*) because it shares the same portion as the functional one.
Having already explained that the *sabhāgatā* (homogeneity) up to the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) is certainly not abandoned by insight (*darśana-prahātavya*),
the following is the eighteenth section on the three types of abandonment.
The first two lines constitute the analysis by way of the realms (*dhātu-vibhāga*).
The final two lines refute divergent views. The *Śāstra* states:
"Up to 'none are to be abandoned,'" which explains the preceding two lines.
"Abandonment" (*prahāṇa*) refers to severing the bonds and realizing dissociation (*visamyoga*).
The *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya* (Exposition of the Treasury), Chapter Four, states:
"First, abandonment by way of intrinsic nature;
second, abandonment by way of the object."
If a phenomenon is a fetter,
or possesses a single fruit and so forth,
it is abandoned when its antidote arises.
This is called the abandonment of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-prahāṇa*). Because that [intrinsic nature] is abandoned,
one attains dissociation (*visamyoga*) from the objective basis (*ālambana-vastu*).
It is not necessary that non-attainment within [the object] be called the "severance of the object-condition" (*ālambana-prahāṇa*). The commentary states:
both intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) and the object-condition are termed "severed" by way of being free from bondage.
The term "and so forth" includes acquisition (*prāpti*).
According to that treatise,
this refers to the four characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) of the afflictions (*kleśa*) and so forth, as well as acquisition.
The non-establishment of the object is also termed the severance of intrinsic nature;
if it is the severance of the fetter that takes [the object] as its condition, this is based on the afflictions directed toward that object.
It is only when they are ultimately exhausted that they are termed "abandoned.
This does not necessarily mean they are non-existent.
For a detailed explanation, see the *Nyāyānusāra*. As for the statement that fifteen elements (*dhātu*) are abandoned solely through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*):
If the five faculties, as well as odors, tastes, and tangibles, are of an undefiled nature;
furthermore, because the bonds of conditions for these material phenomena (*rūpadharma*) have been severed;
and because the two realms of form and sound are directly initiated by a mind abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*).
Furthermore, because the fetters of the object-condition for form-dharmas have been severed;
if the five consciousness-elements are wholesome or indeterminate,
they are so because the fetters of the object-condition for non-affliction have been severed.
These are defiled because they arise from delusion regarding phenomena; therefore, they are all abandoned only through cultivation.
They lack the characteristics of being abandoned through insight and thus do not pertain to abandonment by insight.

None of these are untainted (*anāsrava*), nor do they pertain to what is not to be abandoned (*aprahātavya*). Regarding the latter three [categories], they are associated with the three [types of abandonment];

namely, the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) to be abandoned by insight (*darśana-prahātavya*) and their associated phenomena (*saṃprayukta-dharma*), because they arise from delusion regarding the principles (*tattva*).
The four characteristics and acquisition are abandoned by insight, because they are the direct instigators of those delusions of view.
The characteristic of being abandoned through cultivation does not apply to that which is abandoned through cultivation;
because it is not untainted (*anāsrava*), it does not apply to that which is not abandoned. Furthermore, another interpretation states:
there are eighty-eight afflictions (*kleśa*).
Because they arise from delusion regarding the principles, they are abandoned by insight (*darśana-prahātavya*).
The factors associated with the afflictions are directly related to those afflictions,
because they are bound together through association and because they function as associated causes (*samprayuktaka-hetu*).
Therefore, as the secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*) are abandoned, although these four views do not correspond to those afflictions,
they are nonetheless bound by the same category (*nikāya-sabhāga*) and function as co-existent causes (*sahabhū-hetu*). Thus, they are abandoned simultaneously.
Furthermore, it is abandoned along with the afflictions;
although it is neither associated with nor co-existent with those afflictions, it is nonetheless bound by them because they belong to the same category.
If there is delusion, there is existence; if there is no delusion, there is no existence.
Although these are bonds of conditions, they are also directly related to delusion;
therefore, as delusion is severed, [existence] follows suit.
Because they are not delusions regarding objects and so forth, they are not abandoned through the path of cultivation;
because they are dharmas to be abandoned, they are not non-abandonable.
As for all other contaminated [dharmas], such as those that are wholesome or non-obscured-neutral in the formless realm:
This is because the bonds of non-afflicted conditions have been severed;
for all afflictions and their associated factors arise from delusion regarding objective phenomena.
The four characteristics [of conditioned phenomena] and their acquisition are so designated because they are directly initiated by the mind of that [cultivation];
likewise, virtuous and defiled non-informative matter (avijñapti) are so designated because they are directly initiated by a mind to be abandoned through cultivation.
Furthermore, these are material phenomena (rūpadharma) whose binding conditions have been severed.
All are abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*). They lack the characteristics of being abandoned through vision (*darśana-heya*), and thus do not pertain to abandonment by vision;
nor do they pertain to non-abandonment (*aheya*), because they are not untainted (*anāsrava*).
Since all untainted (anāsrava) phenomena are not bound by fetters, they are all not to be abandoned (*aprahātavya*).
One might ask: "Is it not the case that there are further [phenomena] that are diametrically opposed to the ultimate?
This section below explains the latter half of the verse.
The Sautrāntikas and others object:
Since the nature of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva*) and so forth do not arise in one who has attained the state of an noble one (*ārya*),
they should logically be abandoned through vision (*darśana-prahātavya*), as they are contrary to the state of a noble one.
"Even so, this dharma is definitely not abandoned by insight. Answer: Briefly opening three chapters to demonstrate that it is not abandoned by insight:
first, non-defiled dharmas.
As the *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya* states:
Regarding "non-defiled," this refers to tainted wholesome states and non-obscured neutral states.
These two are not produced by the six [mental consciousnesses].
This refers to the five consciousnesses and so forth.
They are called "not produced from the six" because they arise from the five sense organs;
although they also arise from the mind, this designation is made based on their specific supports.
The *Tri-ratna-vyākhyā* states:
"Form refers to that which is tainted by outflows (*sāsrava*) and not free from defilement. It further offers another interpretation:
"All phenomena that are not free from defilement."
All dharmas that are not produced by the six [senses], all material dharmas,
and all untainted (anāsrava) dharmas.

In principle, it is also certainly not something to be abandoned by insight (*darśana-prahātavya*). Alternatively, the *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya-ṭīkā* (Xianzong lun) may provisionally rely on the perspective of what is abandoned;
however, the principle that untainted phenomena (*anāsrava*) are not to be abandoned is beyond doubt.
Therefore, they are not explained separately.
It should be understood that,
herein, all non-defiled dharmas are certainly not abandoned by insight.
This is stated here as a specific rule;
it does not mean that all defiled states are abandoned through seeing.
Regarding those among them that are defiled:
If those associated with the delusions of view (dṛṣṭi) and so forth are abandoned by seeing (darśana-heya),
the remainder are abandoned by cultivation (bhāvanā-heya). Because they are not fixed [in their mode of abandonment], they are not mentioned.
That which is not born of the six [consciousnesses] is definitely not abandoned by insight;
this is what is specifically stated here.
It does not mean that everything born of the six is entirely abandoned by insight.
Among the six types of arising,
those associated with the delusions of view are abandoned through seeing;
the remaining contaminated [phenomena] are abandoned through cultivation.
If something is untainted (*anāsrava*) or not subject to abandonment (*aprahātavya*), it is not mentioned because it is indeterminate;
here, only that which is matter (*rūpa*) and definitely not abandoned by insight (*darśana-prahātavya*) is specifically discussed.
This does not mean that all non-material things (*arūpa*) are abandoned by insight.
Among those that are not form,
if they are associated with the delusions of view, they are abandoned by insight;
the remainder, being tainted, are abandoned by cultivation.
If it were untainted (*anāsrava*) and not subject to abandonment (*aprahātavya*), it would not be mentioned because it is indeterminate.
As for its being the nature of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva*), it is because it arises from immediate proximity.
Separate Explanation: This nature of being an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva*) is comprised within the category of non-defiled neutral (*akliṣṭāvyākṛta*),
because the bonds of the objects of perception have been severed.
Because it is still possessed by those who have already abandoned desire,
it is clearly known not to be defiled;
because it is still possessed by those who have severed the roots of goodness, [it is known not to be wholesome].
Knowing it is not wholesome,
and since it is not defiled,
one clearly knows it is not abandoned by insight.

Although it is not abandoned by seeing [the truths], because it has already been relinquished previously, one is not called a *pṛthagjana* (ordinary worldling). To counter-argue against the Sautrāntikas and others, he says:
"If this nature of being an ordinary worldling (*pṛthagjanatva*) were abandoned by seeing [the truths]..."
Since the nature of that [state] is already established at the stage of the patience regarding the dharma of suffering (duḥkha-dharma-kṣānti),
one would then be an ordinary person (pṛthagjana) at that time. If it were established then...
There was then a man named Fan-sheng-guo (Ordinary-Saint-Passing).
He was called a "saint" (ārya) because he had accomplished the dharmas of a saint; he was called "ordinary" (pṛthagjana) because he possessed the nature of an ordinary person.

Because it contradicts reason, it is not abandoned by insight (*darśana-prahātavya*). This can be understood as being other than the six [mental factors] that arise with birth (*saha-ja*) and as being form (*rūpa*). That which is previously mentioned as non-defiled (*akliṣṭa*), that which does not arise with the six [consciousnesses], and this form [are not abandoned by insight].
They are certainly not abandoned through insight. Why is this?
Because these three types...
First, it is not deluded regarding the principle of the truths;

second, it is not directly initiated by the afflictions of view (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*). Alternatively, it is non-defiled, not produced by the six [consciousnesses], and not deluded regarding the principle of the truths.
Form (*rūpa*) is not directly initiated by the afflictions of view.
Therefore, it is not abandoned by insight (*darśana-prahātavya*). Furthermore, another interpretation states:
the six [mental factors] previously mentioned, as well as this form (*rūpa*), are certainly not abandoned by insight.
The five consciousnesses do not delude regarding the principles of the truths (*satya*).
This is because form (*rūpa*) is not the direct cause for the arousal of afflictions associated with views (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*).

Furthermore, non-defiled [form] is not abandoned by the path of seeing (*darśana-heya*), as this has already been explained separately. Question: Regarding the form abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya-rūpa*).
The afflictions of the nine grades each arise individually and directly;
since they arise individually and directly,
this form should be severed accordingly, following those respective afflictions.
The commentary states:
This defiled matter is directly produced by the afflictions abandoned through cultivation; therefore, it is abandoned through cultivation.
Because the bonds of conditions are severed,
the nine grades of afflictions must first be eliminated before they can be said to be "severed";
it is not a matter of severing them individually.
If the afflictions of the higher realms, as well as the four characteristics,
were to be abandoned by their own nature,
they would not be analogous to this matter (rūpa).
It should be understood as explained previously:
[this applies] to the dharmas such as the afflictions (*kleśa*).
It is attained together with the four characteristics.
If it is abandonment by way of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-prahāṇa*) or abandonment of the object (*ālambana-prahāṇa*),
it is subsumed under abandonment by way of intrinsic nature.
If there is a bond of association (*saṃprayoga-bandhana*) and a bond of object (*ālambana-bandhana*),
it is subsumed under the bond of object.
This is according to the *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya*, Chapter Four.
To explain these three dharmas:
first, the dharma of non-defilement,
as well as all material (rūpa) dharmas.
That which is not abandoned by seeing refers to those afflictions that are only designated as "abandoned" at the time they are ultimately severed. Furthermore, it says:
Those dharmas that are not born of the six [consciousnesses] and are not abandoned by insight do so because they function externally toward objects such as visible forms (*rūpa*).
Thus it has been explained, up to the point concerning those forms that are obstructed.
Below this is the nineteenth section, the "Gate of Views and Non-Views.
Within it, the first part provides the formal explanation.
Second, the digression.
This is the actual exposition.
The first two lines set forth the essence of the view.
The following six lines resolve objections and refute misconceptions: the Venerable Vasumitra maintains that it is the eye that sees;
the Venerable Dharmatrāta maintains that it is visual consciousness (*cakṣurvijñāna*) that sees;
and the Venerable Ghoṣaka maintains that it is the wisdom (*prajñā*) associated with visual consciousness that sees.

The Dārṣṭāntikas [assert] that seeing is the conjunction of the mental states and mental factors (citta-caitta) simultaneous with eye-consciousness. Question: Works such as the *Vibhāṣā*, the *Pañcavastuka*, and the *Abhidharmahṛdaya* all refute the conjunction of consciousness and wisdom.

Why does this verse refute only consciousness (*vijñāna*)? One explanation is that it refutes [the opponent's position] according to the intention of the author of the treatise. Another explanation is that it also incidentally refutes wisdom (*prajñā*).
The verse states: "The wisdom co-arising with the five consciousnesses is not vision (*darśana*)."
It is already known that [the Sautrāntika] refutes wisdom (*prajñā*) but does not refute the composite whole (*saṃghāta*). This may be so;
for they consider the composite whole to be identical to the Sautrāntika school.
The author of the treatise does not refute [the opponent's position] separately because its meaning is already clear. Furthermore, according to another interpretation, all three types are refuted.
The statement that obstructive matter is not seen is used to refute consciousness by way of its dominant factor;
wisdom and their conjunction are refuted by analogy.
It should be understood that the *Abhidharmasamuccaya* states:
"The eye of the same class sees forms; it is not that eye-consciousness sees them."
It is not wisdom;
it is not a composite [consciousness], because obstructed forms are not perceived. Furthermore, this treatise explains that consciousness is refuted by way of its dominant [characteristic].
The refutation of these three types is extensive, as found in various treatises.
Thus, the first chapter of the *Pañcavastuka-śāstra* asks:
"Who is it that can see form?"
Is it the eye faculty that sees?
Is it the visual consciousness that sees?
Or is it the wisdom associated with visual consciousness that sees?
Is it seen as a combination of mind and mental factors?
How can such a doubt arise?
To have such a doubt is itself a fault.
If it is the eye-faculty that sees,
why is it that when other consciousnesses are active, one does not see forms?
Why do they not simultaneously grasp all objects?
If it is visual consciousness that sees,
then since consciousness has only the characteristic of discernment (*vijñapti*) and not the characteristic of seeing, how could it possibly see visible forms?
If it is held that what is seen is the wisdom associated with visual consciousness,
then one must likewise admit that what is heard is the wisdom associated with auditory consciousness; yet, that [wisdom] is not hearing.
How is this seen? If it is the conjunction of mind and mental factors that is able to see,
then such a conjunction of various minds and mental factors is not determinate.
That is to say, a wholesome visual consciousness is associated with twenty-two mental factors;
an unwholesome visual consciousness is associated with twenty-one mental factors;
and a visual consciousness that is obscured-neutral is associated with eighteen kinds of mental factors.
Since the unobscured-neutral eye-consciousness is not determined to be associated with twelve types of mental factors, how do they combine?
Answer: It is the eye-faculty that sees, but it does so only when conjoined with eye-consciousness, and not otherwise.
For example, the function of visual consciousness in discerning forms exists only by depending upon the eye;
likewise, the functions of feeling and so forth in experiencing and so on must necessarily depend upon the mind.
This case should be understood in the same way.
By this principle,
when other consciousnesses are cognizing [objects], the visual consciousness is already empty and thus cannot see forms;
furthermore, there is no fault of simultaneously apprehending all objects.
Because within a single continuum, two minds do not arise simultaneously.
Question: For what reason are there six bases and six objects, yet no six consciousnesses arise together within a single continuum?
Answer: Because the equal-and-immediate condition (samanantarapratyaya) is singular.
Furthermore, there is another point:
if it is the eye-consciousness that sees, then what else could cognize?
If it is wisdom that sees, who else could know?
If it is the conjunction of mind and mental factors that can see the various distinct functions of each phenomenon,
then within that [conjunction], there is certainly no sense of a "conjoined seeing."
Furthermore, a single entity would have to possess two functions,
namely, the capacity for seeing and the capacity for experiencing and so forth.
Moreover, there is another point.
If consciousness were that which sees, then because consciousness is non-obstructive,
it should be able to see forms that are obstructed;
the same should be understood to apply to wisdom and their conjunction as well.
Therefore, the eye-faculty alone is designated as "that which sees.
The treatise states: "As for the others, none are seeing.
Among the eighteen elements (*dhātu*), the eye-element is entirely seeing.
One part of the dharma-dhātu consists of eight kinds that are views;
the remaining sixteen dhātus in their entirety,
as well as a small portion of the dharma-dhātu, are not views.
None of these constitute "view.
One should know that within this context, there are two kinds of view:
first, that which is termed "view" as discerning observation.
Regarding what is called the eye-faculty (*cakṣur-indriya*):

although wisdom (*prajñā*) is also termed "contemplative observation" (*vipaśyanā*), here we shall provisionally refer to the eye itself as "contemplative observation. Question: When the eye encounters a visible form (*rūpa*), how is it designated as "seeing"?
If you say that light extends to reach the object,
then lamps and the sun should also be called "seeing.
If you say it is the reflection that appears, [then...]
A water mirror should also be called "seeing.
If you say it is because its substance is pure and subtle, then the four faculties of the ear and so forth should also be called "seeing. The explanation says: when the eye sees forms...
They do not emit light to reach their objects, unlike a lamp or the sun;
nor do they manifest reflections, unlike water or a mirror.
Although the substance of the five material faculties is entirely pure, their functional operations are each distinct.
That is to say: the eye sees forms;
the ear hears sounds;
the nose smells odors.
The tongue tastes flavors;
the body perceives tangibles;
the eye confronts forms, yet it is not like tongs grasping an object.
It simply arises as the function of observing form;
therefore, it is uniquely called "view" (*dṛṣṭi*) because it differs from [other mental factors] such as [perception].
Second, that which involves deliberation is called "view."
Within that wisdom, only these eight types [of consciousness] can observe;
the remaining sixteen elements in their entirety and a portion of the dharma-element cannot be observed by it.
Furthermore, it lacks inferential deliberation.
None of these are [correct] views. What are the eight?
Question:
Regarding the statement that the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and so forth differ in terms of clarity and obscurity:
the answer is that worldly views are either defiled or undefiled.
That which is defiled or undefiled is called "worldly"; that which is in training or beyond training is called "views. The simile of a cloudy night illustrates the state of being defiled;
because the five views are tainted by outflows (*āsrava*), they are like the night.
Because these are afflictions, they are like clouds;
the cloudless night serves as a metaphor for being free from defilement;
because right view still possesses outflows (*sāsrava*), it is like the night.

Because they are free from afflictions, they are like a cloudless sky; the daytime with clouds is a metaphor for those in training (*śaikṣa*), as they possess right view that is untainted (*anāsrava*)—thus like day—and yet possess afflictions—thus like clouds.
The daytime without clouds is a metaphor for those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*).
Because right view is untainted (*anāsrava*), it is like the daytime;
because it is free from afflictions (*kleśa*), it is like a cloudless sky.
The remainder of the text may be understood accordingly.
Why is it that right view in the world is associated only with the mental consciousness?
Question:
Because the five [sensory] consciousnesses do not reach this [level], they are not views.

Answer: It can be understood. Question: The five consciousnesses lack investigative discrimination (*abhinirūpaṇā-vikalpa*), and thus may be termed "non-conceptual" (*nirvikalpa*), just as with the contaminated right view (*sāsrava-samyagdṛṣṭi*) within meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
Furthermore, regarding the right view of those in training and those beyond training,
since it is devoid of conceptual calculation and discrimination,
how can it be called "view"?

Because conceptualization (*vitarka*) and discrimination (*vicāra*) consist solely of scattered wisdom (*prajñā*). The commentary explains: although meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*) are not themselves conceptualization and discrimination, they are called "view" (*dṛṣṭi*) because they are capable of investigative deliberation (*santīraṇa*) and decisive judgment (*niścaya*).
"By analogy.
As for the statement 'the remainder of these, up to those that are not views,
should be known,' this is an illustrative explanation."
Among the eighteen elements (*dhātu*), the eye element is entirely seeing, because it observes and illuminates forms.
Eight types within the dharma element are seeing,
because they possess the nature of investigative judgment.
Among those types of wisdom, the wisdom associated with the five sensory consciousnesses is not, in its entirety, "view" (*dṛṣṭi*),
because it does not involve deliberative judgment (*pariccheda*). By this same principle, the remaining defiled wisdoms [are also not view].
