Why, then, is only one designated by the name "contact" (*sparśa*)? The explanation is as follows: the reason why faculties (*indriya*) and objects (*viṣaya*) do not touch one another is that each of the four sides of all phenomena possesses its own specific power and function.
Just as when a person is surrounded on all four sides by conditions such as water or a mirror, their reflection immediately appears;
so too it is with the atoms.
When each possesses its own power and they are in a state of mutual pressure, they obstruct one another so that they cannot come into contact; therefore, they do not touch.
Thus, the *Nyāyānusāra* says:
Although there may be slight intervals between them, they possess the power to obstruct its movement;
thus concludes the treatise. Although the three faculties are all termed "attainment" (*prāpti*), they are not without distinction.
The olfactory faculty perceives fragrance.
For the sake of conventional explanation, a single atom is said to be divided into four parts;
between the nose and the fragrance it perceives, there are three parts of empty space.
The tongue’s apprehension of flavor has two parts that are empty;
the body’s apprehension of touch has one part that is empty.
The reason for this is as follows:
The substance of fragrance is subtle and its power is moreover strong;
therefore, it reaches somewhat further.
The substance of taste is coarser and its power is correspondingly weaker.
The substance of tangibility (*spraṣṭavya*) is the coarsest [of the external objects] yet its power is the weakest;
therefore, that which is in closest proximity is termed the "object touched" (*spraṣṭavya*), while the body is termed the "agent that touches" (*spraṣṭṛ*).
If it is claimed that the object of touch is also capable of touching,
then one must admit that the body-faculty (*kāyendriya*) is also an object of touch;
in that case, the distinction between the object (*viṣaya*) and the subject (*viṣayin*) would become confused.
Nevertheless, there is no confusion.
Having established the object (*viṣaya*) and the subject (*viṣayin*), the other two [objects]—smell and taste—are established somewhat further away.
Therefore, the *Nyāyānusāra*, chapter eight, states:
Although they are similar in their proximity, there are distinctions among them;
for example, although the eyelids and so forth share the common designation of "reaching," there are nonetheless distinctions among them.
It is not that the eyelids and so forth are designated as "reaching" [the object] such that all things would then be indistinguishable in their reaching; for the eyelid,
the probe, the medicinal ointment, and the physician differ in their degree of proximity to the visual faculty within the continuum of categories.
Furthermore, regarding the statement that "aggregated matter [continues] up to a homogeneous succession," this is the second master’s explanation below:
although the various atoms do not touch one another.
Since it is admitted that composite matter possesses spatial divisions (*digbhāga*),
there is no fault in their mutual contact;
for it is by virtue of this that striking produces sound.
If one accepts this principle that the color-form of the aggregate (saṃghāta-rūpa) undergoes contact,
then the textual meaning of the *Vibhāṣā* is well-established;
thus, this name "aggregate" refers to contact.
"Coarse aggregation" indicates the meaning of a gross collection;
"dispersed" refers to that which is non-contacting,
indicating the meaning of a subtle collection.
The coarse object perceived at a distance is not tangible.
If it were otherwise,
then within the motes of dust already present before one's eyes, there would already be an infinite number of atomic clusters.
It should be called "contact.
The first phrase refers to the combination and separation [of elements],
such as when a ball of powder is dispersed into space.
This reveals the meaning of a coarse aggregate giving rise to a subtle aggregate.
The second phrase refers to the combination of dispersed elements,
such as when scattered fibers are gathered to form a ball.
This clarifies the meaning of subtle aggregates giving rise to coarse aggregates.
The third phrase refers to conjunction;
that is, conjunction.
"Just as a ball of flour forms another ball" illustrates the sense that a coarse aggregate arises from a coarse aggregate,
or that [an aggregate] arises from its own kind.
Alternatively, it may transform into coarseness;
although there are slight differences between the preceding and succeeding states,
both are termed "coarse."
If the second case involves what is subtle at first and coarse later,
their essential natures are so vastly different that it cannot serve as an analogy.
Otherwise, if it becomes even more coarse, under which category would it be subsumed?
If it is said that [the object] is subsumed under the second clause,
then there should be no third clause.
If it is argued that the third clause refers to a coarse [object] producing its own kind of coarse [result], then...
Since they are already designated as "contact" when compared with their own kind,
and subsequently give rise to something even coarser,
why is the former contact called "non-contact" in relation to the latter?
The fourth phrase refers to the dispersal of that which is already dispersed,
moving toward motile dust;
this reveals the sense that a subtle aggregate arises from a subtle aggregate.
They may arise as their own kind,
or they may transform and arise as subtle;
although there are slight differences between the preceding and succeeding states, both are termed "subtle."
In the first case, the former is coarse and the latter is subtle;
their essential natures are vastly different,
so this cannot be used as an analogy for the present instance.
This treatise, for the time being, refers to the continuity of similar types. Were it not so,
under which category would the phrase "the arising of subtle matter from previously moving dust" be subsumed?
If you say that it is subsumed under the first category,
then there should be no fourth category at all.
If you say that the production of a subtle [particle] from its own subtle class constitutes the fourth category, then these classes, when compared with one another, are already termed "non-contact."
It transforms and becomes even more subtle.
Why was it not called "contact" (*spraṣṭavya*) previously, yet is now called "contact"?
Venerable Vasumitra says: it persists until the subsequent moment.
This is the explanation of the third master.
This master’s intention is to say that past and future atoms exist in a state of dispersion.
If [the moments] flow from the future into the present without even slightly touching one another,
then their dispersal into the past is easily accomplished. However,
if they touch one another in the present, it is difficult for them to disperse upon entering the past.
It takes some time before they can finally be separated;
like objects stuck together with glue,
even if one tries to force them apart, it still takes some time.
If it were to persist in the present, it would have to continue into the subsequent moment;
if it were to reach the subsequent moment, its nature would necessarily be eternal. Furthermore, another interpretation holds that future atoms abide in a dispersed state;
yet if one were to claim they touch one another...
Just as there is an interval between two atoms when they first reach the present moment,
they perish as soon as they are about to touch;
if they were to traverse this space, they would have reached the subsequent moment.
The time it takes for a single atom (*paramāṇu*) to pass through one [unit of space] is called one *kṣaṇa*.
Although there may be empty intervals where not even a single atom can fit,
when they are about to touch, they return to the subsequent moment (*paścāt-kṣaṇa*).
If it were to reach the subsequent moment, it would necessarily be permanent.
As for the Venerable One’s statement that "reaching" is a metaphorical designation for contact,
this constitutes the fourth interpretation.
Among the four great masters, Dharmatrāta was revered for his virtue;
because his name was not extensively cataloged, he is addressed as "Venerable" (Bhadanta).
To speak according to the truth:
They do not actually touch one another;
rather, the designation "contact" is applied metaphorically because they are situated in immediate proximity.
This intention of the Venerable [Vasubandhu] should be found agreeable.

This is the second [section], describing its length. Although there have been four interpretations above, the Master of the Treatise (Śāstrin) evaluates and adopts the fourth, that of the Venerable (Bhadanta).
In the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 132, there are likewise four interpretations.
The same applies to this treatise.
If it were otherwise, then up to the point where they admit [the object] to be resistant (*sapratigha*),
this section below constitutes the third [part], which refutes its shortcomings.
Among these,
the first refutes the third teacher mentioned previously,
and the second refutes the second teacher mentioned previously.
The third [section] refutes the first master mentioned above,
proceeding from the end toward the beginning;
this constitutes the first part of the text.
For this reason, the third school is refuted first.
The Master’s intention is that the Venerable [Vasumitra] asserts that atoms are immediately adjacent to one another,
whereas he considers the position of the World-Honored Friend (Vasumitra) to be that there is a slight distance between them.
Therefore it is said:
"If one were to speak otherwise than this Great Virtuous One,
these atoms would necessarily have intervals between them."
Since the space between them is empty,
what could obstruct their movement so that they cannot advance and draw near one another?
If they were to abide separately, [how could this be explained]?
If there is empty space in between, they do not obstruct one another.
How, then, can it be maintained that they constitute "obstructive resistance" (*āvaraṇa-pratighāta*)? Furthermore, this passage refutes a divergent view within the *Mahāvibhāṣā*, not Vasumitra.

Because the explanation of Vasumitra contains no contradictions, and because there are gaps within the alternative explanations of the *Mahāvibhāṣā*, we do not follow them here; furthermore, this interpretation also refutes the proponents of the "harmonious combination" (*saṃghāta*).
Therefore, the *Abhidharmamahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 73, states:
"Some say that atoms do not actually touch one another."
Nor is it without an interval;
rather, when they abide in conjunction with one another and are closely proximate, the conventional designation "contact" is established.
Since that treatise states that it is "also not without an interval," [it follows that contact is merely a designation].
"Knowing that they are somewhat distant and not equal to a Great Virtue (bhadanta)"— this is another interpretation refuting the hypothetical [position].
Furthermore, regarding the statement "leaving the atom to reach this point should also be thus," this refutes the second previous assertion.
If one were to concede that composite matter (saṃghātarūpa) undergoes contact,
yet there is no composite matter apart from atoms (paramāṇu),
then the contact of the composite would be the contact of the atoms themselves.
Just as a collection is characterized by resistance (*sapratigha*), so too each individual atom within that collection is called "resistant.
Your proposition that atoms touch one another follows this same principle.
The conjunction [of factors] is called contact (*sparśa*).
Within this conjunction, atoms (*paramāṇu*) facing one another should likewise touch.
Therefore, it is said that just as [matter] is subject to resistance and obstruction, so too should this be the case.
Furthermore, regarding the claim that there is no such fault even if one admits that atoms reach [one another],
this refutes the first master mentioned previously;
the author of the treatise refutes him by means of general reasoning.
Furthermore, it is admitted that if atoms possess spatial dimensions,
then whether they are in contact or not, they must have spatial dimensions;
even if one were to grant that they do touch, provided they lack spatial dimensions, [the following would apply].
Furthermore, there is no fault regarding spatial parts (digbhāga).
Why must one avoid the fault of atoms coming into contact with one another?
The *Nyāya* school offers this defense:

Since "having parts" (sāvayava) and "having directional parts" (digbhāgavattva) are synonymous in meaning, the term "partless" (niravayava) has already excluded [the possibility of] having directional parts.
How, then, can doubt arise regarding this once again?
That is to say, if one grants that atoms possess spatial dimensions,
then since they would lack such dimensions, how could they be subject to contact? Furthermore, [if they were to touch] they would have to touch with their entire substance.
Alternatively, it might touch only one part;
both positions entail faults,
as has already been fully discussed.
How can it be further said that if there are no spatial parts (digbhāga),
even if one grants they touch, there is no such fault? If one were to offer the defense of a Vaibhāṣika master,
one should instead say:
Since you establish that atoms have no spatial parts,
why do they not touch one another? If you say that their touching would result in a logical fault, [then how can they touch at all?]
To say that they do not touch one another also does not avoid the fault,
because they face the six directions differently.
If it is said that each atom possesses its own power and function, [the same fault persists].
Regarding those things that mutually obstruct and prevent one another from touching:
does this functional capacity constitute a separate entity?
If it were a separate entity, [then...]
This is identical to the category of action (karma-pada-artha) in the Vaiśeṣika school.
If it were not distinct from the substance itself,
there would be no function external to that substance.
Why do they not touch?
Thus, this also results in a logical fallacy.
Furthermore, do the sense organs, such as the eye, reach objects that are unequal in size?
Below this, the third section clarifies the size of the sense organs (*indriya*) and their objects (*viṣaya*).
Some schools maintain that the eye and other organs perceive only objects of equal magnitude;
they argue that when one sees a great mountain or the like, it is due to rapid movement, like a whirling firebrand (*alātacakra*).
Therefore, this question arises.
The verse says: "Up to 'only taking objects of equal magnitude'.
The text of the verse is abbreviated.
It speaks only of the three faculties being equal in measure;
by implication, the size of the other three is not fixed.
The treatise says: "Regarding the distinctions in shape and measure..."
Within the prose commentary, there are two parts:
first, the direct explanation of the verse text;
second, the clarification of the shape of the faculties.
The three types of clear knowledge (*vidyā*) share the same category (*sabhāga*), and so forth;
this constitutes the first section.
The three faculties, beginning with the nose, apprehend their objects only when they reach them.
Therefore, consciousness arises from the mutual correspondence of the sense faculty (*indriya*) and its object (*viṣaya*).
Regarding the term "equal" (*sama*) used here:
according to their respective natures, the contact between the sense faculty and the object is termed "equality of measure" (*pramāṇa-sama*).
This is to show that it is not the case that the sense organ can apprehend an object exceeding its own size;
nor is it the case that a partial sense organ cannot apprehend a partial object,
provided that the eye-organ is spread out laterally.
Regarding the skin of a grape: if one says the eye-faculty is like a sphere, it is like the interior and exterior of a grape.

Question: How is it possible to see the color within the grape? Answer: It is because the skin is thin, therefore it is seen. Another explanation states: even if the skin were thick, the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*) would still perceive it.
The *Nyāyabindu* states:
"Just as when one sees grapes, jujubes, and other fruits, the auditory faculty perceives their respective objects, giving rise to various sounds—whether small or large—as appropriate."
If one hears the sound of a mosquito,
the sense organ is large and the object is small;
if one hears the sound of clouds, [the situation is otherwise].
That is, the sense organ is small while the object is large;
in the West, the sound of thunder is called the sound of clouds.
Thunder is named after its basis, just as clouds arise from their basis; if one hears the sound of a lute, it is likewise [a case of] the sense organ, the object, and the magnitude being equal.
Therefore, the *Nyāyapraveśa* (Treatise on Logic), Chapter Eight, states:
"The auditory faculty also perceives mosquitoes, clouds, and the small or large magnitudes of the sound of a lute," and so forth. This concludes the passage from the treatise.
Regarding the phrase "hearing clouds of mosquitoes, etc.," the term "etc.
refers to things of equal magnitude. Alternatively, it is explained that "etc. includes sounds of lutes of equal magnitude.
This is because the five sensory faculties of form are composed of atoms (*paramāṇu*).
One can distinguish objects of perception as large or small;
however, because the mind lacks material obstruction, it cannot be distinguished by shape or dimension through its objects of perception.
Nevertheless, one may still say that its object of focus (ālambana) is either large or small. The rest of the text is clear.
Regarding the question, "What is the distinction in the arrangement and dimensions of the eye and so forth?"—
this section below clarifies the shape and magnitude of the faculties; this is the question.
Regarding the question of whether the atoms of the eye faculty reach the size of a finger-ring in shape,
the answer is that there are two explanations; the former is said to be superior.
It is not said that there is speech [therein].
The ear faculty is like a rolled birch bark;
according to the custom of the Western countries, when first piercing the ears, [the bark is used as a model].
Many layers of birch bark are placed inside a hole with the intention that it gradually expand;
this is used as a metaphor because of its similarity to being close to the ear.
By analogy with this:
The ears have apertures that communicate with the interior of the brain.
As for those who say that the auditory faculty (*śrotrendriya*) is like a lamp-stand,
they are referring to its four lips rather than its base.
The nose can be known by its slight [protrusion].
Regarding these first three faculties,
if one considers their essential substance and location, there is no difference in height.
If one considers their respective bases, there is indeed a hierarchy of height;
therefore, the previous fascicle states that they follow a sequential order according to their positions, such that the tongue is the most subtle and can be known [only by inference].
Regarding the tongue-faculty (*jihvendriya*), there is a portion the size of a hair-tip within it that is not the tongue-faculty itself;
although there is no scriptural or treatise-based statement to this effect,
the ancient masters of the West have traditionally explained it thus.
Medical treatises state that within the tongue-faculty there is a space the size of a hair-tip where no tongue-faculty exists;
this is the *marmānta* (the terminal node of death).
If a needle were to pierce that spot, the person would die immediately.

Furthermore, it is the natural law that within the tongue there is such a hollow space. Moreover, it is explained that within the human brain there is an extremely foul-smelling, filthy, and impure brain-wax (meda).
If one sees the brain-dregs flowing out and dripping onto this empty space,
and if there were no such place to receive these brain-dregs,
they would strike the root of the tongue, causing the person to vomit and making it impossible to eat or drink.

Because the body-faculty (*kāyendriya*) has already been explained, the two faculties of male and female (*puruṣa-strī-indriya*) are clarified here. The remainder of the text may be understood [by the reader].

Regarding the statement, "The atoms (*paramāṇu*) of the eye-faculty are so minute as to be invisible," this marks the third section below, which clarifies the "homogeneous class" (*sabhāgatā*) and so forth.
The first four faculties can be understood [as having both types].
The body faculty is invariably non-deficient (sabhāga);
even in the Extremely Hot Hell (Pratāpana), where the body is enveloped by fierce flames, it remains so.
The Sarvāstivādins traditionally maintain that there still exists a body-faculty (kāyendriya) which is "of the same class" (sabhāga).
[They argue that] if the body-faculty were to produce consciousness throughout its entire extent, the body would necessarily disintegrate.

Because the body-faculty (*kāyendriya*) and its respective objects each consist of a single atom (*paramāṇu*) separated by space, they cannot serve as the basis and object for the arising of body-consciousness (*kāyavijñāna*).
This is because the five groups of consciousness necessarily depend upon a collection of numerous atoms.
Only when they constitute the nature of the support (*āśraya*) and the object (*ālambana*) can they give rise to their own consciousness.
It is precisely by this principle that it is also said that each individual atom (*paramāṇu*) is by nature invisible (*anidarśana*).
Because a single atom is invisible,
it must be accumulated to a great extent before it can be called "visible.
This applies when there is a single layer of sense organ and a single layer of object within the body.
This would entail the fault that consciousness could be produced by a single atom of either the sense faculty or its object.
Furthermore, it would entail the fault that the body-faculty, being obstructed, would become fragmented and destroyed in many parts;
thus it is said that "the body should disintegrate. Question: Do the two faculties of the nose and the tongue also produce consciousness throughout their entire extent?
"Why do they not disintegrate? The explanation says: the two faculties of nose and tongue take the body as their support and manifest pervasively without disintegrating.
The body has no separate support; when it manifests pervasively, it immediately disintegrates. Furthermore, it is asked: do the subtle atoms of the nose and tongue faculties merely spread laterally?
This also applies to the case of vertical accumulation.
If one were to say that they extend horizontally,
then there would be the fault that a single atom of the nose or tongue could simultaneously encounter its object and its own body-faculty.
It does not constitute an accumulation;
if one speaks of a layered succession,
it occurs when consciousness arises universally.

Furthermore, there would be the fault that the sense organs and their objects are separated by a distance of one *paramāṇu* each as their support and condition. The commentary explains: the atoms of the nose and tongue faculties are merely spread out laterally;
although they do not exist in vertical layers, this lateral spreading is termed "accumulation."
Therefore, there is no fault of a single atom giving rise to consciousness.
Furthermore, those whose faculties are sharp do not require such repeated accumulation.

Moreover, the internal basis (the body) and the external support (the object) possess sufficient power [to produce cognition]. An objection is raised: "If the body-faculty contacts objects in successive moments and also accumulates them laterally, it should give rise to consciousness everywhere."

Why, then, is it said that a single atom (*paramāṇu*) of the faculty and a single atom of the object serve as the support (*āśraya*) and the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*), respectively, to produce body-consciousness (*kāya-vijñāna*)? The explanation is as follows:
there are two kinds of accumulation (*saṃcita*).
First, "accumulation" (saṃcita) refers to lateral aggregation;
second, it refers to vertical superposition.
As for the statement that the five consciousnesses necessarily depend on and take as their object an accumulation of many atoms (paramāṇu):
Speaking in terms of general characteristics, as appropriate,
if one distinguishes them individually, the nose and tongue are termed "lateral" and "accumulated."
The body-faculty (kāyendriya) is designated as "accumulated" based on its extension in the directions of front and back, as well as the lateral directions;
therefore, that body-faculty, being merely laterally accumulated, cannot produce consciousness.
Furthermore, the nature of a faculty is dull and must depend upon being layered or aggregated.
Only when they possess the power of mutual dependence can they apprehend objects.

Furthermore, because there is no separate support, they must be layered one upon another. Moreover, it is explained that the faculties of the nose and tongue, though subtle, also extend to being layered.
Although the faculties and their objects alternate sequentially, they are able to produce consciousness universally;
this is because they are termed "accumulated" in their lateral arrangement and because their nature is sharp.
Furthermore, because the internal body and its supporting basis possess power,
they are distinct from the [physical] body due to this difference in meaning;
although there are two interpretations.
The faculties of the nose and tongue seem slightly superior in their initial discernment.
Question: As when entering the third dhyāna, one experiences pliancy and bliss throughout the entire body.
"The body should disintegrate. The commentary explains: when one is correctly entering meditative absorption (*samādhi*), bodily consciousness (*kāyavijñāna*) does not arise.
When bodily consciousness arises, one immediately emerges from absorption;
therefore, there is no pervasive experience of pliancy (*praśrabdhi*) and bliss throughout the entire body.
If, according to the Sautrāntika school, the body-faculty (*kāyendriya*) is capable of universally producing consciousness,
then the *Nyāyānusāra* (Treatise on Correct Reasoning),
fascicle seven, states: "Furthermore, this is what is taught in the school of the Venerable Elder [Vasumitra]."
"The entire body is placed in water that is either cold or warm;
the atoms of the body-faculty (*kāyendriya-paramāṇu*) are capable of producing consciousness throughout [the body]," as stated in the treatise.
Since the author of the treatise follows the Sautrāntika school, he says "it is traditionally said" (*kila*).
Regarding the question, "Is it also the same as previously stated up to the basis?"—
the following fourth section clarifies the temporal inclusion of the bases of the six consciousnesses;
this is the inquiry.
If one follows the Sautrāntika school, the five consciousnesses take only the past as their object;
thus, the *Nyāyānusāra* (Treatise on Reasoning), fascicle eight, states:
"There are those who maintain that the objects of the five consciousnesses are exclusively the past."
As was extensively refuted above.
If it were not so, the answer is as follows.
"What is it? This is the inquiry.
The verse says: "As for the mental factors of the dharma-realm," this refers to what follows.
This refers to the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*). Because it occupies the final position among the six consciousnesses, it relies solely upon the past;
for all six groups of consciousness, having ceased immediately prior, are designated as "mind" (*manas*).
This serves as the supporting faculty (*āśrayendriya*) for the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).

Therefore, the mental consciousness relies exclusively upon the past mind that has just ceased without interval (*anantaranirodha*). Question: In this school, all eighteen elements (*dhātu*) are said to pertain to all three time periods.
How can it be said that the mind exists only in the past? The explanation states: If one considers the actual substance of the mind, it truly pervades all three periods of time;
however, when categorized by period and discussed in terms of its manifest activity, it is said to exist only in the past.
Therefore, the treatise states:
"That which is past is called *manas* (mind-organ);
that which is future is called *citta* (mind)."
That which is present is called consciousness (*vijñāna*).
Regarding the two supports of the five consciousnesses, they may be understood according to the text; this demonstrates that their support is not fixed, as it may be simultaneous with them.
Alternatively, because it relies on the past,

the original text is cited to establish the certainty of the nature of the support (āśrayatva) by means of a question-and-answer regarding its equivalence to the equal-and-immediate condition (samanantarapratyaya).
The sixth [condition], the immediate condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*), is not a mental factor because it functions by way of dominance through its capacity;
furthermore, in terms of the meaning of "opening up" and "yielding," it applies to mental factors but does not apply to material faculties.
The breadth and narrowness differ.

To establish the distinction of the support (*āśraya*), this is cited as a question and answer: "Is not the final mind of an Arhat the support of the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), yet not its equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantarapratyaya*)?"
Why, then, is it said that this is the nature upon which the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) relies?
It is certainly the immediately preceding condition (*samanantarapratyaya*) for the mental consciousness.
To explain: if one considers the meaning of "reliance," in principle it is indeed so.
In this present passage, the support of consciousness (*vijñāna*) is raised as the subject of the question and answer.
The final mind of an Arhat has no subsequent consciousness;

it is not what is being questioned here, as it is subsumed under the category of the "neither" (neither-cause-nor-effect). Furthermore, another interpretation holds that this is explained here according to the essential nature (*svabhāva*) and category (*jāti*) [of phenomena].
Without considering its function,
it is still subsumed under the category of "simultaneous" (*sahabhū*);
the former interpretation seems superior.
Regarding the question, "For what reason does consciousness arise in relation to the eye and so forth, and not elsewhere?"—
the following fifth section clarifies why the eye and other faculties receive the designation of "basis" (*āśraya*).
This may be understood according to the text.
Furthermore, the *Nyāyānusāra* (Treatise on Right Reasoning), fascicle 8, states:
"If that were so, the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) would also shift along with the body;
that is to say, when the body is afflicted by disorders such as wind-disease (*vāta-vikāra*), the mental consciousness immediately becomes disturbed."
When the body is pure and tranquil, the mental consciousness is calm and still.
For what reason does that mental consciousness not take the body as its support?
There is no such fault, because it follows its own respective support.
That is to say, when the body is afflicted by wind-disorders and the like,
a body-consciousness associated with painful sensation arises;
such a body-consciousness is called the "disturbed mind-element."
When this [feeling] together with painful sensation has subsided,
it can cause a distracted mental consciousness to arise in the mental faculty; conversely,
when [the feeling] is contrary to this, the mental consciousness becomes tranquil.
Therefore, the mental consciousness follows its own respective basis. Furthermore, the intent of that treatise is merely to clarify the distinctions of increase and decrease, clarity and dullness;

it does not mean that all [consciousnesses] are identical. Thus, when a tainted (*sāsrava*) mind arises, an untainted (*anāsrava*) consciousness [may arise]. Question: Just as visual consciousness arises...
It is also due to emptiness, clarity, and the capacity to produce mental attention (*manasikāra*).
Why, then, is the question posed only in terms of two conditions? The explanation states:
as the *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra* says, "Furthermore, the arising of visual consciousness necessarily depends upon the power of its support (*āśraya*) and its object (*ālambana*)."
Furthermore, because it is unique [to visual consciousness],
when eye-consciousness arises, it necessarily relies upon the eye and visible form as its support (āśraya) and object (ālambana);
other dharmas are not so determined.
This means that the consciousness of nocturnal creatures arises without depending on light;
the consciousness of aquatic creatures is produced without awaiting space;

These are the bases of the mind,
and all possess the sense of being "faculties" (indriya).
The specific distinctions among these six faculties are due to the female and male faculties.
Furthermore, by means of the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*), these six faculties remain for the duration of a single lifetime.
These six faculties become defiled through the five feeling-faculties (*vedanendriya*).
These six faculties serve as the basis for the purification of the outflow-free (*anāsrava*) state through the five faculties beginning with faith (*śraddhā*).
These six faculties become pure and untainted through the latter three faculties. As for their distinctions:
while the two types of distinct abiding both subsume the six faculties, they differ in terms of defilement, the provisions, and purification.

It exists solely within the mind. Furthermore, it is explained that from this point onward, the five types of distinctions regarding characteristics and so forth all reside in the mind, or rather, in these sentient beings.
By means of these six types, the establishment of the functions of the faculties is brought to completion.
Since ignorance and so forth, as well as the vocal organs and so forth,
lack predominant influence (*adhipatya*) in this context, they should not be established as faculties (*indriya*).
Furthermore, other masters maintain that there are twenty-two faculties.
The following is the second section, which sets forth alternative views.

This is the definition of the sense-faculties (*indriya*) established by the school that maintains that "it is consciousness that sees" and so forth. Regarding the terms "evolution" (*pravṛtti*) and "involution" (*nivṛtti*), the *Nyāyabindu* states:
The continuous succession of birth and death is the meaning of saṃsāra;
the cessation of birth and death is the meaning of nirvāṇa.
This refers precisely to the ultimate eradication of the six sense faculties.
Furthermore, the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* (Vibhāṣā), fascicle 100, states:
"Cyclic existence (*pravṛtti*) refers to taking birth again;
cessation (*nivṛtti*) refers to proceeding toward nirvāṇa."
Regarding the statement that the fourteen faculties up to the point of the basis for transmigration are established:
in the state of transmigration, these fourteen faculties are established based on four meanings.
Within the cycle of birth and death across the three realms, consciousness serves as the primary factor.
The arising of consciousness necessarily depends upon the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*).
The production of these six sense bases is due to the female and male faculties (*strī-puruṣendriya*).
Furthermore, the maintenance of these six sense bases is due to the life faculty (*jīvitendriya*).
The experience of objects by the six sense faculties further occurs through the five feelings (*vedanā*).
Because the six sense faculties apprehend those objects due to those five feelings,
the experience of objects is termed "apprehension" (*anubhava*).
Unlike the case of feeling (*vedanā*),
regarding the sequence established in the sūtra within the context of the stage of cessation (*nirodha*),
the latter eight faculties are established based on four specific meanings pertaining to that stage of cessation.
The intent of the *Nyāyānusāra* clarifies this in terms of the attainment of nirvāṇa;
thus, the ninth chapter of the *Nyāyānusāra* states:
"The cessation of birth and death is the meaning of 'returning to extinction' (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*)."
This is the ultimate cessation of the six sense bases.
Its basis for attainment consists of the five faculties, such as faith,
because they are the most excellent causes for the growth of all roots of virtue.
The first untainted faculty (*anāsrava-indriya*) is able to produce this attainment,
because it is produced for the first time within the group of those fixed in rightness (*samyaktva-niyata-rāśi*).
Subsequently, the [second] untainted faculty causes this attainment to endure.

Because it arises as a long-term continuity, the subsequent untainted faculties (anāsrava-indriya) enable the enjoyment of dwelling in happiness in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharmasukhavihāra*), as this is what they manifest.
Thus concludes the treatise. That is to say, the basis for the attainment of cessation (*nirodha-prāpti*) consists of the five [faculties] beginning with faith (*śraddhā*).
Through the first untainted [dharma], nirvāṇa is brought forth;
through the middle untainted [dharma], nirvāṇa is maintained;
and through the final untainted [dharma], nirvāṇa is experienced as dwelling in happiness in the present life.
The measure of the faculties is established by these four meanings,
neither deficient nor redundant;
it is precisely due to these four causal conditions of the forward progression and the reversal of the cycle of existence.

Regarding the statement that "the sequence of the twenty-two faculties established in the Sūtra should not be [dismissed] on the grounds that speech is only accomplished when the vocal apparatus reaches its object," the following provides a specific refutation.
This is the instrument of divisive speech.
It is not correct that the vocal apparatus serves as the root for speech,
because this speech is established only in dependence upon the distinctions of training, study, and so forth.
Therefore, we know that the vocal apparatus does not exercise predominance over speech.
If the vocal apparatus were able to exercise predominance over speech,
then one who has just been born and possesses a tongue should be able to speak immediately.
As for the claim that hands and feet should not be established as faculties (*indriya*):
this refutes [the inclusion of] hands and feet;
for the hand functions in grasping.
It is sufficient that it exists in the act;
for this grasping and the act are not distinct entities apart from the hand and foot.
That is to say, when the hands and feet move from here to there, it is called "different places.
Raising, lowering, bending, and extending are called "different characteristics.
Because these distinctions arise, they are termed "grasping" and "motion."

Apart from the hands and feet, there is no separate faculty of locomotion; yet, even apart from the hands and feet, there is locomotion, as in the case of snakes and other such belly-crawling creatures, which are able to move despite having no feet.
Although they lack hands, they are still able to grasp and bind; therefore, hands and feet cannot be established as faculties (indriya) in relation to those [functions].
If one insists [on such a definition], then the belly would also [be a faculty] for that reason.
"One should establish the organ of the abdomen" refers to the opening for the expulsion of feces; "until it is drawn out" means until the feces have been led out.
This refers to the fissure for excrement.
The faculty of excretion should not be established as a root, because it is incapable of relinquishing feces,
urine, and other such impurities; heavy objects do not remain suspended in space,
for they fall everywhere, whether internally or externally.
It does not arise from that location.
If one were to insist [on its existence],
then because it would also fall into emptiness, one would have to establish a "root of emptiness."
The impurities within the body are drawn out by the power of the winds; therefore, it is not a matter of their location.
If one were to insist otherwise:
Furthermore, since it is by means of wind that [the organ] is drawn out, one should establish a "wind-root.

As for the statement "because it draws out the place of urine until this pleasure arises," this refers to the production of the pleasure of sexual desire at the place where urine is emitted from the urinary tract.
One should not establish [additional] faculties;
for it is the female and male faculties themselves that give rise to this pleasure.
Why then should one calculate their locations and establish them as separate faculties?
Furthermore, regarding the claim that the throat, teeth, and so forth should not be established as faculties (*indriya*),
this is refuted by citing a counter-example:
just as the throat is [an organ] for swallowing.
The teeth are for chewing;
the eyelids are for opening and closing;
the limbs and joints are for bending and extending.
Each possesses its own functional power and should all be established as faculties (indriya). Or rather, [one might argue that] all causes [should be so established].
Each of all things that produce their own respective effects possesses a functional capacity,
and thus each should be established as a faculty (*indriya*).
Although the throat, teeth, and so forth also possess functional capacity, [they are not faculties].

Regarding the statement that they are not established as faculties (*indriya*) because they lack predominance (*ādhipatya*): this implies that speech, hands, and so forth should also not be established as faculties, as they likewise lack predominance.

By this, the objection concerning ignorance (*avidyā*) and the like is also addressed; for within the category of "and so forth" (*ādi*), ignorance and the rest are also included. Question: Just as there are twenty-two faculties...
If one defines the essential nature [of the faculties] based on the seventy-five dharmas and so forth,
there are only thirteen;
this is because the male and female faculties are included within the body faculty (*kāyendriya*).
The five faculties of feeling are all subsumed under "feeling.

Since the three untainted faculties (anāsrava-indriya) are included within nine faculties, the thirteen are as follows: eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, mind, mindfulness, concentration, wisdom, feeling, faith, diligence, and vitality.
Why, among the seventy-five dharmas, are only thirteen established as faculties (*indriya*) while the others are not?

The explanation states that this is a brief summary based on the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* and other texts regarding their establishment or rejection. First, concerning the eleven material dharmas:
The five faculties are exclusively internal and exclusively bases;
therefore, they are established as faculties.
Form and the other [objects] are not so.

Therefore, masculinity and femininity are not established as separate faculties, as they are already included within the body faculty (*kāyendriya*). Second, mental factors (*caitasika*) are internal and also serve as supports;
they possess predominance (*ādhipatya*) over minds of all three moral natures.

Therefore, they are established as faculties. Among the third category, the mental factors (caitasika-dharma), only mindfulness, concentration, wisdom, feeling, faith, and diligence are established as faculties.
Regarding those not established [as faculties]:

if a factor is preeminent in accordance with purification, it is established as a faculty. Among the universal mental factors (*mahābhūmika*), mindfulness (*smṛti*), concentration (*samādhi*), wisdom (*prajñā*), and feeling (*vedanā*) are established as faculties;
the others are not so established.
Mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom are established as faculties because they are preeminent in favoring purification;
although attention also favors purification, it is not established as a faculty because it is superior at the beginning but inferior later on.
Although resolve (*adhimokṣa*) is predominantly conducive to the pure state of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), it is established as a faculty (*indriya*) only in that stage;
because it is inferior in the stage of training (*śaikṣa*), it is not so established there. Question: Concentration (*samādhi*) is also strong when fixed and inferior when distracted.
Why are they established as faculties (indriya)?
Answer: Concentration is strong even in a state of distraction;
as for perception (saṃjñā), volition (cetanā), contact (sparśa), and desire (chanda), because they are particularly predominant in accordance with defilement, they are not established as faculties.
Although feeling (vedanā) is common to both the defiled and the pure, and is superior in both cases,
it is established as a faculty (indriya) by distinguishing it specifically from the perspective of the wholesome (kuśala).
That it is common to both the defiled and the pure is known from the following:
Therefore, the *Vibhāṣā* states: "Some say that although feeling conforms to the defiled category, it nevertheless communicates with wholesome dharmas;
it is just as when a prison official, though his own station is lowly,"
Because it associates with the noble and the eminent,
among the universal mental factors (*mahābhūmika-dharma*), four are established as faculties (*indriya*) while the remaining six are not.
As for why, among the great wholesome mental factors (*kuśala-mahābhūmika-dharma*), faith (*śraddhā*) and diligence (*vīrya*) are established as faculties while the others are not:
Faith is the root of all virtues;
no category of goodness is accomplished apart from faith.
Diligence is universally capable of inciting and developing all virtues.
No category of wholesome qualities (*kuśalapakṣa*) is accomplished without diligence;

therefore, these two are established as faculties (*indriya*) because they are preeminent in accordance with purification. Although the two types—shame (*hrī*) and dread of blame (*apatrāpya*)—are able to counteract all unwholesome states of mind that are of an exclusively black nature and are inherently unwholesome (*akuśala-svabhāva*), [they are not established as faculties].
They are designated as "virtuous by nature" (*svabhāva-kuśala*) and "virtuous for oneself" (*ātma-kuśala*).

However, because they lack a distinct, superior capacity to produce and grow various wholesome dharmas, they do not possess the meaning of "roots. [These are] non-attachment (*alobha*) and non-hatred (*adveṣa*).
Although that which is to be abandoned by them coexists with the six consciousnesses and is generally abandoned through the five [paths],
it is of the nature of a latent tendency (*anuśaya*).
They are established as unwholesome roots because they possess these five characteristics:
they can give rise to coarse and heavy misconduct of body and speech;
they serve as the primary application for severing the roots of virtue; and so forth.
The three roots beginning with non-attachment are able to counteract those [unwholesome states] and give rise to various scattered wholesome karmas; thus,
they are designated as "wholesome roots."
However, faith and the others are established as faculties because they universally cause all wholesome dharmas to grow and arise;
non-attachment and the others do not function as faculties in this context, as their meanings are distinct.
Serenity, equanimity, heedfulness, and non-harming [are established] by way of their respective counteractive objects, the four secondary afflictions.
Three exist exclusively within defiled minds;
one acts as an associate to evil vitarka, harassing the bodhisattva and obstructing the attainment of bodhi.
Although it is established among the wholesome dharmas as an antidote to that [evil vitarka], it remains [defiled].
However, they have no superior function regarding the growth of various pure dharmas;
therefore, they are not established as faculties (*indriya*).
The two types—delight and aversion—are too distracted and powerful.
They are definitely inferior;
they are not superior in either stage,
nor do they arise simultaneously.
Therefore, they are not established as faculties: six universal defiled mental factors (mahākleśabhūmikadharma),
two unwholesome mental factors (akuśalabhūmikadharma),
and ten minor defiled mental factors (parīttakleśabhūmikadharma).
Furthermore, greed, hatred, pride, and doubt that exist outside the [three] realms are all not conducive to purification.
Because their nature is inferior and lacks the characteristics of a root, they are not established as roots.

Question: If that is so, then defiled feeling (*vedanā*) should also not be established as a root. Answer: Feeling is established as a root because its functional power is predominant within the category of defilement.
The afflictions are not like that, because afflictions arise in dependence upon the various feelings (*vedanā*).
Question: If that is so, then perception (*saṃjñā*) should also be established as a faculty (*indriya*).
It is also because [perception] can give rise to afflictions. Answer: Although perception can give rise to afflictions, it does not surpass feeling in this regard.
For this reason, it is also not included among the members of dependent origination.
Some say that although feeling (vedanā) accords with the defiled category,
it also intermingles with wholesome dharmas;
whereas afflictions accord only with the defiled category and do not accord with the wholesome.
Therefore, it is not established as a faculty (*indriya*).
It is like a prison official who, although his station is lowly, associates with those of noble rank;
he is not like a gatekeeper or jailer, who, despite possessing fierce power, inflicts suffering upon others.
Furthermore, because they are extremely base, evil, and loathsome, those of noble standing distance themselves from them.
Thus, regret, sleep, applied thought, sustained thought, and fear are not established as faculties.
The two types of fearfulness (*bhaya*) and the defiled (*kliṣṭa*) and neutral (*avyākṛta*) states do not extend to the wholesome (*kuśala*).
Although regret (*kaukṛtya*) and sleep (*middha*) also extend to the wholesome nature, they pertain only to the distracted state and not to meditative concentration (*samāhita*).
Vitarka and vicāra, although they occur in both concentrated and non-concentrated states, do not occur in all stages (*bhūmi*).

Furthermore, as they are merely conducive to the wholesome and are not preeminent, they are not established as faculties (*indriya*). [Objection: If that is so, then suffering, pleasure, grief, and joy also do not occur in all stages.
[Question: Should it not be established as a faculty (*indriya*)? [Answer:
Generally speaking, feeling (*vedanā*) pervades all stages (*bhūmi*), because the feeling of equanimity (*upekṣā-vedanā*) is common to all stages.
Since they are established as faculties based on their respective categories, it is likewise established here.
Furthermore, all feelings possess growth, development, and predominance;

fear and so forth do not. [Question: Why is *vitarka* established as a factor of the path (*mārgāṅga*), yet both *vitarka* and *vicāra* are established as factors of meditative concentration (*dhyānāṅga*)?

Is it not the case that they possess superior power for growth and development? Answer: These are established as factors (aṅga) because they possess the power to exert and sustain concentration and wisdom;
they do not have a superior function regarding growth and development.
Therefore, among the factors dissociated from mind (citta-viprayukta-saṃskāra), only vitality (jīvita) is established as a faculty (indriya).
As for why the others are not so established:
vitality is established as a faculty because it possesses three characteristics.
First, it exists only in sentient beings;
second, it is exclusively a result of maturation (*vipāka*);
third, it universally sustains [the body]; and fourth, it lacks all three of these characteristics.
Although the maturation of non-conceptualization possesses the former two [characteristics],
it lacks universal sustenance;
whereas the homogeneous class (nikāyasabhāga) possesses the first and the last, it is not exclusively maturation.
Because they are outflows (*niṣyanda*).
The two mindless attainments (*acittaka-samāpatti*), the sets of names, phrases, and phonemes (*nāma-pada-vyañjana-kāya*), acquisition (*prāpti*), and non-acquisition (*aprāpti*)—
although the first of these meanings applies to them, they lack the latter two meanings.
Therefore, none of these are faculties (*indriya*). Regarding the fifth point, that the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) is not a faculty:
the state where the faculties have ceased is called the unconditioned;
furthermore, because it lacks the function of arising, it is not established as a faculty.
Furthermore, this has been briefly explained above according to one’s inclination;
for a detailed account, see the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*.
Regarding what should now be explained here—namely, that [the mind] reaches the state of sleep and so forth:

Below this, the third section clarifies the essential nature and arising of the faculties (*indriya*). Regarding these, the six faculties beginning with the eye are as previously explained in the Chapter on Elements (*dhātu*) within the [treatise on] Aggregates (*skandha*), Elements (*dhātu*), and Bases (*āyatana*).
The male and female faculties have been explained thus at the beginning of this chapter.
The life faculty will be analyzed later in the section on the dissociated factors (*viprayukta-saṃskāra*).
The five faculties beginning with faith will be analyzed in the section on mental factors (*caitta-dharma*).
These fourteen faculties have been explained previously; since they have already been discussed, they will not be clarified here.
As for the remaining faculties that have not yet been explained, they should now be elucidated.
The verse says: "Based on the nine [faculties] that reach their support, three faculties are established."
A brief explanation of the verse.
The *Śāstra* states, "up to what is called the faculty of grief (*daurmanasyendriya*)," which explains the first five lines.
The term "body" (kāya) has two meanings.
If one speaks of the "six bodies of feeling," then "body" refers to the physical aggregate itself.
If one speaks of "bodily feeling" and "mental feeling," then "body" refers to the sense faculty.
The body is an aggregate of matter;
the term "body" refers to an aggregate of matter.
Here, what is called the "body" as an aggregate of matter refers specifically to the material sense-faculties (*rūpindriya*).
Because it arises based on the body, it is called "bodily sensation" (*kāyikī vedanā*).
It is named after its basis.

The remainder of the text is easy to understand. Question: If the third dhyāna involves an extremely joyful mind associated with pleasure (*sukha*), then might the minds of those in hell, which are extremely displeased, likewise be associated with suffering (*duḥkha*)? Answer: Only that which is extremely joyful and free from conceptual discrimination (*avikalpa*) can be associated with pleasure.
Extreme harm is accompanied by discrimination but is not associated with suffering.
According to the Mahāyāna, even the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) in the hells is associated with suffering.
That which is neither pleasant nor painful is called the faculty of equanimity (*upekṣendriya*).
Regarding the relinquishment mentioned in the sixth phrase:
as for the question of whether this faculty of equanimity (*upekṣendriya*) constitutes a mental feeling (*citta-vedanā*). [Question: What is it?
One should say that it pertains to both.
Answer: This explains the two.
Why are these two established collectively as a single faculty?
[Question:
For what reason are this body and the mind established collectively as the single faculty of equanimity (*upekṣendriya*)?
Regarding the statement that this feeling (vedanā) is established as a faculty (indriya) in its totality because it reaches both body and mind:
the answer is that there is no difference in the explanation.
This equanimity (upekṣā) exists in both body and mind; because it is likewise non-discriminative, it is not established separately [from the mental factor].
Suffering and pleasure differ, and for this reason they are established separately. [The same applies to] suffering and pleasure in the mind.

Sorrow and joy arise from much conceptualization (*vikalpa*). Although the mental pleasure (*citta-sukha*) of the third dhyāna does not involve conceptualization, it is said to "arise from much conceptualization" because it follows upon that state of much conceptualization. Physical pain and pleasure, however, arise without conceptualization.
The arising of what is called suffering or pleasure follows the power of the respective objects;
likewise, for Arhats and those in the three lower fruits, these five feelings arise according to their respective conditions.
This cites the noble ones as being the same as ordinary beings.
Therefore, suffering and pleasure are established as distinct from the body and mind;
equanimity, however, arises spontaneously without discrimination.
Therefore, the faculties are established as the union of body and mind. Furthermore, suffering in the body and its impairment in the mind are distinct;
likewise, pleasure in the body and its benefit in the mind are distinct.
Therefore, they are established as distinct faculties; because equanimity (*upekṣā*) has no differentiated characteristics, it is established as a single faculty in general.

This continues from the mental faculty (*manas*), pleasure (*sukha*), joy (*saumanasya*), and equanimity (*upekṣā*) up until the establishment of the faculty of one who possesses complete knowledge (*ājñātāvīndriya*).
Explaining the latter two phrases:
the three untainted faculties (*anāsrava-indriya*) have nine faculties as their substance;
they are established according to the three paths.
This can be understood from the text as it stands.
As for the question of why these three names were established,
this asks about the reason for their designation.
This refers to one who is on the path of seeing and has reached the stage of "the unknown to be known.
The answer is:
within that [context].
First, it is explained by way of the three paths;
second, the faculties are individually analyzed.
This refers to the establishment of "the faculty of 'I shall come to know the unknown'" (*anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya*) in relation to the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*).
Knowing is wisdom;
this refers to the fifteen moments of the path of seeing (darśanamārga),
consisting of the eight patiences (kṣānti) and the seven knowledges (jñāna).

Regarding the eight truths of the higher and lower realms, there exists for each the turning of the path consisting of "that which is yet to be known" (*ajñātamājñāsyamīti*) and "the act of knowing" (*ājñendriya*).

Therefore, that practitioner is called "one who has the duty to know the unknown" (*ājñātāvī*). Question: Since the eight patiences (*kṣānti*) are not cognitions (*jñāna*), how can they be said to be "the duty to know the unknown"?

Regarding why the seven knowledges that correctly cognize the principles of the truths are also called "the knowledge of what is yet to be known": the explanation states that while these seven knowledges are termed "correct knowledge" from the perspective of their taking their respective truths as objects, [they are so called because they are directed toward what remains to be understood].
Now, with respect to the method of the Eight Truths (*aṣṭasatya*),
because one knows the Eight Truths yet has not fully pervaded them and has not exhausted the knowledge of the truths—
arising in the interim— it is also called "the state of that which is yet to be known" (*ājñātāvyājñāsyāmīndriya*).

If one has reached the stage of the path of cultivation (bhāvanāmārga) and is called "one who has already known" (ājñātāvī), this designation "one who has already known" is established in reference to the path of cultivation; that is,
if one is on the path of cultivation.
Regarding the eight truths of the higher and lower realms, there is nothing previously unknown that remains to be known,
because one has thoroughly and completely understood all eight truths;
it is solely for the purpose of abandoning the remaining latent dispositions (*anuśaya*).
One repeatedly understands those very truths once again;
therefore, that practitioner is said to be "one who has already known.
This occurs at the first moment of the Path-Knowledge of Subsequent Knowledge (*mārgānvaya-jñāna*) during the stage of the Path of Cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*).
Regarding the paths of the higher realms,
at that time one possesses correct knowledge;
although it is like the seven knowledges, [it is distinct].
As for those termed "already known," all the subsequent immeasurable and boundless knowledges are distinct from the preceding ones.
Taking the few according to the many,
they are collectively termed "already known.
Thus, the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 143, states:
Question: The sixteenth moment of mind should be like the seven knowledges;
why is it alone designated as the faculty of "already known" (ājñātendriya)?
Is it not because one knows what was not yet known?
The answer is that this is also stated from the perspective of the majority.
That is to say, although it resembles seven types of knowledge in its initial moment,
all subsequent moments differ from them.
For the most part, these are all termed the faculty of "already-known" (ājñātendriya),
because they share a single nature.
Some say that thereafter there is no longer any path not yet known that could overwhelm or obscure it.
One does not allow those below to overstep those above so that they may not act with autonomy;
because it must necessarily be so,
one knows what should be known and declares it as such.

As it is said in the treatise: "Just as that which is in the process of going is called 'already gone,' so too is this [the case]. Question: When the subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*) takes the second moment as its object, at that time there is correct knowledge (*saṃprajanya*).
Why is it called "already known"? The explanation says: this is established in terms of the [Four] Truths and not in terms of moments (*kṣaṇa*).
Because the part is small compared to the whole, it is designated as "already known."
Just as it cannot be said that a single drop of the great ocean or a single atom of Mount Sumeru has not been traversed when they are equal to the dust [of the earth],

so too, because it is the retinue of the knowledge of the patience regarding the path (mārga-anvaya-kṣānti), it is also called "knowing. Next, [the text] asks concerning the patience regarding the path.
When the subsequent knowledge of the path (mārgānvayajñāna) first takes [the truths] as its object,
how can it be called "already known"? The explanation is that this is established in terms of the [four] truths,
not in terms of individual moments.
Because the few follow the many, they are collectively termed "already known" (*ājñāta*).
Just as a single drop in the great ocean or a single speck of dust on Mount Sumeru,
from this perspective, the seven knowledges are also termed "already known."
Because one has not yet fully exhausted the knowledge of the truths and because [defilements] arise in the interim,
it is not called "already known."
Regarding the statement "in the path of no-more-learning" and so forth, explained at length:
the faculty of one who has full knowledge (*ājñātāvīndriya*) is established in reference to the path of no-more-learning;
this is because within the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), afflictions still remain.
Regarding the principle of the Four Noble Truths, one who has not yet attained the realization that "I have known what was to be known" cannot do so; however,
upon entering the Path of No-More-Learning (aśaikṣamārga), because of the absence of delusion,
one is able to produce the realization regarding the objects of the truths that "I have known what was to be known."
Therefore, it is called "knowledge.
This explains the meaning of knowledge.
One who has accomplished this knowledge is called "one endowed with knowledge" (vijjā-vant).
Regarding the explanation of "endowment" (*ājñātāvin*) by way of accomplishment: one who has repeatedly practiced this knowledge and attained its perfected nature is called "one who has known.
Regarding the explanation of "endowment" by way of practice:
because one has attained the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*), one is called "one who has known."
"I have fully known suffering" is the knowledge of exhaustion;
"there is nothing further to be fully known" is the knowledge of non-arising.
"I have abandoned the origin" is the knowledge of exhaustion.
Not further abandoning the origin [of suffering] is the knowledge of non-arising.
"I have realized cessation" is the knowledge of exhaustion.
Not further realizing cessation is the knowledge of non-arising.
"I have already cultivated the path; this is the knowledge of exhaustion (kṣayajñāna).
I shall no longer cultivate the path; this is the knowledge of non-arising (anutpādajñāna).
Thus it is said, "and so forth," up to the full exposition.
Regarding the phrase "those faculties which lead to the faculty of 'I shall come to know the unknown' (ājñāsyāmīndriya)," this is a specific explanation of the faculties.
It refers to all the faculties possessed by one who practices for the sake of knowing the unknown.
The terms "faculty of 'I shall come to know the unknown'" (*anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya*) and so forth are *tatpuruṣa* (dependent determinative) compounds,
according to the intention of the *Nyāyānusāra*.
The [terms] "that which is yet to be known" (*anājñātamājñāsyāmīndriya*) and so forth are *karmadhāraya* compounds based on the function of the faculties (*indriya*).
Each is established according to a specific meaning. Furthermore, the *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra*, chapter nine, states:
"Although there are twenty-two such names for the faculties..."
However, the substance of the faculties consists of only seventeen,
because the female and male faculties are subsumed within the body faculty,
and the three untainted faculties are subsumed within nine faculties.
Having thus explained [the categories] up to the tainted (*sāsrava*) and untainted (*anāsrava*), here follows the fourth section: the analysis by way of various gates.
In total, there are six gates.
This constitutes the first gate of the contaminated (*sāsrava*) and uncontaminated (*anāsrava*).
Because it is subsumed within the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*), it is called "possessing form" (*rūpin*).
Among the nine faculties beginning with the mind (*manas*), three are subsumed within the uncontaminated.
This is untainted (*anāsrava*);
the rest are called tainted (*sāsrava*).
The remainder of the text may be understood accordingly.
The statement by other masters that [this] reaches the category of external ordinary persons (*bāhya-pṛthagjana*) recounts the tenets of the Mahīśāsaka school;
it is precisely the *Vaibhāṣika* position.
These are called the Vibhajyavādins.
Because they maintain that faith and the other [faculties] are exclusively untainted (anāsrava), the Blessed One said:
If a person is endowed with such faith and so forth, they are called an Arhat;
and so on, until:
if a person is endowed with such faith and so forth.
He is called one who has entered the stream.
Having said this, he further spoke these words:
"If these five faculties, such as faith and so forth, were entirely non-existent..."
I say that they abide among the class of external worldlings (*bāhyapṛthagjanapakṣa*).
From this it is known that faith and the other [faculties] are exclusively untainted (*anāsrava*).
"This is not a valid proof because it was spoken as a statement directed toward those who have reached [the path]"—
thus the Master of the Treatise refutes [the objection]. As for the scriptural statement that "ordinary beings lack faith and so forth," [it refers to their lack of firm resolve].
"It is said that [the faculty] does not exist because it relies on the untainted faculties (*anāsrava-indriya*).
How is this known to be so? This is the challenge posed by other masters (*ācārya*).
Regarding the phrase "because it was previously stated based on the untainted attainment," this is an explanation;
for it is said in the Sūtra:
This statement was made because, having previously established the distinctions among the various noble stages— the four fruits and the four paths— based upon the five faculties,
such as untainted faith and so forth.
If one is entirely devoid of these five untainted faculties, such as faith,
I say that such a person abides among the class of external worldlings and is not included within those who possess the tainted.
Alternatively, regarding those ordinary beings who have reached the category of external ordinary beings: furthermore,
the Sūtra speaks of "external ordinary beings."
This refers to one who has severed the roots of goodness; according to their statement, [the path] does not exist there.
Furthermore, the Sūtra states that "reaching" (prāpti) also extends to the outflow-tainted (sāsrava).
Furthermore, a sūtra is cited as proof that faith and so forth are contaminated (*sāsrava*):
namely, when the Buddha was about to turn the wheel of Dharma,
he first surveyed the world universally with his Buddha-eye.
Sentient beings dwelling in the world are first born and subsequently grow.
There are distinctions among the faculties, such as superior, middling, and inferior faith;
even before the Buddha had yet turned the wheel of Dharma,
he observed that sentient beings possessed these various distinctions of faith and so forth, and thus they were capable of being delivered.
Therefore, it is known that faith and the other [faculties] also pertain to the outflow-tainted (sāsrava),
as was the case before the Buddha had turned the wheel of Dharma.
If there were already those in the world who possessed the untainted faculties (anāsrava-indriya),
the appearance of a Tathāgata in the world would be in vain.
Furthermore, the World-Honored One has taught that even the supernormal powers (abhijñā) can be either tainted (sāsrava) or untainted (anāsrava).
Furthermore, it cites a sūtra to prove that the contaminated [phenomena] such as sensation are "origination" (*samudaya*):
that is, they bring about the accumulation of birth and death, which is the cause of suffering; they are "submergence" (*nirodha*):
that is, they are the place of sinking and drowning; they are "flavor" (*āsvāda*).
That which is the basis for the relish of craving, that is its danger;
that which is the basis for its danger, that is the escape;
and that which is the escape, that is what should be escaped from.

The "aggregates" and so forth are all synonyms for that which is with outflows (*sāsrava*). Furthermore, another interpretation holds that being able to know things as they truly are is the wisdom of contemplation;
this is precisely the Truth of the Path (*mārgasatya*).
Arising, subsiding, and gratification constitute the truth of origination;
their peril constitutes the truth of suffering. Alternatively, arising is the truth of origination;
subsiding, gratification, and peril constitute the truth of suffering. Or else, subsiding and gratification pertain to both suffering and origination.
Renunciation is the truth of cessation.
"Māra" refers to the Māra of the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven; "Brahmā" refers to the Brahmā King; the phrase "and so forth" includes all the heavens above these. Furthermore, the Blessed One said:
If I have not yet known these five faculties, such as faith and the rest,
as they truly are— in terms of their origin, their disappearance, and so forth—
I am unable to transcend this world of gods and humans, including its Māras and Brahmās.
...up to: "Until one has attained unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment," and so forth at length.
It is not the case that untainted (*anāsrava*) phenomena can be observed through such categories as accumulation, disappearance, or gratification.
Thus, it is known that faith and the other [faculties] pertain to both types.
Having thus explained how each one individually pertains to both, what follows below is the second section:
the gate of the ripened (vipāka) and the non-ripened.
The verse provides the answer to the inquiry.
The treatise states: "Up to the point that it is meditative absorption and is a maturation (*vipāka*).
This explains the first phrase.
Among the twenty-two faculties (*indriya*),
only the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) is invariably a maturation (*vipāka*). If this is so, of what is it the maturation?
Question:
If it were solely the maturation [of karma],
how could an Arhat maintain his life-force for a hundred years, a thousand years, or more?
Since all these result from present acts of giving clothing and so forth,
which draw forth and prolong life from the previous existence,
they should not be considered *vipāka* (maturation).
Regarding this life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*),
whose maturation (*vipāka*) is it?
And yet, you say that the life-faculty alone is necessarily a maturation.
Regarding the statement in the root treatise, "up to the fruition of the life-span maturation," within the response,
the first part provides the formal answer according to the school's tenet.
Second, the presentation of divergent views.
Below this follows the correct response according to our own school (*siddhānta*). Within this section, there are two parts;
this first part presents the response of the initial master based on the *Mūla-śāstra*.
As stated in the treatise:
"How does a bhikṣu retain his life-force (āyuḥsaṃskāra)?
The answer consists of six parts.
"Victorious alone" refers to the Arhat; that is,
the ultimate fruit of the Śrāvaka, distinguished from those still in training.
Second is the excellence of liberation:

by accomplishing the supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), one manifests as one liberated in both ways (*ubhayatobhāgavimukta*), thereby distinguishing them from those liberated through wisdom alone (*prajñāvimukta*).
Third is the excellence of cultivation:
attaining mastery over the mind and manifesting the nature of immovability.
Briefly stated, there are four superior fields of merit: [the first three] and,
if among the Saṃgha, [the fourth].
Regarding "an individual" (*pudgala*) and "the Saṃgha"—
the latter meaning four or more persons— the "individual" refers to one who has first entered the meditative concentration of loving-kindness (*maitrī-samādhi*).
The concentration of non-contention,
the concentration of cessation,
and the path of vision.
Regarding the arising of the path of cultivation:
it arises by means of various requisites for sustaining life, such as robes, alms bowls, and needle-cases.
Distributing according to circumstances constitutes giving;
"giving" here refers to the practice of the act of giving itself,
thereby distinguishing it from inferior fields of merit.
Fifth is the excellence of the basis:
having given, one makes a vow,
either vowing to attain mastery in entering the meditative absorption of the ultimate limit (*prāntakoṭika-samādhi*).
Or, wishing that this [merit] should produce a ripened result (*vipākaphala*),
he enters the fourth "limit" (*prāntakoṭika*) dhyāna;
among all meditative absorptions, those of the highest degree are called "limits."
Because the power of this [practice] is most excellent within the state where *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* are balanced, one enters this meditative absorption;
it is distinguished from other absorptions and from those who do not make a formal vow.
The sixth is the excellence of transformative karma;
having arisen from meditative absorption, one forms a mental intention and speaks with the voice:
"May all my karmas that induce the maturation of wealth [be transformed]."

He made the vow, "May all these [merits] instead transform to bring about the fruit of longevity as their karmic maturation," for he feared they might not be sufficient to produce such a result; having thus emerged from meditative absorption, he again carefully confirmed this vow.
Once he had made this vow:
At that time, those karmas capable of producing the maturation of wealth all transform to produce the maturational fruit of longevity;
this is the intended meaning of this treatise, which excludes those karmas that do not transform.
Because at the time of giving, volition associated with non-greed is precisely what brings about the present life-faculty as its maturation;
this occurs by taking the "limiting concentration" (prāntakoṭika-samādhi) and so forth as conditions.
One can transform karma that produces wealth so that it instead brings about the fruit of longevity;
this is precisely the case where present karma produces the fruit of a present life-span. Question: Does the homogeneous character (*nikāya-sabhāga*) also produce its fruit in the present?
Between the life-span and the homogeneous character, which is more comprehensive?
Regarding the distinction between them, the first interpretation states:
the *sabhāgatā* (homogeneity) is the general [factor],
while the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) is the specific [factor].
The homogeneous character (*sabhāgatā*) is not experienced in the present; the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) may be experienced in the present.
This is due to the difference between their collective and individual [modes of experience].
Because there is a distinction between the manifest and the non-manifest,
that which is of the same class (*sabhāga*) may have its longevity extended, even if its life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) is short.
If the *sabhāgatā* (homogeneity) were also short, life could not be extended.
Since this treatise states that it further brings about the fruit of longevity,
one knows from this that it can manifestly induce life.
Furthermore, the treatise below states:
"The four wholesome [karmas] may all be performed together;
however, those that project a homogeneous state (*nikāya-sabhāga*) are only three."
Excluding those [karmas] to be experienced in the present life,
because the homogeneous status (nikāyasabhāga) of the present body is projected by prior karma;
since that text does not mention the life-faculty (jīvitendriya).
Thus, we know that while present karma cannot induce a homogeneous portion (*nikāya-sabhāga*), it can induce the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*).
Furthermore, the subsequent treatise states:
"A single karma projects a single birth."
Many karmas can bring about fulfillment.
Furthermore, it is said that the term "this one life" indicates a single *nikāya-sabhāga* (homogeneous class).
It is further said:
Nor is there a single birth that is projected by multiple karmas,
lest there be a fragmentation of the homogeneous class (*nikāya-sabhāga*).
Although a single karma projects a single homogeneous existence (*nikāya-sabhāga*),
it is admitted that its completion is brought about by multiple karmas;
