"In what state do the four great elements cease without remainder?
He replied, "I do not know."
In this manner, the six heavens of the desire realm pass the responsibility on to one another,
extending even to the Heaven of Controlling Others' Emanations (Paranirmita-vaśavartin). There,
they in turn look upward and pass it on to the Brahma-kāyika devas.
Desiring to go to the Brahma-world and enter a superior meditative concentration,
he again vanished from his palace by means of a concentrated mind and emerged among the gods of the Brahmakāyika realm.
Rising from meditative concentration, he again posed the same question.
The assembly of Brahmās all replied, "We do not know."
Furthermore, he pointed toward Mahābrahmā;
the bhikṣu Aśvajit then questioned that King Mahābrahmā.
At that time, while the Great Brahmā King was dwelling among his own assembly of Brahmās,
he was suddenly questioned by the bhikṣu Aśvajit,
who asked: "Regarding these four great elements of the desire and form realms— "
At what stage are they completely extinguished so that there are no further fetters of affliction?
Brahmā does not know this according to its proper application.

When the afflictions of the fourth dhyāna are completely abandoned by relying on the four fundamental dhyānas, the threshold concentration (*anāgamya*), the intermediate dhyāna (*dhyānāntara*), and the preparatory stage of the sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana-prayoga*),
all the great elements (*mahābhūta*) become ultimately liberated from bondage.
In the state of parinirvāṇa without remainder,
he falsely praises himself to manifest his deceit;
he speaks flattering words of apology to manifest his flattery.
This is a brief summary;
the details are as explained in the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 129.
Question: What is the distinction between this [being] and Mahābrahmā and the others? Answer: Among the Brahmakāyika gods, the one who is the most honored is named Mahābrahmā.
He exercises sovereign mastery over all things, encompassing them entirely.
He is called the "Creator" because he can fashion the vessel-world (*bhājana-loka*),
and he is called the "Transformer" because he can transform the world of sentient beings (*sattva-loka*).
The term "producer" (*janaka*) explains the preceding "agent" (*kartṛ*), further clarifying the meaning of "acting.
That is to say, one who can produce the receptacle world (*bhājanaloka*) is therefore called an "agent.
The section beginning with "nourisher" (*poṣaka*) explains the preceding "transformer" (*pariṇāyaka*), further clarifying the meaning of "transforming."

This means that he who is able to nourish and sustain the world of sentient beings is called a "transformer" (*nirmāṇa*) because he is the father of all sentient beings; this is the interpretation according to the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*. Question: Does Aśvajit further manifest transformations when he arrives there?

Upon arriving there, how many supernormal fruits can further coexist in a single moment? The explanation says: when Aśvajit transported his body to that first dhyāna, he manifested transformations of that stage because he was Mahābrahmā;
therefore, they were able to take each other’s hands and lead one another.
If one does not transform [the object] separately, the coarse grasping of the form of the desire realm cannot be attained.
It should be understood that regarding the supernormal power of moving the body and the supernormal power of transformation,
one first leaves behind a transformed body and subsequently employs the divine eye to see the forms of that level.
Alternatively, one may give rise to the divine ear to hear the sounds of that realm;
these two supernormal powers arise interchangeably. In general terms:
Within a single moment of thought, both may arise simultaneously.
Thus, the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 150, asks:
"In one moment of thought, how many supernormal powers (abhijñā-phala) can arise?"

Answer: Those who maintain that the supernormal powers of the divine eye and divine ear do not possess their respective "homogeneous" (sabhāga) states assert that in a single moment, only one type of supernormal fruit arises.
This refers to any one of the five supernormal powers (*abhijñā*).
For those who maintain that the divine eye and divine ear exist as transformative emanations (*nirmāṇa*) but lack their respective homogeneous counterparts (*sabhāga*),
they assert that two fruits of supernormal power can arise in a single moment.
This refers to the fruit of the supernormal power of the divine realm (*ṛddhividhi-jñāna*), as well as any one of the other four;

furthermore, for those who maintain that there are emanated forms (*nirmāṇa*) that remain, there are their respective counterparts (*sabhāga*) regarding the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*) and divine ear (*divyaśrotra*).
He states that in a single moment one can attain four supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) as fruits: namely,
the fruit of the supernormal power of the psychic basis (*ṛddhivisaya*), the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*), the divine ear (*divyaśrotra*), and either one of the remaining two— namely,
the supernormal power of knowing the minds of others (*paracittajñāna*) or the supernormal power of recollecting past lives (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛti*).
Because their respective objects are distinct and they do not arise simultaneously.
Regarding this explanation,
it should be understood that the second position stated is the correct one.

Because the supernormal powers of the divine eye and divine ear can be retained through transformation, they necessarily lack their respective homogeneous states (*sabhāgatā*); this is because they must manifest simultaneously.
Thus has been explained the distinction regarding the minimum number of parts.
The third major section below clarifies the similarities and differences.
Regarding their essential natures,
they are actually distinct from one another, though there are slight similarities.
Thus, there are four pairs of distinctions in total.
Hereafter, the first two pairs are clarified.
The following verse introduces the preceding inquiry.
Regarding the inquiry into the arising [of phenomena], there are two parts: first, the general;
second, the specific.
This constitutes the general [explanation].
From "lack of shame and lack of dread" up to "what is their distinction?
constitutes the specific [explanation].
The verse states: "As for [the statement] 'it exists only in the Desire and Form Realms,' within the response provided by the verse,
the first two lines clarify the absence of shame (*āhrīkya*) and the absence of dread (*anapatrāpya*)."
The final two lines clarify affection and respect.

The Commentary states: "As for 'the dharmas that serve as their counterparts,' these refer to various merits, namely precepts, meditative concentration, and so forth; [and] those who possess such merit."
This refers to teachers and the like; the four factors beginning with "lack of respect" collectively manifest a lack of reverence.
Regarding the first two objects, there is neither respect nor veneration;
or, regarding their various virtues, there is no respect.
Lacking veneration for those who possess virtue;
or lacking respect for those who possess virtue;
lacking veneration for all meritorious qualities.
Regarding the first two objects, there is no hesitation or difficulty,
nor is there any sense of subordination;
or, regarding all virtues, there is no hesitation or difficulty.
To have no sense of deference toward those who possess virtue is called "lack of shame" (*āhrīkya*).
This is the state of opposition to respect (*gaurava*) and shame (*hrī*); for [it is defined] by means of respect...
Because it has shame as its essence, and because it causes all noble persons to feel dread [regarding it],
this explains the lack of moral dread (*anapatrāpya*) with respect to transgression— that is, sinful karma.
In this regard, not seeing that within these transgressions there is a fruit to be feared is called "lack of shame" (*anapatrāpya*). Here, the word "fear" indicates an undesirable result.
It is called "fear" because it can produce fear.
Regarding the statement that not seeing fear is called "not seeing fear," this is an external objection.
What meaning does the expression "not seeing fear" intend to reveal?
It refers to not being terrified despite seeing the consequences of those transgressions; this is called "not seeing fear."
Not seeing the fruit of fear regarding those transgressions is called "not seeing fear.
Alternatively, it is explained that seeing the transgression yet not fearing it is called "not seeing fear.
This question concerns fear as belonging to the mind.
That is, one feels fear and dread with respect to the object.
Not seeing the fearful consequences of that sinful household is called "fear from not seeing.
This question concerns the fear belonging to the object.
This refers to the very result that is feared.
To the question, "If that were so, what would be the fault?
the Master of the Treatise provides a general answer.
"Both [positions] possess faults up until the point where ignorance should be revealed":
here, the opponent points out a fault,
saying that if one perceives those faults, one will fear their consequences.
Not being terrified is called "not seeing fear";
this should clarify wisdom.
Here, "wisdom" refers to false view.
Because this wrong view negates cause and effect,
the *Nyāyānusāra* states:
"One should clarify what constitutes wrong view."
If one does not perceive the fearfulness of the fruit of those offenses,
this is called "not seeing fear";
it should be understood as ignorance (*avidyā*).

Because of this ignorance, one does not see [the fault] and thus feels no fear. Furthermore, if it were the case that one sees the fault yet feels no fear, it would manifest as wrong view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*).
If one does not see the fault within that [state], then there is no fear regarding its result.
"One should clarify that ignorance [is what is meant];
this statement does not clarify seeing and non-seeing.
Thus the Master of the Treatise replies.
The opponent further challenges: "This statement that 'fear is not seen' does not reveal either wrong view or ignorance.
What, then, does it reveal?"
This shows that there is a phenomenon which is designated as "lack of shame.
The Master of the Treatise replies:
This shows that there exists a phenomenon called lack of shame.
This is a secondary affliction (upakleśa).
It is called "lack of shame" (āhrīkya) because it serves as the cause for both that wrong view and ignorance.
Therefore, the *Nyāyānusāra* states:
"That which serves as the proximate cause for the manifestation of non-wisdom (*ajñāna*) and distorted wisdom (*mithyājñāna*) is designated as 'lack of shame' (*anapatrāpya*)."
Other masters say that [the state] reaching up to what is called "lack of shame" (*anapatrāpya*) describes a different interpretation;
this master distinguishes between the two based on the absence of shame regarding oneself and others.
If that is so, how can these two arise together? This is the objection:
since shamelessness (*āhrīkya*) and lack of dread (*anapatrāpya*) involve distinct perspectives regarding oneself and others, how can they arise simultaneously?
Regarding the statement that these two are not mentioned up to the point where they are called "lack of shame" (*anapatrāpya*),
other masters explain:
it is not that these two— lack of shame and lack of dread (*ahrīkya*)— are not mentioned.
They arise simultaneously.
Lack of shame (*āhrīkya*) specifically observes oneself, while lack of dread (*anapatrāpya*) specifically observes others.
However, when there is a state of shamelessness that observes oneself, its function is predominant; therefore, it is designated as "lack of shame."
At that time, although one may possess a lack of shame (*anapatrāpya*) when observing oneself,
because the function of observing oneself is inferior,
there is also a lack of modesty (*ahrīkya*) when observing the bodies of others.
Because it functions to increase [the lack of shame], it is designated as "lack of dread" (āhrīkya).
At that time, although there is indeed a lack of shame with respect to the bodies of others,
its function is inferior when observing the bodies of others.
Furthermore, the *Nyāya* states:
Some say that to commit transgressions while dwelling alone without shame is called "lack of self-respect" (*āhrīkya*).
If one commits an offense in the midst of the assembly without shame, this is called "lack of remorse" (*anapatrāpya*). This is explained in detail as in that [text].
The *Abhidharmamahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 34, also extensively explains the distinction between these two types.
I cannot describe them in full detail.
Regarding the statement that "the distinction between shame (*hrī*) and dread-of-blame (*apatrāpya*) is such that when it reaches its verbal expression, it is called 'dread-of-blame'":
one should understand that this explains *hrī* and *apatrāpya* as being the opposites of the two [preceding] explanations.
The shame (*hrī*) and dread of blame (*apatrāpya*) were explained previously.
The lack of shame (*āhrīkya*) and the lack of dread of blame (*anapatrāpya*) will be analyzed later;
this refers to that passage.

Having already explained [the factors] from lack of shame (*āhrīkya*) up to "excluding the three preceding characteristics," the following section distinguishes between affection (*preman*) and reverence (*gaurava*).
Affection refers to fondness or endearment.
Its essence is faith.
However, when explaining "affection" (preman) in general, there are two kinds:
the first is with defilement, which refers to craving (rāga).
The second type of non-defilement is faith (*śraddhā*).
Generally speaking, clear faith also has two aspects:
first, the aspect of acceptance (*abhyupagama-lakṣaṇa*).
Alternatively, it is called "trustworthy" (*śraddheya*);
though the names differ, the meaning is the same. Second is the characteristic of aspiration and delight (*pranidhāna-ruci-lakṣaṇa*).
It is sometimes called "faith-joy" (śraddhā-prasāda) and sometimes called "faith-love" (śraddhā-preman);
while the names differ, the meaning is the same.

Based on this, because faith (*śraddhā*) and affection (*preman*) differ in their scope, four permutations (*catuṣkoṭi*) can be established. The first permutation is: there is faith, but not affection.
This refers to faith directed toward suffering (*duḥkha*) and its origin (*samudaya*).
It is called "having faith" because it involves the patient acceptance (*kṣānti*) and conviction that suffering and its origin exist as the foremost truth.
Defiled phenomena (*sāsrava-dharma*) are not objects of endearment;

because they lack a second [mental state], namely faith (*śraddhā*), they are called "non-endearing. In the second phrase, there is "endearment" (*tṛṣṇā*) that is not "faith," which refers to all defiled forms of craving (*kliṣṭa-tṛṣṇā*).
The defiled craving that arises with respect to one’s wife, children,
and so forth is called "craving for existence" (bhavarāga) because it is the foremost form of craving.
Since it is defiled, it is not faith.
The third phrase refers to having faith that is associated with communication and affection;
this refers to faith conditioned by cessation and the path.
Because one accepts cessation and the path as being supreme, it is called "having faith."
The untainted dharmas are objects of endearment;
because there is a second kind of faith, it is called "having craving.
It should be understood that within this context, faith takes cessation and the path as its objects.
This comprehensively includes both types. The fourth phrase excludes the aforementioned characteristics.
Some say that for those who possess faith, [craving] reaches its limit, whereas for those who lack faith, it is not so;
this describes an incorrect interpretation.
This master’s intention is to say that acceptance (kṣānti) and delight (abhinandanā) do not occur simultaneously.
Therefore, affection is not faith.
As for "respect" (*gaurava*), it refers to reverence directed toward the objects of the Path and its Cessation (*nirodha-mārga*).
Regarding "shame" (*hrī*): this is a separate explanation of respect and shame.
Shame (*hrī*) is broad;
respect (*gaurava*) is narrow.
These constitute two distinct categories: the first category consists of that which possesses shame but is not respect.
This means that when a wholesome mind arises taking suffering and its origin as objects, there is a sense of shame and remorse toward that suffering and its origin;
therefore, there is "shame" (hrī).
Phenomena associated with outflows (āsrava) are not to be respected.
Therefore, there is no *hrī* (reverence).

Thus, one feels shame (*lajjā*) with respect to suffering (*duḥkha*) and its origin (*samudaya*), but this is not reverence. The second phrase involves both shame (*lajjā*) and reverence (*hrī*), namely, shame with respect to cessation (*nirodha*) and the path (*mārga*).
When a wholesome mind arises conditioned by that cessation or the Path,
there is shame because of a sense of moral dread;
there is reverence because the untainted (anāsrava) dharmas are worthy of respect.
Therefore, the sense of shame (*hrī*) that takes cessation and the path as its objects is included within reverence (*gaurava*),
because it is essentially reverence. Some say that while reverence is "approaching" [the object], shame is not.
To describe what is not righteous:
reverence for one's predecessors and shame toward those who follow are matters of different times.
Reverence is not the same as shame (*hrī*).
In the eleventh chapter of the *Nyāyānusāra*, the author refutes this teacher, stating:
"That teacher must admit that one who lacks shame and dread of blame (*anapatrāpya*) can give rise to reverence."
Because when reverence first arises, shame has not yet occurred;
thus, one who lacks shame would be able to give rise to reverence.
If it is argued that shame already exists at the time of reverence, [then this is untenable].
Then one should not say that shame arises only preceded by respect.
If it is argued that at the time of respect there is no absence of shame, yet respect is not itself shame; [then this is our position].

This is also unreasonable, because there is no evidence for the claim that respect (*gaurava*) is not a form of shame (*hrī*). Regarding the statement "with respect to the object of perception, reaching [the state of] 'love' excludes the three preceding characteristics":

this distinguishes the fourfold logical alternatives (*catuṣkoṭi*) regarding the presence or absence of love (*preman*) and respect with respect to the object of perception. The first alternative is: there is love, but no respect.
Regarding one's wife, children, and so forth, there is defiled affection (*sneha*) due to lustful attachment;
because they are not objects of veneration, there is no respect (*gaurava*). This constitutes the second case: having respect but lacking affection.
There is reverence (*gaurava*) toward other teachers and the like because they are worthy of respect;
there is no affection (*preman*) because there is no aspiration for them. The third case involves both affection and reverence:
there is affection toward one’s own teacher and the like because they are objects of aspiration.

Because undefiled affection (*anāsravā prema*) is worthy of respect, there is reverence (*gaurava*). The fourth alternative—neither affection nor reverence—is that which excludes the three aforementioned characteristics.
*Pudgala* is translated here as "one who repeatedly undergoes birth" (*saṃsārin*).
It refers to repeatedly taking up various realms of existence;
in general, this applies to all five destinies.
Thus, when love and respect reach their absence even in the formless realm, [they are said to be non-existent].
Regarding the analysis by way of the elements (*dhātu*):
Is it not the case that faith (*śraddhā*) and shame (*hrī*) exist even in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*)?
[This is] an objection.
Affection has faith as its essence;
reverence has shame as its essence.
These factors of the great wholesome ground also exist in the formless realm.
How can it be said that they do not exist?
Regarding the statement that there are two types of affection and respect, which are absent in the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu), the answer is as follows:
If based on the dharma that is the object of the condition, love and respect actually pervade all three realms.
However, the intention here is to state that because they take a *pudgala* (person) as their object, they do not extend to the formless realm.
This is because beings in the desire realm and the form realm possess physical bodies;
because there are distinctions of superior and inferior;
and because their physical characteristics are manifest.
It can be said that there is both affection (*sneha*) and respect (*gaurava*) when viewed in relation to one another;
this is not the case for the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), and therefore these do not exist there.
Question: If [these] pertain to the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), why does the *Vibhāṣā* (vol. 29) state:
"Question: In what places do such affection (*preman*) and respect (*gaurava*) exist?"
Answer: Although [these qualities] may exist within all three realms and five destinies,
what is described here— namely, distinguished affection and respect—
is found only among humans in the desire realm, and not elsewhere.
Only within the Buddha-dharma do such forms of affection and reverence exist.
According to the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, based on a specific intention, it is stated that they exist only in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
Why does this treatise include the realm of form (rūpadhātu)? The explanation states: This treatise includes the realm of form because it relies on what is manifest;
the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* restricts it to the desire realm (kāmadhātu) because it relies on what is preeminent.
Each relies on a single principle, and thus they do not contradict one another.
Thus, having already explained those who possess a mind directed toward the ultimate and are without regard for anything else, this clarifies the latter two pairs.
The first phrase clarifies the third pair: vitarka (applied thought) and vicāra (sustained thought).
The last three phrases clarify the pair consisting of pride (*māna*) and arrogance (*mada*).
The treatise states: "That which is of a subtle nature is called *vicāra* (sustained thought);
the coarse nature of the mind is called *vitarka* (applied thought)."
The subtle nature of the mind is called *vicāra*.
Among the mental factors (*caitta*), it possesses its own distinct substantial entity and is associated with the mind (*citta-samprayukta*).
The essence is not identical to the mind;
the statement that the mind is coarse or subtle is an *tatpuruṣa* (dependent) compound.
How is it that these two are associated with a single mind?
The Master of the Treatise objects:
Vitarka is coarse;
vicāra is subtle.
Because their natures are contradictory,
how could these two be associated with a single mind?
The Sautrāntikas do not admit that the two dharmas of vitarka and vicāra are associated with a single mind.
The proponent of the treatise (śāstrakāra) raises this objection because he follows the Sautrāntika school.
As for the interpretation that "it reaches the point where simultaneous activity exists," there are two explanations provided below by the Vaibhāṣikas.
This refers to the first master.
Because of water, it is not clarified;
because of the sun, it does not congeal.
Water is the cause of condensation;
the sun is the cause of dissolution.
In this way, because the single mind possesses vitarka, it does not become subtle.
Because of the presence of vicāra, one does not transcend coarseness;
vitarka is the cause of coarseness,
while vicāra is the cause of subtlety.
Therefore, how is it logically contradictory for these two to possess their functions simultaneously within a single mind? If that is so,
then what is the reason why vitarka and vicāra do not reach a state where their essence is neither stagnant nor dissipated?
The master of the treatise raises an objection by means of an analogy:
water is the cause of congealing,
while the sun is the cause of dissolution.
Their essence is neither solid nor dissolved;
one should also investigate that vitarka is the coarse cause and vicāra is the subtle cause.
It is not that the coarse and subtle are their essential nature.
Furthermore, regarding the claim that "the natures of coarseness and subtlety are distinguished by vitarka and vicāra," the author of the treatise further refutes this.
Now, the natures of the coarse and the subtle are established in mutual dependence.
This may be understood in terms of the three realms or in terms of the nine stages.
Alternatively, according to the nine grades,
there are differences in their distinctions;
relative to one another, the lower stages are termed "coarse."
The higher stages are subtle;
even the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*) is subtle when compared to the lower stages,
yet it is coarse when compared to the meditative attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*).
There must be vitarka and vicāra. Furthermore, it is explained that the coarse is called "superior" (ūrdhva) and the subtle is called "inferior" (adhas).
Thus, by way of comparing the characteristics of the coarse and the subtle, there must be vitarka and vicāra even up to the Peak of Existence (bhavāgra).
The author of the treatise sets forth the Sautrāntika position as an objection;
thus, the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 52, states:
"Some maintain that vitarka and vicāra exist from the desire realm up to the peak of existence."
As stated in the treatise above regarding the proponents of similes (Dārṣṭāntikas):
furthermore, among all phenomena, the two natures of coarse and subtle do not possess distinct ontological categories.
One cannot rely on these [definitions] to distinguish between the two types, vitarka and vicāra,
in the same way that feeling is manifested by its function of experiencing and perception is manifested by its function of grasping images.
All mental factors possess their own distinct characteristics;
however, this nature of coarseness and subtlety pervades all five aggregates.
Therefore, it cannot be used as a basis for distinguishing between vitarka and vicāra.
Furthermore, as for the explanation given by others asking, "How does this contradict the principle?"—
this is the second explanation provided by the Vaibhāṣikas,
that the word "practice" (caryā) refers to the cause.
Vitarka and vicāra are the two causes of speech,
for they are capable of producing speech.
Within these causes, there are two types.
The coarse is called vitarka (applied thought),
and the subtle is called vicāra (sustained thought).
Within a single moment of mind, both the coarse and the subtle arise together.
What is the logical contradiction?
Regarding the question, "If there is a distinct substantial category, how can it reach a distinct characteristic?
the Master of the Treatise further raises an objection.
Among the mental factors (*caitta*),
if there are two distinct categories of coarse and subtle, it is logically consistent to distinguish them as *vitarka* (applied thought) and *vicāra* (sustained thought);
in reality, there is no contradiction.
However, since there would be no distinction between the two categories of coarse and subtle,
it would contradict reason;
that which is mentioned above is termed "coarse."
The lower [category] is called "subtle.
The lower [categories] are explained accordingly.

Within the same class of the essence of mind, it is impossible for the coarse and the subtle to arise simultaneously. Furthermore, another interpretation holds that within the same class of the essence of mind and mental factors, it is impossible for the subtle and the coarse to arise simultaneously.
If you, O Vaibhāṣika, say that there is also a difference in the essential nature (*svabhāva*) of vitarka and vicāra,
you should explain what the distinct characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) of these different natures are.
When these two natures are brought to manifestation, their distinct characteristics [are as follows]:
The Vaibhāṣika masters reply:
It is difficult to describe the distinct characteristics of the essential natures of *vitarka* (applied thought) and *vicāra* (sustained thought);
they are distinguished only by the fact that the former is coarse and the latter is subtle.
"It is not by way of superior or inferior [states] that they correspond to a single mind.
The Master of the Treatise further objects:
"It is not by way of coarseness or subtlety that the distinct characteristics of *vitarka* and *vicāra* can be manifested."
Within each category of mind and mental factors,
there is both grossness and subtlety based on their mutual relativity; yet,
since there is no distinct characteristic to differentiate them from vitarka and vicāra, [the distinction remains unclear].
From this, it should be understood that the two dharmas of vitarka and vicāra can certainly not be held to be associated with a single moment of mind.
If so, how is it that [the first dhyāna] comes to possess all five factors?
The Vaibhāṣika masters cite a sūtra to raise an objection:
"If you do not admit that those two factors, vitarka and vicāra, are associated with a single moment of mind,
how can the sūtra state that the first dhyāna possesses five branches— namely, vitarka, vicāra, prīti, sukha, and samādhi?"
"Because the statement possesses five members, there is no fault. This is the Master of the Treatise's (śāstrakāra) exegesis of the Sūtra;
he explains that the statement is complete with five members.
This is explained in terms of the preceding and succeeding moments within a single stage (*bhūmi*),
rather than within a single instant (*kṣaṇa*);
therefore, there is no fault.
The author of the treatise follows the Sautrāntika school;
therefore, in accordance with their interpretation, he here omits further defense.
Thus has been explained that which leads to the state of being without regard for anything.
This clarifies the fourth pair.
Pride (*māna*) refers to the mind’s self-exaltation and reliance upon itself when weighing its own qualities against others, thereby looking down upon them with contempt.
In this context, one should also mention the weighing of lineage (*gotra*) and so forth, but these are omitted for brevity.
*Māna* (pride) refers to being stained by attachment to one’s own qualities, such as lineage, physical form, and the like.
It causes the mind to become arrogant and negligent, such that it has no regard for any wholesome dharmas.
Thus, the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* (Vibhāṣā), fascicle 43, states:
"In this context, 'intoxication' (*mada*) refers to not comparing oneself with others."
It is merely the mental state of arrogance and self-satisfaction arising from being stained by attachment to one’s own lineage, physical appearance, strength, wealth, status, wisdom, and so forth.

In this context, "pride" (*māna*) refers to the characteristic of exalting oneself and relying upon one's own lineage, appearance, strength, wealth, status, wisdom, and so forth, in comparison to others. Question: Is pride always directed toward others? Answer: The phrase "in comparison to others" is stated according to the majority of cases.
Therefore, the *Vibhāṣā* states:
The critique says that one should speak thus:
it is not the case that all forms of pride necessarily arise in relation to others.
Due to the power of habitual practice since beginningless time, pride (*māna*) also manifests within one's own continuum;
it is explained as pride (*māna*), excessive pride (*atimāna*), pride beyond pride (*mānātimāna*), and inferiority pride (*ūnamāna*).

These four types of pride—pride (*māna*), excessive pride (*adhimāna*), and false pride (*mithyāmāna*)—arise based on one's own mental continuum. Other masters say that this extends up to the specific characteristics (*viśeṣa-lakṣaṇa*).
The other masters explain *mada* (intoxication/arrogance) as follows:
just as the specific state of exhilaration and elation arising from wine is called "drunkenness," so too is this [state] designated.
Pride (*mada*) is the outflow-result (*niṣyanda-phala*) of craving.
Thus, a specific form of elation and uplift that arises from craving is designated as pride.
*Hṛṣṭatā* (exultation) is broad in scope,
whereas *mada* (intoxication) is narrow;
this *mada* is a specific differentiation of *hṛṣṭatā*.
Thus has been explained the distinction between the names and their meanings.

Below this, the fourth major section clarifies the various designations for the assembly [of dharmas]. Thus has been explained the different categories of all minds, mental factors, the five stages, and so forth.
The third [section] is the determination of the simultaneous arising of the three natures and the mind;

the fourth is the differentiation of the distinct characteristics of the mental factors (caitta) relative to the mind (citta). Now, below the section on the mind and mental factors, a question arises regarding the terms "name" (nāman) and "conceptualization" (saṃjñā).
Some names are derived from the fruit,
while others are established based on the cause; therefore,
they are called "names and concepts" (*nāma-saṃjñā*).
The verse states: "Regarding the meaning of association, there are five.
The first line specifically clarifies alternative names for the mind (*citta*);
the subsequent three lines generally clarify alternative names for both the mind and mental factors (*caitta*).
The Commentary states: "That which reaches [its object] is therefore called consciousness.
This is an etymological explanation of its synonyms;
in Sanskrit, it is named *citta*.
This is called "mind" (*citta*).
It carries the meaning of "accumulating and arising.
That is to say, by the power of the mind, mental factors (*caitasika*) and activities such as karma are accumulated and brought forth.
Therefore, the Sūtra says: "The mind can lead the world;
the mind can universally encompass and sustain it.
Because it is able to accumulate and give rise [to phenomena], it is called 'mind' (citta)."
In Sanskrit it is called *manas*;
here it is translated as "mind" (*yi*).
It carries the meaning of "deliberation."
In Sanskrit it is called *vijñāna*; here it is translated as "consciousness" (*shi*),
which carries the meaning of "discernment."
Furthermore, there is another explanation stating that it is called "consciousness" (*vijñāna*) because it cognizes.
This is the second interpretation provided by the Sarvāstivāda school.
In this context, the term *dhātu* means "nature."
The various distinctions between the natures of purity and impurity,
and the diversity of their modes of activity (*ākāra*), constitute what is called "mind" (*citta*).
This explains the meaning of "mind" through its manifold aspects.
This very mind is called "manas" (the mental faculty) because it serves as the basis for others; thus,
the meaning of "manas" is explained by way of its being a support.
Because it acts as the support, it is called "consciousness" (*vijñāna*);
thus, the meaning of "consciousness" is explained by means of its support.
Therefore, although the terms *citta*, *manas*, and *vijñāna* differ, their essence is one.
The concluding passage may be understood accordingly.
Furthermore, the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 72, in explaining mind (*citta*), thought (*manas*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*), states:
"Some teachers say that there is no distinction between them."
Furthermore, there are those who say that "name" (*nāman*) is itself the differentiation.
Moreover, there is also temporal differentiation:
that which is past is called "mind" (*manas*).
Because that which is future is called "mind" (*citta*) and that which is present is called "consciousness" (*vijñāna*).
Furthermore, there is also a distinction in their conventional designations.
This means that "mind" (citta) is designated within the context of the elements (dhātu), "intellect" (manas) is designated within the context of the bases (āyatana),
and "consciousness" (vijñāna) is designated within the context of the aggregates (skandha).
Furthermore, there is also a distinction in meaning:
"mind" (citta) has the sense of being a seed-lineage,
while "intellect" (manas) has the sense of being a gateway for arising.
Consciousness has the meaning of accumulation.
Furthermore, there is also a distinction regarding karma:
that which travels far is the karma of the mind.
The preceding is the karma of mental action (*manas-karman*).
Rebirth (*pratisandhi*) is the karma of consciousness (*vijñāna-karman*). Furthermore, there are three additional successive explanations of karma that cannot be fully related here.
Regarding the phrase "as the mind, mental consciousness, and so forth, arise through conjunction":
the mind (*citta*) and its associated mental factors (*caitta-dharma*) have four alternative names.
First, they are called "having a support" (*sāśraya*), because they necessarily rely upon the sense faculties as their basis. Second, they are called "having an object" (*sālambana*).
Because it necessarily arises in dependence upon an object, the third [type of cognition] is said to possess an aspect (*sākāra*).
That is to say, regarding all phenomena as its objects,
it possesses various differentiations of categories and types.
Mind and mental factors are called "possessing aspects" because they arise with an aspect in accordance with whichever phenomena they take as objects.
That is to say, the essence of mind and mental factors is luminous and pure;
regardless of what object they encounter,
by their very nature, that preceding object appears entirely upon the mind and mental factors.
That which is manifested is called the "aspect" (ākāra).
Precisely because this manifestation carries the sense of an object,
it is described as the "cognizing subject" (ālambaka) insofar as it resembles the preceding object.
However, this mode of activity (ākāra) has no separate essence;
it is not distinct from the mind and so forth.
It is subsumed within the mind and so forth, and is not an object of cognition (ālambana).
It is just as when a bright mirror faces various forms and appearances, all of which manifest upon the mirror's surface;
yet these manifested images are not the objects being reflected.
Nevertheless, insofar as the images appear, one says that the mirror "is able to reflect"; this case should be understood in the same way regarding the characteristics of speech.

It is called "aspect" (*ākāra*) because it possesses the images and characteristics of its object; alternatively, it is explained as "aspect" because it is the characteristic of that which has an object of activity; furthermore, it is explained that "formation" (*saṃskāra*) means "transmigration."
The manifestation of names and signs upon the mind and so forth is called "aspect" (*ākāra*);

because it proceeds toward names and signs, it is termed "aspected activity" (*ākāra-karma*). Furthermore, another interpretation holds that "activity" (*ākāra*) refers to the process of cognitive engagement, such as discernment (*vijñapti*), while "sign" (*nimitta*) refers to the objective appearance, such as a reflected image.
It is called "aspect" (*ākāra*) because it is the aspect of activity.
An extensive explanation of this aspect is as previously explained. Fourth is "conjunction" (*samprayoga*), because of their mutual harmony and association.
In what sense is it called "equal conjunction"?
Question:
Since "equal conjunction" has already been used to explain "association" (*samprayoga*), [why is this distinction made?]
In what sense is it called "equal conjunction"?
It is because there are five meanings; that this applies to each [of the five] respectively is also the case. Answer:
This refers to the mind and mental factors.
They are said to be "associated" because they are equal and similar in five respects: first, equality of basis, meaning they necessarily share the same sense faculty as their support.
Mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) and its associated mental factors (*caitta-dharma*) have one support (*āśraya*),
namely the immediately preceding ceased mind-faculty (*manas*).
The five sensory consciousnesses and their respective associated mental factors each have two supports.
First, the sense faculty that serves as the simultaneous support;
second, the mental faculty that has ceased without interval.
In each case, they are respectively the supports for equality.
This text intends to subsume two types of bases;
therefore, it does not explicitly state that they share the same basis.
When various treatises speak of mind and mental factors having the same basis, [it refers to this].
Furthermore, based on a different support,
it is said that the six consciousnesses and their associated mental factors each have the same support. Moreover, this explains the equality of the supports,
which demonstrates that the six consciousnesses and their associated mental factors each have the same support.
Therefore, in the explanation of the associated cause (*samprayuktaka-hetu*), it says:
"In this context, the word 'identical' indicates that the basis (*āśraya*) is one.
Although the five consciousnesses also rely upon the mental faculty (*manas-indriya*)," [they are not considered identical in this specific sense].
This text is based for now on the explanation of those who rely on [the doctrine] of simultaneity: second, equality of the object of cognition (*ālambana*).
This means they must necessarily share the same objective referent;
within that object, at times they may take one [aspect] as their object.
Alternatively, they may take many [objects] as their conditions;
in each case, they are all equal with respect to the object of cognition (*ālambana*).
When various treatises state that the mind (*citta*) and mental factors (*caitta*) share the same object, it refers to this.
Furthermore, this is stated according to a specific condition regarding a single dharma.
If it were not so, then—just as in the contemplation of non-self (anātman)—with the exception of its own associated factors, coexistent factors would universally take all things as their objects.
How could these possibly have the same object? Furthermore, the "equality of the object" (ālambana-samatā) is explained as follows:
this demonstrates that the six consciousnesses and their associated mental factors each have the same object.
Therefore, in various treatises, it is said that mind and mental factors share the same object (ekālambana).
Although there are indeed those that take multiple objects,
this text speaks for now based on those that take a single object. Third, the mental states and mental factors (citta-caitta-dharma) are equal in their modes of activity (ākāra).
Its essence is luminous and pure; according to whatever object it encounters, it gives rise to respective modes of activity (*ākāra*).
It may encounter a single phenomenon and give rise to a single mode of activity, or it may encounter multiple phenomena and give rise to multiple modes of activity.
Whether one or many,
their modes of activity are each distinct.
In each case, the aspects (*ākāra*) are equal;
however, because many aspects manifest simultaneously, it is not said that they possess an identical aspect.
When various treatises state that the mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta-dharma*) have an identical aspect, [it refers to this equality].
Furthermore, based on the sense that they share a single object and are similar in nature,
it is logically correct that they are actually distinct. Moreover,
the explanation regarding the equality of their aspects (*ākāra*) demonstrates that the mind (*citta*) and mental factors (*caitta*) take the same object.
They are said to have the same aspect because they share the same mode of activity; therefore, various treatises state that the mind and mental factors possess the same aspect.
Although their modes of activity are each distinct and different,
they are said to have the same mode of activity because they are similar in accordance with their commonality.
Although there are indeed instances where multiple objects are perceived and multiple mental aspects manifest simultaneously,
these do not correspond to one another; for now,
this discussion is based on the case of perceiving a single object, wherein the four moments are equal.
This means that mind and mental factors necessarily exist at the same moment.
This is because they arise, abide, and cease together, and belong to the same temporal period.
Thus, it is said that their time is equal and their five characteristics are equal.
The term "phenomenon" (*vastu*) refers to the essence (*svabhāva*); because each essence is one, they are said to be equal in terms of phenomena.
Within a single associated state of mind and mental factors, just as the essence of the mind is one, so too are the others.
The essential natures of all mental factors (caitta-dharma) are likewise each singular;
there is never the simultaneous occurrence of two distinct natures at one time.
This refers to the equality of their substance within a single moment (kṣaṇa).
It is not that there is a difference between the preceding and succeeding [moments], nor in their categories and numbers;
one should know that the three factors herein— the basis (*āśraya*), the object (*ālambana*), and the mode of activity (*ākāra*)—
have already been explained as before.
The meaning of "time" (*kāla*) is self-evident and thus not explained separately;
however, because the nature of "matter" (*vastu*) is somewhat difficult to understand, it is explained in detail here.

According to the *Pañcavastuka-śāstra*, a further explanation of the meaning of "association" (*samprayoga*) states: furthermore, to have the same time, the same basis (*āśraya*), the same aspect (*ākāra*), the same object (*ālambana*), the same fruit (*phala*), the same outflow (*niṣyanda*), and the same maturation (*vipāka*)—this is the meaning of association.
Having already explained the mind and mental factors, as to what those [factors] are that reach [their objects],
the following section— the second major heading— clarifies the non-associated formations (*viprayukta-saṃskāra*). Within this, first,
there is a general indication of their names and number.
Second, the detailed citation and explanation;
third, the analysis by way of various categories.
This [section] is the first, which provides the general enumeration of names and numbers.

Connecting the preceding section and introducing the next: Question—According to the logical progression of the preceding text, one should here merely conclude the discussion on mental factors (*caitta-dharma*) and inquire about the dissociated formations (*viprayukta-saṃskāra*).

Why, then, is the mind (*citta*) also concluded here? Answer—it is because [the mind] was discussed within the analysis of the concomitant arising and alternative names of the category of mind (*citta-pakṣa*).
Because it also clarifies the mind, it is likewise categorized as "associated with the mind.

The verse says: "Up to those factors dissociated from mental formations (saṃskāra), they are dissociated from the mind. This distinguishes them from the mental factors (caitta). As for "mental formations," [it refers to] the formations dissociated from the mind.

This refers to the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*). It excludes matter (*rūpa*), mind (*citta*), and unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*), as they are not the aggregate of formations. Furthermore, it is explained as being dissociated from the mind (*cittaviprayukta*).
To distinguish the mental factors within the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*):
"formations" refers to the aggregate of formations,
thereby distinguishing it from matter (*rūpa*), feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), consciousness (*vijñāna*), and the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
Because they are not the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*):

the two meditative attainments—namely, the attainment of non-perception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*) and the attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*); the characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), namely the four characteristics; and so forth (*ādi*), which includes the inclusion of the group of phrases (*pada-kāya*) and the group of phonemes (*vyañjana-kāya*). Regarding "categories" (*jāti*): [it refers to] the categories of the aggregates, bases, and elements.
This means that the "categories" (*nikāya-sabhāga*) are themselves [the category of] acquisition (*prāpti*), and so forth.
Now, examining this treatise, there are only fourteen formations dissociated from mind (*citta-viprayukta-saṃskāra*).
However, according to the *Nyāyānusāra*, the nature of combination (*sāmagrī*) is added.
Therefore, the *Nyāyānusāra* (Treatise on Right Reasoning), fascicle 12, states:
"The term 'and so forth' includes the phrase-body (*padakāya*), the phoneme-body (*vyañjanakāya*), and the nature of their conjunction.
Since these two treatises thus state different positions, [the discrepancy remains].
It cannot be that both are [simultaneously] true.
To investigate this by means of a hypothetical dialogue between guest and host, the Abhidharmakośa master asks:
"How is this nature of conjunction (saṃyoga) to be known?"
The Master of Right Reasoning (Nyāyācārya) explains:
"Just as when a saṃgha is split, the nature of harmony is abandoned;
it is clearly known that [this nature] exists separately. The Master of Right Reasoning asks:
Regarding my established position that there exists a distinct intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) which you do not establish,
within what category of phenomena is it subsumed?
The masters of the *Abhidharmakośa* explain as follows:
This nature of combination is subsumed under the *sabhāgatā* (homogeneity). The Master of Right Reasoning (*Nyāyācārya*) objects, saying:
"Whenever one speaks of *sabhāgatā*, it must necessarily be obtained based upon a dharma.
Upon what dharma is this 'combination' obtained as its basis?"
The masters of the Abhidharmakośa explain:
it is obtained based on the precepts;
that is to say, at the time of receiving the precepts, one obtains two types of *sabhāgatā*.
1. The shared portion of communal harmony, which is relinquished at the time of schism in the Saṃgha;
2. The shared portion of the great precepts.
"Because the schism of the Saṃgha is not relinquished, as it constitutes a transgression of the precepts. The Master of Correct Reasoning further objects:
"If [the offense] is acquired based on the precepts..."
Since the precepts have not been relinquished at the time of schism,
how can one relinquish that shared portion with the harmonious community?
The masters of the *Abhidharmakośa* explain as follows:
All phenomena are indeterminate;
why must one necessarily obtain parity with another by depending upon that other?
For example, by means of the ten precepts, one obtains the status of a śrāmaṇera.
When receiving the full ordination (*upasaṃpadā*), one does not abandon the ten precepts,
yet one abandons the status (*sabhāgatā*) of a *śrāmaṇera*,
because one has acquired the status of a *bhikṣu*. The Master of the *Nyāyānusāra* further objects:
Who says that at the time of receiving the full ordination (*upasaṃpadā*), one abandons the homogeneous class (*sabhāgatā*) of a novice (*śrāmaṇera*)?
To cite this as an analogy here would be to rely on something that is not universally established.
The Abhidharmakośa master further retorted:
"If it were not abandoned,
then even a single person should be called a bhikṣu."
He is also called a *śramaṇera*.
The Master of Right Reasoning (*Nyāyācārya*) explains that the designation "bhikṣu" is established based on his predominant [quality].
Because they do not relinquish the homogeneous class (*nikāya-sabhāga*) of those who exert themselves in diligence,
just as within the body of the full precepts (*mahā-śīla*),
one also fulfills the ten precepts and is thus named a *bhikṣu*.
The Abhidharmakośa masters further cite a well-established analogy, saying:
"Just as one obtains the homogeneous status (*sabhāgatā*) of upholding precepts through the act of observing them,
even when encountering conditions for transgressing the precepts, one does not abandon that underlying essence of the precepts."

And since it has been abandoned, one loses the commonality (*sabhāgatā*) of upholding the precepts; this being fully established, it should not be rejected or denied. The Abhidharmakośa master further questions the Nyāya master, saying:
"You posit a nature of conjunction (*saṃyoga-svabhāva*)."
Furthermore, by relying on what dharma is this attained?
The Master of Right Reasoning (Nyāyācārya) explains:
"The nature of my integration is attained by relying upon the precepts."
The Abhidharmakośa master raises an objection, saying:
"If the precepts are not abandoned at the time of causing a schism in the Saṃgha, how can that harmony be abandoned? The Nyāyānusāra master explains:
Just as one acquires the commonality (sabhāgatā) of observing the precepts at the time of receiving them,
later, when one violates the precepts, it is not the case that one loses the commonality of observing the precepts;
rather, it remains identical to your own position regarding the commonality of harmony.
It is obtained by relying on the precepts;
it is not discarded simultaneously with the precepts. The Master of the *Abhidharmakośa* further raises an objection:
"At the time of schism in the Saṃgha, is the shared portion of harmony abandoned?"
The Master of Right Reasoning (Nyāyācārya) replies that it is abandoned. The Master of the Abhidharmakośa (Kośakāra) further objects:
"If, at the time of schism, the concordant portion is not abandoned, one might as well allow that the nature of concordance itself is abandoned separately."
Since, at the time of schism in the Saṃgha, one has already abandoned the homogeneous character (sabhāgatā) itself,
why would it be necessary to separately abandon the nature of harmony?
By this logical proof, we know that the nature of harmony is subsumed within the homogeneous character.
Regarding the nature of this conjunction (*saṃyoga*), various explanations differ;
therefore, it must be investigated.
This refers to the commonality of conjunction.
The school must necessarily admit that wherever there is a composite phenomenon (*saṃghāta*), there exists a corresponding factor of compositeness (*saṃghātatva*).
Therefore, it does not need to be sought separately. Question: Is the non-concordance of a schism in the Saṃgha (*saṃghabheda*) not subsumed under "non-acquisition" (*aprāpti*)?

What prevents the harmony of the Saṃgha from taking that [harmony] as its essence? The explanation says: Generally speaking, when one discusses "attainment" (prāpti), there must necessarily be something attained.

Since harmony has no distinct object of attainment, its essence cannot be subsumed under "attainment. Furthermore, another explanation states that all phenomena do not necessarily exist by way of mutual opposition.

For example, while one may use the ordinary to define the noble—the nature of the ordinary being both existent and non-existent—one cannot use the noble to define the ordinary, for the nature of the noble is exclusively existent.
Nevertheless, all noble dharmas are termed the "noble nature. If one follows the first chapter of the *Prakaraṇapāda*, [it states as follows].
Thirteen [categories] are the same as in the *Abhidharmakośa*;

however, it does not mention "non-possession" (*aprāpti*). Nevertheless, it separately explains "possession based on a support" (*āśraya-prāpti*), "possession of the entity" (*vastu-prāpti*), and "possession of the location" (*sthāna-prāpti*).
That treatise explains:
"What is meant by 'depending on acquisition'? It refers to depending on the basis of acquisition."
What is the acquisition of phenomena?
It refers to the acquisition of the aggregates (*skandha*).
What is the acquisition of bases (*āyatana*)?
That is to say, one attains the internal and external bases (*āyatana*). Furthermore, it is said:

"There are other such dharmas of this kind that are dissociated from the mind. This is found in the tenth fascicle of the *Dharmaskandhapāda-śāstra*, which corresponds to the *Prakaraṇapāda-śāstra*. If one follows the *Saṃyuktābhidharmahṛdaya-śāstra*:
Thirteen [points] are the same as in the *Abhidharmakośa*.
It does not mention "non-acquisition" (*aprāpti*),
but rather speaks of "the nature of an ordinary person" (*pṛthagjanatva*).
Question: Since the various treatises differ, how should they be reconciled? Answer:
It is explained that the *Prakaraṇapāda* states that acquisition (*prāpti*) is categorized according to the dharma as its basis (*āśraya*), object (*vastu*), and locus (*sthāna*).
One should understand that this is subsumed within [the category of] acquisition itself.
It is not said that non-acquisition (*aprāpti*) itself is further subsumed under other dissociated factors (*viprayukta-saṃskāra*);

rather, it is precisely what is included within "non-acquisition" as defined in this treatise. The *Saṃyuktābhidharmahṛdaya-śāstra* refers to it as "the nature of an ordinary person" (*pṛthagjanatva*).
It should be understood that this refers to not attaining even a small portion [of the result],
just as the mind of transformation is a small portion of the fruit of supernormal power (*abhijñā-phala*).
The *Miśraka-śāstra* briefly cites only one side of this.
This is not for the sake of exhausting [the entire] principle; furthermore, it is for the sake of correctly interpreting the word "category" (*jāti*) in the verse.
To say "category" (*jāti*) indicates that other dharmas which are conceptually constructed are of the same kind as those previously mentioned.

That is to say, there are those who conceptually construct that apart from acquisition (*prāpti*) and so forth, there exists a nature of acquisition and so forth belonging to the aggregates (*skandha*). The commentary explains: "other dharmas which are conceptually constructed."
This refers to those within the Sarvāstivāda school who,
in later generations, made improper and arbitrary speculations,
asserting that there exists a "possession of the aggregates" (skandha-prāpti) apart from [the primary] possession (prāpti) and so forth.
Acquisition by way of station, acquisition by way of realm,
and the nature of falling away, and so forth.
Now, it is shown that their respective positions are subsumed accordingly. If the Vaibhāṣika masters of the Abhidharmakośa offer this defense:
the term "similar" (jāti) indicates that these fourteen types belong to the same class.
Therefore, this does not reveal other [erroneous] views.

Within this, first distinguishing the two types of cessation—those that pertain to one's own continuum—the following section is the second part, which specifically cites and explains [the text]. This section contains seven parts.
First, the exposition of acquisition and non-acquisition;
second, the exposition of the homogeneous class;
third, the exposition of the state of non-conception.
The fourth explains the two meditative attainments;
the fifth explains the life-faculty;
the sixth explains the four characteristics.
Section Seven: Explaining Designations, etc. Regarding the first [section], the explanation of acquisition (*prāpti*) and non-acquisition (*aprāpti*), there are two parts:
first, explaining their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*); second, explaining their distinctions (*viśeṣa*). This [first part] explains the intrinsic nature.
The first two lines correctly set forth the essential nature (*lakṣaṇa*);
the latter two lines clarify the basis (*āśraya*).
The treatise states: "As for that which is contrary to this..."
Within the prose section,
there is first the direct explanation of the verse,
followed by an extensive series of questions and answers.
The following explains the verse;
specifically, it explains the first two lines. [It begins with] "Attainment."
"Attainment" and "accomplishment" have the same meaning, yet they are designated with distinct names based on different perspectives.
Therefore, in this text, "attainment" (prāpti) is spoken of collectively;
within it, however, distinct meanings are established as "acquisition" (lābha) and "possession" (samanvāgama).
That is to say, regarding any given dharma:
Never before attained, and having been attained, lost;
now for the first time both are attained.
This Dharma is attained at the highest level.
When [a dharma] first arises and is about to reach its state of manifestation, it is called "attained" (prāpta).
If it continues to flow into the present and, having been obtained, is not lost, it is called "accomplished" (samanvāgata).
At the moment of attainment, it is not yet called "accomplished."
At the time of accomplishment, it is not called "attainment.
Even if there were a textual passage stating that reaching the characteristic of arising (utpādānākṣaṇa) is called "accomplishment," regarding that attainment:
This is because it is explained as "attainment.
Even if there were a textual passage stating that reaching the present is called "acquisition," this is because that acquisition is spoken of within the context of attainment.
Thus, it should be understood that there is a distinction between acquisition (*prāpti*) and possession (*samanvāgama*).
If one has acquired a particular dharma, one necessarily possesses it.
Having reached the stage of the characteristic of arising,
because it is certain to flow into the present world,
there is the accomplishment of phenomena themselves, yet no acquisition [of them].

Just as with the delusions of view regarding the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, because they have been established since beginningless time, there is no initial acquisition [of them]. Question:
Within the state of being established, does the attainment of the characteristic of arising constitute "acquisition"?
Regarding "attainment by name" (nāma-siddhi): the commentary explains that because it is not newly acquired, it is not called "obtained" (pratilabdha);
because it has not yet reached the present, it is not called "possessed" (samanvāgata).
One may simply say that it is attained both before and after; the ancient masters all state that it is established according to the "New" and "Old" [traditions],
while the acquisition is based on the *New Treatise*.
It is not the case that all acquisitions (prāpti) are established as having establishment (siddhi), while some establishments are not acquisitions. This is not so.
The distinction between these two is explained in detail as previously stated:
the former text uses the term "attains" (得),
while the latter text uses the term "acquires" (獲).
One should know that although the names differ, the meaning is the same.
Non-acquisition (*aprāpti*) is the opposite of this;
that is to say, regarding any phenomenon (*dharma*).
Previously it was never lost;
even after having regained it once more,
it is only now that it is lost for the first time.
When this dharma’s non-acquisition first reaches the phase of arising (*jāti-lakṣaṇa*) and is about to become non-existent, it is termed "non-attainment" (*aprāpti*).
If it flows into the present, it is termed "non-possession" (*asamanvāgama*).
When there is no acquisition (*anupalabdhi*), it is not yet termed non-accomplishment (*asamanvāgama*);
when there is non-accomplishment, it is not termed non-acquisition.
Even if there were a scriptural statement that "non-acquisition, up to its reaching the characteristic of arising (*jāti-lakṣaṇa*), is called non-accomplishment," [it would still be incorrect].

Regarding the statement that "non-acquisition" (*aprāpti*) is explained within "non-possession" (*asamanvāgama*): even if there were a textual passage stating that what has not yet reached the present is called "non-acquisition," this is because "non-acquisition" is explained within the context of "non-possession."
It should be understood that regarding those dharmas,

when it is said that one "possesses" them, this necessarily implies "attainment" and "accomplishment"; [furthermore,] non-possession (aprāpti) extends up to the characteristic of birth (jāti-lakṣaṇa).
Because they are definitely flowing into the present,
there are certain dharmas that one does not yet possess and has not yet acquired,
such as the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpāda-jñāna*).

Because that knowledge has no beginning and is not attained [from the outset]. Question: Regarding the state of non-accomplishment, when non-attainment reaches the characteristic of arising (*jāti-lakṣaṇa*), is it termed "non-possession" (*aprāpti*)?
Regarding the phrase "not accomplished by name" (*asaṃprāpta-nāmaka*), the commentary explains:
It is not called "not obtained" (*anadhigata*) because it is not the initial non-acquisition (*aprāpti*);
it is not called "not accomplished" (*asamanvāgata*) because it has not yet reached the present.
It should be understood that one can only speak of "non-acquisition" (aprāpti) in terms of prior and subsequent;
herein, "attainment" (prāpti) and "non-attainment" (aprāpti) are to be known accordingly.
Regarding attainment (*prāpti*) and non-attainment (*aprāpti*), they first reach the characteristic of arising (*jāti-lakṣaṇa*).

Whether they are established or not is determined by attainment and non-attainment as they flow into the present, continuing through the succession [of moments] that have already passed; furthermore, this is according to the *Nyāyānusāra* (Treatise on Following Reasoning), fascicle 12.
To explain these four kinds of distinctions,
there are two types of attainment:
namely, that which was previously unattained.
Regarding that which has already been previously obtained: the acquisition of what was not previously obtained is called "attainment" (prāpti),
while the acquisition of what has already been previously obtained is called "possession" (samanvāgama).
It should be understood that non-acquisition (*aprāpti*) is the opposite of this:
namely, that which has not been previously acquired,
and that which was acquired but subsequently lost.
The non-acquisition of what has not yet been obtained is called "non-attainment" (*anadhigama*);
the loss of what has already been acquired is called "non-possession" (*asamanvāgama*).
Therefore, it is said that the nature of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva*) is the non-attainment of the noble dharmas (*āryadharma*). The commentary explains:
The intention of the *Nyāyabindu* is simply that what was previously unobtained is now for the first time called "attained."
That is to say, regarding the name "not having obtained" for dharmas not yet attained, it refers to non-attainment;
if they have already been attained previously,
even if one has since regressed and now reacquires them, [it is still considered attainment].
However, it is called "attainment" (samanvāgama) because it is acquired anew;
that is, the non-possession (aprāpti) of a dharma already lost is what is termed "non-attainment" (asamanvāgama).
If one understands the correct principle in this way, [there is no contradiction].
Thus, one attains [them]; there is the accomplishment and non-accomplishment of relinquishing.
These four propositions are mutually contradictory, yet they may be so.
That which is attained, acquired, and accomplished is essentially a single entity;
however, depending on the author of the treatise, it is adorned with various perspectives— whether broad or narrow—
and thus these cannot all be made identical by way of analogy.
"In which phenomena do acquisition (*prāpti*) and non-acquisition (*aprāpti*) exist?
This section below explains the latter half of the verse;
this is the introduction of the inquiry.
"Within one's own continuum and within the two types of cessation"—
this is the general answer,
which clarifies the bases upon which acquisition (*prāpti*) and non-acquisition (*aprāpti*) depend.
"Self-continuum" refers to one's own body.

"The two cessations" refer to analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) and non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*). This refers to the state where conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) reach a definitive certainty.
Below follows the detailed explanation.
Within the detailed explanation,
there are two types of bases:
first, the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*).
The second is the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*). This is a detailed explanation of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*);
that is to say, among conditioned phenomena:
If [a dharma] falls within one's own continuum, there exist possession (*prāpti*) and non-possession (*aprāpti*) regarding it;
however, these do not exist for the bodies of other continua, because one does not achieve the dharmas of another's body,
as they do not belong to oneself, and therefore such achievement is not established.
If one were to possess a body that constitutes the continuum of another,
there would be the destruction of the transition, the body, and the karma,
due to the fault of the confusion between self and other. That which is not a continuum refers to external non-sentient things.
Because it is not the internal continuum of the body,
it is said to be neither a continuum nor a non-continuum.
Because there is no such thing as accomplishing non-sentient phenomena;
they are not accomplished because they do not belong to a self.
If one were to accomplish non-sentient things, it would destroy the nature of reality (*dharmatā*).
Are they sentient beings?
Or are they non-sentient beings?
At any rate, conditioned phenomena are definitively thus.
Regarding the phrase "because they are established by reversing the ultimate characteristics within unconditioned phenomena":
this is a specific explanation of the unconditioned. Within the category of the unconditioned, [the following applies].
Only with respect to the two types of cessation are there possession (*prāpti*) and non-possession (*aprāpti*).
Regarding analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*), which is a dharma to be realized, there is both possession and non-possession.

Regarding non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*), which is the obstruction of the arising of dharmas, there is also both possession and non-possession. All that follows [is as stated above].
This establishes the two types of cessation.
Since there must necessarily be a deficiency of conditions for any given moment such that [a phenomenon] does not arise,
all sentient beings certainly achieve the non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) of untainted phenomena (*anāsrava*).
Having previously not yet abandoned the afflictions, one now first enters the state of an ārya;
at the stage of *duḥkha-dharma-jñāna-kṣānti*, one is called a "bound ārya" (*sakalabandhana-ārya*) in the first moment,
because within that person's continuum, the afflictions remain fully present.

Furthermore, ordinary beings who are bound by all fetters (*sakalabandhana*) and have not yet abandoned any of the two types of afflictions—those to be abandoned through seeing and those to be abandoned through cultivation—within the three realms do not achieve analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
With the exception of these two kinds [of persons], all other sentient beings certainly achieve analytical cessation. Below this point...
A separate explanation of space (*ākāśa*) states that it is neither attained (*prāpti*) nor non-attained (*aprāpti*).
Space is not something realized (*sākṣātkṛta*), unlike cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*);
nor is it a dharma that prevents the arising [of others], unlike cessation not through deliberation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
Therefore, there is neither attainment nor non-attainment.
As for the fact that those who possess attainments are not explained separately here, it is because,
when considered according to principle:
For all those who possess [attainment], there is likewise non-attainment;
this principle may be understood by analogy.
Therefore, in the preceding text, only the attainment of the two types of cessation was explained.
The two types of cessation and non-acquisition (aprāpti) are not explained separately.
On what grounds is it known that there exists a distinct entity called "acquisition" (prāpti)?
Below, this is addressed through an extensive dialogue.
"This is the question of the Sautrāntika master.
'Because it is stated in the sūtra,' up to 'and so forth at length,' is the response of the Sarvāstivāda master."
Citing authoritative scripture to prove that [the unconditioned] has a distinct substantial entity:

there are ten factors of one beyond training (*aśaikṣadharma*), namely, the eightfold noble path, along with right knowledge (*samyagjñāna*) and right liberation (*samyagvimukti*) as the fifth member.
That is to say, there are five fetters binding one to the higher realms;
by means of these, the noble ones, through birth, attainment, and possession, [abide] in those ten qualities of one beyond training (*aśaikṣadharma*).
"The five factors have already been severed," and so forth, as explained at length;
thus it is established by the Sūtra.
"If it is known that there is a separate real entity [of non-conceptual contact],
then if that were so, even the reaching of insentient things should be established"—
this is the objection from the Sautrāntika school.
Why is this so? Because the Sarvāstivādins cite the Sūtra;
as it is said in the Sūtra, and so forth, up to the full exposition.
The Sautrāntika school cites a sūtra to expose this error:
the sūtra states that a Wheel-Turning King possesses seven jewels;
if their possession were merely conventional, [the sūtra would be contradicted].
It may be said that [the merit] accomplishes other bodies and insentient things;
if you claim this to be true,
then among the seven treasures—
If it were established as wheels or jewels, there would be the fault that they are insentient (*asattva*).
If it were established as elephants, horses, women, the lord of the treasury, or the commander of the army, there would be the fault that they belong to the mental continuum of another.
Therefore, the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 93, in recounting the statement of the Dārṣṭāntikas, says:
Question: For what reason do they hold this view?
Answer: They hold this view based on the sūtras.
That is to say, the sūtras state that there are wheel-turning kings (cakravartin) who possess the seven jewels.
If the nature of possession were substantially existent,
then because of possessing the wheel-treasure and the jewel-treasure, the dharma-nature would be destroyed. Why is this so?
Because they are both sentient beings and yet not sentient beings,
and because they have perfected the elephant-treasure and the horse-treasure, they must again proceed toward destruction.
Why is this? Because they are both animals and humans.
Because he has attained the jewel of a woman, his body must again perish. Why is this?
For he was originally a male body.
Furthermore, because she is a woman’s body,
and because she has attained the status of a commander-in-chief and a minister of the treasury,
her karma must likewise be exhausted. Why is this so?
Because of the confusion between subject and object,
do not fall into this error; therefore,
the nature of accomplishment (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*) is certainly not substantially existent.
Regarding the phrase "herein, mastery consists in acting according to one's will," this refers to the Universal Monarch (cakravartin) according to the Sautrāntika school of the Sarvāstivāda.
Regarding those seven treasures, one possesses sovereign power over them and enjoys them according to one's pleasure;
based on this sovereignty, it is called "attainment."
It does not have a separate substantial entity.
Since this [entity] is sovereign, if one concludes that there must be a distinct thing,
the Sautrāntika school further objects.
Since this *Cakravartin-sūtra* states that mastery (*vaśitā*) is designated as "accomplishment" (*siddhi*),
by what cause is it known from other sūtras that accomplishment is a distinct entity?
What irrationality is there in admitting that it is a distinct entity?
The Sarvāstivādins further ask the Sautrāntikas:
"If you further admit that there is a distinct entity called 'possession' (prāpti),
what is unreasonable about this?"
"In this way, that which is unreasonable is established as being unreasonable.
This is the Sautrāntika refutation.
Thus far, the argument has been based on the authority of the sacred word (*āptavacana*).
Now, this is refuted by means of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) and inference (*anumāna*).
That is to say, the "acquisition" (*prāpti*) that is clung to has no essence that can be known.
Just as the five consciousnesses directly apprehend form, sound, and so forth,
and just as the knowledge of others' minds directly apprehends greed, hatred, and so on, it would be known that [the direct apprehension of objects by a single consciousness] is useless.
As with the eyes, ears, and so forth; that is to say,
because the eyes, ears, and so forth possess the functions of seeing, hearing, and so on,
one infers the existence of the sense-faculties such as the eye.
Since its apprehension is useless,
how can one know that it truly exists?
It cannot be known through either direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) or inference (*anumāna*).
Therefore, it is unreasonable to maintain that "attainment" (*prāpti*) is a distinct entity; such a view is illogical.
If it is argued that this attainment cannot be established according to the principles of reasoning:
The Sautrāntika school refutes this by saying:

If you claim that "possession" (prāpti) has an active function and serves as the cause for the arising of dharmas, then unconditioned phenomena (asaṃskṛta), which do not arise, would have to lack possession. Furthermore, if you maintain that possession is the cause for the arising of dharmas...
Regarding the dharmas thus attained:
at times they have not yet been attained,
and at times they have already been relinquished.
Whether it be the coming and going and shifting between the three realms and nine stages,
or the departure from defilement—
in all such phenomena, nothing is currently apprehended by him.

Furthermore, when [a dharma] subsequently arises, how could it arise? If you say that although there is no *prāpti* (possession) prior to its arising, there is nonetheless a simultaneous-arising *prāpti* that acts as the cause for its arising, then what function do the "great" and "small" types of *prāpti* perform?
Moreover, since non-sentient dharmas lack *prāpti*, [how could they arise?]

It should certainly not arise; furthermore, for an ordinary person bound by all fetters whose afflictions have not yet been abandoned, there exist nine grades of causes for the arising of afflictions. Since these causes for arising are equal, [the afflictions would necessarily arise].
There would be no distinction in the manifestation of afflictions as inferior, middling, or superior.
Why is this? Because there would be no distinction in their acquisition as causes for rebirth.
Since there is no distinction once [the state] has been attained,
one should not say that the manifestation of superior-grade greed constitutes being "one who acts with greed," while medium or inferior grades do not.
The same applies to hatred and the other [afflictions]. The intent of this objection is that,
