since the causes for their arising are equal,
it is impossible for the three grades [of intensity] to manifest differently.
If you attempt to defend this by saying that the manifestation of afflictions differs due to other causes, [we respond as follows].
In that case, phenomena would arise solely from those other causes;
what, then, would be the use of *prāpti*?
Therefore, it is untenable to maintain that *prāpti* functions as the cause for the arising of phenomena.
The reasoning is not established.
Who has said that this "acquisition" (*prāpti*) acts as a cause for the arising of dharmas?
The Sarvāstivādins offer this defense:
Who says that this "acquisition" (prāpti) acts as a generative cause for conditioned phenomena?
Yet you challenge me with this objection:
"If that is so, what function does this acquisition perform?"
The Sautrāntika school further challenges this by asking: "What is the cause for establishing these distinctions?
To which the Sarvāstivādins reply: "Why is that so?"
The Sautrāntika school further challenges:
"If there were no 'possession' (prāpti), how could distinctions be established?
The Sarvāstivāda school replies:
If there were "acquisition" (prāpti),
one could establish the distinction between the two types of individuals— ordinary beings and noble ones; if there were no acquisition,
[such a distinction would be impossible].
If both ordinary beings and noble ones were to give rise to mundane, out-flowing states of mind, there would be no distinction between the two types. [Objection:
Is it not the case that there must be a distinction because their afflictions differ?
The Sautrāntika school provides this explanation for the distinction:
"Is it not the case that those who have already severed the afflictions are called 'noble ones' (ārya), while those who have not severed them are called 'ordinary persons' (pṛthagjana)?"
Because there is a distinction,
there ought to be a distinction.
If you maintain that there is no attainment because one has either reached detachment or not yet reached it, [then this is incorrect].
The Sarvāstivādins raise an objection:
"We admit that there is 'acquisition' (prāpti), and that it constitutes what is 'abandoned' or 'not yet abandoned.
It is called 'abandoned' because one has become separated from the acquisition of the afflictions."
Because they have not yet been abandoned, they are said to be "not severed.
If one maintains that there is no such thing as "acquisition" (prāpti), how could it be said that afflictions are severed or not severed?
This [distinction] depends upon the state of the basis (āśraya) and is merely conventional, not real.
The Sautrāntika explanation is as follows:

"Severed" and "not yet severed" refer to the power of the path of antidotes (pratipakṣa-mārga), which renders the basis—the body—incapable of causing [the afflictions] to manifest again; this is what is termed "severance."
It is termed "not accomplished.
The opposite of this is termed "not severed" and is termed "accomplished."
If it is called "abandoned" because it is ultimately severed by the power of the noble path,
or if it is called "abandoned" because it is suppressed and subdued by the mundane path—
whether this [abandonment] is established or not, it is all conventional and not real.
In the past there was the seed of delusion;
now that it has been severed, it no longer exists, and is therefore called a transformation different from the original.
Regarding the statement that "there are two kinds of wholesome dharmas" up to "they are also provisional and not real": [this means that although they appear as real, they are ultimately empty].
The Sautrāntika position is more convenient.
Regarding the two types of wholesome states, their establishment or non-establishment,
and their abandonment or non-abandonment, it is established that innate wholesome states are acquired without relying on effortful cultivation.
There is that which is abandoned and that which is not yet abandoned; there is that which is accomplished and that which is not yet accomplished.
As for what is called "abandoned":
That is to say, by the power of wrong view,
one is able to damage the innate seeds of goodness within the body,
rendering them incapable of producing manifest wholesome states of mind.
It should be known that this refers to the abandonment of [defilements]. It is called "abandonment" not because they are ultimately destroyed so as to become non-existent altogether.
That which exists but is useless is called "diminished" (*hāni*).
At the time of diminution, it is termed "severed" (*ucchinna*) and "unestablished" (*asiddha*).

That which has not yet been diminished is termed "established" (*siddha*) and "not yet severed. Wholesome states of application (*prayoga-kuśala*) must be acquired through effort; they are either established or unestablished.
If, within the basis, those seeds of wholesome dharmas have already arisen,
the seeds of the wholesome increase and give rise to their actual manifestation.
When functional capacity is sovereign and its power is undiminished,
this aspect of sovereignty is termed "accomplishment" (siddhi);
that is precisely what is meant by the "sovereign accomplishment" (vaśitā-siddhi) of the Mahāyāna.
Even if those wholesome seeds exist previously,
if they have not yet arisen,

or if having arisen they have regressed and are no longer under one's control, this is called "non-accomplishment. Therefore, within the basis (āśraya), there is no distinct entity [called "possession"].
Since the Sautrāntika school has established its own tenet, it maintains that within the basis of the person there exist only seeds;
these seeds of the afflictions have neither been permanently uprooted by the Noble Path nor suppressed and diminished by the worldly path.
When one has not had the seeds of virtue destroyed or suppressed by wrong views and has acquired them,
and when the virtues of application increase and become autonomous,
at such a stage the designation "accomplishment" (niṣpanna) is established.
It is merely a designation and has no separate entity.
Since the previous debate established its substantial nature, it is now specifically concluded as being established. Regarding this, what dharma is called the "seed"?
This is the question posed by the Sarvāstivādins.
Regarding the statement that "name-and-form (nāmarūpa) possesses the capacity to produce its fruit," the Sautrāntika replies:
"As for 'name-and-form,' 'name' refers to the four aggregates."
"Form" refers to the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*).
According to that school, "name-and-form" (*nāmarūpa*) consists of both the seeds and the perfuming (*vāsanā*);
that is to say, within name-and-form, [these] produce their own results.
The uninterrupted succession of all seeds is called "transmission" (pāramparya).
That which is about to produce its own fruit is called "proximity" (sāmantaka).
The "proximate" (*samanantara*) refers to the taking of a fruit; that which takes the fruit immediately is called "efficacy" (*sāmarthya*),
which is the actual arising of efficacy.
These three are all synonyms for "seed.
This succession occurs because the seeds continue in a stream, thereby proceeding without interruption.
This is "proximate," because it is proximate to the fruit due to the transformation of the seed;
this is its functional capacity.
Due to the differentiation of seeds, they correctly give rise to functional capacity.
These three are also synonyms for "seed.
They explain the three aforementioned types in their respective order. Furthermore, this explains the fruit.
It arises due to the transformation and differentiation of the continuity of seeds.
What is called the second transformation?
It refers to the state within the continuity of seeds when they are about to produce a fruit.
Its seed undergoes transformation such that it becomes different from what it was before,
just as the substance of a seed transforms when it is about to produce a sprout.
What is called the "first continuity"?
That is to say, this seed is the cause in relation to what follows and the effect in relation to what precedes; therefore,
it can comprehensively encompass all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) across the three periods of time.
These are collectively termed "succession" (*saṃtati*). Within this text,
the reason why "transmission" (*pāramparya*) is explained first and "succession" is explained afterward is as follows:

Because the sequential progression is clarified by means of the continuity of the subtle [characteristics], and because the meaning is already explained through the preceding analysis, what need is there for a formal sequence?
What is called the third distinction? It refers to the capacity of the seed to produce its fruit immediately.
Because this subsequent seed-moment differs from the preceding seed-moment, it is called "differentiation" (*viśeṣa*).

According to the Sautrāntikas, because cause and effect differ in their temporal sequence, they speak of a "capacity to produce a fruit immediately" (*anantara-phala-dāna-śakti*). Furthermore, it is explained as "successive capacity" (*pāramparya-śakti*) and "proximate capacity" (*sāmantaka-śakti*).
This refers to the transformation of the continuum and the differentiation of the continuum.
By this, the transformation of the continuum constitutes the remote efficacy,
while the differentiation of the continuum constitutes the proximate efficacy.
However, as for the passages in some places stating that one who has reached [a certain stage] is necessarily unable to cultivate [the path],
the Sautrāntika school provides an interpretation of these sūtras. The reason they must interpret this scriptural passage is as follows:
The Sautrāntika school maintains that although one may possess the seeds of defiled phenomena,
it is still possible to cultivate wholesome states.
However, there is a sutra which states that if one is possessed of greed, one is unable to cultivate the four foundations of mindfulness;
the intention of that sutra is as follows:
One who is attached to and habitually practices greed is said to "possess" it because they cannot renounce the active manifestation of that greedy affliction;
this is due to the period during which the habitual practice of greedy attachment continues to manifest.
They will certainly be unable to cultivate the four foundations of mindfulness.
The Sūtra speaks of "attainment" based on actual manifestation;
thus, it says they are "unable to cultivate."
Based on seeds, I am able to cultivate all wholesome qualities;
therefore, the Abhidharma-śāstra states that there are three kinds of possession (*prāpti*).
First, the accomplishment of the seed;
second, the accomplishment of mastery;
third, the accomplishment of manifestation.
The Sautrāntika school agrees with them. Furthermore, this explains how they respond to the challenge posed by the Sarvāstivādins.
The intent of that challenge is as follows:
"If acquisition has no separate substantial entity..."
For what reason does the Sūtra state that if one is possessed of craving, one cannot cultivate the four foundations of mindfulness?

Since the Sūtra says that being possessed of craving means not cultivating the four foundations of mindfulness, it is clear that "possession" (prāpti) has a distinct substantial entity. The Sautrāntika replies:
However, as for the sutra statement that if one is possessed of greed, one cannot cultivate the four foundations of mindfulness,
the intention of that sutra is to say that those who are addicted to present greed are unable to feel weary of it and relinquish it; therefore, they are said to be "possessed" of it.
Due to being attached to and indulging in the present moment of craving,
one will certainly be unable to cultivate the four foundations of mindfulness;
this does not mean that there exists a separate ontological essence [of these foundations] apart from their accomplishment.
"Thus, even this 'attainment' (prāpti) is merely conventional and not real"—
this is the Sautrāntika's summary of how attainment is established.
Applying this as appropriate across all categories,
it is merely conventional and not real;
it is simply the negation of that [attainment] which is termed "non-attainment."
It is also provisional and not real.
As for the Vaibhāṣika masters who maintain that [the dharmas] are real and not provisional,
they are asserting the fundamental tenet of the Sarvāstivāda school.
Since both of these approaches are well-expounded,
the Master of the Treatise approves of both schools. Why is this so?
I address the Proponent:
In principle, two positions cannot both be correct;
one must necessarily be incorrect.
Regarding the statement, "How is it that all words of praise are well-spoken?
Because they do not contradict reason and because they are what we ourselves accept," this is the Master of the Treatise’s explanation.
The Sautrāntika school asserts that [the designation of] the conventional does not contradict reason;
furthermore, since my own school, the Sarvāstivāda, asserts [the existence of] the real,
the Master’s intention was to side with the Sautrāntikas, and thus he provided this interpretation.
Having already analyzed their intrinsic nature (svabhāva), one should now analyze their acquisition (prāpti).
Below this is the second section, which clarifies their distinctions. Within this:
First, the distinction of acquisition (prāpti) is clarified;
second, the distinction of non-acquisition (aprāpti) is clarified.
Regarding the first, the clarification of the distinction of acquisition:
First, the formal exposition of the distinctions;
second, the detailed explanation according to specific inquiries.
Herein begins the first: the formal exposition of the distinctions.
The inquiry begins with the intent to clarify.
Within this inquiry, there is first a general overview.
There are two distinctions.
This is the general inquiry.
For now, one should analyze that which is attained.
This constitutes a specific inquiry.
The verse states: "Up to those not to be abandoned, there are two kinds.
This is the response provided within the verse.
The first line concerns the gate of the three periods of time;
the second line concerns the gate of the three natures;
the third and fourth lines concern the gates of being bound and not being bound.
The fifth phrase concerns the gate of the three trainings (*triśikṣā*);
the sixth phrase concerns the gate of the three abandonments (*trityāga*).
In this present passage, the specific means of attainment are explained in relation to the dharmas attained.
The Commentary says: "Up to 'each has three acquisitions' [refers to] the section on the analysis of the three time periods.
Regarding past phenomena having past acquisitions:"
They may be prior to the dharma, subsequent to the dharma, or simultaneous with the dharma.
Those acquisitions that are present or future are all subsequent to the dharma;
even though, from a transverse perspective across time, they are all subsequent to the dharma.
If one considers the sequence of the arising and functioning [of dharmas],
there are also prior acquisitions of those dharmas in the future;
that is to say, future dharmas may possess acquisitions belonging to the past or the present.
All these exist prior to the dharma.
There are those future acquisitions that may be prior to the dharma, subsequent to the dharma, or simultaneous with the dharma.
Although there is no sequential order of "prior" and "subsequent" within the future itself, [these distinctions still apply].

The preceding and succeeding [distinctions] are explained in terms of the categories of acquisition (*prāpti*) and the capacity for the arising of function. Regarding present dharmas that possess past acquisition, they exist only prior to the dharma;
regarding those that possess future acquisition, they exist only subsequent to the dharma.
According to the worldly perspective, although [the acquisition] occurs only after the dharma,
from the perspective of the sequence of the arising of its function,
there is also the prior acquisition of that dharma in the future.
Regarding those that are acquired in the present, they are acquired only simultaneously with the dharma itself.

This statement is made provisionally based on the sense of what is possible; their specific distinctions shall be further analyzed later. According to the *Abhidharmamahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 158:
There are four types [of conditions] that can obtain:
first, those prior to that dharma;
second, those subsequent to that dharma.
Third, it is simultaneous with that dharma;
fourth, it is not prior to, subsequent to, or simultaneous with that dharma.
As for the dharmas that are acquired, there are six kinds.
First, for those dharmas that are acquired, there is only simultaneous acquisition (*sahapratilambha*),
such as those born of maturation (*vipākaja*) and so forth.
Second, for those dharmas that are acquired, there is only prior acquisition (*pūrvapratilambha*).
As in the case of the three types of conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*) at the limit [of the path],

some say that these also possess both simultaneous attainment (*sahapratilambha*) and subsequent attainment (*pṛṣṭhalabdha*). Regarding the three categories of acquired phenomena (*pratilabdhadharma*), there is only simultaneous attainment and subsequent attainment.
As with the prātimokṣa vows and so forth,

for the four types of dharmas involving apprehension, there is only simultaneous acquisition (*sahapratilambha*) and prior acquisition (*pūrvapratilambha*), such as in the case of the patience regarding the subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārgānvayakṣānti*) and others.

5. Phenomena that possess obtainment (prāpti) have obtainment prior to, subsequent to, or simultaneous with themselves, as is the case with other phenomena such as the wholesome (*kuśala*) and the defiled (*kliṣṭa*).
6. Regarding phenomena that possess obtainment, it cannot be said that they have obtainment prior to, subsequent to, or simultaneous with themselves, yet they do indeed possess various obtainments.

This refers to cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) and cessation not through deliberation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*). There is no dharma that can be acquired only after the dharma itself has already arisen;

for at the very moment it manifests, its acquisition (*prāpti*) must necessarily exist. The commentary explains: this includes those born of maturation (*vipākaja*) and other neutral (*avyākṛta*) dharmas.
Regarding conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*) and the factors associated with it,
since this knowledge ultimately does not arise,
there is no dharma that co-exists with it, nor any that follows after it.
Some say that there is also simultaneous acquisition [of both],
which should be included in the fourth category:
namely, the prātimokṣa vows and so forth, together with the remaining unwholesome vows and so forth.

Regarding the dharmas associated with the *mārga-anvaya-kṣānti* and so forth: Question: How can there be "attainment prior to the dharma" (*dharmapūrvaprāpti*) for the present *mārga-anvaya-kṣānti*? Answer: It is explained that [this refers to] the present *mārga-anvaya-kṣānti*.
Although there is only simultaneous acquisition (*sahapratilambha*) with the dharma,
the future *dharmajñānakṣānti* also possesses prior acquisition (*pūrvapratilambha*) of the dharma;
it is said to possess prior acquisition because this is stated in reference to the category of *kṣānti*.
This is because the dharmas obtained are explained according to their categories. Furthermore, regarding the present *mārga-anvaya-kṣānti*,
although at this moment there is only the simultaneous acquisition (*sahajā-prāpti*) with the dharma,
if it does not manifest, there is also the prior acquisition (*pūrvaprāpti*) of the dharma.

According to one interpretation, it may be said that there is an acquisition prior to the dharma; furthermore, another explanation holds that, regarding the patience of the subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārgānvayajñānakṣānti*), when considered in terms of time, there is only an acquisition simultaneous with the dharma (*dharmasahaja-prāpti*) and no acquisition prior to the dharma.
Because this present patience (kṣānti) has the acquisition (prāpti) of future dharmas prior to itself,
it is also called "having the acquisition of dharmas prior to them. This is the acquisition of those future [dharmas].
From the perspective of conventional worldly convention, although it actually exists subsequent to the patience regarding the present,
it is called "attained prior to the dharma" and not "attained subsequent to the dharma," because this attainment does not arise immediately [after that realization].
Its arising must necessarily occur prior to that patience (*kṣānti*).
This is because, regarding the acquisition of the acquisition (*prāptiprāpti*), one speaks of its arising before, after, or simultaneously in terms of its potential to function.
Consequently, present patience also possesses a prior acquisition.
Furthermore, regarding the three types of acquisition (*prāpti*) for wholesome and other dharmas up to the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*):
this is the section on the classification by way of the three natures.
Although these acquisitions are largely determined as being of a specific nature based on the dharmas they acquire.
Within this, there is not a lack of some slight distinction;
thus, the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 158, asks:
"For what reason are the nature and category of the attainment (*prāpti*) and the dharma attained (*prāpya-dharma*) sometimes the same and sometimes different?"
Answer: There are three kinds of acquisition (prāpti):
first, the acquisition of conditioned phenomena (saṃskṛtadharma); second, the acquisition of analytical cessation (pratisaṃkhyānirodha).

Third, there is the acquisition of non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyānirodha*). The acquisition of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*) varies according to the specific nature and category of the phenomenon acquired,
because conditioned phenomena possess the functional capacity to induce their own acquisition.
The attainment of cessation through deliberation (pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha) follows the distinctions in the nature and category of the path by which it is attained;
for cessation through deliberation itself possesses no functional activity,
but rather exists simply because that [cessation] is realized at the time when the power of the path exerts its effort.
Because it brings about the acquisition of that [non-analytical cessation], the acquisition of non-analytical cessation follows the specific distinctions of the nature and category of its own basis;
for non-analytical cessation itself possesses no functional activity.
It is not sought by means of the path,
because its manifestation depends solely upon the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) and the homogeneous class (*nikāyasabhāga*).
Furthermore, there are four types of acquisition (*prāpti*) for bound phenomena (*saṃyuktadharma*).
The section on the distinction between being bound and not being bound:
If one acquires dharmas bound to the three realms,
those acquired dharmas in turn belong to the three realms.
Conditioned phenomena are determined by their nature according to the acquisitions (prāpti) of those phenomena they obtain.
If it is an acquisition of an outflow-free, unconditioned phenomenon,
it pertains to both that which is bound to the three realms and that which is unconditioned.
The general characteristics are thus; as for the detailed classification:
all unconditioned dharmas comprise three categories in total. The first is cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
Second is non-analytical cessation (apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha). Third is the truth of the path (mārga-satya).
If non-analytical cessation is acquired, it can pertain to all three realms of existence.
Whichever realm the body belongs to,
the non-analytical cessation (apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha) obtained therein is bound to that same realm; for its nature is determined according to its basis.
If the acquisition of analytical cessation is determined by the nature of the path that realizes it,
then that which is induced by a contaminated path belongs to the realms of form and formlessness.
Because there is no path capable of severing [defilements] within the desire realm;
furthermore, that which is induced by the untainted path (anāsrava-mārga) is itself unconditioned (apratisaṃyukta).
Regarding "clouds" and the "untainted":
if the acquisition of the Truth of the Path is exclusively untainted,
it is unconditioned by the realms.
The Path is conditioned (*saṃskṛta*).
Because the nature of a dharma is determined by the attainment (*prāpti*) of that dharma which is acquired,
the attainment of unconditioned dharmas (*apratisaṃyukta-dharma*) pertains to all three realms and consists of four types of non-bondage.
Furthermore, there are those who attain the dharmas of training (śaikṣa) and are immediately non-trainees (aśaikṣa).
This is the section on the distinction between the three types of training.
The dharmas of training and non-training are conditioned (saṃskṛta).
The attainment of these factors—

whether they be those of training (*śaikṣa*), those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), or those that are neither training nor beyond training (*naivaśaikṣanāśaikṣa*)— is distinguished according to what has been attained.
However, if stated generally, they are common to all three trainings.
If distinguished separately,
all contaminated phenomena (*sāsrava*) and the three unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*) are neither-learner-nor-non-learner (*naivaśaikṣanāśaikṣa*).
Furthermore, contaminated phenomena (*sāsravadharma*) possess only acquisitions that are neither-learner-nor-non-learner (*naivaśaikṣanāśaikṣa*).
This is because the acquisition of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*) is determined according to the phenomenon acquired;
however, the acquisition of cessation not through deliberation (*apratisaṃkhyānirodha*) is determined according to its basis (*āśraya*).
If the acquisition (*prāpti*) of cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṃkhyānirodha*) induced by the noble path is categorized according to the path that realizes it,
then because they are all contaminated (*sāsrava*), they are both neither-learner-nor-non-learner (*naivaśaikṣanāśaikṣa*). If, however,
it is the acquisition of cessation through deliberation induced by the learner’s path (*śaikṣamārga*), then it is a learner’s acquisition (*śaikṣa*).
Because the path capable of realization is that of one in training (śaikṣa),
when the faculties are transformed during the path of no-more-learning (aśaikṣa),
the acquisition of the analytical cessation (pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha) thus induced is itself of no-more-learning.

Because the path capable of realization is that of one beyond training (aśaikṣa). Question: By means of both contaminated and uncontaminated paths, the practitioner of training (śaikṣa) is able to abandon the afflictions of cultivation belonging to the eight stages from the Sphere of Nothingness downward.
Whichever path is employed,
each is capable of inducing the acquisition of two types of dissociation (*visamyoga-prāpti*). Since they mutually induce one another, [the paths are established].
How is the nature [of the faculties] determined according to the path? The explanation says:
although the untainted path (*anāsrava-mārga*), which abandons delusions, can also induce tainted acquisitions (*sāsrava-prāpti*), it is the tainted path that abandons delusions.
Although it can also induce uncontaminated attainment (*anāsrava-prāpti*),
it does not do so directly; rather,
it induces it only incidentally.
Therefore, their nature is not determined by following both paths interchangeably,
but rather by following their own respective path;
even if that path capable of realization does not arise.
Nevertheless, they are cultivated reciprocally;

yet, because the analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) arises through the power of that [cultivation], each is classified according to the path by which it is realized. Question: Why does the verse state only "neither-learner-nor-non-learner" (*naivaśaikṣanāśaikṣa*)?
Why does the prose (*gadya*) fully explain the three trainings (*tri-śikṣā*)? The explanation says: because the verses (*kārikā*) are concise, they discuss only one type;

because the prose is expansive, it fully explains all three. Furthermore, another explanation states that it refers to acquisitions that are neither-learner-nor-non-learner (*naivaśaikṣanāśaikṣa-prāpti*).
There is a distinction;
because it encompasses all three trainings, it is specifically designated as such.
The attainments (*prāpti*) of those in training (*śaikṣa*) and those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) each consist of only one kind.
Because there is no great distinction [between them], they are not explained separately; alternatively, by mentioning the latter, the former is implied.

Furthermore, the statement that "that which is reached through seeing and cultivation is all non-abandonable" constitutes the section on the classification of the three types of abandonment (*prahāṇa*).
The entities of the dharmas abandoned through seeing and cultivation are conditioned;
the acquisitions that correspond to them are likewise abandoned through seeing and cultivation.
All untainted (anāsrava) dharmas are termed "not to be abandoned" (aheya).
There are distinctions to be found.
Generally speaking, there are two types:
those abandoned through cultivation (bhāvanā-heya).
Alternatively, it may not be something to be abandoned.
If one analyzes them individually, the acquisition (*prāpti*) of non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) is abandoned solely by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*),
because it follows the nature of its basis (*āśraya*), which is abandoned by cultivation.
If there is an acquisition of analytical cessation induced by a contaminated path,
it is also abandoned solely through cultivation,
because it conforms to the path that realizes it, which is itself abandoned through cultivation.
If it is the acquisition of analytical cessation induced by the untainted path,
it is called "not to be abandoned" because it follows the nature of the untainted path that realizes it.
If it is the acquisition of the Truth of the Path, since the path is conditioned (*saṃskṛta*), [it is not to be abandoned].

That which is acquired in accordance with its attainment and is likewise untainted (anāsrava) is called "not to be abandoned" (aheya). Question: The verse only clarifies that which is not to be abandoned;
for what reason does the prose commentary clarify all three types of abandonment? Answer: It is said that the verse is concise and provides specific designations.
Alternatively, because it pertains to both types of abandonment, it is explained separately;
or, by mentioning the latter, the former is implied.
Although it was stated previously in general terms that [the attainment] does not arise prior to the desire or form realms, [it is here specified].
The following is the second section: a detailed explanation according to specific questions.
A verse is posed as a question and answered by the treatise, which states: "Acquisition (*prāpti*) is also present."
This explains the first phrase.
Regarding the question, "Is it the case that all unobscured [phenomena] are likewise?"—
this is an inquiry.
If it is not so, [the questioner] asks:
"In what way? [The respondent] answers.
Question:
This excludes those who have attained the supernormal powers of the eye and ear, as well as their co-arising acquisitions (*prāpti*). Explanation: [End of section].
This explains the second phrase: namely,
the two types of supernormal knowledge (*abhijñā*) and the four aggregates that arise simultaneously with the mind capable of transformation (*nirmāṇa-citta*),
because their power is particularly strong.
Because it is accomplished through the distinction of preparatory application (*prayoga*),
although it is neutral (*avyākṛta*), it possesses acquisitions (*prāpti*) that arise prior to, subsequent to, and simultaneously with it.
If it were also admitted that the same applies to the acquisition of the arts and crafts (*śailpasthānika*), [it would lead to the following consequence].
The sphere of craftsmanship has visible form, sound, odor, taste, and tangible objects as its essence.
The sphere of deportment has visible form, odor, taste, and tangible objects as its essence.
This mentions the basis in order to reveal the four aggregates that depend upon it;
thus, the *Vibhāṣā*, fascicle 126, states:
"As for the sphere of crafts..."
That is to say, its substance consists of the five bases of visible forms, sounds, odors, tastes, and tangibles.

That which arises from the sphere of craftsmanship (śailpasthānika) has as its substance the two bases of mental objects (dharma-āyatana) and mind (manas). Furthermore, it is said that the path of deportment (airyāpathika) [is also included].
This means that its substance consists of the four bases (āyatana) of visible form, odor, taste, and tangibility.

That which arises as the path of deportment (airyāpathika) has the two bases of mind and mental objects (dharmāyatana) as its substance. Furthermore, it should be explained that there are also minds of the sphere of craftsmanship (śailpasthānika) and minds of the path of deportment.

The mind is not mentioned here, being omitted for brevity. Furthermore, another interpretation states that the mind is the basis for deportment (*īryāpatha*) and craftsmanship (*śilpa*), and is thus called the "place" (*sthāna*) or the "path of names" (*nāmapatha*).
If one adopts this interpretation, it contradicts the *Abhidharmamahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*.

If one has practiced to the utmost the four aggregates of the spheres of craftsmanship (*śailpasthānika*) and the modes of deportment (*airyāpathika*), there is likewise the attainment of them in the past, future, and present;
except for those specifically excluded above, there is attainment across the three time periods.
Furthermore, all other resultant aggregates of the five skandhas, as well as the aggregates of bodily postures, crafts, and supernormal powers;
and a portion of the four aggregates associated with bodily postures, crafts, and supernormal powers.

Furthermore, those that are neutral by nature (*avyākṛta-svabhāva*) and a portion of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) possess only acquisition coexistent with the dharma (*dharma-sahaja-prāpti*). Therefore,
the *Nyāyānusāra* (Treatise on the Principles of Correct Reasoning), fascicle 12, states:

Furthermore, the acquisition of the four aggregates belonging to the sphere of deportment (*airyāpathika*) is for the most part severed by the world (*bhavaccheda*) and severed moment by moment (*kṣaṇaccheda*),
with the sole exception of the Buddhas, the Bhikṣu Aśvajit, and others who have well-practiced the sphere of deportment.

If it is the acquisition (*prāpti*) of the four aggregates belonging to the sphere of the arts (*śailpasthānika*), it is also for the most part severed by the world (*loka-vicchinna*) and severed moment by moment (*kṣaṇa-vicchinna*), with the exception of the deity Viśvakarman and others who have well-practiced the sphere of the arts. [Question: What about the four aggregates belonging to the sphere of deportment (*airyāpathika*) in the form realm?

There are three types of acquisition across the three periods of time. The commentary explains that in that realm, because it is not extremely habituated, there is no acquisition across the three periods of time.
Furthermore, the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 157, explains regarding the desire realm:
Regarding the four aggregates of the sphere of deportment (*airyāpathika*),
those who are well-practiced are such as the Buddha, Aśvajit, and other sentient beings who have become well-practiced.
Furthermore, regarding those who are well-practiced in the four aggregates of the arts and crafts,
it is as with the Buddha, the Devaputra Viśvakarman, and other sentient beings who have attained such mastery through thorough cultivation.
That acquisition (*prāpti*) is also both temporally mixed (*adhva-saṃkīrṇa*) and momentary mixed (*kṣaṇa-saṃkīrṇa*),
because for each [dharma] belonging to the three time periods, there exists an acquisition belonging to all three time periods.

Furthermore, the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* explains regarding the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) that it consists of all obscured-unspecified (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*) and unobscured-unspecified (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*) aggregates of form, as well as the four aggregates of deportment (*airyāpathika*) and maturation (*vipāka*).
That world is not intermingled with others;
it is not intermingled even for a single moment.
This is because, wherever that world exists, one attains only that very world.
According to the *Vibhāṣā*,
within the desire realm,
one specifically excludes those who are highly practiced in the deportments (*airyāpathika*) and the arts (*śailpasthānika*).
There is acquisition across the three time periods.
Within the form realm (*rūpadhātu*),
there is no separate distinction regarding the modes of deportment (*airyāpathika*) concerning acquisition across the three time periods.

It is known that the four aggregates of deportment in the form realm have no acquisition (prāpti) across the three periods of time. Question: If one is unpracticed in the paths of deportment or the arts and crafts, there is no prior or subsequent acquisition.
For what reason does the *Vijñānakāya-pāda-śāstra* state that when one accomplishes a wholesome mind or an unwholesome mind of the desire realm,

it is said in both cases that one necessarily accomplishes an unobscured-neutral mind (*anivṛtāvyākṛta-citta*) of the desire realm? Since that treatise states that it is "necessarily accomplished" (*niyata-siddha*), [how can this be reconciled with the claim that such minds are not necessarily present]?
This refers to one who is newly born into the desire realm;
such a person necessarily possesses two types of indeterminate minds (*avyākṛta-citta*).

How, then, can it be said that for one who has not practiced them, there is no acquisition (*prāpti*) across the three periods of time? The explanation is that the intended meaning of these treatises differs.

It is difficult to provide a comprehensive explanation. Furthermore, when interpreting this treatise, as well as the *Nyāyānusāra*, the *Mahāvibhāṣā*, and the *Saṃyuktābhidharmahṛdaya*, one must also take into account those who have not yet become habituated to these teachings;
for this reason, there are cases where [certain factors] are not fully accomplished.
The "body of consciousness" (vijñānakāya) refers exclusively to that which is habituated;
therefore, it is said to be "accomplished.
Each [term] relies on a single specific meaning, and thus they do not contradict one another.

Regarding the subsequent attainment (*pṛṣṭhalabdha*), it shall be further analyzed later. As for the four aggregates of the *airyāpathika* (postures) and *śailpasthānika* (arts and crafts), if they have been thoroughly practiced, their acquisition (*prāpti*) pertains to all three time periods.

Why does the verse not distinguish [all supernormal powers], but only distinguishes the two types of supernormal powers (abhijñā) and the power of transformation (nirmāṇa)? The commentary explains: because these two—the supernormal powers and the power of transformation—are accomplished through meditative concentration (samādhi), they are distinguished separately.
Because deportment (*airyāpathika*) and craftsmanship (*śailpasthānika*) are indeterminate (*aniyata*), they are not specifically designated.
[The question is: "Is it only the unobscured-neutral (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*) that arises simultaneously? This is the inquiry.
If it is not so, the answer is: how so?
Question: Regarding the statement that "the acquisition of the obscured-unspecified (nivṛtāvyākṛta) dharmas occurs both before and after [the dharma itself]," this is the explanation.
Explaining the third phrase:
it refers exclusively to the afflictions to be abandoned through cultivation within the first dhyāna of the form realm.
One produces obscured-unspecified bodily and vocal informative matter (*vijñapti-rūpa*).
Its acquisition (*prāpti*) is also as previously described, occurring only simultaneously (*sahaja*).
Although there may be superior-grade afflictions (*kleśa*), [the acquisition is still simultaneous].
Furthermore, because it cannot produce non-informative [matter] (*avijñapti*),
its power is weak; for this reason,
there is certainly no preceding or subsequent attainment (*prāpti*).
Alternatively, although there may be manifest karma (*vijñapti-karman*) of the highest degree,
it should be understood that for all obscured-unspecified (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*) four aggregates (*catuḥ-skandha*),
there are acquisitions (*prāpti*) belonging to the three time periods.
The mind is stronger than form,
and because it is capable of initiating [action], it obtains [the fruits] across the three periods of time;
form is inferior to the mind.
Furthermore, because it is that which is produced [by the mind], it is necessarily simultaneous with the mental factors (*dharma*); therefore, this matter belongs only to the first dhyāna.

This is because, in the desire realm, the two views—the view of self-existence (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*)—when they are obscured-unspecified (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*), are incapable of producing karma.
From the second dhyāna upward, [the mind] is not associated with vitarka and vicāra, nor does it initiate karma. As for the question:
"Is there also a difference regarding the fact that they are indeterminate (avyākṛta) dharmas? [The answer follows: There is indeed a difference.
Question:
Is there also [that which] exists?
Answer: Yes.
"What is it? This is the inquiry.
It refers to those acquisitions (*prāpti*) that are bound to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*), as well as those that arise subsequently (*paścāt-kṣaṇika*).
Explanation:
This explains the fourth phrase,
referring to the wholesome and unwholesome manifest and non-manifest matter (vijñapti-avijñapti-rūpa) bound to the desire realm.
Because these are informative (*vijñapti*), they arise simultaneously with the dharma and are acquired subsequent to the dharma.
Since they do not coexist with the mind, they are not acquired prior to the dharma. Question: Regarding the wholesome bodily and vocal intimation (*vijñapti*) of the first dhyāna...
Furthermore, there are only the simultaneous attainment (*sahābhiprāpti*) and the subsequent attainment (*pṛṣṭhalabdha*).
Why, then, are these not explained separately in both the verse and the prose commentary? The explanation says: taken collectively as a whole.
The acquisition of wholesome form in the realm of form is indeterminate.
If it is the wholesome manifest action of the first dhyāna,
there is both simultaneous acquisition and subsequent acquisition.
If the morality that follows the mind were to be acquired across the three periods of time,
it would not be discussed here at length because it is indeterminate; rather,
the wholesome form of the desire realm is specifically designated because it is determinate.
It should be understood that, excluding the wholesome and unwholesome form of the desire realm,
as well as the wholesome manifest form of the first dhyāna,
all remaining unwholesome four aggregates [constitute this category].
And all other wholesome five aggregates; that is to say,
the four wholesome aggregates— both with-outflows (sāsrava) and without-outflows (anāsrava)—
as well as the aggregate of form (rūpa-skandha) that is wholesome through meditative concentration (samādhi) following the mind.
"If all [dharmas] have acquisitions (*prāpti*) belonging to the three time periods,
is non-acquisition (*aprāpti*) not similar to acquisition in its categories of attainment?
This section below is the second, which clarifies the distinctions of non-acquisition.
The questioner asks for clarification.
If it were not so, the answer would be as follows.
What does this mean?
It is an inquiry.
The verse says: "Regarding the attainment of dharmas, changing stages, and relinquishing."
Commentary:
The first phrase of the verse concerns the gate of the three natures (*trisvabhāva*);
the second phrase concerns the gate of the three time periods (*tryadhvan*).

The third phrase concerns the gate of the realms of existence (*dhātu-bandhana*), while the final phrase clarifies the gate of relinquishment (*prahāṇa*). In this present text, the distinctions of non-acquisition (*aprāpti*) are explained with reference to the dharmas that are not acquired.
This follows the same principle as that applied within the category of acquisition (*prāpti*).
There should likewise be a threefold classification of the three trainings and the three abandonments;
for since the first phrase states that it is not the attainment of pure indeterminate [states],
it is clearly understood to be exclusively neither-trainee-nor-non-trainee (naivaśaikṣanāśaikṣa).
The meaning regarding those abandoned through cultivation alone can be understood by analogy;
therefore, they are not mentioned separately.
The treatise says: "As for being included within the indeterminate nature (*avyākṛta*)."
Regarding the classification by way of the three natures:
all non-acquisitions (*aprāpti*) are non-obscured neutral (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*).
This is because all non-acquisitions follow the nature of the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) and the homogeneous class (*nikāyasabhāga*), which are neutral in nature.
Therefore, the *Vibhāṣā* (158) states: Question:
To which category of nature does non-acquisition (*aprāpti*) correspond?
Answer: It certainly does not correspond to the specific nature of the dharma that has not been acquired.
Because they are contradictory,
and furthermore, they do not conform to the Path,
as they are not what is sought by the Path.
It functions solely in dependence on the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) and the homogeneous class (*nikāyasabhāga*).
Therefore, it varies according to the specific nature of its basis.
[Question: If such is the case regarding all non-attainments (*aprāpti*),...
Regarding the acquisition of non-analytical cessation, it follows the nature of its basis;
that basis is either of the nature of maturation (*vipāka*) or exclusively of the nature of outflow (*niṣyanda*).
Regarding which of these two categories they belong to,
the answer is that they follow the nature of outflow (niṣyanda),
because their meaning is all-pervasive.
Because maturation (*vipāka*) is not universal, it is not established accordingly.
Question: If non-acquisition (*aprāpti*) were to follow the nature and category of the specific dharma that has not been acquired, what fault would there be?
Answer: One who has severed the roots of goodness should possess wholesome states;
one who is already free from the defilement of desire should possess unwholesome states;
and all those who are beyond training (aśaikṣa) should possess defiled states.
Ordinary beings would consequently possess the untainted dharmas of the three vehicles;
those who have fallen from a fruit would become those who have attained a fruit; and those who have abandoned the path of approach would become those who have entered that path.
The non-acquisition (*aprāpti*) of the two cessations (*nirodha*) would consequently have to be unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*). Due to such faults,
it is not possible for non-acquisition to differ according to the specific nature of the entity that has not been acquired.
Regarding the distinction of time, up to "non-acquisition (*aprāpti*) of the three times":
this is the section on the classification by the three times.
There is non-acquisition of past dharmas that belongs to the past.
That is to say, whether it occurs prior to a phenomenon,
subsequent to a phenomenon,
or at the present moment while both are together in the past, it is collectively termed "past non-acquisition" (atīta-aprāpti).
There are cases where non-acquisition (*aprāpti*) exists in both the present and the future;
these are all non-acquisitions that follow after the dharma.
Although, from a trans-temporal perspective, they are all subsequent to the dharma, [they are distinguished by their temporal status].

If one bases this on the sequence of the arising and functioning [of dharmas], then even in the future there exists that prior non-acquisition (aprāpti) of those dharmas. Regarding the existence of a future non-acquisition for a future dharma:
it refers to whichever dharma is prior and whichever dharma is subsequent.
At present, those that coexist in the future are collectively termed "future non-acquisition" (*aprāpti*).
Although these future states have not yet established a sequence of priority or posteriority, they are categorized according to their distinct intrinsic natures (*dharmatā*).
The sequence of before and after is spoken of in terms of the capacity to give rise to function.
There are those who possess non-acquisition (aprāpti) of the past and present.

That is to say: for all dharmas, there is non-acquisition prior to their arising; as for present dharmas, there is non-acquisition of past [dharmas], but there is only non-acquisition prior to their arising for future dharmas.
Only dharmas possess subsequent non-acquisition (*aprāpti*).
Although, from a horizontal perspective across time, they exist only after the dharma,
if one considers the sequence of their arising and functioning, [they may precede it].
There is also non-acquisition (*aprāpti*) prior to those dharmas of the future;
however, for a present dharma, there is definitely no present non-acquisition.
Thus, the *Nyāyānusāra* states:
This is because a present dharma does not coexist with non-acquisition (*aprāpti*).
Some say that there is no present non-acquisition of a present dharma,
because their natures are mutually contradictory.
The *Abhidharmakośa* of old states:
"There are non-possessions (*aprāpti*) of present dharmas that are themselves present.
This translation is erroneous.
According to the explanation of non-acquisition (*aprāpti*) in the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 158,
all non-acquisitions are generally of three kinds;
the first occurs prior to that dharma.
Second, it occurs after that dharma;
third, it is neither before, after, nor simultaneous with that dharma.
The dharmas that cannot be apprehended are likewise of three kinds.
Regarding those phenomena that are not acquired, there is only the aforementioned non-possession (*aprāpti*).
This refers to phenomena that will never arise within the continuum of sentient beings, such as future dharmas,
as well as the final moment of consciousness at the point of entering *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*.
Second, there are non-acquisitions of certain dharmas that possess both prior and subsequent non-acquisition;
these refer to other dharmas belonging to the category of sentient beings as appropriate.
Third, there are non-acquisitions of certain dharmas that lack those prior, subsequent, and simultaneous non-acquisitions.
Yet there is non-acquisition (aprāpti),
namely, analytical cessation (pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha) and non-analytical cessation (apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha).
It is absolutely impossible for non-acquisition to coexist with a dharma.
When a phenomenon manifests before one,
that which is attained must necessarily involve the act of attaining;
that which is not attained is without attainment.
Because there is no non-acquisition (aprāpti), there is likewise no subsequent non-acquisition of that which was previously acquired;
for it has not been the case since beginningless time that one has always possessed it without ever relinquishing it.
This is because one must necessarily give rise to that [non-acquisition] so as to exhaust its category.
However, because the nature of all non-attainments (aprāpti) is weak and inferior,
they are accomplished only for a single present moment.
It should be understood that once it has been attained in a single moment, it is immediately relinquished;

furthermore, this non-acquisition (aprāpti) exists constantly during the states of not yet having attained that dharma and after it has already been relinquished. The commentary explains: three types of non-acquisition are to be known.
It is said that there are cases where a dharma cannot be acquired;
there is only the non-acquisition (*aprāpti*) of that dharma prior [to its arising].
This excludes the future, as well as the past and the present.
The number of mental factors is fewer than those that are non-mental.
These are ultimately non-arising phenomena,
namely the conventional knowledge at the conclusion of the three types of subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*), and so forth.
Since this dharma is ultimately unarisen,
there exists only the non-acquisition prior to the dharma,
as well as the final momentary consciousness of those of the three vehicles at the point of entering nirvana without remainder.
This refers to a certain class of future mind that functions solely as the mind entering final nirvana,
the like of which has never arisen before.
Therefore, there is only non-acquisition prior to the dharma;
there is no non-acquisition subsequent to the dharma.
The term "and so forth" includes associated dharmas and others.
And the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpāda-jñāna*), etc.

Because this knowledge of non-arising, etc., is obtained once and never lost, there is also no subsequent non-possession (*aprāpti*) of these dharmas. [Question: Regarding the final mind and the knowledge of non-arising, etc.

When [a dharma] arises and manifests, there exists in the future a nature of non-acquisition (*aprāpti*) prior to that dharma; why, then, is it not said that there is a non-acquisition subsequent to the dharma? The explanation is as follows: generally speaking, when one speaks of "non-acquisition," [The text continues: ...it refers to the state of not possessing a dharma that has not yet been acquired. Regarding the statement that there is no non-acquisition subsequent to a dharma: this means that once a dharma has already been acquired, its non-acquisition is severed; therefore, there is no such thing as a non-acquisition subsequent to that dharma. Furthermore, since non-acquisition is a state of non-possession, it cannot exist simultaneously with possession. Consequently, it is not established that there is a non-acquisition subsequent to a dharma. As for the statement that there is no non-acquisition prior to a dharma: this means that at the time when a dharma has not yet arisen, its acquisition has not yet occurred; therefore, there is no non-acquisition prior to that dharma. Moreover, since non-acquisition is a state of non-possession, it cannot exist simultaneously with possession. Consequently, it is not established that there is a non-acquisition prior to a dharma. Thus, because non-acquisition is a state of non-possession, it does not exist prior to or subsequent to a dharma. It exists only at the time when the dharma has not yet been acquired. Therefore, it is not said that there is a non-acquisition prior to or subsequent to a dharma. This concludes the explanation.
The former and latter are spoken of in terms of the capacity for the arising of function;
as for non-acquisition (aprāpti) in the future, it exists in the latter period in relation to the temporal sequence of the worlds.
Since it is already established that non-acquisition does not arise [simultaneously],
its arising must necessarily occur prior to the final moment of that state;
therefore, what precedes the dharma is not called "posterior to the dharma."

Regarding the second and third [categories], the dharmas that cannot be attained, as well as those that necessarily do not exist—these can be understood from below. As for the statement, "Furthermore, there is none; it exists only until that category is exhausted," it means:
This is an analysis by way of contrapositive.

It demonstrates that there is no non-acquisition (aprāpti) of a dharma that exists only subsequently; if one has been constantly endowed with that dharma since beginningless time, it must necessarily arise at the moment it is not yet relinquished.
When that category has entered the past and come to an end,
only the subsequent non-possession (aprāpti) of that dharma can be obtained;
it is not the case that one has always been endowed with that dharma since beginningless time.
In the state where [the defilements] have not yet been abandoned or relinquished,
those dharmas of that same category necessarily arise,
causing them all to enter the past.
Because that type [of attainment] is immeasurable and boundless, such that it cannot be produced or exhausted;

therefore, there is no non-acquisition (*aprāpti*) of a dharma that exists only subsequently. Question: Just as there is necessarily no falling back (*parihāṇi*) from the abandonment of the afflictions of the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*), [is this the case for others?]
Regarding those that have already entered the past:

is it not the case that there is only the non-acquisition (*aprāpti*) subsequent to a phenomenon? The explanation says: with respect to the category of phenomena, one speaks of non-acquisition regarding those phenomena that have not been acquired.
The various types of afflictions regarding the Peak of Existence (bhavāgra) have already entered the past;
although there is only the non-acquisition (aprāpti) subsequent to the dharma for those [afflictions] remaining in the future,
there is indeed the non-acquisition prior to the dharma for those [afflictions] that exist in the present.
Regarding the past afflictions of view (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*) at the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*),

it cannot be said that there exists only the subsequent non-acquisition (*prāpti-aprāpti*) of those dharmas; furthermore, even though one explains that for past afflictions of view there is now only the subsequent non-acquisition of those dharmas.
If disjunction (visamyoga) does not manifest, there is non-acquisition (aprāpti) prior to the dharma;

this is stated as "there is non-acquisition prior to the dharma" based on what is possible. Furthermore, regarding past afflictions of view (dṛṣṭi-kleśa), when categorized by time-period (adhvan), there is only non-acquisition subsequent to the dharma.
And there is no non-acquisition prior to the dharma;
because there is a non-acquisition prior to the dharma in relation to future dharmas that exist due to those past afflictions,
it is also called "non-acquisition prior to the dharma."
Regarding this one type of future non-acquisition (*aprāpti*),
although it exists in the past when viewed horizontally across time as being subsequent to the defilements (*kleśa*),
it is called "non-acquisition prior to the dharma" (*pūrvadharmāprāpti*) and is not called "non-acquisition subsequent to the dharma" (*paścāddharmāprāpti*).
Since non-acquisition (*aprāpti*) itself does not arise,
it must necessarily precede the dharma that arises.
This is because the priority or posteriority of non-acquisition is established in relation to its potential to bring about the arising of the dharma’s activity.
Due to this fault, there is also non-acquisition (*aprāpti*) prior to the dharma;
herein, the three interpretations should be understood as being based on what was stated regarding the *mārgānvayakṣānti*.
Regarding the distinction of realms, it is logical that this pertains to the untainted (*anāsrava*).
Regarding the classification by way of realm-connection (*dhātu-bandhana*):
because non-acquisition (*aprāpti*) follows the connection of its basis,
the non-acquisition of each individual dharma pervades all three realms.
It is certain that there is no non-acquisition (aprāpti) that is untainted (anāsrava).
It does not pertain to the unconditioned (asaṃbaddha). Why is this so?
Because it is accepted that the non-acquisition (*aprāpti*) of the noble path is designated as "the nature of an ordinary person" (*pṛthagjanatva*),
and because this nature of an ordinary person is certainly not untainted (*anāsrava*),
since the physical basis (*āśraya*) upon which it depends is itself tainted (*sāsrava*).
The proof from the root treatise can be understood.
Question: Regarding the nature of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva*), it is the non-possession (*aprāpti*) of the noble [states]; this non-possession is contaminated (*sāsrava*).

If one were to claim that the noble ones do not possess the non-acquisition (*aprāpti*) of ordinary beings, it would follow that this [non-acquisition] must be untainted (*anāsrava*). The commentary explains: all non-acquisitions follow their basis (*āśraya*);
since the basis is tainted (*sāsrava*), they are all tainted.

Regarding the statement, "The non-acquisition of which noble dharmas is called the nature of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva*)," this asks: what are the dharmas not acquired by the nature of an ordinary person?
That is to say, if one were to claim that the non-acquisition of all dharmas up to and including those of an Arhat constitutes the nature of an ordinary person, [it would lead to an over-extension].
Answer: If one is at the stage of an ordinary person (pṛthagjana),
one has not attained the non-acquisition of all the noble dharmas (āryadharma) of the three vehicles.
It is called "the state of being an ordinary person" (*pṛthagjanatva*), because it is not separately explained in the *Mūla-śāstra*.
This term "non-acquisition" (*aprāpti*) indicates being separated from acquisition (*prāpti*).
If one attains even a small portion of the noble Dharma, one is called a noble one (*ārya*).
Otherwise, if it were said that one must attain all the noble Dharmas to be called a noble one, [there would be no such person],
O Buddhas, World-Honored Ones.

Furthermore, one who does not accomplish the lineage of the two vehicles should be called an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*). Moreover, this term "not obtaining" (*anadhigama*) indicates being free from attainment.
If one has attained even a small portion [of the noble qualities], one is called a noble one (*ārya*).
Although within the body of a noble one there may still be non-attainments (*aprāpti*) regarding other noble dharmas that have not yet been acquired,
this does not constitute the nature of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva*).

If it were otherwise, then one might claim that the nature of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva*) is merely the non-acquisition of all noble dharmas (*āryadharma*). However, this would mean that all forms of non-acquisition (*aprāpti*) are termed the nature of an ordinary person.
The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, do not possess the noble dharmas of the lineage of śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas;

they should therefore be called ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*). Question: For what reason is the body of an ordinary person not itself designated as "the state of being an ordinary being" (*pṛthagjanatva*)?
The noble body is neither the attainment [of the path] nor the state of being an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva*). Answer: As stated in the *Abhidharmamahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* (Vibhāṣā), fascicle 45:
"Furthermore, there are those who say that the state of being an ordinary person consists in not attaining any of the noble dharmas."
Question: If that were so, then all sentient beings would have to be called ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*), because no noble one (*ārya*) possesses all noble dharmas (*āryadharma*).
Answer: Although no noble one is fully endowed with all noble dharmas, [they are nonetheless not called ordinary persons].
And it is not [the case] for ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), because they do not possess a non-acquisition that is mixed with the acquisition of the noble ones (*ārya*).
That is to say, if there were a non-acquisition of the noble dharmas within the body of an ordinary person...
That which is not mixed with the noble attainments is the state of being an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva*);
it is the non-possession (*aprāpti*) of the noble dharmas within the continuum of a noble one.
Because it is acquired through the attainment of the noble [path], it is not the nature of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva*);
for that attainment and its non-attainment are always co-nascent.
Furthermore, that non-acquisition (aprāpti) is of two kinds:
first, common;
second, uncommon.
That which is "unshared" is the state of being an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva*);
that which is "shared" is not the state of being an ordinary person.
It is the non-possession (*aprāpti*) of the noble dharmas within the continuum of a noble one.
Because it is invariably common [to all], the aforementioned fault does not apply.
Furthermore, that non-acquisition (aprāpti) is of two kinds: first, that which has not yet been destroyed; [the second is that which has already been destroyed].
Two have already been destroyed;
that which has not yet been destroyed is the state of being an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva*),
while that which has already been destroyed is not the state of being an ordinary person.
Since the non-acquisition (aprāpti) of the noble dharmas within the body of a Noble One has been entirely destroyed, the aforementioned fault does not apply.
Furthermore, there are two types of non-acquisition of all noble dharmas.
First, it manifests based on the continuum of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*);
second, it manifests based on the continuum of a noble one (*ārya*).
The former is the state of being an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva*).

Since it is not the case that [the state of] being a non-ordinary person (pṛthagjanatva) exists subsequently, there is no fault of implying that a noble one (ārya) could be called a non-ordinary person. Question:

If the non-acquisition (aprāpti) of the noble dharmas is termed "the state of being a non-ordinary person," then the non-acquisition of the ordinary dharmas should be termed "the state of being a noble one. Explanation: An ordinary person does not possess the noble dharmas.
It may be said that non-acquisition (*aprāpti*) is not the state of being a worldling (*pṛthagjanatva*), because a noble one (*ārya*) necessarily possesses the qualities of an ordinary person.

That non-acquisition is not the state of being a noble one. Question: What is the state of being a noble one? Answer: It refers to all the noble dharmas (*āryadharma*). Objection: If so, then all the noble dharmas would themselves be called the state of being a noble one.
It may also be that all mundane phenomena (*pṛthagjana-dharma*) are termed "the nature of an ordinary person" (*pṛthagjanatva*). The commentary explains:

Noble phenomena do not extend to ordinary persons, and thus they can be established as the "nature of a noble one. However, mundane phenomena do extend to noble ones; therefore, they are not all [exclusively] the nature of an ordinary person.
Therefore, the *Nyāyānusāra* (Treatise on Correct Reasoning), fascicle 12, states:
"Is it not as when the noble dharma itself is called the 'noble nature' (*āryatva*)?
One who accomplishes this nature is therefore called a 'noble one' (*ārya*)."
If it were the case that the phenomena of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) were themselves the state of being an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva*),

This [passage] cites the basis upon which the supported *sabhāgatā* (homogeneity) is revealed.

By means of this *sabhāgatā*, the aggregates (*skandha*), bases (*āyatana*), and elements (*dhātu*) are made mutually homogeneous. This is to be understood by analogy with the *sabhāgatā* of sentient beings.
The "homogeneity of phenomena" (*dharmasabhāgatā*) should also be said to be of two kinds;
however, it is not mentioned here because it is omitted due to brevity.

Whether the homogeneity of phenomena is a single entity or multiple entities should be understood according to the previous explanation. Question: Are the homogeneity of sentient beings (*sattvasabhāgatā*) and the homogeneity of phenomena distinct in their essential nature?
This is the section on the meaning of "single essence. The commentary states: their essential natures are distinct.
That which causes sentient beings to be similar is called the "homogeneity of sentient beings" (*sattva-sabhāgatā*);
that which causes dharmas to be similar is called the "homogeneity of dharmas" (*dharma-sabhāgatā*).
Sentient beings and the meaning of the Dharma-gates differ;
for this reason, although the two share certain similarities, their respective categories (nikāya-sabhāga) are not the same. Therefore, all treatises speak of these two types.
Although there are no sentient beings distinct from the phenomena themselves,
they are differentiated according to their specific meanings, and their respective homogeneity (sabhāgatā) is distinct.

There are also ancient masters who establish that the two types of *sabhāgatā* (homogeneity) have distinct essential natures (*svabhāva*). Furthermore, they explain that while sentient beings have no separate essential nature apart from phenomena (*dharma*),
the designation "sentient being" is established upon those very phenomena.
Based on this, one should understand that the "homogeneity of sentient beings" (sattva-sabhāgatā) is established upon the "homogeneity of phenomena" (dharma-sabhāgatā).
While they share the same ontological essence, they are described as two types of homogeneity by way of their distinct meanings.
Their entities are not distinct.
If one were to aggregate dharmas to constitute a sentient being, one would not speak of a "homogeneity of dharmas" (dharmasabhāgatā);
if one were to set aside sentient beings to discuss dharmas alone, [the same would apply].
That is to say, one does not speak of the "homogeneity of sentient beings" (sattva-sabhāgatā) with respect to those phenomena that are sentient.
Discussing them together, both types of *sabhāgatā* are explained.
For this reason, it is so.
Various treatises either discuss only one [of these] or discuss both types; each is based on a single specific meaning, and thus they do not contradict one another.

Question: For what reason does the verse mention only "sentient beings" (*sattva*)? Answer: It is because it is abbreviated; it does not mention the "homogeneity of dharmas" (*dharmasabhāgatā*). Alternatively, it may be interpreted as follows:
The verse also includes the *dharmasabhāgatā*. The term "sentient beings" (*sattva*) serves to distinguish them from non-sentient things. Regarding the statement "if there were no real entity...
as should be understood according to reason": [this means that if there were no such entity, the continuity of the stream would be impossible].
This is the fourth proof for the existence of a substantial entity; it also refutes the Sautrāntika position that there is no real substance.
Sentient beings are not merely designated as "sentient beings" and "sentient beings";
they share the common designation "sentient being," and thus their names are without distinction.
If there were no real entity characterized by non-differentiation called the "homogeneity of sentient beings" (*sattva-sabhāgatā*),
then among the various sentient beings who differ from one another— such as those in the desire realm and the form realm—
there would be no undifferentiated cognition or wisdom regarding them as "sentient being," "sentient being."
The conventional designation of "sentient being" and so forth as being without distinction would not be possible,
because cognitive awareness necessarily takes an object as its referent.
Since names and phrases necessarily express phenomena,
when wisdom arises and speech is uttered,
it is clearly known that there is a substantial entity.
This is formulated as an objection based on the commonality of undifferentiated sentient beings;
because they are universal, they are cited specifically for the purpose of questioning.
Because differentiated beings are not universal, they are not discussed here. Furthermore, the term "homogeneity" (*sabhāgatā*) is explained by analogy with the same principle.
In this way, regarding the aggregates and so forth,
there is a cognition that is without distinction,
and there are conventional designations and names that are without distinction.
It should not be possible [for such a thing to exist];
therefore, it is said that "it should be understood according to reason.
Is there any case where death and birth occur, excluding the aforementioned characteristics?
This is the fifth [point], clarifying acquisition and abandonment.
By correlating death and birth with acquisition and abandonment of the homogeneous class (*sabhāgatā*), four permutations (*catuṣkoṭi*) should be established.
The first permutation consists of those who die and are born.
There is no relinquishing and no acquisition of the homogeneous class of sentient beings (*sattvasabhāgatā*);

that is to say, wherever one dies, one is reborn in that very same place according to what is appropriate. The second phrase involves both relinquishing and acquiring the homogeneous class of sentient beings.
Neither dying nor being born refers to the moment of entering the state of rightness and separation from birth (*samyaktva-nyāma*),

when one abandons the homogeneous class of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana-sabhāgatā*) and acquires the homogeneous class of noble ones (*ārya-sabhāgatā*). The third case involves both dying and being born.
One also abandons and acquires the *sattvasabhāgatā* (the commonality of sentient beings).
This refers to those who die in one realm and are born in another, and so forth. The fourth alternative refers to cases other than those previously mentioned.
The term "sentient beings" (*sattva*) is used to exclude non-sentient things.
According to what is appropriate, this is the specific homogeneity (*sabhāgatā*),
not the general homogeneity of sentient beings;
for by means of the general homogeneity of sentient beings...
Because it can only be relinquished at the time of entering *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*.
If one were to claim that there exists a separate real entity which reaches another personhood,
this leads to the second question and answer below, which serves to definitively examine and establish the point.
The text contains six sections in total. Below this, the first section presents five difficulties raised by the Sautrāntika school:
(1) the difficulty regarding the non-existence of the nature of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjanatva*), and (2) the difficulty regarding the lack of utility if it were not a vision (*darśana*).
Third, the difficulty regarding insentient things having a commonality (*sabhāgatā*).
Fourth, the difficulty regarding the existence of a distinct *sabhāgatā*.
Fifth, the difficulty that [the Sarvāstivāda] should be identical to the Vaiśeṣika school.
This constitutes the first objection regarding the absence of a distinct nature (*abhinnatva*). Within this, there are two parts:
first, the objection stated based on the literal text;
second, the defense provided by the *Nyāyabindu-ṭīkā*.
The Master of the Abhidharmakośa refutes these three;
other objections should be understood accordingly, as all are treated through the three gates. Regarding the statement, "to describe the objections based on the text":
Since the *pṛthagjana-sabhāgatā* (the homogeneity of ordinary beings) is already distinguished from that of the noble ones (*ārya*),
what is the purpose of establishing a separate entity called "ordinary being-ness" (*pṛthagjanatva*)?
It would be like not establishing a separate "human-ness" apart from the *sabhāgatā* of humans.
Why is the nature of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva*) established separately from the commonality of ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana-sabhāgatā*)? Regarding this, the *Nyāyānusāra* offers a defense:
"Is it not the case that the nature of an ordinary person is simply the commonality of ordinary persons?"
This cannot be so, because their activities differ—
namely, their physical forms, their karmic functions, and their inclinations.
The mutual similarity of causes is termed "homogeneity" (*sabhāgatā*).

That which is incompatible with the attainment of the Noble Path and serves as the cause for being an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) is termed "the state of being an ordinary person" (*pṛthagjanatva*).
Upon entering the stage of "leaving behind error" (*niyāmāvakrānti*), one both relinquishes and acquires this homogeneity.
Regarding the state of being an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva*), it is abandoned and not acquired; such is the meaning of the *Nyāya*.
"Ordinary personhood" (*pṛthagjanatva*) refers to the commonality of ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana-sabhāgatā*).
Because their activities differ,
the nature of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva*) is established separately from the commonality of being an ordinary person; however,
because humans share a commonality, there is no separate "human-nature" (*manuṣyatva*) established apart from that.
Because their activities are identical,
humans are established as a single category [nikāya-sabhāga] beyond their individual distinctions;
furthermore, upon entering the state of a noble one (ārya), they share this same homogeneity.
One abandons the homogeneous character of an ordinary person and acquires the homogeneous character of a noble one;
[this occurs] with respect to the state of being an ordinary person.
One merely abandons the nature of an ordinary person (pṛthagjanatva) and does not acquire [a new] nature of an ordinary person;
one should not say that they do not acquire the nature of an noble one (āryatva).
Because the noble dharmas themselves are designated as the "noble nature" (*āryatva*). Regarding this, the third Vaibhāṣika master objects:
"One who enters the state of a noble one does not abandon their [ordinary] homogeneity (*nikāyasabhāga*);
therefore, it is necessary to establish 'the nature of an ordinary person' (*pṛthagjanatva*) as a distinct entity."
Since one who has entered the state of the noble ones (ārya) has already abandoned the homogeneous character (nikāya-sabhāga),
why is it necessary to establish a separate "nature of an ordinary person" (pṛthagjanatva)?
If you say it is because their respective activities differ, [then that is not a sufficient reason].
One must establish the human *sabhāgatā* as a distinct entity,
for the activities performed by human beings also differ from one another.
Why not likewise establish a distinct *sabhāgatā* for each specific class of similar beings, termed "human *sabhāgatā*"?
"To contradict that which is not a person and yet call it human nature;
furthermore, since it does not reach even the worldly [level], what use would it be?
This is the second objection: the critique of being a non-view and being useless.
Furthermore, this substance of the homogeneous class (sabhāgatā) is not perceived by worldly direct perception (pratyakṣa),
because it is not material (arūpin).
Nor can it be discerned through the principles of inference (anumāna) by means of cognitive wisdom.
Because there is no distinct function [for such a distinction],
although worldly people do not realize that sentient beings exist as real entities through a common conceptualization,
they nevertheless give rise to cognitions and utterances regarding sentient beings as being without difference.
Therefore, even if it were to have a substantial entity, what use would it be? Second, the *Nyāya* rescuer says:
