"Since the *sabhāgatā* (homogeneity) is not form (*rūpa*), how can it be known that it has a function capable of producing distinct categories of things?"
Because one knows that [the cause] exists by seeing its fruit;
just as, upon seeing the fruit obtained from present karma,
one knows that there was karma performed in a previous life.

Furthermore, because the practitioner of meditation realizes it through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). The commentary explains that "homogeneous character" (*sabhāgatā*) is not a material form (*rūpa*) up to the point where it is said there is no distinct category of entity;

this describes the intent of the *Abhidharmakośa* objection. From the phrase "by seeing its fruit" onwards, the *Nyāyānusāra* provides the correct resolution. Thirdly, the master of the *Abhidharmakośa* refutes [the position] as follows:
If causes and conditions were unable to produce their own corresponding results,
it might be necessary for them to arise through a homogeneous faculty (*sabhāgatā*);
however, causes and conditions are inherently capable of producing those results themselves.
What need is there for the arising of a homogeneous class (*sabhāgatā*)?
Even the practitioners of non-Buddhist paths claim to realize a self;
how could one possibly believe that they have realized a substantial entity of a self?
Furthermore, for what reason is it not admitted that [the non-sentient] are similar to one another?
This is the third objection regarding the similarity of non-sentient things:
even insentient entities such as grains are mutually similar.
"Why not establish the 'homogeneous class' (sabhāgatā) therein?
Āmra is the name of a fruit;
its shape resembles that of a jackfruit.
In its beginning and end, its form and color are similar;
it is difficult to distinguish whether it is raw or ripe.
*Bhāṇḍa* is also the name of a fruit.
Its shape is like that of a winter melon;
its flavor is sweet and delicious;
its trees are extremely numerous. Second, the *Nyāyānusāra* rescues [the argument] by saying:
Why not allow for the existence of a commonality (sabhāgatā) among insentient things?
One should not raise such an objection,
for it would lead to an over-extension of the principle.
You also admit that there are destinies such as those of humans and devas,
and modes of birth such as the womb-born and egg-born;
why then do you not also admit [the existence of] destinies such as the mango tree?
Regarding the "unripened" state of mung beans and the like,
it is further said that because those plants and so forth lack mutual similarity in their successive functional activities and volitions,
the *sabhāgatā* (homogeneity) is not separately established for them. Thirdly, the Abhidharmakośa master refutes this, saying:
"Destinies" refers to the five destinies;
"births" refers to the four modes of birth.
Insentient things are neither those destinies nor those births.

Since entities that are similar in nature ought to possess a commonality (sabhāgatā), and since [the Sautrāntikas] refute [the existence of] pleasure, desire, and so forth [as substantial entities], one must separately establish sabhāgatā. If this is so,
why is sabhāgatā not established for mung beans and the like, which are likewise similar?
Furthermore, regarding the question of whether "homogeneity" (*sabhāgatā*) extends to the conceptual designation of awakening:
this constitutes the fourth objection concerning the separate existence of homogeneity,
namely that the essential natures (*svabhāva*) of the phenomena sharing that homogeneity are each distinct.
They attain similarity by virtue of their distinct homogeneous groups (nikāya-sabhāga);
yet these similarities, when compared with one another, are also each different.
How could there then be no further homogeneous group for those similarities?
And there arises no distinct discerning wisdom that takes it as an object;
nor does there arise any distinct conventional designation or verbal expression.
If there were yet another *sabhāga* (homogeneous), [it would be the same].
If one proceeds in this manner, there would be the fault of infinite regress. Second, the *Nyāya* rescuer states:

"Because the various *sabhāgatās* (homogeneities) serve as the causal nature for things that are of the same class, they function as the causes for the designation of mutually similar cognitions regarding those of the same class."
Just as with the eye, ear, and so forth,
they constitute the nature of matter (rūpa) by being derived from the primary elements (mahābhūta);
although the primary elements themselves are not derived from other primary elements.
And the nature of form is established. The third Vaibhāṣika master refutes this, saying:
"If you claim that because they share the same cause, their essence is identical, then [the same would apply to] the homogeneous character (*sabhāgatā*) of its own class and so forth."
There is no separate *sabhāgatā* (homogeneity); rather, the very homogeneity itself serves as the cause for cognition and designation.
Alternatively, it may be that what is common to its own class (*svajāti*) and so forth suffices;
there is no need for a distinct *sabhāgatā* to serve as the cause for cognition and designation.
Furthermore, the analogy cited commits the fallacy of contradicting one's own tenet.
Since the nature of form (*rūpa*) in the eye and other [senses] is eternally fixed throughout the three periods of time,
how can it be said that the nature of form is only established through being produced by the primary elements (*mahābhūta*)?
One should simply say that it is "derived from the primary elements" (mahābhūta-nirmita).
One should not say that it becomes a derivative form (rūpa) only by being derived from the primary elements.
Furthermore, one should clarify that it is established as "reaching" (prāpta) because it arises from these [elements].
This is the fifth point, which should be treated as an objection similar to that raised against the Vaiśeṣika school.
In Sanskrit it is called Vaiśeṣika; in Chinese it is translated as "Superior Discourse" (Shenglun).
The old [translation] says *Vaiśeṣika*;
alternatively, *Vaiśeṣika* is a corruption.
You belong to the Sarvāstivāda school.
They maintain that there exists a distinct "homogeneity" (sabhāgatā) apart from the dharmas themselves;
furthermore, this would clearly establish the tenets of the Vaiśeṣika school,
for they assert the existence of a universal category (sāmānya-padārtha).
It is called "universal" (sāmānya) because it penetrates all phenomena;
it refers to the universal term applied to all phenomena and the universal cognition thereof.
From this, the category-meaning of "universal" (sāmānya) arises.
Furthermore, they maintain the existence of the category-meaning of "particularity" (viśeṣa).
Among many diverse classes, that which is viewed as similar to its own kind is termed "universal."
When different categories are viewed in relation to one another, they are termed "different.
That which is identical is pervasive within the same category;
that which is different is pervasive within different categories.
Regarding many phenomena of diverse categories, there are the expressions of identity and difference,
as well as the cognitions of identity and difference.

From this, the categories of identity and difference arise. Furthermore, your assertion of undifferentiated *sabhāgatā* (homogeneity) should clearly establish the Vaiśeṣika category of the universal (*sāmānya*), while differentiated *sabhāgatā* [would correspond to the category of particularity].

One should clearly establish the Vaiśeṣika category of "generality and particularity" (sāmānya-viśeṣa). According to the ancient masters of the Vaiśeṣika school, six categories (padārtha) are established:
first, substance (dravya).
Second, the two virtues;
third, the three karmas;
fourth, existence.
Fifth, identity and difference;
sixth, conjunction.
Later, the master of treatises Huiyue established ten categories of meaning (padārtha).
As established in the *Daśapadārtha-śāstra*: first, "substance" (*dravya*).
The commentary explains that the essence of all phenomena is real;
it is the substratum for qualities (*guṇa*) and so forth. Second, "quality" (*guṇa*).
4. "Explanation of Reality" (Jieyun): This refers to the moral virtue (*dharma*) of the Real House (*shijia*). 3. "Three Karmas" (Sanye):
Explanation says that movement and action are the karma of the Real House. 4. "Four Identities" (Siting):
Explanation says that because their substance (*ti*) is pervasive and identical to reality, they are called identical. 5. "Five Differences" (Wuyi).
The commentary explains: it exists only upon the real (vastu) and causes the real to be distinct.
Sixth, "conjunction" (sāmagrī):
the commentary explains this as meaning it serves as the cause for the arising [of dharmas] up to their reaching [their effect]. Seventh, "possessing capacity" (samartha).

The commentary explains: when [a cause] such as the "real" (sat) produces its own effect, it can produce that effect only through the assistance of these [conditions]; without them, it lacks the capacity.
The commentary explains: this means excluding the production of other effects. Ninth is the "shared portion" (sabhāga).

The commentary explains that this refers to the categories of substance (*dravya*), quality (*guṇa*), and activity (*karman*), which are both identical and different; therefore, they are called "shared portions" (*sāmānya-viśeṣa*).
"Ten non-expressions" (*daśānirvacanīya*) means that they are said to be non-existent. What is the category of reality (*tattva-padārtha*)?
This refers to the nine kinds of real names, real phrases, and real meanings. What are the nine?
First, the earth.
Second, water;
third, fire;
fourth, wind.
Five voids,
six times, and seven directions.
The eight selves and the nine minds;
these constitute the nine realities.
What is earth? It is that which possesses color, taste, fragrance, and tangibility; this is called earth.
What is water? It is that which possesses color, taste, tangibility, as well as liquidity and moisture; this is called water.
What is fire? It is that which has form and tangibility;
this is fire. What is wind?
That is to say, that which is merely tangibility is wind.
What is space? That which is merely sound is space.
What is time? It refers to that which is designated as "this," "that," "both," "neither," "slow," "quick," "permitted," or "conditioned cause.
This is what constitutes time.
What is direction?
It refers to east, south, north, and so forth.
That which designates and serves as the causal condition for these is direction.
What is "I"? It refers to the cognition that arises from the conjunction of causes and conditions— having as its characteristic the awareness of pleasure, pain, desire, aversion, effort,
formations, the Dharma, and the non-Dharma, and so forth.
This is what constitutes "self.
What do you think?
It refers to perception, pleasure, pain, desire, aversion, effort, wholesome states, and unwholesome states.
The characteristic of the cognition of dependent origination through non-concordant causes and conditions is the mind.
What is the category-meaning of quality (*guṇapadārtha*)?
It refers to the twenty-four qualities, which constitute the category-meaning of quality.
What are the twenty-four qualities?
First, color;
second, flavor.
Third, odors;
fourth, tangibles;
fifth, numbers.
Six measures,
seven distinct entities,
and eight combinations.
Nine: the separation;
ten: that essence; eleven: this essence.
12. Awakening; 13. Pleasure; 14. Suffering.
15. Desire; 16. Anger; 17. Diligence and vigor.
18. Solid substance;
19. Liquid substance; 20. Moisture.
Twenty-one lines; twenty-two dharmas;
twenty-three non-dharmas.
The twenty-four sounds.
These are called the twenty-four qualities (*guṇa*).
For details, see the *Daśapadārtha-śāstra*. What is the category of action (*karma*)?
That which is called the "category of karma" consists of five types of karma.
What are these five? First, the karma of grasping (*upādāna-karma*).
2. the action of contraction;
3. the action of bending;
4. the action of extension.
The fivefold classification of categories (*pañcavidha-padārtha*). A detailed explanation is as found in the *Daśapadārtha-śāstra*. What are the common categories (*sāmānya-padārtha*)?
They are existence (*sattā*).
What is "existence" (sattā)?
It is that which is conjoined with all categories (padārtha) of substance (dravya), quality (guṇa), and action (karman),
and is apprehended by all the sense organs.
That which serves as the basis for the designation and cognition of substance, quality, and action is called "existence" (sattā). What is the category of particularity (viśeṣa)?
It is that which resides in substances.
Based on a single reality,
that which negates the cause for the cognition of those [other things] and expresses the cause for this cognition is called the meaning of the term "difference" (anyatva).
What is the meaning of the term "conjunction" (saṃyoga)?
This refers to the inseparable connection of the real and so forth;
it is the cause for the cognition that expresses this [name],
and furthermore, its nature is one.
What is the meaning of the term "composite" (samavāya)?
It refers to the co-inherence of substance (dravya), quality (guṇa), and action (karman),
whether collectively or not as a single unit.
That which brings about its own specific effect as determined by necessity is called the category of "capacity" (*samartha-pada*). What is the category of "incapacity" (*asamartha-pada*)?
It refers to the inherence of substance (*dravya*), quality (*guṇa*), and action (*karman*).
Whether collectively or individually,
they do not produce other fruits that are necessarily required;
such is called the meaning of the term "incapacity."
What is the meaning of a "shared term" (*sāmānyapada*)?
It refers to the nature of substance (*dravyatva*), the nature of quality (*guṇatva*), the nature of action (*karmatva*), and their conjunction in a single referent (*ekārthasamavāya*),
such as the nature of earth (*pṛthivītva*), the nature of form (*rūpatva*), and the nature of being grasped (*grāhyatva*).
This is called the meaning of the "shared category" (*ubhayabhāga-pada*).
A detailed explanation is as found in the *Daśapadārtha-śāstra*. What is the meaning of the "non-existent category" (*asat-pada*)?
It refers to five kinds of non-existence.
This is called the meaning of the phrase "non-existence through non-utterance. What are the five?
First, non-existence of that which has not yet arisen.
Second, non-existence through having already ceased;
third, non-existence through mutual absence;
fourth, non-existence through non-conjunction.
The five that are ultimately non-existent—these are called the "five absences.

A detailed explanation is as found in the *Daśapadārtha-śāstra*. Question: How do the six categories (*ṣaṭpadārtha*) subsume the ten categories (*daśapadārtha*)? Answer: Within the ten categories, there are three: substance (*dravya*), quality (*guṇa*), and activity (*karma*).
This refers to the categories of substance (dravya), quality (guṇa), and activity (karma) among the six categories.
The fourth category is the same;
it refers to the fourth category, "existence" (sat), among the six categories.
The sixth is the "conjunction" (saṃyoga).
This refers to the sixth "conjunction" phrase among the six phrases.
The fifth is the "difference" (anya) phrase.
The seventh is the category of capability;
the eighth is the category of incapability;
the ninth is the category of both.
This is subsumed under the category of "identity and difference" among the six categories of meaning.
Regarding identity and difference: when things are compared with their own kind, they are termed identical.
The term "different" (anya) refers to mutual comparison between dissimilar categories.
The tenth [category], "the inexpressible" (avaktavya), is not included within the six propositions. This is because:
The first six phrases discuss only those phenomena that possess substantial existence; therefore, only six are mentioned.
The tenth phrase discusses both existence and non-existence; therefore, it is called the tenth.

Each is based on a single specific meaning, and thus they do not contradict one another. The "concordant phrase-meaning" (*sādharmya-pada-artha*) of this treatise is precisely the concordant phrase-meaning within the ten phrase-meanings.
Furthermore, among the six categories of meaning, there is the category of "existence" (astitva).
Because it enables all phenomena to exist,
it shares the same name as the category of "being" (sat), though their specific meanings differ.
This treatise concerns the category of generality (sāmānya).

Among the six categories, it is the fifth, the category of generality. Just as among the nine entities within the category of substance (dravya), those that are mutually similar are termed "general" (samāna).
The term "difference" (*anya*) refers to the mutual relation between dissimilar categories; the remaining [categories] are all to be understood accordingly.

Furthermore, among the meanings of the ten categories (*padārtha*), these include: the fifth, the category of difference (*anyatva*); the seventh, the category of capacity (*śakti*); the eighth, the category of incapacity (*aśakti*); and the ninth, the category of commonality (*sāmānya-viśeṣa*).
Regarding the passage "The Vaibhāṣika masters... up to the full explanation," this constitutes the second defense by the Vaibhāṣikas;
among the five objections raised, they are unable to resolve the first four.
However, the fifth type of dispute is resolved in the same manner as the Vaiśeṣika school.
Their position— that the two phrases differ in their referential categories despite sharing a common locus— is rejected,
for they assert that a single entity can subsist in multiple instances.
I maintain that the *sabhāgatā* (homogeneity) within various phenomena exists as distinct entities;
since the meanings of "many entities" and "a single entity" are fundamentally different,
how could I be made to appear the same as the Vaiśeṣika?
Furthermore, even if one were to concede that for the Vaiśeṣika outsiders this [homogeneity] is either manifest or unmanifest,
nevertheless, this homogeneity (sabhāgatā) must necessarily exist as a real entity (dravya),
because the Sūtra speaks of "homogeneity."
It is clearly known that they are distinct.

Although there is this statement up to the point where it says "is called *sabhāgatā*," this is precisely the third point where the Sautrāntika school again raises an objection against the Vaiśeṣika, as can be understood.
What you have said regarding citing sūtras as proof is not yet acceptable. If that is so,
what is this "homogeneity" (*sabhāgatā*) that you speak of?
This fourth Vaibhāṣika master counters the Sautrāntika by questioning them: "Is it not as I have stated—
that the *sabhāgatā* (homogeneity) is substantially existent?"
If you do not grant this,
then what is the "homogeneity" (sabhāgatā) asserted by that school?
It is precisely such a category [of similarity] as exists among beans and so forth.
This is the fifth response from the Sautrāntika school:
when various conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) of a similar kind arise,
the designation "human homogeneity" (*manuṣyasabhāgatā*) and so forth is metaphorically established therein.
If it is argued that there is no separate substantial entity, just as the commonality (*sāmānya*) of various grains and so forth is not real,
and that this is not a sound statement because it contradicts our own tenets—
This is the sixth Vaibhāṣika master;
having exhausted both reason and expression, he makes this statement.
Thus has been explained [the category] from "homogeneity" (*sabhāgatā*) up to those who "dwell in the result of maturation" (*vipākāvastha*) in the "Vast Fruit" (*Bṛhatphala*) heaven.
Below this, the third major section explains the state of non-conception (*asaṃjñin*).
The first two lines clarify the essential nature of non-conception;
the final line provides a twofold analytical classification.
The higher non-perception is the maturation of non-perception;
the lower non-perception is the Heaven of Non-perception (asaṃjñisattva).
This [state] encompasses both those with mind and those without mind.
The Commentary says: "As for 'one who dams the rivers and streams,' this explains the preceding two phrases.
If one is born in the Heaven of Non-conceptual Beings (*asaṃjñisattva*), there exists a resultant dharma of non-associated formations (*viprayuktasaṃskāra-vipākaphala*)."
That which causes the future mind and mental factors to cease is called "non-conception" (āsaṃjñika).
The essential nature of this dharma is a substantially existent entity.
Thus, it is able to obstruct the future mind and mental factors,
causing them not to arise for even a moment throughout five hundred kalpas,
just as a dam holds back a river.
Thus, we know it exists substantially.
It is called "sentient being" (sattva) for fear of confusing it with grass and the like.
This dharma is exclusively a fruit of maturation (vipākaphala).
The five categories are distinguished as being exclusively maturation (*vipāka*).
To the question, "Of what is this the maturation? [it is replied:]
Regarding the so-called "attainment of non-conception" (asaṃjñi-samāpatti), the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 118, states: [Answer: ...

Some say that the non-ideational attainment (asaṃjñi-samāpatti) brings about the maturation of non-ideation, as well as the life-faculty (jīvitendriya) and the group-homogeneity (nikāya-sabhāga) within the form realm.
This refers to the maturation of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) that possesses mind;
the remaining aggregates are its simultaneous maturations.
Furthermore, there are those who say:
The attainment of non-perception brings about the maturation of non-perception and the maturation of form;
the life-faculty is the maturation of that conscious meditative absorption,
while the remaining aggregates are the maturation of both.
Furthermore, there are those who say that the attainment of non-conception brings about the maturation of non-conception,
while the remaining aggregates are its simultaneous maturations.
Furthermore, there are those who say:
when one possesses a mind, one also experiences the maturation of the various aggregates that are without mind;
and when one is without a mind, one also experiences the maturation of the various aggregates that possess a mind.
The commentary states: It should be explained as follows.
The maturation of non-conceptualization (*asaṃjñika*) is produced solely by the meditative attainment of non-conceptualization (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*).
This includes the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*), the generic similarity (*nikāya-sabhāga*), and the material faculties such as the eye and so forth.
All are induced by karma.
The remaining aggregates are induced together [with it]. This is from the *Nyāyānusāra* (Treatise on the Correct Principles), fascicle 12;
it is the same as the position of the first master in the *Mahāvibhāṣā*, which is not the correct interpretation.

This treatise agrees with the *Vibhāṣā* commentator. Question: If this treatise agrees with the *Vibhāṣā* commentator that life-force and the material faculties (*rūpindriya*) are not produced by the attainment of non-ideation (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*), why does the subsequent section on "producing, projecting, and fulfilling" [state otherwise]?
It merely states that the two meditative attainments (*samāpatti*) and their acquisition (*prāpti*) cannot induce the homogeneous class (*nikāyasabhāga*);
it does not say they do not induce life-force (*jīvitendriya*) or the sense-faculties (*rūpendriya*). The commentary explains:
the following text clarifies the two types of induction—projecting (*ākṣepa*) and completing (*paripūraṇa*).
It is simply said that the two meditative attainments and their acquisition can induce fulfillment,
but they cannot induce projection; nor can they induce everything within that fulfillment.
Regarding the question of where the non-percipient beings reside:
it is asked,
they reside in the Bṛhatphala [heaven], up to what is called the Non-percipient Heaven (asaṃjñisattva-deva).
Answer: To clarify their dwelling place:
among the gods of the Broad Fruit (Bṛhatphala) heaven, there is a high and superior abode.
The non-percipient beings dwell upon it,
just as the Brahmā King of the Intermediate Dhyāna dwells among the Brahmapurohita devas.
They arise on terraces and dwell separately;
this is also like that, and is called the Heaven of Non-conceptualization (asaṃjñisattva-deva).
Regarding the question, "Is that state eternally without perception, or does it also possess perception?"—
the answer is that within the state of birth and death, one eventually returns to the arising of perception.
Sentient beings generally possess perception throughout the long duration of their states of birth and death;
however, they are said to be "without perception" because,
for those sentient beings, there is a period between birth and death during which perception is absent.
Because the perception [of thought] does not arise for a long duration of five hundred great kalpas,
it is called "non-perception" (asaṃjñin) by way of speaking in terms of the majority.
As cited in the Sūtra as proof for the arising of perception, it asks: regarding non-percipient beings (*asaṃjñisattva*), which is more numerous—the preceding minds or the subsequent minds?
The answer is one hundred and fifty-four; the Master of the Commentary (*vibhāṣā-ācārya*) says:
Regarding this statement,
the matter is not fixed;
sometimes the former is greater and the latter is smaller.
Alternatively, there may be little at first and much later,
depending on the differences in one's underlying dispositions (*āśaya*). Furthermore, according to the *Vibhāṣā* masters of the *Vibhāṣā-śāstra*,
the non-conceptual mind (*asaṃjñika-citta*) emerges as being either innate wholesome (*upapatti-lābhika-kuśala*), obscured-neutral (*nivṛta-avyākṛta*), or unobscured-neutral (*anivṛta-avyākṛta*).

[It] is abandoned by the five categories (*pañca-varga*). Question: When entering the mind of non-conception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*), through how many natures (*svabhāva*) and how many categories is it abandoned?
Explanation: Although I have not yet seen the textual passage [for this], [the answer is as follows].
The same applies to the emergence of the mind and the entry of the mind. Question: The Sūtra states that all sentient beings subsist by means of nutriment.
Since the four kinds of nutriment are absent within the state of non-conception (*asaṃjñika*), how can they remain there?
The *Nyāyānusāra* (Treatise on the Correct Principle), fascicle 12, replies:
"They take past karma and the immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*) as their sustaining food (*dhṛti-āhāra*).
That is to say, it is by means of past karma that the commonality of species (*nikāya-sabhāga*) and the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*), etc., are projected."
Because they are projected and supported by the mind at rebirth-linking and the mind that immediately enters the fruit of non-perception,
those beings also possess past contact and so forth as their sustaining nutriment.
In the state of mindlessness (*acittaka*), there is only past contact (*sparśa*) and so forth as nutriment;
in the present, there is none at all.
In the state of having mind (*sacittaka*), both types exist. The commentary explains that past karma serves as the nutriment of volition (*manaḥsaṃcetanāhāra*).

The mind that projects rebirth (*pratisandhi-citta*), which functions as the drawing-in and supporting condition for the subsequent entry-mind, constitutes the nutriment of consciousness (*vijñānāhāra*).
The contact associated with that consciousness constitutes the nutriment of contact (*sparśāhāra*).
Therefore, during the state of mindlessness (*acittaka-avasthā*), there exist only the three past nutriments.
That which is presently non-existent does not exist;
yet among all states of mind, there is also present nutriment,
as is the case with the state of non-conception.
Although it does not arise from them as an immediately preceding condition (*samanantarapratyaya*),
its substance can only be produced through the drawing forth and assistance of their power;
if the preceding moments of mind and so forth were absent, [it could not arise].
Its substance cannot possibly arise. As for the statement,
"having passed away from there, one reaches the karma for rebirth in heaven," this clarifies the place of rebirth following a retrogression.
Having passed away from the Heaven of Non-conception,
one will necessarily be reborn within the Desire Realm among the three realms,
and not in any other place. Why is this so?
The first master explains that because the force of the previously cultivated cause of the attainment of non-ideation has been exhausted,
or because the force of the cause of either the conscious or unconscious attainments has been exhausted,
they are unable to induce a fruit.
When their life there ends, they are reborn again in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*),
because they are unable to further cultivate the attainment of non-conception (*asaṃjñisamāpatti*) there;
or rather, it is because of the existence of both the conscious and unconscious attainments that one is not born in that realm.
Just as an arrow shot into the air falls to the ground as soon as its momentum is exhausted,
one should know that it is likewise when beings are reborn in the desire realm.
This is also the case for those sentient beings who are destined to be born in the Heaven of No-Thought (asaṃjñisattva).
There must necessarily be karma to be experienced in a subsequent life within the desire realm;
just as one born in the Northern Continent (Uttarakuru) must necessarily possess karma to be experienced in a subsequent life that leads to rebirth in heaven.
This is because of the existence of such karma to be experienced in a subsequent life within the desire realm.
It arises only in the desire realm and not in other realms.
Thus, the *Abhidharmamahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* (Vibhāṣā), fascicle 154, states:
"Some say that if one performs karma to be experienced in the next birth (*upapadyavedanīya*) in the Heaven of Non-conception (*asaṃjñisattva*), [it is so]."
By the very nature of things (*dharmatā*), one also creates karma in the desire realm that is to be experienced in a subsequent life (*aparaparyāya-vedanīya*).

Just as when one creates karma for birth in Uttarakuru that is to be experienced in the next life (*upapadya-vedanīya*), by the very nature of things, one also creates karma for the gods of the desire realm that is to be experienced in a subsequent life. Question: In which destiny (*gati*) of the desire realm is one born?
The commentary explains that the five destinies (*pañca-gati*) are not fixed.
Thus, the *Vibhāṣā* (154) asks: "Where are those born of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) reborn?"
Answer: Some say they are born in the hells;
others say they are born in the evil destinies.
According to this explanation, they are certainly born in the desire realm, though the specific location is not fixed.
[The beings] are born either in the evil destinies, or as gods, or as humans.

Question: At what time does one perform the karma that accords with the subsequent [rebirth]? Explanation: It is performed at the time when one is about to cultivate the preparatory stage (*prayoga*) for the state of non-perception (*asaṃjñika*).
Because they are powerful and superior, they receive [the teaching] first;
that is to say, when various non-Buddhists are about to practice the state of non-perception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*),
or give rise to false views to slander the *nirvāṇa* of the Śākya clan.
Or one may give rise to the grasping of views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*), reckoning that [false view] to be true;
or one may give rise to the grasping of precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*), reckoning that [such conduct] to be the path.
Such delusions as these serve as the causes for the miserable realms (*apāya*).
Having cultivated this meditative concentration, one must further abandon desire;
this may arise through birth or through hearing.
Or one reflects:
"Such wholesome [deeds] serve as the cause for a fortunate rebirth (*sugati*).
Although there may be karma to be experienced in subsequent lives (*aparaparyāya-vedanīya-karma*) among other births, [this refers specifically to the present].
Because karma created during the stage of preparation possesses strong force, one takes rebirth by means of it;
alternatively, wholesome karma may also be created during the stage of subsequent action.
It should be understood that this applies when one is about to be born in Uttarakuru.
The karma of the gods of the desire realm is also created among humans at the time of practicing the preparatory application for the contemplation of non-self,
because that [human state] is powerful and superior.
Therefore, it is received first now;
or alternatively, it may also be created during the stage of subsequent arising.
Because the karma for being born in the Northern Continent is purely wholesome, one who dies there is reborn in the heavens.
Because wholesome and unwholesome states arise in alternation prior to birth there,
those who pass away from that realm are reborn throughout all five destinies.
Having already explained the state of non-perception (*asaṃjñika*), what are the two meditative attainments (*samāpatti*)?
Below this, the fourth major section explains the two meditative attainments (*samāpatti*).
Within it, the first part explains the attainment of non-conception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*).
Second, the explanation of the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*).
Third, the distinction based on the supporting body (*āśraya*).
Below this, the explanation of the attainment of non-conception (*asaṃjñisamāpatti*).
To clarify the inquiry: herein, there are two parts—first, the general;
second, the specific.
This constitutes the general question:
"Regarding the attainment of non-perception and the attainment of cessation.
This is the general answer.
Regarding the first [state], the meditative attainment of non-conception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*), what are its characteristics?
This is asked separately.
The verse says: "It belongs to those who have not attained the noble state; it is acquired in one lifetime."
Answered separately:
the first line clarifies the essence; the subsequent "meditative absorption" (dhyāna) clarifies the basis;
"seeking liberation" clarifies the purpose.
Clear attention is wholesome;
it is subsumed under the nature of clarity and is exclusively to be experienced upon rebirth.
It brings about a clear result, yet it is not noble.
One who clearly cultivates this attains it in a single lifetime;
this is the clear accomplishment.
The treatise says: "As for 'reaching a state identical to that of non-conception'..."
As previously stated, there is a dharma that is the maturation of non-conception (*asaṃjñi-vipāka*);
because it causes the cessation of mind and mental factors, it is called "non-conception.
Likewise, there is another distinct conditioned factor dissociated from mind (*citta-viprayukta-saṃskāra*).
That which causes the mind and mental factors to cease is termed the essence of the attainment of non-conception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*).
The absence of conception within the body is termed "one without conception" (*asaṃjñin*);
the meditative attainment of one without conception is termed the "attainment of non-conception."

This is an *adhikaraṇasamāsa* (dependent determinative compound). Alternatively, the name "unconscious absorption" (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*) may be taken as an *karmadhāraya* (appositional determinative compound), meaning that the absorption itself is the unconscious state.
The word "thus" (*evam*) used in the verse indicates that this absorption alone brings about the cessation of mind and mental factors.
This is similar to the aforementioned Heaven of Non-conceptual Maturation (asaṃjñi-saṃskāra-vipāka-deva),
yet not identical in all respects;
this is according to the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 151.
The mind entering the attainment of non-perception and the mind emerging from the attainment of non-perception are both tainted wholesome minds of the fourth dhyāna.
It cannot be described in full detail.
As for the question, "In what place does this reside?"— this is the inquiry.
Regarding the statement that it pertains to the final dhyāna and not to others:
the answer is that it exists only in the fourth dhyāna.
It is not so for the other higher or lower stages.
Thus, the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 151, states:
"Furthermore, the lower stages possess both pleasant and unpleasant feelings."
The modes of activity [of the mind] are coarse and agitated, making them difficult to eliminate.
In the fourth dhyāna,
there is only neutral feeling.
Because its mode of activity is subtle and easy to eliminate, the state of non-ideation does not exist in the lower realms.
Question: For what reason does that absorption not exist in the formless realm?
Answer: Only ordinary worldlings (pṛthagjana) conceive of practicing this meditative absorption as a means to realize the nirvāṇa of non-perception;
however, within the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu), there is no maturation (vipāka) of non-perception to be so conceived.
Therefore, the attainment of non-conception is also absent there;
furthermore, ordinary beings fear total annihilation,
and that realm is formless.
If one were to further extinguish the mind, it would constitute total annihilation;
because this is what they fear, the state of non-percipient absorption (asaṃjñi-samāpatti) does not exist within that realm.
For what purpose is the non-percipient absorption cultivated?
Question:
Regarding those who seek liberation and proceed to cultivate the meditative attainment of non-perception (asaṃjñi-samāpatti). Answer:
Those who cultivate the state of non-perception do so in order to seek liberation and nirvāṇa;
they cling to the maturation of non-perception as being true liberation and nirvāṇa.
Seeking to realize that state, one cultivates the attainment of non-conception as a path of renunciation.
As for what was previously stated— that non-conception results in the maturation of the five aggregates— this refers to that very point.
Since it was previously stated that non-conceptualization (asaṃjñi) is a result of maturation (vipāka),
its inclusion within the category of the indeterminate (avyākṛta) is established as a matter of course, even without being explicitly stated.
Therefore, it is not explained separately.
This meditative absorption is exclusively wholesome;
it can bring about the maturation of the five aggregates within the realm of the non-percipient beings (*asaṃjñisattva*).
It arises at first and ceases later;
because it possesses mind and mental factors, it is complete with the five aggregates.
Since it is of a wholesome nature, to what type of feeling does it correspond?
Question:

Regarding those who proceed from the state of being destined for rebirth (upapadyavedanīya) up to the stage of entering the path of certainty (samyaktvaniyāma), they experience only karma to be felt upon rebirth. Is this so? Answer: Yes, they experience only karma to be felt upon rebirth.
This can be understood according to the text.
The *Nyāyānusāra* has one explanation that agrees with this treatise,
while it also offers another explanation.
A certain class of masters maintains this fixed position,
namely that [karma] is to be experienced in the next life (*upapadyavedanīya*) or is of indefinite timing (*aniyatavedanīya*). Why is this so?
One who has attained this meditative absorption may also enter the state of rightness and departure from birth (*samyaktva-niyāma*); once having entered it,
they will certainly never again manifest this absorption in the present life.
It is in terms of its actual manifestation that the attainment of non-ideation is called the "attainment of ordinary beings," not in terms of its possession.
Furthermore, regarding the admission that this meditative absorption extends even to those who will certainly never practice it:
there is a distinction between ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*) and noble ones (*ārya*); it is attained only by ordinary persons.
By means of the attainment of non-conception,
one brings forth the great fruit of birth and death for five hundred kalpas; yet,
in emptiness, nothing is to be obtained.
Because the Noble Ones feel revulsion toward it as if seeing a deep pit and do not delight in entering it,
they must necessarily grasp the maturation of non-conception.
Regarding true liberation and nirvana,
they give rise to the perception that the state of non-percipient absorption is capable of bringing about escape from birth and death.
Yet, when practicing this meditative absorption,
all noble ones do not grasp at the outflow-tainted state of non-conceptual maturation as being true liberation or nirvana.
Not grasping at the contaminated state of non-conceptual absorption as the true path of transcendence,
one certainly does not practice this absorption.
If the noble ones do not reach the state of non-ideation (asaṃjñi-samāpatti),
this section below clarifies the question regarding their attainment.
If the noble ones...
When one cultivates and attains the fourth dhyāna concentration,
one necessarily attains the mindless concentration (asaṃjñi-samāpatti) regarding all minds of the beginningless past and future.
This is the attainment of non-perception (asaṃjñi-samāpatti).

If one asks: "Is it as with dhyāna that one also attains [the ability to go and come], having practiced the attainment of non-perception (asaṃjñi-samāpatti) since beginningless time? Or do others not attain it as well? The answer is: The answer is: No. It is not like dhyāna. Why? Because the attainment of non-perception is a conditioned state produced by volition; it is not a natural capacity. Furthermore, because it is a state of cessation, it cannot be maintained for a long duration. Moreover, it is a state produced by the power of meditative concentration, and its nature is such that it does not involve the movement of going or coming. Therefore, it is not the case that one attains the ability to go and come through it in the same way as through dhyāna. As for the other attainments, they likewise do not possess this quality. Thus, it is not the case that all [attainments] function in the same manner. This concludes the response.
Other ordinary persons,
when cultivating and attaining the fourth dhyāna,
likewise cannot attain the meditative attainment of non-conception regarding the past or the future.
How much more so for a sage? Why is this? Because...
[the reason].
Although he has previously practiced it, there is no cultivation of it for the future;
even though that state of non-perception has been practiced in the past.
Because it is without mind,
it must be attained through the cultivation of great preparatory effort and skillful means; therefore,
at the moment of its initial attainment, only the present [moment] is acquired.
Just as when one first receives the prātimokṣa vows,
they are established only in the present; having attained this meditative concentration, it is likewise so.
From the second moment of thought onwards, until it has been relinquished,
one also accomplishes the past;
even after emerging [from that state], as long as it has not yet been relinquished.
It is established as belonging only to the past;
because it is mindless, there is no cultivation of the future.
As for the statement that one reaches the thirty-fourth thought-moment by means of the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*):
The following section is the second [part], which elucidates the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*).
The first line elucidates its essential nature; "for the sake of tranquility" elucidates the mental attention (*manasikāra*);
and "abiding at the peak of existence" [indicates its location].
The clear [wisdom] relies on the stages; it is wholesome.
The nature of clear wisdom is subsumed under two feelings and is indeterminate.
Clear wisdom brings forth its fruit. It belongs to noble ones and those who cultivate clear wisdom; it is acquired through preparatory application.
The first two phrases clarify the cultivation of practice; the latter two phrases clarify the attainment of Buddhahood.
The Treatise states: "It is the same up to the meditative absorption of cessation" (nirodha-samāpatti), which is analogous to the case of the non-conceptual state (asaṃjñi-samāpatti).
Regarding the phrase "the same applies here," what is the meaning of this as an illustration?
This asks:
what is the purpose of using the example of the attainment of non-perception (asaṃjñi-samāpatti) to illustrate the attainment of cessation (nirodha-samāpatti)?
Answer: This correctly sets forth the essential nature [of the formations].
Furthermore, there are other distinct formations dissociated from mind (citta-viprayukta-saṃskāra-dharma).
That which can cause the cessation of the mind and mental factors is called the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*).
Furthermore, the *Abhidharmamahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 152, states:
Question: What constitutes the substance of this attainment of cessation?
Some say that this attainment has a single substance as its essence;
when cessation manifests before one, it is then termed "mindless."
Question: What is meant by "the single cessation," wherein the manifestation of a single moment is termed "mindless"?
Answer: The manifestation of a single moment of feeling is termed "possessing feeling."
The manifestation of a single moment of perception is called "having perception";
the manifestation of a single moment of consciousness is called "having consciousness.
In this way, there is a single cessation.
If it manifests in a single moment, it is termed "mindless.
What fault is there in this?
Some say that the substance of this meditative absorption consists of eleven factors.
Because the ten universal mental factors (*mahābhūmika-dharma*) and the mind cease,
some say that this meditative absorption has twenty-one entities as its substance,
because the ten universal mental factors, the ten wholesome universal mental factors (*kuśala-mahābhūmika-dharma*), and the mind all cease.
According to this teaching,
as many moments of mind and mental factors as cease,
so many entities manifest before one.
Regarding this established nature, the commentary explains:
According to the intention of the *pīṭaka* (the master of the school), there are further mental factors (*caitta*) of attraction and aversion;
these correspond to the mind as appropriate to each case, yet they do not arise simultaneously.
Therefore, it differs from the previous school’s position.
The nature of the attainment of non-ideation (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*) should be understood accordingly.
Furthermore, the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 153, states:
Question: When entering the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*), which minds and mental factors (*citta-caitta-dharma*) are ceased?
Are they past or future?
It exists in the present.
If it were past, since the past has already ceased, what further could cease?
If it is future, since the future has not yet arrived, how can it be extinguished?
If it is present, [how can it be extinguished]?
If it does not abide in the present, how can it cease?
For even without the power of meditative concentration (*samādhi*), it would cease of its own accord.
To this, one should reply as follows:
It is extinguished in the future.
Question: Since the future has not yet arrived, how can it be extinguished?
Answer: It abides in the present world.
It is called "cessation" because it obstructs future minds and mental factors so that they do not continue in succession,
just as one might cut off a city road, close the gates, and raise a banner.
To prevent people from entering or exiting is called "eliminating bandits.
This case is also like that.
Some say it also extinguishes [the seeds] of the future and the present.
Question: Since that which is present necessarily does not abide, how then does it cease?
Even in the absence of the power of meditative concentration (*samādhi*), it ceases spontaneously.
Answer: Previously, the mind and mental factors of the present world caused conditioned phenomena to arise in succession and then cease;
now, it is the mind and mental factors of the present world [that function in the same way].
It does not allow conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*) to continue arising and then cease.
By whose power is this? It is by the power of cessation through meditative concentration (*nirodhasamāpatti*). The former interpretation is correct.
Because it is not said that there is an assertion [of such a mind].
Furthermore, according to the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 152,
regarding the mind that enters the attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*):

The wholesome, out-flowing (*sāsrava*) mind of the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*), as well as the minds emerging from the meditative attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*), are both characterized by being both out-flowing and outflow-free (*anāsrava*). Question: What dharma do the minds entering and emerging [from this attainment] take as their object? Answer: As stated in the *Abhidharmamahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 153: [The mind entering the attainment takes the cessation of formations as its object; the mind emerging from it takes the same cessation as its object.]
The commentary states: It should be explained that this mind entering meditative absorption takes the future meditative state as its object;
however, it cannot be specified which particular moment it takes as its object or which moments it does not.
Because future concentration consists of many moments, and since there is no prior or posterior sequence, they do not abide in a state of confusion.
Furthermore, it says: "The critique states that it should be explained as follows."
This mind emerging from meditative absorption takes the past absorption as its object;
however, it cannot be said that it takes one specific moment and not another,
because the past absorption consists of many moments existing in a state of intermingling.

Regarding the statement that "these two attainments are preceded by attention (*manasikāra*)," this distinguishes them from one another based on their differing types of attention; [this refers to] the aforementioned attainment of non-perception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*).
Seeking liberation through the maturation of non-perception (*asaṃjñi-vipāka*), one becomes weary of and destroys perception.

Preceded by the mental attention (*manasikāra*) of the thought of renunciation, the attainment of non-perception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*) is able to bring about escape from birth and death; furthermore, it is understood that this [attainment] can also bring about escape from perception itself.
This meditative attainment of cessation is entered by dwelling in the state of weariness toward and the dispersal of mental agitation for the sake of seeking tranquility,
preceded by the mental application of bringing thoughts to rest.

"Cessation" refers to the cessation of the mind and mental factors. Furthermore, although the perception of cessation also brings about the cessation of feeling and so forth, it is specifically designated here because perception is proximate and predominant.
Regarding the statement "from the prior non-ideational absorption up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception," this is due to the differences in their respective levels (*bhūmi*).
Furthermore, the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 152, states:
Question: For what reason do the lower stages lack this meditative absorption?

One explanation states: Furthermore, because the attainment of cessation is attained by means of extinguishing the most subtle mind and mental factors, the lower stages do not accord with the extinction of the most subtle mind and mental factors. Another explanation states:
Furthermore, all lower stages are termed "possessing perception," as their modes of activity are coarse and restless, making them difficult to still.
This stage is termed the Sphere of Neither-Perception-nor-Non-perception.
Because its mode of activity (*ākāra*) is subtle and easy to cease, the lower stages lack the meditative attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*), as explained at length in that commentary.
As for the statement that "this is the same as the previous attainment because it arises from the wholesome (*kuśala*)": [it means that both arise from a wholesome motivation].

This attainment of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti) is identical to the aforementioned attainment of non-conception (asaṃjñisamāpatti) in that its nature is exclusively wholesome, not indeterminate or defiled;
among the four types of wholesome states, it is a wholesome state by way of origination (samutthāna-kuśala).
Furthermore, because it is neither defiled nor indeterminate, it is not tranquil.
As for the statement that the aforementioned attainment of non-conception results in the maturation of four aggregates,
this clarifies the fruit it summons.

The previously mentioned non-ideational attainment (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*) is exclusively experienced upon rebirth (*upapadyavedanīya*). This attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*), however, pertains to experience upon rebirth, in subsequent lives, or is indeterminate;
it is classified as being experienced upon rebirth with respect to its maturation fruit (*vipākaphala*).
There is that which is to be experienced in subsequent lives.
Among those of indefinite timing, there are two types:
either it is indefinite as to whether it will be experienced at all, or it is indefinite as to the time of its maturation while being definite as to whether it will be experienced.
Or it may not be attained at all;
that is to say, if after arising in this meditative absorption in a lower stage, one does not give birth to a higher stage,
but instead abandons the remaining afflictions and attains parinirvāṇa in that very lower stage.
Among the indeterminate [karmas], this is one for which both the maturation (*vipāka*) and the timing are indeterminate;
it brings about only the maturation of the four aggregates (*catuḥ-skandha*) of the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*).
The *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 90, states:
Question: What kind of ripened fruit (*vipāka-phala*) does the attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*) receive?

Answer: It receives the ripened fruit of the four aggregates (*skandha*) of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*), excluding the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) and the group-homogeneity (*nikāya-sabhāga*).
Because that [state] is solely the fruit of karma.
Furthermore, the *Nyāya* states:
"The aforementioned state of non-ideation (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*) conduces to feeling to be experienced upon rebirth (*upapadya-vedanīya*) and to indeterminate feeling (*aniyata-vedanīya*)."
The remaining text is the same as this.
Regarding the statement that "the previously mentioned attainment of non-perception enters through resolute conviction," this is a distinction between ordinary beings and noble ones.
Only a noble one attains this non-conceptual absorption (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*), which exists in the fourth dhyāna.
In that place there is form.
One who cultivates the non-conceptual state forms this thought:
"Although I have extinguished the mind, there is still form;
I am not afraid of annihilation. An ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) can give rise to this attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*), which exists at the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*).
There, however, they possess no form.
Furthermore, because one fears that by extinguishing the mind it would result in annihilationism,
fear arises and thus [the practitioner] is unable to initiate it. Moreover,
this attainment of cessation is produced solely through the power of the Noble Path.
It belongs solely to the noble ones and not to ordinary persons.
Furthermore, when a noble one is about to enter this meditative absorption,
they enter it with the resolute conviction (*adhimokṣa*) that this absorption is *nirvāṇa in the present life* (*dṛṣṭadharmaparinirvāṇa*).
Because they conceive of nirvana as a state of annihilation,
ordinary beings are unable to enter it,
fearing total extinction.
Therefore, because the function of resolute conviction (adhimokṣa) is particularly strong, it is designated separately.
Furthermore, the *Nyāyānusāra* states:
"Ordinary beings (pṛthagjana) are not capable of giving rise to the meditative attainment of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti)."
Because that [state] has not yet abandoned the obstacles to the attainment of cessation arising from its own level,
and because it has not transcended the afflictions to be abandoned by insight pertaining to the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*),
it is ultimately incapable of entering the attainment of cessation. Furthermore, this treatise is refuted as follows:
That explanation is irrational,
for it is the same in the case of the attainment of non-perception (asaṃjñi-samāpatti);
in both cases, the mind is severed.
Because there is no distinction in the resolute conviction regarding nirvāṇa, the Vaibhāṣika masters of the *Abhidharmakośa* offer this defense:
"While there is indeed no distinction from this perspective,
there is a difference in the basis— the realms of form and formlessness."
The fears are not the same;
they cannot be used as an analogy.
This case, too, is like the previous one: it is not obtained through the separation from defilements.
Regarding this attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*):
as was previously stated, it is not obtained through the abandonment of defilements (*vairāgya*). By what means, then, is it obtained?
Thus is the question.
Regarding the statement that "by means of application one attains it, and it also becomes past," the answer is:
it is attained through application.
Initially, one only possesses the present and does not obtain the past;
nor does one cultivate the future,
because of the absence of mind.
It is only through the power of the mind that one cultivates [the dharma] for the future;
from the second moment onward, until it is relinquished,
it also becomes past.
"If the World-Honored One also attained it through preparatory application (*prayoga*)," this section below explains the attainment upon becoming a Buddha;
this is the question.
If it is not so, the answer is: how so?
Question: Regarding the statement that at the time of attaining Buddhahood, one obtains all [realizations] through the attainment of freedom from defilement (*vairāgya-lābhika*).
Explanation:

It is explained that [this] is attained at the time when the Buddha enters the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*) and becomes free from defilement (*vītarāga*). The *Nyāyānusāra* objects: "Is it not the case that this is the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣaya-jñāna*)?"
Even at the time of attaining Buddhahood, it is not called "attainment," let alone in the case of the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*);
for when Bodhisattvas abide in the diamond-like samādhi (*vajropamasamādhi*), [they have already attained it].
It is called the attainment of the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*). This is because "attainment" (*prāpti*) is defined as the arising of its own substance.
Furthermore, it says:
To provide a general explanation for them according to what is appropriate means,
for instance, speaking of "distant" sounds in reference to something near,
or [speaking thus] at the time of the vajra-like samādhi.
Because he will certainly attain Buddhahood, he is also called "one who has attained Buddhahood.

This is because he is certain to attain Buddhahood in the very next moment (*anantara-ksana*). The commentary explains: the Master of the *Nyāyānusāra* provides this as a reconciliation for the *Abhidharmakośa*;
in reality, it is stated [in that manner].
One attains the rank of a bodhisattva.
Now, regarding the matter of achieving [the goal] in proximity to the Buddha, it is said that the bodhisattva first attains the sound from afar;
therefore, there is no error in saying that one attains it at the stage of Buddhahood.
The Abhidharmakośa masters offer this defense:
"To say that one 'becomes a Buddha' is to apply the name of the fruit to the cause."
Regarding the statement that it is attained at the time of the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*): this means that when the knowledge of exhaustion is in the state of arising (*utpādākāra*),
it is inherently sufficient by itself.
There is no need to trouble that Śākya.
It has never happened that the World-Honored One reached the stage of one liberated both ways (ubhayatobhāgavimukta). Question: [Why is this so?]

Since it was stated that "both parts" refers to one who has attained the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*), how can one be called "possessing both parts" at the moment of the Buddha’s knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) if he has not yet arisen from the absorption of cessation?
Regarding those who arise from the absorption of cessation and become "liberated through both parts" (*ubhayatobhāga-vimukta*): [this applies to them].
Answer: Although the Buddha had not yet arisen from the meditative attainment of cessation at the time of his attainment of the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*),
he possessed mastery over the attainment of cessation.
As for how one who has already [attained] it becomes "liberated in both ways" (*ubhayatobhāgavimukta*), the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 153, states:
Question: Why is it that once the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) has arisen, one is called "liberated in both ways"?
Answer: Because one has already attained the minds of entering and emerging from that concentration, it is called "liberation through both.
It does not refer to the attainment of the substance of concentration itself; rather, by this principle, it is termed "attainment through the removal of defilements" (vairāgya-prāpti).
Because it arises subsequently without depending on preparatory effort (*prayoga*).
Question: At the time of the Buddha’s knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*), if he has not yet attained the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*), what is the correct principle?
It is said that because they have eternally abandoned the obstacles to meditative absorption (*samāpatti-āvaraṇa*) and have relinquished [the attainment] due to its non-accomplishment,
and because they have attained mastery over the arising and cessation of the meditative absorption,
they become "liberated-in-both-ways" (*ubhayatobhāga-vimukta*), just like those who have already arisen from it.
If there is no such thing as "acquisition" (prāpti), how can one speak of "abandoning" or "non-accomplishment"?

For acquisition and non-acquisition are established as being mutually exclusive. The commentary explains that there are generally two types of non-acquisition (aprāpti) regarding the meditative attainment of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti).
One class, based on a body whose obscurations have not yet been severed,
is said to be unaccomplished in the mastery of entering meditative absorption;
another class, based on a body whose obscurations have already been severed, [is accomplished].
It is called the non-attainment of mastery over the arising of meditative concentration (*samāpatti*).
The *Nyāyānusāra* states that it is "abandoned" (*prahīṇa*).
This abandonment refers to the non-attainment [of mastery] based on a body in which the obstacles have not yet been severed.

Furthermore, within the Buddha’s body, there is another category that depends on a body whose obstructions have already been severed but which has not yet attained [the state of] accomplishment, such as the non-attainment (*aprāpti*) of the Noble Path; in total, there are two categories.
The first depends on an ordinary body and constitutes the nature of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva*).

First, it relies on the body of an Ārya and not on the nature of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*). Furthermore, another interpretation holds that before attaining Buddhahood, one should obtain the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*) but does not;
thus, there is a falling away from what has not yet been obtained.
If he does not rely on the Buddha-body, it is called "non-attainment" at the time of becoming a Buddha.

Regarding the Western masters' explanation up to the point where they do not permit that [other] view, the following section explains why it is not among the first thirty-four moments of thought; thus, the divergent views are presented as an inquiry.
The Western Masters are the teachers of Gandhāra, located to the west of Kaśmīra;
this is the intended meaning of these masters.
A bodhisattva in the stage of training first gives rise to this meditative absorption; that is to say,
that bodhisattva first abandons the afflictions of the sphere of nothingness before entering the path of seeing.
Having emerged from the path of vision, one enters the meditative attainment of cessation;
having emerged from the attainment of cessation, one abandons the afflictions of the Peak of Existence and subsequently attains enlightenment.
At the time of the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*), the past attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*) is established.

Why is the position of those Western masters not accepted here? If their view were accepted, it would follow that [the attainment] persists until the subsequent birth-knowledge of exhaustion (*upapattyanantara-kṣayajñāna*).
The Master of the Treatise explains:
If one accepts the explanation of those Western masters,
it will accord with the *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra* composed by the Venerable Upagupta.
That treatise states that the Buddha first enters the meditative attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*) and subsequently attains enlightenment (*bodhi*).
This interpretation was formulated because the author of the treatise aligns himself with the masters of the Western tradition.
Upagupta, translated here as "Close to the Treasury," appeared one hundred years after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa;
he was the preceptor to King Aśoka.
The old transcription "Upagupta" is an error.
Regarding the phrase "in the country of Kaśmīra, up to those who have attained the meditative absorption of the cessation of perception and feeling," the intended meaning is the country of Kaśmīra.
It is not the case that one first enters the meditative attainment of cessation and only afterwards gives rise to the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*),
because enlightenment is attained through thirty-four moments of thought;
within these thirty-four moments, [the attainment occurs].
It is impossible for a non-concordant, contaminated mind of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception to arise;
therefore, Bodhisattvas during their stage of training (śaikṣa) should not give rise to the meditative attainment of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti).
As for the question, "What fault would there be for the foreign masters [to claim otherwise] at this point?"—[the answer follows].
The masters from foreign lands— namely, the masters from India outside Kaśmīra—
hold views identical in intent to those explained by the Western masters.
Therefore, I shall now raise this as a question: if,
during the interval between the thirty-four moments [of the path of seeing],
one were to give rise to a non-concordant, contaminated mind of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception after the path of seeing has arisen;
If one attains the meditative absorption of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti), what fault is there?
If that were so, it would follow that one reaches [the limit] without transcending the intended duration of the mind.
The masters of Kaśmīra maintain that if one gives rise to a thought of a different category, one transgresses the formal resolve (*samādāna-citta*);
however, Bodhisattvas do not transgress their formal resolve.
Regarding the fact that a Bodhisattva actually attains the untainted noble path,
the masters of foreign lands explain:
"In truth, the Bodhisattva does not transcend his initial resolve."
However, it is not that one does not transcend the untainted noble path to give rise to other tainted states.
If this is so, how is it that the intention is not transcended?
The Kashmiris further raise this objection.
If one gives rise to outflows, one immediately transgresses the formal resolve (samaya-citta).
How, then, does one not transgress it?
It is said: "Because I have not yet attained the ultimate perfection of all matters."
The interpretation of the foreign masters may be understood.
As for the statement that "the previous explanation is superior because it is our own school's tenet," [it means as follows].
The Kaśmīris were unable to present a counter-argument and thus returned to their own school's position.

Although it was already stated that "the two meditative attainments extend up to the first [attainment] among humans prior to cessation," the following third section clarifies the physical basis (*āśraya*).
The Commentary states: "That which arises upon arrival" explains the first phrase.
Both meditative attainments arise based on both the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and the form realm (*rūpadhātu*).
Furthermore, the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 152, states:
Question: In which realm can this attainment of non-conception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*) arise?
Some maintain that it arises only in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
Because the mind of the desire realm possesses intensity and the power of verbal expression,
some masters say it arises in the desire realm and the three dhyānas;
others say it can also arise [in the higher realms] because it can be produced through the force of mindfulness regarding previously practiced application.

Furthermore, some say that the fourth dhyāna can also be manifested [in the form realm], with the exception of the Heaven of Non-conception (*asaṃjñisattva*), lest the fruit and its cause be too closely proximate. The commentary states: among these three explanations, the latter two are not contradictory.
The former [position] is not correct,
as will be refuted separately below.
Furthermore, the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 153, states:
Question: For what reason can those born in the desire realm and the form realm give rise to the meditative attainment of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti), whereas those in the formless realm cannot?
Answer: The life-faculty (jīvitendriya) proceeds in dependence upon two factors.
First, form;
second, mind.
This meditative absorption is without mind.
Because it arises from a mind that has been interrupted:
when this meditative attainment arises while one is born in the desire or form realms,
although the mind has been interrupted, the life-faculty continues to function in dependence upon matter.
Although form is severed for one born in the formless realm,
life nevertheless proceeds in dependence upon the mind;
thus, if one is born there and gives rise to this meditative absorption, [it occurs].
Since both form and mind are absent,
the life-faculty has no support;
therefore, it too should be severed.
This should be called death;
it does not refer to entering meditative absorption.

Therefore, one who is born in that realm does not give rise to [the meditative attainments]. The commentary explains: because the cessation-attainment (*nirodha-samāpatti*) is formless, it is distinguished separately from those [formless realms].
Since non-conceptualization resides in form and its principle lies beyond words,
it is not explained therein.
If there were those who did not grant that this is what is called "common characteristic," [it would be so].
If there are masters of our own school who do not allow that the attainment of non-conception arises based on the form realm,
they would contradict what is stated in the *Jñānaprasthāna-śāstra*.
That treatise correlates the existence of form (*rūpa-bhava*) with the five formations (*pañca-saṃskāra*). "Existence of form" refers to existence within the realm of form (*rūpadhātu-bhava*).
The five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) are called the five formations; they are termed "formations" because they are impermanent (*anitya*).
Therefore, the *Vibhāṣā* (Śāriputrābhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra), fascicle 192, states:
"In this context, the various aggregates (*skandha*) are spoken of by the term 'formations' (*saṃskāra*).
The Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas of the past..."
It is said that the aggregates (skandha) are called formations (saṃskāra); now, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Śākyamuni says that formations are the aggregates.

The statement in this Abhidharma regarding the "five aggregates" (*pañca-skandha*) is intended to show that the five aggregates taught by the present Buddha are identical to the "five aggregates" (*pañca-dhātu*) taught by previous Buddhas;
thus ends the treatise. *Zhan* (廛) refers to a marketplace or a residential district.
The three realms are as chaotic and diverse as a marketplace.
As stated in the *Abhidharma-jñānaprasthāna-śāstra*:
"There may be those who possess form and have this form, yet there are sentient beings who do not possess the five aggregates."
This refers to sentient beings of the form realm who are either born in the heavens of those possessing perception and abide in a different realm with a non-concordant mind that is untainted,
or who have entered the attainment of non-perception.
Or one may enter the attainment of cessation,
or be born in the Heaven of Non-conception and have already attained entry into the maturation of non-conception;
such as these possess only the two aggregates of form and formations.
Excluding the remaining three aggregates,
this is what is meant by "matter exists here, but the five aggregates do not.
That treatise already states that sentient beings belonging to the realm of form enter the attainment of non-conceptualization (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*).
To say, however, that they do not enter [the formless realm] would contradict their own teaching.
From this it is proven that both of these meditative attainments arise based upon the desire and form realms.
This is called the "similar characteristic" (*sādharmya*).
As for the statement regarding the "different characteristic" (*vaidharmya*), namely that it is cultivated and arises again later,
this explains the second phrase.
This refers to the attainment of non-percipient absorption (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*). It can first arise within both the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and the form realm (*rūpadhātu*),
having been repeatedly cultivated since beginningless time.
Since it is easy to arise [from it] at that time,
one can first give rise to it in both realms; however,
the first arising of the attainment of cessation occurs only among human beings.
Because it has never been cultivated since beginningless time,
it is difficult when first arising; at the very moment of its initial emergence.
Because it can only arise through the power of exposition and through intense application,
the *Nyāyānusāra* states:
"Only among humans are there those who expound and those who explain."
Furthermore, because there is the force of a powerful preparatory application (*prayoga*), and because one understands the state of non-ideation (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*),
one perceives those non-ideating beings through the supernormal power of the divine eye (*divyacakṣur-abhijñā*) and,
taking that state to be *nirvāṇa*, proceeds to cultivate it immediately.

Regarding the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), there are cases where [the attainment] first arises therein; furthermore, it is explained that although the attainment of non-conception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*) may allow for its initial arising in the form realm, it must first have been preceded by preparatory practice (*prayoga*) initially arising in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
Having created karma in the desire realm to be experienced in a subsequent life,
one is then born in the form realm and gives rise to the supernormal power of recollecting past lives;
knowing that this was previously unattained, one now practices it once again.
Therefore, its initial arising is attained.
Having first cultivated and arisen in this meditative attainment of cessation among human beings, it [is subsequently maintained].
Since one first undergoes retrogression before being born into the form realm,
and subsequently cultivates and gives rise to this attainment of cessation based on a body in the form realm,
does this attainment of cessation also involve retrogression?
Question:
One should also say that there are those who take birth in the form realm (*rūpadhātu*).
This is proven by citing a sūtra concerning falling away (*parihāṇi*).
The general meaning can be understood.
Udāyin is translated here as "Appearance" (Chūxiàn).
Śīla is named "Precept" (Jiè). Samādhi...
"Samādhi" is a synonym for meditative concentration (dhyāna). "Prajñā" is wisdom (prajñā).
"Dṛṣṭadharma" refers to the present life.
This refers to the conditions for the decline of chronic illness and so forth;
"fulfillment" refers to the fruit of no-more-learning (aśaikṣa) and the gods who subsist on solid food (kavaḍīkāra-āhāra);
this refers to the six heavens of the desire realm.
Because they subsist on edible food, the bodies of the mind-made gods—
namely, the gods of the form realm—
are not produced from semen, blood, or other such substances.
Taking birth according to one’s will is called the body of the *manomaya-deva*. If one relies on the full explanation in the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 153, it says:
"The Sūtra states:
Venerable Śāriputra..."
He addressed the assembly of bhikṣus, saying:
"If a bhikṣu is fully endowed with morality, concentration, and wisdom,
he is able to repeatedly enter and emerge from the meditative attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling."
In this present life,
as well as at the time of death,
if they are unable to discern the noble intent of the Tathāgata.
At the end of his life, he transcends the realms of gods who subsist on solid food and is reborn among the gods of mind-made bodies; there,
he is further able to repeatedly enter and emerge from the meditative attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling.
"There is such a possibility;
this should be known as it truly is.
At that time, the Venerable Udāyin—
Sitting in that assembly,
he addressed the Venerable Śāriputra, saying:
"That bhikṣu was reborn among the Manomayakāyika devas."
"It is impossible for him to be able to enter and emerge from the attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling more than once;
this is not possible. The second and third [instances] were also spoken thus.
Question: For what reason, Venerable Udāyin?
Having repeatedly opposed the Venerable Śāriputra,
his answers to those doubts were not without foundation;
he thought to himself:
One who attains this meditative absorption must have already become detached from the defilements of the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*).
Upon the end of life, they should be reborn in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*).
