However, it is impossible for such a person to give rise to this meditative absorption while residing in that latter sphere.
Furthermore, because they did not understand the intention of Śāriputra,
they openly and repeatedly acted in opposition to him,
asking Śāriputra what his underlying purpose was.
"How is it that that venerable one did not understand?
He replied: "Śāriputra spoke of those born in the realm of form;

Although these two meditative attainments both have the cessation of mind and mental factors as their essential nature,

The various non-Buddhists reckon suffering and pleasure to be birth and death;

taking the existence of the desire realm to be suffering.
In the first, second, and third dhyānas, there are the feelings of joy and pleasure;
yet, failing to understand the equanimity of the fourth dhyāna as well as other mental states and mental factors, they speak thus.
Although suffering and pleasure have been transcended within the fourth dhyāna,

Therefore, within the preparatory stage (*prayoga*), that which involves a partial aversion toward perception (*saṃjñā*) is called the "attainment of non-perception" (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*). As for the "attainment of the cessation of sensation and perception" (*nirodha-samāpatti*), at the time of its preparation, there is likewise a partial aversion toward both sensation (*vedanā*) and perception;

Regarding the perceptions of the various dhyānas and the formless attainments,

Therefore, during the preparatory stage (*prayoga*), one specifically cultivates aversion toward feeling (*vedanā*) and perception (*saṃjñā*).

This is just as the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*) also cognizes feelings and so forth.

because the obstructing wind is no different [from that which acts later],
just as in its subsequent stages.
In its subsequent state, this arrow would not fall,
because the obstructing wind remains without distinction,
just as it was in its initial state. Furthermore, there must be some distinct, real entity that exists until this point which is designated as "wholesome."
The Master of the Treatise (Śāstrakāra) adopts the position of the Sarvāstivādins.
Regarding the question of whether death occurs solely through the exhaustion of the life-span or due to other causes as well,
this constitutes the second section of questions and answers for analysis.
This is the question.
As for the statement in the *Prajñapti-śāstra* that it "reaches the conditions of calamity," this is the answer.
The fourfold distinction from the *Prakaraṇapāda-śāstra* can be understood from its text. Furthermore,
one should also state that it is "because of relinquishing the life-force (*āyuḥ-saṃskāra*)."
The Master of the Treatise explains:
Within this fourth phrase,
one should also state that it is because the Buddhas and Arhats relinquish their life-force (*āyuḥ-saṃskāra*).
It is not because [the author] does not speak of them that they are not considered "unjust" conditions;
rather, it is because the author of the treatise bases his analysis on unjust conditions.
As stated in the twentieth fascicle of the *Vibhāṣā* within the section on the "neither-nor" category:
The author of that treatise made this statement to demonstrate that there are untimely deaths; thus,
although the Buddha’s wealth and lifespan were both not yet exhausted, he entered parinirvāṇa.
"However, this is not an untimely death, because it is accomplished through the power of the concentration of the limit (*koṭi-samādhi*). The *Nyāya* refutes this treatise, stating:
"One should not further say that it is because of the relinquishing of the life-force (*āyuḥ-saṃskāra*)."
Since the meaning is already subsumed within the first phrase, the *Nyāyānusāra* states:
"One who practices the relinquishment of life-force causes the karma that projects longevity to instead project wealth and happiness;
because this is the exhaustion of the karma that projects longevity, it should be called 'death through the exhaustion of life-force.'"
The Abhidharmakośa masters offer this defense: "Death due to the exhaustion of merit does not mean that one dies because one's lifespan has been exhausted.
How, then, could it be subsumed under the first category?"
Furthermore, this contradicts the *Vibhāṣā*, which states that because the Buddha’s wealth and lifespan are both not yet exhausted, he is included in the fourth category.
As for the claim that it contradicts the *Abhidharmakośa*—how can this possibly harm your own school?
For even in the state where the lifespan is exhausted, death occurs only when [all conditions] reach total exhaustion.
To provide a further explanation of the third phrase:
between the two types of karma, that which induces longevity is superior;
thus, among the three types of death, death through the exhaustion of the life-span is the subject of this third phrase.
Although merit is exhausted at death and thus lacks further efficacy—
since one dies naturally when the lifespan is exhausted—
it is nevertheless said that death occurs because both [merit and lifespan] are exhausted.
Because when the lifespan is exhausted, the merit is also exhausted;

therefore, when both are exhausted simultaneously, death occurs, which is described as "death due to the exhaustion of both. Furthermore, this interpretation serves to address an anticipated objection.
The intent of that objection is as follows:
When merit is exhausted but life is not yet exhausted, it is possible to continue living while undergoing suffering;
however, when life is exhausted but merit is not yet exhausted, one certainly cannot live further.
Thus, we know that this occurs at the time when both are exhausted.
It is not the case that the exhaustion of merit renders one powerless at death; rather, one should say that death occurs because the lifespan has been exhausted,
and one should not say that death occurs because merit has been exhausted.
This passage exists to resolve this objection:
while the exhaustion of merit has no actual causal efficacy regarding death,
it is simply because death occurs at the point where both [merit and lifespan] are exhausted.
It is said that death occurs because both [the life-faculty and the heat] are exhausted.

Regarding the question, "What is the meaning of the statement in the *Abhidharmajñānaprasthāna-śāstra* that one 'reaches' that [state]?"—this cites the text of the *Jñānaprasthāna* to inquire into its underlying intention. Question: As in the case of the "neither-killing-nor-harming" category, many types are mentioned for the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
The meaning of "abiding together" is the same as that [of the other two attainments].

Why, then, are only the attainment of non-perception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*) and the attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*) mentioned? The explanation is that these two attainments encompass the entirety of the mindless states;
therefore, they are mentioned separately.
The others each possess only a small portion of mind;
therefore, they are not mentioned. Furthermore, it is explained that these two meditative attainments do not diminish the life-span;
for this reason, they are treated separately.
Suppose a person who is destined to live for a hundred years enters those two meditative absorptions at the age of fifty;
even if they remain in absorption for a thousand years, they will only emerge from it then.
Not consuming solid food, he further receives another fifty years of life.
Since the remainder would otherwise shorten his lifespan, it is not mentioned separately. Question: When one enters the two meditative absorptions (dhyānas), the lifespan lasts for a long time.

What is the fruit of this karma? The explanation states: according to the previous case of prolonging life, it is either the fruit of the distant preparatory application (*prayoga*) prior to entering meditative absorption, or the fruit of a present wholesome volition (*cetanā*) belonging to the desire realm.

Alternatively, it is the fruit of residual karma (*avaśeṣa-karma*), or the fruit of indeterminate karma (*aniyata-karma*). Another interpretation holds that through the power of meditative concentration (*samādhi-bala*), past karma is reinforced so as to prolong one's lifespan;
however, this should be further examined against the textual sources.
Furthermore, the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 151, states:
Question: In the desire realm, although one does not enter the two mindless attainments (*acittaka-samāpatti*), there are also [factors] that do not follow along with conditions (*anuvartaka*).
Why is it not taught?
It should indeed be taught;
that it is not taught [is for a specific reason].
One should know that this meaning is not exhaustive.
Some say that what is stated here refers to the definitive [teaching].
That is to say, when one abides in either of the two mindless attainments (*acittaka-samāpatti*),

the life-force (*jīvita*) and formations (*saṃskāra*) definitely do not proceed in accordance with conditions; as for others, they may proceed according to conditions, and therefore these are not mentioned.
Some say that although there are other states in the desire realm that do not function in accordance with conditions,
they are mentioned specifically here to demonstrate the power of the two meditative attainments (*samāpatti*).
If the body upon which [the attainment] relies reaches even a single moment and remains, [it is considered to have arisen].
The author of the treatise replies:
"That which is based upon the physical body is called 'continuity' (*saṃtati*).
Therefore, the *Vibhāṣā* states:"
Some say that the material body is called the "continuum," meaning that for one born in the desire realm who does not abide in the attainment of non-perception or the attainment of cessation,
the life-span proceeds in accordance with the continuum of the material body.
Why is this so? If the body is harmonious and peaceful, one's lifespan will not be cut short;
if the body is impaired and damaged, one's lifespan will be prematurely ended.
In the kingdom of Kaśmīra, there are those who die prematurely;
this is the interpretation of the second Vaibhāṣika master.
The first [master] explains that [the lifespan] proceeds in accordance with the continuum, manifesting that there are obstructions to life.
Furthermore, once they have arisen [in that state], they abide there for the duration of their lifespan without obstruction.
Because of this, it is certain that untimely death exists.
Therefore, the Sūtra states that they "attain parinirvāṇa of their own accord."
Citing scripture to establish this proof:
among the four statements, the first three demonstrate that [the mind] evolves in accordance with the continuity of the stream;
the fourth demonstrates that it abides as soon as it arises.
This explains the first phrase: "The gods of Forgetfulness through Play" (krīḍā-pramoṣaka-deva).
This refers to those who are so attached to play that their bodies and minds become exhausted and they lose their mindfulness.
Due to the predominance of joy, they pass away from there; as for the gods of mental wrath (*manorāga*),
it means that their minds give rise to predominant fury,
and with hearts full of resentment, they stare at one another with narrowed eyes.
Having long harbored resentment that did not subside,
they perished there; these two may be gods of the Heaven of the Four Great Kings.
Or perhaps it is the Heaven of the Thirty-three.
Thus, the *Vibhāṣā* (Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra), fascicle 199, asks regarding these two heavens:
"Question: In what places do these various devas reside?"
Some say they dwell on the terraces of Mount Sumeru;
others say they are among the Trāyastriṃśa gods. Furthermore, in the first of these statements, one should also mention the Buddhas, because they enter parinirvāṇa by shortening their own lifespans.
This is merely a brief indication and does not exhaustively enumerate all cases.
Therefore, the *Vibhāṣā*, fascicle 151, further states regarding the first phrase:
Furthermore, there is another class of beings—whether nāgas, garuḍas, pretas, humans, or others—who can only harm themselves and not be harmed by others;
yet they are capable of harming other sentient beings.
The explanation of the second phrase is a brief indication;
it does not provide an exhaustive enumeration of all cases.
Therefore, the second section of the *Vibhāṣā* further states:
"Furthermore, there is another class [of beings], whether they be nāgas, garuḍas, or ghosts, or humans, or even others."
"That which can be harmed by others but not by oneself" refers to both [types of harm];
"that which can be harmed" refers to sentient beings up to those in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
This explains the third phrase.
One may understand this by reflecting upon it as appropriate;
this has been briefly cited for now and is not an exhaustive enumeration of all instances.
Therefore, the *Vibhāṣā* also states in its third section:
"That is to say, various birds and beasts, or nāgas, garuḍas, or ghosts, humans, or even others."
Regarding those who may harm themselves or others,
and those who harm neither— up until the time of entering the womb of a Wheel-Turning King—
this explains the fourth phrase.
Among these, there are those that must wait for conditions to take birth;
therefore, it is not [a case of] killing.

Furthermore, there is no karma of killing in the form and formless realms. Another explanation is that the bodies of the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) and the form realm are exceptionally sublime.
Neither can be harmed. Because there is no physical body in the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu), it likewise cannot be harmed.
Those bound by the evil karma of the hells (naraka) cannot die through harm. In Uttarakuru, one must necessarily live for a thousand years.
Furthermore, there is no karma of killing; one who has seen the Path will certainly not meet an untimely death during the fifteen moments [of the path of seeing].

This is because those who emerge from the meditative absorption of loving-kindness (maitrī-samādhi) do so for the sake of benefiting and bringing happiness to others. As for the meditative absorption of cessation (nirodha-samāpatti) and the state of non-conception (asaṃjñi), they result from the power of meditative concentration (samādhi).
Neither of these cases involves mutual harm. Regarding the "royal seer" (rājarṣi), it refers to a wheel-turning king who renounces his home to practice the Way;
being endowed with the five supernatural powers, he is called a royal seer. Another interpretation holds that it refers to the crown prince of a wheel-turning king.
Once the consecration has been performed,
one should first train in the holy life (brahmacarya) practiced by the King of the Rishis; therefore,
he is called a Royal Rishi (Rājarṣi).
Because he was destined to succeed to the rank of a Wheel-Turning King (cakravartin),
they did not harm him either; nor did they harm the Buddha’s messenger—
that is, the person sent by the Buddha.
Because he acted by the power of the Buddha’s messenger, his undertaking was not yet finished, nor did he cause both to die;
he was like Jīvaka (translated here as "Life-Sustainer"),
who could effectively treat all illnesses and sustain life.
Formerly called Jīva;
alternatively called Jīvaka, which is a corruption.
The Buddha sent him into the fire to embrace and retrieve Sudīrghaka.
This is called Youming (Vimalakīrti);
the old transcription Shuti-jia (Jyotiska) is erroneous.
His parents were of immense wealth, yet in their old age they had no son.
Suddenly, upon becoming pregnant, she questioned the various non-Buddhist teachers (tīrthikas).
They all declared it would be a girl who would not live long.
When she questioned the Buddha, the Buddha prophesied that it would be a boy who would live a long life and possess every virtue.
Among the non-Buddhists who lack the medicine of skillful means,
a son remains unharmed when his mother’s body is cremated;
yet the Buddha sent Jīvaka into the fire to retrieve her.
There is one who does not die because of the power of the Buddha’s prediction;
there is one who does not die because of the Buddha’s messenger.
The detailed explanation is as in the Sūtra. According to the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 151.
The five men, including Dāmiḷa and the others,
were all those for whom the Buddha had given specific predictions. Dāmiḷa...
This is called *dharmas* (phenomena);
*lā* means "to grasp."
Because he begged from the deity Bhava and was named after the deity from whom he received it, he is called Bhavila.
This son of a householder is called Udraka; this means "Superior."
He was also the son of a householder.
Gaṅgā is the name of a river goddess.
"Rāhula" means "appropriated.
Out of affection for their son, his parents gave him this name based on the deity:
"My son has been appropriated by the deity Khaṅgi."
Other malevolent spirits and deities cannot harm them.
If one calls out their name in a female voice, it is *Gaṅgī*;
if one calls out their name in a male voice, it is *Gaṅgā*.
The old [translation] "Ganges" is an error. Yaśas, the son of an elder—
*yaśas* here meaning "renown"—
entered the Buddha's teaching to leave the household life.
Crossing the deep current at night, he was safe and unhurt. *Kumārajīva*:
*kumāra* means "youth" (*kōtō*), and *jīva* means "to sustain life" (*kakumei*).
He was named the youth Jīvaka;
he was a bodhisattva in his final existence,
meaning the body born within the royal palace.
They will certainly attain Buddhahood because their tasks are not yet completed; furthermore,
when the mother of this Bodhisattva carries the Bodhisattva in her womb...
By the power of the Bodhisattva’s merit, his mother remains unharmed;

this is due to the sustaining power of all the supreme karmic deeds of the universal monarchs, as well as during the time when the mother of this universal monarch carries the future monarch in her womb.
"By the power of the Cakravartin’s merit, his mother was not harmed. This is merely a brief indication and does not exhaustively enumerate all cases.
Therefore, in the fourth section of the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, among the records concerning the Buddha, it further mentions Sudarśana; it also says:
A person abiding in their final existence whose tasks are yet unaccomplished;
humans at the beginning of an eon;
and the nāga kings Ailavila and Sāgara, as well as King Yama, and so forth.
And as for another class who are both non-harming [in body and mind],
if that is so, why does it say "sentient beings who have reached birth"?
The Master of the Treatise cites a sūtra to raise this objection.
If the Vaibhāṣika masters claim that among those who are neither harmed [by themselves nor by others],
all sentient beings of the form and formless realms are likewise neither harmed,
why does the Sūtra mention only the Peak of Existence (bhavāgra)?
Regarding the tradition that the remainder cannot be harmed even by the "neither-perception-nor-non-perception" [state],
the answer is:
the Vaibhāṣika masters maintain this tradition.
The remaining three formless attainments and the four dhyānas have acquired selves that can be harmed by both their own and higher paths.
For the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*), there is no harm from either its own or higher paths.
Based on this, it is said that [the Peak of Existence] cannot be harmed by either [self or others].
Is it not the case that those from the Peak of Existence down should be called "harmed by others"?
The author of the treatise refutes this objection regarding killing.
In this way, one should speak of those who attain rebirth in heaven through supreme bliss.

Regarding the Master of the Treatise’s (śāstrakāra) explanation of the Sūtra’s statement that "even the Peak of Existence (bhavāgra) is neither harmed nor benefited," it should be explained in this same manner.

By citing the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*), the first three formless attainments (*ārūpya*) and the four meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*) are revealed. This can be understood from the examples provided below, such as "or perhaps... and so forth.
Regarding that sūtra, the word "like" (*yathā*) applies until the point where it cannot be analogized to that [case].
The opponent objects: In the sūtra cited,
there is the word "like" (iva), which can clarify the meaning of the metaphor.
To cite one case is to reveal the rest;
however, this *Śāriputra-sūtra* does not contain the word "sound" (*śabda*),
and thus it cannot be cited as an analogy for the *Brahmaparṣad-sūtra* and others.
If it is argued that the illustrative meaning [of the example] is also present in the word "like" (*yathā*),
the Master of the Treatise (Śrīlāta) counters with a refutation: [as stated] in the *Saptavijñānasthiti-sūtra*.
Although the first station of consciousness (*vijñānasthiti*) is not an explicit illustration, it nonetheless possesses the nature of a "likeness" (*yathā-śabda*).
Therefore, one should know that the term "likeness" does not necessarily denote an explicit illustration.
Let this digression cease for now.
The Master of the Treatise has ceased the dispute.
Having already explained the nature of the life-faculty up to birth, duration, change, and cessation,
the following section— the sixth major heading— clarifies the four characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*).
Among these, first is the clarification of the essential nature of the characteristic of light,
and second is the general rebuttal of external objections. Regarding the clarification of the essential nature of the characteristic of light:
First, the explanation of the primary characteristics (*mūla-lakṣaṇa*); second, the explanation of the secondary characteristics (*anulakṣaṇa*).

This [section] clarifies the primary characteristics. "Characteristics" (*lakṣaṇa*) serves as the heading for the chapter; "that which is" (*yad*) and what follows constitutes the formal explanation. That which is produced through causes and conditions is termed [characteristic].
Phenomena such as form and mind arise from causes and conditions.

Because they exist by virtue of those [causes], they are called "conditioned" (*saṃskṛta*). Conditioned phenomena are manifold; these various conditioned phenomena are that upon which characteristics depend.
The characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) is the signifier;

it is that which can represent the fact that all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) have the nature of being conditioned, each possessing its own distinct essence (*svabhāva*), which is termed "nature" (*dhātu*).
A characteristic does not arise in isolation but must depend upon a phenomenon. For full precision, one should say: "the nature of arising of all conditioned phenomena."
"Up to the nature of the cessation of all conditioned phenomena.
Regarding the commentary which states that "nature" (*tā*) means "essence" (*svabhāva*),
this refers to the prose section.
First, the commentary on the root verses;
second, the analysis through questions and answers.
This is the commentary on the verses.
Because these four are the defining characteristics of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*),
any phenomenon that possesses them must be included within the category of the conditioned;
that which is contrary to these is an unconditioned phenomenon (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*).
In this school, the essence of all phenomena is fundamentally existent.

The four characteristics (catur-lakṣaṇa) are described solely with respect to their function regarding phenomena, not in terms of their essential nature. Among these, that which can initiate the function of a phenomenon causes it to enter the present.
It is called "arising. If the characteristic of arising did not exist,
then all conditioned phenomena [would not arise].
Like space and so forth, [phenomena] should originally be unarisen;
yet having reached the present, they abide and cause their respective functions to remain stable for a time, each inducing its own fruit.
Therefore, this is called "abiding" (*sthiti*).
If phenomena that lack the characteristic of abiding were to abide even momentarily,
they would be unable to further project their own results. If, on the other hand, they were to project results repeatedly by the power of abiding itself,
then a distinct factor capable of weakening that capacity to project results would necessarily exist.
It prevents them from being able to repeatedly produce their own results;
therefore, it is called "difference" (*anyathātva*). If this characteristic of difference did not exist, [the result would arise repeatedly].
Their functional capacity is diminished;

for what reason are they unable to repeatedly induce their own results? Or, as for "having a different characteristic," this refers to the continuity of conditioned forces (*saṃskāra*) being different later than it was before its cause.
If one were to abide by the power of persistence,
it would cause all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) to gradually become superior to what preceded them; however,
due to the transformation and decay (*anyathātva*), they cause subsequent states to be inferior to those that precede them.
Although there may be dharmas that are subsequently superior to those preceding them,

this is due to the assistance of other conditions which suppress the capacity of the dissimilar characteristics and bring forth the subsequent superiority. Once the distinct efficacy has already declined and been impaired, [the former state ceases].
Cessation is further able to destroy the functioning of that [dharma] in the present;
because it enters the past, it is called "cessation.
If the characteristic and function of cessation did not exist, there would be no cessation.
If its activity were not to cease, it would have to be eternal.
It should be understood that, according to this school, the characteristic of arising exerts its activity in the future,
while the three characteristics of duration, change, and cessation exert their activities simultaneously in the present.

Although both are established based upon a single dharma, they differ in their respective points of reference and their functions are distinct. Question: The shortest duration of time is called a *kṣaṇa*.
Since their functions are already distinct, why is time called a *kṣaṇa*? Answer: In the *Abhidharmamahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 39, there are two explanations.
One explanation states:
although their essence is simultaneous, their functions occur sequentially;
the completion of the process of arising and ceasing within a single dharma is termed one *kṣaṇa*.
Furthermore, another explanation states:
although the stages of arising and ceasing may span more than a single moment,
each single moment nonetheless possesses three natures.
Therefore, it is said that the three characteristics exist in a single moment.
The former school bases this on their functional activity;
the latter school bases it on the simultaneous possession of the three essences.
Each [definition] relies on a single meaning, yet there is no commentator [to adjudicate]; thus, it is sufficient as one interpretation:
the moment when a function arises is called a "kṣaṇa."
The time during which the three characteristics of the present function is also called a single *kṣaṇa*.
This is an explanation based on the extreme brevity of the moment when their activity arises.
Is it not said in the Sūtras that conditioned phenomena possess the characteristic of "arising"?
The following is the analysis through question and answer. This is the question:
the Sūtra mentions only three.
Question: Why does the treatise state that there are four characteristics? Should it not be stated in this sutra that there are four? Answer:
In this sutra, it would logically have been necessary to explain four [points].
Why are they not explained? This is the inquiry.

Regarding the statement "abiding-characteristic up to conditioned-characteristic," this master explains that the sūtra’s initial exposition does not explicitly mention the so-called abiding-characteristic.
This is his interpretation.
The Sūtra does not mention those who abide [in the stages],
because sentient beings easily grow weary of the faults and defects inherent in the three characteristics; therefore,
the Sūtra speaks of them separately.
Because sentient beings find it difficult to grow weary of abiding and remaining in their current state,
the Sūtra does not mention "abiding. However, the Sūtra’s mention of "abiding-and-changing" (*sthity-anyathātva*) is another name for this very "change," which is explained in relation to abiding.
Because it is the change of abiding, it is called "change of abiding" (*sthity-anyathātva*).
It is just as "arising" (*jāti*) is named "origination" and "cessation" (*nirodha*) is named "exhaustion" (*kṣaya*); these are different names for the same thing, such as "eye" and "organ of sight."
It should be understood in this way.

The term "change-of-abiding" (*sthity-anyathātva*) is used as a distinct name because one fears that the name "change-of-abiding" might be confused with the characteristic of abiding (*sthiti-lakṣaṇa*) among the three characteristics;
therefore, it is explained separately.
The power of arising (utpāda) causes the dharma to enter the present through its function of transition;
the power of difference (anyathātva) and cessation (nirodha) cause it to enter the past through their functions of transition.
That which is currently entering the past is solely due to the power of cessation.
Furthermore, because they speak of distinct characteristics to assist in cessation,
and because these faults are grave, the Sūtra speaks of three;
this can be understood through the analogies provided.

Because it is non-transient, not urgent, and characterized by constant joy and peaceful abiding, the Sūtra does not mention it among the characteristics of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta-lakṣaṇa*), in order to induce worldlings to feel revulsion [toward the conditioned].
Furthermore, because unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*) are already present [as a reality], the Sūtra does not mention them [among those characteristics].
The second explanation:
because "abiding" (sthiti) is confused with the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta), the Sūtra does not mention it.
Some claim that this Sūtra extends [the definition] to what is called the characteristic of abiding-and-change (sthity-anyathātva-lakṣaṇa).
Third explanation: Because "abiding" (*sthiti*) and "alteration" (*anyathātva*) are explained in combination, the Sūtra speaks of three [characteristics].
One might ask: what is the purpose of explaining them in such a combined manner?
Question:
Regarding the statement that "abiding" (sthiti) pertains to sentient beings up to the four characteristics of conditioned phenomena (saṃskṛtalakṣaṇa). Answer:
This is taught by combining the state of abiding in revulsion with its opposite,
just as one might show Kālī together with Śrī;
to inspire revulsion for Śrī, one first shows Kālī.
The two sisters, Kālī and Śrī, are always in each other’s company.
The elder sister is named Śrī;
wherever she goes, she is able to bring about benefit.
Her younger sister was named Kālī;
she was so called because her ears were black.
Wherever she went, she brought about ruin and destruction.
Fools are greedily attached to auspiciousness;
the wise, wishing to cause them to feel revulsion and renounce it, first show them the "Black Ear.
Once they have seen the Black Ear, they abandon even their auspiciousness.
The old [translation] refers to them as "Goddess of Merit" (Puṇyadevatā) and "Darkness Woman" (Tamasī);
this was an error by the translators.
The same applies to duration (sthiti) and change (anyathātva).
In order to cause [the practitioner] to dwell in revulsion, these are explained together with their opposites.

Therefore, there are definitely four conditioned characteristics (*saṃskṛtalakṣaṇa*). As for the statement that "these characteristics, such as arising, reach [their respective objects], such as the characteristic of arising": [it means they apply to each other].

The following clarifies the arising of questions concerning secondary characteristics (*anulakṣaṇa*). Since primary characteristics (*mūlalakṣaṇa*) are conditioned (*saṃskṛta*), they must themselves possess [secondary characteristics] such as arising (*jāti*) and so forth.
If there were further characteristics, it would lead to an infinite regress;
one should say that there are further [characteristics] up to the point where the eighth and first existents have the capacity [to function].
The preceding sentence answers the first question.
The second sentence provides a general response to the second question.
The *Śāstra* states: "Up to 'by means of the four secondary characteristics' (*anulakṣaṇa*)," which refers to the prose section (*gadya*).
First, the commentary on the root verses;
second, the extensive determination.
Within the commentary on the root verses:
This explains the first phrase.
These four primary characteristics (mūla-lakṣaṇa) function as defining marks because they possess secondary characteristics (anulakṣaṇa) that serve as their indicators.
Therefore, they are called "conditioned" (*saṃskṛta*).
Here, it is precisely explained that the primary characteristics (*mūla-lakṣaṇa*) are conditioned by the four secondary characteristics (*anulakṣaṇa*),
while all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are said to be conditioned by the four primary characteristics.
They are spoken of because they mutually condition one another;

although the primary characteristics (lakṣaṇa) themselves are also conditioned by primary characteristics, this discussion here is for the time being conducted in relation to the secondary characteristics (anulakṣaṇa). It should be understood that each of the four primary characteristics—whether great or minor—has three names.
Regarding the three names for the primary characteristics (*mahālakṣaṇa*): the first is called the "primary characteristic" (*mūlalakṣaṇa*),
in contrast to the secondary characteristics (*anulakṣaṇa*).
Alternatively, it is called the "primary characteristic" (mūla-lakṣaṇa) because it is the characteristic upon which this dharma itself is based;
secondly, it is called the "great characteristic" (mahā-lakṣaṇa) in contrast to the "minor characteristics" (parīttaka-lakṣaṇa).
Alternatively, they are called "great characteristics" because they characterize eight phenomena.

The three individual characteristics, such as arising (*jāti*), are called "small characteristics" because they characterize [the secondary characteristics] such as the arising of arising (*jāti-jāti*). As for the three names of the small characteristics:
The first is called "conforming to characteristics" (*anulakṣaṇa*), because it conforms to the primary characteristics (*mūlalakṣaṇa*), or because the characteristics conform to the primary [entity].
The second is called the "minor characteristic" (*anuvyañjana*),
because its form is subordinate to the major characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), or because it characterizes a single dharma.
These are called the "minor characteristics" (anulakṣaṇas).
The third group consists of "the arising of arising" (jāti-jāti) and so forth; they are so named because they correspond to [the primary characteristics] such as arising.
The character "sheng" (生) in the upper instance refers to the Lesser Birth;
the character "sheng" (生) in the lower instance refers to the Greater Birth.
Because it is able to give birth to births, another interpretation holds that the character "sheng" (生) in the upper instance refers to the Greater Birth.
The character "sheng" (生) in "xià shēng" (下生) refers to the "arising" (*jāti*).

Because it is the arising of arising, it is called "the arising of arising" (*jātijāti*). As with the explanation of the arising of arising, the same applies to the remaining three characteristics. [Objection:
Is it not the case that the primary characteristics would lead to an infinite regress?
The following explains the second phrase.

Question: Is it not the case that, just as the primary characteristics (mūla-lakṣaṇa) correspond to the phenomena they characterize (lakṣya-dharma), each one should likewise have four secondary characteristics (anulakṣaṇa)?
These four secondary characteristics (anulakṣaṇas) each further have four [secondary characteristics] of their own, which would lead to an infinite regress;
yet there is no such fault, because they function as distinct capacities.
Answer: They are distinguished by their primary and secondary capacities;
thus, there is no infinite regress.
What is meant by "functionality"?
It refers to the activity of a dharma; that is to say, when a dharma possesses efficacy.
The explanation of functional capacity (*kāritra*) refers to the activity of the eight dharmas;
it is also termed "human effort" (*puruṣakāra*).
"Śramaṇa" refers to a "person" (puruṣa).
It is named after its function, just as one speaks of a "person's use.
It is designated by way of analogy.

The primary characteristics have [functions] with respect to eight [dharmas], while the secondary characteristics have [functions] with respect to one; each has its own specific utility. What is the meaning of this?
Regarding the further objection: "When a phenomenon arises, it reaches [its own arising], which would lead to the fault of infinite regress"—
the explanation of this passage can be understood from the text itself.
Regarding the Sautrāntika masters' statement that the essence of the attainment (prāpti) is substantially real,
the following provides a detailed determination of this point;
specifically, it refutes [the existence of prāpti] by means of the three types of valid cognition (pramāṇa).
The Sautrāntika masters maintain that the four characteristics, such as arising and so forth, have no substantial reality;
their conceptual analysis is like the analytical division of space. This applies to the four objects, beginning with visible form, as well as the five sense faculties and so on.
That is to say, these various characteristics are not established through direct perception (pratyakṣa) like the five objects of the senses,
nor are they established through inference (anumāna) like the five sense faculties.
Its substantial existence is not proven by scriptural authority (*āptāgama*).
That which is the ultimate teaching is called "scriptural authority" (*āptāgama*); it is also termed "the authority of the noble teachings" (*āryāgamapramāṇa*).
This would mean that it is absent from all three means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
How, then, can its existence be known?
If that is so, why is it said that "it can also be cognized through the arrival [of the object]?"
The Sarvāstivādins rebuke the Sautrāntikas, stating:
"Even though there is no knowledge through direct perception or inference, there is scriptural authority;
for it is stated in the sūtras that conditioned phenomena have arising and so forth."
The sixth case-ending further states "clearly knows," which makes it evident that there is a substantial entity.
"O Beloved of the Gods, since the ultimate meaning is what you rely upon,
the Sautrāntikas harmonize this by stating that one must rely solely on the meaning and should not cling to the literal phrasing."
What is meant by the true meaning taught in this sutra? This is the inquiry.
It refers to those of the class of fools up to those who are capable of understanding.
The Sautrāntika school explains the sūtras to demonstrate the absence of substantial reality,
stating that those of the class of fools are blinded by ignorance and lack the eye of wisdom.
Regarding the continuous succession of conditioned formations before and after,
they do not know them to be impermanent; they conceive of them as one and as permanent,
and grasp at them as a self.
Some cling to "mine," and for a long night they develop attachment toward it.
The Blessed One, in order to sever that clinging and destroy that attachment, [taught this].
It reveals that the continuity of activity has as its essence the nature of being conditioned and dependently originated,
and thus the three characteristics are provisionally established.
Therefore, that sūtra states:
"There are three conditioned characteristics of the conditioned;
they do not manifest all conditioned phenomena."
Within a single moment, there exist the three characteristics as substantial entities;
by means of that single moment,
the three characteristics— arising and so forth— are produced.
Because it cannot be known through the observation of wisdom,
that which cannot be known should not be established as a characteristic.
Therefore, that sutra further states:
The arising of conditioned phenomena can be known;
their cessation, duration, and alteration can also be known.
However, since the three characteristics—arising and so forth—cannot be known within a single moment, [how could they be known in succession?]
The Sūtra further states "clearly knowing.
It is clearly understood that this is certainly a provisional designation based on the continuum (*saṃtāna*),
and not based on a single moment (*kṣaṇa*).
Because [the three characteristics] are understood only by way of the continuity (*saṃtāna*),
this citation of the sūtra’s intent proves that the three characteristics do not exist in a single moment (*kṣaṇa*).
While it is established that they exist in terms of continuity, in response to the objection, only a single passage from that sūtra is cited.
In the *Vyākhyā*, two passages from that sūtra are cited in full.
Regarding the passage where the sūtra repeats the statement that "up to the point of manifest [action], it is wholesome or unwholesome," this is the Sautrāntika interpretation of the sūtra.
However, regarding the preceding scriptural passage which states that there are three conditioned characteristics of the conditioned,
the sutra should have simply stated that there are three characteristics of the conditioned.

However, the reason the Sūtra reiterates the phrase "subsequent conditioned existence" (paunarbhavika-saṃskāra) is to make known that these characteristics indicate that the essence of the characterized phenomena (lakṣya-dharma) is itself conditioned.
If one were to speak only of the characteristics of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta-lakṣaṇa*),
one would not know that these characteristics definitively indicate that the essential nature of the characterized phenomenon (*lakṣya-dharmasvabhāva*) is conditioned;
or, one might doubt whether these characteristics indicate that the conditioned exists.
Because [the term] applies to both the wholesome and the unwholesome, etc.,

the phrase "conditioned by subsequent existence" (paunarbhavika) is employed so that one may know that these characteristics indicate that the characterized phenomena (lakṣya-dharma) are necessarily conditioned (saṃskṛta).
Therefore, one should not say that because this mark indicates the existence of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*),
it is like a white heron whose presence indicates that water is not absent;
nor should one say that this mark [is the cause].

Manifesting conditioned phenomena as wholesome or unwholesome is like the physical traits of a young girl that can indicate whether she will become a man or a woman, or whether her future affairs will be virtuous or non-virtuous;
for instance, if her nature is chaste and her ankles are slender and rounded.
With skin that is fine and soft, teeth that are white, and lips that are thin—
one will surely give birth to virtuous children. These marks signify goodness.
If her nature is not chaste, her feet and knees are clumsy and large,
her skin is coarse and rough, her teeth are black, her lips are thick,
and she gives birth to unworthy sons.
This mark indicates that it is not wholesome.
This conditioned characteristic is not like a white heron indicating the presence of water.
The characteristic of a young girl does not indicate whether [the phenomenon] is wholesome or unwholesome;
it merely indicates that the essence of the characterized phenomenon is conditioned— that is,
the continuity of all formations (saṃskāra) which reaches decay, alteration, and destruction.
The author of the treatise describes the Sautrāntika school’s position:
the four characteristics are conventionally established in relation to the continuity (*saṃtati*) of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*),
and do not pertain to a single moment (*kṣaṇa*).
"Continuity" (saṃtati) refers to the continuity of a single lifetime,
or the continuity of a single momentary process,
as appropriate; its initial stage of arising is termed "birth" (jāti).
The state of final exhaustion and cessation is called "cessation" (nirodha).
The uninterrupted continuity and progression during the intermediate period is called "abiding" (sthiti).
The differentiation between preceding and succeeding moments within this very state of abiding is called "alteration of abiding" (sthity-anyathātva).

Because it abides while being distinct, it is called "abiding" (*sthiti*); because it is distinct, the Buddha, the World-Honored One, based upon this continuity, elucidated the meaning of the four characteristics.
At one time, in the midst of a great assembly, he addressed Nanda, saying:
This noble son Nanda well understands that arising, abiding, change, and cessation all depend upon feeling.
Before Nanda had attained the Path, he frequently gave rise to sensual desire;
sensual desire arises because of feeling.
In order to abandon craving,
one constantly contemplates all feelings (vedanā) as arising, abiding, changing, and ceasing; therefore,
even after attaining the Path, one continues to contemplate those feelings.
The Buddha explained this meaning with reference to Nanda.
If one considers it in terms of continuity, it can be well understood;
however, if one speaks of moments (*kṣaṇa*), it is difficult to well understand [the arising, abiding, changing, and ceasing of sensation].
The undergoing of future birth can be known through present cognition;
however, the undergoing of duration, change, and cessation must reside in the present.
It is logically impossible for the wisdom capable of knowing these to exist in the past or the future.
Since both [the cognition and the sensation] are present simultaneously, it is logically contradictory that wisdom within the same associated mental state (*samanvāgata*) could cognize the sensation;
for it has already been stated that one cognizes the arising, abiding, change, and cessation of the sensation.
Knowing that birth and the other [characteristics] do not occur in a single moment,
one should understand that the present cognition arises separately in each moment,
cognizing the four characteristics such as the arising of the continuity of sensation.

This interpretation is not contradictory. Furthermore, it is explained that if arising and so forth possessed substantial entities, how could one contemplate arising, abiding, and so on in relation to feeling?
If arising, abiding, and so forth were present within every single moment, [how could they be observed sequentially?]
How can they be observed simultaneously?
Since they are observed individually according to the sequence of feeling (*vedanā*),
it is known that birth (*jāti*) and the other [links] have no separate substantial entities.
It is not for a single moment;
therefore, the verse says, "up to the statement that it abides in a continuum," which cites the verse as proof.
These three verses are all verses spoken by the masters of the Sautrāntika school.
The first two lines clarify that the characteristics of arising and so forth are established based upon the continuum.
The phrasing differs while the meaning remains the same.
The final verse refutes the Sarvāstivāda position that things abide substantially for a moment;
rather, because phenomena lack substantial abiding for even a single moment, their cessation is merely nominal.
Once those phenomena have arisen, they do not depend on external conditions,
for they perish spontaneously moment by moment.
To maintain that there is a real duration within each moment is irrational.
Therefore, "abiding" is spoken of only with respect to the continuum (*saṃtati*) and not in reference to a single moment (*kṣaṇa*).
For this reason, when the *Abhidharma* speaks of the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) as being momentary,
the Master further says:
Because the meaning of "abiding" is established through this continuity,
the principle explained in the Abhidharma of the Sarvāstivāda school is proven.
Thus, that treatise states:
What is meant by "abiding"?
It refers to the continuity of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) that have already arisen but not yet ceased; this is called abiding.
That which has arisen but has not yet ceased is called the momentary nature of phenomena (*kṣaṇika-dharmatā*).
Because its duration is extremely brief, it is termed a single moment (*kṣaṇa*).
If one were to stop for even longer, it would no longer be extremely brief;
although the Master [Vasubandhu] was personally inclined toward the Sautrāntika school,
he did not extensively refute the original treatise.
Therefore, it is cited as proof.
Although the *Abhidharma-jñānaprasthāna-śāstra* states that [this process] does not occur in a single moment,
the Master [Vasubandhu] reconciles this passage from the *Jñānaprasthāna*.
Although that treatise speaks of characteristics such as arising within a single mind,
it refers to a single mind in a general sense, based on a single moment of mind within the continuity of a homogeneous life-stream (*nikāya-sabhāga*).
It is not the case that a single moment is called "one mind";
therefore, there is no contradiction. Furthermore, it may be explained as follows:

when the three natures (trisvabhāva) arise individually, the continuity of a single movement is termed "one mind. Alternatively, this is stated in reference to ten stages or in reference to a single category.
Regarding the homogeneous character (nikāyasabhāga) as it applies accordingly,
and furthermore, that each and every moment— even down to the four characteristics— is established,
the Sautrāntika masters say:
Why is it that the four characteristics are only provisionally established in relation to a continuum?
They may also be provisionally established according to a single moment (kṣaṇa).
How can this be established?
"Examination" means that each and every moment of thought reaches a state where there is no lack of differentiation. This is the explanation.
That which was originally non-existent now comes into being; this manifestation of its essence is called "arising.
That which, having existed, returns to non-existence at the time of its absence is called "cessation.
That which is able to induce each subsequent moment to succeed the preceding one in arising is [the continuity of conditioned phenomena].
Alternatively, the successive moments following this very thought,
arising in succession from their predecessors, are called "abiding";
this is the provisional characteristic of abiding.
Because there is a distinction between either the preceding moment or the succeeding moment, it is called "change-while-abiding" (*sthity-anyathātva*).
It is termed "change-while-abiding" because change is distinguished in relation to abiding. [The opponent] raises an objection:
If things as hard and solid as diamond are indistinguishable before and after, how can they be called "different"?
To resolve this objection, it is said:
When these vajras and so forth arise in a similar manner across preceding and succeeding moments,
there is no lack of distinction when comparing the preceding and succeeding states.
As for how those distinct characteristics are to be known: this is the inquiry.
It refers to seeing that which is similar [to the object] through the vajra-like meditative attainment (*vajropamasamāpatti*).
Commentary:
This refers to [objects] such as vajras,
because there is a distinction between the time when they have been thrown and the time when they have not yet been thrown.
Therefore, there is also variation;
within the act of throwing, there is further differentiation:
if one throws with great force, it falls quickly.

If thrown with weak force, it falls slowly; alternatively, it is explained that if thrown with strong force, it falls slowly because it travels a great distance, whereas if thrown with weak force, it falls quickly because it travels only a short distance.
Thus, due to the difference in time, there is a difference in their characteristics.
By this principle, the meaning of the transformation and differentiation of the great elements (mahābhūta) is established;
they are called "great" because of their predominance.
Derived matter is not explicitly stated, yet it is established by itself;
all conditioned phenomena are similar in that they arise in a continuous succession from moment to moment.
When viewed in relation to what precedes and follows,
and observed through their coarse characteristics,
although there are not many differences between them, [they are distinct].
If one analyzes them in detail, they are not without distinction.

If that were so, then at the final moment, [the characteristic] would not pervade all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*). This objection concerns the characteristic of difference (*anyathātva-lakṣaṇa*).
If it is said that "abiding" and "change" are named because there is a distinction between the prior and the subsequent,
then [this applies to] the sound of the final moment and the light of the final moment.
Furthermore, at the moment of entering parinirvāṇa without remainder, regarding these final six sense bases,
none of these phenomena possess a subsequent moment that could be distinguished from them; thus,
they should be without duration or change.

If this subsequent moment were devoid of any distinct characteristic, then the established definition of "conditioned" would not apply universally to all conditioned phenomena. Furthermore, regarding the difficulty of abiding and the two characteristics of change:
since there would be no subsequent moment to succeed it, [the phenomenon] could not persist.
There should be no abiding;
since there is no subsequent moment to distinguish,
there should be no difference.
Regarding the statement, "This does not entail the fault of failing to pervade [all cases] up to the state of abiding," the Sautrāntika replies:
This addresses the objection concerning differing characteristics (*vilakṣaṇa*).
When the sūtra speaks of "change while abiding" (*sthity-anyathātva*),
its intention is merely to state that change constitutes a characteristic of the conditioned;
it does not intend to state that abiding itself is a characteristic of the conditioned.

Therefore, the Sūtra says that there are three conditioned characteristics of the conditioned. If one asks what their meaning is, the answer is: because it is the alteration of duration, it is called "alteration of duration.
Thus, wherever there is duration, there must necessarily also be alteration.
Although subsequent moments of sound and so forth lack a succeeding moment to continue the present instant,
they are nonetheless able to succeed the preceding past instant.
It is also called "abiding.
Although there is no subsequent moment that can differ [from itself],
it nevertheless possesses difference because it differs from the preceding moment.
This is the correct explanation of the distinction.
As for the mention of "abiding," it clarifies the distinction in relation to abiding.

By means of this, the definition of the characteristics [of conditioned phenomena] is established without the fault of being non-pervasive. Furthermore, another interpretation holds that this applies to both the characteristics of abiding and change.

Among the two characteristics [of conditioned phenomena] that are revealed, the intention is to establish the characteristic of difference (*anyathātva*) as the characteristic of the conditioned (*saṃskṛtalakṣaṇa*). This does not mention the characteristic of duration (*sthiti*) as a characteristic of the conditioned,
because one wishes to distinguish difference by means of duration.
The preceding section explained "abiding.
You have not grasped my intended meaning and thus rashly challenged the characteristic of abiding;
this was merely a provisional refutation of the challenge regarding that characteristic of abiding.
He then asked, "What is the meaning of this?
The answer was: "It refers to the alteration of duration; therefore, it is called 'alteration of duration' (sthity-anyathātva)."
Therefore, wherever there is abiding, there must also be change.
Although in the case of the final sound and so forth there is no subsequent moment to succeed it or to differ from it,
there is nevertheless a preceding moment that can succeed it or differ from it.
There is the existence of "abiding-and-change" (*sthity-anyathātva*). This correctly clarifies that change is a characteristic of the conditioned;
however, the mention of "abiding" is made in reference to abiding in order to clarify change.
By this, the fault that the definition [of the characteristics] would not be all-pervasive is avoided. If one follows the force of the text, the former interpretation is superior;
if one follows the wording of the response, the latter interpretation is also applicable.
One should understand that if "duration" (*sthiti*) and "alteration" (*anyathātva*) refer to the final moment, [the definition remains consistent].
Although there is no thought that can be succeeded to or differentiated from another,
it is nevertheless able to succeed to what preceded and differ from what preceded,
just as in the case of the initial thought.
Although there is no preceding thought that can be succeeded to or differentiated from,
there is nevertheless a succeeding thought and a subsequent differentiation;
if the intermediate moment possesses both the succession of the preceding and the differentiation of the succeeding.
Even if a single moment differs from its preceding type,
it is also called "change-in-dwelling" (*sthity-anyathātva*). Although this was discussed last within the question-and-answer section,
this has been presented here as a brief illustration of one corner [of the topic].

However, regarding the statement in this sūtra that "arising and so forth are distinct entities," the Sautrāntika school briefly indicates the intended meaning of the sūtra: namely, that within this sūtra,
these four characteristics [of conditioned phenomena]...
Regarding the characteristics of the conditioned as taught by the Blessed One,
to show them briefly:
the arising of conditioned phenomena is defined as their existence now after having been non-existent.
That which exists and then ceases to exist is called "cessation" (nirodha).
The continuous succession [of moments] is called "duration" (sthiti).
The distinction between these preceding and succeeding states of duration is called "alteration" (anyathātva).
In this context, what is the use of distinct entities such as arising (*jāti*)?
How can that which is characterized (*lakṣya*) be established as the characteristic itself (*lakṣaṇa*)?
Thus asks the Sarvāstivāda school.
If there is no separate characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*),
how can the characterized phenomenon (*lakṣya*) itself be established as the characteristic?
How could the marks of a Great Being (*mahāpuruṣa-lakṣaṇa*) or [the characteristics] up to birth (*jāti*) be real entities (*dravya*)?
The Sautrāntika school raises a counter-objection to establish their own position:
how is it that the World-Honored One’s thirty-two marks are not distinct from the Great Being himself?
The three objections regarding the horns and so forth should be understood by analogy with this.
The principle regarding these conditioned characteristics (*saṃskṛtalakṣaṇa*) should likewise be understood in this way:
the characteristics do not exist as something distinct from the characterized (*lakṣya*),
even though one perceives the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of conditioned phenomena such as form (*rūpa*).
...up until one has not yet understood that there is arising from what previously did not exist,
that there is cessation after having existed,
and that there is continued abiding through successive transformation.
Although there are differences between the preceding and succeeding [moments],
it is still not yet known that their essence is conditioned (*saṃskṛta*).
Therefore, the nature of matter (*rūpa*) and so forth is not itself the characteristic of the conditioned.

However, there is no real entity such as "arising" that exists apart from the nature of form and so forth; for the cognition of the characteristic and the characterized are distinct, one cannot say they are identical.
Yet, because there is no separate nature apart from form and so forth, one cannot say they are different either.
One must not say they are separate;
this is the meaning of being neither identical nor separate.
If they were separate from the conditioned, then what would be irrational about that?
The Sarvāstivādins counter-interrogate:
"Because it is admitted that a single dharma reaches [its effect] at one time, they are co-existent.
The Sautrāntikas respond with a refutation to expose the flaw.
A single conditioned phenomenon possesses four distinct characteristics;
for it would follow that at one and the same time,
arising, abiding, alteration, and cessation must be admitted to exist simultaneously.
This objection is not valid; as for the statement that "arrival does not entail contradiction," this is the Sarvāstivāda explanation:
the activity of arising exists in the future.
The three functions exist in the present;
because their times of operation are distinct,
they do not contradict one another despite coexisting.
Furthermore, one should reflect upon whether something is useful or useless.
Below, the Sautrāntika school provides an extensive refutation;
this is an exhortation to reflect.
One must first determine whether the intrinsic nature of future phenomena exists or does not exist;
only then can one discuss their utility or lack thereof.
Since its substance is not yet established,
why is it necessary to speak of its function?
Even if one were to grant that the future exists, one would still have to describe it as having the characteristics of the present.
This is refuted as follows:
Even if one were to concede that the future possesses activity,
once it has initiated activity, it ought to be designated as "present."
How is the future established?
One should explain the characteristics of the future.
When a dharma is in the present time...
If its arising and function have already ceased, it should be called "past.
How then can it be established as "present"?
One must explain the characteristics of the present.
The *Nyāyānusāra* (Treatise on Right Reasoning), fascicle 14, defends the [Vaibhāṣika] position:
"The characteristic of arising (*jāti-lakṣaṇa*) in the future merely initiates its capacity (*śakti*), but it is not yet an activity (*kāritra*).
Only when it initiates the activity of grasping a fruit (*phala-grahaṇa*) in the present is it truly an activity."
Activity necessarily entails functional capacity,
but functional capacity does not necessarily entail activity.
It is on the basis of activity that the present is established.
The future [dharma] merely gives rise to its capacity (śakti) but is not present; the Abhidharmakośa masters refute this, saying:
"Your 'capacity' and 'activity' (kāritra) are merely different names for the eye."
Why is it that the activity of arising (*jāti*) is termed "capacity" (*sāmarthya*),
while the other three are termed "function" (*kāritra*)?
Furthermore, this contradicts the position of the *Vibhāṣā* masters who represent the orthodox school (*vibhajyavādin*).
They state: "There is no equal-and-immediate condition (samanantarapratyaya) that takes its fruit at one time and gives its fruit at another time."
According to the intent of that treatise,
upon entering the two mindless absorptions (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti* and *nirodha-samāpatti*),
one immediately takes up and gives away the past [karmic formations].
If that which has already passed were to take [an object], it should be called "present.
If the Sautrāntikas say that the equal-and-immediate condition (samanantarapratyaya) takes [the object] all at once while being present, yet gives [the result] gradually in the past; then...
This would, moreover, contradict the position of the *Vibhāṣā* commentators.
Furthermore, regarding the claim that the three [characteristics] beginning with "abiding" (*sthiti*) constitute destruction:
this section below refutes these three characteristics of abiding and so forth.
The three characteristics function simultaneously based upon a single dharma.
At that time, is this dharma to be called "abiding" or is it to be called "alteration"?
"It is destroyed by name.
The *Nyāya* proponent says:
"Now, this must be resolved."
Within the state of having already arisen,
the three— staying, change, and cessation— each perform their respective functions,
causing the characterized phenomena [to arise].
At one time, the perspectives differ,
yet they possess three meanings;
how can such a comprehensive explanation be logically contradictory?
The Abhidharmakośa masters refute this, saying:
"Although their functions are distinct,
they ultimately share the same single substratum (dharmin)."
How does it abide? It causes [the mind] to abide securely and attain superior results.
What is difference (*anyathātva*)? It causes deterioration and leads to inferior results.
What is cessation (*bhaṅga*)? It causes destruction and entry into the past.
This contradicts reason.
Those who assert that the moments of meditative attainments (samāpatti) are subject to momentary destruction merely recount their own positions;
in total, they fail to refute the three characteristics, such as duration (sthiti), and so forth.
The masters of the Sarvāstivāda school maintain that although the three characteristics— such as duration (sthiti) and so forth— are all present simultaneously,
their functions do not occur at the same time, but arise sequentially and separately.
That assertion contradicts the principle of momentary destruction (*kṣaṇabhanga*).
A "moment" (*kṣaṇa*) refers to the shortest possible duration of time;
yet, since it is claimed that the three characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) exert their functions separately at the present, prior, and subsequent [moments], [the doctrine is undermined].
This would mean that the [object] remains stationary, which contradicts the principle of momentary destruction (*kṣaṇabhanga*).
If one were to say, "I define 'arrival' as a single moment," this is a restatement of the defense.
Regarding what you say concerning the Sarvāstivāda masters:
if they claim that I define a single moment as the completion of the activity of one dharma and its four characteristics;
"You should now explain why [the characteristics] do not act simultaneously.
This specifically refutes the notion of abiding;
for the three characteristics manifest together."
Why does that which abides arise first in its function,
rather than being something other or ceasing?
If you say it is because its power is strong.
Later, why would they both become inferior and encounter destruction simultaneously?
If you say that the characteristic of duration does not arise again like the characteristic of birth,
then birth should likewise be capable of such [non-repetition].
That which has already been introduced into the present should not be introduced again;
it should not be so for that which abides,
because that which already abides can be made to abide eternally.
The function of arising should occur constantly;
it cannot be analogized such that once it has arisen, it may not arise again.
Furthermore, what obstacle prevents the function of abiding from existing momentarily and then ceasing?
If it were something different [from the obstruction], then the power of that which destroys the obstruction would have to be stronger;
why then does it not arise earlier?
Furthermore, "the function of abiding ceases until there is nothing further to be done" refers to the simultaneous refutation of the two characteristics of difference and cessation.
Moreover, the function of abiding ceases.
The characteristics of alteration and cessation are the very nature of the dharma itself; they do not abide naturally but fall away into the past.
Where, then, do these two characteristics—alteration and cessation—exert their function? Furthermore, what purpose is served by the operation of these two?
Because it sustains them through its abiding,
once phenomena have arisen, they do not perish for a time;
thus, this abiding is required.
Since the function of abiding has already ceased, the dharma cannot remain;
it naturally perishes and falls away into the past.
Therefore, the functions of change and cessation have nothing further to accomplish.
Since they serve no purpose, what need is there for those two?
This is the charge of uselessness.
Furthermore, it would follow that a single dharma could never achieve the establishment of difference.
This specifically refutes the characteristic of difference.
Furthermore, it would follow that when a single dharma has arisen but not yet perished, it is called "abiding";
and when, having abided, it perishes, it is called "cessation."
This principle may indeed be accepted.
Even if one grants that abiding and cessation exist, it is logically impossible for them to be distinct from a single phenomenon when examined from both perspectives.
Generally speaking, what is called "difference" refers to a distinction between preceding and succeeding states.
It is not that this very dharma can be said to be different from itself;
therefore, a verse says:
"The dharma at the time of the characteristic of change is the very same dharma at the time of the characteristic of abiding."
It is not established that they are different.

This is a further challenge: if the dharma at the time of the characteristic of change were different from the dharma at the time of the characteristic of abiding, then it would not be a single dharma;
for abiding and change would then be separate dharmas.
To do so would entail the fault of contradicting one's own tenets;
this is precisely what constitutes a "retracting challenge" (*pratyāyanīya*).
Therefore, the Sarvāstivādins cannot establish difference upon a single dharma.
Although other schools claim that [the concept of] "attainment" (prāpti) is illogical,
this refers to the Sautrāntika refutation of the characteristic of cessation (nirodha-lakṣaṇa) as asserted by the Saṃmitīya school. The Saṃmitīyas maintain:
Fuel and the like persist for a long duration;
at the time of their extinction, they cease due to two conditions:
first, the internal characteristic of cessation.
Second, external fire and so forth abide and cease at different times,
as do the mind and mental factors.
Since it is solely by way of internal cessation and not by external conditions,
[the author] now refutes this,
even though other Saṃmitīya schools [hold such a view].
It is said that when fuel and the like encounter external causes and conditions for extinction, such as fire,
it is the internal characteristic of extinction (*nirodha-lakṣaṇa*) that is able to extinguish the fuel and so forth which are to be extinguished;
yet, this is what they have asserted.
It would be as if one were to say that when taking a purgative, a deity comes and causes the evacuation;
likewise, the causes and conditions for the extinction of fire and so forth should themselves extinguish the fuel and other things to be extinguished.
Why, then, must one separately maintain the existence of a "characteristic of extinction" (*nirodha-lakṣaṇa*)?
Furthermore, phenomena such as fuel are extinguished in dependence upon external conditions;
in your own school, it may be said that their prior abiding and subsequent extinction are not simultaneous.
However, this is not the case for the mind and mental factors.
According to your own tenet that things perish moment by moment,
they do not require any external conditions for destruction; therefore,
at the very time they exercise their functional activity, they must simultaneously give rise to the activity of perishing.
How can their position— that the functions of arising and ceasing occur at different times from the function of abiding— be maintained?
If the function of ceasing were to occur at the very time a phenomenon abides,
then a single dharma would both abide and cease simultaneously within that same moment.
It would also be extinguished,
which is contrary to correct reasoning.
Therefore, one should rely on the continuity [of the stream of consciousness], as this accords with the sūtras.
Having finished the refutation by the Sautrāntika school, [the author] returns to his own school's position;
therefore, explaining the four characteristics of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) based on the principle of continuity does not contradict correct reasoning.
Second, this accords well with the sūtras.
Regarding the question, "If they arise in the future, why do they not all arise together?"—
the following constitutes the second major section, which addresses external objections.
This is the external objection:
"If the characteristic of arising exists in the future and gives rise to the phenomena that are to arise,
then since all future phenomena possess the characteristic of arising, why do they not arise simultaneously?"
The verse says: "Reaching [the state] where it is not separated from the conjunction of causes and conditions.
This is the answer in verse.
The commentary says: "[The states] do not all arise simultaneously. This is the explanation in prose.
Within the prose commentary, there is first the explanation of the verse and subsequently the definitive analysis;
this [section] constitutes the explanation of the verse.
Although there is the characteristic of arising, because it necessarily relies upon causes and conditions, it does not arise instantaneously.
If that is so, then [the arising] occurs through the power of causes and conditions;
this is the Sautrāntika objection from below, which provides a definitive resolution.
The meaning of the text is clear and can be understood.
As for the phrase "all existing phenomena (sarvadharmāḥ) according to their respective applications," this is the explanation provided by the Sarvāstivādins.
How could you, of the Sautrāntika school, know all phenomena that possess an intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*),
for the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is profound and extremely difficult to know?
Although subtle phenomena do exist as entities, they are nonetheless subtle.
That you, followers of the Sautrāntika school, cannot know this is precisely a praise of the profundity of the Dharma.
If the characteristic of arising did not exist, there would be no cognition of arising.
Since there is already the cognition of arising that knows arising exists,
the sixth case-ending (ṣaṣṭhī-vibhakti) indicates a relationship between distinct entities,
such as "the king's minister."
If there were an entity of arising, the sixth case (genitive) construction would be established;
if there were no characteristic of arising, this sixth case expression— namely, "the arising of form" and so forth— would not be possible.
If one were to say that arising is itself form,
then one should not speak of "the arising of form," just as one does not speak of "the form of form.
Yet, since one does speak of "the arising of form," [arising must be distinct from form].
It is clearly known that there is arising distinct from form;
just as it is faulty to demand that what is non-existent should arise,
so too should it be understood by analogy for cessation, and so forth.
If that is so, in order to establish [the realization of] emptiness and selflessness,
the following Sautrāntika objection is raised,
first formulating it as an objection concerning internal phenomena.

If that were so, in order to establish the cognition of emptiness and selflessness, one would have to posit a nature of emptiness and selflessness external to all phenomena; yet, apart from phenomena, there is no separate nature of emptiness and selflessness.
And yet, one gives rise to the realization of emptiness and selflessness.
What prevents there from being a distinct arising and so forth apart from form and the rest,
while one simultaneously gives rise to the realization of arising and so forth?
Regarding the establishment of distinct natures ranging from one or two up to the number of atoms (*paramāṇu*),
the Sautrāntika school raises an objection based on external phenomena.
If we follow the Buddha’s teaching:
Apart from the essence of dharmas, there is no separate entity such as "number" and so forth.
You, who profess the Sarvāstivāda school,
[assert this] in order to establish the cognition of numbers such as one and two.
The cognitions of large and small magnitudes,
the cognition of individual parts, and the cognition of their combination.
Free from perception;
that perception;
this perception.
The phrase "the cognition of existence" (sattva-buddhi) and so forth includes, by way of ellipsis, the cognitions of identity, difference, and so on;
one should [regard this] as being like the Vaiśeṣika non-Buddhists.
Apart from phenomena (dharma), they separately maintain the existence of the nature of number,
the nature of measure, and individuality.
The nature of conjunction,
the nature of separation, and that nature.
"This nature," "possessing nature," and so forth— these terms include, by way of ellipsis, "sameness," "difference," and so on.
The Vaiśeṣika outsiders have six categories (padārtha):
first, substance (dravya);
second, quality (guṇa).
Third, the three types of karma;
fourth, the four modes of existence;
fifth, similarities and differences.
Sixth, the sixfold harmony (*ṣaḍ-sāmagrī*).
Alternatively, some explain ten points of meaning,
all of which are as previously stated.
If all dharmas are subsumed under the categories of substance (dravya) and quality (guṇa),
there are twenty-four qualities in total within the category of quality,
as previously explained.
Among the twenty-four types,
here the number is the fifth and the magnitude is the sixth.
Each individually is the seventh; combined, it is the eighth;
separated, it is the ninth;
and that is the tenth.
This is the eleventh. "The nature of existence" (bhāvatva) is the meaning of the term within the sixfold set of terms;
it is the common meaning within the tenfold set of terms.
The categories of "sameness" and "difference," and so forth, are identical to the category of "generality" (sāmānya) and "particularity" (viśeṣa), etc.
According to that school, apart from substantial entities (dravya), there exist separate essences within the category of qualities (guṇa), such as number (saṃkhyā) and so forth;
and apart from dharmas, there exist separate essences for the categories of existence (bhāva), generality, particularity, and so forth.
Therefore, that [objection] is cited as a challenge: although cognitions of number and so forth arise, there is no separate entity such as "number" apart from the phenomena themselves;
likewise, what prevents the arising of cognitions of "arising" and so forth?
Apart from form and so forth, there is no separate arising and so on.
Furthermore, regarding the establishment of the term "reaching" (*prāpti*), how could it be established?
Thus far, the cognition of arising has been refuted.
This refutes the sixth case-ending.
Furthermore, in order to establish the expression of the sixth case-ending,
