one must maintain that there exists a distinct nature of a collection of forms (*rūpa-samudāya*).
However, apart from form (rūpa), there is no separate nature of aggregation.
Furthermore, as it is said regarding the intrinsic nature (svabhāva) of form:
apart from form, there is no separate intrinsic nature.

How can this sixth-derivative (ṣaṣṭhī-vibhakti) expression be established? According to the difficulty posed by this text, the meaning of the sixth-derivative case is explained as a state of connection;
it does not necessarily require that the entities be distinct from one another in order to be related.
"Therefore, it should also be so for birth and the others up to this point" means that the Sautrāntika school has finished its refutation above and returns to its own tenet to provide an explanation:

"Therefore, the four characteristics are merely established as conventional designations; they have no separate, substantial entities. Thus, the characteristic of birth is that which was previously non-existent and now exists."
Since the categories of phenomena belonging to the five aggregates are numerous,
the genitive case is employed— stating "the arising of form," for instance—
to distinguish them from the other aggregates and prevent confusion with them.
In order to make it known to others that this arising consists solely of form (*rūpa*) and nothing else—such as feeling (*vedanā*) and so forth—it is called "the arising of form.

The explanation for the other four aggregates follows this same principle. It is like how, in common worldly usage, one speaks of "sandalwood fragrance" to distinguish it from the fragrance of aloeswood and other such scents.

The substance of the pebble is identical to the substance of the tile and so forth; furthermore, regarding the fragrance of sandalwood, there is no fragrance that exists apart from the sandalwood itself.
Such is the substance of the pebble.
Apart from the particles themselves, there is no separate entity;
one should know that this is likewise true for the arising and so forth of these forms.
In the same way, one should understand "abiding" and the others as appropriate.
As it is with arising, so it is with abiding and the other [characteristics].
If conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are separate from the characteristic of arising, why do they not arise?
This is the objection raised by the Sarvāstivādins.

If conditioned phenomena (saṃskāra-dharma) were to arise while being devoid of the characteristic of real arising, then why would the three unconditioned phenomena (asaṃskṛta-dharma), which are likewise devoid of the characteristic of arising, not also arise?
Furthermore, regarding the claim that "conditioned phenomena are called 'arising' until they reach the state of non-arising activity": [this is untenable].
The Sautrāntika explanation is as follows:
conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are said to "arise" because they exist now where they previously did not;

since the essence of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) is eternal, how can it be said to arise? Furthermore, according to your own school, *dharmatā* (the nature of things) does not state that all phenomena have arising.
The conditioned is subject to arising, while the unconditioned is without arising.
Thus, you must admit that not all phenomena are capable of arising;
the conditioned can arise, whereas the unconditioned cannot. Furthermore, according to your own school, all conditioned phenomena alike possess the characteristic of arising.
Yet, regarding causal conditions in relation to conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*),
they must either possess the capacity to produce certain things so that those things are produced,
or lack the capacity to produce certain things so that those things are not produced.
Since all phenomena are distinct when viewed in relation to their respective causes and conditions,
one must likewise admit that all conditioned and unconditioned phenomena share the same characteristic of being unarisen.
Regarding those two dharmas, all causes and conditions possess the function of producing the conditioned,
but they lack the function of producing the unconditioned; such is the intent of the *Nyāya* defense.
Although the eye and other faculties arise from karma,
what prevents there being a separate set of four great elements (*mahābhūta*) that produce them? Likewise, although conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) arise from causes and conditions,
what prevents there being a separate characteristic of arising (*jāti-lakṣaṇa*)?
The Abhidharmakośa masters refute this, saying:
"O Sautrāntikas,
that which has no intrinsic nature cannot arise by depending on causes and conditions."
"In your school, the arising of an existent entity should not depend upon causes and conditions.
[This concludes] the section for the Vaibhāṣika masters up to "one who practices in accordance with the truth.
Here, the Master [Vasubandhu] brings the argument back to the fundamental tenets of the Vaibhāṣikas.
The Vaibhāṣika masters maintain that the characteristics such as arising (jāti) and so forth exist as distinct, substantial entities;
this principle can likewise be established.
The remaining text may be understood.

Having thus completed the general explanation of the syllables in the chapter on "Perception" (*saṃjñā*), the following section, the seventh major heading, clarifies the "groupings of names" (*nāmakāya*) and so forth. [The Groupings of Names and So Forth]
The Citation of the Text: "That which is called...

and so forth. The Main Explanation: The "bodies" (*kāya*) of names, phrases, and syllables are their fundamental designations; they are explained through synonymous terms—*saṃjñā*, *pada*, and *vyañjana*—respectively, according to their sequence.
The Commentary states: "As for reaching the 'body of words' (*vyañjana-kāya*),
this refers to the prose section,
wherein one first explains the verse."
2. Question and Answer. Below this is the explanation of the verse.
It specifically explains the word "etc.
One should understand that herein, the phrase "up to the perception of odor, taste, etc. [is used].
This is a specific explanation of the name;
it explains the name by means of "perception" (saṃjñā).
In Sanskrit, it is called *nāma* (pronounced with a departing tone), which in the language of Tang means "name."
This is the meaning of following,
the meaning of returning, and the meaning of proceeding toward.
Summoning (āhvāna) refers to following sounds as they reach their respective objects,
thereby summoning forms and so forth.
A name is that which expresses meaning,
yet it is not conjoined with the object;
sound itself is not that which expresses meaning.
Nor is it a case of the meaning being conjoined [with the sound]. Thus, the second chapter of the *Abhidharma* states:
"It is not that the vocal sounds themselves can directly express the meaning."
Do not say that fire burns the mouth at the very moment one speaks; rather,
it is by depending on speech that names such as "fire" arise,
and it is through these names for fire and so forth that the objects— fire and so forth— are expressed.
"Designation" (ākhyā) refers to that which can produce an awakening of cognition in another regarding the meaning being manifested;

it does not consist in being conjoined with the object itself—this is the treatise. In Sanskrit it is called *saṃjñā* (pronounced *seng-ruo-ri*, with the second syllable reversed), and in the Tang language it means "perception" (*xiang*).
This refers to the sense of grasping at images with exclusive attachment,
or it refers to the sense of establishing a common convention.
Regarding the term "forming a perception" (*saṃjñā-karaṇa*), "forming" (*karaṇa*) means to construct or produce.
Because among the mental factors (*caitasika*), having grasped an image through perception (*saṃjñā*), one establishes and constructs this designation;
thus, that which is produced by perception is called "the construction of perception.
To say that the name is perception is a designation based on its cause. Furthermore, it is explained that by taking the name as an object, one is able to give rise to perception.
Because it is capable of producing a perception, it is called "producing-perception" (*kṛtasaṃjñā*). Furthermore, the word "producing" (*kṛta*) means "to cause to arise.
It is by virtue of names such as "deva" or "human" that perceptions of devas, humans, and so forth are caused to arise.

Therefore, it is called "conceptualization" (*saṃjñā*). To say that "name" is "conceptualization" is to name it according to its result. Furthermore, another interpretation is that this term "conceptualization" is itself a synonym for "name," because names are all essential conventions established as means of expression (*vyañjana*).
Because it is by means of this very perception that there can be expression, it is called "making" (*kṛti*).
To make such a perception is what is meant by "the perception of making.
Regarding the phrase "a sentence (*pada*) is [a collection] up to a chapter (*varga*"):
This is a separate explanation of the term.
It is explained by means of the chapter [itself].
In Sanskrit it is called *pada*, and in the language of Tang it is called "trace" (*ji*).
Just as a single elephant’s body has four footprints,
and just as a single verse (gāthā) is composed of four lines in total,
here "line" (pāda) is translated according to its meaning as a "verse-quarter."
A "phrase" (*pada*) is that which ultimately expresses meaning.
In Sanskrit it is called *vākya*, and in the language of Tang (Chinese) it is called *zhang* (a chapter);
both are that which ultimately expresses meaning.
As stated in the chapter on "All Conditioned Phenomena are Impermanent" and so forth, because their meanings are identical, the chapter is used to explain the phrase;
the chapter is simply another designation for the phrase. Question: If one follows non-Buddhist treatises, the meanings of chapters and phrases are distinct.
How are the chapters used to explain the sentences? The commentary states that regional customs differ:
here [in China], there are few sentences per chapter and many chapters;
such is the system of the Indian country.
Both chapters (varga) and phrases (pada) are ultimate in their expression of meaning;
therefore, a chapter may be used to explain a phrase.
Alternatively, when one is able to discern and realize [the meaning] up to this point, it is called a "phrase" (pada).

Furthermore, according to the analysis of phrases by means of grammatical science (*śabda-vidyā*): "activity" (*karman*) refers to the activity performed; "virtue" (*guṇa*) refers to the virtues of all phenomena.
Each, as appropriate, possesses both virtue and activity. "Time" (*kāla*) is a qualifying adjunct to the phrase.
It means that the sense of "hooking attachment" (*saṃyojana*) is the ability to discern the function, quality, and time [of phenomena].

That is to say, it is the uninterrupted hooking attachment to the names and meanings within that which enables one to discern the function, quality, and time. As for the distinction: whatever phenomenon possesses such a function and quality [is so characterized].
It is called "differentiation" (viśeṣa) because it is distinct from other phenomena. For example, as in the statement: "Devadatta, bring a black cow;
milk her and give it to my preceptor to drink.
Within this context, the movement is termed "functional activity" (karmaprayoga).
The cold nature of black cow’s milk can cure fever; this is called its "virtue" (*guṇa*).
That all names and meanings are uninterrupted is called "correspondence" (*yoga*).
This [substance] possesses such functional activity and virtue.
The differentiation by name is distinct from other dharmas.
If one can discern the differentiation of function, quality (*guṇa*), and temporal correspondence, this chapter is called "Phrases" (*pada*).

Furthermore, it is explained that "action" (*karman*) refers to what is performed; "function" (*vṛtti*) refers to the capacity for action; "quality" (*guṇa*) refers to the moral qualities of all dharmas; and "time" (*kāla*) refers to the three periods of time. If such is the case regarding these dharmas...
Conjunction (*saṃprayoga*) is the name given when [a phenomenon] is conjoined with the activity it performs; non-conjunction with those [other] factors is called differentiation (*viśeṣa*).
If this factor is conjoined with this capacity for action, it is termed "conjoined."
The term "differentiation" (viśeṣa) refers to not being associated with that [other] dharma.
If a dharma is conjoined with this quality, it is called "associated" (saṃprayukta);
not being associated with that dharma is called "differentiation."
If a phenomenon is conjoined with this [time], it is termed "associated" (*saṃprayukta*);
not being associated with that [other time] is termed "distinguished" (*viśeṣa*).
One should know that association and distinction both apply to karma.
The fourfold equality refers to the differentiation according to the correspondence of function, efficacy, quality, and time.
This chapter is called the "Verse. Furthermore, it is explained as being like the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of an atom (*paramāṇu*) within the sense-field of form (*rūpāyatana*).
There is the karma of what is seen;
there is the karma of raising or lowering.

There is the capacity to produce the function of consciousness or the function of grasping the fruit. Qualities such as blue or yellow, [the three] times such as past or future, and their association with the immeasurable are termed "conjunction" (*saṃprayoga*). To distinguish them from those that are not conjoined, they are termed "particularity" (*viśeṣa*).
Alternatively, that which is dissociated is itself termed "differentiation" (*viśeṣa*),
meaning that which can discern and identify that "form is what is seen," and so forth;
this chapter calls such [dissociated factors] "phrases" (*pada*).
"Phrasing" (*vyañjana*) refers to syllables such as *a*, *i*, *u*, and so forth;

this is a specific explanation of phrasing, wherein phrasing is explained by means of syllables. In Sanskrit it is called *vyañjana*, which in the language of Tang (Chinese) is translated as "phrasing."
This is that which manifests meaning; it manifests names and phrases proximately, and meaning distantly.
According to the customs of the Western Regions (India), fans, salt, vinegar, and so forth are also called *piṇḍapāta*.
It is also that which can manifest meaning.
A fan manifests wind;
salt, vinegar, and the like manifest the flavors within food.
The old translation as "taste" (味) is an error. In Sanskrit it is called akṣara; in the language of Tang (Chinese), it means "syllable" (字).
It carries the sense of "not being subject to transmigration," meaning that it does not change or shift according to different directions or locations.
It is also that which can manifest meaning.
It manifests names and phrases to reveal meaning from afar;
therefore, we now explain the text by means of the function of syllables (*vyañjana*).
"Letter" (*akṣara*) is another designation for "syllable" (*vyañjana*).
These letters, such as *a* and *ā*, are subsumed under the category of non-associated formations (*viprayukta-saṃskāra*);
they are not like the written characters of ink found in this region. Furthermore, these letters possess no expressive power (*abhilāpa*).
That which possesses the capacity for expression consists precisely of names and phrases;
it is merely the basis upon which names and phrases rely,
and that which can manifest those two.
"Since the substance [of the word] has no expressive function,
is it not the case that this 'letter' (*akṣara*) is also a name for a division of writing?
This is the question.
Is it not the case that these characters,
such as "A" and "Ai," can also express those portions of ink-written script upon paper,
and are themselves names for those portions of ink-written script upon paper?
Since this [non-manifest] also possesses the capacity for expression, it should also be considered a "name" (nāma).
How then can you say there is no expression?
It is not the case that the term "non-manifest" is used here to exclude those portions of writing that do not constitute the name.
Answer: It is not for the purpose of manifesting the written characters on paper that the letters *a*, *ā*, and so forth are produced;
rather, it is for the purpose of manifesting the letters *a*, *ā*, and so forth that the written characters on paper are produced.
The use of metaphors serves as an illustration;
it is not for the purpose of manifesting a true form by means of fabricating a provisional image,
but rather for the purpose of manifesting the true form by means of fabricating a provisional image.
In ancient times, the various sages deliberated together,
saying: "How might we ensure that others in distant places,
even though they do not hear the words we speak," [understand our meaning]?
They were nevertheless understood;
therefore, they collectively created written characters on paper and transmitted them by sending them afar, in order to manifest these various signs.
Furthermore, syllables (*vyañjana*) are able to manifest both names (*nāman*) and phrases (*pada*), whereby they are understood;
therefore, syllables are not the names for the constituent parts of writing.
This explains the reason for the construction of the constituent parts of writing.
By this analogy, it should be understood that even when sound is not heard,
visible form (rūpa) can likewise manifest the three: syllables (vyañjana), names (nāman), and phrases (pada).
There are some who, although they do not speak, express themselves through bodily gestures;
these also include visible forms, names, and so forth.
What are these "names and so forth" that constitute the body?
Question:
Below this, the body is explained individually;
that is to say, from the general explanation of "saṃjñā" (perception) and so forth, up to "ka-kha-ga," etc.
Answer: The body is explained by way of a general description.
In Sanskrit it is called *kāya*, which in the language of Tang means "body."
This has the meaning of "aggregation.
That is to say, the meaning of "body" (*kāya*) is the aggregation of many names and so forth.
In Sanskrit it is called *samukti*, which in the language of Tang means "general statement."
This is the meaning of "aggregation" (*samudaya*).
It refers to the collective synthesis and general exposition of many names and so forth;
thus, it explains its "body" (*kāya*) by means of this general exposition.
Regarding the statement that the verbal root *uñcha* is taught in the sense of "gathering" (*saṃgraha*):
in the science of grammar (*śabda-vidyā*),
the verbal root *uñcha* is established as a *dhātu* based on the meaning of *samavāya*, which in the language of Tang is translated as "gathering."
"Element" (*dhātu*) is the primary meaning.
Therefore, within the root of the word,
*ud-√ci* should be explained in the sense of "to collect together."
Furthermore, by means of various syllables as conditions,
the *uṣman* element is added,
transforming it into the three *muktitis*.
The Chinese term for this is "general exposition" (zǒngshuō). Since the word for general exposition originates from *uddeśa*,
and *uddeśa* carries the meaning of "compilation" or "collection," [it refers to a summary].
Thus one knows that a collective statement (*uddeśa*) is also a synthesis (*samudāya*).
Therefore, the element *ucchada* is taught within the sense of synthesis in order to prove that a collective statement has the meaning of synthesis.

Thus, by explaining the "body" (*kāya*) through a general definition, we know that it must be the collective aggregation of many names and so forth that constitutes the meaning of "name-body" (*nāmakāya*) and the others. Question: Why does the *Vibhāṣā* ask, "What is the meaning of 'name-body'?"
Answer: These two [terms] have the meaning of "accumulation.

Therefore, a single name is not called a "body" (kāya). The commentary explains: The *Abhidharmamahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* designates a collection of two names as a "body," whereas this treatise designates a collection of many names as a "body."

Each is based on a specific meaning and they do not contradict one another. Question: Why are *ya*, *a*, and so forth cited in the preceding text, while *ka*, *kha*, and so forth are cited in the subsequent text?
Answer: It is explained that *ya*, *a*, and so forth refer to the phonetic sounds of the letters.
Ka, kha, and so forth are the *akṣara* (phonemes).
To clarify the phonetic sounds, all *akṣara* are subsumed under the category of "syllables" (*vyañjana*).
Therefore, the first of each group is cited to include the subsequent ones. Furthermore, it is explained that within these syllables there are also individual letters.
This refers to [vowels] such as *a* and *ā*.
There are also conjunct consonants, such as *ka* and *kha*;
these are identical to the individual letters.
Therefore, they are explained in terms of their scattered [occurrence]. As for the "body of syllables" (*vyañjana-kāya*), it is explained as being connected because it involves many [syllables].
Is it not the case that these three [bodies] do not correspond to mental factors?
The following is a dialogue.
This is the question from the Sautrāntika school:
"Is it not the case that names and so forth have vocal sound as their essence?"
Among the five categories [of phenomena], material phenomena (*rūpadharma*) are subsumed;
how then can it be said that they are "non-associated with mind" (*cittaviprayukta*)?
The three—names (*nāman*), phrases (*pada*), and phonemes (*vyañjana*)—should be subsumed within the aggregate of matter (*rūpaskandha*).
Because speech is their intrinsic nature,
just like false speech.
These three do not bring about the understanding of the meaning through mere arrival.
The Sarvāstivādins reply: This demonstrates the fault of the reason being unestablished (*asiddha*). How so?
It is for the sake of making it understood.
The Sautrāntika challenges this,
saying: "If it is claimed that speech produces a name, which then reaches [the listener] and enables them to understand," this is the explanation given by the Sarvāstivādins.
It is by means of the name that one understands, not by means of the speech itself;
for it is not the case that something is called "speech" only when the sound has reached [the ear].
The Sautrāntika school further explains of its own accord:
"In our school as well,
it is taught that not all sounds are designated as 'speech'."
Speech is defined as that sound by which something is expressed and through which meaning can be understood.
What kind of sound makes meaning intelligible?
"Objection":
This refers to the claim that there exists a distinct, real entity called "name.
This is the Sautrāntika explanation.
Since the beginning of the eon,
all those capable of exposition have collectively established sound as the definitive means of expression for all meanings.
Furthermore, for example, in ancient times,
all wise people collectively established the single term "go" (cow) among nine meanings as a definitive means of expression.
This is the citation of evidence. As for the nine meanings:
first, direction;
second, wild animals.
The third stage,
the fourth light,
and the fifth word.
Sixth, the vajra-jewels;
seventh, the eyes;
eighth, the devas.
Regarding the nine waters:
why do you claim that this universally accepted authoritative means of expression is established only by me?
There are indeed Vaibhāṣika masters [who hold this view].

Those who maintain that real entities exist as names capable of manifesting meanings must also necessarily admit that such names for these various objects are collectively established as the definitive means of expression (*vācaka-pramāṇa*).
Furthermore, the interpretation of these nine meanings [beginning with] "cow" (*go*) is as explained above.
Furthermore, it should be understood that the word *gaur* (cow) signifies these nine meanings;
however, it is called a "name" (*nāman*) because a name is itself a sound.
Alternatively, one might say that within this verse-line, these nine meanings are manifested by means of the name.
Since the function of signification is already accomplished by the sound itself,
why must one gratuitously postulate that there exists a real name distinct from sound?
Furthermore, it remains unexplained to what extent this name depends upon a separate name.
The Sautrāntika school further employs two methods of inquiry to challenge this position:
if it is claimed that this name-sound (*nāma-śabda*) is capable of producing manifestation (*abhivyakti*), then all sounds should be capable of producing manifestation.
Arising is like a seed producing a sprout and so forth;
manifestation is like a lamp illuminating a jar and so forth.
If it is argued that there is a distinction between arising and manifesting sound:
This sufficiently clarifies the meaning;
why wait for another name?
Furthermore, regarding those instances where various sounds reach [the ear] by being produced through speech:
Below this, the Sautrāntika school specifically refutes the designation of "arising.
For example, when the single name "arising" is produced by multiple moments of sound,
the preceding sounds have reached the present while the subsequent sounds are yet in the future.
If the subsequent sound arrives when the preceding sound has already ceased, they cannot be gathered together; how, then, could there be the designation "arising"?
Nor does a single name arise gradually, part by part.
How can it be said that the arising [of non-informative action] is triggered by speech?
And how is it that one must wait for past manifest actions to reach the point where they can produce the non-informative action?
This is the defense offered by the Sarvāstivādins.
Just as at the time of receiving the precepts,
the final moment of informative action arises only by depending on the power of the preceding moments of informative action to produce the non-informative action.
The production of a name is likewise like the sound of the final syllable. If that were so,
then at the final stage, one should be able to comprehend the meaning.
The Sautrāntika objects:
Since the sound arises as the name at the final stage,
this name would therefore exist only in the subsequent moment.
In the preceding stage, one is in the future;
thus, one should be able to comprehend the meaning upon hearing only the final sound.
If you maintain that this is because [the sounds] cannot be accumulated, then...
The Sautrāntika school cites and refutes this:
"If you hold such a view,
I do not say that speech can produce a name."
That is to say, speech gives rise to phrases;
phrases, in turn, give rise to names;
and names then manifest the meaning.
Regarding this, the same objection as previously stated applies: it would constitute the fault of the name arising from speech.
Since the phonemes of successive moments cannot be aggregated, how could a name arise?
Nor does a single name arise gradually part by part;
how, then, could this name be produced from phonemes?
The fault of [the opponent's position] regarding the manifestation of names by speech should be understood as analogous to that of production.
This is a specific refutation of the term "manifestation" (nāman),
which cannot be fully detailed here;
it should be understood as being analogous to the case of "arising" (jāti).

Furthermore, since the various moments of sound cannot be aggregated, and no single dharma is manifested gradually part by part, how could it be that the manifestation of a name is produced by speech? Why?
Because [the alternatives] "if that were so" and "if one holds such a view," and so forth, would follow.
The opposite of the preceding can be understood accordingly.
This can be explained by interpreting "manifestation" (*khyāna*) as "replacement" (*sthāna*).
Furthermore, regarding the statement that it is entirely unreasonable for the phrasing to differ [from the previous], [it is as follows].
The preceding section separately refuted the name;
this section separately refutes the text.
First, it clarifies that the essence cannot be known.
The second is an application by analogy using the same name;
it differs only in substituting the wording for the name,
while all other meanings are identical.
The explanation may be understood by analogy.
Furthermore, regarding those who hold the view that [the self] reaches [the new body] yet should not be admitted [as such],
the alternative positions are set forth and refuted.

Furthermore, if there is an adherence to the view that names arise simultaneously with their referents— just as the four characteristics [of conditioned phenomena] arise together with the phenomena themselves—
it is refuted by stating:
"Names belong to the present time."
The meaning of the eyes going and coming cannot be established,
because they do not exist simultaneously.
It is only when the children and others have gradually grown that their fathers and others establish names for them.
This clearly shows that what is first produced is not simultaneous with its designation.
If it were simultaneous with its designation at the outset, how could it be established later?
It is only for conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*) that possess arising that one may admit simultaneity with their designation.
Since the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) is without arising, it should not possess the designation "name.
To insist on a name for it as if it possessed characteristics such as arising would be untenable.
Nevertheless, the Blessed One spoke of the sequence of reaching and the mind.
The Sautrāntikas interpret the scriptural passage as follows:
the Sūtra states that verses depend upon names and the authors of the verses;
it does not say they depend upon sounds.
Regarding these various meanings,
the sages of antiquity collectively established the limits of the phonemes upon which they rest.
The sound that can express that meaning is precisely the name (*nāman*).
Since the name is conventionally established upon the sound,
the name takes the sound as its essence.
This is called a verse (*śloka*) by virtue of its specific arrangement;
it is said that a verse depends on names (*nāman*) in this sense,
not because the name possesses a separate ontological substance.
This verse is called a "distinction of arrangement" (*vyavasthāna-viśeṣa*).
To maintain that the verse exists as a real entity is contrary to correct reasoning;
it is like a row formed by many trees—apart from the trees, there is no row.
In the case of multiple minds, there is succession; in the case of no mind, there is no succession.
This verse is also like this:
apart from what is designated by the name "separation," there is no separate essence.
Alternatively, for one who maintains that [the phonemes] must reach [the object], it would be useless;
thus, even if the Sautrāntikas admit there is scriptural authority, they further refute names and phrases.
It is the collection of phonemes that constitutes names and phrases.
Furthermore, if one were to insist that there are additional names and phrases, they would then be rendered useless.
As for the statement "the Vaibhāṣikas [hold this] because it reaches what can be understood," the Vaibhāṣikas return to their own fundamental tenet.

Praising the profound nature of the Dharma, which cannot be fully comprehended by all, I shall here briefly explain the three categories of name (*nāman*), phrase (*pada*), and syllable (*vyañjana*) according to the Sarvāstivāda school.
First, I shall clarify these three stages.
2. Analysis through Question and Answer. Regarding the statement that clarifies the three stages, the *Nyāyānusāra* states:
"The *Vibhāṣā* says..."
Names, phrases, and syllables—each of these three has three types.
Regarding the three types of names:
they are the name, the name-body, and the multiple-name-body.
The same applies to phrases and syllables.
Names have many states;
that is to say, they arise from a single syllable.
They may arise from two syllables,
or they may arise from many syllables.
As for those arising from a single syllable:
When one syllable is spoken, there is merely a name;
when two syllables are spoken, it is called a "name-body" (nāmakāya).
Or, it is stated as follows:
When three syllables are spoken,
this is called a "multiple-name-body" (nāmakāya);
or it is stated as follows:
It is only when four syllables are uttered that one speaks of a "name-group" (*nāmakāya*).
As for that which arises from two syllables:
when two syllables are uttered, there can only be a "name" (*nāman*).
When four syllables are spoken, it is called a "name-group" (nāmakāya).
Or it is said that when six syllables are spoken,
it is called a "multiple name-group" (bahunāmakāya).
Some say that it is only when eight syllables are uttered that one speaks of a "name-group" (*nāmakāya*);
among those produced from multiple syllables, there are those produced from three syllables.
When three syllables are spoken, there is merely a name;
when six syllables are spoken, it is called a "name-body" (nāmakāya).
Or, it is stated as follows:
When nine syllables are spoken, it is called a "multisyllabic body" (*nāmakāya*); alternatively,
it is said that only when twelve syllables are spoken is it called a "multisyllabic body."
Because this serves as the gateway,
the remaining many syllables that give rise to name-bodies (*nāmakāya*) and phrase-bodies (*padakāya*) should be explained accordingly.
Phrases also have multiple categories, namely: the intermediate phrase,
the initial phrase,
and the final phrase.
Short phrases and long phrases:
if eight syllables form a name, it is called a middle-length phrase.
Because it is neither long nor short, it is called "the middle way.
Thirty-two syllables give rise to four lines;
these four lines constitute a *śloka*.
The texts and treatises of the sūtras and śāstras mostly rely on these numerical categories.
If a name is formed with six or more syllables, it is called the "initial phrase" (pūrvapada);
if it is formed with twenty-six or fewer syllables, it is called the "subsequent phrase" (uttarapada).
If fewer than six syllables are produced, it is called a short verse;
if more than twenty-six syllables are produced, it is called a long verse.
For now, we shall distinguish three types based on the intermediate length of the verse.
When eight syllables are spoken, there is merely a phrase;
when sixteen syllables are spoken, it is called a "phrase-body" (padakāya).
Or, it is stated as follows:
When twenty-four syllables are spoken, it is called a "multitude of phrases" (*padakāya*);
alternatively, it is said that only when thirty-two syllables are spoken is it called a "multitude of phrases."
Since a *vyañjana* (phoneme) is identical to a *akṣara* (syllable), there is only one category.
When a single syllable is spoken, it can only be a *vyañjana*;
when two syllables are spoken, they are called a *vyañjanakāya* (phoneme-group).
Some say that when three syllables are uttered, it is called a "multitude of phonemes" (vyañjana-kāya). Others say: [the same].
When four syllables are uttered, it is then called a "multisyllabic phoneme-group" (vyañjanakāya).
By this principle, one should state that when a single syllable is uttered, there is a "name" (nāman).
There is no collection of names,
no collection of phrases,
and no sentences.
There is no body of phrases;
there is no body of many phrases;
there are syllables.
There is no phoneme-body (*vyañjana-kāya*), nor is there a plurality of phoneme-bodies.
When two syllables are uttered, there is a name (*nāman*).
There are name-groups (nāmakāya), but no phrase-groups (padakāya) or multiple word-groups (vyañjanakāya).
There are no [other] three, such as phrases and so forth.
There is a syllable;
there is a collection of syllables;
there is no plurality of collections of syllables.
When the four characters are spoken, there are the three beginning with "name" (nāman),
the absence of the three beginning with "phrase" (pada), and the presence of the three beginning with "syllable" (vyañjana).
When the eight syllables are spoken, there are the three [factors] beginning with name (nāman),
as well as the phrase-body (padakāya) and the non-phrase-body (vyañjanakāya).
There is no *pada-kāya* (phrase-group). There are three [categories], beginning with *vyañjana* (phoneme).
When sixteen syllables are spoken, there are three [categories], beginning with *nāman* (name).
There is a phrase;
there is a phrase-body,
but there is no multiplicity of phrase-bodies.
There are three [categories], such as phonemes (vyañjana) and so forth. When the thirty-two syllables are spoken,
each of the three— names (nāman), phrases (pada), and phonemes (vyañjana)— possesses three types.
Taking this as the gateway, the rest should be explained according to reason.
The *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 14, states:
"However, the six syllables constitute the first phrase."
The twenty-six syllables are called the "subsequent phrase.
This does not contradict correct reasoning.
As for the statement that six syllables constitute the "initial phrase":
To cite the first is to reveal the subsequent;
to state that "twenty-six syllables constitute the latter phrase" is to cite the subsequent in order to reveal the preceding.

Second, the analysis through question and answer: Question: As in the case of multiple name-bodies (*nāmakāya*), it is said that when three syllables are uttered, they constitute a multiple name-body. How is this so?
One version states: "When four syllables are spoken, it is called a 'name-group' (nāmakāya).
What is the meaning of this? The explanation says: "Regarding the statement that three syllables produce a name and thus constitute a name-group:
the first and second syllables form one body."
The first and third syllables together constitute one body;
the second and third syllables together likewise constitute one body.
According to the rules of grammatical phonetics (*śabda-vidyā*), it is only from three onwards that they are designated as "many."

If a name consisting of four syllables is called a "name-body" (*nāmakāya*) or a "multiple-name-body," then when they are joined in immediate succession, three such bodies constitute a "multiple-name-body.
Furthermore, another interpretation holds that it is simply called a "multiple-name-body" because there is a plurality of names.

It is not defined by many bodies; alternatively, it is explained that when one body is added to another body, it is called a "multitude of bodies" (*kāyagaṇa*). Question: How are speech, phonemes, names, and phrases formed? Explanation: It is as follows, O Tathāgata.
A single thought gives rise to a single word;
a single word expresses a single syllable.
The mental application is fierce and sharp, and its speech is swift and rapid.
Each lasts for a single moment.
A śrāvaka utters a single word with a single moment of mind.
A single word cannot express a single syllable;
ordinary beings produce a single word through the arising of many moments of mind.
When a single sound is produced, there must necessarily be multiple moments of thought (*citta*).
Within the continuity of speech sounds, a single continuous sound expresses only a single syllable.
It should be understood that, in some cases, a single utterance expresses a single syllable.
There are cases where many syllables express a single phoneme;
there are cases where a single syllable gives rise to a single name;
and there are cases where multiple syllables give rise to a single name.
Either a single name constitutes a phrase, or multiple names constitute a phrase.
Question: Does this name arise from a single syllable, or does it arise from multiple syllables?
Although there may be many syllables upon which it depends, the substance of the name is only one.
Why, then, does the treatise state that "the smallest limit of a name is a single syllable"?
Should not a name consisting of multiple syllables also be considered the smallest limit? The explanation is as follows: "reaching the limit of a single syllable" means...
This is based on the explanation of names consisting of a single syllable; when such a single syllable is spoken, it is termed "minimally small.
However, when two or more syllables are spoken—even if they give rise to a single name—[the situation differs].
If one considers a single word as a "name," then there are name-bodies (*nāmakāya*) consisting of multiple names,
because a single [word] is not the ultimate minimum. Furthermore, another interpretation holds that a name depends upon the ultimate minimum.
A name reaches its limit in a single syllable;
it is called "small" when based on few [syllables], and "large" when based on many.
Furthermore, there are two gates: name (*nāman*) and meaning (*artha*).
Among these, names, phrases (*pada*), and phonemes (*vyañjana*)—the three—are all subsumed under "name.
Within this, names and phrases may sometimes rely upon many [phonemes].
A single unit of a syllable has no further subdivisions;
among these, taking one such unit is called the "extremely small" (paramāṇu).
Otherwise, it would not be so.
One should say that there is one name;
yet what is called "one word" (akṣara) is precisely one "syllable" (vyañjana). Question: Apart from the basis of words and the basis of names, there exists a distinct entity of the phrase (pada);
it is by depending on phrases that verses (gāthā) are formed.
Why is there no separate entity of the verse? The explanation states: the syllable (*akṣara*) manifests the name (*nāman*) and the phrase (*pada*).

The name expresses the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of all phenomena, while the phrase expresses the distinctions among all phenomena; apart from these, there is nothing else to be expressed.
Therefore, there is no separate essence to the verse. Furthermore, Master Kōng (Kumārajīva) said:
"A collection of syllables forms a name; a sentence is that which conveys a complete meaning through its forceful expression, characterized by continuity and uninterrupted succession."
Therefore, there are distinct names and phrases;
four phrases constitute a verse (*gāthā*).
Where the force of the words does not reach one another, they are separated by an interval.

Therefore, there is no separate verse-body [for this]. Question: Just as a single utterance has its name arise, so too, at one time, in accordance with the customs of different regions, it follows the conventions of those various localities.
Each designates a distinct object. [Question:
Is there one name that arises for many objects? [Answer: The explanation is as follows:
although there is but one name, and though its substance is one, it functions as a definitive designator by virtue of being mutually agreed upon as such.
Therefore, according to local customs, each explains different matters.
Regarding the statement, "These names, bodies, and so forth, should all be analyzed here," this marks the third major section of the text: the analysis by way of various categories. Within this:
First, the analysis of the three categories beginning with "name" (nāman);
second, the analysis of "homogeneity" (sabhāgatā). This is the first [section], the analysis of the three categories beginning with "name," which consists of four gates in total.
First, the question concerning the realms of bondage;
second, the question concerning sentient and non-sentient beings;
third, the question concerning the five categories.
The four questions concern the three natures;
in reality, they are exclusively unconditioned,
while momentary [phenomena] are exclusively the patience regarding suffering.
Therefore, no separate questions are posed for the five categories.
The verse states: "Up to 'of the nature of outflow' and 'indeterminate.
This is the response in verse.
The Commentary states: "Up to 'however, it cannot be said'—this treatise presents two positions;
the latter position is not the correct one."
Therefore, the *Mahāvibhāṣā* refutes this, stating:
"The critique says: One should not make such a statement.
It would be better to say that it does not exist than to say that it cannot be described."
It exists but cannot be described because it is useless.
Within the preceding explanation, there are further two assertions.
One assertion names it "bound to both the stage of speech and the stage of following speech."

One explanation names it "bound to the five stages that follow the body. Both the *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya* (Vibhāṣā) and the *Nyāyānusāra* present these two views, yet neither contains a formal critique.
Therefore, the *Nyāyānusāra* states:
These three, beginning with name (nāman),
are bound exclusively to the two realms of desire and form.
Within the realm of form, [they are further classified].
Some say it exists only in the stage of the first dhyāna;
others say it also extends through the three higher dhyānas,
according to the distinctions of what is bound to speech and what is bound to the body.
If these three are said to be bound according to speech,
then even when one is born in the desire realm and utters speech of the desire realm,
the speech, the names, and the body are all bound to the desire realm.
The meaning he has explained is either bound to the three realms or,
alternatively, it is unconditioned;
that is, when he further employs the terminology of the first dhyāna.
Speech, as well as names and so forth, are bound to the stage of the first dhyāna;
the body is bound to the desire realm.
The meaning is as previously explained.
In this way, if one born in the stage of the first dhyāna utters speech belonging to two stages,
it should be understood accordingly.
The same applies if one born in the second, third, or fourth dhyāna stages utters speech belonging to two stages.
This should also be reflected upon according to reason.
If it is said that these three are bound to the body,
then even if one is born in the desire realm or in the four dhyānas...
Names and so forth, as well as the body, are bound to their own respective levels;
speech, however, may be bound either to its own level or to another level.
The meaning is as previously explained. Question: Between these two explanations, which is correct? Answer: Each is correct according to its respective context.
This is because language is directly capable of producing names and other such meanings.

Furthermore, the Sautrāntika masters maintain that the "name-body" (*nāmakāya*) and so forth are themselves speech (*vāk*). Question: For what reason does the text below state that the analytical knowledge of phenomena (*dharmapratisaṃvid*) pervades five stages? Answer: It is explained as follows.
According to the mind that takes them as objects, these [four analytical knowledges] pertain to five stages (*bhūmi*).

However, in principle, names (*nāman*) and so forth actually pertain to two stages, following speech (*vāk*). [Objection: If that is the case, then the analytical knowledge of language (*nirukti-pratisaṃvid*) would be defined according to the mind that takes it as its object.

"Why is it that [the analytical knowledge of eloquence] is said to pertain only to two stages when it actually pervades all five stages? The explanation says: because it is difficult to take words and phrases as its object, it must be based on the mind of its own stage.
Furthermore, another explanation states that the text below says the analytical knowledge of phenomena (dharma-pratisaṃvid) pervades all five stages.
This refers to the "body-bound" (kāyapratibaddha) category;
there is no need for further detailed explanation. Furthermore, the interpretation follows the subsequent passage of that same text.

It should be understood that "body-bound" is the correct term. Question: Does the mind of transformation (nirmāṇacitta) take names and so forth as its objects? Answer: The mind of transformation does not take them as objects.
This is the object of the mind resulting from supernormal powers (abhijñā-phala-citta). It should be known that there are two types of mind resulting from supernormal powers:
first, the mind of transformation (nirmāṇa-citta), which is the mind resulting from supernormal powers.
Regarding the two types of resultant minds that initiate karma:
it is only the second type of resultant mind that can take a manifested person as its object and initiate speech, names, and so forth.

Since the "discriminative activity regarding phenomena" (*dharmavikalpa-karman*) can also accommodate this, it is asked: "If that is so, why does it not take the mind and its associates as its object? The explanation says: "Once it has acquired the name 'object' (*ālambana*), it also takes the mind and its associates as its object."

However, when various treatises state that [the mind] takes four objects as its conditions, this is said with reference to the mind of transformation (*nirmāṇacitta*). Furthermore, it is explained that it does not take names (*nāman*) and so forth as its objects;
if the mind of transformation takes only four objects as its conditions, [then names and so forth are excluded].
If the minds that initiate karma and those that produce its results take only the two types of action— bodily and verbal—

as their objects, yet they are said to "pervade the factors" (dharmas) and be "discriminative," this is because they are called "object-of-factors" (dharmālambana) based on their taking [all] collectively as their object.

It is called "conditioned by dharmas" because it does not take seven kinds of dharmas as its object. Question: Since the *nirhāra-phala-citta* (the mind that issues speech) does not take the three realms as its object, how can names (*nāman*) and so forth be able to express the three realms?
Answer: Although the *nirhāra-phala-citta* that issues speech does not take the three realms as its object, [names and so forth do]. Thus, they are able to express them.
However, because the preparatory stages of the supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) can, by their very nature, give rise to a mind that takes the three realms as its object,
the names produced thereby are said to be designators (*vācaka*) of the three realms.
Furthermore, regarding the statement that "the sets of names and so forth do not manifest the meaning":
these sets of names and so forth consist of the conceptual distinctions between sentient and insentient beings.
This is comprised within the category of sentient beings;
that is to say, because the speaker possesses names and so forth,
it is therefore comprised within the category of sentient beings.
Names and so forth do not achieve their status as being manifested by mountains, rivers, and the like;
therefore, they do not apply to insentient things.
This is because the triad of names and so forth does not exist within the objects that are manifested.
The *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 15, states:
Question: Who accomplishes [the possession of] names and so forth? Is it the speaker?
Is it that which is spoken?
If so, what fault is there?
If it can speak, [then...]
In that case, an Arhat would possess defiled phenomena;
and one who is free from the defilement of desire would possess unwholesome phenomena.
An ordinary person (pṛthagjana) should accomplish the noble dharmas (āryadharma).
One who has severed the roots of goodness (samucchinnakuśalamūla).
One should accomplish wholesome dharmas,
because even Arhats and others speak of defiled dharmas and so forth.
If this is what is being said:
If that were so, then external objects and even non-action (*anabhisaṃskāra*) would also have to be established as possessing names and so forth, since they too are things that are spoken of.
The answer is: only that which is capable of speaking possesses names and so forth.
Question: If that is so, the latter objection is well resolved;
how, then, is the former objection resolved?
Answer: It concerns those such as arhats.
Although they achieve the names "defiled" and so forth,
they do not achieve the actual defiled phenomena and so forth,
because the names "defiled" and so forth all refer to phenomena that are non-obscured and neutral (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*).
Regarding the statement that "the name-body and so forth are exclusively outflows":
among the fivefold classification in the third section,
they are exclusively outflows because they arise from homogeneous causes (*sabhāga-hetu*).
Because they are not atoms (*paramāṇu*), they are not produced through accumulation (*aupacayika*).
Because they arise according to desire, they are not born of maturation (*vipākaja*).
Thus says the *Nyāyānusāra*.
As for the statement that names and so forth arise from karma,
this is because they are the dominant fruits (adhipatiphala) produced by that karma;
since their substance is not unconditioned (asaṃskṛta), they are not real.

Because it arises from a homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*), it is not momentary (*kṣaṇika*). Furthermore, as for its being comprised solely within the category of the non-obscured neutral (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*):
this is the fourth analysis of the three natures (*tri-svabhāva-vibhāga*), wherein it is exclusively neutral.
This is neutral by intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-avyākṛta*) and is not included among the four types of neutrality;
it is neutral solely because its nature as established is not determined based on what is manifested.
Question: For what reason is it called "equal" (*samanvāgata*)?

Why does it not follow the vocal sound (*ghoṣa*), which [itself] permeates all three moral natures (*trividha-svabhāva*)? Explanation: Because of mental attention (*manasikāra*), one intends to produce that vocal action (*vāk-karman*).
Therefore, the vocal sound follows the mind that produces speech and thus permeates all three moral natures.
Because they are not induced by correct attention (*samyak-manasikāra*),
those names and so forth are exclusively indeterminate (*avyākṛta*). Thus, the *Vibhāṣā* (15) states:
Question: Are names and so forth wholesome,
unwholesome, or indeterminate?
Answer: It is indeterminate (*avyākṛta*), because it is not an action (*karma*) and because it arises from intentional thought (*saṃcetanā*).
It is like the four great elements (*mahābhūta*). Question: According to the treatise below...
False speech and so forth arise depending on the basis of name-aggregates (*nāmakāya*) and so on;
this means that speech arises depending on names. The commentary explains: the mind that depends on names is posited as the remote motivating cause (*dūre samutthāpaka*).
This does not depend on the immediate cause (samanantara-pratyaya) or the motivating cause (samutthāna-hetu). If it were based on the immediate cause,
it would only take sound as its object and not names (nāman) and so forth.
Regarding what was stated above, "up to those that are the outflow of non-attainment and meditative concentration," this is the second section clarifying the *sabhāgatā* (homogeneity) and so forth.
The treatise states: "The category of 'reaching' (*prāpti*) applies to two meanings."
The explanation of *sabhāgatā* (homogeneity) is clear from the meaning of the text.
This demonstrates that *sabhāgatā* pervades all three realms (*dhātu*).
It pertains only to sentient beings;
it is exclusively non-obscured and neutral;
and it is categorized as both fruition-born and outflowing.
Because it takes phenomena similar to those of the three realms as its cause,
it pervades all three realms; however,
it pertains only to sentient beings and does not extend to non-sentient things.
As previously explained, regarding the "unobscured-neutral" (anivṛtāvyākṛta):
that which is comprised within maturation (vipāka) is maturation;
the remainder is neutral by nature (svabhāvāvyākṛta).
Among the five categories, it is not a minute atom (paramāṇu) and thus is not something nurtured by food;
because it arises from causes of its own kind (sabhāgahetu), it is not momentary;
and because it is not unconditioned (asaṃskṛta), it is not a substantial entity (dravya).
If it arises from karma, it is a result of maturation (vipāka);
otherwise, it is a result of outflow (niṣyanda).
Therefore, the *Nyāyānusāra* states:
What is maturation? It refers to the destinies such as the hells, and the types of birth such as egg-birth,
as well as the homogeneous classes of beings.
What is meant by "homogeneity" (sabhāgatā)?
It refers to the commonality found among all those belonging to the same realm, level, sphere, lineage, class, [type of] ascetic, brahmin, learner, or non-learner.
Other masters say that among the various types of homogeneity (sabhāgatā),
that which is produced by the projection of prior karma is the maturation-homogeneity (vipāka-sabhāgatā).

The present arising of application is a result of outflow (*niṣyanda*) and belongs to the homogeneous class (*sabhāga*). Question: Since this text states that the maturation-homogeneous class (*vipākaja-sabhāga*) consists of the five destinies (*gati*) and the four modes of birth (*yoni*), what of the five destinies, as well as the womb-born, egg-born, and moisture-born?
None of these include the intermediate state (*antarābhava*).
Furthermore, the treatise below states:
"A single karma projects a single birth."
"Birth" refers to the homogeneous class (nikāya-sabhāga).

It is not yet known whether the intermediate state (antarābhava) belongs to the homogeneous class of the destination (gati-sabhāga) or to the homogeneous class of birth (upapatti-sabhāga). The commentary states:
The *Nyāyānusāra* bases its discussion on the homogeneous class (*nikāya-sabhāga*) of the five destinies and four modes of birth as a horizontal perspective; this treatise, however,
bases its discussion on the total homogeneous class that induces a single lifetime.
This is explained by Śrīlāta. Therefore,
two types of existence (*bhava*) arise within the "intermediate state" (*antarābhava*),
but this is not an instance of birth occurring within the four modes of birth (*catur-yoni*).
Regarding "attainment and the various characteristics up to the outflow and maturation":
this distinguishes attainment (*prāpti*) and the four characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) into five categories.
It comprises the momentary (*kṣaṇika*), the outflowing (*naiṣyandika*), and the ripening (*vipākaja*).
It is momentary because it coexists with the receptivity to the dharma of suffering (*duḥkhe dharmajñānakṣānti*);
it is outflowing because it is produced by a homogeneous cause (*sabhāgahetu*).
It is a maturation because it arises from unwholesome or wholesome-outflowing [karma].
It is not nutriment-produced because it is not composed of atoms.
It is not substantial because it is not unconditioned.
Regarding the statement "non-acquisition, the two meditative attainments, and up to that which is not a result of maturation (*vipāka*)," non-acquisition and the two meditative attainments,
among the five categories [of conditioned phenomena], are exclusively outflows (*niṣyanda*), because they arise from causes of similar type (*sabhāga-hetu*).
Because it is not produced by karma, it is not a result of maturation (vipāka);
because it is not composed of atoms (paramāṇu),
it is not something nurtured (aupacayika).
Because it is not associated with the patience regarding suffering, it is not momentary;
because it is not unconditioned, it is not real.
The phrase "having thus explained the meaning not yet explained" is the conclusion.
Regarding the fact that the life-faculty (jīvitendriya) of non-percipient beings has already been analyzed as before: [this refers to the preceding discussion].
Non-conception exists only in the realm of form;
life-force pervades all three realms.
Both of these belong exclusively to sentient beings.
It is exclusively maturation and exclusively indeterminate,
as has already been explained above.
For what reason is it not stated that [these factors] are included within the category of sentient beings?

Question: For what reason are acquisition (*prāpti*), non-acquisition (*aprāpti*), and the two meditative attainments (*samāpatti*) not stated to be included solely within the category of sentient beings?
Regarding the statement, "Because it has already been explained that [the self] is composed of sentient beings and so forth," the answer is:
the term "and so forth" (ādi) includes that which is not established.
It has already been explained that sentient beings possess [these factors];
it has already been explained that sentient beings do not possess [them].
That is to say, within the preceding analysis of acquisition (*prāpti*) and non-acquisition (*aprāpti*).
Regarding sentient phenomena, there is acquisition (*prāpti*) and non-acquisition (*aprāpti*); regarding insentient phenomena, there is neither acquisition nor non-acquisition.
Thus, both acquisition and non-acquisition are established in relation to the two meditative attainments (*samāpatti*).
Since it is clearly understood that what is not accomplished is comprised solely within the category of sentient beings,
for what reason is it not stated that it extends to those who are not comprised within the category of sentient beings?
Question:
It has already been stated that [all conditioned phenomena] are co-existent.
Answer: [As follows:]
Since it was previously stated that the four characteristics accompany all conditioned phenomena (saṃskṛta),
it is clearly understood that they apply to both sentient and insentient things; therefore,
they are not mentioned [separately] here either.
Regarding those other factors not yet mentioned that should be understood accordingly:
these are acquisition (*prāpti*), the four characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), non-acquisition (*aprāpti*), and the two meditative attainments (*samāpatti*).
These eight are to be analyzed according to their realms (*dhātu*) and their natures (*svabhāva*).
If it is possession (*prāpti*), it pervades the three realms of existence and that which is non-bound;
it pervades the three natures (*trividha-svabhāva*). If it is non-possession (*aprāpti*), it pervades the three realms of existence.
They are exclusively indeterminate.
If the attainment of non-conception belongs to the realm of form,
the attainment of cessation belongs to the formless realm.
The two meditative attainments are both wholesome;
therefore, it is said that "the remainder not yet explained should be understood accordingly.
Since this has already been fully explained previously, it will not be analyzed here.
*Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya-ṭīkā*, Scroll Five. On the fifteenth day of the fourth month of the third year of the Jōan era, completed at the Tōhon-bō (Pagoda Main Hall) of Ishiyamadera Temple.
*Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya-ṭīkā*, Scroll Six.
Narrated by the Śramaṇa Śākya Kō.
In the second chapter on the Analysis of Faculties (Indriya-vibhaṅga), part four,
having thus already explained up to the point where it is stated that [the faculties] act as causes and conditions,
the third major section of this chapter below clarifies the causes and conditions (hetu-pratyaya).
Among these, the first section restates the preceding question to introduce the topic,
while the second section correctly discerns the essential nature.
This concludes the preceding inquiry and introduces the following section.
Regarding the phrase "first, by means of six kinds," this is the second part, which correctly elucidates the essential nature (*svabhāva*). Within this:
First, the explanation of the six causes;
second, the explanation of the four conditions.
Within the explanation of the six causes:
First, the actual clarification of the essence of the cause;
second, the clarification of the cause attaining the fruit;
third, the clarification that phenomena arise from causes. Regarding the section on the actual clarification of the essence of the cause:
First, the general designation of the name;
second, the specific manifestation of the essence;
third, the detailed classification.
The following is the first general heading. Therefore, he first answers by stating: "Briefly, there are six kinds of causes.
The question "What are the six? is an inquiry. The verse says: "Up to these six kinds," and so forth.
Answer: It is asserted that there are only six causes,
thereby distinguishing [this system] from other schools.
Because it can produce an effect, it is called the efficient cause (*kāraṇa-hetu*).
The cause is that which produces;
the effect is that which is produced.
That which is capable of acting is called the efficient cause (*kāraṇa-hetu*);
this is a *karmadhāraya* compound.
Alternatively, the cause of that which is capable of acting is called the efficient cause; this is a *tatpuruṣa* compound.
This is an *adhikaraṇa-samāsa* (possessive compound). That is to say, that which acts as a direct cause (*sākṣāt-kāraṇa*) is the proximate cause,
while those other factors that do not obstruct [the result] are the remote causes.
This remote cause is called the "efficient cause" (*kāraṇa-hetu*) because it is named after its function as an efficient cause;
that is, it serves as a cause through a successive transmission to produce the fruit.
Thus, the *Nyāyapraveśa* (Treatise on Logic), chapter nineteen, states:
Alternatively, this is called the "efficient cause" (*kāraṇa-hetu*) because it is the efficient cause of that;

this refers to the sense that this serves as a cause for that through a continuous succession—this concludes the treatise. Because they possess simultaneous activity, they are called "coexistent" (*sahabhū*).
That which co-exists is called the "co-existent cause" (*sahabhū-hetu*); this is an *karmadhāraya* (appositional) compound.
Alternatively, it is called "co-existent" because the cause and the fruit exist together.
The cause that exists simultaneously is called the simultaneous cause (*sahabhū-hetu*);
this is an *ṣaṣṭhī-tatpuruṣa* compound. That which is similar in cause and effect is termed "homogeneous" (*sabhāga*);
if it is homogeneous and is a cause, it is called the homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*).
This is a *karmadhāraya* (appositional compound). If a cause of the same kind is called a "homogeneous cause" (*sabhāga-hetu*), it is a *tatpuruṣa* (dependent compound).
Mind and mental factors are said to be "associated" (*samprayukta*) because they are equal in five respects.
If "concomitance" itself is the cause, it is called the "concomitant cause" (*saṃprayuktaka-hetu*);
this is an appositional compound (*karmadhāraya*). If it is the cause of that which is concomitant, it is called the "concomitant cause"; this is a genitive determinative compound (*tatpuruṣa*).
This is an *adhikaraṇasaptamī-tatpuruṣa* (dependent compound): it is called "universal" (*sarvatraga*) because it serves as the cause for all defiled phenomena of the five categories;
thus, "universal" itself is the "universal cause," which is an *karmadhāraya* (appositional compound).

One must not say it is the cause of universal factors (*sarvatraga-hetu*), because it also serves as the cause for those that are not universal. The cause of maturation is called the "maturation cause" (*vipāka-hetu*); this is an *ṣaṣṭhī-tatpuruṣa* (genitive determinative) compound.
If one says that the maturation itself is the cause, it is called the "maturation cause" (*vipāka-hetu*);
this is an *appositional compound* (*karmadhāraya*). These six causes cannot all be formed as *possessive compounds* (*bahuvrīhi*).
If one says that the capacity to act as a cause—such as the efficient cause (*kāraṇa-hetu*) and so forth—is the cause, it is called the "efficient cause," and so on.
This demonstrates that the essence of these six is not a cause by depending on another as its cause;
rather, because the essence of these six is itself the cause,
first, regarding the "efficient cause" (kāraṇa-hetu), it refers to all efficient causes with the exception of the thing itself.
Below this, the second section specifically clarifies the essence [of the causes].
Since the six causes differ,
the text is divided into six parts.
This is the first section.
A question is raised, and the response is given in verse.
The treatise says: "up to 'because of abiding without obstruction.'"
Within the prose section,
there is first the explanation of the verse,
followed by the questions and answers.
Regarding the explanation of the verse, there are two parts: first, the determination of its essential nature;
second, the interpretation of its name.
This constitutes the definition of its substance. To state it in brief:
among all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*), with the sole exception of its own self-substance.
All conditioned and unconditioned phenomena constitute the essence of the efficient cause (*kāraṇa-hetu*),
because when their effects arise, they remain present without obstruction;
whereas a thing can never act as an obstruction to its own self.
Therefore, according to our own view, it is not a *kāraṇahetu* (efficient cause).
This is explained at length in the *Nyāyānusāra*. Question: Can it also serve as a cause for non-arising? Master Yue’s commentary states:
It is not a cause; now, this is explained as being incorrect,
for it is indeed a cause.
However, as for the treatise’s statement that [the aggregates] serve as the cause for birth,
this is based on what is explicitly taught;
although other causal natures may be included within the general category, they are here designated by their specific names.
This explains the definition of the term.
Among the six causes, although the other five abide by way of non-obstruction, [the efficient cause alone is defined by its capacity to produce].
It may also be termed the "efficient cause" (*kāraṇa-hetu*).
While each [of the other causes] has its own distinct name established from its specific characteristics,
the efficient cause has no further distinct name.
Just as with the sense-base of form (*rūpāyatana*) and so forth,
the general term is itself the specific name.
Is it not the case that "not yet known" (*ajñāta*) serves as the efficient cause (*kāraṇahetu*)?
The following is a section of questions and answers for analysis. Question:
Is it not the case that the outflows (āsrava) will arise because one has not yet known the principle of the Four Noble Truths?
Because one has already realized the principle of those Four Noble Truths, the outflows (āsrava) do not arise;
wisdom acts as an obstacle to the arising of the outflows.
Furthermore, just as sunlight can obstruct the eye.
When one observes the light of the stars, it can act as an obstacle to the functioning of the eye.
How then can conditioned phenomena, with the sole exception of their own selves,
serve as efficient causes (*kāraṇa-hetu*) for all other phenomena?
Regarding the statement that one should know this "arising" refers to the efficient cause (kāraṇahetu) when it reaches its time,
the answer is:
wisdom arises.
Kāśyapa, regarding those outflows, the eye is indeed capable of acting as an obstruction;
one should know that this occurs when these outflows arise.
Furthermore, when the various stars appear at the time of birth,
that wisdom— the sun— is present without obstruction;
therefore, it is called the "wisdom-sun."
Regarding these outflows (*āsrava*), the eye is the efficient cause (*kāraṇa-hetu*).
If it were to reach a state where it has no obstructive function toward the arising of these [outflows], that would be difficult to maintain.
If a phenomenon arises in dependence upon another,
that [other] phenomenon may be called a cause only if it has the capacity to obstruct or not obstruct;
if it lacks any obstructive function whatsoever, how could it be considered a cause even if it does not actually obstruct?
The analogy makes this clear.
Although it lacks the function of obstruction, the statement that [the seed] reaches the sprout and so forth is applicable.
For example, although things such as *nirvāṇa* lack the capacity to obstruct the arising of those phenomena and prevent them from occurring,
they nonetheless function as causes.
Because when the fruit arises, they are all capable of being without obstruction,
they are called causes. This is like a powerless king who, although incapable of causing harm, [is still designated as such].
One also attains, as previously stated, "peace and happiness through the sovereign as my cause. This is a general explanation of all unobstructed efficient causes (*kāraṇa-hetu*).
If one speaks of the efficient cause in terms of its preeminence:
"It is not that there is no power to produce [the act]; as in the case of the eyes and so forth," and so on—this cites the power of the proximate cause (*pratyāsanna-bala*).
Some raise this objection: "Does this mean that one becomes a perpetrator of killing in all cases?"
The opponent objects:
Since there is no obstruction to their abiding, they should all arise simultaneously;
since there is no obstruction to their abiding, they should all constitute killing.
This objection is not valid; it applies only to those who possess the power of direct agency.
This explains the objection:
[the result arises] simply due to the absence of obstructions.
All phenomena are admitted to be acting causes (*kāraṇa-hetu*),
not because there exists the direct productive power of the other five causes with respect to the arising of an effect;
therefore, all phenomena do not arise simultaneously.

It is not because of the causal motivation (*samutthāna*) or the direct performing force (*sākṣāt-karaṇa-bala*) regarding the act of killing that [all] become established as having committed the karma of killing;
therefore, it is not the case that all who kill are equally established as having performed the karma of killing.
Other masters say that this applies to those who possess the force of capability (*samartha-bala*).
It was previously stated that the efficient cause (kāraṇa-hetu) is both proximate and remote;
the proximate possesses functional power.
"Distant but not obstructive.
This is the intended meaning of this master regarding all efficient causes (*kāraṇa-hetu*).
All possess the capacity to act as a productive cause (*kāraṇa-hetu*) with respect to the arising of their results.
Now, regarding how things such as *nirvāṇa* possess the capacity to act as a productive cause:
[the question is asked].
Regarding the inclusion of non-arising dharmas and so forth:
if the mental consciousness takes them as its object and possesses the power to produce [a subsequent cognition], the answer is as follows.
The mental consciousness arises taking such phenomena as nirvāṇa as its object;
it may give rise to wholesome right views and the like,
or it may give rise to unwholesome wrong views and the like.
Therefore, at a subsequent time, the visual consciousness— whether wholesome or unwholesome—
arises in succession according to its respective conditions.
Because they are indirect causes,
those factors such as nirvana possess the capacity to act as an efficient cause (*kāraṇa-hetu*) for the arising of visual consciousness.
Other dharmas are to be understood accordingly as possessing the power to produce [their effects]. Question:

Since their essential natures (*svabhāva*) are thus broad and pervasive, how do these dharmas relate to one another as cause and effect? Answer: As stated in the *Nyāyānusāra* (Treatise on the Principles of Correct Reasoning), fascicle 15:
Past dharmas act as the efficient cause (*kāraṇa-hetu*) for the other two time periods; those dharmas of the two time periods [likewise act as efficient causes for past dharmas].
Furthermore, [present dharmas] serve as the sovereign fruit (*adhipatiphala*) for the past. As for future dharmas,
they act as the efficient cause (*kāraṇahetu*) for the other two time periods because they do not obstruct them.
Those dharmas of the two time-periods do not coexist, because [the cause] is posterior;
therefore, it does not serve as a sovereign fruit (*adhipatiphala*) for the future.
Since a fruit must necessarily be grasped by its cause, there are only two interpretations: namely, that if the fruit-dharmas were to coexist [with their cause], [it would be impossible].
If it occurs later, there are thus two [types of causes]. As for the "cause" (*hetu*), because it is based solely on the absence of obstruction, it is admitted to pervade all three time periods.
This refers to present dharmas.
It acts as a productive cause (*kāraṇa-hetu*) for the other two time periods.
Within those two time periods, only future dharmas serve as the results of the present.
Conditioned phenomena are both causes and results.
The conditioned and the unconditioned are neither cause nor fruit.
The unconditioned and the unconditioned are neither cause nor fruit.
The unconditioned and the conditioned are cause but not fruit.
For this reason, it is said as follows:
the efficient cause (*kāraṇa-hetu*) is for the most part not an dominant fruit (*adhipati-phala*),
because all phenomena are efficient causes, whereas only conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) are dominant fruits.
Having thus explained that which follows the mind with a focused mind,
the following second section clarifies the co-existent cause (*sahabhū-hetu*).
First, it correctly defines the co-existent [cause].
Second, the analysis of what accompanies the mind (*cittānuvartin*).
This is precisely the analysis of the co-existent (*sahabhū*).
The first phrase explains the meaning of being co-existent.
The latter two phrases point to the essence.
The *Śāstra* says: "As for being a co-existent cause (*sahabhū-hetu*)," this is a general explanation that the meaning of being mutually the fruit of one another is termed the co-existent cause.
As for what its characteristics are:
this asks about its essence.
For example, the four great elements act as simultaneous causes (*sahabhū-hetu*) for one another.
The following is the answer:
The four great elements (*mahābhūta*) are mutual simultaneous causes (*sahabhū-hetu*) for one another.
Therefore, the *Vibhāṣā* masters of the critical school say:
Whether the essential natures of the four primary elements are increased unevenly or not increased unevenly,
earth serves as the co-existent cause for the other three.
Third, the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) act as co-existent causes (*sahabhū-hetu*). Why is this?
Because the primary elements do not depend upon other primary elements when producing derived matter (*upādāya-rūpa*).
Because all phenomena do not observe their own nature (*svabhāva*) or their homogeneous essence (*sabhāga-rūpa*) as being the cause for others;
this applies even to the great element of wind (*vāyu-mahābhūta*).
Regarding the statement that "these various characteristics even act as mutual causes for one another," a question is asked:
Why is it not stated that the primary characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) and their concomitants (*anuvartaka*) each act as mutual causes for one another?
The *Nyāyānusāra* replies:
This is intended to demonstrate that it is only dissimilar factors (*vijātīya*) that are stated to be simultaneous causes (*sahabhū-hetu*),
whereas similar factors (*sajātīya*) are not explicitly stated to be mutual causes, as this is already established by implication.
"This is the simultaneous cause (sahabhū-hetu) up to as is appropriate" is the summary;
or it refers to the mutual relation of the great elements (mahābhūta).
Either the characteristic is viewed in relation to the characterized, or the characteristics are viewed in relation to one another,
or the mind is viewed in relation to the mind that functions in accordance with it.
Alternatively, because they are mutually concomitant with the mind that follows [the primary dharma], it is said "as appropriate.
