Regarding the dharmas and their secondary characteristics (*anulakṣaṇa*), those points to be explained in this context shall now be analyzed.
The author of the treatise points out the error of the Sarvāstivādins:
if one explains the co-existent cause (*sahabhū-hetu*) by means of mutual causality,
then a primary dharma and its secondary characteristics (*anulakṣaṇa*) would not be mutually causal.
Although the primary characteristics (lakṣaṇas) are the fruits of these factors (dharmas), the factors themselves are not the fruits of the secondary characteristics (anulakṣaṇas); therefore,
it is said that they do not serve as fruits for one another.

However, the primary dharma and its secondary characteristics (*anulakṣaṇa*) are simultaneous causes (*sahabhū-hetu*) for one another; it is not the case that the secondary characteristics are simultaneous causes for the primary dharma.
This point should be analyzed here; according to the sixteenth school of commentators in the *Vibhāṣā*, it is said:
The meaning of having a single fruit is the meaning of being a co-existent cause (*sahabhū-hetu*).
Furthermore, the *Nyāyānusāra* (Treatise on the Principles), fascicle 15, states:
"Conditioned phenomena that have a single fruit may serve as co-existent causes."
The intent of the two treatises is the same.
According to the intent of the *Nyāyānusāra*,
they are called "simultaneous causes" (*sahabhū-hetu*) because they serve as mutual effects for one another.
Because this [definition] is flawed, it is further explained:

among conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*), those that possess reciprocal power and together obtain a single fruit are called co-existent causes (*sahabhūhetu*). If one were to offer a defense as a teacher of the *Abhidharmakośa*, saying that "those which have a single fruit are called co-existent causes," [that would be incorrect].
Is this based on simultaneity,
or is it based on difference in time?
If it is based on simultaneity, then they would share the same effect.
Just as the intrinsic natures of the mind and mental factors are not identical with respect to their own nature and thus do not share a single fruit,
they should not be simultaneous causes (*sahabhū-hetu*).
If it is argued that, excluding their own nature, they share a single fruit with other phenomena...
This refers to the secondary characteristics (anulakṣaṇas).
If they are considered in relation to their primary dharmas, since they equally obtain the fruit of one great characteristic (mahālakṣaṇa),
they should be regarded as being mutually co-existent causes (sahabhūhetu) for those primary dharmas.
If one says that having the same effect constitutes a co-existent cause (*sahabhūhetu*),
as in the case of the mind and its mental factors (*citta-caittas*),
there are cases where things have the same effect but are not co-existent causes.
Just as in the case of mutual dependence regarding the fundamental dharma, I have merely stated that things can serve as simultaneous causes (*sahabhū-hetu*) within a single result;
I did not say that all things which share a single result are necessarily simultaneous causes. If one offers this defense:
This statement regarding the "identity of the fruit" is not a definitive proof.
If it refers to attaining the same fruit at different times,
it is like the case where the fundamental dharma and its great characteristics both attain the subsequent single fruit together.
The secondary characteristics (anulakṣaṇas) and the primary characteristics (lakṣaṇas) likewise all attain the same final fruit.
That is to say, the fundamental dharma, its characteristics, and its secondary characteristics,
when viewed in relation to one another, all equally attain the same final fruit.
If that were so, then in relation to one another, they ought to be called simultaneous causes (sahabhū-hetu) with respect to their primary dharmas; yet,
whether one pursues this argument further or retreats from it, many logical fallacies arise.
When investigated through reasoning,
the fault of mutual proof as effect is minimal; however,
that which functions as a mutual effect is necessarily a co-existent cause (*sahabhūhetu*).
It is not said that all things which are co-existent causes (sahabhū-hetu) are mutually effects of one another;
nor does being mutual effects necessarily entail being co-existent causes.
This can also be explained by the definition of "matter" (rūpa) as that which is subject to transformation and resistance.
Although non-informative matter (*avijñapti*) is not subject to transformation or resistance, it is still designated as "matter" (*rūpa*).
Why, then, can this not resolve the difficulty regarding their mutual causality?
It is because [this position] involves numerous faults.
According to the *Abhidharmāvatāra-śāstra*,
there are two interpretations;
therefore, that treatise states:
All conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*) are mutually effects of one another;
those that share a single effect are called co-existent causes (*sahabhūhetu*). The masters of the *Abhidharmakośa* say:
"That treatise was composed later."

It is said that they are mutually fruits; this refers to my teacher, the Venerable Vasubandhu. Question: Regarding the associated cause (*samprayuktaka-hetu*) and the co-existent cause (*sahabhū-hetu*), both take simultaneous efficient fruit (*puruṣakāra-phala*).
What is the specific intention behind each? Explanation: The associated cause takes a simultaneous efficient fruit.
The intention is that they take a single object as their common focal point;
the co-existent cause (sahabhū-hetu) takes the simultaneous efficient fruit (puruṣakāra-phala),
intending to provide lateral support for all simultaneous phenomena so that each may give rise to its own activity.
Either they exercise the function of the efficient cause (*kāraṇa-hetu*),
or they exercise the function of the homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*) and the pervasive cause (*sarvatraga-hetu*),
or they exercise the function of the retributive cause (*vipāka-hetu*), each taking its own respective fruit.
Because these two causes produce different effects, their underlying intentions are distinct.
Question: As explained in the *Pañcavastuka-śāstra* regarding the mental factors (*caitta-dharma*) within the context of "association" (*samprayoga*), [how does this differ from the present case]?
There is one interpretation which says:
"Furthermore, at the same time and with the same basis."
Identical in aspect, identical in object,
and identical in fruit.
Having the same outflow (*niṣyanda*) and the same maturation (*vipāka*):
this is the meaning of "associated. According to that treatise, the mental factors associated with the mind likewise have the same fruit and so forth.

How can it be said that the associated cause (saṃprayuktaka-hetu) intends for [factors] to share a single object (ālambana), rather than supporting one another to grasp a single fruit (phala) and so forth?
The explanation states: the mental factors (caitta-dharma) associated with the mind are both associated causes and co-existent causes (sahabhū-hetu).
If one says they occur simultaneously,
with a single basis and a single mode of activity.
The aspect of having a single object (*ālambana*) is the associated cause (*samprayuktaka-hetu*).
If one says that the aspect of having a single fruit (*eka-phala*) and so forth is the co-existent cause (*sahabhū-hetu*), another interpretation of that treatise states:
"The term 'associated' (*samprayukta*) here does not intend to definitively establish the associated cause and the co-existent cause."
What are called the factors that follow the mind?
Below this, the second section clarifies the factors that follow the mind.
Within this, first, the essential nature of the factors that follow the mind is presented.
Second, the explanation of the meaning of "concomitance with the mind" (cittānuvartin).
This constitutes the first inquiry.
The verse says: "Regarding those dharmas that are concomitant with the mind..."
The first two phrases identify the essence;
the final phrase establishes the name.

This refers to all mental factors (*caitasika-dharma*), the discipline of the path (*mārga-saṃvara*), those dharmas—namely those mental factors and the two types of disciplinary dharmas—as well as the primary characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) such as arising (*jāti*) that belong to the mind.
All such factors are called "concomitants of the mind" (*cittānuvartaka-dharma*),
because these factors and the mind act as mutual effects for one another. Since it mentions "arising" (*jāti*) and so forth,
but does not mention "the arising of arising" (*jāti-jāti*) and so forth, [it follows that the latter do not exist].
This demonstrates that the secondary characteristics (anulakṣaṇas) do not follow the mind, as will be explained separately later.
As for the question, "How does this dharma reach [its state] by way of time, fruit, wholesomeness, and so forth? [it is as follows:]
The following is the second section, which explains the meaning of "concomitance with the mind" (*cittānuvartin*) through both a question and a verse response.
The treatise states: "That which is called 'concomitant with the mind'...
This refers to the initial explanation of the verse within the prose commentary.
Next, the coexistence [of dharmas] is clarified by means of their functions.
The following explains the verse: "fruit, etc."—the "etc.
includes the ripened (*vipāka*) and the outflowing (*niṣyanda* [results]; "wholesome, etc."—the "etc. includes unwholesome and neutral [dharmas]).
This includes the unwholesome and the indeterminate;
the four types beginning with birth are collectively termed "time.
Therefore, these terms [of the sūtra] do not apply to time.
However, regarding the fruit and the wholesome,
and specifically that which pertains to time— up to "belonging to a single world-period"—
the following provides a detailed explanation of time.
Within that interval there are four:
first, arising;
second, ceasing.
One abides; it falls within one lifetime.

This demonstrates that [the characteristics] are called "concomitants" (anuvartaka) only when they exist at the same time and in the same location as the mind. Question: Among the four characteristics, [which...]
Why are the distinct characteristics not mentioned? The explanation is as follows: arising refers to bringing a dharma from the future into the present;
abiding refers to causing a dharma to remain stable while in the present;
and cessation refers to the passing of a dharma into the past.
Each possesses its own specific capacity; therefore, they are explained separately.

Because the destruction of a phenomenon through the mutual assistance of other conditions lacks a distinct, superior capacity, it is not mentioned. Furthermore, another interpretation of this passage holds that "abiding" (*sthiti*) is simply an alternative name for "alteration" (*anyathātva*).
To clarify the distinction regarding their abiding,
the *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 155, states: "In this context,
'arising' refers to birth (*jāti*)."
"Abiding" refers to aging;
"ceasing" refers to impermanence. Furthermore, the *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra* raises an objection, saying:
"Why not simply speak of arising, abiding, and ceasing?"

One immediately knows that this also refers to falling into a single lifetime; the commentary explains that by mentioning "arising," "abiding," and "ceasing" within one life, it has already manifested falling into the future and so forth.

One might ask: "If it has already been stated that they fall into a single lifetime, would it not be redundant to say 'falling into a single lifetime' again? The *Zhengli* (Correct Understanding) explains: "Although it is indeed known that they fall into a single lifetime..."
Furthermore, this dharma and the mind have not yet been fully understood as being inseparable throughout the past and the future.
Alternatively, it is said in order to demonstrate that dharmas are non-arising;
thus, it further states "and falling into one period," which explains that it refers merely to a single lifetime and so forth.
Although he also immediately knows that arising falls into the future world,
while abiding and ceasing fall into the present world,
he has still not yet understood this dharma in relation to the mind.
Because that which has fallen away into the past and that which has not yet reached birth remain inseparable from the remainder of the future world,
it is said that they "fall into one world" to manifest this inseparability.
Or perhaps some may harbor a doubt:
"Since those [dharmas] that have already arisen in the past and those that will arise in the future are not dissociated from the mind, should they not also be called 'concomitants of the mind'?"
That which does not arise in the future should be capable of being dissociated and would not follow the mind.
Furthermore, it is to demonstrate that even those dharmas that do not arise are likewise not dissociated [from one another].
Apart from arising, abiding, and ceasing, it is further stated that [a phenomenon] falls within a single lifetime (*ekajāti*).
Furthermore, the *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra* raises an objection, saying:

If that were so, one should simply say that [the dharma] falls within a single *adhvan*. The explanation is as follows: the term *adhvan* (world/period) is broad in scope, whereas its characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) are narrow;
thus, the *adhvan* may be established separately from its characteristics.
Since [the characteristics] are already subsumed within the world (*loka*),
why is it necessary to speak separately of arising (*jāti*) and so forth as being apart from the world?
The *Nyāyānusāra* states:

No; otherwise, one would not be made to know that [the state] is definitely fixed to a single birth. The commentary explains: "Birth" (*jāti*) and so forth are fixed, whereas "birth-state" (*janman*) is indefinite.
Just as past dharmas consist of many moments,
even though they now likewise fall within the same single period of time,
among them, whichever dharma [is considered]:
Formerly, when there was no distinction between the present and other worlds,
the future dharmas consisted of many moments that had not yet reached the present.
Although they belong to the same world,
whichever phenomenon it may be,
if it flows into the present—
That which coexists with future dharmas belongs to a different time period;
thus, it is neither fixed nor concomitant.
This is intended to make known that [the mind] is necessarily included within a single time period.
Therefore, apart from falling into one lifetime,
it is further stated that there is arising, abiding, and ceasing.
Arising is necessarily falling into the future life.
The abiding and cessation attainments fall within the present world.
If there were no [characteristics] such as arising, they would not cause one to know that these attainments fall within a single time period.
From "by way of the fruit" up to "and by way of the outflow."
Among the fruits, there are three:
first, the fruit of fruition; second, the fruit of maturation.
First, regarding the "same outflow" (eka-niṣyanda):
this indicates that only those factors which share the same fruit as the mind are designated as "concomitant" (anuvartaka).
The *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra* states:
Is it not the case that both outflow (*niṣyanda*) and maturation (*vipāka*) are also subsumed under the single category of "fruit"?

Why, then, are outflow and maturation mentioned as being external to the "one fruit"? The explanation is: the term "fruit" is used in a general sense and should therefore include the other two [types of fruit].
Regarding the statement that there are two [types of] results external to the fruit, what is the intended meaning?
The *Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna-śāstra* states:
It is indeed so.

Regarding the statement here that there is "one fruit," it refers only to the fruit of human effort (*puruṣakāra-phala*) and the fruit of disconnection (*visamyoga-phala*). The commentary explains: if one speaks according to a general definition of the term "fruit," it is indeed so.
This also subsumes the other two.
Regarding the statement that these ten concomitants have "a single fruit," this is discussed from a specific perspective.
It comprises only the fruit of human effort (*puruṣakāra-phala*) and the fruit of disconnection (*visamyoga-phala*).
Furthermore, the *Nyāyabindu* raises an objection:

"Does this statement not apply universally so as to also include the fruits of outflow (*niṣyanda-phala*) and maturation (*vipāka-phala*)? The response explains: "Does this term 'one fruit' [not] apply [to all]?"
The commentary on the *Nyāyabindu* states:
"Although it is said that [the faculty of] penetration also subsumes the other two, this is not what is being elucidated here."
However, there are generally four kinds of virile fruits (*puruṣakāra-phala*):
simultaneous, immediate, remote, and non-arising.
This indicates that it is not a fruit coexistent with its cause.
This is to refute the exclusive attachment to the idea that within the composite aggregate co-arising with its cause, there exists a "human effort fruit" (*puruṣakāra-phala*);
for while the members of this composite aggregate serve as fruits for one another,
the [composite] itself is not a human effort fruit of its own self.
This demonstrates that among the co-arising, combined *puruṣakāra-phala* (human effort results), there is no sense of being a single result.

Therefore, the *niṣyanda-phala* (outflow result) and *vipāka-phala* (ripening result) are mentioned separately. The commentary explains: although the name "single result" applies generally, it also encompasses the *niṣyanda-phala* and the *vipāka-phala*.
However, this is not what is clarified within this discussion of "concomitant transformation" (anuvartana).
Herein, the single fruit consists exclusively of the fruit of human effort (puruṣakāra-phala) and the fruit of disjunction (visamyoga-phala). An external opponent raises an objection:
Regarding the meaning of "concomitant transformation" (*anuvartana*) herein,
the statement that they share a single fruit is sufficient to clarify such concomitance;
why then is it necessary to separately mention "maturation" (*vipāka*) and "outflow" (*niṣyanda*)?
Therefore, I shall now explain this.
To dispel doubts and obstacles, it is necessary to discuss those two points. Why is this so?
Now, the fruits of human effort (*puruṣakāra-phala*) are generally of four kinds.
First is the simultaneous fruit of human effort (*sahaja-puruṣakāra-phala*),
which refers to the reciprocal fruits produced at the same time by co-existent and associated causes.
And those produced simultaneously with it that are acquired [by it] are its two immediate results of human effort (*puruṣakāra-phala*);
namely, those produced by the immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*) and those produced by other conditions occurring in immediate succession.
Third is the fruit of human effort separated by an interval,
which is like the fruit of maturation (*vipākaphala*) and like a farmer who sows in spring and reaps in autumn.
Fourth is the non-arising of the fruit of human effort (*puruṣakāra-phala*),
which refers to the non-arising of the essence of analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
This generally clarifies that there are four types of fruits of human effort in total.
Regarding the statement "one fruit" among these ten types of concomitant factors (*anuvartaka*),
it does not refer to the simultaneous or reciprocal *puruṣakāra-phala* (fruit of human effort),
because a thing itself cannot be its own *puruṣakāra-phala*.
This does not mean they have a single result.
Regarding those who acquire [results] through other simultaneous activities,
among the immediate [successions], one must exclude those of the same nature.
Immediately following [an action] of a different nature,
one takes the remaining results; among those separated by an interval, excluding the ripening result (*vipākaphala*), one takes the remaining results— the distant dominant result (*adhipatiphala*)—
as well as the result of non-arising and the result of analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyānirodha*).
Fearing that those who have not yet understood might,
upon hearing the term "single fruit," claim it encompasses both the co-arising and the successive *puruṣakāra* fruits, or alternatively,
cling to the view that there exists only the co-arising *puruṣakāra* fruit.

Therefore, at this point, [the author] further separately demonstrates that the results of outflow (*niṣyanda*), maturation (*vipāka*), and the determinate [result] do not arise simultaneously with their cause.
This is intended to refute the position that maintains that the efficient fruit (*puruṣakāra-phala*) exists only within the assemblage of factors arising together with the cause.
The term "co-nascent" (sahaja) excludes [factors] such as immediate succession (ānantarya).
The phrase "congregated collection" (saṃghāta) excludes other types of co-nascent production, namely those consisting of volitional activity (abhisamskāra) or acquisition (prāpti).
This refers to the expression "congregated collection."
This is to clarify the meaning that they serve as causes for one another.
It is necessary to exclude this [notion of] "human effort" (puruṣakāra) because it does not result in a single effect;
that is to say, they are mutually effects of one another.
This demonstrates that [the cause] is also the fruit of another;
it is not its own substantial fruit. The member [of dependent origination] demonstrates that it is not its own fruit.
Because one's own fruit is not shared with others,
there is no sense of a single fruit.
Why stop at merely negating the notion that co-arising factors are mutual *puruṣakāra-phala* (fruits of human effort)?
This also serves to clarify the meaning that there is no single fruit.

Because this objection has been refuted, the outflowing fruit (*niṣyanda-phala*) and the ripening fruit (*vipāka-phala*) are explained separately from the single fruit. Question: If one relies on the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 16...
And [the total] is one hundred and fifty-five.
It states that "one fruit" refers to the fruit of dissociation (*visamyoga-phala*).
The *Nyāya* further states:
"A single fruit refers to the fruit of human effort (*puruṣakāra-phala*) and the fruit of disconnection (*visamyoga-phala*).
Is this not contradictory? The explanation says:
As for the *Abhidharmamahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*’s exclusive mention of the fruit of dissociation (*visamyoga-phala*),
this is stated with reference to that fruit alone which is definitive and free from confusion.
The fruit of human effort (puruṣakāra-phala) is termed "broad" and "indeterminate," as it may be either co-nascent (sahaja) or immediate (anantara), and so forth.
The *Abhidharmamahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* should also have discussed the fruit of human effort.
The reason it is not stated [as such] is that one fears it would be confused with the co-nascent (*sahaja*) and reciprocal (*paraspara*) efficient fruits (*puruṣakāra-phala*);
for when a thing is considered in relation to its own self, it does not constitute a single fruit.
The reason the *Nyāyānusāra* speaks of "human effort" (*puruṣakāra*) is to encompass the entirety of the fruit of human effort within a single fruit; therefore,
it is mentioned separately.

Each is based on a specific meaning and they do not contradict one another. Question: Regarding the "single fruit" (eka-phala) in this treatise, with which [system] is it identical? Explanation: It may be identical to the *Vibhāṣā*, or it may be identical to the *Nyāyānusāra*.

None of these present any contradiction. Question: According to the treatise cited below, among the five fruits, it is stated that the fruit of human effort (*puruṣakāra-phala*) is obtained only through the associated cause (*saṃprayuktaka-hetu*) and the co-existent cause (*sahabhū-hetu*).
For what reason does the *Nyāya* state that the fruit of human effort (*puruṣakāra-phala*) is of many kinds and is obtained through other causes as well?
The explanation is that there are two types of the fruit of human effort.
First, the result of specific human effort (*puruṣakāra-phala*),
which is obtained only by the associated cause (*samprayuktaka-hetu*) and the co-existent cause (*sahabhū-hetu*).
Second, the general result of human effort.
However, whatever is attained through the application of effort is termed a "result of human effort" (*puruṣakāra-phala*).
The *Nyāyānusāra* relies on this to explain the term "human effort" in a general sense,
as appropriate to each case.
The four fruits in their entirety and a small portion of the higher [fruit] are attained through six causes;

each is established according to its own specific meaning, and thus they do not contradict one another. One should know that within this context, although the terminology may differ, the underlying meaning is not inconsistent.
It should be understood that herein,
the former [of the two] refers to time, indicating simultaneity;
the latter refers to the fruit, indicating a common fruit.
Because they manifest together and manifest in common, it is said that their meanings are not the same.
Regarding the phrase "from being wholesome up to being indeterminate," this indicates that the nature [of the mental factors] is identical to that of the mind.
Among these, there are three:
first, the wholesome;
second, the unwholesome.
The three [types of] indeterminate [dharmas].
This concludes the summary of why these ten causes are called "concomitants of the mind" (*cittānuvartin*).
Regarding the statement that "herein, the mind-king (*citta-rāja*) acts as the co-existent cause (*sahabhū-hetu*) for the mind":
the following section clarifies the co-existent cause by way of specific dharmas.
This precedes the previous discussion concerning the scope—whether universal or restricted—of the mind-king acting as a cause for mental factors (*caitta*) and so forth.
Furthermore, this is explained in terms of the non-obscured neutral (anivṛtāvyākṛta) mind from the second dhyāna upward.
Therein, there are only the mental king (cittarāja) and the ten universal mental factors (mahābhūmika-dharma).
These eleven types each possess the four primary and secondary characteristics (lakṣaṇa), resulting in a total of ninety-nine dharmas.
In relation to the ninety-eight dharmas,
the mind-king (citta-rāja) has at its very minimum fifty-eight dharmas as its co-existent causes (sahabhū-hetu):
namely, the ten universal mental factors (mahābhūmika-dharma) and their forty primary characteristics (mūla-lakṣaṇa).
The eight primary mental factors and their secondary characteristics constitute fifty-eight dharmas;
this excludes the forty secondary characteristics associated with the universal mental factors.
Because they are separated by distance, their power does not reach that [object], and thus they are not simultaneous causes (*sahabhū-hetu*).
If one considers fifty-eight dharmas in relation to the mind-king (*citta-rāja*),
excluding the four secondary characteristics (*anulakṣaṇa*) of the mind:
Because they are inferior and weak, their power does not reach that [of the primary mind].
The remaining fifty-four [mental factors] act as co-existent causes (*sahabhū-hetu*) for the mind,
just as the mind-king acts reciprocally toward the ninety-eight dharmas.
The ten universal mental factors (*mahābhūmika-dharma*).

One should understand that each subsequent factor is to be treated according to this same principle. If one takes the great ground-factor "birth" (*jāti*) as the subject in relation to the ninety-eight dharmas, it serves as the co-existent cause (*sahabhū-hetu*) for fifty-eight dharmas.
This refers to the ten universal mental factors (*mahābhūmika-dharma*), together with their forty primary characteristics (*mūla-lakṣaṇa*);
as well as the mind-king (*citta-rāja*) itself, along with its three major and four minor characteristics.
This excludes the forty secondary characteristics (*anulakṣaṇa*) belonging to the universal mental factors.
The fifty-eight factors, in relation to the mind, give rise to the "great" [mental factors].
Fifty-five of these serve as the co-existent cause (*sahabhū-hetu*).

This excludes the minor [mental factors] associated with the mind—namely, *sthiti*, *jarā*, and *anityatā*. Furthermore, it is explained that they give rise to the "great" [factors] upon the mind-king (*citta-rāja*).
It is the co-existent cause (sahabhū-hetu) for eighteen factors:
namely, the ten universal mental factors (mahābhūmika-dharma),
the mind-king (citta-rāja), as well as the four great characteristics (mahā-lakṣaṇa)— arising, duration, change, and cessation— and the four secondary characteristics (anulakṣaṇa).
These eighteen dharmas, when viewed in relation to the mind, give rise to fifteen [mental factors] as co-existent causes (*sahabhū-hetu*).
This excludes the minor mental states of duration (*sthiti*), change (*anyathātva*), and cessation (*bhaṅga*). Regarding these two interpretations, each possesses its own underlying intent.
The previous explanation was based on the principle that the great arising (*mahābhūta*) and the mind (*citta*), which it characterizes, possess equal power;
thus, with respect to the forty great characteristics (*mahālakṣaṇa*) belonging to the universal mental factors (*mahābhūmikadharma*),
it may also function as a co-existent cause (*sahabhūhetu*).
The subsequent explanation of the mental factors (*caitasikas*) is like that of the mind-king (*citta-rāja*):
they serve as causes only for the primary characteristics (*mahābhūtalakṣaṇa*) and secondary characteristics (*anuvyañjanalakṣaṇa*) on their back;
whereas if directed forward, they serve as causes only for the associated phenomena (*saṃprayuktadharma*) and the four primary characteristics upon those associated phenomena.
Taking the second layer both behind and ahead,
they cannot serve as causes for the minor four characteristics (*anulakṣaṇa*) of the associated dharmas;
because they are distant, their power does not reach the third layer.
This great arising is likewise able to serve as the cause for the mind-king and its associated mental factors,
but only up to the second stage.
Nor can it serve as the cause for the four great characteristics (*mahā-lakṣaṇa*) that arise subsequently,
because being separated by a distance, its power does not reach the third level.
This is explained in two ways, just as with the "great arising" (*mahā-jāti*) that arises upon the mind-king (*citta-rāja*).
It should be known that there are the [four] great characteristics— arising, abiding, change, and cessation— upon the mind-king (citta-rāja),
as well as the forty great characteristics upon the universal mental factors (mahābhūmika-dharma).
Both [commentaries] provide two interpretations;
one should understand it accordingly.
If [a mental factor] arises slightly upon the mind-king (citta-rāja) in relation to the ninety-eight dharmas:
It acts as a co-existent cause (*sahabhū-hetu*) solely for the great arising.
Conversely, with respect to the small arising,
ninety-eight dharmas have five types of dharmas as their causes.
This refers to the mind and the four great characteristics (mahā-lakṣaṇa) of the mind, which are like the minor characteristics (anulakṣaṇa) of the mind;
one should know that there are likewise the four minor characteristics— subsistence, change, and cessation—
of the mental sovereign (citta-rāja), as well as the forty minor characteristics of the universal mental factors (mahābhūmika-dharma).
Based on this, it should be understood as follows. Question: The minor characteristics (*anuvyañjana*) on the mind do not characterize the mental king (*cittarāja*).

Since they are similar to the major characteristics (*mahā-vyañjana*) of the universal mental factors (*mahābhūmika-dharma*), why is it that the major characteristics of the universal mental factors serve as causes for the mind?
Is the minor mental factor (*caitasika*) not a cause of the mind? Regarding this, the masters of old who commented on the *Dharmapada* explain that,

in relation to the sovereign mind (*citta-rāja*), the universal mental factors (*mahābhūmika-dharma*) possess both the associated cause (*samprayuktaka-hetu*) and the co-existent cause (*sahabhū-hetu*).
Therefore, among the universal mental factors (mahābhūmika-dharma), the universal factors are mutually co-existent causes (sahabhū-hetu) for the mind-king (citta-rāja). Among the universal factors,
the universal factors are merely co-existent causes for the mind-king.

Therefore, the great characteristics (mahābhūmika-dharma) are superior to the minor characteristics (parīttabhūmika-dharma). [The opponent claims that] in relation to the mind-king (citta-rāja), they are not co-existent causes (sahabhū-hetu). Refuting this:
for example, the great characteristics of the morality that follows the mind (cittānuvartin-śīla) are dharmas that follow the mind.
That is to say, the mind is a co-existent cause (sahabhū-hetu) with respect to the precepts; however, with respect to the mind,
those characterized precepts possess only a co-existent cause and lack an associated cause (samprayuktaka-hetu).
"How can those [mental factors] be mutually considered *sahabhū-hetu* (co-existent causes) for one another?

Therefore, it is said that this is unreasonable. Now, the explanation is as follows: regarding the forty great characteristics (*mahābhūta-lakṣaṇa*) upon the universal mental factors (*mahābhūmika-dharma*).
Because the power of the birth-characteristic (*jāti*) is strong and equal to that of the dharma it characterizes,
it serves as a cause in relation to the mind-king (*citta-rāja*), whereas the mind-king is the minor characteristic (*anuvyañjana*).
Because the power of the produced dharma is inferior and it is not a dharma that is coextensive with its characterized object,
it is not a cause in relation to the mind-king. Thus,
the *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya* (Jianzhong lun), fascicle nine, states:
Because the power of the intrinsic characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) and that of the dharma itself are equal. Furthermore, the *Nyāyānusāra* states:
"For what reason is it that the characteristics do not serve as co-existent causes (*sahabhū-hetu*) for the mind?
Because the mind does not arise by virtue of their power."
This is because the mind and those [factors] do not serve as mutual effects;
because they possess functional efficacy toward a single dharma;
and because they do not share the same effect as the mental sovereign (citta-rāja).
Because for the most part within that aggregate, they are not its results;
thus, by virtue of these many stated reasons,
the secondary characteristics (anulakṣaṇas) are not called "concomitant mental factors" (cittānuvartaka-dharma).
If that is so, how can the mind serve as the co-existent cause (*sahabhū-hetu*) for them?

It is because they proceed in accordance with the various states, such as arising, of the mental sovereign (*citta-rāja*). [End of] the treatise. Some say that [the co-existent cause] is the cause of the mind, including the primary characteristics (*mūla-lakṣaṇa*) of the mind.
This is the interpretation of the second master:
when the fifty-eight factors are compared with the mind-king (*cittarāja*),
only fourteen factors constitute its co-existent causes (*sahabhūhetu*).
This refers to the ten universal mental factors (mahābhūmika-dharma) together with the four primary characteristics of the mind;
it does not include the forty secondary characteristics (anuvyañjana-lakṣaṇa) that pertain to the universal mental factors.
This differs from the previous master.

This master’s intention is to say that because the mind follows and is separated from its own fundamental characteristic (*mūla-lakṣaṇa*), it is not a coexistent cause (*sahabhū-hetu*) in relation to the mind.
Therefore, one should know that because the universal mental factors (mahābhūmika-dharma) are mutually exclusive, they are not co-existent causes (sahabhū-hetu) with respect to the mind.
This explanation is not sound; it is known to be incomplete.
The Master of the Treatise refutes the second teacher:
This exposition is not sound. Why is this so?
If one were to say that only fourteen factors are the co-existent causes (*sahabhū-hetu*) in relation to the mind,
it would contradict what is stated in the *Prakaraṇapāda-śāstra*.
Because the text here is abbreviated, the proof is somewhat difficult to discern.
If one consults the tenth chapter, "The Chapter on Three Thousand Questions," of the *Prakaraṇapāda-śāstra*, it asks:
"How many have the view of a self-body (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) as their cause, but are not causes of the view of a self-body?
The answer is: two.
"Neither having the view of a self-identity as its cause, nor being the cause of the view of a self-identity. Explanation:
There are two [factors], namely cessation.
The two truths should be distinguished in two ways. That is to say,
regarding the Noble Truth of Suffering,
there are cases where it has the view of a self-identity as its cause, yet is not itself a cause for the view of a self-identity.
There are things that have the view of a self as their cause and also have the view of a self as their cause;

there are things that neither have the view of a self as their cause nor have the view of a self as their cause. Regarding those that have the view of a self as their cause but do not have the view of a self as their cause:

That is to say: excluding the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) to be abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-satya*) that are past and present, as well as the truths of suffering (*duḥkha-satya*) associated with and co-existent with them; and also excluding the universal latent dispositions (*sarvatraga-anuśaya*) to be abandoned through the vision of the origin (*samudaya-satya*) that are past and present.

And the truth of suffering associated with that [view], as well as the truth of suffering coexistent with it; furthermore, one also excludes the truth of suffering associated with the view of a self-identity in the future, and also excludes the view of a self-identity in the future.
And the associated dharmas of those [afflictions], as well as their arising, aging, duration, and impermanence;
furthermore, all other defiled truths of suffering that have the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) as their cause, and which themselves have the view of a self-identity as their cause.
This refers to those factors previously excluded: those that do not have the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) as their cause, nor are they causes for the view of a self-identity.

This refers to the undefiled *duḥkhasatya* (truth of suffering) and likewise the *samudayasatya* (truth of origination). The commentary explains: That passage examines the relationship between the essence of the four truths and the view of a self-identity in terms of whether they universally or specifically function as causes.
"Condition" refers to the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*) among the four conditions;
it has the five causes as its nature,
excluding the efficient cause (*kāraṇa-hetu*).
Within this context, whichever factors are present in relation to one another may all serve as causes;
it is not necessary for all five conditions to be complete.
Because the two truths of cessation and the path are untainted (anāsrava),
they do not have the view of a self-identity as their cause,
nor are they the cause of the view of a self-identity.
The two truths of suffering and its origin should be distinguished.
First, by correlating the truth of suffering with the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), three propositions are established.
This is because there is necessarily nothing that arises without having the view of a self-identity as its cause.
Regarding that which has the view of a self-identity as its cause:
the reason is that there is nothing that does not have the view of a self-identity as its cause.
It is not the case that the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) alone serves as the cause; this is a single categorical statement.
Furthermore, in all treatises, when formulating arguments, if many [factors] are taken up, the few are excluded.
If one takes up the few, they are immediately designated by name;
this is to economize on discourse.
In the first phrase, one takes up the many and excludes the few.
Since all defiled truths of suffering arise from the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*),
when looking back at that view of a self-identity,
those for which it serves as a cause are few, while those for which it does not serve as a cause are many.
Now, because one wishes to eliminate the many, one first eliminates the few.

Within the process of elimination, there are four sections: the first section eliminates the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*) in the past and present.
And the Truth of Suffering (duḥkhasatya) that is associated with it, co-existent with it, and so forth.
"Associated" refers to the associated dharmas;
"co-existent" refers to the four characteristics (lakṣaṇas).
The term "etc. (ādi) means including acquisition (*prāpti*) and so forth.
If one considers the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) and their associated factors (*saṃprayukta-dharma*) in relation to the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), there are four causes:
the similar-type cause (*sabhāga-hetu*), the universal cause (*sarvatraga-hetu*), the associated cause (*saṃprayuktaka-hetu*), and the co-existent cause (*sahabhū-hetu*).
There is no ripening cause (*vipāka-hetu*).

If the four [aggregates] are viewed in relation to one another, there are the similar-type cause (*sabhāga-hetu*), the pervasive cause (*sarvatraga-hetu*), and the co-existent cause (*sahabhū-hetu*) for the view of a self-identity (*satkāya-dṛṣṭi*).
There is no associated cause or retributive cause;
if acquisition is considered in relation to the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*),
there is only the similar-type cause (*sabhāgahetu*).

There are four remaining causes. In the second section, one also excludes the past and present universal latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) to be abandoned by the vision of the origin (*samudaya*), as well as the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkhasatya*) that is associated with and co-existent with them.
Regarding these latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) in relation to the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), they are exclusively universal causes (*sarvatragahetu*) and lack the other four causes;

since they do not constitute non-universal causes, the term "etc. (*ādi*) is not used. In the third section, one must also exclude the associated suffering-truth (*duḥkhasatya*) that arises from future instances of the view of a self-identity.
The view of a self-identity is not abandoned;
this is because future view of a self-identity takes past and present view of a self-identity as its cause.
Because the future has no priority or posteriority, it cannot serve as a cause for the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*).
That view of a self-identity is subsumed under the category of single-membered [factors].
As for associated factors in relation to the view of a self-identity:

It possesses the associated cause (*samprayuktaka-hetu*) and the co-existent cause (*sahabhū-hetu*), but lacks the homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*), the pervasive cause (*sarvatraga-hetu*), and the retributive cause (*vipāka-hetu*). In the fourth section, one must also exclude the future existence-view (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), as well as its arising, aging, duration, and impermanence.
And regarding the associated factors, there are arising, aging, duration, and impermanence.
This fourth section does not exclude the view of a self-existent body (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*),
because it is subsumed under a single category.
Nor does it exclude the associated dharmas,
because those are excluded by the third section;
it excludes only the four great characteristics (mahā-lakṣaṇa) that reside upon those dharmas.
Since it speaks only of birth, aging, duration, and impermanence,
it is clearly known that these are the four great characteristics (mahā-lakṣaṇa).
If it were the four minor characteristics (anulakṣaṇa), it would have to mention "birth of birth" and so forth.
This refers to the view of a self-identity (satkāyadṛṣṭi) in relation to that [view] itself, to the factors associated with it,
and to the four great elements in relation to the view of a self-identity.
Because the future lacks priority and posteriority, it cannot be said to have homogeneous or pervasive causes.
Because it is not an associated dharma, it cannot be said to have an associated cause.
Its retributive cause consists of unwholesome, wholesome, and contaminated dharmas.
The sensation is an unobscured-neutral maturation fruit;
its four characteristics are essentially obscured,
and the view of a self-identity is furthermore defiled.
Furthermore, it cannot be said that this is a ripening cause (*vipāka-hetu*);
since it has already been included among those excluded,
it is caused by the view of a self-identity (*satkāya-dṛṣṭi*).
There is also the category of being subsumed under the cause that is the view of a self (satkāyadṛṣṭi).
Since it is stated that there is a cause,
and it is not the co-existent cause (sahabhū-hetu), what other kind of cause could it be?
Regarding the great universal characteristics (mahābhūmika-dharma) associated with [the mind],
it should be understood by analogy that, in relation to the view of a self-identity (satkāyadṛṣṭi), they obtain the status of a co-existent cause (sahabhū-hetu).

The forty great characteristics (mahābhūtalakṣaṇa) associated with the universal mental factors (mahābhūmika-dharma) can also serve as co-existent causes (sahabhū-hetu) in relation to the mind-king (citta-rāja). By this, it is known.
It is certainly unreasonable to claim that only fourteen dharmas serve as co-existent causes (sahabhū-hetu) for the mind.

It should be understood that the *Abhidharmakośa* merely cites the fourth section of the *Prakaraṇapāda* as proof. Regarding "all other defiled truths of suffering," it should be understood [as follows].
These are the defiled dharmas abandoned through the vision of cessation, the vision of the path, and the path of cultivation across the three periods of time;
as well as those abandoned through the vision of the origin in the past and present,
including the non-universal latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) that are associated (*samprayukta*), co-existent (*sahabhū*), and so forth.
Furthermore, there is the acquisition (prāpti) upon the universal proclivities (sarvatraga-anuśaya) and their associated and co-existent dharmas;

as well as the minor four characteristics (lakṣaṇa) and their acquisitions upon the view of a self-identity (satkāya-dṛṣṭi), which is to be abandoned through the vision of suffering (duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya) in the future.
Furthermore, it includes the minor four characteristics (lakṣaṇas) associated with the view of a self (satkāyadṛṣṭi), as well as their acquisitions (prāpti),
and those factors associated with and co-existent with the remaining nine latent dispositions (anuśaya) to be abandoned through the vision of suffering (duḥkhadarśana-prahātavya).
And those future phenomena abandoned through the vision of the origin (*samudaya-darśana-prahātavya*):
these are all caused by the view of a self-identity (*satkāya-dṛṣṭi*),
but they do not themselves act as causes for the view of a self-identity.
This is called the second category of all other defiled truths of suffering:
those that have the view of a self-identity as their cause and also serve as the cause for the view of a self-identity.
That is to say, it refers to those aforementioned dharmas excluded [in the first two phrases].
Regarding the third phrase: "neither having the view of a self-identity as its cause, nor being the cause for the view of a self-identity."
This refers to the non-afflicted truth of suffering (*duḥkhasatya*) abandoned through cultivation; it should be understood to be the same as the noble truth of suffering.

The noble truth of origination (*samudayasatya*) should also be understood in the same way with respect to the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), with the only difference being that the term "origination" replaces the position of "suffering."
The remaining meanings are all the same,
because the truths of suffering and its origin are one and the same entity.
Since this is established according to the essential nature of the truths, there is no difference in their breadth or narrowness.
The masters of recent times state that the truth of origination is not without distinctions; specifically,
it excludes the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*).
That [opponent] claims that delusion regarding the truths gives rise to afflictions;
this assertion is incorrect—
it is a profound error.
The *Prakaraṇapāda* cites only the first and second phrases as proof;
the remaining [phrases] are included because their wording is identical.
The *Prakaraṇapāda* corresponds to the old *Saṃghabhedavastu*.
That text is somewhat erroneous;
for the passage concerning the first section on the past merely states:
"except for the proclivities (*anuśaya*) abandoned through the vision of suffering in the past and present."
That [suffering] associated with it is the Truth of Suffering;
it is not said to be "coexistent" (sahabhū) and so forth,
which means that coexistent factors and acquisitions (prāpti) are not excluded.
The text of the second section merely states that one excludes all pervasive latent dispositions (*sarvatraga-anuśaya*) abandoned through the vision of the origin (*samudaya-darśana-prahātavya*),
as well as the suffering truths (*duḥkha-satya*) associated with them;
furthermore, it does not exclude their co-existent factors (*sahabhū-dharma*).
The remainder of the text is the same as in the *Prakaraṇapāda*.
There are other masters who,
wishing to establish that only fourteen dharmas serve as co-existent causes (*sahabhū-hetu*) for the mind, [state as follows].
Therefore, one does not recite those associated dharmas; rather,
it is simply stated that there is the exclusion of the future arising, aging, duration, and impermanence of the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*),
as well as the four great characteristics (*mahālakṣaṇa*) of the dharmas associated with the view of a self-identity.
Since they do not enter among those [factors] to be excluded,
by this it is known that there are forty great characteristics (mahālakṣaṇa) upon the universal mental factors (mahābhūmika-dharma).
Nor does it serve as a co-existent cause (sahabhū-hetu) for the mind.
The Vaibhāṣika masters of Kaśmīr say:
"The Prakaraṇapāda must certainly be recited in this manner."
Excluding the future view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and the arising, aging, duration, and impermanence of its associated factors;
this is a provisional hypothesis according to that treatise.
There are no associated dharmas that reach [that state],
or one should understand that the statement is incomplete according to the principle of the co-existent cause (*sahabhū-hetu*),
for all treatises state that the four great characteristics (*mahā-lakṣaṇa*) exist upon associated dharmas.
These factors that follow the mind are precisely those that stand in the sense of being mutual co-existent causes (*sahabhū-hetu*) with the mind.
Regarding the phrase "all those [factors] by virtue of being co-existent (sahabhū) or co-arising (sahaja)":
this explains the co-existent cause (sahabhū-hetu),
further clarifying which co-existent factors are causes and which are not.
Whatever phenomena function as causes by virtue of being co-existent causes (sahabhū-hetu),
those phenomena are necessarily co-existent;
or, they may be co-existent.
They do not constitute causes by virtue of being simultaneous causes (*sahabhū-hetu*).
In total, there are eight pairs.
The first refers to how each of the secondary characteristics (*anulakṣaṇa*) relates to its respective primary dharma (*mūladharma*).
2. These various secondary characteristics (anulakṣaṇas) are mutually related to one another;
3. the secondary characteristics of the dharmas that follow the mind are related to the mind;
4. these various secondary characteristics are related to one another in turn.
5. All co-arising obstructive derived matter (upādāya-rūpa) is mutually relative;
6. a small portion of non-obstructive derived matter co-arising with non-informative matter (avijñapti);
7. the limbs [of the body] are mutually relative.
Seventh, all co-arising derived matter and primary elements are mutually related to one another.
Eighth, all co-arising acquisitions (prāpti) and their acquired objects (*prāpya*). Such are these various dharmas.
Although they are said to be co-existent, they do not constitute causes by virtue of being co-existent causes.
Why is this? Because those [characteristics], such as the secondary characteristics (anulakṣaṇas), in relation to the primary dharma and so forth...
Speaking from a horizontal perspective,
it is not because they can equally take on one fruit, one maturation, and one outflow;
for fear that there might be an objection.
The "attainment" (prāpti) and the "thing attained" (prāpya), like [the characteristics] such as arising (jāti) and so forth,
should be called simultaneous causes (sahabhū-hetu), because they arise together with the dharma.
Now, the explanation is given that the attainment and the dharma attained do not necessarily function simultaneously;
rather, the attainment may exist either prior to or subsequent to the dharma.

Or, there may be dharmas that arise together, yet because they do not arise simultaneously in the same manner as other determinate factors, they cannot be considered simultaneous causes (sahabhū-hetu) with respect to those dharmas. This applies to all cases regarding the principle of cause and effect as far as it extends.
The Sautrāntika asks:
All that has been established above regarding cause and effect may indeed be logically tenable for the time being.
Even granting this for the sake of argument,
in the world it is observed that prior seeds and such serve as causes for the production of subsequent fruits, such as sprouts.
In all worldly matters where cause and effect are universally established as arising in succession,
such simultaneous causality has never been observed;
therefore, it must now be explained.
How can there be the principle of simultaneous cause and effect within a collection of worldly phenomena that arise together?
Is it not evident that even the "reaching" [of an object by a sense organ] functions as both cause and effect?
The Sarvāstivādins reply:
Is it not clearly observed that light arises from a flame and a shadow arises from a sprout, such that cause and effect are simultaneous?
This should be examined in detail until we reach the point where the shadow takes the sprout as its cause;
the Sautrāntika counters this by asking:
"This must be examined in detail."
Is it as your own school asserts:
that the lamp-flame and its illumination take one another as causes,
such that cause and effect are simultaneous?
It is as in our Sautrāntika school:
through the conjunction of causes and conditions— namely, the human effort of the preceding moment and the lamp, its vessel, oil, and wick—
the subsequent momentary flame and light arise together.
The reason the Sautrāntika school raises this objection is that if you grant that light is produced from a flame, [then...]
I do not allow this,
because the Sautrāntika school does not admit that cause and effect are simultaneous.
If the subsequent flame and light are produced from the prior conjunction of causes and conditions, [then they must arise sequentially].
Because both parties agree on this,
it is cited as a universally established proof that the cause precedes the effect,
just as when the sun first rises, its light illuminates the eastern side of a sprout.
On the eastern side of this [seed], there are other objects that obstruct the light; on the western side of the sprout, its own shadow appears.
Although the atoms (paramāṇu) on the eastern side of the sprout obstruct the light, they do not manifest as a shadow, whereas the atoms on the western side of the sprout do.
Although it manifests as a shadow,
it does not obstruct the light.
If one were to say that this shadow arises from the eastern side, [it would be a contradiction].
Since an immeasurable number of atoms intervene in the middle,
how could [the sound] arise?
If it is claimed that it arises from the western side, [then...]
Since the sun does not shine,
how can it manifest a reflection?
Furthermore, if there were no time when the sun shines, reflections should also manifest at all times.
Therefore, one should know that this reflection is not produced by the preceding momentary sprout acting as its cause;
rather, it arises simultaneously with the subsequent momentary sprout, which is produced solely from the preceding momentary sprout.
How can it be said that this reflection has the sprout as its cause?
Such a principle is untenable. This is the Sarvāstivāda defense regarding the establishment of cause and effect according to ultimate reality.
You are not now my simultaneous cause and effect;
logically, this cannot be so,
because the existence or non-existence of the nature of the fruit follows the existence or non-existence of the cause.
One who is skilled in the treatises on logic (*hetuvidyā*) has no partisan bias in their mind when explaining the characteristics of cause and effect.
If it is said that when this cause exists or does not exist,
that effect accordingly exists or does not exist,
then this phenomenon is certainly the cause.
That dharma is certainly a fruit;
I say it is likewise.
Among co-existent dharmas, they exist together.
The principle that cause and effect are established through simultaneous arising—
even extending to their being mutual causes and effects— is likewise non-existent.
The Sautrāntika objects:
While the principle of simultaneous cause and effect may indeed be plausible,
how can it be said that they are mutually cause and effect?
Regarding the statement that there is no contradiction with what was previously explained, the Sarvāstivādins respond:
"Precisely because of what was previously stated— that when one exists, all exist."
If everything were non-existent, there would be nothing at all;
yet, the principle that they mutually function as cause and effect is not contradicted.
If this is so, then as previously stated, it refers to that which connects and causes [the continuum] to persist.
The Sautrāntika objects:
If that is so, then as previously stated,
there would be derived matter (bhautika-rūpa) consisting of visible form, sound, odor, taste, and tangibility.
They are mutually inseparable according to their respective natures;
such is the relationship between derived matter and the four great elements.
The mind and its concomitants, such as the mental factors corresponding to the characteristics [of the aggregates],
are never dissociated from one another;
they exist together and cease together.
They should be mutual causes. If it is argued that, just as three staffs stand supporting one another through their reciprocal power,
so too do all dharmas existing simultaneously exert causal efficacy in relation to one another.
The meaning of cause and effect is established as the co-existent cause (sahabhū-hetu).
Although these derived [matter] and so forth lack power when viewed in relation to one another despite being simultaneous, [they still function as such].
It is not a co-existent cause (*sahabhū-hetu*).
The Sautrāntika cites [the opponent's] defense and, having finished refuting it, says: "This should be considered."
Regarding these three staffs:

do they remain by virtue of the power of simultaneous arising and mutual dependence, as you have stated; or rather, do they remain by virtue of the power of causes and conditions consisting of the accumulation of human effort from a prior moment?
Does this mean that the latter three staffs arise and abide together?
According to what I have said, the Sautrāntika school maintains that these three staffs abide [in this manner].
It abides solely by the power of the causal conditions of the preceding thought-moment,
not by means of simultaneity;
for they maintain that the cause precedes and the effect follows.
Furthermore, within that [system], do the three staffs merely stand supported by one another? No;
there are also other things, such as ropes and hooks, capable of connecting them.
Furthermore, the earth is able to support them and cause them to abide securely;
why then do you speak only of the three staffs leaning upon one another?
The non-Buddhist practitioners of the West carry three staffs,
which are linked together by ropes and joined with hooks.
Because one places the staff on the ground while crossing it and sets down belongings such as those carried on the person,
the three staffs are cited as a metaphor;
here too, the sense of being "provisional" (*paryāya*) until the cause is reached is established.
The Sarvāstivādins offer this defense:
when coexistent dharmas arise,
they do not merely exert influence upon one another simultaneously.
It constitutes a co-existent cause (*sahabhū-hetu*).
Within this context, there are also other causes such as the similar-type cause (*sabhāga-hetu*).
Therefore, the meaning of the co-existent cause is established.
Just as those three staffs do not merely abide through the power of mutual dependence,
but are also held together and made to stand by means of ropes, hooks, the ground,
and so forth; so too has it been explained regarding [the stages] beginning with those consisting of hearing and reflection.
The following section is the third, which clarifies the homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*).
The treatise states: "Up to 'none serve as causes,'" which explains the first phrase.
It is well established that the five aggregates of the wholesome and the defiled serve as causes for one another;
there is no other explanation. Regarding the five aggregates of the indeterminate, there are four differing views. The first view holds that they serve as causes for one another.
Because their natures and categories are equal, the second [treatise] states that five are the effects of matter (rūpa-phala),
while manifest color (varṇa-rūpa) serves as the cause for five;
four are not causes of matter.
This clarifies that the four [aggregates] do not produce matter (*rūpa*).
The intention of this master is to say that because the four aggregates are superior, they are not the cause of matter;
whereas the aggregate of matter is inferior, it serves as the cause for the four. The third [position] states that the five [aggregates] are the fruit of the four.
The manifest [matter] acts as the five causes for [the four great elements], whereas visible matter does not act as the cause for the four.
Furthermore, visible matter does not give rise to the four.
The intention of this master is that because the power of the four aggregates is strong, they can serve as causes for matter (*rūpa*);

whereas because the power of the aggregate of matter is weak, it does not serve as a cause for the four [mental aggregates]. The fourth master asserts that matter and the four aggregates do not serve as causes for one another.
Because both are indeterminate (*avyākṛta*), inferior, and of different categories.
All treatises present these four views without a formal adjudication (*anirṇaya*). For now, my interpretation takes the latter master’s view as correct;
thus, the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 131, states:
How many conditions do the great elements serve as for the sphere of mind?
Answer: They serve as the object-condition (ālambana-pratyaya) and the dominant condition (adhipati-pratyaya). How many conditions does the sphere of mind serve as for the great elements?
Answer: By way of cause and predominance.
As for "cause," it refers to one cause, namely the maturation cause (*vipāka-hetu*).
As for "predominance," it is as previously explained. The commentary states:
Since the indeterminate four great elements,
when compared to the sense-base of mind (*manāyatana*),
do not mutually possess a homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*), it is said that they have no such cause in relation to one another.
By this analogy, it should be understood that the indeterminate aggregate of form,
in relation to the four indeterminate aggregates, [is not a cause].

It is correct that when they are viewed in relation to one another, they do not constitute a homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*). Question: If it is said that the indeterminate aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) does not have the indeterminate aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) as its homogeneous cause; [is this so?]
For what reason does the *Vibhāṣā*, fascicle 131, state:
"How many conditions do the great elements (*mahābhūta*) serve as for the sphere of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*)?
Answer: "As causes, as objects of perception (*ālambana*), and as predominant conditions (*adhipati*)."
The causes are sevenfold:
namely, the cause of arising and so forth, the co-existent cause, the homogeneous cause,
and the object-condition.
This refers to the phenomena associated with body-consciousness (*kāyavijñāna*) and those associated with mind-consciousness (*manovijñāna*), which serve as the objects of perception (*ālambana*).
As for their predominance (*adhipatitva*), it is as previously explained; this is according to that treatise.
The four primary elements (mahābhūta) are co-existent causes (sahabhū-hetu) for the four characteristics within the sphere of mental objects (dharmāyatana).
As for what is called the homogeneous cause (sabhāga-hetu),
generally, when things are viewed in relation to one another at the same time, they constitute co-existent causes.
When viewed across different times, they can also function as similar causes (*sabhāga-hetu*).
Therefore, the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) can serve as similar causes for the four characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) within the sphere of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*).
The four great elements are the aggregate of form (rūpaskandha).
The four characteristics are the aggregate of formations (saṃskāraskandha).
These constitute the indeterminate (avyākṛta) aggregate of form.
If one considers that the indeterminate aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) can serve as a homogeneous cause for [other] indeterminate aggregates,
why then is it said that the indeterminate aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) is not a homogeneous cause for the four [mental] aggregates?
Regarding the correct interpretation, it is explained:
the mention of the indeterminate aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) within this treatise is made in relation to the four indeterminate aggregates.
Regarding the statement that "mutually observing one another is not a homogeneous cause," this refers to the observation of mind and mental factors,
and not to the observation of the four characteristics (lakṣaṇas).
The aggregate of form (rūpaskandha),
when compared to the four characteristics within the aggregate of formations (saṃskāraskandha),
is invariably a homogeneous cause (sabhāgahetu) in relation to one another.
This is not to be doubted; furthermore, it is explained that this is stated from the perspective of the majority,
even though the aggregate of form (rūpa-skandha) includes indeterminate (avyākṛta) factors.
In relation to the neutral formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*), the four characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) can act as similar causes (*sabhāga-hetu*).
However, in relation to the three— neutral feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*)—
as well as the formations (*saṃskāra*) excluding those four characteristics, they cannot.
Regarding other dharmas:
since this refers to the majority of cases when speaking of non-homogeneous causes (*sabhāga-hetu*),
it is stated that the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) is indeterminate (*avyākṛta*).
Viewed in relation to the four indeterminate aggregates (*avyākṛta-skandha*),
they are not homogeneous causes (*sabhāga-hetu*).
Herein, the analysis is conducted by viewing them collectively in relation to the four aggregates.
Furthermore, regarding the phrase "within a single body, up to the stage of cause-increase" (*hetu-vṛddhy-ādi*), there are ten stages.
That is to say, there are five within the womb:
first, the *kalala*.
2. Arbuda; 3. Peśī; 4. Ghana.
The five *prasākhā* (stages outside the womb):
first, the infant;
second, the child.
Third, youth; fourth, middle age; fifth, old age.
Among the ten manifestations of the body, all subsequent stages exclude the preceding ones.
If one considers the ten stages of other future bodies of the same kind, each and every one serves as a cause for all ten stages.
(Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra, vol. 18)
There are many masters who explain the homogeneous causes (*sabhāga-hetu*) across the ten stages;
I cannot describe them all here.
In this treatise, we shall follow the position of one master that is not considered orthodox.
Therefore, the *Vibhāṣā* masters of the critical evaluation say:
"The critical evaluation states that one should speak thus:
the remaining ten stages of the body."
Each [moment] of these ten stages of this body serves as a homogeneous cause for the ten stages of the other bodies, as well as for the ten stages of this very body.
The ten stages of this body...
Each [moment] serves as a homogeneous cause for the ten stages of this body and the ten stages of other bodies;
furthermore, because a dharma that has already arisen in a later stage also serves as a homogeneous cause for a dharma that has not yet arisen in an earlier stage. Another interpretation states:
This treatise is likewise consistent with the *Vibhāṣā*’s commentator (*pūrvapakṣa*).
This treatise explains the ten stages of the present body based on their actual manifestation;
therefore, a subsequent stage is not the cause of a preceding stage.
If one considers the ten stages of other future bodies of the same kind,
each and every one serves as a cause for all ten stages.
This is the position of the *Vibhāṣā* commentators.
The ten states of the manifest body are explained by taking into account both those that are currently manifesting and those that are not. Therefore,
these constitute the ten states of the manifest body.
One should understand that these ten stages,
when considered in relation to one another, can also function as homogeneous causes (*sabhāga-hetu*) and so forth;
however, these ten stages are spoken of only with respect to being of the same level (*bhūmi*) and the same realm of existence (*gati*).
Therefore, the *Vibhāṣā* (131) states: Question: Regarding those who share the same destiny (*gati*) and the same level (*bhūmi*), what are the distinctions in their locations?
Are they mutually related as having causes?
Some say they have no cause;
this is not reasonable.
There must be primary elements (mahābhūta) that are momentary;
namely, those belonging to the five Pure Abodes,
which have never arisen throughout beginningless saṃsāra.
Question: According to the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 131,
within the same realm (*gati*) and the same level (*bhūmi*),
the left eye is a homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*) for the left eye.
The right eye, as well as those that are nurtured (*aupacayika*) or resultant (*vipāka*),
each act as a homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*) in relation to its own respective category.
This is according to the *Abhidharmakośa* and other treatises.
It is said that each stage, such as the kalala and so forth,
can serve as a homogeneous cause (sabhāga-hetu) for all ten stages;
this means it also serves as a cause for factors that are not of a similar nature.
Furthermore, for example, in the *kalala* stage,
there exists only the body-faculty (*kāyendriya*) and the primary elements (*mahābhūta*).
How, then, could it possess the four faculties, such as the eye, among the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*)?

Regarding the statement that [each] acts as a homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*) for the ten stages: the explanation says that this is stated according to their general characteristics (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*).
It is not that each one individually serves as a pervasive cause.

For example, within the stage of the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*), the four faculties such as the eye take their preceding counterparts, such as the eye, as their homogeneous causes (*sabhāga-hetu*). Question: If the eye and the other [faculties] serve as causes for their own respective categories within the same destiny (*gati*), [how does this apply]?
The wholesome and unwholesome [karmas] of the five destinies serve as causes for their respective future destinies. The commentary explains:

because the power of wholesome and unwholesome [karma] is strong, it can serve as a cause for a different destiny within the same level (*bhūmi*). By this principle, [the same applies to other cases].
One should extensively investigate external grains, rice, and so forth,
each within its own respective category. If the Dārṣṭāntikas do not admit that material phenomena (*rūpadharma*) serve as homogeneous causes (*sabhāgahetu*) for other material phenomena.
That position contradicts what is stated in the original treatise; therefore,
the original treatise says:

Past primary elements, in relation to future primary elements, serve as causes such as the homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*) and others. "Cause" here refers to the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*), that is, the homogeneous cause;
it does not refer to the other four conditions.
"Predominant" refers to the predominant condition (*adhipatipratyaya*).
By this it is clearly known that matter (*rūpa*) is a similar cause (*sabhāgahetu*) with respect to material phenomena.
Regarding the statement that "those which are similar serve as homogeneous causes" (sabhāga-hetu),
a question is asked: Is it not so?
Answer: What is it? This is an inquiry.
Regarding the meaning of "from one's own category and level up to those that have no cause":

this explains "one's own category and level. "Category" refers to the five categories (*pañca-varga*); "level" refers to the nine levels (*nava-bhūmi*). These fifty-four types (five times nine) each function as causes for themselves respectively.
Therefore, the *Vibhāṣā* (17), representing the position of the commentators (*pūrvapakṣin*),
states: "Defilements arising in the same level but in different locations are mutually bound to one another."
They function as homogeneous causes (*sabhāga-hetu*) by proceeding in succession according to their respective categories;
however, different classes (*nikāya*) are excluded because there are distinctions in the limits of the fetters (*saṃyojana*) of the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*).
Furthermore, regarding the phrase "not all of these":
this means that within one's own school and one's own level,
not every [dharma] serves as a cause for every [other dharma].
What is this? It is asked:
that which has arisen previously and serves as a homogeneous cause (sabhāga-hetu).
Answer: This correctly explains "previous births," meaning exclusively those that occurred in the past.
It acts as a homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*) for dharmas that are similar to it and which have either already arisen or have not yet arisen.
How is this known to be so?
Regarding the statement, "Because the root treatise explains it, all [cases] should be explained in detail":
this cites the root treatise as proof that [dharmas] arise from their own preceding class.
Serving as a cause for what follows. Question:

How is it that the characteristic of arising (*jāti-lakṣaṇa*) in the future is not subsumed under the preceding [moment of] birth? Explanation: Although one has reached the characteristic of arising, one has not yet transcended the future.
In terms of the world, their sequence is fixed;
therefore, it is not subsumed by what precedes it.
However, as for that same treatise’s statement regarding "that which is not a cause":
Below this, it is explained that if there were no homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*) in the future, there would be six difficulties:
first, the difficulty of [all things] being non-causes at all times;
second, the difficulty regarding the defiled Truth of Suffering (*duḥkha-satya*).
3. The objection regarding the determination of cause and effect;
4. The objection regarding that which was previously non-existent now coming into being;
5. The objection regarding phenomena that are not caused by the mind.
Six Difficulties Concerning Defiled Eye-consciousness: Among these six general difficulties,
the first addresses the first four difficulties according to the literal text,
while the second addresses the final two difficulties beyond the text.
Proceeding according to the text, this section addresses the first of the four preceding difficulties:
the objection that there is no time when something is not a cause.
This specifically concerns the objection regarding the production of wisdom (*jñāna*).
"Condition" (*hetu*) here refers to the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*) among the four conditions;
this is because the *Jñānaprasthāna-śāstra* poses questions and provides answers in successive order according to the four conditions.
This introduces the opponent's objection:
if one says that there is no homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*) in the future, [then...]
If [a dharma] exists only in the past and present,
then this dharma would at times not be a cause for that dharma; how, then,
can you answer that there is no time when it is not a cause?
Regarding the claim that "there is no fault because this depends on simultaneous possession (*sahabhū-prāpti*)," the Master replies:
"There is no time when it is not a cause."
This is based on the three causes— coexistent, associated, and maturation—
because these produce their results directly and operate across the three time periods;
therefore, there is no fault.
Therefore, the *Vibhāṣā* states in general:
"Some say that he [the author] composed this treatise based on the co-existent cause (*sahabhū-hetu*),
because of the co-existent cause."
Because all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*) are capable of directly producing their results across the three time periods,
some say that this treatise is composed based on the two causes— associated cause (*saṃprayuktakahetu*) and co-existent cause (*sahabhūhetu*).
This is because these two causes both pervade all three moral natures (*tridharmatā*).
Because the direct causes (*pratyaya*) are able to produce their results across the three time periods.
Some say that this treatise is based on the three causes— associated cause (*samprayuktaka-hetu*), co-existent cause (*sahabhū-hetu*),
and maturation cause (*vipāka-hetu*)— because these three causes are directly able to produce their results across the three time periods.
Some say that he composed the treatise based on the four causes— associated, co-existent, ripening,
and enabling— because these four causes pertain to all three time periods.
Others say that he composed the treatise based on five causes.
With the exception of the efficient cause (*kāraṇa-hetu*),
all factors are not excluded, as they are universally present in all phenomena.
Regarding this, some say that the pervasive cause (*sarvatraga-hetu*) is also to be excluded.
Because its essence and function are narrow,
one should state that it is composed based on the six causes (*ṣaḍ-hetu*),
