for the term "cause" (*hetu*) encompasses all six types. According to that *Vibhāṣā*, there are seven explanations in total.
In this treatise, the third [position] is considered incorrect,
whereas in that [other] treatise, the seventh is stated to be correct;
for these are spoken according to the specific intentions of their respective authors.

Furthermore, according to the masters who uphold the correct doctrine of the *Vibhāṣā*, the efficient cause (*kāraṇa-hetu*) possesses causal conditions (*pratyaya*), namely the five causes such as arising (*jāti*) and so forth.
Question: Since there is no homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*) in the future, [how can this be so]?

Regarding the correct principle of the *Vibhāṣā*: "How is the treatise based on the six causes? The commentary explains: "Although [the future] does not exist, the intended meaning is that it can function as a cause;
it is not the case that it is not a cause at a later time when it no longer exists."
Alternatively, it may be said that [a dharma] is definitely able to function as a cause at the stage of its actual arising;
based on this, it is cryptically stated that "there is no time when it is not a cause.
Some claim that in the future there is a time when it is not a cause.
The second response to the objection:

This likely refers to the three masters following the *Mahāvibhāṣā*, or perhaps to the masters of the orthodox school (*siddhāntavādin*) who composed treatises on the six causes; there were indeed *Vibhāṣā*-masters among them.
That is to say, dharmas in the state of being currently arising in the future must necessarily enter the present;
they are certainly able to serve as homogeneous causes for those preceding dharmas characterized by birth.
Therefore, that passage from the *Jñānaprasthāna* provides this answer—
that there is no time when [a dharma] is not a cause— by way of a cryptic reference to the state of the final moment of arising in the future.
Speaking in terms of the three periods of time, there is no time that is not a cause;
this intention reveals that there is no fourth period.
Therefore, the stage of the "presently arising" within the future is called the final stage.
The period prior to the arising of future, endless birth and death is called the "future.
If there is a flow that reaches the characteristic of birth (*jāti-lakṣaṇa*), it is called the "final stage of the future.
This is based on the sequential progression of phenomena as they move through time.
If one clarifies priority and posteriority based on cause and effect,
then the preceding phenomenon is termed the cause and the subsequent phenomenon is termed the effect.
Regarding the opponent's objection concerning that which has already arisen, whether it has reached its destination or not yet reached it,
the Master [Vasubandhu] does not accept the explanation of the second teacher;
that explanation of the opponent's objection is not a sound interpretation.
Because future dharmas, prior to the stage of actual arising, are not similar causes,
and only become such causes when they subsequently reach the characteristic of arising,
it follows that there are times when they are not causes.
How can you answer that there is no time when it is not a cause?
Furthermore, it is difficult to establish the inducing cognition (*ākṣepaka-jñāna*),
just as in the case of the homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*) and the immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*).
They are established as such only when they reach the present. Why,
then, does the answer regarding conditions refer to what has not yet arrived or what has already arisen,
while the answer regarding causes refers to that which is never not a cause?
They should also be equal; why then are they not the same?
As for the further explanation that "it should also be so when reaching there," this is the second master’s resolution of the objection.
However, that master further explains this by means of two approaches:
the presentation of the reflection and the brief exposition.
This is as in the response given regarding the condition of immediate succession (*samanantarapratyaya*) concerning what has not yet arisen after it has already been produced.
In this context of causal conditions (*nidāna*), one should likewise answer that there is no time when [the state] has not yet arisen or has already arisen.
Just as in this context of causal conditions it is answered that there is no time when it is not a cause,
so too in those cases of the immediately preceding condition (*anantara-pratyaya*), one should answer that there is no time when it is not a condition.
Regarding the statement that it is better to compose the text as previously explained,
the Master of the Treatise (Śāstrakāra) adopts the former interpretation.
What merit is gained by composing the text in this manner?
This merely reveals that the author of the *Jñānaprasthāna* was not skilled in composition;
therefore, one should know that the first three reasons for the explanation are superior in principle.
By this principle, the cause is answered by the fact that there is no time when it is not a cause;
the condition is answered by the fact that it has not yet arrived or has already arisen.
If the Master of the Treatise (Śāstrin) were to interpret it in this way,
he would not be taking the *Vibhāṣā* commentators as authoritative.
If that is so, why does he say, "as for those factors that are to be excluded"?
The following passage addresses the second objection concerning the defiled truth of suffering (*duḥkhasatya*).
This citation from the third section of the *Prakaraṇapāda* serves as the objection:
since the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) in the future has already been included among those things to be excluded.
This is subsumed under both categories.
It arises from past existence and manifests as the view of a self-body (satkāyadṛṣṭi),
and it is capable of producing the view of a self-body in the future.
Since the view of a self-existent body (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) has already arisen in the future,
it is clearly known that there is a homogeneous cause (*sabhāgahetu*) for the future; that is,
the view of a self-existent body in relation to the view of a self-existent body.
It is not the associated cause, the coexistent cause, or the retributive cause.
Since it is stated that there is a cause,
it is clearly evident that it must be the homogeneous cause.

Regarding the passage that should state, "It should be understood through the meaning that it is not [the case]," the Master [Vasubandhu] correctly explains the text from the third section of that *Prakaraṇapāda*.
It should be stated that this excludes the truth of suffering associated with the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) in its future state.
This text does not intend to exclude the view of a self-identity itself,
but rather excludes only those factors associated with the view of a self-identity.
The two characters "and that" (及彼) are not present in the original text.
The intention behind the external objection was to eliminate the view of a self-entity (satkāyadṛṣṭi);
therefore, the two characters "and that" were added within the text of the third section.
In the *Prakaraṇapāda*,
although the two words "if" (*sacet*) and "that" (*tat*) appear as stated there,
one should know by the meaning that they are not [to be applied here].
Because in the future world there is no sequence of before and after,
how much less could there be the addition of the view of a self-existent body (satkāyadṛṣṭi)? Since it is not something to be eliminated by entering [the path], [it does not exist].
Knowing that there is no homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*) in the future,
one should understand that regarding the co-existent cause (*sahabhū-hetu*),
the opponent cites the fourth section of the passage from the *Prakaraṇapāda* which excludes [certain factors] as a challenge.
That is to say, one does not recite the five syllables of that [text] and its associated dharmas. If,
within the context of the homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*),
one raises an objection by citing the third section of the passage concerning what was excluded.
One must add the two characters "jiā" (plus) and "bǐ" (that).
The preceding and following passages each cite different texts;
since many people do not realize this, one should reflect upon it carefully.
Furthermore, how is it that [the mind] reaches its support (*āśraya*) and its object (*ālambana*)?
Below this, the third objection regarding the determination of cause and effect is addressed;
this first section sets forth that objection.
If there were no similar cause (sabhāga-hetu) in the future state,
and it were only designated as a similar cause upon reaching the state of having already arisen,
how could this be determined with certainty?
Since it has already been stated that [the cause] is determinate,
it is clearly known that there exists a homogeneous cause (sabhāga-hetu) in the future.
One should understand that the passage concerning "the six objects, such as visible form," refers to this.
This addresses the general objection:
the statement that "the cause is determined" refers to the four causes, such as the efficient cause (kāraṇa-hetu) and so forth,
and does not pertain to the homogeneous (sabhāga) or pervasive (sarvatraga) causes.

When it is said that the result is "determined," this refers to the three results beginning with the predominant result (*adhipati-phala*), and not to the result of outflow (*niṣyanda-phala*). If that were so, one might object:
"In that case, a homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*) would have to arise where none previously existed."
The following section addresses the fourth objection regarding "that which was non-existent now existing.
This is the statement of the objection itself.
The *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* states: "In that case, there would be existence without a cause, yet there would also be a cause."
Furthermore, it would follow that there is an effect where there is no effect,
which would destroy one's own tenet.
Since [the opponent] accepts this, there is no fault up until the point where it becomes a non-substantial effect.
This addresses the general objection.
Since it is admitted that homogeneous causes (*sabhāga-hetu*) are "previously non-existent but now existent," there is no fault.
Homogeneous causes are established in terms of their functional states (*kāritra*) in the past and present.
It is not established by way of its essence;
for although an essence does not exist,
it is not posited because there is no sequence of before and after.
That which, having reached the past or present state, functions through cooperation is called a homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*).
It is capable of producing subsequent outflow fruits (*niṣyanda-phala*);
these are the subsequent outflow fruits.
This is the fruit of the preceding stage, not the fruit of its own essence. Above, we have addressed the four difficulties based on the text;
below, we shall address the two subsequent difficulties outside the text, namely the fifth difficulty: that which is not a cause of mind.
Regarding the sixth difficulty concerning the defiled eye-consciousness and the response to the fifth difficulty concerning phenomena that are not causes of mind:
the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* states,
"Furthermore, if it did not exist..."
How, then, is the *Prakaraṇapāda-śāstra* to be reconciled?
As it says: "What are the phenomena that do not have mind as their cause?
Answer: Those who have already entered into the state of rightness and departure from birth (*samyaktva-niyāma*)."
The first untainted mind of a person,
as well as the first untainted mind of other ordinary beings who are certain to enter the state of rightness and departure from birth.
However, all future untainted minds (*anāsrava-citta*) belonging to that ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) do not have mind as their cause; why, then,
is it said that only the first untainted mind [is so described]?
The answer is: That [text] speaks only of those phenomena that are ultimately not caused by mind.
Although they have not yet entered the state of rightness and departure from birth (*samyaktva-niyāma*), all their untainted minds (*anāsrava-citta*) are likewise not caused by mind.
However, if one enters the state of rightness and departure from birth (samyaktva-niyāma),
there is only the initial untainted mind (anāsrava-citta),
which is a phenomenon that does not have mind as its cause.
There is no other mind that does not have mind as its cause.
Other masters say that the aforementioned text does not distinguish the meaning of the homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*).
What are these? They are the distinction between only two kinds of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*):
namely, those with the nature for parinirvāṇa and those without the nature for parinirvāṇa.
Although the text does not explicitly mention those who lack the nature for parinirvāṇa,
the meaning is established by logical inference (*nyāyamukha*) as being understood to exist.

That is to say, since it states that there are certain other ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) who will certainly enter the state of rightness and departure from birth (*samyaktva-niyāma*), this logical implication establishes their existence.
There are also ordinary beings who are determined never to enter the state of rightness and departure from birth;
these are precisely what is called those "lacking the nature for parinirvāṇa.

That which is termed "lacking the dharma of nirvāṇa" is explained as being not caused by the mind, whereas those possessing the nature for parinirvāṇa are so named because they are caused by the mind.
There is the first untainted mind (*anāsrava-citta*),
which serves as the "attaining cause" (*prāpti-hetu*) for the realization of nirvāṇa; thus,
the mind is designated as the cause.
If one lacks the nature of nirvāṇa,
there will be no initial untainted mind;
such a person does not possess the "attaining cause" (prāpti-hetu) for realizing nirvāṇa.
It is said that "non-mind" is the cause.
The remainder of the text is understandable.
In the previous explanation, the cause of mind is a cause that functions as a condition (*pratyaya*).
This refers to the homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*).
Regarding the objection that there are no other four causes for the sixth defiled visual consciousness,
the *Mahāvibhāṣā* states:
Furthermore, if [past entities] did not exist,
how would one reconcile the *Vijñānakāya-śāstra*,
which states: "Regarding all latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) associated with past defiled visual consciousness"?
Regarding this mind, it may be a cause for that [mind] but not something that increases in accordance with it;
or it may be something that increases in accordance with it but cannot be its cause;
or it may be both a cause and something that increases in accordance with it.
Or there are those that can serve as causes but are not objects of increase. Regarding those that can serve as causes but are not objects of increase:
these refer to the various underlying tendencies (anuśaya) that, prior to this mind, are of the same class or are universal (sarvatraga).
That is to say, those proclivities which do not take this as their object, or which have been abandoned even if they once did,
and for which the associated proclivities have already been abandoned— such that they no longer increase [the defilement] and cannot act as a cause.
This refers to those latent dispositions (anuśaya) that are of the same class or are universal (sarvatraga), which follow after this mind;
that is, those very latent dispositions which take this [mind] as their object, have not yet been abandoned, can act as its cause, and also increase in accordance with it.
This refers to those latent dispositions (anuśaya) that are of the same class or are universal (sarvatraga) and precede this mind;
namely, those latent dispositions which take this [mind] as their object and have not yet been abandoned,
as well as the associated latent dispositions which have not yet been abandoned— [in such cases], they cannot act as causes nor can they increase through association.
This refers to those proclivities that, following this mind, are of a similar type and are universal; that is,
if those proclivities do not take this [mind] as their object,
or if they do take it as their object but have already been abandoned.
If it is an object of other [cognitions],
or if it is an underlying tendency (anuśaya) of another,
or if it is a universal underlying tendency (sarvatraga-anuśaya) belonging to a different realm— just as in the case of that past defiled eye-consciousness.
The same applies to future defiled eye-consciousness. While the logic of the four alternatives (catuṣkoṭi) may hold for the past, how can they be applied to the future?
If there were a sequence of before and after, how could there be no cause?
Answer: Regarding those [dharmas] in the future, three cases should be established.
Excluding those that increase by following along (*anuśerate*) and cannot act as causes, because they have no subsequent [moment].
However, the statement that the future is like the past has a specific underlying intention:
namely, that at the very moment of arising, it necessarily enters the present.
It is determined to be either a homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*) or a pervasive cause (*sarvatraga-hetu*).
In relation to other [dharmas] that have not yet arisen, it may be said to be "prior," because in contrast to these, the others may be called "subsequent. Thus say some masters.
Regarding the future as well, there are four propositions.
It is not said that the mind exists in the future with temporal priority or posteriority as it does in the past.
For now, consider that which can serve as a cause but is not something that increases through being followed.
This refers to those latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) associated with it that have already been abandoned;
they cannot act as causes for further increase because they are no longer present.
That is to say, there are similar and pervasive latent dispositions existing in the future.
Regarding future defiled visual consciousness,
that which has been conditioned but not yet abandoned can serve as its cause and also increase accordingly.
This refers to those associated latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) that have not yet been abandoned,
which neither function as causes nor undergo further increase.
This refers to those of the same class and the universal (*sarvatraga*) latent dispositions that exist in the future.
If it does not take this as its object,
or even if it has taken it as its object, that object has already been severed; as for whatever other objects remain.
Regarding "if it is a latent disposition (anuśaya) of another" and "if it is a universal latent disposition (sarvatraga-anuśaya) of a different realm," the explanation states:
"cause" refers to the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*).
According to their respective natures, these are associated, co-existent, homogeneous, and universal causes.
They lack a ripening cause.
Contaminated visual consciousness is abandoned through cultivation.
Regarding that which is "increased by following" (*anuśayita*): it means that these latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) are those which accord with and cause the growth of that visual consciousness;
they are of the same class as those abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) and serve as homogeneous causes (*sabhāga-hetu*).
Suffering and its origin, when they function as universal mental factors, serve as the universal cause (sarvatraga-hetu).
The latent dispositions (anuśaya) that coexist with the mind serve as the associated cause (samprayuktaka-hetu) and the coexistent cause (sahabhū-hetu).
These together are capable of acting as causes.
In the center, one does not take it as an object;
even if one were to take it as an object, that [object] has already been severed, and the corresponding latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) have also been severed.
These are not objects that increase through association;
they are subsumed under the first category.
If the mind takes them as its preceding object and its associated factors are not abandoned, then they are increased through association.
This is subsumed under the third category.

All remaining latent dispositions (anuśaya) do not act as causes for the subsequent moments of that same mind; rather, they are those which increase through association with their own kind, universal [factors], and objects of perception, and which are not abandoned.
This is subsumed under the second clause.
If, following other minds, there are similar and pervasive [causes] that do not take [those minds] as objects,
or which have already been abandoned— these fully encompass all similar and pervasive causes.
If the remaining objects of perception refer to those abandoned by the path of cessation and the path of the way, they are suffering and origination that are not universal,
because they are determined as remaining objects of perception for those [defilements]. This applies if they are other latent dispositions (*anuśaya*).
This refers to all latent dispositions (anuśaya) belonging to other stages;
those universal latent dispositions that do not belong to the same realm;
and the nine latent dispositions of one's own stage that take the higher stages as their objects.
All of these are subsumed under the fourth alternative.
The remainder of the text may be understood through reflection.
As for what fault would arise if the homogeneous cause were to reach [its effect], [the answer follows].
The following clarifies that if a homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*) were to exist in the future, there would be two difficulties:
first, the difficulty that it is not mentioned in the root treatise;
second, the difficulty of mutual causality.
The following section addresses the first objection not raised in the root treatise;
it introduces the inquiry by asking:
"If a homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*) were to exist in the future, just as a retributive cause (*vipāka-hetu*) does, what fault would there be?"
If there is a fundamental treatise (mūla-śāstra) that should be stated regarding the future,
the answer is:
if there is a fundamental treatise that should be stated regarding the future, [it shall be stated].
This treatise states only that the past serves as a homogeneous cause for the present and the future, and that the present serves as a homogeneous cause for the future;
it does not state that the future serves as a homogeneous cause.
Knowing clearly that there is no similar cause (*sabhāga-hetu*) in the future,
this is precisely what our own treatise does not state.
Since the treatise speaks only of "reaching" [the result], there is no error.
This accords with the root treatise (*mūla-śāstra*).
The root treatise speaks only of homogeneous causes (*sabhāga-hetu*) that "take" and "give" their fruit as being in the past and present;
it does not speak of future homogeneous causes that neither take nor give their fruit, and therefore there is no error.
Regarding the claim that there is no such principle as reaching the point where a homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*) does not exist,
the Master of the Treatise refutes it,
stating: "There is no such principle."
The homogeneous cause (sabhāga-hetu) draws forth its concordant fruit (niṣyanda-phala).
It is logically impossible for this homogeneous cause to exist in the future,
because there is no distinction between prior and posterior in the future.
How can a similar cause (*sabhāga-hetu*) in the future produce a result of uniform outflow (*niṣyanda-phala*)?
Since there is no result of uniform outflow in the future,
past and present dharmas that have already arisen should not be considered the results of uniform outflow for those dharmas yet to arise.
It is not said that [the dharma] is currently arising; this is either omitted for brevity, or stated according to the majority of cases, or by mentioning the subsequent to reveal the preceding.
Furthermore, another interpretation holds that past and present dharmas that have already arisen should not be considered as the outflow (*niṣyanda*) of future dharmas that are yet to arise.
That which is currently arising and that which has not yet arisen are included by the term "arising," just as past dharmas are not present fruits.
Otherwise, there would be the fault that the effect precedes the cause.
Therefore, in the future, there is no homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*).
If it is argued that this is because the retributive cause (*vipāka-hetu*) does not exist prior to or subsequent [to its effect], [we reply:]...
The following point constitutes the second objection concerning the mutual relationship of cause and effect.
To introduce the inquiry:
if that were so, the ripening cause (*vipāka-hetu*) would not exist in the future.
It is not possible for a cause of maturation fruit to exist prior to or simultaneously with its effect,
because dharmas in the future lack priority and posteriority. There is no such fault [in our position],
as it does not follow that [the cause] would be non-existent upon reaching the future.
The author of the treatise replies:
This correctly eliminates the fault of mutual causality;
such a fault does not exist.
Although there is no sequence of before and after in the future world,
because the ripening cause and the ripening fruit are not similar,
the future exists.
Because the homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*) is similar to its resultant flow (*niṣyanda-phala*), it does not exist in the future.
If there were no sequence of before and after within the future, they would have to act as causes for one another;
and since they would thus be mutual causes, they would also have to be mutual results.
If they were mutually cause and effect, it would contradict reason;
for while a homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*) draws forth a subsequent fruit,
a retributive cause (*vipāka-hetu*) does not produce a retributive fruit that is similar in nature to itself.
Although future [dharmas] are devoid of priority and posteriority,
there is no fault of mutual causality among those that are simultaneous or superior;
therefore, the homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*) is established in relation to the sequence of the stage of manifest activity.
The future does not exist [as a substantial entity].
However, if the retributive cause (vipāka-hetu) is established according to its essential characteristic,
the future is not non-existent.
Furthermore, the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* states:
Question: If there were a homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*) in the future, then two moments of mind would necessarily exist as mutual causes and effects for one another.
Answer: Just as the four aspects each have their respective associations, so it is with the remaining factors;
therefore, there is no such fault.
That is to say, regarding the aspect of impermanence in future time:
there are four aspects of practice that arise immediately prior to it; these are what is cultivated as being connected to this [state], and the aspect of impermanence serves as their cause.
Because that [impermanence] is not bound to this [suffering] as its cause,
the aspect of impermanence must necessarily arise first;
the same applies to the aspects of suffering, emptiness, and non-self.
Other conditioned phenomena should be understood in the same way.
Therefore, two minds do not serve as cause and effect for one another.
If this were asserted:
There are those who, relying on the fourth dhyāna, attain the fruit of arhatship and are able to cultivate the untainted (anāsrava) states of the nine stages in the future;
all the untainted states they cultivate are bound to this [fourth dhyāna].
Subsequently, when the noble path of another stage manifests,
one can no longer cultivate future untainted [dharmas],
because the noble paths of other stages are not connected to this [stage].
It would follow that [the cause] must exist in the past or present;
it cannot be a non-homogeneous cause (asabhāga-hetu).
This would contradict what is stated here.
"Virtuous roots produced in a prior life serve as the homogeneous cause for those produced in a subsequent life," and so forth,
as explained at length;
let there be no such error.
Therefore, it is logically sound that there is no homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*) in the future.
As for the statement regarding the homogeneous cause reaching its certainty, upon what basis is it said?

Answer: It was previously stated that the meditative concentrations (*samādhi*) of their own respective stages depend upon the contaminated (*sāsrava*).
However, if it concerns the uncontaminated path (*anāsravamārga*), the nine stages act as causes for one another in mutual relation.
The desire realm lacks meditative concentration,
while the Peak of Existence is dull and inferior;
neither can give rise to the untainted noble path.
Therefore, it relies solely on nine [stages]. Question: If the noble paths of the nine stages serve as causes for one another, why does the *Nyāyānusāra* (16) state:
"In relation to its own [stage] and those above"?
Regarding the absence [of cultivation] based on lower stages, that treatise states that each of the nine stages can cultivate the noble path of all nine stages,
as appropriate, together with that cultivated based on its own stage.
Because that which is cultivated based on a higher stage serves as a similar cause for [the cultivation] based on its own [stage],
it is said: "with respect to what is based on itself, there is that which is cultivated based on a higher stage."
Because that which is cultivated based on a lower stage does not serve as a homogeneous cause for [the cultivation] of a higher stage, it is said that there is none "based on a lower stage.
For example, the noble paths cultivated based on the *anāgamya* (preliminary) concentration pertain to all nine stages.
It acts as a homogeneous cause for the eighty-one types of noble paths cultivated in reliance upon the nine stages.
In this manner, it continues up to the noble paths cultivated in reliance upon the nine stages [beginning with the first] up to the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*).
It serves as a homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*) only for the ninefold noble path cultivated in dependence upon the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*).
According to the *Nyāyānusāra*,
this refers to that which is cultivated based on the aforementioned [sphere].
It is not the case that what is cultivated based on a lower stage acts as a similar cause (*sabhāga-hetu*) for this [higher stage].

How, then, can it be said that the noble paths (*ārya-mārga*) of the nine stages act as mutual causes? To explain: when it is said that the noble paths of the nine stages act as mutual causes, [it refers to their relationship within the same category].
Relying upon a single stage, one can cultivate the noble paths of all nine stages;

because they are cultivated within the same stage, they serve as homogeneous causes (*sabhāga-hetu*) for one another. It is not the case that the noble paths cultivated across all nine stages universally function as causes for one another.
To speak of "nine stages" is not a statement that exhausts the principle; if one were to speak exhaustively of the principle, [it would be otherwise].
How could a path based on a higher stage serve as the cause for a dull path based on a lower stage?
According to the intention of the masters of the *Nyāyānusāra*,
although they are equal in being of the same lineage and the same category, [they do not stand in a causal relationship].
That which relies on a higher stage is superior,
while that which relies on a lower stage is inferior;
therefore, that which relies on a higher stage does not serve as a cause for that which relies on a lower stage.
It serves as a cause for those that depend on its own level and higher levels.
According to the interpretation of the master Guṇaprabha,
each of the nine levels can cultivate the noble path of all nine levels.
The eighty-one types of noble paths, when viewed in relation to one another, can all serve as causes for one another.

This is because they are explained according to those of the same nature and category who should practice based on the nine stages; therefore, they are able to serve as causes for one another in succession.
Question: If, as you say, the knowledge of others' minds arising from a lower stage does not know the minds of a higher stage, how can the nine stages serve as causes for one another?
Answer: The explanation is that their meanings regarding the objects they take as conditions are distinct.
Since the meanings of "cause" (hetu) differ,
this cannot be raised as an objection.
Although there have been two different interpretations above, [the former] remains superior.

There is no contradiction whatsoever with this treatise. Furthermore, regarding the correct principle, it is explained according to a single aspect: because one gradually advances through the superior dharmas of the various stages, it is said that what is above is not the cause for what is below.
In terms of reality, it is also identical to Virtuous Light (*Guṇaprabha*).
However, the phrase "because there is nothing superior to what has been attained" serves to distinguish it from other specific [attainments].
The explanation that [the dharmas] such as the equal and superior are the results,
while the equal and superior are the causes—
rather than the inferior being the cause— is because they arise from preparatory effort (*prayoga*).
The method of designation can be understood from this.
Furthermore, regarding those dharmas that have already arisen and serve as homogeneous causes (*sabhāga-hetu*),
they are explained as causes in terms of being equal or superior with respect to the three paths.
The path of seeing is the cause for three [results],
the path of cultivation is the cause for two,
and the path of no-more-learning is the cause for one; this is according to the intention of the *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya*.
The three paths act as causes for one another in succession.
For example, the dull path of cultivation produced in a previous life also serves as the homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*) for the sharp path of seeing that will not arise in the future.

Furthermore, a previously arisen dull path of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣamārga*) is also a similar cause (*sabhāgahetu*) for a future sharp path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) that will not arise, or for a path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*); or when one falls back from the state of no-more-learning to the state of training (*śaikṣa*) and transforms one's faculties (*indriya*).

It also serves as the cause for the cultivation of the path that has already arisen. Regarding the statement that [a dharma] acts as a homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*) for three, two, or one [subsequent moments], this is explained according to the sequence of their actual manifestation.

Question: Is the intent of this treatise the same as that [of other systems]? Answer: One interpretation states they are the same. Another interpretation states that the intents of the various treatises differ.
The treatise states that the path of seeing serves as the cause for three [paths],
the path of cultivation serves as the cause for two,
and the path of no-more-learning serves as the cause for one.
It is clearly known that the subsequent path is not the cause of the preceding path.
If it were the preceding cause, why is it not so stated? Furthermore, within this context, [the path] serves as a homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*).

because the latter is coarse and easily understood.
There is no fault of contradiction; the above is the treatise (*śāstra*).

For this reason, it is known that the two types of action—bodily and vocal—cannot produce life-force (*jīvitendriya*) or the homogeneous class (*nikāyasabhāga*). Question: Does this treatise accord with the *Nyāyānusāra*? Answer: It is explained that there is no separate statement in this treatise [to the contrary].
This is consistent with the correct principle (*yukti*).

Question: If it is said that only mental karma (*manas-karman*) can induce life-force (*jīvita*) and the homogeneous class (*nikāya-sabhāga*), why does the Karma Chapter (*Karma-nirdeśa*) speak of four types of wholesome [karma]?
Both [the *āśraya* and the *sabhāgatā*] act together;
however, according to that treatise, only three [factors] induce the homogeneous class (*sabhāgatā*).
Simultaneously, they can induce three types of *nikāya-sabhāga* (homogeneous class): those pertaining to birth, those pertaining to subsequent existence, and those that are indeterminate.
It cannot be said that a single moment of mental karma can induce the *nikāya-sabhāga* of three lifetimes.
Furthermore, it cannot be said that within a single moment three mental karmas arise to project the three types of group-homogeneity (nikāya-sabhāga).
Nor can it be said that the volition (cetanā) originating from the three past causes projects the three types of group-homogeneity.

"Because a ripening cause (*vipāka-hetu*) must necessarily take its fruit in the present. The commentary explains: "That text merely clarifies that among the four types of karma—past, future, and indefinite—it is possible for [karma] to produce a homogeneous portion (*sabhāga-bhāga*) in the present, but it cannot produce [a fruit] in the present."
It does not state that a single moment can simultaneously induce three types of *nikāya-sabhāga*.
Therefore, the subsequent treatise asks:
"How many karmas are able to project the *nikāya-sabhāga*?"
Only three [types of karma] are capable of projecting;

that which is to be experienced in the present life is excluded, because the present existence and its homogeneous character (nikāya-sabhāga) have already been projected by prior karma. Furthermore, it is asked: if one says that bodily and vocal actions of the desire realm cannot project the life-span or the homogeneous character?
Why is this? Because the text below states that the two mindless attainments (*acittaka-samāpatti*) and acquisitions (*prāpti*) cannot project other [results].

Since it mentions "other [results]," it is clearly understood that the two types of karma—body and speech—of the desire realm can also project life-span and homogeneity (*nikāya-sabhāga*). The commentary explains: "To say they 'can project' means they may potentially project those [results]."
It does not state that all [karmas] are capable of producing results;

rather, it means that if they are bodily or vocal karmas of a subsequent existence (*pāratantrika*), they can produce results, whereas if they are bodily or vocal karmas of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), they cannot produce results. Furthermore, this interpretation of the treatise differs from the *Nyāyānusāra*.
In the desire realm, bodily and vocal karma can also induce the life-span and the homogeneous class (*nikāya-sabhāga*).
Within such karma, numerous atoms (*paramāṇu*) arise according to their respective functions;
some of them induce only the projecting fruit (*ākṣepaka-phala*).
There may be cases where only the fruit of completion (*pūrṇa-phala*) is experienced;
or there may be cases where one part induces the projecting karma (*ākṣepaka*) and another part induces the completing karma.
If it is said that these arise from the same single moment of mind:
It is not permitted for the projecting cause (*ākṣepaka-hetu*) and the completing cause (*paripūraka-hetu*) to arise from the same moment of mind. For if they did,
which [cause] would project the visible form and which would project the odor and so forth?
Although they arise from the same single mind, there are differences such as the fact that some result in *nirmāṇa-rūpa* (manifested form) while others do not;
how could this prevent the same single mind from arising [to produce] both the projecting (*ākṣepaka*) and the completing (*paripūraka*) [karmas], which differ in their temporal sequence?
If one interprets it in this way, it differs from the *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra*.
It should be understood that at times the four aggregates reach and arise therein;
likewise, it should be understood that within the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), they reach and arise therein.
This is distinguished according to the form and formless realms;

it can be understood by reflecting upon this. Question: Herein the terms "attainment" (*samāpatti*) and "equipoise" (*samāhita*) are used, while in other passages the term "concentration" (*samādhi*) is used instead.
What is the distinction between these three types? The explanation states: the Sanskrit name is *samādhi*, which is translated here as "equipoise" (*dengchi*).
It encompasses both meditative concentration (*samāhita*) and the distracted state (*vikṣipta*), and it includes all three moral natures.
There is only mind. Because it holds the mind with equanimity and causes it to proceed toward its object, it is called *samādhi*.
The Sanskrit name is *samāpatti*, which is translated here as "equilibrium" (*dengzhi*).
They encompass both states with mind and states without mind;
they exist only in meditative concentration and do not extend to the distracted state.
If it is a state with mind, it is termed "attainment" (*samāpatti*).

This means that by means of the mind preceding meditative concentration (*samādhi*), one becomes free from dullness (*laya*) and agitation (*auddhatya*) and attains equilibrium (*samatā*) within this concentration.

This name is established based on its preparatory application (*prayoga*). Alternatively, it is explained that the concentration itself, being free from dullness and agitation, is called "equilibrium."
To be able to reach equality of body and mind is called "attainment" (*samāpatti*).
If one speaks of "attainment" (*samāpatti*) without reference to the mind, it is further explained in two ways;
this may be understood by analogy with the case where the mind is present.
The only difference is the absence of mind (*acittaka*). The Sanskrit term is *samāhita*, which is translated here as "equipoise" (*ting*);

it encompasses both states of meditative concentration with mind (*sacittaka*) and without mind (*acittaka*). It is generally explained in reference to concentrations with mind, and does not apply to the state of distraction (*vikṣepa*).
If there is a state of mental concentration called "equipoise" (samāhita), it means that the mind preceding the concentration is free from lethargy and agitation; this is termed "equi-" (sama).
That which can induce this concentration is termed "inducing" (-āhita).

This name is established based on its preparatory application (*prayoga*). Furthermore, another interpretation is that it is called "equanimity" because the meditative absorption itself is free from lethargy and agitation;
it is called "inducing" (*āneñjya*) because it can induce a state of equilibrium in body and mind.
If the meditative absorption of the mindless state is termed "equanimity" (samāhita),
it should be understood by analogy with the explanation of the absorption of the conscious state, as being interpreted in two ways.
The only difference lies in being without mind (*acittaka*).
Regarding the statement that "there is karma that only brings about [rebirth] as soon as it reaches [the new existence], namely the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) and so forth":
from here below, the distinctions among karmas are revealed by way of the greater or lesser number of bases (*āyatana*) they bring about.
Among the twelve bases (*āyatana*), sound is excluded because it is not a result of maturation (*vipāka*).
Among the remaining eleven, if they are determined to be of the same nature as the karma that produced them, [they are considered homogeneous].
Their substance must necessarily coexist.
For those who possess these two meanings, they will experience [retribution] in whichever place corresponds to their karma;
at the very least, one [type of retribution] will certainly be experienced.
At most, they definitely induce four [results].
If it is admitted that karma of distinct natures can induce them,
their substantial entities need not necessarily coexist.
If there is any deficiency, it is indeterminate;
otherwise, it can induce maturation in five up to eleven places.
If a karma induces maturation in only one place, [it is determinate].

This refers to that which constitutes the sphere of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*), namely the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) and so forth. The phrase "and so forth" includes the homogeneous character of beings (*nikāyasabhāga*).
Thus, the *Mahāvibhāṣā* states:
Furthermore, there is karma that results in maturation in only one location;
namely, the karma that acquires the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) and the commonality of species (*nikāyasabhāga*).
That karma results in maturation solely in the sphere of phenomena (*dharmāyatana*). Another interpretation holds that it also includes birth (*jāti*) and so forth.
Because they are determined to be experienced together;
the other ten bases are not so determined.
If one enters the mindless state, there is no mental base (manāyatana).
If one is born in the higher realms, odor and taste are necessarily absent;
if one is born in the formless realm, visible form and tangibility are also absent.
Although these—visible form, odor, taste, and tangibility—may at times arise simultaneously with life-force and the other [mental factors], they are not so in these cases.
They may be produced by distinct karmas;
for example, such things as human and celestial lives are produced by wholesome karma,
whereas these five [unwholesome states] are summoned by unwholesome karma.
If the five [faculties], such as the eye,
are compared with those [faculties] such as life,
regardless of which realm of existence they reside in.
Although these four faculties, such as the eye, are definitely produced by karma of the same nature,
if they exist in the desire realm, [they are so].
Because that which has not yet been attained or has already been lost is not established;
and because if one is born into the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu),
the five faculties beginning with the eye are entirely unestablished.
Because the five material faculties, life-force, and the homogeneous character (*nikāya-sabhāga*) are the bases of birth and are produced by karma of a similar nature,
they are not fixed; therefore, these ten bases are not necessarily experienced in common.
If it is said that "the same should be understood for the sense-sphere of mind," this means that if one experiences the sense-sphere of mind, one necessarily experiences two spheres:
namely, mind and mental objects (dharmas).
"Dharmas" refers to the mental factors that accompany the sphere of mind (*manāyatana*), as well as the dharmas of arising and so forth.
The remaining nine are indeterminate.
As for the four faculties, such as the eye, if they arise in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*)...
Because that which has not been attained or has already been lost does not constitute [the possession].
If one is born in the form realm (rūpadhātu), there is no odor or taste.
If one is born in the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu), the remaining nine are entirely absent.
Although these nine [bases] may sometimes be produced by distinct karmas even when coexisting with the mind-base (*manāyatana*),
they do not necessarily produce it. However, if they produce the touch-base (*spraṣṭavyāyatana*),
they necessarily produce both the touch-base and the dharma-base (*dharmāyatana*).
That is to say, birth and so forth.
The other nine are indeterminate.
If the four faculties, such as the eye, arise in the desire realm...
Because that which has not yet been attained or has already been lost is not established as such;
because the sense-sphere of mind (manāyatana) does not exist when one enters the mindless states;
and because fragrance and taste do not exist in the higher realms.
Although these nine [bases] may, at times, be produced by distinct karmas even when co-arising with contact,
they are nonetheless associated with the body and form when producing contact. Therefore,
the location where contact is produced does not necessarily produce those nine bases.
If it is said that "the same should be understood for the sense-bases of the body," this means that when the sense-base of the body is experienced, three bases are necessarily experienced:
namely, body, tangibles, and mental objects.
The sphere of tangibles refers to the four great elements that act as the formative causes;
the sphere of mental objects refers to [factors] such as birth;
the remaining eight are indeterminate.
Although the four bases, such as the eye, and the body base are produced by the same karma,
they are not possessed [as accomplished] when one is born in the desire realm and has either not yet acquired or has already lost them.
As for the mind base, it is absent whenever one enters a state of no-mind.
This mind sometimes arises together with the body as a result of a distinct karma;
however, fragrance and taste do not exist in the higher realms.
When present in the desire realm, they induce the body.
Although fragrance and taste may both be produced by distinct karmas,

they are nonetheless necessarily co-existent with matter; for while it is possible that the locus of the body itself may be produced by distinct karmas, it is likewise possible that fragrance and taste are produced by distinct karmas while remaining co-existent with matter.
If one experiences the body-base, one does not necessarily experience those eight. Question: As stated in the *Nyāyānusāra* (Treatise on the Sixteen Bases):
"If one experiences the body-base, one necessarily experiences four bases, namely:
the body-base, the visible-form base, the tangible-base, and the mental-object base."
Why does that treatise state that [karma] produces the body and also produces matter? The explanation is: this treatise is based on what is produced by the karma that produces the body;
it also includes the production of the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) which constitute the tangible objects within the sphere of touch.
Because they are proximate, they must be produced by the same karma;
although visible form and the body-faculty necessarily arise together,
because they are not proximate, they may be produced by separate karmas.
Therefore, it is not necessarily experienced.
The correct principle— that which experiences the body necessarily experiences matter—
is based on the fact that matter is invariably associated with the body and is common to both the desire realm and the form realm.
Therefore, when the body is projected, color is also necessarily projected. If that were so, then when color is projected, the body should also be projected. It is not so;
because the sense-sphere of the body (*kāyāyatana*) is the basis of birth, when the body is projected, color is also projected.
Because it is produced by common karma,
form is not the fundamental basis of birth;
therefore, while it produces form, it does not necessarily produce the body.
This is because they may be produced by distinct karmic causes;

thus, these two treatises each rely on one specific interpretation. Furthermore, it is explained that the *Abhidharmakośa* is correct, as it accords with the statement of the first master in the *Mahāvibhāṣā*.
Furthermore, other treatises do not state this:
if that which is inseparable from something were to induce it,
then at the time of inducing matter, one should also induce the body.
It is clearly known that these are not primary [elements].
One should know that the same applies to the perception of color, odor, and taste;
each is determinately perceived as a triad.
Each is designated as one [aggregate] by its own name;
to each, "contact" (sparśa) and "phenomena" (dharma) are added.
As for the term "specifically explained":
If one is reborn with the sense-base of form (*rūpāyatana*), one necessarily acquires the sense-bases of form, tangibles (*spraṣṭavya*), and mental objects (*dharmāyatana*).
The remaining eight are not certain.
This is because the four bases beginning with the eye do not exist for those born in the desire realm who have not yet obtained them or have already lost them.
The sense base of mind (manāyatana) does not exist when one enters the meditative absorption of non-mentation; furthermore,
odor (gandha) and taste (rasa) do not exist in the higher realms.
Although these seven [bases] may sometimes be produced by distinct karmas even when coexisting with form,
and although the production of the base of form may sometimes be produced by distinct karmas even when it is necessarily coexistent with the body, therefore,
the production of the base of form is necessarily restricted to producing all three together.
The remaining eight are indeterminate.
If one experiences the sphere of odors, one necessarily experiences the spheres of tangibles and mental objects;
the remaining eight are indeterminate.
The four bases beginning with the eye, as well as the mind base (*manāyatana*), are explained as before.
These five exist in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
Although they may at times be produced by distinct karmas together with the odor base (*gandhāyatana*), they are nonetheless capable of being so induced.
Although when perceiving an odor it is certain that [the sense organ] is accompanied by the body, visible form, and taste, it is possible for them to be produced by distinct karmas;
therefore, the locus where an odor is perceived necessarily produces those three loci,
while the remaining eight are not so determined.
If one experiences the sense-base of taste, one necessarily experiences the sense-bases of taste, touch, and mental objects (*dharmāyatana*).
The remaining eight are not fixed;
they should be explained by analogy with the case of odor.
Regarding the statement "if one experiences the sense-base of the eye, it should be understood that it is likewise for others":
if one experiences the sense-base of the eye, one necessarily experiences the sense-bases of the body, tangibles, and mental objects (*dharmāyatana*),
as explained previously.
The remaining seven are indeterminate.

Although the three faculties of ear, nose, and tongue are likewise produced by the same karma, they do not constitute [faculties] if one is born in the desire realm having not yet acquired them or having already lost them.
Furthermore, the two bases of odor and taste simply do not exist in the higher realms.
If the mind-base enters a state of no-mind, it ceases to exist.
These [bases of] odor, taste, and mind may, at times,
arise simultaneously with the eye-base, yet they can be produced by distinct karmic causes.
Although form is necessarily co-existent with the eye, it may be produced by distinct karmic forces; therefore,
while the production of the sense-base of the eye necessarily entails the production of the other four bases,
the remaining seven are not so determined.
The [karmic results] for the ear, nose, and tongue should be explained by analogy with the eye. Question:
According to the *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra*, if one is reborn with the four bases such as the eye, does each determinately result in the acquisition of five bases, including the base of visible form?
Why does this treatise state that [karma] does not necessarily produce form? The explanation says: This treatise does not speak of producing form, whereas that treatise speaks of producing form;
each is based on a different point of view.
This is as explained in the *Madhyamakahr̥daya-vṛtti-tarkajvālā*. Furthermore, the interpretation of the *Abhidharmakośa* as being correct accords with the initial statement in the *Mahāvibhāṣā*;
however, upon thorough investigation, this specific statement is entirely absent from the *Mahāvibhāṣā*.
It should be understood that this is merely what the master of the *Nyāya* school has conceptualized himself:
namely, that if something is not separate [from the cause], it must be produced by that [cause].
If that were so, he would have to say that what produces matter (*rūpa*) must also produce the body (*kāya*).
Since it is not experienced by the body, it is said to be illogical;
yet there is karma capable of bringing about rebirth in the Nirmāṇarati heaven and so forth,
which brings about five bases up to eleven.
According to what is appropriate,
the quantity of the fruits induced by the power of karma is indeterminate. Why is this so?
Karma may have either few fruits or many fruits,
just as the fruit produced by external seeds may be few or many; that is, when the fruit produced from a seed is small.
Just as grains such as rice and wheat are harvested once a year;
furthermore, their roots and stalks are few;
and moreover, each pod contains only a single seed.
Regarding the names "few fruits from the seed" and "many fruits produced from the seed":
examples include the lotus, the pomegranate, and the *nyagrodha* tree;
from a single seed, one harvests [fruit] for many years.
Furthermore, there are many roots, stalks, and so forth;
and furthermore, a single pod contains many seeds—this is called "abundance of seeds and fruits.
Moreover, it is explained that if one considers these eleven locations in relation to one another, [the same principle applies].
Regarding those that are strong and predominant:
according to what is experienced in this place, one will also certainly experience the others;
therefore, one will certainly experience one, up to and including four.

If, when viewed in relation to one another, they are not strong relatives, then although they may exist simultaneously, they do not necessarily produce a result. Question: Why are the aggregates (*skandha*) explained in terms of causes, while the bases (*āyatana*) are manifested in terms of results?
Answer: It is said that because all five aggregates are capable of acting as causes, they are distinguished by way of their causality.
Since twelve bases (*āyatana*) for the most part cannot function as causes, they are explained here in terms of their results;
this is because all eleven bases can potentially serve as results. Question: As it says in the *Vibhāṣā* (19):
Furthermore, there is karma that results in maturation in only one location;
namely, the karma that acquires the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) and the commonality of species (*nikāyasabhāga*).
That karma results in maturation solely in the sphere of mental phenomena (*dharmāyatana*).
There is karma that ripens as retribution in only two bases (*āyatana*).
That is to say, there is karma pertaining to the mind-base (*manāyatana*);
such karma ripens only as retribution in the mind-base and the phenomena-base (*dharmāyatana*).
Karma that results in the acquisition of the sphere of tangibles (spraṣṭavyāyatana) also receives the maturation of two spheres,
namely the sphere of tangibles and the sphere of phenomena (dharmāyatana).
Karma that results in the acquisition of the sphere of the body (kāyāyatana) receives the maturation of three spheres.
That is to say, the sense bases of body, tangibles, and mental objects.
The same applies to the karma that results in the sense bases of visible forms, odors, and tastes.
Each receives its own respective maturation within the sense bases of body, tangibles, and mental objects.
The karma that acquires the eye base undergoes maturation as four bases:
namely, the eye base, the body base, the tangible-object base, and the mental-object base.
The same applies to the karma that acquires the ear, nose, and tongue bases.
This refers to the maturation of each respective sphere: the sphere of the body, the sphere of tangibles, and the sphere of mental objects.
Other masters state that all primary elements produce both visible form and sound.
The various forms of the desire realm are not separate from odor and taste;
thus they say that the karma which acquires the sense-base of the eye undergoes maturation as seven bases.
The eye base, the body base, and the bases of visible forms, odors, tastes, tangibles, and mental phenomena are the result of maturation (vipāka).
The same applies to the karma that acquires the ear, nose, and tongue bases.
That is to say, each experiences the maturation of its own respective bases: the bases of body, form, odor, taste, tangibility, and mental objects.
Through the karma that acquires the basis of the body, one experiences the maturation of the six bases.
That is to say, it is the maturation of the sense-base of the body, as well as the sense-bases of visible forms, odors, tastes, tangibles, and mental objects.
When one performs an action that results in the maturation of the sense-base of visible forms, one receives the maturation of five sense-bases;
namely, the maturations of the sense-bases of visible forms, odors, tastes, tangibles, and mental objects.
The same applies to the karmas that result in the acquisition of the spheres of odor, taste, and tangibility;
that is, each receives the maturation (vipāka) of the spheres of visible form, odor, taste, tangibility, and mental objects (dharmāyatana).
What has been stated thus far refers to those [karmas] which necessarily result in acquisition.
Regarding those whose attainment is indeterminate, their number is not fixed;
however, there are karmas capable of undergoing maturation in eight locations.
There is karma that can experience the maturation in nine bases;
there is karma that can experience the maturation in ten bases;
and there is karma that can experience the maturation in eleven bases.
With the exception of the sense-base of sound (*śabdāyatana*), according to the *Vibhāṣā* text,
there are further masters who state that [karma] definitely results in five, six, or seven [bases]. How should these differing views be reconciled?

"What constitutes the correct [view]? The explanation states: This treatise and the earlier masters of the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* maintain that [karma] definitely brings about one, two, three, or four [rebirths].
Regarding the indeterminate [karma] that brings about [rebirth], it is said to bring about five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten, or eleven [rebirths].
Other masters of the *Vibhāṣā* state that the acquisition of five, six, or seven [objects] is likewise necessarily acquired;
the intention of those masters is that color, fragrance, taste, tangibility, and mental phenomena (*dharma*) are invariably inseparable from one another.
The four [bases] beginning with the eye each definitely produce seven;
the body-base definitely produces six;
and the bases of visible form, odor, taste, and tangibility each definitely produce five.
Between these two explanations,
this treatise and the *Abhidharmamahāvibhāṣā* consider the first explanation to be correct,
while the other masters' views are incorrect.
What is the meaning of this?
It means that one [karma] necessarily results in rebirth in one, two, three, or four realms.
This is the same in both the *Abhidharmakośa* and the *Mahāvibhāṣā*.
Furthermore, the *Saṃyuktābhidharmahṛdaya-śāstra*, in its "Chapter on Miscellaneous Mental Activities," is also identical to this treatise,
with no differing explanations.
As for the two [other] views mentioned in the *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* regarding the attainment of five, six, or seven [faculties], they are as follows:
This is the incorrect position of other masters.
Since it is stated that all primary elements (*mahābhūta*) produce both visible form and sound,
it is clearly known that this is not the correct principle.
Third is the refutation based on principle:
If you say that they definitely do not separate and thus must induce one another,
then there should be no induction of the five [aggregates].
Since the body must necessarily be present when perceiving visible form, odor, taste, or tangibility, these [objects] are certainly not dissociated [from it]; therefore,
they should also be experienced by the body.
If it is argued that the body and its objects such as form are produced by different karmas,
then at the time of producing that body, why would one not also produce those forms and so forth? For this reason, it is known [that they are produced by the same karma].

Regarding this treatise and the first master of the *Vibhāṣā*, the latter is correct. Question: If five, six, or seven [factors] are indeterminate, why did the former masters of the *Vibhāṣā* not explain them separately?
Answer: It is logical that they should have been explained as being among the indeterminate.
The reason they are not distinguished separately is that other masters state [they exist] within meditative concentration (*samāhita*).
Because these divergent views differ, they are omitted and not specifically displayed;
according to the text of the *Abhidharmakośa*, they are subsumed under the category of "indeterminate" (*aniyata*). Master Tai’s commentary on the *Abhidharmakośa* states:
To claim that the sense-base of touch experiences two bases or three bases,
or four bases, is entirely incorrect.
All other cases involve experiencing one base, two bases, or five bases and beyond.
This is the correct interpretation.
The general intent of the Dharma Master is the same as that of the other masters in the *Vibhāṣā*,
explaining it in terms of non-separation.
This is refuted by the same critical analysis as before. Furthermore, regarding the *Vibhāṣā*, the two masters—the former and the latter—each rely on a different principle.
The former school speaks from the perspective that those who maintain that karma of a determinate nature necessarily entails the simultaneous existence of its substantial entity (*dravya*).
The Master [Vasubandhu] subsequently bases his argument on the principle of inseparability.
As for his statement that [karma] produces matter and so forth but does not mention the production of the body and so forth,
it is because the five material sense-faculties are the fundamental basis for birth.
When one projects that [rebirth], one also projects form and so forth,
because form and the like are not the primary basis of birth; however,
while projecting those forms and so forth, one does not necessarily project the body and its faculties.
If one adopts this interpretation,
the *Abhidharmakośa* maintains that [karma] may result in five, six, or seven [rebirths],
thus partially agreeing with other masters of the *Mahāvibhāṣā*.
Because there are differing explanations regarding five, six, and seven [factors],
this treatise does not explain them separately.
Regarding the statement "there is karma of one time that reaches [its result] as described above," it should be understood accordingly.

This refers to the distinction between time-periods (*adhvan*) and moments (*kṣaṇa*), clarifying that the fruit is manifold while the cause is few. There is karma of one time-period with maturation in three time-periods;
this refers to the "small" three time-periods.
For example, when a single moment in the present creates karma to be experienced in the present, it is called "karma of one time-period."
The fruit induced by karma that has already fallen away is called past maturation (*vipāka*);
that which continues to manifest is called present maturation;
and that which has not yet arisen is called future maturation.
There is no instance where karma from three time periods collectively induces a single lifetime of maturation, lest the fruit be less than the effort exerted and thus diminish the cause.
There is, however, an instance where karma created in a single moment induces a maturation result spanning many moments.
One does not experience a single moment of maturation as the result of karma created over many moments,
lest the fruit be diminished relative to the labor expended in its cause.
The preceding [explanation] was presented in terms of time.

Regarding the subsequent explanation based on mindfulness (*smṛti*), although the general meaning is the same, it is explained according to the distinctions between the gates. Furthermore, one interpretation holds that "world" refers to the three great periods of time, whereas "mindfulness" refers to a single moment (*kṣaṇa*).
Question: If many moments are required to create karma...
If multiple moments [of karma] were to produce a single fruit within one moment, this would mean that many moments of karma produce a fruit within a single moment.

How then can it be said that there is no experiencing of a single moment’s fruit by means of many moments of karma? The explanation says: This demonstrates that there is no such thing as performing karma over many moments and then collectively experiencing a single fruit within one moment.
This clarifies that the fruit does not diminish the cause;

it does not preclude the possibility of experiencing distinct fruits within a single moment for karma created over many moments. Question: For example, as when a Bodhisattva cultivates the karma for the maturation of the marks and signs (*lakṣaṇa-vyañjana*) over a hundred eons.
How can a single body-experience result from so much [causality]? Is it not because the fruit is small? The explanation says:

regarding the karma that brings about the most excellent physical marks of a Buddha, through long-term cultivation, one gives rise to a final, supreme karma that manifests and is able to induce the extraordinary maturation of a Buddha’s body.
If the former [karma] is inferior and does not produce [the result], what contradiction is there in this principle?

If it were otherwise, there would necessarily be a case where the causes are many but the results are few. Furthermore, another interpretation holds that although one may perform [actions] for a hundred kalpas, they all ripen into a single body-experience.
However, the atoms of the resultant maturation (*vipāka*) produced by these [karmas] differ from moment to moment,
being distinct in each preceding and succeeding instant;
it is not the case that the karma of a hundred eons collectively produces a single fruit.
Because it is not a co-existent cause (*sahabhū-hetu*).

As for the statement that "the ripened fruit (*vipāka-phala*) can only be distinguished when it arrives," this indicates that the fruit and the cause are not simultaneous; rather, they require a continuity of the stream [of moments] as an intermediate condition. Thus, the ripened fruit does not coexist with the karma.
It is not the case that the very moment this thought is produced, this same thought receives its fruit;
therefore, it does not arise simultaneously with its cause, nor does it arise immediately thereafter.
This is because the subsequent moment exists as a phenomenon in the state of arising (*jāyamāna*).

Because this is induced by the power of the immediately preceding condition (samanantarapratyaya), it is not due to the power of the ripening cause (vipākahetu). Furthermore, another interpretation holds that it is not immediate;
for once the karma has been performed in the first moment, [the result does not follow instantly].
Because it is drawn forth by the power of the immediately preceding condition (*samanantarapratyaya*) of the second moment,
its fruit arises only in the third moment.
This explanation is stated here with reference to the mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*).

In reality, form and the other aggregates are likewise not immediate [successors]. Furthermore, it is explained that within the category of matured results (*vipākaphala*), there are those that are sharp, namely mind and mental factors;
and there are those that are dull, namely form and non-associated formations.
If the faculty is sharp, because it is induced by the power of the immediately preceding condition (*samanantarapratyaya*) in the second moment and so forth,
the fruit arises in the third moment.
If the faculty is dull, even at its swiftest, it still requires the induction of the power of the third moment.
It manifests only in the fourth moment.

Here, because the explanation is given in terms of the swiftest possible case, form and so forth are not mentioned; however, another interpretation holds that this text also implies form and so forth.
Because they are induced by the power of the immediately succeeding moment,
visible color and so forth are not without an interval;
because they are induced by the power of the equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantarapratyaya*) of the immediately succeeding moment.
This demonstrates that the mind and so forth are not without an immediate antecedent.
Furthermore, it is difficult for a ripening cause to produce a ripening fruit;
it must necessarily depend upon a continuity in order to bring about the result.
It is neither simultaneous nor immediate.
According to the *Śāsanaprakaraṇa* (Treatise on the Wheel of the Teaching),
these are divergent tenets of the later schools, such as the Mahāsāṃghika and others.
Karma and its maturation (vipāka) may exist simultaneously;
thus, regarding these six causes up to those that do not pertain to the time periods—
this is the third classification according to the time periods.

Since the verse does not specify the temporal locus of the efficient cause (*kāraṇa-hetu*), it should be understood by implication that it extends across the three time periods and the non-temporal (*adhvanya*).
The *Nyāyānusāra* states: "It cannot be said that its specific time period is fixed," and thus it is not mentioned in the verse.
Having already explained the six causes up to the establishment of those causes,
the following section— the second major heading— clarifies how causes obtain their fruits. Within this,
the first part provides a general definition of the essence of the fruit.
Second, the correlation of causes with fruits;
third, the specific manifestation of the characteristics of the fruits;
fourth, the timing of the cause’s grasping and giving. Below this, the first section provides a general definition of the essence of the fruit.

Having already explained the distinctions in the essential characteristics of the six causes as determined by the three time periods, [the author] now poses a question regarding which effects correspond to those causes.
The verse states: "Up to the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta), there is neither cause nor effect."
The first phrase reveals the essence;
the second phrase resolves doubts.
There are two kinds of fruits.
First, conditioned fruits, namely:
maturation, outflow, human effort, and dominance.
Second, unconditioned fruits.
This refers to disjunction itself.
As for the fruit, it has two meanings:
first, it is that which is induced.
That is, it is a conditioned fruit,
because it is produced by those six causes;
secondly, it is that which is realized.
That is to say, the fruit of dissociation (*visamyoga-phala*) is that which is realized by the Path;
the Path is the cause of realization (*sākṣātkāra-hetu*), not the cause of production (*janana-hetu*).
Therefore, it is not subsumed within the six causes.
The other two unconditioned phenomena (asaṃskṛta) are not results that are "drawn forth" because they do not function within the world;
nor are they results that are "realized" because they are indeterminate (avyākṛta) in nature.
Fearing that one might doubt whether the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) is a fruit and thus should arise from a cause,
or whether it is a cause and thus should be able to produce a fruit, he now explains:
Although the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) is called a "fruit" because it is a realized result,
it is not produced by the six causes,
as it does not function within the world.
Although the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) is a cause, it is called a "cause" only in the sense that it does not obstruct;
it does not obtain the five fruits.
Because it is not something that can be realized [as an attainment], it does not obtain the fruit of the unconditioned.
Because there is no grasping and no giving, one cannot obtain conditioned fruits.
For this reason, it is said that the unconditioned has neither cause nor fruit.
The old translation states: "The unconditioned is neither cause nor fruit."
This is a great error. The *Śāstra* states:
"As for 'reaching up to' and 'with analytical cessation,'" this refers to the prose commentary (*gadya*).
First, the explanation of the verse;
second, the definitive analysis.
Hereafter follows the explanation of the verse.
Citing the commentary on the preceding verse from the root treatise:
disconnection (*visamyoga*) and analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) are one entity with two names.
That which is manifested by the removal of bonds is called "disconnection."
Because that which is attained through the path is called "cessation through deliberation" (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*),
cessation through deliberation is used to explain "disjunction" (*visamyoga*).
If that is so, as for the statement that the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) serves as a cause in this context:
The following explains the second phrase.
Two points of inquiry raise an objection:
among the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), only cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) is designated as a fruit.
The three unconditioned phenomena are all termed efficient causes (*kāraṇa-hetu*).
Thus, the *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya-ṭīkā* (Xianzong lun), fascicle 9, states:
"Therefore, analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) is a cause but has no fruit."
This fruit has no cause.
The other two unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*) are causes but not fruits.
That there are neither causes nor fruits [in these cases] is established as the ultimate principle. Furthermore, the *Nyāyānusāra* (Treatise on Right Reasoning), fascicle 18, states:
There is a phenomenon that can function as a single cause-nature,
namely unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*).
There is no phenomenon that is not a cause, nor is there any phenomenon that is not an effect.
Regarding the statement that "space and non-analytical cessation [are not fruits],
because only conditioned phenomena can possess the five fruits": the answer is as follows.
Only conditioned phenomena possess six causes and five fruits;
unconditioned phenomena do not.
Why is this so? Because the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta) is eternal in essence and is not produced by the six causes;
furthermore, it does not obtain the five fruits.
For what reason is it not admitted that reaching [the object] constitutes an efficient cause (*kāraṇahetu*)?
Question:
Should the path of immediate succession (*ānantaryamārga*) not be called an efficient cause?
What is it that does not obstruct the arising of the path to its destination?
Answer: Because it is unconditioned and eternal.
The Path is not an agent.
If that is so, one might ask: "Whose fruit is it? and "In what sense is it a fruit?
First, [the question] asks whose fruit it is.
Second, the question regarding the meaning of the fruit:
"Because it is obtained through the power of the path as the fruit of the path.
The answer: "It is indeed the fruit of the path."
Answering the first question: "Because it is obtained through the power of the Path.
Answering the second question:
"If that is so, then the fruit of the Path would reach [the state of] non-attainment, but not cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*)."
Question:
If that were so, the fruit of the path would consist solely of the acquisition (*prāpti*) of that very analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*);
the path would then have the capacity to induce its arising within that [acquisition].
It is not because analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) is eternal by nature;
rather, it is because there is a distinction regarding the attainment (*prāpti*) of its presence.
This is the answer.
