Because it is capable of distinguishing between attainment (*prāpti*) and the path to cessation (*nirodhamārga*).
How does it have efficacy regarding the attainment of the path? [Question: What is meant by this?
Regarding the phrase "because it is able to produce":
the answer is that it means because it serves as the cause for production.
What is meant by "having efficacy regarding cessation and the path"?
Question:
It refers to being able to realize [cessation], such that one reaches analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) as the fruit of the path.
Answer: Because one is able to realize cessation through the power of the Path;
it is for this reason.
Although the Path does not destroy the six kinds of causes for arising,
it can nonetheless be said that analytical cessation (pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha) is the result attained through the Path as its cause.
Since all unconditioned phenomena (asaṃskṛta-dharma) function as enabling causes (kāraṇa-hetu).
Question:
Regarding the statement that "all unconditioned phenomena [function] by way of yielding the activity of results," the answer is as follows:
That which does not obstruct arising may be called the "efficient cause" (*kāraṇa-hetu*).
Because it lacks the functions of grasping or bestowing, it has no fruit.
It should be understood that there are two types within the efficient cause.
First, the function of that which has arisen,
namely past and present phenomena.
Second, the function of that which has not yet arisen.
This refers to future phenomena and all unconditioned (asaṃskṛta) phenomena;
they are called efficient causes (kāraṇa-hetu) solely because they do not constitute an obstacle.
Regarding the Sautrāntika masters’ statement that [the term] "reaches" refers only to conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*):
the following section provides a definitive analysis (*viniścaya*). This marks the formal thesis (*siddhānta*) of the Sautrāntikas.
The unconditioned is not a cause.
This concludes the citation of scriptural evidence.
As for the question, "In which sūtra is this stated? [the following is provided].
The Sarvāstivādins ask: "As it is said in the Sūtra that this applies even up to consciousness, so it is.
The Sautrāntikas reply:
Since it has already been stated that all things such as form (*rūpa*), which are produced by causes and conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*),

are impermanent (*anitya*), it is clearly understood that the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) is not subsumed under causes. This follows from the preceding text concerning impermanent causes and conditions.
If that were so, and unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*) were to serve as objective conditions (*ālambanapratyaya*), the Sarvāstivādins ask:
The Sūtras state that all conditions are impermanent.
If the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) is eternal,
it should not serve as an object-condition (*ālambanapratyaya*) for consciousness and the like; yet,
since [the opponent] asserts only that it can produce [consciousness] and that it reaches [it], this objection is not established.
The Sautrāntika replies:
When the sūtras state that various causes and conditions can produce consciousness,
these causes and conditions are all impermanent.
Since it is not asserted that everything which serves as an object-condition for consciousness is impermanent,
the objection is not established.

By virtue of this unconditioned [dharma], it can serve as an object-condition (ālambana-pratyaya) for consciousness. Furthermore, it is explained that not everything that serves as one of the four conditions for consciousness is necessarily impermanent.
Is it not also said that "the ultimate" (*paramārtha*) acts as the efficient cause (*kāraṇa-hetu*)?
The Sarvāstivādins ask: by analogy with causes, this applies to conditions (*pratyaya*) as well.
Does not the Sūtra state that only that which can take up a fruit and is a cause for the arising of a fruit is impermanent?
Thus, although unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*) are not causes of arising,
they are nonetheless acting causes (*kāraṇahetu*) by virtue of merely not constituting an obstruction.
Regarding the statement in a sūtra that [the cause] is merely "not being an obstacle," the Sautrāntika replies by citing a sūtra as proof.
The unconditioned (asaṃskṛta) is a condition, not a cause.
Regarding the statement, "Although there is no sūtra that says so, does it mean there is no sūtra that says so?
the Sarvāstivādins say: [it is so].
Although no sūtra explicitly states that unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*) can function as a creative cause (*kāraṇahetu*),
nor is there any place where this is prohibited,
they are for the most part obscured.
How can it be definitively determined that there is no scriptural statement [to this effect]?
If that were so, what dharma would be called "disjunction" (visamyoga)?
Thus asks the Sautrāntika.
Since the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) has already been designated as the efficient cause (*kāraṇahetu*),
it remains to be known which dharma is termed "disjunction" (*visamyoga*).
This refers precisely to that which is called "cessation through deliberation" (*pratisaṃkhyānirodha*) in the root treatise.
The Sarvāstivādins reply:
"Is it not the case that we previously asked [this] until the nature [of things] was revealed?
The Sautrāntikas then reprimand them.
Second, because the self-nature [of these] is difficult to know through mutual questioning and answering,
one should elucidate the self-nature through a separate method.
This self-nature of this dharma is also called "disentanglement" (*visamyoga*).
The Sarvāstivādins reply:
Permanently abiding dharmas do not fall within the three periods of time;
they are not the basis for verbal expression.
Therefore, it is said that there truly exists something ineffable, realized only internally by the noble ones (ārya),
which can be described only in general terms as being virtuous and eternal,
and which possesses its own distinct substantial reality.
The Sautrāntika masters state that these do not exist;
this describes the Sautrāntika position regarding the three kinds of unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*).
It is not the case that all [unconditioned phenomena] exist substantially like the five [aggregates], such as form, which have distinct substantial entities;
for these unconditioned phenomena lack such [entities].
If this is so, why are they called "space" and so forth?
The Sarvāstivādins ask: "Since there is no substantial entity, why is it called 'emptiness' and so forth?
It refers merely to the absence of contact and reaching, [occurring] when those with premature death have their remaining aggregates [dissolved]."
The Sautrāntika replies:
Space is merely a conventional designation for that which is not encountered through tactile contact;
that is to say, it is that which is not encountered through tactile contact in the midst of darkness.
Thus it is said: "This is space. To speak according to reality, that which is unobstructed within illumination is also space.
It is simply because the eye cannot see in the dark that the characteristic of emptiness is easily manifested;
whereas analytical cessation consists merely in the non-arising of afflictions and suffering.
It constitutes their essential nature.

That is to say, when past afflictions that have already arisen have infused seeds into the body, they are termed "arisen latent dispositions" (*anuśaya*). It is precisely these latent dispositions [that constitute the nature of the afflictions].

That which can induce successive afflictions is called the "seed of birth. Furthermore, the seeds of the past are termed "arisen latent dispositions" (*anuśaya*), while the seeds of the present are termed the "seed of birth."
This refers to the present seeds produced by the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) that have already arisen in the past;
the text abbreviates this by simply stating "produced seeds" (*utpanna-bīja*). Alternatively, it is explained that the seeds of present afflictions are termed "arisen latent dispositions."
This capacity to produce what follows is called the "seed of arising. As for the state of cessation,
it refers to this very seed of affliction being devoid of the functional capacity to produce subsequent afflictions or future existence.
Therefore, it is called the state of cessation. Furthermore, according to another interpretation of the Sautrāntika school, the three characteristics exist in the present;
the characteristic of cessation exists in the past.
This refers to the time when the seed of arising is present.
This refers precisely to the phase of cessation when [the dharma] has passed away.

Just as on a scale one end descends while the other rises, it is called the "phase of cessation" because they are equal in their state of equilibrium. Furthermore, it is explained that this is called the "phase of cessation" because one realizes *pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha* (cessation through analytical discernment) at this time.
If the seeds have not yet been eliminated by the power of discernment,
they can give rise to subsequent afflictions and future existence;
however, through the power of discernment, others no longer arise.
This means that the path of uninterrupted transition (ānantarya-mārga) still coexists with the seeds [of the afflictions] and perishes together with them; nevertheless,
it is by virtue of the power of discernment (pratisaṃkhyāna) of the path of uninterrupted transition [that the seeds are abandoned].
It causes the seeds of afflictions in subsequent states, as well as the afflictions that are currently active or will arise, never to be produced again in future existence;
this perpetual non-arising is termed "cessation."
Cessation through the power of discernment is called "cessation through discernment" (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
If one is apart from the power of discernment,
it occurs merely through the deficiency of necessary conditions.
That which does not arise again thereafter is called "cessation" (nirodha).
This cessation that occurs without analytical discernment is termed "cessation not through deliberation" (apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha).
It is like a person who is destined to live for a hundred years [but dies before reaching that age].
At fifty, one dies; the remaining fifty years are called the "residual commonality of existence" (*nikāya-sabhāga*).
Those who die prematurely have their remaining aggregates fail to arise due to a deficiency of conditions.
The masters of other schools (nikāyāntarīya) state that "attainment" (prāpti) is called non-analytical cessation (apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha).
This describes the tenets of the Sthavira school and others regarding the two unconditioned phenomena (asaṃskṛta-dharma):
they define analytical cessation (pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha) in terms of the non-arising of latent dispositions (anuśaya).
The Sautrāntika school refutes the claim that "non-analytical cessation" (apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha) is defined by the non-arising of the fruit of suffering,
and that when it occurs through the power of detachment from analytical discernment, it is subsumed under "analytical cessation" (pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha).
The cessation of this fruit of suffering through non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) cannot be established apart from the power of analytical discernment (*pratisaṃkhyā*).
It is by the power of analytical discernment that the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) are prevented from arising;
once the latent dispositions do not arise, subsequent suffering does not occur.
The loss of causes and the disappearance of effects are both due to the power of wisdom (*prajñā*).
Therefore, the non-arising of these results of suffering is subsumed under analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
Some say that when dharmas reach the point where they are no longer named, this is called non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
The Mahāsāṃghika school asserts that once all phenomena have arisen in the present,
they necessarily cease spontaneously and enter the past.
This cessation is called "cessation not through deliberation" (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
Regarding the claim that such a [non-existent] entity persists until its destruction,
the Sautrāntika school refutes it.
The essence of the non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) as it is thus conceived would have to be impermanent;
for its essence does not exist while the phenomenon has not yet ceased,
but its essence exists only when the phenomenon subsequently ceases.
"Is it not the case that analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) would also be impermanent because it is preceded by analysis?
This is the objection raised by the Mahāsāṃghikas.
This cessation, being previously non-existent and subsequently existent,
would likewise be impermanent.
It is not the case that it exists only upon reaching [a state] preceded by non-discernment (apratisaṃkhyā) and does not arise otherwise.
The Sautrāntika replies:
It is not the case that analytical cessation (pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha) exists only after non-analytical cessation has preceded it;
how then can you reproach me for claiming that the essential nature of analytical cessation is also impermanent?
Why is this? It is not that there is first a discernment,
and subsequently the future, unarisen dharmas fail to arise.
Non-arising is precisely cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*). Why is this?
[This is] the question.
Regarding the statement "non-arising up to non-produced non-arising," the Sautrāntika replies:
the principle of non-arising exists inherently from the very beginning.
If there were no noble path and the wisdom that discerns phenomena,
all things would arise; however, when they arise through the discernment of noble wisdom, [they do not].
Because the cause perishes, the fruit is lost, and the dharma never arises again.
Regarding this principle of non-arising, one discerns its functional capacity;
that is to say, at a prior time, there was no obstruction to the arising of various dharmas.
Now, the arising of noble wisdom serves to manifest the principle of non-arising by creating an obstacle for the birth of dharmas;
it does not newly produce non-arising.
If one asks: "If there is only non-arising, would this not be contradictory? [The answer follows: No, it is not contradictory.
The Sarvāstivādins raise an objection based on scripture:
"If nirvana were merely the non-arising of future dharmas,
why does the Sūtra speak of the five faculties, such as faith?"
Whether it be the path of seeing,
the path of cultivation, or the path of no-more-learning, one extensively cultivates and practices them.
Or, one may practice it at the beginning,
cultivate it in the middle,
and perform many deeds with it at the end.
"Cultivation" refers to the cultivation of attainment (*pratilambha-bhāvanā*); "practice" refers to the cultivation of habituation (*niṣevaṇa-bhāvanā*);
and "frequently performed" means that what is to be remedied is further removed.
Therefore, the *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya* states: "Whether it be practiced (*abhyasta*),
cultivated (*bhāvita*),
or frequently performed (*bahulīkṛta*)."
Regarding the distinction of meaning, it is intended to demonstrate that through the cultivation of practice (*āsevanā-bhāvanā*) and the cultivation of attainment (*pratilambha-bhāvanā*),
that which is to be countered becomes even more remote.
As stated in the preceding treatise (*śāstra*), this [cessation] brings about the eternal severance of all suffering of the past, future, and present.
This essence of eternal severance is itself *nirvāṇa*.
According to this scriptural passage, while it universally severs the past and present, its sense of "non-arising" applies specifically to the future.
Is it not contradictory that this does not apply to the past and present?
Although there is this text, the Sautrāntikas interpret the sūtra as being intended for the purpose of causing [defilements] to cease.

Regarding the scriptural statement that it "can cause the severance of all sufferings of the past and present," the intended meaning of this sūtra is that it can cause the severance of those afflictions (*kleśa*) that take past and present suffering as their objects and will arise in the future.
When the capable cognizer is severed, it is said that the object of cognition is also severed; present suffering is likewise called "severed.
One should speak of severing craving, yet one speaks of severing form;
one should speak of the full comprehension of craving, yet one speaks of the full comprehension of form.
To speak further in terms of the objects of focus (*ālambana*):
the abandonment of form (*rūpa*) is the path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*),
while the full knowledge (*parijñā*) of form is the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*).
The detailed exposition continues up to:
"The aggregate of consciousness is also thus.

The meaning of the abandonment of past and present suffering should also be understood according to this principle. Question: Since the abandonment of past and present suffering has already manifested the abandonment of the afflictions that take them as objects, [what further is to be explained?]

Regarding the statement that "the future suffering is abandoned," by what is this meant? One explanation says that the abandonment of future suffering also indicates the abandonment of the afflictions (*kleśa*) that take it as their object, because it is so stated in a sutra.

Another explanation holds that causing the substance of future suffering not to arise is called "abandonment. Yet another explanation holds that causing future afflictions and suffering not to arise is [what is meant].
Both are termed the abandonment of suffering.
As for other sūtras that speak of abandoning the afflictions of the three periods of time,
they should be explained according to the principle established above.
This interpretation is also not contradictory,
because future afflictions can take the afflictions of the three periods of time as their objects.
When it is said that one abandons the three time periods upon abandoning the future defilements that take them as objects,
this refers to the actual abandonment of the future;
or perhaps this sūtra has a different underlying intention.
Past afflictions refer to the delusions that were previously aroused during past lives;
present afflictions refer to the afflictions aroused during the present life,
such as the eighteen modes of craving within the category of craving-based conduct (*tṛṣṇā-carita*).
Based on the six objects of the past, future, and present, eighteen [mental factors] arise;
thus, the afflictions arising in these two periods of the past and present act as the perfuming causes.
In order to give rise to future afflictions,
it induces the seeds of perfumed results within the present continuum of the body.
Because the seeds that are the fruits of this perfuming are severed,
it is said that the causes— the delusions capable of perfuming in the past and present— are also severed.
This is just as when the fruit of maturation (vipāka-phala) is exhausted, it is also said that the karmic cause is exhausted.
Because of the abandonment of the fruit, one speaks of the abandonment of its cause;
this is precisely the cessation through the loss of the fruit and the disappearance of the cause.
This applies to future suffering as well as all afflictions.
Because seeds lack causes, they are ultimately non-arising; this is what is called "severance.
Because the cause is severed, its fruit is said to be severed.
This is precisely the severance wherein the cause perishes and the fruit is lost.
If, as I maintain, the future entity is severed [in its very nature],
then since the past has already ceased and the present is currently ceasing,
what need is there to sever them?
The meaning here is to clarify that the past and present are termed "severed" because the fruit does not continue;
the future is termed "severed" because its substance does not arise.
Regarding the results of abandonment and the causes of abandonment in their respective order,
if the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) dharma were established as the foremost,
the Sarvāstivādins would cite a sūtra as an objection.
Since the sūtra states that being free from defilement is supreme,
it is clearly known that nirvāṇa possesses a distinct substantial reality.
Nor do I say that reaching this state constitutes supremacy.
The Sautrāntika replies:
"I do not say that unconditioned phenomena (asaṃskṛtadharma) are entirely non-existent in essence, like the horns of a rabbit."
It should simply exist as I have described it. That intention [of yours] is to say that the principle of nirvāṇa being without intrinsic nature must necessarily exist;
because it exists as something without intrinsic nature, it is called "nirvāṇa exists," just as one speaks of "this present sound."
There is sound prior [to its arising],
which does not exist in the future; there is sound subsequent [to its ceasing].
The past does not exist;
it cannot be transcended. The future does not exist;
yet it is spoken of as existing.
Therefore, the meaning of "having an essence" is established,
because the expression "exists" does not necessarily refer exclusively to reality,
as it also refers to non-existence.
It should be understood that the same applies to the statement regarding the existence of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
To say that the unconditioned exists does not mean that it possesses a substantial entity;
rather, there exists the dharma-body of nirvāṇa.
Although they do not exist, they may still be praised;
there are many such cases.
If wholesome dharmas did not exist, they could be censured and disparaged.
If calamities and misfortunes were non-existent, they could be praised;
therefore, the ultimate non-existence of calamities and misfortunes such as the various afflictions is called "detachment from defilement."
This nature of nirvāṇa is the most preeminent among all things that possess substantiality and those that lack substantiality.
The World-Honored One, in order to cause the sentient beings to be converted to give rise to profound joy,
specifically extols Nirvana as supreme.
If unconditioned phenomena (asaṃskṛtadharma) are designated as the noble truth of cessation (nirodhasatya),
the Sarvāstivādins raise an objection:
first, what is the meaning of "noble truth" (āryasatya)?
The Sautrāntika counters with a reductio ad absurdum:
"Is it not the case that this statement pertains to the meaning of 'non-erroneous'?
The Sarvāstivādin replies:
Regarding the question of what contradiction there is in the noble ones seeing both existence and non-existence as ultimate reality,
the Sautrāntikas explain that the noble ones' vision of both existence and non-existence is entirely free from error.
That is to say, when the Noble Ones perceive suffering, they call it "existent"; when they perceive that which is not suffering, they call it "non-existent.
How does this contradict the meaning of the Noble Truths? Furthermore, another interpretation holds that the Noble Ones perceive suffering, origin, and the path as existent.
To see cessation as non-existent is entirely without inversion.
This is the general heading; what follows is the specific explanation.
That is to say, the noble ones perceive suffering as merely suffering,
and they perceive what is non-existent within suffering as merely non-existent.
How does this contradict the meaning of the Noble Truths?
In the separate explanation,
only suffering and cessation are mentioned, while origination and the path are not.
How is it that one does not reach the third noble truth?
The Sarvāstivādins raise an objection:
"Because it reaches the second [moment] without interval, it becomes the third.
The Sautrāntikas resolve this.
Because the Noble One perceives the Truth of Cessation immediately after the second Truth of Origination,
and because it is so stated in the Buddha’s sūtras, it is established as the third.
If unconditioned phenomena were to reach [the mind], they would have to take a non-existent object as their cognitive domain.
The Sarvāstivādins raise an objection:
If the essence of unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*) were merely non-existence,
then how could consciousness take space (*ākāśa*) or nirvāṇa as its object?
The mind should arise by taking a non-existent object as its condition.
Regarding this point— that taking a non-existent object as a condition will be extensively analyzed later—
the Sautrāntika school explains it as follows:
There is no fault in [the position that] consciousness is conditioned by an object that does not exist;
this shall be extensively analyzed and deliberated upon later in the "Examination of the Three Times" within the "Investigation of Delusion."
If it is granted that unconditioned phenomena (asaṃskṛta) possess [the quality of] reaching [their object], what fault would there be? The Sarvāstivādins ask.
What further merit would there be? The Sautrāntikas counter-ask.
If one grants that [unconditioned phenomena] are protected [as real], they are then called "virtuous" (*guṇa*).
The Sarvāstivādins reply: If one grants that unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*) exist as distinct substantial entities (*dravya*), [then...]
Even if one upholds the Vaibhāṣika school,
this is called a virtue;
yet if there is something that ought to be upheld which results in what is called a fault, [then it is not a virtue].
The Sautrāntika master Saṃghabhadra says:
"If this unconditioned entity has a protective deity who guards it of its own accord, [then it would be subject to protection]."
However, to assert that [these] exist substantially while falsely imagining them to be so is to be identical to the various non-Buddhists;
this is called a fault.
Why is this so? The Sarvāstivādins argue that this is because [cessation] is designated as "destruction" even though it lacks any substantial entity (*bhāva*).
The Sautrāntika replies:
This unconditioned (asaṃskṛta) has no real substantial entity that can be apprehended,
unlike the five objects such as visible form and so forth.
The five consciousnesses do not apprehend through direct perception (pratyakṣa) mental states and mental factors such as feeling,
nor does the knowledge of others' minds (paracittajñāna) apprehend them through direct perception;
furthermore, no utility for such apprehension can be found.
Just as the eye, ear, and so forth exist because they possess seeing, hearing, and so on—
known through inference— so too does this unconditioned [phenomenon] exist.
If there were a separate entity apart from craving and so forth,
how could one establish that it is the "cessation" of those things such as craving,
using the sixth case-ending (ṣaṣṭhī-vibhakti) to denote a possessive relationship?
In the science of grammar (śabda-vidyā), the sixth case-ending (ṣaṣṭhī-vibhakti) expresses the relation of belonging to a possessor.
Phenomena that are related must necessarily be interconnected.
Greed, hatred, and so forth are conditioned phenomena (saṃskṛta).
Cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*). It does not stand in a relationship of mutual dependence,
because this and that do not bear the relationship of cause and effect when viewed in relation to one another.
This cessation, when viewed in relation to that entity, is neither its cause nor its effect.
Even though this cessation may be considered an efficient cause (*kāraṇa-hetu*) with respect to that entity, [it is not so in the sense of being a productive cause].
Furthermore, that which does not take up the fruit is also termed "non-cause.
Since phenomena (*vastu*) cannot realize the Path, cessation (*nirodha*) is not the realization of the fruit.
Moreover, because cessation is eternal, it is also not the cause for the arising of the fruit.
Therefore, it is called "not an effect.
"Not a cause" indicates that it is not something to which [another] belongs;
"not an effect" indicates that it is not something that belongs [to another].
Since this and that, when compared with one another, are neither cause nor effect,
they are not mutually related;
how then can it be said that the cessation of that entity belongs to the referent of the possessive suffix?
From this, it is known that cessation has no separate essence;
it is merely the aspect of negating the arising of those phenomena.
It is called the cessation of phenomena.
Cessation has no separate essence,
for it is simply the non-existence of the phenomenon itself that is termed "cessation."
It may be said that this cessation belongs to that entity, whereby the sixth [case-ending] is established;
this is in accordance with the rules of grammar (*śabdavidyā*). Now, based on this passage:
The sixth, the genitive case, has two types. First, when distinct entities are viewed in relation to one another,
as in the statement, "the cessation of that entity" (tasya bhāvasya nirodhaḥ) regarding the Sarvāstivādins.
It is also like the servant of a noble lady;
the two are not different entities.
As the Sautrāntikas say, that phenomenon ceases.
It is also like the substance of a pebble;
although cessation is distinct, that which pertains to that specific entity is explained by the Sarvāstivādins as follows:
Although cessation exists as something distinct,
when the afflictions that take those contaminated things as their objects are abandoned, [that cessation is attained].
One attains this cessation only upon the liberation from those objects;
thus, one may say that this cessation belongs to those objects.
This "belonging" is predicated in terms of attainment.
"For what reason does this cessation belong specifically to this attainment?
Thus the Sautrāntika objects:
"If the essence of cessation were distinct [from the object], it would not be the mere non-existence of that thing."
Since the substance of cessation is manifold and its acquisitions (*prāpti*) are likewise not unitary,
for what reason is this cessation definitively attributed to this specific acquisition? Why,
then, do you say that it is "attributed to the entity" based on its acquisition?
Regarding the statement in the sūtra that "attainment can be spoken of," the Sarvāstivādins cite this scripture to resolve the objection:
"A bhikṣu attains nirvāṇa in the present life."
Because it is attained in the present life, it is called "nirvāṇa in the present life" (*dṛṣṭadharma-nirvāṇa*).
Since one has already attained nirvāṇa, it can be said that [the state] belongs to that attainment.
Furthermore, he challenges him, saying:
The Sautrāntika replies: How can that which does not exist be said to be "attained"?
It is by attaining the antidote that one reaches what is called nirvāṇa.
By attaining the path that serves as the antidote,
one thereby attains a body that is forever opposed to the basis of the afflictions;
and by so doing, one attains a body that is forever opposed to the basis for future existence.
The sense that afflictions and future existence no longer arise is called attaining nirvana;
yet it possesses no substantial entity.
This is the proof by reasoning. Furthermore, there is scriptural proof from the lower teachings that [the person] lacks intrinsic nature.
As a sūtra states: "For one who has reached this nirvāṇa, all fruits of suffering are abandoned without remainder; the cessation of suffering is designated as 'cessation'."
Cessation has no separate substantial entity.

Alternatively, by citing the fruit, the cause is revealed: when the fruits of affliction and suffering are exhausted, all causes of affliction are severed. Or, it refers to severing each individual cause of affliction such as craving;
or, it refers to abandoning each individual fruit of suffering.
It may pertain to both cause and fruit: either because the causes of all afflictions are exhausted, or because the fruits of all suffering are exhausted.
Or it may pertain to both cause and fruit: being "free from defilement" (vairāgya) means being far removed from bondage, whereby the causes of all afflictions are extinguished.
Either it is the cessation of the fruit of suffering,
or it is common to both cause and fruit; or it is the stilling of the cause,
or the stilling of the fruit of suffering.
Either both cause and effect are extinguished, or the cause is eternally extinguished,
or the fruit of suffering is eternally extinguished,
or both cause and effect are extinguished; furthermore, the remaining future fruits of suffering will no longer continue and will not be taken up again.
They will not arise again;
or else other bitter fruits will not continue,
or they will not take up fruit.
Or else, it will not arise again; this nirvāṇa is supremely tranquil, this nirvāṇa is supremely sublime.
This is a general praise: that is to say, by relinquishing all bases of existence, it reveals that nirvāṇa is devoid of the fruits of suffering.
The relinquishing of all craving reveals that nirvāṇa is devoid of the causes of all afflictions.
Craving is singled out for mention because it is the most prominent;
one relinquishes all dependencies and cravings.
The exhaustion, detachment from passion,
and cessation are called nirvāṇa,
yet they possess no separate substantial entity. Furthermore, regarding the ten names [of nirvāṇa], the first five types are briefly cited here as explanations of nirvāṇa.
This means: "Abandoning" refers to the complete abandonment of all bases, as explained previously regarding suffering;
"giving up" (prahāṇa) refers to the individual relinquishing of all craving, as explained previously;
"exhaustion," "detachment," and "cessation" are according to their respective names.
The sequence refers to the subsequent three types;
the final five types are omitted for brevity,
or perhaps by citing the former, the latter is implied.
"What does it mean to say that [a thing] is not produced because it has already reached [its state of existence]?
This is the challenge posed by the Sarvāstivādins.
How do the Sautrāntikas respond?"
Regarding the statement that the Sūtra does not permit [the term] "unborn":

it is because this analytical cessation possesses the power of non-arising that one says "suffering does not arise. Alternatively, when it is said "unborn," this refers to the power of analytical cessation which causes suffering to be non-arisen.

Therefore, it is said that suffering does not arise; or, based on this analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*), because suffering does not arise, it is said that analytical cessation does not arise.
Since it has already been stated that it is "based on this analytical cessation," [it follows that the non-arising of suffering is due to its cessation].
The Sautrāntikas respond: "We see that these [entities] exist as having a substantial nature,
yet you claim they lack intrinsic nature."
We observe that this sound, which serves as the basis for the seventh transformation,
possesses no efficacy whatsoever toward the realization of analytical cessation (pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha).
For what reason do you hold such a view?
Regarding the statement "depending on this, there is non-arising":
if the phrase "depending on this" refers to that which already exists, namely nirvāṇa,
then all sufferings would have originally not arisen.
Since nirvāṇa is eternal and primordially existent, if one relies on this statement, it would pertain to the meaning of nirvāṇa already attained;
in that case, one would have to reckon that the attainment of nirvāṇa is induced by the path. Furthermore, there is the exhortation: [text continues]
This suffering does not arise;
or it depends solely on the Path, because suffering does not arise when the Path arises; or it depends on the attainment of Nirvāṇa induced by the Path.
Because its arising prevents suffering from occurring,

you should accept this. Furthermore, if one interprets this statement as referring to the sense of "already attained," then one must consider that it refers to the attainment of the path superior to the [current] stage.
Because suffering does not arise once this path is attained, he further exhorts:
"Whether relying solely on the path, or by attaining [the cessation] based on the path, you should have faith and accept that suffering will not arise.
This provides an excellent explanation for what follows below.
Citing scripture to prove that nirvāṇa has no substantial entity:
although nirvāṇa is termed "extinction," it lacks any substantial entity,
just like a lamp.
When the lamp of nirvāṇa has extinguished, it is without substance;
when the mind attains liberation, the aggregates cease and are without substance.
How could it be that only the sūtras state they are without substance?
The Abhidharma also states:
What are phenomena that lack a basis?
They are all unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛtadharma*).
The Sautrāntika commentary states:
"Regarding the phrase 'without a basis' (avastuka),
the term 'basis' (vastu) refers to the substantial entity (svabhāva)."
That is to say, it has no intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
Those Vaibhāṣika masters who do not accept this interpretation likewise do not accept the Sautrāntika interpretation.
If that is so, what is the meaning of their explanation regarding "entities" (*vastu*)?
The Sautrāntikas ask this, and they reply:
"That which is called an 'entity' extends even to that which is without cause and without effect."
The Sarvāstivādins reply:
Those things spoken of as "entities" (vastu) are, in brief, of five kinds.
First, the entity of intrinsic nature (svabhāva-vastu).
That is to say, the intrinsic nature of all phenomena is itself called the "entity" (*vastu*).
Second is the "entity as object," which refers to that which is the object of the mind.
That which is the object of focus is called the "entity.
Third is the entity of bondage,
meaning that which is bound by craving and so forth.
That which is bound is called the "phenomenon" (vastu).
There are four kinds of causal phenomena;
these are called the "phenomena that are causes."
The fruit is that which possesses the cause;
the cause is that which is relied upon.
The fruit arises in dependence upon that which is relied upon.
It is like a son being born because of a father:
the father is the cause, and the son is that which possesses the cause.
This means that all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*) arise from causes and are thus called "phenomena with a basis" (*savastuka*).
The term "basis" (*vastu*) refers to a cause.
The five things comprised [of possessions]:
fields, houses, and so forth, are what are possessed by persons;
thus, that which is possessed is termed a "thing" (*vastu*).
Although, in general, there are five kinds of "factors" (vastu),
that which is referred to as a "factor" here in this Abhidharma is as follows:
Based on the fourth previously mentioned "cause as a thing" (*vastu-hetu*),
it is shown that unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*) have no cause whatsoever;
it is not based on the first [category], "intrinsic nature as a thing," that one says unconditioned phenomena are "without a thing."
Therefore, although the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta) is indeed a real entity,
because it is eternally without function, it is called "causeless" since it does not arise from causes;
and it is called "fruitless" since it cannot produce an effect.

The general discussion is concluded. As for "the activity of mutual correspondence," this marks the second section below, which pairs causes with their results. Herein, it is explained that results arise from causes; therefore, only four [causes] are mentioned.
The fruit of dissociation (*visamyoga-phala*) is eternal and is not produced by the six causes;
therefore, it is not mentioned here.
The treatise says: "That which is obtained through these causes..."
The first phrase is explained as follows:
"Regarding the preceding causes... up to what is called the dominant fruit" explains the second phrase.
This means that the efficient cause (kāraṇa-hetu) possesses sovereign power;
the fruit of this sovereignty is called the sovereign fruit (adhipati-phala).
It is named after its cause.
Regarding the question, "What is the predominance of abiding solely in the absence of obstructions?
it is asked:
"One should consider that it is precisely by virtue of the absence of obstructions that one reaches suchness."
Answer: If a cause were to act as an obstruction, the fruit would not arise;
because the fruit can only arise when the cause is unobstructed, it is therefore called "predominant" (*adhipati*).
This refers to the universal efficient cause (*kāraṇa-hetu*). Alternatively, it is an explanation of the third phrase:
"Because the similar cause, the pervasive cause, and so forth are all like causes," which separately sets forth the superior function of the efficient cause.
If the similar cause (sabhāga-hetu) takes only its own realm, its own stage, its own category, and its own nature as its outflow fruit (niṣyanda-phala);
if the pervasive cause (sarvatraga-hetu) takes only its own realm, its own stage, its own nature, and defiled phenomena as its outflow fruit.
Because the fruits obtained from these two causes both resemble their respective causes, although there are two causes, their fruit is only one.
Question: For example, when false view gives rise to the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), although their natures are different...
Because they are equally defiled,
they are the outflowing fruit (*niṣyanda-phala*).
From the wholesome arises the non-obscured [neutral].

Although their natures differ, since they are equally pure, they should be considered *niṣyanda-phala* (outflow fruits). The commentary explains: defiled phenomena are easily made identical [to their cause], and thus can serve as fruits;
pure phenomena are difficult to make identical, and thus do not serve as such fruits.
Regarding the statement that "simultaneously existing and associated [causes] extend to being called the fruit of human effort (*puruṣakāra-phala*)," this explains the fourth phrase.
These two causes both obtain the superior fruit of human effort that arises simultaneously with them.
Although all six causes take the fruit of human effort (puruṣakāra-phala),
it is the associated (saṃprayukta) and co-existent (sahabhū) causes that can take a superior fruit of human effort occurring at the same time.
This is explained here specifically to refute the Vaiśeṣika position that functional activity exists separately from the substance of a phenomenon; therefore,
it is said that there is no distinct "human function" (puruṣakāra) apart from the human substance itself.
The fruit obtained through the human effort (*puruṣakāra*) of these two causes is called the "fruit of human effort" (*puruṣakāraphala*).
It is named after a metaphor:
just as the activity of a person (*puruṣa*) is called "human effort," so too is this fruit.
The fruit of human effort is called the "fruit of human effort" (*puruṣakāra-phala*).
Regarding this term "human effort," what phenomenon does it designate?
This is the question.
Regarding the statement, "all dharmas up to the general Intoxicated Elephant," the answer is:
they refer to the associated cause (*samprayuktaka-hetu*) and the co-existent cause (*sahabhū-hetu*).
The name is established based on its function,
just as it receives the name "human activity" (puruṣakāra) because of its human-like function;
it is like the medicinal herb called "crow-foot" (kāka-pada).
Because the medicinal herb resembles a crow’s foot,
it is called the "crow-foot" medicinal herb;
because the general resembles a rutting elephant capable of entering the ranks, he is so named.
He is named General Drunken Elephant.
Because he can enter the ranks by means of an elephant made intoxicated, he is called "Drunken Elephant.
Furthermore, it is explained that the Drunken Elephant resembles a general who is capable of entering the ranks.
The name is General Mad-Elephant (*matta-hastin*).
Regarding the question: "Is it only these two [who do so], or is it the same for others as well?"—this is the inquiry.
Is it only for the associated and co-existent causes that there is an efficient fruit (*puruṣakāra-phala*),

or do the other four causes also have one? Some say that the other causes possess [this fruit] up to the point of the ripening cause (*vipāka-hetu*), but that this is not the case for the ripening cause itself.
The answer consists of two parts;
this is the first master’s position.
The other three causes—homogeneous, pervasive, and enabling—likewise possess the fruit of human effort (*puruṣakāra-phala*).
Excluding the ripening cause (*vipāka-hetu*), there are two general types of virile fruit (*puruṣakāra-phala*): first, that which arises simultaneously with its cause;
[and second, that which arises subsequently].
Second, [the cause] is that which is immediate to the cause,
associated, co-existent, capable of grasping,
co-arising, of the same class, and universal.
If the fruit is contiguous, it can be grasped by an immediate [cause];
as for the efficient cause (*kāraṇahetu*), it universally grasps both simultaneous and immediate [causes].
Therefore, these five causes obtain the fruit of human effort (*puruṣakāraphala*).
The ripening cause (*vipāka-hetu*) is not like this;
because its nature differs from that of the fruit it produces, the production of the fruit is somewhat difficult.
It requires a continuity (*saṃtati*) for the fruit to then manifest.
It is neither simultaneous nor immediate;
therefore, there is no "human effort" (puruṣakāra). Furthermore, another interpretation holds that the ripening fruit (vipākaphala) is not so:
because it is neither simultaneous with its cause nor immediate, it is not human effort.
Other masters say that it reaches the fruit that is harvested;
this is the second master’s interpretation of this ripening cause (*vipāka-hetu*).
There are also cases where the result of human effort (*puruṣakāra-phala*) is separated by a temporal interval,
such as when a farmer plows and sows in the spring and reaps the fruit in the autumn.
If one considers the general designation, all six causes may be said to obtain this result.
Now, this second master’s explanation is based on this [verse]. The verse clarifies that *puruṣakāra-hetu* (the cause of human effort) refers only to that which arises simultaneously (*sahaja*),
thereby excluding the other four causes.
Therefore, it is said that there are two types of attainment.
Thus, the *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya-ṭīkā* (Xiǎnzōng lùn), fascicle nine, states:
"The co-nascent efficient fruit (*sahaja-puruṣakāra-phala*) definitely exists and is moreover superior."
Therefore, it is said that the associated cause and the co-existent cause are obtained;
[as for] the immediate [cause], it may be present,
separated, or absent.
Furthermore, there are those that are not superior and which overlap with other fruits;
for this reason, it is not said to be obtained through other causes. Question: There are four types of the term "virile activity" (*puruṣakāra*).
That is to say: simultaneous, immediate, separated, and non-arising;
these encompass all five fruits. Now, one might ask:
does the mention of "virile fruit" (puruṣakāra-phala) not lead to confusion with the others? The explanation says: the other four are established by names based on their specific characteristics.
This is a name established based on a general category;
although it indicates a general designation, it simultaneously receives a specific name,
just as in the case of the "sphere of form" (*rūpāyatana*) and so forth.
Regarding the statement "from the ripening fruit up to the dominant fruit of conditioned phenomena," this section below is the third,
which specifically elucidates the characteristics of the fruits.
The first two lines clarify the ripening fruit (*vipākaphala*).
The third phrase clarifies the fruit of outflow (*niṣyandaphala*);
the fourth phrase clarifies the fruit of disjunction (*visamyogaphala*).
The subsequent two phrases clarify the fruit of human effort (*puruṣakāraphala*).
The latter two lines clarify the dominant fruit (*adhipati-phala*). Regarding the explanation of the names of the five fruits, the second chapter of the *Abhidharmāvatāra-śāstra* states:
"Because the fruit does not resemble the cause, it is called 'dissimilar' (*visabhāga*)."
"Ripening" (pakva) means being matured so as to be fit for enjoyment.
"Fruit" refers specifically to the maturation [result], which is called the "maturation fruit" (vipākaphala).
Furthermore, it is said that because the fruit resembles its cause, it is termed "equal" (sabhāga).
Because they arise from causes, they are further described as "outflows" (*āsrava*).
Since the fruit is itself an outflow, it is termed the "outflowing fruit" (*niṣyanda-phala*).
Furthermore, it is said:

Cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*), which is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), is called the fruit of dissociation (*visamyoga-phala*). This is obtained by means of the Path, not produced by the Path;
since the fruit is itself dissociation, it is termed the "fruit of dissociation."
It is further said:
"Because they arise by the power of this [cause]."
This is called "human effort" (puruṣakāra) and that is called the "fruit.
Furthermore, it is said:
"By means of the preceding dominant condition (adhipati-pratyaya), the subsequent phenomenon arises."
The fruit of predominance is called the "predominant fruit" (*adhipatiphala*); the preceding [explanations] in the treatise follow that commentary.

Furthermore, the first three [terms] are *karmadhāraya* (appositional compounds), while the latter two are *tatpuruṣa* (determinative compounds). Another explanation is that the fruit of maturation is called the "maturation fruit" (*vipākaphala*).
Thus, the cause is termed "ripening" (vipāka),
and the effect is termed "fruit" (phala);
alternatively, an effect that is a similar outflow is termed a "flowing-forth fruit" (niṣyanda-phala).
Because the cause and its fruit are similar in their category or nature, they are called "outflow" (*niṣyanda*).
Alternatively, the fruit of dissociation is called the "fruit of dissociation" (*visamyoga-phala*);
that is to say, because the untainted path (*anāsrava-mārga*) brings about dissociation from bondage, it is also termed "dissociation."
Alternatively, the fruit itself is called the "fruit of human effort" (*puruṣakāra-phala*) because the fruit is like the activity of a person. Alternatively,
the fruit itself is called the "dominant fruit" (*adhipati-phala*) because it is the dominant [condition].
Because the fruit is manifold and its essence is predominant,
although this latter interpretation has not been seen in the formal treatises,
there is no contradiction in the explanation of its meaning.
However, in all the treatises, they rely on entering the Abhidharma;
in no case may it be analyzed as a *bahuvrīhi* compound. If it were analyzed as a *bahuvrīhi* compound, [it would be incorrect].
This refers to those dharmas that do not manifest as results.
The treatise states: "Regarding those that possess a ripening result (*vipākaphala*), among the three natures (*trisvabhāva*)."
The ripened fruit (vipākaphala) exists only within non-obscured neutral (anivṛtāvyākṛta) phenomena,
and not within those that are wholesome or defiled;
for this reason, it also extends to those things not included among sentient beings.
Question:
Why is it restricted exclusively to sentient beings? Answer:
Regarding those that are outflows (*niṣyanda*) and those that are nurtured (*aupacayika*):
Question:
What of this fruit of maturation (*vipākaphala*)?
Among the five categories,
one should know that those which exclusively possess the characteristics of the ripened fruit (*vipākaphala*) are neither out-flowing (*naiṣyandika*) nor nurtured (*aupacayika*).
Answer: This fruition of maturation differs from its cause;
it is exclusively that which arises from a determinate [action].
It does not pertain to outflow (*niṣyanda*) or nourishment (*aupacayika*).
Outflow is not exclusively of a determinate nature (*avyākṛta*),
because it pertains to all three moral natures (*trividha-svabhāva*).
That which is nurtured (*aupacayika*) is also not exclusively of a determinate (*avyākṛta*) nature;
for although its substance is indeterminate, it arises from [causes] belonging to all three natures (*trividha*).
As the preceding treatise states: "Food, assistance, sleep, and meditative concentration (*samādhi*)."
That which is benefited by superior conditions is called "nourished" (*aupacayika*). Furthermore, it is explained that among the five categories,
those not fully subsumed under "maturation" (*vipāka*) are then established as "nourished" and "outflow" (*niṣyanda*).
If [all phenomena] were subsumed under the category of maturation (vipāka),
then nurtured (aupacayika) and outflowing (naiṣyandika) [phenomena] would not be established as separate categories,
because the essential substance would be entirely subsumed within the fruit of maturation.
Regarding the question: "Why are they not called 'nourished' (*aupacayika*) or 'outflowing' (*naiṣyandika*),
and why is it that when they are not included among sentient beings, they are nonetheless not considered 'maturation' (*vipāka*)?"—
this is the inquiry.
They are not included among sentient beings,
yet they arise from wholesome and unwholesome karma; why, then,
are they not considered maturation (vipāka)?
Regarding the statement that "because it is shared, one experiences the ripening fruit," the answer is:
the ripening fruit is not something experienced in common.
Because it is experienced collectively by both sentient and non-sentient beings, it is not a maturation fruit (*vipāka-phala*).
Regarding the question: "To what extent does its dominant fruit (*adhipati-phala*) extend so that it may be experienced collectively? [This is] the inquiry.
If the external dominant fruit is also produced by karma,
how can it be experienced in common?
[It is so] because it is produced by collective karma.
Answer: Because they arise from collective karma (*sādhāraṇa-karman*), they are experienced collectively.
Furthermore, the *Nyāyānusāra* (Treatise on the Principles), fascicle 18, states:
Is it not the case that the non-sentient environment inhabited by the Great Brahmā is itself the fruit of distinct karma?
Should this not also be called "maturation of karma" (*karmavipāka*)? Why, then, do you say it is not?
Some say: "The abode of Mahābrahmā is produced through the sovereign power of all the karma of Mahābrahmās."
Others further say:
"Since the continuity of the Great Brahmā’s abode has not yet been destroyed,
it is logical that others may experience enjoyment therein."
"Therefore, it is not non-common" refers to the fact that dharmas resembling their own causes extend to the two causes, namely the universal cause;
this explains the third phrase.
That which is necessarily similar to its own cause is called a result of outflow (*niṣyanda-phala*).
Although the simultaneously arising activity (*puruṣakāra*) is also necessarily similar to its own cause,
there is also the activity that occurs immediately thereafter (*anantara-puruṣakāra*).
Because it is dissimilar to its cause,

this result-of-outflow (*niṣyanda-phala*) is not confused with the result-of-human-effort (*puruṣakāra-phala*). Although the omnipresent cause (*sarvatraga-hetu*) also takes [factors] from different categories as its objects, [it differs in that the result-of-outflow is similar to its cause].
This is because they share the same nature as a result of outflow (*niṣyanda-phala*).
If the nature of the fruit of human effort (*puruṣakāra-phala*) were different,
and if the universal cause (*sarvatraga-hetu*) were designated as a homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*), [it would lead to logical inconsistency].
Question:
Is this fruit attained solely by eliminating the aforementioned characteristics?
Answer: [It is].
This universal cause and effect is shown to pervade all five categories solely because they belong to the same level;
it is shown not to extend to the pure because they are equally defiled.
It resembles its cause not by way of the five categories or the three natures; rather,
if the fruit also resembles its cause by way of the five categories and the three natures,
then the cause of that fruit is called "homogeneous" (sabhāga).
In contrast, four permutations should be established.
Regarding the first permutation:
a non-universal dharma acts as a homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*).
It is called a "homogeneous cause" (sabhāga-hetu) because it produces [its effect] within its own category;
it is not a "pervasive cause" (sarvatraga-hetu) because it does not universally produce defiled [states].
As for the second clause:
Taking the pervasive dharmas of other categories as pervasive causes (sarvatragahetu),
they are termed pervasive causes because they universally produce defiled states;
they are not similar-cause (sabhāgahetu) because they do not produce [dharmas] of their own category.
Regarding the third phrase:
that which takes the pervasive dharmas of its own category as a pervasive cause (sarvatraga-hetu) is called a similar cause (sabhāga-hetu) because it produces [dharmas] of its own category.
It is called the pervasive cause (*sarvatraga-hetu*) because it universally produces defilement;
this should be understood as the fourth phrase.
Regarding the statement that "by means of wisdom, the exhaustion of phenomena is termed the fruit of dissociation" (*visamyoga-phala*):
This explains the fourth phrase.

Because afflictions are exhausted by means of wisdom (*prajñā*), the unconditioned dharma (*asaṃskṛtadharma*) that is realized is called the fruit of dissociation (*visamyogaphala*). Furthermore, it is explained that this is due to the discernment (*pravicaya*) exercised by wisdom.

The dharma of the extinction of afflictions is called the fruit of dissociation (*visamyoga-phala*). Furthermore, it is explained that by taking the discernment of wisdom as the cause, one becomes free from all fetters and realizes the dharma of extinction;
this is called the fruit of dissociation.
Cessation attained through wisdom is called "cessation through discernment" (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
This very cessation through discernment is also termed "disjunction" (*visamyoga*),
because it is realized by means of being disjoined from fetters.
If a phenomenon reaches its state through that [cause] by virtue of the power of the path,
this explains the fifth and sixth phrases,
clarifying the fruit of human effort (*puruṣakāra-phala*).
If a phenomenon arises solely through the power of another,
that phenomenon is called a "virile fruit" (puruṣakāra-phala),
such as [the states] of a lower stage and so forth.
To indicate the specific category:
one should know that there are many types of *puruṣakāra* (human effort).
The non-arising of cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) is termed the "non-arising *puruṣakāra*."
It should be said that it is realized through the power of the path.
The *Nyāyānusāra* (18), explaining the fruit of human effort (*puruṣakāraphala*), states:
"This is of four kinds."
Simultaneous, immediate, separated, and non-arising have been explained as before.
"Simultaneous" means occurring at the same time.
They arise through the power of being mutual causes for one another.
The term "immediately" (anantara) refers to the subsequent moment.
It arises through the power of the preceding moment as its cause,
just as the "receptivity to the knowledge of the dharma of suffering" (*duḥkhe dharmajñānakṣānti*) arises from the "highest mundane dharmas" (*laukikāgradharma*).
As for the term "interrupted":
This refers to a distant temporal sequence,
wherein [phenomena] arise through the successive power of causes,
such as farmers [producing] rice, wheat, and so forth.
That which is called "non-arising" is what is known as nirvāṇa;
because it is attained through the power of the path of uninterrupted realization (*ānantarya-mārga*), it does not arise.
How can it be said that because it arises through the power of that [human effort], it is called a "result of human effort" (*puruṣakāraphala*)?
We observe that the term "arising" (*utpatti*) is also used in the sense of "acquisition" (*prāpti*);
for example, when one says, "My wealth has arisen," the meaning is "I have acquired wealth."
If it is the path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*) that severs the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*), the analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) realized thereby [is the fruit].
Thus, analytical cessation (pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha) is called both the fruit of disconnection (visamyoga-phala) and the fruit of human effort (puruṣakāra-phala).
This refers to the analytical cessation realized at the time of re-attaining [the path] when the uninterrupted path (ānantarya-mārga) does not abandon the latent dispositions (anuśaya).
Thus, analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyānirodha*) is not a fruit of disjunction (*visamyogaphala*);

it is solely a fruit of human effort (*puruṣakāraphala*). The aforementioned passage from this treatise—and the preceding text of this same treatise—refers specifically to the preeminent fruit of human effort that arises simultaneously [with its cause].

This merely explains that [the fruit] is obtained through the associated cause (*samprayuktaka-hetu*) and the co-existent cause (*sahabhū-hetu*); however, because the subsequent text refers to the universal fruit of human effort (*puruṣakāra-phala*),
it states that [the fruit] is obtained through all six causes.
Regarding the phrase "the dominant fruit (adhipatiphala) of all conditioned phenomena," this explains the latter two lines. Generally,
the fruit in relation to its cause may be simultaneous with it.
Either subsequent, where the cause is the dharma in relation to the fruit;
or simultaneous; or prior.
Because a preceding dharma is not the fruit of a subsequent dharma.
Among conditioned dharmas, one excludes those that have already arisen,
because a preceding dharma is not the fruit of a subsequent one.
These others are either simultaneous with or subsequent to it;
they are the dominant fruits (*adhipatiphala*) of conditioned phenomena. Question: By what cause and by what dominance?
The arising of its fruit is called the dominant fruit (*adhipatiphala*);
other fruits likewise arise because they are produced through the dominance of their causes.
It should be called the *adhipati-phala* (dominant fruit). The commentary explains: other fruits are established by names derived from their specific characteristics;
since this is not established from a general category, it is not called the *adhipati-phala*.
The predominant [factor] has no other specific designation; its name is established based on the general category.
Although it is designated by the general term, it nevertheless receives a specific name, just as in the case of the "sense-base of form" (*rūpāyatana*) and so forth.
Regarding the distinction between the two fruits— the fruit of human effort (*puruṣakāra-phala*) and the dominant fruit (*adhipati-phala*):
the question is,
since these two fruits are numerous, what is their difference?
What is the difference between their essential natures and characteristics?
Regarding the question of why the term "fruit of human effort" (*puruṣakāra-phala*) extends only as far as the "dominant fruit" (*adhipati-phala*), the answer is as follows:
The "function of the noble person" (puruṣakāra) is opposed by that which possesses power and predominance;
this is understood by way of non-obstruction,
as can be known from the examples cited.
Regarding what was stated above— that [the mind] reaches one [moment] and is exclusively past—
the following fourth section clarifies the appropriation of causes and their timing.
A verse is posed as a question and then answered.
The Commentary states: "Up to this point,
these are not mentioned" means that among the six causes, excluding the efficient cause (*kāraṇa-hetu*),
the remaining five causes grasp their fruits only in the present.
The past has already taken [the fruit];
the future is without utility. It should likewise be said that the efficient cause (*kāraṇa-hetu*) takes its fruit in the present;
yet it is not so stated because the efficient cause does not necessarily possess a dominant fruit (*adhipati-phala*).
Therefore, these are not mentioned in this verse;
that is to say, although unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛtadharma*) and future phenomena (*anāgatadharma*) are indeed efficient causes (*kāraṇahetu*), they are excluded here.
However, because it cannot produce a dominant fruit (*adhipatiphala*),
the *Nyāyānusāra* (Treatise on Right Reasoning), chapter eighteen, states: "Nevertheless,
as for the efficient cause (*kāraṇahetu*)."
That which can produce a fruit is necessarily only present.
Regarding its relationship with the past and the present, if one follows the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* (Vibhāṣā), fascicle 21, it states that the efficient cause (*kāraṇa-hetu*)...
Some say that [karma] takes its fruit in the present,
while [other karma] gives its fruit in the past and the present.
Other masters say that this efficient cause (kāraṇa-hetu) takes up its fruit in the past and the present.
Regarding the past, the present, and the fruit, there is indeed no proponent [of such views].
This treatise follows the *Vibhāṣā* masters of the former school in its correct reasoning; furthermore, it is explained that this treatise accords with the *Vibhāṣā* masters of the latter school.
Regarding the statement that the efficient cause (*kāraṇa-hetu*) takes up its fruit in the present like the other five causes,
this is said from the perspective of the majority of cases.
As for the statement that the co-existent (*sahabhū*) and associated (*samprayukta*) causes must necessarily be simultaneous, it is because they exist at the same time.
The second phrase is explained:
association (*samprayukta*) and coexistence (*sahabhū*) also bestow their fruit in the present,
because these two types of grasping necessarily occur simultaneously.
"Similarity, pervasive [causality], and reaching across time apply to both the past and the present" explains the third phrase:
similarity, pervasive [causality], and reaching across time [apply] to the past and the present.
Regarding the statement that "the past may [still] grant up to the outflowing fruit (niṣyandaphala)":
[Question:
Is there an outflowing fruit that has reached the point where it should no longer be granted?
Answer: Because it has reached the present,
there is a resultant flow (niṣyanda-phala) that continues without interruption.
When it reaches the stage of the characteristic of arising (*jāti-lakṣaṇa*), it immediately manifests and gives its fruit.
If the fruit reaches the present, the cause then becomes past; this is called "having already given its fruit."
"One should not give further" means that when explaining the wholesome similar cause (*sabhāga-hetu*), one excludes the aforementioned characteristics;
this constitutes a separate explanation of the wholesome similar cause through a fourfold permutation (*catuṣkoṭi*).
The first case is that which is acquired but not relinquished.
This refers to the acquisition (prāpti) relinquished at the final moment when the roots of virtue are severed;
it is called "acquisition" because it can serve as the seed for those [roots].
The second case is that which is given but not received;
this refers to what is first obtained at the moment of reconnecting the roots of virtue.
That which was acquired at the moment of its final relinquishment in the past is now attained;
at this present time, the fruit has reached the phase of arising (*jāti-lakṣaṇa*).
It is correctly said that they are "given" by virtue of being given that power;
however, because they were already acquired in the past, they are not called "acquired.

The Master of the Treatise [Vasubandhu] fears that if this were the case, one would be said to acquire again all those things previously obtained at the very first moment of their existence when the acquisition resumes.
Now, to explain the statement: "At that time, the continuity is what was previously acquired.
"Previously acquired" refers to the acquisition of the very last [moment] that was relinquished in the past.
The *Nyāyānusāra* (Treatise on Right Reasoning), chapter eighteen, refutes this, asking: "How so?
How could multiple moments in a prior state, having become a homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*), all take up the present acquisition (*prāpti*)?"
Yet at this present time,
one speaks only of attaining [the fruit] in the very last moment,
which is simultaneous with the attainment of the fruit now.

Therefore, it should be understood as excellent according to the original text. If one were to offer a defense on behalf of the master Vasubandhu as a teacher of the *Abhidharmakośa*, [one might argue as follows].
This refers to those dharmas that have never previously been given.
Although all past acquisitions (*prāpti*) bestow their fruits at the time of their continuity, [they do not do so for those dharmas].
All previous moments of thought have already yielded their results;
because they are subsumed under the category of "simultaneous" (sahabhū), they are not mentioned here.
It is only the attainment of the single moment that is finally relinquished which is discussed.
Now, at the time of reconnecting the roots of goodness, it is the initial [wholesome state] that bestows its fruit;
therefore, it is specifically mentioned.
Furthermore, at the time of reconnecting the roots of goodness, past wholesome states other than this are also capable of bestowing their fruit.
Why is it said that [attainment] is obtained exclusively?
Since it is stated separately that it is obtained, it is clearly understood that only the final moment is taken. Furthermore, this is the interpretation of the Master of the Treatise.
It should be said that what continues at that time was previously acquired;
that is to say, all prior past acquisitions of wholesome states are termed "the first acquisition."
Who says that the acquisition (*prāpti*) of what is relinquished belongs only to the final [moment]?
This acquisition of what is relinquished extends across the three time periods;
it is not the case that everything subsequent is capable of yielding its fruit.
Therefore, the preceding statement briefly selects the past.
Thus, the *Vibhāṣā* (18) states:
"There are times when [a cause] yields its fruit but does not grasp it."
This refers to the time when one reconnects the roots of goodness;

that is, abiding in the past, one acquires the wholesome states previously abandoned—this is as stated in the treatise above. Therefore, it specifically employs two simple propositions regarding "acquisition."
Regarding "not being bound by roots of goodness":
when one is about to sever the roots of goodness,
those roots of goodness no longer manifest.
Only acquisition (*prāpti*) is said to function [in this context], and therefore it is specifically mentioned as such.
The third case involves both taking up and relinquishing.
This refers to all wholesome dharmas within a single lifetime,
as appropriate for each case,
during the remaining stages prior to the severance of the roots of goodness.
The "grasper" and the "giver" are designated as the remaining states.
The fourth alternative is neither grasper nor giver;
that is to say, it excludes the aforementioned characteristics.
Furthermore, whatever wholesome dharmas are appropriate to the case— whether they are non-appropriated or appropriated— are all included. Moreover,
regarding unwholesome [dharmas] up to the point of excluding the aforementioned characteristics,
four permutations (catuṣkoṭi) are established in relation to the similar class of unwholesome [dharmas].
This can be understood through reflection.
Regarding the second statement,
the correct reasoning should be applied by analogy to the previous refutation.
The Abhidharmakośa masters again provide an explanation consistent with the previous one.
Regarding the phrase "the obscured-unspecified [states] should be explained accordingly," this refers to the final acquisition that is relinquished at the moment of attaining the fruit of Arhatship.
It is acquired but not given;
at the time of retrogression from that state, it is the first acquisition obtained.
It is given but not acquired.
Those who have not yet attained the stage of no-more-learning (aśaikṣa) both take up and relinquish;
others in the stage of no-more-learning neither take up nor relinquish.
Therefore, it is said that one should speak in accordance with the principle:
"The unobscured-neutral [states] persist until the final aggregates.
These refer to the final aggregates.
This refers to the time when one is about to enter *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*.
The remaining volitions (*cetanā*) can be understood;
as for those with objects of perception (*sālambana*), they should be explained by analogy according to the established rule.
The preceding section clarified that there is no object of cognition; this section clarifies that there is an object of cognition.
The phrase "having an object of cognition" (sālambana) indicates the mind and mental factors.
The distinctions between moments clarify the preceding and succeeding instants;
this can be understood by reflecting upon the three natures and the four propositions.
As for the meaning of "taking the fruit" and "giving the fruit," what do they signify?
Question:
Is that which is capable of acting as the seed for that [result] until it reaches [its destination] called "giving the fruit"?
Answer: No.
The "seed" (bīja) has the meaning of being able to produce;
because the cause possesses the capacity to produce a fruit, it is called "grasping the fruit" (phalagrahaṇa).
That which is produced by it is the fruit.
Because its cause exerts its power precisely at the time of that fruit,
it is called "giving the fruit.
As for the statement that "the ripening [cause] gives its fruit either immediately or after an interval," [it means as follows].
The fourth phrase is explained as follows:
the retributive cause (vipāka-hetu) exists only in the past with respect to its fruit,
because the fruit and the cause are neither simultaneous nor immediate.
Furthermore, there are other masters who, regarding the fruits of the dhyānas,
present alternative views.
The *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 121, states that the masters of the Western regions [say as follows].
It is said that there are nine fruits;
that is, to the five previously mentioned, four additional fruits are added, as stated in the treatise above. The wind-mandala and so forth are able to establish the water-mandala and so forth;
the fruit of such establishment is called the "establishment fruit" (*pratisthā-phala*).
The contemplation of impurity and so forth serve as remote preparatory practices (*prayoga*) for the arising of the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*) and other such insights.

The fruit of these preparatory practices is called the "fruit of preparation" (*prayogaphala*). Furthermore, visual consciousness and the like arise through the gathering and conjunction of the sense faculties, objects, and other conditions.
The fruit of conjunction is called the "fruit of conjunction.
Through the cultivation of meditative absorption (*dhyāna*), one attains the mind of transformation (*nirmāṇacitta*) and so forth;
this fruit of cultivation is called the "fruit of cultivation."
Regarding the inclusion of these four fruits within the category of dominant fruit (*adhipatiphala*),
the masters of Kaśmīr provide a general explanation:
all four of these fruits are comprised within both the fruit of human effort (*puruṣakāraphala*) and the dominant fruit.
If it is considered to be obtained through the power of the cause, it is called the fruit of human effort (*puruṣakāra-phala*);
if it is considered to be obtained through the causal capacity of the agent (*kāraṇa-bala*), it is the dominant fruit (*adhipati-phala*).
Since it is not produced by wholesome or unwholesome karma, it is not a ripened fruit (*vipāka-phala*).

Because they are dissimilar, they are not results of outflow (*niṣyanda-phala*); because they are not attained through realization, they are not results of disjunction (*visamyoga-phala*). Furthermore, according to another interpretation, the first and third are exclusively dominant results (*adhipati-phala*), while the second and fourth are both results of human effort (*puruṣakāra-phala*).
The dominant fruit (adhipati-phala).
As for the fruit of human effort (puruṣakāra-phala), it is obtained through exertion;
thus, when the treatise states that "all are fruits of human effort and the dominant," it is speaking in terms of their general characteristics.
Having explained cause and effect, [the text asks] "to how many causes does it arise?
Below this, the third major section clarifies that phenomena arise from causes; this serves as a concluding summary that introduces the following inquiry.
Regarding the statement that "dharmas are briefly of four types, down to three,
with the remainder being other dharmas," the answer is: among all conditioned dharmas.
Briefly, there are four kinds:
first, defiled phenomena;
second, phenomena born of maturation.
Third, the initial untainted dharmas.
Fourth, the remaining dharmas other than those three preceding categories.
What are these remaining dharmas?

Question: What is meant by "excluding the maturation [result] and all other wholesome dharmas"? Answer: [It refers to the following: *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya*, Chapter 5, Verse 21: "Wholesome [dharmas] acquired through effort, those born of cultivation, the unwholesome, and the neutral [dharmas] of the desire realm; these are the dharmas that have a ripening result. This means that the wholesome dharmas acquired through effort (*prāyogika*) and those born of cultivation (*bhāvanāja*), as well as the unwholesome (*akuśala*) and the neutral (*avyākṛta*) dharmas of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), are the dharmas that possess a ripening result (*vipāka-phala*). This excludes the wholesome dharmas acquired through birth (*upapattilābhika*) and the neutral dharmas of the form and formless realms (*rūpa-ārūpya-dhātu*), which do not produce a ripening result. Furthermore, it excludes the dharmas that are themselves the ripening result, such as the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) produced by past karma. Thus, the phrase "excluding the maturation and all other wholesome dharmas" refers to those wholesome dharmas that are distinct from the aforementioned categories of ripening results and those acquired through birth.
Among indeterminate dharmas,
excluding those that are fruition-born, the remainder are indeterminate.
Among wholesome dharmas...
Excluding the first untainted [factors] and taking the remaining wholesome factors—
thus, these four categories, including those that reach others and excluding those associated with them—
correctly explain how phenomena arise from causes.
The first five phrases clarify the associated dharmas (*saṃprayukta-dharma*);
the sixth phrase clarifies matter (*rūpa*) and the non-associated [dharmas] (*viprayukta*).
The Commentary says: "As for those produced by the remaining three causes..."
This explains the first verse.
All conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*) are comprised of four types;
within these four types, each has two varieties.
1. Factors associated with mind;
2. Factors dissociated from mind;
and among those associated with mind, all defiled factors.
Excluding the ripening cause (*vipāka-hetu*),
they arise from the remaining five causes;
for the phenomena produced by the ripening cause are not defiled (*kliṣṭa*).
