because there is no distinction [between them].
"Just as in the previous position, furthermore, regarding the claim that he is called Rudra because he has attained mastery (*īśvara*),
this is the second refutation based on futility:
what benefit or purpose does the Lord gain by producing phenomena?"
If he brings about the arising of various worlds by generating joy,
then he must depend on other joys for their arising and would not be sovereign.
Since he is not sovereign over joy, [he cannot be the creator].
The same principle should apply to other phenomena as well;
for no distinct causal conditions can be found to differentiate between Īśvara and the arising of joy.
Furthermore, what is the use of taking pleasure in the infliction of suffering upon sentient beings by causing them to be born in the hells and other realms?
Based on the verses spoken by those non-Buddhists, I also believe this to be well-said: [Insert relevant verse here] I likewise accept this as a well-spoken teaching.
The master of the treatise is mocking those non-Buddhists.
The meaning of this verse as explained by the non-Buddhists is that Maheśvara manifests various transformations to teach and transform sentient beings.
Regarding those who should be delivered by means of the "perilous and sharp" [forms]:
he manifests these perilous and sharp bodies to deliver them.
That which is capable of performing perilous and evil deeds is called "perilous."
It cuts through and severs the fame and profit of sentient beings;
it can burn sentient beings, thus it is called "the burner";
it manifests a terrifying body, thus it is called "the terrifying."
Because he constantly afflicts and harms sentient beings with instruments of suffering, he is called "Constantly Afflicting" (Nityakrodha).
Alternatively, because he sometimes delights in eating blood,
flesh, and marrow, he is called Rudra.
This is called Pāpabhūti,
an alternate name for Maheśvara.
Maheśvara has a total of one thousand names.
Currently, there are only sixty extant [texts] in the world;
Rudra is simply one of its names. Furthermore, the explanation of the ash-smearing non-Buddhists (Kāpālikas) states that Maheśvara transcends the three realms and possesses three bodies.
First, the Dharma-body pervades the entire dharma-realm.
Second, the Enjoyment-body resides in the palaces of the Sovereign Heaven (Īśvara) above the Form Realm;
this is what is referred to in the Buddha-dharma as the Mahesvara Heaven.
He has three eyes and eight arms, and his body is sixteen thousand *yojanas* in height.
His three transformation bodies (*nirmāṇakāya*) assume forms according to the six realms of existence to teach and transform beings in various ways.
This verse describes the Heaven of Transformation Bodies (*nirmāṇarati-deva*): "By means of that which is sharp and perilous, capable of burning..."
There were three asura generals leading their three kingdoms who flew through the air above the Heaven of Mastery (Īśāna-deva).
The gods there, unable to endure this, shot flaming arrows at them.
The three realms are burned away simultaneously and utterly consumed;

the fierce and sharp iron arrows are capable of incinerating the three realms. As for those who are constantly threatened and harmed by fearsome beings, they have human skulls pierced by dragons and fastened upon their heads.
Furthermore, regarding his binding of the arm with a dragon, his killing of elephants, and his taking of their skins to smear with blood while wearing them backward—these manifest what he consumes.

Since those who delight in eating flesh, blood, and marrow now perform sacrifices using these very things as offerings, he is named Rudra. Moreover, this applies to those who believe in and accept the deeds and powers of the Supreme Person (Tathāgata).
The third section below refutes [the opponent's view] by contradicting worldly consensus.

If phenomena were produced solely by the cause of Īśvara, then one would be denying such things as human effort in the world. If it is argued that when Īśvara acts, he must not be Īśvara, [then the following applies].
This is a refutation by restating and turning back the opponent's argument.

If it is claimed that Īśvara depends on other causes and conditions—such as human effort and so forth—to assist in the manifestation of his functional capacity before he can become a cause, this is merely an expression of partiality toward the god Īśvara; for apart from other causes and conditions, no distinct function of Īśvara is observed.

Alternatively, [if it] waits for causes and conditions, it should not be Maheśvara. This refutes the counter-argument by restating the position that "if one holds that its initial arising is like that of Maheśvara.
If it is said that it does not depend on other causes at its initial arising but depends on causes later on, [then...]
That which first arises would then be beginningless,
as it does not depend on any other cause, just like Īśvara.
Regarding the statement, "The meditative attainments such as 'I am superior' arise from a single cause," this serves as an example for the refutation and summary.
As for the passage, "How strange that worldly beings [seek] Ishvara and other causes," the author of the treatise expresses lamentation over their false attachments.
Now, having ceased the refutation of heterodox views, we shall establish the correct meaning.

Regarding the previous statement that other dharmas serve as mutual causes and conditions: *Note: This text contains the phrase "zhǐpò biànzèng" (止破辨正), which translates to "ceasing the refutation and establishing the correct [meaning]," and "yúfǎ zhì hùwéi yīnyuán" (餘法至互為因緣), which translates to "other dharmas up to being mutual causes and conditions."*
The following is the second section, the detailed explanation according to specific questions.
It introduces the preceding inquiry with the verse:
"That which reaches [its object] acts as the single cause for the great [elements]."
The first phrase refers to the great [elements] in relation to the great [elements];
the second phrase refers to the great [elements] in relation to that which is produced;
the third phrase refers to that which is produced in relation to that which is produced.
Regarding the fourth phrase, "the derived [matter] in relation to the great [elements]," the treatise says:
"As for the meaning of reaching the similar cause (*sabhāga-hetu*)," which explains the first phrase.
The *Nyāyānusāra* states: "When viewed in relation to one another, they possess the cause of coexistence (*sahabhū-hetu*).
Although their natures and categories differ, because they are mutually concordant with respect to a single function, they possess the cause of similar type (*sabhāga-hetu*)."
"That which is greater than its created effects can act as five causes" explains the second phrase. The five causes,
such as arising (*jāti*), are termed "causal conditions" (*hetu-pratyaya*).
The two explanations are as previously stated.
Alternatively, it is subsumed under the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*) among the four conditions.
The *Vibhāṣā* also states that the ten causes constitute the causal condition; according to this text, it is therefore not the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*).
The ancient masters explain that regarding "the cause created by great expectation" and "the predominant [condition]":
some say that "cause" refers to the co-existent cause (*sahabhū-hetu*).
Whether it is said that [the cause] is only the homogeneous cause (sabhāga-hetu), or whether it is said to be both the co-existent (sahabhū) and homogeneous causes,
neither is reasonable.
Both the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* and this treatise state that the five causes, such as arising (*jāti*), are the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*).
Furthermore, since the *Jñānaprasthāna* composes its discourse based on the four conditions,
these causes are indeed causal conditions.
Former teachers did not realize that the five causes, such as "arising" (utpāda), are subsumed under the condition of "causal condition" (hetu-pratyaya);
this is why there are various differing interpretations. What are these five?
Question:
What is meant by "the nature of being the cause for the arising, supporting, establishing, reaching, abiding, and increasing [of phenomena]"? Answer:
Within these causal conditions, there are five causes, such as "arising" (janana) and so forth;
however, among the six causes, this refers only to a portion of the efficient cause (kāraṇa-hetu) and not the other five causes.
This is because the primary elements (mahābhūta), when considered in relation to derived matter (upādāya-rūpa), do not share the same fruit.
Because their natures are not necessarily identical;
because it is possible for them to be created in different time periods; and because it is possible for them to be possessed [by sentient beings] in different ways.
Therefore, it is not a co-existent cause (*sahabhū-hetu*).
Because it is neither mind nor mental factors (*citta-caitta*), it is not an associated cause (*samprayuktaka-hetu*).
Because it is not defiled (*kliṣṭa*), it is not a universal cause (*sarvatraga-hetu*).
Because it is indeterminate (avyākṛta), it is not a ripening cause (vipāka-hetu).
Because it arises simultaneously, it is not a homogeneous cause (sabhāga-hetu);
even if it were to arise later, it would not be a homogeneous cause because it is not of the same class.
Although they are alike in being indeterminate (*avyākṛta*), they differ in their categories (*jāti*).
Thus, although feeling (*vedanā*) and so forth differ in category from the mind,
they can serve as causes because they share the same fruit.
They are not instances of the primary elements acting as causes for derived matter.

Regarding the five remaining causes that act upon what is produced by the primary elements, they are explained in detail as in the *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra*. Derived matter arises from the primary elements.
Just as a mother is said to be the cause of birth for her child because the derived [matter] continues to evolve following the primary elements once it has been produced;
and just as disciples and others are said to be the causes of reliance upon their teachers and so forth because they can sustain that derived matter.

Just as a wall is said to be the supporting cause for a painting, so too is it called the "supporting cause" (*dhṛti-hetu*) because it is the cause for the non-interruption of derived matter (*upādāya-rūpa*), and it is called the "nourishing cause" (*puṣṭi-hetu*) because it is the cause for the growth of that derived matter. In this way, it is revealed that the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) function as the originating nature for derived matter, which is precisely their generative cause (*janana-hetu*).
The nature of the transformative cause (*pariṇāma-hetu*) is the supporting cause (*niśraya-hetu*);
that is to say, when the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) undergo transformation, derived matter (*upādāya-rūpa*) likewise undergoes transformation accordingly.
The nature of the sustaining cause (*dhṛti-hetu*) is the establishing cause (*pratisthā-hetu*).
The nature of the cause of abiding (*sthiti-hetu*) is itself the cause of maintenance (*dhṛti-hetu*), because it maintains the continuity of the derived matter (*upādāya-rūpa*).
The nature of the cause of growth (*vṛddhi-hetu*) is itself the cause of nourishment (*puṣṭi-hetu*). Furthermore, the correct understanding of these five causes is stated as follows:
Alternatively, "productive cause" refers to all primary elements (mahābhūta) producing derived matter (upādāyarūpa),
because derived matter does not arise apart from the primary elements.
Once derived matter has arisen, it continues in a homogeneous succession without interruption.
Fire acts as the causal condition of dependence (*āśraya-hetu*), for it enables drying and prevents decay.
Water acts as the causal condition of establishment (*pratisthā-hetu*), for it provides moisture and prevents dispersal.
Earth acts as the causal condition of support (*dhṛti-hetu*), for it sustains those [elements] and prevents them from falling.

Wind is the sustaining cause (*puṣṭi-hetu*), for it can induce those [derived forms] to grow; the commentary explains that the generative cause (*janma-hetu*) pertains to all four great elements, while each of the other four causes corresponds to one great element respectively. Regarding "all derived forms" up to the result of the eye faculty and so forth:
The third phrase can be understood.
Regarding the statement "because that which is derived [matter] reaches the great elements as their fruit": this means that derived matter arises from the great elements and takes them as its cause.
Explaining the fourth phrase:
according to this verse, the ten causes are termed "causal conditions" (*hetu-pratyaya*).
Therefore, the preceding question states:
How do the primary elements (mahābhūta) and their derivatives (upādāyarūpa), whether belonging to oneself or another, mutually function as causes and conditions?
This treatise is composed in accordance with the *Vibhāṣā* based on ten types of causes.
While this was previously explained in general terms, it shall now be definitively established.
Below this, the second major section specifically clarifies the equal and immediate [condition] (*samanantara-pratyaya*).
Within this, first, the arising of various minds is clarified;
second, the number of minds attained is clarified. Below this, the arising of various minds is clarified.

How many minds can it produce? Furthermore, from how many minds does it arise, and what kind of mind arises [therefrom]? This constitutes the inquiry regarding from how many minds [a given mind] arises.
Regarding the statement that, "to speak briefly, there are twelve minds," within the response,
the first part clarifies these twelve minds.
II. Explaining the Twenty Minds. Regarding the twelve minds:
first, the listing of the twelve minds;
second, the formal analysis of their mutual generation.
Below this, twelve types of mind are listed;
this is the answer given by stating the total number. What are these twelve?
Question:
The verse states, "Up to the combination, they total twelve. Answer:
The number can be known.
Regarding these twelve minds, from the others four arise from five:
hereafter, the actual process of mutual arising is correctly analyzed.
To provide a brief summary by citing the verses:
the first four lines concern the four minds of the desire realm;
the subsequent six lines concern the three minds of the form realm.
The next four phrases refer to the three types of mind in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*),
and the final two phrases refer to the two types of untainted (*anāsrava*) mind.
To clarify how these various minds arise from one another, they are briefly analyzed according to twenty minds and three categories.
The twelve [bases] and the twenty [elements] differ in their inclusion and exclusion;
however, their essential nature (svabhāva) has no distinction of breadth or narrowness.
Because the enumeration of twenty is more extensive, it is explained by means of that.
Regarding the three gates: first, the mind that arises from the states of concentration and distraction;
second, the mind of the preparatory means for guarding concentration;
and third, the mind at the time of death and rebirth. As for "the mind that arises from the states of concentration and distraction":
Among these,
there are three modes of arising:
first, the arising of wholesome concentration.
Second, the mutual generation of the scattered and the self-arisen;
third, the mutual generation of the concentrated and the scattered. Regarding the first, the mutual generation of the wholesome and the concentrated, there are further two types.
First, contaminated concentration (*sāsrava-samādhi*).
There are two types of untainted meditative absorptions (*anāsrava-samādhi*). Regarding what is called tainted meditative absorption (*sāsrava-samādhi*):
if the mind of tainted preparatory concentration (*prayoga-samādhi*) belonging to the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) can produce four types of minds.
That is to say: the preparatory and meditative minds of one's own realm;
the preparatory and meditative minds of the formless realm;
and the outflow-free minds of those in training and those beyond training.
Furthermore, these arise from these four minds.
If it is a contaminated meditative mind of the formless realm, it can produce four minds;
these four minds, in turn, arise from those four.
As it was explained regarding the defiled preparatory concentration (*prayoga-samādhi*) of the form realm,
so too regarding the untainted concentration (*anāsrava-samādhi*):
if a mind of one in training (*śaikṣa*) can produce four types of minds.
This refers to the defiled meditative minds of the form and formless realms,
as well as the minds of those in training (*śaikṣa*) and those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*).
Excluding the mind of one beyond training, these arise from three types of minds.
If an *aśaikṣa* mind can produce three minds—excluding the *śaikṣa* mind from among the aforementioned four—it arises from four minds, including the *śaikṣa* mind.
Second, regarding those that arise from their own scattered characteristics (*svabhāva*): [the text continues].
This means that they arise in relation to their own realm as scattered states of mind.
Among the eight minds of the desire realm,
the *abhijñā-phala-citta* (resultant mind of supernormal power) arises only from a concentrated state of mind.
It does not arise from the other seven minds.
Each of the other three types of neutral minds can give rise to six minds,
excluding the mind of supernormal fruition and the preparatory mind.
Each arises from seven minds, excluding those that are the result of supernormal powers (*abhijñā-phala*).
If a wholesome mind of application (*prayoga-kuśala*) is added, it can produce seven, excluding the result of supernormal powers.
It arises from four minds, excluding the four types of neutral (*avyākṛta*) minds.
If it is a wholesome mind acquired at birth, or either of the two defiled minds,
each can produce seven; furthermore, seven minds can arise from them, excluding the fruition-of-superknowledge mind.

The arising of scattered states in the form and formless realms should be explained according to this principle. Regarding the mutual arising of the three meditative absorptions and the scattered state:
eight types of consciousness can act as the entry-point for a mind entering a contaminated meditative absorption.
That is to say: the preparatory wholesome mind and the mind of supernormal power (abhijñā-phala-citta) of the desire realm;
and the preparatory wholesome, innate wholesome, and obscured minds, as well as the mind of supernormal power, of the form realm.
The innate wholesome states (*upapatti-lābhika-kuśala*) of the formless realm and the obscured mind (*nivṛta-citta*).
The reason we know that the innate wholesome states of the form realm are capable of entering meditative absorption is that,
just as the innate wholesome states of the formless realm are already able to enter meditative absorption.

The wholesome states acquired at birth (*upapatti-lābhika*) in the form realm are also capable of entering meditative absorption. Furthermore, it is explained that the wholesome states acquired at birth in the form realm cannot enter meditative absorption;
as for the wholesome states acquired at birth in the formless realm, there is no separate wholesome state of preparation (*prayoga*) in the distracted state through which one could enter absorption.

In the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), there are additionally the scattered preparatory stages of wisdom derived from hearing (*śrutamayī-prajñā*) that are capable of entering meditative absorption (*samādhi*);
innate wholesome states (*upapatti-lābhika-kuśala*) cannot enter absorption.
If this interpretation is adopted, then only seven types of mind can serve as the minds that enter impure (*sāsrava*) meditative absorptions.
Twelve types of consciousness can produce the consciousness of a contaminated meditative absorption (*sāsrava-samādhi*):
namely, the preparatory wholesome, the innate wholesome, and the supernormal-resultant consciousnesses of the desire realm;
and the six consciousnesses of the form realm.
There are three types of mind in the formless realm;
the preparatory stage is excluded because the preparatory stage is itself meditative absorption.
This is why the meditative absorptions of the form realm do not give rise to lower-level defiled states or other neutral states.
Even from the formless attainments (*ārūpyasamāpatti*), the innate wholesome states (*upapattilābhika-kuśala*) of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) do not arise,
because they are not clear or sharp;
how much less could the form attainments give rise to the defiled (*kliṣṭa*) or neutral (*avyākṛta*) states of a lower realm?

Furthermore, the reason we know that from a tainted meditative state (*sāsrava-samādhi*) of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), minds of maturation (*vipāka*) and deportment (*airyāpathika*) of its own realm arise,
is because it is like how a mind in a formless realm meditative state (*ārūpyadhātu-samādhi*) can produce a mind of maturation of its own realm.
It should be understood that the mind in the form realm can also produce both resultant and functional minds;
these two types of mind can serve as the entry point for the mind of untainted meditative absorption—
namely, the preparatory wholesome mind of the desire realm.
The preparatory wholesome mind of the form realm and three types of minds can produce the mind of uncontaminated meditative absorption;
namely, the preparatory wholesome mind of the desire realm and the innate wholesome mind.

The preparatory (*prayoga*) non-informative wholesome states of the form realm do not give rise to the non-informative wholesome states of the formless realm that are dissociated from meditative concentration (*asamāhita*). This is because there are no preparatory wholesome states in the state of being dissociated from concentration;
although innate wholesome states do exist there, they are inferior and thus do not give rise to them. Second, regarding the mind that employs the means for guarding meditative concentration:
Four minds can act as the preparatory application for the concentration of restraint (*saṃvarasamādhi*):
namely, the two defiled minds of the form and formless realms, which,
as appropriate, can give rise to wholesome minds of the lower stages.
Namely: the acquired virtue of application in the desire realm, the innate virtue of the desire realm,
the acquired virtue of application in the form realm,
and the acquired virtue of application in the formless realm.
It should be understood that this serves only to prevent [the arising of] a concentrated mind.
After a defiled mind of a higher stage, a wholesome mind of a lower stage may arise;
others necessarily do not. Third, regarding death and rebirth:
Twelve types of consciousness can function as the death-consciousness:
namely, the innate wholesome, unwholesome, obscured, functional, and resultant [consciousnesses] of the desire realm;
and the innate wholesome, obscured, functional, and resultant [consciousnesses] of the form realm.
The wholesome mind acquired at birth, the obscured, and the unobscured minds of the formless realm—
these four types of mind can serve as the mind of rebirth.
This refers to the four defiled minds of the three realms.
If one is to be reborn through a mind at the moment of death,
within this context, the single thought-moment of death is called the "mind of passing away."
There is the initial moment of the intermediate existence (*antarābhava*) in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and the form realm (*rūpadhātu*),
as well as the initial moment of the birth-existence (*upapattibhava*) in all three realms, including the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).
All are termed "minds of taking birth" (*upapatticitta*),
because this treatise states that the first moment of consciousness in the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) is called "taking birth.
A mind of taking birth does not give rise to the mind of death (*cyuticitta*).
Because they are separated by a great distance,
the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 154,
states: "Is there any place where there is mind for only two moments?"
Does this refer to the time of linking rebirth (*pratisaṃdhi*) and the time of death?
One should answer: "No.
This is the statement of the Venerable Ghosaka.
There is. That is to say, the Heaven of Non-conception (*asaṃjñisattva*).
Is there any place where the mind at rebirth-linking arises as the immediately preceding condition for the mind at the moment of death?
Vasumitra says it is non-existent;
the Venerable Ghosaka says it exists.
This refers to the passage in the *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya* concerning the Heaven of Non-conception (*asaṃjñisattva-deva*) and above; the former explanation is taken as correct. Question:
If the former explanation in the *Mahāvibhāṣā* is taken as correct, it would contradict the *Nyāyānusāra*, chapter twenty-one.
Therefore, that treatise states:

"That is to say, while it may be possible for the death-existence (*cyuti-bhava*) to manifest immediately after the birth-existence (*upapatti-bhava*), it is not possible for the fundamental existence (*mūla-bhava*) to arise;
furthermore, there is absolutely no possibility for [the intermediate existence] to exist on the plane of the intermediate state (*antarābhava*)."
The existence at birth (upapattibhava) manifests immediately after the existence at death (maranabhava);
therefore, the name "intermediate existence" (antarābhava) does not overlap with the other forms of existence.
The commentary explains that what is stated in the *Nyāyapravēśa* is precisely the meaning of Guṇamati.
There is no need for further elaboration.
If one follows that explanation, it can be understood by analogy that the mind at birth may also serve as the mind at death;
the former explanation is correct.
If the mind at the end of life can produce the mind that takes rebirth—
wherein the four defiled minds of the three realms are called the "mind that takes rebirth"—
then in the desire realm, there are two such defiled minds that take rebirth.
The universal [mental states] arise from the twelve types of death-moment consciousnesses of the three realms.
If it is a defiled mind at rebirth in the form realm,
it arises from ten types of death-moment consciousnesses.
Among the twelve [minds], excluding the two defiled minds of the desire realm,
the defiled mind of one born in the formless realm arises from nine minds at the moment of death.
Regarding the twelve [minds], excluding the two defiled minds of the desire realm and the one defiled mind of the form realm.
The Commentary says: "As for the arising of wholesome and defiled minds, it means that nine [minds] arise immediately after a wholesome mind of the desire realm."
That is to say: the four [minds] of its own realm,
and two minds of the form realm—
namely, the wholesome mind that arises at the time of entering meditative absorption.
At the stage of rebirth, one gives rise to a defiled mind.
Furthermore, the *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra* (Treatise on the Principles), fascicle 20, asks:
"What kind of wholesome mind arises [at that time]?"
Furthermore, by which stage is it subsumed?
This arises as a mind of preparatory application (*prayoga-citta*) in the initial stage;
at a later time, it arises as the attainment of freedom from desire (*vairāgya-prāpti*).
Because one dwells in accordance [with that state], there is no possibility for that innate wholesome mind (*upapatti-lābhika-kuśala-citta*) to arise;
even if born in this realm, one cannot cause it to manifest.
Some say that this mind is subsumed under the *anāgamya* stage.
Some say it is also included within the first dhyāna;
others say it is also in the intermediate dhyāna.
The Venerable Ghoṣaka has stated this as follows:
This extends even to the second dhyāna; it is like when one enters the leap-concentration (*vyutkrāntaka-samāpatti*), arising from a different level.
Some say that a non-equipoised mind lacks the power to draw forth the arising of a mind from a different level.
Therefore, that explanation is certainly not logical; according to the text of the *Nyāyānusāra*,
one knows that when the body is in a lower stage, it cannot give rise to a wholesome mind acquired through birth (*upapatti-labdha-kuśala-citta*) belonging to a higher stage.
Regarding "the one [mind] of the formless realm at the time of entering meditative absorption":
this refers to the wholesome mind of the desire realm;
it gives rise only to one defiled mind of the formless realm.
Those wholesome states do not arise there because they are extremely remote;
the formless realm is remote from the desire realm in four ways. This is why.
A wholesome mind of the desire realm cannot give rise to that [wholesome mind].
Therefore, the *Nyāyānusāra* (Treatise on Correct Reasoning), fascicle 36, states:
"That which is distant in terms of its basis refers to the states of entering and emerging from meditative attainments (*samāpatti*)."
Because there is no possibility for the equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*) to serve as its supporting substance;

and because the mode of activity (*ākāra*) is remote, meaning that a mind belonging to the formless realm is ultimately incapable of forming modes of activity such as "suffering" or "coarse" with respect to phenomena of the desire realm.
The meaning of "remoteness of the object" (*ālambana-dūratā*) should be understood in this same way.

Because the mind of the formless realm can only take the contaminated phenomena (*sāsrava-dharma*) of the fourth dhyāna as its objects through the aspects (*ākāra*) of suffering, coarseness, and so forth.
Regarding remoteness by way of antidote (*pratipakṣa-dūratā*): when one has not yet abandoned sensual desire,
it is absolutely impossible for one to give rise to the formless attainments (*ārūpya-samāpatti*),
which can serve as the antidote to unwholesome conduct and other such phenomena of the desire realm.
Because there are two types of antidotes: the antidote of revulsion and the antidote of abandonment.

It is not that [the formless realm] is incapable of taking [the desire realm] as an object; rather, it is simply that the formless realm, in relation to the desire realm, lacks the antidotes of abandonment and revulsion. *Jieyun* (Exegesis) explains: "The formless realm, when compared to the desire realm, has no antidotes of abandonment or revulsion."
Therefore, it is said that they are distant as antidotes;
however, there exists a "possession-antidote" (prāpti-pratipakṣa),
because it can maintain that [attainment] so that it is not lost.
There is also the antidote of distancing (*dūrabhāga-pratipakṣa*),
because it prevents those afflictions from arising by keeping them at a distance. Furthermore,
there is no antidote of abandonment (*prahāṇa-pratipakṣa*).
Because one is unable to abandon the dharmas of the desire realm,
if we consider the mind at the moment of death and rebirth,
a mind of the desire realm can also serve as the support for a mind of the formless realm.
"Furthermore, this [attainment] again proceeds until it is said 'at the time of emerging from meditative absorption'":

this explains the second phrase. Question: When one is in a lower realm and gives rise to a defiled mind of a higher realm, and subsequently gives rise to a wholesome mind of a lower realm, can that [lower wholesome mind] prevent the higher meditative absorption?
It is not yet known how many defilements of the higher realms arise for one whose body resides in a lower realm. Answer: As stated in the *Abhidharmamahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* (Vibhāṣā), fascicle 53:
"This refers to one who dwells in the desire realm without dying or being reborn, yet for whom the fetters (*saṃyojana*) of the form and formless realms manifest."
And that [knowledge] pertains to both ordinary persons (pṛthagjana) and noble ones (ārya).
If it pertains to an ordinary person,
any one of the sixty-two underlying tendencies (anuśaya) of the form and formless realms is present.
This refers to those who have attained the higher dhyānas— whether they be ordinary persons or noble ones—
when any one of the six proclivities to be abandoned through cultivation in the form and formless realms, namely: craving, views, doubt, or pride, becomes manifest.
This refers to those who have attained higher dhyānas through craving or pride.
After that concentration, the afflictions manifest;
after the afflictions, the concentration manifests again.
This is called having fetters belonging to the desire realm that do not fall within the desire realm. Furthermore, it is said:
"Abiding in the two lower realms, one does not undergo birth or death, yet the fetters of the formless realm manifest before one."
That [defilement] pertains to both ordinary persons (pṛthagjana) and noble ones (ārya).
If it pertains to an ordinary person,
any one of the thirty-one proclivities (anuśaya) of the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu) manifests.
This refers to those who have attained the higher dhyānas— whether they be noble ones (ārya) or others—
and in whom any one of the three latent proclivities (anuśaya) to be abandoned through cultivation in the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu), namely craving, views, or doubt, has become manifest.
For one who has attained the higher dhyānas through attachment or pride,
after that concentration, afflictions manifest;
after those afflictions, the concentration manifests again.
This is called a fetter that exists but is not located in the formless realm;
yet that fetter does not fail to fall within the formless realm.
According to that treatise, when one’s body is in a lower realm, both ordinary persons and noble ones give rise to afflictions of a higher realm.
When higher-level afflictions arise, they all emerge from and enter into a concentrated mind.
If one considers the prevention of the concentrated mind by means of these afflictions,
then according to their respective correspondences, after an affliction of a higher realm, one enters a wholesome mind of a lower realm.
The thirty-one [factors] of the form realm all enter into the wholesome mind of the desire realm;
the thirty-one [factors] of the formless realm are all capable of entering into the wholesome mind of the form realm.
This text does not mention ignorance (avidyā).
"Because they necessarily exist, they are established without being explicitly stated.
Regarding "defilement refers to the unwholesome up to the state where there is no further possibility of arising," this explains the third phrase.
The *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* states:
It is called "obscured" (*nivṛta*) because it can obstruct the Noble Path and its preparatory practices;
it is called "indeterminate" (*avyākṛta*) because it does not bring about a ripened fruit (*vipāka-phala*).
The "remainder" refers to those from the fetters of the desire realm up to that which can produce their defilements;
this explains the fourth phrase.
It refers to wholesome minds of the form realm up to those that produce the defilements of the desire and formless realms.
This explains the three minds of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*).
As for "the wholesome [minds] of the formless realm reaching down to [and including] those defiled by desire and form," this explains the three minds of the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).
Regarding the statement that "the mind of one in training (śaikṣa) arises from four [minds] up to and including the single mind of one beyond training (aśaikṣa)":
this clarifies how the minds of those in training and those beyond training arise in conjunction with various other minds,
because they are not mutually contradictory like the defiled minds of the three realms.
It is not because the various non-obscured ignorances (*anivṛta-avidyā*) are sharp; therefore,
those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) do not give rise to those still in training (*śaikṣa*),
for the latter are not their fruit.
Regarding the statement that the twelve minds are explained up to other enumerations as previously described:
this section below is the second, which clarifies the arising of the twenty minds.
This involves dividing the twelve minds into twenty.
The Commentary states: "Because there is a distinction between those acquired at birth and others.
Within this prose section, the first part provides the direct explanation of the verse.
Second, the arising of the twenty mental states is explained;
third, their arising according to different categories is explained.
Hereafter follows the formal exposition.
This explains the second and third phrases.
Regarding "the non-obscured [states] of the desire realm up to the four fruits of penetration":
this explains the following three phrases.
"From the non-obscured mind of the form realm up to the mind of craftsmanship" explains the seventh phrase.
"Thus, these twelve become twenty" [explains] the eighth phrase.
Explaining the first and last phrases:
The *Nyāyānusāra* states that because there are no activities such as walking and so forth in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), there are no modes of deportment (*airyāpathika*).
Because there is no samādhi that involves grasping, there is also no supernormal power (abhijñā-phala).
Regarding the twelve bases (dvādaśāyatana) as the objects of the modes of deportment (airyāpathika) and so forth:
this specifically clarifies the objects of the three types of neutral (avyākṛta) states.
The mind born of maturation (*vipākaja*) can take the twelve bases (*āyatana*) as its object;
since this is already known, it is not specified separately.
The minds of deportment (*airyāpathika*), craftsmanship (*śailpasthānika*), and the three types of neutral resultant minds (*avipāka-avyākṛta*) [take] the bases and the spheres as their objects.

All [of these] take visible form, odor, taste, and tangible objects as their objective conditions (*ālambana*). The "artistic skills" (*śailpasthānika*) and so forth include the mind resulting from supernormal powers (*abhijñā-phala-citta*);
these two types of neutral minds also take sound as their object.
Because there is skillful craftsmanship in speech,
the mind of craftsmanship takes sound as its object;
because a manifested person utters speech, the mind of supernormal transformation takes sound as its object.
Because sound is not a deportment, the mind of deportment does not take it as an object.
Thus, these three minds are exclusively mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).
[They are] the application of the paths of deportment and the paths of craftsmanship.
Not only the mental consciousness,
but it also extends to the four [sensory] consciousnesses and the five consciousnesses.
Now, there are two types of *nirmāṇacitta* (fruition-of-mastery mind).
First, there are the supernormal powers (abhijñā-phala) involving the five sensory consciousnesses,
namely the supernormal power of the divine eye and the supernormal power of the divine ear.
Second, there are the supernormal powers involving the mental consciousness (manovijñāna).
These are the mind of transformation (*nirmāṇa-citta*) and the minds of the supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) and their fruition (*phala*).
Here, based on the second type—the mind of the fruition of supernormal power—it is said that it is "only mental consciousness" (*manovijñāna*).

However, if one considers both types of supernormal power, they also exist in the five sensory consciousnesses (*pañca-vijñāna*). Question: How is it known that these two types of supernormal power are called "minds of the fruition of supernormal power"? Answer: As stated in the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* (Vibhāṣā), fascicle 95: [text follows].
Among these, the wisdom associated with the five consciousnesses is of three types:
first, wholesome;
second, defiled.
The three are the non-obscured neutral, the wholesome, and the defiled. The wholesome refers exclusively to that which is acquired at birth (*upapatti-pratilambhika*).
The defiled refers exclusively to that which is associated with greed, hatred, and delusion (*lobha-dveṣa-moha*) and is abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*).
The non-obscured and neutral [states] refer to those born of maturation (*vipākaja*).

There are also small portions associated with the minds of deportment (*airyāpathika*), the arts and crafts (*śailpasthānika*), and the supernormal powers (*abhijñā-phala*). Regarding the aforementioned treatise which states that if the mind of deportment belongs exclusively to the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*):
According to the explanation based on the mind that initiates deportment (*airyāpathika*),
if the preparatory stage (*prayoga*) of the path of deportment were restricted to the mental consciousness alone,
it would not be correct; for it also extends to the four consciousnesses, as they take the four objects as their spheres.
Because sound is not a mode of deportment (*īryāpatha*), one does not take sound as an object.
Thus, [the *Śāriputrābhidharma-śāstra*] 126 states:
"The four consciousnesses of the eye, nose, tongue, and body..."

This refers to the preparatory stage (*prayoga*) for the modes of deportment (*airyāpathika*), not the actual arising of the modes of deportment themselves. The mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) is both the preparatory stage for the modes of deportment and that which gives rise to them;
this is the conclusion of the treatise. If the mind of the sphere of craftsmanship (*śailpasthānika*) consists solely of mental consciousness...
According to the explanation based on the mind of the stage of craftsmanship (*śailpasthānika-citta*),

if the preparatory application (*prayoga*) for the stage of craftsmanship occurs not only in the mental consciousness but also extends to the five sensory consciousnesses, because they take the five objects as their conditions.
Therefore, the *Vibhāṣā* states:

"The five consciousnesses, such as the visual consciousness, are applications (*prayoga*) for the sphere of craftsmanship (*śailpasthānika*), but they do not give rise to the sphere of craftsmanship itself. The mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) is both an application for the sphere of craftsmanship and that which gives rise to the sphere of craftsmanship."
Furthermore, regarding the treatise on the arising of the *śailpasthānika* (artistic) mind and those above it:

if the preparatory stage (*prayoga*) of the *nairmāṇika* (fruition-of-mastery) mind consists solely of a concentrated mind, it is associated with the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) and does not extend to the five sensory consciousnesses.
Therefore, the treatise does not mention it.
Other masters say that there are two types of indeterminate (avyākṛta) consciousness induced [by karma],
because they belong to the categories of deportment (īryāpatha) and craftsmanship (śailpasthānika).
It is capable of fully apprehending the objects of the twelve bases (*āyatana*).
The *Abhidharmamahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* also contains this statement.
Generally speaking, there are three types of minds associated with the modes of deportment (*īryāpatha*).
The first type of deportment-mind is exclusively the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).
The second type of deportment-mind has two objects of perception.

The [first] three are similar to the mind of deportment (*airyāpathika*) and thus pertain to all six consciousnesses; the [fourth], the mind of craftsmanship (*śailpasthānika*), pertains to the four sensory consciousnesses as well as the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).
Just as one casually attends to external objects such as forms and sounds,
if it is said that the mind of the path of deportment is exclusively the mental consciousness,
this is stated with reference to the arising of the mind of the path of deportment.
If the preparatory application (*prayoga*) of the modes of deportment (*airyāpathika*) pertains not only to the mental consciousness but also to the four [sensory] consciousnesses,
this is stated with reference to the mind that takes the modes of deportment as its object.
If it is said that the mind of the modes of deportment takes all twelve bases (*āyatana*) as its objects, [then...]
According to what is taught regarding the mental states associated with the path of deportment (*airyāpathika*),
when explaining the sphere of craftsmanship (*śailpasthānika*) in general, there are briefly three types:
first, the mind that initiates craftsmanship (*śailpasthānika-citta*).
Only the mental consciousness (manovijñāna).
Second, the mind directed toward the sphere of arts and crafts (śailpasthānika) involves both the five sensory consciousnesses and the mental consciousness.
The third type, the mind resembling that of the arts and crafts (*śailpasthānika-citta*),
also extends across the six consciousnesses;
it is like the casual perception of external forms, sounds, and so forth.
If it is said that the mind of the arts and crafts (*śailpasthānika-citta*) is exclusively the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*),
this is stated with reference to the arising of the mind of the arts and crafts itself.

If it is said that the preparatory application (*prayoga*) for the arts and crafts pertains not only to the mental consciousness but also extends to the five sensory consciousnesses (*pañca-vijñāna*), [this refers to the preliminary stages].

This is stated based on the mind that takes the bases of craftsmanship (*śailpasthānika-citta*) as its object. If it is said that the mind of craftsmanship takes all twelve bases (*dvādaśāyatana*) as its objects, this is stated based on a mind that resembles the mind of craftsmanship.

Question: What is meant by the "mind of deportment" (*airyāpathika-citta*)? Explanation: Walking, standing, sitting, and lying down are called "deportments" (*iryāpatha*). The mind associated with these is the mind of deportment.
It has as its nature manifest form (*rūpa*) characterized by length, shortness, and so forth.
Its substance consists of visible form, odor, taste, and tangibility.
It is called a "path" because it is that upon which postures (*iryāpatha*) depend.
"Path of deportment" is a *tatpuruṣa* (dependent determinative) compound.
The mind that belongs to the path of deportment is called "the mind of the path of deportment."
This is an *adhikaraṇa-samāsa* (dependent determinative compound).
If interpreted in this way, visual consciousness is the preparatory stage (*prayoga*) for the course of deportment (*airyāpathika*), taking the course of deportment as its object;
it takes only a small portion of the course of deportment as its object.
The three consciousnesses of nose, tongue, and body are the preparatory stages for the path of deportment;
each takes a small portion of the path of deportment as its object and is thus called a "mind of the path of deportment.
The mental consciousness is both the preparatory stage for the path of deportment and that which takes the path of deportment as its object.

The mind that, conditioned by the path of deportment (*airyāpathika*), can give rise to the path of deportment, is called the "mind of the path of deportment. Alternatively, it is explained that the "path" (*patha*) itself is the "deportment" (*iryāpatha*);
this is a *karmadhāraya* (appositional) compound.
It has visible form, odor, taste, and tangibility as its substance.
Therefore, the *Vibhāṣā* states:
"The path of deportment (*airyāpathika*)..."

The treatise states that its substance consists of the four bases of form, odor, taste, and tangibility; this is because the four modes of deportment are never separate from these four objects, and thus they take these four objects as their substance.
The mental concomitants rely upon the bases, which are termed "paths.
If one interprets it in this way,
each of the four consciousnesses takes a portion of the path of deportment as its object.
This is called the mind of deportment (*airyāpathika-citta*).
The rest is as explained previously.
Question: What is meant by the "mind of the sphere of craftsmanship" (*śailpasthānika-citta*)? Explanation: There are two types of the sphere of craftsmanship.
First, the sphere of bodily craftsmanship;
second, the sphere of vocal craftsmanship.
Regarding the sphere of bodily craftsmanship: activities such as carving and engraving are termed bodily craftsmanship.
The physical bases have matter as their essence;
the locations have color, fragrance, taste, and tangibility as their essence.
Regarding the "locations of vocal and manual arts," vocal arts refer to things such as singing and chanting.
Sound constitutes its essence;
the bases constitute their essence through the five sense objects.
These are called the "bases of craftsmanship" because they are the locations upon which craftsmanship relies.
"Artistic skill" (*śailpasthānika*) is a *tatpuruṣa* compound.
The mind that pertains to artistic skills is called "the mind of artistic skill."
This is an *adhikaraṇa-samāsa* (dependent determinative compound). If one explains it in this way,
visual consciousness is the preparatory application (*prayoga*) for the sphere of bodily craftsmanship.
The mind associated with bodily craftsmanship, which takes as its object a portion of the bases of craftsmanship, is called the "craftsmanship-mind.
The consciousnesses of nose, tongue, and body constitute the preparatory application for the bases of bodily craftsmanship.
The mind that takes as its object a small portion of the field of bodily craftsmanship is called the "craftsmanship-mind.
Ear-consciousness is the preparatory stage (*prayoga*) for the field of vocal craftsmanship;
that which takes as its object vocal craftsmanship or a small portion of the field of vocal craftsmanship is called the "craftsmanship-mind."
The four consciousnesses, beginning with the visual consciousness, are the preparatory stages (*prayoga*) for the craftsmanship of speech;
because each takes a small portion of the craftsmanship of speech as its object, they are called "minds of the craftsmanship of speech.
The mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) is the preparatory stage for craftsmanship [in general].

That which can give rise to the sphere of arts and crafts (śilpasthāna) by taking the sphere of arts and crafts as its object is called "the mind of the sphere of arts and crafts. Alternatively, it is explained that the sphere itself is the art; thus, it is called "the sphere of arts and crafts" through a *karmadhāraya* (appositional compound).
If manual skill (*śilpa*) has the four objects as its essence, it is because when manual skill arises, it does not depart from the four objects; thus, it takes the four objects as its essence.
If verbal skill (*vāc-śilpa*) has the five objects as its essence, [it is because it arises in dependence upon them].
Because when verbal skillfulness arises, it does not depart from the five sense objects,
it takes the five sense objects as its essence.
This is the "base" (āyatana) so named because it is the locus upon which the mind relies for its cognitive object.
Therefore, the *Vibhāṣā* states:
"The sphere of craftsmanship (*śailpasthānika*) has as its essence the five objects—visible form, sound, odor, taste, and tangible objects.
If one interprets it in this way, [it would involve] the four consciousnesses and the five consciousnesses.
Each of these takes a portion of the *śailpasthāna* (arts and crafts) as its object and is thus called a *śailpasthāna-citta*.
The remainder is as explained previously.
Thus, from the twenty [minds] up to the two minds pertaining to one's own form (*sva-rūpa*).
Below this, the second section clarifies the arising of mental states (*cittānuvartana*).
This refers specifically to the mutual arising of the eight minds of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
Next, it explains the transition from the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) to two minds within its own realm.

This explains the mutual arising of the six minds of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*). Next, regarding the statement "the formless [minds] arise from four of their own realm," this clarifies the mutual arising of the four minds of the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).

Question: Can one whose body is in a lower stage give rise to the innate wholesome mind (*upapattilābhika-kuśala-citta*) of a higher realm? Answer: According to the passage from the *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra* cited previously, it is not possible.
It certainly cannot arise. Since antiquity,
all the virtuous masters have maintained that it can arise,
just as in the case of those beyond training (aśaikṣa).
When one abiding in the desire realm regresses and gives rise to afflictions of the formless realm,
from what kind of mind do they arise?
Since such afflictions cannot arise from a non-defiled mind, [they must arise from a defiled one].
Those three types of neutral minds—the deportment, the craft, and the supernormal—do not arise in a different plane;
nor does the mind born of maturation arise in a different plane.
For this reason, it is known that [the mind in question] does not arise from a neutral state of consciousness.
Nor can it be said that a wholesome mind can produce [defilements];
rather, only the *parihāṇika-bhāgīya* concentration can produce defilements,
because at the time one attains the state of *aśaikṣa*, [the parihāṇika-bhāgīya] is no longer possessed.
The remaining three abodes and so forth cannot produce afflictions.
When one falls away from the innate wholesome states of the higher realms, what kind of mind arises? For this reason, it is known [that the innate wholesome mind of the desire realm arises].
One whose body is on a lower stage can give rise to a wholesome mind acquired at birth belonging to a higher stage;
furthermore, one may fall back and give rise to afflictions.
It is also said that one whose body is in the desire realm can give rise to the supernormal power of the divine eye.
When returning from the supernormal power of the divine eye to enter meditative absorption,
if there is no innate wholesome mind (*upapattilābhika-kuśala-citta*), one cannot produce an acquired wholesome mind (*prāyogika-kuśala-citta*).
According to various treatises, with the exception of the mind of transformation (*nirmāṇacitta*),
no other unobscured-neutral (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*) mind is permitted to arise immediately prior to a mind of applied virtue (*prayoga-kuśala*).
This is because it is not permitted for a mind of innate virtue (*upapatti-lābhika-kuśala*) belonging to a higher stage to arise [from such a neutral state].
The essence of the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*) is non-obscured and indeterminate (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*).
How, then, can it give rise to a mind that is virtuous through application (*prayogika-kuśala*)?
One should understand this by analogy.
Regarding the claim that one in a lower realm can give rise to a wholesome mind acquired at birth (*upapatti-lābhika-kuśala-citta*) belonging to a higher realm—this interpretation is incorrect.
One in a lower stage cannot give rise to a wholesome mind acquired at birth belonging to a higher stage.
As in the case of the regression of one beyond training (aśaikṣa), although there is no concentration belonging to the category of regression,
such is the intended meaning of both the *Abhidharmamahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* and the *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra*.
It is admitted that the *sthitibhāga* (the portion of stability) within meditative concentration can also give rise to afflictions;
yet the ancient masters did not realize that the *sthitibhāga* could produce them,
and thus they engaged in various kinds of forced interpretations.
Furthermore, following the supernormal power of the divine eye (divyacakṣur-abhijñā), one can also produce a mind of applied virtue (prayoga-kuśala-citta),
because the supernormal power of the divine eye is itself a mind that is the fruit of such a power (abhijñā-phala-citta).
If it is argued that the transformative mind (nirmāṇa-citta) is narrow in scope...
If one says that the "resultant-of-attainment mind" (abhijñā-phala-citta) is broader [in scope],
and that it is translated merely as "mind of transformation" (nirmāṇa-citta) without being called "resultant-of-attainment," this is an error on the part of the translator.
The ancient masters failed to realize that these two supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) are subsumed under the "resultant consciousnesses" (*phala-citta*),
which is why they fell into this erroneous interpretation.
Next, it explains the untainted [consciousness] up to those belonging to the stages of training (*śaikṣa*) and beyond training (*aśaikṣa*).
This clarifies the arising of two types of untainted minds;

for an untainted mind of one beyond training (aśaikṣa-citta) necessarily arises from a mind of one in training (śaikṣa-citta). Thus, an untainted mind of one beyond training arises from a mind of one in training.
Since it is absolutely impossible for one to fall away from an *aśaikṣa* mind and give rise to a *śaikṣa* mind,
there is no case where an *aśaikṣa* mind gives rise to a *śaikṣa* mind.
Furthermore, for what reason would it ever arise as a wholesome state of application (*prayoga-kuśala*)?

The following explains the objection: Why is it that the preparatory stage (*prayoga*) gives rise to the three types of neutral states (*avyākṛta*), but those neutral states do not give rise to the preparatory stage?
It is because their power is inferior; [only when they reach a state] capable of giving rise to them [does this occur].
Answer: Because the mind born of maturation has inferior power,
and because it is not produced through the exertion of effort.
Because the [minds] of pleasure (*sukha*) function by inducing the transformation of craftsmanship (*śailpasthānika*) and deportment (*airyāpathika*),
these three cannot give rise to the wholesome mind of application (*prayoga-kuśala-citta*).
This is because the emerging mind (*vyutthāna-citta*) functions without the exertion of effort (*anabhisamskāra*).
Therefore, immediately following the preparatory stage (*prayoga*), those three can be produced.
If it is argued that this is because the defiled states are mutually incompatible, that constitutes an objection.
If that were so, wholesome states resulting from application (*prayoga-kuśala*) should not arise immediately after a defiled state,
because the attachment to objects is incompatible with them. Nevertheless,
it is possible for one who has become weary of such attachment to give rise to application.
Answer: Although they are not mutually concordant,
the afflictions manifest repeatedly, leading to weariness and aversion.
In order to fully understand the objects that give rise to faults,
it is possible for preparatory effort (*prayoga*) to arise immediately after the afflictions (*kleśa*);
this refers to the mind acquired at birth (*upapatti-pratilambhika*) in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) which leads to the production of those [afflictions].
Because the distracted states of the Desire Realm are acquired through distraction and are strong, clear, and sharp,
they arise immediately after the two types of untainted [attainments] and the preparatory stage of the Form Realm;
this is because they are not induced by superior effort.
These three minds cannot arise from this [state] and proceed to that [state],
because the formless realm is a state of meditative concentration (samāhita-bhūmi), whereas those acquired through dispersal (vikṣipta-pratilabdha) are inferior.

Because these are dull and inferior, they are neither of the learner (*śaikṣa*) nor the non-learner (*aśaikṣa*); they arise immediately after [the thought of] another realm through preparatory effort (*prayoga*),
for they are not produced by the exertion of deliberate application (*abhisamskāra*).
It cannot induce that mind from this state.
Furthermore, the statement that "the desire-realm innate [mind] arises immediately after [death]" serves to demonstrate that the desire-realm innate mind is clear and sharp.
It is possible for that which can prevent the higher meditative absorption to arise immediately after the defilement of the form realm (*rūparāga*).
Because the innate [attainment] of the form realm (*rūpadhātu-upapatti-labdha*) is not sharp, it lacks this capacity.
There are three types of mental attention (*manasikāra*); regarding the mental attention associated with arrival (*prāpti-samprayukta-manasikāra*):
Below this is the third section, which explains the arising [of states] according to different categories. Within it:
first, an explanation of the three types of mental attention (*manasikāra*) for entering and emerging from the Noble Path;
second, an explanation of the mind that emerges from the nine stages of those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*).
The three knowledges (*vidyā*) and four wisdoms (*prajñā*) enter and emerge from the noble path. Below this, the three modes of mental attention (*manasikāra*) are explained.
Within this section, the first explains these three modes of mental attention.
2. Narrating Alternative Explanations: This clarifies the three types of attention (*manasikāra*).
Because the function of attention is predominant, it is specifically designated as "attention," though this does not mean that feeling (*vedanā*) and the other mental factors are absent.
Within the contemplation of conventional characteristics (*parikalpita-lakṣaṇa*), because resolute conviction (*adhimukti*) is also strong, it is designated as "resolute conviction.
In principle, attention to common characteristics (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa-manasikāra*) actually extends to both the contaminated (*sāsrava*) and the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*).
Since this section clarifies the entry into and emergence from the noble path,
it is made clear that all three types of mental attention (*manasikāra*) are with outflows (*sāsrava*).
Furthermore, the [meditations on] impurity, the immeasurables, the spheres of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*), and the spheres of totality (*kṛtsnāyatana*) are exclusively conceptual constructions.
Within liberation, both the provisional and the real are encompassed;
the statement that "there is liberation with form" designates the first three liberations.
Because it is merely a conceptual construction (*parikalpita*).

Since the formless liberations (*ārūpya-vimokṣa*) apply to both the conceptual and the real, they are said to "possess form" (*sārūpya*). Question: As explained in the *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya* (or *Mahāvibhāṣā*), fascicle 11, regarding the attention of resolute conviction (*adhimukti-manasikāra*).
It speaks only of "liberation.
Why does it not speak of "having form"? The *Vibhāṣā* explains that "liberation" refers to the conceptual liberation within [the state of] liberation.
It may be acceptable to say that not all liberations (vimokṣa) are merely conceptual constructs.

The "liberation with form" mentioned in this treatise is precisely what is referred to as liberation in the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*. Question: Regarding the "attention consisting of resolute conviction" (*adhimukti-manasikāra*) in the *Vibhāṣā*...
Mindfulness of breathing (ānāpānasmṛti) is also taught [elsewhere]. Why is it not mentioned in this treatise?
Furthermore, in the latter part of this treatise, mindfulness of breathing is said to be "correct mental attention" (yoniśomanasikāra).
Therefore, the subsequent treatise states:
"Regarding form, other masters say that the exhalation extends to a very great distance."
This would not be logical, whether it refers to the wind-circle (vāyu-maṇḍala) or the Vairambha winds.
Since this mindfulness is conjoined with true mental attention (*tattvamanasikāra*), the treatises differ;
how, then, should this be reconciled? The explanation states that mindfulness of breathing (*ānāpānasmṛti*) is of two kinds.
First is the provisional characteristic, which refers to the preparatory stage (*prayoga*);
second is the ultimate reality, which refers to the fundamental stage (*maula*).
This treatise is based upon the fundamental stage.
The *Abhidharmamahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* relies on preparatory application (*prayoga*), while each [text] relies on a distinct meaning;
thus, they do not contradict one another. Furthermore, the intended meanings of the treatises are each different.
In this treatise, both the preparatory stage (*prayoga*) and the fundamental stage (*maula*) are considered real;
however, in the *Abhidharmamahāvibhāṣā* and according to other masters in this treatise, the preparatory stage is also admitted to be conventional (*prajñapti*).
The fundamental basis is reality.
Regarding these three types that lead to the cultivation of the factors of enlightenment such as mindfulness,
the following is the second section, which records alternative explanations.
There are three masters in total;
this is the first teaching:
three entrances and three exits.
If one speaks of the three entrances,
it accords with the scriptural statement that one cultivates the factors of enlightenment, such as mindfulness, which are untainted and accompanied by the contemplation of impurity.
In this context, the word "simultaneous" (*saha*) signifies the sense of "immediately following," meaning that they occur in immediate succession. This passage serves, for the time being,
as proof that the mental application of resolute conviction (*adhimukti-manasikāra*) can enter the Noble Path.
If one enters the path of seeing (darśanamārga) by means of the universal characteristic (sāmānyalakṣaṇa) alone,
one exits through all three [types of liberation].
If one is on the path of cultivation (bhāvanāmārga) or the path of no-more-learning (aśaikṣamārga), one enters and exits through all three.
Other masters state that one reaches the cultivation of the factors of enlightenment, such as mindfulness;
this is the second alternative explanation. One enters [the meditative absorption] three times and emerges from it once.
Including the preceding cited sūtra,
the phrase "concomitant" (*sahagata*) refers to being distant and successive, rather than being immediate and simultaneous.
Others further state that it extends up to the attention to common characteristics (*sāmānyalakṣaṇamanasikāra*).
This concludes the third section on differing opinions regarding the simultaneous entry and exit.
If that is so, there are those who maintain that it extends up to the path of preparation (*prayogamārga*).
The Master of the Treatise refutes the third teacher’s position that only the universal aspect (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*) arises;

for since the three [stages] beginning with the "not-yet-reached" (*anāgamya*) are proximate, it is possible for the universal aspect of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) to arise. Question: In *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* 11, how is this teacher further challenged?

Why is it said that one has not yet reached even a single stage (*bhūmi*), rather than three? The commentary explains: A master of the *Abhidharmakośa* should state that [the path] relies solely on the "not-yet-reached" (*anāgamya*) stage;
as for the mention of "three stages," this is merely a concession granted for the sake of argument.
This is precisely the identity of the three.

If one interprets it in this way, it not only accords with the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, but also accords with the fact that the mind emerging from the state of an Arhat arises solely by relying on the *anāgamya* (not-yet-arrived) stage to produce a mind of the desire realm. Question: As stated in the seventy-second [section] of the *Vibhāṣā*...
The first explanation states that the desire realm and the preparatory concentration (anāgamya-dhyāna) arise in immediate succession.
The second explanation states:
The desire realm and the threshold concentration (anāgamya) arise in immediate succession with the first dhyāna;
this is the third explanation.
The desire realm, the threshold concentration, the first dhyāna, and the intermediate dhyāna arise in immediate succession [with one another].

The fourth explanation states that the desire realm arises immediately after the threshold concentration (*anāgamya*), the first dhyāna, the intermediate dhyāna, and the second dhyāna. Although there are these four explanations,
[the former three are rejected].
The *Vibhāṣā* masters of the critical evaluation accept the second teacher’s position.
If it is said that one emerges from the Path of Seeing based solely on the *anāgamya* concentration,
and that immediately after emerging from the mind of an Arhat (*aśaikṣa-citta*) based on the *anāgamya*, one is able to produce a mind of the desire realm:

This directly contradicts the position of the *Vibhāṣā* commentators. The explanation states that because it is difficult for a mind of a different stage to emerge at the initial moment of the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*) and the Path of No-More-Learning (*aśaikṣamārga*), one can only give rise to a mind of the desire realm by relying on the *anāgamya* (not-yet-arrived) concentration.
Because they arise in immediate succession.
If one relies on another stage,
one can also give rise to a mind of the desire realm immediately after relying on the first dhyāna.
Therefore, this does not contradict the *Vibhāṣā* masters either. Furthermore, the interpretation that the three are identical to the "one" is as explained previously;
however, this is the position of the first master among the four explanations in the *Mahāvibhāṣā*.
This is not the *Vibhāṣā-śāstra*’s own commentary (*vibhāṣā-vibhājaka*). Question:
According to the *Vibhāṣā-śāstra*, it is correct that one enters the mind of the desire realm from the minds of the two [upper] stages.
Why, then, does it state this within the context of emerging from the mind of the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*)?

This raises the objection that the "not-yet-arrived" (*anāgamya*) stage is not the first ground. The explanation states: according to the true meaning of the *Vibhāṣā*, the two grounds are indeed correct.
As for the term "not-yet-arrived," it refers to...
Furthermore, let us raise an objection based on other masters:
the *Abhidharmakośa* does not take the *Mahāvibhāṣā* commentators as its authority, so there is no need for reconciliation.
Moreover, in explaining the *Vibhāṣā*, one should state that it relies upon the three stages beginning with the *anāgamya*.
The statement "not yet reached" (*aprāpta*) mentions the first [moment] to indicate the subsequent ones;
this is thus one that subsumes the three.
This is the position of the third master among the four explanations in the *Vibhāṣā*. Question: For what reason does the *Abhidharmakośa* [state this]?
Emerging from the mind of the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*),
one immediately says that the three stages beginning with the "not-yet-arrived" (*anāgamya*) can give rise to the mind of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
Emerging from the mind of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*).

It is simply said that one who has not yet reached [the higher stages] can give rise to a mind of desire. The commentary explains: because the mind emerging from the Path of Seeing is sharp and intense, the mind of the third stage can enter the Desire Realm;
whereas the mind emerging from the state of No-More-Learning (aśaikṣa) does so because it is characterized by cessation.
Therefore, only the *anāgamya* (not-yet-arrived) stage can enter into a mind directed toward the desire realm.
Question: If the *Vibhāṣā* commentators consider it correct that a mind arising from two stages enters into a mind of the desire realm, [how is this to be understood]?

Why is it that, when emerging from the mind of the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*), one raises an objection based on the principle of non-arising in the three stages? The explanation says: according to the correct tenet of the *Vibhāṣā*, the two stages are indeed the correct [position].

Regarding the statement "the three stages," this is raised as an objection based on the views of other masters. Furthermore, the interpretations of the *Ekabhūmi-śāstra* and the *Tri-bhūmi-śāstra* differ in their underlying intent.
The *Ekabhūmi-śāstra* corresponds to the first master of the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*.
Regarding the third stage, it corresponds to the third master in the *Mahāvibhāṣā*.
The questions and answers that resolve these difficulties may be understood as previously explained.
If one relies on the second, third, or fourth [dhyānas], because they are distant,
they cannot give rise to the desire for the common characteristics (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*);
such is the attention to common characteristics (*sāmānyalakṣaṇamanasikāra*).
If it belongs to the stage of meditative concentration (*samāhitabhūmi*), it is subsumed under the "stages leading to penetration" (*nirvedhabhāgīya*);
once the fruit of an ārya has been attained, there is no possibility of giving rise to those wholesome states of the stages leading to penetration.
If it does not belong to the stage of meditative concentration, it is subsumed under the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
Since one cannot give rise to the universal mental application (*sāmānyalakṣaṇamanasikāra*) of the desire realm while relying on the two meditative attainments (*dhyāna*),
it follows logically that one must give rise to the other two types of mental application;
for although one has previously cultivated the superior roots of goodness of the universal mental application in those stages during the past.

That which arises in this life after having been abandoned through rebirth is subsumed under the *nirvedhabhāgīya* (stages conducive to penetration). Question: Why is it that within those stages one cannot achieve the common-attention (*sāmānyamanasikāra*) of the stages prior to *ūṣmagata*? Answer: Because one enters the state of a noble one (*ārya*) in this very life.
This body gives rise only to the "warmth" and subsequent stages upon entering the state of a noble one;

it does not give rise to the preparatory attention to common characteristics (*sāmānyalakṣaṇamanasikāra*) of the preceding stages. Even if such were to arise, because it would be subsumed under the category of applied effort (*prayoga*), it could not [lead to the realization of the path].
If you claim that there is a distinct attainment (*prāpti*) which brings that [object] into manifestation,
this is a restatement of your defense; if you say that it occurs during the intermediate stage of the process of discernment (*viniścaya*).
One attains the cultivation of three types of similar-class and common-characteristic contemplations;
because these are tied to those [contemplations] and do not take the truths as distinct objects,
they are not called "stages leading to penetration" (nirvedhabhāgīya).
Because it is cultivated at that stage, it is subsumed under what has been previously attained;
it is a contemplation of common characteristics (sāmānyalakṣaṇa) that brings [the object] into manifestation.
As for the Vaibhāṣika position, it contradicts correct reasoning.
Refutation and defense:
The meaning is that one performs the sixteen aspects of analytical observation by means of the stages of penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*).
One cultivates only the sixteen aspects of their own corresponding type.

Although those three are universal characteristics (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*), because they are too general and are not cultivated, it is said that this contradicts reason. Furthermore, another explanation is that since these [aspects] belong to that same category and are connected to it, it is also illogical for them to arise [independently].
This statement contradicts correct reasoning.
Thus, the *Viṃśatikā-vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states:
"This defense is irrational."
The attention cultivated through preparatory application (*prayoga*) is bound to it; it does not manifest after the fruit has been attained because it belongs to that same category.
Among these three explanations in this treatise, the view of the first master is correct.
Since this is the position of the *Vibhāṣā* (Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra), Chapter 11, according to the masters of the critical school (*viniścaya-vādin*),
the interpretation of the second master— which maintains that one enters the three [realms] and emerges from them simultaneously based on the path of vision (*darśana-mārga*)—
may also be considered correct.
However, regarding the path of cultivation and the path of no-more-learning,
since it is stated only that they "enter together and emerge three times," this too is not correct.
However, this treatise merely refutes the third master’s position that [the attainment] arises solely from the universal characteristic (sāmānyalakṣaṇa).
If one relies on the view that it arises only from the *anāgamya* stage and not from other stages, it would be solely its own [attainment].
This clarifies the emerging mind from the nine stages of the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*).
If one is in the desire realm and, relying on the threshold concentration (*anāgamya*),
attains the fruit of arhatship, the mind that emerges from meditative observation (*vyutthāna-citta*) thereafter is as follows:
If one has attained mastery over that concentration,
one remains in that very stage;
if one has not attained mastery over that concentration, one arises in the desire realm.
If one is born in the first dhyāna stage and attains the fruit of arhatship, the mind that emerges from meditative absorption subsequently arises only in its own stage.
If one is born in the Peak of Existence (bhavāgra) and relies upon the sphere of nothingness (ākiṃcanyāyatana), [the same applies].
Having attained the fruit of arhatship, when subsequently emerging from the meditative absorption of the mind, it must be the Peak of Existence (bhavāgra).
One can certainly not give rise to a lower, out-flowing (sāsrava) state of mind. Why is this?
A mind born of maturation does not arise from a different level;
for the afflictions of lower levels have already been abandoned and do not manifest,
nor does it give rise to wholesome or contaminated minds of lower levels.
One arises from meditative absorption with a wholesome mind of the Peak of Existence (bhavāgra) stage;
if the body is born in a lower stage,
one relies upon the sphere of nothingness (ākiṃcanyāyatana).
One attains the fruit of arhatship either in that very stage and not in any other stage,
because one has attained mastery over that stage.
If one attains the fruit of Arhatship based on the intermediate state or other stages,
the mind that emerges from meditative absorption arises only as a mind of its own stage, not of any other stage.
Because one attains mastery over those very stages,
the mind emerges from that specific stage and not from the mind of another stage. If,
for instance, one attains the fruit of Arhatship while relying on the second dhyāna or others, [the mind emerges from that same stage].
Later, one emerges from contemplation of the mind.

Why does one not [emerge] either in that same stage or by arising in a lower stage? The explanation says: if the distracted mind of the desire realm is powerful, it is because sentient beings have, since beginningless time, been born many times therein and have repeatedly cultivated it through habituation.
It is easy to arise [from that state] at that time.
For those who rely on the *anāgamya* concentration but have not attained mastery, it is possible for them to give rise to a distracted mind of the desire realm;
however, for those in the two higher realms, there is only the meditative absorption and the distracted mind.
Sentient beings have not been born there many times since beginningless time; thus,
