it is difficult for them to give rise to [a mind] in a different stage after their initial attainment of the state of no-more-learning,
whereas it is easy when they are in that very same stage.
Therefore, having attained the fruit of arhatship (*aśaikṣaphala*) by means of the two meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*) and so forth,

the subsequent mind that emerges from contemplation relies solely on its own level (*svabhūmi*), not on a lower-level absorption or a distracted state of mind (*vikṣiptacitta*). This is because within the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), [the mind] is clear and sharp.

This is the third [point], clarifying that the four types of wisdom enter and exit the noble path; because it belongs to the scattered stage of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), there is no wisdom of cultivation (*bhāvanāmayī-prajñā*).

As for the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), there is no wisdom of reflection (*cintāmayī-prajñā*), which can be understood according to the text. In the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), there is no wisdom of reflection.
As explained in the case of the Form Realm (rūpadhātu),
because they lack the hearing of the ear, they possess no wisdom derived from hearing (śrutamayī-prajñā). In summary:
Among these eight, five are entry [into the path] and six are exit [from it]. Question: As stated in the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* (vol.

11), there are three types of attention (*manasikāra*) in the desire realm: namely, that acquired through hearing (*śruta-maya*), that acquired through reflection (*cintā-maya*), and that acquired through birth (*upapatti-labdha*).
In the realm of form (rūpadhātu), there are three types—namely, those acquired through hearing (śrutamaya), cultivation (bhāvanāmaya), and birth (upapattilabdha).
In the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu), there are two types—namely, those acquired through cultivation and birth.
In the desire realm (kāmadhātu), volition enters into three and emerges from them.
Regarding the two types of entry into the cultivation of the form realm and the emergence from it, as well as the entry into and cultivation of the emergence from the formless realm—

why does that treatise not state that the wisdom derived from hearing (*śrutamayī-prajñā*) in the desire and form realms can enter the noble path? The explanation is that the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* speaks according to those of dull faculties.

This treatise and others generally explain this in terms of those with sharp faculties; furthermore, the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* explains it in terms of those who first cultivate [the path] and [realizations] arise in succession.
Since this treatise and others generally explain it in terms of the stage of full maturity, there is no contradiction between them.
Regarding the question previously raised as to how many minds can be attained:
the following section, the second major heading, clarifies the number of minds attained,
restating the preceding inquiry to introduce it.
The verse says: "As for 'reaching the others, all are obtainable by oneself,'" this refers to the first part of the response,
which correctly explains the attainment of the mind.
Second, the narrative explanation and refutation of errors;
third, the general elucidation of the meaning of the preceding verses.
From here below, the actual attainment of the mind is clearly explained.
The first three phrases clarify simultaneous accomplishment;
the final phrase clarifies individual accomplishment.
The Treatise says: "Because it reaches [the goal], it is called 'attainment' (prāpti). This refers to the sixth [category].
The intended meaning here is that,
among the twelve types of mind,
"acquisition" (prāpti) refers to the attainment of what was previously not possessed.
Although one subsequently newly acquires a mind of its own kind, it is not termed "acquisition," because it has already been acquired previously.
This is stated here according to the general characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*).
Because it is not established as a universal [attainment], it is said that "it may be obtained.

Regarding the attainment of the six [roots] through desire-taint (*rāga*), this occurs generally by way of three stages: first, the restoration of the roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*) following a period of doubt.
Second, falling back from the two realms;
third, falling back due to the arising of afflictions.
A wholesome mind of the desire realm is acquired through two conditions.
First, by reconnecting the roots of goodness through doubt;
second, by falling back from a higher realm.
The two types of defiled minds of the desire realm are acquired through these two conditions.
First, by falling away due to the arising of afflictions;
second, by falling back from the higher realms.
The obscured mind of the form realm is also acquired through two conditions.
First, by falling away due to the arising of desire-afflictions;
second, by returning from the formless realm.
[These include] the obscured-neutral mind of the formless realm and the mind of one in training (śaikṣa).

It is said that one attains six [minds] solely by virtue of falling away due to the arising of afflictions. Question: When falling back from a higher realm, one attains the wholesome mind of the desire realm.

Does one attain only the innate (upapatti-lābhika) wholesome mind, or does one also attain the acquired through application (prāyogika)? Explanation: One interpretation holds that one attains only the innate wholesome mind. Another interpretation holds that one who has practiced the acquired through application also attains it.
The *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* contains these two views,

yet there is no evaluative commentary [on them]. Regarding the statement, "Because the defiled mind of the form realm reaches [the fruit], it is said that six are acquired," this clarifies that the defiled mind of the form realm acquires six [dharmas].
It is attained through two states:
first, falling back from a realm;
second, falling back due to the arising of afflictions.
The desire-realm mind that is unobscured-neutral and associated with fruition, as well as the wholesome and unobscured-neutral minds of the form realm,
are acquired through the regression from the formless realm;
those defiled by the form realm are acquired through two conditions.
First, by falling away from a realm;
second, by arising from afflictions.
[This applies to] the obscured-unspecified mind of the formless realm and the mind of one in training (śaikṣa).
However, because they are acquired through falling away from the afflictions (*kleśa*), they are said to "attain six.
As for the statement that one "attains two" when reaching a defiled mind of the formless realm (*ārūpya-dhātu*): [it refers to the attainment of the minds of the two lower realms].
One obtains two types of mind when an afflicted mind of the formless realm arises:
namely, the afflicted mind of the formless realm itself and the mind of one in training (śaikṣa).
This occurs solely through a single state, namely, falling away due to the arising of afflictions. Question: Does this falling away involve the arising of afflictions belonging to all three realms?
From what kind of mind does that affliction arise immediately? The explanation says: as stated in the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 61:
"What kind of mind arises immediately before an affliction manifests?"
If one who has completely become detached from the defilements of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception should fall away because the fetters of that stage manifest before them,
then immediately after that wholesome mind of that stage, afflictions will manifest.
If one has not yet completely abandoned the perception of compassion and the state of being neither in nor out of meditative equipoise,
and thus falls away because the fetters (paryavasthāna) of that stage manifest before them,
then immediately after that stage— whether it be a wholesome mind or a defiled mind— a defilement manifests.
It should be understood that the same applies up to the first dhyāna.
If one falls away from detachment due to the arising of a defilement (paryavasthāna) of the desire realm,
it occurs immediately after either a wholesome mind or an unobscured-neutral mind of the desire realm.
When afflictions arise and manifest before one—
if one falls away because of the arising of a fetter of the desire realm due to not having completely abandoned the defilements of the desire realm—
then immediately following that [falling away], there is either a wholesome mind of the desire realm, a defiled mind, or an unobscured-neutral mind.
Afflictions arise and become manifest. In this context,
if one has not yet attained the fundamental wholesome meditative absorptions (dhyāna) or formless attainments (ārūpya-samāpatti),
and these are not currently manifest, one cannot fall away because the obsessions (paryavasthāna) of the form and formless realms have not become manifest.
However, one falls away only when the fetters of the desire realm arise and become manifest;
this does not occur when a fundamental wholesome dhyāna—
rather than an absorption of the formless realm— is manifest.
He cannot fall away because the fetters of the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) manifest before him;
rather, he falls away only because the fetters of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) manifest before him.
This applies if he has attained the fundamental wholesome dhyānas.
Regarding the manifestation of the formless attainments (*ārūpya-samāpatti*):
because they can cause the fetters (*paryavasthāna*) of the three realms to manifest, one falls away from them.
The *Mahāvibhāṣā* states that this occurs at the time of falling away from the desire realm.
Regarding the fact that a defiled mind can arise immediately after an indeterminate mind:
one tradition asserts three types of indeterminate minds,
while another tradition asserts two types of indeterminate minds.
Excluding the result-of-maturation (vipāka).
However, there is no commentary on this.
Regarding the phrase "the wholesome mind of the form realm up to that which arises from spiritual progress":
This clarifies that wholesome form can obtain three minds;
it is obtained through two stages:
first, by entering meditative absorption.
Second, by way of detachment from defilement:
this refers to when ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), having first suppressed the desire realm and entered the *anāgamya* concentration, attain a wholesome mind of the form realm;
subsequently, through the further abandonment of the defilements of desire, they attain the fundamental dhyāna via the ninth path of liberation.
One attains the two types of fruition-minds of the desire and form realms.
Thus, in these two stages— entering the form realm from the desire realm,
and entering the fundamental state from the preparatory stage— it is all termed "ascending progress."
The reason it is not called "attaining the mind of one in training" (śaikṣacitta) is as follows:
when the Supreme Mundane Dharma (laukikāgradharma) is present, it has not yet become the mind of one in training;
furthermore, when the Receptivity to the Dharma of Suffering (duḥkhadharmajñānakṣānti) reaches the present, it is likewise not a wholesome mind of the form realm (rūpadhātu) manifesting at that time.
Therefore, the wholesome mind of the form realm does not attain the mind of one in training (*śaikṣa*).

By this, it is known that in this context, the term "attainment" (*prāpti*) signifies possession (*samanvāgama*). If the mind of one in training reaches the state of being free from the defilements of the form realm...
This clarifies that the attainment of the mind of training is fourfold;
it is attained through two stages:
first, by entering meditative absorption (samāpatti).
Second, by means of detachment from defilements:

through the initial realization of entry into the state of rightness (samyaktva-niyāma), when the patience regarding suffering (duḥkha-kṣānti) manifests, one attains the mind of a learner (śaikṣa-citta);
this occurs by means of entering meditative absorption.

Furthermore, by means of the Noble Path, one attains the fundamental dhyāna through the ninth path of liberation from the defilements of the desire realm, and thereby acquires the two types of fruition-minds of the supernormal powers belonging to the desire and form realms.

If, by means of the Noble Path, one becomes free from the defilements of the form realm and attains a wholesome mind of the formless realm—[the question is: at what time is that wholesome mind of the formless realm acquired? The explanation is: it is at the time of the ninth path of liberation when one becomes free from the defilements of the fourth dhyāna by means of the Noble Path.
One attains the wholesome mind of the formless realm;
although the preparatory stage (*sāmantaka*) of the sphere of infinite space possesses the same antidote for contaminated phenomena (*sāsrava-dharma*),
its attachment to the level is firm and it has not yet abandoned the defilements of the lower stage.
One cannot cultivate the higher [stages].

If one interprets it thus, being completely free from the defilements of the form realm (*rūpa-rāga*) is called "freedom from the defilements of the form realm. Furthermore, another interpretation holds that when one abandons the defilements of the fourth dhyāna by means of the Noble Path (*ārya-mārga*), at the moment of the first path of uninterrupted transition (*anantarya-mārga*).
One immediately attains the wholesome mind of the preparatory stage (*sāmantaka*) of the sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*).
Since a wholesome preparatory mind necessarily involves cultivation through the same antidote (*pratipakṣa*),
if one interprets it in this way, the separation from the defilements of form is called "separation from the defilements of form" (*rūparāga-virāga*).
The *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya* also offers two interpretations,
which will be cited in full when explaining the cultivation [of the path] below.
As for why one cannot obtain wholesome states of mind belonging to the form realm:
Because one must first accomplish the state of a learner (śaikṣa) before attaining it;
nor can there be a non-learner (aśaikṣa),
because when the state of a learner is manifest, one necessarily has not yet accomplished the state of a non-learner.
"Others" refers to what was previously stated up to "only obtainable by oneself"; that is,
the minds other than those previously mentioned as defiled and so forth—
namely, the three types of non-obscured-neutral minds of the three realms.
Regarding the wholesome minds of the desire and formless realms, as well as the mind of one beyond training (aśaikṣa),
we do not describe the distinctions of the minds acquired when those six minds are manifest; for in those cases,
they are acquired solely by themselves.
Not Attaining Others: Question— If it is said that when a defiled mind of the desire realm arises,
one only attains six [minds] and does not attain the non-obscured minds of its own realm,
this would contradict the *Vijñānakāya-śāstra* and other such texts.
As stated in the *Vijñānakāya-śāstra* (Treatise on the Aggregates of Consciousness), Chapter 13:
"If one accomplishes an unwholesome mind, does one also accomplish a non-obscured, neutral mind bound to the desire realm?
If one accomplishes an unwholesome mind, one necessarily accomplishes a non-obscured, neutral mind bound to the desire realm."
Or, one may possess a mind that is unobscured and neutral (anivṛtāvyākṛta) bound to the desire realm,
but not an unwholesome mind;
this refers to one born and raised in the desire realm who has already become detached from the greed of the desire realm.
Alternatively, for a person born and raised in the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*), according to that treatise regarding the stage of retrogression from that realm,
at the moment they give rise to desire-tainted attachment (*kāmarāga*), they necessarily possess an unwholesome mind (*akuśalacitta*).
Once the unwholesome has been established,
one necessarily accomplishes the desire-realm non-obscured-neutral state.
However, among the four types of neutral states within the desire realm:
However, because the two types— dignified deportment (*airyāpathika*) and craftsmanship (*śailpasthānika*)—
possess strong force, they can be acquired across the three periods of time;
therefore, when they become unwholesome (*akuśala*), they necessarily become fixed as such.
Therefore, the other two types of indeterminate [minds] are not established.
Since it has already been established that they are unwholesome, there is no principle by which they could produce a ripening fruit;
furthermore, the mind born of ripening lacks both preceding and succeeding [moments], and even if it were to arise subsequently, it would certainly not be established [as such].
According to the *Vijñānakāya-śāstra*,
the minds of deportment (*airyāpathika*) and craftsmanship (*śailpasthānika*) in the desire realm have acquisitions (*prāpti*) belonging to the three time periods.
This means that at the stage of returning to a lower realm, within a mind defiled by desire, these necessarily constitute the unobscured-unspecified (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*) states of the desire realm.
Regarding a mind defiled by desire, one should say that seven [minds] are acquired;
why then is it said that six are?
Furthermore, regarding a wholesome mind of the form realm, one should say that two are acquired.
One should say that the mind of training (śaikṣa-citta) attains three [types of minds],
each excluding the non-obscured neutral (anivṛtāvyākṛta) of the desire realm.
When first attaining those two types of minds, the body is necessarily situated in the desire realm.
Because the unobscured-neutral [states] of the desire realm are already established beforehand,
one should not say that those two minds are acquired [within them].
The *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya* (Jñānaprasthāna-śāstra), chapter eleven, agrees with the *Vijñānakāya*.
Therefore, the *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya* (Xianzong lun) revises the verse,
stating: "The defilements of the three realms are acquired, in order, in seven, six, and two types."

The wholesome [states] of the form realm consist of two types of training; three are acquired without remainder. Regarding the phrase "two are without": [Note: The provided text fragment appears to be a technical commentary on Abhidharma categories, specifically concerning the wholesome factors (*kuśala*) of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), the two types of training (*śikṣā*), and the acquisition of states without remainder (*anupadhiśeṣa*).]
The *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya* states:
"The two refer to the unobscured-neutral [states] of the desire and form realms;
within these two types of mind, nothing at all is apprehended."
This also shares the same general intent as the *Abhidharmakośa*,
though it specifically designates two types of neutral states (*avyākṛta*) as distinct.
Although the *Nyāyānusāra* does not alter the verse, it provides a detailed commentary.
The meaning of the prose section is the same as that of the *Vijñānakāya*. Since this treatise contradicts the texts of the *Vijñānakāya* and other works, how should it be reconciled?

The explanation states: in the desire realm, the two types of neutral minds—those of deportment (*airyāpathika*) and those of craftsmanship (*śailpasthānika*)—for the most part do not possess acquisitions (*prāpti*) across the three time periods.
However, for those born in the desire realm, one who gives rise to [a state] with mastery is said to "possess" it;
one who does not give rise to it is said to be "not possessing" it.

It is not necessary to have obtained [the state] in order to be said to possess it. An objection is raised: "If that were so, then when the resultant-neutral mind of the formless realm is not present..."
It should be called "attainment" (*siddhi*),
because it is the arising of mastery. Furthermore, if this [mastery] is already designated as "attainment" due to its sovereignty,
for what other reason would one know that there exists a separate entity?
Therefore, it is said that there is an error. Furthermore, another interpretation states that the two types of neutral minds possess acquisitions (*prāpti*) across the three time periods;
however, when one descends from a higher realm to a lower one, these must necessarily manifest before their acquisition can arise.
Since that which first arises therein is a defiled mind,
at that time it is not yet designated as "unspecified" (avyākṛta);
it later arises due to present causes.
Once it has been attained throughout the three periods of time, its subsequent continuity is always termed "accomplishment";
the initial mind, however, has not yet attained it.
This does not contradict this treatise.
Furthermore, it is definitively established that the first minor [category] was not mentioned;
from this perspective, it also does not contradict the *Vijñānakāya-śāstra*. An objection is raised: "If that is so, then regarding wholesome form and the mind of one in training (*śaikṣa*,"
One should not say that the "unobscured" (*anivṛta*) of the desire realm is attained, for since it was already established previously, there would likewise be a fault.

Now, I shall briefly provide three interpretations to explain that passage comprehensively. The first interpretation states: The intent of the treatise is distinct in each case; there is no need for laborious reconciliation.
How could one use the *Abhidharmakośa* to refute its own source text?
The Master of the Treatise does not take his own treatise as the sole authority.
This is the intention of the *Vijñānakāya-śāstra*.

Because the power of deportment (*iryāpatha*) and craftsmanship (*śailpasthānika*), though they are neutral (*avyākṛta*), is so strong, they are necessarily established as belonging to the three time periods.
According to the intent of this treatise and others,
deportment is like that of the Buddha, the Bhikṣu Aśvajit, and others who have well practiced it.
If one is as skillful as Viśvakarman or other well-trained practitioners, then success will be achieved through meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
However, if one lacks such superior familiarity with the practice, then success will not be achieved. A second interpretation states that these two treatises are likewise not contradictory.
Among many sentient beings, there are those who have cultivated mastery in deportment and crafts,
and those who have not. This is because treatises such as the *Vijñānakāya-śāstra* speak from the perspective of those for whom such cultivation is predominant.
It is said that they definitely possess the non-obscured [neutral] states of the desire realm;
this treatise speaks according to those who have not practiced them habitually,
or it says they do not possess the non-obscured states of the desire realm because it is speaking from the perspective of the majority.
Each occupies its own side and is without contradiction or harm.
If explained in full detail, some may be established and others not;
however, for one who has practiced it repeatedly, it is immediately established.
If one holds the view that [the result] is not accomplished for those who have not practiced habitually,
then by correlating the textual passages of the *Vijñānakāya* with the *Abhidharmakośa*, the third interpretation states that the two treatises are likewise not in contradiction.
Each and every sentient being possesses numerous modes of deportment and crafts;
among these many, those with which one has practiced habitually are accomplished,
while those with which one has not practiced habitually are not accomplished.
The text of the *Vijñānakāya-pāda* states that it is definitely established as an unobscured-neutral state of the desire realm based on those who are habituated; this treatise, however,
states that it is not established as an unobscured-neutral state of the desire realm based on those who are not habituated.
Speaking exhaustively according to principle:
if one relies on those who have familiarized themselves with this treatise, it is also definitively established;
if one relies on those who have not so familiarized themselves, [it is not].
The text of the *Vijñānakāya-pāda* also contains inconsistencies.
If one adopts this interpretation, one may reconcile the *Abhidharmakośa* with the *Vijñānakāya*.
If one adopts this interpretation, there is no need to laboriously alter the verses of the *Prakaraṇapāda*.
Although I have offered this interpretation, I fear the Sage’s intention may be difficult to discern.
I nevertheless hope that those of high wisdom will examine these humble views in detail.
Should there be alternative explanations, I would be grateful for them to be set forth. As for the remaining [categories], they are exclusively indeterminate (*avyākṛta*).
The following is the second section, which sets forth and refutes erroneous views.
This refers to the Master of the Treatise (the author),
who recounts the position of the *Saṃyuktābhidharmahṛdaya* master, who asserts that a defiled mind can possess nine mental factors.
This does not contradict the present treatise.
This treatise is based on the defiled minds of the three realms and further accounts for their repetition;
that is to say, the defiled mind of the desire realm can attain six [types].
The defiled mind of the form realm attains six;
the defiled mind of the formless realm attains two.
As previously stated, these combined total fourteen.
The *Saṃyuktābhidharmahṛdaya* excludes the repeated [categories] and relies on the single [instances], stating only that nine are attained.
Regarding the statement "nine minds," this refers to the four minds of the desire realm.
The three minds of the form realm,
the defiled mind of the formless realm,
and the mind of one in training (śaikṣa).
These are called the nine.
Within these fourteen [categories] discussed in this treatise, five instances of repeated mental states are excluded.
As for what is meant by "five instances of repeated mental states":
This means that the defiled mind of the form realm is acquired twice:
it is acquired at the time of the defiled mind of the desire realm,
and it is acquired at the time of the defiled mind of the form realm.
Excluding one type of mind—
the defiled mind of the formless realm and the mind of one in training (śaikṣa)— each is acquired three times; that is,
each is acquired at the moment of attaining the defiled minds of their respective three realms.
Each excludes two minds;
added to the previous, they become five.
Therefore, this treatise speaks of fourteen.
The *Saṃyuktābhidharmahṛdaya* speaks of nine [types],

each based on a single meaning, which likewise presents no contradiction. Regarding the statement that "the wholesome mind attains six," this treatise’s preceding text also takes into account the case of repeated recitation.
In total there are seven:
namely, three wholesome [states] of form,
and four of the learner (śaikṣa).
The names are as previously explained.
In the *Saṃyuktābhidharmahṛdaya*, with the repetitions removed and based on the single instances, there are six kinds.
As for these "six kinds":
That is to say: the non-obscured [neutral] of the desire realm;
the wholesome and the non-obscured neutral of the form realm;
and the wholesome of the formless realm.
Together with those of the learner (*śaikṣa*) and the non-learner (*aśaikṣa*), they are thus called the attainment of six.
Within these seven [categories] discussed in this treatise, two types of mental states are excluded as being redundant.
Regarding the statement that two minds are "heavy," this refers to the fact that the non-obscured minds of the desire and form realms are each acquired twice; namely,
the wholesome mind of the form realm.
When the mind of training becomes detached from the defilements of desire,
it respectively acquires two types of non-obscured minds— those of the desire realm and the form realm—
and, excluding one type of non-obscured mind from each, it takes up the remaining five types of minds.
Including the mind of one beyond training (aśaikṣa), they are thus called the six types. Regarding "the indeterminate is only indeterminate":
this refers to when the three kinds of non-obscured indeterminate minds (anivṛtāvyākṛta) of the three realms are present.
It merely establishes its own nature and cannot encompass others because its power is inferior;

therefore, it is said that the indeterminate is only indeterminate. Question: Why are the numbers not separately enumerated for the indeterminate? Explanation: Within the indeterminate, one should also say that three [categories] are obtained.
This refers to the unobscured [neutral] states of the three realms;

it should be understood that the term "intermediate" (*madhya*) has already indicated the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*). Furthermore, because within the wholesome and defiled there are cases where other factors are also acquired, their numbers are cited separately.
Within the indeterminate [states], there are only those that are self-referential and not others;
no separate enumeration is provided.
Thus concludes the Master’s exposition.
Regarding the statement that "one should know the characteristics [of the mind] up to the point of being within a wholesome state," this is the author of the treatise refuting an incorrect view;
he asserts that defiled minds are categorized as nine types based on their individual, singular nature.
There is no contradiction in the case of the indeterminate [mind], as it only acquires its own [category].
Regarding the wholesome mind, acquiring only six is too few;
one should state that seven are acquired within the wholesome mind.
This means that when one reconnects the roots of goodness through right view,
the stage at which a wholesome mind of the desire realm arises is called "attainment" (prāpti);
this constitutes the first [case].
In the final stage of the ninth path of liberation from the defilements of the desire realm,
one simultaneously attains two types of non-obscured minds belonging to the desire and form realms;
together with the previous one, these constitute three.
When one attains the two meditative absorptions (dhyāna), those two wholesome minds are said to be "attained.
Together with the previous [three], these constitute five.
At the moment of first entering the stage of being "born apart from birth" (*vairāgya*), one attains the mind of a learner (*śaikṣa*).
When one attains arhatship, one acquires the mind of one beyond training (*aśaikṣacitta*).
Together with the preceding [six], these constitute seven.
The masters of the *Abhidharmahṛdaya-śāstra* do not state that the aforementioned right view reconnects the roots of goodness.
To say that only six are attained is both too few and excessive.
The remaining defiled and neutral [states] are explained by analogy with what preceded.
One should know that the meaning of its characteristics is likewise not contradictory.
The *Nyāya* [school] offers this defense:
"In principle, one should also attain wholesome minds of the desire realm."
This means that by means of right view, one continues all roots of goodness;

although one adds the desire for goodness to eliminate the unconcealed mind, the Master of the Sūtra (Sautrāntika) should not raise the objection that this results in obtaining seven [factors]. The commentary explains: that treatise is identical to the *Vijñānakāya*.
One who is free from the defilement of desire cannot attain the non-obscured [neutral] states of the desire realm.
The *Abhidharmakośa* refutes this,
as explained extensively above.
Even if one were to assume that there is no unobscured-neutral mind in the desire realm,
the author of the *Abhidharmasamuccaya* would still incur the fault of not stating that a wholesome [mind] exists in the desire realm;
if you can resolve this, then proceed.
"Why does he not rescue them and speak of a virtuous mind?
This is because the preceding meaning has not yet been established.
This constitutes the third verse, which reiterates the previous meaning.
To summarize the preceding meaning and clarify the distinctions among the attainments of mind,
another verse is spoken:
"First, by way of the time of taking rebirth."
That is to say, by falling back from a realm;
and second, by entering meditative absorption—
that is, by means of a wholesome, trained mind of the form realm.
Third, by way of the time of detachment from passion,
namely, detachment from the passions of the desire realm and the form realm;
fourth, by way of the time of falling away.
That is to say, at the time of falling away due to the arising of afflictions;
and fifth, by way of the stage of reconnecting with the roots of goodness, namely, when one reconnects with the roots of goodness through doubt.
Among these five, the first and the last two are exclusively defiled minds;
the middle two types, occurring during meditative absorption and the state of freedom from passion, are exclusively wholesome minds.
Thus, the distinctions among the minds attained in these five stages are as fully explained above.
Regarding the statement here that "attainment" (*prāpti*) is not something previously established, it is because it is now being established as such.

3. *Lokanirdeśa-vibhāga*, Chapter Three, Part One.
Regarding the "Chapter on the Analysis of the World" (*Lokadhātu-vibhaṅga*): "World" (*loka*) refers to the world (*lokadhātu*),
because it is subject to destruction.
Because there are antidotes (*pratipakṣa*),
this chapter explains them extensively and is therefore called "Discrimination" (*vibhaṅga*).
The reason the "Chapter on the World" (*loka-varga*) is explained next is as follows:
The preceding two chapters generally clarify the contaminated (*sāsrava*) and the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*).
From here on, the following six chapters specifically clarify the contaminated and the uncontaminated;
these [preceding chapters] constitute their foundation.
Therefore, the general explanation is presented first to clarify the basis for the specific explanation, which is presented later.
Within the specific explanation, six categories are elucidated.
The first three chapters specifically clarify contaminated (*sāsrava*) phenomena,
while the latter three chapters specifically clarify uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) phenomena.
Contaminated phenomena are explained first because they are coarse and manifest.
The untainted (*anāsrava*) and subtle [dharmas] are explained last for that reason.
Within the separate exposition of the tainted (*sāsrava*),
the World Chapter (*Lokadhātu-varga*) elucidates the fruits of the tainted.
The Chapter on Karma elucidates the causes of outflows (āsrava), while the Chapter on Latent Tendencies (anuśaya) elucidates the conditions for outflows.
Within these three chapters, the characteristics of the fruit are coarse and manifest; therefore, they are explained first.
Regarding the question of how many distinct destinations within the three realms have already been established:
in the Chapter on the World (*Lokadhātu*),
the first [section] clarifies the world of sentient beings (*sattvaloka*).
Second, the explanation of the receptacle world (*bhājanaloka*). Within the explanation of the sentient world (*sattvaloka*), there are two parts:
first, a general classification of sentient beings;
second, a determination of their group distinctions. Regarding the general classification of sentient beings: [the following follows].
First, it clarifies the birth of sentient beings;
second, it clarifies the abiding of sentient beings;
third, it clarifies the passing away of sentient beings.
Regarding the birth of sentient beings, this section clarifies two points:
first, the three realms;
second, the five destinies.
The third [treatise] elucidates the three knowledges and the seven stations of consciousness; the fourth elucidates the nine abodes of sentient beings;
and the fifth elucidates the four stations of consciousness.
Sixth, the clarification of the four modes of birth;
seventh, the clarification of the intermediate state (*antarābhava*); eighth, the clarification of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*).
9. Clarifying the Four Existences (*catur-bhava*). Below this, first, the three realms (*tridhātu*) are clarified.
This serves as a transitional inquiry linking back to what preceded;
at the end of the previous chapter, the various states of mind were already analyzed in accordance with the three realms.
Now it should be explained what the three realms are, and how many distinct locations there are within each respective realm.
The verse says: "That which causes the mind and its concomitants to continue in succession..."
This constitutes the formal analysis:
the first verse clarifies the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*),
and the second verse clarifies the form realm (*rūpadhātu*).
The third verse clarifies the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).
It answers the two preceding questions according to their respective order.
The treatise says: "Up to the Heaven of Making Use of Others' Emanations" (*paranirmita-vaśavartin*).
Within this prose section, there are two parts: first, an explanation of the verse;
second, a detailed analysis through questions and answers.

Hereafter follows the actual explanation of the verse. The six heavens that possess desire are called the Six Desire Heavens (*ṣaḍ-kāmāvacara-deva*). As stated in the *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya* (XVI): "Only the Six Desire Heavens experience the objects of exquisite desire."
Regarding the six heavens of the desire realm (*ṣaḍ-kāmadhātu-deva*):
first is the Heaven of the Four Great Kings (*cāturmahārājika*).
This refers to the presence there of the four great kings and the hosts they govern.
Alternatively, those celestial hosts serve the Four Great Kings,
for they are governed by the Four Great Kings;
[there are] twenty-three such heavens of the Trāyastriṃśa.
That celestial realm is the abode of the thirty-three classes of devas.
On each of the four sides of the summit of Mount Sumeru, there are eight groups of celestial hosts,
and in the center is one, namely Śakra, the Lord of Devas.
Thus, there are thirty-three [devas].
Next is the Yāma Heaven;
this is translated as "Time-Portion" (Shifen).
That is to say, in that celestial realm, for the most part at all times, they exclaim, "How joyful!
Fourth is the Tuṣita Heaven;
this is translated as "Contented with Joy."
This refers to those celestial realms where beings mostly give rise to a mind of contentment with what they themselves have received.
These are the gods who delight in the transformation of desires (*nirmāṇarati-deva*), meaning that in those celestial realms, beings take pleasure in frequently transforming objects of desire.
Therein they experience pleasure.
Sixth are the Paranirmita-vaśavartin devas;
that is to say, those devas experience pleasure with mastery over the objects of desire manifested by others.
Regarding the question, "How many distinct locations are there within the desire realm (kāmadhātu)?
it is asked:
from the various hells and continents up to all that is subsumed under the desire realm.
Answer: The *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra*, fascicle 31, explains the first seven hells as follows:
"Various sufferings oppress the body, causing frequent fainting spells as if dead."
Upon searching, they return to life as before;
therefore, it is called Saṃjīva (Reviving).
This refers to those sentient beings.
Although they were subjected to various forms of cutting, stabbing, grinding,
and pounding, as soon as they encountered a cool breeze, they immediately revived and returned to their original state.
It is named Saṃjīva (Reviving) because beings there are restored to life as before.
It is named Kālasūtra (Black Line) because one first measures the limbs with black cords and subsequently cuts and saws them.
Numerous instruments of suffering come together to oppress the body;
because those who have formed factions slaughter one another, it is named Saṃghāta (The Crushing).
Oppressed by manifold sufferings, beings of various kinds wail in lamentation.
It is called "Screaming" (Raurava) because the inhabitants emit cries of resentment;
it is called "Great Screaming" (Mahāraurava) because, oppressed by intense suffering,
they utter great and agonizing sounds of lamentation and wail against their grievances.
Fire revolves around the body, blazing intensely on all sides;
because the heat and suffering are unbearable, it is called the "Blazing Heat" (Tapana).
This occurs both internally and externally.
Both one's own body and the bodies of others all emit fierce flames that burn and harm one another;
because the heat therein is extreme, it is called "Extreme Heat" (Pratāpana). Furthermore, this treatise explains the eighth hell in its later section as follows:
It is called "uninterrupted" (ānantarya) because suffering is experienced without interruption;
it is called "uninterrupted" because there is no interval of pleasure between the sufferings. Regarding the "four continents," they are Jambudvīpa in the south.
Some derive their names from forest groves;
others are designated by fruits. As for Pūrvavideha, it is so called because the bodies of its inhabitants are superior;
or, because the bodies there are superior to those of Jambudvīpa, it is named "Superior Body."
In Sanskrit, it is called Videha; the western continent of Aparagoyānī is named Goyānī because goods are traded there using cattle.
In Sanskrit, it is called Godānī; the northern continent of Uttarakuru is translated into Chinese as "Superior Place" (Shengchu).
Because it occupies the most preeminent position among the four continents, it is called "Preeminent Birth" (*jyestha-janman*);
alternatively, because birth therein is the most preeminent among the four continents, it is so named. The rest of the text may be understood accordingly.
"From this desire realm up to the eight [levels] ending with Akaniṣṭha" explains the seventeen heavens of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*).
The *Nyāyānusāra* (Treatise on Proper Reasoning), fascicle 21, explains the names of these various heavens as follows:
Because it is produced from extensive goodness, it is called *brahman*.
Since this *brahman* is great, it is called the "Great Brahma" (*mahābrahmā*).
This is because he has attained the intermediate dhyāna (*dhyānāntara*).
Because they arise first and because they perish last,
their majestic power and other qualities are preeminent.
Therefore, they are called the Mahābrahmās; because they are emanated and governed by the Mahābrahmā, they are called the Brahmakāyikas.
Because they stand in ranks before the Mahābrahmā and serve as his attendants, they are called the Brahmapurohitas.
Within the devas of its own level, the light is minimal; therefore, it is called "Limited Light" (Parīttābha).
Because the light becomes increasingly superior and its measure is difficult to fathom, it is called "Immeasurable Light" (Apramāṇābha).
Because pure light universally illuminates the entire region of its own level, it is called "Utmost Purity of Light" (Ābhāsvara).
The experience of pleasure on the mental level (*manobhūmi*) is termed "pure" (*śubha*).
Within its own level, this purity is the most inferior and is therefore called "limited purity" (*parītta-śubha*).
When this purity increases and becomes immeasurable, it is called "immeasurable purity" (*apramāṇa-śubha*).
This [heaven] is called "Universal Purity" (Śubhakṛtsna) because its purity is all-pervasive;
this indicates that there is no other pleasure that can surpass it.
It is the ground where the devas of the lower space-dwelling realm reside.
Because they are like clouds densely gathered, they are called "Clouds" (Abhraka).
Above these heavens, there are no further grounds of cloud;
because they are at the head of those without clouds, they are called "Cloudless" (Anabhraka).
Furthermore, there is a superior merit for ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*);
because it is a specific location where one can be reborn, it is called "Merit-Born" (*puṇyaprasava*).
It resides in a particular location.
Because this is the most excellent among the fruits of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), it is called "Vast Fruit" (*Bṛhatphala*).
Because the noble ones (*ārya*) who have abandoned desire wash away the stains of afflictions with the water of the Noble Path, it is called "Pure" (*Śuddha*).
They are called "Pure Abodes" (Śuddhāvāsa) because they are the dwelling place of those with purified bodies;
alternatively, they are called "pure" because those who dwell here reach the ultimate limit of saṃsāra,
just as one is called "pure" when a debt has been fully repaid.
They are called "Pure Abodes" (Śuddhāvāsa) because they are the dwelling place of those who are pure;
alternatively, they are called Pure Abodes because within these heavens there is no admixture of ordinary beings (pṛthagjana), and they are inhabited solely by noble ones (ārya).
"Prolixity" (prapañca) means either "confusion" or "extensiveness.
Among those that lack confusion, this is the first.
Because this [heaven] is the most inferior among the Śubhakṛtsna deities, it is called "Unadorned" (Aśubha). Alternatively,
it is called "Without Seeking" (Apraṇihita),
because its inhabitants do not seek entry into the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu).
Having already well-subdued and eliminated the superior and middling obstacles to the mixed cultivation of dhyāna,
it is called "Without Heat" (*atapa*) because the mental disposition is pliant and free from all feverish afflictions.
Alternatively, that which causes the arising of lower-tier afflictions is termed "heat."
This initial detachment receives the name "free from heat" (*atapa*).
Alternatively, "heat" (*tāpa*) signifies "intense burning," referring to the cultivation of the highest degree of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) and its fruit.
This stage is still not yet realized and is therefore called "Without Heat" (Atapa).

Having attained the superior degree of meditative cultivation through alternating practice (*vyavakīrṇa-dhyāna*), the qualities of its fruition are easily manifested; hence it is named "Well-Appearing" (Sudṛśa).

Because the remaining grades of the obstacles to meditative concentration have been mixed and thinned until they are extremely subtle, and because vision is utterly clear and penetrating, it is called "Excellent Vision" (Sudarśana).
Since there is no other place within the realm of form that can surpass this, it is named "Ultimate Form" (Akaniṣṭha).
Alternatively, this refers to the ultimate limit of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), which is the final boundary of the body that serves as the basis for all suffering.
Some say that "form" (*rūpa*) refers to accumulated form;
reaching its final boundary is called the ultimate limit of name-and-form.

Regarding the passage from "In the kingdom of Kaśmīra" to "surrounded by the fourfold assembly," the Master of the Treatise (Śāstrin) states in his verses that there are seventeen [realms] according to the interpretation of the Western Masters.
Thus, the *Mahāvibhāṣā* says: "The Western Masters state that there are seventeen realms in the Form Realm (*rūpadhātu*)."
That teacher’s intention is to say that because the Great Brahmā King differs from the other two heavens in terms of lifespan, measurement, and abode,
three distinct heavens are established within the first dhyāna.
Therefore, the *Vibhāṣā* states:
"The masters of the West (the Westerners) maintain this teaching:
there are three distinct locations within the stage of the first dhyāna."
1. The abode of the Brahmā gods;
2. the abode of the Brahmapurohita gods;
3. the abode of the Mahābrahmā gods.

This very place is the intermediate dhyāna (*dhyānāntara*). That master did not establish the heaven of non-perception (*asaṃjñisattva*) because its lifespan, dimensions, level, and so forth are indistinguishable from those of the Heaven of Vast Results (*bṛhatphala*).
Furthermore, the *Nyāyānusāra* states:
"There are others who provide a different enumeration of seventeen bases (*sthāna*),
establishing two bases in total within the first dhyāna."

Regarding the separate mention of the "non-conceptual" (*asaṃjñin*) within the fourth dhyāna: the commentary explains that the intention of that master is to establish a distinct fruit induced by a specific type of cultivation;
thus, he does not establish the Great Brahmā as being part of the first dhyāna, but rather speaks of them as two.
Furthermore, the *Nyāyānusāra* states:
"The Sthavira establishes eighteen bases (*āyatana*) within the form realm (*rūpadhātu*). The commentary explains that these eighteen are established due to two distinct causes.
Now, our National Preceptor does not establish either of these two.
Because there are no distinct levels [within them], there are only sixteen.
Thus, the *Mahāvibhāṣā* states:
"The masters of Kaśmīra say that in the level of the first dhyāna, there are only two locations."
Regarding the statement that "within the formless realm there are distinctions of superior and inferior":
this section below explains the formless realm to clarify the two preceding phrases,
demonstrating that the meditative absorptions of the formless realm are entirely devoid of spatial location.
However, due to differences in excellence and inferiority arising from the homogeneous character (*nikāya-sabhāga*), life-force (*jīvita*), and maturation (*vipāka*), there are four distinctions.
When first practicing the formless attainments (*ārūpya-samāpatti*), one must first cultivate revulsion toward form and contemplate infinite space.
One forms the perception of infinite space; next, becoming weary of external space, one further contemplates internal consciousness, and thus forms the perception of infinite consciousness;
next, becoming weary of consciousness as well, one further contemplates nothingness.

It is understood as being "nothingness. Next, because it lacks the coarse perceptions of the seven lower meditative absorptions, it is called "neither-perception-nor-non-perception" (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñā*).
It is not "non-perception" because it differs from the state of mindlessness. It is a "station" (*āyatana*) because it is a place where sentient beings are born and grow.
The first three receive their names based on their preparatory stages (*prayoga*),
while the fourth receives its designation according to its essential nature.
Therefore, the *Samādhipaṭala* states:
The names of the three [formless attainments], beginning with "Infinite Space," are established based on their preparatory practices (*prayoga*).
The name "Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception" is established because it is dull and inferior;
this will be explained in detail below.
Furthermore, how is it known that it has no spatial location?
Question:
It is because the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) arises at this very place.
Answer: Regarding the phrase "in this place," it refers to obtaining that meditative absorption in whichever realm—desire or form—is appropriate.
Although one obtains that absorption in this place, [the following applies].
One may also pass away in other locations;
here, for the time being, the explanation is based on passing away in this very place. "Or in that location" refers to whichever state, province, or similar region it may be.
This indicates the general location;
for one who attains that meditative absorption in this place may also pass away in another location.
Therefore, we know that the statement regarding "place" refers to the location in general and not to a specific one.

Since it is said that one takes birth in a certain place and that the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) manifests in that same place, it is clear that the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) has no distinct spatial location. If there were a distinct location, one would have to go to that place to take birth, and the intermediate state would manifest there.
This is the position of the Mahāsāṃghika school.
They maintain that the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) possesses a distinct location.
If there were no location, how could one speak of "this place"? [The opponent] asks: Since it is said that one is "born in this place," [it must have a location].
Since it is stated that the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) is present in this location, it follows that the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) must have a spatial location. The commentary explains:
"This location" refers to the place where one attains the formless meditative absorptions (*ārūpyasamāpatti*).
This does not mean that formlessness (*arūpya*) exists as a separate location,
like the eye-consciousness which depends on the eye-faculty;
whereas the faculty has a location, the consciousness lacks a location.

Based on this principle, it can be said that consciousness is transmitted and takes birth in the intermediate state (*antarābhava*). Furthermore, the explanation that "it arises in this place" indicates the absence of a fixed location;
it does not mean that there is a distinct location existing apart from that.
As it says regarding the "sphere of empty space," the *Abhidharmamahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* (Vol. 68) states:
"One who passes away from the desire realm and is born in the formless realm..."

Since the birth-existence (*upapatti-bhava*) in the formless realm does not arise at the place of death in the desire realm, as stated in the treatise above, when one passes away from there and is born into the desire or form realms,
the intermediate existence (*antarābhava*) arises precisely at the place where one is to be reborn.
Therefore, the *Vibhāṣā* (Treatise on the Great Exposition), fascicle 68, states:
"Question: For one who dies in the formless realm and is reborn in the desire or form realms, which of those two intermediate existences (*antarābhava*) manifests before them?"
Some say that it exists in the fourth dhyāna.
The critique says: one should not say that. Why is this so?
If the formless realm possessed spatial location, one could speak in this way;
however, the formless realm has no spatial location.
For what reason, then, does it reach as far as the fourth dhyāna?
Other masters say: if one passes away from that realm and is reborn in the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu),
the intermediate state (antarābhava) manifests in that very same location.
He, too, should not speak in such a manner. Why is that?
If he were to speak thus:
Regarding those who pass away from the formless realm and are reborn in the formless realm:
how could this be possible?
One should state it as follows.
If one dies in the desire realm or the form realm to be reborn in the formless realm,
or dies in the formless realm to be reborn in the formless realm;
and when such a person dies in the formless realm to be reborn in the desire or form realms—

That intermediate state (*antarābhava*) of those two appears right where they are to be born. Question: If it is as in the latter interpretation, it may accord with the *Vibhāṣā* masters’ final judgment;
but if it is as in the former interpretation, would it not be contradictory? Answer: The Master of the Treatise takes reason as his primary authority.
One should not take the *Vibhāṣā* commentators as the authoritative standard;

why then trouble oneself with a comprehensive explanation? Question: If it is explained as previously stated, one may say that consciousness is transmitted through the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) to receive birth.

If it is as explained later, why would an intermediate state (*antarābhava*) be necessary when one is to be reborn in a particular place? Answer: The *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 69, states:
Question: When one passes away from the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) and is born into the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) or the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), [why is an intermediate state required]?

Once the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) has appeared in accordance with the place where one is to be born, since that [place] involves no coming or going, what use would there be for an intermediate state?
Answer: Because one has previously already created the karma that brings about the intermediate state.

Although there is no coming or going, one still undergoes the intermediate state (*antarābhava*), for it must necessarily arise as projected by the power of karma. Furthermore, another interpretation holds that the four modes of birth (*yoni*) in the desire and form realms necessarily depend upon the intermediate state for their arising.
Through skillful means, one takes birth in accordance with defilement,
just as there is a continuity of mind and so forth up to the form realm.
This section below explains the latter two phrases.
The Master of the Treatise asks:
The desire and form realms are both called "possessing form" because they possess matter.
Sentient beings possessing form must depend upon matter for the continuity of the mind, body, and so forth.
By what does the mental continuum of sentient beings in the formless realm depend?
This question regarding the formless realm is posed by analogy with the two lower realms.
According to the masters of Abhidharma, [the continuum] persists until it attains [a new basis].
The Sarvāstivādins reply:
Although the formless mind and so forth lack a physical body,
they obtain continuity by depending upon the homogeneous character (*sabhāgatā*) and other such factors.
If that were so, then material form would reach these two continuities;
thus the Master of the Treatise objects:
"Material form, mind, and so forth."
"Why not rely on these two— homogeneity (*nikāya-sabhāga*) and life-force (*jīvitendriya*)?
Because these two are inferior for those born in the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*)," so says the Sarvāstivāda school.
Regarding the statement that the two inferior minds of the form realm and so forth do not rely [on them],
and that these two [minds] of the formless realm are strong for what reason,
the author of the treatise further raises an objection.
Regarding the statement that "those two realms can suppress the perception of form from the point of arrival," the Sarvāstivādins reply:
Because they arise from superior meditative concentration (*samādhi*), those two are powerful.
Because concentration suppresses form, it is said that concentration is superior; or, because concentration suppresses form, one does not rely on form but relies solely on these two.
If this is so, what is the purpose of having a distinct basis for those [two]?
The Master of the Treatise objects:
"Since that [homogeneity] is established as superior, the mind and other factors should depend upon it;
what need is there for a separate entity such as the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*)?"
Furthermore, it must now be explained upon what "reaching" (prāpti) depends.
The author of the treatise asks:
For sentient beings in the realms of desire and form, the homogeneous character (nikāya-sabhāga) and the life-faculty (jīvitendriya) necessarily function in dependence upon matter (rūpa).
What serves as the basis for these two in the formless realm?
Following the pattern below,
these two proceed by depending upon one another.
The Sarvāstivādins reply:
"The homogeneous character (sabhāgatā) and the life-faculty (jīvitendriya) are mutually dependent.
Why, then, do these two not [mutually] depend on one another when they possess form?"
The Master of the Treatise raises an objection:
"Because these two are inferior for those born in the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*).
The Sarvāstivādins respond.
The inferior does not depend [on the superior].
For what reason are these two stronger in the formless realm?
The author of the treatise further inquires.
Regarding the statement that these two types of attainment in that realm can suppress the perception of form (*rūpa-saṃjñā*), the Sarvāstivādins reply:
because the cause is superior, its fruit is likewise powerful.
It was previously stated that this concentration is superior because it can suppress the perception of form (*rūpa-saṃjñā*), or because,
having suppressed the perception of form, it does not rely upon form.
This, however, returns to the same difficulty regarding the continuity of the mind (*citta-saṃtati*).
The Master of the Treatise refutes the argument for killing by pointing out that it has already been demolished previously.
If it is argued that because meditative concentration (*samādhi*) is superior, the two [the mind and the body] are mutually dependent due to their strength, [this is also untenable].
This would then be identical to the previous difficulty regarding the continuity of the mind.

One should say: if, in that case, the life-faculty (jīvitendriya) continues to evolve within that homogeneous class (nikāyasabhāga), why rely on mutual dependence when it depends solely upon the superior meditative absorption (samādhi)?
Regarding the claim that mind and mental factors depend solely upon one another,
the Master of the Treatise further challenges this with reasoning:
"If you say that the formless [spheres] consist of mutual dependence between the homogeneous character (*nikāya-sabhāga*) and the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*)," [he asks].
Alternatively, the mind and mental factors of the formless realm depend solely upon one another and do not require a separate basis. Furthermore, since their causes are superior,
the mind and mental factors should depend solely upon one another.

Thus, through these skillful means of objection, [the Sautrāntika] intends to clarify that the *sabhāgatā* (homogeneity) and the *jīvitendriya* (life-faculty) do not possess real substantial entities. Therefore,
when the Sautrāntika master reaches the point of [the argument] that [the mind] does not proceed in dependence upon matter,
he cites the scriptural teaching as proof.
Therefore, the Sautrāntikas say:
In the formless realm, the continuity of mind and mental factors depends solely upon one another;
there is no separate basis such as a homogeneous character (*nikāya-sabhāga*) or life-force (*jīvita*).
That is to say, if there is a cause that has not yet abandoned craving for form, it gives rise to effects such as the mind;
because the cause has not abandoned craving for form,
the resulting effects, such as the mind, [are likewise affected].
It arises together with form and evolves in dependence upon form; yet, because one has already attained detachment from form as the cause and has become weary of and averse to form,
it does so by virtue of that causal detachment from form.
The fruits, such as the mind and its concomitants, which are induced [by these], do not arise simultaneously with matter and do not function in dependence upon matter;
this demonstrates that in the formless realm, the mind and mental factors depend solely upon one another.
As for why they are called the three realms, such as the realm of desire (*kāmadhātu*), the following provides an analysis through question and answer regarding the names of these three realms.
Question: What are the names of the three realms?
Regarding the statement that "it can maintain its own characteristic until the simile is explained as before," the answer is:
the term *dhātu* (element) may carry the meaning of "maintaining."
Alternatively, it has the sense of "lineage" (*gotra*);
the two explanations are as before. The term "element" (*dhātu*) is the general [designation], while "desire" (*kāma*) and so forth are the specific [designations].
The term "desire realm" (*kāmadhātu*) and so forth are derived from the general name by depending on its specific instances;
strictly speaking, one should say "the realm belonging to desire," but for brevity,
the word "belonging to" is omitted and it is simply called the "desire realm."
Desire is that which possesses [the realm],
while the realm is that which is possessed.
Because they are discussed as the possessor and the possessed in combination, it is called the "desire realm" (kāmadhātu).
Because desire is so predominant, it is discussed separately for the time being;
this is to indicate the general realm by means of a specific instance,
just as one might refer to the district to which a person belongs.

A person is that which possesses [a realm], and a district is that to which one belongs. It should be understood that the same applies to the "form realm" (*rūpadhātu*), which is so named because it is the realm to which form (*rūpa*) belongs.
A drink containing black pepper is called a "black pepper drink."
On the ring there is a vajra-jewel named Vajrakaṭaka.
To be precise, it should be called "the drink belonging to pepper" or "the ring belonging to the vajra."
This statement is made by omitting intermediate words;

in all cases, the specific is subsumed under the general. Because that realm lacks form (*rūpa*), it is called "formless" (*ārūpya*). That which is termed "form" has the meaning of being subject to transformation and obstruction (*rūpaṇā*).
That is, the ten kinds of form.
Alternatively, the meaning of "manifestation" is itself the sense base of form (*rūpāyatana*).
This is because one might otherwise suspect that "formless" means having non-existence as its essence.
Therefore, I shall now explain that the four formless [realms] (ārūpya) are designated as "formless" because their essential nature is not form;

it is not that these formless realms take as their essence the mere absence of form or the non-existence of phenomena. The explanation of the formless realm and the two analogies are both to be understood according to what was previously stated.
Furthermore, regarding the statement that "it should be known that the same applies up to the realm of desire" (*kāmadhātu*):
this second explanation follows the *tatpuruṣa* (dependent determinative) analysis.
This realm is the realm of desire, and is therefore called the "desire realm."
This is precisely the support of desire,
because this realm (*dhātu*) is able to support desire; thus,
the realm is that which sustains.
Desire is that which is supported;
because the subject and object are discussed in combination, it is called the "desire realm" (kāmadhātu).
The same applies to the other two realms.
Regarding the question, "What phenomena are intended by the term 'desire' herein?
it is answered:
"Briefly stated, from edible food up to exquisite form."
Answer: Briefly stated, desire refers to the greed induced by sexual intercourse and by edible food (*kavaḍīkārāhāra*).
Furthermore, a verse is cited below to prove that desire is indeed greed.
The general meaning may be understood.
As stated in the sixth fascicle of the *Dharmaskandhapāda-śāstra*:
"However, the five kinds of exquisite sensual pleasures (*pañca kāmaguṇāḥ*) are not the true essence of desire."
The essence of true desire is that which conditions craving for those objects.
As the Blessed One said:
"The various exquisite objects of the world are not true desire."
True desire refers to the greed of human conceptualization;
while the exquisite objects remain as they are in the world,
the wise have already eliminated desire for them.
The meaning of this verse is as follows:
desirable and exquisite forms, sounds, odors, tastes, and tangibles are not the true nature of desire.
The true nature of desire refers to the conceptual attachment that arises in dependence upon them.
The objects of desire remain as they were;
it is because the wise one is detached from them therein that he is called "one who has left desire" (*vītarāga*). Thus said the Venerable Śāriputra.
On one occasion, while he was speaking these verses to people,
a certain heterodox practitioner of wrong livelihood (mithyājīvin) stood nearby and challenged Śāriputra with a verse.
If the exquisite objects of the world were not true desire,
and true desire is defined as the greed of human conceptualization,
then a bhikṣu would have to be called a person who indulges in desire.
Because they give rise to evil conceptualizations and discursive thoughts,
Śāriputra then replied to the non-Buddhists:
"To give rise to evil discursive thoughts is truly what is called indulging in sensual desire."
It is not the case that all bhikṣus give rise to unwholesome conceptualizations and discursive thoughts regarding the sublime objects of the world;
therefore, you should not raise such an objection.
He then countered that non-Buddhist with a verse:
If the sublime objects of the world were truly desire,
then it would not be said that desire is the greed of human conceptualization;
your teacher would then have to be called a person who experiences desire.
"Because he constantly contemplates pleasing and wondrous forms, that non-Buddhist teacher remained silent and was unable to answer;
for he was truly contemplating desirable forms.

From this it is known that desire is craving (*rāga*) and not the object itself"—this concludes the treatise. Question: Why is the object called "desire"? Explanation: It is called "desire" because it is the basis (*upakaraṇa*) for desire.

"Just as it is called 'pleasure' because it possesses the instruments of pleasure," [it is asked,] "for what reason is it called 'sublime'? The answer is as stated in the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 173.
One explanation says:
"Furthermore, while all desires are base, those who are greedy for them conceptually exaggerate them and grasp at them as pure and sublime."

Therefore, it is said to be "exquisite," as explained extensively in that commentary. Question: Why are only the five objects of exquisite desire mentioned, and not the *dharma*? Answer: As the *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya-ṭīkā-vibhāṣā* (*Vibhāṣā*) states:
"The *dharmas* cognized by the mind..."
Why are "exquisite desires" (kāmaguṇa) not established [as a separate category]?
Answer: Only those objects of craving are established as exquisite desires;
these are the phenomena cognized by the mind.
Because there are objects that are unattractive,
the "exquisite desires" are not established as such, as explained at length in that [text].
If a phenomenon does not pertain to those [objects] bound to the three realms, [it is not so established].
Question:
Are the dharmas that manifest within the three realms necessarily bound to those three realms? If not, why is this so?
Answer: "What is it? is an inquiry.
Regarding the statement that they increase accordingly up to being bound to these three realms,
the answer is:
within those dharmas currently manifesting in those three realms.
That which conforms to and increases craving for the three realms is "bound to the three realms.
Herein, what dharma is called "craving for the three realms"?
Thus, craving for the three realms is further questioned.
Regarding the phrase "that which increases respectively within each of the three realms," the answer is:
that which respectively accords with and increases the out-flowing (āsrava) dharmas within each of the three realms.
This is called "craving for the three realms.
Regarding the statement, "Now, as for what is said here, it reaches the point where none can understand," this is an external objection.
Those in the West who do not clearly understand the meaning of this passage will mock one another, saying it is like the "horse-tying" answer (*aśvabandha-prativacana*).
The Master of the Treatise now states that this [objection] is like the "horse-tying" answer: when non-Buddhists slaughter a horse to sacrifice to the gods, they tie the horse to a pillar.
Someone asked, "Who is it that binds the horse?
He replied, "The owner of the horse. [The questioner asked,] "Who is the owner of the horse?"
He replied, "I am bound.
These two answers both failed to bring about understanding;
it was not known who he was by name or for what reason he was bound, and thus they remained uncomprehending.

The Master of the Treatise should be understood to answer the question in the same way: when I ask the Master about the phenomena bound to the three realms, he replies that those among them which increase the greed of the three realms [are so called].
I then ask again: what phenomena are termed "greed of the three realms"?
Again, he replied to me by saying that [the afflictions] increase respectively within each of the three realms. Neither of these two answers allows for understanding;
one does not know which phenomena are bound to the three realms.
It is not known which dharma constitutes the craving of the three realms.
The answer is indistinct, similar to the response regarding the tethering of a horse.
Now, as for what is here called "bound to the formless realm":
The Master of the Treatise replies:
What is stated here now is not the same as the "bound horse" analogy you cited.
It refers to the twenty locations of the desire realm previously described.
The greed of one who has not yet abandoned greed is called "greed of the desire realm.
Those phenomena which are conducive to and increase this greed are called "phenomena bound to the desire realm" (*kāmadhātu-pratisaṃyukta-dharma*).
Regarding the seventeen locations of the form realm previously mentioned,
the craving of one who has not yet abandoned craving for them is called "craving for the form realm.
These are the locations that are conformed to and increased by this craving.
Regarding the factors bound to the realm of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa-dhātu*),
the greed for those four bases of the formless realm previously mentioned that has not been abandoned by one who is not free from craving is called "greed for the formless" (*ārūpyarāga*).
Those states which are conducive to this craving and serve as its basis for increase are called "phenomena bound to the formless realm" (*ārūpyadhātu-pratisaṃyukta-dharma*).
There is a vast difference in breadth between "craving" and "bound phenomena," and their essential natures (*svabhāva*) are clearly distinct.
How could this be the same as tethering a horse? Second, regarding the explanation based on the indeterminate and so forth, it should be understood according to what preceded.
As for how desire and greed arise with respect to the mind that intends to transform [others]:
Question:
One who has attained the mind capable of transformation has already severed desire and greed;
if greed has not been severed, one does not attain the mind capable of transformation.
Regarding how craving arises toward a mind intended for transformation:
as for the statement that it arises from hearing about another [object] and thereby generating craving, the answer is as follows.
Either because one hears from others about the future mind of transformation and thus develops a relish for it;
or because one has personally regressed and thus develops a relish for the past mind of transformation;
or because one contemplates the sovereign power of the transformer and thus gives rise to craving and attachment for the present mind of transformation.
If it is argued that the mind can transform itself to produce transformed odors and tastes,
then this meaning is already implicitly clarified.
As for the question, "Are there thus only three realms?"— it is as follows.
Question: Regarding the number [of realms], it is said that the three realms are boundless, reaching as far as empty space. Answer:
The three realms are boundless;
therefore, it is difficult to exhaustively deliver all sentient beings.
According to the Mahīśāsaka school, however, there are sentient beings who first arise.
Defilements do not arise from karma;
rather, it is only from the second existence onward that they arise from both defilements and karma.
Because they arise repeatedly, the Buddha’s deliverance of them is inexhaustible.
Regarding the question of how the world should be said to abide:
is it spread out horizontally? This is the inquiry.
Regarding the statement that they are "superimposed," it should be said that they exist "side-by-side" up to the point where "above and below" is not mentioned;
this is the response of the Sarvāstivādins.
It is taught that there are worlds in the eight directions situated horizontally.
Since the sūtras mention the four cardinal directions but do not mention above or below, it is clear they are distributed horizontally.
The sūtra’s mention of the "four directions" includes the four intermediate points as well. Furthermore, it states that the raindrops fall without interval or interruption.
This metaphor illustrates that the world is boundless, continuous, and uninterrupted, undergoing neither destruction nor formation for even a moment’s rest.
Some say that there are also [worlds] that have reached [destruction]; one should know that this is likewise the case.
Some say that there are also the two directions of above and below,
because other *tantra* scriptures of the Secret Mantra (*guhyamantra*) speak of the ten directions.
Within these ten directions, in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*),...
If there are sentient beings who, at the moment they abandon the craving for one desire realm,
attain the cessation and abandonment of craving for all desire realms throughout the ten directions,
because their characteristics are identical.
It should be understood that the same applies to the formless and the formless-free realms. That which is illuminated by the sun and moon is called a single world-system (*lokadhātu*).
Within a thousand such world-systems, there is one Brahmā King.
Although the Brahmā King generally serves as the lord of a thousand worlds, when he gives rise to supernormal knowledge based on the first dhyāna,
the supernatural powers he manifests enable him to travel only as far as the thousand worlds in which he himself has been born.
And they are able to go to the Brahma-world that arises from themselves,
but not to other worlds or other Brahma-worlds, because of the distinction between their respective locations.
If one relies on the remaining [levels], such as the second dhyāna, when arising in supernormal knowledge (abhijñā), it should be understood that the same applies accordingly.
Furthermore, it should be understood that the same applies to the remaining four types of supernormal knowledge.
This is based on ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*).
If based on noble ones (*ārya*), this is not fixed. This is based on those possessing the five supernormal powers (*pañcābhijñā*).
If one relies on the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya*), it can also comprehensively establish the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) of other realms.
Having already explained that the three realms extend to sentient beings but not to the intermediate state (*antarābhava*),
the following second section clarifies the five destinies (*gati*).
The first two lines provide the direct answer;
the latter two lines distinguish the specific dharmas.
The *Śāstra* states: "Up to one portion of the heavenly realm (*devagati*)."
Beneath the earth there is a prison called "earth-prison" (dìyù);
this is a semantic translation.
Its Sanskrit name is *naraka*.
If one follows the *Nyāyānusāra*, its explanation of the names of the five destinies states:
*nara* means "human being," and *ka* means "evil."
Many people commit evil deeds and fall into it;

for this reason, it is called the *naraka-gati* (the realm of hell-beings). Alternatively, it is called *naraka* because it is near humans, for those who have committed grave offenses fall there swiftly.
Or again, *ka* is a synonym for pleasure (*sukha*). [In this case, it is called *naraka* because there is no pleasure for humans.]
"Na" means "non-existent.
"Loka" has the meaning of "to fall.
Thus, that which possesses the characteristic of falling into non-existence is called *naraka*. Alternatively, *loka* has the meaning of "rescue."
That which cannot be [endured] is called *naraka*. Alternatively, *nara* means "to delight in";
