that which is not to be delighted in is called *naraka*. In the *Vibhāṣā*, it is also said to be named *nalaka*.
"Na" is a short vowel;
it refers collectively to that realm of rebirth.
"Nā" is a long vowel.
This is that which belongs to the particular.
The former is general and the latter is particular;
the particular is that which belongs to the general.
Based on these distinct meanings, separate names are established. Regarding the term "animals" (*tiryag-yoni*):
it is because in that realm of rebirth, beings for the most part dwell with their bodies horizontal;
or because within that realm, there may be some who move horizontally.
Furthermore, because their species are numerous and they are largely ignorant,
they are called "animals" (tiryagyoni). As for those called "hungry ghosts" (preta):
This refers to those who, in other lifetimes, delighted in stealing the property of others and were habituated to stinginess and greed;
furthermore, they were mostly ancestors to whom sacrifices were offered,
and they frequently harbored aspirations for their own survival and sustenance.
Furthermore, they are often timid and weak, their forms emaciated and exhausted;
because their bodies and minds are flighty and restless, they are called "hungry ghosts.
They are called "humans" because they cause devas to give rise to pride upon encountering them.
Among these types of beings in the higher realms, I am the most honored;
or, because their own minds are characterized by much overweening pride or much deliberation, they are called "human" or "deva."
That is to say, their radiance and majestic power are blazing and intense;
they sport and converse with boldness, vying with one another,
or else they are noble and exalted, possessing sovereign spiritual efficacy.

The above is the treatise on the prayers and petitions of the multitude for the sake of the heavens. The *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* also explains the names of the five destinies (*pañca-gati*), though it cannot be described in full detail. The *Vibhāṣā*, fascicle 172, speaks of the asuras.
Some say it is included within the realm of gods;
others say it is included within the realm of hungry ghosts.
According to the Saṃmitīya and Mahāsāṃghika schools, however, [it is otherwise].

The asuras constitute the sixth realm of existence. Regarding the question of the physical forms and languages of the five realms: the commentary explains that their bodies stand upright and they all speak the refined language of the noble ones (*ārya-vāk*).
Human forms are clearly perceived.
At the beginning of the eon, all spoke with the speech of the noble ones;
later, they produced various languages according to their respective locations.
At the beginning of the kalpa, ghosts all spoke with the speech of noble beings;
later, their forms diverged according to their respective locations and their speech became indeterminate.
As for animals, their physical forms are directly perceived.
At the beginning of the kalpa, all beings spoke the noble language;
later, they produced various dialects according to their respective locations.
The sentient beings in the hells have forms like those of humans.
Upon first birth, all utter noble speech;
subsequently, having experienced suffering, they emit various cries of pain.
This is a brief explanation of the forms and speech of the five destinies according to the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*.
Regarding the statement that there are three realms up to the teaching that there are five destinies (*gati*),
the following explains the third phrase of the inquiry.
"Existence" (*bhava*) refers to wholesome or defiled states up to those whose essence is not the intermediate state (*antarābhava*).
Answer: The destinies (*gati*) are exclusively indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) and do not extend to the wholesome or the defiled; this is the position of the *Vibhāṣā* commentators.
If it were otherwise, and if they were said to extend to the wholesome and the defiled, then the destinies would become intermingled.
Within a single realm of existence (*gati*), the karma and afflictions that bring about all five realms are fully present.
The five realms consist exclusively of sentient beings (*sattvākhya*) and do not extend to the external vessel-world (*bhājanaloka*),
because that external vessel-world is also subject to the common enjoyment of those belonging to the five realms.

Because it would otherwise result in confusion, the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) is not the essence of a realm of rebirth (*gati*). The essence of the five realms of rebirth is not the intermediate state;
for a realm of rebirth is that which is gone toward, whereas the intermediate state is not that which is gone toward as a realm.
Because it is a means for proceeding [to rebirth], it is not included within the destinies (*gati*).
Thus, the *Prakaraṇapāda-śāstra* states: "That which is called the intermediate state (*antarābhava*)..."
For this reason, it is known that the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) is not a destination (*gati*).
The *Dharmaskandhapāda-śāstra*, in the section on "the accomplishment of the intermediate state through cultivation," further cites scriptural evidence: "This is the eye."
Distinguishing it from the ear and other faculties:
among the twenty-two faculties, this is the eye faculty;
among the twelve bases, this is the eye base.
Among the eighteen elements, this refers to the eye-element,
as well as the eyes of the five destinies and the divine eye produced through cultivation.
Furthermore, since the intermediate state (antarābhava) possesses eyes and is taught separately from the five destinies (gati),
it is clear that the intermediate state is not subsumed within the five destinies.
The sūtra also distinguishes those in the intermediate state from those going to other realms.
To provide scriptural proof, one asks: "Which sūtra is this?"
Question:
Regarding the statement that the *Saptabhava-sūtra* refers to reaching various different realms of existence (*gati*),
what is the answer?
This refers to the *Saptabhava-sūtra*.
In that sūtra, the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) is explained separately from the destinies (*gati*),
as it is the means for reaching those destinies.

Thus, one knows that the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) is not included within the five destinies (*gati*). This is the direct proof that the intermediate state is not a destiny; by extension of this principle, it is also shown that the essential nature of a destiny is exclusively neutral (*avyākṛta*).
That sūtra distinguishes between the destinies (*gati*) and separately explains that karmic existence (*karma-bhava*) is the cause of the five destinies;
thus, one knows that the five destinies are the fruit of maturation (*vipāka-phala*).
Therefore, the principle that the destinies are exclusively non-obscured neutral (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*) is thoroughly established.
Because the Sūtra distinguishes the causes of karma as being different from the various destinies (*gati*),

and because it further cites a Sūtra stating that "all outflows (*āsrava*)" extend up to the non-obscured neutral state (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*), [it is established that] the destinies are exclusively neutral.
This reveals the karma and afflictions that result in rebirth in hell;
it precisely reveals their causes: "crookedness" refers to flattery, and "filthiness" refers to...
Regarding "hatred" and "turbidity":
this refers to greed (*lobha*). Because those actions of body, speech, and mind arise from deceit, hatred, and greed, they are called the crooked, defiled, and turbid karma of body, speech, and mind.
This precisely clarifies the karma that leads to experience in hell.
Because one has committed this evil karma, one undergoes the ripened fruit (*vipāka-phala*) of the five aggregates within the *naraka* (hell).
Once the ripening has arisen, it is called *naraka*.
Apart from the phenomena of the five aggregates, that hell cannot be found at all.
Because of this scriptural statement, the destinies (*gati*) are exclusively non-obscured neutral (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*),
since the fruit of maturation (*vipākaphala*) is exclusively neutral.
If it were as you say, then [the afflictions] would be "increased" (anuśayita) wherever they reach; this is an objection,
for the treatise states that all latent dispositions (anuśaya) are increased throughout all five destinies (gati).
Clear knowledge also extends to the defiled;
if it were exclusively an indeterminate fruit of maturation (*vipāka-phala*),
that treatise should have stated that the five destinies are abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*).
Furthermore, the universal latent dispositions (sarvatraga-anuśaya) increase [in these states];
one should not say that they pertain to all [states].
Since it is stated that they pertain to "all," it is clearly known that they extend through both the defiled and the undefiled.
Regarding his statement that the five destinies up to what is collectively termed a "village" are included: this is generally applicable;
for it is possible for various afflictions to arise during the process of rebirth within the five destinies, which is called the "mind of entry."
The destinies (*gati*) and the entry into the mind (*cittapraveśa*) are collectively termed "destinies," and there is no contradiction or error in this.
An analogy can clarify this.
Some say that because the essence of a destiny extends [to these states], they are mentioned separately.
The Mahāsāṃghika school asserts that the essential nature of the destinies (*gati*) also extends to both the wholesome and the defiled.

However, regarding the *Sūtra on the Seven Existences* (*Saptabhava-sūtra*), which distinguishes "karmic existence" (*karma-bhava*) from the five destinies, this does not constitute a separate statement asserting that karma is definitively not subsumed under the destinies. [Furthermore, there are] the five corruptions (*pañca-kaṣāya*).

That is to say: the *kalpa-kaṣāya*, the *āyuḥ-kaṣāya*, the *sattva-kaṣāya*, the *kleśa-kaṣāya*, and the *dṛṣṭi-kaṣāya*. Just as among these five corruptions (*pañca-kaṣāya*), afflictions (*kleśa*) and views (*dṛṣṭi*) are mentioned separately as corruptions, it does not follow that because they are mentioned separately, those views are necessarily not included within the afflictions.
Since all ten latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) are afflictions (*kleśa*), although karma is the cause for manifesting rebirth (*gati*), it is mentioned separately.
If that is so, one might object that the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) should also be considered a rebirth. This is the challenge.
Although *karmabhava* is mentioned separately, it is said to be included within the destinies (*gati*).
Since *antarābhava* is also mentioned separately,
it too should be included among the destinies.
Regarding the statement, "Otherwise, the meaning of *gati* would entail that death and birth are simultaneous," this is a refutation of a divergent view.
A *gati* is that which is gone toward.
Among these, the "one who goes" can be established;
however, it cannot be said that the "place to which one goes" is the same as the "one who goes," because the place of death is the very place of birth.
If it is argued that this is because one reaches and takes birth in the formless realms, [we respond: This objection is invalid;
for the intermediate state (antarābhava) that dies at its place of birth is not included within the [five] destinies (gati).
The death-place and birth-place of the formless realm (*ārūpya*) should likewise not be included among the destinies (*gati*). If that is so,
then regarding the intermediate state (*antarābhava*), which is designated as such when it arrives [at its destination],
provide a better interpretation.
Because it is called "intermediate existence" (antarābhava), it should not be called a "destination" (gati).
Since it is born in the interval between two destinations, it is named "intermediate existence.
If this were included within a destination, it could not be called "intermediate."
However, as for that Venerable One making such a statement intentionally,
the Mahāsāṃghikas and others further cite the aforementioned sutra;
yet that Venerable Śāriputra stated that it is only after the maturation has arisen that one is called a hell-being.
Because it is not merely a result of maturation (*vipāka*), it is categorized as both wholesome and defiled.
That sutra further states that "apart from the phenomena of the five aggregates, that *nāraka* cannot be found.
This was said in order to refute the false attachment to a truly existent *pudgala*—a real self-entity—that travels to the various realms of existence.
This statement was made because it does not exclude wholesome or defiled [states], but refers to the remaining aggregates.
When the Vaibhāṣika masters say "it also extends to the nurtured (*aupacayika*)," they are returning to their own fundamental tenet.
Among these, the former explanation of the two masters is correct.
Thus, the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 172, states:
"Question: It is already known that the essence of the destinies (*gati*) is exclusively non-obscured neutral (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*)."
In this regard, is it solely of the nature of maturation (vipāka),
or does it also include that which is nurtured (aupacayika)?
If it were solely of the nature of maturation, [then...]
How should one reconcile the statement in the *Prakaraṇapāda*?
It says that the five destinies (*gati*) comprise the five aggregates (*skandha*), the twelve bases (*āyatana*), and the eighteen elements (*dhātu*).
If these were to include the "nourished" (*aupacayika*) [matter], then the essential nature of the destinies would become confused.
Because within the human realm (*manuṣyagati*), one also gives rise to the growth of the sense faculties (*indriya*) and the great elements (*mahābhūta*) nurtured by the form realm (*rūpadhātu*).
Therefore, it should be stated that the essence of a realm (*gati*) is exclusively maturation (*vipāka*). [Objection: How then should one reconcile this with what is stated in the *Prakaraṇapāda*?
The answer is that the text should have stated that the five destinies comprise a portion of the five aggregates, eleven bases,
and seventeen elements; since it does not say this,
one should know that the reciter has made an error.
Some say that the treatise refers to the retinues of all five destinies,
as well as the karma that brings about those destinies and the factors that provide protection;
since it does not refer exclusively to the destinies themselves, there is no fault.
However, because there are distinctions among the realms of afflictions and because there are distinctions among the destinies of the aggregates of maturation,
the essence of a destiny consists solely of maturation.
"Regarding 'there are seven abodes of consciousness within the three realms':
this third section below clarifies the seven abodes of consciousness.
Within the three realms and five destinies, from bottom to top, there are seven such abodes of consciousness in their respective order."
What are these seven? Question:
The verse says: "Reaching others, there is no further impairment."
The first phrase clarifies the first station of consciousness (*vijñānasthiti*);
the second phrase clarifies the second station of consciousness;
reversing this [indicates] the third station of consciousness.
That is to say, reversing this second phrase, there is "one body and different perceptions.
"One body and one perception" is the fourth station of consciousness (*vijñānasthiti*).
The fourth phrase refers to the latter three stations of consciousness, which are the lower three formless realms (*ārūpya*).
The fifth phrase provides the conclusion;
the sixth phrase distinguishes the dharmas.
The *Śāstra* says: "Up to what is called 'difference in perception' (*saṃjñā-viśeṣa*)."
This clarifies the stations of consciousness.
That is to say, those sentient beings possess a physical body;
therefore, they are called "sentient beings with form."

The first station of consciousness (*vijñānasthiti*) consists of those whose bodies and perceptions are both different, such as the entirety of the human realm (*manuṣyagati*) and a portion of the gods.

Regarding "a portion of the gods," this refers to the entirety of the gods of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and, within the first dhyāna, all except for those who arose at the beginning of the eon (*kalpādya*), including the remainder of that period thereafter. Question: According to the *Vibhāṣā* (137), it says that "a portion of the gods" refers to the gods of the desire realm, but does not mention the first dhyāna. Why is this?

Furthermore, the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* states that because the first station of consciousness is bound exclusively to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), it is extinguished based solely on the threshold concentration (*anāgamya*).

Because the second station of consciousness is bound to the first dhyāna, it is extinguished based on the first dhyāna, the threshold concentration, and the intermediate concentration (*dhyānāntara*).
The preparatory stage (*sāmantaka*) of the second dhyāna ceases it.
Since that treatise states that the first station of consciousness (*vijñānasthiti*) ceases based on the *anāgamya* concentration, and does not say it ceases based on the first dhyāna and so forth,
it is clear that it does not apply to even a portion of the first dhyāna.
Furthermore, the ninth chapter of the *Prakaraṇapāda* states:

"The first station of consciousness is known by seven knowledges, excluding the knowledge of analogies (*anvaya-jñāna*), the knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-jñāna*), and the knowledge of the path (*mārga-jñāna*)."
If it were to include the first dhyāna, one should say that "subsequent knowledge" (anvaya-jñāna) knows it. The commentary explains:

the phrase "a portion of the heavens" (deva-ekadeśa) logically includes the first dhyāna, because a portion of the heavens of the first dhyāna is subsumed within the first station of consciousness (vijñāna-sthiti).
One portion is subsumed under the second station of consciousness;
because it is indeterminate, it is not mentioned.
The six heavens of the desire realm in their entirety constitute the first station of consciousness; because they are determinate, they are specifically mentioned.
That treatise explains the second station of consciousness (*vijñānasthiti*) as referring only to the initial arising at the beginning of the eon (*kalpa*), and not to later times;
therefore, there is no contradiction.

Furthermore, the statement that the first consciousness-dwelling (*vijñāna-sthiti*) ceases upon reaching the preparatory concentration (*anāgamya-samādhi*) is made on the basis of the complete category;
for one part of the first dhyāna is severed by being combined with the second consciousness-dwelling.
Because it is not complete, it is omitted and not mentioned.
At the beginning of the *Prakaraṇapāda*, the "abodes of consciousness" (*vijñānasthiti*) should also be stated as being known by subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*);
this is because that text speaks of the whole and does not refer to a partial portion. As for the phrase "difference of body" (*kāyabheda*):
This means that all those physical bodies are distinct; they are distinguished by their bodies.
This is explained in terms of their essential nature (*svabhāva*). Alternatively, there may be distinct bodies, which is stated in terms of their possession (*samanvāgama*).
Therefore, those sentient beings are said to have "different bodies" (*nānātva-kāya*). Regarding "different speech and perceptions" (*nānātva-vāk-saṃjñā*):
the three types of perception are not identical. The "perception of suffering" and so forth are divided into three kinds based on the associated constituent parts of feeling (*vedanā*).
If one is in the desire realm, all three perceptions are present; if in the first dhyāna, there are two, excluding the perception of suffering.
These are distinguished by way of their nature according to the differences in perception, or there may be different perceptions.
According to the *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya*,
those sentient beings are said to have "diversity of perception" (*saṃjñā-nānātva*).
As for those "sentient beings possessing form who have reached diversity of body" (*rūpiṇaḥ sattvāḥ kāyena nānātvaṃ gatāḥ*):
Explaining the second phrase:
when the Brahmakāyika devas speak, they cite the first to represent the subsequent;
this collectively subsumes the three heavens, referring only to the beginning of the kalpa and not to later times.
At the beginning of the eon, when the Brahma-multitude first arose, they conceived the notion: "We have all been born from Mahābrahmā.
And Mahābrahmā conceived the notion: "All these members of the Brahma-multitude have been born from me."
Because the Brahmā King and his retinue alike maintain that they are born from a single cause, they are called "those of uniform perception" (*ekasaṃjñin*).
Thus, the *Nyāyānusāra* (Treatise on the Principles of Correct Reasoning), chapter twenty, states: "Is it not the case that the retinue of Brahmā says, 'I was born from him'?"
Furthermore, the Great Brahmā King says, "I am able to produce them.
Since their perceptions differ, how can they be said to be one?
This objection is unreasonable.
This is because the Brahma-hosts and the Brahma-king alike conceive the notion [of self] based on a single cause;
or, it is because they perceive the created beings as a single unity. The commentary explains: "Alike they adhere to a single cause, and alike they take the created beings as their object."
Since there is no difference in their perception, it accords with the intent of this treatise. Furthermore, the *Nyāyānusāra* states:
"For what reason do the Brahmakāyika gods collectively give rise to this perception?
It is because they see that the Great Brahmā’s abode, physical form, and supernormal powers are all preeminent."
Furthermore, because they observe that Mahābrahmā already existed previously, while the other gods were born only later,
they are unable to see him passing away from the higher plane;
thus, relying on the first dhyāna, they develop the supernormal power of recollecting past lives (*pūrvanivāsābhijñā*).
Because they cannot clearly perceive the objects of the higher realms, for what reason does Mahābrahmā also give rise to this notion?
It is because as soon as he forms the thought, the assembly appears; thus, he claims it was created by himself.
Because they do not perish quickly;
or because they are ignorant of the principles governing the arising of karmic fruits;
or because they perceive their own physical form, stature, power, lifespan, majesty, and so forth, to be superior to those of other beings.
The Brahma-multitude and the Brahma-king differ in body, yet they give rise to a single perception. As for "difference of body":
because the bodies of the Brahma-king and the Brahma-multitude are each distinct, it is called "difference of body."
This passage clarifies the difference in bodies by contrasting the Great Brahmā with the Brahmakāyika gods;
it also shows that there is a difference in body when the Brahmapurohita and Brahmakāyika gods are compared within their respective realms.
Thus, the *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya-ṭīkā* (Xianzong lun), fascicle 12, states:
Regarding the statement "difference in body":
in the first dhyāna, there are informative and non-informative [karma], as well as vitarka and vicāra;
because many consciousnesses act as causes that produce differences in the body, there is a distinction.
The Sūtra speaks of those from the Brahmakāyika gods up to those who have previously seen a Brahmā king;
this is based on the Sūtra that gives rise to the question.
Other masters say it refers to those who will come to be born here.
Answer: There are three explanations;
this is the position of the first master.

The Master of the Treatise refutes [the opponent's position]: "In the past, while in the two meditative absorptions (dhyāna), you once saw the Brahmā King; how is it that at this present time you have fallen into the grasping of rules and observances (śīlavrataparāmarśa)?"
When one is born into the first dhyāna, one has not yet attained the second dhyāna;
how, then, can one recollect the events of that [higher] stage?
When one attains the second dhyāna, the afflictions of the first [stage] have already been abandoned.
How is it that one still gives rise to the grasping of rules and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) even when taking Mahābrahmā as an object?
Other masters say that this refers to one who dwells within the intermediate state (*antarābhava*).
The second master explains [it as follows].
In the past, while dwelling in the intermediate state (*antarābhava*), one once saw the Brahmā King.
Regarding those who dwell in the intermediate state and remain there for a long time until their lifespan is exhausted,
the Master of the Treatise refutes this.
In the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), there are those who undergo birth from a womb and so forth;
since the conditions for birth have not yet converged, it is possible for them to remain for a period of time.
In contrast, all intermediate beings of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) undergo miraculous birth (*upapāduka*); their taking of birth is unimpeded.
Since the conditions for its existence are not lacking, it cannot remain for long;
how, then, can it be said that the Brahmā King was once seen to live for a long time?
Therefore, it is from the Brahma assembly that such a thought arises.
The third [position] is the correct interpretation of the Master of the Treatise:
having first seen a being at birth, when seeing it again later, one forms the thought:
"We have previously seen such a sentient being living for a long time."
Furthermore, the *Nyāyānusāra* (Treatise on the Principles of Correct Reasoning), fascicle 22, states: "Other masters say:
'Because there are those who dwell in the Ābhāsvara Heaven and, passing away from that heaven, come to be born here.'"
Having passed away from that realm and been reborn here,
how is it that one who has not yet attained the second dhyāna is able to recollect those various past lives?
Who says that they have not attained the second dhyāna?
If they had attained it, they would have abandoned craving for the first dhyāna;
how then could they still give rise to the view of ritualism and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) regarding the first dhyāna?
What fault is there in asserting that one is born only after having fallen away?
Is it not the case that there is no falling away in the form realm?
Some say that there is no obstacle to falling away for those who have just been born [there].
Other masters claim that while dwelling in the intermediate state (*antarābhava*), one has previously seen Brahmā.
This is not reasonable,
for the Sūtra states that he sees him because he has long resided in the world.
Since those gods exist within that heaven,
and because there is no possibility for them to remain long in the world once they have been born there without lacking the necessary conditions,
one should say that the Brahmakāyika gods themselves, while residing in their own heaven, previously saw the Brahmā King.
Because those who have passed away from the Ābhāsvara Heaven and first undergo rebirth there have previously seen him;
that is to say, when the Brahmā-pariṣadya gods first descend to be born,
they see the Great Brahmā King’s majestic radiance blazing intensely.
Although I harbored deep reverence and a desire to go in person to receive his instruction,
I was constrained by his majestic spiritual power and could not approach him;
thus, as time slipped away, a great deal of time has passed.
Thereafter, exerting single-minded sincerity, they approached to behold him; having arrived, they all together formed this thought:
"We have seen him before," and so forth, as extensively described.
That is to say, when they draw near to the sight of Mahābrahmā,
they are immediately able to recollect and know the things previously seen,
and furthermore, they are able to clearly comprehend the various lower beings who have appeared before them.
Only the Brahmā King and his mental aspirations [remain];
or perhaps he was previously in the Ābhāsvara Heaven,
where he once saw the Brahmā King and now, seeing him, is able to remember.
This means that in the past, while he was in the Ābhāsvara Heaven,
he saw the Brahmā King dwelling alone on the lower plane,
yet he also knew that through his aspirational mind, the Brahmā wished to dwell together with the assembly.
Out of compassion, he immediately gave rise to a transformation-body in the first dhyāna,
causing the assembly of transformed beings to attend upon the Brahmā King as his retinue.
In an instant, once the transformation was produced, his own merit was exhausted.
Upon the end of his life, he is reborn in the first dhyāna.
The body and mind of Mahābrahmā, as well as the phenomena emanated by him,
are all objects of the supernormal knowledge (abhijñā) of the first dhyāna.
Upon seeing him now, they immediately gave rise to the recollection of their former abodes;
therefore, those Brahmā-pariṣadya deities thought to themselves:
"We have seen him before," and so forth, as described at length.
Other masters say that the eye-consciousness arising within the second dhyāna,
which is able to take the Brahma-world as its object,
is subsumed under the factors of the first dhyāna stage.

Therefore, one can now also recollect those dharmas by means of mindfulness; since the two preceding teachers both gave rise to the recollection of past lives (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛti*) based on dharmas that had previously arisen, it is said that they "saw them as having existed. Thus some have explained it.
Those gods of the Brahmakāyika realm do not undergo gestation in a womb and have severed the suffering of the final moment of death (*antimamaraṇa*).

Because they possess mindfulness free from forgetfulness, they remember such matters as what they saw in their previous lives. Thus far, there are six explanations according to the correct principle (*yukti*).
The first three are the same as here;
the latter three are not. Furthermore, in the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 98, there are five interpretations;
the first three are the same as this treatise.
The fourth interpretation states:
Other masters say that he recalls past events previously seen by means of the innate knowledge of recollecting births (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛtijñāna*).
Question: Is it not the case that the realm of form (rūpadhātu) lacks the innate knowledge of recollecting past lives (pūrvanivāsānusmṛtijñāna)?
Answer: At the time of the initial formation of a kalpa, those in the realm of form also possess the innate knowledge of recollecting past lives.
The fifth explanation states:
Some say that the Brahmā King first enters the intermediate dhyāna and remains there for a long time;
then those various Brahma-assembly beings pass away from the higher realms and are born within the Brahma world.
Seeing that the Great Brahmā King lived for a long time with a majestic radiance so brilliant that he did not dare to draw near,
[the Buddha], after emerging from meditative concentration, commanded the assembly of Brahmās to offer mutual greetings and inquiries.

At that time, the assembly of Brahmās said to one another, "We have previously seen such sentient beings who were long-lived and remained for a long duration. Furthermore, the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* states: [It] asks the Great Brahmā King.
For how long a duration does he dwell alone?
For how long a duration does he dwell together with the community,
and then again separate from the community?
The commentary states: It should be explained thus:
for half an eon he dwells alone, and for half an eon he dwells together with the assembly.
After half a kalpa had passed, he again parted from the assembly.

Twenty intermediate kalpas constitute the measure of a half-kalpa. Regarding "sentient beings with form who again experience sensual pleasure," this is the third station of consciousness (vijñānasthiti), which, when explained in reverse, is called the Ābhāsvara [Heaven].
Regarding the statement that the latter [heaven] subsumes the first two heavens and that their "bodies are one":
because they are produced by no different causes and their bodies are identical, it is said that their bodies are one.
However, when compared across the three heavens of the same level—looking from the lower to the upper—their bodies are also distinct.
Furthermore, it is said that the body is a single entity when viewed in relation to its location.
Thus, the *Nyāyānusāra* (Treatise on the Principles of Correct Reasoning), fascicle 22, states:
"In those heavens, there is no distinct bodily form produced by causes such as informative action (*vijñapti-karman*)."
Therefore, it is said that their bodies are one;
this means that the deities dwelling in the same location share identical forms and appearances, such that there is no distinction between them.
However, in the Sūtra spoken by the Venerable Anuruddha, it says:
The Ābhāsvara devas and others have bodies that vary in height and possess degrees of excellence or inferiority;
because they occupy distinct locations as their support, this statement is made.
It is not that there is a difference in the bodies within a single heaven;

rather, they are said to have "different characteristics" because of the distinction between pleasure (*sukha*) and equanimity (*upekṣā*), and "different perceptions" (*saṃjñā*) because of the clarification of the three feelings (*vedanā*).
Joy (*prīti*) and pleasure (*sukha*) are both termed "pleasure. This can be understood through analogies.
"Is it not the case that the same should apply to the perception of universal purity?
This is an objection.

"Is it not the case that because the two perceptions of pleasure and equanimity in the sphere of universal purity are also intermingled, it should likewise be called 'diversity of perception' (saṃjñā-nānātva)?"
Regarding the statement "because the gods of the Śubhakṛtsna [heaven] up to the Ābhāsvara [heaven] have agitated minds," the answer is:
within the three dhyānas, there is never a time when their bliss is not experienced with satiety.
Joy is not so; because it agitates the mind, there is a distinction between the two.
The Sautrāntika masters say that "attainment" (*prāpti*) is merely a different name for "conception" (*saṃjñā*).
The Sautrāntika school cites a sūtra to explain that the third station of consciousness is named "diversity of perception," as can be understood from the text.
This is the intended meaning of the critique in the *Nyāyānusāra*.
The gods of the third dhyāna heaven see the calamity of water occurring in the lower realms;
among the newly born and long-established gods, there are those who conceive fear and those who do not.
Thus, they should be designated as having "different perceptions."
If the Abhidharmakośa masters offer this defense:
because joy (*prīti*) is agitating within the second dhyāna,
one perceives the fear of the fires of the lower realm as the perception of fearlessness.
In the third dhyāna, because bliss is tranquil and still,
one does not give rise to fear even when seeing the calamity of water;
this is because the perception of non-fear and the verbal expression of that perception are one and the same.
Regarding "there are sentient beings with form who, because their perception is uniform, are called 'those of uniform perception'":
this explains the fourth station of consciousness (*vijñānasthiti*) concerning those of uniform body and perception.
"Sentient beings with form" and "uniformity of body" are both explained as before.
Because this ripening pleasure is never subject to satiety, it is called "one-pointed perception" (*ekasaṃjñā*).
Although the feeling of equanimity (*upekṣā-vedanā*) also arises within the three dhyānas, [the first dhyāna] is so designated because of its predominance.
Because one does not weary of relying [on it],
it is said that "perception is one.
Regarding the statement that "perception is one" because it reaches [this state] within the first dhyāna:
This generally clarifies the distinctions among the three types of perception.
The phrase "the lower three formless realms, up to this point,
are called the seven" explains the fourth and fifth lines.
From among the four formless realms, one takes the first three types;
that is to say, the gods of the Sphere of Infinite Space constitute the fifth station of consciousness,
and the gods of the Sphere of Infinite Consciousness constitute the sixth station of consciousness.
The sphere of nothingness is the seventh station of consciousness;
these are called the seven.
Among these, what dharma is designated as a "station of consciousness"?
Question: Regarding the essence of the stations of consciousness (*vijñānasthiti*), it is said that "those things to which one is bound are called the stations of consciousness. Answer:
If it is [the state] of desire, its substance consists of the five aggregates bound to the realm of form;
if it is [the state] of the formless, its substance consists of the four aggregates bound to the formless realm.
In each case as appropriate, it is a phenomenon belonging to the category of sentient beings.
Because consciousness dwells with pleasure and attachment therein,
it is called a station of consciousness (*vijñānasthiti*). Why, then, are the remaining [factors] not stations of consciousness?
The sixth phrase is raised as a question.
Regarding the statement that "in other cases there are factors that impair consciousness," the verse is cited as the direct answer.
What are the "other places"? This is the inquiry.
It refers to the various evil realms; because one arrives there, they are not stations of consciousness (*vijñānasthiti*).
The explanation is clear.
What are those factors that are called "deteriorating the consciousness"?
Question:
Regarding the statement that the various evil realms are not abodes of consciousness because one arrives there [by force],
the answer has two parts.
This is the first explanation.

Among the three evil destinies, the fourth— consisting of the states where suffering is diminished and consciousness is impaired— and the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*) are not abodes of consciousness (*vijñānasthiti*),
because there exists a dharma that causes the cessation of consciousness.
Furthermore, it is said that where [the mind] reaches but is not a station of consciousness (*vijñānasthiti*).
This is the second interpretation:
that which possesses both characteristics is established as a station of consciousness.
Because the others lack these [factors], they are not abodes of consciousness.
One seeks to enter the heaven of non-perception,
or seeks to enter the meditative attainment of non-perception.
Because the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*) is dull and inferior,
it is not a station of consciousness (*vijñānasthiti*). Thus, having distinguished the nine abodes of sentient beings (*navasattvāvāsāḥ*),
this fourth section below clarifies those nine abodes of sentient beings.
What is the ninth? Question:
The verse says: "Reaching the others, it is not that they do not dwell in joy."
Answer: The first three phrases reveal the essence;
the final phrase distinguishes the phenomena.
The Commentary says: As explained in the section on the stations of consciousness (*vijñānasthiti*),
sentient beings are conventional designations (*prajñapti*),
whereas "abiding" refers to the real dharmas— the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*)— in which they reside.
The provisional abides within the real.
That which sentient beings inhabit is called a "sentient-being habitation" (*sattvāvāsa*).
Herein, the intended meaning clarifies the phenomena that constitute the inhabited.
In brief, one takes [the object] from among sentient beings, not from another's body, nor from insentient matter, nor from the intermediate state (*antarābhava*).
Thus, the *Nyāyapraveśa* (Introduction to Logic), chapter 22, states:
This refers to the physical forms and so forth that serve as the basis for sentient beings to abide in their own happiness;
they are real entities and nothing else,
because sentient beings exist only as conceptual designations.
However, since all real entities are that which are inhabited by the provisional,
the "abodes of sentient beings" consist solely of the phenomena belonging to sentient beings.
This is because the attachment of sentient beings to their own supporting bodies is more intense than their attachment to physical locations.
Furthermore, if one were to establish sentient abodes based on physical locations,
those abodes would necessarily become confused;
yet there is no confusion regarding abodes, for they exist only within the internal body.
Therefore, the abodes of sentient beings consist only of the factors pertaining to sentient beings.

Since it is stated that those who have already been born are called "abodes of sentient beings," we know that the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) is not included within the abodes of sentient beings.
Furthermore, because the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) is not a place where one dwells for long,
sentient beings do not take pleasure in abiding there;
moreover, it must necessarily be so.

The *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya* states that "sentient abodes" (*sattvāvāsa*) are established to manifest the places of birth. Furthermore, the *Nyāyānusāra* clarifies the distinction between the seven stations of consciousness (*vijñānasthiti*) and the sentient abodes, stating:
"Within the cycle of birth and death, the stations of consciousness are established to show how the various consciousnesses abide through attachment driven by craving."
It is shown that because all sentient beings delight in and dwell securely within their own bases of existence, they are established as "abodes of sentient beings.
Thus, these two categories have been distinguished and established above in the treatise. *Rākṣasa*.
It should be stated in its full form as *rākṣasa*,
which here means "protector.
Furthermore, the *Abhidharmamahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 137, states that there are seven stations of consciousness (*vijñānasthiti*).
Regarding the nine abodes of sentient beings:
do the seven subsume the nine,
or do the nine subsume the seven?
Answer: The nine encompass the seven, but the seven do not encompass the nine.
What is not encompassed?
Namely, the Heaven of Non-perception and the Sphere of Neither-Perception-nor-Non-perception.

In this regard, the reason why it should be understood as previously stated is that, according to these characteristics of inclusion, the seven stations of consciousness (*vijñānasthiti*) also consist exclusively of those counted among sentient beings (*sattvasaṃkhyāta*).
As for the sūtra cited earlier, what are its four points?
The following fifth section clarifies the four stations of consciousness (*vijñānasthiti*).
Based on the sutra, a question is raised.
The verse says: "Included within the four lines up to 'with outflows' (*sāsrava*)."
The first three phrases,
as well as the outflowing (sāsrava),
clarify the essence; these are subsumed within four categories.
Clarifying the broad and the narrow.
The *Śāstra* states, "Up to this point, these are called the four kinds," which enumerates the names of the four stations of consciousness (*vijñānasthiti*).
Regarding these four types, what is their essential nature?
This is the question.
It refers to that which, in successive order, results in dependence upon and attachment to them.
Answer: It is with outflows (*sāsrava*).
This excludes that which is without outflows (*anāsrava*). It consists of four aggregates (*skandha*). This excludes the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñānaskandha*).
Within the four contaminated aggregates (*sāsrava-skandha*), one grasps only those belonging to one's own level (*svabhūmi*) and not those of other levels.

Within one's own level, one grasps that which belongs to one's own person (*ātma-bhāva*) and is categorized as sentient (*sattvasaṃkhyāta*), and does not grasp that which belongs to another person or is non-sentient (*asattvasaṃkhyāta*).
Therefore, the *Nyāyānusāra* (Treatise on Correct Reasoning), fascicle 22, states:

"Furthermore, within one's own level (*svabhūmi*), only that which is comprised of sentient beings (*sattvasaṃkhyāta*) and only that which belongs to one's own continuum (*svasaṃtāna*) is established as a station of consciousness (*vijñānasthiti*).
This does not include that which is comprised of non-sentient things (*asattvasaṃkhyāta*) or that which belongs to the continua of others."

"Consciousness dwells according to its pleasure, as in its own continuum"—this is the treatise cited above. These four contaminated aggregates (*skandha*) of one's own level and one's own person are the support (*āśraya*) of consciousness;
they are that upon which consciousness relies and to which it is attached.
This refers to the co-arising support of consciousness;
because it acts as a simultaneous auxiliary that causes consciousness to arise,
and because it is most intimately associated with it, it is called a "support" (*āśraya*).
It is not necessary for something to be the sense organ upon which consciousness relies in order to be called a "basis" (*āśraya*).
This term "basis" indicates the sense of being that which is directly relied upon. "The object of attachment" refers to the objective field (*viṣaya*) to which consciousness is attached.
They are called "abodes of consciousness" because they both induce and do not induce the arising of consciousness;
furthermore, all contaminated consciousnesses, according to the power of craving, depend upon and adhere to them.
Because these two meanings apply, they are named "abodes of consciousness."
Because one also cherishes one’s own body or craves pleasure within the hells, there is likewise a station of consciousness (vijñānasthiti) in the hells.
As for non-sentient things and the four aggregates of another's body, although they may serve as objects of perception, they can be called "objects of attachment."
Furthermore, because they do not depend on what is neither-self nor associated with it, they are not stations of consciousness (*vijñānasthiti*).
If they belong to a different level (*bhūmi*) or are untainted (*anāsrava*), both conditions are absent;
thus, consciousness does not depend upon them or cling to them through the power of craving.
Because craving does not take uncontaminated (anāsrava) phenomena or phenomena of a different level as its object;
even if it were to arise toward phenomena of a different level,
or even if it were to arise with a mind of a different level.
Alternatively, even at times when there is no mind, the two present aggregates are also called "abodes of consciousness" because they share the same characteristics as the abodes of consciousness.
Although the various consciousnesses of the same category do not arise due to the absence of other conditions, [they are still designated as such].
It is not that [consciousness] cannot arise therein.
Why, then, is consciousness itself not described as a station of consciousness?
Question:
Regarding the passage from "by being free from that which can abide" up to "it is as has been explained," the answer is:
whatever is called a "station of consciousness" (vijñānasthiti).

Because the four aggregates that constitute the "abode" are established separately from the consciousness that constitutes the "dweller," and because the dwelling consciousness itself cannot be termed a "consciousness-abode," it is impossible to say that consciousness is a consciousness-abode.
Just as one cannot call that which is not the king himself the "king's throne," so too,
if there were four aggregates of phenomena that consciousness rides upon and controls, they would be called "abodes of consciousness."
This analogy is like the principle of a person riding in a boat:
consciousness does not pilot consciousness, and therefore consciousness does not abide in consciousness.
If that is so, why is it said that [the mind] has the five aggregates as its substance?
This is difficult.
The Sūtra states that because there is joy and defilement within consciousness, consciousness dwells therein;
it is that which consciousness mounts and directs.

Furthermore, it is said that the substance of consciousness constitutes the seven stations of consciousness (*vijñānasthiti*). This clarifies that the substance of consciousness itself is also that which is inhabited.
Although this statement exists, as for other points that could be discussed:
Answer:

Although this is stated in the sūtras, within the five aggregates comprised by the place of birth (*upapatti-sthāna*), one does not separately distinguish them; rather, the sense of consciousness (*vijñāna*) which gives rise to joy and defilement as a whole is termed "consciousness-food" (*vijñānāhāra*).
In terms of the sense of being conditioned by the five aggregates, they are called the seven stations of consciousness (*vijñānasthiti*).
Since the term "arising" (*vartate*) means "to emerge," when consciousness emerges, it is not only the four aggregates that are called the stations of consciousness.

The aggregate of consciousness is also called a station of consciousness (*vijñāna-sthiti*). It is not only said that consciousness alone gives rise to joy and defilement and is thus termed a "station";
rather, each of the other four aggregates—form and so forth—is individually capable of giving rise to various kinds of joy and defilement.

Because consciousness causes [the other aggregates] to become attached, it is called a "station of consciousness" (*vijñānasthiti*). Consciousness alone is not so; therefore, it is not that which is stationed.
Thus, within these four stations of consciousness, consciousness itself is not a station of consciousness.
Regarding the other four nutriments and the seven stations of consciousness (*vijñānasthiti*), one may say that consciousness abides in consciousness.
Furthermore, the Buddha’s intention—that such is the meaning of the authoritative teaching—is as follows.
Moreover, he cites scriptural authority to prove that consciousness is not itself a station.
Furthermore, regarding the statement that "dharmas are not stations of consciousness because they reach [consciousness]":
while the four aggregates can arise simultaneously with consciousness, serving as a fertile field for consciousness and thus being established as stations of consciousness,
there is no instance where consciousness arises simultaneously with consciousness itself.
Therefore, consciousness itself, when viewed in relation to consciousness, is not a station of consciousness (*vijñānasthiti*). Thus, the *Vibhāṣā* (137) states:

"If there is a dharma that is mounted and governed by consciousness, which co-exists with consciousness and is intimately associated with it, these are established as the four stations of consciousness."
Consciousness does not stand in such a relationship toward consciousness;
therefore, it is not established as one of the four stations of consciousness (*vijñānasthiti*).
This is because a phenomenon must either serve as the cause for consciousness or be its effect.
Through mutual support in a continuous succession, the seven stations of consciousness are established.
Consciousness relates to consciousness in this manner;
therefore, they are established as the seven stations of consciousness.
Regarding the statement "as thus explained, reaching the point of excluding the aforementioned characteristics," this clarifies the mutual breadth and narrowness,
as well as the fourfold logical distinctions (*catuṣkoṭi*), between the seven stations of consciousness (*vijñānasthiti*) and the four stations of consciousness.

The substance (*tattva*) of the seven stations of consciousness (*vijñānasthiti*) is broad while their scope (*sthāna*) is narrow; the scope of the four stations of consciousness is broad while their substance is narrow.
The four alternatives (*catuṣkoṭi*) may be understood according to the text.
Since the third statement specifies that four of the seven consist of the four aggregates (*skandha*),
and the *Nyāyānusāra* further states that the four stations of consciousness (*vijñānasthiti*) pertain exclusively to sentient beings,
it is clearly understood that the seven stations of consciousness likewise pertain only to sentient beings.

If the nine abodes of sentient beings are compared with the four stations of consciousness, they mutually possess both breadth and narrowness, thus forming four permutations (*catuṣkoṭi*). The first permutation consists of those that are nine but not four;
this refers to consciousness among the nine. The second permutation consists of those that are four but not nine.
That is to say: the three miserable realms; and those among the deities of the fourth dhyāna not included within the Heaven of Non-perception (asaṃjñisattva).

The third phrase consists of nine [factors], which are also four—namely, the four aggregates of form, feeling, perception, and formations. The fourth phrase consists of that which is neither nine nor four.
This means setting aside the aforementioned characteristics.
Regarding the four types of birth briefly mentioned in the preceding section,
the following sixth [section] clarifies these four modes of birth.
Regarding the three realms and five destinies previously described, one should know that there are, in brief, four kinds of birth.
What are these four? Where do they occur? And what are they?
First is the question of number.
Second, a specific inquiry concerning the realms.
The verse states: "Reaching the hungry ghosts, they are born through both womb and transformation.
The first two lines answer the initial question.
The final four lines answer the subsequent question.
The Treatise states: "Regarding 'birth and the types of beings,' etc.:
birth refers to the categories of the four modes of birth."

Although among sentient beings there are various different forms and appearances that intermingle with other categories, they are nonetheless equal according to their respective types of birth (*yoni*).
Furthermore, the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 120, states:
Question: What constitutes the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of these four modes of birth?
Answer: They have the four aggregates (*skandha*) or five aggregates as their intrinsic nature;
that is, the five aggregates of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and the form realm (*rūpadhātu*).
The four aggregates of the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).
Regarding these, some say that their intrinsic nature consists solely of the maturation (*vipāka*) aggregates;
others say they also include those nurtured by food (*aupacayika*).
This is called the intrinsic nature of the four modes of birth (*yoni*).
Of the two explanations given in the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, the former is correct,
because [it is consistent with] the inclusion of the four modes of birth within the five destinies (*gati*).
It is said that the four modes of birth encompass the five destinies, but the five destinies do not encompass the four modes of birth.
What is it that is not so encompassed? It is the intermediate state (*antarābhava*).
If this were not the case, [the two would be coextensive].
One should further state that it does not include the "nourished" (aupacayika).
If one were to argue that there is no such fault because the five destinies (gati) also extend to the nourished,
this defense is untenable.
According to the correct principle of the *Vibhāṣā*, the essential nature of the five destinies (*gati*) is exclusively that of maturation (*vipāka*).
How is it that those born from eggs and so forth are called "transformed" (*nirmāṇa*)?
This explains the meaning of these four names.
"That humans and animals each possess four types" explains the third line;
this is a general enumeration.
Regarding the phrase "humans born from eggs may have as many as five hundred sons" and so forth:
this clarifies that humans can be egg-born. Śaila means "Mountain" in the language of Tang; Upaśaila means "Little Mountain."
Because they differ in size, he was distinguished by the smaller one. Both brothers were Arhats;
as they were born near a mountain, they were named after the mountain.
Therefore, the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 120, states:
"Regarding those born from eggs among humans:
formerly, in this region, there was a merchant who entered the sea and obtained a female crane."
His form and features were magnificent and extraordinary, inspiring delight.
Subsequently, two eggs were produced;
later, when the eggs opened, two boys emerged who were handsome, intelligent, and wise. When they grew older, they left the household life to become renunciants.
All attained arhatship.
The younger was named Upasīla and the elder was named Sīla; the above is from the treatise. As for Mṛgāramātṛ:
This is Lady Viśākhā. Viśākhā is the name of a lunar mansion in the second month; she was named after this asterism.
In the Chinese language, it means "Nurturing."
This refers to the growth of merit.
She was the daughter of the householder Migāra;
her husband had a son named Mṛga, so she was called Mṛgī (the Deer Woman) after her son's name.
He gave birth to thirty-two eggs,
and from each egg emerged a child.
Thus, the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 124, states:
Viśākhā Mṛgāramātṛ; Pañcāla is the name of a country, which in the language of Tang means "Holder of Five.
This king was named after the land, and when the queen gave birth to five hundred eggs, she felt ashamed and feared they would portend a calamity.
He placed them in a small casket and cast them into the Ganges River,
where they drifted downstream.
Beneath the water, a neighboring king, while observing the river, sent men to retrieve them and found the eggs.
After they had returned home for several days, each gave birth to a son.
As they grew up, they were fierce and brave; wherever they went, all submitted to them, and none dared to oppose them.
At that time, the king of a neighboring country had long harbored enmity toward their father, the king.
Desiring to dispatch an army for punitive action, he first sent a letter declaring his intent to engage in a decisive battle.
Soon thereafter, his troops arrived and surrounded the city, intending to crush it.
King Pañcāla became extremely anxious and terrified.
The queen asked for details and comforted the king, saying,

Others further state that one who reaches this point is called an "intermediate-attainer" (antarāparinirvāyin).
An account of differing tenets.
The *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* (Vibhāṣā), fascicle 69, refers to them as the Vibhajyavādins (*fenbie lunzhe*).
Among them, there are two [subdivisions].
First, a general explanation;
second, a detailed exposition.
Within the general explanation, there are two alternative interpretations.
First, during the intermediate period of one's lifespan:
that is, having been born in the form realm and not yet having completed that lifespan,
one abandons the remaining afflictions during that intermediate period of the lifespan.
Attaining arhatship [in this state] is called "attaining parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state" (antarāparinirvāyī).
Second is "near the heavens in the intermediate state," meaning being born in the form realm (rūpadhātu) in the intermediate space near the fundamental heavens.
Having dwelt somewhat in a remote region,
as soon as they are born, they proceed toward the celestial hosts;
yet while still on the way, before reaching their original heaven, midway along the path—

To sever the afflictions and become an Arhat immediately [upon rebirth] is called "one who attains parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state" (antarāparinirvāyin). This is the general explanation. Regarding the statement that there are three grades because the stage of the field, the arrival, and the realm are reached: 1. **The Field**: This refers to the excellence of the Buddha-field where one is born. 2. **The Arrival**: This refers to the excellence of the time of arrival at the place of birth. 3. **The Realm**: This refers to the excellence of the meditative absorption (dhyāna) or the realm of rebirth. Because these factors vary in their degree of excellence, there are three distinct grades.
The following is a detailed explanation.
This commentary on the duration of life consists of three parts.
The first concerns the stage of reaching the realms.
The "element" (dhātu) refers to the seeds of afflictions.
Second, it is by reaching the stage of perception;
"perception" here refers to defiled perception.
Third, by virtue of reaching the stage of investigation (*vitarka*).
"Investigation" refers to seeking;
because one attains parinirvāṇa [at this stage], there are three grades.
Therefore, the *Nyāyānusāra* (Treatise on the Correct Principle), fascicle 24, states:
"Some say that those who sever the remaining afflictions during the interval of their lifespan are all termed 'attaining parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state' (*antarāparinirvāyin*).
Because they attain parinirvāṇa upon reaching the stage of the realm (*dhātu*), or the stage of perception (*saṃjñā*), or the stage of vitarka, three grades are taught."
This means that the stage of cultivating the preparatory application for abandonment while the afflictions remain as latent tendencies (anuśaya) is called the "stage of reaching the realm" (dhātu).
Here, the intention is to show that when the seeds exist but have not yet become active, it is designated as the "stage of the fruit."
That is to say, those of sharp faculties who,
upon the initial arising of afflictions, are able to diligently apply themselves to the preparatory practice for their abandonment are said to have reached the stage of "perception" (*saṃjñā*).
Herein, the intention is to clarify that the first occurrence of defiled perception is designated as the "stage of perception."
This refers to those of middling faculties.
Having long been subject to the arising of afflictions, they are only able to apply themselves with diligence to the preparatory practice for abandonment once they have reached the stage of vitarka.
Here, the intent is to show that because the power of the afflictions causes the mind to seek variously toward its objects, it is called the stage of vitarka.

That is to say, for those of dull faculties; furthermore, it is explained that there are three types of those who attain parinirvāṇa near the heavens. These three are distinguished based on the realms (*dhātu*), perceptions (*saṃjñā*), and levels of discursive thought (*vitarka*).
Alternatively, they are designated as "attaining parinirvāṇa upon rebirth" (*upapadya-parinirvāyin*) because they reach the Form Realm (*rūpadhātu*).

This is a detailed explanation of the three distinctions among those who attain parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) near the heavens: First, one who, having taken up the homogeneous class (*nikāya-sabhāga*) of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), attains parinirvāṇa immediately upon arrival is called the first. Second, one who, after subsequently experiencing celestial bliss, attains parinirvāṇa only after entering the assembly of the Dharma (*dharmasāṃkathya*) is called the second. Third, one who, following that, enters the assembly of the Dharma for the first time and attains parinirvāṇa before returning to his original heaven is called the third.

The three types of those who attain parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state (*antarāparinirvāyin*) among the aforementioned three [categories] are each divided into three, as they all attain parinirvāṇa in the intermediate stage (*antara-bhava*) close to the fundamental heavens (*mauladhyāna*). By way of context, the term "attaining parinirvāṇa upon rebirth" (*upapadyaparinirvāyin*) is explained:

having entered the assembly of the Dharma, one attains parinirvāṇa only after a long period has elapsed; this is called "attaining parinirvāṇa upon rebirth. Alternatively, it is explained that "upon rebirth" refers to those who have diminished [their lifespan]. Furthermore, these three types within this category are also understood to pertain to the intermediate stages of the life-span (*āyus*). Moreover, these three types are also explained according to their respective order as corresponding to the three [obstacles]: the realm (*dhātu*), perception (*saṃjñā*), and discursive thought (*vitarka*).
Regarding the statement, "Thus, what has been explained reaches the point of non-differentiation," the author of the treatise refutes it below:
although there are distinctions of near, middle, and far in terms of time, [the essence remains the same].
Regarding those in the form realm, when analyzed by way of their locations, there is no distinction in their mode of movement;
that is to say, having passed away from the desire realm, they undergo the intermediate existence (antarābhava) of the form realm,
proceeding from here to those near, intermediate, or distant locations.
Because they proceed swiftly toward rebirth, their activity does not abide; thus,
depending on the difference in location and activity, they may be distinguished as being near, intermediate, or far— just like sparks from a fire—
yet there is no distinction whatsoever in their movement toward those respective locations.
Even if one were to divide those near the heavens into three types,
how could it be that once born there, they would constantly move without staying, as is the case with the intermediate state (*antarābhava*)? Therefore,
the analogies of the firebrand regarding the distinctions of near, intermediate, and distant are all inconsistent.
Furthermore, regarding the claim that everything up to the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) is entirely false,
it is also refuted.
If one says that it is called "attaining parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state" (*antarāparinirvāyin*) because of attaining parinirvāṇa during the interval of one's lifespan, [that is incorrect].

Since those in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) also attain parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state (*antarāparinirvāyī*) during their lifespan, they ought to be called "those who attain parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state.
However, it is not said that there are those who attain parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state within the formless realm.
As it is said in the *Udānavarga*: *Udāna* means "Collection of Exclamations" (*udāna*) and *varga* means "Verses" (*gāthā*).
Because the Buddha collected essential meanings and composed them as verses to bestow upon all sentient beings, it is called the *Udānavarga*. Noble one.
That is to say, the noble ones are called "the virtuous," while ordinary persons are called "the commoners.
For example, there is one who, having become detached from sensual desires and unwholesome, evil states, attains the first dhyāna.
Yet, conceiving a mind of attachment and delight toward the first dhyāna, they do not seek transcendence from the world;
or, by creating superior-grade causes, they are born in the realm of Mahābrahmā,
or by creating middling-grade causes, they are born in the realm of Brahmā-purohita.
Alternatively, one who creates an inferior-grade cause may be reborn among the Brahmakāyika gods;
these constitute three types of persons.

Or, there may be a person who, having attained the first dhyāna, does not consider it sufficient, and thus gives rise to a mind of wearying detachment toward all contaminated phenomena within that first dhyāna.
By joyfully dedicating all roots of goodness pertaining to nirvāṇa toward the pursuit of bodhi,
one is able to plant the roots of goodness conducive to liberation (*mokṣabhāgīya*);
together with the preceding three, these constitute four.
Furthermore, there is another person who, having attained that concentration, realizes the fruit of non-returning;
being able to sever all outflows within a body belonging to the desire realm, they are called one who attains parinirvāṇa in the present life.
Together with the previous ones, these constitute five.
Furthermore, there are five types of persons who, having attained the first dhyāna, either attain parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state,
or attain parinirvāṇa upon rebirth,
or attain parinirvāṇa through effort.
Either those who attain parinirvāṇa without exertion (anabhisamskāra-parinirvāyin) or those who attain parinirvāṇa by going upstream (ūrdhvasrotas)—
these are the five types of non-returners (anāgāmin).
The preceding [nine] together with this make ten. Thus, these ten types all rely upon the first dhyāna;

as there are ten based on the first dhyāna, so it is for the second, third, and fourth dhyanas—by this standard, there are ten in each. Question: Since the number of heavens in the fourth dhyāna is so great, how can you say they are the same as those below, numbering only ten? Answer: It is explained that the five Śuddhāvāsa (Pure Abode) heavens are inhabited exclusively by noble ones (*ārya*).

It should be understood that these are subsumed within the categories of those who attain parinirvāṇa upon rebirth (*upapadya-parinirvāyin*) and so forth. It must be known that "those with no fixed destiny" (*aniyata-gotra*) are necessarily those born among non-Buddhists;
this clarifies that the noble ones (*ārya*) and sages are exclusively disciples of the Buddha.
Therefore, it is not mentioned;
for the Great Brahmā, as a disciple of the Buddha, must necessarily attain the fruit of concentration without vitarka (applied thought).
Therefore, they are explained separately;
thus it is said that each of the four dhyānas has ten [types],
while for the first three formless attainments, one excludes the "intermediate parinirvāṇa" from each of the ten previously mentioned.
Because those who attain that meditative concentration have no intermediate state (*antarābhava*),
and because— excluding the two types of birth—
that place is singular, there are seven types in each case.
Therefore, it is said that there are seven for each of the three formless realms.
Within the non-percipient stage (*asaṃjñī-bhūmi*), one further excludes the "Upstreamer" (*ūrdhvasrotas*) from among the previous seven,
because once that meditative absorption has been attained, there is no higher rebirth.
If one speaks from a horizontal perspective,
there are also those who attain parinirvāṇa by flowing upward within the Sphere of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception; however,
since that sphere cannot give rise to any higher stage, it is said here that there is no "upward-flowing" [attainment].

Therefore, it is said that there are only six, namely excluding those in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*). Furthermore, another interpretation holds that the karma of the first dhyāna constitutes one person;

having attained the first dhyāna and planted the roots of merit conducive to liberation (*mokṣabhāgīya-kuśalamūla*), this constitutes the second person; and having attained that dhyāna and attaining parinirvāṇa in the present life, this constitutes the third.

And there are the seven destinations of the virtuous persons (*satpuruṣagati*): namely, the three types of those who attain parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state (*antarāparinirvāyin*), together with the four types beginning with those who attain parinirvāṇa upon rebirth (*upapadyaparinirvāyin*).
These, added to the previous [seven], constitute ten.
The second, third, and fourth dhyānas, as well as the formless attainments,
should be understood by analogy.
By this it is proven that there is no intermediate parinirvāṇa in the formless realm.
Therefore, all that they maintain is false and illusory.

Furthermore, if one does not recite [the passage] up to "it is established as truly existent," the Master laments that there is a "house" within what is non-existent, thereby establishing the Unsurpassed Dharma King.
Regarding what is called the Tathāgata— the great generals of the Dharma such as Śāriputra and others—
it has come to pass that various schools have formed differing views, which now flourish ever more extensively.
Up to the present time, nine hundred years have passed since the treatise was composed.
If one asks at what period the various schools were divided, the *Samayabhedoparacanacakra* (Treatise on the Different Tenets of the Schools) states:
"More than one hundred years after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa."
During the time of King Aśoka,
the community was first divided into two schools:
the first was the Mahāsāṃghika.
Second, the Sthavira school.
Subsequently, within this same second century, three schools branched out from the Mahāsāṃghika:
first, the Ekavyāvahārika school; [and so forth].
Second, the Lokottaravāda;
third, the Kukkutika.
Furthermore, during this second century, another school emerged from within the Mahāsāṃghika, named the Bahuśrutīya.
Next, during this second century, another school named the Prajñaptivāda emerged from within the Mahāsāṃghika.
When the second century was completed, the Mahāsāṃghika further split into three schools.
1. The Haimavata school; 2. The Aparaseliya school;
3. The Uttaraseliya school.
Thus, the root and branch divisions of these schools are separately enumerated as nine in total:
first, the Mahāsāṃghika;
second, the Ekavyāvahārika.
Third, the Lokottaravāda school;
fourth, the Kaurukullaka school;
fifth, the Bahuśrutīya school.
Sixth, the Prajñaptivāda school;
seventh, the Caitīya school;
eighth, the Aparaśaila school.
The nine Northern Mountain Dwellers (*Uttarāpathaka*): the Sthavira school remained in a state of uniform harmony for some time;
however, at the beginning of the third century, within the Sthavira school, it split into two sects.
First, the Sarvāstivāda, also known as the Hetuvāda;
second, the Mūlasarvāstivāda, which was subsequently renamed the Haimavata.
Furthermore, during this third century, another school emerged from within the Sarvāstivāda, named the Vātsīputrīya.
Furthermore, in the third century, four schools further emerged from within the Vātsīputrīya:
first, the Dharmottarīya;
second, the Bhadrayānīya.
Third, the Saṃmitīya school;
fourth, the Mahīśāsaka school.
Furthermore, during this third century, another school named the Mahīśāsaka emerged from within the Sarvāstivāda.
Next, during this third century, a school named the Dharmaguptaka branched out from within the Mahīśāsaka school.
At the end of the third century, another school named the Kāśyapīya—also known as the Suvarṣaka—further emerged from within the Sarvāstivāda school.
At the beginning of the fourth century, another school emerged from within the Sarvāstivāda, named the Sautrāntika, also known as the Saṃkrāntika.
Thus, including both the primary schools and their branches, there are eleven schools in total.
1. The Sarvāstivāda school;
2. The Haimavata school;
3. The Vātsīputrīya school.

The four schools of the Uttarīya branch: 1. the Mahīśāsaka school; 2. the Dharmaguptaka school; 3. the Kāśyapīya school; and 4. the Sautrāntika school. The five schools of the Bhadrayānīya branch: 5. the Bhadrayānīya school; 6. the Sammitīya school; [and others]. The six schools of the Saṃmatīya branch.
7. The Mahīśāsaka school;
8. The Mahīśāsaka school;
9. The Dharmaguptaka school.
Tenth, the Kāśyapīya school;
eleventh, the Sautrāntika school.
If this is so, how is it that [beings] reach the Avīci Hell?
The absence of an intermediate state (*antarābhava*) is challenged by citing a sūtra as proof.
If an intermediate state exists, why does the sūtra say that one's present body falls directly into the Avīci Hell? [Furthermore,] Māra is named Dūṣin.
The *Dūṣaka* (Corrupter) refers to this as "ruination," while *Māra* refers to it as "killing. Thus,
the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 125, states:
When Krakucchanda Buddha rebuked Māra, that Māra immediately fell into hell.
It is heard that this Buddha had a single attendant named Zhiyuan (Vīradatta).
Entering the village of Bārāṇasī to beg for alms in sequence,
Māra’s messenger transformed himself into a young boy and hurled a stone from afar to strike him.
The attendant’s head was split open and blood flowed down his face as he followed behind the Buddha.
At that time, the Buddha turned to the right, looking back like an elephant king.
Seeing these events, he rebuked Māra, saying:
"Why do you, unwarrantedly, commit such evil karma?
At that moment, Māra’s karma being exhausted, he fell into hell. The commentary explains that when Śākyamuni Buddha was still the King of Māras, his name was Pāpīyān.
The Māra of Krakucchanda Buddha was named Duśī.
The intent of this sūtra is to explain that [the recipient] will receive [the teaching] upon taking birth in a future life.
The Master of the Treatise (Vasubandhu) thus interprets the sūtra.
Due to the predominant power of his evil karma, Māra currently experiences the fierce flames of hell encircling his body;
as the signs of suffering have already arrived and he undergoes them before him,
it is said that his present body falls headlong on account of these preceding signs.
It is not that very same Avīci Hell itself.
Why, then, does the Sūtra say, "having gone to birth in a hell"?
[The opponent] further cites a Sūtra to raise an objection, stating that there is no intermediate state (antarābhava).
Since it is stated that after committing the five heinous crimes (*ānantarya*) one is reborn in the *naraka* hell without interval, this clarifies that there is no intermediate state (*antarābhava*).
If an intermediate state were to exist, there would necessarily be an interval.
The intention of this sutra is to explain that "arriving" constitutes birth-existence (*upapattibhava*).
The Master of the Treatise cites a sūtra:
"One who commits an immediate transgression will certainly fall into hell;
there is no other realm intervening."
Furthermore, this reveals that there is no intervening karma between [the cause] and the arising [of the result].
If one were to hold the literal text as definitive,
then one would have to maintain that one is born in hell only when all five factors are complete, and not if even one is missing.
If one were to commit one, two, three, or four [of these], they should not give rise to rebirth there;
furthermore, it would follow that only these five immediate karmas (*ānantarya-karma*) could cause birth in hell, and no other karmic causes could do so.

If it were not produced, it would entail a great error; furthermore, it would mean that one is born in hell immediately after performing the karma that leads to the Avīci hell, arising in the second moment without waiting for the destruction of the body.
However, there are cases where, after having committed an immediate (ānantarya) karma, one is reborn in an immediate hell only after ten or twenty years have passed;
thus, one should not adhere strictly to the literal meaning of the text.
I maintain that the intermediate state (antarābhava) may also be designated as "birth" (jāti).
Because it is produced through skillful means,
it is also called *naraka*. *Naraka* is here translated as "unpleasant."
Because the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) of hell is likewise not to be desired,
the Sūtra states that one is "born" (*upapadyate*) in the Avīci hell;
it does not say that at that very moment one is already born.
What is the contradiction?
If that were so, then according to the verse of the Sūtra, "there would be no one to whom it applies.
