However, as long as one has not yet produced wholesome or unwholesome karma for the sake of future existence (*punarbhava*), this is the stage of grasping. Regarding the distinction between craving and grasping in the original treatise: that which first arises is called craving.
Because the continuity [of existence] is established as "grasping" (upādāna) due to its intense flourishing,
the *Nyāyānusāra* (Treatise on Right Reasoning), fascicle 28, asks:
"How is it that the two factors of craving (*tṛṣṇā*) and grasping (*upādāna*) are established separately?"

The Vaibhāṣika masters maintain that the craving of the first moment is designated by the term "craving" (tṛṣṇā), whereas this same [craving], when it has become continuous, expanded, and intensified, is established as "grasping" (upādāna).
This is because the continuity of grasping at objects becomes increasingly firm and violent. Alternatively, "grasping" is explained as "clinging" (parigraha).
This refers to the four types of clinging (*upādāna*).
Thus, the *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra*, fascicle 26, states:
"It is the state of running about everywhere in pursuit in order to obtain various desirable objects."
This stage is called "clinging" (upādāna).
There are four kinds of clinging, namely:
desire and views.
The distinctions among the grasping at precepts and observances and the grasping at a theory of self.

Because it is capable of grasping, it is called "grasping" (*upādāna*). To explain: although the branch of grasping actually encompasses all four types of grasping, it is designated as "grasping" primarily because of the predominance of craving (*tṛṣṇā*);
this is stated in contrast to the preceding [branch of] craving.
Because of this pursuit, reaching this stage is called "existence" (bhava).
Furthermore, as one gradually grows up, due to the excellence of grasping and pursuit,
one accumulates karma capable of drawing forth the fruit of future existence.
The five aggregates (pañca-skandha) existing at the stage when this karma arises are collectively termed "existence" (bhava).
Karma is called existence because it has the capacity to bring about [future results];
in this stage, karma is predominant.
It is designated by the term "existence" (*bhava*).
Thus, the *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya* states: "One should know that herein, because [the cause] is able to produce a future fruit by means of this and depending on this, it is established as 'existence.
There are two kinds of existence: namely, karma."
Regarding maturation (*vipāka*):

here, we take only the "existence of karma" (*karmabhava*) and above; according to the treatise, prior to these members of existence (*bhavāṅga*), one has mostly performed completing karma (*paripūrakakarma*) and has not yet mostly performed projecting karma (*ākṣepakakarma*).
If, in the present, craving, grasping, and becoming do not arise,
it should be understood that [the consciousness] is nonetheless subsumed under the link of feeling (*vedanā*).
By this karmic force, it reaches the very state of consciousness as it is now.
Thus, by the power of present karma, at the very moment one passes away from this life and is about to take rebirth, all the five aggregates that exist for a single kṣaṇa are termed "birth" (*jāti*).
This branch of birth (*jāti-aṅga*) is precisely like the present consciousness, each lasting for a single kṣaṇa.
The name is designated based on the excellence of the future birth;
the present consciousness is given its designation according to its own essential nature.
From the moment after birth until the four branches of contact and feeling:
All the five aggregates existing during the intermediate stages from the moment after birth until the position of the future *vedanā* link are collectively termed "aging and death" (*jarāmaraṇa*).
Thus, this aging and death is equivalent to the four [links] beginning with name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) in the present life; the designation "aging and death" applies across these four positions.
It may be said, in brief, that birth serves as the condition;
because the characteristics of old age and death become manifest following the branch of birth, it is designated by that name.
Such is the analysis of the distinct natures of the twelve branches.
Summary: Furthermore,

regarding the statement that "the various dependent originations extend up to four [links] as a distant succession," the following constitutes the third major section of the text, which clarifies the intended meaning of the original teaching.
Among these, the first clarifies the explanation according to stages;
the second clarifies the elimination of ignorance and delusion.
This is the first section.
It introduces the general exposition of the four types of dependent origination:
momentary (*kṣaṇika*), which refers to a single moment; and continuous (*sāmbandhika*).
"Succession" refers to the sequential connection of preceding and succeeding states.
"Phases" refers to the twelve preceding and succeeding phases.
"Continuity" refers to the uninterrupted succession through intervening periods.
This is a general enumeration of names.
What is meant by "moment" (*kṣaṇa*)? [This is] the question.
That which is called "death" refers to the moment of reaching destruction. Answer:
It means that within a single moment, one who kills out of desire possesses all twelve links [of dependent origination], including ignorance (*moha*).
That is to say: ignorance associated with craving; volition associated with craving—this is *saṃskāra*;
consciousness that discerns objects while associated with craving is called *vijñāna*;
and the three aggregates coexisting with that consciousness.

This means that, within the five aggregates, with the exception of consciousness and feeling—which are established as separate factors—the aggregate of perception in its entirety and a portion of the aggregates of form and formations are included.
As for the portion of the aggregate of form:
This means that within the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*), with the exception of the five sense faculties and the bodily and vocal informative and non-informative actions—
which are established as separate factors— one takes the remaining form associated with consciousness.
Regarding "a portion of the aggregate of formations" (*saṃskāra-skandha*):

this refers to excluding ignorance (*avidyā*), volition (*cetanā*), contact (*sparśa*), craving (*rāga*), as well as lack of shame (*āhrīkya*), lack of dread (*anapatrāpya*), lethargy (*styāna*), and restlessness (*auddhatya*) from within the aggregate of formations.
It arises, differs, and ceases together [with consciousness],
because it is established as a distinct factor and because it includes the remaining aggregates that coexist with consciousness.
The three aggregates together with consciousness are collectively termed "name-and-form" (*nāmarūpa*).
"Name-and-form" is the general category,
while the sense faculties (*indriya*) are its specific instances.
Because the specific [bases] are subsumed under the general,
it is said that the name "abiding" refers to the sense-faculties (*indriya*). Although the number is fewer, the five material sense-faculties are explained as the six bases (*āyatana*).

As explained regarding name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*): because it is by the power of that [name-and-form] that the six [senses] can be fulfilled, the *Nyāyānusāra* states that the material sense-faculties are called the "six bases" (*ṣaḍāyatana*). Furthermore, another interpretation holds that the mind's abiding is called the "faculty."
The five faculties, such as the eye, abide in the material faculties;
therefore, it is said that they abide in name-and-form (nāmarūpa) and are called the six sense bases (ṣaḍāyatana).
Although the mind (manas) is past while the other five are present, they are designated as the "six sense bases" based on their majority presence.

It may be so. If the manifest consciousness (*vijñāna*) is designated as "mind" (*manas*) in relation to what follows it, then the aggregate of feeling (*vedanā-skandha*) would also be designated as "name-and-form" (*nāmarūpa*) in relation to that [consciousness].
Why, then, is this not stated? The explanation is as follows: both "name" (*nāma*) and "form" (*rūpa*) each possess distinct dharmas that constitute the essence of name-and-form.

Since there is no other distinct dharma in the present that serves as the mind (*manas*), consciousness (*vijñāna*) itself is taken as the mind. When the six sense bases (*ṣaḍ-āyatana*) encounter their respective objects, a distinct contact (*sparśa*) arises from the triadic conjunction with consciousness. The experience of contact is called feeling (*vedanā*). Craving (*tṛṣṇā*) is itself attachment (*rāga*). The outbursts (*paryavasthāna*) associated with attachment—namely, lack of shame (*āhrīkya*), lack of dread (*anapatrāpya*), lethargy (*styāna*), and restlessness (*auddhatya*)—are called grasping (*upādāna*). The manifest (*vijñapti*) and unmanifest (*avijñapti*) actions of body and speech that arise simultaneously with craving in the same moment are called becoming (*bhava*). These various dharmas, when they are about to arise in the future, are called birth (*jāti*). When they reach the present and undergo transformation through the maturation of distinct characteristics, it is called aging (*jarā*).
The moment the characteristic of cessation undergoes destruction is called death.
"Abiding" is subsumed within name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*). Question: Birth exists in the future, while old age and death exist in the present.

They are distinguished at that very moment. How can a single *kṣaṇa* possess twelve factors? One explanation states: this is based on the fact that a single *kṣaṇa* is defined by the completion of the activity of the four characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*); therefore, it possesses all twelve branches. Another explanation states: the characteristic of arising (*jāti-lakṣaṇa*) does not depend on its activity, but is spoken of as the "branch of birth" simply because it manifests in the present. This teaching of momentary dependent origination (*kṣaṇika-pratītyasamutpāda*) applies exclusively to sentient beings and is limited to the conditioned (*sāsrava*).

Furthermore, there are those who say that "pervasive throughout all conditioned phenomena" refers to the momentary and the continuous; this explains what is pervasive throughout all conditioned phenomena.
Sentient and non-sentient;
with outflows and without outflows;
because they differ moment by moment, these divergent explanations are set forth.
Because the meaning of "conjunction" (*saṃyojana*) is the same [as that of "bond"], it is not explained separately.
"Conjunction" (*saṃ*) means "uninterrupted," and "bond" (*yojana*) means "to join together. Alternatively, "conjunction" (*saṃ*) means "immediately following."
Being bound together is called "bondage.
Therefore, the *Nyāyānusāra* states:
"Dependent origination as continuous bondage refers to the arising [of phenomena] through the uninterrupted connection of causes and effects of both similar and dissimilar classes."
Regarding the statement that "the twelve links of dependent origination are all subsumed under the category of states":
this refers to the five aggregates (pañcaskandha) existing throughout the sequential stages of the twelve links, which, through their uninterrupted continuity, are termed "states" (avasthā).
This is explained with reference to birth, indeterminate karma, and afflictions;
therefore, the *Nyāyānusāra* states:
"The dependent origination of stages."
This refers to the uninterrupted succession of the twelve factors of the five aggregates across three lifetimes.
That which is thus separated by a great distance is designated as "distant succession" (*viprakṛṣṭānuvartana*).
This state of dependent origination, being remote in its continuity, is called "distant succession."
This is explained in terms of subsequent [rebirth] and indeterminate [karma].
Thus, the *Nyāyānusāra* states that it is the "distant continuity of dependent origination" (*dūra-anvaya-pratītyasamutpāda*).

This means that because there are karmas to be experienced in subsequent lives and indeterminate karmas, as well as afflictions, throughout the prior and subsequent limits [of time], one revolves in saṃsāra without beginning. One should understand that these are the four distinct types of dependent origination.
Momentary dependent origination refers to that which is explained in terms of mutual relation within a single moment.
According to the previous interpretation, this pertains exclusively to sentient beings and is characterized by outflows (*sāsrava*).
If one follows the latter master, [the dependent origination of] non-sentient things and the untainted (anāsrava) are also included.
The other three types of dependent origination are all explained in terms of mutual relation between preceding and succeeding factors.
Among these, the "bound-together" (*sambaddha*) type applies to both sentient and non-sentient things.
There are the contaminated (*sāsrava*) and the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*).
Regarding the state (*avasthā*) and the distant succession (*dūra-anubandha*), these apply only to sentient beings and are exclusively contaminated.

If it is a continuous connection (*prabandha*), it refers to the immediate adjacency of preceding and succeeding moments in a continuous stream. If it is a state (*avasthā*), [it refers to the various conditions within that stream].
Regarding the uninterrupted succession arising through the twelve stages, it is also taught as being indeterminate.
If it is a distant succession, it is based on the latter part of the stages, and it is also taught as being indeterminate.
What is the intended meaning of the Blessed One in this regard?
This is the statement of the formal inquiry:
among these four types of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*), what is the one intended by the Blessed One?
The verse says: "Regarding the establishment of the names of the members based on their predominance":
the first line provides the direct answer, while the second line clarifies the rationale for establishing those names.
The Commentary states: "Up to the point where there are twelve branches" is a tradition accepted by the Vaibhāṣika masters.

They maintain that among the four types of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*), the Blessed One spoke of the twelve branches of dependent origination solely with reference to the sequential stages (*avasthā*).
If it is the case that within each link [of dependent origination] one arrives at names such as "ignorance" (avidyā) and so forth,
a question arises:
since there is no fault in the fact that the names differ according to the various stages, why is this so?
Answer: Ignorance is predominant because it is the root of all existence and because it arises both independently and in association [with other factors].

Because it is difficult to discern once the various afflictions have been extinguished, as it resembles ignorance, the Sūtra states that it "shatters the grain of ignorance. Next, regarding the excellence of *saṃskāra*:
*saṃskāra* refers to volitional formation (*abhisamskāra*).

Because karma is the most predominant among the factors that bring about the ripening of results when performing an action, one speaks of "past karma" when observing present results. Next, regarding the predominance of consciousness:
because consciousness is the most predominant at the moment of initial conception.
The Sūtra states that a sentient being is constituted by the six elements;
although the other five exist, they are not as dominant as consciousness,
for consciousness is the sovereign of the body.
It is called the "mind-king" because [it is predominant];
next, it is called the "predominance of name-and-form" because, in this stage, both name and form are predominant; next, it is called the "predominance of the six sense bases."
In this stage, the six sense bases (ṣaḍāyatana) are first perfected because the characteristics of the faculties become manifest. Next, contact (sparśa) is predominant;
for once the six faculties are complete, the union of faculty, object, and consciousness first gives rise to the fruit of contact.
First, contact (sparśa) is predominant because its function is to touch the preceding object. Next, feeling (vedanā) is predominant;
since one has already made contact with the object, feeling subsequently experiences and assimilates it, and thus its function is predominant. Next, craving (tṛṣṇā) is predominant.
Having already received them, because the craving for the requisites of enjoyment is predominant and the characteristic of craving is manifest, one next grasps at what is superior.
Once craving has arisen, it may gradually increase and grasp at preceding objects;
because its grasping function is predominant,
the past aspect is obscured and is collectively termed ignorance (*avidyā*).
In the present phase, craving (*tṛṣṇā*) and grasping (*upādāna*) are explained separately because they possess superior characteristics.
Once grasping has arisen, existence (*bhava*) immediately follows;
"existence" means having the capacity to produce results in a future life.
This is precisely the nature of karma.
Because karma is predominant at this stage, it is designated by that name;
because manifest karma is preeminent in its initial seeking of future results, it is designated by that name.
Past karma is not designated by its own name because it is no longer being newly sought; rather, that which produces excellence in the subsequent birth is so called because,
once the present karma has been performed and the future fruit is certain to be experienced,
the phase of "arising" (jāti-lakṣaṇa) becomes manifest as that future fruit is about to come into existence.
Because the characteristic of arising is predominant,
those who perform actions all say, "In the future, where shall I be born?
Because the present consciousness is predominant, it is designated by the name "consciousness."
Regarding the future birth being designated by its excellence: after one has been born, aging and death necessarily follow;
because the characteristics of aging and death are most prominent at this stage, it is designated by their excellence.
In the present [life], because the four functions of name-and-form and so forth are each predominant and their characteristics are clearly manifest,
each is established as a separate limb.

Although old age and death are manifest in the future, they are somewhat more difficult to discern in comparison to the four branches of the present; thus, "old age and death" is given as a collective designation. As for why "abiding" is not established as a separate branch:
The Sūtra does not state that [the unconditioned] exists within the three realms of existence (tridhātu),
because it would then be confused with the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta) and because it does not induce revulsion.
Regarding the question, "For what reason does the Sūtra say 'up to' and so forth, as explained in detail?"— it asks:
for what reason does the Sūtra speak of twelve stages?
Regarding the statement in the treatise that "all conditioned phenomena" and the expression in the Sūtra "up to this is called the distinction," the answer is:
[the word] "etcetera" (ādi).
The term "and so forth" includes both the contaminated (*sāsrava*) and the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*).
While the Sūtra speaks with a specific intent regarding only the states (*avasthā*), the continuity (*prabandha*), sentient beings (*sattva*), and the contaminated and so forth, the Śāstra,
following the general principle of the Dharma, applies it to each moment (*kṣaṇa*).
The continuous bond [applies] to sentient and non-sentient beings,
as well as to the out-flowing and the out-flow-free, and so forth.
This is called the distinction.
Why does the sutra speak only of "sentient beings"?
Below this, the second section clarifies the dispelling of delusion and confusion.
Based on the sūtra, a question is raised.
The verse says: "Up to 'only among sentient beings.
This means that it is only said that sentient beings sever the delusions and confusions of others.
Ordinary beings are deluded regarding their own internal bodies across the three time periods;
the Buddha, in order to sever that [delusion], taught dependent origination across the three time periods with reference to sentient beings.
How is it that sentient beings are deluded regarding the prior limit?
Question:
Regarding the passage from "Concerning the past" up to "How did I exist?"— Answer:
This reveals doubt concerning the prior limit (*pūrvānta*), namely: "Did I exist, or did I not exist, in the past?
This is the first doubt regarding whether the self exists; if one asserts that it existed, then one must specify: "In what way did I exist? Thus, non-existence is beyond verbal expression.
Is it identical with the aggregates?
Is it distinct from the aggregates?
Or is form the self?
Is it feeling, perception, and so forth?
This is the second doubt regarding my own self-nature: if one adheres to any one among these as being the self, how could there be [the thought], "I have existed"?
"Is it permanent or impermanent?
Is it male, female, and so forth?
This is the third type of doubt concerning the distinctions of the self.
Regarding how sentient beings are deluded concerning the future limit:
it is asked, that is, from [the thought] "What will become of me in the future? up to "How shall I come to exist?"?
Answer: This clarifies ignorance regarding the future limit (*aparānta*).
It may be understood by analogy with the explanation provided for the past.
How is it that sentient beings are deluded regarding the middle limit?
Question:
It refers to [the thought] regarding the middle limit: "Who will I become? or "What will I become?"
Answer: This clarifies delusion regarding the intermediate state (*madhyānta*).
Because one definitively knows that [the self] exists in the present, one does not doubt its non-existence. [One wonders: "What is this 'I'?"
Doubt regarding the self-nature [of the self] is: "What is this self?
Doubt regarding the specific distinctions of the self follows the explanation provided for the prior limit.
Regarding this present self, what was its cause in the past?
Regarding this present self, what will be its fruit in the future life?
One does not doubt the prior limit because the causal essence is indeed a cause.
One does not doubt the fruit because it is known through its manifestation;
one does not doubt the future cause because it is known through its manifestation;
and one does not doubt the essence of the fruit because it is the fruit itself.
Therefore, there are two doubts regarding cause and effect in the middle period,
and two doubts regarding existence and non-existence in the prior and subsequent periods;
it is for the purpose of eliminating such [doubts] that [the Buddha taught] "up to" "existence and non-existence," and so forth.
This is the summary.
Because it eliminates delusion regarding the three time periods, the Sūtra speaks only of the dependent origination of sentient beings;
it explains past ignorance and formations in their respective order to eliminate delusion regarding the prior limit.
The teaching on future birth, aging, and death removes delusion regarding the future limit (*aparānta*).
The teaching on the eight [factors] from consciousness to existence removes delusion regarding the intermediate limit (*madhyānta*).

The dependent origination of the three time periods consists solely of the mutual connection between cause and effect across the preceding and succeeding moments; it lacks autonomy and truly has no self.
The Sūtra states that one can eliminate ignorance regarding these three periods by observing them with right wisdom.
The statement by other masters that [ignorance] pertains to the cause of the future limit (*aparānta*) is a citation of a divergent view; for craving (*tṛṣṇā*),
grasping (*upādāna*), and existence (*bhava*) are the causes of the future, and thus ignorance regarding the future is excluded from the causes, which follow from their effects.

The *Nyāyabindu* refutes this, stating: "One should also say that from consciousness up to feeling [are taught] for the purpose of eliminating others' delusions regarding the prior limit (*pūrvānta*).
Since these five are all results of the prior limit, there would then be no intermediate limit (*madhyānta*)."
This would contradict the sūtras;
alternatively, they should have provided the specific reasons for the distinction,
yet they were unable to do so.
Therefore, the preceding argument for superiority is established; furthermore, the above treatise provides an additional objection:
if causes are derived from effects, then since the two past causes would follow from the five present effects, there would be no prior limit (*pūrvānta*).
If one considers the fruits from the perspective of their causes,
then by taking the two future fruits from the three present causes, there would be no end to the succession.
If one considers the three present causes from the perspective of the two future fruits, [the same fault follows].
Since the five present fruits arise from two past causes, there would be no intermediate state;
for this reason, it should be known that the previous explanation is correct.
Furthermore, it should be understood that "this reaching" refers to the fruit and the cause.
Below this is the fourth section, which summarizes the extensive by means of the concise, condensing the twelve extensive points into two or three concise ones.
This constitutes the general heading.
As for its meaning: what is it?
Question:
The verse states, "Reaching [the limit] through the middle, one can infer the two.
The first two lines correctly clarify the inclusion.
The final two lines resolve an objection.
The *Treatise* states: "Because [the afflictions, karma, and things] constitute the intrinsic nature. This refers to the afflictions (*kleśa*), karma (*karman*), and the objective entities (*vastu*).
Furthermore, it should be understood that these are subsumed within cause and effect, comprising twelve [categories].
Because one creates causes based upon the fruit of a foundational entity, it is called the "foundational entity" (*vastu*).
Alternatively, because afflictions and karma arise in dependence upon this fruit of the foundational entity, it is the "foundational entity" upon which they rely.
Regarding the phrase "for what reason, in the middle period, [the afflictions] reach only one":
this asks why,
because the middle period is extensive, it would be useless to speak further.
Answer: The characteristics of the middle period are explained extensively because both cause and fruit are manifest;
the preceding and succeeding periods are explained briefly because they are difficult to discern.
Since the broad meaning has already been established through the middle and the last [of the three types of inference],
if one were to argue that the links of dependent origination lead to the fault of infinite regress,
this section below provides the fifth explanation to resolve such doubts and difficulties.
This is the statement of the doubt:
if there were no result-link (phala-aṅga), there would have to be a beginning and an end;
if one were to further establish additional links, it would result in the fallacy of infinite regress (anavasthā).
Regarding the statement that one should not further establish [a category] because its meaning is already manifest:
the answer is that one should not further establish anything outside of the twelve links.
However, there is no fault of having a beginning or an end, nor of being infinite, as previously stated;
for the Blessed One has already revealed this within these twelve [links] by way of their meaning. How has he revealed it?
Exegesis:
The verse says, "As for the principle of the factors of existence (bhavāṅga), it is only this.
This is the answer in verse.
The Commentary states: "As for the phrase 'its principle is simply this,' it can be understood from the explanation of the verse.
Since [the process] from birth to old age and death has already been revealed, what is the purpose of the statement 'up to this'?"
If name-and-form gives rise to the six sense bases,
the six sense bases give rise to contact,
and contact gives rise to feeling.
It has already been shown that old age and death are the causal basis for the factors of existence;
it has also been shown that birth and craving are the causal basis for delusion regarding old age and death;
furthermore, birth and craving are manifested as the resultant effects of ignorance.
If craving gives rise to grasping, this already reveals ignorance as the fruit of affliction;
for past ignorance is presently of the nature of the two afflictions of craving and grasping,
while future old age and death are presently of the nature of the four factors of name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, and feeling.
By this, it has already been demonstrated that old age and death are the cause and ignorance is the fruit;
what need is there to further establish other members of dependent origination?
Therefore, there is no fault of having a beginning or an end.
Therefore, the Sūtra states regarding the twelvefold dependent origination: "In this way, there is the arising of this entire great mass of suffering.
By citing the intent of this Sūtra, it is proven that ignorance is also an effect, and old age and death are also causes.
The twelve links of existence all pertain to both suffering (*duḥkha*) and its origin (*samudaya*).
The sense of being the fruit of these links is termed the aggregate of suffering;
the sense of being the cause of these links is explained as the origin.
If it is not admitted that ignorance is the fruit and old age and death are the cause,
what is the purpose of this sutra’s statement?
Regarding the statement, "There is another explanation which says: 'As for those [passages] in this sūtra,'" this below records alternative interpretations.
This is the ancient explanation of Vasubandhu.
This is the later Vasubandhu, the master;
that is to say, in the commentary on the first fascicle of the *Abhidharmasamuccaya*, it states that Vasubandhu was a divergent teacher within the Sarvāstivāda school.
Since this has already been refuted herein, it is not contradicted by correct reasoning.
As ignorance arises from the cause of improper attention (*ayoniśomanasikāra*),
it is known that beginningless improper attention is also subsumed within the link of grasping (*upādāna*).
Because these four types of grasping (*upādāna*) encompass a broad range of phenomena—
encompassing not only the various afflictions (*kleśa*) but also improper mental attention (*ayoniśo-manasikāra*)—

and because it is stated that [improper mental attention] is included within this Sūtra on the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination, no further links of dependent origination are established. Alternatively, the passage beginning with "or improper mental attention" serves as a response to anticipated objections.

The objection raised here intends to ask: if improper mental attention (*ayoniśo-manasikāra*) were the cause of ignorance (*avidyā*), why does the Sūtra on the Twelvefold Dependent Origination (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda*) not establish it as a separate limb?

Therefore, it is now stated generally that not only the various afflictions are subsumed under the limb of grasping (*upādāna*), but improper mental attention (*ayoniśomanasikāra*) is also subsumed under the limb of grasping;
for this reason, it is also taught within the *Pratītyasamutpāda-sūtra* and is not established separately.
Regarding the claim that this improper mental attention (*ayoniśomanasikāra*) serves as the condition for the link of origination (*pratītyasamutpādāṅga*),
the Master refutes it:

if one says that because this improper mental attention is associated with those four types of grasping (*upādāna*) and afflictions, it is therefore subsumed under the link of grasping, [that is incorrect].
If craving and ignorance were also associated with the four graspings (upādāna) and should likewise be subsumed within the four graspings,
then other members of dependent origination (pratītyasamutpāda) should not be established separately.
Even if it were granted that they are subsumed under the member of grasping, how could this prove that they are the causes of ignorance?
If you say that merely being included within the four types of grasping (*upādāna*) proves the existence of cause and effect,
then since craving (*tṛṣṇā*) and ignorance (*avidyā*) are also included within the four graspings, they would likewise prove the existence of cause and effect; thus,
craving and ignorance should not be established as separate factors.
Another further explains, saying "up to the defiled attention (*kliṣṭamanasikāra*).
This is the interpretation of Śrīlāta within the Sautrāntika school;
he is known as Zhisheng (執勝).
The *Nyāya* [school] calls this the "Elder" (*sthavira*).
Since improper mental attention (*ayoniśo-manasikāra*) has ignorance as its cause and is subsumed under the factor of contact (*sparśa*),
another sutra states that at the stage of the six sense bases (*ṣaḍ-āyatana*), an afflicted and turbid mental attention born of delusion arises with the eye and visible forms as conditions.
In the preceding moment at the stage of the six sense bases, delusion (*moha*) is that which gives rise [to the subsequent state];
in the succeeding moment at the stage of contact (*sparśa*), defiled attention (*kliṣṭamanasikāra*) is that which is produced.
Therefore, it is said that "delusion gives rise to the defiled attention that is produced."
Citing the intent of this sūtra as proof, it is stated that improper mental attention (*ayoniśo-manasikāra*) occurs at the time of contact (*sparśa*).
This improper mental attention at the time of contact serves as the cause,
which necessarily induces ignorance (*avidyā*) at the subsequent stage of feeling (*vedanā*).
This precisely clarifies that ignorance has a cause;
thus, other sūtras state that through the contact of ignorance, it is revealed that at the time of contact there is improper mental attention (*ayoniśomanasikāra*).
The various feelings that arise serve as conditions for the arising of craving;
this further demonstrates that the stage of feeling necessarily involves ignorance.
Citing the intent of this sutra, it is proven that ignorance arises from improper mental attention (*ayoniśo-manasikāra*).
He then summarizes by saying:

Therefore, at the time of the preceding moment of contact, irrational mental attention (ayoniśomanasikāra) together with the subsequent moment of feeling functions as the condition for ignorance (avidyā).
By this, ignorance is not subject to the fault of being causeless.
Because it arises from improper mental attention (*ayoniśo-manasikāra*),
there is no need to establish further members of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*),

as improper mental attention is subsumed within the member of contact (*sparśa*). Furthermore, by explaining below that improper mental attention arises from ignorance (*avidyā*), the fault of infinite regress (*anavasthā*) is avoided.
Since the Sūtra states that defiled attention arises from delusion (*moha*), it is clear that improper attention (*ayoniśomanasikāra*) arises from ignorance (*avidyā*).
This citation from the Sūtra proves that improper attention is said to exist at the time of contact (*sparśa*).
Now, this sūtra is cited to prove that improper mental attention (*ayoniśomanasikāra*) arises from ignorance (*avidyā*).
Although the same sūtra is cited in both cases,
the intended meaning in each instance is distinct.
Although other sūtras contain statements that should have been further explained,
the Master of the Treatise refutes them,
noting that although other sūtras contain such sincere words, [they are incomplete].
"However, there are things that ought to be further explained in this Mahānidāna Sūtra,
and things that need not be further explained," the Elder replied.
Regarding how this is known through realization,
the author of the treatise further inquires:
"It is known through reasoning."
The Elder replied:
"What constitutes the principle?
The Master of the Treatise then further questioned him.
"As for the statement that 'it is known because feeling apart from ignorance serves as the proof,' the Elder replied:
'Feeling that is not associated with ignorance cannot serve as a condition for craving.'"
Because an Arhat experiences feelings without craving arising,
it is clear that whenever craving arises upon experiencing a feeling, ignorance must necessarily be present simultaneously.
Furthermore, a non-erroneous contact cannot serve as the condition for defiled feeling,
nor can it become erroneous apart from contact associated with ignorance;
this is because the contact of an Arhat is not erroneous.
Since perverted ignorance-contact can serve as the condition for defiled feeling,
it is clearly known that at the same time as contact, there must necessarily be irrational mental attention (*ayoniśo-manasikāra*).
Herein, the intended meaning is that at the moment of contact, irrational mental attention acts as the condition to produce ignorance at the stage of feeling.
This demonstrates that ignorance arises from causes and is also subsumed within the contact of improper mental attention;
it is known through such reasoning as proof.
If that were so, then the objection raised by the commentator—
that it would result in the failure to establish [the position]— would entail a great fault;
for [the point] can be established through correct reasoning.
In that case, it would follow that all the factors [of dependent origination] need not be further established by scriptural evidence.
Thus, the Elder’s explanation does not resolve the objection.
Nevertheless, what the Elder said was intended primarily to dispel the delusions of others.
The Master of the Treatise restates the objection and further explains the intent of the Sūtra:

the World-Honored One, in order to eliminate the delusions regarding the three time periods of sentient beings, briefly taught the twelve links of dependent origination as cause and effect across the three times.
That he teaches the Dharma according to the capacities of his audience has already been analyzed above.
In principle, this is complete.
It is not that within this sutra one intends to demonstrate that old age and death have a fruit or that ignorance has a cause;
rather, it is spoken from the perspective of reasoning.
The former is infinite because birth and death have no beginning;
the latter can be exhausted because once one attains the Way, they cease to exist.
As the World-Honored One has taught, what is the difference between these two?
Below this, the sixth major section explains the scriptural text.
It begins by posing questions based on the sutra.
First, regarding the main treatise’s statement, "because it reaches all phenomena":
Answer: For now,
according to the original treatise, there is no distinction between these two,
because both terms encompass all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*).
Regarding the question, "How can that which has reached the future be called 'dependently arisen'?
an external objection states:
"The past and present have already arisen and may thus be termed 'already arisen'; [but how so for the future?]
How can that which has not yet arisen in the future be called "already arisen"?
And how can that which is in the future be designated as "conditioned" (*saṃskṛta*)?
[The author] thus raises a counter-objection against the opponent.
That which has already been produced through volitional effort is called "conditioned" (*saṃskṛta*).
How can future maturation (*vipāka*), which has not yet been produced through volitional effort,
be said to be "conditioned" in the same way as the past and present?
However, in the Sanskrit original, the term for "conditioned" (*saṃskṛta*) contains the sense of "already" (*saṃ*). Thus,
it should properly be stated as "already conditioned" (*saṃskṛta*),
because it has been produced by the power of volitional effort (*cetanā*).
The opponent explains:
Future ripening fruits are called "conditioned" because they have already been produced by the power of present wholesome or unwholesome volitions (*cetanā*).
If that is so, how can the untainted (*anāsrava*) be conditioned?
The master of the treatise further objects:
Since future untainted phenomena are not maturation,
how can they be conditioned?
Regarding the phrase "because it has already been produced by the power of wholesome volition," the non-Buddhist (bāhyaka) explains:
that future untainted [dharma] is also called conditioned because it has already been produced by the power of present wholesome volition.
If it were the case that one would likewise attain *nirvāṇa*, the Master of the Treatise further objects:

"The name 'future untainted phenomena' is applied because they have already been produced by the power of wholesome volition; thus, the arising of their acquisition (*prāpti*) constitutes what is called 'conditioned' (*saṃskṛta*)."
Nirvana also arises through the power of wholesome reflection; thus, one attains Nirvana.
Consequently, Nirvana should be called conditioned (*saṃskṛta*).
Therefore, it is said: "If that were so, then the attainment of Nirvana would likewise be so."
"In reality, one should say that there is no fault in [the term] reaching what has been explained," is the Master’s correct interpretation;
he explains that the future is called "dependently arisen."
In truth, one should say that this is spoken in terms of "category" (*jāti*).
Because it belongs to the category of that which has already arisen in the past and present, it is also called "already arisen.
This is illustrated by means of a metaphor.
"Transformation and decay" refers to form (rūpa).
Just as future form, although not yet subject to transformation and decay,
is still designated by the name "form" because it belongs to the same category as form that has undergone transformation and decay in the past and present.
The future is called "already arisen" because it is identical in kind;
thus, there is no fault in this explanation. Furthermore, "form" (*rūpa*) is explained as that which is subject to transformation and decay.
Just as future form, although not yet transformed or decayed, still receives the designation "form."
Because of this, the categories of form (*rūpa*) in the past and present are identical;
thus, there is no fault in what was said regarding the future having already arisen.
However, the current explanation is intended to establish that [form] possesses the nature of cause and effect (*hetu-phalatva*).
The Master of the Treatise correctly explains two phrases from the Sūtra.
"If that were so, the establishment [of the two] would not be simultaneous"—
this is an objection.

Since cause and effect have no distinct substantial entities, the establishment of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) and that which has arisen dependently (*pratītyasamutpanna*) would not be possible simultaneously. This is not so;
for when one examines the referents of such names as "father" and "son," [they are established].
Explanation:
They differ according to their mutual dependence.
That is to say, if one considers this prior cause, it is called "dependently arisen."
It is not that observing this prior cause is itself termed "dependent origination" (*pratītyasamutpāda*);
rather, it is when one observes this subsequent effect that it is termed "dependent origination.
Nor is it that observing this subsequent effect is itself termed "dependently arisen" (*pratītyasamutpanna*).
Although the perspectives regarding a single phenomenon differ,
it is just as when a single object is called a "cause" in relation to what follows and a "result" in relation to what precedes;
the same applies to father and son.
Regarding the Venerable Vaṅgīsa’s statement that "all unconditioned phenomena (asaṃskṛta-dharma) are dependently originated" (pratītyasamutpanna):
Vaṅgīsa meant that if something has arisen from causes, it is called "dependently originated," which comprehensively includes all phenomena of the past and present.
If something serves as a cause for others, it is called "dependent origination" (*pratītyasamutpāda*).
This includes all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*) of the three time periods, with the sole exception of past and present phenomena and the final mind of an Arhat.

Since the substance of dependent origination is narrow while the time period is broad, and the substance of "that which has arisen dependently" (*pratītyasamutpanna*) is broad while the time period is narrow, four logical alternatives (*catuṣkoṭi*) are established. The first alternative consists of those things that are dependent origination but not "that which has arisen dependently."
This means that future dharmas are called "dependent origination" because they can function as causes;
however, those not yet reached—the past and present—are not "dependently arisen. The second category consists of those that are dependently arisen but are not dependent origination.
This refers to the final moment of consciousness of an Arhat, which takes past and present phenomena as its object;

because it reaches back to the past and the present, it is "dependently arisen" (pratītyasamutpanna) but cannot function as a cause, and thus is not "dependent origination" (pratītyasamutpāda). The third category is both dependent origination and dependently arisen.
That is to say, with the exception of the final mind of an Arhat, all other [phenomena] of the past and present are called "dependent origination" (pratītyasamutpāda) because they can act as causes;
they are called "dependently arisen" (pratītyasamutpanna) because they have reached the past and present. The fourth alternative is that which is neither dependent origination nor dependently arisen.
That is to say, all unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*) cannot serve as causes to take up effects; therefore, they are not dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*).
Because their essence is eternal, they do not arise from causes and are not "arisen from conditions" (*pratyayaja*).
Regarding the point where the Sautrāntika masters reach a contradiction with the meaning of the sūtras,
the following section provides a definitive resolution.
This specifically recounts the Sautrāntika critique that the dependent origination of the temporal states has the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*) as its substance.
Since the sūtras state that ignorance and the others have the lack of knowledge regarding the three time periods as their essence,
it is clear that they do not have the five aggregates as their essence.
This [position] contradicts the sūtras, for the sūtras are of definitive meaning (*nītārtha*).
Regarding the statement that "it should not be the case that all sūtras are likewise [definitive]," the Sarvāstivādins offer this defense:
Not all sūtras are of definitive meaning (*nītārtha*); there are also those spoken according to what is predominant (*yathāpradhāna*).
As stated in the *Hastipadopama-sūtra*: "What is the internal earth element? It refers to hair, body hair, nails, and so forth.

Although these things—hair, body hair, nails, and the rest—are not devoid of other qualities such as color, odor, taste, tangibility, and the other three great elements (*mahābhūta*), they are designated by their predominant characteristic.
Because the earth element in hair, body hair, nails, and so forth is solid,
hair, body hair, and the like are used to explain the internal earth element.
The principle regarding the factors such as ignorance taught in this sutra should also be understood in this way.
Although it is not that other aggregates such as form do not exist therein,
they are designated by names such as "ignorance" (avidyā) because of their predominance.
As for the cited passage, it does not prove that [ignorance] is the only thing remaining until nothing else exists.
The Sautrāntika school refutes this,
stating that the cited passage is not proof;
for in the *Hastipadopama-sūtra*, the internal earth element was intended to be used to distinguish hair, body hair, and so forth.
This is an incomplete explanation of how [the body] is formed;
that is to say, the earth element is narrow,
whereas the hair, body hair, and so forth are broad.
It possesses visible form, odor, taste, and tangibility. If that sutra asks,
"What are the hair, body hair, and so forth called?"— referring to the internal earth element—
it may be answered by citing the most prominent [characteristic], as you suggest.

Although hair, body hair, and so forth possess color and other qualities, because the earth element is predominant therein, that sutra distinguishes hair, body hair, and so forth as internal earth-derivatives; it does not mean that the earth element transcends hair, body hair, and so forth.
Therefore, the *Hastipadopama-sūtra* is a complete exposition;
this *Pratītyasamutpāda-sūtra*, which explains ignorance (*avidyā*) and the other factors,
is likewise established as a complete exposition, just like the *Hastipadopama-sūtra*.
Therefore, apart from the factors such as ignorance that have been mentioned, there is no other dharma.
This demonstrates that the cited sūtra contradicts one's own [position] and accords with that of others.
Is it not the case that the earth element exists even in its essential nature?
The Sarvāstivādins raise an objection:
"Is it not the case that the internal earth element also exists within hair, body hair, snot, tears, and so forth?
If so, then hair and the like would not be fully subsumed under the category of 'earth'."
This is not an exhaustive explanation;
rather, it is spoken of in terms of what is predominant.
As for [the statement] that "nasal mucus and so forth should likewise be displayed until now," [it refers to the following].
The Sautrāntikas resolve this objection:
mucus, tears, and so forth are also said to be included in that *Hastipadopama-sūtra*,
just as it says, "Furthermore, there are other things within the body."
"Other things" refers to substances such as mucus and tears.
Even if one were to grant that there is a distinct earth element within mucus, tears, and so forth—just as there is in hair, body hair, and the like.
Apart from the factor of ignorance (*avidyā*), there must be some other form of ignorance that should now be demonstrated.
However, apart from ignorance, there is no separate ignorance.
If one were to bring in something of a different category here, what benefit would it serve?
The Sautrāntika school further rebukes:
"If one brings in five aggregates of a different category and places them within ignorance, what benefit is there?
Even if, in all stages, it were exactly as described," [it would still be flawed].
The Sautrāntika school establishes a reasoning that universally explains and confirms their own position:
although all twelve links possess the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*),
they do not take those very five aggregates as their essential nature (*svabhāva*).
Only that which is mutually dependent can be established as a constituent member (*aṅga*).
However, when the presence or absence of a particular effect is determined by the presence or absence of a particular cause,
that causal factor may be established as a constituent member of that resultant factor.
Just as an arhat, although possessing the five aggregates, lacks formative activity (saṃskāra)—
namely, meritorious, non-meritorious, or imperturbable formative activities— and so forth,
up to having the five aggregates while lacking craving and the rest.
Therefore, it is known that the twelve links are not established by the power of the five aggregates alone.
If you were to say that the five aggregates of one beyond training (aśaikṣa) are not established as links because they lack ignorance and the other factors, [then we reply:]...

This is precisely because the factors [of dependent origination] are established by the power of ignorance and so forth, rather than being established by the power of the five aggregates; therefore, the meaning of the *Pratītyasamutpāda-sūtra* is exactly as it is stated in the text.
Alternatively, as I have explained,
it takes only ignorance and so forth as its essence.
Regarding the four propositions mentioned, which extend to the three time periods that have been established:
The Sautrāntika school refutes the four alternatives regarding the fulfillment of expectations.
Since the Sūtra states that all factors already arisen pertain to all twelve links,
does not the restriction to only the past and present contradict this?
Alternatively, birth and aging would not exist in the future,
because you maintain that what has already arisen exists only in the past and the present.
If these two were not in the future, the three time periods previously established would be undermined.
As for the claim that dependent origination (pratītyasamutpāda) reaches the eternally abiding nature of phenomena (dharmatā),
according to the *Śāsanodbhāvana* (Treatise on the Wheel of the Teachings), this is the tenet of the Mahāsāṃghika school and others.
Furthermore, the *Mahāvibhāṣā* (Vol. 23) refers to them as "Proponents of the *Vibhajya-vāda*" (*Vibhajyavādin*).
This is merely a restatement of their tenets;
for the Sūtras already state that such a nature of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda-dharmatā*) is eternally abiding.
Therefore, it is known that the essence of dependent origination (pratītyasamutpāda) is unconditioned (asaṃskṛta).
Regarding the claim that, according to such an intention, the ultimate principle is not so,
the Master of the Treatise refutes it as a whole.
Regarding the question of how such mental engagement (*manasikāra*) and its impossibility [are established],
the Mahāsāṃghikas raise this inquiry:
"If it is said that there is no logical principle for mental engagement through reaching [the object]," [how can it be established?]
The Master of the Treatise replies:
"It is according to my own intention that I speak of whether a Buddha appears or does not appear."
Formations and other resultant phenomena always arise conditioned by causes such as ignorance;
they do not arise conditioned by other phenomena.
If ignorance were severed, formations would have no condition and thus would be said to be eternally abiding.
When the Sūtra states that the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) is eternally abiding,
it reveals the sense of the certainty of cause and effect.
Such an intended meaning is indeed logical.
If you claim that, according to your own intention, there exists a distinct, real, and substantial entity called dependent origination (pratītyasamutpāda) which is serene and eternally abiding,
this interpretation is logically untenable.
That school's position is unreasonable.
Why is this so? Because it contradicts the words of the Buddha.
"Arising" (*jāti*) and "origination" (*samudaya*) are synonyms;
both are conditioned characteristics (*saṃskṛtalakṣaṇa*),
and are not distinct unconditioned, eternal phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-nityadharma*)."
It is consistent with correct reasoning that [unconditioned phenomena] possess the characteristic of impermanence,
because they assert that unconditioned phenomena are dependently originated.
Furthermore, the arising of a fruit’s function must necessarily be established based on the cause from which it arises.
This unconditioned, eternally abiding dharma and those impermanent dharmas such as ignorance—
one is eternal.
What does impermanence have to do with it?
Yet you say that this eternally abiding dharma is established based upon ignorance and so forth.
They arise with ignorance and so forth as conditions;
furthermore, ignorance and so forth are themselves called "dependent origination" (pratītyasamutpāda).
You, however, claim that the eye is permanent.
In this way, the meaning of the term "dependent origination" (pratītyasamutpāda) is not logically inconsistent with permanence.
Herein, the Mahāsāṃghikas ask: what is the meaning of the term "dependent origination"?
Regarding the meaning of *pratītyasamutpāda* (dependent origination),
the Sautrāntikas respond,
or alternatively, the Sarvāstivādins respond.
According to the treatises on grammar (śabdavidyā), there are phonemes (vyañjana) and verbal roots (dhātu).
If a verbal root is assisted by the arrival of a phoneme, [it becomes a word].
Thus, there arise various meanings: *prati* has the meaning of "reaching" (*prāpti*) and is the etymological prefix (*upapada*).
The root *iti* has the meaning of "going" (*gati*) and is the etymological base (*prakṛti*). A "base" (*dhātu*) has the meaning of "essence" (*svabhāva*).
This *iti*-boundary (the suffix) undergoes a semantic transformation into "condition" (*pratyaya*) through the assistance of the preceding *pra*-*ati*.
If it has been assisted and thus becomes a condition, one should say *pratyaya*; this is translated as "condition."
The reason for this is that conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are so named because they arise as effects through the power of various conditions;
before they have arrived, the status of being a condition is not yet established.
If the power of the conditions reaches the fruit,
or if the characteristics of the conditions reach it,
only then can they be called "conditions."
Therefore, the founders of the script added the auxiliary phoneme *ji* (至) to the syllable *xing* (行) so that it would convey the meaning of "condition" (*pratyaya*).
The character *can* (參) carries the meaning of "conjunction" or "integration," while *wu* (嗢) carries the meaning of "ascending."
These two are the conditions for the syllable.
