within this stage, the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*) and so forth are established.
He then cites scriptural evidence from such texts as the Mahānidāna-sūtra and the Pratītyasamutpāda-vibhaṅga-sūtra,
all of which state that name-and-form (nāmarūpa) comprises the five aggregates (pañcaskandha) throughout the entire course of a single lifetime.
Regarding the statement "thus, from name-and-form up to what is called the six sense bases," this clarifies the essence of the six sense bases:
within the stage of name-and-form, the eye and the other [senses] gradually come into being, which are termed the six sense bases.
Next, regarding "the conjunction with the object leading to contact that is pleasant and so forth," this clarifies the essential nature of the factor of contact (*sparśa*).
Once the six sense faculties have arisen and subsequently conjoin with their respective objects, consciousness then arises.
When the sense faculty, object, and consciousness come together, there are three types of contact conducive to pleasant feeling and so forth;
based on these, the three feelings of pleasure and so forth arise— this explains the essential nature of the "feeling" factor (vedanā-aṅga).
Based on this contact, there arise the three feelings of suffering, pleasure, and equanimity.
From these three feelings up to the arising of craving for the formless realm constitutes the limb of craving.
From these three types of sensation, three types of craving are induced.
That is to say, because of the affliction caused by suffering in the desire realm,
craving for the desire realm arises toward pleasant sensation.
Or, there may be those who, regarding the bliss of the first, second, and third dhyānas of the form realm,
or the neither-painful-nor-pleasant sensation of the fourth dhyāna,
give rise to craving for the form realm.
Or there may be those who, regarding only the sensations that are neither-painful-nor-pleasant within the formless realm,
give rise to craving for the formless realm;
from this craving for pleasant sensations, they then give rise to grasping for desire and so forth.
Below this, the essential nature of the link of grasping (*upādāna*) is set forth. Within this,
first is the general designation.
Second, the detailed explanation.
This is the general heading:
following the craving for pleasant and neutral feelings previously mentioned.
Next, the four graspings, beginning with the grasping for sensual desire, arise.
According to the Sautrāntika school, these four graspings have craving as their essence;
this is the same as the Mahāyāna.
If it is said that the Sarvāstivādins take the one hundred and eight afflictions as their essence,
and regarding the phrase "herein, 'desire' refers to the statement of 'self' based upon [the aggregates]," this is the second section: the detailed explanation.
First, the clarification of the four objects;
second, the exposition of the essence of grasping.
This [second section] clarifies the four objects: first, desire.
The five objects of the exquisite desires, namely form and so forth;
and the two views refer to the sixty-two views,
as explained in detail in the Brahmajāla Sūtra.
This will be enumerated, indicated, and explained in the Chapter on Latent Tendencies (*Anuśaya-varga*). Regarding the three types of "vows of ascetic observances" (*śīla-vrata*):
"vow" (*śīla*) refers to the restraint of conduct;
that is, within our own tradition, it refers to the avoidance of unwholesome conduct.
"Vow" (vratam) refers to the practice of prohibitions;
that is, the vows of non-Buddhists such as those involving dogs or oxen.
For example, various Nirgrantha non-Buddhists observe and maintain various practices such as being naked or plucking out their hair.
Because he is far removed from the bonds of clothing and other such things, he is called a "Liberated One" (vīta-rāga). As for the Brahmins and non-Buddhist outsiders:
they maintain and carry staffs in their hands, wear garments of bird and deer skins, and there are the Pāśupatas—non-Buddhists who are here translated as "Cattle-Masters."
"Lord" refers to the Lord of Heaven (Indra) or Maheśvara.
Because he travels mounted upon an ox, he is named "Ox-Lord" (Vṛṣabha-pati).
Furthermore, this non-Buddhist practitioner studied the dharma of that deity;
because he was named after that [deity], he is called "Lord of the Bull" (Vṛṣabha).
This non-Buddhist maintains a single topknot upon his head and smears his body with ash. The Pāñcarātrika non-Buddhist—here translated as "Pervasive Emanation" (Biànchū)—is so named.
This reveals the meaning of "renunciation.
These are renunciants who follow external paths;
they receive, maintain, and carry the triple staff (tridanda).

The term "and so forth" includes such practices as preparing to place clothing, water flasks, alms bowls, and other items [therein], as well as the meaningless asceticism of shaving one's hair and beard;
all such various other heterodox practices are collectively termed "prohibitions. Fourth is the "doctrine of self" (*ātmavāda*).
This is called "discourse on self" (*ātmavāda*) because it refers to the body within the three realms as the basis for speaking of a self;
it is not like the Sarvāstivādins, who speak of a self based solely on the two upper realms.
Other masters say that "extreme views" (antagrāhadṛṣṭi) are called "discourse on self" (ātmavāda).
As for the Sautrāntika dissenters,
why are these two alone termed "discourse on self"?
Question:
By means of these two kinds [of views], one arrives at "I" and "mine. Answer:
Because these two types [of views] speak of a self, they are called "self.
Since the self does not exist, it is merely a verbal expression; therefore, it is called "discourse on self" (*ātmavāda*).
As the Sūtra says: "Ordinary worldlings give rise to the grasping of a self in accordance with conventional discourse."
Within this, there is truly no self or what belongs to a self;
one clearly understands that the essence of a self does not exist,
but is merely a linguistic convention.
Regarding the aforementioned four kinds, that which is called "desire and greed" constitutes the second essential nature of grasping (*upādāna*).
The four kinds previously mentioned are the objects of grasping (*upādānīya-viṣaya*).
Now, that which is precisely presented as the substance of the apprehending subject is what is called "desire-attachment" (kāmarāga); that is,
"desire" (kāma) is a name for attachment (rāga).
Greed (rāga) pervades all three realms;
it is not merely the greed of the desire realm.
The Sūtra states that "desire-greed" is called grasping (upādāna).
It is clearly understood that [craving] does not extend to other factors;
rather, by taking [craving] as a condition, it leads up to what is called "existence" (*bhava*).
This explains the essential nature of the limb of existence and cites scriptural evidence.
Karma capable of summoning the fruit of future existence is called "existence" (bhava).
Because it serves as the condition for existence, that which reaches [the next life] is called "birth" (jāti), which refers to the production of the physical constituents.
Due to conditioned factors as conditions,
consciousness flows on in succession toward future birth,
according to the principle explained previously regarding the link of consciousness.
The intermediate existence (antarābhava) hastens toward the place of rebirth;
the body of the existence at conception (pratisandhibhava),
endowed with the five aggregates (pañcaskandha), is called birth (jāti).
Although they are largely similar, there is no lack of distinction between the member of consciousness (*vijñāna*) and this [member of] birth (*jāti*).
The term "consciousness" is narrow, referring only to the six consciousnesses;

the term "birth" is broad, as it encompasses all five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*). Furthermore, some explain that this member of birth is like the previous members of consciousness and name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*).

Since it has already been stated that the continuity of consciousness is the same as the branch of consciousness (*vijñāna*), and further stated that it is complete with the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) just like name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*),
this term "birth" (*jāti*) generally indicates the beginning of future existence, starting from the first moment of the intermediate state (*antarābhava*).
This extends up to the end of life, which constitutes a single lifetime.
Within this state of birth, one establishes aging and death. Furthermore, it is explained that the term "aging and death" is preceded by "birth";
with birth as a condition, [the process] continues as extensively described in the sūtra.
The essence of old age and death emerges;
thus, old age and death are established immediately following birth. Furthermore, it is explained that old age and death are established within the stage of the link of birth.
The characteristics of old age and death consist of such things as white hair and wrinkled faces.

The various distinctions are explained at length as in the Sūtra. Furthermore, it is explained that from the onset of such things as the greying of the hair onwards, it is called "aging," and what follows is called "death.
Thus, the word "purely" refers to the arising of the entire mass of suffering aggregates.
The above has set forth the essential nature of the twelve links according to the Sautrāntika school.
It further explains the scriptural passage, "Thus is the origination of this entire mass of suffering," based on the Sūtra's statement that "ignorance conditions volitional formations."
Up to birth as the condition for old age and death;
thus occurs this entire great mass of suffering.
Therefore, it is explained.
Regarding the statement that "the Vaibhāṣika school is as previously explained":
the above has been the Sautrāntika explanation of the twelve links of dependent origination;
as for the Vaibhāṣika explanation of the twelve links of dependent origination, it is as previously explained.
*Abhidharmakośabhāṣya-ṭīkā*, Fascicle Nine.
*Abhidharmakośabhāṣya-ṭīkā*, Fascicle Ten.
Narrated by the Śramaṇa Shi Guang.
Regarding the third part of the third chapter, "The Analysis of the World":
as for the meaning of ignorance (*avidyā*),
from this point onward is the second major section, which specifically clarifies the definitions and meanings of the terms.
Among these,
there are four distinct analytical sections. Regarding the first of these four distinct analytical sections:
First, the analysis of ignorance;
second, the analysis of name-and-form;
third, the analysis of contact.
4. Distinguishing Appropriation. Below this, ignorance is distinguished.
Within this section:
first, the explanation of its meaning.
Second, the establishment of proof.
Below this is the explanation of the meaning; this is the question.
That is to say, its essence is not clarity. Answer:
Because its essence is not clarity, it is called ignorance (*avidyā*).
If that were so, it would follow as a logical objection that ignorance (*avidyā*) must be the eye and so forth;
for the nature of the eye, ear, nose, and other [senses] is likewise not knowledge (*vidyā*),
and thus they too ought to be ignorance.
If that is so, this point should be called "clarifying non-existence. [The opponent] explains:
[this allows for] the possibility of shifting one's position when faced with a challenge.
The absence of knowledge is called ignorance (*avidyā*).
If that were so, it would follow that the essence of ignorance does not exist;
thus, he raises a further objection.
The absence of knowledge is called ignorance (*avidyā*);
its essence should therefore not exist.
To demonstrate that it does possess an essence—just as in the case of "non-relative" or "untruth" and so forth—[the following is stated].
Regarding the two previous [objections] concerning the fault [of non-existence], the Master provides the correct explanation:
it is to demonstrate that ignorance (*avidyā*) possesses a substantial entity and is not a mere non-entity.
This meaning does not overlap with other [defects], such as the fault of lacking eyes or the like. That which is the direct opposite of clear knowledge (*vidyā*) is termed "ignorance" (*avidyā*).
Regarding "not being a relative" and so forth, the *Śāstra* states: "As for 'neither different nor non-existent,' this explains the second phrase.
An enemy is called "not a relative"; deceptive speech is called "not true"; and that which is contrary to the Dharma is [called "not right"].
That which is unwholesome phenomena is "non-benefit. That which is the meaning of unwholesomeness is "non-activity.
That which is the activity of unwholesomeness is the category of things opposed to friends and so forth, termed "non-friends" and the like.
It is not that there are no non-friends distinct from friends; rather, it is simply that there are no [entities] other than friends.
Ignorance (*avidyā*) is likewise:
ignorance is the phenomenon that is the counter-correlative of knowledge (*vidyā*).
"It is neither different from clarity nor is it non-existent as ignorance.
How is this known to be so?
The following establishes the proof through an interrogative inquiry.
Regarding the statement "because it is taught as the condition for volitional formations" (saṃskāra-pratyaya),
the answer is:
because this ignorance is taught as the condition for volitional formations, it is clearly known that it possesses substantial reality (svabhāva).
Furthermore, regarding the scriptural evidence stating that [ignorance] is able to defile wisdom:
the first phrase provides the direct proof,
while the following three phrases refute divergent views.
The Commentary says: "Regarding the statement 'it is called ignorance' (*avidyā*):

The Sūtra states that ignorance is included among the nine fetters (*saṃyojana*), the three bonds (*bandhana*), the ten latent tendencies (*anuśaya*), the three outflows (*āsrava*), the four yokes (*yoga*), the four floods (*ogha*), and so forth.
Therefore, one knows that it exists as something distinct,
neither being other [faculties] such as the eye nor being entirely non-existent in essence.
To say that it is called "fetter" (*saṃyojana*) and so forth—
just as a wicked wife or son should be called "ignorance" (*avidyā*)—
is a statement of a divergent interpretation.
Just as a wicked wife or son who lacks the qualities of a wife or son is said to be "without a wife" or "without a son," so too,
faulty wisdom that lacks the quality of clarity should be called "ignorance."
Regarding the statement, "Because they do not reach that which is non-ignorance, they are not non-ignorance," the Master of the Treatise cites this verse to directly refute [the opponent's view]:
those various forms of faulty wisdom (kuprajñā) are not ignorance (avidyā).
Among the types of unwholesome wisdom (*kuprajñā*), there are five that are defiled wisdoms (*kliṣṭaprajñā*) which are by nature views (*dṛṣṭi*).
Because they are by nature views—characterized by investigation, intensity, and decisive judgment—they are not ignorance (*avidyā*).
If that is so, then one must admit that those forms of wisdom which are not views are ignorance.
External objection:
If that is so, since greed and the like are not among the five views,
and since wisdom (prajñā) is not of the nature of view, one must admit that ignorance (avidyā) is likewise [not a distinct entity].
Regarding the statement "it is not so, because ignorance reaches [the point of] being associated with [other factors]," this is explained by the third phrase:
since ignorance coexists with views, it is known not to be wisdom (*prajñā*).
Because the essence of non-dual wisdom is associated with [it],
and because it is further stated that ignorance reaches up to "dissimilar wisdom" (*vipaśyanā*) and is able to defile it;
thus, by means of this fourth phrase, it is proven that [ignorance] is not itself wisdom.
The Sūtra states that ignorance can defile wisdom;
therefore, we know that the essence of wisdom is not identical to ignorance.
How could wisdom itself further defile wisdom?
Regarding the question, "Why is it not permitted? What logical contradiction exists?"—this is the Sautrāntika's salvific intent:
why is it not permitted that there is a seed of defiled wisdom (*kliṣṭa-prajñā*)?
It refers to the statement that wholesome wisdom can defile unwholesome wisdom, or that unwholesome wisdom currently manifesting can be defiled by wholesome wisdom occurring before or after it;
or it refers to the seeds of unwholesome wisdom, as well as its preceding and succeeding manifestations.
It is said that defiled wisdom (kliṣṭa-prajñā) is that which contaminates wholesome wisdom;
this is like a mind defiled by greed being associated with greed.
In reality, however, it is contaminated even if it is not associated [with greed].
A mind is said to be defiled by greed either because the seeds of greed are interspersed within it,
or because greed is manifested in its preceding and succeeding moments and thus interspersed within it,
or because both the seeds of greed and its preceding and succeeding manifestations are interspersed within it.
Subsequently, when the seeds of craving are extinguished, the mind is liberated.
It is said that ignorance defiles wisdom; it is not that [ignorance] is associated with wisdom.
Because the seeds of ignorance are interspersed within wisdom, it is said that they are able to defile wisdom.
Alternatively, it is said that ignorance defiles wisdom because it is interspersed with wisdom through its manifestation before and after;
or else, it is because of the seeds of ignorance as well as its manifestation before and after.
If it is argued that among those [afflictions] associated with wisdom, some are able to defile wisdom,
then what logical contradiction is there in such a distinction?
Furthermore, who could possibly prevent this from being considered a sound teaching?
The author of the treatise is not a Sautrāntika; he critiques and adopts the Sarvāstivāda position.
Regarding those who hold that the afflictions reach the object, this is refuted by reasoning.
There is also the position held by certain other masters.
The lack of understanding regarding objects on the part of all afflictions is termed "ignorance" (avidyā); this,
too, should be refuted by the same reasoning as before.
If the afflictions were not given a collective name, then the specific enumeration of their faults would not be established; this is refuted by the same reasoning as before.
Furthermore, among the nine fetters (*saṃyojana*) and so forth, ignorance (*avidyā*) is mentioned separately.
It is clearly known that ignorance (*avidyā*) is not a general designation [for all afflictions]. Furthermore, if ignorance were identical to all afflictions,
it should not be associated with views (*dṛṣṭi*) and so forth,
because a factor cannot be associated with itself.
In the sūtra, it should have been stated that "ignorance defiles the mind," rather than stating that "desire defiles the mind.

This is because ignorance is more comprehensive and also subsumes desire. If you argue that this sūtra’s statement that "desire defiles the mind" is made from the perspective of specific distinctions, [then...]
Regarding defiled wisdom, one should not speak of it using the general term "ignorance" (avidyā);
rather, it should be explained according to its specific distinctions.
Since you have granted that ignorance exists, what then are its characteristics?
The outsider asks:
"What is meant by 'those who do not understand the truths, the jewels, and the results of karma'?
The Sarvāstivādins answer.
The failure to comprehend the Four Noble Truths, the Three Jewels, wholesome and unwholesome karma, and their resultant maturation is called ignorance (*avidyā*).
As for the specific characteristics of this ignorance, they are as explained in the section on ignorance.
The opponent further objects:
If it were distinct from cognition, it would have to be the eye and so forth;
if cognition were non-existent, then its substance would not exist either.
The two faults are as previously stated.
This refers to one who understands the distinct phenomena that are to be remedied. Answer:
This "ignorance" refers to a distinct dharma that is the antithesis of the wisdom of thorough comprehension;
furthermore, it is difficult to fathom what its specific characteristic is.
The opponent further challenges:
"In such cases, it is the nature of things that one can only discern the function.
[The author] replies:
The eye is translucent matter that serves as the basis for visual consciousness;
this is distinguished in terms of its function.
Ignorance is likewise so.

Regarding the statement that "the non-realization of the truths and so forth can only be distinguished by their function," when the Venerable Dharmatrāta says "relying on the nature of the self-group" (*ātma-varga-svabhāva*),
the intention of this Venerable one is that "relying on the self" means relying on the self to give rise to pride (*māna*).
That which is called "relying on the self" is precisely the conceit of "I am";
its essential nature is ignorance.
This ignorance is of the same nature as the category of pride;
therefore, ignorance is manifested by way of pride.
This principle also applies to its being of the same nature as other afflictions.

Furthermore, it is provisionally designated as "pride" (māna) for the sake of clarification; moreover, because this ignorance is associated with all other afflictions and resembles them, it specifically receives the name of that "category.
As for what the essential nature of this category, distinct from pride, actually is: [it is]...
The master of the treatise asks:
"The nature of 'category' (*jāti*) is precisely the conceit of self (*asmimāna*).
Because the conceit of self is a category of the view of a self (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), it is called the 'nature of category.'"
Therefore, it is said that [this] is different from the category of *asmimāna* (the conceit "I am"). What is its nature?
The Sūtra says: "I have now reached that which is different from *asmimāna*.
The Venerable One cites this Sūtra as his response.
The Sūtra says: "Having known thus, I now cultivate the path;
having seen thus, I have realized the path. Or: "Having known thus, these are the various knowledges (jñāna);
having seen thus, these are the various patiences (kṣānti)."

Through knowledge and vision, craving and the other [afflictions] are forever severed. Alternatively, knowing thus is the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*), and seeing thus is the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*).
Because it is contemplative observation, it is also called "vision. Alternatively, knowing thus is the knowledge of exhaustion and non-arising.
Having seen thus, this is the knowledge of right view of one beyond training (aśaikṣa).
This is because exhaustion (kṣaya) and non-arising (anutpāda) are not [merely] views. All that exists as craving—“craving” here meaning greedy craving—is [abandoned].
Because craving is the basis for delusion, it is designated separately by name.

"All views" refers to the remaining four views among the five views, excluding the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*). "All categories of existence" refers to all types of generic properties (*jāti*).
This means that ignorance (avidyā) is universally present along with all other afflictions;
because it is predominant, it is mentioned separately as "ignorance" and so forth.
This separate mention serves to reveal its nature as a representative of that entire class.
Therefore, the *Nyāyānusāra* states:
"Among the predominant afflictions (*kleśa*), ignorance (*avidyā*) has not yet been mentioned;
to distinguish it specifically, the term 'of the same nature' (*jātīyatva*) is stated."

Because it is universally associated with the afflictions and universally proceeds toward all realms of existence, it is called "category-nature" (*nikāyatva*). "Category" (*nikāya*) has the meaning of "conditioned formations" (*saṃskāra*);
the essence of this category receives the name "category-nature. It consists of all forms of grasping at a self and what belongs to a self.
This means that because the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) is preeminent, it is explained separately;
thus the *Nyāyānusāra* states:
"The grasping at 'I' and 'mine' is the root of all views."
Therefore, within the category of views (*dṛṣṭi*), two distinct types are specifically revealed: the conceit of self (*asmimāna*) and the latent tendency (*anuśaya*).

Regarding the conceit of self: among the seven types of conceit (*māna*), it is singled out because it arises with the notion of "I" and because it is preeminent. Regarding the latent tendency: [it is singled out] because...
That is to say, doubt and hatred.
Therefore, the *Nyāyānusāra* states:
"The term 'latent tendency' (*anuśaya*) is used to include both doubt and hatred, because they are abandoned through full knowledge (*parijñā*)."
That is to say, when all afflictions are severed and one attains the knowledge of exhaustion,
this is *sopadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa* (nirvana with remainder), which is shadowless and quiescent cessation.
This refers to *anupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa* (nirvana without remainder).
Since the Sūtra speaks of the nature of "clinging" (*nikāya-sabhāga*) separately,
we know that the nature of clinging is distinct from the conceit of "I" (*asmimāna*).
How, then, can it be known that the nature of clinging is itself ignorance (*avidyā*)?
The Master of the Treatise challenges the Venerable One regarding the statement that it cannot be said to be "other afflictions.
The Venerable One replies:
"It cannot be said [that it is] other greed and so forth.
To the objection, "Could it not be said that it is other pride and so forth?
the Master of the Treatise further refutes this.
Could the nature of this category of sūtras not be described as the other six types of pride?
By "pride and so forth," one includes the five types beginning with *atimāna* (excessive pride).
If pride and the others constitute its essential nature, [then it is so].
Because it is a category of other afflictions, it is called "generic nature" (*jāti*).
The masters of the Sautrāntika school do not believe that ignorance (*avidyā*) has a separate substantial entity.
Since the author of the treatise sides with the Sautrāntikas, he raises this objection.
The intention of the *Nyāyānusāra* is the same as that of the Venerable [Vasubandhu].
As for the phrase "if one were to further pursue this point here, it would be best to desist," the author of the treatise stops the debate.
Regarding the meaning of "name-and-form" (*nāmarūpa*):
this section below is the second [part], which analyzes name-and-form.
As for "form," it has been analyzed previously; as for "name," it refers to the four formless aggregates.
Answer: Form (*rūpa*) has been analyzed previously;
that is, it was analyzed in the preceding "Chapter on Elements" (*dhātuvarga*) within the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*).
Now, only its name is being analyzed.
Although the preceding text also analyzed the other four aggregates,
it did not yet state that they constitute "name";
therefore, they are now distinguished here.
The treatise asks: "Why is it called 'name' (*nāman*)?
This is a question regarding "name" among the dissociated factors (*viprayukta-saṃskāra*).
Why are the four formless aggregates called "name" (*nāman*)?
It is said that they are called "name" because they conform to whatever name has been established and reach it. The answer is as follows:
If a name undergoes a transformation in its meaning through the power of the designation established by common convention since ancient times,
it is therefore called a "name" (nāman).
If the four formless aggregates transform with respect to their objects according to the power of the faculties and their respective objects,
they are called "name" (nāma) because they undergo transformation; thus, they are designated as "name."
Because these four aggregates necessarily depend upon the sense faculties and take objects as their conditions,
it is said that they follow the power of the faculties and the objects.
How do they undergo transformation by following the power of names?
Question:
What is meant by "transforming according to the power of names"?
That is to say, [it refers to] following various names such as "form," "taste," and so forth.
Answer: It refers to the time at the beginning of the eon,
when names were established by worldly convention for various phenomena.
By virtue of their power,
names subsequently undergo transformation to express various meanings,
just as in the case of names such as "ox" and so forth.
Furthermore, for what reason are these designated by the name "name"?
Question:
For what reason, moreover, are these four aggregates designated by the name "name"?
Regarding that which transforms and conditions various respective objects:
the answer is that it is the formless aggregate (ārūpya-skandha) that transforms and conditions various respective objects.
Because transformation occurs according to their names,
they are designated as such; although other dissociated factors lack transformation,
they are included because they likewise possess transformation within the formless realm.
There is no fault in the designation [of "matter" (*rūpa*)] as being inclusive;

it is like the case where that which is subject to transformation and resistance is called "matter" (*rūpa*). Although non-informative matter (*avijñapti*) and so forth lack transformation and resistance, they are nonetheless included under "matter" because they share in the quality of being subject to transformation and resistance within the category of matter.
There is no fault in including it within form (*rūpa*).
Furthermore, regarding the term "resembling" (*sadṛśa*),
this is the second interpretation.
The four aggregates and "name" (nāman) belong to the same category of formless phenomena;
because they resemble name, they are designated by the term "name."
Therefore, the *Vibhāṣā*, volume fifteen, in explaining the reason why the four aggregates are called "name" (*nāman*), answers:
"The Buddha generally divides conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*) into two categories:
namely, form (*rūpa*) and non-form (*arūpa*)."
Form is the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*).
That which is non-form consists of the other four aggregates, such as feeling (*vedanā*) and so forth.
Within this collection of non-form, there exists that which can manifest the names of all phenomena (*sarvadharmāḥ*).
Therefore, it is not that a collection of form is collectively designated as "name" (nāma).
Regarding the phrase "because it manifests according to name," this is the third interpretation.
The four aggregates of the formless realm have obscured characteristics that are difficult to discern;
because they are manifested according to their names, those names are used as designations.
Thus, the *Mahāvibhāṣā* states:
Some say that material phenomena (*rūpadharma*) are called "form" (*rūpa*) because they are coarse and manifest;
non-material phenomena (*arūpa*),
being subtle and hidden, are called "name" (*nāman*) because they are manifested by names.
Other masters say that the name is designated because it reaches [the next life];
this is the fourth explanation.
Having abandoned these four aggregates of the formless realm after leaving this body, they proceed to another place of rebirth in the future.
Because transformation corresponds to its name, it is designated as such.

Although the four untainted aggregates (*anāsrava-skandha*) do not undergo rebirth, they are included within this category without error because they belong to the same class. Regarding the first definition, "transformation" refers to the change of the object.
The subsequent explanation regarding the ease with which names arise is termed "transformation" (*pariṇāma*).

Although there are distinctions in meaning, both are explained as being based on transformation. Furthermore, the *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra* (Treatise on the Principles of Correct Reasoning), fascicle 29, states:
"The Buddha taught that the four formless aggregates are called 'name' (*nāman*)."
Why is it called "name" (nāman)?
Because it is able to designate and summon;
that is to say, it is able to designate and summon various objects of cognition.
If that were so, it would not fully include the formless [realms],
because non-associated dharmas lack an object of cognition.
It is not the case that such designation exists only in the formless [realms].
There is no fault in the explanation given when defining the term "matter" (rūpa).
The Buddha stated that it is called "matter" because it is subject to transformation and resistance (varṇa-vikāra-pratighāta).
This applies to past and future matter, non-informative matter (avijñapti), and all atoms (paramāṇu).
Although it lacks resistance and obstruction, it is nonetheless designated as "form" (rūpa),
because within the formless realm (ārūpya) there is no resistance or obstruction.
That resistance and obstruction constitute "form" is not at all unestablished.

In this way, while there may be the possibility of "manifestation" (vijñapti) within the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu), since it does not exist within the realm of form (rūpadhātu), there is likewise no logical contradiction.
Therefore, there is no fault in including [the dissociated factors] under the name "dissociated" (viprayukta). Furthermore, there are three other interpretations which cannot be fully recounted here.
Regarding the meaning of "contact" (*sparśa*):
the following section is the third [part], which analyzes contact. Within this, [it is explained as follows].
First, the explanation of the six contacts;
second, the explanation of the two contacts;
third, the explanation of the eight contacts.
The following clarifies the inquiry regarding the six types of contact (*ṣaṭ-sparśa*).
The verse says: "Contact arises from the meeting [of three] and from the conjunction of the six and the three.
This answers the question: what is contact?
This indicates the essence [of consciousness].
Regarding the six divisions based on their supports, the phrase "arising from the threefold conjunction" cites the cause to reveal the essence.
The Commentary states: "From 'up to' and even 'mental contact'":
this refers to the initial explanation of the verse within the prose section.
The subsequent determination.
Below this, the verse is explained, which is to say, the six types of contact are explained.
Furthermore, what are these?
Question:
What, moreover, is the nature of this contact?
Is it that which arises from the coming together of the three, or is there a distinct contact that arises?
Answer: To explain that which arises from the conjunction of the three:
because of the coming together of the three, a distinct contact arises; this is what is designated as "contact."
Furthermore, regarding how the five types of contact arise through conjunction, the following section provides a definitive analysis.
It asks: how do the contacts associated with the five consciousnesses arise?
The three can be in conjunction,
because it is admitted that the sense faculty, the object, and consciousness are all simultaneous; thus,
contact arises associated with the mental consciousness.
The three—faculty, object, and consciousness—may each exist in different time periods.
How, then, can they be combined? Since dharmas may also exist in the past and present, the word "or" (vā) is used.
Regarding the statement, "This is called 'conjunction' because it leads to the arising of contact in accordance with [the object]," the answer is:
conjunction is not defined by being in the same world-period (*adhvan*).
The triad of faculty, object, and consciousness,
though each resides in its own distinct moment, is precisely what is called "conjunction" (saṃnipāta);
that is to say, the principle of cause and effect is established.
The mind and mental objects serve as the cause, and mental consciousness serves as the result.
Furthermore, the triad of faculty, object,
and consciousness is termed a "conjunction" (saṃnipāta) because they collectively and harmoniously give rise to the single result of contact (sparśa).
There are two kinds of conjunction (*sāmagrī*):
first, that which arises simultaneously is called conjunction;
second, that which produces a fruit through mutual compatibility is called conjunction.
Among these six, the first five possess both types of conjunction (*sāmagrī*),
while the last one is termed conjunction because it arises in accordance with its result.
Thus, the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* (Vibhāṣā), fascicle 197, states:
The answer to this question states:
There are two kinds of conjunction (*sāmagrī*).
First, that which arises simultaneously and is inseparable is called conjunction.
The non-contradiction of two [factors] in accomplishing a single object is termed "conjunction" (saṃnipāta).
This is the characteristic of the five consciousnesses, which must be associated with contact (sparśa).
It is called "conjunction" (saṃnipāta) because of the conjunction of these two;
it is the contact associated with the mental consciousness.
It is called "conjunction" because it establishes the conjunction of a single function. Question: In all cases where cause and effect are viewed in relation to one another...
If a cause is considered in relation to its fruit, it may be simultaneous with or prior to it;
if a fruit is considered in relation to its cause, it may be simultaneous with or posterior to it.
For example, when the past mental faculty (*manas*) gives rise to the present fruit of mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).
It may be logically sound that the past faculty of mind (*manas*) gives rise to the present consciousness (*vijñāna*), which in turn produces the fruit of present contact (*sparśa*).

However, how can future dharmas as objects give rise to present consciousness and the fruit of present contact? The explanation states: generally clarifying the term "attaining the fruit" (*phala-prāpti*), there are briefly three types.
Taking [the result] and giving [the result] are called "result" (phala).
This result, in relation to its cause,
may be either simultaneous with it or subsequent to it.
These are the four conditioned fruits.
They are called "fruits" because they are realized through two types of realization;
that is to say, they are the fruit of unconditioned analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
Because it conforms to the three characteristics,
and because the characteristic arises in dependence [upon them], it is called a "result. This result,
in relation to its cause, may be prior, subsequent, or simultaneous.
It encompasses both the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
For example, the present mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) is called a "fruit.
Among the three types of fruits, in relation to the past mental cause (*manas-hetu*), it possesses both the first and the last fruits.
Regarding the future dharma as a cause, there is only the subsequent result.
This is like the present contact-result among the three results.
Regarding the past mental faculty (*manas*) as a cause for the present mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), there are both the initial and subsequent results.
Regarding the view that in the future dharma there is only the cause and no subsequent fruit: as for this "fruit" which follows the prior cause,
it is provisionally named "fruit" because its characteristics accord with one another and because those characteristics depend upon and rely upon one another.

It is not one of the five fruits. Furthermore, it is explained that the present mental consciousness and the present contact, in relation to future phenomena and objects, are also sovereign fruits (*adhipatiphala*).
There are two kinds of dominant results (*adhipatiphala*):
first, the dominant result consisting of the grasping of the fruit (*phalagrahaṇa*) and the giving of the fruit (*phaladāna*).
This fruit necessarily does not exist prior to its cause.

The second [type of fruit] is neither the fruit of appropriation (*ādāna-phala*) nor the fruit of giving (*datta-phala*), but rather the sovereign fruit (*adhipati-phala*). This fruit may exist prior to its cause;
it is with reference to this that I speak now.
Regarding the passage from "The various masters, concerning this... up to "...is called contact," the following section describes their differing views.
The various masters differ regarding this contact in terms of its nature as sensation (*vedanā*) or discernment (*prajñā*).
There are Sautrāntika masters who say that the mere conjunction of the three—faculty, object, and consciousness—is itself called contact (*sparśa*).
This can be known from scriptural evidence.
Others say that because [the three] meet, there exists a distinct entity called contact.
The masters of the Sarvāstivāda school state that, apart from the sense faculties, objects, and consciousness, there exists a distinct entity of contact (*sparśa*).
This can be known through scriptural evidence. A sutra says: "As for the body..."
This refers to its essence (*ātman*). Furthermore, it is explained that the accumulation of multiple moments of consciousness and so forth is called a "body" (*kāya*).
Thus, the *Abhidharmamahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* explains the "six bodies of craving" (*ṣaḍ-tṛṣṇākāya*), asking:
"For what reason are they called 'bodies'?"
Answer: It is called "body" (*kāya*) because it is an accumulation of many [factors].
That is to say, it is not a single moment.
As for the statement that it "extends from the conjunction of the three up to being included within the non-dharma bases," [it refers to this].
The Sautrāntikas maintain that the *Ṣaṭṣaṭka-sūtra* is comprehensive;

although "feeling" (*vedanā*) and "craving" (*tṛṣṇā*) are mentioned separately, they are subsumed within the sphere of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*). Although "contact" (*sparśa*) is also mentioned separately, it is nonetheless subsumed within those three [aggregates].
To say that there is no such fault because [the teaching] is stated with reference to specific distinctions is the Sarvāstivāda’s rebuttal of the Sautrāntika’s counter-objection;
it is according to our own tenet.
Apart from craving, feeling, and contact, other factors can be found within the sphere of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*) that can be distinguished and described.
Since, according to your own school, there are no three [feelings] distinct from contact,
how can you claim that contact and those three are distinguished and described?
"Even though there are faculties and objects, they would become useless if [contact] were merely reaching them.
This statement restates and refutes the opponent's defense.
The intent of the opponent's defense is that there are also cases where the faculty and object cannot give rise to consciousness.

Therefore, since the sūtra speaks of the faculties (indriya) and objects (viṣaya) separately, how can you challenge me by claiming that there is no distinct third element apart from contact (sparśa)? Thus, [the opponent] restates and refutes [this position], saying: "Even though faculties and objects exist, they do not give rise to consciousness."
Furthermore, there is no consciousness that does not rely upon sense bases and objects;
thus, it can be said that the three [bases, objects, and consciousness] subsume contact.
To speak of contact separately would therefore be redundant.

Another offers this defense: "When they are collectively established as contact (*sparśa*)," the Sautrāntika masters defend [their position] by stating that they are spoken of separately as three based on their respective sense faculties (*indriya*), objects (*viṣaya*), and consciousnesses (*vijñāna*).

If one bases this on the three factors of the sense faculty, object, and consciousness—which are subsumed under the causes and effects of the "homogeneous portion" (sabhāga)—then contact is established as their totality.
It is said that apart from the coming together of these three, there is the manifestation of pleasure and so forth.
Regarding the Sautrāntika citation of a sūtra from the preceding [text], the Sarvāstivāda school offers two interpretations:
first, that the wording I recite differs;
second, that even if this passage does exist, [it should be understood differently].
The name "contact" is applied metaphorically to the three causes; therefore,
it is said that the gathering and conjunction of these three factors is called contact,
just as it is said that the appearance of the Buddhas is blissful.
"Establishing the effect within the cause;
thus proceeding by such successive stages until it reaches the [original] point— this should now be set aside," says the Master of the Treatise,
thereby bringing the dispute to an end.
However, when the Abhidharmikas assert that there is a distinct contact (*spraṣṭavya*),
they are returning to the fundamental tenet of the Sarvāstivāda school; namely,
that the aforementioned six contacts culminate in the sixth, which is associated with the designation (*adhivacana*).
Below this, the second section clarifies the two types of contact (*spraṣṭavya*).
These are divided into two kinds based on their respective bases (*āśraya*) and so forth.
The treatise states: "Because the [tangible object] serves as the basis (*āśraya*)."
This explains the first phrase.
Contact associated with the five consciousnesses, such as the visual consciousness, is called "with resistance" (*sapratigha*).
Because it takes resistant faculties (*indriya*) as its basis (*āśraya*), it is named after that basis.
"Contact with resistance" (*sapratigha-sparśa*) is explained according to the *tatpuruṣa* (dependent) compound.
However, according to the *Nyāyānusāra*, it also takes into account the object;
thus, that treatise states:
Because it takes the resistant sense faculties as its support and has only resistant phenomena as its object,
the sixth mental contact is called "the elder" (āyusmat).
This explains the second phrase.
Contact associated with the sixth consciousness is called "designation" (*adhivacana*).
The reason it is termed "designation" is as follows:
Speech consists of sounds, yet it lacks the capacity for signification;

the "name" (nāman), however, possesses the capacity for signification and excels speech, and is therefore called the "designation" (adhivacana). Furthermore, another interpretation holds that this name is called the "designation" because it can signify [its object] only when speech serves as its augment (adhika). Yet another interpretation holds that "augment" (adhi) means "to increase."

Because it takes names as its object, it increases verbal expression. Furthermore, another interpretation is that because the power of names causes speech to become superior, it is called "designation" (*adhivacana*).
These names are the extensive objects apprehended by the mental consciousness.
Therefore, it is called "designation-contact" (adhivacana-saṃsparśa) with respect to its object;
this is an *ṣaṣṭhī-tatpuruṣa* (genitive determinative) compound meaning "the contact of designation.
It is called the "extended object" (*prabhūta-viṣaya*) for the following reason:
Just as visual consciousness can only cognize blue but cannot cognize the name "blue," mental consciousness cognizes both blue and the name "blue.
After mental consciousness has shared the same object of perception as the five sensory consciousnesses, [it further cognizes the name].
Furthermore, it is called "long" by virtue of its name; thus,
when "contact with resistance" (*pratigha-saṃsparśa*) is established in relation to its object (*ālambana*),
these two types of contact are combined under a single name.
As for the statement that "the mental consciousness is established based on its association with [mental factors]," this records a divergent view.
This position asserts that the mental consciousness only engages with its object by virtue of being dominated by specific linguistic expressions.
The five consciousnesses are not like this;
this is stated for the most part.
Furthermore, there is also mental consciousness that is able to apprehend objects without being dependent on speech.
Therefore, the mental consciousness alone is called "designation" (adhivacana),
because it has speech as its predominant condition;
this is a possessive compound (*bahuvrīhi*).

That which is associated with this is called "designation-contact" (*adhivacana-saṃsparśa*). This is an etymological explanation (*nirukti*) based on its association. Furthermore, in the *Nyāyānusāra* (Treatise on the Correct Principles), fascicle 29, there is another explanation of "designation": [The text continues: "Furthermore, what is the meaning of 'designation' (*adhivacana*)? It refers to the name (*nāman*), for it designates the object. Because it is superior to other [forms of] speech, it is called 'designation. Or, because it is the most excellent among all names, it is called 'designation. Or, because it is the most excellent among all words, it is called 'designation. Or, because it is the most excellent among all designations, it is called 'designation. Or, because it is the most excellent among all expressions, it is called 'designation. Or, because it is the most excellent among all conventions, it is called 'designation. Or, because it is the most excellent among all designations of objects, it is called 'designation. Or, because it is the most excellent among all designations of things, it is called 'designation. Or, because it is the most excellent among all designations of meanings, it is called 'designation. Or, because it is the most excellent among all designations of principles, it is called 'designation. Or, because it is the most excellent among all designations of dharmas, it is called 'designation. Or, because it is the most excellent among all designations of phenomena, it is called 'designation. Or, because it is the most excellent among all designations of entities, it is called 'designation. Or, because it is the most excellent among all designations of substances, it is called 'designation. Or, because it is the most excellent among all designations of bases, it is called 'designation. Or, because it is the most excellent among all designations of supports, it is called 'designation. Or, because it is the most excellent among all designations of causes, it is called 'designation. Or, because it is the most excellent among all designations of conditions, it is called 'designation. Or, because it is the most excellent among all designations of origins, it is called 'designation. Or, because it is the most excellent among all designations of sources, it is called 'designation. Or, because it is the most excellent among all designations of bases, it is called 'designation. Or, because it is the most excellent among all designations of supports, it is called 'designation. Or, because it is the most excellent among all designations of causes, it is called 'designation. Or, because it is the most excellent among all designations of conditions, it is called 'designation. Or, because it is the most excellent among all designations of origins, it is called 'designation. Or, because it is the most excellent among all designations of sources, it is called 'designation.'"

Some say that the mental consciousness (manovijñāna) is called "designation" (adhivacana) because it exercises sovereignty over the production of speech. This interpretation holds that it is called "designation" because it is the sovereign factor for speech;
this is an *ṣaṣṭhī-tatpuruṣa* (genitive determinative) compound. Furthermore, in the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 129, there are two further interpretations:
Question: Why is this contact called "designation" (*adhivacana*)?
Answer: Because the nature of this contact is augmented by speech, it is therefore called "designation.
Question: In what way is the nature of this contact augmented by speech?
Answer: Contact with resistance (*pratigha-saṃsparśa*) is bound only to the realms of desire and form.

This contact, however, extends to all three realms as well as that which is unbound, as explained at length in that [text]. Some say this contact is called "designation-contact" (*adhivacana-saṃsparśa*) because its object is designation.
Question: What is the designation for the object-condition (*ālambana*) of this contact?
Answer: Contact involving resistance (*sapratigha-sparśa*) takes only material phenomena (*rūpa-dharma*) as its object-condition;
this contact, however, universally takes both material and immaterial phenomena as its objects, as explained at length therein.
Regarding the aforementioned six types of contact that accord with the three feelings, such as pleasure and so forth:
hereafter, thirdly, the eight types of contact are explained.
These are divided into eight kinds based on their different modes of association.

The Commentary states: "Up to 'unobscured-neutral'" explains the first two phrases. Regarding "within the contact of ignorance... because it is associated with them": *Note: This excerpt corresponds to the commentary on the *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya*, specifically the section concerning the three types of contact (ignorance-contact, purity-contact, and neither-purity-nor-ignorance-contact) and their association with various mental factors.*
The third phrase is explained:
that which collectively encompasses all "arrivals" (prāpti) is termed "conducive to feeling" (vedanīya).
The fourth phrase is now explained.
The names can be understood from their enumeration.

Regarding the statement that these three types of contact are "conducive to feeling" (*vedanānukūla*), it means that these three contacts serve as causes capable of inducing the results of pleasant feelings and so forth;
thus, they are the inducers of that which is to be induced.
This contact is experienced by feeling because it is what is apprehended by the three types of feeling, such as pleasure; thus, feeling experiences contact, as explained in detail previously.
Although all mental factors arise from contact, [feeling alone is so designated].
Because it is that which is experienced through grasping, it is precisely what is experienced as being conducive to the act of experiencing.
Alternatively, contact serves as the basis for the aspect of experience;
this is because the aspect of experience necessarily arises in dependence upon contact.
This means that the basis conforms to what depends upon it.
Because it conforms in this way, it is called "conducive to feeling" (*vedanīya*).
How is it that contact is the basis for the formations (*saṃskāra*) experienced by feeling?
Question:
How is it that contact occurring simultaneously is experienced by feeling?
And how is it that contact occurring simultaneously serves as the basis for the activity of feeling? This can be understood from the first of the three previous explanations.
Therefore, they were not questioned separately.
As for the latter two, because they are somewhat obscure, they are now specifically investigated.
Regarding the statement, "The mode of activity (*ākāra*) is extremely similar to contact (*sparśa*), as it arises in dependence upon contact":
Answer: Because the mode of activity (*ākāra*) of feeling (*vedanā*) is extremely similar to that of contact (*sparśa*),
contact is what is experienced by feeling.
Just as a son resembles his father and inherits his father’s charm,
so too does he answer the preceding question:
this feeling arises in dependence upon contact.
Therefore, contact (*sparśa*) is the basis for the occurrence of feeling (*vedanā*).
This answers the subsequent question.
Thus, these combine to form sixteen types of contact.
Summary. Regarding the meaning of "feeling" (*vedanā*):
the following section is the fourth, which clarifies feeling.
Among these, there are two types:
first, the general;
second, the specific.
This is the general summary.
It summarizes the preceding inquiry as follows:
"Up to 'because it relies solely upon the mind.'"
Answer: Based on the distinctions among the causes of contact, it is divided into six types;
yet, with respect to the difference in their supports, they are further subsumed into two categories.
All [these terms] are *tatpuruṣa* (dependent) compounds.
Regarding whether "rebirth" (*upapatti*) occurs subsequent to or simultaneously with "contact" (*sparśa*),
the Sautrāntika master asks.
Regarding the Vaibhāṣika position that [feeling] exists up to the point of the co-existent cause (sahabhū-hetu),
the answer is:
contact and feeling arise together.
Because they are co-existent causes (*sahabhū-hetu*).
Regarding how the meaning of these two dharmas can be established,
the Sautrāntika school further objects.
How is it that the two phenomena of contact (sparśa) and feeling (vedanā) arise simultaneously, such that contact is established as the producer and feeling as the produced?
This meaning can be logically established.
Regarding how [the Sautrāntika] does not establish [this]:
the Vaibhāṣika counters the Sautrāntika by asking,
"Because it lacks functional capacity, it cannot reach other dharmas."
The Sautrāntika school further presents a logical refutation:
once a feeling has already arisen, other dharmas of contact have no power over it,
just as two horns of an ox grow simultaneously.
When these two look at one another, who can be designated as the "agent" (the subject) and the "object" (the recipient)?
As for the question, "What is the use of establishing a thesis and stating it so emphatically?",
the Vaibhāṣikas are not, moreover, of the Sautrāntika school.
The two difficulties presented earlier and later differ in wording but are identical in meaning.
What is the use of stating them again?
If that were so, there would be the fallacy of mutual production.
The Sautrāntika school further objects:
"Since both touch and feeling occur simultaneously, there is the fault that they would arise from one another.
If you accept this, it is not a fault; for even things that are simultaneous can be mutual causes."
The Vaibhāṣika masters reply:
We accept that contact and sensation are mutually cause and effect.
Although you grant this, as for the point regarding "the mind first and consciousness later," and so forth:
The Sautrāntika school further refutes the simultaneity of cause and effect.
The sūtra states only that contact gives rise to feeling;
it does not state that feeling gives rise to contact.
Thus we know that the preceding cause and the subsequent effect do not refer to things existing simultaneously as mutual causes and effects;
to say they arise mutually would contradict the teachings.
Furthermore, at this same time, the principle of mutual causality is not tenable;
because it would transcend the nature of that which produces, both this contact and feeling would simultaneously reach the present as already arisen.
How can it be said that they mutually act as producers?
Therefore, this interpretation is irrational, as it exceeds the nature of a producing dharma.
Generally speaking, when one speaks of cause and effect, the former must be considered in relation to the latter.
If this causal phenomenon is universally established in the world as being able to produce that resultant phenomenon,
then it is universally established that there is a temporal distinction between this causal phenomenon and that result,
just as in the case of the seed preceding the sprout.
Regarding the statement "from prior cause to subsequent effect, up to derived matter (*upādāya-rūpa*)," the Vaibhāṣika masters accept that the cause precedes the effect,
and they also accept simultaneous cause and effect.
Just as the effects such as visual consciousness coexist with their causes such as the eye and visible forms,
and the effect of derived matter coexists with its causes, the four great elements—
so too, in this case, what reasoning could possibly prevent you from accepting [this coexistence]?
The Sautrāntika school explains this away as follows:
here too, cause and effect are not simultaneous;
rather, it is the prior conditions of the sense organ and the object that can give rise to the subsequent result, which is consciousness.
The preceding thought acts as the cause that produces the four great elements;
how can it be obstructed from producing the subsequent fruit of derived matter?
Is it not the case that, like a shadow and a sprout, they exist simultaneously?
The Vaibhāṣika masters put forward the theory of simultaneous cause and effect;
the reason the Sautrāntikas do not refute it here is that it has already been refuted previously within the discussion of the co-existent cause (*sahabhū-hetu*).
Some say that feeling arises from contact through the condition of "posteriority" (*paścātpādaka*);
this is the interpretation of the Sthavira within the Sautrāntika school.
[They hold that] contact acts as the cause prior [to the feeling], and the subsequent fruit, feeling, arises.
Just as the sense faculty and its object precede it in the first moment,
consciousness arises immediately thereafter in the second moment; when consciousness arises,
it necessarily depends upon the faculty and takes the object as its condition.
This conjunction of the three is itself designated as contact;
it has no separate essence.
Alternatively, it consists of the preceding sense organ and object, together with the subsequent consciousness.
The conjunction of these three is conventionally designated as "contact" (sparśa).
In the third moment, with the preceding moment's contact as its condition, this present moment's sensation (vedanā) arises as its fruit.
If that is so, one might object: "Should not all instances where consciousness reaches [an object] be considered contact?"
The Vaibhāṣika masters raise an objection:
If they arise sequentially,
then at the time of contact in the second moment, consciousness would not necessarily be accompanied by feeling.
Because it is through this contact of the first thought-moment that the feeling of the subsequent thought-moment arises,
the various consciousnesses simultaneous with the feeling of the third thought-moment should likewise not all be contact.
The Sautrāntika school resolves this objection by stating that because this feeling arises from a preceding moment of contact,
there is no such fallacy [of infinite regress], nor is there anything that is not contact.
There is no such fault,
because the second moment of contact arises from the first moment, wherein the faculty, object, and contact occur simultaneously. Subsequently,
in the stage of the second moment of contact, feeling arises.
Therefore, whenever contact arises, it is invariably accompanied by feeling.
This explains the first objection.
Regarding the third point: there is no instance where the substance of consciousness existing simultaneously with feeling is not contact.
Because consciousness arises necessarily depending on the sense faculty and in relation to an object, these three are termed "contact" (sparśa).
Although this contact cannot produce a simultaneous feeling (vedanā),
it can produce a feeling in the fourth moment that follows it.
This explains the subsequent objection.
That this "is not reasonable" is the position of the Vaibhāṣikas.
Regarding what is contradictory in principle,
the Sautrāntika asks in return:
"Is it not the case that at times [the mental states] reach [their objects] and focus upon the same object?"
The Vaibhāṣika masters offer this rebuttal:
just as one single contact may have visible form as its object and another single contact may have sound as its object,
it is therefore said that there may be two contacts with distinct objects.

If the sensation (*vedanā*) in the subsequent moment, which takes sound as its object and arises from contact (*sparśa*) in the state of taking sound as its object, is produced by the contact in the preceding moment that took form as its object and was in the state of taking form as its object,
how can it be a sensation with a different object?
It arises from contact with a different object;
or else, one must admit that feeling is associated with a mind that takes sound as its object,
rather than being associated with a mind that takes the same single-sound object.
Because it arises from contact with a different object,
it should have the same object as the preceding moment of contact that took color as its object.
If this were so, what fault would there be in admitting such a case?
The Sautrāntika school counters:
Since there is the aforementioned fault, we now offer another explanation.
If it is granted that there is a tactile consciousness that arises from contact, [then our position holds].
This contact is without feeling (*vedanā*).
Just as the first moment of contact conditioned by sound can produce a subsequent moment of feeling belonging to its own category,
this consciousness is called "contact" and is therefore said to be contact.
Because it arises subsequent to contact with a different object,
there is no feeling (vedanā) at this stage prior to the initial moment of the sound-object.
Just as in the final moment of perceiving a form,
there is consciousness and feeling, yet their essence is not contact;
for consciousness exists because it cognizes the object.
Because sensation arises from contact of a preceding moment with its own kind, there is sensation;
however, a preceding moment cannot produce the initial moment of sensation that takes sound as its object,
for its essence is not contact.
It is so because the conditions differ;
what fault is there in this?
If, after having taken sound as an object, one subsequently takes form as an object...
The consciousnesses that take form as their object during the penultimate moment are designated as "contact" (*sparśa*),
because they are capable of producing the subsequent feeling (*vedanā*) that shares the same object.
If this were so, it would contradict the principle that [the mental factors] are always co-present within the category of the mind.
The Vaibhāṣika masters raise an objection:
if one says that contact (*sparśa*) and feeling (*vedanā*) do not always occur simultaneously,
then the category of the universal mental factors (*mahābhūmika-dharma*) is undermined.
"Because they must necessarily coexist with the mind.
"Upon what scriptural authority is that certainty established as always coexisting?
Thus the Sautrāntika challenges.
Regarding the establishment based on the root treatise:
the Vaibhāṣika masters reply that it is based on the six *pāda* (foot) treatises of the root *Abhidharma*.
We maintain that because it is not essential for [the object] to pervade all moments of mind,
the Sautrāntika position does not fail to be established by the scriptural authority (*āgama*) of the Sautrāntika school.
Furthermore, he explains:
Regarding the meaning of "universal mental factors" (mahābhūmika-dharma): it is not necessary that they must arise simultaneously with all minds.
If so, what is the meaning of the term "universal mental factors"?
The Vaibhāṣika asks: "That there are three stages [of consciousness] which were not originally recited in the sūtras.
The Sautrāntika replies:
If a dharma exists in all stages, including those with vitarka and vicāra, it is called a "universal mental factor" (mahābhūmika-dharma);
it does not need to arise simultaneously with the mind in a single moment to be designated as a universal mental factor.

The meaning [of this] also includes the explanation of the "great wholesome mental factors" (mahābhūmika-dharma) and so forth. As for why the "great unwholesome mental factors" (mahā-akuśala-bhūmika-dharma) are not explained, other masters say:
"Such great unwholesome mental factors as these..."
However, later Vaibhāṣika masters,
because they recited "greatly wholesome," cited "unwholesome" [as a parallel];
this is what has been added by them.
This is not recited in our own treatise;
therefore, it is not explained separately.
The reason why the minor afflictions (*upakleśa*) are not explained is as follows:
Because it is not universal.
If [it were argued that] feeling, perception, and volition arise simultaneously with contact,
the Vaibhāṣikas cite a sūtra as an objection.
The Sūtra states that contact (sparśa) arises simultaneously with feeling (vedanā), perception (saṃjñā), and volition (cetanā).
How then can it be said that feeling arises after contact?
Since the Sūtra merely says they arise together (sahaja), it does not serve as proof for [the claim that] it is not so.
The Sautrāntikas offer this explanation:
the sutra merely states that feeling (vedanā), perception (saṃjñā), and volition (cetanā) arise together;
it does not say that feeling and the others arise simultaneously with that contact (sparśa).
One must explain what contradiction this poses to our own school.
Furthermore, it is explained again:
within the arising of moments in immediate succession, one also finds the term "simultaneous" (*saha*).
As stated in the Sūtra: "One cultivates the awakening factor of mindfulness in conjunction with the meditative concentration of loving-kindness (*maitrī-samādhi*).
This term "conjunction" (*saha*) refers to immediate succession (*anantara-sahatva*).
It should be understood that the same applies to the statements regarding conjunction with contact (*sparśa*) and feeling (*vedanā*).
Because they are stated to be simultaneous, that [scriptural passage] is not a proof.
If so, why does it say, "up to the point of being separated from feeling and the rest"?

The Vaibhāṣikas cite this sūtra as a refutation, proving that [mental factors] arise simultaneously; the sūtra states that feeling and the other [factors], though distinct entities, are intermingled and certainly not separate.
Therefore, there is no consciousness that is separate from feeling and the other [mental factors].
This proves that feeling and the others are universal mental factors (*mahābhūmika*).
Since feeling and the others must necessarily exist whenever consciousness arises, [they are established as such].
This also demonstrates that feeling arises simultaneously with contact;
for when consciousness arises, the triad is conjoined, and thus contact necessarily arises.
Even if the Sautrāntika school asserts that contact is merely nominal (prajñapti), [the fact remains].
Furthermore, one must certainly admit that feeling (vedanā) and the other [mental factors] arise simultaneously,
because consciousness itself is contact (sparśa).
Thus, the Nyāyānusāra states:
The school that maintains that contact (*sparśa*) is a mere designation (*prajñapti*) must also admit that feeling (*vedanā*) and the other [mental factors] arise simultaneously with contact.
This is because this sutra states that consciousness is associated with feeling and the rest.
Since consciousness is a constituent of contact,
one should now carefully consider why it is stated [in the sūtra] as such.
The Sautrāntika school further cites scriptural passages to pose this question of indeterminacy.
Now one should reflect carefully:
in what sense are they "intermingled"?
Furthermore, this sūtra states that "whatever is felt is also what is thought," and so forth.
One has not yet understood the two preceding and following passages in the sūtra:

whether "intermingling" (saṃsṛṣṭa) refers to the arising [of cognitions] in succession with respect to the same object, or whether it refers to the arising [of them] simultaneously at the same moment. Thus it is said.
Regarding the determination that life-force (*āyus*) and warmth (*uṣman*) exist for a fixed number of moments,
the Vaibhāṣikas explain it as follows:
just as in the Sūtras there is a statement regarding the simultaneous arising and mutual intermingling of life-force and warmth.
It is known from examples that this sutra speaks of "fixed" (niyata) specifically in terms of moments (kṣaṇa).
Therefore, the Nyāyabindu-ṭīkā explains:
"The former [refers] to moments."
Furthermore, regarding the object of focus,
its principle is definitive.
Moreover, a sutra states that [contact] arises simultaneously with feeling and so forth.
The Vaibhāṣika masters cite a sūtra as an objection to show that [the factors] arise simultaneously within a single moment (*kṣaṇa*). Furthermore,
the aforementioned sūtra states that the conjunction of the three— faculty, object, and consciousness— is called contact (*sparśa*).
How could there be consciousness that is not contact through the triad?

Or how could there be a conjunction of the three—sense faculty, object, and consciousness—that is not termed "contact"? Therefore, one must certainly admit that all consciousnesses are invariably accompanied by contact.
There is no contact whatsoever that does not arise simultaneously with feeling and the other [mental factors].
Having concluded this incidental discussion, we now proceed to the second section: the detailed analysis according to the differences among the mental applications (*manopavicāra*).
Among these, first is the fixed number of categories,
and second is the analytical exposition of their meanings.
This is the first section:
the summary question and the response in verse.
The Treatise says: "From this point until 'the preceding gives rise to the subsequent'..."
Because the characteristics of bodily sensation (*kāyikī vedanā*) are manifest, they will not be further explained;
because the meaning of mental sensation (*caitasikī vedanā*) is obscure, it is clarified again here.
Within the single category of sensation briefly mentioned previously, it is divided into eighteen types.
One should understand that the word "furthermore" (punar) at the beginning of this verse indicates that the subsequent text arises following the preceding [section on] "appropriation" (upādāna).
What are these eighteen mental explorations (manopavicāra)?
