It is called "mixed" when it produces both pure and impure results;
it is called "pure" when it produces only pure results. Alternatively, it is called "mixed" when wholesome and unwholesome karma are intermingled;

it is called "pure" when it consists solely of wholesome karma. Alternatively, it is called "mixed" because, although one performs wholesome karma such as that of a human being, the defilements are so potent that one is frequently overwhelmed by them.
Although delusions may still arise even when performing wholesome karma for rebirth in the heavens,
it receives the designation "pure" because the wholesome is superior and the unwholesome is inferior.
What is the essential nature of this karma by which that result is produced?
The second phrase is explained.
This constitutes the question:
"That which is intended by the mind, up to that which is performed through volition."
Answer: Volitional action (*cetanā-karman*) refers to that which is intended by the mind;
because volition itself is action, it is called volitional action. Action subsequent to volition (*cetayitvā-karman*) refers to that which is produced by volition.
The two types of action—bodily and vocal—are performed by volition (*cetanā*).
Because they are performed after volition has arisen, they are called "actions subsequent to volition" (*cetayitvā-karma*).
These two types of action, along with mental action, constitute the actions of body, speech, and mind.
The commentary explains the latter two lines by dividing the two into three.
Regarding the question, "How are they established? it refers to their basis upon motivation (*samutthāna*).
Question:
Are these three types of action established in reference to the body that serves as their basis,
or are they based on their own intrinsic nature?
This is because it refers to the actual motivation (*samutthāna*). Even so, what contradiction is there?
This addresses the doubts of the opponent.
If it is argued that [the non-restraint] extends to the basis, the mental motivation, and the origination,
the outsider expresses his doubt:
"The Vaibhāṣika masters maintain that it extends by means of the latter three causes."
Answer: Bodily action (kāyakarman) is established by virtue of the body as its basis (*āśraya*). The aggregate of matter and form is collectively termed "body";
because this action depends upon the body, it is called bodily action. Verbal action (vākkarman) is established by virtue of its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
Because the nature of karma is speech, it is called vocal action (*vākkarman*); because it arises from [the mind], mental action (*manaskarman*) is established.
"Mind" refers to the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), and "action" refers to volition (*cetanā*). As for "arising," it means that which is able to give rise [to the action].
That which is in the mind (*manas*) but not volition (*cetanā*), or that which is originated by it;
that which is volition but not in the mind, or that which is both the agent and the object;
that which is both in the mind and volition, or that which is originated by the mind and so forth—these are what is meant by "in the mind."
Arising is itself volition (*cetanā*).
Because it is originated by the mind, it is called mental action (*manas-karman*). Therefore, the *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra* (Treatise on the Principles of Correct Reasoning), fascicle 33, states:
"That is to say, because karma depends upon the body, it is called bodily action (*kāya-karman*)."
Because the nature of karma is speech, it is called vocal karma (*vākkarman*).
This karma relies upon the mind;
furthermore, because it arises together with the mind and initiates body and speech, it is called mental karma (*manaskarman*).
The phrase "because it is that which the mind intends and from which it arises" explains the latter two lines.
The Master of the Treatise uses the word "however" (ran) because he is describing the three types of action according to the Sarvāstivāda school.
Volition is mental action;
volition is that which performs and that which originates [action].
Body and speech are that which is performed and that which is originated.
What is the intrinsic nature of these two types of action, bodily and vocal?
Below this, the second section clarifies the five types of karma. Within it:
first, a general explanation of informative and non-informative [karma];
second, a specific explanation of bodily and vocal informative [karma].
Third, the separate proof for the existence of non-informative [matter] (*avijñapti*). Below this, first, there is a general explanation of informative (*vijñapti*) and non-informative matter.
Mental action (*manas-karman*) is volition (*cetanā*), as has already been established previously.
The intrinsic nature of bodily and vocal [action] has not yet been explained; it is now asked.
The verse says: "Reaching that which has the nature of both informative and non-informative.
One should know that among these aforementioned three types of action, the two actions of body and speech both have the nature of being informative and non-informative.
Both are of the nature of form and action;
one is called "informative" (*vijñapti*) because it can manifest its own mind’s states, such as virtue, so that others may know them,
while the other cannot manifest its own mind and is therefore called "non-informative" (*avijñapti*).
Based on these distinctions, two types of names are established. Mental action (*manas-karman*) is non-material (*arūpin*);
because it cannot be manifested, it is not called "informative" (*vijñapti*).

Since there is no informative action, non-informative action (*avijñapti*) also does not exist; for the term "non-informative" is used to exclude that which is similar in kind to material things, namely the manifestations of body and speech.
Furthermore, as for what the characteristics of bodily and vocal intimation (*kāya-vāk-vijñapti*) are like:
this section below is the second part, which specifically clarifies bodily and vocal intimation.
This question is raised in order to introduce the explanation.
The verse says: "Regarding the statement that vocal intimation is admitted to be speech and sound," there are ten lines in this verse;
the first nine lines clarify bodily intimation.
The final phrase clarifies the expression through speech.
Regarding the preceding nine phrases,
the first one states that the Master of the Treatise [Vasubandhu] describes the Sarvāstivāda position that bodily form constitutes bodily intimation (*kāyavijñapti*).
The next five sentences constitute the Master’s refutation of the Saṃmitīya position that bodily motion constitutes bodily intimation (*kāyavijñapti*).
He refutes this first because both the Sautrāntika and the Sarvāstivāda schools do not accept the existence of such a moving form (*rūpa*).
Next, in three sentences, the author of the treatise refutes the Sarvāstivāda position that shape constitutes bodily intimation (*kāyavijñapti*).

According to the Sautrāntika school, both bodily and vocal intimations are explained as manifestations of a state (*avasthā*) within a continuous stream (*saṃtati*) of multiple entities—namely, matter (*rūpa*) and sound (*śabda*)—that have accumulated together.
First, there is no capacity for non-manifest action (*avijñapti*), because a single entity cannot manifest [an action] alone;
for it is taught that a single moment of wholesome or unwholesome [mind] lacks the capacity to benefit or harm.
Because it arises from a continuum and is an accumulation,
it is conventional and not real— this is according to the Saṃmitīya school.
Since it is accepted that among conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*) there exists informative action (*vijñapti*) over a long duration rather than perishing moment by moment,
both bodily and vocal informative actions are capable of manifesting [their meaning] based on the continuous movement of a succession of atoms (*paramāṇu*).

It is precisely because of this movement that [action] can manifest benefit or harm. According to the Sarvāstivāda school, the two types of manifest action—bodily and vocal—consist of distinct atoms (*paramāṇu*) and possess the nature of real existence (*dravyasat*).

Here, the Master [Vasubandhu], aligning himself with the Sautrāntika position, refutes both of those systems. Regarding vocal manifest karma, it is explained by analogy with bodily manifest action, and therefore is not discussed again here.

The commentary states: "Up to 'the informative action of the group of names' (*nāmakāya-vijñapti-karman*)," which explains the first phrase and describes the Sarvāstivāda school to clarify its own master’s tenet.
Therefore, the preceding verse states that bodily intimation is admitted to be a distinct shape.
A collection of hair, body hair, and so forth is collectively termed the "body.
Since the bodily form is not unitary, it is described as being "such-and-such" [a shape].
Within this body, by the power of volition (*cetanā*),
a specific bodily form arises; that which is capable of representing the mind is called bodily informative action (*kāyavijñapti-karma*).
Other masters state that [the term] "up to" (yāvat) refers to the statement that [motion] is not movement;
this explains the second phrase.
Other masters of the Saṃmitīya school say:

The Saṃmitīya school maintains that there is a distinct form called "bodily informative action" (*kāyavijñapti*), which consists of the movement of a collection of matter from one location to another;
for when the physical body moves, it is by means of this karmic matter that the body is able to move to that other place.

Among conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*), because the mind (*citta*), mental factors (*caitasika*), sound, light, and so forth perish in each moment (*kṣaṇa-nirodha*), they necessarily lack motion. Non-associated formations (*viprayuktasaṃskāra*), bodily intimation (*kāyavijñapti*), matter (*rūpa*), the body, mountains, fuel, and so on, do not perish in each moment but endure for a long duration.
According to their respective conditions, there is arising at the initial stage and cessation at the final stage,
while in the intermediate state there is abiding and transformation.

Since it does not undergo birth and cessation, it could be admitted that it has the sense of movement by passing from this place to another location; in order to refute this attachment, the verse states that there is no movement, because all conditioned phenomena (saṃskṛta) are momentary (kṣaṇika).
The following explains the third and fourth phrases by establishing the reason that there are moments (*kṣaṇa*) therein,
thereby providing a formal refutation.
To prove that there is no motion: the inference is that the matter of bodily intimation (kāyavijñapti-rūpa) certainly lacks motion,
because it is momentary,
like sound, light, and so forth.
Regarding the question "What is meant by a *kṣaṇa*?",
the Saṃmitīya school asks:
Regarding the statement that "the acquisition of its own essence, its immediate cessation, and its movement are called bodily intimation," the Master replies:
When a phenomenon that previously did not exist first arises, it is termed the "acquisition of its own essence.
This essence necessarily ceases immediately thereafter and returns to non-existence.
Because these conditioned phenomena possess this moment, they are called "momentary.
To illustrate this by means of a metaphor:
just as a person who possesses a staff is called "one with a staff," so too do all conditioned phenomena, upon reaching the present, merely acquire their own essence for a single moment.
From this present moment, it will necessarily cease and return to non-existence without interval;
as soon as it arises in this place,
it immediately perishes in this very place.
It is impossible for it to move from this place to another location before ceasing;
therefore, the Saṃmitīya school cannot claim that motion is what constitutes bodily intimation (*kāyavijñapti*).
If the meaning of a conditioned phenomenon (*saṃskṛtadharma*) were to be established as reaching [another place], then [this might be possible].
The Saṃmitīya school offers this defense:
If all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*) are momentary,
then the principle that a cause does not reach another location is logically established.
Since conditioned phenomena exist, there is no moment [of duration];
as in the case of bodily intimation and so forth, this cause of momentariness falls into the fallacy of being unestablished.
For all conditioned phenomena perish immediately upon their very arising.

The author of the treatise rescues [the argument] from the fault of non-establishment by explaining the two characters "exhausted" (kṣaya) in the fourth line: "Form and the non-associated [conditioned factors] necessarily possess momentariness,
because they must necessarily be exhausted later."
Like a lamp or other such things, the Master of the Treatise further demonstrates that cessation does not depend on a cause.
That is to say, conditioned phenomena necessarily cease moment by moment;
their cessation does not depend on a cause.
Why is this so? From the perspective of principle,
that which depends on causes is called the effect.
Cessation is a non-entity.
Since a non-entity is not a fruit, it does not depend on a cause. The inference is as follows:
cessation does not depend on a cause.
Because this [destruction] does not exist, it is like the horns of a rabbit; or, one may formulate the formal argument (*pramāṇa*) as follows:
destruction does not depend upon a cause.
Because it is not an effect, like a tortoise’s hair. Alternatively, one may formulate the formal argument (*pramāṇa*) as follows:
cessation does not depend upon a cause.
Because it is not non-resultant, it is like a flower in the sky;
since cessation does not depend on a cause, it ceases immediately upon arising. Herein, "cessation" is spoken of.
This means that conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*) cease once they have arisen.
This cessation is without intrinsic substance (*niḥsvabhāva*), as is universally established among all schools. Next, we shall generally explain the arising and ceasing of all conditioned phenomena;
there are two kinds of causes for this.
The first is the primary cause (*mukhya-hetu*).
This refers to the characteristic of arising and ceasing which is always concomitant with phenomena; because its causal function is powerful and preeminent, it is called the primary cause.
The second is the secondary cause (*āgantuka-hetu*).
That is to say, because other causes and conditions—whether present or absent—do not possess a preeminent causal function, they are called "guest causes" (*āgantuka-hetu*).
According to the Saṃmitīya school, the arising of all phenomena is difficult to account for except by means of both primary and guest causes.
When all phenomena cease, this applies equally to what is difficult and what is easy.
If mind, mental factors, sound, light, and so forth, cease solely through their primary causes and not through external conditions, [then they are easy to cease].

If [the cause] were non-associated, or other [factors] such as matter (rūpa) and fuel (indhana), then by means of both the primary and secondary causes, the arising of all phenomena (dharma) would be difficult to establish according to the Sarvāstivāda school.
This is because [their arising] depends upon both the primary and secondary causes.
The cessation of all phenomena occurs easily solely through their primary cause and not through external causes.
According to the Sautrāntika school, when phenomena arise, they do so by means of external causes;
however, when phenomena cease, they do not cease by means of external causes.
Since the primary cause lacks intrinsic nature, it cannot be called a "cause.
Furthermore, according to another interpretation of the Sautrāntika school, although arising and ceasing lack substantial reality, they are conventionally said to exist.
When phenomena arise, they do so by means of both primary and secondary causes.
When all phenomena cease, they do not cease by means of a cause.
It is like throwing an object into the air:
its upward motion depends on human effort, but its downward fall does not.
Furthermore, it is explained that the Sautrāntika school is similar to the Sarvāstivāda in asserting that when phenomena arise,
they do so through primary and secondary causes, and when phenomena cease, they do so through primary causes.
It does not arise from adventitious causes.
Although the primary cause lacks a distinct substantial entity, it may be conventionally designated as a cause. Furthermore, there are non-Buddhists who maintain this view.
"When all phenomena arise, they do so without cause;
when all phenomena cease, they do so without cause. This is a brief summary of the divergent tenets of various schools.
If it were not the case that they cease from the very beginning, it would necessarily contradict ultimate reality.
He restates that position and refutes it with a challenge:
"If dharmas such as form do not perish in their initial state,
they should likewise not perish in their subsequent states."
Since its substantial nature (svabhāva) in the subsequent state is identical to that in the initial state, the formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows:
At the time of the subsequent state, it ought not to perish,
because it possesses existence (*sattva*) and other such qualities.
It is just like the initial state; since there is subsequently the knowledge of exhaustion, one knows that what preceded has ceased. One establishes the formal argument (*pramāṇa*) as follows:
At the time of the initial state, there must also be cessation, because it possesses the nature of existence (*sattva*), and so forth.

It is just as in the case of a subsequent state: if you attempt to rescue [your position] by claiming that the substance of form and so forth exists in the subsequent state but is different from the prior one, such that it can then perish—then, regarding what is called "difference," at the time of the subsequent state, two phenomena are being compared.
It is not the case that the very same entity of the preceding state should be called by a different name;
it is logically impossible for the characteristics of that very same entity to be different.
Is it not the case in the world that everything ultimately does not depend on causes?
The Saṃmitīya school offers this defense:
it is evident that the cessation of all phenomena depends upon adventitious causes.
Is it not observed in the world that firewood and the like cease through the power of adventitious causes, such as contact with fire?
Therefore, one brings about cessation and non-existence.
Among the three types of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), one realizes all phenomena through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*);
there is certainly no room for inference (*anumāna*) or scriptural authority (*āgama*, *śabda*), as these cannot surpass direct perception regarding the present.
Therefore, it is not the case that the cessation of all phenomena does not depend on adventitious causes.
How do we know that fuel and the like cease because of contact with fire?
Thus the author of the treatise questions.
Regarding the statement, "Because fire is no longer perceived after it has come into contact with fuel and so forth," the Saṃmitīya school replies:
"One should together reflect upon this until it is established through inference."
The Master of the Treatise exhorts the Saṃmitīya school to consider this:
Is it as your own tenet holds—that these preceding pieces of fuel and so forth are no longer seen because they have been extinguished through the power of an external cause, namely contact with fire?

Or is it as our own tenet holds—that these preceding pieces of fuel and so forth, having arisen, perish of their own accord and are not extinguished by fire, such that subsequent fuel does not arise and is therefore not seen?
One should understand that when fuel and such are in contact with fire— or even when not in contact—
they perish of their own accord moment by moment due to their primary cause.
If the fuel and such possess the power to project a subsequent effect before being in contact with fire, then at the time they do come into contact with the subsequent fire, [the effect arises].
This fire merely renders the fuel and other factors powerless to project a subsequent effect;
furthermore, it prevents the subsequent fuel and other factors from arising, rather than destroying them.
This is like the wind coming into contact with a lamp flame in your own school of thought.
The hand and the sound of the bell are conjoined;
furthermore, it is admitted that fire and sound are not extinguished by adventitious causes such as wind or the hand.
Rather, at every moment, whether conjoined or unconjoined, they perish through their own primary cause.
When they have not yet conjoined, the flame and the sound possess the power to draw forth their subsequent effects;
however, once the hand and the wind have conjoined, the hand and the wind merely cause the flame and the sound to lack the power to draw forth their subsequent effects.

Furthermore, since one can obstruct the subsequent flame such that it does not arise, yet this does not mean the preceding flame has been extinguished, the principle that all these phenomena are momentary must be established through inference (*anumāna*). Moreover, it is explained that the principle that the cessation of these phenomena does not depend on a cause is thus established.
"What is meant by inference (anumāna)?
The Saṃmitīyas ask:
'As previously stated, because it has already arrived, it does not depend on a cause.'"
The Master of the Treatise cites the preceding text as the answer.
The formal syllogism (*pramāṇa*) is as stated before.
Furthermore, if that which awaits the arrival of causes were itself not dependent on causes, [it would follow that it exists eternally].
The explanation of the fifth phrase is that there should be no such thing as causeless destruction.

If you stubbornly insist that destruction must depend on adventitious causes such as firewood, then it would follow that all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*) undergo destruction only by depending on adventitious causes. To establish this, the formal argument (*prayoga*) is stated as follows:
Cessation, like arising and so forth, must depend on external causes, because it is included within the category of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*),
just as fuel and the like [depend on causes]; this is by analogy with arising.
Just as the arising of conditioned phenomena all depends on adventitious causes and none occurs without a cause,
so too should the principle of their cessation be understood:
they all depend on adventitious causes and none occurs without a cause.
If the cessation of all phenomena necessarily depended on adventitious causes, it would contradict direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
However, as is commonly observed in the world,
cognition, flames, and sound do not depend on adventitious causes for their cessation.
Because the mind and mental factors (citta-caitta-dharma) are capable of being cognized as perishing spontaneously at every moment, they are collectively termed "cognition" (*buddhi*).
This is stated by way of a formal syllogism (*upanyāsa*):
therefore, the extinction of fuel and so forth does not depend on external causes. The formal inference (*pramāṇa*) is as follows:
When fuel and so forth perish, they do not depend on external causes;
for they possess momentariness.
Regarding cognitions, flames, and so forth,
there are those who maintain that a cognition perishes after its preceding cause.
The following section sets forth and refutes these divergent views.
This is the view of a dissenting teacher of the Vaiśeṣika school:
the cause for the cessation of the preceding cognition of sound is the arising of the subsequent moment,
because the latter is of a nature contrary to the former.
It is just as a subsequent body of water pushes against a preceding flow of water;
that teacher does not establish four characteristics,
but maintains that the preceding momentary cognition is extinguished solely by the arising of the subsequent one.
"That too is irrational; by what, moreover, would it be extinguished?
Thus the Master of the Treatise refutes [the opponent], stating: "That too is irrational."
If two [cognitions] were to arise simultaneously, one could say that this ceases for the sake of that; however,
because the two preceding and succeeding cognitions,
as well as the two preceding and succeeding sounds, do not arise together.
If the subsequent [moment] has reached the present while the preceding one has not yet arisen,
it lacks substantiality and thus cannot extinguish the preceding dharma.
If the subsequent [moment] has reached the present while the preceding one has already passed away, [it likewise lacks the capacity].
How can a subsequent dharma extinguish a preceding one?
It is like the two dharmas of doubt and knowledge,
or the two dharmas of suffering and pleasure.
Regarding the two dharmas of greed and hatred and so forth,
since their specific characteristics (svalakṣaṇa) are mutually contradictory,
there is no logical possibility for them to coexist. How, then, can it be said that the latter ceases after the former?
Even if it were granted that a subsequent moment could destroy the preceding one,
how could a subsequent cognition and sound that are not clearly manifest destroy a preceding cognition and sound that are clearly manifest?
Even if it were granted that a subsequent inferior [state] could extinguish a preceding superior one,
such that a later [moment] in a continuous stream could extinguish an earlier one,
by what would the final cognition or sound be extinguished?
There are those who maintain that the extinction of a lamp’s flame is caused by non-existence (*abhāva*);
this is the position held by the Sthaviras and the Saṃmitīyas.
"Abiding" refers to the characteristic of abiding (*sthiti-lakṣaṇa*). If the characteristic of abiding were present in a dharma, its cessation would be impossible;
it is precisely because abiding is absent that a dharma can be ceased.
Therefore, that lamp-flame ceases by taking non-existence (*abhāva*) as its cause.
As for those who maintain that at the time of the flame's cessation it occurs through the power of *dharma* and *adharma*,
this is a divergent tenet of the Vaiśeṣikas.
Dharma and non-dharma are subsumed under the categories of virtue and meaning.
That which is beneficial to persons is called dharma;
that which is not beneficial to persons is called non-dharma.
By these two powers, one is able to give rise to all phenomena and able to extinguish all phenomena. It is like a bright lamp within a dark room;
for one who intends to make use of it, the presence of the lamp is beneficial.
This is the arising of dharmas;
the extinguishing of the lamp is of no benefit.
This is not the cessation of dharmas.
If one anticipates theft, the lamp is useless;
thus, non-dharma arises.
When the lamp is extinguished, it is beneficial.
"This is precisely the extinction of the Dharma.

Regarding the phrase "both are irrational because they are respectively concordant and discordant," the Master [Vasubandhu] simultaneously negates both attachments. To refute the former attachment, he says:
Now, to say that "abiding" is non-existent means that it lacks an intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).

Since a phenomenon lacking intrinsic nature cannot serve as a valid reason (*hetu*), it is said that "non-existence" is not a reason. To establish this through formal logic (*pramāṇa*), one states the syllogism as follows:
Abiding is not non-causal,
because it lacks intrinsic nature,
just like a rabbit’s horn. To refute the subsequent attachment, it says:
It is not that, according to the Vaiśeṣika school, both dharma and adharma act as causes for arising,
nor do both act as causes for cessation,
within a single moment; rather, this occurs moment by moment.
Dharma is conformity;
non-Dharma is opposition.
This is because the two are mutually contrary.
What are the causes for the simultaneous arising and ceasing of two dharmas? Furthermore, the *Nyāya* states:
"Neither dharma nor adharma are causes for cessation.
This is because one observes flames flickering within an empty cave; thus it is explained.
A flame within an empty cave neither harms nor benefits;
since there is nothing to oppose it and no dharma exists,
what could serve as the cause for its extinction?
"Or because every [entity] reaching its destination possesses momentariness" is a further refutation of the Vaiśeṣika position,
because [the motion] arises dependent upon that [substratum].
O Vaiśeṣika teacher, you may perhaps conceive that within all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*),
at every single moment, there exists the principle that "this dharma" and "non-dharma" act as the causes for arising and ceasing.
Even though you maintain that the causes for the arising and ceasing of phenomena and non-phenomena are distinct,
you nonetheless concede that conditioned things arise and cease moment by moment.
Since this constant arising and ceasing is precisely what the Sāmmitīyas dispute— namely, the absence of momentary destruction— your argument must now cease.
Because it is accepted that all things, without depending on other causes for cessation such as fire,
possess momentariness; furthermore, this explains the double refutation of the two types of grasping,
or [it applies] to all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*).
In every moment, it can be calculated that there exists the sense of a cause for this persistence and the absence of cessation,
and the sense of a cause for the cessation of this dharma or non-dharma.
Since this is so, the original dispute regarding the absence of momentary cessation should be brought to rest.

It is likewise admitted that [these] do not depend on other causes for extinction, such as fire, because they all possess momentariness (*kṣaṇikatva*). Furthermore, this is another interpretation refuting the Saṃmitīya school:
"You Saṃmitīyas [assert that] among all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*),..."
Since it can be determined at every moment that there is this sense of a primary cause for cessation,
the dispute with the Saṃmitīya school regarding the absence of momentary destruction should now cease.
This is because all things, such as fire, perish without depending on any other cause of destruction and exist for only a single moment (*kṣaṇa*).
Furthermore, if the conjunction with fire were the cause for the destruction of fuel and so forth,
then— as explained below regarding the sixth point— the cause of production would itself be capable of causing destruction.
Regarding the refutation of the thesis:
as for the claim that among those things produced through transformation by heat (*pākaja*), that which has reached the stage of low or medium maturation ceases [at that point],
this is precisely what is being refuted.
If you insist that fire is the cause for the destruction of fuel and so forth,
then the very essence of the cause of production would become the cause of destruction.
For example, when fire burns wood, there are three distinct grades— low, medium, and high— in the process of its transformation as it develops.
The first, being yellowish, is called "inferior";
the next, being black, is called "middling";
and the last, being entirely black, is called "superior."

The very substance that serves as the cause for arising would then become the cause for cessation. Why is this so? It is because the conjunction of the cause of fire with fuel and so forth can bring about the production of three distinct types of transformation through heating within that fuel.
The arising of the medium-maturity [state] is the cessation of the inferior-maturity [state]; the arising of the superior-maturity [state] is the cessation of the medium-maturity [state].
It follows that the cause for the arising of the medium-maturity [state] must be identical to the cause for the cessation of the inferior-maturity [state].
Because the middle ripening perishes at the very moment the superior ripening arises,
the cause for the arising of the superior ripening must be the same as the cause for the perishing of the middle ripening;
for the middle ripening perishes at the very moment the superior ripening arises.
Therefore, it is said that the very entity which is the cause of arising becomes the cause of cessation;
or that it is either identical to or resembles [the cause] when it reaches the stage of maturation prior to cessation.
This explains the meaning of the opponent's proposed defense.
Either that which produces the ripening of the lower grade acts as the cause for the cessation of the ripening of the lower grade;

it is not the case that the cause which produces the ripening of the middle grade can cause the cessation of the ripening of the lower grade; or rather, it is that which produces the ripening of the middle grade [which acts as the cause].

That which can serve as the cause for maturation in the intermediate state is not the cause for maturation upon being born in a higher realm; rather, it is that which can cause cessation in the intermediate state.
Therefore, it is said that they are either identical or different. This is the calculation of identity or difference;
furthermore, it is the calculation of transformation, whereby a cause for ripening in the lower realms appears as a cause for extinguishing ripening in the lower realms.
The ripening cause during the phase of arising resembles the ripening cause during the phase of cessation;
although the two causes for the arising and cessation of a flame are distinct,
they appear similar because they are intermingled simultaneously.
One serves as the cause for arising,
and one serves as the cause for cessation;
it is not that a single dharma acts as the cause for both arising and cessation— such is their [the opponents'] calculation.
In a continuous succession of flames that remains uninterrupted and similar from beginning to end,
the preceding moment serves as the cause of arising, while the succeeding moment serves as the cause of cessation.

It is not that a single dharma serves as the cause for both arising and ceasing; rather, it is like how the cause that produces a lower degree of maturation is simultaneously capable of being the cause that extinguishes a lower degree of maturation, whereas the cause that does not produce a lower degree of maturation cannot extinguish that lower maturation.
Although they appear similar, their natures are distinct.
Or, that which is the cause for maturing within the state of being "unripe" can itself act as the cause for destroying the "middling" degree of ripening.
The cause that ripens during birth is not the same as that which extinguishes during the intermediate state;
although they appear similar, because their natures are distinct, it is said that they are "perhaps similar."
"This is either a [false] conception or something resembling one; thus, the causal substance arises, or it is non-existent in this regard"—
this refutes the two preceding conceptions.
If the nature of the causes for the arising of the lower and middling [fruits] were identical to the causes for the destruction of the lower and middling [fruits],
how could that which is a cause of arising be a cause of destruction?
This refutation may be understood as follows: either [the cause] is identical to the maturation, destruction, and production causes;
or, in the case of medium-grade maturation, destruction, and production causes, their essential natures must be similar and indistinguishable from one another.
Since their natures are similar, how can it be said that one is the cause of arising and the other is the cause of cessation?
This refutation may appear to be based on a misconception; from "it should not" onwards, both schools are refuted simultaneously. That is to say:
This is either the conceptualization of "similarity," or it is the expression "there is similarity," or the expression "arising is not existent."
Extinction should not occur through this very flame; nor do those lower and middle ripenings exist by means of this very flame.
Furthermore, those lower and middle ripenings do not exist through this very flame.
This refutation may be formulated as follows: It is not tenable that those inferior or middling ripenings exist by virtue of this or a similar flame;
nor is it the case that those inferior or middling ripenings do not exist by virtue of this or a similar flame.
This refutation may appear to be a mere conceptualization; this passage intermingles a dual refutation of both schools.
The author’s phrasing is skillful, so one should reflect upon it well.
Even if one were to argue that the flames differ from the causes of their arising and ceasing:
Even granting that the critical analysis and refutation might momentarily arise with respect to the flames.
Suddenly they subside;
sometimes they merge,
sometimes they disperse.
At times long,
at times short;
or perhaps less.
Alternatively, within the various distinctions of arising, one might consider that the causes of production differ and the causes of cessation differ; however,
in the six substances such as ash and so forth, there are no distinct characteristics such as fluctuation or non-fluctuation.
Since contact with fuel and the like can cause the fuel and so forth to undergo transformation and ripening within the process of arising,
how can you calculate that the causes of arising and ceasing are distinct?
If that were so, what would be the purpose of observing "reaching" (prāpti) as it is actually perceived?
The Saṃmitīya asks: "If that is so, we observe directly that when water is boiled, it diminishes until it is exhausted;
by this, it is clearly known that fire is the cause of its cessation."
If it were not so, what function would the conjunction with fire perform therein?
For it is by means of the actual conjunction with fire that the principle [of combustion] can be established.
The author of the treatise replies:
Through the conjunction with the external fire-element,
the power of the primary fire-element increases.
Due to the increase of the primary fire element,
it causes the mass of water to gradually diminish and cease its continuity;
this is called the action performed by the conjunction with fire within [the mass].
Fire merely causes the preceding water to lose its power and prevents it from drawing in subsequent water;
furthermore, it obstructs the subsequent water so that it cannot arise.
It does not extinguish the preceding water. Therefore, there is no external cause (*āgantuka-hetu*) that brings about the cessation of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*).
Conditioned phenomena do not remain still for even a single moment;
their own essence perishes because they are of a disintegrating nature and because they cease spontaneously.
Arising and ceasing simultaneously,
the meaning of "moment" (kṣaṇa) is established;
because there are moments, there is certainly no motion.
"Motion" is a mere conventional designation for [an entity] appearing in successive locations;
it is a false claim of motion, a conceit of overestimation (*abhimāna*). After the Master has refuted this, he further permits the transmission of the following statement:
"By this reasoning, it is established that according to the Saṃmitīya school, motion certainly does not exist."
The Sarvāstivāda position that bodily intimation (*kāyavijñapti*) is shape is thus logically established; having briefly stated this provisional admission, it is now refuted in succession.
However, as for the Sautrāntika claim that [intimation] consists of a distinct category of matter (*rūpa*):
Below this, the author of the treatise sets forth the Sautrāntika position to refute the Sarvāstivāda claim that shape (*saṃsthāna*) is substantially real.
This explains the seventh phrase of the verse: "Shape, too, is not substantially real."
Since there is no real form, it is conventionally established based on color.
That is to say, various colors arranged in different ways are conventionally designated as the forms of long, short, square, and round.
This can be understood from the text itself. Regarding the remaining shapes that should be understood accordingly:
among these, the color "high" is conventionally established based on the arising of a convex surface, while the color "low" is conventionally established based on the arising of a concave surface.
Within the midst of the composite (samsthāna-rūpa), one conventionally designates "correct color" (samyak-varṇa);
within the midst of the irregularly produced, one conventionally designates "incorrect color" (asamyak-varṇa).
In reality, when one perceives manifest color (varṇa-rūpa), what is intended [by the designation] are [dimensions such as] length and so forth.
This is illustrated by a metaphor:
it is like seeing a whirling firebrand,
where its rapid movement makes it appear long.
"Perimeter" refers to circularity.
This length and circularity are provisionally established based upon the fire-brand;
in reality, one perceives the fire-brand itself as being long and so forth.
The principle that shape depends upon color should likewise apply here;
therefore, shape has no real, distinct substantial entity as a type of matter.
If it is argued that there exists a real capacity to perceive shape, [that too is untenable].
This explains the eighth phrase of the verse: "because it is to be apprehended by two sense-faculties.
The Sautrāntika master says:
"If you maintain the position that shape is real, then [it would follow that]..."
Then it would follow that a single shape-color (saṃsthāna-rūpa) is apprehended by two color-faculties;
that is, the eye-faculty is able to see the distinctions such as length and so forth within a collection of matter.
The body faculty is capable of touching,
yet it simultaneously perceives [qualities] such as length;
by this, the fallacy of two faculties apprehending the same object would be established.

From the perspective of reasoning, among the twelve bases (*āyatana*), there is certainly no single base of form (*rūpāyatana*) that is apprehended by two faculties of form. Having finished refuting [the opponent's view] through reasoning, he states the correct principle:
"However, it is just as when consciousness arises in dependence on the tangible (*spraṣṭavya*)."
Within that [color], one apprehends the conventional [notion] of length and so forth;
likewise, based on color, the mental consciousness apprehends the conventional form within it.
Since shape depends on touch and is established as a conceptual construct,
it is said that the mind apprehends it.
But would it not be the case that when touch reaches the shape, one is able to recollect the color of the flower?
The Sarvāstivādins offer this defense: "The statement that [the body] exists [only] through action is not correct, for touch and form coexist within a single aggregate;
thus, the body takes touch as its object, while the mind is able to recollect the forms and colors previously seen."
It is not that the body directly perceives form within the contact;
therefore, there is no fault of the sense-field of form being apprehended by two faculties. This is illustrated by way of analogy:
just as the eye sees the red color of fire.
The mind then recollects the prior sensation of the warmth of fire;

it does not directly perceive the tactile object within the visible form. Or again, as when the nose smells the fragrance of a flower, the mind is able to recollect the prior sight of the flower's color.
The nose does not directly perceive color within the fragrance;
rather, it is these two factors [smell and color] that reach the object and enable the recollection of its shape.
This is the Sautrāntika objection.
In this context, the red color of fire and the heat-tangible quality of fire,
as well as the fragrance of a flower and the color of that flower,
are two phenomena that are invariably inseparable.
Therefore, by perceiving one [quality], one can recollect the others.

There is no such tangible object (*spraṣṭavya*) that can be perceived as being invariably associated with or inseparable from such a shape (*saṃsthāna*), because a smooth tangible object may possess length and so forth.

At times, roughness and other [tangibles] may also possess length and other [dimensions]. How, then, can one apprehend a tangible and subsequently recollect its shape? Furthermore, even granting this, it is argued:
if the tangible and the shape are not necessarily co-located, yet one apprehends the tangible and recollects the shape, [this would be impossible].
Furthermore, tangibility is not necessarily co-present with visible color;
likewise, visible color should also be recollected through tangibility.
Moreover, just as visible color does not invariably belong to tangibility, [tangibility does not invariably belong to visible color].

At the time of touch, one cannot discern the manifest color (*varṇa*), because it does not invariably belong [to the same object]. Alternatively, shape (*saṃsthāna*) would likewise, like manifest color, not invariably belong to touch;
thus, at the stage of perceiving touch, shape should be indiscernible. However, in reality, this is not the case according to the principles of logic.
When touching with eyes closed, one can only discern shape and not color;
by this, it is known.
Since the form is provisional while the color is real, you should not say that one can recollect a previously seen real form by grasping the touch.
If one were to recollect the real form, why would one not recollect the color? Since one does not recollect the color, [the former claim is untenable].
It is understood that shape is provisional; furthermore, it is explained that color-form (varṇa-saṃsthāna) is not so [provisional]. Why is this?
If there were a real shape, the body would also directly perceive it.
Therefore, one should not say that because of grasping at contact,
one is able to recollect a previously seen real form;
nor [should one say this] regarding things such as brocades, which do not possess a truly existent substance.
The Sautrāntika school further refutes this,
stating that within a piece of brocade or similar fabric, one may see a horse when looking from the left,
yet see an ox when gazing from the right.
Those who see correctly perceive people,
while those with distorted vision see ghosts;
their various forms and images are of different kinds and not the same.
It would follow that there must be multiple real forms in a single location, which is logically impossible.
Just as various manifest colors (varṇa) possess multiple real entities without undergoing change, so too [the same applies here].
Therefore, shape (saṃsthāna-rūpa) does not exist as a real entity.
Furthermore, regarding all those things that reach [the senses] and are conventionally designated as "long" and so forth,
the Sautrāntikas raise another objection:
moreover, all those five sense-faculties and five objects which are resistant and substantial matter.
One must necessarily admit that there are real, distinct types of atoms when investigated through reasoning;
however, no atom exists that can be designated as "long" and so forth.
Therefore, it is precisely the plurality [of atoms] that manifests as the subtle atom (*paramāṇu*).
Within such a differentiated arrangement of characteristics, "length" and so forth are conventionally established. The formal argument (*prayoga*) is stated as follows:
Shape is not substantially existent.
Because there are no distinct atoms;
it would be like a flower in the sky and so forth.
If it is argued that [the object] exists simply by means of a collection and arrangement, [then...]
The Sautrāntika cites the Sarvāstivāda’s defense against this refutation:
"If you claim that it is simply the arrangement of shape-atoms (*saṃsthāna-paramāṇu*) that is called 'long' and so forth,
this exposes the aforementioned fault that there is no distinct atom as a cause, resulting in the fallacy of non-establishment."
This is merely a partisan bias;
I do not accept it, because it is not universally established (*aprasiddha*). Furthermore, this interpretation belongs only to the partisan school of the Vaiśeṣika masters.
That school’s position—that the nature of manifest color (*varṇa*) and shape (*saṃsthāna*) are distinct—is not universally established.
If the shape-atoms were mutually established as distinct entities,
they could be arranged to constitute length and so forth; however,
shape-atoms are not mutually established as distinct entities in the same way that visible colors are.
How are they arranged? The *Nyāyānusāra* explains that the Sarvāstivādins offer this defense:
"Has it not already been stated that the atoms themselves possess shape?

It is based on such an arrangement that the eye-consciousness perceives a collection of distinct [atoms], which is then conventionally designated as 'long' and so forth. According to the intent of this defense in the *Nyāyānusāra*:

The establishment of [concepts such as] length and so forth is known by mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) and not apprehended by the five sensory consciousnesses (*pañcavijñāna*). If one were to refute this from the perspective of a Vaibhāṣika master, [the opponent would argue:
"In your own system, you originally established that length and so forth are real;
only when pressed by our objection do you claim that length and so forth are merely conventional (*prajñapti*)."
[Sautrāntika: "Is it not evident that things which have reached [the same location] can have different forms?
[Sarvāstivādin: The Sarvāstivādins offer this defense:
"Is it not evident that various objects, such as earthenware vessels, [differ in form despite being in the same place]?"
Some are blue,
some are yellow;
they have similar manifest characteristics.
Since the forms of jars, basins, and so forth differ from one another,
we know that external objects possess distinct, real shapes.
If you argue that this has not yet established the ultimate truth and that it must likewise be so [for all things], [we reply:]...
The Sautrāntika school further refutes this:
"Has this point not already been established previously?

It has been clearly demonstrated that 'long' and so forth, as well as the distinctions such as 'jar' and 'bowl,' are merely conventional designations based on the specific arrangements of many substances. [The opponent] now employs a metaphor to illustrate this."

Just as a multitude of ants and the like possess black color and other such characteristics without distinction, yet at times they may be arranged in different shapes, such as long lines or circular wheels;

apart from the characteristics of the ants themselves, there is no separate "line" or "wheel" shape. By the same principle, it should also be understood that [the shape] does not exist apart from the manifest color and so forth.
Apart from color and so forth, there is no separate shape. [The phrase] "color and so forth" includes tangibility by way of the term "and so forth.
Is it not the case that in the dark, what is perceived as an arrangement [of parts] constitutes shape?
The Sarvāstivādins offer this defense:
"Is it not the case that when one perceives a log or similar object with the eye in the dark or at a distance,
one only discerns its shape, such as length, and does not discern its manifest color, such as blue?"

The Sautrāntika provides this general explanation: "If one clearly knows that there is a real shape distinct from the manifest colors, how could it be that the arrangement of those very manifest colors constitutes the shape?
For in cases of darkness or distance, one perceives only a general mass."
Because visible forms are not clearly perceived when viewed from a distance or in darkness, they are not entirely unperceived;
for this reason, the mental consciousness merely gives rise to conceptual discriminations such as long, short, square, or round.
It is not that one perceives their actual form; rather, they are illustrated by means of a metaphor.
For example, when people view a grove of trees from a distance or in the dark, their mental consciousness merely apprehends the conventional designation of "a grove of trees."
The multitude of people, relying on the army, does not know the multitude of trees.
The multitude of people perceives them as distinct from one another; furthermore, they understand that consciousness merely cognizes the rows of trees and the human army.
Visual consciousness does not know the specific characteristics (*viśeṣa-lakṣaṇa*) of trees or persons;
the analogy of an army represents the shape (*saṃsthāna*), while the specific characteristics represent the manifest color (*varṇa*). This principle must necessarily be so.
What is the reasoning for this? It is because at times the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) does not discern the distinctions between color and shape;

it only cognizes the general aggregate as a conceptual mark (*prajñapti-nimitta*). Furthermore, it is understood that the visual consciousness (*cakṣurvijñāna*) does not discern these two types: color and shape.
Mental consciousness (manovijñāna) cognizes only the general, collective, and provisional characteristics; because it is not clear, it is called "not manifesting" (anabhivyakta).

Because it does not take shape as its object, it is called "not manifesting shape" (anākṛty-abhivyakta). Furthermore, another interpretation holds that visual consciousness is called "not manifesting" because it is not clear and distinct, and thus "not manifesting"; it is not entirely non-cognizing.
The mental consciousness does not comprehend form;
because it does not differentiate form, it is said to "not comprehend form.
The mental consciousness only knows the general, collective, and provisional characteristics.
Having thus refuted [the opponent's position], he asks what is established as bodily intimation (*kāyavijñapti*).
He concludes the inquiry by stating that he has already refuted the Saṃmitīya masters' claim that "motion" (*gati*) is called bodily intimation.
Furthermore, while the Sarvāstivādins maintain that actual shape constitutes bodily intimation (*kāyavijñapti*),
what do you Sautrāntikas posit as bodily intimation?
If you posit shape as bodily intimation, it is merely conventional and not real.
The Sautrāntika replies:
They establish shape (*saṃsthāna*) as bodily intimation (*kāyavijñapti*), which differs from the Saṃmitīya school;

yet they maintain that it is merely conventional and not substantial, which differs from the Sarvāstivāda school. In the tenet of those Sautrāntikas, both bodily and vocal intimations are merely conventional designations upon matter and sound.
Regarding the question, "Since you maintain that only the movement itself constitutes bodily action," the Sautrāntika asks:
"If you maintain that only the conventional form serves as the substance of bodily intimation (kāyavijñapti), [how can this be so?]"
Furthermore, what dharma is established as bodily action (*kāyakarman*)?
If it is asked, "Should one not know that the same applies to an action that depends on the body?
the Sautrāntika replies: "If an action proceeds by way of the bodily door (*kāyadvāra*)."
That is to say, it arises by taking bodily intimation as its object; the same explanation applies to vocal action.
Other than these, the remainder proceeds together with the mind and arises based on the mental level (*manobhūmi*);
therefore, they are called "dependent on the mental door" (*manomukha-pratibaddha*).
Although the other two gates also rely on the mind (*manas*),
they establish distinct names based on specific meanings;
this [gate of] feeling (*vedanā*) takes the general term as its specific designation.
As with the sense-base of form and so forth,
it should be stated in full as "karma based on the body" and "karma based on speech."
Regarding the karma of the mind: according to the Sautrāntika school, all three types of karma have volition (*cetanā*) as their essence.
If that is so, why is it said [in the sūtras] that there are two? What is the difference between these two?
Thus the Sautrāntika is questioned.
Citing the teachings to distinguish the contradiction:
if the substance of his three karmas were all volition (*cetanā*),
how could the Sūtra say, "having willed" (*cetayitvā*)?
What is being referred to?
Since it has already been stated that [the action] is "having intended," it is clearly understood that the two types of karma are not volition itself.
Regarding the statement that "the preceding preparatory action up to the point of naming it 'completed action' [is so called]," the Sautrāntika school provides a comprehensive explanation:
volition (*cetanā*) and reflection (*manasikāra*) are the remote causes and motivations (*samutthāna*).
The *Mahāyāna-karmasiddhi-śāstra* states that the volition of performing an action (*kṛtya-cetanā*) is the proximate cause of origination (*samutthāna*).
It identifies two types: first, the volition of deliberation (*santīraṇa-cetanā*), and second, the volition of determination (*niścaya-cetanā*).
In this treatise, volition that is encompassed by reflection is categorized as the karma of volition;
volition that initiates movement is categorized as the volition of performance. This refers to the karma subsequent to volition; it does not refer to the momentary origination (*kṣaṇasamutthāna*).
At this time, the nature of the mind need not be identical,
for the two gates of sin and merit are not determined by it; thus,
one does not rely on that [nature] to explain the distinctions among karmas.
If, at that stage, a corresponding volition arises, it is subsumed under two types of volition as appropriate:
bodily and vocal karma are the volition of performance (*kṛtya-cetanā*), while mental karma is called the volition of having intended (*cetayitvā-karma*).
If that were so, it would lead to the great error that manifest karma (vijñapti-karma) persists;
this is the objection. The response is: the volition (cetanā) that performs an action is called "karma after having intended" (cetayitvā-karma).

If informative action (*vijñapti-karman*) consisting of form and sound were definitively non-existent, then since informative action does not exist, uninformative action (*avijñapti-karman*) in the desire realm would likewise not exist.
This is because uninformative action in the desire realm arises dependent upon informative action; [if it did not,] it would result in a great logical error.
Regarding the question, "What fault is there in such a great error reaching this point?
the Sautrāntika replies:
"Such a great error can be refuted by reason."

This refers to the various distinct manifestations of volition that arise from the power of the active volition—superior due to its remote and proximate causes—that initiates the two types of informative action previously described:
bodily movement and vocal utterance. These distinct manifestations of volition are termed "differentiation of volition."
Alternatively, it is called "discrimination of volition" because it is distinct from the seeds of other volitions;
since it is provisionally established upon the seeds of volition, it is termed "unmanifest" (*avijñapti*).
What fault is there in this? Regarding the explanation of the term:
This seed of volition, which cannot move the body or initiate speech to manifest the internal mind, is called "unmanifest action" (avijñapti-karman).
According to the Sautrāntika school, both bodily and vocal manifest actions are neutral (avyākṛta) in nature.
Because volition (*cetanā*) permeates all three natures (*trisvabhāva*), only the karma of volition can perfume and form seeds; manifest action (*vijñapti*) cannot.
Thus, the *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra* (Treatise on Following Reason), fascicle 34, states:
"They [the Vaibhāṣikas] maintain that bodily and vocal actions are exclusively neutral (*avyākṛta*)."
Regarding the statement, "This should be called that which arises together with a sincere mind," there is a further objection:
if the seed of volition is what is termed the unmanifest (avijñapti), [how can it be so called?].
The seeds of that volition constantly adhere to the mind;
this should be termed "unmanifest karma that follows the mind" (*cittānuvartin-avijñapti-karman*),
because it functions in conjunction with the mind, just as the unmanifest karma associated with meditative concentration (*samādhi-sahaja-avijñapti*) does.
Regarding the statement "there is no such fault because [the mind] is dull by nature," the Sautrāntika school further explains:
"I do not have such a fault of being subject to the fluctuations of the mind."

The non-informative [matter] (*avijñapti*) arising from the distracted mind of the desire realm is produced by being drawn forth by the distant causal motivation (*dūre-hetv-utthāna*) of prior active reflection, superior volition, and decisive superior volition,
as well as by the proximate causal motivation (*āsanne-hetv-utthāna*) of the initiating superior volition.
There are also [unmanifest actions] that exist without consciousness; these are not called "actions that follow the mind" (*cittānuvartin*).
If a determinate unmanifest action is not induced by that volition, it does not follow the mind.
However, because it is only conceptually established upon the volition that accompanies the concentrated mind,
it exists while one is in meditative absorption and ceases to exist once one has emerged from it.
Therefore, it is called "action that turns according to the mind.
Thus, this does not constitute a valid precedent. Suppose I were to adopt your position and agree with the Sarvāstivādins that there exist two types of manifest action: bodily and vocal.
Furthermore, it depends on the power of volition as previously described to bring about the non-informative (avijñapti);

the informative (vijñapti) itself cannot produce the non-informative, because the nature of bodily and vocal informative matter is dull. Moreover, even if one were to grant, for the sake of argument, that you have a distinct informative [action], [it still would not suffice].

You too must wait for the two types of volitional force—the distant and the proximate—as previously described, before they can induce non-informative matter (*avijñapti*), because the nature of informative matter (*vijñapti*) is dull.
Furthermore, it is explained that it is not only non-informative matter that depends on the induction of prior volition.
Even if one were to grant the existence of informative action (*vijñapti*),
it too would depend upon the power of volition (*cetanā*) as previously described,
because the nature of informative action is dull.
Regarding the statement that "the Vaibhāṣikas hold that it has shape as its essence":
this refers to the Vaibhāṣikas returning to their own fundamental tenet,
asserting that the essence of vocal informative action (*vāgvijñapti-karman*) is simply the sound of speech.
This explains the tenth phrase.
According to the explanation of the Sarvāstivāda school,
bodily informative action (*kāyavijñapti*)— including hair, body hair, nails, and so forth— is collectively termed "the body."
The manifestation of colors such as long and short that represent the internal mind is called *vijñapti* (informative action).
Because this *vijñapti* involves volitional activity, it is termed *karman* (action).
It arises based on the body.
This indicates that it is called "karma";
therefore, it is named "bodily informative karma. Regarding "vocal informative karma," "speech" refers to vocal sound.
Sound that can express the internal mind is called *vijñapti* (manifestation).
Because manifestation involves volitional activity, it is called *karman* (action).
Speech itself is precisely this manifestation.
Because the manifest [action] is itself karma, it is called vocal manifest karma. Regarding "vocal and mental karma":
"mental" refers to the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).
Karma is volition (*cetanā*).
Because karma arises from the mind, it is called mental action (*manas-karman*).
Thus, the *Nyāyānusāra* states:
Why is it that the essence of vocal intimation (*vāgvijñapti*) is identical to speech,
whereas bodily intimation and mental karma are not identical to the body or the mind?
Because apart from speech, there is no other sound capable of manifesting [intention].
Since there are bodily and mental informative acts (*vijñapti*) as well as volitional acts (*cetanā-karman*),
the designation "bodily karma" is established based on its support (*āśraya*),
while "vocal karma" is established according to its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
Mental action arises in accordance with its motivation;

thus, there is no fault of contradiction therein. The above is the treatise’s own explanation. If, however, one follows the Sautrāntika interpretation, bodily action is [defined as] informative (*vijñapti*).
The body is explained as before.
It is designated by taking the provisional form as its substance;
that is to say, the continuity of form is able to represent the internal mind.
This informative [action] is a conventional designation established upon form (*rūpa*).
"Action" refers to movement and bodily volition (*kāya-cetanā*).
Because this action arises by depending on the door of the body, it is called "bodily informative action. Regarding "vocal informative action":
"Speech" refers to sound.
Its manifestation has sound as its essence;
that is to say, the continuity of sound is able to express the internal mind.
This informative [action] is a provisional designation established upon sound.
"Action" refers to the volitional action of initiating speech; because it can give rise to informative [action] by means of the gateway of speech, it is called vocal informative action.
Mental action is the same as previously described.
Regarding the statement "the characteristics of non-informative action (avijñapti-karman) have already been explained above":
this refers to the third section below, which specifically clarifies the characteristics of non-informative action by referring back to the previous explanation.
The verse does not explain them separately, but rather establishes their actual existence through realization.
Regarding the statement, "The Sautrāntika school also says it reaches the formless (ārūpya) aspect," this recounts the Sautrāntika interpretation.
The Sautrāntikas also say [this].
This unmanifest karma (avijñapti-karma) does not possess a real, substantial nature.
Because one refrains from committing various evils due to a prior vow or restriction, the term "non-doing" expresses the avoidance of doing;
it does not have a separate ontological entity. Furthermore, the nature of that unmanifest karma is also designated based upon past primary elements (mahābhūta).
However, since the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) upon which it formerly depended have already ceased and lack substantiality, how could the dependent unmanifest (*avijñapti*) actually exist?
Furthermore, all unmanifests lack the specific characteristic (*sva-lakṣaṇa*) of matter, which is to be subject to change and obstruction (*rūpaṇā*).
How can it be said that this form (rūpa) truly exists?
It would pose no obstacle [to our position] if one were to merely establish the non-informative (avijñapti) as a conceptual designation upon the seeds of volition (cetanā-bīja).
Regarding the statement that "the *Vibhāṣā* says this also exists substantially," this recounts the interpretation of the *Vibhāṣā*-masters.
How is it known to be so?
Question: Regarding the verse which says, "Because it reaches increase and is not produced, etc.," the answer is as follows:
In this verse, there are eight proofs in total that establish the existence of non-informative matter (*avijñapti*).
First, the proof of the statement that there are three types of matter; second, the proof of the statement regarding untainted matter (*anāsrava-rūpa*).
Third, the proof of the increase of merit through repeated recitation;
fourth, the proof that [karma] is not produced as a completed act;
fifth, the proof of matter within the sphere of phenomena (*dharmāyatana*).
Sixth, the realization of the eight branches of the path;
seventh, the realization of the Prātimokṣa;
eighth, the realization of the precepts as a dam.
The first four verses explain how the latter four [categories] are subsumed.
The Treatise says: "Up to 'invisible and non-obstructive'":
this is the first explanation of the three types of matter as proof.
These three serve as the general categories that encompass all form (*rūpa*). "Possessing form" means there is a certain class of form.
"Visible" means this form-base is limited by vision.
"Resistant" refers to the resistance of obstruction. There is a certain class of form that is not the object of the eye-faculty; it is called "invisible."
It is called "with resistance" (*sapratigha*) because it possesses obstructive resistance;
this refers to the five sense faculties and four of the objects. A certain class of matter that is not an object of the eye faculty is called "invisible" (*anidarśana*);
because it lacks obstructive resistance, it is called "without resistance" (*apratigha*).
This refers to non-informative matter (avijñapti-rūpa).
Since the Sūtra states that it is "invisible and non-obstructive," it is clearly known that there exists a distinct entity called non-informative matter.

Furthermore, when it is stated in the sūtra that "that which has reached [this state] is called an uncontaminated (anāsrava) dharma," this is the second proof for the existence of uncontaminated form.
The intention of this sūtra is to reveal that the five aggregates (pañcaskandha) throughout the three periods of time constitute all uncontaminated dharmas.
Since the Sūtra states that there is untainted (anāsrava) form,
it is clearly known that there exists a distinct unmanifest form (avijñaptirūpa).
This excludes [the view that] there is no unmanifest form up to the point of asserting that there is no untainted form.
These two sūtras together demonstrate the existence of non-informative matter (avijñapti).
Excluding non-informative matter, what dharma is designated as "invisible and non-obstructive" in the first sūtra?
And what dharma is designated as "outflow-free matter" (anāsrava-rūpa) in the second sūtra?

Furthermore, when the sūtra speaks of the increase of meritorious actions that lead to great fortune, this is the third proof of the increase of merit: the accomplishment of the seven bases of meritorious action that have a physical support.
First, giving to travelers;
second, giving to those on the road;
third, giving to those who are ill.
Fourth, giving to those who attend to the sick;
fifth, giving gardens and groves;
sixth, giving to those who constantly beg for alms.
Seventh is giving according to the occasion,
as explained separately below.
One who accomplishes these seven bases of meritorious action—

Constantly and continuously succeeding the preceding meritorious karma, it gradually increases; because there is a subsequent arising of meritorious karma, it is called "having a continuation. Thus, these seven types are called "with support" (*sopadhi*) because they have a supporting basis (*vastu*). They are called "merit" (*puṇya*) because they are wholesome. They are called "karma" (*karman*) because they are performed. They are called "basis" (*vastu*) because volition (*cetanā*) relies upon them.
Regarding merit (*puṇya*), action (*karman*), and the basis (*vastu*), these three are explained separately below.

"The same applies to that which is without a basis" means that it is called "without a basis" because it lacks those seven bases as its support. Nevertheless, when one gives rise to a profound mind of sympathetic joy (*anumodanā*) and reverence, merit continues to arise within the context of practice and so forth.

The same principle applies because they possess a basis (*sāśraya*); thus it is said that "it is likewise. Excluding non-informative action (*avijñapti-karman*), if one gives rise to other defiled or neutral states of mind, or during a state of mindlessness (*acittaka*), with respect to what dharma could it be said that the meritorious action increases?

If one explains it in this way, then only the mental state of sympathetic joy and reverence arises, and there is no bodily informative action (*kāyavijñapti*). Furthermore, regarding the explanation of merit that does not depend on material things:
it is not merely the arising of the mind, but rather the merit of the act of reverence through both body and mind increases.
It is called "without basis" simply because there is no object of giving; if there were no unmanifest [action], how could merit increase and grow?
Furthermore, as for the claim that it is not self-performed and thus lacks this nature of being distinct: [this is incorrect].
This is the fourth proof that one does not perform actions oneself:
furthermore, one does not personally perform two types of bodily action and four types of vocal action,
but rather dispatches others to do them.
If there were no unmanifest karma (*avijñapti-karman*), it would not constitute a course of action (*karmapatha*).
This is because the manifest act (*vijñapti*) of commanding another is not included within that course of action;
therefore, such manifest acts are merely preliminary applications (*prayoga*).
Because one has not yet correctly performed the action to be done,
after causing another to perform an act such as killing,
the nature of the informative action (*vijñapti-karman*) dispatched by this instructor remains no different [from that of the actual perpetrator].
Since no distinct types of bodily or vocal karma arise [in such cases],
it would follow that there should be no courses of action (*karmapatha*) when one dispatches another to act; yet,
in reality, they do constitute courses of action.
Therefore, we know that at that time, a separate unmanifest (avijñapti) course of action is further induced.
Furthermore, regarding the statement in the sūtra that [the path] would become useless upon reaching [the object],
this is the fifth proof for the existence of form within the sphere of mental objects (dharmāyatana-rūpa).
Furthermore, a sūtra states:
"Bhikṣus, you should know that among the twelve bases (āyatana), what is called the 'base of mental phenomena' (dharmāyatana) refers to the external base."
These eleven bases do not include these phenomena.
Because they are not seen by the eye, they are called "non-visible" (*anidarśana*);
because they are without obstruction, they are called "non-resistant" (*apratigha*). In this sutra, it is not stated that they are "formless" (*arūpa*).
It is clearly known that within the sphere of phenomena (dharmāyatana) there exists unmanifest form (avijñaptirūpa).
If one does not take into account this unmanifest form within the sphere of phenomena,
this sūtra would be deficient and thus rendered useless.
It should further be stated that they are "formless" (ārūpya).
This is what the *Nyāya* calls the *Pratyekasthāna-sūtra*.
Furthermore, if there were no unmanifest [form] (*avijñapti*), it would not exist in speech and so forth.
This is the sixth proof for the eightfold path.

If there were such a thing as unmanifest form (*avijñapti*), one could say that while in meditative concentration, those possessing right speech, right action, and right livelihood would be endowed with all eight branches of the path.
If non-informative action (*avijñapti*) did not exist, there would be no eight branches of the path;
there would instead be only five,
because the three— right speech and so forth— are entirely absent during meditative absorption.
If that is so, why does it say "up to being pure and bright"? [This is] an objection:
if there were unmanifest form (avijñapti) concomitant with the Path within untainted meditative absorption (anāsrava-samādhi), [then this would follow].
These are called right speech, action, and livelihood.
Why, then, does the sutra state:
"To know thus is wisdom"?
He views it thus as patience;
or he knows it thus as the path of seeing;
he views it thus as the path of cultivation.
Alternatively, when one knows in this way, that is the path of cultivation;
when one sees in this way, that is the path of vision.
One cultivates the five factors beginning with right view until they all reach perfection.
Right speech and the other two [right action and right livelihood] were already obtained prior to this;
yet, since this sutra does not mention right speech, right action, or right livelihood within the untainted concentration (*anāsrava-samādhi*),
it further states that right speech, right action, and right livelihood were already obtained previously.
Since it is clearly known that these three do not exist within the very substance of untainted concentration (*anāsrava-samādhi*),
how can they serve as proof for the existence of unmanifest form (*avijñapti-rūpa*)?
As for the argument that this relies on a prior time [of action], it falls into the error of contradiction with the state of signlessness (*animitta*).
The mastery of the scriptures, right speech, and right livelihood were already attained at an earlier time;
this is explained according to the mundane path of detachment previously attained,
and does not rely upon the untainted (anāsrava) path.
Because one has previously attained that contaminated path and thus no longer gives rise to the three types of wrongness,
the subsequent uncontaminated contemplation is said to attain only five [factors].
This does not mean that these three— right speech and so forth— are absent from the uncontaminated meditative absorptions.
Therefore, there is no contradiction with that sutra.
Furthermore, if one were to deny the existence of "arrival" (prāpti) while still being designated as a bhikṣu and so forth,
this would constitute the seventh proof for the existence of the prātimokṣa.
Furthermore, if one were to deny the existence of non-informative matter (avijñapti-rūpa), there would be no essence of the precepts.

It would not be the case that after receiving the precepts, one continues to possess the continuity of those precepts such that one is still designated as a bhikṣu and so forth, even when arising with minds of evil or neutral states due to other conditions.
Once the precepts have been received, there is a continuity of the moral discipline;
thus, even when one gives rise to minds of an evil or neutral nature through different conditions,
one is still designated as a bhikṣu and so forth.
It is clearly known that there exists a separate unmanifest form (*avijñapti*) as the essence of this precept.
Furthermore, the Sūtra states that there is a substantially existent unmanifest matter (*rūpa*);
this serves as the eighth proof for the precept being a dam or embankment.
Since morality serves as a dam, it is clearly understood that the non-manifest (avijñapti) exists as its distinct substance.
From these eight proofs, one knows that non-manifest form (avijñaptirūpa) truly exists.
This concludes the summary.
Regarding the Sautrāntika master’s statement that "reaching" (prāpti) is the same as non-informative matter (avijñapti):
the following section refutes the previous eight proofs.
This specifically refutes the first proof.
The former constitutes a general negation,
while the latter provides a specific explanation.
