First, regarding the statement in the Sūtra that among the three kinds of form there is that which is invisible and non-obstructive:
The Yogācāras state that when one cultivates dhyāna, there is a form produced by the power of meditative concentration which constitutes the objective sphere of that concentration;
this refers precisely to the forms of the first eight *kṛtsnāyatana*s (totalities), and so forth.
It is called "non-visible" because it is not the object of the eye-faculty;
it is called "non-obstructive" because it does not occupy physical space;
yet it is not non-informative matter (*avijñapti*).

If it is argued that, being thus invisible and non-obstructive (*anidarśana-apratigha*), how can it be called "matter" (*rūpa*), this objection is explained in the same way as [the case of] unmanifest matter (*avijñapti*): your own unmanifest matter is likewise invisible and non-obstructive.
How is it that "name-and-form" (nāmarūpa) is associated with this term "yoga"?
It is simply another name for the practitioner of meditation.
Furthermore, regarding what the Sūtra says—that which reaches [the state of] suchness is called "outflow-free" (anāsrava)—it refers to this.
The following refutes the second proof.
Regarding the second scripture’s mention of "untainted form" (anāsrava-rūpa), the Yogācāras say:
Within the matter produced by the power of meditative concentration, there are two kinds of matter.
That matter which arises based on impure (sāsrava) concentration is said to be impure;
that matter which arises based on pure (anāsrava) concentration is said to be pure matter.
It is not that the term "uncontaminated matter" (anāsrava-rūpa) refers to non-informative matter (avijñapti).
As for the statement by other masters that the term "uncontaminated" refers to acquisition (prāpti), this is a citation of an alternative interpretation.
Other Dārṣṭāntikas say:
"All forms within the body of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), as well as all forms within the external vessel-world (*bhājana-loka*), are untainted (*anāsrava*).
They receive the name 'untainted' because they are not the basis for the increase of the various taints (*āsrava*)."
"It is not based on an increase in conditions.
As for why the Sūtra says "up to" and so forth at length,
this is the objection raised by the Sarvāstivādins.
Why does the Sūtra state that "outflowing dharmas" refer to fifteen elements (*dhātu*),
and that they receive the name "outflowing" because they are not the antidote to outflows? This refers to the *Dārṣṭāntika* school’s interpretation of the sūtras.
"Since these fifteen elements are not antidotes to the outflows (*āsrava*), they possess the designation 'with-outflow' (*sāsrava*).
Thus, one should say that these are both with-outflow and without-outflow (*anāsrava*).
This is the objection raised by the Sarvāstivādins.

In that case, one should say that within the single substance of a phenomenon (dharma), it is called "with outflows" (sāsrava) and also called "without outflows" (anāsrava). If one asks, "What fault is there in this?
the Dārṣṭāntika answers with an analogy.
Regarding the fault of confusion:
the Sarvāstivādins further challenge this,
stating that if a single dharma-entity were called both "with outflows" (sāsrava) and "without outflows" (anāsrava), there would be the fault of confusion.
If, according to this principle, the same applies to sound and so forth,
the Dārṣṭāntika replies:
"According to this principle, that which is not an antidote to the outflows (āsrava) is designated as 'with outflows' (sāsrava)."
It has never been taught that this [state] is untainted (anāsrava) on the basis of such a definition;
the same applies to the untainted.
If it is according to this principle—that it is not a basis for the outflows (āsrava)—that it is called untainted, [then so be it].

It has never been taught that these are "with outflows" (sāsrava) based on this [principle]. A single dharma receives different names depending on its correlative relationship, just as with the terms "father" and "son";

how could there be any confusion here? If, according to your own school’s doctrine, the fifteen elements such as the sense-base of form (rūpāyatana) and so forth are exclusively "with outflows," [then your position is untenable].
For what reason does this sutra teach with such distinctions?
It says that "all contaminated and grasping forms are capable of giving rise to those mental weeds and coverings. Here, "weed" (karṣa) refers to a sprout or a plant.
"Concealment" (*mrakṣa*) refers to obscuration. "Planting" (*vāsanā*) and "concealment" are two synonymous terms for affliction (*kleśa*). It acts as a "planting" for the mind;
it can obscure the mind.

Because it grasps various forms and is the object of the mind's planting and concealment, it is called the "object of the mind's planting and concealment. Since the Sūtra has already explained these six objects of the mind's planting and concealment:
It is said that "tainted and grasped" forms are matters that obstruct and cover the mind;
therefore, we know that there exist separately "untainted and ungrasped" forms which are not matters that obstruct and cover the mind. Otherwise, for what reason would they be explained as distinct?

If the sūtra refers only to that which is with outflows (sāsrava), it should simply state that "all forms and minds are the matter of obstruction and concealment. Furthermore, another interpretation is that the very essence of the mind itself is the obstruction of birth and death, capable of concealing the Noble Path.
The matter is as explained previously; the same applies to sound and so forth.
Furthermore, regarding the statement in the Sūtra that "meritorious karma continues to arise," this section below refutes the third proof. As for "the increase of merit":

The former masters of the Sautrāntika school explain that through the power of the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), the seeds of perfuming increase as meritorious karma; thus, for each and every donor who is not singular, there is a recipient who is likewise not singular.

It is designated as "thus and thus" because, through the recipients' enjoyment of the donated objects, they are able to cultivate meritorious qualities such as loving-kindness (*maitrī*), thereby benefiting their bodies and minds;

this is due to the distinctions in the strength and well-being of body and mind. Furthermore, it is explained that through the recipients' enjoyment of the donated objects, they attain various meritorious qualities such as the meditative absorption of loving-kindness (*maitrī-samādhi*), which brings about distinctions in the benefit accorded to sentient beings. Subsequently, even if the donor's mind gives rise to unwholesome or neutral states associated with other mental objects.
Furthermore, the seeds perfumed by the volition of giving directed toward the preceding object of support reside within the body of the donor;
their mode of activity is subtle,
yet they continue in an uninterrupted succession.
Subsequently, through gradual transformation, it arises with a superior capacity to produce its fruit immediately, distinguished from its prior state.

These five are all synonyms for "seed. Because this seed of volition (*cetanā*) is able to bring about various fruits such as wealth in the future, it is taught with intentional meaning (*saṃdhyābhāṣita*) that the seeds are perfumed by volition.
Constantly and continuously,
meritorious karma gradually increases;
meritorious karma arises in succession.
This is not an explicit teaching.
As for the question of how it is that the unmanifest (avijñapti) dharma arises,
the Sautrāntika school cites the objection and refutes it through inquiry.
If you argue that this is because the body within the continuum of the recipient possesses qualities that provide a specific benefit, thereby causing a mind—
even though it has arisen as evil or neutral due to other conditions— to arise within the body of the donor’s own continuum;
As for the claim that there is production through the transformation of seeds, this explanation of the difficulty is identical to your own position regarding the unmanifest (*avijñapti*).
Furthermore, how could it be [produced] by the distinctions in the merits and benefits derived from the continuum of another recipient’s body?

It causes another kind of truly existent unmanifest dharma (*avijñapti*) to arise within the continuum of the body of other donors. Regarding the increase of merit in the case of "meritorious action not based on a physical object" (*anāśraya-puṇyakriyāvastu*), the question is asked:

If there is merit based on the recipient, it is reasonable that the meritorious karma of the donor increases because there is a distinction in the benefit derived when the recipient enjoys the object.
If, regarding those meritorious deeds that lack a physical basis,
one merely hears that Buddhas have appeared in other directions and gives rise to a sense of reverence from afar, the distinction in merit is superior to that of giving material gifts to them.
"How can merit and karma increase within the continuum of the body?
It is also through repeated practice until it becomes constant and persists throughout one's life.
Thus the Sautrāntika replies.
It is not only in the case of those with a physical basis that merit and so forth increase by virtue of the power of volition;
this merit of action without a physical basis also increases through the power of superior volition directed toward those Buddhas and others, which arises from repeated practice.
"Even in dreams, the seeds of respectful reflection continue to grow and persist in succession.
For one who argues for the existence of non-informative matter (avijñapti), how could such a thing not exist?
Thus the Sautrāntika counters the objection.

According to those who propound the doctrine of permanence and establish the theory of non-informative action (*avijñapti*), non-informative action arises dependent upon informative action (*vijñapti*).

However, in the case of merit that is independent [of physical or vocal action], one merely gives rise to a mind of reverence; since there is no informative action, [non-informative action cannot arise].
Is there not, then, non-informative [action] (*avijñapti*)? The *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya* (Chapter 18) offers this defense: "Who says that there is no informative action (*vijñapti-karman*) here?
It should logically exist.
For instance, one hears that in such a place, within such a district or town, the Tathāgata or his disciples are currently residing."
Regarding the statement, "Because one gives rise to joy, merit constantly increases":
that person must necessarily possess superior faith and, from afar, respectfully offer salutations and praise toward that direction,
thereby giving rise to meritorious manifest action (*vijñapti-karma*) and meritorious non-manifest action (*avijñapti-karma*).
Yet, because one adorns oneself with the hope of personally attending upon [the Buddha], it is said that merit increases constantly based on the unmanifest (*avijñapti*).
The intent of the *Nyāyānusāra* is the same as that of the *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya*. This follows the defense provided in the *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya* and other texts.
Non-informative action (*avijñapti*) necessarily arises based on informative action (*vijñapti*).
How then can this treatise state that it does not? The Master Vasumitra refutes this, saying:
"In your own system, non-informative action does not arise from informative action."
Because they were pressed by these difficulties, they said that [the mind] arises from the manifest (*vijñapti*) and extends far to offer prostrations and praise;
it may be entrusted to the manifest to arise, but one merely gives rise to faith.

From what manifest action does it arise? Furthermore, another interpretation holds that the Sautrāntika school uses their own tenets to challenge the argument regarding non-manifest action (*avijñapti*).
Regarding merit that does not rely on material things (*anupādhi-puṇya*), according to reason,
since there is no manifest action (*vijñapti-karman*),

how could there be non-manifest action (*avijñapti*)? Furthermore, the school that maintains [merit] is always present explains that there is no such thing as merit from actions not relying on material things.
Some maintain that [karma] arises from manifest action (vijñapti),
while others maintain that it does not arise from manifest action.
I now challenge those who claim it does not arise from manifest action.
As for the objection arising from the surface [of the argument],
why is it necessary to offer a defense?
Some say that there is dependence upon the point at which [the seed] reaches the continuum and begins to increase.
Regarding the different teachers' views on the section on the Sūtras:
some say that when the various meritorious actions based on material things increase,
it is not solely due to the material goods that were given.

Furthermore, it is due to the donor’s repeated cultivation of a superior volition directed toward the objects associated with that [gift] that merit is said to increase continuously at all times. Moreover, this master’s intention is explained as follows:
not only does merit increase perpetually through the repeated cultivation of volition directed toward those objects even without a physical basis, but [it is so] for this reason as well.
There are those who rely on various merits, and through repeated cultivation, the mental continuum of volition directed toward those objects increases.
If that is so, the Master [Vasubandhu] cites a sūtra to refute the claims of other teachers regarding the statement that "it reaches concentration" (samādhi) being logical.
When any bhikṣu, having accepted a gift from another, enters the meditative absorptions of the four immeasurables and personally realizes these absorptions to their full perfection,
it should be understood that by this cause and condition, the donor’s merit increases immeasurably.
At that time, the merit of the donor increases constantly.
How could it be that this increase only begins when there is a volition directed toward that gift?
Therefore, the former master’s statement—that there is a subtle continuity perfumed by volition—is correct.
It is certainly logical that [merit] arises through gradual transformation and differentiation; however,
merit constantly increases solely due to the seeds perfumed by the volition (*cetanā*) following the act of giving.
It is not the case that [merit] increases only through the donor's repeated mental engagement with the object;
nor is it the case that one must personally perform the bodily and vocal courses of action.
This concludes the refutation of the fourth proof.
The commentary on the scriptural proof states: "It should be explained in this way.

Because at the time the teacher originally instructs another, they have already been able to infuse the seeds of preparatory volition (*prayoga-cetanā*) into their mental continuum, which then persists."
When the messenger has completed the act of killing or other such deeds according to the instructions,

it is by the very nature of things (*dharmatā*) that it causes the seeds of volition (*cetanā-bīja*), which were previously perfumed by the preparatory effort (*prayoga*) within the body of the instructor, to [ripen].
Furthermore, the seeds of volition (*cetanā*) pertaining to the fundamental courses of action (*mūlakarmapatha*) arise again;
they emerge through a subtle, continuous transformation and differentiation,
persisting in successive stages until an occasion for their abandonment is encountered.
Moment by moment it gradually increases;

through this seed of volition (*cetanā*) from the fundamental path of action, one will be able to bring forth manifold fruits in a future life. The same principle applies when the deed is accomplished by oneself.

It should be understood that these very seeds, such as the subtle ones and so forth, are called "paths of action" (*karmapatha*). As for this designation of the seeds of volition (*cetanā*) as "paths of action," it is a case of metaphorically applying the name of the cause to the effect.
Regarding the expression "cause and effect": the volition (*cetanā*) that initiates the preparatory action (*prayoga*) which perfumes and sets in motion bodily and vocal karma is called the cause.
The seeds of volition (*cetanā-bīja*) that are perfumed and induced by this are called the effect.

Because that manifest, initiating volition involves purposeful activity (*abhisamskāra*), it is termed "karma" (*karman*); because it is the path traversed by the two preceding types of volition—deliberation (*vitarka*) and determination (*vicāra*)—it is termed the "path" (*mārga*).
Alternatively, it is called the "path" (*mārga*) because it can lead to birth in all realms, whether virtuous or non-virtuous.
When the active volition (*cetanā*) is the cause, it is the "right path of action" (*samyak-karmapatha*);

when the seed-volition is the fruit, it is termed a "path of action"—this is a case of metaphorically applying the name of the cause to its fruit. The first chapter of the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* also states that the motivating volition is called the "path of action."
Therefore, that treatise states: "The volitions (*cetanā*) of body and speech that perform an action are called karma (*karma*),
because they are traversed by deliberative and decisive volition,
and because they universally produce the maturation fruits (*vipākaphala*) of suffering and pleasure."
It is also called the "path" (*mārga*).

Therefore, as stated in the treatise: "The preceding seven paths of action also have volition (*cetanā*) as their intrinsic nature. Furthermore, it is explained that the seed of volition is called the "path" because it is able to lead one through to birth in the realms of both good and evil.
Regarding the designation "karma," this is a case of applying the name of the cause to its result.
This is because it is the result induced by bodily and vocal karma.
That is to say, the preceding preparatory effort and the manifest volition are the causes, while the bodily and vocal karma are the results.
The volition that constitutes the seed is the cause, not the bodily or vocal action;

yet it is designated as "action" because the name of the cause is metaphorically applied to the fruit, which is the volition itself. Furthermore, another interpretation holds that it is called "action" metaphorically because it is produced by the volition that initiates the preparatory effort (*prayoga*) of bodily and vocal intimation (*vijñapti*).
Because it is that which volition (cetanā) traverses, it is also called a path of action (karmapatha).
The manifest [action] is the path of action;
because volition arises by means of it, it is the cause.
Volition (*cetanā*) is the seed and [thus] the cause;
therefore, the name "cause" is metaphorically applied to the fruit. Thus, the first chapter of the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* also states:
"Alternatively, because bodily and vocal intimation (*vijñapti*) are issued by volition, they are metaphorically designated as 'action' (*karman*)."

Because it is that which is traversed by volition (*cetanā*), it is called a "path of action" (*karmapatha*). Furthermore, another interpretation holds that the volition which initiates the performance of the preliminary application (*prayoga*) is called "action" (*karman*), while the body and speech thus initiated are called the "path" (*patha*).
Because it is that upon which the karma of volition relies for its activity, it is called the "path" (*mārga*).
Through the assistance of the path, karma is perfumed so as to form seeds;
both this karma and the path are termed "causes."
This is the path of right action.
As for the designation "path of action" applied to the fruit of volition (cetanā) that has been perfumed by it,
this is a case of metaphorically applying the name of the cause to its effect.
According to the school that maintains that unmanifest action exists as a distinct entity, unmanifest action is also called a path of action of body and speech.
Manifest action is properly named the path of action of body and speech;
unmanifest action is called the path of action of body and speech because it arises from the paths of action of body and speech.
This is also a case of metaphorically applying the name of the cause to the effect. Furthermore, it is explained that the manifest [karma] is properly termed bodily and vocal action;
the unmanifest [karma] is called bodily and vocal action because it arises from bodily and vocal action.
This, too, is a case of applying the name of the cause to the effect by way of metaphor.
Because it brings forth [right] thought, it is called the "path" (*mārga*). Furthermore, some explain that the manifest (*vijñapti*) is precisely body and speech;
since the unmanifest (*avijñapti*) arises from body and speech, it is named "body" and "speech."
This is also a case of metaphorically applying the name of the cause to the effect.
That which performs an action is called "karma" (action);
that which expresses intention is called "mārga" (path).
The name "cause" is applied metaphorically to the fruit according to its correspondence.

According to the Sautrāntika school, wholesome and unwholesome ethical discipline (*śīla*) and so forth perfume the seeds of the seven volitions of the preparatory stage (*prayoga*) during the stage of application (*prayogāvasthā*).
Having encountered superior conditions, from these seeds of preparatory volition (*prayoga-cetanā*), one further perfumes them to produce seeds of fundamental volition (*maula-cetanā*).
Together with the preceding seeds of preparatory volition, they simultaneously give rise to the seeds of the seven factors of the first moment of thought.
In the second moment of thought, the seeds of the two sets of seven factors [arise];
in the third moment of thought, the seeds of the three sets of seven factors [arise].
Thus, until one encounters a condition for relinquishment, the seeds of volition regarding the seven factors increase in every successive moment.
If it encounters conditions for relinquishment, it does not increase;
this is termed "equanimity.
The fundamental seeds are capable of summoning their respective maturation (*vipāka*).
Because volitions (cetanā) of subsequent bodily and vocal actions arise separately following the fundamental [volition], they perfuse and establish seeds for subsequent volitions.

Alternatively, the first moment is called the "fundamental," while from the second moment onward it is called "subsequent. Another interpretation holds that within a single seed of volition, the functional capacity of the seven branches increases moment by moment.
The Mahāyāna is likewise; however, in the Mahāyāna, the eighth consciousness is perfumed, whereas in the Sautrāntika school, both matter and mind are perfumed.
In the Mahāyāna, seeds arise simultaneously with one another.
In the Sautrāntika school, seeds produce subsequent [moments] from preceding ones; in the Mahāyāna, the perfumed seeds correspond with the perfuming agents.
In the Sautrāntika school, seeds are perfumed such that a preceding moment perfumes a succeeding moment.
However, when the Venerable says, "having reached the point of killing and having killed," he is recounting a divergent opinion. The Venerable—
namely Dharmatrāta— maintains that the appropriated aggregates (*upādānaskandha*) are what constitute the sentient being who is killed.
Regarding the taking of life, volition arises during three moments:
first, "I shall kill"; second, the actual act of killing; [and third, the completion of the act].

The Master [Vasubandhu] refutes [the opponent's view], stating that it is only after the threefold act of killing has been completed that one incurs the transgression; it is not merely by this [initial intention] that one reaches a state where it would be irrational for the offense not to apply.
The completion of the course of action consisting of volition does not occur solely through these three moments;

otherwise, one might incur an immediate retribution (*ānantarya*) karma by generating the volitions of the three moments within a dark room, even though one’s own mother or others have not actually been killed.
However, regarding the act of killing committed by oneself, one incurs the offense of killing through the three moments of volition;
if it were based on this [text], it would not be unreasonable.
But to claim that the offense is incurred merely by giving rise to the three volitions while the victim has actually not yet been killed is indeed unreasonable.
Regarding the question of why there is a transformational distinction in the unmanifest (*avijñapti*):
the Sarvāstivādins ask, "Why do you categorically deny the existence of the unmanifest,
while the Sautrāntikas accept the 'seed-unmanifest' (*bīja-avijñapti*)?"
As for the statement, "However, this and that have already been explained previously," the Master of the Treatise (the author) replies by presenting the evaluations of both schools.
However, this avijñapti (non-informative action) taught by the Sarvāstivādins, as well as that taught by the Sautrāntikas,
are both difficult to comprehend.
Alternatively, both this Sautrāntika school and that Sarvāstivāda school are difficult to fully comprehend;
regarding them, my mind maintains equanimity and is truly free from any malice or envy.

However, the Sarvāstivādins themselves maintain that the non-informative (avijñapti) karmic paths are wholesome; they are of the same nature as the mind because this non-informative [action] is their origination.

Since it is acquired by the mind, it is of the same category as that mind. Furthermore, another interpretation states: "I allow that those seeds of volition (cetanā) which constitute the karmic paths are of the same category as the mind, for they are both immaterial (arūpin); thus they are said to be of the same category. This is what the masters of the Sarvāstivāda school say.
When that person who has received the instruction, through physical application, carries a weapon or the like from this place to that place and completes acts such as killing,
there arises within the body of the instructor a distinct non-informative dharma (*avijñapti*), which is separate from both body and mind.

The Sautrāntika master says: "If, by means of this [intention], the instructor causes the instructed person to produce an application—such as grasping a weapon—that leads them from here to there, [then that intention is the cause]."
When an act such as killing reaches its completion,
it is precisely because that which was commanded has reached its completion that the fundamental path of action (*maula-karmapatha*) arises;
this occurs through a specific transformation and differentiation within the continuity of the volition-seed (*cetanā-bīja*), which does not exist apart from the body and mind.

Such a tenet may be made to inspire joy, for according to the Sautrāntika school, it is solely due to the transformation of a specific continuity of the seeds of volition (*cetanā-bīja*) within the mind and body that future fruits are produced.
It is not produced by a separate unmanifest [form], as has already been stated previously.
What was stated previously? [The following] question:
Regarding the statement, "Since manifest action (*vijñapti-karman*) does not exist, how could non-manifest action (*avijñapti*) and so forth exist?
the answer is:
"This refers to the passage on 'merit without a basis' (*anupādhiṣṭa-puṇya*)," and so forth.
This refers back to all preceding passages;
since this passage occurs later, it mentions the latter to imply the former.
Furthermore, regarding the statement that "that which belongs to the sphere of phenomena (dharmāyatana) is included within the sphere of phenomena as form":
This refutes the fifth proof.
Furthermore, regarding the statement that the sphere of phenomena (*dharmāyatana*) is invisible and non-obstructive but not said to be formless:

this is because there exists, as previously described by the yogācāras, a form included within the sphere of phenomena that constitutes the meditative object (*samāpatti-viṣaya*), which is both invisible and non-obstructive.
This is why it does not mention "formless" (ārūpya).
Furthermore, regarding the statement that the factors of the path (mārgāṅga) extend to seeking clothing and so forth:
this below refutes the sixth proof. Furthermore, regarding the statement that there should be no eight factors of the path: [this is the seventh proof].
Furthermore, you should explain how right speech, right action, and right livelihood can exist while one is actually in the untainted path (*anāsrava-mārga*).
Is it because, in this state, there is the utterance of correct words that is called right speech?
Engaging in right action is called right action (*samyak-karmānta*); seeking clothing, food, and so forth is called right livelihood (*samyag-ājīva*). Is this not so? It is not so. Why? Because...
[the text continues].
The Sarvāstivādins reply: "What is it?
This is the master of the treatise posing a question.
Regarding the statement that "one obtains what is designated as vocal action," the Sarvāstivādins explain:
because those noble ones obtain such a type of untainted non-informative matter (*avijñapti*) that is co-existent with the Path.
Therefore, after emerging from meditative observation, by the power of the previously attained untainted non-informative matter (avijñapti),
one is able to give rise to the three types of correctness and not the three types of error;
yet it is said that while in meditative concentration, there are these three kinds.
Because the names of the three fruits— speech, action, and livelihood— are established among the causes of non-manifestation (avijñapti) that coexist with the path,
the names of speech, action, and livelihood are likewise established for non-manifestation itself.
If that is so, how is it that one reaches the eight branches of the noble path?
The Sautrāntika master says: If that is so, why do you not accept my position?
According to our school’s tenet, although there is no separate substantial entity of unmanifest form (*avijñapti*), [the path is established].

And while one is in that untainted path (anāsrava-mārga), one attains such an intention (āśaya) and basis; this intention has desire as its essence, or it has resolute conviction (adhimukti) as its essence.
Alternatively, it has desire (*chanda*) and resolve (*adhimokṣa*) as its essence.
Thus, the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* states that desire has resolve as its essence.
Because it is a pleasure associated with the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), it is called "mental pleasure" (*manorati*).
The basis has as its essential nature the volition that is simultaneous with the intention;

because it serves as the basis for that intention, it is called the "basis of intention" (*āśaya-saṃniśraya*). Alternatively, it is explained that the intention itself has the present volition as its essential nature.
Because it serves as the basis for the three [virtues] that follow after emerging from meditative absorption, it is called the "basis";
because the mental disposition itself is the basis, it is called the "basis of mental disposition. In brief:
The volition that arises simultaneously with the path is called the non-informative (avijñapti); it is termed the morality concomitant with the path (mārga-sahaja-śīla).
It has no separate substantial entity.
Because one has attained that precept as a basis,
after emerging from meditative absorption, by the power of the aforementioned untainted (anāsrava) precept,
one is able to give rise to the three types of correctness and not give rise to the three types of error.
While on the path, although there is no verbal expression,
one initiates right action by seeking clothing, food, and so forth.

Because the name of the subsequent result is established based on the preceding cause, one may fully establish the eight branches of the noble path at that stage of the path. Furthermore, "intention" refers to all forms of mental inclination.
The basis refers to the body that serves as the support.
His statement means that within meditative concentration, the three [types of] actual entities do not exist;
rather, through the power of the path, one attains the mental disposition (*āśaya*) and the superior physical basis (*āśraya*).
These are able to abandon the three perversions at a later time;
thus, the names of the results are used to designate the seeds, establishing the three correct [roots].
Paramārtha’s intention is the same as this interpretation.
As for the statement by other masters that "it should also be so in this case," this recounts a divergent view of the Sautrāntika school.
The intention of this master is that only the non-commission of wrong speech, wrong action, and wrong livelihood are taught as the three path-factors.
That is to say, while one is actually in that untainted meditative absorption,
through the power of the Noble Path, one is able to attain the certainty of not committing wrong speech and so forth, which constitutes right speech and so on.
It does not have a separate substantial entity. If it has no separate entity, how can it be called "outflow-free" (anāsrava)?
To resolve this anticipated objection, it is said:
"This concentration does not [arise] as such."
It is called "untainted" (anāsrava) because it is established by means of the untainted path.
The intention of the former master is that the "path-concomitant restraint" (mārga-sahabhū-śīla), which is conventionally designated based on volition (cetanā),
constitutes the three actual entities.
The intention of other masters is that non-action (akaraṇa), though lacking substantiality, is nonetheless attained through the Path;
it is not a separate basis,
for non-action itself is stated to be the threefold essence of the right [limbs].
It is not the case that names and categories must always be established based on the existence of a substantial entity;
rather, it refers to specific instances, such as the second of the eight worldly dharmas, which is the failure to obtain food and clothing.
It is not the case that a name and number are established only when there is a distinct substantial entity.
Among the eight worldly dharmas, it is impossible for a number to exist therein without a substantial entity.
This should likewise apply to Right Speech and the others among the Eightfold Path. As for what is called "worldly dharma":
The *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* states:
"Because they are followed and conformed to by sentient beings in the world, they are called 'worldly dharmas' (*loka-dharma*).
This is explained in detail in the forty-fourth [section] of the *Vibhāṣā*."
And one hundred and seventy-three explanations. Regarding what is called the "eightfold":
first is acquisition (*lābha*), which refers to obtaining clothing, food, and so forth;
the *Mahāvibhāṣā* calls this "benefit" (*artha*).
"Benefit" refers to obtaining benefits such as robes;
the names differ but the meaning is the same. "Non-benefit" refers to not obtaining [benefits] such as robes, food, and so forth.
In some places in the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, it says "decline" (*parihāṇi*).
"Decline" refers to being destitute and unable to obtain clothing and other necessities.
In other places in the *Vibhāṣā*, it says "lack of gain" (*alābha*).
This refers to not obtaining benefits such as robes;
these are all identical in meaning despite the different terminology. Third is "slander," which refers to slandering someone behind their back.
In some places in the *Vibhāṣā*, it says that "non-praise" (*a-yaśas*) and "praise" (*yaśas*) differ in name but are identical in meaning. There are four kinds of praise:
namely, praising someone behind their back or in their presence. There are five kinds of acclaim (*praśaṃsā*).
This refers to praising someone in their presence.
In some places in the *Mahāvibhāṣā*, it is called "praise" (*praśaṃsā*);
though the names differ, the meaning is the same. Sixth is "reviling."
This refers to reviling face-to-face.
In some places in the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, it is called "destruction" (*kṣepa*);
though the names differ, the meaning is the same. These are the seven sufferings.
This refers to painful sensations of body and mind.
In one section of the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, it is stated that "suffering" refers to the suffering of body and mind within the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
Others say that it refers exclusively to the suffering associated with the five sensory consciousnesses (*pañca-vijñāna*). [The eight types of] pleasure (*sukha*) are as follows:
This refers to pleasant sensations of body and mind.
In certain passages of the *Abhidharmamahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, it is stated that "pleasure" refers to the bodily and mental pleasure of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
Others say that it refers exclusively to the pleasure associated with the five sensory consciousnesses (*pañcavijñāna*).
In some places, this also extends to the bliss of *praśrabdhi* (pliancy).
Regarding the phrase "the prātimokṣa restraint reaching the prātimokṣa restraint," this below refutes the seventh proof.
The distinct nature of the prātimokṣa restraint should also be understood accordingly.
That is to say, by the power of the volition and aspiration that constitute the proximate cause and motivation,
one first establishes a formal commitment and vow not to commit evil.
One is able to definitively restrain and prevent the evil karma of body and speech;
having perfumed the seeds of volition (*cetanā*) during the stage of preliminary application (*prayoga*), one reaches the third refuge,
or at the time when the third *karmavācanā* (formal ritual act) is completed.
From the previous volitional seeds, sevenfold volitional seeds are further perfumed and increase moment by moment;
it is on account of this that the prātimokṣa restraint is established.
These volitional seeds are provisionally designated and possess no separate substantial entity.

Regarding the phrase "if one gives rise to a mind directed toward other objects, it ceases upon reaching recollection," this restates the objection raised by the Sarvāstivādins and provides a comprehensive explanation. Your previous objection was:
"If precepts have no separate substance, then when one gives rise to an unwholesome or neutral mind directed toward other objects, there should be no restraint."
This objection is irrational.
For one who has received the precepts, the power of the precepts— which consists of the seeds of volition perfumed moment by moment within the body and mind—
causes [unwholesome thoughts] to cease immediately upon recollection when they arise.
"Precepts are a dam; those who break them reach [the water].
This refutes the eighth proof.
It negates the meaning you previously stated regarding precepts as a dam.
The Prātimokṣa restraint should also be explained according to this principle.
That is to say, through the volition of preliminary application, one establishes a verbal vow and limit, "I shall certainly not commit evil," which perfumes and establishes seeds of volition.

By the power of the growth of these seeds of volition, one subsequently repeatedly brings to mind a sense of shame and dread of blame; thus, being present before the mind, they enable one to exercise self-restraint and prevent the violation of the precepts.
Therefore, the meaning of a dike or embankment arises from being maintained by the mind and has no separate substance.
You say that in the Sarvāstivāda school, if there were a distinct real entity called the unmanifest (avijñapti) which,
manifesting at every moment, is able to prevent the commission of transgressions.

There should be no one who, through loss of mindfulness, breaks the precepts; for according to the Sautrāntika school, the seed of reflection is designated as "precept," yet this seed has no separate substantial entity.
If one possesses the power to remember and thus does not transgress, [the precept is maintained].
If the seeds lack power, they cannot maintain mindfulness and thus one commits a transgression;
since there is no distinct entity that could undergo such a transgression, let us cease these numerous debates.
The author of the treatise stops the dispute.
As for the statement "the Vaibhāṣikas hold this as our own tenet," the Sarvāstivādins conclude by returning to their own fundamental school.
Regarding the previous question, "Is there a difference in the extent to which the unmanifest (avijñapti) reaches?"—
the following section is the second [part], clarifying the great primary elements (mahābhūta) that constitute it. Within this:
1. The great difference between manifest (vijñapti) and non-manifest (avijñapti).
2. The similarity and difference regarding the time of their being derived from the primary elements (mahābhūta).
3. Clarifying the primary elements as the producers according to their respective levels (bhūmi). The first [section] below concerns the great difference between manifest and non-manifest.

Question: Regarding the previous statement that the unmanifest (avijñapti) is derived from the primary elements (mahābhūta), does that which produces the manifest (vijñapti) also produce the unmanifest, or is there a different set of primary elements that produces the unmanifest? The verse says: "Because it would not be reasonable [to claim otherwise]."

Answer: This unmanifest [form] (*avijñapti*) has a set of primary elements (*mahābhūta*) for its creative cause that differs from the set of primary elements upon which manifest action (*vijñapti*) relies. Why is this so?
From a single cause consisting of the harmonious combination of the four great elements,
there arises a subtle result, which is non-informative (avijñapti), and a coarse result, which is informative (vijñapti).
Because it would be illogical;
for example, as in the case where the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) and derived matter (*upādāyarūpa*) are distinct.
Hereafter, the second section clarifies the inquiry regarding the similarities and differences in the timing of the primary elements and their derivatives.
Regarding the statement that "all derived matter (upādāya-rūpa) up to that which relies on the past [is co-existent with the primary elements]," the answer is:
speaking from the perspective of the majority, all derived matter is for the most part co-existent with the great elements (mahābhūta).
However, there are also instances where present and future derived matter (*upādāyarūpa*) depend upon past primary elements (*mahābhūta*).
What are these few instances? This is the inquiry.
The verse says: "That which reaches the hand has the earth as its basis.
The answer is:
it refers exclusively to all non-informative matter (*avijñapti*) belonging to the Desire Realm (*kāmadhātu*), beginning from the second moment onward after the first moment.
It arises from past primary elements (*mahābhūta*).
These past primary elements act as its formative cause (*abhinirvartaka-hetu*), serving as the direct basis for the five factors such as arising (*jāti*) and so forth,
by virtue of which the subsequent moment of non-informative matter (*avijñapti*) is able to arise.
From the second moment onward, the primary elements (mahābhūta) of the present body are not the creators of the simultaneous non-informative matter (avijñapti);
nor do they possess the five causes, such as arising and so forth.

However, it is only by means of past primary elements (*mahābhūta*) acting as the direct generative cause (*abhinirvṛttihetu*) that the unmanifest (*avijñapti*) arises; "generative" here means "arising. Because it arises from them, the present bodily primary elements act as the indirect sustaining cause (*anuvartakahetu*).
Because it proceeds in accordance with that non-informative [matter],
it is called a "concomitant cause" (anuvartaka-hetu), as the concomitant is itself the cause.
Alternatively, the non-informative [matter] proceeds in accordance with the primary elements (mahābhūta).
The cause that functions in accordance [with another] is called the *anuvartaka-hetu* (concomitant cause).
It is like a wheel moving upon the ground;
the hand is the basis for its turning, which serves as a metaphor for the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) being exceeded.

The earth element serves as the metaphor for the "concomitant basis" (*anuvartaka-āśraya*), manifesting as the primary elements (*mahābhūta*). Question: Why is it not said that "the non-informative [matter] (*avijñapti*) of the subsequent moment of form," but rather "the non-informative [matter] of the subsequent moment of desire"? Explanation: In the Form Realm (*rūpadhātu*), the precepts that follow the mind (*cittānuvartin*) are necessarily produced by the four primary elements that exist simultaneously with them.
Furthermore, in that realm there is no non-informative matter (avijñapti) of distraction;
thus, the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 122, states:
"The definitive meaning explained herein is as follows:"

In the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), there is necessarily no non-informative action (*avijñapti*) that follows along [with a primary action]. In the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), there is necessarily no non-informative action produced based on informative action (*vijñapti*).

Question: Why is this so? One explanation says: Furthermore, some say it is because the mind capable of producing karma through innate acquisition (*upapattilābhika*) in the desire realm is earnest and intense.
The manifest action (*vijñapti*) that is produced can produce non-manifest action (*avijñapti*).

However, the karma-producing mind acquired at birth in the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) cannot produce non-manifest action because it is neither earnest nor intense. Furthermore, another interpretation states: there are also those who say that if one is born in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), one lacks the concentration of meditative absorption (*samādhi*).
Because the indeterminate mind is superior,
the manifested [action] can produce the unmanifested;
this is because those born in the form realm possess a concentrated mind.
Because an indeterminate mind is weak, the manifest [action] it produces cannot produce the unmanifest.
This is explained at length in that [text]. Question: Does the unmanifest of subsequent moments also arise based on present primary elements?

Why does this passage state that [the great elements] arise from the past? The explanation is that because this text is concise, it refers for the time being only to the present activity from the subsequent moment onward;
therefore, it says they are "past great derivatives."
If one analyzes them in detail, the three time periods are not fixed.
Therefore, the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 132, states:
"All derived matter that possesses resistance (*sapratigha*) and all matter that evolves in accordance with the mind (*cittānuvartin*), regardless of which time period they belong to..."
These are produced by the primary elements of that very world.
Furthermore, regarding the various unmanifest forms (*avijñapti-rūpa*) arising from manifest form (*vijñapti*), there are three categories whose times of production are unequal;
namely, those of the first moment, such as those with resistance (*sapratigha*), and so forth.
Each is produced by the primary elements (mahābhūta) belonging to its own time;
if it occurs in the second moment, whether in the past or the present,
it is in both cases produced by past primary elements.
If [the restraint] is in the future, it is generally produced by the primary elements (mahābhūta) of the present and the future;
for subsequent moments, those of the past and present are as previously described.

If [the restraint] is in the future, it is generally produced by the primary elements of all three time periods. Question: When one undertakes the Prātimokṣa vows of the future, [by what elements are they produced?]
Since the precepts have not yet been attained, how can they be produced? The commentary explains: the meaning of "producing" various non-informative (avijñapti) factors is not fixed.
There are cases where one attains them without producing them, such as the future precepts that follow the mind (*anuparivartin*).
There are cases where one creates [an action] but does not acquire [the result], such as future *prātimokṣa* vows.
There are also cases where one both acquires and creates [it].
As in the case of the first moment of the prātimokṣa vows and so forth, there are some that must necessarily be produced.
That is to say, excluding the aforementioned cases. Question: Do the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) of the first moment produce all subsequent non-informative matter (*avijñapti*)?

Is it that the very same great elements (*mahābhūta*) used to produce the first moment of non-informative matter (*avijñapti*) also produce the subsequent moments, or do separate great elements arise to produce the later non-informative matter? The first explanation states: "The great elements that produce the various subsequent moments of non-informative matter are precisely those same great elements that produced the first moment of non-informative matter. [Objection: If that were so, would it not mean that a single set of the four great elements produces multiple types of derived matter (*upādāyarūpa*)? [Response: The explanation states: "A single set of the four great elements cannot produce many types of resistant matter (*sapratigha-rūpa*)."

There is no fault in the production of many unobstructed forms. Question: If many [forms] are produced, then the produced non-informative matter (*avijñapti*) would be produced by the same four great elements;
as they stand in relation to one another, they ought to be simultaneous causes (*sahabhū-hetu*). Explanation: It can be said that many [forms] are produced because they are unobstructed.
Because they differ in time and because they are not mutual effects,
they are not co-existent causes.
If one were to hold such an interpretation— that the present four great elements (mahābhūta) produce those present and future non-informative forms (avijñapti)—
it would be untenable, because there are no present great elements that produce present derived matter (upādāyarūpa). Therefore, the *Vibhāṣā* (132) states:
If one is endowed with present primary elements (mahābhūta), is one also endowed with the derived matter (upādāyarūpa) of the present?
Answer: It is so. Furthermore, if one is endowed with the derived matter of the present, is one also endowed with the primary elements of the present? Answer: It is so.
Answer: It is so.

This is because present primary elements (*mahābhūta*) do not lack results, nor do present derived matter (*upādāyarūpa*) lack causes. The commentary explains: "Because present primary elements do not lack results."
Therefore, it must be derived matter of the present;
nor can it be derived matter of the present without a cause.
Consequently, it must be the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) of the present.

For this reason, it is known that there is no separate set of primary elements (*mahābhūta*) in the present that creates future non-informative matter (*avijñapti*). Furthermore, another interpretation states: a single set of the four primary elements creates the non-informative matter of the first moment;
at that very same time, there is a separate set of the four primary elements that creates all those subsequent moments of non-informative matter.

Therefore, in the twentieth chapter of the *Nyāyānusāra*, while explaining that the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) are not simultaneous causes (*sahabhū-hetu*) with respect to derived matter (*upādāya-rūpa*), it says:
"There are those who possess derived matter but do not possess the four primary elements."

There may be that which is capable of producing the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) but not the derived matter (*upādāyarūpa*). This passage serves as proof that there exists that which can produce [matter] without being itself produced.

Therefore, we know that there are also cases where the primary elements are manifest while the derived matter is not manifest, such that the former produces the latter in the future from afar. If one adopts the former interpretation, it will also accord with the subsequent proof.

Regarding the statement that "there is that which is produced capable of creating the non-derived matter," this refers to the first moment creating the subsequent non-informative matter (*avijñapti*).

Since the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) of that [non-informative matter] are definitely established in the first moment, it is said that there is that which is produced capable of creating the great elements.

At that time, although one produces future non-informative matter (*avijñapti*), because it is future, it is said not to be derived matter (*upādāya-rūpa*). If one adopts the latter interpretation, it applies to the preceding proof as follows:
the statement "because there is no fruit from present primary elements (*mahābhūta*), and because there is no cause for present derived matter" [is established].
This is because it is stated from the perspective of the majority,
and because it refers to the creation of obstructive [matter].
If one were to say that it includes the unmanifest (*avijñapti*), [it would be incorrect].
The treatise also states that it is not the case that a created form (*rūpa*) of the present moment is produced without a cause;
for how could there be a second moment of present created non-informative matter (*avijñapti*) that has simultaneous great elements (*mahābhūta*) as its producers?
For this reason, it is known that [this statement] is made based on the presence of resistance (*sapratigha*).
If one were to provide the former interpretation of these words, namely that "each and every [element] is also not matter produced in the present because it lacks a cause," [that would be incorrect].
There are two kinds of present causes:
first, the proximate cause;
second, the remote cause.
If one considers present resistant form and the first moment of non-informative matter (*avijñapti*),
the simultaneous primary elements (*mahābhūta*) serve as the direct cause. If one considers [them] from the second moment onward, [the primary elements of the preceding moments serve as the cause].

The primary elements (*mahābhūta*) within the body that manifest as the unmanifest (*avijñapti*) serve as its indirect cause (*pratyaya*). Furthermore, another interpretation states that while one set of the four great elements produces the first moment of the unmanifest, at that very same time, numerous other sets of the four great elements arise separately.
The future non-manifest (avijñapti) is projected;

it is produced separately by the four great elements at every single moment. Question: If, at the first moment, many great elements arise and produce [the non-manifest] separately at each and every moment...

In a single lifetime, the number of non-informative (avijñapti) forms is extremely great. How can a body existing at a single present moment accommodate so many primary elements (mahābhūta) that act as its creators? The explanation is: because the retribution-born [elements] are sparse and porous, they can coexist without any fault.
The citation of evidence and the explanation for resolving [the objection] are as stated by the second school;

I shall not further elaborate. Question: Regarding the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) of the present body that can serve as a basis, do they serve as a basis for the created [derived] body-elements (*bhautika*) and so forth?
It is said that a separate set of primary elements (*mahābhūta*) arises as a basis; this means that the primary elements which constitute the body and so forth serve as the remote basis.
It is not the five [factors] such as arising (*jāti*).

The detailed question and answer regarding this is as explained in the section on non-manifest action (*avijñapti*). Question: If past primary elements are called the "transformative cause" (*pariṇāma-hetu*), [how is this so]?
Present primary elements (mahābhūta) are called "concomitant causes" (anuvartaka-hetu).
Why, then, does the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* (Vibhāṣā), fascicle 133, state:
"There are material phenomena that are present but are not produced by present primary elements"?
This refers to present primary elements (*mahābhūta*).
As for matter that is present yet produced by past primary elements, how is this so?
It refers to the unmanifest (*avijñapti*) arising from present manifest action (*vijñapti*), which is produced by past primary elements.
As before, one might ask: "Does this non-informative matter (avijñapti-rūpa) also have present primary elements (mahābhūta) as its support?
Why, then, is it not so stated? The answer is: "Because those [present primary elements] are the basis for its transformation (pariṇāmāśraya), not the basis for its production (nirmāṇāśraya)."
This unmanifest form has two kinds of bases:
first is the basis of transformation,
meaning that the present primary elements are transformed by its power.
The second is the basis of production (*nirvṛtty-āśraya*).
This refers to the past primary elements (*mahābhūta*), because [the derived matter] is produced by their power.
Here, only the basis of production is mentioned, not the basis of transformation (*vivartty-āśraya*).

Therefore, it is not said that the five causes capable of producing [the derived matter] are all past. The commentary explains: when this treatise refers to "past primary elements" as "transformative causes" (*pariṇāma-hetu*), it refers to the direct transformative cause.
The *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* states that the "great elements" (*mahābhūta*) of the present are called the "basis of transformation" (*āśraya-parivṛtti*).
This is a remote basis of transformation;
"transformation" here refers to the transformation of the continuum.
The name "conforming" (*anuvartin*) used here has the same meaning as that in the preceding treatise.
Regarding the question of which levels of bodily and vocal karma reach the stage of arising as outflow-free (*anāsrava*):
this third section below clarifies the creative causes (*abhinirvartaka*) by way of their levels (*bhūmi*).
Regarding the question and the response in verse,
the treatise states: "Up to that which is derived from the primary elements (*mahābhūta*)," which explains the first phrase.
Because they are bound by outflows (*sāsrava*), bodily and vocal actions are produced by the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) of their own level.
Furthermore, the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 134, states:
"Question: If one is born in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), when the primary elements of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) manifest..."
Where does it manifest?
Some say it is between the eyebrows;
others say it is at the tip of the nose.
Some say it is at the edge of the heart;
some say it is at the edge of the navel;
others say it is at the tips of the toes.
Some say that it manifests in whichever place was previously established through preparatory application (*prayoga*).
Other masters say that the great elements (*mahābhūta*) of the desire realm are coarse,
while those of the form realm are subtle.
It enters coarse apertures with subtlety,
like oil entering sand; yet,
when the fundamental dhyānas manifest, [the subtle mind does not emerge].
The great elements (mahābhūta) of the form realm arise pervasively within the entire body;
however, when the preparatory concentration (sāmantaka-dhyāna) manifests,
the great elements of the form realm arise only at the periphery of the mind.
Some say that when the preparatory concentration (*sāmantaka-samādhi*) manifests,
the great elements (*mahābhūta*) of the form realm also arise throughout the entire body;
however, they nourish the body not as effectively as those of the fundamental [dhyāna].
Suppose there are two people who both go to a pond to bathe.
One stays by the side of the pond and bathes his body by scooping up water;
the other enters the pond and bathes with his body submerged.
Although both individuals use water that completely covers their bodies, the one who enters the pool for the sake of nourishing the body is superior.
Question: Within the body of the desire realm, there are already existing interstices.
Do the great elements (*mahābhūta*) of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) enter into it? Answer: No.
The future body of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) itself possesses two kinds.
First, there are only the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) of the desire realm;
second, the primary elements of the form realm are mixed [with them].
This occurs when one encounters conditions for entering a meditative absorption (*samādhi*) of the form realm.
Because those belonging solely to the desire realm cease,
while those mixed with the form realm arise; therefore,
it cannot be said that there was first an interval and later [beings] came to dwell within it— as explained extensively in that [text].
"If bodily and vocal actions reach the state of being untainted (*anāsrava*)," explains the latter phrase;
that is, if bodily and vocal actions are untainted.
Whatever arises accompanying the body in a particular stage must be brought into manifestation;
that is, it is produced by the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) of that very stage. Why is this? Because untainted phenomena (*anāsrava-dharma*) do not fall within the realms of existence.
Therefore, it is not produced by the great elements (*mahābhūta*) of those stages; for there can never be great elements that are untainted (*anāsrava*).
Nor is it produced by great elements that are unbound (*apratisaṃyukta*), because it arises from the power of the supporting body within the untainted realm (*anāsravadhātu*).
Therefore, it employs those great elements that accompany the body;
this indicates that both the manifest (*vijñapti*) and unmanifest (*avijñapti*) reach the level of being derived from the great elements.
Below this is the second section: the analysis of karma through various categories.
Among these, first is the explanation by way of categories;
second is the explanation of nature, realm, and stage. Herein, the first is the explanation by way of categories. Among these:
First, the categories of the appropriated and the non-appropriated are clarified;
second, the categories of the five things are clarified;
third, the categories of the sentient and the non-sentient are clarified.
The general categories of similarities and differences in the four explanations constitute the inquiry itself.
First, it asks what the category of these manifest and unmanifest [karmas] is.
Second, it asks by what kind of primary elements (mahābhūta) they are derived.
The verse says: "Reaching those belonging to the body that are appropriated.

In this response, the first two lines clarify the various non-informative [moralities] (*avijñapti*), while the subsequent two lines clarify the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) upon which the non-informative [morality] of the distracted state depends.
The next two lines clarify the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) upon which non-informative matter (*avijñapti*) depends;
the final two lines clarify all informative matter (*vijñapti*).
The Treatise says: "Because it arises depending on the internal... [and so forth].
The first two lines are explained to clarify its unmanifest nature;
in this verse, the unmanifest is first distinguished.

Whether in a state of meditative concentration or in a distracted state, all non-informative matter (*avijñapti*) is without appropriation (*anupātta*), because it lacks resistance (*apratigha*). Among the five categories [of conditioned phenomena], it is also of the nature of outflow (*niṣyanda*). The word "also" (*api*) is stated in the verse.
This demonstrates that this non-informative [matter] (avijñapti) is momentary.

Specifically, the non-informative matter arising simultaneously with the first untainted (anāsrava) stage of the receptivity to the knowledge of the dharma of suffering (duḥkhe dharmajñānakṣānti) is momentary because it does not arise from a cause of similar type (sabhāgahetu). All remaining non-informative matters are of the nature of outflow (niṣyanda).
This means it arises from a homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*), not from a ripening cause (*vipāka-hetu*); therefore, it is not born of maturation (*vipākaja*).
Because there is no accumulation of atoms (*paramāṇu*), it is not nurtured (*aupacayika*).
Because these are conditioned (*saṃskṛta*), they are not ultimately real; because they arise based on the internal, they belong only to the category of sentient beings (*sattva-saṃkhyāta*).
Since they do not depend on external factors, they do not extend to non-sentient things.
Among these, those in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) that are derived from the primary elements (*mahābhūta*)—
Explanation of the third and fourth phrases: This clarifies the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) upon which the non-informative matter (*avijñapti*) of the dispersed type depends.

Because the primary elements upon which the non-informative matter of the desire realm’s dispersed type depends arise from causes of the same class (*sabhāga-hetu*) among the five categories, they are of the nature of outflow (*niṣyanda*).
It is not born of maturation because it does not arise from a ripening cause;
it is not nurtured because there is no distinct, superior condition for its growth;
and it is not momentary because it arises from a homogeneous cause.
Because it is conditioned (*saṃskṛta*), it is not real; because it is appropriated (*upātta*), the *Nyāyānusāra* (Treatise on Reasoning), fascicle 35, states:
"The great elements (*mahābhūta*) upon which the non-informative matter (*avijñapti*) of the dispersed stage (*vibhūmi*) relies are appropriated."

Because they are the fruits of a distracted mind, and because one clings to them with a mind of craving as being the internal self in the present, the aforementioned treatise may also be subject to refutation.
Since external objects, when contacted, can produce suffering or pleasure, the seven factors of desire are not concomitants of the mind.
Because one also obtains the precepts at times when there is no [active] mind;
furthermore, the seven [mental factors] do not stand in the relation of co-existent cause (*sahabhū-hetu*) to one another,
because they do not share a single common fruit.

Therefore, the seven branches each have their own distinct primary elements (*mahābhūta*). Question: Why do the primary elements not distinguish between the sentient and the non-sentient? Answer: It is explained that it has already been stated that the unmanifest (*avijñapti*) belongs to the category of sentient beings.

The fact that insentient things do not constitute the great elements or the matter of sentient beings can be understood by analogy; therefore, it is not stated separately. Furthermore, another interpretation holds that since the term "appropriated" (upātta) is used, it definitely refers to sentient beings, whereas the term "unappropriated" (anupātta) applies to both sentient and insentient things.
Because there is a fear of over-extension, the term "sentient being" (*sattva*) is not explicitly stated in the definition of non-informative matter (*avijñapti*).

Regarding the phrase "the non-informative matter born of meditative concentration (*samādhi-ja*) reaches a state of no distinction," this explains the fifth and sixth lines, clarifying the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) upon which the non-informative matter of meditative concentration depends.
Among the five categories [of derived matter], there is that which is nurtured (aupacayika), because it encounters specific, superior conditions.
Therefore, the *Nyāyānusāra* asks:

"For what reason is the great primary element (*mahābhūta*) that constitutes all unmanifest form (*avijñapti*) in the realm of the unconcentrated (anāgamya) of exclusively of the nature of outflow (*naiṣyandika*)?"

The non-informative [matter] (*avijñapti*) produced by the meditative state (*samāhitabhūmi*) is nourished [by the great elements], because at the moment when a particularly distinguished mind is present, it is necessarily able to nourish the great elements and the sense faculties.

A mind in meditative concentration is invariably accompanied by particularly distinguished great elements that can act as the productive cause (*janakahetu*) for creating all the non-informative matter associated with that meditative mind.
In the stage of non-concentration (*asamāhita-bhūmi*), the unmanifest (*avijñapti*) does not arise simultaneously with the motivating mind (*samutthāpaka-citta*),
because it also arises during states of mindlessness (*acittaka-avasthā*). Furthermore,
its fundamental elements (*mahābhūta*) are exclusively of the nature of outflow (*niṣyanda*).

Because the motivating mind (*samutthāpaka-citta*) cannot nourish the great elements (*mahābhūta*) that give rise to the unmanifest (*avijñapti*), as stated in the above treatise; for this reason, it is known that there are no "nourished" (*aupacayika*) great elements.
Because they do not arise from a ripening cause (*vipāka-hetu*), they are not "born of ripening" (*vipākaja*).
Among the five categories [of phenomena], those that are "outflowing" (*niṣyanda*)—
not included within the categories of ripening (*vipāka*) or nurtured growth (*aupacayika*)— are termed "outflowing."

Since the great elements produced by maturation (*vipākaja*) are fully subsumed within those produced by formative effort (*abhisamskārika*) and those nurtured by food (*āhāra-saṃbhūta*), the great elements of outflow (*naiḥṣyandika*) are not established separately.
Because they arise from causes of similar kind (*sabhāga-hetu*), they are not momentary.
Because they are conditioned (*saṃskṛta*), they are not substantial. They are non-appropriated (*anupātta*).
Therefore, the *Nyāyānusāra* (Treatise on the Principles of Correct Reasoning), fascicle 35, states:
"The primary elements that serve as the basis [of the mind] are non-appropriated (*anupātta*),
because they are the fruit of a concentrated mind."
This is because there is necessarily no affectionate mind that would grasp these primary elements as its own internal self in the present;
furthermore, these primary elements lack any other characteristic of being appropriated.

Having been designated as "without appropriation," the aforementioned seven branches of body and speech are composed of the four great elements; because their supporting primary elements are, like the meditative mind, exclusively one and without distinction.
Therefore, while the great elements that produce the *anuśaya*-concomitant precepts (*cittānuparivartin-śīla*) are likewise produced by a single set of four great elements,
the non-manifest karma (*avijñapti*) of the desire realm, although its causal motivating mind (*samutthāpaka-citta*) may also be a single one,
is not concomitant with the mind and is produced by distinct sets of great elements.
Furthermore, the *Nyāyānusāra* states: "The seven members arise through mutual, reciprocal force;
because they share a single fruit, they are produced solely from one set of the four great elements (*mahābhūta*).

Since scattering [the atoms] would contradict this, they depend on different great elements. This is the aforementioned treatise. As for why it does not mention "sentient beings" (*sattva*), it is as explained previously.
Alternatively, it should be understood that once [the body] has been nourished and manifested as a sentient being,
there is informative action (*vijñapti*) up until the point where it is appropriated (*upātta*).
This explains the latter two phrases, which clarify informative action (*vijñapti-karman*).
Because it arises from a homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*) among the five categories, it is a result of outflow (*niṣyanda*). The word "only" excludes the other four types [of causes].
Because it does not arise from a ripening cause (*vipāka-hetu*), it is not a result of ripening (*vipākaja*).
Because there is no other superior condition, it is not something nurtured (*aupacayika*).
Because it arises from a cause of its own kind (*sabhāga-hetu*), it is not momentary.
Because it is conditioned (*saṃskṛta*), it is not substantial. There are two types of informative action (*vijñapti-karman*).
That is to say, bodily and vocal intimation: if it belongs to the body, because it arises in dependence upon the sense faculties, it is appropriated (*upātta*);
if it belongs to speech, because it does not depend upon the sense faculties, it is non-appropriated (*anupātta*). Question: If bodily informative action is appropriated...

Why does the *Prakaraṇapāda-śāstra* state that all informative actions (*vijñapti-karma*) are non-appropriated (*anupātta*)? The explanation says: the intention of the author of the treatise is different, making it difficult to provide a consistent interpretation.
Furthermore, another explanation holds that the *Prakaraṇa*’s discussion of informative action refers to its temporary arising within the body.
It is like a guest staying temporarily;

because the mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta-dharma*) do not possess the capacity for appropriation (*upādāna*), it is said that manifest action (*vijñapti-karman*) is non-appropriated (*anupātta*).
Treatises such as the *Abhidharmakośa* maintain this based on the fact that [manifest action] arises in a continuous stream within the body over a long duration.
Because the mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta-dharma*) are capable of appropriation (*upādāna*), it is said that manifest action (*vijñapti-karman*) is possessed of appropriation.

Each [explanation] relies on a single specific meaning, and thus they do not contradict one another. As for why "sentient" and "non-sentient" are not explicitly mentioned: since manifest action arises based on the internal [mind], it is already evident that it pertains to sentient beings; therefore, they are not stated separately.
Regarding the fact that all other meanings are the same as those for non-manifest [karma] in a scattered state: this serves as an analogy;
namely, that the four great elements of the manifest [karma] are the same as the four great elements that constitute the non-manifest [karma] in a scattered state.
These are of the nature of outflow (niṣyanda),
are appropriated (upātta),
arise from distinct primary elements (mahābhūta), and are further explained as being included within the category of sentient beings (sattvasaṃkhyāta).
And because it can produce a great similarity to the non-manifest (avijñapti) of the dispersed state,
the *Nyāyānusāra* states: "The remaining meanings are all the same as those of the non-manifest of the dispersed state."
That is to say: belonging to the category of sentient beings, being a basis,
being a result of outflow,
and being appropriated.

Arising from distinct primary elements (*mahābhūta*). Question: As stated in the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* (Vibhāṣā), fascicle 122, regarding the transformation of speech (*nirmāṇa-vāc*), there are two theories.
One says: "That is vocal action (*vāk-karman*), because it is produced by the mind."
Other masters say that this is not vocal action but merely the sound of speech, because the manifested body lacks appropriation (*anupāttaka*).
The intention of the former masters is that although it is not appropriated, it is produced by the great elements (*mahābhūta*) as its cause.
Because it is initiated by the mind,
the emanated speech is an action (*karman*).
According to the intention of the later masters, the emanation body (*nirmāṇakāya*) is without appropriation (*anupātta*).
This clearly demonstrates that emanated speech does not arise from the four great elements that are appropriated.
Since it does not arise from the four great elements that are appropriated,
it is evident that emanated speech is not karma.
However, that which arises from non-appropriated primary elements (*mahābhūta*) is not at all karma.
If it were karma, it would arise from appropriated primary elements;
yet there is no definitive assessment by the Master [Vasubandhu] as to whether the transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*) is karma or not-karma.
Although this passage is not seen in the text,
based on the *Parivarta*, there should likewise be two explanations.
Upon which of these does this treatise rely?

The commentary states: This treatise’s position corresponds to that of the later masters of the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, because it asserts that informative action (*vijñapti-karman*) arises from appropriated primary elements (*mahābhūta*).
Regarding the question, "When informative action arises, does it not reach [the object]?"—it is indeed so.
Question:
When manifest karma arises, must it necessarily destroy the dimensions of the original body produced by maturation, or not?
If one asks, "What fault would there be if that were so?
the answer is:
"If it were to be destroyed and then reach the measure of the two sexual organs, [it would constitute a formal offense]."
A dual inquiry.
There is a distinct new production that does not destroy its own substance.
Explanation.
If that is so, one might object: how can the informative action (*vijñapti*) arise pervasively based on the atoms (*paramāṇu*) it occupies?
For if both the informative action and its maturation (*vipāka*)—the two types of matter—were to arise together, they would have to be larger than their original substrate.
If they do not increase pervasively, how can they produce pervasive informative action (*vijñapti*)?
As for the argument that they can coexist because the body has pores and interstices,
this is refuted.
Because the body resulting from maturation (*vipāka*) is porous and possesses interstices,
it can accommodate the *niṣyanda* (outflow) and *vijñapti* (informative) matter;
thus, the *Abhidharmamahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 122, states:
However, both manifest and unmanifest [karma] arise based on the body;
some depend on only a single part,
such as the snapping of fingers.
One part of the body, such as the lifting of a foot, moves to perform wholesome or unwholesome karma.
Another type relies on the whole body,
as in prostrating before a Buddha or pursuing an enemy, where the entire body moves to perform wholesome or unwholesome karma.
In this regard, the number of atoms of the manifest action corresponds to the number of atoms of the body upon which it depends;
as is the number of atoms of the manifest, so too is that of the unmanifest.
Having already distinguished the categories of karma, as for the question "What are their differences?",
the following section secondly clarifies their nature (*svabhāva*), realm (*dhātu*), and stage (*bhūmi*). Within this,
the first part correctly elucidates their nature, realm, and stage.

Second, explaining the basis for the three natures (*trisvabhāva*). Below this, first, the actual explanation of the natures, realms, and stages (*dhātu-bhūmi*) arises as a response to the preceding inquiry.
Having already distinguished the categories of action (*karman*), which are of two kinds—namely, volition (*cetanā*) and action following volition (*cetayitvā karman*)—[the discussion proceeds].
Alternatively, there are three types, namely the distinctions of bodily, vocal, and mental karma.
