Alternatively, there are five types, namely the two of bodily and vocal karma—each consisting of informative and non-informative [karma]—along with the distinction of volitional karma. These constitute the five types of karma.
Regarding the distinctions among the three natures (*trisvabhāva*), the three realms (*tridhātu*), and the nine stages (*navabhūmi*), the verse states: "Up to 'because of the absence of origination'.
The first line provides the analysis of the three natures.
The final five phrases concern the classification by realm (*dhātu*) and level (*bhūmi*).
The treatise states: "Up to 'wholesome,' 'unwholesome,' and 'indeterminate,'" which explains the first phrase.
Non-informative [action] (avijñapti) pertains exclusively to the wholesome and unwholesome natures; there is no indeterminate (avyākṛta) [non-informative action]. Why is this?
Because it is originated by a mind and mental factors of powerful force.
Because the power of an indeterminate mind is weak, it cannot induce a strong unmanifest action (avijñapti) to arise;

however, at the moment that [the manifest action] ceases, its fruit continues to arise in each subsequent mental state and even during periods of non-conception. As for the others—namely, manifest action and volition—they all pertain to the three moral natures.
Regarding the phrase "because unwholesome [karma] therein is not specifically excluded":
this explains the second clause.
Among these, unwholesome informative and non-informative karma, as well as volition, exist only in the desire realm and not in the other two realms.

Because the unwholesome roots—namely, lack of shame (*āhrīkya*) and lack of dread (*anapatrāpya*)—have already been severed, there is no unwholesomeness in the higher realms. Wholesome states and neutral (*avyākṛta*) states exist in all stages as appropriate to each.
Because the verse does not exclude it,
the statement that "in the desire and form realms, there is restraint of body and speech" explains the third line.
Non-manifest form (avijñapti) is necessarily derived from the great elements (mahābhūta).
Since the great elements capable of acting as its source exist in both the desire realm and the form realm, non-manifest form derived from them exists in both.

Because the great elements capable of acting as its source do not exist in the formless realm, non-manifest form derived from them does not exist there either. Furthermore, wherever the activity of body and speech occurs, it is only in that place that the discipline (saṃvara) of body and speech exists.
Because bodily and vocal activity exist in the two realms of desire and form, both obtain bodily and vocal restraint (*kāya-vāg-saṃvara*).
Since bodily and vocal activity do not exist within the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), it lacks bodily and vocal restraint.
If that were so, then it would be difficult to explain how an untainted non-informative action (*anāsrava-avijñapti*) could arise within the body. If that were so...

When one born in the desire or form realms enters an immaterial absorption, although there are no immaterial primary elements (mahābhūta), there must nevertheless exist an immaterial restraint (avijñapti) that is derived from the primary elements of the body.

This is just as when one born in the desire or form realms gives rise to an outflow-free mind (anāsrava-citta): although there are no outflow-free primary elements, there exists an outflow-free non-informative matter (avijñapti) derived from the primary elements of the body.
This constitutes a difficulty regarding the primary elements (*mahābhūta*). Furthermore, it is explained:
if that were so, when one born in the desire or form realms enters an immaterial attainment (*ārūpyasamāpatti*), although there is no immaterial body or speech, [the same principle would apply].
There must be an immaterial restraint (ārūpya-saṃvara) consisting of the primary elements (mahābhūta) that accompany the body;
just as when one born in the desire or form realms gives rise to an outflow-free mind (anāsrava-citta), although there is no outflow-free bodily or vocal action,
there exists an outflow-free non-informative matter (avijñapti-rūpa) accompanying the primary elements of the body.
This is the refutation of [the position regarding] body and speech; furthermore, it explains how the refutation applies to both types.
Otherwise, the statement "because that [consciousness] relies upon the primary elements (mahābhūta) as its basis" is the explanation.
Not so; because that untainted (*anāsrava*) non-informative matter (*avijñapti*) does not fall within the realms (*dhātu*).
Although there are no untainted primary elements (*mahābhūta*), it arises based on the body and is thus composed of the great elements belonging to that body. Another interpretation says: "Not so."

Because that untainted (anāsrava) non-informative matter (avijñapti) does not fall within the realms (dhātu), although it lacks an untainted body or speech, it arises in dependence upon the body; therefore, it is composed of the same primary elements (mahābhūta) as the body. Furthermore, another interpretation explains both types [of non-informative matter] together. This serves to resolve the objection by way of a counter-argument.
If there were unmanifest form (*avijñapti*) in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*),

there would have to be an unmanifest form not produced from the great elements (*mahābhūta*), namely that which they [the opponents] imagine exists as a defiled (*sāsrava*) unmanifest form belonging to that specific realm and stage (*dhātu-bhūmi-saṃbandhin*) within the formless realm.
It stands to reason that it should arise from the great elements (*mahābhūta*) of that realm.
In the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), the four great elements do not exist.
If there were unmanifest form (*avijñapti*) there, it would follow that there is unmanifest form not produced from the great elements.
Furthermore, it cannot be said that contaminated non-informative matter (*avijñapti*) is the same as uncontaminated precepts (*anāsrava-śīla*),
because it relies upon the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) of a distinct realm and stage.
Thus, the *Vibhāṣā* (17) states:

Question: Just as there is untainted (*anāsrava*) morality even though there are no untainted great elements (*mahābhūta*), so too, what prevents there from being morality in that realm (*dhātu*) even though the great elements are absent? Answer: Untainted morality does not become untainted through the power of the great elements.
However, because it is originated by the mental factors concomitant with the outflow-free mind through the power of that mind, it is similar;
whereas impure morality, being bound to a specific realm and stage by the power of the primary elements, is not similar.
Furthermore, regarding the phrase "turning one's back on all forms up to the subduing of the perception of form," this can be understood through another interpretation.
As for the Vaibhāṣika masters' statement "up to the point where there is no non-informative matter (*avijñapti-rūpa*)," [it is explained as follows].
Furthermore, he recounts alternative interpretations:

"In order to eliminate unwholesome discipline (*duḥśīla*), morality (*śīla*) arises; since unwholesome discipline exists only within the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), wholesome morality arises in both the desire and form realms (*rūpadhātu*) to serve as its antidote."
The formless realm is distant from the desire realm by way of four types of distance;
thus, there is no non-informative matter (*avijñapti-rūpa*) within the formless realm. These four distances have been explained at length in the *Vyākhyāyukti*.
Informative matter (*vijñapti-rūpa*) exists only in the realm of contact (*prāpti*); that which can be called "informative" exists solely therein.
Explaining the fourth phrase:
The three natures of manifest karma all pertain to the desire realm and the first dhyāna.
If one says that it includes only those with vitarka (applied thought) and excludes the intermediate dhyāna, [it is as follows].
The statement "possessing vicāra" is made in order to include the intermediate [state].
Regarding the phrase "concealed-neutral (nivṛtāvyākṛta) informative action (vijñapti) up to feigning and self-praise," this explains the fifth clause.
This briefly distinguishes the differences.
Manifest action (vijñapti) that is obscured-unspecified (nivṛtāvyākṛta) is definitely non-existent in the desire realm;
it exists only in the first dhyāna. The passage beginning with "I have heard" below cites scriptural evidence.
Deceptive and sycophantic speech constitutes manifest vocal intimation (*vāgvijñapti*).
Inducing others outside the assembly constitutes manifest bodily intimation (*kāyavijñapti*).
Since there is no speech in the higher realms, how could there be the sphere of sound (*śabdadhātu*)?
Question:
Since there is no vocal intimation (*vāg-vijñapti-karma*) in the higher realms, how can there be sound?
Question: Is there sound produced with external primary elements as its cause? Answer:
There is sound because there is sound produced with external primary elements as its cause.
Although there is an internal great element acting as the cause for producing sound,
it is explained as being external and manifest,
or perhaps it is implied by way of reflection.
As for the statement by other masters that "[it is] because it is inferior and because it is abandoned," this recounts a divergent view;
there are also unobscured-neutral (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*) informative actions (*vijñapti-karman*) in the three higher dhyānas.
It can only give rise to a mind that is non-obscured and neutral (anivṛtāvyākṛta) which expresses manifest karma;
it is neither wholesome nor defiled.
One born in a higher stage cannot give rise to wholesome or defiled minds of a lower stage to produce bodily or vocal intimation (*kāya-vāk-vijñapti*).
This is because the wholesome states of the lower stage are inferior, and the defiled states of the lower stage have been abandoned.

Therefore, the former school’s intention is that bodily and vocal informative actions (*kāya-vāk-vijñapti-karman*) are bound to the level (*bhūmi*) of the body itself, not to the level of the motivating mind.
The latter school’s intention is that bodily and vocal informative actions are bound to the level of the mind that motivates them.
It is not bound to the stage that accompanies the body (*kāyānuparivartin*).
Regarding what was previously stated to be wholesome,
the Master of the Treatise (*śāstrakāra*) adopts the position of the former school that it is bound to the stage that accompanies the mind (*cittānuparivartin*).
The mind is intimate and powerful;
the body is distant and weak.
Therefore, all material actions are judged in terms of their nature according to the mind.
If various material actions (rūpa-karma) are bound to the same level as the body,
then the nature of these material actions should also be bound to that same body;
"body" here refers to the life-faculty (jīvitendriya), the group-homogeneity (nikāya-sabhāga), and so forth.
Their nature is neutral (*avyākṛta*).
If these various material karmas were all to follow the body in being of a neutral nature, they would not apply to the wholesome or the defiled, which would result in a great error.
For this reason, it is known that [this is not the case].
It is well said that [the mind] is bound according to the level of the mind.
Furthermore, for what reason does it reach the state of neutral manifest karma?
The following explains the sixth line, which poses a double question;
this may be understood.
This is because there is no [action] that initiates karma and yet results in a non-manifest (avijñapti) action that is obscured-unspecified (nivṛtāvyākṛta).
The double response: "Because there is no mind that initiates or motivates karma" is the general answer.
A mind accompanied by vitarka and vicāra is capable of manifesting manifest karma (*vijñapti-karma*).
Above the two meditative attainments (*dhyāna*), this mind does not exist at all;
therefore, manifest action (*vijñapti-karman*) is entirely absent in the three higher stages.
Question: Why is it that the higher stages lack the minds of vitarka and vicāra?
The *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* states: "Vitarka and vicāra are coarse and agitated, lacking tranquility;
because the higher stages are subtle and tranquil," as cited in the aforementioned treatise. Furthermore, the mind that expresses [speech] is abandoned only through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*).

Because they operate through external objects, the afflictions abandoned by insight (darśana-heya) cannot incite karma; because they operate through internal objects, [the afflictions abandoned by cultivation] can.

Although the two views—view of self-existence (satkāya-dṛṣṭi) and view of extremes (antagrāha-dṛṣṭi)—exist within the desire realm and are categorized as obscured-unspecified (nivṛta-avyākṛta) and abandoned by insight, [they do not incite karma].
Because it operates through internal doors, it cannot initiate karma;
since there are no obscured-unspecified (nivṛtāvyākṛta) afflictions to be abandoned by cultivation within the realm of desire,
there is therefore no obscured-unspecified manifest action (vijñapti) in the desire realm.
This clarifies the distinction.
As for the question, "Is it solely by virtue of the motivation (*samutthāna*) that [an action] reaches the nature of being wholesome, unwholesome, and so forth?"—
the following section is the second part, which explains the basis for the three natures.
Among these, first is the direct clarification of the basis for the three natures;
second is the clarification of the two kinds of origination. Below this is the first section: the direct clarification of the basis for the three natures. Question:
Is it solely by virtue of the motivating mind (*hetu-samutthāna-citta*) that phenomena become virtuous, non-virtuous, and so forth?
No; this is the answer. "How so? is the inquiry.
Regarding the statement that "by four kinds of causes, [the nature of] the wholesome and so forth is established through the fourfold origination," the answer is:
the nature of being wholesome and so forth is established by means of four kinds of causes.
Regarding the question of what phenomena possess what nature and by what causes they are established, three further questions are posed:
first, among all phenomena, which are designated as "ultimate" (*paramārtha*) and so forth? These constitute four [questions].
Second, it asks: among the three natures, what nature does this ultimate reality (paramārtha) and so forth belong to?
Third, it asks: by what cause is this ultimate reality and so forth established as being wholesome and so forth?
The verse says: "The supreme, the indeterminate, and the two constants.
Answer: Regarding this within the verse:
The first four lines clarify the four wholesome states; the fifth line clarifies the unwholesome;
and the sixth line clarifies the indeterminate.
Regarding the preceding four lines:
The first phrase clarifies ultimate goodness;
the second phrase clarifies intrinsic goodness;
the third phrase clarifies associated goodness.
The fourth phrase clarifies wholesome states by way of motivation (*samutthāna*).
Reversing these four types of wholesomeness,
there are likewise four types of unwholesome states, and one type of indeterminate state.

Regarding what is called the ultimate meaning: [Question] Why are there four types each for the wholesome and the unwholesome, while the indeterminate is only one? [Answer] It is explained that among the mental factors (*caitta*), there is no separate mental factor that is indeterminate by nature (*svabhāva-avyākṛta*).
Because they lack intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), association (*samprayoga*) is not established;
because association is not established due to the non-establishment of intrinsic nature, its origination (*samutthāna*) is likewise not established.
Furthermore, even if these three were established as a comprehensive categorization of phenomena (*dharmasaṃgraha*), it would still not be exhaustive.
The *Nyāyānusāra* (Treatise on Correct Reasoning), fascicle 36, states: "There is no distinct intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), association (*samprayoga*), or origination (*samutthāna*).
This is because there is no single mental factor (*caitta*) that is exclusively indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) and universally associated with an indeterminate mind."
Even if one were to establish three types, such as the "self-nature" (svabhāva) and so forth, as a skillful means,
they would still not encompass them exhaustively because the indeterminate (avyākṛta) is so manifold. Therefore, the indeterminate consists of only two kinds.
First is the ultimate truth (paramārtha);
second is intrinsic nature (svabhāva).
That which is conditioned and indeterminate is subsumed under intrinsic nature.
Because it is established as indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) without depending on any other cause, unconditioned indeterminate phenomena are subsumed under the ultimate (*paramārtha*).

This is because their nature is permanent and lacks any alternative modes [of designation]. Thus concludes the treatise. The intent of this treatise is the same as that of the *Nyāyānusāra*, which also maintains two types [of indeterminate phenomena].

The intrinsic nature (svabhāva) will not be discussed here as it is too brief to treat in detail. Question: If, according to the *Nyāya*, all conditioned indeterminate (avyākṛta) phenomena are of intrinsic nature, why does the *Mahāvibhāṣā* (Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra), fascicle 87, state regarding the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) that: [text missing] ?
There are five types of indeterminate [dharmas]:
first, dharmas born of maturation;
second, dharmas of deportment.
Third, the dharmas of the sphere of arts and crafts; fourth, the indeterminate dharmas resulting from fruition;
fifth, the indeterminate dharmas by their own nature. Furthermore, it is said that within the form realm (rūpadhātu), there are four types of indeterminate [dharmas].
Excluding those arising from craftsmanship, the rest are as explained for the desire realm. Furthermore, regarding the formless realm, it is said that there are two types of neutral (avyākṛta):

first, those born of maturation (vipākaja), and second, those neutral by nature (svabhāva-avyākṛta). The commentary explains: according to the *Nyāyānusāra*, among conditioned phenomena, all whose essence is neutral are termed "neutral by nature."
Within the conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*), the *Mahāvibhāṣā* further opens up five types based on distinctions in meaning;
one should know that what is not included within the first four is termed "intrinsic nature" (*svabhāva*).
The various treatises on the indeterminate differ.
Some speak of one kind, namely the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).
Others speak of two kinds, namely the ultimate truth and...
As for their intrinsic nature,
some say there are four types: namely, maturation, deportment, [functioning, and transformation].
The skillful (śailpasthānika) and the fruition-of-mastery (abhijñā-phala);
alternatively, it is said there are five types when the intrinsic nature (svabhāva) is added.
Alternatively, it is said that there are six types, with the addition of the ultimate (paramārtha).

Thus, there is no contradiction in the differences between the extensive and the concise, or in their being analyzed or synthesized. Question: If this treatise establishes four kinds of wholesomeness and so forth...
Why does the *Vibhāṣā*, in its second [section], state:
"Now one should question him: if only the five faculties are wholesome by intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-kuśala*), what is the intrinsic nature of the remaining wholesome dharmas?
If it is claimed that they are also called 'wholesome' because they are mixed with the five faculties—which are themselves unwholesome or neutral—[then this is untenable]."
In this way, these five faculties are intermingled with those [other factors].
Why, then, are they not designated as unwholesome or indeterminate?
However, the five beginning with faith [are distinct] from the remaining dharmas.
They have the same basis,
the same aspect, and the same object.
Arising together,
abiding together,
and ceasing together.
They have a single fruit;
they share the same outflow and the same maturation.
To say that the five faculties are inherently virtuous (*svabhāva-kuśala*), while others are designated as virtuous only through association (*saṃprayoga*), would be a mistake;
for such a view merely accords with deluded sentiments and does not conform to correct reasoning. Do not fall into this error.

Therefore, one should state that the roots of the "supreme mundane dharmas" (laukikāgradharma) possess both the nature of being roots and the nature of not being roots. According to the critique of the *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya* regarding the intention [of the *Mahāvibhāṣā*], all mental factors (*caitta*) and so forth share the same basis (*āśraya*) and other such commonalities;

how then can the five faculties alone be designated as having their own specific nature? This is precisely what the *Mahāvibhāṣā* establishes as the general definition of "specific nature" (*svabhāva*).
Just as it is with the wholesome, so it should be understood for the unwholesome and the indeterminate; these too should be explained solely in terms of their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).

Would it not be contradictory to further establish three other types, such as those associated (*samprayukta*)? The commentary explains: since the *Vibhāṣā* already refutes the establishment of the five faculties as being intrinsically wholesome by means of the "single basis" (*ekāśraya*) and other arguments.

Regarding the statement that there are four kinds of wholesomeness, this describes the interpretation of other masters. Furthermore, according to the explanation by the Bodhisattva Sthiramati in his *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya-ṭīkā*, if one speaks according to the ultimate reality, all of these are wholesome by intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-kuśala*).
However, when the Master Vasubandhu establishes four types [of wholesomeness],
he designates different names according to the relative superiority or inferiority of their meaning.
That which is the most powerful and supreme among the wholesome is "wholesome in the ultimate sense" (paramārtha-kuśala).
Next, the stronger [factor] establishes the intrinsic nature (svabhāva);
next, the weaker [factor] establishes the association (saṃprayoga);
and the weakest is called the origination (samutthāna).
The unwholesome is also established as fourfold according to its meaning;

thus, in the *Abhidharmamahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* (144), in the section on the analysis of the three natures regarding the twenty-two faculties (*indriya*), one master also states that there are four kinds of wholesome and unwholesome.
It is the same as this treatise.

However, no refutation is seen there. Furthermore, the preceding passage of the *Vibhāṣā* merely refutes the heterodox masters who establish the five faculties (*pañcendriya*) as being intrinsically wholesome (*svabhāva-kuśala*).
Since Vasubandhu establishes that non-attachment and so forth constitute the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of the wholesome, there is no contradiction between his earlier and later statements.
The Treatise says: "It is just like one who is free from illness."
The first phrase clarifies that which is virtuous in the ultimate sense (*paramārtha-kuśala*). The ultimate sense is *nirvāṇa*.
This indicates that *nirvāṇa* is called "virtuous" because it is secure;
just as a person who is free from illness and suffering is secure.
Furthermore, one interpretation in the *Nyāyānusāra* (Treatise on the Correct Principle), volume thirty-six, states:
"Alternatively, true liberation is supreme;
thus, it receives the name 'ultimate meaning' (*paramārtha*)."
"Victorious" (parama) means most supreme, having no equal.
"Meaning" (artha) refers to a distinct, truly existent essence.
This indicates that because nirvāṇa is unequaled and substantially existent, it is called the "ultimate meaning" (paramārtha).
Thus, that which is supreme, ultimate, and secure is called "wholesome.
Since such nirvana is wholesome and eternal,
its essence is the most venerable among all phenomena.
Therefore, it is uniquely designated as "virtuous in the ultimate sense.
Regarding the passage from "virtuous by nature" up to "like excellent medicine," this explains the second phrase,
clarifying what is virtuous by nature (*svabhāva-kuśala*).
That which is good by its very nature is called "intrinsically good" (*svabhāva-kuśala*).
It is like a potent medicine;
because the medicine itself is efficacious and wholesome, it is called a "potent medicine. Question: Why are these five specifically designated as "intrinsic"?
Are the other wholesome dharmas not intrinsic natures (*svabhāva*)? The explanation says: these five, being powerful and superior, are called intrinsic natures;

the others, being neither powerful nor superior, are not so called. Furthermore, another explanation holds that the three [wholesome roots] such as non-attachment reverse the three unwholesome roots, while the two—shame (*hrī*) and dread of blame (*apatrāpya*)—reverse the great unwholesome ground-dharmas (*mahā-akuśala-bhūmika*).
Because the dharmas being negated are powerful and predominant, the five dharmas that can negate them are termed "virtuous by nature" (*svabhāva-kuśala*).
Other virtuous dharmas and so forth cannot negate those [five], and therefore they are not termed "virtuous by nature."
Regarding the phrase "associated wholesomeness is like water mixed with medicinal herbs," this explains the third line,
clarifying associated wholesomeness through the analogy of water mixed with medicinal herbs.
Water mixed with medicine is called "medicinal water.
Other minds and mental factors become wholesome only when they are associated with that which is wholesome by nature; therefore, they are termed "wholesome through association" (*samprayoga-kuśala*).
Regarding "wholesome by origination" up to "that which is produced [by it] like milk":
this explains the fourth phrase, clarifying wholesome by origination.

This refers to bodily and vocal actions, as well as formations dissociated from mind—namely, the four characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), acquisition (*prāpti*), and the two meditative attainments (*samāpatti*).
This is because it is virtuous by nature and arises from association with the virtuous.
This arising virtue is like milk produced by the infusion of medicinal decoctions;
that is to say, just as when a cow drinks the juice of sweet licorice, the milk produced through its power is sweet and delicious.
Regarding the point that "if a mind of a different class reaches this state, the meaning should be considered," it is difficult to establish the origination of the wholesome.
A defiled mind is called a "mind of a different class" because it is distinct from the wholesome.

For example, when a wholesome state follows a state of doubt, it can subsequently induce the acquisition of the wholesome and the arising of its four characteristics (birth, subsistence, decay, and impermanence).
How can the acquisition (*prāpti*) and so forth that arise [simultaneously] be established as wholesome?
This point should be considered.
Furthermore, the *Nyāyānusāra* (Treatise on the Correct Principle), fascicle 36, states:
Acquisitions (*prāpti*) also arise due to minds of a different category;
for example, when a mind resulting from supernormal powers (*abhijñā-phala-citta*) is attained through meditative absorption (*dhyāna*),
or when defiled phenomena (*kliṣṭa-dharma*) are acquired because a superior neutral mind (*viśiṣṭa-avyākṛta-citta*) has become manifest.
Since wholesome dharmas are acquired when a superior defiled mind manifests, how do these [defiled minds] come to possess a wholesome nature?

This is because they arise simultaneously with the acquisition (*prāpti*) of those dharmas; thus, it was said that there is no fault, as a mind of a different category does not act as a causal condition (*pratyaya*).
Although minds of different categories also arise through conditions to become wholesome and so forth, they do not depend on those [other] minds; or rather,
because they arise from the various acquisitions (*prāpti*) and so forth based on those [minds],
they attain the nature of being wholesome and so forth precisely by depending on them.
Therefore, it is established that their nature as wholesome and so forth differs by virtue of their motivation (*samutthāna*).
To explain: in the question, there are generally three distinct types of minds.
First, the mind of supernormal power (*abhijñā-phala-citta*) obtained through dhyāna.
This means that when a wholesome mind—which is distinct from the neutral state of non-acquisition—is present, one obtains all defiled dharmas because two superior neutral minds are manifesting;
this is based on the principle that one possesses defiled dharmas through a neutral mind.

This refers to the acquisition (*prāpti*) of an indeterminate mind that is distinct from the defiled; furthermore, it is explained that when one falls away [from a higher state], the obscured-indeterminate minds of the view of self-existence (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*) belonging to the desire realm manifest before one.

The acquisition of various defiled and unwholesome dharmas is the acquisition of a mind that is obscured-neutral (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*) rather than unwholesome; this occurs because one falls back from a superior state and brings a defiled mind into manifestation, thereby acquiring various wholesome dharmas.
This refers to the acquisition (*prāpti*) of wholesome factors that is distinct from the defiled mind.
How do these [factors] come to possess the nature of being wholesome and so forth? In the response, two interpretations are given: [they are wholesome] by way of their motivation (*samutthāna*).
First, it can be said that both [the acquisition and the dharma] are acquired together.
This means that because the acquisition arises simultaneously with a dharma of the same nature, it is stated cryptically in this way.
The nature—whether wholesome and so forth—is established by the motivating cause (*samutthāna*); a mind of a different category does not act as the motivating condition.
Therefore, there is no fault.

Although minds of different categories act as conditions to produce acquisitions of a different category, resulting in the attainment of virtue and so forth, this does not depend upon that [specific] mind; rather, it is explained in terms of the acquisition occurring before or after the dharma itself.
Alternatively, it is because the various acquisitions (*prāpti*) that arise prior to or subsequent to those dharmas obtained thereby— depending upon those very dharmas—
establish their nature as virtuous (*kuśala*) and so forth.
The distinction between the natures of wholesome and so forth is established by way of their motivation (*samutthāna*).
As it is said, "the nature of the wholesome extends to that which is contrary to this," the fifth phrase explains the four types of unwholesome states as being the opposites of the wholesome.
What is the contradiction?
Question:
From "ultimately unwholesome" up to "like a chronic illness."
Answer: To clarify what is ultimately unwholesome:
it refers to the phenomena of saṃsāra, which have the nature of the Truth of Suffering.
That which is extremely unstable is called ultimately unwholesome (*paramārthākuśala*).

It is like a person with a chronic illness who is constantly suffering and lacks peace; cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*) is the opposite of nirvāṇa, because nirvāṇa is ultimately wholesome (*paramārtha-kuśala*).

Birth and death are ultimately unwholesome (*paramārthato 'kuśala*). Question: Since the opposite of the wholesome is unwholesome, ultimate unwholesomeness would thus encompass all three natures (*tridharmaka*).

Likewise, since the opposite of the unwholesome is wholesome, ultimate wholesomeness would also encompass all three natures. Answer: It is explained that because ultimate unwholesomeness pervades all contaminated (*sāsrava*) phenomena, it can encompass all three natures.
Ultimate wholesome phenomena are exclusively analytical cessation;
they are solely wholesome and do not pertain to the three natures.
As for those that are unwholesome by their own nature, up to "being like poison," [it refers to]...

It should be understood that these are unwholesome by their very nature (*svabhāva-akuśala*). Question: Among the contaminated (*sāsrava*) factors, why are only these five designated as being unwholesome by nature? Answer: Because they are preeminent, they are established separately.
The three unwholesome roots possess five superior characteristics:
namely, they pervade the five categories [of afflictions] and extend throughout the six consciousnesses.
This is the nature of the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*).

At the time when the roots of virtue are severed, they exert a firm and powerful application, capable of producing coarse and evil actions of both body and speech. In this regard, lack of shame (*āhrīkya*) and lack of dread (*anapatrāpya*) possess both meanings in a superior manner.

This means that only what is unwholesome and what is universally unwholesome are established [as such], because the remainder do not possess these qualities in their entirety; therefore, they are not so designated.
Regarding "associated unwholesomeness" up to "that which is produced by being induced":
this explains associated [unwholesomeness] and its origination.
This can be understood.
If it were so, then there would be no "reaching" [of the object], because everything would be subsumed under birth and death;
thus, the objection regarding the ultimate meaning of unwholesomeness is invalid.
If all contaminated (*sāsrava*) birth and death were ultimately (*paramārthatas*) unwholesome, then within them there would be no wholesome or neutral states.
If you argue that there is no fault because this is based on the ultimate sense,
we reply:

If one relies on the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), it is indeed as you say that there is no such twofold nature; however, within these contaminated phenomena (*sāsrava-dharma*), "wholesome" and "indeterminate" are established in relation to their maturation fruit (*vipākaphala*).
Among all contaminated phenomena (*sāsrava-dharma*),
those for which a ripened fruit (*vipāka-phala*) cannot be designated are established as "indeterminate" (*avyākṛta*).
Among contaminated phenomena, those for which a desirable ripened fruit can be designated are called "wholesome" (*kuśala*).
"Therefore, there is no fault.
Regarding "the ultimate indeterminate has no further alternative formulations," this explains the sixth phrase.
This can be understood from the text itself.
The citation from the *Nyāyapraveśa* has already been explained as before.
Regarding the statement, "In this regard, one should consider that the same applies to the subsequent examples," the following is a question-and-answer analysis.
Question:

If the body and speech were to become wholesome or unwholesome by the power of their motivation (*samutthāna*), then the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) that serve as the basis for those bodily and vocal actions would themselves have to be wholesome or unwholesome,
because they are all equally originated from a single mind.
Regarding the argument that the analogy does not hold because the mind of the agent is involved,
the answer is as can be understood from the text.
Although the four characteristics that arise with all conditioned phenomena do not arise intentionally but are established based upon those phenomena,
they may still be called "co-arising" (samutthāna) because they arise following the power of those phenomena. If this were so,
one would have to exert effort to bring about a concentrated mind (*samāhita-citta*).
The master of the treatise further objects:
If that is so, then the non-informative matter (avijñapti) that follows a concentrated mind is neither produced by the attention (manasikāra) of one currently in meditative absorption,
nor is it induced by the preparatory effort (prayoga) of a distracted mind.
Because the distracted state and the state of conformity (anuvartaka) are of different types;
or because the distinction between the concentrated and the distracted is of different types,
it should not arise from the mind in the same way as the primary elements (mahābhūta).
How is it that this becomes wholesome?
The *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra* (Treatise on Following Right Reasoning), fascicle 36, provides the following defense:
"The non-informative [action] (*avijñapti*) associated with meditative concentration arises through the power of that concentration and so forth."
It follows logically that it should also be established as being "wholesome by origination" (*samutthāna-kuśala*).
The Abhidharmakośa masters refute this, saying:
"If it is called 'wholesome by origination' because the meditative non-informative [matter] arises through the power of meditative concentration, then..."
The great elements (*mahābhūta*) are also produced by the power of the mind; therefore, they should be designated as having a virtuous or non-virtuous nature of origination (*samutthāna*).
If you say that the great elements are not produced by attention (*manasikāra*), then how could this discipline (*saṃvara*) and unmanifest form (*avijñapti*) arise from volition?
Alternatively, the divine eye and ear would have to be of a virtuous nature, just like virtuous bodily and vocal actions,
because they are originated by a virtuous mind.
This objection applies to both the two faculties or both the two supernormal powers.
Alternatively, the objection applies equally to both the faculties and the [matter] they accompany;
therefore, the previous explanation is superior,
as it identifies the similar matter as the motivating cause (*samutthāna*).
To advance or retreat and to demand an account of this is, in principle, difficult to reconcile.
One ought to apply diligent effort to seek an alternative interpretation. The *Nyāya* (Correct Principle) offers this defense:
This objection is unreasonable,
because those two— the path of liberation and the mind— are indeterminate (*avyākṛta*),
and because those two arise simultaneously with the Path.
If one penetrates this apparent difficulty, what need is there for such strenuous effort? The master of the *Abhidharmakośa* refutes it, saying:

"If the divine eye and ear arise simultaneously with an indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) path, then since they are indeterminate, they ought—by virtue of the power of that path—to be designated as 'co-arisen' (*samutthāna*)."
If it is claimed that it is not by the power of that path that the state of being "unspecified" (avyākṛta) is established,
then how can the expression "arising together with the path" (mārga-sahaja) be explained?
This genuine objection remains unresolved.
The labor thus becomes wasted.
Regarding the phrase "as stated above, up to and including wrong livelihood," etc.,
this section below is the second part, which clarifies the two types of co-arising (samutthāna).
False view is itself an affliction abandoned through seeing.
Yet the Sūtra states that it can give rise to false speech, action, and livelihood.
How is it that you previously stated that afflictions abandoned through seeing cannot manifest [karmic] expression?
Regarding this lack of contradiction:
the response is as follows. "Why is this?
is a critical inquiry. The verse states: "Up to the indeterminate, it follows whichever is virtuous."
The verse provides the response.
The first verse generally clarifies the two types of motivation (*samutthāna*).
The second verse distinguishes their differences in relation to the six consciousnesses.
The third verse distinguishes [the three natures] by way of their specific characteristics.
The treatise states: "Up to the point where it is called 'conforming' (anuvartaka)," which can be understood as the explanation of the first verse.
As for what functional capacity it possesses in conforming to karma:
Question: Although there are prior causes, it follows that karma such as that of death should not exist. Answer:
Although there are prior causes, they serve as the conditions for the elicitation of karma.
If there were no accompanying mental states and mental factors (*citta-caitta*),
then karma would be non-existent, just as in the case of a dead person.
If that were so, how could one generate ethical discipline (*śīla*) in a state of mindlessness?
Question:
Regarding those who possess mind and for whom karma has utility—does this apply universally? Answer: It applies universally.
It is not that one cannot produce the precepts without a mind;
rather, it is said that because the arising of karma is distinct for those who possess a mind, the concomitant mind (*anuvartaka-citta*) is functional with respect to that karma.

The *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra* (Treatise on Following Right Reasoning), fascicle 36, states: "If there were no concomitant mind, even though a prior cause exists as an inducer, [the result would not follow]."
As in the state of being without mind, or as with a corpse,
informative action (*vijñapti*) should not arise.

The manifest action (*vijñapti*) possesses the functional capacity to follow along [with the mind], whereas the unmanifest action (*avijñapti*) does not depend upon such following along to function, because the unmanifest action continues to function even during states of mindlessness (*acittaka*). The Vaibhāṣika masters raise an objection: "In a state of mindlessness, although there is no manifest action to follow along, the prātimokṣa [vow] still functions."
If it is argued that "the first moment must possess both the manifest (vijñapti) and the non-manifest (avijñapti), and thus, like the state of mindlessness,
the manifest should not arise"— this statement is flawed.
If one claims this is not based on the acquisition of the manifest in the first moment, but rather refers to other states of mindlessness, [that too is incorrect].
Since it was stated that there must be a distinction [between types of consciousness] yet no such distinction was made,
a fault consequently arises;
for the consciousnesses to be abandoned by insight (darśana-heya) do not exist at this stage.
Explaining the fifth phrase:
[vitarka and vicāra] are seen to function solely as the "transformative" (pravartaka) factors;
they serve as the necessary provisions for the arising of vitarka and vicāra, which in turn give rise to informative action (vijñapti).

Because it assists in the arising of that [action], it is called the "distant motivating cause" (*dūre-samutthāna*). Therefore, it can function as the "primary motivator" (*pravartaka*) but not as the "concomitant motivator" (*anuvartaka*).
Since it operates through an internal door (*antarmukha-pravṛtta*), it cannot initiate karma.
Only a mind that operates toward external objects (*bahirmukha*) is capable of initiating karma.
At the very moment such an externally directed mind initiates karma, this [mind]—which is to be abandoned by insight (*darśana-heya*)—does not exist.
Therefore, the *Vibhāṣā* (117) states:
Furthermore, a mind that functions through the external doors (*bāhyadvāra*) can produce bodily and vocal actions as momentary origination (*kṣaṇasamutthāna*).
Because this [present] mind functions through the internal doors (*antaradvāra*), it cannot produce them.

This is explained at length in that [text]. Moreover, regarding "that which is abandoned by seeing (*darśanaheya*) is [only] abandoned by seeing": [this refers to the fact that] once a state has become abandoned by seeing, it remains so.
The second interpretation:
Furthermore, if that which is abandoned by insight (*darśana-heya*) were to manifest as physical form (*rūpa*), then such form would also have to be abandoned by insight.
If it is granted that [form] is abandoned by vision, what fault would there be?
The Sautrāntika asks:
"What fault is there in granting that contaminated form (*sāsrava-rūpa*) is also abandoned by vision?"
"What fault is there in this?
This would contradict [the principle] that [defilements] are not abandoned by insight.
Thus the Sarvāstivādins respond.

If impure form (*rūpa*) were to be abandoned by insight (*darśana-prahātavya*), it would contradict the *Abhidharma-mūla-śāstra*, which states that form is not abandoned by insight; this would thus contravene the scriptural authority. "Clarity" (*vidyā*) refers to wisdom (*prajñā*).
Ignorance (avidyā) refers to delusion (moha). Delusion necessarily coexists with confusion;
it is designated as "ignorance" specifically because it is the opposite of knowledge (vidyā). Since knowledge and ignorance are mutually exclusive, they cannot arise simultaneously.
However, they may be distinguished into categories and subsequently severed.
Leakage-tainted (sāsrava) karma and matter are not in contradiction with either clarity (vidyā) or ignorance (avidyā);
therefore, they are not abandoned through insight (darśana-prahātavya). Rather, it can only be said that they are abandoned because of the bondage of their objects (ālambana-bandhana).
The formal syllogism is stated as follows:
The matter of contaminated karma is not abandoned by insight,
because it is not in contradiction with either clarity or ignorance.
This contradicts reason, as in the case of the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) and so forth.
Therefore, the *Mahāvibhāṣā* asks: "For what reason are the nine grades of defiled minds and mental factors abandoned gradually, whereas [the defilements of] form..."
Are the tainted wholesome states and the unobscured-neutral states of mind and mental factors abandoned all at once by the power of the ninth path of immediate succession?
Answer: Because clarity (*vidyā*) and ignorance (*avidyā*) are mutually contradictory.

That is to say, the arising of the lowest-of-the-low clarity eliminates the highest-of-the-high ignorance, and so on, until the arising of the highest-of-the-high clarity eliminates the lowest-of-the-low ignorance.
The contaminated wholesome [dharmas] and the non-obscured neutral [dharmas] of the form realm are not in contradiction with either clarity or ignorance.
Regarding the statement that "this principle should be further established," the Sautrāntika master rebuts this by pointing out that the reason provided is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*). For instance,

just as life-force (*jīvitendriya*) and so forth are not abandoned through vision (*na darśana-prahātavya*) because they are not incompatible with clarity (*vidyā*) or ignorance (*avidyā*), [so too might these factors be].

If it is argued that [the four characteristics] are not abandoned by insight (*darśana-heya*) because they do not contradict clarity (*vidyā*) or ignorance (*avidyā*), this reasoning is not yet exhaustive;
therefore, it must be further established that such a principle holds. Alternatively, it may be that contaminated (*sāsrava*) karma and matter (*rūpa*) are not abandoned by insight.
Regarding the subordinate responsibility for the text,
it may apply to both locations;
in meaning, there is no contradiction in either case.
"If that is so, [the karma] is led by the power of the primary elements (mahābhūta)," says the Sarvāstivāda in rebuttal.
According to the Sautrāntika, if contaminated karma (sāsrava-karma) were abandoned through the path of vision (darśana-heya), [it would follow that it could not produce results].
That which creates it (the great elements) should also be abandoned by insight (*darśana-prahātavya*),
because both the agent and the object are produced by the power of the mind that is abandoned by insight.
There is no such fault, nor does this contradict the ultimate principle.
The Sautrāntika replies:
There is no such fault of being abandoned by insight,
just as the four great elements are not rendered wholesome or unwholesome by the influence of the mind.
Because they arise from the great elements (mahābhūta) produced by non-defiled minds,
and because their nature differs from that which can induce a defiled mind,
they are not abandoned by insight (darśana-prahātavya).
Because tainted material karma is defiled by the same [afflictions] as the projecting mind, it is abandoned through seeing (*darśana-prahātavya*).
This is an uneven interpretation;

however, there is no logical contradiction in allowing that the four great elements (*mahābhūta*), which are projected by what is abandoned through seeing, are themselves abandoned by the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*).
"The reason why it should not be admitted as such, because it would lead to contradiction," is the objection raised by the Sarvāstivādins; that is to say,
from the perspective of reasoning, it should not be admitted as such.
Because the primary elements (mahābhūta) are certainly neither abandoned by insight (darśana-prahātavya) nor abandoned at all, but are abandoned only through cultivation (bhāvanā-prahātavya);
for non-defiled phenomena do not contradict either clarity (vidyā) or ignorance (avidyā).
"Therefore, it is not abandoned by insight;
that sutra merely refers to what has been reached, so there is no contradiction"—
this is the Sarvāstivāda interpretation of the scriptural passage.
That which arises simultaneously with its cause is called "simultaneous motivation" (*sahaja-samutthāna*);

that which arises at a subsequent moment is called "subsequent motivation" (*paścāt-kṣaṇika-samutthāna*). The Sūtra states that wrong view gives rise to wrong speech and so forth; these two are [examples of] motivation.
That sutra speaks thus based solely on the antecedent motivation (*pūrvakāraṇa-samutthāna*) and not on the momentary motivation (*kṣaṇika-samutthāna*);
therefore, there is no contradiction.
As for the statement that "the five groups of consciousness function toward external objects," it is because they turn toward the external.
This explains the sixth phrase:
because the five consciousnesses are devoid of discrimination, they cannot act as the primary driver;
because they arise directed toward external objects, they can act as the secondary follower.
Regarding the phrase "because the consciousness to be abandoned by cultivation arises toward external objects," this explains the seventh point:
because the consciousness to be abandoned by cultivation possesses conceptual discrimination (*vikalpa*), it is capable of acting as a transformation (*pariṇāma*).
"Because it arises from an external door, it can act as a concomitant transformation (anuvartaka).
Because all untainted [states] reach the point of spontaneous operation"—
this explains the eighth phrase.
All untainted minds (*anāsrava-citta*) are neither primary movers (*pravartaka*) nor concomitants (*anuvartaka*),

for they operate solely within the internal door due to being in meditative concentration (*samāhita*) and thus lack the capacity to impel karma. Likewise, minds born of maturation (*vipākaja-citta*) are neither primary movers nor concomitants.
Because it operates spontaneously without relying on preparatory effort, its nature is weak and inferior;
thus, it lacks the capacity for karma. The *Nyāyānusāra* raises an objection:
"However, it is said to be untainted (*anāsrava*)."
If it were not a maturation (vipāka), there would be the faults of over-negation and over-extension;
for even the contaminated meditative mind (sāsrava-samādhi-citta) would likewise be neither [of those two].
The various ripening consciousnesses can only be non-transformative;
what reasoning could possibly prevent them from acting as the concomitant transformatives?
Furthermore, it is said:
"Because the mind born of maturation (vipākaja-citta) functions toward external objects, it can act as a concomitant.
It is also said:

One should simply state that because the mental force (*citta-vega*) produced by maturation (*vipākaja*) is weak, it cannot be a motivating cause (*hetu-samutthāna*); one should not say that it is because it proceeds spontaneously (*svarasavāhin*) without application (*prayoga*).
Otherwise, even the innate wholesome states (*upapatti-lābhika-kuśala*) would not function as causes to initiate informative action (*vijñapti-karman*).
Furthermore, it is not because [the mind] operates through application (*prayoga*) or spontaneously (*anābhoga*). The Vaibhāṣika masters of the *Abhidharmakośa* offer this defense:

"The mental states of impure meditative concentration (*sāsrava-samādhi*) are identical in nature to those that are pure (*anāsrava*); they are neither 'operating' (*pravartaka*) nor 'concomitant' (*anuvartaka*).
The mere mention of 'being in concentration' (*samāpanna*) already excludes and clarifies [these distinctions]."
Therefore, they are not explained separately.
Although the mind born of maturation (*vipākaja*) functions toward external objects,
it arises spontaneously without effort, being induced by wholesome or unwholesome karma rather than by preparatory application (*prayoga*).

Because their nature is weak and inferior, they do not undergo transformation or follow along with transformation; how could the acquired wholesome minds (*upapattilābhika-kuśala-citta*) be the same as those?
First, these [acquired wholesome minds] are not produced from karmic maturation (*vipākaja*).
The second [position] holds that its very nature is forceful;
therefore, it is not difficult [to refute].
This, however, contradicts reason.
Furthermore, it contradicts the scriptural teachings; thus, the *Abhidharmamahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 117, asks:

Answer: A powerful mind initiates bodily and vocal karma;
because the nature of a mind born of maturation (*vipākaja*) is weak and inferior, it cannot initiate them.
This is explained at length as stated there. Furthermore, another interpretation holds that although the mind of maturation functions toward external objects, [it does not initiate karma].
Because its nature is weak and inferior, it does not transform or follow along.
Although the mind in a contaminated meditative concentration (*sāsrava-samādhi*) operates internally,

One is able to remain constantly in meditative concentration throughout the four modes of deportment;

however, it is not that the three types of indeterminate minds do not exist during the state of non-concentration. As for the mind of craftsmanship (*śailpasthānika-citta*), the Buddha does not frequently give rise to it, and therefore it is omitted from discussion.
It is not that they do not arise at all;
for this reason, in the *Vibhāṣā*’s explanation of the deportment and artisanal consciousnesses,

As previously cited in full, this treatise and others do not mention the Buddha among the arts and crafts (*śilpa*), as they are omitted for brevity. Furthermore, the explanation of the three types of neutral states (*avyākṛta*) is based on their active manifestation (*samudācāra*).

Although the Buddha of Artistic Skill (śilpa-buddha) possesses [these qualities], they are not mentioned because they do not manifest in his conduct. Furthermore, it is explained that the Buddha of Artistic Skill does not even possess them, because for the most part they constitute wrong livelihood (*mithyājīva*) and so forth.
Therefore, in this treatise and in the accomplishment of right understanding regarding the indeterminate,
it is stated that deportment is "just like that of the Buddha, the Bhikṣu Aśvajit, and others who are well-practiced."
Regarding craftsmanship, it is merely said to be like that of Viśvakarman and other well-trained practitioners;
it does not mention the Buddha. If this is so, does this not contradict the statement in the *Abhidharmamahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*?
The commentary explains that the meanings of the various treatises differ.
Although there are three interpretations, the first interpretation is taken as correct;
for it is not only supported by textual evidence, but also accords with reason.

Regarding the statement that "all manifest actions (vijñapti-karma) persist as long as their corresponding motivating factors (anuvartaka) persist," this is the question for the subsequent analysis through dialogue. This, then, is the question.
Regarding the phrase "If that were so, what fault would there be?": this is a rhetorical question intended to challenge the opponent's position.
It means: "If it were as you describe, then one would have to exert great effort [to achieve the result]."
This correctly articulates the intent of the inquiry,
posing two critical challenges: if,
for instance, the manifestation of the mind were to constitute virtue and so forth.

In that case, there would have to be obscured-unspecified (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*) manifest karma within the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), because the two views—the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*)—are capable of acting as its instigators (*pravartaka*).

If you were to defend [your position] by saying that the view of a self-identity and the view of extremes in the desire realm are of an unspecified nature (*avyākṛta*) and therefore cannot act as instigators; [we reply: ...
One should distinguish that the two views—the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*)—cannot act as the turning point;
other false views (*mithyādṛṣṭi*), etc., can act as the turning point.
It is not the case that all minds abandoned through the vision of the truths (*darśana-prahātavya*) are capable of acting as the turning point.
If, as you claim, the manifest action (*vijñapti*) acquires the nature of being wholesome and so forth by conforming to the mind that initiates it,
then the manifest action of the Prātimokṣa obtained simultaneously with an unwholesome or neutral mind should not be wholesome in nature. Thus,
one faces a dilemma whether one advances or retreats.
One should apply diligent effort to seek an alternative interpretation.
As for the statement that it is "like the turning of the mind being separated by an interval," this is the Master's correct explanation.
It should be said that it is like the manifestation of a mind that has turned [toward virtue], whereby it becomes virtuous in nature and so forth;
however, it is not like the distant causal motivation (*dūre-samutthāna*) of a mind that has been abandoned by insight (*darśana-heya*). Why is this?
Because it is separated by the immediate cause and motivation (*samanantara-hetu* and *samutthāna*) of the mind that undergoes transformation through cultivation and abandonment,
it is distant from the manifest action (*vijñapti*) when viewed from afar, yet proximate to the manifest action when viewed from near.
Manifest action (*vijñapti*) becomes wholesome and so forth by following a mind that operates in the immediate vicinity;
it does not become wholesome and so forth by following a mind that operates at a distance.
If manifest action were not produced through the arrival [of the motivating mind], it would be neutral (*avyākṛta*).
The Master of the Treatise reveals the error in the previous Vaibhāṣika’s interpretation of the sūtra:

if it were the case that the manifestation [of karma] as wholesome and so forth is not established by the power of the concomitant mind, then your previous attempt to explain the sūtra on the initiation of action by wrong view would be untenable; you could no longer claim that the sūtra refers only to the preceding motivating cause (*pūrva-samutthāna*) and not to the momentary cause (*kṣaṇa-samutthāna*).
If one were to establish this interpretation,
first, it would result in confusion with the intermediate state (*antarābhava*);
second, it would effectively amount to conceding [the existence of] moments (*kṣaṇa*).
If one were to rely solely on the aforementioned "causal motivation" (*hetu-samutthāna*) as the definition of the intermediate state (*antarābhava*), there would be an overlap with other categories.
For motivation is of two kinds: first, causal motivation; [and second, immediate motivation].
Second, simultaneous origination (*sahabhū-samutthāna*).
With respect to subsequent moments of origination, the causal origination (*hetu-samutthāna*) is called "prior" because it precedes them; thus, it is termed "prior causal origination."
The motivating cause (samutthāna-hetu) is further divided into two types:
first, the proximate motivating cause;
second, the remote motivating cause.
The proximate motivating cause (*samanantara-samutthāna*) is capable of manifesting [the action], whereas the remote motivating cause (*dūre-samutthāna*) is not capable of manifesting it.
Since it has already been stated that the prior motivating cause is not capable of manifesting it.
Both proximate and remote causes are designated as "prior causes.
Within this designation, the exclusion of other factors is not exhaustive; otherwise, it would redundantly overlap with the "proximate cause" (*samutthāna-hetu*).
This is not based on a single moment (*kṣaṇa*), for if it were, one would effectively be conceding that a momentary manifest action (*vijñapti*) constitutes virtue and so forth.

If you do not accept that the manifest [action] (vijñapti) is established as virtuous and so forth based on its momentary origination (samutthāna), why do you say it is not based on the moment? If it were based on the moment, would you not also allow it to be called "momentary"?
If one says that this also admits the fault of contradicting one's own tenets (*siddhānta-virodha*),
then although the preceding text of this treatise does not explicitly state that it is not based on moments (*kṣaṇa*),
it should be added according to the underlying meaning within the subsequent objections. Alternatively, it may be so.
Although this was not stated in the preceding text,
since other treatises that accord with the sūtras state that they are all present,
the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 117, says:
Answer: This statement was made based on the *hetu-samutthāna* (causal origination) and not the *kṣaṇa-samutthāna* (momentary origination).
Therefore, there is no fault. [End of] the treatise. Consequently, in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), there is definitely no obscured-unspecified (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*) manifest karma (*vijñapti-karman*).
This is established as a formal conclusion based on the underlying principle, as there is no explicit textual authority for it previously;

perhaps it may be found in another passage. Furthermore, another interpretation states: if a manifest action (*vijñapti*) were not rendered wholesome or otherwise by the power of the concomitant mental force (*anuvartaka-citta*), [it would follow that it could never be so].
However, since it is by means of the mind acting as the instigator (*pravartaka*) that there can be obscured-unspecified (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*) manifest action (*vijñapti-karman*) within the desire realm—
and because bodily [action] and the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*) are capable of acting as such instigators—
it should not be said that the aforementioned sūtra refers only to the antecedent motivation (*pūrva-samutthāna*) and not to the momentary motivation (*kṣaṇika-samutthāna*).
One should not say, therefore, that there is definitely no obscured-unspecified (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*) manifest karma within the desire realm;
rather, one should simply state that it extends to unspecified manifest karma.
The Master, having demonstrated that the previous argument was applicable, now instructs him to correctly interpret the scriptural passage.
One should simply say that the sutra speaks only with reference to other proximate causes—the mind being separated by them—as the remote cause and motivation (*dūre-samutthāna*).
Thus, the mind abandoned through seeing (*darśana-heya*) is the remote cause and motivation.
Because it is separated from the proximate cause for cultivation through abandonment by other means,
although the mind abandoned by seeing can act as a precursor,
there is absolutely no obscured-unspecified (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*) manifest karma in the desire realm.
Change "but" (但) to "only" (唯), and change "prior" (前) to "intervened by other mental factors" (餘心所間);
thus there will be no impediment. Question: The manifestation of the three natures is determined based on the evolving consciousness (轉心).

Question: From what is the nature of the non-informative action that follows the mind (*anuvartaka*) determined? The explanation says: its wholesome nature is determined by the following mind (*anuvartaka-citta*).
Therefore, the *Nyāyānusāra* (Treatise on Correct Reasoning), volume thirty-six,

The quality of wholesomeness is established by the power of the concomitant [mental factors], because they arise as necessarily belonging to this mind. Completed at Seoyon (West Hall). Gwanggyeong.

The answer: It can obstruct;
that is, it can obstruct the continuity of unwholesome conduct. It can extinguish.

it is explained that the prātimokṣa vows can obstruct the continuity of unwholesome precepts,

Therefore, it is called "restraint" (*saṃvara*). "Law" (*vinaya*) refers to legal codes; "rite" (*īryā*) refers to ritual procedures. It is not mentioned here because its manifestation is not universal.

Question: Regarding the introductory verse, it says, "up to 'each is individually non-contradictory'. Answer:
The first phrase distinguishes the name;
the following three phrases distinguish the essence.
The treatise says: "Regarding the prātimokṣa restraint..."
Explanation of the first phrase: *Bhikṣu* is translated into Chinese as "alms-seeker" (*qǐshì*).
The older transcription *bǐqiū* is an error. *Bhikṣuṇī*:
*Bhikṣu* is explained as above.
*Ni* is a feminine term; in Sanskrit it is called *śikṣamāṇā*, which in the language of Tang means "one in formal training.
"Formal" refers to one who is formally training in the six rules.
The six precepts are:

abstaining from sexual misconduct, abstaining from stealing, abstaining from killing, abstaining from false speech, abstaining from drinking intoxicants, and abstaining from eating at improper times—Sanskrit: *śīlavrataparāmarśa* (though here referring to the specific observance of *śīla*, moral discipline).
In the language of Tang, it is called *qínsè* (勤策),
meaning that one exerts diligent effort (*śramaṇera*) for the sake of becoming a *bhikṣu*.
The character "luò" (洛) is a masculine sound.
The old term "śrāmaṇera" is a corruption. In Sanskrit it is *śrāmaṇerikā*; in the language of Tang (Chinese), it means "female diligent-courager.
Its explanation of the name is as previously stated.
The term *li* (理) is a feminine sound;
it is an erroneous transcription of the old term *shami-ni*. In Sanskrit, it is called *upāsaka*;
in the language of Tang, it means "lay follower."
"Suo" (索) is a masculine pronunciation;
it is an erroneous transcription of "upāsaka.
Regarding the term "near-attendant" (jìnshì), the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 123, states: [text follows].
Question: For what reason is one called an *upāsaka*?
Answer: Because of drawing near to and practicing all wholesome dharmas.
That is to say, because his body and mind are habituated to wholesome dharmas, he is called an *upāsaka*.
Other masters say it is because of associating with and serving virtuous persons (*satpuruṣa*).
Others say it is because of associating with and serving the qualities of the Buddhas (*buddhadharma*).
The details are as explained in that [commentary]. In Sanskrit it is called *upāsikā*;
in the language of Tang, it means "female lay follower" (*jìnshì nǚ*).
The explanation of its name is as before.
This refers to the female voice.
The old [translation] "upāsikā" is a corruption; in Sanskrit it is "upavāsā," which in the language of Tang means "near-dwelling."
Regarding the term "near-dweller" (*upavāsaka*):
the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 124,
states that one dwells near an Arhat.
Because one receives this discipline and trains accordingly, some say it is called "near-abiding" (*upavāsa*) because it abides near the lifelong precepts;
others say it is called "near-abiding" because the precept abides for a limited time. Among these eight [precepts], the first five are the precepts of the renunciants.
The latter three are precepts for laypeople;
the former seven are lifelong precepts;
the latter one is a precept for a single day and night.

Although these eight are distinct, they are collectively termed the "first prātimokṣa restraint. Question: Why are these eight established based on the prātimokṣa restraint, rather than being established based on the dhyāna or the untainted (anāsrava) restraints? Answer: It is explained as follows:
Because the prātimokṣa restraint is acquired gradually,
it is established progressively;
based upon that, eight distinct types can be established.

The seven factors of dhyāna and the untainted [factors] are acquired instantaneously; one cannot establish eight distinct categories based upon them. Furthermore, it is explained that the Prātimokṣa vows belong exclusively to the eight assemblies among humans in the desire realm.
Furthermore, it occurs only among humans in the desire realm;
therefore, it is established based on them.
Meditative absorption (*dhyāna*) and the untainted (*anāsrava*) [attainments], however, can also arise among the celestial realms of the higher worlds.
Therefore, the eight distinctions are not established based upon them.
Although there are eight names, they do not differ from the laywoman's (upāsikā) vow;
this explains the second phrase.
Although there are eight names based on differences in the individuals [who receive them], in terms of their actual substance, there are only four types:
there is no separate bhikṣuṇī discipline apart from the bhikṣu discipline; and there is no separate discipline for the śikṣamāṇā or the six rules of training apart from the śrāmaṇera discipline.
Regarding the ten precepts of the śikṣamāṇā discipline:
the śikṣamāṇā first receives the ten precepts and subsequently receives the six dharmas.
Although she further acquires the six dharmas, these are identical to the six precepts contained within the ten precepts.
Therefore, the ten precepts of a śrāmaṇerī and the six rules of a śikṣamāṇā are not different from the ten dharmas of a śrāmaṇera;
furthermore, it is explained that when one becomes a śikṣamāṇā, one does not acquire six additional dharmas distinct from those already held.
However, the emphasis is on the practice of receiving the instructions.
Since these six dharmas are based on maintaining what was previously received, they are identical to the six [precepts] within the ten precepts of the *śikṣamāṇā* and the *śrāmaṇerī*.

Thus, it is said that the ten precepts of the *śikṣamāṇā* and the *śrāmaṇerī* do not differ from the ten precepts of the *śrāmaṇera*. The eight precepts of the *upavāsa* last for only one day and night.
Because time was short, and because there was no distinction between male and female, they were treated as a single group.
How is this known? The following passage explains the third phrase.
This is the question.
The phrase "because the transformation of form reaches that which is not different from the three substances" provides the formal answer by citing the verse.
Just as when the faculties are transformed, there is neither the relinquishing nor the acquisition of the precepts;
rather, only the designation changes. This refers to the state of the transformation of the faculties.
If a bhikṣu undergoes a change of gender to become female,
his original bhikṣu vows are termed bhikṣuṇī vows;
if a bhikṣuṇī undergoes a change of gender to become male, [her vows are likewise transformed].

This causes the original *bhikṣuṇī* vows to be designated as *bhikṣu* vows. Question: What is the difference in the number of precepts between a *bhikṣu* and a *bhikṣuṇī*, and how can it be said that their names differ while their substance remains the same when there is a transformation of gender (*indriya-parāvṛtti*)? Explanation: It is because male and female are distinct.
There is a distinction between what is permitted and what is prohibited,
as they differ according to circumstances;
alternatively, it is said that there are two hundred and fifty rules.
Some say there are five hundred precepts;

however, when discussing the essential nature (*śīla-ātmaka*) of the seven branches, they are all equal. Furthermore, another interpretation holds that based on the original seven branches, the precepts for the two assemblies (*saṃgha*) are equal;
yet, if one discusses the number of prohibitory precepts (*pratikṣepa-śīla*), there are differences.
Although it is denied that there is any difference [in the recipient],
at the time one first receives the precepts, both assemblies obtain them. Why is this so?
When both bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs make the vow that all evils shall be severed,
by the power of this aspiration they mutually obtain the prohibitions against transgression.
Although they both mutually obtain them, it is because their respective conditions differ.
The maintenance and violation [of precepts] differ,

and the offenses established by prohibition (pratikṣepaṇa-śikṣāpada) are distinct. Furthermore, it is explained that there are differences in the quantity of the essential nature (svabhāva) of these prohibited precepts before one has undergone a change of gender (indriya-parāvṛtti).
If one receives a precept of this kind,
one immediately obtains that very kind of precept;
at the stage of the transformation of the faculties (*indriya-parāvṛtti*), one does not separately obtain or lose it within that category.
Although there is no formal prohibition regarding the vows,
one still incurs that offense due to violating the instructions. If a śrāmaṇera undergoes a change of gender to become female,
his original śrāmaṇera discipline is designated as the śrāmaṇerī discipline.
Because she has not yet acquired the six dharmas,
or because she has not yet formally undertaken the training in the six dharmas,

she is not called a *śikṣamāṇā*. However, if a *śrāmaṇerī* or a *śikṣamāṇā* undergoes a transformation of their sexual organs (*indriya-parivṛtti*) and becomes male, [they are no longer so designated].
The original śrāmaṇerī discipline and the śikṣamāṇā discipline are designated as the śrāmaṇera discipline,
because those ten precepts, together with the six rules, are identical to the ten types of śrāmaṇera precepts. This applies if an upāsaka changes gender and becomes a woman.

It causes the original upāsaka restraint to be called the upāsikā restraint; if an upāsikā undergoes a change of gender to become male, it causes the original upāsikā restraint to be called the upāsaka restraint. [This applies to] the one-day-and-night fast (upavāsa).

Although there is a transformation of the faculties (*indriya-parāvṛtti*), because male and female are not established as two distinct categories, they are not mentioned separately; nor is there any cause or condition for abandoning the previously obtained discipline (*saṃvara*) at the stage of such transformation.
Because the four causes and conditions for relinquishing [the precepts] are absent,
there is no cause and condition for obtaining a previously unobtained discipline at the stage of changing one's faculties;
this is because the causes and conditions for receiving the precepts are absent.
The four types of restraint—those of the bhikṣuṇī, śrāmaṇerī, śikṣamāṇā, and upāsikā—are not distinct from the three entities of the bhikṣu, śrāmaṇera, and upāsaka.
"If one attains the full ordination (*upasampadā*) directly from the status of a lay follower (*upāsaka*)," this section below explains the fourth phrase.
Question: If one receives the *śrāmaṇera* precepts from a lay follower, and then receives the *bhikṣu* precepts from a *śrāmaṇera*, [how does this occur]?
These three types of restraint are synonyms for the morality of abstinence (*virati-śīla*), because they consist in the increase of abstinence and the increase of the means for abstinence,
as they involve the abstaining from evil.
The skillful means for seeking the precepts are so called because they involve seeking the subsequent precepts;
they differ from the former by being further augmented and perfected.
Distinct names are established for each stage:
those who increase the five precepts by five to become ten precepts are called *śrāmaṇeras*;
those who increase the ten precepts by two hundred and forty to become two hundred and fifty are called *bhikṣus*.
Just as adding one to a single unit makes it "two," adding five to five makes ten,
and adding ten to ten makes twenty— is the substance of each of the three precepts produced instantaneously, complete and distinct from one another?
Regarding the phrase "the three types of restraint arise according to what is appropriate," the answer explains the verse individually:
the three types of restraint arise separately and instantaneously, each according to its own greater or lesser extent.
This can be understood through reflection. The eight precepts (*aṣṭāṅga-śīla*) should also be addressed through questions and answers within this context;
however, they are omitted here for brevity due to the constraints of time.
If that is so, since they are of the same category when compared with one another, what is their distinction?

Answer: They differ when compared to one another due to the distinction between internal causes and external conditions.

Question: Regarding the statement, "Because one seeks to receive [the precepts] according to each [occasion], the three are distinct," this is an explanation:

the recipient of the precepts is not a single person, which is termed "according to each" (yiruyi); the substance of the precepts is not a single entity, which is termed "thus and thus" (yisayi yisayi).
Just as one seeks to receive various types of training rules (śikṣāpada) according to what is appropriate— where "training rules" refers to ethical discipline—
in that same way, according to what is appropriate,
one is able to abstain from various kinds of high and wide beds and seats.
When one abstains from intoxicants such as various liquors— the basis for arrogance and negligence— at that very moment,
one abandons the numerous conditions for killing, stealing, and so forth, thereby giving rise to this precept.
This is because all forms of abstinence arise based on internal causes and external conditions.

Regarding the distinctions among causes and conditions for the separate observance [of precepts]: as for the term "distinction of causes," it refers to the distinction in the mind seeking the precepts— namely,
seeking the five precepts [or others].
Some seek the ten precepts, while others seek the full precepts;
thus it is called "distinction by cause. As for "distinction by condition":
This refers to the differences in the conditions for receiving the precepts,
namely the upādhyāya, ācārya, and others; for instance,
when receiving the five precepts, one does so in the presence of a single person.
If one receives the ten precepts before two people,
or if one receives the full ordination (*upasampadā*) before ten people and so forth,
it is therefore called "distinction by condition" (*pratyaya-bheda*).
Because these causes and conditions are distinct, there is separation and difference. To raise an objection by means of reasoning:
if this [distinction] did not exist, then the three [vows], such as non-killing and so forth, would gradually increase and become complete [without distinction].
At the time one relinquishes the bhikṣu vows,
