one would then have to relinquish all three vows— the upāsaka, śrāmaṇera, and bhikṣu—
since the first two, the upāsaka and śrāmaṇera, are subsumed within the latter, the bhikṣu. Since this is not permitted, the three are distinct.
Due to these three distinctions, one who has relinquished the bhikṣu precepts is still called a śrāmaṇera;
furthermore, one who has relinquished the śrāmaṇera precepts is still called an upāsaka.
However, when these three types [of practitioners] reach a point where they are no longer upāsakas and so forth—
This explains their lack of contradiction.
However, the three [vows], such as non-killing and so forth, are mutually non-contradictory within a single mind;
they arise simultaneously in one and the same moment.
One does not abandon the previous lay devotee (upāsaka) and novice (śrāmaṇera) vows by undertaking the subsequent monk (bhikṣu) vow;
for there is no cause for such abandonment.
Otherwise, one would cease to be a novice upon abandoning the bhikṣu precepts.
One does not cease to be a lay follower (*upāsaka*) merely by relinquishing the *śrāmaṇera* precepts, because even after their relinquishment, one may still be designated by that name.
Therefore, it is known that all three types of precepts are present within a single body; although within one body one may possess only two of these precepts.
Or, one may possess all three precepts;

because the latter precept is superior, it is designated by its superior name. Question: Is it possible to receive the latter precept without having received the preceding ones? Answer: As stated in the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 124: [text follows].
Question: If one first does not receive the lay practitioner's (upāsaka) discipline and then receives the novice (śrāmaṇera) discipline, does one obtain the novice discipline?
Some say that one does not.
Because the lay practitioner's discipline serves as the gateway,
the basis, and the preliminary application for this discipline.
Some say it is not fixed;
that is, if one does not clearly understand that one has previously received the lay practitioner's (upāsaka) vows before subsequently obtaining the novice (śrāmaṇera) vows.
Because he places his trust in the preceptor,
when he receives this discipline, the other obtains that discipline;
[otherwise], the preceptor incurs an offense.

If it were the correct procedure for one to first receive the lay devotee (upāsaka) vows and subsequently receive the novice (śrāmaṇera) vows, yet out of pride they are unwilling to undertake and train in the lay devotee vows; [then this would be a fault].
He spoke these words:
"What is the use of receiving these inferior precepts of a lay follower?
Because his mind was entangled in pride, although he received them, he did not truly obtain them.
Just as it is said that one may receive the śrāmaṇera vows without having received the upāsaka vows,
so too one may receive the bhikṣu vows without having received the śrāmaṇera vows.

The detailed explanation is likewise. Question: If one were to receive the preceding vows from among the subsequent ones, would one obtain the precepts? Answer: As stated in the *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra* (Treatise on Following Right Reasoning), fascicle 36:
"If there is a śrāmaṇera who receives the upāsaka discipline..."
Suppose there is a bhikṣu who receives the first two types of precepts; does he receive them as they are taken?
Some say that this need not be questioned:
if they already exist beforehand, there is no principle by which they could be received again.
Because it has already been obtained previously.
If it did not exist previously, one would not be a *śrāmaṇera*, nor a *bhikṣu*;
for there is no principle by which one who has not previously received the lay devotee (*upāsaka*) vows could necessarily receive and obtain the *śrāmaṇera* precepts.
If one has not previously received the śrāmaṇera vows, there is likewise no principle for receiving the bhikṣu precepts;
thus, it would be impossible to establish those two names.
By investigating in this manner:
It should not be accepted [that one can receive it].
Other masters say that there is a principle whereby even one who has not received a preceding discipline (*saṃvara*) is nonetheless able to receive and obtain a subsequent precept.
Therefore, those who uphold the Vinaya recite this: "Even though one did not previously receive the *śrāmaṇera* precepts..."
Nowadays, even one who merely receives the full ordination (upasaṃpadā-śīla) is said to have properly received the full ordination.
By virtue of this, it is possible for a śrāmaṇera to receive the lay follower’s (upāsaka) discipline.
It is possible for a bhikṣu to receive the precepts of a śrāmaṇera or an upāsaka;
however, would it not be improper for a śrāmaṇera to declare of himself, "I wish only to be known as an upāsaka"?
It is the same for a bhikṣu:
he should not claim for himself, "May you know me as one of the former two.
There is no principle for attaining the precepts of an upāsaka or śrāmaṇera apart from such self-proclaimed designations.
This objection is unreasonable, for both [identities] can be designated.
That is to say, one may declare: "I am a śrāmaṇera and also an upāsaka; I pray that you bear witness to this."
The bhikṣu should also speak accordingly.
However, there is no fault in designating those two names based on their predominant precepts.
If that is so, then regarding the śrāmaṇeras, bhikṣus, and so forth—
One should likewise be able to receive the upavāsa precepts;
what fault would there be in granting this as one does for the upāsaka?
However, it is because they are inferior and lack the aspiration to receive them.
Regarding the lay devotee (upāsaka), the one-day precept holder (upavāsastha), up to the fully ordained monk (bhikṣu) discipline:
this constitutes the second establishment of the four disciplines,
wherein the application of ointments and the wearing of garlands constitute one [category].
Watching the dance and listening to the song constitute one [offense]. Furthermore, it is explained that one must not dance,
must not sing, must not watch,
and must not listen.

Therefore, among the ten, two are distinguished as separate categories. Question: Why are eight combined while ten are distinguished? Explanation: Because for laypeople, their transgressions are light, these two are combined into one.
Because the censure directed at the monastic community was particularly severe, what was originally one [precept] was expanded into two.
Furthermore, the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* states:
"That is to say, abstaining from the application of ointments, perfumes, and garlands."
Abstaining from song, dance, performers,
and musicians is established as a single factor because it functions similarly in relation to places of adornment.
Furthermore, the *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra*, fascicle 36, states:
In order to encourage lay sentient beings who are timid and fearful of numerous precepts, and to demonstrate that they are easy to undertake, the eight precepts combine two items into one. Question:

Why is the acceptance and possession of gold and other such things not established within the *upavāsa* (near-dwelling) precepts, but rather within the ten precepts? Answer: It is because laypeople are attached to treasures such as gold and silver, and are unable to remain far removed from them.
Therefore, this precept is not prescribed for the *upavāsa* (near-dwelling) discipline.

Since those who have undertaken the *śrāmaṇera* (novice) vows and those who have gone forth should not be attached to treasures such as gold and silver, which would obstruct and cause the abandonment of the cultivation of the path,
it is established separately as one [precept] among the ten.
If one undertakes the abstention from all bodily and verbal misdeeds that ought to be avoided, this constitutes the fourth precept.
The remainder of the text may be understood accordingly.
As for why the Pratimokṣa restraint is called *śīla*: [it is because it cools the heat of non-virtue].
This is the third section, clarifying the specific alternative names.
It is called *śīla* because it can level out all perilous and evil unwholesome karmas;
this is its first name.

Observing the precepts can cause the body and mind to be cool and refreshing because it brings peace and happiness; violating the precepts can cause the body and mind to suffer from feverish distress because it leads to regret. This may be understood by citing the verse.
Because it is praised by the wise, it is called "wonderful conduct.
This is the second [point].
Furthermore, the *Nyāya* states:
Alternatively, because one practices this and thereby obtains a desirable fruit,
and because it constitutes the very essence of what is performed, it is called "action" (*karma*);
this is the third [explanation].
Since the very essence of the precept is what is performed, it is called "action" (karman). [Objection:
Is it not the case that the unmanifest (avijñapti) reaches the state of being the essence of what is performed? [Question: Why is this so?
It is correct that the manifest [action] is called "karma.
But is it not the case that the unmanifest is also called "non-doing" (akriyā) in the sūtras?
How is it that what is now described as the "substantial entity of the performed" (kṛtya-svabhāva) receives the name "performed" (kṛtya) by those who possess a sense of shame? Answer:
The Sūtra says "non-action" (*akaraṇa*):

those who possess a sense of shame (*hrī*) and dread of blame (*apatrāpya*) receive the power of non-informative matter (*avijñapti*), and because they do not commit various evils, it is called "non-action. The Śāstra says "action" (*karaṇa*).
Because it is produced by bodily and vocal intimation as well as by mental volition (*cetanā*),
it receives the name "that which is performed" (*kṛta*).
Others explain that there is no fault in applying the term "performed" even to that which has not yet been completed.
To explain the different interpretations:
the unmanifest (avijñapti) is named after its result, as it is the cause for the subsequent category of "result of what has been done" (kṛta-phala);
the manifest (vijñapti) is named after its cause, as it is the result for the preceding category of "cause consisting of volition and action" (cetanā-karma-hetu).
It is called "without fault.
Because it can restrain body and speech, it is termed "discipline" (saṃvara);
this is the fourth [type].
Because it is able to guard body and speech so that they do not commit transgressions, it is called "restraint" (*saṃvara*).
One should understand that the terms "preparation" (*prayoga*) and "consequent action" (*pṛṣṭha*) apply accordingly.
This explains the fifth and sixth names.
The following two lines are explained:
In this way, one should understand that the prātimokṣa vows bear the same name throughout both the initial moment and all subsequent moments without distinction;
however, it is only during the first instant that they consist of both informative (*vijñapti*) and non-informative (*avijñapti*) action.
It receives the name of the fifth *prātimokṣa* and the name of the sixth course of action (*karmapatha*). Why is this so?
This refers to the initial moment of the manifest and unmanifest [karma] at the time of receiving the precepts.

Because one individually abandons various evils such as the karma of killing through the specific precepts against killing and so forth, it is designated by the name "Prātimokṣa" (Individual Liberation) based on the meaning of individual abandonment.

At the very moment of the initial thought, all virtuous deeds performed reach their completion; based on the causal motivation (*samutthāna*) and the full extent of the intended meaning, the term "path of action" (*karmapatha*) is established. That volition (*cetanā*) which, as the causal motivation, performs the act is called "action" (*karman*).

Because the initial manifest and unmanifest [actions] are the paths traversed by volition (*cetanā*), they are called "paths of action" (*karmapatha*). Therefore, at the first moment, the initial distinct abandonment of evil is called "distinct liberation" (*prātimokṣa*);
it is the initial distinct restraint and prevention.
It is also called the prātimokṣa restraint; it thoroughly clarifies the limits of its meaning.
It may also be termed the fundamental path of action (*mūlakarmapatha*), from the second moment until it is relinquished.

It is not that the initial separate abandonment of evil is not called "individual liberation" (*prātimokṣa*); rather, because it is able to obstruct and prevent [evil], it is named "restraint" (*saṃvara*).
Thus, it is called the "individual liberation restraint" (*prātimokṣa-saṃvara*) because it is the restraint of individual liberation, and not because it expresses [the intention] through thought.

These are not called courses of action (*karmapatha*); they are termed "subsequent" (*pṛṣṭha*) because they occur after the fundamental act. Regarding the question of who accomplishes which restraint (*saṃvara*), the following section secondly provides a general explanation of accomplishment.
Among these, first, the three types of vows are established in general;
second, their possession is clarified according to the time periods. Regarding the establishment of the three types of vows in general:
First, the explicit explanation of the general accomplishment;
second, the explanation of the discipline of abandonment;
third, the correlation with the two disciplines of the sūtras. This is the first: the explicit explanation of the general accomplishment.
The preceding question is raised by the verse.
The verse says: "Up to the last two, which follow the mind.
This is the answer.
The first phrase clarifies the accomplishment of the prātimokṣa;
the next two phrases clarify the accomplishment of the śīla of meditative concentration and the path;
the final phrase reveals their distinctions.
The Commentary states: "From 'up to' and 'even including the upavāsa'":
this explains the first phrase, clarifying that the eight classes of practitioners constitute the prātimokṣa.
[It asks: "Do non-Buddhists not possess any received precepts?"
Question:
Although they exist, they are not called "reliance" because they involve attachment to existence. Answer:
Although non-Buddhists may observe precepts such as the vow of non-killing,
these are merely termed "precepts of the middle way" and are not called "prātimokṣa precepts."
Because that which is received lacks the capacity for the permanent separation and liberation from all unwholesome dharmas,
and because it relies upon and is attached to the matured fruit (*vipāka-phala*) of the three realms of existence,
it is therefore not called the *prātimokṣa* vow.
Regarding the phrase "those born of dhyāna should also be understood in this way," this explains the second and third lines of the verse: those who have attained dhyāna accomplish dhyāna;
it clarifies that the restraint of dhyāna is what is referred to in the verse by the term "born of dhyāna."
That is to say, this restraint arises from meditative absorption (*dhyāna*);
it is explained in terms of its cause of arising, or it is understood in terms of its basis,
namely meditative absorption.

Therefore, it is called the restraint born of meditative concentration (*dhyāna-ja-saṃvara*). One who attains meditative concentration necessarily accomplishes this restraint of meditative concentration.
The preparatory stages (*sāmantaka*) of all meditative concentrations are also termed "meditative concentration."

Just as fields of rice and so forth located near a village or town receive the name "village" or "town," the principle regarding these preparatory stages (*sāmantaka*) should be understood in the same way.
As for the arising of the restraint of the path, it extends to those who are both learners (*śaikṣa*) and non-learners (*aśaikṣa*).

Commentary on the Verse Two. Regarding the third phrase, "attaining the noble ones, accomplishing the path, and giving rise to the untainted restraint (*anāsrava-saṃvara*"): "path" refers to the untainted noble path (*anāsrava-āryamārga*).
Because it is capable of producing restraint, it is called "restraint born of the path."
Regarding the previous analysis up to the second [point], what is it?
This explains the fourth phrase,
restating the preceding question to introduce the topic.
Regarding the statement "because those born of dhyāna and so forth also constantly revolve," the answer is:
the two types born of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and the path (*mārga*) are concomitants of the mind (*cittānuvartin*), whereas the prātimokṣa is not.
Why is this? Because this prātimokṣa continues to function constantly even during states of mind that are unwholesome or neutral, as well as during states of non-consciousness;
therefore, it is not called "precept that follows the mind."
If this prātimokṣa restraint were called "conforming to the mind," it could be said to conform when a wholesome mind arises; however,
when an unwholesome or neutral mind arises, [it would not].
Furthermore, because it must be abandoned even in the state of mindlessness (*acittaka*),
the term "discipline of abandonment" (*prahāṇasaṃvara*) refers to the dhyāna and untainted (*anāsrava*) states;
this is the second instance where the discipline of abandonment is explicitly clarified.
Since it is explained within the section on "Accomplishment" (*niṣpatti*), it is also categorized as belonging to the "Gate of Accomplishment.
The remaining passages may be understood accordingly. "Abandonment" refers to the antidote of abandonment (*prahāṇa-pratipakṣa*).
Thus, the *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 119, states:
Question: Why is this alone called the restraint of abandonment (*prahāṇasaṃvara*)?
Answer: Because it serves as the antidote that abandons both the breaking of precepts and the afflictions that give rise to the breaking of precepts.
Specifically, this refers to the two types of concomitant morality (*anuvartaka-śīla*) within the first eight paths of immediate succession (*ānantarya-mārga*).
It serves exclusively as the antidote for the abandonment of both the breaking of precepts and the afflictions that give rise to such breaking.

Within the ninth path of immediate succession (*ānantarya-mārga*), the two types of concomitant morality (*anuvartaka-śīla*) serve as the antidotes for the abandonment of both the breaking of precepts and the afflictions that give rise to them. Based on these passages from the treatise, it follows that only the concomitant morality within the nine paths of immediate succession of the *anāgamya* (preparatory) concentration [functions in this manner].
The desire realm, the unwholesome precepts, and the afflictions that give rise to them serve as the antidotes for abandonment;
although the first dhyāna and the other four do not serve as antidotes for abandonment regarding transgressions of the precepts and the like,
they possess the antidote of revulsion and destruction, and therefore there exists the "concomitant precept" (anuvartaka-śīla).

In the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu), because both abandonment (*prahāṇa*) and revulsion (*vidūṣaṇā*) are absent with respect to the breaking of precepts and so forth, there is no "concomitant morality" (*anuvartaka-śīla*).

Although in the form realm (rūpadhātu), the path belonging to the category of subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna-pakṣa-mārga*) lacks abandonment and revulsion as two types of antidotes with respect to the breaking of precepts and so forth [it still possesses them].

Because there are two kinds of remedies—possession (*dhāraṇa*) and distancing (*dūra*)—there is the "conforming precept" (*anuvartaka-śīla*). Question: In relation to the desire realm, the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) likewise possesses these two kinds of remedies, namely possession and distancing, with respect to such things as the breaking of the precepts.

"There should be concomitant morality. The commentary explains: although there is the maintenance [of morality], because it is remote from aversion toward form (*rūpa*), it is called the Formless Realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).
Therefore, there is no concomitant morality. In summary:
There are five remedies:
first, equanimity;
second, abandonment.
Third, maintaining;
fourth, distancing;
fifth, aversion.
In the case of those who aspire to break the precepts and so forth, the five [factors] have not yet been attained.
In the first dhyāna and the other four, there is no equanimity; there is abandonment, maintenance, distancing, and aversion.
In the formless attainments, there is no equanimity, abandonment, or aversion; there is maintenance and distancing.
These five antidotes are explained according to the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 17;
they are explained in detail therein.
Consequently, some may even attain the untainted restraint (*anāsrava-saṃvara*).
The fourfold permutation (*catuṣkoṭi*) regarding the relationship between the dhyāna restraint (*dhyāna-saṃvara*) and the restraint of abandonment (*prahāṇa-saṃvara*) should be understood.
Likewise, it should be known that there may be cases where [the former] extends [to the latter], as is appropriate.

The fourfold permutation of the untainted restraint (*anāsrava-saṃvara*) in relation to the restraint of abandonment follows the same principle as before. Regarding the first permutation: it excludes the untainted restraint of the nine paths of immediate succession (*ānantarya-mārga*) of the threshold concentration (*anāgamya-dhyāna*).

Regarding the remaining untainted (*anāsrava*) restraints: the second phrase refers to the tainted (*sāsrava*) restraint based on the nine paths of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*) of the threshold concentration (*anāgamya-dhyāna*); the third phrase refers to the untainted restraint based on the nine paths of uninterrupted transition of the threshold concentration; the fourth phrase refers to all other tainted restraints, excluding the tainted restraint of the nine paths of uninterrupted transition of the threshold concentration.
If that is so, as for what the Blessed One takes as their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*),
this section below is the third [section], which provides a general explanation of the two types of vows (*saṃvara*) based on the Sūtras;
it introduces the inquiry by relying upon the Sūtras.
If only bodily and verbal actions were called "restraint" (saṃvara),
why did the Blessed One, when speaking of the brief summary of the precepts, praise them by calling the triad of body, speech, and mind all "restraint"?
Regarding what is called "universal restraint" (*sarva-saṃvara*), it is generally said to be of three kinds.
Furthermore, for what reason does the sutra speak again of "restraint of the eye faculty" (*cakṣur-indriya-saṃvara*)?
This preceding sutra spoke of "restraint of the mind" (*manas-saṃvara*).
Regarding the subsequent scriptural teaching on the restraint of the eye faculty (*cakṣurindriya-saṃvara*):
what is its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*)?
If these two [restraints] do not have non-informative matter (*avijñapti-rūpa*) as their intrinsic nature, [what then is it?]
Answer: If that is so, what then is it? This is an inquiry.
The verse says: "Up to 'manifest,' do not [apply] in successive order.

The commentary explains: this means that the restraint of the mind (*manasaḥ saṃvara*) and the restraint of the faculties (*indriyasaṃvara*)—both of these have right awareness (*saṃprajanya*) and right mindfulness (*smṛti*) as their essential nature.

Therefore, in the verse, after first listing the names of right knowledge (*saṃprajanya*) and right mindfulness (*smṛti*), the word "combined" (*sahita*) is further stated; that is to say, it briefly explains that the restraint of the mind has right knowledge and mindfulness as its essence.

Thus, wisdom (*prajñā*) and mindfulness (*smṛti*) are combined [with the preceding] to constitute "restraint of the eye faculty" (*cakṣurindriya-saṃvara*) in the subsequent sūtra; therefore, they are separated first and then joined later.

This indicates that one should not assign them to the two types of restraint in their respective order. As for why wisdom and mindfulness are called "restraint": [it is because they function as such].
Discernment (*pratisaṃkhyā*) is able to select;
mindfulness (*smṛti*) is able to recollect.
These two powers are strong enough to guard and restrain the mental faculty and the visual faculty.
It is called "restraint" (*saṃvara*) because it prevents various faults from arising with respect to objects; it is not, however, non-informative matter (*avijñapti-rūpa*).
One should also fully state the six faculties, such as the eye and so forth;
the reason why the ear and others are not mentioned is due to brevity.
Therefore, the *Nyāyānusāra* (Treatise on Right Reasoning), fascicle 36, states: "Thus the Sūtra says:
'Having seen forms with the eye, one does not rejoice.'"
He is without anxiety,
dwelling constantly in equanimity, clear comprehension, and mindfulness;
thus it continues until he has cognized mental phenomena with the mind.
Now, one should reflect upon and discern up to what point in time [the attainment] lasts.
This is the second section below, which clarifies possession (*prāpti*) in relation to the time periods (*adhvan*). Within this:
First, the question;
second, the answer.
This, then, is the question.
Now, one should reflect upon this:
who possesses which manifest (*vijñapti*) and unmanifest (*avijñapti*) actions,
and for how long a duration within the three periods of time?
Furthermore, regarding the analysis of the accomplishment of non-informative discipline (*avijñapti-śīla*) and non-discipline (*aśīla*),
the following provides the answer.
Within this answer:
First, the accomplishment of non-informative action (*avijñapti*) is explained; second, the accomplishment of informative action (*vijñapti*) is explained;
third, the alternative names for non-restraint (*asaṃvara*) are explained.
Regarding the fourfold establishment of manifest and non-manifest [karma], within the first [section] clarifying the establishment of non-manifest [karma]:
first, its establishment as wholesome or unwholesome according to the time periods;
second, its establishment as intermediate (neutral) according to the time periods.
The three abodes of goodness and evil constitute the middle; this is the first [section], which establishes goodness and evil according to the world.
Within this, the first is the statement of the fundamental tenet.
Second, the formal explanation.
This marks the core thesis.
The verse says: "From the attainment of the path of meditative concentration, one becomes established in the middle."
This is the formal explanation.
Regarding the verse,
the first three lines clarify the prātimokṣa restraint.
The fourth phrase clarifies non-restraint (*asaṃvara*);
the fifth and sixth phrases clarify the restraint of meditative concentration (*dhyānasaṃvara*);
and the seventh phrase clarifies the untainted restraint (*anāsravasaṃvara*).
The eighth phrase clarifies both meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and the path (*mārga*).
The Commentary states: "Because their power is weak" explains the first three phrases.

For one abiding in the Prātimokṣa, as long as the precepts have not been relinquished, it is always established in the present. From the second moment onward, after the first moment, it is also established in the past. In the second clause, the phrase "as long as they have not been relinquished" applies universally to the subsequent cases, such as non-restraint (*asaṃvara*) and so forth. There is no unmanifest form (*avijñapti*) in the scattered stages (*vikṣipta-bhūmi*) of the desire realm that is established in the future. This is because it is matter that does not follow the mind, is not a single fruit with the mind, and its force is weak.
By this same principle, it is also impossible to establish that morality (śīla) exists in a previous life.
This explains the fourth phrase, as it was said: "Abiding [in the present], one also accomplishes the past."
For one who abides in non-restraint, from the moment of undertaking that evil discipline until it is relinquished, one always possesses it in the present;
furthermore, from the second moment onward, one also possesses it in the past.
Regarding the phrase "those who have obtained [it] will necessarily obtain it again":
this explains the fifth and sixth lines, concerning those who have obtained the dhyāna-restraint (dhyāna-saṃvara) and,
until they have relinquished that precept, [will continue to possess it].

It would always entail the fault [of being both] past and future. This is because the past discipline (dharma-vinaya) that was previously lost must necessarily be reacquired at the very first moment [of its restoration].
Question: As stated in the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* (Vibhāṣā), fascicle 17: "The heat-accompanying precept (uṣmagata-anuvartaka-śīla) serves as the antidote for abandoning transgression."
Furthermore, the *Nyāyānusāra* (Treatise on Right Reasoning), fascicle 61, states:

"There are those who, having previously not yet abandoned the defilements of desire, rely upon the wisdom produced by reflection (*cintā-mayī-prajñā*) to induce the arising of the 'heat' (*uṣmagata*) root of goodness.

Moreover, the *Mahāvibhāṣā*, fascicle 7, also says that for one who has not yet abandoned the defilements of desire, the 'heat' can be induced immediately following the wisdom of reflection. Based on these three texts:
There are those who enter the stage of "Heat" (*uṣmagata*) for the first time through the wisdom of reflection (*cintāmayī-prajñā*).
Furthermore, the roots of goodness of "Heat" cultivate only their own kind and do not cultivate other kinds;
this is because such a person who enters "Heat" for the first time through the wisdom of reflection does not cultivate other kinds.
Furthermore, one should not claim that there is no concentration lost since beginningless time;
this would mean it is indeterminate (*aniyata*) in the past.

How then could the initial attainment of concentration definitively establish it as belonging to the past or the future? The explanation says: from the moment of entering the "Heat" (*uṣmagata*) stage through the power of reflection (*cintāmayī prajñā*), at the very first instant.

Furthermore, because one also cultivates dissimilar types [of moments], one obtains that which was previously lost since beginningless time; thus, it is established as a certainty that from the second moment onward, one cultivates only similar types.
This is stated in terms of the majority of cases, meaning one does not cultivate dissimilar types. Alternatively, it is explained that this is said according to the portion of merit (*puṇya-bhāga*).
When first attaining meditative concentration (*samādhi*), one necessarily accomplishes both the past and the future [attainments].
However, if one refers to the initial attainment of concentration during the stage of the aids to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*), one does not accomplish the past [attainment].
Therefore, the *Nyāyānusāra* (Treatise on the Principles of Correct Reasoning), fascicle 36, states:
All those who have attained the restraint of meditative concentration (dhyāna-saṃvara) constantly possess it from the past until they relinquish it; furthermore,
they always possess the past restraint of concentration that was previously lost.
Since one necessarily reacquires that [discipline] at the very first moment,
a distinction must be made here in the explanation:
within the first moment of the discipline included in the levels conducive to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*), the past [moment] is not established.
That which was obtained in other lives is relinquished at the time of death;
in this life, there is no possibility of obtaining it again. This concludes the treatise.
Regarding the statement, "Because all noble ones have not previously arisen [in that state]": [it means that they have not yet produced it].
The explanation of the seventh phrase can be understood.
If there are those who currently abide until they achieve completion, these are called "present."
Explaining the eighth phrase:
regarding the restraint of meditative concentration (*dhyāna-saṃvara*) and the restraint of the path (*mārga-saṃvara*), if one currently abides in meditative absorption (*dhyāna*),
one accomplishes the present restraint of meditative concentration.
If one currently abides in the untainted path (anāsrava-mārga),
one accomplishes the restraint of the present path;
it is not the case that the present restraint is accomplished at times other than when one is in meditative equipoise (vyutthāna).

Because the meditative discipline (*dhyāna-saṃvara*) and the path discipline (*mārga-saṃvara*) function in accordance with the mind; for when the distracted mind is manifest, these two disciplines necessarily do not exist. Question: For what reason is *dhyāna* called "meditation" (*samādhi*), and why is the untainted (*anāsrava*) called the "path" (*mārga*)? Answer: It is explained that although both meditation and the path equally encompass these two [types of discipline], they are so designated based on their predominant characteristics. Specifically, because the power of concentration is predominant in *dhyāna*, it is termed "meditation"; because the power of the path is predominant in the untainted state, it is termed the "path. Furthermore, since the former is associated with the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), it is called "meditation," while the latter is associated with the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), and thus is called the "path. Alternatively, because it is the basis for the arising of the eight liberations (*vimokṣa*), it is called "meditation," whereas because it serves as the means for abandoning the afflictions (*kleśa*), it is called the "path. Moreover, because it is the basis for the arising of the supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), it is called "meditation," while because it is the means for attaining Nirvana, it is called the "path. Finally, because it is the basis for the arising of the four immeasurables (*apramāṇa*), it is called "meditation," whereas because it is the means for attaining the fruit of Arhatship, it is called the "path. Therefore, although both are common to both [realms], they are distinguished by their respective predominance. Thus, the former is named "meditation" and the latter is named the "path. This concludes the explanation.

To distinguish their specific differences, each is established with its own name. Furthermore, it is explained that the untainted (anāsrava) dharmas are those in which the various noble ones (ārya) travel, the path for emerging from birth and death, and the ultimate departure from suffering;
although they also include meditative concentrations (samādhi), they specifically receive the name "Path" (mārga). The tainted (sāsrava) dharmas are not like this.
Although it also follows the general principle, a specific designation has been established.

Having already explained that which abides until the second moment as non-informative (avijñapti), this is the second [section] concerning its establishment according to the time periods (*adhvan*). As for the term "abiding in the intermediate": [Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly; the translation reflects the portion available.]
This refers to that which is neither an extremely wholesome restraint (*saṃvara*) nor an extremely unwholesome non-restraint (*asaṃvara*);
therefore, it is called "intermediate" (*madhyama*).
Regarding the karma initiated by such states, it is not necessarily the case that all of it possesses non-informative action (*avijñapti*).
If one performs wholesome deeds that are not pure or commits unwholesome deeds that do not cause extreme affliction, there is no non-informative action (*avijñapti*).
If one performs wholesome deeds that are pure or commits unwholesome deeds that cause extreme affliction, then there is non-informative action.
The non-informative [matter] within the wholesome sphere is subsumed under the category of virtuous restraint;
the non-informative [matter] within the unwholesome sphere is subsumed under the category of non-virtuous restraint.
The meaning of "non-informative" is the same in both cases.
Because they are similar in kind, it is said that they are "subsumed under their kind. Regarding the intermediate non-manifest (avijñapti), it is accomplished in the present at its first moment;
from the second moment onward, until it is abandoned, it constantly accomplishes the non-manifest of both the past and present two time-periods.
Regarding the question of how long one remains established [in a state]:

this is the third section below, concerning the formation of good and evil within the "abiding. Question: Does a person who abides in restraint (saṃvara) ever form a neutral (madhyama) non-informative action (avijñapti)?
Does a person who dwells in non-restraint (asaṃvara) ever possess the intermediate virtuous non-informative (avijñapti)? If so, for how long?
The verse says: "Until the end of the force of defilement or purity.
The first two lines answer the initial question.
The last two lines answer the subsequent question.

The *Śāstra* states: "As for 'reaching through to establish [karma] as past and present,' it is like a bhikṣu or others who abide in the vows and commit acts such as killing due to intense afflictions."

There is non-informative [matter] (*avijñapti*) of the intermediate type that is unwholesome, such as that of those with non-restraint (*asaṃvara*), like sheep-slaughterers and the like, who perform acts such as prostration out of pure faith.
There is also wholesome intermediate non-informative [matter], which, as long as the two minds have not been severed, continues in constant succession; it becomes manifest at the first moment.
Following the previous section on the unmanifest (*avijñapti*),
which has already been analyzed up to the point where one possesses only the present [unmanifest],
the following second section clarifies the possession of the manifest (*vijñapti*).
The first two lines clarify the manifest karma of good and evil;
the latter two lines clarify the manifest karma of the indeterminate.
The treatise says: "As for the explanation of non-manifest [karma]..."
Explaining the first two lines:
those who abide in discipline (*vinaya*), non-discipline (*avinaya*),
or as neutral persons (*madhyastha*) constantly accomplish present manifest action (*vijñapti*) while they are actually performing it.
It is neither produced nor accomplished; from the moment after its first instant until it is relinquished, it is always accomplished as past.
If it is relinquished, it is not accomplished; there is absolutely no one who accomplishes a future manifest action (*vijñapti*).
As explained in the commentary on non-informative [action] (*avijñapti*) that is "scattered," this is because its force is weak as it does not follow the mind.
Regarding the statement "the obscured and unobscured [non-informative actions] are completed by retroactive application even up to the point of a transgression":
The following two lines explain [the previous point].
Second, there is the fault that an indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) informative act (*vijñapti*) cannot be established, whether it has arisen or not;
for since the power of the dharma itself is weak, the power it acquires is likewise slight.
Therefore, it is impossible to retroactively establish the future or retrospectively establish the past.
As for this inferior power of dharmas, by whom was it produced?
Question:
What is it that acts as the mental concomitant? Answer:
If that were so, there would be the fault that obscured [neutral] [action] could not constitute the past or future.
This objection means that since this neutral manifest action cannot constitute the past or the future...
That [mind] is able to project [the body].
Furthermore, the two types of neutral minds (*avyākṛta-citta*) should also be unable to accomplish that;

"and so forth" (*ādi*) refers to including strong neutral minds, namely those of habitual practice (*ābhyāsika*), deportment (*airyāpathika*), craftsmanship (*śailpasthānika*), and supernormal powers (*nairmāṇika*).
This criticism is unreasonable. As for the point that [the distinction] is established through their having differences:
it is explained that because manifest form (vijñapti-rūpa) is dull and insentient, and because it arises dependent upon another's mind.

The mind and so forth are clear and sharp, and do not arise in dependence on others. "And so forth" means including all mental factors (*caitta-dharma*). The two types of neutral minds are inferior when compared to wholesome and unwholesome minds.
Non-defined manifest karma arising from an inferior mind possesses a power twice as weak as the mind that gives rise to it;
therefore, it does not constitute the past or the future.
Consequently, there is a distinction between the manifest karma and the mind, such that they cannot be treated as analogous cases.
Furthermore, the *Nyāyānusāra* states:
"This objection is unreasonable,
because that which is produced is inferior to the mind that produces it."
The reason for this is that while an indeterminate mind can manifest a manifest action (*vijñapti-karman*),
the manifest action so manifested does not give rise to an unmanifest action (*avijñapti*).
Thus, it is known that the inferior [state] which is produced is the mind capable of producing it.
As previously stated, up to the point where "four other names are established," this constitutes the third section clarifying the alternative names for non-restraint (*asaṃvara*).
This is clarified incidentally by the discussion on the accomplishment [of karma];
it should be understood accordingly. Alternatively, regarding the accomplishment of manifest action (*vijñapti-karman*), one should apply the fourfold logical permutation (*catuṣkoṭi*).
Below this is the fourth section, which establishes the manifest (*vijñapti*) and the unmanifest (*avijñapti*).
This constitutes the statement of the thesis. As for what its content is:
Question:
The verse says, "Upon reaching completion, it becomes non-informative (avijñapti), not informative (vijñapti).
The verse answers:
The Commentary states: "Up to and including the completion of the karmic path" explains the first two phrases;
that is, in the first phrase, the manifest action is established, while the non-manifest action is not.
This means that when a person of intermediate capacity performs wholesome or unwholesome deeds with a weak and inferior volition,
they produce only manifest karma (*vijñapti-karma*) and not even non-manifest karma (*avijñapti*).
How much less could manifest karma produced by neutral (*avyākṛta*) volition give rise to non-manifest karma?

By citing the superior to illustrate the inferior: with the exception of the seven types of merit based on material things (*aupadhika-puṇya*) and the formation of wholesome or unwholesome courses of action (*karmapatha*), even those of neutral character who possess weak and inferior volition can give rise to non-informative action (*avijñapti*); therefore, these are distinguished separately.
"Only the unmanifest (avijñapti) is accomplished until it is either abandoned upon birth" explains the latter two phrases; that is,
the second phrase concerns the accomplishment of the unmanifest rather than the manifest (vijñapti).
This refers to noble ones who have been reborn in the three realms:
if they are born in the desire or form realms, they possess both the path and the formal non-informative [matter];
if they are born in the formless realm, they possess only the non-informative [matter] of the path.
There are cases where manifest action (*vijñapti*) is not established.
For example, when one is in the womb and so forth, manifest karma has not yet arisen;
or, once manifest karma has arisen, it is subsequently abandoned due to encountering certain conditions.
Regarding the phrase "one should understand that both constitute non-positions as appropriate," the latter two lines of the verse do not provide a separate explanation; therefore,
in the prose commentary, the Master exhorts the student to study them.
The explanation according to their respective meanings should be understood as appropriate.
The third category consists of those that accomplish both, namely both the manifest (*vijñapti*) and the unmanifest (*avijñapti*),
such as those abiding in the *prātimokṣa* vows and so forth.
The fourth, the "neither-nor" category, refers to that which is neither established as either the manifest (*vijñapti*) nor the unmanifest (*avijñapti*).
This is like being within an eggshell or similar states. As stated in the *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra*, Chapter 36, regarding the refutation of the second category: [text follows].

Is it not the case that an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) who has already attained meditative absorption (*dhyāna*), but whose manifest action (*vijñapti*) has not yet arisen or has already been lost,
would also possess non-manifest action (*avijñapti*) rather than manifest action?
Why, then, does the verse mention only the noble ones (*ārya*)?
It is also logical that those who are not easily reborn [should be mentioned];
why, then, does the commentary specifically designate those who are easily reborn?
The masters of the *Abhidharmakośa* explain this as follows:
The principle should also apply to the second statement;
it is either explicitly clarified for emphasis or implied by contrast.
Alternatively, one may be mentioned while the others are omitted for brevity;
thus, the *Abhidharmamahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 122, states:
"If one accomplishes bodily intimation (*kāyavijñapti*), does one also accomplish its non-intimation (*avijñapti*)?"
It can be answered in four propositions.
There are cases where one accomplishes bodily intimation (*kāyavijñapti*) but not this non-intimation (*avijñapti*).
This refers to those born in the desire realm who abide in a state that is neither discipline (*saṃvara*) nor non-discipline (*asaṃvara*).
One who currently possesses bodily intimation does not acquire this non-intimation;
or, one who previously possessed bodily intimation and has not lost it does not acquire this non-intimation.
Regarding "one who currently possesses bodily intimation":
That is to say: not sleeping,
not being intoxicated,
and not being dazed.
One who does not abandon their application and seeks to produce a bodily intimation (*kāyavijñapti*),
yet fails to obtain this non-intimation (*avijñapti*), is said to lack earnest faith and to lack intense fetters (*paryavasthāna*).
Although one may produce a bodily intimation (*kāyavijñapti*), one does not necessarily obtain this non-intimation (*avijñapti*).
Alternatively, if a prior bodily intimation has been produced and has not been lost—
meaning that the manifest action (*vijñaptikarman*) is not relinquished due to three conditions— [then it continues].
First, because the intention does not cease;
second, because one does not abandon the application of effort;
third, because the momentum is not exceeded.
The meaning of "not obtaining this non-informative [matter]" is as previously explained. There are those who possess bodily non-informative matter but not this informative matter;
namely, those noble ones (ārya) dwelling within the womb.
If one is born in the desire realm and abides in restraint,
yet does not obtain the prātimokṣa restraint,
there is no bodily intimation; even if it were present, it would be lost.
If one is born in the form realm, bodily intimation does not exist; even if it were present, it would be lost.
Furthermore, if noble beings (*ārya*) are born in the formless realm, such noble beings are unable to produce intimation while dwelling in the womb.
The manifest karma (*vijñapti-karma*) from previous lives has already been lost;
however, one who abides in the restraint (*saṃvara*) accomplishes only the meditative (*dhyāna*) and untainted (*anāsrava*) non-manifest karma (*avijñapti*).
This refers to one who abides in meditative concentration (dhyāna) or the untainted restraint (anāsrava-saṃvara).
One who lacks bodily intimation (kāya-vijñapti) is,
for instance, one who is asleep.
Either due to intoxication or fainting,
one abandons all preparatory efforts and does not seek to initiate informative action (*vijñapti*).
Regarding that which exists but is lost:
it refers to the abandonment of bodily informative action (*kāya-vijñapti-karman*) due to three conditions.
First, because the underlying intention (*āśaya*) has ceased.
Second, because the preparatory effort (*prayoga*) has been relinquished;
third, because the momentum (*vega*) has passed.
If one is born in the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), there is no bodily intimation (*kāyavijñapti*).
This means that because they have abandoned preparatory effort and do not seek to initiate manifest action (*vijñapti*),
even if such action were present, it would be lost as previously explained.
This applies to those noble ones (*ārya*) who are born in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).

One who is a learner (śaikṣa) accomplishes the learner’s non-informative [action] (avijñapti); one who is beyond learning (aśaikṣa) accomplishes the non-learner’s non-informative [action]. There are those who accomplish bodily informative [action] (kāya-vijñapti) as well as this non-informative [action]:
namely, those born in the desire realm (kāmadhātu) who abide in restraint (saṃvara), yet have not obtained the prātimokṣa restraint.
One who currently possesses bodily intimation also acquires this non-intimation; or,
having previously possessed this intimation without losing it, one also acquires this non-intimation,
provided one abides in the prātimokṣa restraint.
If one abides in non-restraint,
or if one abides in that which is neither restraint nor non-restraint,
and currently possesses bodily intimation (*kāyavijñapti*), one also acquires this non-intimation (*avijñapti*).
Either one previously possessed bodily informative action (*kāyavijñapti*) and has not lost it, and also acquires this non-informative action (*avijñapti*);
or, if born in the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), one currently possesses bodily informative action;
or one previously possessed bodily informative action and has not lost it.
In this context, one who currently possesses bodily intimation also acquires this non-intimation.
The phrase "and so forth" means that one also acquires non-intimation by manifesting intimation through either earnest faith or intense fetters (*paryavasthāna*).
If one abides in the prātimokṣa restraint,
or if one abides in non-restraint,
that person necessarily accomplishes both bodily intimation and non-intimation.

If one is born in the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) and currently possesses bodily intimation (*kāyavijñapti*), this refers to one who has not relinquished their preparatory effort (*prayoga*) in seeking to initiate an intimated action.
The rest is as previously explained. There are those who neither possess bodily intimation nor its non-intimation (*avijñapti*).
This refers to those dwelling within an eggshell;
or ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) residing in the womb;
or those born in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) who abide in a state that is neither restraint nor non-restraint and lack bodily intimation (*kāyavijñapti*).
There is also the case of having possessed [an action] and then losing it. For instance, when ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) are born into the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*),

or when such ordinary beings abide within the womb or egg, they have already lost the manifest and unmanifest karma (*vijñapti-avijñapti-karman*) from their previous lives and are currently unable to produce it.
This should be understood as previously explained:
having been born in the formless realm, one has already abandoned the contaminated [states] but has not yet attained the uncontaminated,
because there is no form in that stage.
The remainder is as previously explained.
Regarding the statement "abiding in the restraint," as for how it is obtained,
the following section— the third major heading— clarifies the specific conditions for obtaining the precepts.
Among these, the first clarifies the attainment of the three types of discipline,
and the second clarifies the temporal limits of their attainment.
1. Explaining the observance of the threefold training (*tri-śikṣā-saṃvara*). 2. Explaining the observance of the lay follower (*upāsaka-saṃvara*).
3. Explaining the distinctions between the three observances. This is the first [section], explaining the attainment of the three observances.
The preceding question is raised as a preface.
Regarding the verse which states, "Attainment arises from the instruction of others," etc.,
the following is the response provided within the verse itself.
The first phrase clarifies meditative concentration (dhyāna);
the second phrase clarifies the untainted (anāsrava);
the final two phrases clarify individual liberation (prātimokṣa).
The Commentary states: "Because it arises together with the mind" explains the first phrase.
Since the dhyāna-restraint (*dhyāna-saṃvara*) is born of meditative concentration (*samādhi*), the verse refers to it as "born of concentration."
The remaining text is understandable.
Regarding the phrase "the untainted restraint (anāsrava-saṃvara) will be explained later," this explains the second line [of the verse].
The verse mentions "that sound" to indicate the preceding dhyānas;
it further uses the term "noble" (ārya) to select the untainted minds (*anāsrava-citta*) of the six stages.
Because the untainted restraint (*anāsrava-saṃvara*) arises from the Path, the verse refers to it as "born of the Path" (*mārgaja*).
Regarding the Prātimokṣa restraint obtained through the instruction of another,
the explanation of the following two lines may be understood accordingly.
Regarding the statement "these further comprise two types up to five types of precepts," this clarifies the distinctions between the two kinds of *saṃgha*:

a group of four or more persons is called a *saṃgha*, because among the eight classes of practitioners, the three beginning with the *bhikṣu* obtain [the precepts] from such a group; whereas a *pudgala* refers to an individual person.
This means that the other five types obtain it from these two;
if one is a śrāmaṇera or a śrāmaṇerī, they obtain it from both persons;
if one is an upāsaka, an upāsikā, or one observing the upavāsa vows, they obtain it from a single person.
Regarding the phrase "the various Vinayas up to 'furthermore it is said,'" this is a separate explanation of the word "etc. (ādi).
This is the explanation of the Vinaya-vibhāṣā masters.
There are ten ways of obtaining full ordination (*upasampadā*).
To include these, the word "etc. (*ādi*) is further stated in the fourth phrase. What are these ten?
Question:
One [type] arises spontaneously and issues forth as manifest karma (*vijñapti-karman*).
Answer: One [type] arises spontaneously.
This means that when the Buddhas and Pratyekabuddhas attain the mind of the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) spontaneously and without a teacher, they obtain full ordination (*upasampadā*).
Thus, the *Nyāyānusāra* (Treatise on Correct Reasoning), fascicle 37, states:
"Spontaneous refers to knowledge."

First, by realizing this wisdom without relying on a teacher, one obtains full ordination; second, by entering the state of rightness and departure from birth, as in the case of the five bhikṣus, such as Ājñāta-Kauṇḍinya and others.

Furthermore, the *Nyāyānusāra* states that one obtains the full precepts through the realization of the path of vision; thirdly, by the Buddha’s command, "Come, Bhikṣu," at which time the precepts are obtained—referring to Yaśas and others.

Yaśas (here translated as "Renown") states in the *Nyāyānusāra* that it is due to the power of his original vows and the majestic empowerment of the Buddha. Fourth, one obtains the precepts at that time by accepting the Buddha as the Great Teacher.
That is to say, Mahākāśyapa [was so called] because of his skillful answering of questions.
As for Sūdayin— Sūdayin means "Good Giver"—
he was only seven years old, yet because of his intelligence, he answered the Buddha's question well, satisfying the Buddha's mind.
Although he was not yet twenty years of age,
the Buddha permitted the community of monks to confer the full ordination upon him through a formal ritual (*karmavācanā*);
because of his intelligence, he was skillful in providing answers.
A separate condition is established:
the precept is not conferred at the very moment of replying.
Regarding "replying," it refers to when the Buddha asks him, "Where is your home?"
Sudāyin replied: "In the three realms there is no home; it is by respectfully receiving the eight rules of respect that one then attains the precepts.
This refers to Mahāprajāpatī; the old translation "Mahāprajāpatī" (Great Loving Path) is erroneous.
In Sanskrit, she is called Mahāprajāpatī.
*Mahā* here means "great," and *prajāpati* here means "giver of birth."
*Bhava* here translates as "Lord.
This is one of the thousand names of the Great Brahmā King (*Mahābrahmā*). Because sentient beings are numerous, he is called "Great Being" (*Mahāsattva*).
The Brahmā King is able to give birth to all sentient beings.
Because she was the mistress of Mahāmāyā, she was named Mahāmāyāvī;
furthermore, she was given this name by the deity from whom she had requested [a son].
She was the Buddha’s maternal aunt.
The Buddha dispatched Ānanda to explain the eight dharmas of respect for him;
he then reverently accepted them,
and at that moment, he obtained the precepts.
These eight are called "dharma-s to be honored" because they are dharmas that ought to be respected.
Regarding the fact that she was the first among the community of nuns to go forth,
it is explained in detail as set forth in the Vinaya.
The eight rules of respect (aṣṭau gurudharmāḥ), formerly called the eight reverences; seven are obtained through delegation,
namely, the "Dharma-giver Nun" (dharmadinnā bhikṣuṇī)— a nun named Dharma-giver is called a "Dharma-giver Nun."
This nun was upright and dignified; fearing there might be obstacles on the road as she went among the monks, she did not face the great assembly (bhikṣusaṃgha) when receiving full ordination.
Instead, the great assembly dispatched one nun to receive the ritual on her behalf and transmit it to her for ordination.
Therefore, by means of sending [a messenger], one becomes endowed with full ordination (*upasampadā*).
Because nuns were modest and decorous, the Blessed One separately established this provision. Eighth, regarding the preceptor of discipline (*vinayadhara*) as the fifth person:
this refers to border regions where, due to the absence of a quorum of monks, even the absolute minimum must consist of five persons.
Since the preceptor does not count toward the quorum, the remaining four constitute the assembly;
if fewer than that, it does not constitute an assembly.
Among these five persons, one must necessarily be a holder of the Vinaya who performs the formal ritual (karmavācanā).
Therefore, it is said that the fifth [requirement] is the upholder of the Vinaya.
Fewer than five do not constitute a quorum;
more than five does not obstruct [the validity]. Ninth, by means of a group of ten: this refers to a place where the Sangha is numerous, namely the Middle Kingdom.
At the very least, ten people are required;

more than that is not prohibited. These ten consist of three who recite the taking of refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha, and seven who constitute the assembly of the sixty virtuous and harmonious members.

The Buddha dispatched an arhat to explain the three refuges and the reception of full ordination for him. Thus, the ten types of prātimokṣa discipline obtained above do not necessarily arise based on informative action (vijñapti-karman).

That is to say, the first two kinds do not arise from informative action (*vijñapti*), while the latter eight arise from informative action. Question: It was previously stated that the prātimokṣa is obtained through the instruction of another or spontaneously.

Regarding the question of how one obtains precepts through the path of seeing (darśanamārga) without relying on the instruction of another: the commentary explains that the preceding passage refers specifically to obtaining them through the instruction of another, whereas the subsequent passage refers generally to obtaining them without such instruction.
Therefore, the word "etc. (ādi) is said to include this distinct meaning. Question: It may be acceptable that this meaning is not obtained from another;
however, how is it that the unmanifest (avijñapti) does not arise from the manifest (vijñapti)?
As the treatise says below:
If the seven paths of wholesome action arise from undertaking [the precepts], they necessarily possess both the manifest (*vijñapti*) and the unmanifest (*avijñapti*).

This is because the morality arising from undertaking must necessarily depend upon the manifest. The commentary explains: "Arising from receiving [the precepts] from another necessarily depends on the manifestation of the manifest."
If it is not received from another and does not arise dependent on manifest action (*vijñapti*), what contradiction is there? This must be explained. Question:

If there is such an unmanifest action (*avijñapti*) that does not arise from manifest action, why does the Master [Vasubandhu] pose a challenge later in the text, saying: "In the desire realm, there is no unmanifest action that arises apart from manifest action"? Answer: It should be understood that in the latter passage, the Master is stating the position of other teachers (*ācārya*) to raise an objection. Alternatively, the latter passage may be taken as referring generally to both the preparatory (*prayoga*) and fundamental (*maula*) stages, because in both cases manifest action necessarily exists.
Therefore, it is said that desire can exist without unmanifest action (*avijñapti*), which arises independently of manifest action (*vijñapti*).

If this were not the case, what manifest action would there be at the moment the fundamental path of action (*mūla-karma-patha*) is completed in instances such as killing by dispatching an agent? It cannot be said that [the manifest action] occurs spontaneously.

Regarding the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*): since the acquisition of the fundamental non-informative (*avijñapti*) discipline necessarily arises dependent upon the informative (*vijñapti*), there is no contradiction.
Furthermore, it is explained that the ten types of prātimokṣa discipline obtained thus far [are as follows].
The sevenfold non-informative [action] does not necessarily arise based on the sevenfold informative action.
For example, when receiving the precepts through ritual (karma), non-informative action of speech also arises from the three types of bodily informative action;
likewise, when receiving the precepts through the triple refuge, non-informative action of body also arises from the four types of vocal informative action.
It is not necessarily the case that [the acquisition of precepts] arises based on the manifestation of one's own kind.
If this interpretation were adopted, the ten ways of obtaining the precepts would all arise based on manifestation,
just as in the case of the self-arisen (svayaṃbhū).

Regarding the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*): it is also acquired through the arising of informative action (*vijñapti-karman*), which brings about non-informative action (*avijñapti*). This interpretation intends to explain that the Path of Seeing occurs spontaneously.

This means that for such a person, there was previously a determined continuity of manifest action (*vijñapti*) that remained uninterrupted, until—in the state of an Arya—unmanifest discipline (*avijñapti-saṃvara*) is produced from that manifest action. Question: As the treatise states, "If the seven wholesome courses of action arise from undertaking [the precepts], they necessarily possess both [aspects], namely manifest and unmanifest."
Since the morality of undertaking rebirth must necessarily rely upon informative action (*vijñapti*),
according to this passage,
the statement that "one who undertakes rebirth possesses both" means that the undertaking of rebirth relies upon informative action.
Why is it not said that the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*) is also naturally endowed with both?
The commentary explains: the lower treatise, relying on what is manifest, speaks only of "receiving birth" (*upapatti*).
It does not preclude spontaneous [attainment].
Upon seeing the Path, one obtains the precepts; this relies on both [the mind and] the manifest [action], or it is spontaneous.
The path of seeing (darśanamārga),
because it involves the intentional undertaking of rebirth and belongs to the category of those who take rebirth.
It is also called "receiving birth" (*upapatti*).

If one interprets it in this way, it accords well with the following passage which states that desire arises without non-informative matter (*avijñapti*) apart from informative matter (*vijñapti*); furthermore, there are also two such explanations within the *Nyāyānusāra*.
As that treatise states:
"Other masters say that it is not the case that all unmanifest [form] in the desire realm arises based on manifest [form],
as is the case at the time of attaining the fruits [of the path]."
The five bhikṣus and others obtained the prātimokṣa vows;

however, it was previously determined that they possessed *vijñapti*. The commentary explains that this is the opinion of other masters (*anyācārya*) in that treatise, who assert that in the realm of desire (*kāmadhātu*), there exists *avijñapti* that arises independently of *vijñapti*. The passage beginning with "However, they... represents the position of the master of the *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra*.
It is not the case that non-informative action (*avijñapti*) arises independently of informative action (*vijñapti*).
For those who have attained the fruit— such as the five bhikṣus and others—
there must previously have been a continuous stream of informative action that was determined and uninterrupted.
Up to the stage of the noble ones (*ārya*), from that [moment] onward, there is the unmanifest restraint (*avijñapti-saṃvara*) issued forth from the manifest;

this former explanation accords with the *Nyāyānusāra*, while the latter explanation accords with the intent of the *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya*. Furthermore, in the *Mahāvibhāṣā* (vol. 122), it clarifies that one may possess a present unmanifest [action] without possessing its manifest; regarding this as well, there are two explanations.
If one abides in the prātimokṣa restraint or in non-restraint (asaṃvara) and currently lacks bodily intimation (kāyavijñapti),
some say that this refers to the second moment and thereafter.
Because that [non-restraint] must necessarily possess informative action (*vijñapti*) at its initial moment.
Some say that this initial moment is also what is being discussed,
because there exists the present non-restraint (*asaṃvara*) even when bodily informative action is absent.

And because one obtains full ordination while in meditative concentration (*samādhi*). Regarding the explanation in that treatise which says, "Because there is present non-restraint (*asamvara*) without bodily intimation (*kāyavijñapti*)," this means that when one undertakes the ritual act, one acquires non-restraint even though there is presently no bodily intimation.
Regarding the statement that one obtains full ordination while in meditative absorption:
this refers to Buddhas and Pratyekabuddhas.

As well as for the five bhikṣus, when they attain the precepts while in meditative concentration, there is likewise no bodily intimation (*kāyavijñapti*). The intention of the former master is that in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) there is no non-informative matter (*avijñapti*) that arises apart from informative matter (*vijñapti*).
The intention of the latter master is that in the desire realm there is also non-informative matter that arises apart from informative matter.
However, there is no commentator [to adjudicate]. The former interpretation accords with the *Vibhāṣā* masters of the later period;
the latter interpretation accords with the *Vibhāṣā* masters of the earlier period.
Furthermore, regarding the statement "up to half a month" and so forth:
Below this, secondly, the delimitation of time periods is clarified.
Within this, first,
the delimitation of the Prātimokṣa is clarified.
Second, the clarification of the limits of non-restraint (*asaṃvara*). This is the first [section], clarifying the limits of individual liberation (*prātimokṣa*).
There are two types in total, as can be understood from the text.
The meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*), the untainted (*anāsrava*), and those within the intermediate states (*antara*) do not have fixed times,
unlike the two types of vows of individual liberation (*prātimokṣa*),
which are fixed to specific times. Therefore, when discussing the time of the discipline of logic (*hetuvidyā-śīla*), it is shown that time is not ultimately real.
This is not like the non-Buddhists who cling to the notion that time exists as a substantial reality;
rather, it is an interpretation of the scriptural statements.
The reason the sūtras speak of days and nights repeatedly, and mention periods such as half-months and so forth, is that these do not possess any separate intrinsic substance.
The Master Paramārtha’s commentary states: This passage addresses an anticipated objection.

The objection is as follows: "If the boundaries of the time for observing the precepts consist of only two types, why does the Sūtra speak of receiving the eightfold precepts for a period such as half a month?"
To resolve this objection, we now offer this explanation:
although the sūtras state that the precepts of the half-month and so forth must be received daily,
this is because the eightfold precepts have only the duration of a day and night as their limit.
It is stated again that day and night constitute a half-month and so forth;
this does not contradict the sūtra because it is not the case that one receives the eight precepts for the duration of a half-month or similar periods.
As for what kind of dharma is designated by the term "time":
Question:
At the time of understanding, what dharma is that which is called the "expressive name"? Furthermore, at the time of understanding, what dharma is this "name"?
Since this [treatise] clarifies time (*kāla*), it asks about the essence of time.
The *Nyāyānusāra* (Treatise on the Principles), chapter thirty-seven, also states:
"What dharma is designated as 'time'?"
The *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 135, also states:
"What dharma is called a 'kalpa'? Furthermore, what are the nature of the time that is expressed and the name that expresses it?"
In this context, because it is the time of understanding, the essence of time is questioned.

Having clarified the meaning of time as a causal condition, the inquiry proceeds to its designation: that is, the metaphorical designation for all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*), which extends to the establishment of the names "day" and "night."
Answer: It is the "designation" (*adhivacana*), which refers to the "name" (*nāman*).
As explained previously, that which designates all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) is called a designation.

The state of light is designated by the name "day," and the state of darkness is designated by the name "night. Furthermore, it is explained that time has no separate substantial entity; rather, conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are called "time.
That is to say, the conditioned phenomena manifested by a metaphorical designation (*adhivacana*) are what are called "time."
One should say that it refers to the conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) manifested by the designation (*adhivacana*).
Thus, the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* (Vibhāṣā), fascicle 135, states:

"The answer is: these [terms] manifest half-months, months, seasons, and years. Furthermore, another interpretation holds that the conditioned phenomena are the answer to what is expressed by the time.
"An answer by way of a designation (*adhivacana*) refers to a name that expresses [the meaning].
Regarding the statement 'in the two limits, even non-arising can occur':
this is a question from the Sautrāntikas."
Regarding the two limits, it is possible [to undertake the precepts] for the duration of one's life;
however, after death, even if there is a formal commitment, the precepts are not generated.
This is because the precepts are abandoned upon death due to the change in the physical basis (āśraya) upon which they depend.
In a separate basis-body (*āśraya*), the precepts do not arise because there is no application of effort (*prayoga*) to seek their reception;
furthermore, once the precepts have been received, they must be maintained through mindfulness and awareness,
and since such mindfulness is absent in a separate basis-body, it can be said that they are not produced.
It is accepted here that one may undertake the vows of the Upavāsa (fasting) precepts after an interval of one day and night,
or five days and nights,
or ten days and nights, and so forth, even if they have been separated by a subsequent birth.
"What dharma acts as an obstacle such that the precepts do not arise? Since the Sautrāntikas maintain that the *upavāsa* (fasting) precepts can be received for many days, they raise this question:
"There must necessarily be some dharma that limits [the duration] to exactly one day and night."
The Sarvāstivādins reply:
When the dawn breaks at daybreak and the light of the sun appears,
it constitutes an obstacle that causes one to relinquish the precepts.
The scriptural citations can be understood [from other sources].
Regarding the point that "the precept lasts for one day and night" in this sense, the Sautrāntika masters say:
"In this matter, we should investigate together whether the Buddha, having correctly perceived [the duration] as one day and night..."
It is logically impossible for the *upavāsa* (near-dwelling) discipline to arise [in the manner] you have described;
therefore, it is stated in the Sūtra that it lasts for one day and night, in order to accommodate those whose faculties are difficult to subdue.
In the sutras, this is based on the precepts for a single day and night;
however, if one's faculties are easily disciplined, it is also permissible to receive many more, as I have stated.
As for the question of by what reasoning and scriptural authority such a statement is made, the Sarvāstivādins respond:
"Because it is not contrary to reason that this precept arises even beyond [the moment of death]."
The Sautrāntika replies:
Although there is no scriptural passage stating that the precept arises beyond this day and night, it does not contradict reason that it should arise.
As for the Vaibhāṣikas who do not accept this point:
The Sarvāstivādins further raise an objection:
"Any established tenet must rely upon the authoritative scriptures (āgama);
how could a principle be established by reason alone in the absence of scriptural proof?"
Therefore, our school does not accept this position.
As for the question of what limit constitutes reaching the point of engaging in reprehensible and loathsome karma,
this refers to the second division of non-restraint (*asaṃvara*).
It lasts only for the duration of one's life and not for even a single day and night,
because there is no such thing as receiving the unwholesome precepts (duḥśīla) in the presence of a teacher.
If that were so, then there would likewise be no one who acquires non-restraint (asaṃvara).
Difficult.
The evil precepts last for as long as one's life,
and they are not received from a teacher.
How is it that they are obtained?
Although there is no teacher present, why is it not established that they exist? Answer:

Although one who observes the precepts of non-restraint for as long as life lasts does not have a teacher present, the transgression of destroying wholesome roots is grave, and thus they incur non-restraint (*asaṃvara*).

This is not because the destruction of wholesome roots is merely temporary, nor because the lack of a teacher causes them to incur non-restraint; therefore, there is no such thing as [non-restraint] lasting for a day and night. However, regarding the *upavāsa* (fasting) precepts, by the power of having a teacher present, even if one destroys the wholesome roots, the transgression is light, and one still incurs restraint (*saṃvara*). Even if it were hypothetically possible for someone to temporarily receive non-restraint in the presence of a teacher, they would necessarily still incur it.
However, because it has never been observed, its existence is not established.
When the Sautrāntika masters say "because it reaches the *āśaya*," they are stating the tenet of the Sautrāntika school.

The Sautrāntika masters say that non-informative action (*avijñapti*) is a designation for the seeds of virtuous restraint and volition (*cetanā*), and does not exist as a separate substantial entity.
"Intention" (*āśaya*) is volition;
alternatively, "intention" refers to one's underlying purpose.
It may have desire as its essence,
or it may have resolve as its essence,
or it may have both desire and resolve as its essence. By this same principle, non-restraint (asamvara) should also not be considered a real entity, just as virtuous restraint (kuśala-saṃvara) is.

The perfuming that results in the continuous succession of the seeds of the intention and volition (*cetanā*) to commit evil and unwholesome acts, which is not relinquished, is called non-restraint (*asaṃvara*). Alternatively, it is explained as being perfumed by the power of the volition to manifest evil through the force of a formal undertaking (*samādāna*).

The non-relinquishment of the seeds of volition (*cetanā*) characterized by an unwholesome intention (*āśaya*) is called non-restraint (*asaṃvara*). Regarding the first two interpretations, the "intention" has volition as its essential nature. Furthermore, another interpretation holds that it is the non-relinquishment of the continuity of the seeds of volition associated with the unwholesome intention of wishing to commit evil, which have been perfumed (*vāsita*). Yet another interpretation holds that it is the perfuming produced by the power of the manifest volition of the commitment (*samādāna*) to wish to commit evil.

The continuity of the seeds of volition (*cetanā*) associated with an unwholesome intention (*āśaya*), which is not relinquished, is called non-restraint (*asaṃvara*). In the two previous explanations, the intention was distinguished separately because it is more predominant than the volition itself. Consequently, even if a wholesome mind subsequently arises at a later time, [the seeds of that unwholesome volition persist].

Yet they are called persons who have accomplished non-restraint (*asaṃvara*), because they do not abandon this *āśaya*—*āśaya* being translated here as "intention" (*i-yüan*). It is said that [this lasts] for one day and night, up until the night when one ceases from adornment.
Below this, thirdly, the upavāsa discipline is explained.
Within this, first,
the method of receiving it is explained.
Second, it clarifies the possession of the eight branches;
third, it clarifies the person receiving the precepts.
