This is the first [section], clarifying the method of receiving [the precepts].
The Commentary states: "As for 'failing to achieve the near-dwelling,' this explains the preceding three phrases;
it may be understood according to the text."
To show that receiving this restraint becomes profoundly useful,
the fourth line is explained:
because of [the desire for] adornment, one extensively commits various transgressions.
Therefore, it is specifically prohibited and termed a "basis of negligence. Regarding "excellent conduct," this refers to intermediate excellent conduct;
because it is practiced throughout the day, one is able to restrain oneself from slaughter and hunting.
Because it lasts throughout the night, one is able to restrain against fraud and theft.
Furthermore, this explanation is made from the perspective of the majority;
in reality, both day and night enable one to abstain from these two. This precept for day and night is also capable of causing one to abstain from false speech and so forth.
If it is not mentioned, the fault is minor and thus not discussed;
alternatively, it may refer specifically to the body,
or cite the first instance to illustrate the subsequent ones.
Regarding the term "near-dwelling" (*upavāsa*), it refers to one who dwells in the precepts for as long as life lasts;
this explains the meaning of the name "near-dwelling.
Furthermore, the *Nyāyānusāra* states: "Some say that these precepts dwell near [the time]."
Thus, regarding the statement that this restraint is called "nurturing" (*poṣadha*),
it describes another name for the *upavāsa* (fast-day observance).
*Poṣadha* is translated into Chinese as "nurturing."
The old translation "posadha" is an error. Therefore, a verse is cited to prove that the name signifies "nurturing" (poṣadha).

As for the question, "For what reason does one undertake this [vow] until the point of losing mindfulness and succumbing to arrogance and negligence?"—this is the second section, which clarifies the possession of the eight branches.
Regarding the question and the response in verse,
the *Śāstra* states: "Up to the point of attaining a mind of weary detachment (*nirveda-citta*)," which explains the two preceding lines.
"For what reason does one fully receive these three branches?
This explains the latter two phrases.
The "three branches" refer to the branch of ethical discipline (*śīla*), the branch of heedfulness (*apramāda*), and the branch of restraint (*niyama*).
This is the question.
To answer it by citing a verse, [it says]: "Because one does not possess the factors, lacks a sincere mind, and dwells in negligence."
One should perform what ought to be done and refrain from what ought not to be done; conversely, one should not do that which should not be done.
One who eats at the proper time is able to restrain the practice of eating at all times.
First, one immediately recalls having received the *upavāsa* vows;
second, one is able to give rise to a profound sense of weary detachment toward the world.
The remainder of the text may be understood accordingly.
The statement by other masters that "it is because the observance (*upavāsa*) is divided into two" cites a divergent opinion;
the intention of this master is to say that abstaining from eating at improper times constitutes the essential substance of the fast (*upoṣadha*).
In the customs of the Western lands, abstaining from food is called *zhāi* (fasting).
The remaining eight types are not called *zhāi*, as they do not possess the full meaning of fasting;
they are merely termed "limbs of fasting" (*zhāizhī*).
This can be understood as divided into two parts.
If one follows this interpretation, there are nine precepts;

yet, when they are referred to as "eight precepts," this is not stated according to their essential nature (*dravya*), but is discussed merely in terms of their constituent branches (*aṅga*). Question: Are the Sanskrit names for *upoṣadha* (fasting) and *upavāsa* (near-dwelling) the same? Answer: They are the same.
Since the text explains them separately, it is clear that they are distinct. Furthermore, regarding the etymology of the Sanskrit term *upavāsa*,
it is sometimes translated as "fasting" (*zhāi*) and sometimes as "near-dwelling" (*jìnzhù*).
The names differ while the meaning remains the same.
If one holds this view— that [the agent] extends even to the follower and the executor—
the Sautrāntika refutes it by citing a sūtra.
I now follow the training of the noble Arhats.
Whatever the Arhats practice and whatever they do,
I shall follow that practice.
One should act in accordance with that.
The rest of the text is self-evident.
If this is so, what constitutes the factors (aṅga) that give it the name "fast" (upoṣadha)?
[Objection:

It is difficult. Other masters ask: since the name "fast" (*upoṣadha*) originally derives from abstaining from eating at improper times, if one does not take that very abstention from eating at improper times as the essence of the fast, [how can it be so called?]
What is the distinct essence of the fast (upavāsa), such that it is designated by eight names as the "limbs of the fast" (upavāsāṅga)?
According to the older treatises,
upavāsa is also translated as "fast."
The *Gujilun* (Treatise on Old Friends) states:
"If that is so, what distinct dharma is named *upavāsa*?
To summarize, the designation 'fast' (*zhāi*) should be understood to apply in this same way."
The Sautrāntika replies:
Fasting has no separate essence; it is constituted by taking up the eight [precepts].
The aggregate itself is the fast.
The distinct [factors] are themselves called "limbs" (*aṅga*).
For example, a chariot is formed by the synthesis of its various constituent parts;
likewise, an army is formed by the synthesis of its four branches: elephants, cavalry, chariots, and infantry.
Just as a chariot, an army, or a powder is formed by gathering and combining five components,
so too should one understand that the eightfold fast (aṣṭāṅga-upavāsa) is likewise a mere designation.

Adopting eight parts constitutes "fasting" (*upavāsa*), yet even this fasting is merely conventional; it differs from common parlance, for here "fasting" (*upavāsa*) refers solely to the act of not eating.
From "the Vaibhāṣika masters up to those who have not attained meditative concentration" (*dhyāna*), [this section] sets forth the explanation of the Vaibhāṣika masters.

Now, as for what is called "fasting" (*upavāsa*), it refers to abstaining from eating at improper times; thus, abstaining from eating at improper times is the fast itself. Furthermore, because it is one among the eight [factors], it is a limb of the fast.
The remaining seven limbs are each one among the eight, and are therefore limbs of the fast.
It is not that abstaining from eating at improper times is not called a fast; just as right view and the path are both of the nature of wisdom, one may say that right view is the path.
Furthermore, because it is one among these eight, it can be called a "limb of the path" (*mārgāṅga*); likewise, each of the other seven limbs is a limb of the path because it is one among the eight.
However, since their essential nature (*svabhāva*) is not wisdom (*prajñā*), they are not the path itself.
Since both the investigation of phenomena (*dharmapravicaya*) and awakening (*bodhi*) are in essence wisdom (*prajñā*),
it can be said that the investigation of phenomena is awakening.
Furthermore, because it is one among the seven [factors], it can be called a factor of awakening (*bodhyaṅga*).
The remaining six factors are each one among the seven [factors of enlightenment], and thus they are limbs of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*).

However, because their essential nature (*svabhāva*) is not wisdom (*prajñā*), they are not [themselves] enlightenment. This is just as, among the factors of meditative concentration (*dhyānāṅga*), the meditative absorption (*samādhi*) and the essence of meditative concentration are both simply concentration (*samāpatti*).
It can be said that samādhi is dhyāna;
furthermore, because it is one among the five [factors], it is a limb of dhyāna.
Likewise, the remaining factors such as vitarka and vicāra are limbs of dhyāna because they are each one among the five.
"Because its nature is not fixed, it is not dhyāna.
This is the objection raised by the Sautrāntikas regarding the aforementioned statement that [the stages] up to the Peak of Existence possess eight branches, and so forth.

Now, the term "limb" (*aṅga*) carries the meaning of a constituent part; it cannot be said that [the factors] such as right view are limbs when considered in relation to other [factors], but they are indeed limbs when considered in relation to themselves. The phrase "and so forth" includes the awakening factor of discrimination of phenomena (*dharmapravicaya-saṃbodhyaṅga*) and the limb of concentration (*samādhy-aṅga*). If you claim that previously arisen right view and so forth serve as limbs for subsequently arisen right view and so forth, [this is not tenable].
In that case, prior to the noble path such as the *duḥkhe-dharma-jñāna-kṣānti* at the first moment, right view and the other factors would not exist;

thus, the eightfold [path] and so forth would not be complete. The Sautrāntika position is that while the names "path," "enlightenment," and "dhyāna" are stated collectively, they are explained as having constituent members (*aṅga*) when analyzed individually.
In general, there is no contradiction if they are distinct branches.
The *Nyāyānusāra* offers this defense: it is not the teaching of the *Vibhāṣā* that the substance of right view and so forth is itself the branch of right view and so forth.
Nor is it the case that previously arisen right view and so forth serve as the factors for subsequently arisen right view and so forth.
Rather, among the eight co-arising factors such as right view, only right view alone has the capacity to investigate the characteristics of all phenomena and can be designated as the "path."
Because it is able to seek out the meaning of the Path,
this right view itself is called a "limb" (aṅga) as it can further accord with right thought and the other factors.
As for the remaining seven limbs, they are called limbs because they accord with the co-arising dharmas in relation to them.
That which is not capable of seeking cannot be called the Path;
such is the true meaning.
However, from the perspective of conventional designation, all other factors are able to nurture right view.
Contemplation and the others also receive the name "path," and it does not contradict reason for "view" to be called a "limb of the path.
Thus, all of them are both the path and its limbs.
The rest should be explained accordingly as appropriate.
By this same method of interpretation, the eight branches of the *upavāsa* (fasting discipline) are explained.
Against this, what does the Master of the Sūtras rely upon to state his criticism? The Vaibhāṣika master refutes [this position], saying:
If one speaks according to the ultimate meaning (*paramārtha*), right view (*samyagdṛṣṭi*) alone should be called the path;
the other factors such as right thought (*samyaksaṃkalpa*) should not be called "factors of the path" (*mārgāṅga*).

Since they are nonetheless called "factors of the path," if we consider them from their own perspective, then according to conventional designation (*saṃvṛti-nāman*), the remaining seven should also be called the path.
Why is it said that these are "limbs of the path" (*mārgāṅga*) rather than the "path" itself?
It is because they apply only to lay practitioners (*upāsaka*), excluding those who are ignorant.
This constitutes the third [section], clarifying the person who receives the precepts.
Even one who has not received the status of a lay follower (*upāsaka*) may receive the one-day precepts (*upoṣadha*).
However, because the precepts cannot be obtained without first receiving the three refuges (*triśaraṇa*), it is said that they do not exist [for such a person].
If a person does not know that they must first receive the three refuges before the precepts can arise, [the precepts are not obtained].
Alternatively, if the preceptor forgets and does not confer the ordination,
yet merely recites the precepts for them, they still obtain the precepts;
through the power of their intention (*āśaya*), the restraint (*saṃvara*) is likewise generated.
Therefore, the *Vibhāṣā* (44) states:
"Some say it is also obtained;
that is to say, if one does not know whether the three refuges were received before or after the restraint."
Furthermore, if one forgets or errs and fails to confer the Three Refuges,
yet confers only the vows of discipline (*śīla*), the one who confers them incurs an offense. If, out of arrogance,
one does not receive the Three Refuges but receives only the vows of discipline, that person will certainly not obtain them.
Regarding the statement in the Sūtra that one becomes a lay follower (*upāsaka*) upon merely arriving [at the presence of the teacher],
this section below is the fourth, which clarifies the discipline (*saṃvara*) of the lay follower.
First, it clarifies the time when the precepts are generated.
Second, the interpretation of the scriptural text;
third, the elucidation of the three categories of precepts;
fourth, the elucidation of the essence of the three refuges.
Fifth, it clarifies abstaining from improper conduct;
sixth, it clarifies marrying without transgression;
seventh, it clarifies abstaining from falsehood and deception.

The eight prohibitions consist solely of abstaining from alcohol. Below this, the first section clarifies the time of receiving the precepts. From "Sogaka" onwards, all is the scriptural text. According to the scripture, it asks:
"If one has only received the Three Refuges but has not yet undertaken the Five Precepts, does one immediately become a lay follower (*upāsaka*)? Paramārtha says:
Mahānāman was a kinsman of the Buddha, being the son of Aniruddha’s paternal uncle.
When his elder brother, King Śuddhodana, renounced the world, he entrusted the kingdom to him.
The Buddha then taught Mahānāman the Dharma of the Three Refuges.

Regarding the statement that "the masters of foreign lands say that this alone constitutes [the status of a lay follower]," this recounts the response of the masters of foreign lands. These masters of foreign lands—namely, the masters of the Sautrāntika school from the Gandhāra region outside of Kaśmīra—maintain that by merely receiving these three refuges, one becomes a *triple-refuge upāsaka*.

When one receives the three refuges but has not yet undertaken the five precepts, it is only after the characteristics of the precepts are subsequently explained that one separately generates the specific precepts; these are called the five precepts of an *upāsaka*.
According to that school, the five precepts may be received in varying numbers, and in all such cases, the generation of the precepts is attained.

According to the account of the Master of that country, those in the kingdom of Kaśmīra hold that one who does not possess the five lay precepts (*upāsaka-saṃvara*) is not a lay follower (*upāsaka*). Thus,
apart from the five lay precepts, there is no such thing as being a lay follower.
"One must possess the five precepts to be called an upāsaka.
If that were so, it would contradict this sūtra.
Thus the foreign masters raise an objection.
If one must necessarily undertake the fivefold preceptual discipline (*pañca-śīla-saṃvara*) to be called an upāsaka,
then this would contradict the *Mahānāma-sūtra*.
That sūtra states that after receiving the three refuges and so forth, it simply says "up to" (*yāvat*).
This is what is meant by an upāsaka; it does not mean that one is called a lay follower (upāsaka) only upon the arising of the precepts.
This is not contradictory, because [the precepts] have already arisen.
The Kaśmīrī reply is:
What I have now stated does not contradict this *Mahānāma-sūtra*,
because at the time of receiving the three refuges and so forth, one has already undertaken the five precepts.
Regarding the time when the precepts are generated,
the masters of foreign lands ask whether it is fixed to a specific moment.
The verse says: "As for the statement 'up to those such as bhikṣus,' the verse answers.
The commentary says: "Because [the vow] is generated immediately upon [reaching] them."
This explains the first phrase.
It cites the *Mahānāma-sūtra* to clarify the time when the precepts are generated:
at the moment one is protected by the compassion [of the Buddha], one simultaneously generates the lay follower (*upāsaka*) discipline.
"This explains the sūtra, showing that at the time of manifesting the precepts, by uttering such terms as 'lay follower' (*upāsaka*), the discipline (*saṃvara*) is immediately produced.
This explains the verse clarifying the moment the precepts are generated. Furthermore, it interprets the preceding [verse] as citing the sūtra to provide a general exposition.
This concludes the brief summary. Furthermore, to resolve and re-explain this: at what point is the precept generated?
By what reasoning is it known that the precept is generated at that time?
It is known that the five precepts are generated at that very moment because of his own declaration using such terms as "lay follower" (*upāsaka*) and so forth.
If one does not undertake the precepts, how could they rightly call themselves a lay follower (*upāsaka*) and so forth? Furthermore, this passage is understood as belonging to what follows;
since he intends to further cite scriptural evidence, he first states his thesis.
According to this scriptural passage, even after one has received the three refuges, the precepts have not yet been generated;
it is only upon reaching the state of being protected by compassion that the precepts finally arise.
This is because the sutra further states, "having attained the five precepts."
How is it known that the mere utterance of the words "lay follower" (*upāsaka*) and so forth gives rise to the vow?

It is because another sutra states that after one has received the three refuges and been called a "lay follower," one further makes the personal vow: "From this time forth until the end of my life, I renounce living beings. The intention of this sutra is to explain that one renounces the five types of evil karma, such as killing; thus, the two characters for "killing" and so forth are omitted, and only "renouncing living beings" is stated.

Since one subsequently vows to abandon killing and so forth after the three refuges and other rites, one already obtains the five precepts at the time of receiving the three refuges and becomes a lay follower (*upāsaka*). It is not the case that merely taking the three refuges constitutes being a lay follower.
The scriptural passage cited here is abbreviated.
As stated in the *Abhidharmamahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 124, citing a sūtra:
"As it is said: 'I, so-and-so, take refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha; may the Honored One remember me.'"
"I am a lay follower (*upāsaka*).

From this day forth until the end of my life, I shall protect living beings and take refuge in purity. Furthermore, the *Prakaraṇapāda* of the *Abhidharmahṛdaya-śāstra* says: "As it is said: 'I, [name],'" and so forth.
I take refuge in the Buddha, the Honored One among two-legged beings;
I take refuge in the Dharma, the Honored One free from desire;
I take refuge in the Saṅgha, the Honored One among assemblies.
"I am an upāsaka. May it be known that for as long as life lasts, I renounce all killing of living beings and receive the three refuges with a pure mind.

Up to this third verbal utterance, one obtains the upāsaka discipline (*upāsaka-saṃvara*). The commentary explains: The *Abhidharmakośa* cites this in brief; it does not mention the first two sets of refuges and so forth, nor the purity of the subsequent refuge.
It should be understood that this refers only to the intermediate period;
from this point forward, etc.

It should be understood that following these three refuges and prior to the exposition of the characteristics of the precepts, the *Mahānāma-sūtra*— because it refers to the moment of formally undertaking the precepts— states only "one who calls himself a lay follower (*upāsaka*), etc."
Furthermore, because other sūtras state that after the precepts have been generated, one must make a formal vow and commitment,
they further say, "From this time forth," and so on.
Although such a person has already attained the state of necessarily possessing the discipline (*vinaya*), [the sūtra speaks thus].
Explaining the second phrase:
although he has already obtained the precepts at an earlier time by virtue of his own vow,
he has not yet fully understood the distinctions among the characteristics of those precepts.
In order to cause them to understand the training precepts of the five precepts,
he further explained the characteristics of the five types of precepts, such as abstaining from taking life, so that they would recognize and firmly uphold them.
Once they had received the full ordination (*upasampadā*) of a bhikṣu through one motion and three proclamations (*jñapti-tricarma*), [the procedure was completed].
Furthermore, he taught them the four grave rules of training (śikṣāpada) so that they would recognize and firmly uphold them; the same applied to the śrāmaṇeras.
First, they received the three refuges; although they had already obtained the precepts, [the teacher continued].
Furthermore, he explains ten kinds of precept-features to them so that they may firmly uphold them; this same principle should apply to the precepts of a lay follower (*upāsaka*).
Therefore, a lay follower must necessarily possess the five precepts.

One is not called a *upāsaka* (lay follower) merely by having received the three refuges without having undertaken the five precepts. Question: What is meant by "training rules" (*śikṣāpada*)? Answer: As stated in the first fascicle of the *Dharmaskandhapāda-śāstra*:
What is called "training" (*śikṣā*) refers to the state of one who has not yet perfected the five bases;
because they constantly, diligently, firmly, and correctly cultivate the application of effort (*prayoga*), it is called training.

What are called "bases" (*sthāna*) are precisely the abstention from killing and so forth; because these are the foundations upon which training relies, they are called bases of training (*śikṣāpada*). Furthermore, the very abstention from killing and so forth is itself called training.
It is also called a "basis" (*sthāna*), and thus it is called a "basis of training" (*śikṣāpada*).
The verse says: "The term 'reaching' (*prāpti*) refers to what is spoken in terms of that which can maintain [the training].
This is the second interpretation of the scriptural text.
The first two phrases constitute the Sautrāntika’s challenge based on scripture;
the third phrase provides the Sarvāstivāda’s comprehensive explanation. The treatise states:
"Up to the fourth [stage], one is able to train in the full measure."
This explains the first two lines.

The Sautrāntikas raise an objection, saying: "If all lay followers (upāsaka) possess the full restraint (saṃvara), for what reason did the Blessed One state in the context of the five precepts that there are four kinds of upāsakas?"
First, one who can train in one part,
meaning they train in one precept;
second, one who can train in a small portion.
That is to say, one trains in two precepts;
third, one is able to train in most parts,
namely training in three or four precepts.
Fourth, the ability to fulfill the training:
this refers to training in the five precepts.
Because one is able to maintain them to the full extent, one is called an upāsaka (lay follower).
This explains the subsequent phrase.
In the Sarvāstivāda school, which is consistent with the sūtras,
the term "learning" (śikṣā) is said to mean "upholding" (dhāraṇa).
This means that four types are taught in terms of their capacity for maintenance.
Although one may have previously fully received the fivefold discipline (*pañcāṅga-saṃvara*),
it may later be impaired or deficient due to encountering certain conditions.

Among them, some are able to uphold a single portion of the training rules (*śikṣāpada*), and so on, up to some who fully uphold all five branches; it is for this reason that such a statement is made.
Because they are able to uphold what was previously received, the term "able to train" (*śikṣate*) is used. Otherwise, this sutra would have stated "receiving a single portion" and so forth.
Why, then, is it said that they "train in one part" and so forth?

These four types [of upāsakas] are designated as such based merely on their ability to uphold [the precepts]. In reality, however, one is called an *upāsaka* (lay follower) by virtue of having received the three refuges and being fully endowed with the five precepts.
Regarding this point that such a tenet contradicts the sūtras,
the Sautrāntikas pose the challenge:
"In what way does it contradict the sūtras?"
The Sarvāstivādins raise an objection:
"Because no sūtra states that [the intermediate state] persists until the relinquishing of life.
The Sautrāntikas reply:
This means that no sutra states that the mere utterance of the words "I am a lay follower (*upāsaka*)" and so forth immediately brings about the five precepts.
Furthermore, this *Mahānāma-sūtra* does not state: "From this day forward, until the end of my life, I renounce [taking] life."
As for how the Sūtra explains this:
the Sarvāstivādins ask, "In the Mahānāma-sūtra,
it is said that [the opponent] contradicts the Sūtra by going beyond it."
The Sautrāntika response can be understood. However,
other sūtras state that this applies even to those who have already undertaken the five precepts.
The Sautrāntika school further cites other scriptural passages:
"Renouncing life" means that one would rather give up one's own life than abandon the True Dharma;
"taking refuge" means taking refuge in the Triple Gem; and "purifying."
This refers to the purification through pure faith in the Three Jewels; that is, the four purifications through realization (*catvāri avetyaprasādāḥ*).
Since they are now being cited in somewhat greater detail, "refuge" and "purification" have been added.
The rest of the text may be understood.
Furthermore, regarding the passage concerning "a portion" (*ekadeśa*) and so forth in relation to the observance or violation of the precepts,
the Sautrāntika school refutes the preceding interpretation that attempts to reconcile it with the sūtras.
Furthermore, regarding the explanation of "a portion of the training" and so forth in terms of upholding or violating the precepts:
that person who has received the precepts should not even question the Buddha,
much less should the Buddha provide an answer for them.
Why is this so? For who, having already understood the lay devotee’s (upāsaka) discipline as necessarily consisting of five branches,

would later— when observing or violating it— not understand the points of training (*śikṣāpada*), such that one might claim that observing only one and not the others constitutes "a single part" (*ekadeśa*) and so forth?
"Because he has already understood it himself, he should not be questioned.
Regarding the phrase "because he has not yet understood," and so forth up to the full explanation,
this is the Sautrāntika school’s own commentary on the scriptural text.
Because those who wished to receive the precepts did not understand the extent of the few or many rules of the upāsaka discipline, they questioned the Buddha:
"In how many ways can an upāsaka be able to train in the training rules?"
The Buddha replied, "There are four types of upāsakas, namely those who can train in one part, and so forth.
Those who had received the precepts were still unable to understand this;
they asked the World-Honored One again, "What is meant by 'one who can train in one part,' 'a small part,' and so on?"
The Blessed One answered at length as follows:
The intention of this sūtra is to explain four types [of precept-holders] for the sake of those who receive the precepts;
it does not refer to "a single portion" and so forth in terms of whether one upholds or violates them.
"If it were the case that one who lacks the restraint [of a lay follower] should also be subject to this [classification]," so says the Sarvāstivāda school,
using the examples of the bhikṣu and śrāmaṇera to refute the upāsaka.
For what reason is the number of precepts for a lay follower fixed at these specific limits?
The Sautrāntikas counter-charge that it is so because they are established by the power of the Buddha's teaching.
The Sarvāstivādins reply: "By the power of the Buddha's teaching, all [vows] possess their constituent parts.
If that is so, for what reason does it reach the point where one is no longer a bhikṣu and so forth?
The Sautrāntikas explain by way of analogy:
"I too, through the power of the Buddha's teaching, am called an upāsaka even though I lack the formal restraint."
Regarding those who are not bhikṣus and so forth:
according to the tradition of Kaśmīra, one becomes a lay follower (*upāsaka*) upon reaching [the age of] attainment.
This is the established tenet of the Kaśmīra school.
One must possess all five precepts to be designated a lay follower (*upāsaka*);
it is not permitted to become a lay follower while lacking any of the precepts.
Among these lay followers, some may even attain the superior grade (*adhimātra*).
This is the third [section], clarifying the three grades of precepts.
Because there are three grades of precepts corresponding to the three grades of the mind,
there are cases where a noble one (ārya) fulfills the lower grade, while an ordinary person (pṛthagjana) fulfills the higher grade.
Therefore, the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 117, states: "Thus it is asked:
Is it possible for a newly ordained bhikṣu to be endowed with the highest degree of restraint (*adhimātra-saṃvara*)?"
But does an Arhat achieve an inferior grade of restraint?
Answer: Yes.
That is to say, there is a newly ordained bhikṣu who, with a superior mind, initiates informative action and undertakes the various restraints.
There are Arhats who, by means of an inferior state of mind, initiate informative action and receive various vows;
likewise, a newly ordained bhikṣu may achieve a superior state of discipline.
Since an Arhat achieves only the lowest grade of restraint (*saṃvara*), according to this text, an Arhat does not obtain the precepts spontaneously.
Is it possible that one merely receives [the vows] until they become a lay follower (*upāsaka*)?
Below this, the fourth section clarifies the essence of the three refuges.
Question: Can one become a lay follower (*upāsaka*) by merely receiving the precepts for a lay follower without receiving the three refuges? Answer: No.
One does not become a lay follower (*upāsaka*), except in the case of one who is ignorant. Answer:
If a person knows they have received the three refuges (*triśaraṇa*) yet does not formally undertake them, they do not become a lay follower.
If a person does not know that they have previously received the three refuges,
and the preceptor who administers the precepts does not confer them for them,
the status of an upāsaka is not established. Thus, the *Vibhāṣā* (124) states:
Question: Can one obtain the vows of the upāsaka discipline without receiving the three refuges?
Some say that one cannot, because the reception of the three refuges serves as the gateway to this discipline.
It serves as a basis and as an application; thus,
some say it is indeterminate.
That is to say, if one does not know that one must first receive the three refuges before receiving the precepts,
yet receives the discipline out of faith in the precept master, that person obtains the discipline,
while the precept master incurs a transgression.
If one understands this correctly, the proper procedure is to first receive the three refuges and subsequently receive the vows of discipline;
yet, out of pride, they do not receive the three refuges and speak as follows:
Furthermore, one who should receive the precepts must rely on faith in the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha;
yet for one whose mind is entangled by pride,
even if they receive them, they do not truly obtain them.
Regarding those who take refuge, it is said that they are "endowed with the three refuges.
This clarifies the essential nature of the Three Jewels to which one takes refuge.
The treatise states: "As for taking refuge in the Buddha, [it refers to] 'the Buddha who is able to awaken to all things.'"
The commentary on the verse explains that taking refuge in the unlearned (*aśaikṣa*) dharmas that constitute Buddhahood clarifies the essence of the Buddha-jewel.
This means that one takes refuge solely in those untainted (*anāsrava*) unlearned dharmas by which one becomes a Buddha;

because these dharmas are preeminent, the body receives the name "Buddha. Alternatively, it is called "Buddha" because, by attaining those unlearned dharmas, the Buddha is able to awaken to all phenomena (*dharma*). As for "awakening to all": *(Note: The provided text ends abruptly with "As for awakening to all," indicating the source material was incomplete.)*
That is to say, untainted wisdom (*anāsravaprajñā*) that illuminates principles with clarity is called "awakening to all.

This refers to a limited portion of "all," because untainted wisdom takes only the [Four] Truths as its object. Alternatively, it is explained that all tainted wisdom (*sāsravaprajñā*) can awaken to all, because it exhaustively takes all phenomena as its objects.
This is because, by attaining the dharmas of one beyond training (aśaikṣa),
one possesses outflow-tainted wisdom (*sāsravaprajñā*) capable of awakening to all things. Furthermore, it is explained that both tainted and untainted wisdom (*anāsravaprajñā*),
according to their respective capacities, are termed "awakening to all."
Because one has attained the dharmas of one beyond training (aśaikṣadharma), these two kinds of wisdom are able to train in all things.
What are called the Buddha’s dharmas of one beyond training?
Question:
Regarding the statement "because they are equal before and after the attainment of the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) and so forth," the answer is: it refers to the knowledge of exhaustion,
the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*), and others within the Buddha’s body.
Furthermore, the five untainted aggregates (anāsrava-skandha) that accompany it are called "beyond training" (aśaikṣa); they do not refer to the tainted five aggregates of the physical body.
This is because [the state] prior to attaining Buddhahood and the state after attaining Buddhahood are similar [in this regard].
Regarding the question of whether one takes refuge in a single Buddha or all Buddhas,
the answer is: in principle, one should say that because their ultimate characteristics are without distinction.
In truth, one should say that one takes refuge in all Buddhas of the three periods of time.
Because the essential nature and characteristics of the untainted noble path of those Buddhas are no different,
taking refuge at one moment is itself taking refuge in all.
Regarding the phrase "those who take refuge in the Sangha do so because it is indestructible":
this explains the two kinds of dharmas that constitute the refuge in the Sangha, clarifying the essence of the Sangha Jewel. As for "taking refuge in the Sangha": [it refers to...]

This means that one universally takes refuge in the two types of untainted dharmas—those of the learners (*śaikṣa*) and those of the non-learners (*aśaikṣa*)—which constitute the Saṃgha; it is by virtue of attaining these dharmas that the Saṃgha is established as the eight kinds of persons (*pudgala*) consisting of the four paths and four fruits.
Question: Since the Sangha of those who have attained the purity of conviction (avetyaprasāda) is by its very nature indivisible,
does one take refuge in the Sangha of a single Buddha or in the Sangha of all Buddhas?

"Is it that you take refuge in the Saṃgha of disciples of the single Buddha Śākyamuni, or do you take refuge in the Saṃgha of disciples of all Buddhas of the three periods of time? Because they are the Saṃgha of the Buddha, it is called the Buddha-Saṃgha."
Regarding the statement that, in reality, one universally takes refuge in the Saṅgha-treasure as far as those who have attained direct vision,
the answer is:
in reality, one universally takes refuge in the Saṅgha of all Buddhas of the three periods of time.
This is because the Buddhas and the Saṃgha do not differ in essence or characteristic from the untainted (anāsrava) noble path.
Nevertheless, the Sūtra states that when the Buddha first attained enlightenment, there was as yet no Saṃgha.
The merchant caravan encountered the Buddha and received the Three Refuges from him.
The Buddha said to them,
"In the future, there will be a Saṃgha to whom you should take refuge."
That sutra merely demonstrates the Saṃgharatna as it will appear in the future:
the five bhikṣus, namely Ājñātakauṇḍinya and the others. Question: There are many kinds of Saṃgha; which Saṃgha is being referred to here?
Is the Buddha also included within that Saṃgha to which one takes refuge? The explanation states: among the Three Refuges, "Saṃgha" refers to the Śrāvaka Saṃgha.
Although the Buddha is likewise a member of the Noble Saṃgha, he is not a Śrāvaka Saṃgha.
Therefore, the *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya* (Xianzong lun), chapter twenty, states:
"There are many kinds of Saṃgha, namely: sentient beings, Śrāvakas, fields of merit, and the noble Saṃgha, etc.
Among these, the Buddha is not the Śrāvaka-Saṃgha; he may be considered another kind of Saṃgha."
Because it is naturally awakened, that which is now taken as refuge is the Saṃgha of Śrāvakas.
Regarding the taking of refuge in the Dharma, this refers to those who have reached the ultimate; thus, it is a universal refuge.
This explains the third phrase, clarifying the essence of the Jewel of the Dharma. As for "taking refuge in the Dharma": [it is]...
That is to say, taking refuge in nirvāṇa is precisely analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
It is the single characteristic of the quiescent extinction of the afflictions and the fruits of suffering within the continuums of oneself and others; it is virtuous and eternal.
Therefore, it is generally said that one takes refuge in the cessation [of suffering]. This indicates the cessation of the tainted (*sāsrava*) phenomena of sentient beings;
however, in reality, it also applies to taking refuge in the cessation of non-sentient phenomena.
Therefore, the *Vibhāṣā*, fascicle 34, states:
"One should say that [the object of refuge] is the cessation of all aggregates—both those within one's own and others' continuums, as well as those categorized as insentient.

If it were only the dharmas of those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) that constituted the attainment of the offense of immediate retribution (*ānantarya*)," [it would follow that such an offense could not be committed by a layperson].
The Master of the Treatise raises an objection,
or alternatively, the Sautrāntika school raises an objection:
"If the Buddha-body consists solely of the dharmas of one beyond training (aśaikṣa-dharma) and is not the birth-body (janma-kāya),..."
How is it that merely damaging the birth-body (*janma-kāya*) of the Buddha constitutes an immediate transgression (*ānantarya-karma*)?
Regarding the Vaibhāṣika statement, "Because one follows and destroys that [body]," the answer is as follows:
Because when that basis—the body born of an Aśaikṣa—is destroyed, those Aśaikṣa dharmas are also destroyed accordingly;
thus, by harming the body of birth, one incurs the immediate transgression (ānantarya).
However, upon consulting the root treatise regarding the Aśaikṣa dharmas of a Buddha:
The master of the treatise further raises an objection—
or rather, presents the objection of the Sautrāntika school—
yet upon examining the fundamental texts such as the *Ṣaṭpādābhidharma* (Six-Legged Treatises), one finds...
It is not seen that the mere unlearned dharmas (*aśaikṣadharma*) are called the Buddha;
rather, it is said that the unlearned dharmas can bring about the Buddha.
Since this does not exclude the body-born nature (*janmakāyadharmatā*) of the Buddha, [the Buddha's physical body is not denied].
It should be understood that the supporting basis (*āśraya*) and the birth-body (*janma-kāya*) are also both subsumed under the term "Buddha.
Therefore, within this context, the aforementioned objection—that damaging the Buddha’s birth-body would constitute an immediate transgression (*ānantarya-karma*)—is untenable.

Because it is admitted that the birth-body (*janma-kāya*) is also the Buddha; for if, according to my [opponent's] view, the birth-body which serves as the basis were not the Buddha, then when the Buddha and the Saṃgha abide in their present birth-bodies with mundane, outflow-tainted minds (*sāsrava-citta*), [they would not be Buddhas].
At that time, the manifest absence of the five untainted aggregates (anāsrava-skandha) would neither be the Saṃgha nor the Buddha.

Although it constitutes an offense, it does not fall within the category of phenomena because it is not a sentient being. Furthermore, one would have to maintain that the very possession of the bhikṣu precepts is itself the bhikṣu.
If you say that the precepts are the bhikṣu, then consider one who wishes to make offerings to a bhikṣu.
He merely makes offerings to fulfill the śīla of a bhikṣu;
he should not offer the four requisites to the physical body that serves as the basis for that śīla.
Since he is now making offerings to the body upon which the śīla depends, [he should do so].
Therefore, one should know that the body upon which [the precepts] rely is also a bhikṣu.
If one were to say that it is not an object of veneration because it is the physical basis for the precepts,
this would contradict worldly convention.

Because the world makes offerings to that body which is the basis for the precepts; likewise, those who desire to take refuge in the Buddha should also take refuge only in the dharmas of one beyond training (*aśaikṣadharma*) that constitute Buddhahood.
If it is said that one takes refuge only in the dharmas of the Buddha’s state beyond training (aśaikṣadharma),
this would again contradict worldly convention,
for we observe in the world that one pays homage by taking refuge in the person who produced the Buddha.
This would entail the fault of contradicting the world as understood by the Sarvāstivādins.
The author of the treatise maintains that the essential nature of the Buddha Jewel consists of the conditioned and untainted dharmas (*anāsrava-dharma*) within the Buddha’s body.
Furthermore, some teachers maintain that all contaminated (*sāsrava*) phenomena within the Buddha’s body constitute the essence of the Buddha Jewel;
others state that it extends up to the eighteen unique qualities (*āveṇika-dharma*).
These represent alternative views.
The intention of this master is to say that the essence of the Buddha Jewel consists of both the conditioned,
untainted virtues within the Buddha’s body and the tainted virtues within the Buddha’s body.
One does not take up the birth-body,
as it is not a merit; this differs from the position of the Master of Treatises.
Furthermore, regarding the inclusion of *āsrava* (outflows), this differs from the Sarvāstivāda school.

According to the *Śāsanapravartana-saṃgraha-śāstra* (*Zonglun lun*), the Mahāsāṃghika and other schools maintain that all Tathāgatas are devoid of *āsrava*-dharmas. Although there have been various differing explanations above, [the conclusion remains as follows].
A General Clarification of the Essential Nature of the Three Jewels to Which One Takes Refuge. Question:

Within the objects of refuge, why does the Sarvāstivāda school not mention the Pratyekabuddhas and Bodhisattvas? Explanation: As stated in the *Nyāyānusāra* (Treatise on the Principles), fascicle 38: [The text continues...]
That which is to be taken as refuge consists of the entirety of the truth of cessation and a portion of the truth of the path,
excluding the untainted merits of those in training belonging to the vehicle of the solitary realizers and the vehicle of the bodhisattvas.
For what reason are those dharmas not a refuge?
Because they cannot rescue one from the fear of birth and death;
that is to say, the pratyekabuddhas are unable to preach the Dharma or provide instruction to sentient beings to enable them to leave behind the fear of birth and death.
Because those in the stage of training (śaikṣa) do not transcend their initial resolve,
and because they lack the capacity to instruct others,
the dharmas of training and beyond-training within their own bodies cannot rescue or protect them, nor can they serve as a refuge; this is explained at length therein.
Regarding what constitutes the essence of this refuge: the question concerns the essence of that which takes refuge;
its essence is vocal intimation (*vāgvijñapti*).
Answer: This is based on the view that its essence consists of the vocal intimation (*vāgvijñapti*) by way of its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
If, however, its retinue is included, its essence consists of the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*).
Therefore, the *Nyāyānusāra* (Treatise on the Correct Principles), fascicle 38, states:
"Among these, the vocal intimation (*vāgvijñapti*) constitutes the essence [of the refuge],
because its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) consists in establishing a self-imposed vow."

If [the refuge] together with its retinue has the five aggregates as its substance, then since all verbal expressions of taking refuge are originated by the mind and are not separate from the mind—[one might ask: if the vocal intimation (*vāgvijñapti*) is taken as the substance of the refuge...
This directly contradicts the position of the *Vibhāṣā* commentators.
As the *Vibhāṣā*, fascicle 34, states:
"Regarding those who are able to take refuge..."
Some say it is name and so forth;
some say it is vocal action;
others say it is also bodily action.
Some say it is faith.
It should be stated as follows: it consists of the bodily and vocal actions, as well as the mental states and mental factors that give rise to them, along with their concomitants.
In all such cases, the wholesome five aggregates are the substance of the refuge; this is how it should be stated. This is the position of the *Vibhāṣā* commentators (*vibhāṣā-vādin*).
In the *Abhidharmakośa* and other texts, this corresponds to the "unorthodox" (non-definitive) view of the second master in the *Vibhāṣā*.
Regarding the attempt to reconcile [the views]: the explanation states that the intention of the commentator differs because he speaks according to his own inclination;
thus, the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* (Vibhāṣā) is not taken as the ultimate authority.

There is no need for such laborious reconciliation. Furthermore, it is explained that the master Vasubandhu, in order to instruct future disciples on what is right and wrong, recounted the incorrect tenets of the *Vibhāṣā*.
The Venerable Saṅghabhadra was unaware of this text and instead relied upon this very commentary.
If one follows the correct interpretation, which accords with the *Vibhāṣā*’s critical school (*pūrvapakṣa*), then what is the meaning of such refuge?
Question: Regarding the meaning of taking refuge, it is said that its meaning is "rescue" because it extends to all suffering. Answer:
To rescue, deliver, and liberate is the meaning of taking refuge;
for it is by means of those Three Jewels as the objects of refuge that all sentient beings are able to attain eternal liberation from all suffering.
Furthermore, the *Nyāyānusāra* (Treatise on the Correct Principle), fascicle 38, states:
"How can the noble dharmas of another's body and unconditioned wholesome phenomena serve as a refuge for one's own self?
It is because by taking refuge in them, one is able to extinguish the great terrors of the boundless wheel of birth and death."
Regarding the Blessed One’s statement that [this refuge] leads to liberation from all suffering:
this passage cites Buddhist sūtras as proof to contrast the false with the true.
The first two verses reveal the false refuges.
The final three verses clarify the correct refuge.
Driven by fear, most people in the world take refuge in various seers and spirits, garden deities, forest deities, deities of solitary trees, and *caityas*.
*Caitya* refers to the stūpas and temples of non-Buddhists; the phrase "and so forth" (*ādi*) includes other objects of false refuge as appropriate.
This object of refuge is neither superior nor venerable. Furthermore, it is explained that it is not superior because it cannot liberate one from the suffering of the three evil destinies.
Because they cannot liberate one from the suffering of the realms of humans and devas, they are called "non-supreme. Why is this?

It is because by relying upon these refuges, one cannot achieve ultimate liberation from all sufferings. Furthermore, it is explained that some, when oppressed by the suffering of enemies or bandits, flee into mountain valleys to escape such suffering.
Some, encountering the suffering of separation from loved ones, wander through gardens to dispel their grief and sensual desires;
others, driven by the pain of hunger, enter the thickets to gather what they can for survival.
Some, suffering from the inability to obtain what they seek and desiring to fulfill their wishes, pray to deities of solitary trees;
others, weary of present suffering and seeking future happiness, make offerings to the stūpas and temples of non-Buddhist heretics.
"Et cetera" means that those not yet mentioned are included here as appropriate.
The rest is explained as before. "All those who take refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha..."
Constantly observing the Four Noble Truths and so forth with wisdom, one knows suffering—that is, the truth of suffering;
one knows the origin of suffering—that is, knowing the origin of suffering is the truth of the origin; and one knows the permanent transcendence of all suffering.
To know this as the Truth of Cessation and to know the Eightfold Noble Path as the Truth of the Path—this Truth of the Path leads to the secure state of Nirvana; it is the most supreme refuge.
"Most Honored" (*agra*) means that one who is able to liberate [beings] from the suffering of the miserable realms is called "Most Victorious" (*jina*).

One who is able to liberate [beings] from the suffering of the happy realms is called "Most Honored. Because one can ultimately be liberated from all sufferings by relying upon this refuge, it is said that the meaning of "refuge" (*śaraṇa*) is "protection" (*trāṇa*).
It can liberate one from all sufferings;
therefore, taking refuge is the ultimate gateway to skillful means. (This concludes the section.)
Therefore, taking refuge serves as the preliminary gateway that leads to all the various sets of vows received from the eight classes of practitioners;
by means of it, one can give rise to the precepts and be forever liberated from all suffering.
Because if one does not take refuge, the precepts will not arise.
For what reason did the World-Honored One state that it is easy to avoid [sexual misconduct] and attain the status of a non-doer?
This is the fifth question clarifying the avoidance of sexual misconduct.
Among the eight classes of followers, for what reason did the Blessed One establish the training rule of abstaining from unchaste conduct specifically for the other six classes,
or for other bhikṣus, śrāmaṇeras, and upavāsakas?

Since only sexual misconduct is prohibited within the single restraint of the lay follower (*upāsaka*), the same principle should also be questioned regarding the precepts for a female lay follower (*upāsikā*). For now, let us take the male lay follower as the subject of inquiry;
alternatively, this may be understood by implication.
Alternatively, the term "lay follower" (*upāsaka*) also includes the female lay follower (*upāsikā*), because the essence of their precepts (*śīla-skandha*) is identical.
This answers the three points in the verse.
The Treatise says: "Up to 'one who does not engage in non-celibacy' (*abrahmacarya*)."
The first interpretation is most worthy of censure;
for sexual misconduct alone is universally condemned by the world, as the karmic path of illicit lust—such as violating another’s wife—induces rebirth in the evil destinies. Etc.
This refers to taking concubines and the like; it is not non-celibacy.
That is to say, when one engages in sexual desire that does not constitute non-celibacy, such bodily misconduct is not severely censured by the world.
It does not lead to rebirth in the miserable realms.
Furthermore, regarding the transition from sexual misconduct to the abandonment of unchaste behavior,
the verse is easy to explain.
Because sexual misconduct is easy to abandon, the Buddha prohibited it;
because abstaining from non-celibacy is difficult, he did not prohibit it for laypeople.
Furthermore, regarding those noble ones who have reached the stage where they will certainly never commit such acts again:
"Abstinence from [unwholesome acts] is attained" means that because the bodies of all noble ones (ārya) are endowed with untainted dharmas (anāsrava-dharma),
they invariably attain the restraint of abstinence (*virati-saṃvara*) regarding all sexual misconduct. This is the restraint of abstinence.
This refers to the vow not to engage in sexual misconduct and so forth;
it does not possess a separate substantial entity,
just as when people in the world have a nature that does not drink alcohol, this does not constitute a separate substantial entity.
Because noble ones (*ārya*) who have been born [in the world] also do not engage in such sexual misconduct;

since all noble ones, by their very nature, do not transgress that precept of a lay follower (*upāsaka*), it is said that noble ones can maintain natural morality (*prakṛti-śīla*). This is not the case, however, regarding the abstention from unchaste conduct (*abrahmacarya*).
Since noble ones who have not yet abandoned desire still possess wives,
the lay follower's precept (upāsaka-śīla) restricts one from sexual misconduct. If, however,
you persistently maintain that abstaining from non-celibate conduct constitutes the lay follower's precept, [then this would be untenable].
A noble one who has not yet transcended birth does not violate the lay follower’s discipline (*upāsaka-saṃvara*),
because they possess a wife.
Therefore, the *Nyāyānusāra* states:
If it were otherwise, those in training who have undergone rebirth would be unable to maintain the precepts of a lay follower (*upāsaka*).
This applies to all those who have previously received the attainment of restraint (*saṃvara*), as well as those who have not.
The following section concerns the sixth case where taking a wife does not constitute an offense;
this is the question itself.
In principle, one should indeed be able to attain the prātimokṣa vows.
Answer: It is acquired through that [rebirth-linking].
If that is so, why is one not a transgressor of the precepts later on?
Difficult.
The verse says: "As for reaching the point of violating the preceding precepts," the answer can be understood from the text.
Furthermore, the *Nyāyānusāra* (Treatise on the Principles of Correct Reasoning), fascicle 38, states:
"If one first marries a wife or concubine and subsequently receives the vows (*saṃvara*), the precept is still generated with respect to one's own wife and others.
This is because the Prātimokṣa vows of the upāsaka and other categories are acquired in relation to all sentient beings."

If it were otherwise, one would also not be transgressing the precept against sexual misconduct when engaging with one's own wife or concubine, or in an improper place, at an improper time, through an improper organ, or in an improper manner.
Since there would already be violations regarding what was previously undertaken,
there should be non-violations regarding what is newly undertaken;
for what reason, then, is it prescribed that one becomes a lay follower (*upāsaka*) through the observance alone?
Below this, the seventh section clarifies the avoidance of false speech.
Question:
Since there are four faults of speech, why is only one of them proscribed?
Regarding the statement, "It is also because of what was previously explained, namely, reaching the point of non-doing," the answer is:
it is because the three preceding causes only prohibit false speech.
The first cause is as explained previously.
Furthermore, the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 123, explains the second cause, stating:
"Some say that it is easy to guard against [the precept] by remaining free from false speech."
It is not apart from the other three;
that is to say, while living as a householder and managing servants and so forth,
it is difficult to distance oneself from the three [mental actions] such as divisive speech, as well as physical acts such as beating and the like.
Furthermore, the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* explains the third cause, stating: "Others further say:
if noble ones (*ārya*) do not violate the lay follower's precepts (*upāsaka-śīla*) throughout their successive births..."
A noble one (ārya) will certainly distance himself from the karma of false speech throughout his successive births, but not from other types of verbal karma. Why is this?
Because there are three other [types of] speech.
That is to say, they arise from greed, hatred, and delusion.
Although noble ones who have been reborn do not commit transgressions arising from delusion,
this is because such delusion is subsumed under the category of views (*dṛṣṭi*).
Because the Noble Ones have already severed [the defilements], those offenses arising from greed and hatred are not established for them.
Furthermore, there is another reason: because it is capable of preventing future transgressions, the fourth cause—the restraint of the eight classes of persons—is called "universal."
The remainder of the text may be understood.
Furthermore, for what reason does it reach the level of the lay practitioner's (upāsaka) discipline?
From here below, the eighth section prohibits the exclusive abstinence from intoxicants.
This is the question.
Who says that within this [context] one does not depart from the prohibitive offenses? Answer:
Regarding "abstaining from what constitutes a prohibitory offense": this is an inquiry.
It refers to abstaining from drinking alcohol.
[The] Explanation:
For what reason is it that, regarding those [precepts], one merely prohibits the drinking of intoxicants? [This is] the Objection.
The *Nyāyānusāra* asks:
"For what reason, among all those things that are free from natural transgressions (*prakṛti-sāvadya*),
are four established as the training rules (*śikṣāpada*) for a lay follower (*upāsaka*)?"
Nevertheless, among all the prohibitions against transgressions (*pratikṣepaṇasāvadya*), the lay practitioner's vow (*upāsaka-saṃvara*) prescribes only the abstention from drinking alcohol.
As the verse says: "As for the requirement to abstain from drinking alcohol..."
The answer can be understood from the text.
Among the prohibitions, the consumption of intoxicants is specifically restricted for lay followers (*upāsaka*) because of its grave nature;
the other prohibitions are not like this.
"How is it known that drinking alcohol is subsumed under the category of prohibitive offenses (*pratikṣepaṇa-sāvadya*)?
This is the question.
[The answer is: "Because within this [act], there is no actual [affliction] capable of producing a defiled mind."
Answer: This is because drinking alcohol lacks the characteristic of a natural transgression (*prakṛti-sāvadya*).
This is because all natural transgressions are committed only with a defiled mind (*kliṣṭa-citta*) and do not apply to other states of mind.
Drinking alcohol for the purpose of treating illness cannot be considered an intrinsic transgression (*prakṛti-sāvadya*) because it does not involve a defiled mind;
therefore, the *Nyāyānusāra* (Treatise on Right Reasoning), fascicle 38, states:
"Because within this [act] there is no characteristic of an intrinsic transgression."
What are the characteristics of natural offenses (*prakṛti-sāvadya*) and proscribed offenses (*pratikṣepaṇa-sāvadya*)?
The characteristic of a natural offense is that it is definitely not committed by those who have abandoned desire even before the precepts were established.
If one still commits such an act, it is called a *pratikṣepaṇa-sāvadya* (prohibited offense).
Furthermore, if an act is committed solely by relying on a defiled mind (*kliṣṭa-citta*), it has the characteristic of a *prakṛti-sāvadya* (inherent offense).
If it is also committed by relying on a non-defiled mind, it is called a *pratikṣepaṇa-sāvadya*.
"Is it not the case that one knows beforehand that [this] is precisely a defiled mind?
This is an objection.
"This is not a defiled mind because... This is the response: therefore, it is not a defiled mind.
Answer: Regarding those Vinaya-holders who say that one goes there to drink alcohol,
this is a statement of the Vinaya-holders' own words.
Drinking alcohol is a natural transgression (*prakṛti-sāvadya*).
Four proofs are cited in total;
this is the first proof establishing that drinking alcohol is a natural transgression.

The Buddha permitted [the consumption of intoxicants] as a secondary rule for those who were ill, except in cases of natural transgressions (*prakṛti-sāvadya*). Since there are instances where drinking alcohol is not permitted even for the sick,
one should know that drinking alcohol is subsumed under natural transgressions, O Upāli.
This is called "taking what is near.

Furthermore, the statement in the sūtra that this is subsumed under natural transgressions (*prakṛti-sāvadya*) serves as the second proof for the fact that even the very least amount must not be drunk.
There are extremely few cases where [the Buddha] did not explicitly forbid it, clearly knowing them to be natural transgressions (*prakṛti-sāvadya*).
Furthermore, regarding such acts as killing, even for the noble ones (*ārya*), [they remain prohibited].
The third is the proof through scriptural authority that there is no offense [in drinking].
This one is proven by reason:
drinking alcohol is a natural transgression (*prakṛti-sāvadya*).
This is because even noble ones (*ārya*) who have undergone rebirth do not commit such acts,
as in the case of killing and so forth.
Furthermore, it is because the Sūtra states that these constitute bodily misconduct (*kāyaduścarita*).
The fourth is the proof regarding bodily misconduct.
The Sūtra states that drinking alcohol is bodily misconduct.
If one possesses a mind free from defilement, how can it be termed misconduct?
Therefore, it is known that drinking alcohol is subsumed under the category of natural offenses (*prakṛti-sāvadya*).
Thus, the *Nyāyānusāra* (Treatise on Correct Reasoning), fascicle 38, states:
"The Sūtra says that there are four types of unwholesome conduct of the body."
From killing up to drinking alcohol,
those that are not to be obstructed (anāvṛta) are subsumed under misconduct (*duścarita*).
According to the masters of the Abhidharma, this is because they constitute the commission of natural transgressions (*prakṛtisāvadya*).
From this point downward, the masters of the Abhidharma synthesize the preceding four proofs.
This specifically synthesizes the first proof concerning the exclusion of the drinking of intoxicants as a natural transgression (*prakṛti-sāvadya*);
that is to say, the drinking of various intoxicants is not a natural transgression.
However, for the sake of the sick, all prohibitions except for those concerning natural transgressions (*prakṛti-sāvadya*) are universally relaxed.
This implies that drinking [alcohol] is permitted as it is not a natural transgression;
were it a natural transgression, the Buddha would not have permitted it.
Furthermore, at another time, the Buddha prohibited the drinking of alcohol.
There were members of the Śākya clan who, being afflicted by illness, were unable to drink;
however, because they might commit a natural transgression (*prakṛti-sāvadya*) as a consequence, the Buddha prohibited drinking for their sake.

Furthermore, regarding the statement that it causes intoxication even when the amount is as small as what might stick to the tip of a blade of *kuśa* grass, this refers generally to the second proof of the minimum quantity not being drunk.
Because the degree of intoxication is indeterminate, the minimum quantity is prohibited; for example, just as with one's natural disposition, drinking even a small amount may lead to intoxication.
The purpose of the prohibition against drinking in the Sūtras lies herein:
it does not mean that drinking is a natural transgression (*prakṛti-sāvadya*) merely because the Sūtras prohibit it.
For instance, there are types of liquor which, even when consumed in large quantities, do not cause intoxication.
The principle that drinking a small amount when ill should also be understood as permissible applies here as well.
Furthermore, regarding the statement that "for all noble ones (*ārya*), there is no fixed measure," this explains the third sūtra,
establishing that one does not incur an offense through birth [in such a state].
Because the noble ones possess a sense of shame and dread,
and because they fear losing right mindfulness,
all noble ones refrain from drinking alcohol.
One should not drink even a small amount,
because, like poison, its dosage is indeterminate;
it is not a natural transgression (prakṛti-sāvadya) that noble ones (ārya) would not drink.
Therefore, the *Vibhāṣā* (123) states:
"Other masters say that a noble one (*ārya*) will certainly never drink alcohol even after being reborn.
Even in the state of infancy or nursing, though a foster mother might forcibly drip [liquor] into his mouth with her finger..."
Because one lacks self-mastery, there is no fault [in the case of unintentional consumption].
However, as soon as one possesses the capacity for discernment, even if encountering powerful external conditions, one would never drink it even for the sake of protecting one's body or life;
therefore, among the prohibitive offenses (*pratikṣepaṇa-sāvadya*), the precept against alcohol stands alone.
Furthermore, the sutra states that all these [prohibitions] are natural offenses (*prakṛti-sāvadya*).
This universally establishes the fourth [category] as a physical misconduct (*kāya-duścarita*).
As the sūtra says, drinking alcohol is a physical misconduct.
Alcohol is the basis for all heedless and unwholesome conduct;
because of drinking alcohol, one gives rise to physical misconduct.
Therefore, it is said that drinking alcohol is a bodily misconduct (*kāyaduścarita*).
It is not a bodily misconduct by virtue of being a transgression by nature (*prakṛtisāvadya*);
rather, it is designated as a distinct "basis for negligence" (*pramādasthāna*) specifically because of drinking alcohol.
The other four [unwholesome actions], such as killing and so forth, are not established as "bases of negligence" because they are all natural transgressions (*prakṛti-sāvadya*).
Therefore, the *Nyāyānusāra* (Treatise on Reasoning), fascicle 38, states:
"Alternatively, the drinking of various liquors is called a 'misdeed' (*duścarita*) because it is a basis of negligence."
Because it is not an intrinsic offense (*prakṛti-sāvadya*), this alone is designated by the name "basis of negligence" (*pramāda-sthāna*);

whereas killing and so forth are intrinsic offenses. Furthermore, another interpretation of the sūtra holds that only that which arises from a defiled mind (*kliṣṭa-citta*) is called "bodily misconduct" (*kāya-duścarita*).
Although it may appear that drinking alcohol is free from defilement and is clearly not an unwholesome act,
it is nevertheless said that through repeated practice, it increases and becomes more intense.
The above constitutes four proofs that apply generally to those who uphold the Vinaya;
now, furthermore, it applies generally to the obstacle of falling into the evil destinies.
Thus, the *Nyāyānusāra* (Treatise on Right Reasoning), fascicle 38, states:

Some maintain that because the sūtras state that habitual practice can cause one to fall into the evil destinies—as is the case with killing and so forth—drinking various types of alcohol is therefore subsumed under natural transgressions (*prakṛti-sāvadya*).
To this, we now respond: when the sūtras state that habitual practice leads to falling into the evil destinies, [it refers to specific cases].
It is shown that frequent drinking of alcohol causes various unwholesome states within the body to continue and evolve, thereby leading to rebirth in the evil destinies;
furthermore, it can trigger the karma for the evil destinies, thereby leading to rebirth in those evil destinies.
Or it may cause the already arisen karma leading to the miserable realms to increase and flourish;
by means of alcohol, one gives rise to karma that causes falling into the miserable realms.
In reality, however, drinking alcohol itself does not directly summon rebirth in the miserable realms.
Furthermore, the *Nyāyānusāra* states:
"We also observe that some say that cutting green grass and the like causes one to fall into the evil destinies;
therefore, this provides no proof that drinking various types of alcohol is subsumed under the category of natural transgressions (*prakṛti-sāvadya*)."
It is as explained extensively therein.
Regarding the statement in the Sūtra, "up to for what purpose is it spoken," this is because,
in order to explain the drinking of alcohol, the various synonyms for alcohol are interpreted.
Regarding whether it is permissible or impermissible to drink, the Sūtra speaks of *surā* and other liquors; by what meaning is this explained?

Based on the Sūtra, a question is raised: furthermore, it is interpreted as citing the Sūtra to prove that alcohol is a basis for negligence (*pramāda-sthāna*) and is capable of producing manifold evils.
Therefore, the question arises:
"Because the fermented food becomes wine and reaches its locus of dependence.
The answer is: "The fermented food becomes wine."
Rice, barley, and the like are called *sura*;
those produced from other substances, such as roots and stalks, are likewise [called *surā*].
It is called *madya* (intoxicating liquor).
This refers to the aforementioned two types of liquor when they are either not yet fermented,
or when, having been fermented, they have deteriorated and can no longer cause intoxication.
This is not what is prohibited;
it is not called *madya*.
That which causes intoxication is called *madya* liquor.
To eliminate the redundant position, one should re-establish *madya*. There should be an objection: "In this context, one should have spoken only of *madya* (intoxicant);
why speak separately of *sura* and *maireya*?"
To resolve this objection, it is said: "However,
although betel nut, millet, and the like can also cause a slight,
momentary intoxication, they do not lead to heedlessness."
Because it is permitted to eat,
there is no violation of the precepts;
it is for the sake of distinguishing that case [that this is stated].
Next, the *surā* and *maireya* liquors are explained.
Because they cause extreme intoxication, the first fascicle of the *Dharmaskandha-pāda-śāstra* states:
"As for all 'liquors,' this refers to *surā* liquor."
Regarding *meraya* liquor and *madhu* liquor:
*surā* liquor refers to rice,
barley, and so forth, that have been steamed or boiled according to the prescribed method.
Mixing it with the juice of yeast and malt,
one throws in various medicinal ingredients;
through fermentation, it is fully prepared.
Regarding the flavors of alcohol—
its color, aroma, and taste— drinking it so as to become dazed and intoxicated is called *surā* liquor.
*Maireya* refers to the juices of various roots, stalks, leaves, flowers, and fruits.
Without using malt or yeast,
yet through the process of fermentation, the color, fragrance, and flavor of wine are fully realized.
That which, when drunk, causes stupor and intoxication is called *madya* (intoxicating liquor). The term *madhu* refers to grape wine;
alternatively, *sura* and *madya* liquors that cause intoxication when drunk are collectively termed *mada*.
The *Nyāyānusāra* (Treatise on Right Reasoning), fascicle 38, explains the names of various liquors;
while there are not no slight differences,
it is largely identical to the *Dharmaskandha* (Aggregate of Dharmas).
Although drinking these various liquors constitutes a prohibited offense (*pratikṣepaṇa-sāvadya*),
it leads to negligence and the extensive commission of manifold evils;
therefore, the World-Honored One strictly prohibited the drinking of all liquors in order to effect their thorough cessation.
Therefore, it is said that this alcohol is a basis for heedlessness (*pramāda*).
All unwholesome actions are called heedlessness;
because alcohol is the locus upon which heedlessness depends, it is termed a "basis for heedlessness."

The Third Part of the Fourth Chapter on the Analysis of Karma.

Regarding the phrase "this distinct liberation [extends] even to the other two," this marks the fifth major section below, which distinguishes the acquisition of the three types of restraint (*saṃvara*).
Among these, first, it clarifies the similarities and differences regarding the attainment of states;
second, it clarifies the factors and causes for sentient beings;
third, it clarifies the attainment of evil and intermediate states. Below this, it clarifies the similarities and differences regarding the attainment of states.
Question: When one obtains one of these three types of restraint from that source, does one also obtain the other two? If not, [why is this so?]
Answer: "What is it? is an inquiry.
The verse says: "Regarding the attainment of dhyāna and the untainted [attainments]. Answer:
The first two lines clarify prātimokṣa.
The final two lines clarify the meditative absorption (*samādhi*) and the path (*mārga*).
The *Śāstra* states: "As for 'attained subsequently,' this explains that [the restraint] is obtained from all [beings], distinguishing it from the *prātimokṣa*."
This is obtained from the point of departure regarding the root, the preliminary application, and the subsequent conclusion of all that is evil;
that is to say, by undertaking virtuous precepts and thereby abandoning the root, the preliminary application, and the subsequent conclusion of evil.
One can still obtain virtuous restraint even from a basis for generating evil.
Regarding "obtained from two," this refers to obtaining it from both natural transgressions (*prakṛti-sāvadya*) and proscribed transgressions (*pratikṣepa-sāvadya*).
This explains what is obtained from the two.
This means it is obtained from two categories:
first, from the category of sentient and non-sentient objects;

second, from the category of fundamental transgressions (*prakṛti-sāvadya*) and prohibitory transgressions (*pratikṣepaṇa-sāvadya*). Furthermore, another interpretation states that the "two categories" refers to: [the rest of the sentence follows].
There are two types of pairs:
first, the category of sentient beings;
second, the category of non-sentient things.
First, the category of natural offenses (*prakṛti-sāvadya*);
second, the category of proscribed offenses (*prajñapti-sāvadya*). Furthermore, another interpretation states that the two categories consist of:
first, the category of sentient beings who can commit both natural and proscribed offenses.
There are two types of non-sentient objects that can give rise to natural transgressions (*prakṛti-sāvadya*) and proscribed transgressions (*pratikṣepa-sāvadya*).

Now, because one who receives the virtuous precepts is able to remain free from both natural and proscribed transgressions, the virtuous precepts are generated anew in relation to those two types of objects from which natural and proscribed transgressions would otherwise arise.
Therefore, the *Nyāyānusāra* (Treatise on Correct Reasoning), fascicle 39, states:
"Regarding sentient beings, natural offenses refer to actions such as killing;
prohibitive offenses refer to such things as staying in the same room with a woman."
Non-sentient natural transgressions refer to stealing external property;
prohibited transgressions refer to such acts as digging the earth or cutting living grass.
Regarding the phrase "from those obtained in the present to the realm of sentient beings": it refers to [the fact that] these extend from the present life to the sphere of sentient beings.
The Śrāvaka obtains this prātimokṣa from the present;
that is to say, it is acquired from the present aggregates (skandha), bases (āyatana), and elements (dhātu) within the three periods of time,
and not from the past or the future.

Why is this? Because this restraint operates toward presently existing sentient beings, and it also operates toward the bases upon which presently existing sentient beings depend. Regarding "it operates toward presently existing sentient beings":
This means that the precepts are generated from the side of sentient beings.
For example, one incurs an offense by failing to protect sentient beings through such acts as sexual misconduct;

conversely, one generates the precepts by refraining from sexual misconduct and so forth through the protection of sentient beings, as appropriate to each case. This applies to those [precepts] that function with respect to the current bases of sentient beings.
The basis for sentient beings refers to the internal body;
it is the place upon which sentient beings depend.
This refers to the external vessel-world as the locus for the support of currently existing sentient beings.
One acquires this precept from the internal body that serves as the support for currently existing sentient beings;
it is just as one incurs an offense from its locus when performing acts such as killing.
If one receives the precepts by abstaining from killing and so forth based on their respective supports,
then according to the case: if it concerns the dwelling places of currently existing sentient beings,
one acquires these precepts with respect to the external receptacle-world that serves as the dwelling place for those currently existing sentient beings.

Just as one incurs an offense from the place where one dwells when digging the earth and so forth, if one does not dig the earth and so forth, the precept arises from that same place of dwelling according to what is appropriate. Coming and going are not themselves sentient beings.
Furthermore, it is not a place upon which sentient beings rely;
therefore, one cannot generate the prātimokṣa vows.
Thus, the Nyāyānusāra states:
The "abodes of sentient beings" refers to all sentient beings and the bases upon which they rely,
manifesting as the aggregates (skandhas), sense bases (āyatanas), and elements (dhātus).
The internal refers to that which sentient beings rely upon;
the external is called that in which sentient beings dwell.
This is because it does not pertain to the past or the future. Question: If one acquires [something] from a present sentient being, is it like stealing an object belonging to a present stūpa?
The *Vibhāṣā* (113), in the opinion of the master of the definitive interpretation (*viniścayavādin*), states:
