"One who speaks thus incurs an offense in the presence of the Buddha; according to that correct principle, the offense is incurred in the presence of a past Buddha."

How can it be said that the offense is incurred toward the currently existing sentient being? The commentator explains: according to the reasoning of the *viniścaya* (the adjudicating school), the offense should logically be incurred in relation to the present guardian;
yet, it is stated that the offense is incurred toward the Buddha.

Because the gift was made to the Buddha, the object is manifested as being of great importance; thus, it is attributed to the Tathāgata. Furthermore, another interpretation explains that the intention of the commentator is to state that the two gates of demerit and merit are not always equal.
If one discusses the arising of the precepts, they are obtained in the presence of sentient beings.
If one discusses the determination of the offense, there is no hindrance; it may also be obtained from a past Buddha.
If one has attained meditative absorption (dhyāna), how much more so from a prohibited offense (pratikṣepaṇa-śīla)?
This explains that [the vow] is obtained from the root [offense].

If one attains meditative concentration or the path, it should be understood that the ethical discipline of concentration or the path is acquired solely from the point where the fundamental courses of action (*mūlakarmapatha*) are initiated;
it is not even acquired from the points of the preliminary application (*prayoga*) or the subsequent conclusion (*pṛṣṭha*) of those actions.

Moreover, since this restraint is obtained even from the point where one commits a *pratikṣepaṇa-sāvadya* (prohibited offense), this is an instance of citing a heavy case to illustrate a light one. Furthermore, it is explained that because the training rules for the *prātimokṣa-saṃvara* (individual liberation restraint) are established by the Teacher’s prohibition of prohibited offenses.

From the point of a prohibited offense (*pratikṣepaṇa-sāvadya*), one acquires the restraint of prohibition (*pratikṣepaṇa-śīla*). Because the non-informative (*avijñapti*) restraints of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) and the path (*mārga*) do not prohibit prohibited offenses by their very nature, there is no separate restraint of prohibition for them;

since there is no separate restraint of prohibition, one does not acquire it from the point of a prohibited offense. Question: Why is it that the Prātimokṣa restraint is also acquired from the points of preliminary action (*prayoga*) and subsequent action (*pṛṣṭha*), whereas the restraints of meditative concentration and the path are not? Answer: It is explained that the Prātimokṣa restraint prohibits offenses through the formal preceptual injunctions regarding preliminary and subsequent actions.

The non-informative [action] (*avijñapti*) of the meditative and path restraints (*dhyāna-mārga-saṃvara*) arises from the preparatory (*prayoga*), the subsequent (*pṛṣṭha*), and the actual state (*maula*).

Therefore, it is not acquired during the preparatory or subsequent stages of the non-restraint (*asaṃvara*). Furthermore, regarding the restraint in the state of distraction (*vikṣiptāvasthā*), within that distracted state, there are three phases: the preparatory, the fundamental, and the subsequent.
In all cases, it is possible for the observance of a distinct restraint (*virati-saṃvara*) to be present,
just as the restraints of a *śrāmaṇera* and so forth exist during the preparatory stages (*prayoga*) of receiving the full ordination (*upasaṃpadā*).
At the moment of acquiring the precepts, one obtains them even in relation to the three types of occasions where evil arises.
The restraint of meditative concentration (*samādhi-saṃvara*) arises solely during the fundamental state (*maula*) within meditative concentration;
because it is restricted to the fundamental state itself, it does not exist during the preparatory (*prayoga*) or subsequent (*pṛṣṭha*) stages,
as this precept does not exist prior to or after the concentration.
Therefore, at the time of obtaining the precepts, they are acquired solely with respect to one type of unwholesome locus.
Thus, the *Nyāyānusāra* states:
"If one obtains the dhyāna-restraint or the untainted (anāsrava) restraint, it should be known that this occurs only from the fundamental courses of action (*maula-karmapatha*)."
Because within meditative concentration (*samādhi*), there exists only the fundamental path of action (*maula-karmapatha*);
it is not obtained from the preceding or succeeding preparatory stages (*sāmantaka*).

This is because when one is in a state of concentration, only the fundamental [path] exists, whereas in a non-concentrated state, this restraint (*saṃvara*) does not exist. Furthermore, regarding the restraint in the state of distraction, it exists within the distracted state itself.
Because there are the preparatory, the fundamental, and the subsequent stages,
the attainment of the precepts occurs throughout these three types of arising;
the restraint of the meditative state is present within that meditative state itself.
There is no preparatory action (*prayoga*) or subsequent action (*pṛṣṭha*), because the arising [of the act] is itself the fundamental action (*maula*).

At the time of obtaining the precepts, one obtains them only with respect to a single type of unwholesome basis. Furthermore, both the precepts of liberation (*prātimokṣa-śīla*) and the precepts of meditative concentration (*dhyāna-śīla*) are alike in their opposition to and elimination of evil.
Because evil and the non-restraint of scattering both belong to the desire realm,
they are close to one another in character and are difficult to guard against.
Therefore, one obtains the *prātimokṣa* (discipline of restraint).
This is obtained in relation to the three types of occasions for the arising of evil,
because evil and the discipline of meditative concentration (*dhyāna-saṃvara*) do not belong to the same realm (*dhātu*).
Because they are far removed from one another and because they are easy to guard against,
one attains the precepts of meditative concentration.
"Only from one kind does it arise; it is obtained at the place of evil.
From "from that which is constant" up to "obtained from the aggregates, bases, and elements" explains how it is obtained from that which is constant.
This means that because it is obtained from the aggregates (skandha), bases (āyatana), and elements (dhātu) of the three times, it is called "obtained at all times. Question:

Why is it that the prātimokṣa is obtained only in the present, while the two types of restraint—meditative (dhyāna) and path (mārga)—pertain to the past and future as well? Answer: The prātimokṣa discipline is obtained by relying on the formal instruction of the teaching.
The intent of the teaching is solely to prevent [unwholesome conduct] in the present; therefore, it arises only in the present.
The two types of restraint—those of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and the Path (*mārga*)—are not received based on formal instruction.

Because they arise in accordance with the mind, they extend to all three periods of time. Furthermore, another interpretation holds that the power of the restraint that functions in accordance with the mind is particularly strong.
Because it universally protects the three periods of time, it is acquired with respect to the aggregates (skandha), bases (āyatana), and elements (dhātu) of the three periods;

because the specific vows are not thus, they are acquired only with respect to the present. Furthermore, another explanation is that this precept is accomplished together with the mind throughout all three periods of time.
The morality concomitant with the mind (citta-samprayukta-śīla) is acquired in relation to the aggregates, bases, and elements (skandha-āyatana-dhātu) across all three time periods;
because the prātimokṣa is not so, it is acquired only in the present.
Therefore, the *Nyāyānusāra* states: "From that which is constant."
This means it is obtained from the aggregates (skandha), bases (āyatana), and elements (dhātu) of the past, future, and present.
Alternatively, it is explained that the mind concomitant with this precept is able to take the three periods of time as its object.
The precept coexistent with the mind can prevent [unwholesome conduct] across the three periods of time by the power of the mind;
this is because the precept exists simultaneously with that mind as its cause,
and its power is consequently strong.
The vows pertaining to the three periods of time encompass the aggregates, bases, and elements;
the Pratimokṣa is not like this,
as it prevents only the present.

It is obtained only in the present moment. Furthermore, it is explained that just as with the mind associated with the precepts, both the mind and the precepts sever [the defilements] across the three periods of time;
for it is said that the restraint of discipline severs the unwholesome precepts of desire and the afflictions that give rise to them.
By this clear knowledge, one knows that the precepts sever the three periods of time;
for it is through the precepts conjoined with the mind that one is able to sever the three periods of time.
It also extends to the attainment of dharmas of the three periods of time;
the prātimokṣa is not so, and therefore it is attained only in the present,
as it is not capable of severing [defilements].
Regarding this distinction concerning the preparatory (*prayoga*) and subsequent (*pṛṣṭha*) stages:

one should formulate four logical alternatives (*catuṣkoṭi*) based on the difference in the spheres of origin for the Prātimokṣa restraint in relation to the two restraints of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) and the Path (*mārga*).
There are aggregates, bases, and elements from which one can obtain only the prātimokṣa restraint, but not the other two restraints—those of meditative concentration (dhyāna) and the Path (mārga).
This can be understood by reflecting upon it through the four logical alternatives (catuṣkoṭi).
In the fourth statement, the nature of prohibitory offenses (*pratikṣepaṇa-sāvadya*) is not mentioned, as it is omitted for brevity.

Furthermore, in the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 120, regarding the first statement of the fourfold classification, the mention of prohibitory offenses is likewise omitted and not discussed.
Regarding the phrase "not [protecting] the present while correctly attaining [the restraint]," the author of the treatise rebuts the first and third clauses, stating:
"At the time one is correctly attaining the wholesome restraint (*śīla-saṃvara*), it is impossible for a present unwholesome course of action (*akuśala-karmapatha*) to exist."
Furthermore, why is it said that [the first category] includes the preparatory acts, the subsequent acts,
and all prohibitive offenses (*pratikṣepaṇa-sāvadya*)?
The third phrase refers to the present fundamental paths of action,
as well as the preliminary applications,
the subsequent consequences, and all prohibitive offenses (*pratikṣepaṇa-śikṣāpada*).
Having finished the recitation, he says correctly:
"Therefore, the first phrase should state:
from the present preparatory stage, the subsequent stage, and the points concerning various prohibitory offenses."

The third phrase should be stated as "from the present fundamental path of action. Herein, for now, regarding the first and third phrases, in actual fact, the word "place" (*sthāna*) should be added to all four phrases.

The second phrase should be stated as: namely, the fundamental paths of action (*maula-karmapatha*) of the past and future. The fourth phrase should be stated as: namely, from the preliminary (*prayoga*), the subsequent (*pṛṣṭha*), and the prohibited offenses (*pratikṣepaṇa-sāvadya*) of the past and future.
Immediately after the conclusion, it further states:
"If one considers the arising of the precepts, they pervade the three periods of time;
however, if one discusses their function of guarding, one should speak only of guarding against the future."
It should certainly not be said that [the meditative absorption] protects against past or present faults;
for the past has already ceased and the present has already arisen.
Because there is no need for such a defense, the *Nyāyānusāra* (The Correct Principle) offers this rebuttal:
"Since the terms 'course of action' (*karmapatha*) and so forth are applied to the courses of action themselves,
there is no fault in the meaning of the preceding four propositions."
By this same principle, it also applies to the protection against past and present courses of action (*karmapatha*),
and not merely to the future;
for the term "courses of action" and so forth refers to their bases (*adhiṣṭhāna*).
If it were otherwise, one would have to say that restraint merely protects against the future;
for restraint is only able to prevent future offenses from arising, and does not protect against those of the past or the present.

Because restraint that has already ceased or has already arisen lacks the function of prevention with respect to those [objects], it is explained that the term "unwholesome courses of action" (akuśala-karmapatha), which refers to the dependent,
is used here for the objective bases (ālambana) that serve as the support for the arising of such unwholesome courses of action.
Because the precepts are generated from the objective bases that serve as the supports for unwholesome courses of action and so forth,
it is said that the precepts are generated from unwholesome courses of action and so forth;
therefore, there is no fault in the meaning of the preceding four propositions.

In this way, the principle that the objective bases for unwholesome courses of action pertain to all three time periods also applies to the prevention of unwholesome courses of action in the past and present;
for when one generates restraint toward the objective bases of unwholesome courses of action in the past and present, [the restraint is established].
That is to say, one guards against the bases and objects of unwholesome courses of action in the past and present,
so as not to allow unwholesome karma and the like to arise.
It also speaks of the protection against unwholesome courses of action (*karmapatha*) in the past and present;
for by the term "courses of action" and so forth,
it refers to the objective spheres that serve as the bases for those unwholesome courses of action.

If one were to explain the guarding of the unwholesome paths of action solely in terms of their essential nature as dependent factors, rather than in terms of the bases and objects upon which they depend,
then it would follow that one should say only future phenomena guard only future phenomena.
The ethical discipline (*saṃvara*) is able to prevent future transgressions from arising; it does not,
however, prevent the actual entities of unwholesome paths of action (*karmapatha*) in the past or present,
for those of the past have already ceased.

[The opponent argues: "Since [the unwholesome state] has already arisen in the present, restraint has no function of prevention regarding it, as it cannot cause it not to arise. The *Abhidharmakośa* master refutes this, saying:
"There is no doubt regarding the meaning if one simply adds the word 'occasion' (*sthāna*). Why then do you labor so extensively to provide an alternative interpretation?"
Could one possibly obtain restraint by arising from those worldly dharmas,
such that it would prevent those worldly evil courses of action and so forth?

Although the arising of the precepts extends throughout the three periods of time, while the prevention of transgressions exists in all times, the actual prevention occurs only with respect to the future.
To raise an objection and thereby prevent it in the future:
this is indeed exactly as you have stated.
Regarding those who have attained [realization], is there any difference among them?
This is the second [section], clarifying the factor of sentient beings as the cause.
Question: Do all those who acquire restraint (*saṃvara*) or non-restraint (*asaṃvara*) do so with respect to all sentient beings and with respect to all seven branches of body and speech?
Is there a difference based on all superior, middling, and inferior causes?
Furthermore, regarding the interpretation that restraint (*saṃvara*) and non-restraint (*asaṃvara*) arise toward all sentient beings,
is there a difference in terms of their factors (*aṅga*) and causes (*hetu*)?
This is the response from one who maintains that there is indeed a distinction.
"What are the characteristics of this difference?
is the inquiry.
The verse says: "Regarding sentient beings, factors, and non-causes.
Within this response in verse form, the first two lines clarify the discipline (*saṃvara*).
The final two lines clarify non-restraint (*asaṃvara*).
The *Śāstra* states: "As for what is explained up to the last three causes," this is an explanation of the preceding two lines.
The Prātimokṣa restraint is necessarily obtained from all sentient beings; there is no principle for it to be obtained from only a few.
As for the seven branches of body and speech, these are not fixed: some are obtained from all seven branches of body and speech.
This refers to the bhikṣu restraint.
The term "bhikṣuṇī" is not mentioned because the seven branches are the same, or because it is implied by the mention of the other.
It is obtained through four types of branches: three from the body and one from speech.
This refers to the other six types of restraint, such as those of the śrāmaṇera and so forth;
for herein, only the seven fundamental courses of action are designated as the "limbs of restraint. Furthermore, whether these are superior, middling, or inferior is likewise not fixed.
Although there are two types of causes, this verse refers to the latter three causes;
because they do not arise simultaneously, their distinctions can be discerned.
Alternatively, there is a class [of persons] who reach the level of the *śrāmaṇera* vows.
The explanation regarding the person is now clearly presented;

the correlation and interpretation may be understood [thereby]. Question: As stated in the *Saṃyuktābhidharma-hṛdaya-śāstra* and the *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* (117), if one obtains the restraint (*saṃvara*) with respect to all sentient beings...
As for the claim that there is no such category as "arising from all causes but not consisting of all factors," does this not contradict the present treatise?
The explanation is: the *Mahāvibhāṣā* states that there is none because it specifically refers to those who live out their full lifespans.
This treatise states that it exists because it applies generally to both day and night. Furthermore, the Sanskrit name *upavāsa* is translated as "fast" (*zhāi*) in meaning;
it is also called "near-dwelling" (*jìnzhù*).
In the West, there are those who observe a single day of fasting, which is also called *upavāsa*;
if one receives the eight precepts of fasting, it is likewise called *upavāsa*.
This name for "fasting" is common throughout the Vinaya and is not restricted to a specific context.
If lifelong precepts are excluded from the *Vinaya-vibhaṣā* because they are not fixed within the category of restraint (*saṃvara*),
this treatise states that they do exist because it refers generally to the one-day fast (*upavāsa*) precepts.
Therefore, the *Mahāvibhāṣā* states:
Question: If one receives the *upavāsa*, *upāsaka*, and *śrāmaṇera* precepts respectively with inferior, middling, and superior minds...
This is precisely what is meant by attaining restraint toward all sentient beings;
it is due to all causes, yet not through all branches.
Why, then, do you say it does not exist?
Answer: Herein, the treatise is composed solely in reliance upon [vows] lasting for the duration of one's life, and not in reliance upon [vows] of a day and night.
Why is this? Because that [latter] is designated as "fasting" (upoṣadha).
Because it is not determinate within the context of restraint (*saṃvara*).
Regarding the phrase "there is nothing that does not pervade or that is not completely ceased," this is the explanation.
One must be universally expansive toward sentient beings and not limited to a few;
if a person does not practice sublime conduct that reaches its full extent, [they will not attain the goal].
This demonstrates that because these five types of restraint are not universal, one does not obtain formal discipline (*saṃvara*);

rather, one obtains a semblance of it, namely intermediate virtuous conduct (*madhyama-prasāda-karma-patha*). The phrase "and so forth" includes stealing and other such acts. Although the one-day fast (*upavāsa*) is restricted by time, one nevertheless obtains formal discipline through it.
This statement that one "cannot" [attain it] is based on the fact that it lasts for the remainder of one's life;

however, the mention of periods such as "one month" already excludes durations of day and night—this can be understood by reflecting upon these five certainties. Furthermore, according to the Sautrāntika school, one may also attain the restraint through these five certainties.
Regarding how one can obtain restraint (*saṃvara*) with respect to objects that are not within one's power:
the question is asked—
if it is the principle that one obtains [restraint] toward all sentient beings without exception, [how is this possible]?
If one cannot harm beings in other regions, how does one obtain the restraint?
Regarding the statement that one obtains the restraint by reaching [the state of] universal regard for all sentient beings, the answer is as follows:
Because that recipient of the precepts possesses a benevolent intention toward sentient beings, they extensively obtain the restraint (*saṃvara*);
therefore, it is illogical for it to be partial toward any sentient being.
This is precisely what accords with the correct tenet of the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*: that one universally generates the basis of the precepts toward all sentient beings.
Regarding the point that the Vaibhāṣika masters fall into the error of [the mind] being acquired and then abandoned,
the second master replies:
"In the *Vaibhāṣya*, there is a statement made as follows."
The restraint that is acquired must necessarily arise universally.

If one were to claim that one acquires the prātimokṣa solely with respect to objects capable of causing harm, but does not acquire it with respect to objects incapable of doing so; [that would be incorrect].
This very restraint must therefore undergo increase and decrease:
when one becomes capable of what was previously incapable, the restraint should increase;
when one becomes incapable of what was previously capable, the restraint should decrease.

If there is increase or decrease, there is the fault of obtaining through separation and abandoning through conditions; there is the fault of obtaining through conditions and abandoning through excess.
When there is increase, it is called the fault of obtaining through separation and obtaining through conditions.
When there is decrease, it is called the fault of abandoning through separation and abandoning through conditions.
The conditions for acquisition refer to the preceptor and others;

the conditions for relinquishment refer to the four or five conditions and so forth. This corresponds in meaning to the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*’s discussion on the "unjustified" position regarding the distinct arising of the precepts within various sentient beings.
Because it is unjust, the following provides a specific refutation.
Regarding the statement, "That which they say is not so; this should also apply by analogy," the Master of the Treatise raises an objection.
Their assertion that there is increase and decrease is unreasonable.
For instance, when grass and such things arise where they previously did not exist, those precepts do not increase;
or when they have arisen and then wither, those precepts do not decrease.
Because a single prohibitory precept is issued collectively for things such as living grass, there is neither increase nor decrease [in the number of objects].
This same principle should also apply when the objects of the restraint obtained with respect to those capable objects and incapable objects undergo change.
That which is capable of producing [an effect] should not decrease;
that which is incapable of producing [an effect] should not increase.
This is how it is known.
Regarding the correct principle that one generates a single, collective precept with respect to all living plants and so forth, the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 120, states:

"According to those who speak thus, restraint is also obtained with respect to external phenomena. Question: If this were so, there would be an increase or decrease in restraint. Answer: There is neither increase nor decrease.
Because it is acquired collectively.
That is to say, this restraint acquires a single non-informative (avijñapti) entity collectively with respect to all grass and so forth;

yet, in the world, there is no time when grass and such things do not grow. Furthermore, another interpretation holds that although the intention is generated separately toward individual sentient beings, even though it is generated separately, it is accepted as being generated collectively with respect to growing grass and the like.
Therefore, I cite an example accepted by both parties to refute their position.
As for their statement, "It is not so, because the natures [of the two] are different," this is the defense offered by the Pṛthaktvavādins (the proponents of distinctness).
He said: "Not so;
for all sentient beings, when dying here and being born there, their preceding and succeeding natures are identical."
There is increase and decrease.
If that which is capable of producing [a result] cannot do so, it may be said that its capacity has decreased;
this is because the category of the capable has become diminished.
It cannot increase through analogy,
because it cannot be multiplied by analogy;
if it cannot produce capacity, [it cannot increase].
That which can be spoken cannot be reduced by its counterparts;
because it cannot be reduced by its counterparts, it increases through them;
and because its counterparts are numerous.

Grass and other such things undergo different stages— initial growth, subsequent growth, and withering— and thus it would be possible for them to collectively produce precepts without the fault of increase or decrease; however,
this cannot be taken as an analogy [for the case at hand].
If that were so, then regarding sentient beings who are virtuous according to principle,
the Master further objects:
if one obtains the precepts by generating them individually according to each sentient being, yet has not attained nirvāṇa.
When one dies here and is born there, it can be said that for sentient beings, their preceding and succeeding natures and precepts neither increase nor decrease.
Even when certain sentient beings have attained parinirvāṇa,
such categories as they formerly possessed no longer exist at present.
Since sentient beings are few, there would be a lack of the specific conditions for its separate arising;
how then could that restraint not be diminished? Therefore, this latter explanation—that the separate arising of restraint [occurs through the vow]—is logically untenable.
The cause previously explained— generating a benevolent intention toward all sentient beings—
is logically sound for the general undertaking of the vow;
although it was not asked whether the undertaking is general or specific.
According to the first school’s interpretation, [the vow] should be generated collectively;
according to the second school’s interpretation, it should be generated individually.
If that were so, would there not be the aforementioned fault regarding the previous Buddha reaching the state of non-decrease?
It is difficult to resolve this collectively.
If that were so, then regarding those such as Kāśyapa Buddha and the beings he delivered who have already entered nirvāṇa,
the later Śākyamuni Buddha and others would not have obtained the distinct discipline of the prātimokṣa from those former Buddhas and others.
"How is it that ethical discipline (*śīla*) does not fall short of the transgressions of previous Buddhas?
To this, the general response from the perspective of the entire family [of practitioners] is: "Because all Buddhas have reached the state where there is no falling short of previous transgressions."
Because the Prātimokṣa vows of the Buddhas of the three times are obtained collectively from all sentient beings as their objects,
even if those sentient beings were still present at that time,
a subsequent Buddha would likewise obtain the Prātimokṣa vows collectively from them.
Therefore, there is no fault of the subsequent śīla being diminished by what preceded it;
although the objects may be diminished, the essence of the precept remains unimpaired.
Thus, in the *Abhidharmamahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 120:
The masters of the Nyāya school answer this question, saying:
"It should be stated that although there are differences in the extent of the objects of restraint, [the nature of the restraint remains the same]."

The essence of the restraint (saṃvara) is without difference before and after, because it is acquired in its entirety from all sentient beings and locations; this is explained in detail as stated therein. Question: There are two differing views regarding whether the restraint is acquired in its entirety or acquired individually.
Is it in reference to the seven branches?
Or is it in reference to the twenty-one types?
The commentary states: first the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* is cited, and only then is the explanation provided.
As stated in the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 120: "If one were to distinguish them according to their continuity and moments, there would be immeasurable types of restraint (*saṃvara*).
Now, they are summarized as seven kinds, namely:
abstaining from taking life."
Up to and including abstaining from frivolous speech. Regarding this,
some say that each of those seven branches is acquired with respect to all sentient beings, and what is thus acquired is a single [abstention].
According to that [other] teaching, when one violates a single branch of the precepts with respect to a single sentient being,
this single branch of the precepts is severed toward all sentient beings, while the remaining six continue to function.
This would then properly explain what the Blessed One said:
"If one violates a training rule,
one is no longer a bhikṣu."
They are not śramaṇas;
they are not of the Śākya lineage.
Some say that these are the seven branches of the precepts.
Each one is obtained with respect to all sentient beings,
yet what is obtained differs for each according to the number of sentient beings.
The same applies to the precepts one has acquired.
They say that even when one violates a single branch of the precepts with respect to a single sentient being, [the entire set is affected].
Thus, in the case of this single sentient being, while one branch of the precepts is abandoned, the remaining six still function;
in the case of other sentient beings, all seven branches function.
Question: If that is so, how does one reconcile this with what was said by the Blessed One?
If one has violated the training rules and is thus not a bhikṣu and so forth,
the answer is that they are called "not a bhikṣu" in terms of the ultimate sense (paramārtha),
because they are unable to proceed toward that state.
Other masters say that the prātimokṣa restraint is established as twenty-one types according to the distinctions of its causes. Among these,
some say that each of the twenty-one types is acquired with respect to all sentient beings, and the nature of what is acquired does not differ.
He explains that due to the affliction of greed,
when one commits a transgression against even a single precept toward a single sentient being,
it constitutes a violation toward all sentient beings.
The single factor of ethical discipline produced by non-greed is abandoned;
the remaining twenty types continue as before.
This provides a thorough explanation of what the Blessed One taught.
If one violates a training rule and is no longer a bhikṣu or the like,
some say that these twenty-one types [of offenses] are each incurred in relation to every sentient being.
Yet what is obtained differs according to the number of sentient beings;
the precepts obtained are likewise so.
He explains that when one commits a transgression against a single sentient being by means of the affliction of greed,
the single factor of the precept produced by non-greed is severed with respect to that very same sentient being.
The remaining twenty types continue to function as before.
In the remaining abodes of sentient beings, all twenty-one types function in their entirety.
Question: If this is so, how does one reconcile this with what the Blessed One has said?
If one has violated a training rule and is thus not a bhikṣu and so forth,
the answer is that "not a bhikṣu" is stated with reference to the bhikṣu in the ultimate sense,
as previously explained. The masters of the treatises from Kaśmīra say:
Although one may violate the code of discipline (*vinaya*), the discipline itself is not severed;
by repenting and eliminating the offense according to the Dharma, one is again called a "holder of the precepts.
This is because there is no such thing as receiving [the vows] all at once and then abandoning them partially.
In the state where one has not yet repented and eliminated [the transgression], both names apply.
If one has already repented and eliminated it, one is merely called "one who maintains the precepts. The above is the explanation from the treatise; the *Vibhāṣā* contains five general explanations.

The first master holds that with respect to all sentient beings, one generates the three roots—non-attachment and so forth—and the seven branches collectively; thus, they are abandoned individually upon the commission of a specific offense.

The second master holds that with respect to each individual sentient being, one generates the seven branches separately; thus, they are abandoned individually upon the commission of a specific offense.
The third master asserts that one generates twenty-one branches collectively toward all sentient beings, and they are relinquished individually upon transgression.

The fourth master asserts that one generates twenty-one branches individually toward each sentient being, and they are relinquished individually upon transgression. Although the fifth master speaks of receiving them all at once, he does not speak of generating them individually.
Some agree with the first master;
others agree with the third master’s explanation.
There is certainly no separate abandonment [of the precepts]. Examining these five explanations regarding the characteristics of the relinquishment of the precepts:
The first four masters are not correct,
as they all claim that one abandons the precepts separately from committing an offense.
The fifth master represents the correct tenet.
This is because it clarifies that one does not abandon the precepts by transgressing them separately.
As for the attainment of the precepts, the second and fourth masters are incorrect.
This is because they speak of the distinct arousal [of the precepts]. The first master says that one arouses all seven branches collectively toward all sentient beings;
this means that the three roots of goodness together arouse the seven branches.
The third master asserts that for all sentient beings, twenty-one factors are universally produced.

This is because, due to the distinctions among the causes of the three roots of goodness, seven factors are produced by each, resulting in twenty-one factors. Question: Among these two explanations, which is correct? Answer: It is said that the first master’s view is correct.
Because it is stated at the very beginning in the *Vibhāṣā*,
it further says, "Some say," which refers to the statement of the third master, namely, that other masters say.
Furthermore, the principle that the mind and mental factors together give rise to the seven limbs is also superior.
What logic is there in saying that, within a single aggregate of phenomena, three distinct roots of goodness each separately give rise to the seven limbs?
The commentators on various treatises describe the views of other masters; furthermore, they explain that the third master’s position is correct.
Why must the initial statement "some say" necessarily represent the correct meaning?
In the *Abhidharmamahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, there are also instances where an initial statement "some say" does not represent the correct meaning.
There are also other masters who say that this is the correct meaning;
however, since it is simply the meaning that is correct, why discuss whether it is at the beginning or the end? Some say: "Other masters."
Furthermore, all treatises state that each of the three roots of goodness gives rise to seven branches.
The *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra*, fascicle 39, says:
"That is to say, sentient beings, according to the distinctions of causes such as non-greed and so forth, give rise to different types of branches."
The two types of factors each possess one non-informative [matter] (*avijñapti*), which is acquired in relation to all sentient beings.
Furthermore, among the four explanations provided by various treatises,
they all state that the three roots of goodness separately give rise to material karma (*rūpakarma*).
There is no textual evidence for the simultaneous undertaking of the seven branches;

therefore, it is known that the twenty-one [vows] constitute the correct view. Furthermore, although the two explanations differ in their enumeration, both state that the vows are undertaken collectively with respect to all sentient beings.
The interpretations of the commentators and the correct principles do not contradict one another.

Furthermore, since there is no distinct establishment [of a separate position] among the various treatises, any [position] may be considered correct according to what one prefers. Alternatively, the mention of the "seven branches" in the various treatises describes the view of the first master.
As for the various treatises that speak of twenty-one factors,
these recount the position of the third master;
it should be understood that this treatise’s definition of the forfeiture of precepts accords with that of the fifth master.
Regarding the attainment of the precepts, it may be the same as the first master,
or it may be the same as the third master;
there is no contradiction in any of these three interpretations.
Regarding the statement, "Having explained [the case] from that, one should know that this applies by analogy," this explains the latter two lines.
It clarifies that non-restraint is necessarily acquired with respect to all sentient beings, and not with respect to a limited portion of objects.
One who lacks discipline (asaṃvara) necessarily acquires it through all seven courses of action—three of body and four of speech.
There is no one who lacks any of these branches of non-discipline.
Furthermore, this [acquisition] certainly does not occur through all three grades of causes—low, medium, and superior.
Because minds of inferior grade and so forth do not arise simultaneously, it is for this reason that the three causes are not mentioned. The passage beginning with "If there is...
explains why the three grades do not coexist.
If one possesses a low-grade intention and thus incurs non-restraint,
yet later at another time kills with a high-grade intention,
that person achieves only the low-grade non-restraint.

It also constitutes the upper-grade manifest and non-manifest actions of the path of karma for killing, as well as the intermediate [path of karma], because there is no repeated arising of non-restraint (*asaṃvara*). One should also speak of killing with intermediate and lower-grade minds.
It is not mentioned here because it is abbreviated;

however, one should understand that the medium and superior grades follow this same principle. Question: Why are there three grades of restraint, and why is it that some do not possess all seven branches?
Non-restraint does not have three grades; it necessarily possesses seven branches. Answer: Restraint is difficult to obtain.
Because there is such a thing as receiving it gradually, there are three grades, and there are cases where one does not possess all the branches.
Because non-restraint is easily acquired and acquired instantaneously,
it does not have three grades nor is it incomplete in its constituent parts.
Thus, the *Abhidharmamahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 117, states:
Regarding those who speak thus, discipline is acquired gradually and not all at once.
Why is this? Because discipline is difficult to obtain.
Because it is difficult to obtain, non-discipline (*asaṃvara*) is acquired and received gradually;

because it is easy to obtain, it is acquired and received all at once. Question: In this context, if it is said that for a person of non-discipline, the factors (*aṅga*) may be complete or incomplete—what does this mean?
This directly contradicts the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*; as stated in the *Vibhāṣā* (117):
"There are those who acquire non-restraint (*asaṃvara*) toward all sentient beings, yet not by means of all its constituent parts (*aṅga*), nor by means of all its causes (*hetu*)."

That is to say, one takes the life of a living being with a weak, middling, or strong degree of entanglement (*paryavasthāna*), and not otherwise; nor does one give rise to other factors [of non-restraint].
There are those who obtain non-restraint (*asaṃvara*) toward all sentient beings by means of all factors, but not by means of all causes.
This refers to taking the life of a living being with weak fetters (*paryavasthāna*),
up to and including engaging in frivolous speech;
it is done with either middling or superior [fetters], and not by others.
There is one who incurs non-restraint toward all sentient beings through all causes,
but not through all factors; that is, by means of weak, medium,
or intense fetters (*paryavasthāna*), one takes the life of a living being without undertaking the other factors [of non-restraint].
There is one who incurs non-restraint toward all sentient beings by means of all factors and all causes; that is to say,
through the lower, middle, and upper fetters, they take the life of a living being, up to and including engaging in frivolous speech.

The commentary explains: The *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* speaks of "limbs" (*aṅga*) based on the conditions that give rise to non-restraint; thus, it states that the causes may be either complete or incomplete.
This treatise, however, speaks of the limbs being complete based on the attainment of the actual substance of non-restraint.
It is because the causes are incomplete.
Regarding the phrase "In this context, who is called one of non-restraint?"—
this is a question concerning persons of non-restraint.
Regarding the statement, "It should be understood that this applies likewise to those who slaughter sheep," the answer is:
those who slaughter sheep, for the sake of their own livelihood, make a vow to harm sheep throughout their entire lives and thereby acquire non-restraint (*asaṃvara*).

If one kills a sheep for a brief period rather than for as long as life lasts, one incurs an intermediate evil state that is not a non-restraint (*asaṃvara*). Other cases should be explained accordingly.
As for the expression "binding dragons": [it refers to those who, though having committed such acts, do not incur full non-restraint].
This refers to those who, by means of incantations, bind dragons and snakes, seeking objects for amusement and sustenance to maintain their own lives.
As for the phrase "cooking dogs," it refers to the *caṇḍālas* and other base, evil persons who commit various types of wicked deeds.
In the Western Regions, they are called "dog-cookers," though it may not be that they constantly cook dogs;
rather, they likely cook dogs to serve as their food.

The name "Western" (Paścima) is used as its designation because of the *sārameya* dogs; the other names can be understood accordingly. The word "etc. (*ādi*) serves to indicate the kings and so forth. "Kings" refers to wicked rulers who, contrary to the law, inflict lethal punishment.
This refers to those who administer legal codes and punish offenders;
it refers to those who investigate and deliberate, such as the Censorate;
and it refers to those who adjudicate cases, such as the Supreme Court (Dali). In terms of major categories, there are twelve in total.
Regarding those not yet mentioned, the word "etc.
(ādi) includes them; one is called "possessing non-restraint" (asaṃvara) simply by constantly harboring a harmful intent, and it is not necessary to carry out the act of killing with one's own hand.
This is explained with reference to the mind:

if one possesses a compassionate mind and lacks the constant intent to harm, even while occupying this state, one is not "unrestrained" (*asaṃvara*). Alternatively, it is because certain individuals who abide in unrestraint are themselves designated as "those who possess unrestraint."
This is explained by way of abiding; that is, there are those who, by virtue of possessing non-restraint, are called "those with non-restraint.
This is an explanation based on possession (*samanvāgama*).
It applies universally throughout the realm of sentient beings until one has acquired non-restraint.
The Sautrāntika asks:
It may be so that one obtains the wholesome restraint (saṃvara) with respect to all sentient beings,
because it is acquired through a universally superior intention (āśaya).
It is not that butchers and others cause harm to their own close relatives;
rather, how is it that they incur non-restraint (asaṃvara) toward all sentient beings?
It is because those very same close relatives may become objects toward whom they harbor a harmful intent.
The Sarvāstivādins reply:
Since one might harbor a harmful intent even toward a close relative who has passed away—such as by intending to sacrifice them as a sheep—the [unwholesome restraint] applies universally.
Thus, it is known that even those very close to one can incur non-restraint (*asaṃvara*).
The Sautrāntika school further objects:
"If one's own close relative has already died and can be slaughtered as a sheep,
why would there be any malicious intent toward those who are currently not sheep and so forth?"
The name applies to all sentient beings.
While an ordinary person who has personally acted as a sheep might harbor harmful intent [toward others],
it is logically impossible for a noble being (ārya) to have ever been born as a sheep or the like.
How does one incur non-restraint with respect to them?
If it is argued that although one has attained the state of an Arya and is no longer a sheep,
one nevertheless perceives the future self-essence of those sheep and so forth.
If one were to obtain non-restraint within the present continuum of the body of a noble one (ārya),
then it would follow that sheep and the like currently possess the bodies of relatives or noble ones in future lives,
and thus one would certainly lack any intention to harm them.
In that case, one should consider the future bodies of close relatives and noble beings;
for one does not incur non-restraint with respect to sheep, chickens, pigs, and so forth in their present state.
As for those who do incur non-restraint with respect to the current bodies of sheep and the like:

The Sarvāstivādins raise an inquiry based on reasoning regarding those who possess the full set of factors for non-restraint (*aśubhasamvara*) while remaining in their present bodies as mothers and so forth; the Sautrāntikas,
in turn, counter-argue by posing the difficulty concerning the performance of such actions.
Furthermore, how can those who lack restraint (asaṃvara) possess all seven branches throughout their entire lives, given that they lack two bodily and four verbal [non-restraints]?
As for the claim that they possess the branches because they have completely damaged their wholesome [roots]: this is not so.
The Sarvāstivādins reply:
Because his wholesome intention (*āśaya*) is completely impaired, he may possess all the constituent factors [of the offense],
even though he is mute and does not speak.
Because the body can express speech, it is able to possess the full constituent parts [of the precepts].
If that were so, then for such a person, there would be up to seven branches of unwholesome conduct (*duḥśīla*).
Thus, the Sautrāntika school further objects.
If that were so, it might be argued that such a person has previously undertaken the wholesome karma of two or three training rules (śikṣāpada), such as the abstention from taking life;
furthermore, since the Sautrāntikas maintain that the five precepts do not necessarily include all constituent parts (aṅga) of morality, this question is raised again.
Between these two interpretations, the former is considered superior.
According to the latter, one merely commits the act of killing while leaving the underlying virtuous intention (*āśaya*) regarding other precepts undamaged;
how, then, could one fully give rise to the sevenfold unwholesome discipline?

Regarding the statement "the *Vaibhāṣikas* [hold that] even for one who has entered into non-restraint," the *Vaibhāṣika* masters explain that there must necessarily be no deficiency in its constituent parts.
One must possess all seven [factors],
as well as a portion of other objects, and accept the responsibility [for them], in order to be called a person who dwells in non-restraint (*asaṃvara*).
Therefore, the *Nyāyānusāra* says:
If one has previously made a formal commitment to undertake the precepts of virtuous training,
yet later— due to encountering specific circumstances and without having completely impaired the virtuous intention (*āśaya*)—
only undertakes the act of killing, one incurs a middling offense (*madhyama-āpatti*) and does not incur non-restraint (*asaṃvara*).
However, because one who acquires non-restraint necessarily and completely damages the wholesome *āśaya*, they acquire all seven branches.
As for the Sautrāntika masters' statement regarding "mutual exclusion": [text continues].
The masters of the Sautrāntika school state as follows:
it depends on the limit set by the person committing the evil deed,
or it may consist of all seven branches.
Or they may not possess all seven;
within a single factor,
they may be complete with respect to their object.
Or, one may acquire non-restraint with respect to only a portion of the objects;
this applies equally to the lay devotee's restraint within the context of worldly precepts, as it does to the case of evil.
With the sole exception of the eight precepts,
because the time is brief, the factors,
the requisites, and the objects are complete.
If it were not so, a weak and inferior wholesome mind would not give rise to the precepts.

This is because, depending on that person’s intention regarding the scope and duration, the wholesome and unwholesome *śīla* within a single continuum are mutually contradictory and thus exclude one another.
This means that within a single body, if one undertakes a single branch of virtuous discipline (*śīla*), it correctly prevents the arising of a single branch of unvirtuous discipline,
while simultaneously preventing the arising of the remaining branches of unvirtuous discipline;
likewise, if one undertakes a single branch of unvirtuous discipline, it correctly prevents the arising of a single branch of virtuous discipline.
Furthermore, this simultaneously precludes the arising of the wholesome restraint of the remaining factors.
The cases of receiving the second or third [vows] should be explained by analogy with this.
There is certainly no single person who is called both "one of non-restraint" (*asaṃvara*) and "one of restraint" (*saṃvara*).

Because virtuous and non-virtuous precepts are mutually contradictory; furthermore, since the Sautrāntika school already admits that there can be those who do not possess all the branches or only a portion of them, what prevents a single person from being called both "one with restraint" (*saṃvara*) and "one with non-restraint" (*asaṃvara*)?
The ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya) intends this explanation: because virtue and non-virtue, being of many or few [instances],
are mutually exclusive due to their contradictory essential natures and characteristics,
they are determined by those respective measures.
Between these two interpretations, the former is intended as superior.
Regarding the statement "it has already been explained from that point up to what has not yet been explained,
which shall now be explained," the following third section clarifies the attainment of the unwholesome and the intermediate state.
The preceding inquiry is introduced.
The verse states: "Up to: 'Due to the field, the undertaking, and the gravity of the act.
Within the response provided by this verse:
The first two lines clarify non-restraint (*asaṃvara*);
the latter two lines clarify the intermediate state (*madhyama*).
The treatise states: "Upon reaching [the object], one immediately gives rise to evil discipline."
The various forms of non-restraint (asamvara) are acquired through two causes:
first, being born into a family of non-restraint and,
by means of the initial performance of the preparatory application (prayoga) of killing and so forth, such as striking or binding.
At that time, one immediately incurs unwholesome precepts (duḥśīla).
Second, even if one is born into another family,
by virtue of the initial vow and commitment to commit acts such as killing, [one incurs them].
That is to say: "I shall perform such deeds as killing and so forth in order to seek wealth and sustain myself.
At that very moment, one incurs non-virtuous discipline (*duḥśīla*). Question: Why is it not stated that one undertakes a vow when born into a family of non-discipline (*anairyāṇika*)?
"Born into another family, one does not speak of performing [such] actions. The commentary explains: this refers to being born into a family of non-restraint (*asaṃvara*).
From childhood until adulthood, one constantly witnesses evil deeds such as killing within the family trade.
It is not necessary to take a formal vow.
Even if one were to take a vow for oneself, because the mind would be characterized by disrespect, the unwholesome precepts (akuśala-śīla) would not arise;
it is only through actually committing acts such as killing that one acquires the unwholesome precepts.
It is not said that one receives it through a vow.
When one is born into another family and intends to become a person of non-restraint,
one must first receive it through a vow.
From childhood until adulthood, one has not witnessed such evil deeds as killing within the family business.
Because the initial vow was made with a heavy heart, it gives rise to unwholesome precepts (*akuśala-śīla*);

however, because subsequent acts of killing and so forth are not performed with such gravity, they are not described as "karmic action" (*karman*). Question: As stated in the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 117:
Question: Just as one must formally undertake [the vows] to obtain the various types of restraint (*saṃvara*), is it the same for non-restraint (*asaṃvara*)? Some say that it is.
It is also acquired through formal undertaking;
that is, grasping the instruments of killing and vowing:
"From this day forth until the end of my life, I shall constantly perform this action as my means of livelihood."
At that time, one thereby acquires this non-restraint (*asaṃvara*).
Furthermore, there are those who say that although one may grasp the instruments of killing and make a vow for oneself,
one does not thereby acquire this non-restraint.
It is obtained through two conditions:
first, through the performance of action;
second, through the undertaking of the matter.
By way of action: this refers to when one is born into a family of non-restraint and first performs such actions as killing;
at that moment, one obtains this non-restraint.
Regarding the recipient of the act:
it refers to one who, having been born into another family for the sake of livelihood,
conceives a mind of harmful intent and goes before those engaged in the non-virtuous occupations of sheep-slaughterers and the like, making this vow.
"From this moment until the end of my life, I shall constantly perform the work that you perform to sustain my livelihood.
At that time, one thereby acquires this non-restraint (*asaṃvara*).
Furthermore, there are those who say that this non-discipline (*asaṃvara*) is acquired only at the very moment one first performs that action;
they maintain that non-discipline is acquired through a single condition. This is stated in three ways in the *Mahāvibhāṣā*.
The first [type] is said to arise from formal undertaking;
the latter is said to arise from actual action;
the second is said to arise from both.
"What is the correct [position]? The commentary explains:
Although there is no adjudicating authority, we shall take the second master as correct.

All treatises state that [non-restraint] is acquired through two conditions. Question: According to the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, regarding the undertaking of non-restraint through a vow, [is it acquired by both conditions or not?]
Why does this treatise not explain it? The explanation is:
this treatise explains it briefly and does not discuss it;
or perhaps it may be so.
The intent of the treatises differs.
Although the two conditions are the same, the intent of the vow to receive them is distinct.
The text of the *Nyāyānusāra* is identical to this treatise.
"Obtaining other non-manifest [karma] up to the various meritorious actions":
this below explains the latter two phrases.
One obtains other neutral non-manifest [karma] by means of three causes.
First, it is by way of the field (*kṣetra*).
Because the fields are not one, they are called "various fields.
That is to say, when one gives gardens and so forth to such various fields of merit (*puṇyakṣetra*), that wholesome non-informative matter (*avijñapti*) arises immediately upon the initial gift.
As it is said regarding the seven bases of meritorious action that depend on a physical basis,
this is here stated according to the neutral category of wholesome states;
however, by logical extension, there are also unwholesome and neutral [bases] with respect to the field.
This means that regarding the field of activity, unwholesome non-informative matter (*avijñapti*) arises immediately upon the initial act of setting snares, nets, and so forth.

Because their underlying vows differ, these [specific acts] such as snares and nets are distinct from [general] non-restraint (*asaṃvara*). That it is known to pertain to the unwholesome is because...
Therefore, the subsequent section on the relinquishment of the "intermediate" states says:
"Fourth, it is relinquished due to the destruction of the object-base.
What is the object-base?"
That is to say, it refers to what is given as monasteries, dwellings, bedding and furniture, shrines (caityas), and groves;
as well as things such as nets and the like that are provided for these purposes. One should know that this is called a "field" because the dharma it encompasses is broad.
Therefore, the subsequent treatise states:

"The fields differ because there are distinctions in terms of rebirth-state (*gati*), suffering (*duḥkha*), kindness (*upakāra*), and virtue (*guṇa*). Furthermore, it should be understood that in those neutral cases, even if the wholesome or unwholesome courses of action (*karmapatha*) are weak in mental force, they nevertheless give rise to non-informative matter (*avijñapti*) by the power of the field.
Second, by undertaking [vows] such as the constant giving of food and so forth;
that is, by undertaking, meaning making a personal vow such as: "I shall not eat first until I have paid homage to the Buddha," and so on.
Alternatively, one may make a vow or restriction regarding days of fasting (*upoṣadha*) and so forth, such as by constantly giving food;
although the intention may be weak, because of the power of that undertaking, the unmanifest (*avijñapti*) continues to arise. "Days of fasting" refers to the six *upoṣadha* days.
"Half-month" refers to the half-month,
namely the fifteenth day and the final day of the month.
"Month" refers to one full month.
"Year" refers to one year. Furthermore, "fasting days" refers to the six fasting days;
"fasting months" refers to the three fasting months;
and "half-month" means taking half of a month from within a single month.
"Year" refers to one year.
Herein, the explanation is given in terms of wholesome [karma] for the sake of brevity;
unwholesome and neutral [karma] are omitted and not discussed.
It is also reasonable that such a thing should exist;
for example, as when someone makes a vow regarding an enemy, saying:
"If I do not strike or revile him, or do not eat first [of my meal], and so forth."
Or, having made a vow or restriction such as "on a certain day and so forth,
I must strike or scold [someone]," even if the mind is weak, the non-informative (avijñapti) arises in continuity due to the force of that undertaking.
Third, by means of a weighty action, one gives rise to another non-informative.
Third, by means of earnest practice:
that is, giving rise to such a reverent mental attention (*manasikāra*) when performing wholesome deeds, such as having pure faith while making offerings to the Buddha and so forth.

If one commits an evil act while under the influence of intense obsessions (*paryavasthāna*), such as striking others with a club and so forth, the non-informative (*avijñapti*) arises in continuity because the mind is heavy. Having thus explained [the first cause], he concludes by stating:
"By these three causes, other non-informative [actions] arise."
Thus has been explained what was previously stated and what remains to be stated.
Hereafter, in the fourth major section, the distinctions regarding relinquishment (*prahāṇa*) are clarified. Within this:
First, the relinquishing of the Prātimokṣa;
second, the relinquishing of the dhyāna- and path-precepts;
third, the relinquishing of non-restraint.
Fourth, the precepts within the four bases of equanimity;
fifth, the relinquishing of all that is non-material. Herein, the first section clarifies the relinquishing of the Pratimokṣa;
within this, there is one question.
Part Two: The Response. Within the questions, there are two:
first, the general question;
second, the specific question. This is the general question.
This concludes the preceding section and introduces what follows. Now, as for how one relinquishes the Pratimokṣa vows—
this constitutes a specific inquiry.
The verse says: "Upon reaching the point of committing the two [offenses], it is like being burdened by wealth.
This is the answer. Within the answer:
The first verse states the author’s own position;
the subsequent verses describe divergent views.
The treatise says: "Up to 'it is abandoned through four conditions'..."
The following explains the first verse.
"Discipline" (*vinaya*) is a synonym for restraint (*saṃvara*);
by means of this, one is able to discipline the six sense faculties.
Regarding the eight types of restraint, with the exception of the one-day fast (upavāsa),
the remaining seven are relinquished through four conditions among the five ways of relinquishment.
First, by way of the intention of reaching the point of abandoning the training precepts.
It is abandoned by means of an intentional act;
that is to say, one abandons the restraint through an intentional formal action.
Originally, it was acquired by means of an intentional mind.
Now, the relinquishing [of the precepts] occurs through the original intention that led to their abandonment;
therein are three factors.
First, it is because the mental disposition does not take delight in the precepts.
Second, because there is mutual understanding with a person who possesses comprehension;
third, because it issues in manifest karma (*vijñapti-karman*) which contradicts the undertaking of manifest karma;
and fourth, because all three conditions are fulfilled for the relinquishing of the training rules (*śikṣāpada*).
If any [of these] is lacking, the renunciation is not established.
Thus, the *Nyāyānusāra* (Treatise on the Principles of Reasoning), fascicle 39, states:
"First, by intentional renunciation."

This refers to the undertaking of a distinct type of informative action (*vijñapti-karman*) that is contrary [to the vow], toward a person capable of understanding, for the purpose of relinquishing the training rules (*śikṣāpada*),
while lacking any inclination (*āśaya*) toward the discipline (*vinaya*).
It is not merely by generating the intention to relinquish the training rules;
for, as with the attainment of restraint, the mind lacks such capacity,
and furthermore, because relinquishment is not accomplished while dreaming.

It is not merely by the arising of the differentiation of informative action (*vijñapti-karman*) that [the abandonment of precepts] is established, because [precepts] are not lost even when one is angry, insane, or deranged;
nor is it established by these two alone.
Because it is impossible for one to generate a mind of equanimity toward animals and so forth [at the moment of death].
Second, "by abandoning the homogeneous class" (*nikāyasabhāga*) explains [the phrase] "due to the end of life."
The precepts are acquired through the predominant influence of a homogeneous basis (*nikāya-sabhāga*).
Because one dies, the homogeneous basis that serves as the support is relinquished, and the precepts that depend upon it are likewise relinquished.
Therefore, the *Nyāyānusāra* states:
Second, by the end of life;
that is, because one acquires the restraint through the predominant power of the homogeneous class of beings (*nikāyasabhāga*).
Third, by the simultaneous arising of both sexual organs.
The *Nyāyānusāra* states:
"Third, it arises due to the simultaneous production of both sexual organs;
that is to say, at the time when the body undergoes transformation."
Because the mind undergoes transformation;
furthermore, because those with both sexual organs lack predominance.
Fourth, regarding "due to the severance of the roots of goodness which are the cause": the foundation of morality is acquired through the roots of goodness.
Now, because the roots of goodness are severed, one abandons those precepts.
Thus, the *Nyāyānusāra* states:
"Fourth, [the abandonment occurs] due to the severance of the roots of goodness that are their cause."
This means that because the motivating mind for manifest and non-manifest karma has ceased, one relinquishes the *upavāsa* (fasting) precepts.
Regarding the relinquishment of the *upavāsa* precepts through five conditions:
it is relinquished by the first four conditions.
Furthermore, because the night has ended, it is said that there are five conditions for the relinquishment of the *prātimokṣa*.
What is meant by "the end of the night"?
The *Nyāyānusāra* states:
"The end of night" refers to the time when the dawn light appears.
For what reason is the precept relinquished through these five conditions?
Question:
Regarding the phrase "because it contradicts the undertaking and reaches the limit of the period," the answer is:
because a manifest action (*vijñapti-karman*) arises that contradicts the undertaking.
This is abandoned at the beginning because its basis is abandoned;
it is abandoned at the end of life because its basis has changed;
and it is abandoned by the appearance of both sexual organs because its cause has been severed.
This is relinquished through the severance of the roots of goodness or by the expiration of the time limit;
it is relinquished at the end of the night.
Other schools state that it continues until the attainment of the bhikṣu vows.
Explaining the fifth phrase:
some masters of the Sautrāntika school state that one who commits a grave offense (pārājika) relinquishes the precepts.
Regarding the four most grave offenses that entail falling into hell,
if one commits even one of them, one abandons the *śrāmaṇera* and *bhikṣu* renunciant vows.
Other schools state that this occurs because [the vows] cease entirely upon reaching [the commission of such an offense].
Explaining the sixth phrase:
there are others who say it is the Dharmaguptaka school;
in Chinese, this is called the Dharma-mi (Dharma-honey) school.

The extinction of the True Dharma can also cause one to relinquish the prātimokṣa vows, because when the True Dharma perishes, all training rules (*śikṣāpada*), ritual boundaries (*sīmābandha*), and formal acts (*karmavācanā*) cease; for this reason, the precepts are abandoned.
From the statement in the *Kāśmīra* [Vinaya] up to "merely named rich persons," the latter two phrases refute the Sautrāntika masters:
when one commits those four root pārājika offenses, one does not lose the monastic precepts.
The reason for this is that,
from the perspective of principle,
if one were to transgress even a single aspect among the four grave offenses, one would have to relinquish the entirety of the monastic discipline.
This demonstrates that committing a grave offense does not constitute the forfeiture of the essence of the precepts;

since it is cited as an example of committing other offenses that do not forfeit the precepts, it implies that committing other offenses such as *saṃghāvaśeṣa* does not sever the essence of the precepts.
Because other transgressions can be expiated through repentance, one returns to being a good person;

it is clearly understood that the essence of the precepts (*śīlaskandha*) is not relinquished at the time of committing such offenses. Since the precepts have not been relinquished in this case, [the status of the practitioner remains].
The same should apply to the commission of a grave offense:
because they are equally violations of the precepts, they are both termed "violation of the precepts";
yet, in one case, the precept is lost.
First, there is no loss of the precepts,
because that would contradict the underlying principle.
However, there are two designations for a person who has committed a grave offense.
The first is named "upholding the precepts," and the second is named "violating the precepts";
the analogy can be understood accordingly.
If one confesses and eliminates what has been transgressed, and is without a mind of concealment— just as in the case of the monk Cūḍapanthaka who was merely called "one who upholds the precepts"—
the analogy can likewise be understood.
Thus, the *Nyāyānusāra* states:
It is not the case that when one commits any one of the root offenses, there is the sense that all forms of discipline (*vinaya*) are abandoned.
However, for one who has committed a grave offense, there are two designations: first, they are called "one who possesses ethical discipline" (*śīlavant*); [the second is...]
The second is called "one who has violated the precepts.

If, regarding what has been transgressed, one confesses and purifies it through disclosure and repentance, they are said to possess the precepts alone; this is like a wealthy person who, when owing a debt to another, is called both a rich man and a debtor.
If one has repaid a debt and is merely called a wealthy person,
this case should be understood in the same way; therefore, it does not constitute the forfeiture of the precepts.
Furthermore, the Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra, fascicle 119,
states: "The masters of the treatises in the kingdom of Kaśmīra say that when one commits a transgression against the code of discipline, one does not thereby relinquish the discipline."
Yet one attains that which is neither restraint nor non-restraint;
therefore, at that time, one is said to abide in neither restraint nor non-restraint,
and is also called one who abides in restraint.
If, at that time, one confesses openly with a mind free from concealment and repents according to the Dharma,
one then abandons what is neither discipline nor non-discipline;
one is then simply called one who abides in discipline.
For example, when a wealthy person owes another a debt, they are called both a debtor and a wealthy person;
once the debt has been repaid, they are simply called a wealthy person.
If explained in this way, it provides a thorough resolution.

The ritual for confessing and repenting one's transgressions to restore one’s abiding in the discipline (*vinaya*) is not without utility; the *Abhidharma-nyāyānusāra* explains that this treatise maintains that the correct principle applies only to cases where one has committed a grave offense but has not yet abandoned the precepts.
The *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* states in general that those who have merely transgressed the precepts do not lose their ordination.
If this is so, for what reason is the term "defeat" (*pārājika*) applied?
Thus the Sautrāntika masters raise an objection.
If it is said that committing a grave offense does not constitute the loss of the precepts,
for what reason did the Buddha state that one who commits the four pārājika offenses is no longer called a bhikṣu?
For the bhikṣu takes the precepts as his very essence.
One is not called a bhikṣu;
it is clearly understood that one has abandoned the precepts.
Since the precepts can destroy evil, they are called "śramaṇa."
One cannot be called a śramaṇa;
it is clearly understood that one has abandoned the precepts.
Since the precepts arise from the teachings spoken by the golden mouth of Śākyamuni, one is called a son of Śākya.
They are not disciples of Śākyamuni;
it is clearly known that they have abandoned the precepts,
because they have destroyed the essence of the bhikṣu’s vows.
Therefore, they are not called bhikṣus,
because they have harmed the essential nature of the śramaṇa precepts;
for this reason, they are not called śramaṇas.
Because within the observance of the precepts, this constitutes a breach, a destruction, a fall, and a downfall;
therefore, one is not a son of the Śākya.
It is by the commission of the four pārājika offenses that the designation "defeated" (pārājika) is established.
In Sanskrit it is called *pārājika*;
this is translated here as "defeated by another.
One's own wholesome dharmas are termed "self."
Unwholesome dharmas are called "the other.
If wholesome dharmas overcome unwholesome dharmas, it is called "victory over oneself";
if unwholesome dharmas overcome the wholesome, it is called "victory over the other."

Therefore, one who commits a grave offense is called "defeated" (pārājika). Regarding the statement made with the underlying intention that this refers to a bhikṣu in the ultimate sense, the Sarvāstivādins reply:
there are two kinds of bhikṣus.
First, the conventional bhikṣu,
which refers to ordinary worldlings (pṛthagjana);
second, the ultimate bhikṣu.

It refers to the fact that among the noble ones (*ārya*), there is one who possesses the prātimokṣa vows and is called a "conventional bhikṣu," and there is one who possesses the dharma-concomitant vows (*mārga-sahabhū-śīla*) and is called a "bhikṣu in the ultimate sense" (*paramārtha-bhikṣu*).
When the Sūtra states that one who commits a grave offense is no longer a bhikṣu, this is said with the underlying intention (*abhiprāya*) of referring to the bhikṣu in the ultimate sense.
To say one is "not a bhikṣu" does not mean they are not a bhikṣu according to worldly convention; rather,
it means that although a person who has committed a grave offense (pārājika) possesses the essence of the precepts,
they are ultimately incapable of realizing any of the noble dharmas.
One cannot be established as a bhikṣu in the ultimate sense by being called "non-bhikṣu.
Nor does one become a "non-bhikṣu" merely by completely relinquishing the precepts.
The designation "bhikṣu" encompasses two types.
Because the ultimate bhikṣu is not explained separately, it is said that there is an underlying intention (*abhiprāya*).
The śramaṇas and Śākyaputrīyas should be understood according to this principle;
therefore, they are not explained separately.
Regarding this statement that it is "contradictory," the Sautrāntika school challenges it:
what is meant by "contradictory"?
The Sarvāstivādins pose a counter-question regarding the circumstances under which the Blessed One declared an offense to be a grave transgression (*sthūlātyaya*).
The Sautrāntikas respond as follows:
That is to say, regarding the definitive teachings spoken by the Blessed One, one who has committed the four pārājika offenses is no longer called a bhikṣu;
this is explained through a distinct, superior sense so as to render those [other] statements non-definitive.
If it were said that one who commits a grave offense relinquishes the precepts...
He fears losing his protection of the precepts and thus maintains them without transgression;
yet if one says that committing a grave offense does not relinquish the essence of the precepts,
this provides a condition for those with many afflictions to commit grave sins.
Because he heard this yet did not relinquish [the precepts] despite repeatedly committing grave offenses,
to say that he committed a grave offense and thus did not relinquish the precepts is a violent and contradictory statement.
How do you know that this statement is of definitive meaning (*nītārtha*)?
The Sarvāstivādins inquire:
How do you know that the words of this sūtra regarding those who are not bhikṣus are of definitive meaning?
Regarding the statement that "the Vinaya itself explains this as a definitive teaching," the Sautrāntika replies:
"The body belongs to a layperson."
He is called a "bhikṣu by name";

thus it is said he is a "bhikṣu by designation. Furthermore, another interpretation holds that he receives the name "one endowed with full ordination" (*upasampadā*) and so forth through the *jñapti-caturtha-karman* (the formal ritual of motion followed by three proclamations).
Because one establishes the designation "bhikṣu" for such a person,
they are called a "bhikṣu by name and conception.
The name arises from conception.
Alternatively, it is called "name-and-conception" because it can give rise to conception;

one who has committed a grave offense is not actually a bhikṣu, yet he claims for himself, "I am a bhikṣu," and thus it is called "claiming oneself to be a bhikṣu. Another interpretation is that when performing formal ritual acts, one claims for oneself, "I, the bhikṣu so-and-so."
Therefore, it is said that they "call themselves bhikṣus.
The former explanation is superior:

those who have left the household life and sustain themselves by begging are called *bhikṣu-kaṣāyins* (begging bhikṣus). Furthermore, another explanation holds that this applies whether one is a monastic or a layperson.
Those who wander from door to door begging for alms are all called *bhikṣus* by virtue of their mendicancy.

Those Arhats who have destroyed all delusions are called *bhikṣus* by virtue of having destroyed delusions. Furthermore, it is explained that all noble ones (*ārya*) who have attained the untainted path (*anāsrava-mārga*) [are so called].
Because he truly destroys delusions, he is called a "delusion-destroying bhikṣu";
that is, a bhikṣu in the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*).
