Since the Vinaya itself explains that one who commits a grave offense is not actually a bhikṣu, even though they claim to be a bhikṣu.
It is clearly known that one who commits a grave offense lacks the essence of the precepts (*śīla-sarīra*).
Although the text cites four points, it specifically takes the second—self-declaration—as its proof;
this is thus a proof by means of the teaching (*āgama*). Within the meaning of this sutra, it says:
Alternatively, regarding the meaning of "one who has committed a grave offense" (*gurudharma*),
the phrase "not a *bhikṣu*" refers either to one who is no longer a *bhikṣu* through the loss of the precepts,
or to one who is not a *bhikṣu* by way of having received full ordination through the *jñapti-caturtha-karman*, yet is merely designated as such by name and concept.
This does not mean that, according to the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*), he is not a bhikṣu;
the other interpretations are as before.
If this bhikṣu who has committed a grave offense was previously a bhikṣu in the ultimate sense, [then...]
Later, due to committing a grave offense, one becomes a non-ultimate bhikṣu;
thus, one may say that based on the term "ultimate bhikṣu," he is not a bhikṣu.
It is not the case that this bhikṣu who has committed a grave offense was previously an ultimate bhikṣu.
Later, due to committing a grave offense, one becomes a non-ultimate bhikṣu.
How can you explain that, based on the term "ultimate bhikṣu," one is [thereby] not a bhikṣu?
If an ultimate bhikṣu were definitively incapable of committing a grave offense, [your argument would hold].
If, in the conventional sense, whether a bhikṣu commits an offense or not is neither ultimately real, how can it be said that one who has committed a grave offense is called "not ultimately real"?
This is the proof by means of reasoning. By virtue of both this scripture and this reasoning, we know that when the sūtra speaks of one who is "not a bhikṣu," it refers to this.
This is an explanation of definitive meaning (*nītārtha*).

However, regarding the statement that "the same applies even up to the point of committing a grave offense," this is the Sautrāntika school citing and refuting the position previously asserted by the Sarvāstivāda school.
The tāla tree can be known;
its shape resembles the *shuilu* (Phragmites) tree here in this land,
yet it does not exist here.
Regarding what meaning the Great Master illustrates through this analogy here,
the Sarvāstivādins ask:
it is intended to illustrate that one reaches all forms of restraint through the precepts.
The Sautrāntika replies:
the meaning of the text is likewise clear.
Furthermore, regarding the statement that even one who has committed a grave offense (pārājika) is still called a bhikṣu:
The Sautrāntika masters further cite a sūtra to demonstrate that one who commits a grave offense loses their vows. "Saṃgha" refers to the *saṃgha*;
this is translated as "assembly. "Kevalam" means "possessing" or "entirely."
That which belongs to the Saṃgha is called saṃghika;
that is, food belonging to the assembly is called saṃghika food.
Vihāra is translated in meaning as "temple" (si).
This refers to the meaning of "the place where one dwells. A person who has committed a grave offense is not a true bhikṣu, yet they call themselves a bhikṣu;
by this, it is known that in the Vinaya, those who call themselves bhikṣus are persons who have committed a grave offense.
The remainder of the text may be understood.
Regarding what the characteristics of that bhikṣu’s nature are,
the Sautrāntika asks.
What is the nature of that bhikṣu who has committed a grave offense?
Regarding what those characteristics may be, up to the point of being a "śramaṇa who has fouled the path," the Sarvāstivādins respond as follows:
As for that person who has committed a grave offense, regardless of what their specific characteristics may be,
the essence of the precepts must necessarily still exist.
For the sutras state that there are four types of śramaṇas and no fifth.
If one knowingly commits a grave offense while possessing the precepts within one's person,
one is then subsumed under the category of a "defiled-path śramaṇa.
If one does not possess these four [types], one is not so subsumed.
A fifth type, the "semblance śramaṇa," should have been established;
since it was not established separately,
one should know that this refers precisely to the "corrupter of the path" śramaṇa.
If one lacks the essence of the precepts (śīlaskandha), one is not called a śramaṇa;
since one is called a śramaṇa, it is known that the essence of the precepts exists.
This intention cites the fourth [case] as proof.
The others come because their texts are the same. Cunda—here translated as "the young one"—is an error for the old transliteration "Chuntu.
The *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 66, explains:
"A śramaṇa who has surpassed the path..."
This refers to the Buddha, the World-Honored One, who has awakened by himself;
it should be understood that all Pratyekabuddhas are likewise so. As for the "Śramaṇa who shows the path," this refers to the Venerable Śāriputra, because he is without equal.
Because they are the guardians of the Great Dharma and are always able to follow the Buddha in turning the wheel of Dharma,
it should be known that all śrāvakas beyond training (aśaikṣa) are likewise so. As for the "Śramaṇas of the Path of Life":
That is to say, although the Venerable Ānanda dwells in the stage of training (śaikṣa), he is equal to those beyond training (aśaikṣa); he is learned,
having heard and retained the teachings, and is fully endowed with pure ethical discipline and prohibitions.
It should be understood that all those in training (śaikṣa) are likewise so.
As for the "defiled path śramaṇa," this refers to the bhikṣu Mahāloka.
"Delighting in stealing the property of others and so forth. The commentary explains:
This refers to Buddhas and Pratyekabuddhas, because they are able to awaken by themselves.
Because its path is superior,
it is called the "Superior Path.
Śāriputra and others who teach the Dharma and transform sentient beings are called "those who show the path."
Ānanda and others are called "those whose life is the path" because they take precept, concentration, and wisdom as their life.
Those who have committed grave offenses are called "defilers of the path" (mārgadūṣaka) and are destined for the Avīci hell.
This refers to "the aged," meaning an elderly bhikṣu. When asked whether he is included among these four categories—excluding those who have committed a grave offense—he is a common bhikṣu.
To which of these four is he subsumed?
As for the statement that there is no fifth type of śramaṇa, the commentary explains that this is subsumed under the śramaṇa of the life-path (jīvitamārga-śramaṇa),
because he takes the precepts as his life.
The *Abhidharmamahāvibhāṣā* speaks of this specifically regarding those in training (śaikṣa).
Ordinary persons are not mentioned here in brief, though they may be implied.
Furthermore, it is explained that those who defile the path are subsumed under the category of śramaṇas;
although they have not committed a grave offense, because they inevitably commit other minor transgressions, they are also called "defilers of the path."
The *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* speaks here of those who have committed a grave offense;
other cases not yet mentioned are included within the word "etc. Furthermore, another interpretation holds that they are subsumed under both categories:
if they possess pure precepts, they are subsumed among those who live the path of a śramaṇa.
If one commits other minor offenses, one is subsumed under the category of "defiled śramaṇas.
The resolution of this objection is as previously explained. Furthermore, another interpretation holds that they are not so subsumed.
At one time, the World-Honored One...
He taught the Dharma according to the occasion,
specifically addressing the various noble ones and those who have committed grave offenses;
therefore, those who have not committed grave offenses are not included among these four types of persons.
If one were to offer such an interpretation, the scriptural text should be explained as follows: "Cunda, you should know that there are four kinds of śramaṇas;
this is the wording of the sūtra. There is no further statement from the Sarvāstivāda school establishing a fifth."
Regarding this statement concerning those who die by the wheel of fire,
the Sautrāntikas explain the sūtra as follows:
the intended meaning of the sūtra is that a śramaṇa who defiles the path is called a "śramaṇa."
Although this has been said, they are called śramaṇas only because they have shaved their hair, dyed their robes, and possess the other outward marks of a śramaṇa;
it is not because they possess the essence of precepts that they are called śramaṇas. To explain this by means of a metaphor: it is like charred timber, which is no longer truly timber.
Because it resembles timber, the name "timber" is applied to it metaphorically; it is like carving wood into the shape of a parrot’s beak—
it is not actually that beak,
yet it resembles it.
The name "well" is provisionally established for that which has water;
the name "pool" is provisionally established for a dried-up pool because it resembles such a pool. That which produces sprouts is called a "seed," and even a decayed seed is called a "seed."
Because it resembles that seed, the name "seed" is metaphorically established. That which revolves on all sides is called a "wheel"; a whirling firebrand is called a "wheel.

Because it resembles such a wheel, the name "wheel" is metaphorically established. One who reflects is called a "person"; after death, one is still called a "person" because the deceased resembles that person. One should know that the defiled śramaṇa is likewise so named.
One who possesses the name of a śramaṇa but has committed a grave offense is called a śramaṇa only because he resembles a śramaṇa; thus,
he is given the name "śramaṇa" by way of metaphorical designation.
Regarding the case of one who has committed a grave offense (pārājika) down to a monk under training (śikṣādattaka),
the Sarvāstivādins raise an objection:
if one who has committed a grave offense is no longer a bhikṣu because he lacks the precepts, [then how can he be so designated?]
Thus, there is no one who, having committed a grave offense (*pārājika*), must observe the precepts for the rest of their life; however,
it is stated in the Vinaya that although the bhikṣu Cūḍapanthaka had committed a grave offense, [he was still ordained].
With a mind free from concealment,
the Blessed One sent him away to train in the precepts for as long as he lived.
Having been sent to train in the precepts, [he remained].
Even if one clearly knows that a grave offense has been committed, the precepts are not relinquished.
It is not said that for a person who has committed a grave offense, the precepts are established as being thus [lost].
The Sautrāntika school replies:
It is not said that all those who commit grave offenses necessarily incur the offense of pārājika; rather, it is only when one incurs the offense of pārājika [that they are so designated].
Because of concealment,
it is definitively stated that one is no longer a bhikṣu.
That is to say, there may be someone whose mental continuum and physical body possess an exceptional sense of shame (hrī) and dread of blame (apatrāpya).
Although they have committed a grave offense,
it does not constitute a *pārājika* defeat,
because they lack even a single moment of concealed intent, such as that held by Cūḍapanthaka and others.
The World-Honored One, the Lord of Dharma, established it thus:
if one who has committed a pārājika offense goes forth and receives the precepts,
this is difficult to reconcile for the Sarvāstivādins.
If one who has committed a pārājika offense is no longer a bhikṣu because he lacks the precepts,
why not allow him to go forth again and receive the precepts?
This is because his mental continuum has reached such a state that he is no longer fit to be a bhikṣu.
The Sautrāntika replies:
Because the body has already been corrupted by shamelessness and lack of moral dread,
it lacks the power to give rise to the precepts.
Just as a scorched seed does not sprout again,
even if one who has committed a grave offense still calls himself a bhikṣu,
he has abandoned what was to be learned.
Furthermore, since he did not permit him to go forth again,
Śikṣānanda said: "What is the use of laboriously saving one who has no meaning in terms of the precepts?"
If one who has committed a grave offense still possesses the essential nature of the bhikṣu’s discipline,
you should personally take refuge in and pay homage to such a bhikṣu;
for when the time comes that the True Dharma is extinguished, there will be no further possibility of relinquishing it.
This is the *karmavācanā* (ritual procedure) of the Dharmaguptaka school;
*karman* here means "action.
According to the *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 117: [text follows].
The holders of the Vinaya say that the time when the Dharma is extinguished and disappears constitutes the fifth condition;
they speak as follows.
When the Dharma perishes, one abandons the precepts;
at the time when the True Dharma is extinguished, although all boundary demarcations (*sīmā*), ritual procedures (*karmavācanā*),
and the Vinaya no longer exist.
There is no principle for newly acquiring the vows if they have not already been obtained,
because the Prātimokṣa is derived from the instruction of others; however,
for those who have previously acquired the precepts, there is no possibility of relinquishing them when their dharma ceases.
According to the treatise cited below,
there are two aspects of the True Dharma:
first, the teaching (śāsana).
Second, regarding scriptural authority: the scriptures state in general that [the Dharma] will abide for only a thousand years.

There is further evidence that the *dharmavinaya* will abide for only a thousand years, while the period during which the *śāsana* abides exceeds this. Furthermore, the *Abhidharmamahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 183, also states:
The True Dharma lasts for a thousand years,
as previously explained.
If one follows the previous explanation:
At present, less than a thousand years have passed,
because the recitation of the *Prātimokṣa* and the performance of *karmavācanā* have not yet ceased.
According to the latter explanation, it may exceed a thousand years.
"Since it has been a long time since the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, how could one ever abandon the meditative absorptions (dhyāna) and the untainted [attainments]?
This concludes the second section below: the abandonment of the dhyāna and the path-precepts (mārga-śīla).
The term "etc. (ādi) refers to the inclusion of other contaminated wholesome factors and uncontaminated dharmas, in addition to the two types of restraint;
within this context, the textual flow primarily elucidates restraint.
For the sake of convenience in exposition, other dharmas are also clarified.
The verse states: "Up to the refinement of the faculties and the loss [of the path].
The first two lines clarify the relinquishing of contaminated precepts (*sāsrava-śīla*) and so forth.
The final two lines clarify the relinquishing of untainted precepts (*anāsrava-śīla*) and so forth.
The *Śāstra* states: "As for 'reaching that which differs from the form realm' (*rūpa-dhātu-viśeṣa*), this explains the first two lines: 'superior wholesome roots' (*viśiṣṭa-kuśala-mūla*)."
This refers to the four [stages] beginning with "heat" (ūṣmagata).
When a sentient being dies and abandons their homogeneous character (nikāyasabhāga),
if they are born into the desire realm (kāmadhātu):
If one is born into a higher stage, one necessarily abandons those [lower factors];
the rest of the text may be understood accordingly. In summary:
The precepts born of meditative concentration (*dhyāna-ja-śīla*) and so forth are relinquished through three conditions:
first, by changing one's level of rebirth (*bhūmi-saṃcāra*); second, by falling away from attainment (*parihāṇi*).
Third, at the end of life,
the precepts that follow the mind are acquired in accordance with the mind;
because the mind is relinquished, the precepts are likewise relinquished.
Therefore, there are three conditions for the relinquishing of the mind of equanimity, and likewise, there are three conditions for the relinquishing of the precepts.
Thus, it is said in the *Abhidharma-śāstra*:
The dhyāna restraint is acquired through the acquisition of the wholesome mind of the form realm and relinquished through the relinquishment of the wholesome mind of the form realm,
because it is contingent upon that mind. The same applies to the acquisition and relinquishment of the untainted restraint.

Because one attains relinquishment (*tyāga*) in accordance with the untainted mind (*anāsrava-citta*), the aforementioned treatise states that, as in the case of the formless realm (*ārūpya-dhātu*), there is relinquishment through changing stages or through falling away (*parihāṇi*).
However, there is no relinquishment of the precepts (*śīla*). The *Nyāyānusāra* (Treatise on the Principles), fascicle 39, criticizes this by saying:

When one abandons the homogeneous class (*nikāyasabhāga*) and when one becomes free from passion (*vairāgya*), one also abandons "Heat" (*uṣmagata*) and so forth, as well as the meditative absorption of the stage of decline (*hānabhāgīya*).
To include these cases, the word "etc. (*ādi*) is stated again.
In the Master’s commentary, the phrase "becoming free from passion" (*vairāgya*) should be added.
Just as wholesome states of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) are abandoned through three causes— changing levels (*bhūmi-saṃcāra*), falling away (*parihāṇi*), and detachment from passion (*vairāgya*)—

the same applies to those of the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*). The Abhidharmakośa masters defend this by stating that although one may abandon the "part conducive to decline" (*hānabhāgīya*) upon becoming detached from the ninth grade of defilement, [this does not contradict the rule].
If one is separated from the preceding eight stages, one cannot abandon them.
I did not mention the term "separation from defilement" (*vairāgya*) because I feared it might lead to confusion;

however, I did mention it for the case of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), because although the roots of goodness such as "Heat" (*uṣmagata*) and so forth are abandoned at death only in minor instances, they are nonetheless certain to be abandoned.
Furthermore, some explain this briefly without further discussion. Now,
according to this treatise and the *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra*,

it is held that only the four aids to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*), such as "heat" (*uṣmagata*) and so forth, are called the "excellent roots of goodness" (*kuśalamūla-viśeṣa*), and these are what are relinquished at the end of life.
The remaining factors conducive to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*) are not so distinguished that they are not relinquished at the time of death.
First, the *Nyāyānusāra* simply states that "heat" (*uṣmagata*) and the others [are not relinquished].
Second, the *Abhidharmakośa* uses the two conditions for the form realm as an analogy for the formless realm.
If other forms of *nirvedhabhāgīya* are also abandoned at death,
and since the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) also possesses the *nirvedhabhāgīyas*,
why is it not stated that they are abandoned at death?
The *Nyāyānusāra* applies the three conditions of the form realm by analogy to the formless realm and does not mention "death.
For this reason, we know that the other factors conducive to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*) are not particularly superior and are not abandoned at death.
Only the four names beginning with "warmth" (*ūṣman*) refer to the preeminent roots of goodness, because it is taught that they are abandoned solely at the death of an ordinary being (*pṛthagjana*).
Although Noble Ones (*ārya*) also abandon these roots of goodness such as warmth,
this occurs through the transition to another stage (*bhūmi-saṃcāra*), not through death.
If one dies in a particular realm and is reborn in that same realm, one does not relinquish [the precepts].
Question: If it is said that the *niyata-śīla* (fixed precepts) are relinquished at the end of life, this treatise states there are three conditions for relinquishment.
Furthermore, the *Nyāyānusāra* states there are four conditions for relinquishment through the abandonment of defilements (*vairāgya*).
If one speaks of three conditions or four conditions, it contradicts the *Pañcavastuka-śāstra*.
That treatise asks: "By what condition is the dhyāna-restraint obtained?
By what condition is it relinquished?"
Answer: Regarding the wholesome mind of the form realm, if it is acquired, it is acquired;
if it is relinquished, it is relinquished.
Furthermore, this is of two kinds.
First, due to falling back;
second, due to the shifting and changing of realms and stages.
The commentary explains:
The *Pañcavastuka* explains two types because it refers to total relinquishment;
this treatise and the *Nyāyānusāra*, however, explain three types because they refer to partial relinquishment as well.
Alternatively, three types are taught.
Or it is said that there are four kinds.
Question: The prātimokṣa-śīla and the dhyāna-śīla are both contaminated (sāsrava) and both are wholesome (kuśala).
Why are the conditions for abandonment different? The explanation is as follows:

if one considers the five conditions for the Prātimokṣa in contrast to those for meditative discipline (dhyāna-śīla), the Prātimokṣa precepts are acquired through informative action (vijñapti-karman); therefore, they are acquired by the mind and received through formal undertaking.

Furthermore, it is because of manifest action (*vijñapti-karman*) that the mind relinquishes those [precepts]; because they exist, there is relinquishment. The discipline of meditative concentration (*dhyāna-śīla*) is not obtained through manifest action by means of a deliberate mind;

therefore, there is no relinquishment [of it] by such means. Regarding the discipline of individual liberation (*prātimokṣa*), since it depends upon the body, when the basis changes, the mind also changes accordingly.

Therefore, there is no abandonment through the appearance of both sexual organs (*ubhayavyañjana*). Since the discipline of meditative concentration (*dhyāna-śīla*) depends on the body, when that basis changes, the mind also changes accordingly;
thus, there is no abandonment through the appearance of both sexual organs. As for the acquisition of the *prātimokṣa*, it arises from causes such as the motivating mind (*samutthāpaka-citta*).
Because one severs that wholesome mind by giving rise to wrong views,
and because one loses that precept upon losing that wholesome mind,
there is the severance of wholesomeness and the relinquishment of concentration-precepts; these concentration-precepts are obtained through the mind of concentration.
There is certainly no wrong view capable of severing the concentrated mind;

for various treatises state that only the wrong view of sensual desire severs the innate wholesome states of the desire realm, and thus there is no abandonment of the wholesome through such [wrong view]. Furthermore, the *prātimokṣa* vows have temporal limits of day and night.
There is that which is relinquished at the end of the night; the discipline of meditative concentration (*dhyāna-śīla*) has no such temporal limit.
There is that which is not relinquished at the end of the night; it is relinquished only at death, just like the discipline of meditative concentration.
However, the discipline of individual liberation (*prātimokṣa*) is entirely relinquished at death.
Regarding the abandonment of the precepts of meditative concentration (*samādhi-śīla*) at the end of life and the abandonment of warmth (*ūṣman*) and so forth: in summary,
while there are four points of difference between the prātimokṣa and the precepts of meditative concentration, there is one point of agreement.
If one compares the three conditions of the dhyāna-precepts with those of the prātimokṣa-precepts:

because the dhyāna-precepts are lost when one undergoes a change of level through being born in a higher or lower realm, they are abandoned by a change of level; whereas the prātimokṣa-precepts are necessarily abandoned at death, and thus are abandoned solely by death.

There is no loss of the meditative precepts through changing one's stage, because they are not lost by such a change; rather, the meditative precepts are lost through falling away due to the arising of afflictions.
Because one falls away from that meditative concentration, one consequently falls away from the meditative precepts.

Therefore, there is relinquishment through falling away; however, the separate [vows] are not lost through the arising of afflictions due to falling away, because the mind seeking the precepts has not been abandoned.
Thus, there is no relinquishment through falling away. According to the *Nyāya*, furthermore, there are different conditions for relinquishment through the separation from defilement (*vairāgya*).
This means that when one abandons the dhyāna conducive to decline at the time of becoming free from defilement,
because one abandons that dhyāna,
one simultaneously abandons the morality concomitant with that dhyāna.

Therefore, the dhyāna-precepts are relinquished through the abandonment of defilements; the prātimokṣa-precepts are not relinquished through the abandonment of defilements, because they depend on the mind that seeks the precepts.
Thus, there is no relinquishment through the abandonment of defilements;
there is only relinquishment at the end of life.
Regarding the classification into shared and distinct *prātimokṣa*: in summary,
when comparing the morality concomitant with meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samvara*) to the *prātimokṣa*,
according to this treatise, there are two that are distinct and one that is shared.
If one follows the correct principle that there is one generality and three distinctions,
the phrase "because uncontaminated wholesome dharmas reach the path of superior fruit" explains the latter two lines.
Untainted wholesome dharmas are abandoned through three conditions: first, by attaining a fruit;
that is, at the time of attaining a fruit, one abandons the preceding path of application as well as the path of the fruit itself. Second, by refining the faculties (*indriya*).
Acquisition of the sharp and abandonment of the dull; thirdly, by way of falling away (*parihāṇi*).
This means that at the time of falling away, one falls away from the path of the fruit as well as the path superior to the fruit. Regarding "falling away from acquisition" (*pratilambha-parihāṇi*):

having previously accomplished this dharma and subsequently falling away so that it is no longer accomplished is called falling away from acquisition. As for the "path of the fruit" (*phalamārga*): [it refers to the path by which the fruit is attained].
This refers to the path of fruition and the path of superior fruition.

Having attained the fruit, the arising of other untainted states that are superior to the preceding fruit is called the path of superior fruition; alternatively, that which leads toward a superior fruit is called the path of superior fruition.
If viewed in relation to a preceding fruit, it is called the path of superior fruit (*viśeṣa-mārga*);

if viewed in relation to a subsequent fruit, it is called the path of approach (*pratipannaka-mārga*). Furthermore, another interpretation holds that the path of superior fruit is broad in scope, such that any path arising from a fruit is termed a path of superior fruit.
The path directed toward the fruit is called the "path of approach" because it advances toward the subsequent fruit;
between these two interpretations, the former is superior.
Upon attaining the fruit, one abandons the previous path of approach.
How could one not abandon the path of superior fruits?
In brief, untainted wholesome dharmas are abandoned through three conditions.
First, by attaining the fruits;
second, by refining the faculties;
third, by falling away from the correct principle. (The *Sanlun xuanyi* [Treatise on the Meaning of the Three Treatises], fascicle 39, states: "It says: ..."
The Master of the Sūtra (Sūtrakāra) should have stated two conditions here,
because the mention of "attaining the fruit" includes the refinement of the faculties (*indriya-saṃcāra*).
That is to say, at the stage of refining the faculties, one necessarily regains the fruit.
Because one abandons both the path of dull faculties and the path of superior faculties.
Furthermore, it says:
"In this regard, I should provide a brief analysis."
If one considers the abandonment of the Path of Seeing and the Knowledge of the Type of the Path (mārgānvaya-jñāna),
it should be understood that this occurs solely through the attainment of a fruit and not through falling away;
however, for those of immovable dharma (akopyadharman) who are both [in the state of] No-More-Learning (aśaikṣa), neither exists.
The remaining untainted [attainments] may possess both types. The Abhidharmakośa masters offer this defense:

when the Master [Vasubandhu] separately mentions the two types of abandonment—namely, upon attaining a fruit and through the refinement of the faculties—the abandonment upon attaining a fruit refers to abandonment by way of a homogeneous [succession].
As when proceeding from the fruit of stream-entry to the fruit of once-returning:
if one is of dull faculties, one abandons the previous path of dull faculties and attains the path of dull faculties that constitutes the fruit;
if one is of sharp faculties, one abandons the previous path of sharp faculties and attains the path of sharp faculties that constitutes the fruit.
If the abandonment of faculties through refinement is based on abandonment by way of a different category—
just as one abandons the path of dull faculties to obtain the path of sharp faculties—
then although one necessarily also obtains the fruit at the stage of transforming the faculties, [the abandonment of the path occurs through this change of category].
Because it is not an abandonment of a dissimilar type, it is not designated by the term "attainment of the fruit.
This is the intention behind the Master’s separate explanation regarding the refinement of the faculties (*indriya-saṃskāra*).
As stated in the *Pañcavastuka-śāstra*, three types are likewise established.
Therefore, that treatise states:
"Question: By what conditions is the untainted restraint (anāsrava-saṃvara) obtained?
By what conditions is it relinquished?"
Answer: Regarding the statement that one attains [the fruit] together with the Path and does not completely abandon it:
if one abandons it partially, this occurs due to three conditions.
First, due to falling away (*parihāṇi*).
Second, by way of attaining the fruits;
third, by way of refining the faculties. Although the masters of the *Nyāyānusāra* wish to contradict my teaching, why do they instead refute their own school?
Furthermore, although this is a distinction, it does not fully accord with reason.

It should be understood that even those of sharp faculties who are still in training (śaikṣa) during the stage of the path of cultivation (bhāvanāmārga) do not fall away from their attainment of the fruit.
Why is this not stated?
If it were to be properly distinguished, one should say:
"If one abandons the path of vision (*darśanamārga*) and the subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārgānvayajñāna*)."
Furthermore, it should be understood that for those of sharp faculties on the path of cultivation who are still in training (śaikṣa),
[the attainment] occurs solely through the acquisition of a fruit and not through falling away;
for those of immovable dharma (akopyadharman) who are beyond training (aśaikṣa), both are absent.
The remaining untainted [precepts] may possess both types.
If one intends to analyze them, what fault would this entail? Question: Regarding the prātimokṣa precepts and the untainted precepts...
Although the contaminated (*sāsrava*) and uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) are different, both are wholesome.
For what reason do their objects (*ālambana*) differ? The explanation says: if one considers the five distinct conditions in contrast to the precepts of the Path (*mārga-śīla*).
Regarding the distinction between the precepts of meditative concentration (*dhyāna-śīla*) and the precepts of the Path (*mārga-śīla*):
the precepts of meditative concentration are relinquished at the end of life, whereas the precepts of the Path are not relinquished by the end of life.
Because they are not bound [to specific objects], taken as a whole;

however, if one analyzes them individually, the five conditions for the path-precepts (mārga-śīla) are distinct from those of the prātimokṣa-precepts. If one compares the three conditions of the path-precepts with the prātimokṣa-precepts:

The path-precepts (*mārga-śīla*) are abandoned through the attainment of a fruit; this is abandonment by attainment of a fruit because one abandons the previously inferior path upon attaining [a higher] fruit.

The discrete vows (*prātimokṣa*) are not abandoned through the attainment of a fruit, and therefore there is no abandonment by attainment of a fruit for them. The path-precepts are acquired by virtue of the mind.

At the time of refining the faculties (*indriya*), because one abandons the mind associated with the precepts, the precepts are also abandoned accordingly; thus there is abandonment of the precepts through the refinement of the faculties.

However, the Pratimokṣa [precepts] are not abandoned by the refinement of the faculties, as the mind seeking the precepts is not abandoned by the refinement of the faculties. As for the path-precepts (*mārga-śīla*), there is abandonment through falling away (*parihāṇi*).
There is no retrogression or relinquishment of the *prātimokṣa* [vows] distinct from those previously mentioned regarding meditative concentration and ethical discipline.

In summary, the ethical discipline of the Path differs from the *prātimokṣa* in three respects: its object, its cause, and its state (whether concentrated or non-concentrated). Regarding the differences between the *prātimokṣa* and the ethical discipline of the Path—concentrated versus non-concentrated—the conditions for their relinquishment are distinct.

Although the precepts of meditative concentration (*samādhi-śīla*) and the precepts of the Path (*mārga-śīla*) are distinguished as being with outflows (*sāsrava*) and without outflows (*anāsrava*), both are precepts that follow the mind (*cittānuparivartin*).

Why, then, are their conditions for relinquishment (*prahāṇa-pratyaya*) not equal? The explanation states: If one compares the three conditions of the precepts of meditative concentration with those of the precepts of the Path:
Because the *dhyāna-śīla* (meditative precepts) are contaminated (*sāsrava*) and are lost through changing levels (*bhūmi*), they involve relinquishment by changing levels.

Because the *mārga-śīla* (path precepts) are uncontaminated (*anāsrava*), they are not lost by changing levels, and thus there is no relinquishment by changing levels. The *dhyāna-śīla* is relinquished at the moment of death; because it is associated with factors such as *uṣmagata*, it is relinquished at the time of death.

Because the path-precepts (*mārga-śīla*) are not abandoned separately at the end of life, there is no abandonment through death. According to the correct principle (*nyāya*), the meditative precepts (*dhyāna-śīla*) are indeed abandoned through the separation from defilements (*vairāgya-parihāṇi*), because at the stage of detachment one abandons the factors conducive to decline (*hānabhāgīya*).
Because the factors conducive to decline (*hānabhāgīya*) enter into and exit from those afflictions (*kleśa*), when one abandons the afflictions, one also abandons the factors conducive to decline;

and by abandoning the factors conducive to decline, one also abandons the morality co-arising with those factors conducive to decline. Since both the morality of meditative concentration (*samādhi-śīla*) and the morality of the path (*mārga-śīla*) are subject to retrogression (*parihāṇi*), there is abandonment through retrogression in both cases. In summary:

Regarding the relationship between the morality of meditative concentration (*samādhi-śīla*) and the morality of the path (*mārga-śīla*), according to this treatise, there are two points of difference and one point of agreement;

however, according to the *Nyāyānusāra*, there is one point of agreement and three points of difference. If one considers the morality of the path in relation to the morality of meditative concentration through three conditions: first, the morality of the path is acquired by attaining the fruits [of the path] and by refining the faculties (*indriya-pariśodhana*), whereby one acquires the superior and abandons the inferior.

There is abandonment through attaining a fruit or through refining the faculties (*indriya-saṃcāra*), but not through the abandonment [of the restraint] of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) or morality (*śīla*) by means of attaining a fruit or refining the faculties.
There is no abandonment through attaining a fruit or refining the faculties;
rather, it is solely through the conditions for retrogression (*parihāṇi-pratyaya*), as explained previously. In summary:
The path-precepts (*mārga-śīla*) and the concentration-precepts (*samādhi-śīla*) differ in two respects and are identical in one.
Thus has been explained the acquisition of the precepts for those born with both sexual organs.
This concludes the third [section] on the relinquishment of non-restraint (*asaṃvara*).
The verse provides the answer to the inquiry.
The treatise states: "Up to 'because of abandoning the basis,' non-restraint is abandoned through three conditions."
First, because one abandons the basis through death.
Since non-virtuous discipline is originally acquired based on the homogeneous class of beings (*nikāya-sabhāga*),
that basis— the homogeneous class— is now abandoned.
This is because the basis for the non-virtuous precepts is also relinquished accordingly.
Second, "due to the power of attaining the precepts" refers to relinquishment by means of attaining the precepts.
This means that upon obtaining the two types of restraint— prātimokṣa and dhyāna— one abandons non-restraint (duḥśīla).
Due to internal causes and external conditions,
non-restraint is severed at the moment one attains the vows of discipline (saṃvara).
Because the nature and characteristics of wholesome and unwholesome precepts are mutually contradictory, they can never arise simultaneously.

Since the wholesome precepts, upon their initial arising, possess a predominant and powerful force, they are able to abandon the unwholesome precepts. Question: Among the three types of restraint (*saṃvara*), why is it not stated that the untainted restraint (*anāsrava-saṃvara*) abandons the unwholesome precepts? Explanation: Prior to the Path of Seeing (*darśana-mārga*), one necessarily attains the restraint of meditative concentration (*dhyāna-saṃvara*), which abandons those unwholesome precepts.
Because it has already been abandoned previously,
it is not said that the morality of the path is able to abandon it.
Third, it is because the continuity [of the mind] reaches a transformation of its basis (*āśraya*).
Third is the abandonment of both sexual organs.
This occurs because both sexual organs arise simultaneously within the continuum of the body,
and because of the transformation of the physical basis.
The mind also undergoes change accordingly.
Furthermore, because those with both sexual organs lack predominance (*adhipatya*), they are able to relinquish unwholesome precepts (*duḥśīla*).
Moreover, the *Nyāya* states:

However, the arising of both sexual organs causes one to relinquish both virtuous and non-virtuous discipline (*śīla*), because both rely upon the extreme predominance of sensual desire (*kāmacchanda*).
This does not apply to those such as eunuchs (*ṣaṇḍha*) and the like; they do not relinquish virtuous or non-virtuous vows (*saṃvara*).
The arising of these two [roots] is based on greed that is not extremely heavy.

Regarding the statement that "one who abides in immoral conduct is difficult to cure even when ill until death," this clarifies that immoral conduct is easily acquired and is obtained through a formal vow.
The unwholesome precepts are difficult to relinquish; even when the conditions for their abandonment arise, they are not abandoned.
One must first obtain the wholesome precepts before being able to abandon those [unwholesome ones].
This can be understood through an analogy.
Regarding the statement, "The non-restrained person extends even to those called 'intermediate'":
Question:
Other masters say that it extends because it is acquired based on informative action (*vijñapti*).
Answer: The former master’s intention is that the unwholesome mental disposition (*āśaya*) for non-restraint has not been permanently abandoned.
Just as when heated iron is set down, the red color ceases and the blue color arises, so too should one understand the two types of restraint—wholesome and unwholesome.
When the wholesome restraint ceases, the unwholesome restraint arises; such is the intention of the latter master.
Because one acquires wholesome discipline (*śīla*) by abandoning unwholesome discipline (*aśīla*),
and because there is no further cause for the acquisition [of non-discipline] if one does not act again— since non-discipline arises based on the manifest action (*vijñapti*)—
it is merely intermediate (*madhyama*).
According to the *Vibhāṣā*, fascicle 117, the former masters were the teachers of Gandhāra,
while the latter masters were the great commentators of Kaśmīra.

Although that treatise lacks a commentator and takes the later master as authoritative, the *Nyāyabindu-ṭīkā* (Treatise on Right Reasoning), at section thirty-nine, takes the former master as authoritative.
Thus, that treatise states:
The previous explanation is more reasonable, because at the time one first received the precepts, the underlying disposition (*āśaya*) toward evil was not permanently abandoned;
thus, based on that prior manifest action (*vijñapti-karman*), the unwholesome restraint (*duḥśīla*) arises once again. The masters of the *Abhidharmakośa* offer this defense:
All the masters state that one loses the precepts upon acquisition [of a new status].
Since these have already been acquired as precepts,
how could they not be lost?
Since it is not produced again later,
how could it arise anew? Therefore,
we know that the latter explanation is correct.
The *Nyāyānusāra* contradicts the *Abhidharmakośa*;
this [contradiction] actually harms the masters of our own school. Question: This treatise states that there are three conditions for the relinquishment of non-virtuous discipline (*dauḥśīlya*).
Why, then, does the *Mahāvibhāṣā* state that there are four conditions for its relinquishment?
Therefore, the *Vibhāṣā* (117) states:
"All non-restraint (*asaṃvara*) is relinquished through four conditions.
First, by undertaking the prātimokṣa restraint."
Second, obtaining the dhyāna-prātimokṣa restraint;
third, the arising of both sexual organs;
fourth, abandoning the homogeneous class (*nikāya-sabhāga*). The commentary explains that both the prātimokṣa and dhyāna precepts are termed "obtaining the precepts" (*prāpti-śīla*).
This treatise combines [the two] into one type.

The *Mahāvibhāṣā* distinguishes them as two because they differ in being either fixed or non-fixed; thus, their opening and closing differ. Question: How is "individual liberation" established as the opposite of "bad discipline"?
Why is it that the distinctions among the conditions for relinquishing [the precepts] differ?

The explanation is as follows: if one considers the distinct explanations of the five conditions in relation to unwholesome discipline (*duḥśīla*), it is difficult to acquire [the wholesome precepts] but easy to relinquish them.

Because it is acquired through the performance of a ritual procedure, its relinquishment is easy; however, since the ritual procedure for non-virtuous discipline (duḥśīla) is not established— being inherently evil— it is difficult to relinquish.
Because it no longer exists, there is relinquishment. Specifically, the prātimokṣa is acquired through the mind that seeks the precepts;

therefore, by giving rise to wrong views and severing the mind that seeks the precepts, that mental state is not established, and the precepts are likewise relinquished. There is also relinquishment through the severance of the roots of goodness. However, this is not the case for unwholesome discipline (duḥśīla).

Regarding the absence of the "abandonment through severance" (*prahāṇa-parityāga*) for unwholesome precepts: Why is there no "abandonment through severance" among the unwholesome precepts? The explanation states: The mind that seeks unwholesome precepts is an unwholesome affliction (*kleśa*). When that affliction is severed, one necessarily attains the precept of meditative concentration (*dhyāna-śīla*). Therefore, [the abandonment of unwholesome precepts] is not categorized as "abandonment through severance."
Having attained the precepts of meditative concentration (*samādhi-śīla*), one necessarily abandons the precepts of misconduct (*duḥśīla*).

Since there is no case where one has severed those afflictions (*kleśa*) yet has not attained the precepts of meditative concentration, there is no abandonment of misconduct that does not involve severing them. Furthermore, the meaning of attaining the precepts should be understood as the abandonment of misconduct upon its severance.

When one attains the precepts of virtue (*śīla*), although one may still harbor the intention to seek the precepts of non-virtue, because the essence of those non-virtuous precepts is not established, it is called "the abandonment of evil.

Regarding the abandonment through the relinquishing of evil: although the intention to seek the precepts of non-virtue remains present, because one has attained the precepts of virtue, one is able to relinquish the non-virtuous precepts; this is called "the abandonment of evil through relinquishing. [Likewise,] there is the abandonment of virtue and the relinquishing of virtue.
One does not abandon virtuous discipline (*śīla*) by means of immoral discipline;

rather, it is due to wrong view that both the mind and the discipline fail to be established. Because the *prātimokṣa* has temporal limits of day and night, there is abandonment at the end of the night; because immoral discipline lacks such temporal limits of day and night, there is no abandonment at the end of the night. [It is abandoned] upon death.
Regarding those of both sexual organs, both good and evil are identical;
this meaning should be understood. In summary:

Regarding the distinctions between the three types of non-restraint and the prātimokṣa vows: two are the same. If one compares the three conditions for non-restraint with the prātimokṣa, non-restraint is easy to acquire but difficult to relinquish;
there are cases where one acquires the vow but does not relinquish it.
Since it is difficult to acquire and easy to relinquish through separate acquisition,
its abandonment is accomplished immediately;
it is not because one becomes a person of non-restraint due to the undertaking of evil discipline.
One must first abandon what is old.
If one does not first abandon such things as the occupation of a sheep-butcher, it is merely remaining in the intermediate state;
thus one passes away.
The two forms [of sexual misconduct] are identical, so there is no contradiction.

In general, regarding the relationship between the specific vows (*prātimokṣa*) and the unwholesome precepts (*dauḥśīlya*), these two points are the same. Question: Why do the conditions for relinquishing the meditative vows (*dhyāna-śīla*) and the unwholesome precepts differ? Answer: If one compares the three conditions for relinquishing the meditative vows with those of the unwholesome precepts:
Because the *dhyāna-śīla* (meditative precepts) are lost when one changes levels, there is relinquishment through changing levels.

Since the *akuśala-śīla* (unwholesome precepts) are definitely relinquished at the end of life and not by changing levels, there is no relinquishment through changing levels for them. As for the *dhyāna-śīla*, because it is lost when one falls away due to the arising of afflictions (*kleśa*), the precepts are also relinquished accordingly; thus, there is relinquishment through falling away.
The non-virtuous precepts (*duḥśīla*) and the afflictions (*kleśa*) are fully established;
since there is no further ground for regression, there is no regressive relinquishment.

They are relinquished only at the end of life, sharing the same mode of abandonment as the non-virtuous precepts. However, according to the *Nyāya* (Correct Principle), there is a further distinction regarding the separation from defilement (*vairāgya*).

Regarding the restraint of meditative concentration (*samādhi-śīla*), there is relinquishment through detachment (*vairāgya-parityāga*) because one relinquishes the factors conducive to decline (*hāna-bhāgīya*) at the stage of becoming free from passion.
Since non-restraint (*akuśala-śīla*) has necessarily already been relinquished when one first attains meditative concentration, there is no relinquishment through detachment for it. In summary:
The meditative precept (dhyāna-śīla) stands in contrast to the unwholesome precept (akuśala-śīla).
If one follows the distinctions made in this treatise, there is one point of agreement and two points of difference;
if one follows the *Nyāyānusāra*, there is one point of agreement and three points of difference. Thus, the three conditions of the unwholesome precept are contrasted with the meditative precept.
Because one who possesses unwholesome precepts may obtain wholesome precepts,
there is the relinquishing of those precepts; however, for one established in the precepts of meditative concentration (*dhyāna-śīla*), there is necessarily no obtaining of unwholesome precepts.

When one acquires the unwholesome precepts (*duḥśīla*), the meditative precepts (*dhyāna-śīla*) necessarily first lapse. When the meditative precepts lapse, the unwholesome precepts have not yet been acquired.

Therefore, there is no acquisition of the unwholesome precepts while abandoning them. Within the body where the unwholesome precepts exist, it is possible for two sexual organs (*dviliṅga*) to arise; when the two sexual organs arise, [the unwholesome precepts] are abandoned.

Within the category of the body of meditative discipline (*samādhi-śīla*), because the birth of both sexual organs does not occur, there is no abandonment [of the discipline] through the possession of both organs. As for unwholesome discipline (*duḥśīla*), it is entirely abandoned at the end of life;
as for meditative discipline, it is partially abandoned at the end of life.
Thus, they are identical only in that they are both partially abandoned at the end of life. In summary:

Regarding the distinction between the precepts of immorality (*duḥśīla*) and the precepts of meditative concentration (*dhyāna-śīla*): two are distinct, while one is the same. Question: Why do the conditions for the relinquishment of the precepts of the path (*mārga-śīla*) and the precepts of immorality differ? Answer: If one compares the three conditions for the relinquishment of the precepts of the path with those of the precepts of immorality:
The path-precepts (mārga-śīla) possess three [conditions]: the attainment of fruit, the refinement of faculties (indriya-saṃskāra), and falling away;
thus, there can be relinquishment through the attainment of fruit, relinquishment through the refinement of faculties, and relinquishment through falling away.

Since the unwholesome precepts (akuśala-śīla) lack all three of these meanings, they do not have these three types of relinquishment. This is when the three conditions of the unwholesome precepts are contrasted with those of the path-precepts.
At the time of death, one must necessarily relinquish unwholesome precepts;

they are relinquished at the end of life. As for the precepts of the Path, they remain established even after death; they are not relinquished at the end of life. Unwholesome precepts may be acquired, and wholesome precepts may be acquired; there is the relinquishing of precepts.

In the case of the path-precepts (*mārga-śīla*), there is absolutely no principle by which one could obtain evil precepts (*akuśala-śīla*), nor is there any principle by which one could abandon them. Within a body possessing evil precepts, it is possible for two sexual organs (*dviliṅga*) to arise;

thus, there is abandonment [of the precepts] due to the arising of two sexual organs. However, within a body possessing path-precepts, two sexual organs do not arise; therefore, there is no abandonment due to the arising of two sexual organs. To state it in summary:
Regarding the mutual relationship between the moral precepts (*śīla*) and the immoral precepts (*duḥśīla*), the three conditions for each are distinct.
As for how one abandons the intermediate non-informative matter (*avijñapti*):
this concludes the fourth section on the abandonment of the intermediate non-informative matter.
Because it is neither restraint nor non-restraint, it is called "intermediate.
The verse says: "Upon reaching [another stage], completing the task, the end of life, and the severance of the faculties.
Intermediate non-informative matter (*avijñapti*) is relinquished through six conditions.
First, abandonment through the relinquishing of the mind that undertakes [the vow];
second, abandonment through the loss of its force;
and third, abandonment through the completion of the action.
Fourth, by the relinquishment of objects;
fifth, by the relinquishment of life-span;
sixth, by the relinquishment of the basis of the faculties.
The former is abandoned by the path of seeing; the latter is abandoned by the path of cultivation;
both apply to the six intermediate stages.
The commentary states: "Regarding 'cessation occurs through six conditions,' this indicates the title and enumerates the number.
Question: As it says in the *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya* (or *Vibhāṣā*) regarding the abandonment of neutral wholesome and unwholesome [states]:
"This is called the brief *vibhāṣā* on the previously mentioned manifest and non-manifest karma (*vijñapti-avijñapti-karman*)."

If that treatise also speaks of manifest action (*vijñapti-karman*), why does this treatise speak only of non-manifest action (*avijñapti*)? The explanation is: this treatise specifically elucidates non-manifest action and does not discuss manifest action.

The *Abhidharmamahāvibhāṣā* explains both [types of karma] because they both involve clear comprehension; thus it speaks of both. Furthermore, another interpretation holds that when one abandons the unmanifest (*avijñapti*), one necessarily also abandons the manifest (*vijñapti*);

since the latter is known by its shadow-like appearance, it is not mentioned separately. Yet another interpretation holds that this treatise speaks only of the unmanifest because it refers specifically to the abandonment of active manifestation (*samudācāra*).
The *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* explains both [types of abandonment]—possession (*prāpti*) and manifestation (*samudācāra*)—because it treats them comprehensively.

First, regarding "abandonment by means of the mind that accepts [the precepts], which discards what was previously accepted": this refers to abandonment through the severance and destruction of the mind that accepted [them].
This unmanifest [action] is acquired through undertaking;
that is to say, by first making a vow, one undertakes with a virtuous or non-virtuous mind, making this aspiration: "I shall act thus."
At certain times, one constantly performs wholesome or unwholesome deeds;
wholesome deeds include such acts as offering praise and so forth,
while unwholesome deeds include such acts as beating and so forth.
The non-informative [action] (avijñapti) that follows [the vow] would be deficient if the initial commitment were not fulfilled and the original vow were to fail,
should one suddenly feel regret midway and abandon the virtuous or non-virtuous resolve originally undertaken, thinking thus: [I shall stop].
From this time forth, I renounce what I previously received; thus, the non-informative [action] is abandoned.
Originally, this non-informative [action] was acquired through the mind of undertaking;
now, by abandoning that mind of undertaking, the non-informative [action] is also abandoned.
If it is through the mind of equanimity that one abandons [the discipline], this is called "abandonment" (*tyāga*); it is not the case that it is not accomplished.
If it is through the abandonment of the unmanifest (*avijñapti*) that it is no longer accomplished, this is designated as "abandonment."
Furthermore, the *Nyāyānusāra* (Treatise on Right Reasoning), fascicle 39, states:
"First, it is relinquished due to the abandonment or destruction of the accepting mind (*samādāna-citta*).
That is to say, one previously vowed to accept [the precept] to always pay homage to a caitya at a certain time."
As well as [engaging in] praises and hymns.
Now he thinks: "Henceforth I shall no longer do so.
From that point on, his underlying intention (*āśaya*) ceases.

Because that person has abandoned their original intention (*āśaya*), or because they perform another action with an intensified force that contradicts the previously manifest activity, the non-informative matter (*avijñapti*) ceases once the original intention has subsided.

According to the *Nyāyānusāra*, it is stated that within the state of receiving [the precepts], there is also the performance of an action; however, evil actions are not mentioned here, being omitted for brevity, or perhaps subsumed under the word "etc. Furthermore, it is said that one performs another action with an intensified force.
This contradicts the previously established practice.
At that time, when the originally inferior intention ceases, the non-informative [action] (*avijñapti*) is severed.
To claim that one attains the superior and abandons the inferior is a point that differs from this treatise.
In this context, because feeling and mind are severed and destroyed, it is "equanimity" (*upekṣā*) in the sense of being appropriate;
it is called "cessation of mental inclination" (*manas-kāma-śānti*) in the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, and "cessation of longing" (*abhilāṣa-nirodha*) in the *Saṃyuktābhidharmahṛdaya-śāstra*.
The names differ, but the meaning is the same.
Regarding "the two cease when their force is exhausted":
the two are relinquished because they are severed and destroyed by their own force.
That is to say, the non-informative [action] (*avijñapti*) is produced by the two forces of pure faith and intense affliction;
when those two forces are severed or destroyed, the non-informative [action] is then relinquished.
The analogy can be understood through this comparison. Question:
As stated in the *Nyāyānusāra*, "Secondly, it is abandoned because of being severed by force;
that is to say, the non-informative [matter] (*avijñapti*) induced by the force of pure faith or the afflictions [is abandoned]."
When the force that limits those two is severed or destroyed, the non-informative [action] (*avijñapti*) is relinquished,
just like a released arrow or a potter’s wheel;
therefore, the Master (*ācārya*) has stated this.
Because it is induced by the power of the motivating impulse (*samutthāna*),
even though the preparatory effort (*prayoga*) and the underlying intention (*āśaya*) have ceased,
the unmanifest (*avijñapti*) may continue to persist for the duration of one's life.
It should be understood that the same applies even to striking birds and beasts with extremely intense fetters of passion.
Alternatively, if one has previously established a limit for such a duration,
the non-informative [matter] (*avijñapti*) is severed once that force of the limit has passed.
Furthermore, the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 122, states:
The limit of their duration has not yet passed;
this refers to the pure mind and the intense fetters.
Whichever wholesome or unwholesome actions are performed,
the non-informative [matter] (avijñapti) continues uninterrupted according to their force.
For example, as when one kills *kuṇḍa* ants— here called "foot-breaking ants"— due to intense obsession (*paryavasthāna*).
Some say it refers to "eggs and ants.
This name contains two meanings;
therefore, it is not translated.
It is not the case that the non-informative [action] (*avijñapti*) arising from shamelessness (*anapatrāpya*), which is intended to harm or kill, continues in a series for as long as one lives.
The same applies to that which is performed with pure faith (*śraddhā*).

For example, suppose there is someone who, having given rise to profound faith, prepares ritual implements and offers them to the Sangha, making various offerings such as burning incense and scattering flowers.
Or, on such days as those taught by the Buddha— the anniversary of the birth, the enlightenment, or the parinirvāṇa, or the five-year assembly (pañcavārṣika), and so forth—
one invites the community of monks and makes various offerings,
giving rise to a mind of pure faith and initiating actions of body and speech.
As long as the intention has not ceased or the application has not been relinquished,
the non-informative [action] (avijñapti) is not severed.
If the intention ceases and one relinquishes the preparatory effort,
the non-informative [action] is then severed.
The detailed explanation regarding the intermediate course in other places is also like this.

The *Nyāyānusāra* states: "Although one may abandon the application (*prayoga*) and the intention (*āśaya*), the non-informative [action] (*avijñapti*) may still continue to persist for the duration of one's life."
The *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* states: "If the mental inclination ceases and the preparatory effort is relinquished, the non-informative [action] is then severed.
Both [texts] explain that the power [of the action] is severed and abandoned;
why, then, do these two treatises differ?
Furthermore, what does the *Abhidharmakośa* state? The commentary explains that pure faith (*śraddhā*) and intense obsession (*tīvra-paryavasthāna*) each have three grades:
namely, the highest-of-the-high (*adhimātrādhimātra*), the middle-of-the-high (*madhyādhimātra*), and the low-of-the-high (*mṛdv-adhimātra*).
If one gives rise to the highest-of-the-high degree of pure faith and intense obsession...
During that interval, although the mental intention has ceased and the application of effort has been relinquished,
the unmanifest [action] is not severed;
this remains so even if one gives rise to superior or middling degrees of pure faith, or to intense fetters of the highest degree.
In the interim, when the intention ceases and one abandons the application,
the non-informative [action] is immediately severed;
this is explained according to the three grades in the *Nyāyānusāra*.

If [the defilement] arises as the highest of the high (adhimātra-adhimātra), it persists for the duration of one's life; if it arises as the high-middling (adhimātra-madhya) or the high-low (adhimātra-mṛdu), it does not persist for the duration of one's life.
Therefore, it is said "or possibly" (vā syāt) to indicate that this is not fixed.

Regarding this passage from the *Vibhāṣā*, if one relies on the two grades of pure faith—namely, the "middling-superior" and the "superior-superior"—it is because of the forceful entanglements (*paryavasthāna*) that it states:

"The unmanifest (*avijñapti*) of the application, the intention, the cessation, and the relinquishment is severed. Alternatively, this may be because the intentions of the various authors of the treatises differ.
Since there is no explicit statement in the *Abhidharmakośa*,
one may follow either the *Nyāyānusāra* or the *Mahāvibhāṣā*.
Some may say that these two treatises are identical;
in that case, there is no contradiction.
In the *Vibhāṣā* and the *Abhidharmahṛdaya*, the names differ—such as "limiting power" (*nāma-śakti*) versus "transgression" (*atikrama*)—but their meaning is the same.
Third, it is abandoned through the cessation and destruction of the action by which it was produced;
for this non-informative matter (*avijñapti*) is acquired through the performance of an action.
This refers to performing virtuous actions or unvirtuous actions;
virtuous actions include such things as paying homage and offering praise.
Evil [actions], such as striking with a club and so forth,
involve non-informative matter (*avijñapti*) that follows along, just like previously undertaken wholesome or unwholesome karma.
Now, one forms the thought, "I shall not do this again," and the non-informative matter is thereby relinquished.
Originally, this non-informative [matter] (avijñapti) was acquired through an action;
now, when the action is abandoned, the non-informative matter is also abandoned.
Therefore, the Nyāyānusāra states:
Third, it is relinquished through the abandonment or destruction of the performed action;
that is, although one has not relinquished the fundamental mind of undertaking, one no longer performs the actions undertaken,
except for those instances where one fails to act due to forgetfulness.

By means of this non-informative [action] (avijñapti), one undertakes a commitment; when the preparatory effort (prayoga) ceases, the non-informative [action] is then relinquished. Question: The mind of undertaking also involves a commitment, and the performance of the action likewise involves a committed mind.

What is the distinction between these two? One explanation states that the undertaking of the mind is discussed in terms of the mental faculty, whereas the performance of the action is explained in terms of body and speech.
Another explanation states that by the very act of pledging to undertake the mind, one immediately acquires it.
Action is accomplished only through performance; furthermore, although the mind of undertaking (*samādāna-citta*) also possesses that action,
the mind of undertaking is more powerful and preeminent,
because the unmanifest (*avijñapti*) arises solely from the mind of undertaking.
It is merely called the "mind of undertaking" and not the "performance of action.
Although the performance of action also involves that preliminary intention,
the performance of action is more powerful and predominant.
Because non-informative matter (avijñapti) is acquired solely through the performance of an action,
it is termed "action" (karma) and not "receiving-mind" (samādāna-citta).
In the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, it is called the "abandonment of preparatory effort" (prayoga-prahāṇa).
The *Abhidharmasamuccaya* calls this "the skillful means of equanimity" (*upekṣā-upāya*); the names differ, but the meaning is the same.
Fourth, regarding the matter of things reaching the nets and so forth:
The *Nyāyānusāra* explains:
"Originally, the non-informative [action] (*avijñapti*) arises induced by that object;
when that object perishes, the non-informative [action] is thereby severed."
In the *Vibhāṣā*, it is called "dharmas" (vastu);
in the *Saṃyuktābhidharmahṛdaya*, it is called "if there is a thing" (yadi vastu). The names are all similar.
Regarding "the fifth is due to the transformation of the life-span up to existence": the fifth is abandonment due to the severance and destruction of the life-span.
The originally acquired intermediate wholesome and unwholesome non-informative matter [is abandoned] by virtue of the supporting body.
Because of the relinquishing of life,
and because the basis upon which that [unmanifest action] depends— the homogeneous body— undergoes transformation,
the unmanifest action is thereby severed.
The *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* names it after its basis (*āśraya*),
while the *Saṃyuktābhidharma-hṛdaya-śāstra* names it as "body" (*kāya*);
in meaning, there is no contradiction between them.
Sixth, regarding the abandonment of the non-informative [matter] induced by the roots of goodness:
it is abandoned through the severance and destruction of the roots of goodness.
That is to say, when one initiates the preparatory effort to sever the roots of goodness.
At the stage of preparatory application (*prayoga*), one abandons the unmanifest (*avijñapti*) induced by the intermediate roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*).
The *Nyāyānusāra* raises an objection, stating:
"The sixth [type of abandonment] occurs because the basis—the sense faculties—is severed or destroyed."
This means that at the time one initiates the preparatory effort (*prayoga*) to sever the roots of goodness or when committing an evil act,
one respectively abandons the non-informative matter (*avijñapti*) induced by those respective roots.

However, it is not until the time of attaining meditative absorption (*dhyāna*) after having severed the roots of goodness that one abandons the intermediate wholesome or unwholesome non-informative matter.
Because they are weak and inferior,
when one initiates an application of effort (*prayoga*), one immediately abandons the intermediate unmanifest (*avijñapti*) states of both good and evil.
How is it that the Master of the Sūtras (Sthiramati) speaks of the sixth condition in this context as being "the severance of the roots of goodness" (*kuśalamūla-ccheda*)?
If one were to say that the preparatory stage for abandoning the roots of goodness is also called "abandoning the roots of goodness" and thus constitutes the sixth condition,
then one should likewise say that the preparatory stage for dhyāna is also called "dhyāna," which would result in there being seven conditions.
Because one abandons unwholesome non-informative matter (*avijñapti*) during the preparatory stage (*prayoga*) of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*),
it should be said that "roots" here refers to both wholesome and unwholesome roots.
The term "abandonment" (*prahāṇa*) mentioned is the abandonment occurring during the preparatory stage.
Because the abandonment based on the faculties serves as the sixth condition,
this interpretation of the verse is logically sound.
The *Nyāyānusāra* states that each of these six intermediate conditions is individually capable of relinquishing both the wholesome and the unwholesome.
Regarding what is called "severing the roots":
the roots encompass both the wholesome and the unwholesome;
"severing" refers to the severance of the preparatory application (*prayoga*).
If one abandons the preparatory application for wholesome states that are intermediate,
or abandons the preparatory application for unwholesome states that are intermediate,
this constitutes the preparatory application for dhyāna. The Vaibhāṣika masters offer this defense:
In reality, the severance of the faculties as described in the verse follows the explanation given in the *Nyāya* (Principles);
however, in the prose commentary, the specific mention of "severing the wholesome" serves as an implicit indication of the severance of the unwholesome.
Alternatively, it may be so.
The Master of the Treatise intends for later students to discern between what is awakened and what is unawakened;
one should know that herein, wherever a wholesome state arises through the acquisition of the wholesome, it is [awakened].
Furthermore, those [roots] arising from preparatory wholesome states are all abandoned at the time of the preparatory effort for abandoning the roots of goodness; likewise,
those intermediate unwholesome states are abandoned at the time of the preparatory effort for abandoning evil.

This refers to the mental state of equanimity (*upekṣā*) during the intermediate stage of the preparatory application (*prayoga*) for meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), which is termed "abandoning the preparatory application for evil.

That which is called "abandoning" during the preparatory stage means that if the wholesome preparatory application is not accomplished, one abandons and relinquishes the non-informative (*avijñapti*) [matter].
If wholesome states acquired at birth,
as well as unwholesome states,
are suppressed so that they do not manifest, this is termed "abandonment."
The unmanifest (*avijñapti*) can be relinquished;

it is not the case that its substance is not established. Question: Why is it that neutral wholesome and unwholesome [actions] are relinquished only at the time of the preliminary application (*prayoga*)? Answer: Because they are weak, they are relinquished only through the preliminary application. Objection: Since the wholesome [action] of the preliminary application gives rise to the Prātimokṣa vows, it is strong.
How is it that one also abandons [the roots of goodness] during the stage of application (*prayoga*)? The explanation says:

although those [roots] are strong, because they are abandoned at this stage due to the abandonment of the ability to generate the mind [of awakening], they are also abandoned accordingly. An objection states: what about the innate wholesome [roots] that give rise to the intermediate wholesome [roots]?

Furthermore, regarding the stage of intermediate unwholesome preparatory effort (*prayoga*) from which an unwholesome mind arises—since that [unwholesome mind] has not yet been abandoned, how can the mind that produces it be abandoned?

The explanation says: Although the mind that produces it has not yet been abandoned, because its nature is inferior, it is abandoned. Question: When one abandons the preparatory effort for meditative absorption (*dhyāna-prayoga*), is it also possible to abandon the preparatory effort for undertaking the vows of restraint (*saṃvara-śīla*)? The explanation says: It cannot be abandoned.
The treatise states that one abandons [the preparatory stage] during the application (*prayoga*) of dhyāna.

Furthermore, because its nature is neutral (*madhya*), it does not conflict with the undertaking of the precepts; since one does not abandon it even at the fundamental stage (*maula*), how much less so during the application? Objection: Since its nature is neutral, why would it not be compatible with dhyāna? Response: Because dhyāna correctly abandons evil, it abandons the state of evil and abides in the middle. Objection: Individual liberation (*prātimokṣa*) is not primarily capable of abandoning the afflictions (*kleśa*).
How can one abandon non-restraint (*asaṃvara*)? One explanation is that it is abandoned by means of its direct opposition and contradiction with the evil precepts (*duḥśīla*).

Although this is not called "abandonment" in the sense of attaining restraint through the severance of afflictions (*kleśa-prahāṇa*), it is nonetheless an abandonment. Another explanation is that one is indeed able to abandon it.
Just as one who attains meditative absorption (*dhyāna*) is able to relinquish immoral conduct (*duḥśīla*),

so too should it be understood that in the stage of preparatory application (*prayoga*), one relinquishes both evil and neutral states when attaining the discipline of individual liberation (*prātimokṣa*).
Since one has already abandoned the unwholesome restraint (*akuśala-saṃvara*) at the very moment of correctly obtaining the [pure] precepts,
one must also abandon the preparatory application (*prayoga*) and the intermediate state (*madhyama*).
How could it be that one is about to receive the *prātimokṣa* vows?
One does not abandon the intermediate state of evil while receiving those wholesome precepts;
for since one must first abandon [the unwholesome] at the time of reception,
the statement that the intermediate state of evil does not contradict the wholesome precepts refers to the period after the precepts have already been obtained.

If one were to violate the precepts immediately upon first receiving them, it would contradict the arising of correct principle; thus, I shall not provide a brief summary nor discuss this further. It should be understood that among the various treatises explaining the grounds for relinquishing the precepts, the texts are often incomplete.
This treatise, according to the *Nyāyānusāra*, fully explains six types [of non-informative action (*avijñapti*)], which may be said to be comprehensive.

Question: Why do the conditions for abandoning the distinct types of non-informative action (*vijñapti*) and the intermediate type differ? Answer: If one compares the five conditions for abandoning the distinct types with those for the intermediate type:
The increase and excellence of distinct wholesome dharmas do not depend on having two sexual organs;
rather, they are abandoned by the presence of two sexual organs. Those who abide in the intermediate state of neutrality are not in contradiction with having two sexual organs.
There is abandonment through the loss of both sexual organs; for the *prātimokṣa* vows, there are fixed limits of day and night, so there is abandonment at the end of the night.
For those who abide in the intermediate state (*madhyama*), there is no such fixed limit.
There is no relinquishing at the end of the night;

therefore, the meaning of "relinquishing" (prahāṇa) should be understood as the cessation of the mind. The terms "cessation" (nirodha) and "relinquishing" (prahāṇa) are identical in both name and meaning when referring to the cessation at the end of life.
The severance of the roots of goodness is similar in its basis and involves the severance of a portion;

in summary, there are two distinctions regarding the intermediate state of the Pratimokṣa, while three aspects are common. If one correlates the six conditions of the intermediate state with the Pratimokṣa, [the following occurs].
In the intermediate state (*antarābhava*), because there is a cessation of power, activity, and objects, these three types of equanimity (*upekṣā*) exist.
It is not so in the case of the separate [vows], for which these three types of equanimity do not exist.
Regarding the abandonment of feeling and mind, it is because their meaning is equivalent to abandonment.
The severance of life-span and the relinquishment [of roots] share the same name and meaning.
Regarding the severance of the faculties, they are likewise severed together with the abandonment of the wholesome roots; in brief, this is the case.

Regarding the differences and similarities between the three types of distinct vows and the intermediate [vow]: Question: Why do the conditions for relinquishing the meditative vow (*dhyāna-śīla*) and the intermediate non-informative action (*avijñapti*) differ? Answer: If one compares the three conditions for relinquishing the meditative vow with those of the intermediate [vow]...
Because the morality of meditative concentration (dhyāna-śīla) is lost when one changes levels,
it is relinquished by changing levels;
intermediate morality is relinquished by death.
Alternatively, there is abandonment through preparatory effort (*prayoga-prahāṇa*), because it is not lost by changing levels;
