thus, there is no abandonment by changing levels. However, because there is retrogression regarding the meditative concentration and the precepts, there is abandonment through retrogression (*parihāṇi-prahāṇa*).
If one abides in a wholesome state, it is not abandoned through the arising of afflictions due to falling away;
if one abides in an unwholesome state, it is because the afflictions were already established previously,
and thus it is not abandoned through falling away.
It is taught that there is no loss or relinquishment while in the intermediate state;
it is only at death that relinquishment occurs in the same manner. However, this applies to the relinquishment of the portion of meditative concentration and ethical discipline.
Regarding the complete relinquishment of the intermediate state:

in summary, while the meditative restraint (dhyāna-śīla) and the intermediate state differ in two respects and agree in one, if one compares the six conditions of the intermediate state with the meditative restraint:
Only the relinquishment at the end of life is explained as before;
the relinquishment due to the remaining five conditions occurs only within the intermediate state (*antarābhava*).
Regarding the meditative and ethical precepts, there is nothing further to be known. In summary:

Regarding the five differences between the path-precepts (*mārga-śīla*) and the intermediate-unmanifest (*anivṛtāvyākṛta-vijñapti*), one point is the same: the question asks why the conditions for the relinquishment (*tyāga-pratyaya*) of the path-precepts and the intermediate-unmanifest differ. The explanation states: if one compares the three conditions of the path-precepts with those of the intermediate [unmanifest], [the difference lies therein].
The path-precepts (mārga-śīla) possess these three types of relinquishment because they involve attaining fruits, refining the faculties, and falling away;
the intermediate [precepts] are not like this and thus lack these three forms of relinquishment.
Therefore, the three are distinct.

If one contrasts the six conditions for the intermediate [neutral] state with the precepts of the Path (mārga-śīla), since the latter possess neither [of these conditions], the six are all distinct. Question: Why do the conditions for relinquishing unwholesome precepts (akuśala-avijñapti) and those for the intermediate non-informative [neutral] state differ? Answer: If one contrasts the three conditions for unwholesome precepts with those of the intermediate state:
Because it is difficult to relinquish unwholesome precepts, their relinquishment does not constitute the acquisition of [wholesome] precepts;
intermediate [precepts], however, are easily relinquished.
The ritual procedure is thus completed.

Alternatively, because the preparatory effort is relinquished, there is no acquisition or relinquishment of the precepts. Regarding the evil precepts (*duḥśīla*), they are superior among the unwholesome; they do not depend on the two sexual organs. There is relinquishment [of them] through the presence of both sexual organs (*ubhayavyañjana*).
Abiding in the middle, the neutral state does not conflict with having two sexual organs;
it is relinquished through the absence of two organs.
It is relinquished solely at the end of life, which is the same for all. To summarize: [the neutral state is relinquished by these three causes].

Regarding the distinction between the intermediate [neutral] state and the two [types of] non-virtuous precepts: they are identical in one respect. If one applies the six conditions of the intermediate state to the non-virtuous precepts, the relinquishing of the intermediate state is easy;
it is accomplished through the performance of the ritual procedure, or by the severance of the mind that undertook the vow.
The abandonment of unwholesome discipline (*duḥśīla*) is difficult.

It is abandoned through the non-reception [of the vow], the severance of the mind, the loss of the basis, or the presence of intermediate states; there are these four types of abandonment due to the severance of the basis, the influence, the activity, the object, and the faculties.
The unwholesome precepts (*duḥśīla*) are not like this;
they lack these four ways of relinquishment.
They are relinquished solely through the end of life, which is the same as the general case.

Regarding the abandonment of non-virtuous discipline (*duḥśīla*) while abiding in the intermediate state, there are five points of distinction, one of which is the same: the meaning of abandoning non-virtue through the severance of the faculties or the severance of the intermediate state.
When one attains discipline within the state of non-virtuous discipline, one abandons that non-virtuous discipline, because by attaining virtuous discipline, one severs non-virtuous discipline.
If one understands it thus, one partially attains the precepts even within the severance of the faculties (*indriya*).

Regarding the question: "How is it when non-material wholesome states (*arūpa-kuśala*) of the desire realm are relinquished?"—this is the fifth section below concerning the relinquishment of all non-material phenomena. Question: [Regarding] the non-material wholesome dharmas of the desire realm...
Furthermore, how is it that all other non-material defiled dharmas (*rūpa-asaṃprayukta-kliṣṭa-dharma*) of the three realms are abandoned?
The preceding textual sequence has primarily clarified the abandonment of the wholesome, the unwholesome, and the neutral;
now, by posing this question, the meaning is conveniently extended to clarify the wholesome non-material dharmas of the form and formless realms as well.

The meaning regarding the abandonment of meditative concentration and the precepts has already been clarified; therefore, this is not questioned here. Question: Why is the abandonment of indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) dharmas not questioned? Answer: It is explained that other wholesome and defiled dharmas are of the same category as wholesome and unwholesome form (*rūpa*), and for this reason, they are asked about separately.
Other indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) phenomena are not of the same category [as those under discussion], and therefore they are not questioned.
The verse states: "Up to the abandonment of all non-material defilements.
The first two lines answer the preceding question.
The last two lines answer the subsequent question.
The *Śāstra* states, "As for those who go up to the second birth in the upper realms," which explains the first two lines.
All non-material wholesome dharmas of the desire realm—
namely, those acquired at birth, those derived from hearing, and those derived from reflection, along with their attendants—
are abandoned through two conditions: first, by severing the roots of virtue.

This means that when one gives rise to wrong views and severs those roots of goodness, it is called "abandonment through severing goodness" (*kuśalamūla-ccheda-tyāga*). When innate goodness (*upapatti-labdha-kuśala*) is completely severed, its relinquishment is termed "abandonment through severing goodness.

When acquired goodness (*prāyogika-kuśala*) is severed during the preparatory application, its relinquishment is termed "abandonment through severing goodness. Second, being born into a higher realm is termed "abandonment through changing the stage" (*bhūmi-saṃcāra-tyāga*).
This means that when one shifts to another stage (bhūmi), one necessarily abandons those wholesome [roots].
The *Nyāyānusāra* objects:
"One should say that even a portion is abandoned through detachment from defilement (*vairāgya*)."

Regarding the statement that the faculty of grief (*daurmanasyendriya*) and other non-material wholesome phenomena are included, the commentary explains that "and others" refers to the inclusion of the wholesome *kaukṛtya* (remorse) co-arising with the faculty of grief, as well as their associated attendants. The Vaibhāṣika masters offer this defense.
The severance of the roots of goodness and rebirth in the higher realms are explained in full detail;
however, the abandonment [of defilements] through detachment is not fully discussed here as it is summarized.
Regarding the fact that all [levels] of the three realms are reached by nothing other than these means:
The two following lines are explained:
all non-material defiled phenomena (*dharma*) within the three realms that are to be abandoned through seeing (*darśana-heya*) and cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) are relinquished by a single condition.
This means that it occurs solely through the arising of the uninterrupted paths (*ānantarya-mārga*) which serve as the respective antidotes; that is to say,
whenever the uninterrupted path capable of abandoning a particular category of phenomena arises, [that category is abandoned] accordingly.
One should abandon all afflictions of this category along with their attendants;
only the arising of this path can abandon those defilements, and no other means can abandon them.
Question: Thus far, it has been clarified that [this path] abandons the non-material wholesome dharmas of the desire realm.

As for the non-material defiled dharmas of the three realms, why are they not analyzed through a question-and-answer format as is done with the Prātimokṣa and so forth? The explanation is that while it would logically be possible to establish them by pairing each one individually in contrast to its opposite, they are not mentioned separately because they are not the primary subject of exposition.
"From the wholesome and unwholesome restraints up to the exclusion of the intermediate dhyāna and the non-percipient beings":
this constitutes the fifth major section, which establishes [the restraints] by way of their respective locations.
The first two phrases clarify the unwholesome restraint.
The final six phrases clarify virtuous discipline (*śīla*).
Since there is a distinction between the spheres of these virtuous and non-virtuous disciplines, they are established by way of their spheres; this constitutes the intermediate sphere.
Regarding the phrase "no distinction in location":
because it generally applies to all locations, it is not explained separately.
The commentary states, "up to those possessing both sexual organs," which explains the first two lines [of the verse].

In the northern continent, there are no coarse courses of action such as killing, nor is there non-restraint; those known as *śaṇḍha* and *paṇḍaka*, namely the two types of eunuchs, have been explained previously.
The rest of the text may be understood.
"The same applies to restraint" up to "where restraint may exist" explains the third phrase:
"the same applies to restraint."
This refers to those among human beings— excluding those previously excluded, namely the inhabitants of Uttarakuru,
the *śaṇḍhas*, the *paṇḍakas*, and the hermaphrodites—
who possess the remaining human destinies.
This is analogous to the case of immoral conduct (*duḥśīla*);
it exists not only among humans in the three continents, but also among the gods.
Question: It is possible for those in the human realm and the heavenly realms (*deva-gati*) to possess restraint (*saṃvara*).
For what reason, then, does it extend even to those who are not the basis for restraint? Question: [Why is this so?]
It can be known that "continuity" refers to the body. This is because,
according to the Sūtras and Vinaya, [the state] exists even among those who do not belong to that [specific] class.
Answer: The sūtras state that one must possess the male faculty (*puruṣendriya*), while the vinaya states that those such as *śaṇḍhas* (eunuchs) and others are excluded.
Therefore, it is known that the restraint (*saṃvara*) does not exist for such persons.
The remainder of the text may be understood.
Furthermore, by what reasoning is it that they lack restraint?
This is the question.
Although there is a scriptural teaching [to that effect], by what reasoning is it that they lack restraint (*saṃvara*)?
It is because their two bases have not reached the state of a mind possessed of shame (*hrī*) and dread of blame (*apatrāpya*).
This is the answer.
First, it is based on the fact that within a single continuum, two types of greed cannot arise simultaneously to trigger wholesome discipline (*śīla*).

This is because the afflictions arising from the bodies that serve as the bases for the two faculties (male and female) exert a dominant influence over the body of that single continuum at the same time.
One who has not yet generated virtuous discipline,
but possesses the capacity for correct discernment,
may generate virtuous discipline.
Because the *śaṇḍha* lacks the capacity for correct discernment through hearing, reflection, and cultivation,
they do not give rise to virtuous discipline (*śīla*).
Only an extremely profound sense of shame and remorse can give rise to virtuous discipline.
Because paṇḍakas lack an extremely profound sense of shame and dread of blame, they do not give rise to virtuous discipline.
Furthermore, it is explained that paṇḍakas lack the capacity for correct discernment.

The *śaṇḍha* lacks the most profound sense of shame (*hrī*) and dread of blame (*apatrāpya*). Furthermore, some explain that [the *śaṇḍha*] is common to both types; others explain that it is common to all three types.
If this is so, why is there no one among them who possesses non-restraint (*asaṃvara*)?
"Difficult.
"Because it is established by reaching the point of mutual inversion within evil" is the explanation.
Indeed, one who possesses a resolute mind regarding good or evil obtains the vows of good or evil.
This is because those two faculties [of the indeterminate] are not fixed in their intent even when directed toward extremely evil objects.
Furthermore, the vows of good and evil are established as opposites within a single continuum.

Since that body cannot obtain virtuous precepts, it likewise cannot obtain those unvirtuous precepts. Question: Is it only through the two sexual organs that one abandons virtuous and unvirtuous precepts?
It is not through the *śaṇḍha* or *paṇḍaka*.

Why is it that one cannot obtain either the good or the evil precepts in all three cases? The explanation is as follows: the good precepts are the most excellent among good things, and the evil precepts are the most excessive among evil things.
At the moment of initial acquisition, they are difficult to attain and must arise based on a superior physical basis (*āśraya*).
Therefore, those three types of persons are all unable to acquire [the precepts].

As for those who subsequently undergo the transformation of being a *śaṇḍha* or a *pandaka*, their transgressions are not grave; they are unable to relinquish either their virtuous precepts or their unwholesome precepts.
Precepts depend upon that body; because the fault of being hermaphroditic is grave, one is able to abandon both virtuous precepts and unvirtuous precepts.
Precepts do not depend upon that [hermaphroditic state].
Thus, the *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra*, fascicle 39, states:

However, the arising of both sexual organs causes one to abandon both virtuous and non-virtuous precepts, because the two bases [of male and female] are characterized by the extreme predominance of sensual desire.
This does not apply to those such as *śaṇḍhas* (eunuchs) and others; for them, there is no abandonment of virtuous or non-virtuous discipline (*saṃvara*).
The arising of these two [types of non-restraint] is due to their lack of extreme gravity regarding greed.
As for the statement that "people of Uttarakuru possess neither virtuous nor unvirtuous precepts," this specifically indicates that the Northern Continent lacks both virtuous and unvirtuous precepts.
Because the people of Uttarakuru do not receive the precepts,
they lack the prātimokṣa restraint; because they do not enter meditative absorption, they lack the dhyāna restraint.
Since there is neither the restraint of meditative concentration (*dhyāna-saṃvara*) nor the untainted restraint (*anāsrava-saṃvara*),
and because there is no superior intention (*adhyāśaya*) to commit evil,
there is no non-restraint (*asaṃvara*).
"Therefore, they possess neither virtuous nor non-virtuous precepts,
because their intense shame and dread of blame extend even to the point of non-restraint.
This indicates that there are no virtuous or non-virtuous precepts in the miserable realms.
Because intense shame (*hrī*) and dread of blame (*apatrāpya*) are absent within the three miserable destinies, neither restraint (*saṃvara*) nor non-restraint (*asaṃvara*) exists there either.
Restraint arises only when one is endowed with superior shame and dread of blame; it is incompatible with those who possess the opposite of superior shame and dread of blame.
Non-restraint (asaṃvara) exists in association with the superior forms of lack of shame (āhrīkya) and lack of dread (anapatrāpya).
Furthermore, the comparison regarding "the kaśmala grass reaching the excellent seed" is a metaphorical illustration.
This can be understood.
If that is so, why is it said that one must reach the fast-day precepts (upavāsa)?
This is an objection.
If it is said that restraint does not exist in the evil destinies,
why does the Sūtra state that nāgas observe the eight precepts for half a month—
namely, on the fifteenth day and the eighth day?
This refers to the eighth day of the month; alternatively, it is explained as the half-month, namely the fifteenth day of the waxing moon and the fifteenth day of the waning moon.
"The eighth" refers to the eighth day of the waxing moon and the eighth day of the waning moon; alternatively, it is explained as the eighth day within the half-month.
This refers to the eighth day of the waxing moon and the eighth day of the waning moon.
Regarding the statement that these attainments of sublime practice exist only among humans and devas, the answer is as follows:
Although dragons receive the precepts, they only attain the path of excellent conduct situated between [the formal vows] and do not attain the discipline (*saṃvara*).

Therefore, discipline exists only among humans and devas, and not in the three evil destinies. Question: If they do not obtain the precepts, for what purpose do they receive them? Answer: It is said that it causes the arising of excellent conduct so that they may obtain superior fruits.
Therefore, the *Vibhāṣā* (Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra), fascicle 124, states:
"Do those who are *śaṇḍha*, *paṇḍaka*, sexless (*avyañjana*), or hermaphrodites (*ubhayavyañjana*) obtain the restraint of the *upavāsa* (fast-day) vow when they receive it?"
It is not permitted to grant it.
Why is this? Because the physical basis upon which that person relies is of weak and inferior disposition, and is not a fit vessel for the Vinaya.
Nor can they serve as a vessel for the non-restraint;
just as in a field of salt-encrusted soil, neither fine grain nor weeds will grow.
Nevertheless, one should still confer upon them the *upavāsa* (near-dwelling) restraint.

It causes one to give rise to sublime conduct and shall lead to the attainment of supreme fruits. Question: Why does this treatise not speak of the formless? Answer: This treatise does not speak of it because it is abbreviated and not discussed in detail.
However, only humans possess both the supreme dhyānas and the untainted states (*anāsrava*).
This explains the fourth phrase.
As for the statement that if one is born in the desire-realm heavens (*kāmadhātu-deva*), those [states] will certainly not exist there:
Explanation of the fifth and sixth phrases:

The *Nyāyānusāra* states that those born among the gods of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) as well as those born in the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) are all capable of possessing the dhyāna-restraint (*dhyānasaṃvara*).
However, in the case of the gods of non-conception (*asaṃjñisattva*), they are only capable of its possession (*samanvāgama*).
"In those born in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*),
both are absent" explains the first two phrases; "the untainted restraint (*anāsrava-saṃvara*) will certainly not manifest" explains the latter two phrases.
The untainted restraint (anāsrava-saṃvara) exists not only in the desire realm and the form realm,
but also in the formless realm;
that is to say, even if one is born among the gods of the desire realm.
And those born within the realm of form (rūpadhātu),
excluding those in the intermediate dhyāna, the Brahmā kings,
and the heaven of non-conception (asaṃjñisattva).
Because those two places consist exclusively of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*),
the remaining sixteen places can all possess uncontaminated restraint (*anāsrava-saṃvara*).
One born in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) attains only the accomplishment of the uncontaminated restraint belonging to the six lower stages.
Because they are formless, they necessarily do not manifest.

Having distinguished the various karmas up to those specifically designated as "various karmas," the second major section of this chapter below shall now explain the various karmas mentioned in the Sūtra.
Among these, first is the restatement of the preceding general heading;
second is the detailed explanation. This [first section] is the restatement of the preceding general heading.
Furthermore, regarding the statement in the Sūtra, "What are their characteristics?"—
this is the second section below, which provides a specific explanation. Within this:
First, the explanation of karma according to the three natures;
second, the explanation of the three types of karma, such as merit; third, the explanation of karma according to the three types of feeling.
Fourth, it clarifies the karma of the three times.
Fifth, it clarifies the karma of bodily and mental sensation.
Sixth, it clarifies crookedness, filthiness, and turbidity.
7. Explaining the black-and-black [karma] and so forth;
8. Explaining the three purities of the sages (muni);
9. Explaining the three types of misconduct and good conduct.
10. Explaining the ten courses of action (*karmapatha*).
11. Explaining the three types of misconduct. Below this, first, the explanation of actions according to their three natures (*trividha-svabhāva-karman*). Within this:
First, the question;

Because it is conducive to feeling within the associated [factors], it is called "associated with what is conducive to feeling" (*saṃprayukta-vedanīya*);
this can be understood by citing the sūtra.
Third, regarding "object-condition conducive to feeling" (*ālambana-vedanīya*), it refers to that which reaches the object of feeling.
This means that all objects are the objective conditions (*ālambana*) of feeling (*vedanā*).
Because these objective conditions are conducive to the feeling that takes them as its object, they are called "objects conducive to feeling" (*ālambana-vedanīya*).
As it is said in the Sūtra:
Having seen a form with the eye, the mental consciousness experiences only the form;
it does not experience the craving conditioned by that form. Furthermore, "having seen a form with the eye" means that the eye sees the form.
This refers to the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*). The remaining explanations are as before;
it should be understood that this applies likewise up to the sphere of mental objects (*dharmaviṣaya*).
It correctly takes the six objects as its domain.
It is included here because the text regarding "not being subject to craving for form" is identical.
As for the passage beginning with "the four types of maturation that accord with feeling," and so forth, it is explained at length.
That is to say, karma that brings about all types of ripened results (*vipāka-phala*) is called "karma conducive to experiencing ripening" (*vipāka-vedanīya*).
As for why such karma is termed "ripening," it is because the cause is distinct from the result; this distinction is what constitutes "ripening."
Alternatively, it is called "different" because at the time of experiencing the fruit, it differs from what preceded;

it is called "ripening" because at the very moment of experiencing the fruit, it has the capacity to bring it to maturity. Alternatively, it is named after its fruit. This can be understood by citing the relevant sūtra.
Regarding "five types of experience that are favorable when present" up to "experiencing pleasant sensation":
this means that when a sensation is currently active and manifesting in the present, being non-contradictory to its manifestation is called "favorable when present."
As it is said in the Sūtra: "When experiencing a pleasant feeling, one manifests the experience of the present;
the other two feelings then cease," and so on at length. Regarding the Sūtra's statement, "when experiencing a pleasant feeling":
It is not that when this pleasant feeling is present, there is another feeling capable of experiencing this pleasant feeling;
rather, it is simply based on the manifestation of the pleasant feeling itself that the Sūtra speaks of "feeling" or "pleasant feeling."
Regarding the statement here that "only those [karmas] leading to pleasant feeling and so forth are discussed":
although five types have been generally explained above,
within this context of karma conducive to the three feelings, [the focus is restricted].
However, it speaks only of the fourth [category], the "retribution-feeling" (vipāka-vedanīya),
because karma is capable of inducing the experience of retribution;
thus, although the nature of the causal karma differs from that of the resultant fruit of feeling.
Thus they are designated as "conducive to pleasant feeling" and so forth.
Regarding these three types of karma, what are their characteristics?
Hereafter, the fourth section clarifies karma pertaining to the three times.
Within this, first,
the four kinds of karma are clarified;
second, the distinctions among the four karmas are clarified.
The third knowledge concerns the karma of having performed actions; the fourth knowledge concerns the characteristics of karma that will definitely be experienced;
and the fifth knowledge concerns karma that bears fruit in the present life.
Sixth, the clarification that karma is itself the fruit of experience. This is the first [section] clarifying the four types of karma.
It introduces the preceding inquiry;
since the three types of karma for the three feelings are clarified as a means to clarify the four types of karma, the scriptural citation is not provided.
The verse says: "As for the statement by other masters regarding the four alternatives,
the first two lines provide the direct answer,
while the latter two lines present alternative views."
The Commentary states: "Up to 'in total there are four kinds'":
this explains the two preceding phrases.
It is taught that there are four types of karma, all established based on whether their timing is fixed or unfixed. There are three types of fixed timing.
That is to say, the timing—whether in the present, the next life, or subsequent lives—is not fixed as one.
One should understand that the meaning of "not fixed" has many aspects; for instance, it may refer to the fact that the fruit is not necessarily experienced [at a specific time].
Either because it is not certain that [the result] will be experienced at this time;
or because it is not certain that it will be experienced in this realm of existence (gati); or because it is not certain that it will be experienced in this location.
Alternatively, it is because the fruit of this class is not necessarily experienced;
for example, heavy karma may be transformed into light experience, or light karma may be transformed into heavy experience.
Such categories as these are all termed "indeterminate" (aniyata). The reason they are distinguished according to time is as follows:
In general, when discussing the formation of karma, the timing is difficult to determine;
however, if the timing were fixed,
the maturation would also be fixed.
If the time [of ripening] is indefinite,
the maturation is also indefinite,
because there is no distinct nature apart from the timing of the ripening.
Because time is a distinction of the stage of maturation,
some wish to include [the factor of] reaching [the result] so as to constitute five types;
this explains the third phrase and clarifies the meaning of the five functions.

Alternatively, there are those who maintain that indeterminate karma (aniyata-vedanīya-karma) is further divided into two types: first, that which is determinate in its maturation (vipāka-niyata) but indeterminate in its timing.
Regarding this, there are four cases that are not fixed within the three periods of the present life, the next life, or subsequent lives.
Alternatively, they may be indeterminate with respect to two times;
when combined, there are three.
Or, they may be indeterminate with respect to three times; when combined, the three become one. There are two types of maturation (*vipāka*).
Indeterminate both by time and by occasion;
this also has four types.
Or, it may be indeterminate with respect to both the ripening and the timing.
There are three [types] combined as two,
or the maturation at three times, and that which is indeterminate both in time and simultaneous;
these three combined constitute one.
Now, the timing [of maturation] is not fixed;
if the timing were fixed, the ripening would necessarily be fixed.
Therefore, there is no case where the timing is fixed while the ripening is not.

Together with the three types of determinate karma, these constitute five kinds. Question: Are the four types of karma and the five types of karma the same or different? Explanation: They are both the same and different.
As for the three types of determinate karma:
Regarding the indeterminate [karma], both schools agree that there is indetermination of both the maturation (*vipāka*) and the time. However,
if within the indeterminate there is indetermination of the time but determination of the maturation, [the schools differ].
It is said that five karmas exist,
while four karmas do not;
this is the difference.

Therefore, the school of five karmas divides the indeterminate [karma] into two types. Question: Why is it that in the school of four karmas, there is no distinction within the indeterminate regarding the certainty of maturation or the uncertainty of timing? Explanation: [It is because]...
The four types of karma are distinguished as determinate or indeterminate with respect to time.
Time and its maturation (vipāka) do not possess distinct substantial natures.
If [the karma] is determinate regarding maturation, it is also determinate regarding time.
This is precisely what is meant by being "determined" (*niyata*).

Therefore, regarding those that are undetermined (*aniyata*), there is no fixed time for their maturation; thus, those whose timing is undetermined are called "undetermined. Furthermore, the masters of the four types of karma explain the undetermined as follows: they are designated with the name "undetermined" because they are not necessarily to be experienced.
For this reason, it is known that the maturation (vipāka) induced by indeterminate karma may or may not be experienced.
As stated in the *Pañcakarmavarga*: "Among indeterminate [karma], there is that which is determinate in its maturation but indeterminate in its timing."
Thus, we know that the two explanations differ.
Furthermore, since the subsequent section evaluates and adopts the explanation regarding the four types of karma as being correct,
it is clearly evident that this differs from the fivefold classification.

Question: If, among the four types of karma, those that are determinate in ripening but indeterminate in time are not fixed, why does the Master of the *Nyāyānusāra* refute the analogy of the eight types of karma by saying:
"It is like karma that is determinate in ripening but indeterminate in time"?
Because the time [of ripening] is indeterminate.

Since it is commonly accepted as being "conducive to indeterminate ripening," and so forth—the treatise states that it is "commonly accepted as indeterminate"—it is clearly known that there are also cases where the maturation is determinate but the time is indeterminate. The commentary explains:
They say it is commonly accepted;

it is commonly accepted by those who maintain five types of karma, or commonly accepted by those who maintain eight types of karma. Furthermore, another interpretation states that the meanings of four types of karma and five types of karma are essentially similar.
The difference lies in the expansion and contraction [of categories].

Within the category of the indeterminate (*aniyata*), the school of the five karmas expands it into two types: first, that which is determinate in its maturation (*vipāka*) but indeterminate in its timing; and second, that which is indeterminate in both its maturation and its timing.
Second, those with indeterminate maturation and indeterminate timing;
although these are divided into two types based on maturation,
from the perspective of timing, both are indeterminate.

Therefore, although two types are opened up within the indeterminate (*aniyata*), their meaning is not different. If one explains it in this way, there are likewise two types within the indeterminate among the four types of karma.
Generally speaking, when it is said that "the timing of the commission of karma is difficult to determine," [it refers to this].
If the time is fixed, the maturation (vipāka) is necessarily fixed,
because time has no separate essence apart from maturation,
and because time depends upon that fruit of maturation.
There are certain karmas whose maturation (*vipāka*) is determinate,
yet whose timing is indeterminate;
this is because the substance of the maturation fruit itself exists.

Because the fruit of maturation (vipāka-phala) does not depend on time, for this reason, two types may be spoken of within the category of indefinite timing. Furthermore, the subsequent passage explaining present karma states:
Regarding those whose timing is indefinite within the category of maturation, this karma will necessarily produce results in the present life.
Furthermore, the masters of the *Nyāyānusāra* and the *Abhidharmasamayapradīpikā*, refuting the proponents of eight types of karma, state:

This means that, for example, regarding karma fixed by ripening but indefinite as to time (*aniyata-kāla*), because it is indefinite as to time, it is already commonly accepted as being "karma to be experienced at an indefinite time" (*aniyatavedanīya*), and so forth; since that treatise states it is "commonly accepted," [it must be so].
It is clearly known that this is accepted by the proponents of the eightfold karma theory.
Furthermore, when the *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra* refutes the proponents of the eightfold karma theory, it refutes only the view that [karma] is determinate in its ripening but indeterminate in its timing;
it does not refute the proponents of the eightfold or fivefold karma theories who hold that [karma] is determinate in its timing but indeterminate in its ripening.

For this reason, it is known that the fourfold and fivefold classifications of karma differ through the process of opening and closing. Regarding the system of four karmas, those who say that the name "indeterminate" (*aniyata*) is established because [the result] is not necessarily experienced,
or that the name "indeterminate" is established because the maturation (*vipāka*) is not necessarily experienced.

This is designated as "indeterminate" (aniyata) either because its maturation may or may not be experienced, or because it is not fixed among the three periods of time as to when its maturation will be experienced; thus, it is given the name "indeterminate."
This refers to the "indeterminate" (aniyata) because the three times of experiencing the maturation (vipāka) are not fixed;
therefore, there is no contradiction.
As for the subsequent passage which evaluates and takes up four types of karma without mentioning five, it is as follows:
Because their meanings are identical,
it is stated that the four karmas are simply the five karmas, and thus they are not explained separately.
Although there are two interpretations, the latter is superior.
In the case of maturation (*vipāka*),
one may say that both the time and the maturation are determinate; however,
maturation is not established by means of time.
It cannot be said that [the karma] is determinate both with respect to its maturation and its timing;
furthermore, according to the various treatises, within the category of the indeterminate, there are always these two types, and there is no other explanation.
Regarding "that which is to be experienced in the present life" and "that which ripens subsequently in the sequence":
these are distinct explanations of the names of the three concentrations.
First, "that which is to be experienced in the present life."
"Present life" refers to the present body.
"Experience" refers to maturation (*vipāka*).
This means that karma created in this very life results in its maturation fruit within this very life.
"Birth" refers to the homogeneous class of beings (*nikāya-sabhāga*).
"To be experienced in the next birth" means that karma created in this life will yield its maturation fruit (*vipāka-phala*) in the very next lifetime.
"Birth" refers to the place of birth. Regarding "karma to be experienced in subsequent lives":
this refers to karma created in this life;
from the third birth onward, through many successive births, it is all termed "subsequent."
Because it occurs after the second birth,
in this subsequent stage the fruit does not arise all at once,
but ripens sequentially.
Other masters say that it reaches as far as the fruit of maturation (*vipākaphala*) when it is slight.
Other Sautrāntika masters say that it refers to karma to be experienced in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharmavedanīya-karman*).
Although karma from other births, such as the second birth and so forth, may also receive its maturation,

it is designated as "to be experienced in the present life" (kṣepaṇīya) because the name of the karma is established according to its first stage of ripening; thus, it is called "to be experienced in the present."
One should understand that subsequent karma (*upapadyavedanīya*) and subsequent-subsequent karma (*aparāpariyavedanīya*) can also bring about many births;
they are designated by their initial names.
This should be explained according to the present case:

let it not be that an action of superior strength, such as one pertaining to the present life, yields a small ripened fruit. According to the Sautrāntika school, it is admitted that a single action can bring about multiple births.
If karma to be experienced in the present life is of the strongest force, it must necessarily be experienced in a future birth;
if karma to be experienced in the next life is of somewhat weaker force,
it will not be experienced in the present— this is what is meant by "weaker in the present."

That which necessarily results in a subsequent rebirth is superior to those that result in later rebirths. If it is karma to be experienced in a subsequent life (aparaparyāya-vedanīya), its power is the weakest because it does not result in the present or the next life;
thus, it is inferior to the previous two types, as it results in rebirth only in a later stage.
Regarding the Vaibhāṣika claim that [the fruit] ripens only when the grain reaches the stage of maturation:
the Vaibhāṣikas do not accept this position of the Sautrāntikas.
Why must an action be superior simply because its fruit is near?
Karmas are not fixed; for some karmas have results that are near but not superior, while others have results that are distant yet superior.
For example, among external seeds, the *kai* (malva) plant produces fruit after only three or four weeks.

This refers to the fruit being near, but not yet superior; "three and a half months" means one month and a half, or three full months plus another fortnight. It takes six months for the wheat to ripen and bear fruit.
This means that the fruit is both distant and superior.
When the Dārṣṭāntikas say that "arrival" (prāpti) also has two kinds,
they are explaining the fourth phrase.
The Dārṣṭāntikas say that there are four categories of karma: the first category consists of karma that is determinate with respect to three times,
but indeterminate with respect to its maturation.
This refers to the three types of karma—such as that to be experienced in the present life—which do not necessarily yield their maturation.
Among these, there are three;
first, that which is certain to be experienced in the present life.
The maturation is indeterminate;
the two [other types] are determinate at the time of birth,
while their maturation is indeterminate.
Third, it is certain in its subsequent timing,
but indeterminate regarding its maturation;
this is the intended meaning of this school.
Regarding "certainty of the time of action but uncertainty of maturation":
this refers to being certain with respect to three times.
The maturation is indeterminate:
if it is to be experienced at this time, it is experienced then;
if it is not to be experienced at this time, it is never experienced. The second category consists of karma whose maturation is determinate.
The three times are indeterminate;
that is to say, there are indeterminate karmas that definitely obtain maturation.
Among these, there is only one such case.
That is to say, there is karma whose fruition is fixed but whose timing is not fixed. The third category consists of karma that is fixed in both timing and fruition;
this refers to karma such as that to be experienced in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharmavedanīya*), which is certain to yield its fruition.
In this regard, there are three types.
First, those that are determinate with respect to both the present time and the simultaneous ripening of the result.
Second, at the time of birth,
both the timing and the maturation are fixed;
third, subsequently.
At that time, [there is karma] determinate both in terms of timing and maturation. In the fourth case, there is karma that is indeterminate both in terms of timing and maturation;
that is to say, indeterminate karma for which maturation is not fixed to be obtained.
Among these, there is only one that is indefinite with respect to both time and maturation. They state that, in total, there are eight types of karma:
namely, the four types consisting of those to be experienced in the present life, the next life, subsequent lives, and the indefinite.
Because each has both determinate and indeterminate aspects, they constitute eight types.
The three [factors] in the first clause are indeterminate within the determinate;
the one [factor] in the second clause is determinate within the indeterminate.
The third phrase refers to the three types of "concentration within concentration.
The fourth phrase refers to the one type of "non-concentration within non-concentration.
Regarding what has been explained here, this includes those who fall away from the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*) as well as those in the desire realm.
This is the second [section], clarifying the distinctions among the four types of karma.
Within this explanation of the distinctions among the four types of karma,
further differentiations are now analyzed.
The Commentary states: "Regarding the phrase 'up to the characteristics of the four types of karma,' this marks the core thesis.
As previously stated, there are three schools concerning the general classification of karma."
Some speak of four karmas;
some speak of five karmas;
and some speak of eight karmas.
The author of the treatise, in order to evaluate and select among the four types of karma, states that these are explained as "wholesome.
Within these four types of karma, he clarifies only the distinction between those with fixed timing and those with indefinite timing,
thereby explaining the different characteristics of the four kinds of karma as taught in the Sūtras.

Therefore, those with fixed timing are divided into the first three [types of karma], while those with indefinite timing are collectively designated as the fourth. The masters of the *Nyāyānusāra* treat them as five types of karma;
although this is not the correct interpretation, it is their position.

Because these represent the doctrines of different masters within the same school, they are not refuted separately. Furthermore, regarding the five karmas, there are differences in how they are categorized through the opening and closing of categories;
however, since it is stated that the four karmas are simply the five karmas, they are not explained separately.
It should be understood that among the five types of karma that are indeterminate, two are determinate in terms of their maturation (*vipāka*) but indeterminate in terms of time;
[the remaining three] are indeterminate in both maturation and time.
These are thus subsumed under the category of "indeterminate in time" within the fourfold classification of karma.
Since those [karmas] with fixed time have a definite maturation, they are divided into three categories based on their temporal certainty;
whereas for those with indefinite time, the maturation may be either definite or indefinite.
Thus, among the five types of karma, two are of indefinite time.
This is subsumed within the "indeterminate time" category among the four types of karma;
the difference lies in whether they are categorized as distinct or unified. Furthermore, the *Nyāyānusāra* does not refute the existence of five types of karma.
However, among the eight types of karma, the first category—consisting of three kinds—is determinate in its timing but indeterminate in its maturation (*vipāka*).
This is because there is no distinct time apart from the moment of maturation itself. Thus, the *Nyāyānusāra* (Treatise on the Principles of Correct Reasoning), fascicle 40, states:
In principle, there can be no such thing as a determinate karma whose maturation is indeterminate;
for determinate timing is merely a distinction of stage within determinate maturation.
There is no temporal essence that exists apart from maturation.
"How is it that determinate [karma] is not of the nature of maturation?"—this concludes the treatise. Although there are two interpretations, the latter is superior.
Is it possible for four types of karma to be performed simultaneously?
The following explains the first phrase.
The question is raised:
"It may be possible."
Answer: What is being questioned?
It is the point that after dispatching the three messengers, they reach their destination simultaneously.
Explanation:
It is like dispatching three messengers,
one of whom kills.
First, stealing;
second, practicing deception;
and third, engaging in sexual misconduct oneself.
These four courses of action (karmapatha) that reach completion simultaneously are called the "four beginning with the present" (*pratyutpannādi-catuṣka*).
As for how many karmas are able to project a commonality of group (*nikāyasabhāga*):
This explains the second phrase.
This is the question itself:
"Why can only three [causes] project [a result], whereas prior karma projects [it]?"
Answer: It may be understood that,
according to this text, manifest karma is not of the same category as feeling.
It does not obstruct the production of the life-faculty;

therefore, the previous [passage] on "extending life" refers only to the extension of the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) and does not mention the homogeneous character (*nikāyasabhāga*). Furthermore, this text is explained according to the general conventional teaching.
Present karma does not induce a homogeneous portion (*sabhāga*).
However, according to the principle of prolonging life through the power of other conditions, present karma also induces a homogeneous portion.
Yet, within the context of prolonging life, it is stated only that it induces the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) and not the homogeneous portion.
This is merely a partial enumeration.
To speak according to reality, they are also similar in their constituent parts (*sabhāga*).
Question: As stated in the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 114:
Question: How many types of karma can project a homogeneous class (*nikāya-sabhāga*), and how many can fulfill it?
Some teachers say:
Second, there are those that can project a commonality of group (*nikāya-sabhāga*) and also fulfill it—
namely, karma to be experienced in the next birth (*upapadya-vedanīya-karman*) and karma to be experienced in subsequent births (*aparaparyāya-vedanīya-karman*).
Second, there are those that can fulfill a commonality of group but cannot project it.
There is karma to be experienced in the present life and karma to be experienced at an indefinite time.
Furthermore, some say that three types [of karma] can both project a commonality of group (nikāya-sabhāga) and fulfill it.
That is to say, excluding those [karmas] to be experienced in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharmavedanīya*):
one type can fulfill the homogeneous class (*nikāyasabhāga*) but cannot project it;
this refers to karma to be experienced in the present life.
Furthermore, there are those who wish to maintain that even karma to be experienced in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharmavedanīya*) can project a homogeneous class (*nikāyasabhāga*).
If one were to say this—
that all four types of karma are capable of both projecting and completing a homogeneous class— then among these three explanations in the *Mahāvibhāṣā*:
With which of these explanations does this treatise agree?
Which is correct? The explanation says:
This treatise agrees with the second master.
Thus, the second master’s view is taken as correct. Furthermore, another interpretation holds that since the *Abhidharmamahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* contains no formal adjudication (*viniścaya*),
both the second and third positions among the three explanations may be considered correct.
The second master relies on the general explanation;
therefore, he says that present karma does not experience its corresponding homogeneous portion (*sabhāga*).
The third master also relies on specific conditions.
Therefore, it is said that present karma can induce a corresponding homogeneous part (*sabhāga*).
According to the general rule, this treatise accords with the second master;
however, according to specific conditions, it also accords with the third master.
Regarding which realms (*dhātu*) and which destinies (*gati*) can produce how many types of karma:
this explains the third and fourth lines. This is the question:
"In all realms and all destinies, up to the general opening of such [possibilities]?"
Answer: It refers to the three realms and five destinies,
whether wholesome or unwholesome.
In general, it is accepted that all [beings] may perform the four kinds of karma according to their respective capacities. However,
when specific prohibitions are set aside, they are all permitted to perform them.
The following sections of this treatise all clarify specific prohibitions.
Among them, it is stated that hell-beings do not create karma that results in the manifestation of wholesome [rebirths],
because there are no desirable fruits within the hells.
"All others are capable of creating" explains the fifth, sixth, and seventh phrases, concerning those of the non-retrogressive lineage up to those who are unobstructed.
An ordinary person does not fall back from a stage free from passion;
because there is no subsequent rebirth [in that same life], they do not create karma for birth.
Because they will later return to be born [again], they create karma to be experienced in a future life.
Because a non-retrogressive noble one will certainly not undergo rebirth in the lower stages,
they do not create karma for rebirth or for subsequent existence,
whether they be ordinary persons or noble ones.
In whatever place one is born, it is possible to perform karma to be experienced in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharmavedanīya*).

Regarding the performance of indeterminate karma (*aniyata-karman*), there is no restriction in any location. However, as for the various noble ones (*ārya*), this will be explained later as appropriate.
The eighth phrase can be understood by distinguishing its specific differences. Regarding the question,
"Does one also create karma while abiding in the intermediate state (*antarābhava*)?",
the following third section clarifies that karma is created within the intermediate state.
The preceding section clarified the formation of karma during birth-existence (*upapattibhava*), fundamental existence (*mūlabhava*), and death-existence (*maraṇabhava*).
The following section clarifies the formation of karma during intermediate existence (*antarābhava*).
This is now posed as a question.
"Furthermore, as for the creator. Answer: "In what way?"
Question.
The verse says: "Because it is induced by the force of karma. Answer:
While abiding in the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) within the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*),
one may be capable of creating twenty-two types of karma;
that is to say, while in the intermediate state.
Together with the five stages within the womb and the five stages outside the womb,
there are eleven in total.
While abiding in the intermediate state (*antarābhava*), one can create eleven types of fixed karma (*niyata-karma*) and eleven types of unfixed karma (*aniyata-karma*); thus, there are twenty-two.
It should be understood that the eleven fixed karmas created during this intermediate state are all necessarily categorized as karma to be experienced in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharmavedanīya*).
This is because there is no distinction in their homogeneous class (*nikāya-sabhāga*);

that is to say, this state of intermediate existence (*antarābhava*) and the ten states of its own kind’s birth-existence (*upapatti-bhava*) share one and the same homogeneous class, as they are projected by a single karma.
Therefore, all are called "karma to be experienced in the present life" (*dṛṣṭadharmavedanīya-karman*).

For this reason, karma to be experienced in the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) is not mentioned separately, because it is subsumed under those [categories of] karma to be experienced in the next life (*upapadyavedanīya*), subsequent lives (*aparaparyāyavedanīya*), or at indefinite times (*aniyatavedanīya*). In this context, the term "homogeneous class" (*nikāyasabhāga*) refers to...
This demonstrates that they belong to the same category.
Thus, the *Nyāyānusāra* states:
"As for the homogeneous class (*nikāya-sabhāga*):"
This means that categories such as humans are neither *gati* (destinies) nor *upapatti* (births).

This is because the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) and the state of birth (*upapattibhava*) differ in their commonality (*nikāyasabhāga*) when categorized by destiny and birth. If there are eleven types of indeterminate karma (*aniyata-karman*), [they are as follows:]...
Either it is experienced by this body during its eleven stages,
or it is experienced by another body during its eleven stages,
or it is not experienced at all.
It can be said that this is an indefinite-karma (*aniyata-karman*) because our school does not admit the existence of karma that is definite in its timing but indefinite in its maturation (*vipāka*).

Therefore, these eleven types of indefinite karma are not necessarily experienced during these eleven stages of this very life. Question: If an Arhat (*aśaikṣa*) creates indefinite karma, since they have no further rebirths, [how can it ripen]?

If, at the time of receiving the fruit, it is received only in the present life, what prevents an indeterminate karma of the intermediate state from also being received only in the present life and not extending to other stages?
The explanation says: Generally speaking, when we say "indeterminate," we mean that its timing is indeterminate.
Even if an indeterminate karma of one beyond training (aśaikṣa) were to arise in a subsequent life, it would still be possible for that person to experience its result;
however, because there are no further births, it is experienced only in the present life.
It is nonetheless called "indeterminate."
Among these, there are those who are not yet beyond training (aśaikṣa),
as there is still further birth to come; therefore,
indeterminate karma (aniyata-karma) is not necessarily experienced only in the present life.
It may apply to other births, but it cannot be taken as a general rule.

Question: Among the three types of determinate karma (*niyata-karma*), why is it that during the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) one creates only karma for the present life (*dr̥ṣṭadharma-vedanīya*), and not karma for the next birth (*upapadya-vedanīya*) or subsequent lives (*aparaparyāya-vedanīya*)? Answer: It is explained as follows.
Furthermore, the duration of their intermediate existence is brief, and their bodies are frail and thin;
this is because the determinate karma manifesting in the present life is easily produced.
Therefore, one performs determinate karma that manifests in the present life.
Because it is difficult to perform, determinate karma of a different body does not produce results in the next life or subsequent lives.

Since it is difficult to maintain that this body alone is created by indeterminate karma, how can this be reconciled with the experience of other bodies? The explanation is as follows: because it is indeterminate, it is easily created, and thus may be experienced by other bodies.

Furthermore, since it is said to be indeterminate, why is it restricted solely to this life? Question: Why is it not stated that the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) is capable of creating karma? Explanation: It is not mentioned because it is omitted for the sake of brevity.
Regarding "all karmas that are definitely experienced [reaching] other [stages] which are not definitely experienced":
this is the fourth [point], clarifying the characteristics of definitely experienced karma. It refers to the superior fruit, namely, the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpatti-phala*).
Because one first emerges from the path of vision (darśanamārga) when the afflictions of vision (dṛṣṭiheya) are completely abandoned;
and because one first emerges from the path of cultivation (bhāvanāmārga) when the afflictions of cultivation (bhāvanāheya) are completely abandoned in the fruit of arhatship.
The once-returner (sakṛdāgāmin) and non-returner (anāgāmin) have not yet completely abandoned both types of afflictions.
It is not that what first emerges is not called a "superior fruit" or a "superior meditative absorption"— namely, the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*) and so forth—
as will be explained in due order below.
The rest of the text may be understood.
Regarding "karma with results in the present life" up to "that which definitely brings about results in the present life":
this is the fifth [section], clarifying karma with results in the present life.
The first phrase reveals karma to be experienced in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharmavedanīya-karman*);
the following three phrases reveal the determinacy within the indeterminate (*aniyata*).
The treatise states: "As for 'the object is also not one'..."
The explanation of the first phrase is clear.
Although the mind was initially slight, it became grave due to the gravity of the object.
Although the object may later be light, it is heavy due to the mind;
the rest of the text is clear.
Or, from being born in this stage until one no longer undergoes maturation.

The following three phrases explain that within the category of the indeterminate (*aniyata*), there is a determinate ripening (*vipāka-niyata*) whose timing is indeterminate, yet which receives its present fruit.
This refers to those who have attained the fruit of Arhatship and the fruit of Non-returner (*anāgāmin*).
Having been born in a particular stage, one is forever free from the defilements of that stage;
yet, within that stage, according to what is appropriate,
one may perform wholesome or unwholesome karma while not yet free from those defilements.
Furthermore, regarding those who have become free from passion and have performed various wholesome karmas—
whether their maturation is fixed or unfixed—
it is because they have attained permanent freedom from passion.
Because one is not reborn again within this very state of existence (*bhava*), this karma is necessarily able to produce results in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharma-phala*).

Since all [results] are experienced in this body, they are called results in the present life. Question: Just as there are times when one has not yet permanently abandoned defilements (*kleśa*) during the present life, [is it the same for karma]?
One may say that one can create karma of determinate ripening with respect to time and indeterminate karma; however,
since there is no longer any birth [in that state] once one has reached the stage of being permanently free from the defilements of this level,
how can it be said that one also creates karma of determinate ripening with respect to time and indeterminate karma?

It should be called "determined by time" (*kāla-niyata*). The commentary explains: although there is no [fixed] birth and so forth for those who have permanently abandoned the defilements of this stage, it is nonetheless called "determined by maturation" (*vipāka-niyata*) while being "undetermined by time.
This is because, even if one possesses such karma, if a birth or other conditions should occur, it is still possible for the fruit to be experienced again through the power of that karma.

Because [karma] such as that which is "unborn" (*anutpatti*) is experienced only in the present life, it differs in its distinction from "fixed karma" (*niyata-karman*). Furthermore, it is asked: regarding the various wholesome karmas performed by one who has not yet abandoned [defilements] versus one who has permanently abandoned them, can it be said that the fruit is experienced at the stage of having permanently abandoned defilement?
Because it has been accomplished, an evil karma does not become established at the stage of being free from defilement;
how, then, could it bring about its fruit? The explanation says: It is not necessary that a karma must be established in order to bring about its fruit.
Just as when one dies from a higher realm and is about to be born into a lower one,
although the various wholesome and unwholesome karmas of the lower realms have not yet been accomplished, they nevertheless induce their results;
and furthermore, just as homogeneous and pervasive causes (*sabhāga-hetu* and *sarvatraga-hetu*) can function as causes even when they have not yet been accomplished.

If there is another birth in this very stage, then for those karmas that are to be experienced subsequently and with certainty, there is necessarily no possibility of permanently abandoning defilement, because their maturation must necessarily be experienced in that subsequent birth.
However, if [the karma] is indefinite regarding its timing, it is also indefinite regarding its maturation.
Because one has permanently abandoned defilement, one will certainly not experience the ripening [of karma].
Regarding the question of what kind of field gives rise to karma such that the very act of harming or benefiting results in immediate retribution—
this is the sixth point, clarifying that the karma is experienced immediately.
Regarding the question and the response in verse, the treatise states: "Upon reaching meditative concentration, one immediately receives the fruit.
This serves as a general summary of the meaning of the verse.
Regarding the present karma, it further clarifies that the retribution is immediate.
"Field of merit" refers to the Buddha and the preeminent Sangha;
this explains the first phrase.
The Buddha is the foremost among the Saṃgha;

thus, this very community of monks is called the "Saṃgha with the Buddha as its Foremost. Furthermore, it is explained that because the Buddha is the most excellent within the field of merit (saṃghakṣetra), he is called the "Foremost."
That is to say, the Buddha is the foremost among the Saṃgha.
Although the Buddha is not included within the category of the Śrāvaka Saṃgha,
he is nonetheless part of the Noble Saṃgha (āryasaṃgha) and so forth.
Therefore, the *Nyāyānusāra* (Treatise on Right Principle), fascicle 38, states:
"If the Buddha were not included within the Saṃgha,
why would the Sūtra speak as follows?"
If you are able to offer even a small amount of material goods as an offering to the Buddha and the foremost assembly of monks in due order,
you will thereby obtain the merit of a comprehensive and pure gift within the field of the Sangha.
The *Nyāyānusāra* explains:
"There are many kinds of Saṃgha, namely:
the Saṃgha of sentient beings, the Śrāvaka Saṃgha, the Saṃgha as a field of merit, and the Noble Saṃgha (*āryasaṃgha*), and so forth."
Within this [category], the Buddha is not a śrāvaka-saṃgha;
he may be another kind of saṃgha, because he has attained awakening spontaneously. This is explained at length as stated therein.
Based on this textual evidence, it is known that the Buddha is also called the Saṃgha.

Regarding the phrase "concerning the *pudgala* who returns after having attained [the cessation]," the following explains the second and third lines by further analyzing the distinctions through the perspective of specific individuals; there are five such distinctions. This explains the emergence from the meditative attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*).
This means that within this meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*), because the mind has ceased, one attains tranquility of mind.
Since this absorption is tranquil and resembles *nirvāṇa*,
it is said to be "similar" because, like [nirvāṇa], the mind is equally extinguished.
Because it is still subject to accomplishment and because one will eventually be reborn from it, it cannot be called "ultimate.
If, upon first emerging from this meditative absorption, the mind is extremely tranquil,
it may be illustrated by the metaphor of one who has entered nirvana and yet emerges from it once more.
Regarding the second point, "from emerging from the state of non-contention (*araṇā*) until it proceeds as a continuous succession," this explains the emergence from non-contention.
When entering this meditative absorption, one prevents the arising of afflictions in others.
It is called being accompanied by the intention for benefit;
upon emerging from this meditative absorption, there is again the perfuming of the body with immeasurable superior qualities,
which continues in succession.
"Third, 'emerging from the concentration of loving-kindness and proceeding in a continuous succession' explains the emergence from the concentration of loving-kindness.
This concentration is for the purpose of bringing happiness to sentient beings;
the rest is as in the case of the 'absence of conflict' (araṇā)."
Regarding the fourth point, "emerging from the path of seeing and arising in the continuum of a purified body":
this explains emerging from the path of seeing.
It means that within this path, one permanently abandons the afflictions of seeing and attains the superior transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*).

This refers to having attained the superior basis of the body for seeing the Path, and furthermore, having attained the superior basis of the body for the fruit of Stream-entry through the abandonment of the delusions of views.
From this point, one emerges from the Path of Seeing.
It arises from the continuum of the body purified by the stream-enterer (*srotāpanna*).

Although they have not yet been able to abandon the afflictions to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*), they are ultimately never again a basis for the afflictions of views (*dṛṣṭi-heya*); thus it is called the "purified body. This [body] transcends the fruits of the once-returner (*sakṛdāgāmin*) and the non-returner (*anāgāmin*).
The first section, from "emerging from the path of seeing" up to "is called a field of merit," explains emerging from the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*).
This means that within this path, one eternally abandons the afflictions to be abandoned through cultivation;
although there may be temporary regression, because they will inevitably be abandoned again, it is called "eternal abandonment.
One thereby attains a superior transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*).

This means that one attains the superior basis for the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*). Furthermore, it is explained that by having abandoned the afflictions of the path of cultivation, one attains the superior basis of an Arhat.
Upon emerging from this path of cultivation, the continuum of the Arhat’s pure body arises.
Because they do not serve as a basis for the afflictions of the path of cultivation, they are called "pure bodies.

Although there may be temporary retrogression, because one will inevitably sever [the afflictions] again, they are called "pure bodies"; therefore, these five are termed "fields of merit" (*puṇyakṣetra*).
These five refer only to the stage of initial emergence from meditative equipoise;
therefore, the *Nyāyānusāra* states:
"From among these five stages of initial emergence."
Riding upon the momentum of the superior merits previously cultivated,
his mind still looked back with focused mindfulness that he did not abandon;
his faculties were tranquil and exceptionally distinct from the ordinary.
Whether mundane or supramundane,
whether their merit is fixed or unfixed,
there is nothing capable of surpassing, overcoming, eclipsing, or outshining it.
Therefore, these five are called "fields of merit.
Regarding the fourth line of the verse, it explains that if one acts within these fields such that it is capable of summoning immediate results, [the retribution follows swiftly].
If one performs either harmful or beneficial karma toward any of the first six types of fields,
this karma will necessarily bring about its fruit in the very same life. This is not the case,
however, when one proceeds from another state of meditative concentration to a field that is not a superior field of merit.
Brief distinction of the remaining concentrations:
this refers to all concentrations other than the first five. Regarding the remaining fruits:
this refers to those among the four fruits excluding the first and the last.

These others—the once-returners and non-returners—arise sequentially. When they emerge from other meditative concentrations, it is because the concentration previously cultivated was not particularly superior;
likewise when they emerge from other fruits of the path.
Because the afflictions to be abandoned by seeing (*darśana-heya*) have already been abandoned,
while the afflictions to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) are not yet completely exhausted,
that mental continuum is not a supreme field of merit at the stage of initial emergence. Furthermore, when [the recipient] causes harm or benefit, the fruit is not received immediately.
Although a stream-enterer (srotāpanna) cannot completely abandon the afflictions to be abandoned through cultivation (bhāvanā-heya),
because he has completely exhausted the afflictions to be abandoned through seeing (darśana-heya);
likewise, although an arhat has already abandoned the afflictions to be abandoned through seeing.
Because the afflictions to be abandoned through cultivation have been completely severed,
one experiences the karma that brings either harm or benefit immediately upon first emerging from that state.
This refers to the two types among the superior [attainments] of the stream-enterer (srotāpanna).
According to the first emergence, it is superior;
however, if one considers the four fruits in relation to one another at other times,
then the two fruits are superior to the stream-enterer (srotāpanna).
Regarding the question, "Does [the ripening fruit] extend even to non-mental feelings within the category of ripening fruits?"—
this section below is the fifth, which clarifies the karma of the two types of feeling. Within this:
First, the karma of two types of experience;
second, the karma of mental derangement.
This is the first inquiry concerning the karma of two types of experience.
Among the five aggregates that constitute the fruit of maturation (*vipāka*), feeling (*vedanā*) is preeminent.
This should now be investigated:
among the various types of karma, is there any that brings about only the maturation of mental feeling and not bodily feeling?
Is there that which brings about the maturation of bodily feeling but not mental feeling?
There is. Answer: [as follows].
"What is it? This is the inquiry.
The verse says: "As has already been explained above."
Because bodily sensation must necessarily be accompanied by vitarka and vicāra,
there is no bodily sensation in the higher stages due to the absence of vitarka;
furthermore, it cannot produce bodily sensation belonging to a lower stage.
Therefore, the *Nyāyānusāra* states:
"In those stages, there is no bodily sensation (*kāyika-vedanā*);
bodily sensation is necessarily associated with applied thought (*vitarka*)."
Karma that is without vitarka does not produce a result with vitarka.
All unwholesome karma produces only bodily sensation (kāyika-vedanā) and not mental sensation (caitasika-vedanā), as can be understood from the text.
As for wholesome karma with vitarka:
It can immediately give rise to both types of sensation;
however, as this was not the subject of the question, it is not explained here.
Regarding the question of which consciousness serves as the cause and basis for the derangement of a sentient being’s mind:
This is the second [section], clarifying the karma of mental derangement.
Question: In which consciousness does the mental derangement of sentient beings reside?
By what cause is it induced?
Based on what location do they arise?
The verse says: "Reaching [all places] except for the Northern Continent, among those in the Desire Realm.
The first phrase answers the first question.
The next two lines answer the second question, and the following line answers the third question. The *Śāstra* says:
"Because it reaches the state of non-conceptualization (*avikalpa*)."
The first phrase can be understood as explained previously.
From "due to five causes" up to "capable of causing the mind to become deranged," the following explains the second and third phrases.
Sentient beings become deranged in mind due to five causes;
this is the first cause: being born from the ripening of evil karma as a result of evil deeds.
Based on this karmic maturation (*vipāka*), it can cause the mind to become deranged;
the rest of the text may be understood accordingly.
Second, regarding "due to terror... resulting in mental derangement":
The commentary on the verse explains that this is known through fear.
Third, regarding "from injury to eventually resulting in mental derangement": [it refers to] the process by which harm leads ultimately to the loss of sanity.
The commentary on the verse [explains] "due to harm.
Regarding the phrase "four [types of madness] arise due to discord," the commentary on the verse [explains] "due to conflict."
"5. By means of sorrow and grief, as in the case of Vasiṣṭha and others" explains the verse’s reference to "by means of grief.
For instance, the minds of Vasiṣṭha and others became deranged due to sorrow and grief.
Therefore, the *Vibhāṣā* (126) states:
"As it is said in the Sūtra regarding the Brahmin woman Vāsisthī."
Because he had lost his six sons, his mind became deranged and he ran about naked;
upon seeing the World-Honored One, he regained his original sanity.
Regarding the question, "If it is in the mental consciousness, does it not extend to that which is non-retribution?"—
the answer is:
the meaning of "mental" can be understood.
Regarding the statement that "insanity does not extend to an unpolluted mind," the answer is:
it refers to the fact that unwholesome karma causes the maturation of discordant primary elements (*mahābhūta*).
Because the mind loses mindfulness due to the power of these primary elements (*mahābhūta*), it is said to be "deranged" (*unmāda*).
Its nature is not that of maturation (*vipāka*), for both wholesome and unwholesome minds can be subject to derangement.
Thus, the *Nyāyānusāra* states:

Because this mental derangement is not itself a result of maturation (*vipāka*), as both wholesome and unwholesome states of mind can be subject to derangement; such is the treatise. Regarding this mental derangement in relation to mental confusion (*vikṣepa*), one should formulate four permutations (*catuṣkoṭi*). The first permutation is: deranged but not confused.
This refers to one who is insane with a non-defiled mind;
because they have lost mindfulness, they are called "insane," yet because it is not defiled, it is not called "deranged. The second case is being deranged but not insane.
This refers to the defiled minds of those who are not insane;
they are called "distracted" because they are defiled, yet they are not "insane" because mindfulness is not lost. The third category consists of those who are both insane and distracted.
This refers to the defiled minds of those who are insane.
They are called "insane" because they have lost mindfulness, and they are called "deranged" because they are defiled. The fourth category consists of those who are neither insane nor deranged.
This refers to one who is not insane having an undefiled mind; because mindfulness is not lost, he is not insane, and because it is undefiled, he is not deranged.
It should be understood that in this context, "defilement" is what is termed "derangement."
"Losing mindfulness is called madness" refers to [the state] from the northern continent of Uttarakuru up until the realization of the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*);
this explains the fourth phrase.
Within the desire realm, with the exception of Uttarakuru,
other sentient beings of the desire realm may experience derangement of mind;
that is to say, even among the gods of the six classes of the desire realm, there are those whose minds are still deranged.
How much more so for humans; those in the three evil destinies are free from mental derangement.
This is an illustration by means of the superior to illustrate the inferior:
in the hells, there is constant derangement, as can be understood from the text. Among the noble ones of the desire realm, only the Buddhas are excluded.
The Buddha has no derangement of mind through his own volition; other noble ones may possess the fourth [type].
Since the primary elements can become discordant, there may be derangement of mind, but not the first type.

Regarding those born of maturation (*vipākaja*), if there are determinate karmas with respect to the three times and indeterminate karmas with respect to time but determinate with respect to maturation,
one must necessarily first experience their matured fruits before subsequently attaining the state of an Arya.
When, at a certain time, both the maturation and the non-deterministic karma become fruitless because one has attained the state of an Arya,
due to not experiencing them at all.
Furthermore, the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 126, states:
Question: In what realms does this mental derangement occur?
Answer: It occurs in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
It does not exist in the form realm or the formless realm;
however, it is absent in the hells because the mind is constantly distracted there.
Regarding those with deranged minds:
this refers to times that are not constant.
Ghosts and animals may also have deranged minds.
They also exist among humans and devas,
