If one digs up and takes [the earth], one incurs the offense of theft.
Because all that exists upon the great earth belongs to the king; furthermore, the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 113, states:
"If a treasure hidden between two kingdoms is discovered, it shall belong to the Wheel-turning King (*cakravartin*) when he appears in the world."
If there were no Universal Monarch (cakravartin), it would not exist anywhere at all.
If someone were to steal it and take it elsewhere, one should consider that this applies to other cases as well;
the property of a deceased bhikṣu is termed "reverted property" (parivartaka-vastu).
Because one may cause [the property] to be diverted to other bhikṣus, it is called "diverting.
Having already explained taking what is not given up to engaging in improper conduct,
this third section clarifies the characteristics of sexual misconduct.
The meaning of sexual misconduct likewise entails five conditions:

first, the volition to engage in sexual intercourse, which excludes the absence of such volition—this should be understood according to the previous [explanation on killing]; second, engaging with an improper object.
This distinguishes [the object] from that which one ought to practice.
Within the verse, there are these three notions of what should not be practiced,
which distinguish them from the notion of what should be practiced.
If one forms the perception that an improper act is proper, the course of action (karmapatha) is not established;
this is because the perception must necessarily exist, as in the previous cases. Fourth, the preparatory stage (prayoga) for engaging in sexual misconduct.
"Without preparation" (*anabhisamskāra*) is excluded;
by analogy with what precedes, there should be [the qualification] "without error. One engages in sexual intercourse without error, thereby excluding that which is done with error.
It has flowed down from of old,
as explained in the prose section.
Sexual misconduct is established by the completion of the act.
It should be understood as before.
The *Śāstra* states: "Reaching [a place] is called 'improper time' (akāla)";
first, regarding an improper object (*aviṣaya*).
1. Because of harboring the intent to invade and deeply afflict others; 2.
Regarding improper means, because although one does not invade others, one’s heedlessness is grave; 3.
Regarding improper places, because one lacks shame for base and loathsome acts; 4. Regarding improper times.
Because she was pregnant,
because of the child,
and because she had violated the precepts.
Because these transgressions are grave, they all constitute courses of action (*karmapatha*). Some say that if one has formally undertaken the fast and precepts (*upavāsa-śīla*),
a violation constitutes a non-timely act.
If one accepts [an offering] despite not being permitted to do so,
and later commits an offense,
it does not constitute a full course of action (*karmapatha*). This is the intended meaning of the former masters.
Whether one grants or does not grant [the offense], if there is a transgression,
it all constitutes a course of action (*karmapatha*).
Since it is stated that even if there is no error, it is not a course of action, [this must be the case].
The following section provides a detailed analysis,
demonstrating that an action does not constitute a full course of karma (*karmapatha*) when committed with a mistaken mind.
If one approaches another's wife [under such a misconception], does it still constitute a full course of karma?
Question:
The meaning may be understood.
As for the statement that "it is also established because it reaches the ultimate in other cases," [what is meant by this?]
In the response, two explanations are given;
the latter is superior because it is an inclusive [interpretation]. Therefore, it is said: "the enjoyer."
This refers to the culmination of the result; the remainder of the text may be understood accordingly.
Regarding the question, "Does one attain the path of action (karmapatha) in the case of a bhikṣuṇī?"—this is the inquiry.
Since a nun does not belong to another, toward whom would she incur an offense?
Regarding the statement "from the king down to, let alone those who have left the household life," the answer is as follows:
There are two interpretations. The first states that this refers to incurring guilt before the king, because he would not tolerate the performance of unrighteous acts.
The second interpretation states that one should not engage in such acts even with one's own wife or concubine while observing the eight precepts.
How much more so for those who have left the household life?
Using the light to illustrate the heavy,
even a slight act of aggression constitutes a full karmic path.
Although the offenses are identical,
for a wife and others it is an improper time,
whereas for a nun it is an inappropriate object.
Although there are two interpretations, the latter is superior;
thus the *Nyāyānusāra* states:
"Just as bhikṣuṇīs and others have wives who possess the precepts."
If there is an act of aggression or violation, it also constitutes a path of action (karmapatha).
Some say that this offense pertains to the king residing therein,
because he is capable of providing protection and yet fails to prohibit such acts.
If the king himself commits [the act], the course of action is likewise established.
Therefore, what was stated previously is superior in principle. Furthermore, it may also be explained that this master’s view is correct.
If a king personally commits an offense regarding such matters as judicial investigation,
he incurs guilt because he upholds the law.
If it concerns a young girl, does one incur the path of karmic action upon reaching her?
Question:
If it has already been granted that all who come to him obtain [their desires] from the king, answer:
The meaning is clear.
If one commits sexual misconduct with this girl or other women,
one incurs an offense against the king.
If a master of logic were to raise this objection— asking,
"When a king commits an offense, against whom is the charge to be adjudicated?"—
the answer is as previously explained in the general commentary.
Having already distinguished sexual misconduct up to the meaning of false speech (*mṛṣāvāda*),
the following fourth section clarifies the characteristics of false speech.
Within this:
First, the explicit explanation of false speech;
second, the analysis based on what has been seen, heard, and so forth.
This [first section] is the explicit explanation of false speech.
The Commentary says: "Up to 'it constitutes false speech'":
this clarifies that false speech constitutes a karmic path when four conditions are present. First, one speaks with a perception different from the actual state of the object being described.

"Seeing while saying one does not see," and so forth—second, the deceived person understands and comprehends the meaning of what was said; third, the arousal of a defiled mind; fourth, being without error.
These first three [conditions] are present in the verses.
It does not flow forth erroneously.
If the four conditions are complete, it constitutes false speech.
If the person being deceived asks, "What is this that you have said? [the conditions are met].
Question:
What is frivolous speech? Answer:
Regarding when false speech constitutes a full course of action (*karmapatha*):
this asks at what point it becomes a *karmapatha*.
Is it at the moment of the final syllable, or does it extend to all the preceding preparatory actions?
Answer: Although false speech is composed of many syllables,
it constitutes this course of action through the manifest and unmanifest karma that arise simultaneously with the final syllable.
Alternatively, because the person being deceived is by nature intelligent,
they may comprehend the subsequent meaning upon hearing only a brief deceptive statement. Such a person, at whatever time—
When the meaning has been understood by the one being deceived, the manifest and unmanifest karma constitute the actual path of action (*karmapatha*).
The manifest and unmanifest karma occurring simultaneously with the preceding syllables are all its preliminary application (*prayoga*);
the manifest and unmanifest karma occurring simultaneously with the subsequent syllables are all its aftermath (*pṛṣṭha*).
Regarding the statement that one who understands the meaning and is capable of understanding the name is called "one who understands":
this is a critical inquiry.
At what specific time, according to the deceiver, does the one being deceived claim to understand the meaning?
Is "understanding" (vijñāna) named as such based on the correct comprehension of the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) regarding what has already been heard?
Or is it named as such based on the ear-faculty correctly hearing and the auditory consciousness (*śrotravijñāna*) being able to understand?
If that were so, what would be the fault?
Answer: If one were to claim that someone who has already heard [the teaching] up to the point where they can be called "capable of understanding" is such a person,
then further inquiry is required.
If one bases this on the consciousness that has already been deceived, the correct understanding [of the object] by the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) is called "understanding.
It is said that the meaning expressed (*abhidheya-artha*) is what is known by the mental consciousness;
meanwhile, the vocal intimation (*vāgvijñapti*) of the deceiver perishes simultaneously with the auditory consciousness (*śrotravijñāna*) of the deceived.
At the time when the consciousness deceived by [the speech] correctly understands it, that deceiver manifests no informative intimation (*vijñapti*);

therefore, this path of action (*karmapatha*) should be established as consisting solely of non-informative intimation (*avijñapti*). If, however, one bases the definition on the ear-faculty of the deceived person correctly hearing and the ear-consciousness being able to understand, then it is called "understanding."
Although there is no fault of [the action] becoming a karmic path consisting solely of unmanifest action (*avijñapti-karman*),
one has not yet understood how it is that the ear faculty,
while actually hearing, can be called the ear-consciousness (*śrotra-vijñāna*) capable of understanding.
Regarding the statement that one who is skilled in the meaning of words is called "one capable of understanding," the answer is:
for one skilled in the meaning of words, the ear-consciousness has already arisen within the stage of the present.

Because it is free from the conditions of delusion, it is called "capable of understanding. Furthermore, while the ear-consciousness itself is not understanding, it is called "capable of understanding" because it can give rise to the mental consciousness that understands.
Although there are these two interpretations, the former is considered superior.

Regarding the statement, "That which is without fault should be accepted as the thesis," this means that the author of the treatise approves of that which is without fault among the two preceding objections as the thesis.

Specifically, he takes "understanding" to mean the capacity for understanding through correct hearing, because at that time both manifest action (*vijñapti-karman*) and non-manifest action (*avijñapti-karman*) are present. Thus, it is said to be "without fault."

He thus seals these words. Furthermore, the commentator explains that the Master [Vasubandhu] has evaluated them through their general characteristics using reasoning; if there is no fault, one should adopt this as the thesis.
As for the explanation of the accomplishment of the path of action (*karmapatha*), how can this also be considered definitive?
If there is auditory consciousness free from confusion and error,
then being able to understand based on correct hearing constitutes "understanding.
In this case, both the manifest and the unmanifest constitute the path of action.
If auditory consciousness encounters conditions that cause confusion, it is not termed "understanding";
only when subsequent mental reflection (manas) examines them can there be correct understanding.
It is precisely based on this correct understanding following what has been heard that it is called "understanding."
Only the unmanifest (*avijñapti*) alone also constitutes a course of action (*karmapatha*).
Because it is not fixed [in this regard], the Master of the Treatise says: "That which is without fault should be accepted as the thesis.
Furthermore, the *Nyāyānusāra* states:
If one speaks while facing the assembly but with the intention of turning one's back on them,
or falsely claims to have seen what was not seen and so forth among those who are deceived,
the manifest (*vijñapti*) and unmanifest (*avijñapti*) karma at the very moment the deceived person understands this is called the "fundamental path of action" (*mūlakarmapatha*).
Some say that deception is only established when it is approved [by the victim].
If that were so, there would be no principle for deceiving the noble ones (ārya).
However, since the fault of deceiving the noble ones is profound, [the definition must be otherwise].

From this, one should know that what was stated previously is correct: the act of understanding constitutes the completion of the path of action (*karmapatha*), and it is not necessary for the victim to give their consent for it to be established.
Question: Just as the path of action of killing is completed only after the killing has been done, [is this the same for deception?]
The completion of the karmic path of false speech is established through the understanding [of the lie].
Why, then, is it not said that it is completed only after the understanding? The explanation is: killing refers to the severing of life;
it is only when the present life no longer continues that it is designated a karmic path.
Therefore, it is said that once the killing is completed, the act constitutes the path of karma (*karmapatha*) at the very moment the victim understands the deception;
it does not require that they have already "understood" [the intent].
Regarding the statement in the Sūtra that "all words reach the characteristics of what is seen and so forth," this is the second section below,
which clarifies what is seen and so forth.
The inquiry arises based on the sūtra.
The sixteen [points] within the sūtra may be understood according to the text.
If one analyzes in detail,
there are cases where seeing is called "seeing" and so forth,
or where not seeing is called "not seeing" and so forth; these are termed non-noble speech (*anāryavāda*).
There are cases where one says "I have not seen" when one has actually seen, or says "I have seen" when one has not seen;
such instances are termed "noble speech. Therefore, the tenth fascicle of the *Saṃgītiparyāya-pāda-śāstra* states:
If one has actually seen something and so forth, yet gives rise to the perception that one has not seen it and says, "I have already seen it," and so on—
although such speech is called non-noble speech,
it is not called "saying one has seen what one has not seen."
Because he has actually seen [the object] and so forth; furthermore, it is said:
"There is one who, though not having actually seen [the object] and so forth, gives rise to the perception and speech of having seen it, saying, 'I have not seen it,' and so on.
Although such cases are termed "non-noble speech," they are nonetheless included here.
Yet one does not say "I see" when it is called "not seeing," and so forth, because in reality one has not seen and so on. Furthermore, it says:
there are those who, having actually already seen and so forth, give rise to the perception that they have not seen and speak, saying, "I did not see," and so forth.
Although such [statements] are called "noble speech," they are not called "not seeing and saying one does not see," and so forth,
because he has actually seen and so on. Furthermore, it says:
If one does not actually see something, yet gives rise to the perception and thought of seeing it, and says, "I have seen it," and so forth—
although this is called a noble utterance (*āryavāda*),
it is not called "seeing" when one says "I see," and so forth.
"Because he does not actually see [the object] and so forth"—this concludes the treatise.
It should be understood that all speech uttered in contradiction to one's perception is not the speech of an Arya;
conversely, all speech uttered in accordance with one's perception is the speech of an Arya.
Furthermore, the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 171, explains the terminology as follows:
"Question: For what reason is this speech called 'non-noble' (*anārya*)?
Answer: It is called non-noble because it is unwholesome (*akuśala*)."
Furthermore, it is called "non-noble" because it manifests within the mental continuum of those who are not noble.
Furthermore, it is called "non-noble" because it is accomplished by those who are not noble.
Furthermore, it is called "non-noble" because it is spoken by those who are not noble.
Furthermore, they are called "non-noble" because non-noble ones obtain this name by means of them. It is also said:
Question: For what reason is this speech called "noble"?
Answer: It is called "noble" because it is wholesome.
Furthermore, it is called "noble" because it manifests within the continuum of the noble ones;
furthermore, it is called "noble" because it is accomplished by the noble ones;
furthermore, it is called "noble" because it is spoken by the noble ones.

Furthermore, they are called "Noble Ones" (ārya) because they attain the name "Noble One" by virtue of this; that treatise further cites the *Saṃgītiparyāya-pāda-śāstra* to explain this, which cannot be related in full detail here.

The verse answers.

This describes the explanation of the Vaibhāṣika masters:
seeing, hearing, smelling, and knowing are the faculties (indriya) and not the consciousnesses (vijñāna).
Here, the term "consciousness" is employed to indicate the supported faculty by means of the supporting consciousness.
Therefore, the *Vibhāṣā* (Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra), fascicle 21, states:
"Seeing, hearing, smelling, and knowing are faculties (*indriya*), not consciousness (*vijñāna*).
Nevertheless, consciousness is mentioned [here]."
It is evident that the sense organs, such as the eye, can apprehend their objects only when assisted by consciousness;
for it is the *sabhāga* (homogeneous) organs that possess functional activity, not the *tatsabhāga* (non-homogeneous).
This is because [the term] "cognition" (*buddhi*) is established specifically in reference to that which has reached its full development.
The reason why three objects are designated by the same term "that which is cognized" (*vijñeya*) is as follows:
these three objects are called "that which is cognized" because they are equally indeterminate (*avyākṛta*).

For what reason are the objects experienced by the three consciousnesses—eye, ear, and nose—each established as a distinct type, whereas the objects experienced by the three consciousnesses of nose, tongue, and body are combined and established as one type called 'apperception' (*vitarka*)?"
The Venerable Vasumitra said:

"Because the objects of the three consciousnesses are exclusively indeterminate (avyākṛta) and are themselves indeterminate, the faculties are designated by the name 'cognition' (buddhi). Furthermore, because these three faculties apprehend only objects that are reached and are in contact with their objects, they are designated by the name 'cognition'."
The Venerable One said:
"Only these three faculties have objects that are dull and obscure, like a corpse;
therefore, they can give rise to consciousness, which is called 'awakening' (bodha). This is explained at length in that [text].
How is this known to be so?

The general answer consists of two parts: first, by means of scripture;
second, by means of reasoning.
Regarding the statement "by means of the sūtra," as for the question "to what does 'that which is to be awakened' refer?"—
this clarifies that it refers to the sūtra.

thus we know that what is perceived consists of the three [objects], such as odor and so forth.

This is called the principle.
This is precisely using the sūtra to demonstrate the correct principle.
Regarding the argument that this proof fails to establish the characteristics of the desirable and the undesirable,
the Sautrāntika school generally rejects it.
The intent of the sūtra’s explanation is distinct;
it is not that, within these two preceding and following sūtras, the Blessed One intended to definitively determine the characteristics of the "seen" and so forth among the four, such as seeing.
The characteristic of speech as it is heard;
the characteristic of speech as it is perceived;

it means that the Buddha exhorted him [to focus] upon the six objects.
And regarding the four beginning with seeing:
the referential object of what is seen,
and the referential object of what is heard.
The objects of what is awakened to and the objects of what is known;
"object" (vastu) here refers to the essential substance (svabhāva).

Regarding the phrase "whatever is seen," one should not superimpose upon it the characteristics of the pleasant or unpleasant that give rise to greed, hatred, and so forth. [Question: If this is not the case, then...

"Does the mind know dharmas? The commentary explains: The scriptural text merely states that form is not seen by the eye, sound is not heard by the ear, and dharmas are not known by the mind.

the ear alone can hear,
and the mind alone knows phenomena.

This is the question posed by the *Vibhāṣā*.
Regarding the statement that "other masters say that reaching [the object] is also irrational," the Sautrāntika replies:
"Other Sautrāntika masters say..."
If the five objects are directly perceived by the five sense faculties,
they are called "seen" because they are distinct and clear;
if the six objects are derived from the authority of scripture through oral tradition from others, they are called "heard."
If one employs one's own mind through inference (*anumāna*) to deduce the six objects as they are conventionally accepted by means of various reasonings, these are called "the cognized" (*vijñeya*).
If the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) realizes the six objects through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), these are called "the knowable" (*jñeya*).
If the mental consciousness arises immediately following the five sensory consciousnesses,
it directly perceives the five objects;
if it is a mental consciousness within meditative concentration, it directly perceives dharmas.
Alternatively, through direct perception within a state of meditative concentration,
one can also universally realize the six objects;
among these, regarding the five [sensory] objects:
Each [of these] can give rise to the four terms beginning with "view" (*dṛṣṭi*).
Within the four types regarding the sixth object,
those seen by the five sense-faculties are excluded.
There are other [factors] such as what is heard and so forth;
thus, the name "cognition" (*buddhi*) is not without a referent,
for it refers to the six objects that are cognized.
Since the three objects such as fragrance and so forth are common to all four types of verbal expression,
they are not non-existent; they may be called "seen" or they may be called "heard."
It is sometimes called "that which is perceived" and sometimes called "that which is known"; therefore,
that statement regarding the principle is also irrational.
Regarding the statement by the former masters that "that which is called the knowable" refers to those who study the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*,
the former masters speak as follows.
The forms perceived by the direct perception of the eye are called "the seen.
The reason why only the act of seeing is termed "the seer" is that the manifestation of the objective realm of form is most distinct therein.

Therefore, that which is seen by the eye alone is [the object of sight]. If one relies on scriptural authority (*āgama-pramāṇa*) and hears the six objects from another, it is called "that which is heard" (*śruta*).

If one relies on inference (*anumāna-pramāṇa*) and applies one's own mind to conceive and construct the six objects, they are called "that which is cognized" (*mata*). Furthermore, according to direct perception (*pratyakṣa-pramāṇa*), the four objects internally experienced by the ear, nose, tongue, and body are [the objects of touch].
Furthermore, the six objects, which are realized internally through the direct perception of the mental faculty (*manas*), are all termed "objects of knowledge" (*jñeya*).
According to this interpretation, seeing pertains exclusively to the eye,
while hearing and cognizing pertain exclusively to the mind.
It is known that [this applies] to the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind.
Among the six objects, the object of form (rūpa) may give rise to four types [of consciousness], while the five objects beginning with sound may give rise to three: hearing, sensing, and cognizing.
In this context, because the six sense-faculties, the six consciousnesses, and the dharma-object are already included [within the aggregates], they cannot be discussed separately.
Let us now set aside these incidental remarks and proceed with the main argument;
thus, the author of the treatise brings the dispute to an end.
"Is there such a case where one comes to utter false speech by means of the body?
This is the question that follows the preceding section of questions and answers. This, then, is the inquiry.
It is said that there are those who attain the ultimate and those who practice *prasāda* (generosity).
This is the response to the text concerning the elicitation of wisdom (*jñāna*).
There are three questions and answers.
This correctly adopts the second answer to the preceding question;
it is included here because the preceding and following questions and answers share the same text.
Thus, the *Jñānaprasthāna-śāstra* states:
Is it possible to incur the offense of killing without moving the body?
The answer is: yes; that is, when one incurs the offense by speaking words or dispatching a messenger to kill.
Question: Is there any instance where one incurs the offense of lying through speech without having initiated physical movement?
Answer: Yes; that is to say, by moving the body, pointing with a finger, or writing.
Question: Is there anyone who, without moving the body nor uttering a word, is touched by the two offenses of killing and false speech?
Answer: There is.
This refers to sages who, through the fury of their minds, kill various sentient beings.

Without moving the body or uttering a word, one incurs the offense of killing; likewise, when performing the *prasādhana* (confession), if there is any transgression, the preceptor asks and the respondent indicates purity by remaining silent.
Without moving the body or uttering a word, one incurs the offense of false speech.
*Posatha*—translated here as "nurturing"—means that by hearing the recitation of the precepts, one nurtures one's roots of goodness.
The old term "posadha" is a corruption.
Regarding the statement that one need not move the body to where labor must be performed,
the Master of the Treatise raises an objection.
If that seer, at the time of the *pauṣḍhika* offering,
neither moves his body nor utters a word;
In the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), there is no non-informative action (*avijñapti*) that arises independently of informative action (*vijñapti*).
How, then, can killing and false speech constitute courses of action (*karmapatha*)?
One should apply diligent effort to resolve this difficulty through careful investigation.
The *Nyāyānusāra* (Treatise on Reasoning),
chapter 42, offers this defense: "However, when I first explained the *poṣadha*,
it was like how, by means of bodily movement, one can express the meaning of speech and thereby produce the path of action of vocal karma."
Even if the body does not move, a karmic path can still arise through the expression of verbal meaning;
however, when the precepts are being recited, if one has committed an offense, remaining silent expresses purity so that the assembly may all know it.

How is it that the karmic path of false speech does not arise? When a rishi, out of mental indignation, instructs others according to the Dharma and so forth, he has no regard for the minds of sentient beings;
yet non-humans revere him and know that he possesses an evil mind.
Moving the body constitutes the path of action (karmapatha) of killing that living being.
By what means does the seer (ṛṣi) manifest [his intent] so as to make the ghost understand?
Through mental agitation, his body and speech necessarily undergo transformation.
Alternatively, through incantations or curses, the body and speech are necessarily moved.
Other masters say that not all unmanifest [form] in the desire realm arises based on manifest [action].
Just as when the fruit is attained, the five bhikṣus and others obtain the prātimokṣa-śīla,
so too should it be for unwholesome [karma]. However,
in those cases, there was previously a determinate manifest action (vijñapti).
The same should apply to the others as well.
As for the "seer" (ṛṣi), it is as previously stated.
Regarding the one who incurs the offense of lying at the time of the *prasāthana* (distribution of food):
This refers to those who, being impure, falsely enter the midst of the Saṃgha,
assuming a dignified demeanor while seated or making some discourse.
This refers to the preceding manifest [action].

The remaining examples should be understood accordingly. The commentary states: "Thus, from 'I have already' down to 'must move body and speech,' this is the explanation by Saṃghabhadra regarding the time of the *poṣadha*."
Furthermore, when the intention of the seer becomes enraged, two courses of action are established. Second, the presentation of alternative views:
other masters state that not all non-informative matter (*avijñapti*) in the desire realm arises based on informative matter (*vijñapti*).
Among the ten ways of obtaining the precepts previously mentioned,
it is like when the Buddha and the Pratyekabuddhas attained their fruits,
as well as when the five bhikṣus and others obtained the prātimokṣa precepts.
It does not arise based on informative [action].
The principle for unwholesome karma should be understood in the same way: even if one does not move the body nor utter speech, there is no informative [action].
It is established that even where there is only non-informative action (*avijñapti-karma*), the path of action is accomplished. What contradiction is there in this?

How is it that the Master of the Sūtras (Sautrāntika) raises the objection: "In the desire realm, there is no non-informative action that arises apart from informative action (*vijñapti*)"? [This concludes] the third section: the correct explanation.
The master of treatises, Saṃghabhadra, does not accept this interpretation; therefore, he says:
"However, they do attain the fruit."
For the five bhikṣus and others,
there must necessarily be informative action (*vijñapti*) during the preparatory stage,
continuing until they attain the fruit and enter the Path.
Just as the prātimokṣa vows are produced based on this informative action (vijñapti),
it stands to reason that the unwholesome paths of action [arising] when other sages become enraged and utter curses must likewise arise based on informative action.
As previously explained, when a practitioner teaches others through such means as the meaning [of the teachings],
at the time of the preparatory application,
their body and speech will inevitably undergo transformation due to mental agitation.
Alternatively, due to curses or incantations, the body and speech necessarily move;
if there is a bodily intimation, it arises from a bodily intimation,
and if there is a vocal intimation, it arises from a vocal intimation.
This is based on the fact that the preparatory stage (*prayoga*) necessarily involves informative action (*vijñapti-karma*), and not on the fundamental stage (*maula*). Therefore,
the preceding treatise states that when one instructs another through signs and so forth during the *poṣadha* ceremony, one incurs the offense of lying.
That is to say, one who is impure feigns entry into the midst of the Saṃgha and sits there manifesting dignified deportment;
from this bodily informative action, non-informative action arises in the form of speech,
or there is something spoken.
From the informative karma of speech, the non-informative [karma] of speech arises;
this is what is called the "prior informative" (pūrva-vijñapti). Other examples should be considered accordingly. Regarding the term "prior informative":
Alternatively, it may arise from a prior continuity of manifest action (*vijñapti*) that remains uninterrupted until the attainment of non-manifest action (*avijñapti*),
such as in the case of obtaining virtuous vows or performing the *poṣadha* ceremony;
or it may occur even when there is fundamentally no manifest action at all.
Because in the preceding stage of preparatory application there must necessarily be manifest action (*vijñapti*),
such as when a seer’s mind is incensed or when he dispatches someone to kill.
The intention of the *Nyāyānusāra* is that non-informative action (*avijñapti*) in the desire realm necessarily arises based on informative action (*vijñapti*). That is,
there must either be an informative act at the fundamental stage (*maula-karman-patha*),
or there must be an informative act during the preparatory stage (*prayoga*).
Because, as appropriate for each case, there must necessarily be informative action (*vijñapti*) within both stages;
therefore, it is said that non-informative action (*avijñapti*) necessarily arises based on informative action.
It is not required, however, that there be definitive informative action at the root moment of speech.
If it were not so, then at the very moment the fundamental act— such as killing by dispatching a messenger— is accomplished, what informative [action] (vijñapti) would there be?
If one adopts this interpretation, it accords well with the challenging argument that there is no non-informative [action] (avijñapti) arising apart from informative action in the realm of desire.
My position is inherently sound;
your objection is merely a hollow fabrication.

If you claim that the fundamental [unmanifest] must necessarily have a manifest [action] as its cause, and thus raise the objection that desire cannot exist as an unmanifest action arising independently of a manifest one:

When the fundamental act of ordering someone to kill and so forth is completed, what kind of informative intimation (*vijñapti*) exists at that moment? The Abhidharmakośa master refutes this by saying:
"In your own school, there is the opinion of other masters who hold that there is an uninformative intimation (*avijñapti*) which arises independently of informative intimation."
Just as when the fruit was attained,
for the five bhikṣus and others,
as well as for Ṛṣyaśṛṅga.
In the case of *prasādhana* and so forth,
because the body does not move and speech is not uttered.
I have made this statement in order to challenge that teacher:
one does not maintain that non-informative action (*avijñapti*) arises independently of informative action (*vijñapti*).
According to reason, there must necessarily be informative action throughout both the preparatory (*prayoga*) and the fundamental (*maula*) stages.

The masters of the *Nyāyānusāra* are unable to resolve the objections raised against them; they merely follow my own arguments. Furthermore, it is explained that the fundamental tenet of your school is that the sages' wrath of mind [produces non-informative matter].
And the unmanifest karma of the *poṣadha* [ceremony],
because one does not move the body nor utter speech.

The Master of the *Nyāyānusāra* (Sthiramati), pressed by this objection, resorts to another master’s view to counter my own objection. He asks: "If the author of the treatise intends for this passage to establish that non-informative action (*avijñapti*) can arise independently of informative action (*vijñapti*), then [it would follow that]..."

Regarding the statement in the preceding text, within the ten ways of acquiring the precepts, that "the prātimokṣa restraint does not necessarily arise based on manifest action" (vijñapti-karman): the commentary explains that the preceding text records the position of other masters (pūrvācāryas).
The subsequent passage describes this according to our own school’s tenet; furthermore, this interpretation is not contradictory.
When it says that [an action] does not necessarily depend on the manifestation of manifest karma (*vijñapti-karman*), it means it does not necessarily depend on a manifest action of its own kind.

This reveals their mutual production. Question: If it is said that in the realm of desire there is no unmanifest [action] arising apart from manifest action, why does the preceding text state that among the seven wholesome courses of action, those arising from undertaking necessarily possess both?
This refers to manifest (*vijñapti*) and unmanifest (*avijñapti*) [karma].
Since the morality born of undertaking (*samādāna-śīla*) necessarily depends upon the manifest,
the statement that it is "born of undertaking" makes it clear that the fruit is attained.
The five bhikṣus and others do not arise from [that] reception,
nor do they depend on the manifestation [of the act].

This is contrary to that; the explanation states that the preceding passage sets forth the position of other masters (*pūrvācārya*), while the subsequent passage presents a critique based on the correct meaning (*samyagartha*). Furthermore, another explanation holds that they are not mutually contradictory, as this refers to Buddhas and Pratyekabuddhas.
Furthermore, the five bhikṣus obtained the Prātimokṣa because they made a formal commitment to receive it and because they underwent the ritual of taking birth [into the saṃgha].

It is also called "receiving birth. Furthermore, regarding the subsequent statement, "desire arises without unmanifest [action] apart from manifest [action]," this refers generally to both the preparatory (*prayoga*) and fundamental (*maula*) stages, wherein manifest action necessarily exists and is capable of producing unmanifest action.
If one considers the fundamental [action], there is also non-informative action (*avijñapti*) that arises independently of informative action (*vijñapti*).
Otherwise, when the fundamental [action] such as killing by dispatching a messenger is accomplished, what informative action would there be?
If one interprets it in this way, it accords well with the preceding text regarding how the ten ways of obtaining precepts do not necessarily arise based on manifest action (*vijñapti-karman*).
It also accords with the fact that among the seven wholesome courses of action (*karmapatha*), those not consisting of formal undertaking (*samādāna*) do not arise from manifest action.
In summary, regarding the ten ways of acquiring precepts and the seven paths of wholesome action, as well as in the subsequent text, two interpretations are given:
some say that in the desire realm there exists non-informative matter (*avijñapti*) that arises without being preceded by informative matter (*vijñapti*).
Some say that all unmanifest [karma] (*avijñapti*) in the desire realm arises based on manifest [karma] (*vijñapti*).
Having already explained [the cases] from false speech through to flattery, song, and evil treatises,
this fifth section clarifies the characteristics of the remaining three types of vocal karma.
The first two lines clarify divisive speech;
the next line clarifies harsh speech;
and the final three lines clarify frivolous speech.
The Commentary states: "Reaching this point from the preceding flow" explains the first two lines,
clarifying that divisive speech constitutes a full course of action (*karmapatha*) only when four conditions are met.
There are two factors: first, a defiled mind; second, the utterance of words intended to cause dissension in another.
If the other person is divided—or even if they are not divided, provided they merely comprehend the meaning—then divisive speech (*paiśunya*) is established.
Therefore, the *Nyāyānusāra* (Treatise on Correct Reasoning), fascicle 41, states:
The moment the vocal expression of divisive speech is uttered and understood by the other party, the manifest and unmanifest karma is termed the "fundamental path of action" (*maula-karmapatha*).
Other masters say that it is only when the other party is actually divided that it is established.
If this were so, then how could it be said that noble ones (*ārya*) are firm, stable, and difficult to divide?
One should not commit the offense of divisive speech against the noble ones;
however, since the offense incurred for harming a noble one is profound,
one should know this from it.
The previous explanation is correct;
the *Abhidharmamahāvibhāṣā* is likewise in agreement with the *Nyāyānusāra*. This constitutes the third interpretation of the meaning.
Fourth, there is no error.
Among the four conditions, the first two are present in the verse;
the latter two follow from what precedes.
If it is held that [an action] becomes a course of action (*karmapatha*) only when accompanied by a defiled mind,
this explains the third phrase:
it clarifies that harsh speech (*pāruṣya*) also constitutes a course of action only when it possesses four conditions.
First, a defiled mind;
second, uttering unpleasant speech that disparages others, which is termed harsh speech (*pāruṣya*).
From the first phrase of the preceding [category], the three characters "defiled mind" (*kliṣṭa-citta*) flow down to the third phrase of the [category of] harsh speech.
It should be said that harsh speech is defined as unlovely speech uttered with a defiled mind.
It has four characteristics: (1) it is understood by the listener; (2) it is not mistaken.
It should be understood that these two subsequent conditions are also the same as the preceding [condition] regarding divisive speech, flowing from it:
namely, that the path of action is only completed when the one intended to be reviled by the original intention understands the meaning of what was said.
It does not necessarily require that one intentionally cause distress; if another person is distressed or not, both cases constitute harsh speech.
Therefore, the *Nyāyānusāra* states:
At the very moment another understands the coarse and evil speech one has uttered, the manifest and unmanifest karma is called the "fundamental path of action" (*maula-karmapatha*).
Other masters say that it is only when the other person is actually distressed that it is established as such.
If this were the case, then since noble ones (*ārya*) who possess the power of patience cannot be distressed, [the path of action would not be established for them].
Abusing [others] should be without fault;
however, since one incurs profound guilt by abusing the noble ones and sages,
one should know from this that the previous explanation is correct.
The *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* is likewise consistent with this correct principle.
The statement "all defiled minds that reach up to this point" explains the fourth phrase.
According to this passage,
there are two conditions for frivolous speech:
first, any defiled state of mind.
Second, the various utterances produced [by it].
Why is this? Because all speech produced by defilement is frivolous chatter (*sambhinna-pralāpa*).
Following the previous pattern, the word "speech" (*vāk*) from the first sentence should be carried over to the fourth sentence.
It should be stated: "All defiled states of mind that express speech are designated as frivolous speech (*saṃbhinnapralāpa*).
According to this master’s intention, although frivolous speech may arise independently, [it is still subsumed under the category of unwholesome mental states].
If the first three types of speech arise, they necessarily involve frivolous speech;
however, if such frivolous speech is not understood by another,
it is not subsumed under the four paths of vocal karma.
Therefore, the *Vibhāṣā* (107) states:
"Suppose there is someone who,
being alone in a secluded place, speaks as follows:"
There is no giving;
there is no endearment;
there is no sacrifice.
Regarding such verbal misconduct,
sentient beings in the world do not develop understanding of it, nor is it subsumed under the four [bases]. According to that treatise,
one further condition is added.
Regarding what is called "understanding the meaning," other masters state that it is subsumed under frivolous speech (*sambhinna-pralāpa*);
this explains the fifth and sixth phrases.
The intention of this master is to say that speech other than the three previously mentioned is designated as "corrupt" (miśra-pralāpa) only when it is produced by a defiled mind; thus,
all such instances are cases of corrupt speech arising independently.
When the first three types of speech arise, they are not mixed with impurity;
because there is this difference, the divergent explanations are set forth.
The meaning of the text is clear and can be understood.

It may be so. Even among those that are mixed and defiled, there are cases where there is no error; for instance, if one intends to be sycophantic toward a specific person but instead sycophantically deceives another, the path of action (karmapatha) would likewise not be established.
If one relies on this meaning,
there may be four conditions;
however, the previous interpretation is superior.
Regarding the statement that [the path of action] extends from the time a Wheel-Turning King appears up until the inclusion of frivolous speech:
Question—
By what means does that speech proceed from [the point of] not being associated with a defiled mind?
Answer: That which is produced by a defiled mind is called "impure.
This speech, however, arises from a wholesome mind of renunciation.
It praises all that is wholesome and censures all that is unwholesome,
because it is capable of inducing the excellence of renunciation.
A mind that is not pre-polluted is not called "defiled.
The statement by other masters, "until it constitutes a course of action," records a divergent opinion.
At that time, there may also be speech uttered with a defiled mind;
however, because the fault is slight, it does not constitute a full course of action (*karmapatha*).
Therefore, the aforementioned verbal courses of action do not include the preliminary (*prayoga*), the subsequent (*pṛṣṭha*), or what is slight among the verbal misdeeds (*vāg-duścarita*).
This is the position of this master:

during the time of a wheel-turning monarch, frivolous speech that is light and mixed, even if understood by another, is not subsumed under a course of action (*karmapatha*) and does not give rise to non-informative matter (*avijñapti*).
Therefore, the *Nyāyānusāra* states:
Some say that such speech as "he has married" and so forth is subsumed under frivolous speech (*sambhinna-pralāpa*) but is not included among the paths of action (*karmapatha*),
because it belongs to the category of those with diminished defilements (*tanu-rajas*) and thus does not induce non-informative matter (*avijñapti*).
It is not that there is no non-informative [action] (avijñapti) that can be subsumed under the paths of action (karmapatha).
Having already explained the three verbal [paths] up to what is called the path of action of wrong view,
this now clarifies the characteristics of the sixth path of action, that of the mental [path].
The Commentary states: "Regarding the phrase 'designated as the karmic path of greed,' this explains the first clause, clarifying the karmic path of greed.
The term 'another's property' distinguishes it from one's own."
Since greed for oneself is not established, it should also be stated according to reason that greed arises toward sentient beings;
yet, because it is not so stated, it is to be understood through implication.
Alternatively, the mention of the light case serves to reveal the heavy one.
If even generating greed toward insentient things is called a karmic path,
how much more so toward sentient beings?
Or perhaps it may be so.

Others say that this also includes sentient beings; however, because greed arises with particular intensity toward non-sentient things, it is termed a "path of action" (karmapatha) as greed, while the treatises do not mention sentient beings [in this context].

The former interpretation is superior. This means that regarding another's property, there is an improper and evil desire to make it one's own rather than another's. "Force" refers to physical power; "stealth" refers to private pilfering. Thus, by employing force or a stealthy mind, one covetously seeks another's property.
Such evil desire is called the karmic path of greed (*lobha*). This greed is exclusively that which is abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*);
among those abandoned through cultivation, the attachment to one's own possessions is not a karmic path.
Therefore, the *Nyāyānusāra* states:
"Only the arising of malicious desire and greed for another's property is designated as the karmic path of greed.
Were it otherwise, the karmic path of greed would also have to apply to one’s own property."
The case of the Cakravartin regarding Uttarakuru is likewise difficult.
Other masters say that this extends up to the general statement concerning "craving for desire" (*kāmarāga*);
the intention of these masters is as follows.
Within the desire realm, all five categories of craving constitute the karmic path of greed.
Based on the *Pañcanīvaraṇa-sūtra*, the Buddha taught that one should abandon this worldly greed by means of the hindrance of sensual desire.
Therefore, it is known that "greed" (lobha) is a general term for all forms of craving (tṛṣṇā) belonging to the five categories within the desire realm (kāmadhātu).
Some teachers say that "desire-craving" (kāmatṛṣṇā) constitutes the karmic path of greed;
the intention of this master is as follows:
Although the five classes of craving within the desire realm are all termed "greed" when they are exhausted, not all of them constitute a path of action (*karmapatha*).
This greed that constitutes a path of action is so designated because it subsumes the coarse categories among the unwholesome courses of action.
In the era of a Wheel-Turning King,
as well as in Uttarakuru,
the desire-greed that arises toward one's own possessions does not constitute the karmic path of greed.
Because they are minor transgressions,

the preceding treatise states that the unwholesome paths of action of the mind do not include unwholesome intentions (*cetanā*) or minor forms of greed (*lobha*) and so forth within the category of unwholesome conduct of the mind;
this is precisely the position of this master.
The preceding text has already stated this.
Between these two views, the latter master is correct,
because greed abandoned through insight does not take wealth as its object.
Regarding the phrase "among sentient beings" up to "is called the path of action of hatred," this explains the second line:
desiring to cause harm to other sentient beings.
It is called a path of action for anger because its transgression is grave;
if one feels anger toward oneself or toward non-sentient things,
it is not a path of action for anger because the transgression is slight.
Regarding the phrase "concerning the paths of action of wrong view toward the wholesome and the unwholesome," this explains the final two lines,
clarifying the path of action of wrong view: "wholesome" and "unwholesome."
This refers to wholesome and unwholesome karma; "and so forth" includes the ripening of fruits, the noble ones, and so on.
To deny what is directly perceived among these—such as wholesome phenomena—and hold such a view is called the path of action of wrong view (*mithyādṛṣṭi-karmapatha*).
As the Sūtra says, the phrase "up to and including" (yāvat) includes what follows.
By citing this Sūtra, it is shown that those wrong views deny [the existence of] these [factors].
In total, there are eleven distinct points within the Sūtra.
It is said that there is: first, no giving;
second, no affection;
and third, no sacrificial offerings.
These three are all false views that slander the cause; they are abandoned through the vision of the origin (*samudaya-darśana-prahātavya*).
As explained in the *Mahāvibhāṣā* (vol. 98) regarding these three:

first, it is explained that there is no difference [between them], as they collectively manifest a single meaning; furthermore, it is explained that their names themselves constitute the differences. An externalist proponent says:
"Without giving" means there is no giving of the three types of merit.
"Without affection" means...
This means there is no merit for giving specifically to a single Brahmin, nor is there merit for one who performs sacrifices;

it means there is no merit for giving to a multitude of Brahmins. There are further interpretations in non-Buddhist treatises as explained at length therein. As for the internal treatises (Buddhist texts), they say:
"One who does not give" means there is no merit from the past;
"one who does not delight" means there is no merit for the future.
"One who performs no sacrifices" means one who possesses no present merit.
Furthermore, "one who gives no gifts" [is meant].
This means there is no merit from bodily action,
nor is there any delight therein;
it means there is no merit from verbal action.
"Those who do not perform sacrifices" refers to those who lack the merit of mental action (*manas-karman*).
Furthermore, "those who do not give" refers to those who do not practice generosity (*dāna*).

This refers to merit consisting of giving that lacks the nature of generosity, and merit consisting of morality that lacks the nature of ethical discipline. It refers to those who lack loving joy. This refers to merit consisting of morality that lacks the nature of ethical discipline.
"Those who do not perform sacrifices" refers to those who do not cultivate meritorious virtue.
Furthermore, "those who do not give" refers to those who do not practice generosity.
This means there is no merit from giving to the field of compassion,
as there is no one who feels affection; it means there is no merit from giving to the field of gratitude, as there is no one to whom one owes kindness.
"Those who do not perform sacrifices" means those who do not give to the field of merit (*puṇyakṣetra*).
There are further interpretations, as explained at length there. "Those who neither perform sublime conduct nor engage in evil conduct."
This is a wholesale denial of both wholesome and unwholesome conduct;

it is also a wrong view that denies causality, abandoned through the vision of the origin [of suffering]. It consists of five types: denying that there are results of maturation (vipāka) induced by wholesome and unwholesome karmic actions.
This is the total denial of the fruit produced by karma.

The false view that denies the fruit is abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*). [The two views: (6) "There is no this world" and (7) "There is no other world"—these two both involve the denial of cause and fruit.

If one slanders the cause, it is abandoned through the vision of the origin (*samudaya-darśana-prahātavya*); if one slanders the result, it is abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*).
Therefore, the *Vibhāṣā* explains:
Question: It may be said that since the other world is not perceived through direct observation, its non-existence is plausible;
but why say it does not exist when this world is directly perceived?
Answer: Those non-Buddhists are blinded by ignorance.
One also denies things that are directly perceived;
it is not appropriate to blame the ignorant and the blind for falling into a pit.
Furthermore, there are those who say:
Those non-Buddhists merely deny cause and effect, but do not deny the essence of phenomena (*dharmatā*).
To say "this world does not exist" means they claim that this world does not exist as the cause for another world,
or that this world does not exist as the effect of another world.
The view that there is no other world means either that there is no other world as the cause of this world, or that there is no other world as the fruit of this world.

(8) There is no mother; (9) there is no father—these two are wrong views that deny causes (*hetu-apavāda*), which are abandoned through the vision of the origin of suffering (*samudaya-darśana-prahātavya*).
Therefore, the *Vibhāṣā* states:
Question: Parents in the world are all directly perceived;
on what basis do they slander them by saying they do not exist?
The answer is: "Those various non-Buddhists are blinded by ignorance," and so forth, as explained at length.
Some say that those non-Buddhists deny the existence of parents and the karma that brings about a child, but they do not deny their actual substance.
Some say that those non-Buddhists slander the meaning of parents but do not slander their substance, as explained at length in that [text].
Regarding the ten [points], there are no sentient beings born by transformation (*upapāduka*).
This [view] generally subverts both cause and fruit:
if it subverts the cause, it is abandoned through the vision of origination;
if it subverts the fruit, it is abandoned through the vision of suffering.
The *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* explains:
"There are certain non-Buddhist outsiders who assert that the birth of all sentient beings is caused by present factors such as semen and blood."
There is nothing that arises suddenly without conditions.
For example, the growth of a sprout necessarily depends upon seeds, water, fire, and the seasons;
there is nothing that can arise without conditions.
Therefore, it is certain that there are no beings born by transformation (*upapāduka*).
This [view] either denies the karma that produces birth by transformation,
or else it denies the birth by transformation that is produced.
Some say that the beings born by transformation— namely, those in the intermediate state—
neither belong to this world nor to another world.

To deny that there are beings born by transformation is to slander [the existence of] birth; to deny that there are beings born by transformation is to slander [the existence of] intermediate existence (*antarābhava*).
There are certain non-Buddhists who claim that there is no intermediate state (*antarābhava*).
They assert that one must simply proceed from this world to that world,
and that no third world can be found between them.
This [view] either denies the karma that brings about the intermediate state (*antarābhava*),
or it denies the intermediate state itself which is so brought about,
or it denies that the intermediate state is the cause of the existence at birth (*upapattibhava*).
Alternatively, to deny that the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) is the fruit of the existence at death (*cyuty-bhava*) constitutes a denial of both cause and effect.

This [view] is abandoned through the vision of suffering and its origin (*duḥkha-samudaya-darśana-prahātavya*). There are eleven [such views]: the worldly view that there are no śramaṇas, no brāhmaṇas, and no arhats.
This is the wrong view of slandering the noble ones (*ārya*),
which is abandoned through the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*).
According to what is appropriate, that sutra fully reveals the wrong view of slandering action, slandering the fruit, and slandering the noble ones.
This verse cites the initial denial of wholesome and unwholesome karma;
the word "etc. includes the subsequent denials of the fruits [of action] and the denials of the noble ones (ārya).
This is according to the texts such as the *Abhidharmamahāvibhāṣā*.
Furthermore, it explains the false view that denies cessation.
As that treatise states, "There is no right attainment," this is the false view that denies cessation.
That which is abandoned through the vision of cessation refers to that which is to be reached, namely nirvāṇa and so forth,
because it is what should be reached by the untainted path (*anāsrava-mārga*).
The details are as explained therein.

In the sixteenth fascicle of the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya-ṭīkā*, on the twenty-third day of the sixth month in the first year of the Hōen era, at Ōdōji in Tahanri, I, Jōshu, a Provisional Junior Sōjū, finished reading it. It is said that this year’s famine is unprecedented since ancient times; alas, the number of those who die of hunger makes travel along the roads difficult. How tragic! What can be done for such a degenerate age? Yet, while I alone have tasted the flavor of the Dharma, my life has been sustained and my Dharma-body has grown stout. How laughable, how truly laughable!

(Postscript) On the twenty-fourth day of the second month in the second year of Ten’yō, at the hour of the Dragon (7–9 a.m.), I finished reading this once at Seishan-ji Temple. I have attained a profound realization of the Way of Cause and Effect.
Recorded by the Śramaṇa Śākyamuni Kō, Volume Seventeen of the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya-ṭīkā*.
In the fifth section of the fourth chapter,
"The Analysis of Karma," having thus already established that up to seven types of karma are also paths,
this constitutes the second major heading: the explanation of the term "karmic path" (*karmapatha*).
The first phrase clarifies the three [types] of mental [action];
the second phrase clarifies the seven [types] of bodily and vocal [action].
The treatise says: "Because they are produced upon reaching [the object]."
Explaining the preceding sentence:
Among the ten unwholesome courses of action,
the final three— greed, hatred, and wrong view— are paths alone.
The term "path of action" (karmapatha) is established because it is the path of volitional action (cetanā).
That volition associated with greed and so forth is called "action," because that greed and so forth proceed from it.
It is the transformation of volition, because it functions as that which is characterized by greed and so forth; thus,
it is the activity of volition.
Just as with the force of craving and so forth,
because volition (cetanā) performs its activity,
craving and the rest are called "paths of karma" because they serve as the basis upon which volition relies.
Regarding the statement that "the first seven are karma, and they receive the designation 'paths of karma'":
this explains the latter part of the verse.
Among the ten unwholesome paths of karma, [the first seven are so designated].
The first seven in substance are karma,
because their nature is that of bodily and vocal karma;
they are also the paths of karma.
Because it is that which is traversed by the volition of karma,
and because the volition that gives rise to bodily and vocal karma through its causes operates by taking bodily and vocal karma as its object, it is called the "path of karma."
Superior karma consists of bodily and vocal karma;
inferior karma consists of mental karma (*cetanā-karma*).
Karma and the path of karma are collectively designated by the term "paths of action" (*karmapatha*).
Therefore, regarding the phrase "because it is established as such for both parties" (*ubhayasiddhatvāt*) within this context:
this indicates that the commonality of the name subsumes various distinct categories;
thus, it is used in this explanation of the names of the paths of action (*karmapatha*).
The term "paths of action" (karmapatha) fully reveals the latter three paths of action;
as for the former seven, they possess the meaning of both "action" (karman) and "path of action.
If one speaks of "paths of action," it refers to volition (cetanā) associated with greed.
The path consists of greed and other afflictions associated with volition.
If one speaks of "action" as the "path of action," then superior action refers to bodily and vocal [actions].
The lower karma is the volition that constitutes the causal motivation;
the path consists of body and speech.
This is what is meant here.
A single karma reveals many karmas;
a single path reveals many paths.
Although the nature and categories of these karmic paths differ, [they are nonetheless revealed].
Because the names of the karmas are identical, yet one karma is designated as another;
because the names of the paths are identical.
Furthermore, because a single path is designated as "other paths," such categories exist within the world and within the scriptures.
Because both are universally established. Regarding what is universally established in the world:
for example, when one speaks of "chariots" or "oxen," although there are many different types and categories of chariots and oxen.
The names for "chariot" and "ox" are identical,
yet because the ox of one chariot is called the "ox of another chariot," it is established by convention.
For example, regarding the "abodes of consciousness" (vijñānasthiti): although the four abodes of consciousness differ in their essential natures, they share the common name "abode of consciousness";
thus, one abode of consciousness is designated as such because it serves as the basis for the other abodes of consciousness.
Regarding the statement, "The seven [paths], beginning with abstaining from killing, should be explained by analogy to the others":
this refers to the analogical explanation of the wholesome courses of action (*kuśala-karmapatha*).
As for why their preliminary applications (*prayoga*) and subsequent activities (*pṛṣṭha*) are not considered courses of action—what is the reason for this?
Question:
The preparatory stage (*prayoga*) and the subsequent stage (*pṛṣṭha*) should also be called paths of action (*karmapatha*),
because volition (*cetanā*) also proceeds by taking them as its objects.
For what reason is it said that these are not paths of action (*karmapatha*)?
Regarding the statement, "Because they depend on this, because they are based on this, and because they do not go beyond this," there are three parts to the answer.
First, because the preparatory stage (*prayoga*) proceeds only by depending on this as its root, and the subsequent stage (*pṛṣṭha*) proceeds only by depending on this root;
therefore, the preparatory and subsequent stages are not the root itself. Second, as previously stated, this [root] subsumes the coarse category of the paths of action (*karmapatha*).

The preparatory and subsequent stages are not included among the paths of action because they are not of a coarse nature. Furthermore, if through these evil paths of action there is a decrease, it causes a decrease in unwholesome things both internal and external.
Due to the increase of unwholesome courses of action,
internal and external unwholesome things increase; likewise,
due to the decrease of these wholesome courses of action, [unwholesome things increase].
It causes the depletion of internal and external excellent things;
by the increase of the wholesome paths of action,
it causes the increase of internal and external excellent things.
That which possesses this function is established as a course of action (*karmapatha*);

other than this, because it is not so before or after the root [action], it is not a course of action. Furthermore, another interpretation states: if by means of this evil course of action there is a decrease [in merit].
It causes the increase of excellent internal and external things through the increase of unwholesome courses of action;
it causes the decrease of excellent internal and external things through [the increase of] unwholesome courses of action.
If, due to these wholesome courses of action, there is a decrease [in them],
it causes internal and external unwholesome things to increase; conversely,
through the increase of wholesome courses of action, [unwholesome things decrease].
Only when internal and external unwholesome things are diminished does the designation "path of action" (karmapatha) apply;

otherwise, it is not so. Furthermore, another interpretation holds that if, by means of this unwholesome path of action, there is a diminution of unwholesome things—such that internal and external unwholesome things decrease and wholesome things increase—it is then designated as such.
Due to the increase of unwholesome courses of action,
internal and external unwholesome things increase while wholesome things decrease; likewise,
if there is a decrease in these wholesome courses of action [the same occurs].
It causes internal and external good things to decrease and evil things to increase;
yet, because the paths of wholesome action increase,
it causes internal and external good things to increase and evil things to decrease— thus the name "path of action" (karmapatha) is established.
Otherwise, it would not be so. Regarding the statement "internal and external things," the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 113, states:
"That which is inhabited is called 'external'."
Life-span and so forth are called "internal.
When the Dārṣṭāntika masters reach that point where it is called a "course of action" (karmapatha),
they ask:
The Vaibhāṣika masters maintain that greed and the other [unwholesome roots] have distinct substantial entities apart from volition,
and they explain the paths of action accordingly.
The Dārṣṭāntika masters maintain that greed,
hatred, and so forth are themselves mental volition (cetanā) and possess no separate entity.

Regarding the question, "One should ask that teacher why [all these] are called paths of action," the Master of the Treatise replies:
"One should ask that teacher; it is not my concern. If I were to explain it for him..."
Nevertheless, it may also be said that those [afflictions] such as greed and hatred are themselves mental karma,
because they have no separate substance.
Furthermore, it is said that "paths" refers to how one falls into the various evil destinies by means of these [afflictions] such as greed.
They are designated as "paths of action" because they serve as the path leading to the miserable realms;
for either greed and so forth may arise immediately followed by anger and so forth,
or anger and so forth may arise immediately followed by greed and so forth.
The former is able to produce the latter;
the latter arises depending upon the former.
It is said [that the former] serves as the path for the latter.
Alternatively, when they mutually ride upon one another, all are termed paths of action (*karmapatha*).
Regarding what has been stated thus far, as for the distinction [to be explained],
the third point of the main text below clarifies the severance of the roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*) by way of context.

The verse says: "Up to the sudden manifestation, excluding those who commit transgressions.

Only superior, fully perfected wrong view can sever the roots of goodness.

Question.
If it is said that wrong view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*) can sever the roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*),
how is it that the fundamental treatise states that the unwholesome roots (*akuśalamūla*) can sever the roots of goodness,
or that they are the first to be eliminated at the stage of detachment from desire?
These are also the superior grades of unwholesome roots (*akuśalamūla*).
Regarding the passage from "unwholesome roots" up to "a village being burned by bandits," the answer is as follows:
Because the fruit of false views is induced by unwholesome causes,

"What roots of goodness are severed by this?
This explains the second phrase; it is a question.

it refers specifically to the innate wholesome roots (*upapatti-lābhika-kuśala-mūla*) of the desire realm that are what is severed.

because they were not previously established [as such], they are not subject to abandonment.

why does the treatise state that the wholesome states of all three realms are abandoned?

which states that one can sever the wholesome [roots] of the three realms.
Based on the superior realms, it is further explained that one attains greater distance;
this is because the body of the desire realm is gradually rendered no longer a suitable vessel for the acquisition of those superior wholesome states.

Within the desire realm,

this explains that the preparatory roots of goodness consist of the two types of wisdom— those arising from hearing and those arising from reflection.

Only that which is abandoned through birth (*upapatti-lābhika*) is not abandoned through application (*prayoga*); it is not abandoned through application. Morality is that which severs and abandons wholesome states;

this is because wrong view severs only those wholesome states acquired at birth (*upapattilābhika*). as for those who are strong and superior, they remain firm and do not abandon them. Third, it is said that the preparatory stage gives rise to the precepts (*śīla*).
When one is about to sever the roots of goodness,
one must first perform an act of renunciation to relinquish those precepts;

These three interpretations are all contrary to correct reasoning (*nyāya*).
Thus, the *Nyāyānusāra* (Treatise on Correct Reasoning), fascicle 42, states:

There are cases arising from a wholesome mind acquired at birth; however,
if it arises from a wholesome mind produced through effort (*prayoga*),

It refers to one who definitively denies the cause and effect of the Four Noble Truths.

this subsequent section explains everything.

second, the statement of the correct meaning.

one universally includes all objects of cognition,

although false views do not increase in accordance with their objects,

Because wrong view possesses great power, it is also able to sever the roots of goodness. Furthermore, although [the object] does not increase in accordance with it, the associated and co-existent causes also increase;

This section below explains gradual abandonment.

this is a divergent view,

Furthermore, another explanation notes that since the text does not specify otherwise, [the abandonment occurs at that stage].

"If that were so, it would contradict the statement 'the same applies to reaching'";
this refutes an alternative interpretation.
It is stated in the *Mūla-śāstra*:
The minimum number of faculties possessed by a person in Jambudvīpa is eight;
that is, the minimum number possessed by one who has severed the roots of virtue is eight, namely:
the body faculty, the life faculty, the mind faculty, and the five feeling faculties.
As stated in the "Chapter on the Faculties" (Indriya-varga),
since it is said that the same applies to the eastern and western continents,
it is clearly understood that those continents are also capable of severing the roots of goodness.
Regarding the question, "Upon what kind of body does one thus sever the roots of goodness?"—
this refers to the explanation of male and female; this is the inquiry.
Regarding the statement, "Only those with male or female bodies have a stable mind," the answer is:
other masters say this is because [the minds of others] are all dull and obtuse.
Regarding the presentation of alternative views: it is also not the female body,
because [in that state] the arousal of desire, diligence, wisdom, and so forth are all dull and obtuse.
If it is argued that wrong view is sharp and clear,
and if that were so, it would contradict the statement that "the same applies even to the male organ," this refutes the divergent explanation.
The present treatise states:
"If one possesses the female faculty, one necessarily possesses at least eight faculties—namely, the female, body, life, mind, and four sensations (excluding sorrow).
The same applies to the male faculty."
Excluding women while including men— since it has already been stated that one becomes a woman,
yet it does not say that one definitely acquires the five faculties such as faith—
it is clear that even a female body can sever the roots of goodness.
If women cannot sever the roots of goodness,
how could they possess only eight faculties?
For what kind of practitioner is it possible to sever the roots of goodness?
"Regarding the abandonment of those who practice through vision: this is the question.
"Only those who practice through vision go as far as the evil destinies," and so forth.
Answer: It is restless and unstable,
unable to maintain firm persistence.
Inability to penetrate deeply is called the conduct of craving; that which is firm, deep, and immovable— if one can maintain such steadfastness—
[is the conduct of views].
If one can penetrate deeply,

they are called a practitioner who sees; by this principle, those such as *śaṇḍhas* (eunuchs) are unable to sever the roots of goodness, because they belong to the category of those whose conduct is dominated by craving (*tṛṣṇā-carita*).
Because they are like those in the evil destinies.
Therefore, the *Nyāyānusāra* states:
"Only those who follow through vision, not those who follow through craving."
Because the evil *āśaya* (intent) of those who practice various views is extremely firm and deep:
it is called "extremely firm" because that evil inclination seeks out and pursues a continuous succession;
it is called "extremely deep" because the views enter into and follow along with it for a long duration.
Because it is extremely firm and deep, it is able to sever the roots of goodness.
This is because the underlying disposition (*āśaya*) of those who act out of craving is extremely restless.
As for what the nature of this severed root of goodness is: [it is the non-possession (*aprāpti*) of that root].
Regarding the explanation of non-acquisition (*aprāpti*): it should be understood that the term "abandonment" (*prahāṇa*) in the verse refers exclusively to the lower [realms],
and this explains the abandonment of non-acquisition.
"Or it extends both upward and downward. This is the question.
"It should be known that 'skillful severance' has non-acquisition (*aprāpti*) as its essence."
Answer: This severance of the roots of goodness has non-possession (*aprāpti*) as its essence within the category of dissociated factors.
The remainder of the text may be understood.
Regarding the question of how the roots of goodness (kuśalamūla), once severed, are restored:
this explains the doubt concerning the restoration of the roots of goodness for those with views (dṛṣṭi).
This is the question. It is asked because there is doubt as to whether one who has reached the stage of "vision" (dṛṣṭi-prāpta) can be said to have reconnected their roots of virtue.
This is the answer.
From doubt there arises the view of existence; that is, from doubt there are two [aspects]:
first, doubt regarding existence.
Second, there is doubt regarding non-existence:
one who doubts existence is able to reconnect the roots of goodness,
whereas one who doubts non-existence cannot reconnect them.
In this context, it is based on the existence of certain statements regarding doubt that it is said:

"Regarding cause and effect, at times one may have a doubt as to whether this [result] might exist; that is, the restoration of the roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla-pratisaṃdhāna*), or the arising of right view (*samyagdṛṣṭi*). It is certain that it exists and not non-existent. This right view is capable of restoring the roots of goodness; because it is well-acquired for the first time, it is called 'restoration of the roots of goodness. Thus, the verse says 'doubt, existence, and view.'"
There are those that exist only in doubt, or only in views,
or that pertain to both the higher and lower [realms].
Furthermore, the *Nyāyānusāra* states:
