"Due to doubt and views, it is said that [the roots of goodness] are reconnected at the stage of reconnecting the roots."
Either through the power of causes or by relying on a virtuous friend,
one may suddenly give rise to doubt regarding cause and effect once again.
Regarding whether what is summoned in future lives is non-existent or existent:
when one suddenly gives rise to right view concerning cause and effect, one becomes certain that future lives exist.
The previous adherence was erroneous.

At that time, the roots of goodness that were unaccomplished are accomplished and arise again, while those that were accomplished are extinguished; this is called the "reconnection of the roots of goodness."
Other masters state that the nine grades [of afflictions] continue gradually;
this explains the verse.
First, the presentation of alternative views.
Second, the presentation of the correct meaning.
This section describes divergent views.
Regarding the statement, "Thus it is said... until his strength gradually increases": [this refers to the period] from the time he has been born until his physical power begins to increase.
This explains the correct principle:
that after the roots of goodness are suddenly reconnected, they gradually manifest.
The analogy can be understood accordingly.
Regarding the question of whether one can continue the roots of goodness in the present life,
the phrase "releasing those who have committed the immediate transgressions" (*ānantarya*) is the answer to this very inquiry.
Furthermore, there are those who are able to reconnect [the roots of goodness] in states other than the remaining ones.
Answer: There are also those who can reconnect the roots of goodness within their current existence (*dṛṣṭadharmika*).

Except for those who have committed an immediate transgression (*ānantarya*), that [interruption] does not occur within their present continuum. To prove this, he cites a sutra stating that for one who has committed an immediate transgression, the severance of the roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*) occurs in the present body-continuum.
As for the statement, "It should be understood that the same applies to the stage of being about to be born," it means that the same principle holds true there as well.
Regarding the two ways of reconnecting the roots of virtue explained in the sutras,
if one has severed those roots due to the power of wrong views— the internal cause of past habitual tendencies—
they will reconnect them at the time of death.
Because the cause is powerful:
if one has severed the roots of goodness due to the force of external conditions such as present false teachings,
they will be reconnected when that [state] is about to arise.
Because the conditions are weak;
whether by the power of one's own deliberation and investigation,
or by the power of another evil friend providing instruction.
It should be understood that it is likewise so.

Furthermore, regarding the phrase "the corruption of intention should also be understood as being likewise so," this explanation concerns whether the continuum of one who has committed a *ānantarya* offense is currently interrupted or not.
The corruption of intention and the corruption of view refer to the arising of wrong views;
it is not a corruption of application, for the precepts remain uncorrupted as they are guarded within the proper conduct and demeanor.
The preparatory application is ruined;
the precepts are also ruined;
and one does not maintain proper deportment.
Therefore, the *Nyāyānusāra* states:
"There are people in the world who deny the existence of future lives; this is called the corruption of intention (*āśaya-vipatti*).
However, it is not a corruption of application (*prayoga-vipatti*), because they do not act in accordance with that corrupted intention."
One whose views are destroyed but whose precepts are not destroyed;
one whose views are destroyed and whose precepts are also destroyed— the case of one who has severed the roots of goodness should be understood to be likewise.
It is not during the destruction of a kalpa or at the initial formation of a kalpa that one severs the roots of goodness; for [in those periods],
the dominant force of the destruction of the physical world (bhājanaloka) causes the continuum [of the roots] to be moistened,
and those who practice sublime conduct do not sever their roots of goodness.
Because the mind is firm and possesses something to delight in.
Regarding the statement that there are those who sever the roots of goodness up to the point of excluding the aforementioned characteristics,
this is the contextual meaning within this section.
The severance of the roots of goodness is analyzed in relation to falling into wrong determination through a fourfold classification.
One who gives rise to false views is said to have severed the roots of goodness.
Those who commit the heinous crimes of immediate retribution (ānantarya) are said to fall into "wrong fixedness" (mithyātva-niyata).
The first case refers to Pūraṇa. Pūraṇa means "Full";
he is Pūraṇa Kāśyapa.
The former term "Pūrṇa" is a corruption.
One is called a "severer of the roots of goodness" because they have given rise to false views;

however, because they have not committed an immediate transgression (*ānantarya*), they have not fallen into the fixed state of perversion (*mithyātva-niyata*). The second category refers to those such as Ajātaśatru.
Ajātaśatru is none other than King Ajātaśatru;

because he committed a heinous crime (ānantarya), he fell into the state of fixed wrongness (mithyātva-niyata), yet because he placed faith in the Triple Gem, his roots of goodness were not severed. The third category refers to Devadatta and others.
His name in Sanskrit is Devadatta,
which in Chinese means "Heaven-Bestowed.
Because he gave rise to false views, he is called "One Who Severs the Roots of Goodness."

Because one has committed an act of immediate retribution (*ānantarya*), one falls into wrong certainty (*mithyātva-niyata*). The fourth phrase refers to cases other than those previously mentioned. Furthermore, the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* (Vibhāṣā), fascicle 35, states:
"If one severs the roots of goodness, it includes all acts of immediate retribution as well as other acts that cause a schism in the Saṃgha."
They will certainly suffer in the Avīci Hell.
As for those who do not sever their roots of goodness,
they [commit] the other four ānantarya karmas, or [suffer] in the Avīci Hell.
"Or one may experience the ripening fruit (*vipākaphala*) in other hells. The commentary explains:

"Because one who gives rise to wrong views (*mithyādṛṣṭi*) is certain to fall into the Avīci hell, those who give rise to wrong views and commit the various heinous crimes (*ānantarya*) are certain to fall into Avīci. Therefore, the *Nyāyānusāra* states:

One should know that the severing of the roots of virtue through wrong view and the false speech that causes a schism in the Saṃgha will certainly bring about the retribution of the immediate (ānantarya) hell;
as for other immediate karmas, they may or may not bring about such retribution.
Or it may bring about the maturation of other hells.
Having followed the context of the meaning up to the point where [the path of action] operates simultaneously with volition (*cetanā*),
the following section— the fourth major heading— clarifies how the paths of action operate simultaneously with volition.
This connects what preceded to what follows and introduces the inquiry.
The verse says: "Up to the specific prohibition of one, eight, and five."
The first two lines clarify that unwholesome courses of action (karmapatha) operate simultaneously with volition (cetanā);
the latter two lines clarify that wholesome courses of action operate simultaneously with volition.
Regarding the statement here that "the courses of action operate simultaneously with volition":
This refers to their simultaneous occurrence at the same moment;
it does not refer to the preceding and succeeding moments of the volition that originates the cause,
for it is not stated in the context of the fourfold or sevenfold precepts that one can receive the precepts without a mind.
Therefore, it is known that this is definitely stated in reference to a single *kṣaṇa*. Question: As stated in the *Abhidharmamahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* (Vibhāṣā), fascicle 113:
"If one abides in a defiled mind, or abides in an indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) mind..."

Or, at a time when one is without mind, the volition that arises simultaneously with the seven wholesome courses of action brings them to completion. The *Saṃyuktābhidharmahṛdaya* also speaks of being "without mind"; since that treatise states that one is without mind [in such cases], [it follows that the courses of action are completed].
It is clearly understood that even when [the two] operate simultaneously, this is explained in terms of the "arising by cause" (*hetusamutthāna*).

Why, then, is it said that it must necessarily be in terms of a single moment (*kṣaṇa*)? The explanation states: the *Mahāvibhāṣā* and the *Abhidharmahṛdaya* refer to those who are "without mind" (*acittaka*).
This interpretation incidentally clarifies that there is "receiving precepts without mental engagement" (*acittaka-śīla-samādāna*),
yet it is not the correct understanding that [the restraint] arises simultaneously with volition (*cetanā*).
In reality, simultaneous arising must necessarily be understood in terms of a single moment (*kṣaṇa*).
In this treatise, among the seven types of simultaneous occurrence (*sahabhū*), the state of being without mind (*acittaka*) is not mentioned. Furthermore, there are two kinds of simultaneity:
the first is parallel simultaneity (*pāriśuddha-sahabhū*), which refers to arising together at the same moment within a single *kṣaṇa*.
The second is "existence through coexistence," meaning the coexistence of the preceding and the succeeding.
Because that preceding phenomenon exists, this succeeding phenomenon comes to exist.

The *Abhidharmakośa* does not mention the state of being without mind (*acittaka*) because it bases its argument on the simultaneous occurrence [of both factors]. The *Mahāvibhāṣā* and the *Saṃyuktābhidharmahṛdaya*, however, take into account both the simultaneous and the non-simultaneous cases, and thus include the state of being without mind.
Each relies on a single specific meaning, and thus they do not contradict one another.
The Commentary states: "From 'up to' (yāvat) to 'only up to eight' (yāvad-aṣṭamāt)" explains the two preceding phrases.
First is the general indication;
second is the detailed explanation.
This is the general heading.
From "one [mental factor] occurring simultaneously" up to "until any one reaches completion," the following provides the detailed explanation.
It is explained that one course of action (karmapatha) operates simultaneously with volition (cetanā). Regarding "one [course of action] operating simultaneously":
this refers to being free from the remaining seven types of unwholesome courses of action of body and speech.
Any one of the three— greed and so forth— arises and functions simultaneously with the corresponding volition (*cetanā*).
If, through prior preparation, one dispatches an agent to carry out killing or other such acts,
one creates the six types of unwholesome material karma (*rūpa-karma*).
When the mind is untainted (*anāsrava*), one [karmic path] reaches its culmination;
likewise, one karmic path operates simultaneously with volition (*cetanā*).
This refers to the simultaneous operation of volition.
The *Nyāyabindu* refutes this, saying:
"If it were the evil karma previously created through preparatory effort,
or other defilements such as greed..."
Furthermore, when a non-defiled mind manifests, any one [of these] reaches completion.
The Master of the Sūtras (Sūtrakāra) speaks only of the non-defiled mind;
this is excessively deficient.
Because when defiled minds such as pride and doubt arise,
the path of action is also established through the prior application (*prayoga*).
Furthermore, it is stated that one performs unwholesome material karma through application.
The term "form" (rūpa) is overly expansive.
In the formless realm (ārūpya), there is no possibility of first performing preparatory action;
it is only when an action-path is produced by a non-defiled mind that it is established.
Because they must be distinguished [from the primary afflictions], one should likewise refute and reject such categories by explaining them as "other defilements," namely pride, doubt, and so forth.
There is no form.
That is to say, [the Vaibhāṣikas] maintain that greed, hatred, and wrong view are abandoned together. The Master [Vasubandhu] objects:
"Form would not increase excessively."
This is because it speaks of the karma of form (*rūpa*). If it did not speak of form, it would not definitively manifest that karma is form.
If one were to say that the preparatory application (*prayoga*) is definitively form, then there would be no need to mention "form."
Furthermore, it is unnecessary to state that the preparatory stage (*prayoga*) is necessarily karma, as this would result in an excessive proliferation of the term "karma.
One should simply say: "If it is evil committed during a prior preparatory stage..."
The proponents of the theory of non-defiled mind (akliṣṭa-citta-vādin) hold different views:
they maintain that a non-defiled mind necessarily arises simultaneously with only one [mental factor],
whereas for a defiled mind, this is not determinate.
Although pride, doubt, and so forth function in conjunction with only one [other mental factor] when they manifest,
when greed, hatred, and so forth manifest, they function in conjunction with two;
this is because defiled minds are treated as a single category for the sake of brevity and are not described in detail.
Furthermore, regarding this simultaneous occurrence, it is established by citing any one instance as proof;
it is not necessary to state every case exhaustively.
If one provides such an explanation, there is no need for further refutation.
Regarding "the two turning together" up to "or [involving] frivolous speech," this clarifies that two courses of action turn together with volition (*cetanā*).
As for "the two turning together," it refers to the completion of the course of action of killing at the very moment one gives rise to a mind of hatred. Regarding the term "completion":
That is to say, when this act of killing is brought to completion by means of a mind of hatred, it is termed the culmination [of the path of action].
If one personally gives rise to greed, at that stage it constitutes either taking what is not given or sexual misconduct.
Or it may constitute frivolous speech (*sambhinna-pralāpa*);

in all such cases, both [mental factors] operate together. Question: Why are the three [unwholesome paths of action], such as deception (*mṛṣāvāda*), not mentioned? Explanation: There is frivolous speech that exists apart from the three beginning with deception.
If the three [unwholesome roots] such as deception are due to being untimely, they necessarily involve impurity.
Since this section clarifies that two [factors] operate simultaneously, it mentions only "impurity" and does not specify "deception" and the other two.
The *Nyāyānusāra* refutes this, saying:
"The simultaneous occurrence of both refers to engaging in unwholesome conduct;
that is, if one personally commits killing, stealing, or sexual misconduct."
Or one may cause another to act on one's behalf;
in either case, one of the states—greed, hatred, or wrong view—manifests.
This applies even to evil karma previously committed through preparatory effort.
When other defiled minds, such as greed, or non-defiled minds are present,
[the action] reaches its culmination according to those two.
Regarding this, the Master of the Sūtras (Sautrāntika) says the following:
This means that when one acts with a mind of hatred, the karmic act of killing is completed;
if one arises in a state of greed, the taking of what is not given or sexual misconduct is accomplished.
Or [it might be argued that] it is frivolous speech (*sambhinna-pralāpa*). This too is unreasonable;
for if the act were completed by oneself, then one need not laboriously state "hatred" (*dveṣa*) in the case of killing.
Because there is no further possibility for another ultimate [result] here;
the same applies to greed regarding stealing and sexual misconduct.
It is taught that when greed arises, it constitutes frivolous speech (*sambhinnapralāpa*).
This statement is deficient, as it could allow for three possibilities.

If the preliminary application (*prayoga*) were to occur at the time of the final completion (*niṣṭhā*), one would have to state for each case that it is associated with any one of the [three roots], such as greed (*lobha*). The Vaibhāṣika master of the *Abhidharmakośa* offers this defense:
In the ultimate analysis, there must be hatred (*dveṣa*) for suicide;
thus, it is established that both [mental factors] occur together.
If hatred were not mentioned, it would not be evident within the statement.
The *Nyāyānusāra* does not state that [the completion of these acts] is hidden and difficult to discern;
by analogy with this, the cases of theft and sexual misconduct are explained accordingly.
In reality, the "impure" (misconduct) may involve all three as its culmination.

Since the discussion of greed (*lobha*) was presented by way of a partial statement, it is clarified here that among the three [mental factors] that arise together, greed or one of its equivalents is present.

By implication, this also shows that among the two [factors] that arise together previously mentioned, greed or one of its equivalents is likewise present. Furthermore, it has already been stated that the first type of simultaneous arising involves a non-defiled mind (*akliṣṭa-citta*).
In the "Manifestation of the Shadow" (*chāyā-prakāśana*), among the two that occur simultaneously, there is also a non-defiled mind (*akliṣṭa-citta*).
Because the Master’s prose is skillful, he does not provide a separate explanation for the shadow within the preceding and succeeding sections, wishing to avoid prolixity.
Regarding the "threefold simultaneous occurrence," it refers to the case where killing and stealing occur at the same time;
this clarifies that three courses of action (karmapatha) operate simultaneously with volition (cetanā). As for the threefold simultaneous occurrence:
it means that with a mind of hatred, one [kills] chickens, ducks, and so forth belonging to another person.
Because once life has been correctly terminated, one is also separated from its original location,
at that time the three— hatred, theft, and killing— proceed together with volition (*cetanā*).
If that were so, the principle you have stated would not be established.
Question:
If it is said that an act of stealing is also brought to completion by a mind of hatred (*dveṣa*),
how does this accord with the previous statement that the path of action of stealing is brought to completion by greed (*lobha*)?
It should logically not be established.
Regarding the statement, "Based on [the fact that it] is not different from the mind, up to the point of definitive judgment, it should be known," the answer is as follows:
Regarding the previous statement that "the path of action of stealing is completed by greed," this refers to completion being achieved through an uninterrupted mental state;
that is to say, there are two kinds of greed involved in this stealing.
First, the causal motivation (hetu-samutthāna);
second, the momentary motivation (tatkṣaṇa-samutthāna).
It is at the moment when greed reaches its culmination that the subsequent momentary motivation occurs.
Because it is the same greed as the preceding greed that arises from the cause,
it is called "the completion of the act performed by a non-different mind.
As for the subsequent statement, "hatred also completes the theft," [it refers to the case where] hatred arises from the cause of greed.
The completion of the act is brought about by a distinct mind;
that is to say, this theft is completed by hatred,
because the greed that constitutes its motivating cause (*samutthāna*) is different from the greed that constitutes the actual execution (*prayoga*).

It should be understood that the designation "the completion of what is done by a different mind" is made because the preceding and succeeding [passages] each rely on a distinct meaning; thus, such a definitive judgment is established. Furthermore, it is explained that in the subsequent text, it is stated that hatred (*dveṣa*) is capable of bringing [an action] to completion.
The two types of action— killing and stealing— are brought to completion based on a non-differentiated mind;
that is to say,
both killing and stealing are brought to completion by the same single mind of hatred.
It is said that the completion [of the act] occurs based on a non-different mind.
In the preceding text, it was stated that the completion of theft and greed occurs based on a previously different mind.
This means that stealing is brought to completion by greed,
while killing is brought to completion by hatred;
each is based on a single mind, yet greed and hatred differ.
One should know that this definitive judgment is made because [the action] is completed based on a different mind. If, however,
one first applies effort and subsequently reaches the culmination of either of the two [paths], [it is as follows].
If one first employs an agent through preparatory effort to commit evil physical karma such as killing or stealing, then when greed,
hatred, or wrong view actually arise, they bring those two [physical actions] to completion.
Furthermore, three courses of action may also proceed simultaneously with volition (*cetanā*).
Among these cases of simultaneous occurrence, two categories have been presented for now;
the others not yet mentioned should be understood according to reason.
Therefore, the Nyāyabindu states:
"The three [mental factors] arise simultaneously" means that when non-virtuous karma previously committed through preparatory effort arises, accompanied by greed and so forth.
The two [paths of action] reach completion simultaneously:
if one dispatches an agent to commit an act such as killing while one personally commits an act such as sexual misconduct,
both reach completion at the same time.
If one acts as both [the agent and the instigator], it should be considered according to reason.
If it is an evil karma previously committed through preliminary application (*prayoga*),
or other defilements such as greed (*lobha*) and so forth.
Furthermore, when a non-defiled mind is present, [the action] is completed according to the three criteria.
When other defiled minds such as greed arise, they are naturally included within the [category of] completion.
One should reflect accordingly on how actions such as divisive speech and false speech are likewise brought to completion through instigation and so forth.

Regarding "four concurrent" up to "culminating in accordance with three," this clarifies that four courses of action (karmapatha) operate concurrently with volition (cetanā). As for "four concurrent":
it refers to divisive speech (paiśunya) intended to cause dissension among others.
Fearing that he might speak false and deceptive words without having abandoned them,
these two are added to the previous [unwholesome roots] to make four;
because it is an improper time, it necessarily involves the inclusion of frivolous speech (*sambhinna-pralāpa*).
With the three [physical] paths of action as the preceding factors and the three paths of verbal action, plus one path of mental action, there are four that proceed together.
This refers to the case where one intends to cause dissension in another,
yet speaks harsh words for fear that the dissension will not be achieved.
Adding the preceding [two] makes two;
because it is not the proper time, it necessarily includes frivolous speech (*sambhinnapralāpa*).
Adding the preceding [three] makes three; thus, there are three paths of vocal action and one path of mental action, totaling four that proceed together.

Because the three [types of speech]—slander, lying, and harsh speech—are necessarily accompanied by frivolous chatter due to their untimely nature, they are not mentioned separately, as their completion does not depend on its explicit mention.

Question: Are the manifest (vijñapti) and unmanifest (avijñapti) karmas arising from the first three types of speech necessarily accompanied by frivolous chatter, or are the four distinct? The masters such as Dhārmika-Śubhagupta explain:
There are two kinds of impurity:
namely, solitary impurity and mixed impurity.
These are designated by the term "impurity" based on the meaning of the three preceding verbal expressions.
That is to say, frivolous speech (*sambhinnapralāpa*) is distinct from the [other] three types of speech;
it refers specifically to the arising of flattery, song, and so forth, which is termed "isolated frivolous speech. This interpretation is incorrect;
the meaning of "isolated" should be understood according to the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra*.
This is not the position of this school.
According to this school,
when the first three types of speech arise simultaneously, there exists a distinct entity of frivolous speech (*sambhinnapralāpa*).
These are termed "co-arising frivolous speech.
If one engages in flattery, song, and the like apart from the three preceding types of speech, these are termed "unshared frivolous speech.
Generally speaking:
If three utterances arise simultaneously, there are three manifest actions (*vijñapti*) and three non-manifest actions (*avijñapti*).
If four utterances arise simultaneously, there are four manifest actions and four non-manifest actions.
Therefore, it is clear from these various matters that one who receives the five precepts obtains all five manifest actions and five non-manifest actions at once.
Just as those wholesome courses of action can arise simultaneously,
the same principle should apply to unwholesome courses of action. For instance,
if one first employs an agent through preparatory effort to commit an unwholesome material action, such as killing, and so forth.
When greed, hatred, or wrong view are present, they each reach their culmination according to three [factors],
and they may also arise together with four.
Among these cases of simultaneous arising with four, three categories are here presented.
Other points not yet explained should be reflected upon according to reason.
Regarding the statement that "in this way, five, six, and seven should all be understood according to reason," these three cases are not explicitly stated here;
rather, they are intended as an exhortation to study and reflect upon them accordingly.
Just as when an unwholesome material karma is performed through prior preparation, if it arises from greed and so forth, it is called "concomitant with five" when four factors complete it,
and called "concomitant with six" when five factors complete it.
According to the six ultimate cases, they are called "sevenfold co-occurrence.
Other unmentioned cases should be investigated through deliberation.
As for "eightfold co-occurrence," it extends up to that point; there are no ninefold or tenfold cases.
It is explained that eight courses of action (karmapatha) may operate simultaneously with volition (cetanā).
Regarding the operation of eight:
this refers to when, through a prior preliminary effort (prayoga), one dispatches another to commit the remaining six unwholesome material courses of action.
When one personally engages in sexual misconduct, the preceding six factors constitute seven;
because greed is necessarily present at the time of engaging in sexual misconduct,
the treatise does not mention it separately.
The first eight are completed simultaneously;
since the latter three cannot necessarily proceed together by their own power, there are no nine courses of action. Ten courses of action may coexist with volition (*cetanā*).
Having thus explained the exclusion of one, eight, and five [paths of action],
the following two lines are now interpreted to clarify how the wholesome paths of action operate simultaneously with volition (*cetanā*).
This concludes the preceding summary of the thesis.

Regarding the section from "those that both operate together" up to "up to seven non-distracted wholesome [paths]," the following provides a detailed explanation clarifying how the two courses of action operate simultaneously with volition (*cetanā*).
Regarding the simultaneous occurrence of both:

this refers to when wholesome fivefold sensory consciousnesses arise, as well as when the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*) based on the formless realm are present;
in these cases, the seven branches of the scattered wholesome [action] belonging to the preceding desire realm do not exist.
There is only non-greed and non-hatred;
because the five consciousnesses are without discrimination,
and because the knowledge of exhaustion and the knowledge of non-arising are the cessation of seeking.
Since none of these are views, there is no right view.
Because there is no restraint based on the formless absorptions (*ārūpya-samādhi*), there is no morality that conforms to the mind (*cittānuvartin-śīla*).
Regarding the simultaneous occurrence of all three [factors], this extends up to the point where the seven material wholesome factors are absent.
It is explained that the three paths of action operate simultaneously with volition (*cetanā*).
Regarding their simultaneous operation:
it refers to when the mental consciousness associated with right view—whether in a state of meditative concentration or in a distracted state—is present before one.
In the indeterminate, scattered, and sevenfold wholesome precepts,
there are only non-attachment, non-hatred, and right view.
Regarding those that arise together with four [mental factors], up to the *śrāmaṇera* vows:
It is explained that four courses of action proceed together with volition (*cetanā*).
Regarding those four that proceed together:
this refers to obtaining the *upavāsa* (near-dwelling) and other precepts at the moment when an unwholesome or neutral mind is present.
There are cases where only three bodily and one vocal course of action (karmapatha) proceed simultaneously.
Regarding the case of six proceeding simultaneously, which occurs up to the attainment of the higher threefold restraint,
this clarifies that six courses of action proceed simultaneously with volition (cetanā).
Regarding the sixfold simultaneous occurrence:
this refers to when the five wholesome consciousnesses are present and one receives the three types of restraint— the Upāsaka, Upavāsa, and Śrāmaṇera precepts.
When five consciousnesses arise simultaneously, there are non-attachment and non-hatred,
as well as three bodily and one vocal [karmic paths], totaling six courses of action.
Regarding the case of seven concurrent [courses of action], this refers to one who has attained the bhikṣu precepts.
It clarifies that the seven courses of action (karmapatha) operate simultaneously with volition (cetanā).
Regarding their simultaneous operation:
this refers to wholesome mental consciousness (manovijñāna) accompanied by non-concentrated paths of action, wherein form (rūpa) follows the mind.
When right view arises in the present moment, one obtains the three higher types of restraint;
with the addition of right view to the previous six, seven courses of action proceed simultaneously.
Alternatively, when an unwholesome or neutral mind arises in the present moment, one obtains the sevenfold restraint of a bhikṣu.
They also turn together with seven.
Regarding "turning together with nine when [the path] manifests before one":
this clarifies that nine courses of action turn together with volition (*cetanā*); the phrase "turning together with nine" refers to this.
There are three types of ninefold simultaneous occurrences:

those involving the five consciousnesses, the exhaustion-knowledge (*kṣaya-jñāna*), and the non-arising-knowledge (*anutpāda-jñāna*). Because they are not of the nature of vision (*darśana*), they lack right view (*samyag-dṛṣṭi*).
If the five consciousnesses, as well as the knowledge of exhaustion and the knowledge of non-arising based on the formless realm,
are associated with mundane wholesome states, there are seven types of material [form].
If the knowledge of exhaustion and the knowledge of non-arising are based on dhyāna, they necessarily possess morality that functions in accordance with the mind (*cittānuvartin-śīla*).
At that time, if one obtains the great bhikṣu precepts, one also obtains the form of the wholesome factors of the scattered state;
because these seven wholesome forms are identical, they are not distinguished separately.
Regarding the "ten simultaneous occurrences," this refers to the stage when the mind is correctly aroused.
It is explained that the ten courses of action (karmapatha) operate simultaneously with volition (cetanā).
Regarding these ten simultaneous occurrences,
there are two categories.
This can be understood according to the preceding explanation.
Regarding the statement that "distinctly based on manifest characteristics, there are one, eight,
and five," this section below provides a further analysis.
If one refers specifically to the vows (*saṃvara*), the prohibited characteristics are as stated above.
If one refers generally to the vows, including those that are intermediate and implicit, there is nothing prohibited.
Intermediate courses of action (*karmapatha*) are not called "vows," nor are they termed "abstinence from vows."
Based on this implicit characteristic, there is one instance where eight, five, or all ten courses of action (*karmapatha*) proceed simultaneously.
According to our own school’s correct analysis, the formal undertaking of the five precepts and so forth must be complete in order to be designated as a restraint (*saṃvara*).
If one does not receive [the precepts] in their entirety, it is not a formal vow (saṃvara),
but merely an intermediate course of action (madhyama-karmapatha),
such as when a person is unable to fully undertake the five precepts and so forth.
According to the extent of one's commitment, one may undertake the precepts such as abstaining from taking life;
although these are not formally categorized as part of the formal restraint (*saṃvara*), they are nonetheless termed "intermediate paths of action" (*madhyama-karmapatha*).
Among these, for the sake of completing the wholesome paths of action (*kuśalakarmapatha*),
there are ten types that may arise simultaneously.
For now, regarding the intermediate [wholesome] states, one, eight, and five are explained.
In reality, all ten types are present within the locus [of action].
Therefore, the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 113, states:
"When one is in a state that is neither restraint (*saṃvara*) nor non-restraint (*asaṃvara*)."
The seven wholesome courses of action of body and speech vary in number according to what is undertaken; they may be many or few and are not fixed.
As for the three wholesome courses of action of the mind, they may or may not be present.
It may be absent;
it may be many;
or it may be few.
Regarding "arising together in one" up to "abstaining from one branch," this is explained individually below:
that is, when an unwholesome or neutral mind is present.
One obtains one branch of the path of action within the state of seclusion.
Regarding the statement "five [factors] operate together" up to "obtaining two branches," this refers to when a wholesome mental consciousness—
accompanied by non-concomitant matter and associated with right view— is present.

When one attains the two factors of the path of action consisting of abstention from the intermediate [unwholesome] acts, together with the mental path of action, these three are said to proceed simultaneously as five.
"Etc. refers to including the cases of three or five factors.

Alternatively, when wholesome fivefold consciousnesses and so forth are present, one attains three factors of the path of action of abstention from [unwholesome deeds] along with the intermediate state; these likewise operate simultaneously with the five [consciousnesses].
This also occurs when unwholesome or neutral minds are present.
When one attains the fivefold abstention from the intermediate course of action, five [mental factors] also operate simultaneously.
Regarding "up to eight operating simultaneously" and so forth:
this means that when the mental consciousness associated with right view is present, one attains the fivefold abstention from the intermediate course of action, and so on.
This refers to the inclusion of all six;
that is, when the five wholesome consciousnesses are present,
one acquires the six branches of the path of action consisting of abstention from the intermediate [unwholesome] deeds.
It should be understood that regarding the first seven unwholesome [paths],
the initial moment of non-restraint is termed a "course of action" (*karmapatha*). Therefore,
this treatise states within its fourteen explanations of the various names for non-restraint (*asaṃvara*):
They are called paths of action (karmapatha) because they are comprised within the fundamental [actions].
Even when neutral unwholesome states reach the stage of the fundamental [action], they are likewise called paths of action.

As with killing and so forth, this treatise explains them in full. Regarding the first seven wholesome [paths of action], if they are vows (*saṃvara*), their initial moment is called a path of action (*karmapatha*).
Therefore, the preceding text states that only the initial moment of manifest (*vijñapti*) and unmanifest (*avijñapti*) [action] is designated as the distinct vow (*prātimokṣa*) path of action.
If one abides in the intermediate [state], the first moment of wholesome [action] is also called a path of action (*karmapatha*),
as previously cited from the *Vibhāṣā* regarding those who abide in the intermediate state.
Furthermore, because these four categories possess coarse aspects, they are subsumed under the paths of action.
Furthermore, because these four categories possess non-informative [matter] (*avijñapti*), they are subsumed under the paths of action (*karmapatha*).
How could there be a non-informative [matter] that does not constitute a path of action?
Among those [paths of action] that arise simultaneously with volition (*cetanā*) within unwholesome paths of action...
Furthermore, this is based on the intermediate course of action (*madhyama-karmapatha*) and not on the course of non-restraint (*asaṃvara-karmapatha*),
because within the unwholesome intermediate course there are distinctions such as one, two, and so forth;
since these allow for an increase in the number of attainments, it is explained here specifically with reference to that.

Because non-restraint (asamvara) must necessarily possess all seven [types], and because there is no distinct attainment of one, two, or more [of them] individually, it is not explained in relation to those [partial cases]. Master Tai and others explain as follows:
In the case of killing and so forth committed while abiding in the intermediate state, they only constitute a course of action (*karmapatha*) when all the requisite conditions are present.
Regarding non-restraint (*asaṃvara*), the presence of such conditions is not explicitly stated;
although it involves killing and so forth, this non-restraint is not itself an unwholesome course of action consisting of killing and so forth.
Therefore, regarding the simultaneous occurrence with unwholesome volition,
this is explained solely in terms of the intermediate state and not in terms of non-restraint; however, we maintain that this is not the case.
There are two types of unwholesome courses of action (*karmapatha*).
First, that which is acquired through non-restraint (*asaṃvara*) is called a course of action;
because it applies universally to all sentient beings, its specific conditions are not enumerated.

Second, those unwholesome states that obtain a middle position are called courses of action (*karmapatha*) because they are reckoned in relation to a specific individual; therefore, it is said that they possess all the requisite conditions.
Furthermore, in various treatises, non-restraint (*asaṃvara*) is also termed a course of action.
Since the [mental] factors are not identical,
how could the fact that they are not mentioned separately among those that arise simultaneously with volition prove that they are not courses of action?
Regarding their simultaneous arising, let us discuss them for now by way of a single characteristic of differentiation.
This is not a comprehensive explanation.
Furthermore, one might argue that even subsequent moments could be said not to be paths of action;
why then should the first moment alone be excluded from being a path of action?
If it is argued that although these are non-restraint (asaṃvara) such as killing, they are not unwholesome courses of action (karmapatha) such as killing,
then it may likewise be argued that although wholesome restraint (saṃvara) consists of restraints such as non-killing, they are not wholesome courses of action such as non-killing.
Since this is not the case, how could that be so?
Here, it is not clarified whether there is killing or no killing;
rather, it clarifies that the path of action (karmapatha) operates simultaneously with volition (cetanā).
Since non-restraint is called a "path of action," it may also be said to arise simultaneously with volition;
or alternatively, it may be so.
Among the eight simultaneous occurrences (*aṣṭa-samprayukta*), the paths of unwholesome action (*asaṃvara-karmapatha*) are also included.
Who says they are not included?
If Master Tai and others interpret it in this way, [it is correct].
This not only contradicts reason but also contradicts the treatise. Furthermore, an ancient master stated:
"Intermediate wholesome karma is not a course of action (*karmapatha*).
He maintained that intermediate karma is not subsumed under the coarse categories.
That is also not the case; for example,
although acts such as killing are intermediate [in nature], they are still [unwholesome].
Because they subsume coarse categories, they are called "paths of action" (*karmapatha*).
What prevents intermediate wholesome karma from also being subsumed under the paths of action?
It is due to deluded attachment that one considers intermediate karma not to be a coarse category.
This is a profound error on your part.
The *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* also states that wholesome karma situated between [the primary paths] is called a "path of action" (*karmapatha*).
As previously cited in full, another ancient master stated:
"Regarding unwholesome [karma], it is explained that volition (cetanā) operates in conjunction with karma of the intermediate category;
it does not clarify non-restraint (asaṃvara)."
Among the wholesome paths of action (*kuśala-karmapatha*),

this is explained solely in terms of restraint (*saṃvara*) and not in terms of intermediate [action] (*madhyama*), because the mutual manifestation of volition (*cetanā*) and its co-arising is intended. However, this is also not the case.
This is because the intermediate [paths of action] are mentioned among the wholesome paths of action;
or, because non-restraint is also included within the eightfold simultaneous occurrence of unwholesome paths of action.
Thus, both wholesome and unwholesome paths of action extend to those that are currently manifesting.
Below this is the fifth section, which establishes the paths of action according to their locations.
Question: In which realms and which destinies do the wholesome and unwholesome paths of action exist?
In what places are these [unwholesome factors] accomplished and active?
The verse says: "Extending to those who exclude the hells and the northern continent.
The first six lines clarify the unwholesome.
The final six phrases clarify the wholesome.
The Treatise states: "Up to 'free from divisive speech,'" which explains the first three phrases.
In the hells (*naraka*), the three types—coarseness, impurity, and anger—are both manifest and fully established.
Because they are oppressed by suffering and revile one another, there is coarse speech (*pāruṣya*).
Driven by suffering and because of wailing cries, there is frivolous speech (*sambhinna-pralāpa*).
Driven by suffering, with body and mind becoming coarse, violent, and unrestrained due to mutual hatred, there is malice (*vyāpāda*).
Greed and wrong view are possessed but do not manifest.
They are possessed because one has not yet abandoned them;
they do not manifest because there is no desire-greed for desirable objects as one's own possession.
The karmic path of greed does not manifest [in this case]: although a cool breeze touches the body and arouses greed, it is minor and thus not a karmic path.
This is like the greed of a Wheel-Turning King or that of the inhabitants of Uttarakuru, which, being minor, is not a karmic path.
Only when there is the desire for another's wealth and the actual covetousness does it constitute a path of action (*karmapatha*). Therefore,
beings in the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) of hell possess the knowledge acquired at birth (*upapattilābhika-jñāna*),
by which they know that they have come to be born here due to the karma they created in their previous lives.
Because one directly perceives the fruits of karma,
there is no manifestation of the path of action consisting of wrong view; furthermore, the remaining five paths of action are neither accomplished nor manifested.
Why is this? Because death occurs when karma is exhausted, there is no path of action consisting of killing;
and because there is no appropriation of material goods, there is no taking what is not given.
Because they do not take women as their own, there is no sexual misconduct.
Since the mirror of karma appears before them and cannot be denied or concealed, and because it serves no purpose, there is no false speech.
Thus, the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states:

King Yama manifests the very bodies of the offenders to testify to their own deeds; therefore, there is no false speech. Furthermore, it is explained that "deception" refers to seeking to fulfill one's desires through falsehoods;
however, in that place, there is no such thing as seeking one’s ends through artifice.
Because they have no purpose, there is no false speech.
Thus, the *Vibhāṣā* states:
"One who has no false speech does not engage in the undertaking of false speech. Furthermore, the *Nyāyānusāra* states:
Alternatively, false speech causes another’s perception to become inverted;
however, since that person’s perception is already constantly inverted, there is no false speech.
Furthermore, for this very reason—that it would be useless—and because in the hells the mind is constantly distracted by the pressure of suffering, there is no divisive speech.
"From the continent of Uttarakuru up to 'as appropriate'" explains the fourth and fifth phrases. On the northern continent,
the unwholesome courses of action— greed, hatred, and wrong view— are all invariably accomplished.
Because it has not been abandoned, it does not manifest.
Because one does not grasp at "mine," greed does not manifest.
Although desire and so forth may still occur, there is nonetheless no defilement of greed.
The light [afflictions] are not paths of action.
Because body and mind are supple and pliant, there is no occurrence of harm or injury;
therefore, the path of action of hatred does not manifest.
Because there is no malicious intention, the path of action of wrong view does not manifest;
only frivolous speech manifests and is accomplished,
because at times they sing with a defiled mind, and thus there is frivolous speech.
The remaining six courses of action are neither accomplished nor manifest. Why is this?
Because there is no malicious intention; thus, those [beings] lack the six [actions] such as killing.
This is the general explanation.
Furthermore, another explanation states:
because the lifespan is fixed at one thousand years, there is no path of action consisting of killing;
because there is no appropriation of one's own or others' property, there is no path of action consisting of stealing.
Because they do not take women as wives or concubines, there is no path of sexual misconduct.
Because their bodies and minds are gentle, there is no harsh speech.
Furthermore, the *Nyāya* states:
Because their speech is pure and beautiful, they have no harsh or abusive words.
Because there is no purpose for them to do so, they have no false speech or divisive speech.
Furthermore, the *Nyāya* states:
Because he has no deceitful mind, there is no false speech;
because he is always harmonious and conciliatory, there is no divisive speech. The phrase "as appropriate" means that the explanation is applied according to the specific meaning.
How could such a person engage in unchaste conduct?
Question:
Regarding the statement that "those men and women, having reached [that point], depart together in mutual shame," what is the answer? Answer: [As follows:]
This can be understood.
The sixth phrase is explained as excluding those who go from the aforementioned hells to other realms through acts of killing.
Within the desire realm— excluding the hells and the northern continent—
the remaining beings, namely devas, pretas, animals, and humans of the three continents,
all possess both the possession (*parigraha*) and the active manifestation (*samudācāra*) of the ten paths of unwholesome action; however, there are distinctions among them.
That is to say, among gods, ghosts, and animals, the first seven courses of action are comprised solely of intermediate [neither-restraint-nor-non-restraint];
there is no non-restraint (*asaṃvara*) among them. Within the three continents of the human realm, both intermediate and non-restraint exist. Furthermore, according to this text:
Non-restraint (*asaṃvara*) is called a course of action (*karmapatha*).

It is not said that it is not a course of action; rather, this is understood by carefully examining the text. Although the hosts of devas do not kill other devas, this is because they cherish their own class (*svavarga*).
Furthermore, there are times when they kill other asuras belonging to the realm of ghosts;
this refers to the alternative explanation by other masters that their lives are only severed at that point.
This records a divergent opinion.
Even devas harm other devas;
because they recognize their enemies from past lives,
their lives are only severed when their heads are cut off or their waists are sliced through.
Therefore, the *Nyāyānusāra* states:
"Other masters say that gods also kill gods;
although the limbs of a god's body may be severed, they grow back again."
If one cuts off the head or severs the middle, it will not grow again.
Having explained [the section] from the unwholesome up to the statement regarding the accomplishment of what is presently active,
the seventh and eighth phrases are now interpreted.
The latter three paths of wholesome action may be understood through this explanation.
Regarding the seven branches of body and speech up to "all are fully accomplished":
Explanation of the ninth and tenth phrases:
The seven branches of body and speech may arise in the formless realms and among the gods of non-conception;
they can only be possessed [as latent seeds], but never manifest.
This refers to noble beings born in the formless realm who possess past and future untainted discipline (*anāsrava-saṃvara*);
and beings born in the Heaven of Non-conception (*asaṃjñi-sattva*) who necessarily possess past and future dhyāna-discipline (*dhyāna-saṃvara*) of the fourth meditative absorption (*dhyāna*).
However, when noble beings are born in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) in the present life,
they possess that past untainted restraint (*anāsrava-saṃvara*) which arose and ceased in dependence upon whatever basis (*āśraya-kāya*) it had in previous births.
If that which has never arisen were not established as the past,
then if one were born in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) with future untainted restraint (*anāsrava-saṃvara*),
it would have to depend upon the bodies of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) or the four dhyānas and five stages (*pañca-bhūmi*).
The untainted restraint (anāsrava-saṃvara) is fully accomplished in both cases.
Therefore, the *Nyāyānusāra* states:
"In both instances, there is no sense of its manifest activity."
Because the formless realm consists only of the nature of the four aggregates;
because non-percipient beings lack a concentrated mind (*samāhita-citta*);

and because restraint (*saṃvara*) must depend upon both the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) and a concentrated mind—since these two conditions are mutually absent there—it does not manifest [in those realms]. This concludes the treatise. One should know that this refers to noble ones (*ārya*) born in the formless realm.
The future [attainments] will definitely be established in five stages,
whereas the past is not fixed;
thus, the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 134, states:
When a disciple of the Blessed One is born in the formless realm,
if they are an Arhat, they possess only the uncontaminated matter derived from the primary elements (mahābhūta) of the five stages in the future,
because it does not arise in the present.
It is not past, because it has already been relinquished.
If one is a non-returner (anāgāmin), they also possess the future uncontaminated matter (anāsrava-rūpa) derived from the primary elements (mahābhūta) of five stages;
however, it is not present.
Because it does not arise,
the past is indeterminate.
Depending on the body in the five stages (*pañca-bhūmi*), there is variation in the number [of moments] that arise.
Or because it is entirely absent; for this reason,
it should be stated that there are some trainees born in the formless realm who possess the future five stages of reliance upon the precepts.
In the past, there is none at all;
that is to say, previously relying on a body of the desire realm or the four dhyānas,
one [attained] the third fruit and the fourth path.
When various untainted paths have neither arisen nor ceased,
one passes away from that state and is reborn in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).
Alternatively, there may be a learner (*śaikṣa*) born in the formless realm who accomplishes five future [paths] and one past [path].
This means that previously, while practicing the four dhyānas of the desire realm,
one relied upon a single body to attain either the third fruit or the fourth candidate stage.
When all untainted paths have already arisen and have already ceased,
one passes away from that state and is reborn in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).
Alternatively, there may be a trainee (*śaikṣa*) reborn in the formless realm who possesses five future [untainted dharmas] and two past [untainted dharmas].
That is to say, when previously in the desire realm or during the four dhyānas,
depending on either of two bodies,
one was at the stage of the third fruit or the fourth candidate.
When all untainted paths have already arisen and ceased,
one passes away from that state and is reborn in the formless realm.
Alternatively, there may be a trainee reborn in the formless realm who accomplishes five future [paths] and three past [paths].
This refers to when, during the stages of the desire realm and the four dhyānas,
one relies on any of the three bodies and is either in the third fruit or the fourth candidate stage.
When all untainted paths have already arisen and ceased,
one passes away from that life and is reborn in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).
Alternatively, there may be a learner (*śaikṣa*) reborn in the formless realm who accomplishes five future [untainted dharmas] and four past [untainted dharmas].
This refers to when, previously, during the time of the desire realm or the four dhyānas,
one— relying on any of the four bodies—
was at the stage of the third fruit or the fourth candidate.
When all untainted paths have already arisen and have already ceased,
one passes away from that state and is reborn in the formless realm.
Alternatively, there may be a trainee reborn in the formless realm who accomplishes five future and five past [paths].
This refers to one who, relying on a body belonging to the desire realm or to the four dhyānas,
has already arisen and already ceased the various untainted paths pertaining to the third fruit or the candidate for the fourth fruit.
Having passed away from that state, they are reborn in the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu).
Some maintain the following view:
there is no learner (śaikṣa) who is reborn in the formless realm.
One does not possess past form because,
when one previously existed in the desire realm or the form realm,
one must have already produced and already ceased [the path] of either the third fruit or the candidate for the fourth fruit before passing away.
Therefore, the root treatise states:
"If those in training (śaikṣa) are born in the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu), they possess past and future derived matter (upādāya-rūpa).
If they attain the fruit of arhatship there, they possess future derived matter, but not past derived matter."
If one were to say that this is not so,
then the *Mūlaśāstra* should have stated that a learner (*śaikṣa*) born in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) does not possess past created matter (*rūpa*).
Furthermore, the *Vibhāṣā*, fascicle 132, also records two such views, saying:
Question: Is there also a learner (śaikṣa) born in the formless realm who does not possess past conditioned form?
That is to say, one who previously, while in the desire or form realms, had not yet arisen or ceased any untainted paths (anāsrava-mārga).
Having ended their lives, they are reborn in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) and do not at all possess the past matter (*rūpa*) they previously created. How, then,
can it be said that "if those who are trainees (*śaikṣa*) are born in the formless realm..."?
Is there the accomplishment of past derived matter? Answer: This is stated with reference to one who possesses it.
That is to say, for a learner (*śaikṣa*), there are the various untainted paths (*anāsravamārga*) previously arisen and subsequently ceased within the desire and form realms.
Because he has accomplished the derived matter (*upādāya-rūpa*) produced in the past.
Some say that when he was in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) or the form realm (*rūpadhātu*),
he had necessarily already arisen and already ceased various untainted paths (*anāsrava-mārga*).
As with the path of superior progress (*viśeṣamārga*),
it necessarily arises and manifests before one, for there is no such thing as passing away while abiding in the fruit.
Furthermore, in the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 122, there are also two explanations which state:
Question: If a trainee (śaikṣa) attains the fruit of non-returner (anāgāmiphala) by means of the mundane path (laukikamārga) and,
without ever manifesting the untainted restraint (anāsravasaṃvara), is reborn in the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu),
how does he possess past unmanifest bodily karma (kāyāvijñapti)?
If it is not established, why does this text state as follows:
"Do those in training who are born in the formless realm possess past bodily non-informative matter?"
Some say that there are also learners (śaikṣa) born in the formless realm who do not possess past bodily non-informative karma (kāyavijñapti). However,
this passage speaks only with reference to those who do possess it.
Therefore, there is no fault. Other masters say that once one has attained a noble fruit,
one must necessarily give rise to the noble path of a superior fruit so that it manifests before one.
Therefore, when those who are practitioners are born in the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu),
they necessarily accomplish past unmanifest bodily karma (kāyavijñapti-avijñapti).
As for the other realms and destinies, all possess both types [of unmanifest karma] as long as they are present.
He explains the latter two phrases:
"In other realms, destinies, and locations,
excluding the hells and the northern continent."
Because those [beings] lack the first seven paths of wholesome action, they are specifically excluded.

In other realms and so forth, all seven wholesome paths are both manifest and possessed; however, there is a distinction: namely, among ghosts (*preta*) and animals (*tiryagyoni*), there are intermediate paths of action that are free from formal restraint (*saṃvara*).
Because that body lacks restraint (*asaṃvara*), there is only intermediate action (*madhyama-karman*).
In the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*), however, there is only restraint and no intermediate courses of action (*karmapatha*);
thus, bodily informative action (*kāyavijñapti*) is produced within the first dhyāna.

However, these are excellent conduct (*sucarita*) rather than courses of action (*karmapatha*). The restraint of discipline (*saṃvara*) exists in the three continents and among the gods of the desire realm; the intermediate [conduct] exists in both.
That is to say, humans of the three continents possess the three types of discipline.
And the intermediate wholesome courses of action.
If there are celestial beings in the desire realm who possess the discipline of restraint,
they also have the intermediate courses of action.
"There is no separate liberation" refers to the fact that unwholesome and wholesome courses of action lead to the severing of life and the destruction of majesty;
this is the sixth [section], clarifying the three fruits of the courses of action.
The first two lines clarify the attainment of the three fruits;
the latter two lines clarify the causes for those three fruits.
The Treatise says: "Each respectively brings about the three fruits."
This is a general enumeration of the number;
since they shall be explained in detail later, the word "provisionally" (qie) is used here. What are these three?
Question:
Regarding the statement, "Because of the distinctions between maturation, outflow, and dominance," the answer states:
First, the general;
second, the specific.
This constitutes the general response.
Regarding the ten types that constitute the fruit of maturation (*vipākaphala*),
the following provides the specific answers.
"Initial arising" is termed "cultivation" (*vāsanā*).
Next, "arising" refers to cultivation;
subsequently, "arising" refers to what is produced.
This clarifies that the unwholesome paths of action produce the fruit of maturation (*vipākaphala*).
The total maturation (vipāka) extends throughout the three evil destinies;
however, this text mentions only hell because it refers specifically to the most severe cases.
Once one has emerged from there, one reaches the distinct result of outflow (niṣyanda-phala).
This explains the fruit of outflow (*niṣyanda-phala*).
Having emerged from those hells, one is born among human beings by virtue of past wholesome karma to experience the fruit of outflow. "Outflow" means the sense of similarity.
Just as taking the life of another results in a short lifespan, so too is one's lifespan short in the present life.
The same principle applies to stealing and other such acts. Furthermore, those who gave rise to wrong views in a previous life experience an increase in delusion in this life.
Why is this? Because that category of wrong view is more intense than the other afflictions of greed, hatred, and delusion.
Therefore, the arising of wrong view in the past can cause delusion to increase in the present; this is because it is the outflow fruit (*niṣyanda-phala*) of wrong view.
Therefore, the *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya* states:
"For one with wrong view, delusion is predominant;
its immediate dominant fruit is also called a 'similar outflow' (*niṣyanda*). Furthermore, it is explained as follows:
Alternatively, that wrong view can cause delusion to increase;
this indicates the intensification of wrong view.
This is because when wrong view arises, delusion necessarily increases.
The remainder of the text may be understood.
Regarding the statement that a short lifespan among humans is the outflow (niṣyanda) of killing: [Question: What is meant by this?
Regarding the statement that human life does not endure for long:
the answer is that this does not mean that human life itself is the fruit of the unwholesome karma of killing.
It is merely said that because of killing, the lifespan is shortened; the karmic act of killing acts as an obstructive cause for life, preventing it from enduring long.
As for the specific distinctions among the sovereign fruits obtained by these ten [non-virtues]:
This clarifies the dominant fruit (*adhipatiphala*).
It may be understood from the text as it stands.
Regarding the question of whether it is a single act of killing or whether there are further [acts]: [the answer follows].
Regarding the cause of the two fruits, another master says: "It reaches until it produces these [results] as its outflow.
This master’s intention is as follows:
If one says that a single fundamental path of action for killing can induce two fruits,
why does the treatise state:
"Because it causes others to suffer, one experiences the ripening fruit of suffering"?
Since that life no longer exists at the time of the fundamental path of action (*maula-karmapatha*),
one cannot say that it causes another to suffer; therefore,
it is known that the experience of suffering occurs during the stage of preliminary application (*prayoga*).
Since this contradicts the treatise,
it is known that this explanation is not correct. Furthermore, another interpretation is offered regarding the term "a single act of killing."
These fully encompass the three types of karma that cause others to suffer, take their lives, and destroy their majesty.
These three are all capable of first inducing maturation (*vipāka*);
these same three are also capable of subsequently inducing outflowing results (*niṣyanda*).
The subsequent passage states that the three [karmas] produce distinct results;
this is spoken of in terms of their predominant influence, as will be explained below.
Now, regarding the discussion on the strength and weakness of universal retribution:
among the three types of karma, the first and last are the preparatory stages (*prayoga*),
while the middle one is the fundamental stage (*maula*).

Regarding the statement that the fruit of the preparatory application (*prayoga*) is also called the fruit of the path of action (*karmapatha*): because it is the fruit of the preparatory application for a path of action, it is also termed the fruit of the path of action.
If one interprets it in this way, it accords with the treatise.
It may also be considered correct.
In this context, the question and answer do not mention "predominance" (adhipati),
because since it must necessarily be experienced, it is not a matter of doubt.
Sometimes it is omitted and not mentioned;
the *Nyāyānusāra* explains it fully.
Thus, that treatise says:
Other masters say:
"That very same karmic act of killing first undergoes its maturation (vipāka),
and subsequently [undergoes] the near-dominant [result]."
Next, because of the increase of the remote superior [condition], there are three fruits.
Others further say that it extends to the fundamental [roots] and their attendants;
yet others further say:
The causes for the two fruits—maturation (*vipāka*) and outflow (*niṣyanda*)—are distinct.
First, regarding the maturation fruit that is induced: it refers to the karma of intensified action;
because one causes others to suffer, one undergoes the maturation of suffering within the hells.
Subsequently, the resultant fruit of uniform outflow (niṣyanda-phala) refers to the fundamental karma;
since his life has already ended, it does not cause him to undergo suffering,
but rather causes the lives of others to be shortened.

Therefore, when born among humans, one’s lifespan is short. Although the sutra speaks generally of the single term "killing," it actually encompasses the fundamental path of action (*maula-karmapatha*), as well as its preliminary application (*prayoga*) and subsequent consequences (*pṛṣṭha*).

The reason the fruit of the preparatory application (*prayoga*) is also called the fruit of the path of action (*karmapatha*) is that it is the fruit of the preparatory application for that path of action;
thus, it is also termed the fruit of the path of action. This explanation by the Master is well-aligned with the treatise.
Because the preparatory action (*prayoga*) causes others to suffer, and because the fundamental act (*maula*) has the sense of intending to take another’s life;
since the text and the reasoning thus accord, this may be taken as correct. Herein, one should also explain the distinction between the dominant fruit (*adhipatiphala*) and its cause.

Because it was not asked, it was also not answered separately; this refers to the dominant fruit (*adhipatiphala*) which destroys majestic power and induces [retribution], as will be explained in sequence.
Each question and answer is fully clarified below.
Regarding the statement here that [the fruit] "reaches up to being a conventional designation of an outflow" (*niṣyanda*),
since the nature of an outflow is somewhat obscure, it is now explained again.
This refers to the term "outflow fruit" (*niṣyandaphala*) mentioned herein.
It does not transcend the ripening fruit (*vipākaphala*) and the dominant fruit (*adhipatiphala*).
A short lifespan among humans is the ripening fruit when viewed in relation to wholesome karma;
it is the dominant fruit when viewed in relation to the karma of killing.

Its flow-on result (niṣyanda-phala) does not transcend these two [fruits]. Regarding these two fruits, it is metaphorically designated as a "flow-on" based on a slight similarity. As for what is meant by "similarity":
it refers to causing others to shorten their lifespan by commanding them to do so.
Having experienced the maturation [of karma] within the hells,
one is reborn among humans with a short lifespan;
because it resembles that [suffering], it is called "resemblance."
Based on this sense, it is conventionally designated as "outflow" (*niṣyanda*), yet it is not a real outflow.
If it were a real outflow, it would arise from its own kind. Furthermore, this passage is interpreted as comprehensively clarifying all ten types of outflows.
The term "concordant result" (*niṣyanda-phala*) mentioned here does not transcend the results of maturation (*vipāka-phala*) and dominance (*adhipati-phala*).
If the concordant result of killing is indeed a result of maturation, it is also a dominant result.
The other nine are outflowing results (*niṣyanda-phala*) and dominant results (*adhipati-phala*);
they are conventionally designated as "outflowing" based on a slight degree of similarity.
Regarding the statement that the other nine are conventionally designated as both outflowing and dominant: [this refers to their dual nature].
This has been stated in general terms according to the majority of cases.
If one were to distinguish them individually and in detail,
among these nine, two of the body and four of speech are merely metaphorical designations based on predominance.

If greed, hatred, and non-universal wrong view are compared to the greed, hatred, and ignorance that increase in other categories, these are all metaphorically designated as "outflow" (niṣyanda) with respect to their predominant fruit (adhipatiphala).
If greed, hatred, or views increase the greed and hatred of their own category,
or if pervasive wrong views increase the ignorance of the five categories,
then these are actual outflows (niṣyanda) and not merely figurative designations.
Regarding the question, "For what reason do these ten each bring about three fruits?"—
this section below explains the latter two lines of the verse;
this, then, is the inquiry.
Furthermore, regarding the response to the inquiry as to how one should reflect upon the initial act of killing among the ten unwholesome courses of action:
at the moment of killing another, this constitutes the first act of killing.
First, causing others to suffer;
second, causing others to lose their lives;
third, causing others to lose their majesty.
This means that at the time of killing, because one causes another to experience suffering during the stage of preliminary application (*prayoga*),
one falls into hell to experience the ripening fruit (*vipākaphala*) of suffering;
it is not [the result] at the time of actual death.

Because at the time of death there is no painful sensation (*duḥkhā-vedanā*) but only neutral sensation (*upekṣā-vedanā*), and because one has taken the life of another during the fundamental state (*maula-avasthā*),
one emerges from hell to be born among human beings.
A short lifespan is the concordant result (*niṣyanda-phala*). When about to commit killing, one grasps a sword, staff, or other weapons;

because this destroys the majesty of the being to be killed, it results in external objects having little luster as the dominant result (*adhipati-phala*). This destruction of majesty is based on the remote preparatory action (*prayoga*).
The experience of suffering is based on the proximate preparatory stage (*prayoga*);
alternatively, the destruction of majestic dignity (*pratibhāna*) also pertains to the proximate preparatory stage. Master Tai said:
It is not so that one causes another to lose their majesty through a subsequent action;
since even the fundamental [action] is not permitted because there is no life-force,
how much less so a subsequent action?
By the time one reaches the stage of subsequent arising, since that life-force no longer exists,
who would be deprived of its majesty?
Therefore, the *Nyāyānusāra* states:
In reality, at the time of killing, one causes the victim to experience suffering,
brings about the severance of life,
and destroys their majestic radiance.
Because one causes others to suffer, one is born in hell;
because one takes the lives of others, one’s lifespan is short among humans.
These are the results of the preliminary application (*prayoga*).
The latter is the fundamental fruit.
Both the fundamental and the preparatory stages are termed "killing.
By destroying majestic splendor, one brings about the acquisition of unfavorable external conditions.
Therefore, the karma of killing results in three types of fruits.
Other paths of unwholesome action should be considered accordingly. Based on this treatise and the *Nyāyānusāra*, the causes for these three fruits are distinct.

Question: Since both taking life and destroying majestic dignity (*pratibhāna*) are unwholesome and should result in maturation (*vipāka*), why is it said that one experiences only the sensation of suffering?
Answer: It is explained that, in principle, they are indeed capable of producing such results.
As for why it is not mentioned:

it is because the specific characteristics of suffering in others are being emphasized for the sake of others. Question: Since the outflowing fruit (*niṣyanda-phala*) is subsumed within the dominant fruit (*adhipati-phala*), the experience of suffering and the loss of majesty should also be able to induce [those results].
Why is it said that only the taking of life can bring about [retribution]? The explanation is:
although, from the perspective of its predominant influence (*adhipati*), other factors could also bring it about, they are not mentioned here.

Because the karma of taking another’s life has a distinct and superior function in relation to that person’s short lifespan, it is specifically mentioned [as a cause for that result]. Question: Since the category of "dominant" (*adhipati*) is broad and general, all three [types of karma] should equally induce [results].

Why is it that only the destruction of majestic power (*tejas*) induces [this specific result], and not the other two? Answer: It is explained that, according to principle, the other two types of karma are also capable of inducing dominant results.

The reason they are not mentioned is that [the text] intends to manifest a distinct teaching by undermining the majestic appearance of others. From this, one should understand accordingly up to the point where it says "it should be explained as is appropriate.
This explains the three fruits of wholesome [actions]; one should reflect upon how these are the reverse of those for unwholesome [actions].
The remaining dominant fruits (*adhipatiphala*) and the remaining wholesome paths of action (*kuśalakarmapatha*) are the opposites of those mentioned above.
The rest should be explained accordingly; the further details may be understood from the text.
Therefore, the *Nyāyānusāra* states:
From this, one should understand by analogy the three fruits of the wholesome paths of action.
For instance, regarding abstention from killing, whether it is practiced or cultivated:
If one performs many such deeds,
by the power of this, one is born among the devas to experience the ripening fruit;
having passed away from there, one is born among humans to experience an extremely long life.
The proximate dominant fruit is that,
by means of this very [virtue], one brings about external objects of great majestic radiance;
this is the remote dominant fruit.
The three fruits of other wholesome [actions] should be explained by reversing those of the unwholesome.
Furthermore, regarding what the Sūtra says about "reaching wrong livelihood" (*mithyājīva*),
the following section, the eleventh major heading, specifically clarifies wrong livelihood.
Regarding the question raised based on the Sūtra:
"Even if one were to depart from that [position], it would not contradict the Sūtra; therefore, [your objection] is irrational," the answer is as follows:
The first two lines clarify the point directly;
the latter two lines refute attachment.
The Treatise says: "Up to 'because the requisites belong to others'."
However, the vocal karma arising from hatred and delusion each has four branches,
which are collectively termed wrong speech (*mithyāvāc*).
Since speech itself is action, it is not referred to as "action" [separately];
rather, there are three types each for bodily actions arising from hatred and delusion.
These are collectively termed "wrong action" (*mithyākarma*).
Since the body itself is not an action, it is not mentioned as such; rather, it refers only to the two types of action—bodily and vocal—that arise from greed.
These consist of the three bodily actions and the four vocal actions.
Because it is difficult to eliminate, wrong livelihood is established separately.
That is to say, greed is subtle and capable of eclipsing the minds of sentient beings;
the karma arising from it is difficult to restrain and guard against.
Because the Buddha intended for them to practice right livelihood with earnest cultivation,
he distinguished wrong livelihood from the previously mentioned wrong speech and wrong action,
as can be understood from the cited verse.
The latter two lines are cited as proof.
The former two lines are included because they share the same text.
Thus, the *Nyāyapraveśa* says:
It is difficult for householders to sever wrong views,
because they cling excessively to such things as auspicious omens.
It is difficult for those who have left the household life to eliminate wrong livelihood.
