Because all conditions for life depend upon others;
as for the claim by other masters that [the body] reaches [death] because it no longer sustains life,
this merely recounts a divergent opinion.

Other masters maintain that it is only the bodily and vocal actions arising from greed directed toward those requisites for livelihood by which one subsists that are termed wrong livelihood (*mithyājīva*).
Bodily and vocal actions arising from other forms of greed are not subsumed under wrong livelihood.
Why is this? Because performing songs, dances, and so forth for one's own amusement and pleasure does not serve to sustain one's life.
"It is not that wrong livelihood is wrong verbal action;
this contradicts the Sūtra because it [wrong livelihood] merely extends life through falsehood" means that by citing the Sūtra,
he refutes the attachment to receiving external objects through false means to extend one's life.
However, it should be understood that all bodily and vocal actions arising from greed are termed wrong livelihood (*mithyājīva*).
The opposite of these—right speech, right action, and right livelihood—should likewise be known;
this meaning is clarified incidentally here.
The *Nyāyānusāra* states:
"For what reason are body and speech listed first and last among the paths of action (*karmapatha*),
whereas within the eight branches of the path (*aṣṭāṅgamārga*), speech is listed first and body last?"
This is explained according to the relative coarseness or subtlety within the paths of action.
The sequence of the factors of the path is established based on their natural order of arising;
as the Sūtra says: "Having engaged in vitarka and vicāra, one utters speech."
Regarding the question raised previously as to how many fruits there are,
from this point onward, within this chapter, the third major section provides a miscellaneous explanation of various karmas. Within this:
First, clarifying that karma obtains its fruit;
second, explaining the terminology of the original treatise;
third, clarifying the causes of projection and fulfillment.
The fourth clarifies the threefold obstructions;
the fifth clarifies the obstructions of the three times;
the sixth clarifies the characteristics of a bodhisattva.
Seven, clarifying generosity, ethical discipline, and cultivation;
eight, clarifying actions that accord with the three categories; nine, clarifying the nature of writing and so forth;
ten, clarifying the various synonyms for phenomena. Regarding the first [section], clarifying how karma obtains its fruit:
First, a general explanation of the fruits of all karmas;
second, the fruits in relation to the three natures;
third, the fruits in relation to the three periods of time.
Fourth, the fruits corresponding to the various stages (*bhūmi*).
Fifth, the fruits corresponding to the three trainings (*śikṣā*).
Sixth, the fruits corresponding to the three abandonments (*prahāṇa*). This constitutes the first [section], which provides a general explanation of the fruits of all karmas.
The preceding question is restated and introduced.
The verse says: "Up to the third [category], excluding what was previously excluded.
Within this response in verse, there are four general categories.
The first two lines constitute the first category; the next two lines constitute the second category;
the following two lines constitute the third category;
and the final two lines constitute the fourth category.
The Commentary states: "Regarding 'up to' (yāvat) [the categories of] contaminated (*sāsrava*) and uncontaminated (*anāsrava*)," this explains the name of the path of abandonment (*prahāṇamārga*).
The path is able to realize the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) abandonment.
Furthermore, it is capable of severing the afflictions of the conditioned;
possessing these two types of abandonment, it receives the name "path of abandonment.
That is to say, the path of uninterrupted transition (ānantarya-mārga) is that which can induce the acquisition of abandonment.
When it reaches the moment of arising (*utpāda-lakṣaṇa*), it is called "capable of realizing" (*sākṣāt-karaṇa*);
when it is capable of severing the acquisition of afflictions (*kleśa-prāpti*) before reaching the moment of arising, it is called "capable of severing.
Thus, this path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*) both realizes and severs.
If the path of liberation is realization (*sākṣātkriyā*) rather than abandonment (*prahāṇa*),
although it lacks the functional capacity to induce the acquisition of abandonment,
it is nevertheless termed "realization" because it coexists with that acquisition of abandonment.
It is not because that power causes these afflictions to fail to reach the state of arising that it is called "able to sever. There are,
in total, two kinds of paths of abandonment that differ from one another.
This refers to the distinction between contaminated (*sāsrava*) and uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) karma.

Regarding contaminated karma on the path, it possesses three fruits— maturation (*vipāka*), outflow (*niṣyanda*), and dissociation (*visamyoga*)— excluding only that which has already arisen previously.
This may be understood according to the text. Regarding the fruit of human effort (*puruṣakāra-phala*):
first, it refers to the simultaneous fruit of human effort (*sahaja-puruṣakāra-phala*) which is drawn forth by the Path;

that is to say, the fruit of human effort that arises together [with the Path]. Second, it refers to the fruit of human effort of liberation (*vimukti-puruṣakāra-phala*) which is drawn forth by the Path.
That is the immediate *puruṣakāra-phala* (fruit of human effort). Third, that which is cultivated by the Path refers to the merits cultivated in the future;
this is either the delayed *puruṣakāra-phala*. Fourth, that which is realized by the Path.
This is precisely because it does not produce a "virile fruit" (*puruṣakāra-phala*).
Thus, the *Nyāyānusāra* states:
"The virile fruit refers to that which is drawn forth by the Path—namely, the coexistent, the liberated, the cultivated, and the abandoned."
"Co-existent" refers to dharmas that arise simultaneously.
"Liberation" refers to the path of liberation arising immediately [after the path of seeing].
"That which is cultivated" refers to cultivation in the future.
"Cessation" refers to analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*);
it arises only through the power of the Path. The dominant fruit (*adhipati-phala*) may also be understood in this way. Furthermore, the *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra*, fascicle 43, states:
"As for the dominant fruit..."
There is this teaching:
that conditioned phenomena other than intrinsic nature exist, with the sole exception of those previously arisen. Some say thus.
Cessation (*prahāṇa*) should also be the dominant fruit (*adhipatiphala*) of the Path,
because the dominant power of the Path is able to realize it.
If that is so, why does the *Vibhāṣā* state...

It is taught that the abandonment of the ten proclivities (*anuśaya*) of the desire realm is the fruit of human effort (*puruṣakāra-phala*) resulting from the receptivity to the knowledge of the dharma regarding suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-jñāna-kṣānti*).
Has it never been stated that this is also its sovereign fruit (*adhipati-phala*)? It is not the case that something is not a fruit simply because it has not been so stated.

For that very text states that the knowledge of the dharma of suffering (*duḥkha-dharmajñāna*) is the outflow fruit (*niṣyanda-phala*) and the fruit of human effort (*puruṣakāra-phala*) of the receptivity to the knowledge of the dharma of suffering (*duḥkha-dharmajñānakṣānti*),
and it never says that it is its dominant fruit (*adhipati-phala*).
Nevertheless, in reality, the knowledge of the dharma of suffering is indeed its dominant fruit.
That it is not explicitly stated is because its meaning is already established; this case should be understood in the same way.
By mentioning the fruit of human effort (*puruṣakāra-phala*), the dominant fruit (*adhipati-phala*) is logically already included.
Therefore, it is not only that which can arise [through effort] that is the dominant fruit (*adhipatiphala*).

This is because non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyānirodha*) is said to be the fruit of the mind, and there is no other sense of "fruit" apart from this. The *Nyāyānusāra* provides two interpretations.
The former master is correct,
as he accords with this treatise.
Furthermore, all other treatises state that analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) is a fruit of disjunction (*visamyoga-phala*), and do not say it is a sovereign fruit (*adhipati-phala*).
Furthermore, in various treatises, when the nature of the sovereign fruit (*adhipatiphala*) is presented,
they all state that it is conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and do not say it is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*). Moreover,
it is explained that since there is neither establishment nor refutation regarding this in the *Nyāya*, [the point is settled].
According to these differing interpretations, there is no contradiction;
although there are two explanations, the former is superior.
In future lives, it is not only those dharmas that are subject to arising which constitute the predominant fruit (*adhipatiphala*).
Furthermore, there are passages stating that the dharma of non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) is the fruit of the mind.
For this reason, it is known that all dharmas that do not arise are also results of dominance (*adhipati-phala*).
The rest of the text is self-evident.
The passage "In the path of abandonment... up to 'excluding the maturation'" explains the third and fourth lines.
Because these are untainted (*anāsrava*), the ripened fruit (*vipākaphala*) is excluded;
there are the remaining four fruits,
which may be understood by analogy with the previous explanation of the tainted (*sāsrava*) case.
Regarding the statement that "other tainted wholesome [dharmas] should be explained by analogy with this," this explains the fifth and sixth phrases:
because they are not paths of abandonment (*prahāṇa-mārga*), the fruit of dissociation (*visamyoga-phala*) is excluded.
The remaining four fruits should be explained according to the preceding [analysis].
That is to say, regarding the remaining untainted acquisitions (*anāsrava-prāpti*) and dissociations (*visamyoga*):
this explains the latter two phrases.
Because it is untainted (anāsrava) and because it is indeterminate (avyākṛta),
the fruit of maturation (vipākaphala) is excluded.
Because it is not a path of abandonment (*prahāṇa-mārga*), the fruit of disjunction (*visamyoga-phala*) is excluded.
The remaining three fruits are also explained according to the previous analysis.
Thus, the general classification of actions into the three categories of wholesome (*kuśala*) and so forth has been completed.
Below this is the second section: the results corresponding to the three natures.
This introduces the preceding inquiry.
First, the general introduction of the inquiry.
Second is the specific inquiry regarding arising.
The verse says: "Reaching the latter two, three, and three fruits.
This is the verse's answer.

The Commentary states: Regarding the meaning of the section on "pervading all preceding gates," that which is explained last among the various alternative formulations (paryāya) is expressed in accordance with the sequence [of the preceding].
This clarifies the meaning that applies pervasively across the preceding five gates as appropriate.

Regarding "wholesome, unwholesome, up to and including those dissociated [from outflows]," this explains the abundance or scarcity of results by correlating each of the three natures of karma with the phenomena of the three natures respectively.
If the three natures (trisvabhāva) are understood narrowly,
they take a portion of the two aggregates of form (rūpa-skandha) and formations (saṃskāra-skandha) as their essence.
If the three natures are understood broadly, they take all five aggregates as well as the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta) as their essence.
The breadth and narrowness are unequal: if unwholesome karma takes neutral phenomena as its outflow fruit,
it refers to suffering and the universal unwholesome [causes] within the origin of suffering.
Furthermore, the remaining unwholesome karma abandoned through the vision of suffering [produces results],
because the indeterminate factors belonging to the categories of the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*) are its outflow results (*niṣyandaphala*);
or alternatively, it is the outflow result of the omnipresent cause (*sarvatragahetu*).

Or it may be a homogeneous cause with a result of uniform outflow (*niṣyanda-phala*): if an indeterminate action has unwholesome factors as its result of uniform outflow, this refers to those indeterminate actions belonging to the categories of the view of a self-identity (*satkāya-dṛṣṭi*) and the view of extremes (*antagrāha-dṛṣṭi*).
The various unwholesome dharmas of the five classes serve as outflow fruits (*niṣyanda-phala*):
either as outflow fruits of universal causes (*sarvatraga-hetu*) or as outflow fruits of homogeneous causes (*sabhāga-hetu*).
The remaining passages can be understood by reflecting upon them.
As for the statement, "Having already distinguished the three natures up to the subsequent karmic results," this refers to the third [category]: the relative fruits across the three periods of time.
By correlating the karma of the three periods with the dharmas of the three periods, one clarifies the greater or lesser extent of their results.
The karma of the three periods is narrow,
having as its essence only a small portion of the two aggregates of form (*rūpa*) and formations (*saṃskāra*).
The dharmas of the three periods of time are broad;
they take the five aggregates as their substance.
The rest can be understood through reflection.

Having already distinguished the three time periods up to the point where "outflow" (niṣyanda) is not excluded, this constitutes the fourth [category]: the mutual results of the various stages (*bhūmi*).

By means of this text, it is proven that the result of dissociation (*visamyoga-phala*) is not included among the factors belonging to the stages. Furthermore, another interpretation holds that this passage generally cites the karma of the nine stages, taking those factors belonging to the same stage as the four results.
If one distinguishes them separately,
the karma of the upper eight stages takes the dharmas of its own stage as five fruits; thus,
the *Samyuktābhidharmahṛdaya-śāstra* says:

If one correctly contemplates that the stages (bhūmi) also possess the fruit of liberation (vimukti-phala), then according to the text of the *Saṃyuktābhidharmahṛdaya*, the fruit of dissociation (visamyoga-phala) is likewise included among the factors of the stages. Since dissociation is unconditioned (asaṃskṛta), [it follows that it is not comprised within the stages].
Since it does not arise in dependence upon the earth element,
how can it be said to be subsumed under the dharmas of the earth?
Therefore, one knows that what is stated in this treatise is correct.
The remaining thoughts can be understood by inference.
Having already distinguished the various stages up to their fivefold fruits, this constitutes the fifth [section]: the fruits in relation to the three trainings.
The distinction of the fruits is established by correlating the karma of the three trainings with the dharmas of the three trainings.
If the karma of training has as its essence a portion of the two aggregates— form and formations— at the stage of training,
then the karma of no-more-training has as its essence a portion of the two aggregates— form and formations— at the stage of no-more-training.

Non-learner and non-non-learner karma has as its essence a portion of the two aggregates of contaminated form and formations (*saṃskāra*). Learner dharmas have as their essence the conditioned, uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) dharmas belonging to the stage of a learner.
If the dharmas of one beyond training (aśaikṣadharma) take as their essence the conditioned, untainted (anāsrava) dharmas belonging to the stage of one beyond training;

and if the dharmas that are neither of training nor beyond training (naivaśaikṣanāśaikṣadharma) take as their essence all other dharmas, excluding the conditioned, untainted dharmas—taken collectively.
The karma of the three trainings is narrow;
the dharmas of the three trainings are broad.

This can also be understood from the text. The *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra* states: "The karma of one beyond training (aśaikṣa) takes the dharmas of training (śaikṣa) as a single fruit, namely, the dominant fruit (*adhipati-phala*)."
In principle, one should say there are two;
that is, adding the outflowing cause (*niṣyanda-hetu*). The commentary explains:

the meaning of the *Nyāya* (Principles) is that the dull path of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa-mārga*) serves as the homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*) for the future sharp path of learning (*śaikṣa-mārga*).
This refers to cases where [the faculty] does not manifest.
Alternatively, when one who is liberated by occasion (samayavimukta) falls away and transforms their faculties to become one who has attained vision (dṛṣṭiprāpta),
they take the past dull path of no-more-learning as its homogeneous cause.
The "learning through vision" (*śaikṣa-darśana-prāpta*) constitutes the outflow fruit (*niṣyanda-phala*).
This statement refers to its actual manifestation; thus, it is said to be "equal to the outflow," which differs from the *Abhidharmakośa*.
This constitutes a distinct intent of the treatise,
making it difficult to reconcile. Furthermore, another interpretation holds that according to the *Abhidharmakośa*, because factors of the same category arise sequentially from one another,
those in training (*śaikṣa*) and those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) serve as causes for each other.
That which is beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) does not serve as a cause for that which is in training (*śaikṣa*).

According to the *Nyāyānusāra*, because they are considered from the perspective of their differing natures, it is said that even that which is beyond training serves as a cause for that which is in training. Each statement is based on a single specific meaning, and thus they do not contradict one another. Having already analyzed the general principles regarding those in training and so forth, such should be the case.

This is the sixth [category], the result of the mutual correspondence between the three types of abandonment (*prahāṇa*). It consists of the differentiation of results based on the relationship between actions of the three abandonments and phenomena of the three abandonments: If an action to be abandoned by seeing (*darśana-heya*) has as its substance a small portion of the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) abandoned by the four truths; If an action to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) has as its substance a small portion of both the aggregates of form (*rūpa-skandha*) and formations abandoned by cultivation; If an action that is not to be abandoned (*aprahāṇa*) has as its substance a small portion of both the aggregates of form and formations that are conditioned and untainted (*anāsrava*); If a phenomenon to be abandoned by seeing has as its substance the aggregates of feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), formations, and consciousness abandoned by the four truths; If a phenomenon to be abandoned by cultivation has as its substance the five aggregates abandoned by cultivation; If a phenomenon that is not to be abandoned has as its substance all untainted phenomena (*anāsrava-dharma*). In summary:
The three abandonments of karma are narrow;
the three abandonments of dharmas are broad.
Once one knows the broad and the narrow, they can be understood through discerning reflection. Regarding the sixth phrase, "all are respectively as follows":
These [explanations] should be applied accordingly throughout all the preceding sections.
At the end of each verse, one should state that "all should be understood in their respective order.
Such is the nature of this abbreviated method.
Regarding the section "Distinguishing Various Karmas up to the Third [Type] of Mutual Contradiction," this constitutes the second major section of the text,
which explains the karma of the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya*. A question is posed,
and a verse is offered as the response.
The Commentary states: Regarding the distinction between the two explanations, each of the three—*karaṇīya* (to be done), *akaraṇīya* (not to be done), and the third—has two interpretations.

According to the intention of the first master: the three types of defiled karma are called *akaraṇīya*; the three types of wholesome karma are called *karaṇīya*; and the three types of non-obscured neutral karma are called the third. According to the intention of the latter master: [the three types of defiled karma...]
Furthermore, among the non-obscured [neutral states], all bodily and vocal actions that violate established norms and fail to conform to proper decorum,
as well as the volitions that motivate these two types of action,
are all termed "unfit to be done" (akaraṇīya).
This refers to all defiled [actions],
a portion of the non-obscured [neutral actions], and all wholesome threefold karmas;
as well as, within the non-obscured, those bodily and vocal karmas that do not violate established norms and accord with worldly etiquette.
Furthermore, the volition that motivates these two types of action is also called "to be performed" (*kārya*);
this refers to wholesome action in its entirety.
The "unobscured" category is a partial [classification]; within the unobscured, one excludes the three types of karma—those that ought to be done and those that ought not to be done.
The remaining three types of karma are termed the third [category] among the two teachers.
The former [statement] was spoken in terms of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*) and exhausts the principle;
the latter is spoken in terms of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti*) and does not exhaust the principle.
Therefore, the *Nyāya* states:
If one relies on the conventional truth, the latter case may also be so;

if one proceeds from the ultimate truth, the former explanation is superior. Since the preceding treatise has already clarified the breadth and narrowness [of these positions], the interpretation of the text can be understood.
Regarding whether it is by one karma or by many karmas that [rebirth] is projected:
hereafter, thirdly, the causes of projection (*ākṣepa-hetu*) and completion (*paripūri-hetu*) are explained. Within this:
First, it clarifies the multiplicity and scarcity of karmic results;
second, it clarifies the essential nature of the projecting and completing causes. This first section clarifying the multiplicity and scarcity of karmic results raises two general questions.
The verse says: "Up to the maximum, karma can bring about fulfillment.
If it is said that a single karma projects one birth, it cannot project many births.
Answering the first question: If it is said that one birth is projected by one karma and not by many karmas;
answering the second question: the latter phrase resolves the objection.
The treatise says: "When it comes to what is called 'birth' (jāti), according to our own school, the Sarvāstivāda, one should state as follows:
it is manifested by a single karma, not by multiple karmas; it projects only a single birth."

This demonstrates that [a single karma] does not project multiple births. If multiple karmas were to project a single birth, there would have to be repeated deaths and births, because the fruits of the karmas are distinct.
If, on the other hand, a single karma were to project multiple births...
In that case, karma determined by time would become confused.
If so, for what reason does it happen that one attains much happiness? [This is] difficult to explain.
If it is said that a single karma induces only one birth and does not induce many births,
for what reason is it not extinguished?
Such is the statement made.

In the past, by virtue of the single cause of giving food to a pratyekabuddha, he experienced the ripening fruit of being reborn seven times among gods and humans; or rather, that single gift of food served as the ripening cause.
Because he experienced seven births alternating between the heavens and the human realm,
it is established that a single karma can project many lifetimes.
Aniruddha (in Sanskrit, *Aniruddha*).
The old translations "Aniruddha" or "Aniruddhaka" are both erroneous.
He attained great wealth and happiness through a single karmic act.
There are two explanations regarding this;
this is the first explanation.
According to that, a single karma brings about only a single birth.
The remaining six causes are produced through successive differentiation based on this.

It is said that "a single gift" is due to the power of the first [cause]. The analogies can be understood accordingly. As for those with wisdom from previous lives, it may arise either through the maturation of karma.
Or it may not be produced by karma;
herein, we take only that which is produced by karma.
Furthermore, there are those who say [the process continues] until the differentiation of each part.
This is the subsequent explanation:
by means of a single act of giving food, many thoughts and vows arise,
resulting in distinct rebirths among gods and humans.
The moments are not identical;
there is a sequence of priority and posteriority.
It is spoken of as "one" with reference to the basis upon which the food is bestowed.
According to the principle that the volition capable of giving food is actually manifold, a single karma cannot project multiple births;
if it were to project multiple births, it would result in confusion. Furthermore, there is no case where a single birth is projected by multiple karmas.
"One does not die and be born repeatedly with various distinctions because the karmic fruits of the *nikāyasabhāga* (homogeneous class) differ.
This explains the second phrase, clarifying that although it is a single karma, there may be many instances of deficiency.
Although the projecting karma (*ākṣepaka-karma*) is singular,
the completing karma (*paripūraka-karma*) is manifold.
A single color serves as a metaphor for the projecting karma.
The various colors are a metaphor for completing karma (*paripūri-karman*); therefore, the following passage reveals that there are many types of completing karma.
Furthermore, the *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra*, fascicle 43, states:
"In this context, a single color serves as the metaphor."
It constitutes a single type of karma and a single moment;
if one were to use a single type as an analogy, it would contradict the principles of this school.
The statement that "a single birth is projected by non-unitary karma" may be understood in reference to a single category [of karma],
because within such a category there must necessarily be many [karmic instances];
for it is illogical that many [distinct] karmas should project a single birth.
If one were to say that a single color represents a single moment,
then since a single moment cannot delineate a shape,
the proposed analogy would lack the power to prove the point.
Now, this illustration refers to a certain class of karma.
How can it be established that projecting karma is categorized by type?
For there are many karmas that project a single realm of existence.
The meaning of this statement is as follows:
within a single category of karma, only one moment projects the generic similarity (nikāyasabhāga);
however, because multiple moments of karma—whether of the same or different types—can bring it to completion, they are said to be "many."
Therefore, it is as when one first sketches the outline of a form with a single color and subsequently fills it in with various hues;
this statement accords with reason. It is not merely because the power of karma has reached a state of inferiority.
Furthermore, to provide a detailed analysis:
the two causes of projection (*ākṣepa*) and completion (*paripūri*) are not limited to karma alone, but also extend to other phenomena;
they differ in terms of being superior or inferior.
This can be understood according to the text.
As for what the essence of these two categories is:
the following second section clarifies the essence of the two causes—namely, the drawing-in cause and the fulfilling cause.
This is the question.
The verse says: "Up to 'all lead to both the projecting and the fulfilling'.
This is the answer.
Because the two mindless attainments are wholesome,
although they possess maturation (*vipāka*), they lack the power to project a homogeneous class of beings (*nikāyasabhāga*),
as they are not co-existent causes (*sahabhūhetu*) with other karmas.
Acquisition also lacks the power to project a homogeneous class (*nikāyasabhāga*),
because it does not share the same fruit as the various karmas.
This applies to all remaining unwholesome and wholesome contaminated (*sāsrava*) phenomena.

Because it acts as a co-existent cause (*sahabhū-hetu*) for all karmas and possesses functional power, it pertains to both projecting (*ākṣepa*) and completing (*paripūraṇa*). Furthermore, the *Abhidharmamahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* (vol. 19) also states that the homogeneous character (*nikāya-sabhāga*) is a projected fruit (*ākṣepa-phala*).

The remainder are the fruits of fulfillment (*paripūri-phala*). Furthermore, according to the intent of the *Abhidharma-nyāyānusāra*, volition (*cetanā*) brings about both projection (*ākṣepa*) and fulfillment;
the remainder bring about fulfillment only. Question: Regarding the two meditative attainments (*samāpatti*) and acquisition (*prāpti*)...
If it is not induced by a cause of attraction, how can it fulfill the result? Answer: As stated in the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 19, the critique says: "One should state this:
the maturation of the non-conceptual realm (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*) is exclusively the result of the meditative attainment of non-conception (*asaṃjñi-samādhi*)."

The life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*), the group-homogeneity (*nikāyasabhāga*), and the five material faculties (*rūpendriya*) that are karmic maturations (*vipāka*) belong exclusively to the mental karma of the fourth dhyāna.

The maturation of its remaining aggregates is a common fruit (*sādhāraṇaphala*). Question: What kind of maturation fruit does the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*) receive? Answer: It receives the maturation fruit of the four aggregates of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*).
Excluding the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) and the homogeneous character of a group (*nikāyasabhāga*), because these are exclusively the fruits of karma. Question:

What kind of ripened fruit (*vipākaphala*) do the various acquisitions (*prāpti*) and sensations (*vedanā*) produce? Answer: The various acquisitions and sensations produce as their ripened fruit matter (*rūpa*), mind (*citta*), mental factors (*caitasika dharma*), and formations dissociated from mind (*cittaviprayuktasaṃskāra*).
"Form" refers to visible form,
odor, taste, and tangibility; it does not refer to the five physical sense-faculties.
Due to the fruit of that karma,
the mind and mental factors consist of painful feeling,
pleasant feeling, and neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling.
And their associated dharmas.

As for the formations dissociated from mind (*citta-viprayukta-saṃskāra*), these refer to acquisitions (*prāpti*), birth (*jāti*), aging (*jarā*), duration (*sthiti*), and impermanence (*anityatā*). Furthermore, it says: "Question: Do those who perform karmic actions first perform the karma that draws forth the homogeneous class (*nikāya-sabhāga*)?"
Is it that one first creates the karma that completes the *nikāya-sabhāga*? Those who speak thus say that this is not fixed;
for there are cases where one first creates the projecting karma (*ākṣepaka-karman*) and subsequently creates the completing karma (*paripūraka-karman*).

There may be cases where one first creates the completing karma (*paripūri-karman*) and subsequently creates the projecting karma (*ākṣepa-karman*), because it arises according to the intention of the agent.
Regarding this, the Blessed One said: "As for what its substance is... [and so forth].
Below this, the fourth major section explains the threefold hindrances.
Within it, the first part provides a general explanation of these three hindrances.
Second, the specific explanation of karmic obstructions (*karmāvaraṇa*). Within the general explanation of the three obstructions, there are two parts:

first, the presentation of the essential nature of the three obstructions; second, the analysis according to realms and destinies. This is the first: the presentation of the essential nature of the three obstructions.
The question arises based on the Sūtra. This chapter extensively elucidates the various types of karma;
since the meaning of karma is closely related to the three obstacles (*āvaraṇa*), it proceeds to explain the three obstacles by way of contextual relevance.
The verse says: "Reaching the Northern Continent and the Heaven of Non-conception.
This is the response in verse.
The commentary says: "Reaching what is called 'karmic obstruction'."
The essential nature of the karmic obstacles can thus be understood.
Regarding the statement that "afflictions are of two kinds" up to the point where they are called "affliction-obstacles": [this refers to the following].
Regarding the essence of the obstacle of afflictions (*kleśāvaraṇa*): in general,
there are two types of afflictions.
First is habitual practice,
which refers to the constant arising of afflictions.
Second is intensity.
This refers to intense afflictions (*adhimātra-kleśa*).
In relation to this, four permutations (*catuṣkoṭi*) should be established: 1. Frequent occurrence but not intense:
this refers to afflictions of a weak grade (*mṛdu*) that manifest repeatedly. 2. Intense but not frequent occurrence.
That is to say: (1) intense afflictions do not manifest frequently; (2) they manifest frequently but are not intense;
(3) intense afflictions manifest frequently; and (4) they neither manifest frequently nor are they intense.

That is to say, when afflictions of a weak grade do not manifest frequently; one should know that, among these, only those [afflictions] that manifest frequently are termed "afflictive obstructions" (kleśāvaraṇa), as indicated by the first and third phrases.
Just as the afflictions that frequently manifest in those such as the *śaṇḍha* are difficult to subdue and eliminate,
they are therefore described as obstacles;
for even though superior-grade afflictions may be intense and sharp, [they are not as persistent].
Because they do not arise constantly, they are easily subdued and eliminated;
thus, they are not described as obstacles. Among the inferior grades, although the afflictions that frequently manifest are not intense, they are difficult to subdue and eliminate.
Because those [defilements] are constantly active and it is difficult to find an opportunity [to counteract them],
that is to say, when one is born from a lower realm into a middle realm, or from a middle realm into an upper realm,
they cause the seven preparatory paths of suppression to arise.

Because the path cannot arise unless the patience regarding suffering and so forth have already eliminated it, among the afflictions, those that manifest repeatedly according to their respective grades— whether superior or inferior—
are designated as the essence of the afflictive hindrance (*kleśāvaraṇa*).
In total, the sections are divided into two categories, referred to only as "upper" and "lower";
therefore, "middle" is not mentioned.
Alternatively, the mention of "upper" and "lower" implies the "middle" by contrast.
This can be understood.
It should be known that these constitute the substance of the hindrances solely by virtue of their active manifestation (*samudācāra*), and not by virtue of their latent possession (*prāpti*).
Therefore, the *Mahāvibhāṣā* states:
Question: How is this afflictive hindrance established?
Is it based on possession (*samanvāgama*) or on active manifestation (*samudācāra*)? Answer: It is based on active manifestation.
It is not based on accomplishment.
If it were based on accomplishment, then all sentient beings would be without distinction, as they equally possess the accomplishment of all afflictions.
Thus, the entirety of the three evil destinies is designated as the obstacle of maturation (*vipāka-āvaraṇa*).
The nature of the obstacle to rebirth consists of the three evil destinies in their entirety and,
within the human destiny, the northern continent.
Within the realm of gods, taking birth in the Heaven of Non-conceptualization (asaṃjñisattva-deva) constitutes an obstacle to maturation (vipāka-āvaraṇa).
What kind of phenomenon is this obstacle?
Question:
Regarding that which obstructs the noble path up to the roots of goodness of application (*prayoga-kuśalamūla*). Answer:
That is to say, it obstructs the noble path and the roots of goodness that constitute the preparatory application for the noble path;
it may also obstruct an ordinary person from becoming free from defilement.
Therefore, the *Nyāyānusāra* (Treatise on Correct Reasoning), fascicle 43, states:
"Because it obstructs the Noble Path, its provisions, and the state of being free from defilement. The aforementioned treatise follows this principle.
Regarding the fact that Mahābrahmā is not mentioned among the obstacles of maturation (*vipākāvaraṇa*), it is because one can abandon defilements through the path with outflows (*sāsravamārga*).
Furthermore, regarding the reason why he is not mentioned among the obstacles of karma (*karmāvaraṇa*) up to this point,
the preceding section clarifies the establishment and exclusion of these obstacles.

Within the context of karmic obstructions, it is also logical to speak of other determinate karma; that is, all other karma certain to result in the miserable realms, because Noble Ones are not reborn in the three evil destinies.
The Noble Ones (ārya) also do not undergo birth from eggs or moisture-born birth.

Although there are indeed those born from eggs or moisture who have entered the Noble Path, such as Śaila and others, it is absolutely impossible for one who has attained the state of a Noble One to undergo those two modes of birth. Once they have attained the state of a Noble One, they no longer receive a female body.

Although there may be women who can enter the Noble Path, once they have attained the state of a noble one, they will certainly never again receive a female body. Having attained the state of a noble one, they will definitely not undergo an eighth existence within the desire realm, nor will they take birth in a single location or for two lifetimes in the form or formless realms. All that has not been explicitly mentioned is included here by way of analogy. Such are the various types of determinate karma.
It can also act as an obstruction, preventing one from entering the state of a noble being (*ārya*).

It should likewise be said that it is subsumed within the category of karmic obstructions (*karmāvaraṇa*). However, if there is karma that is easy to perceive and easy to know due to five causes and conditions...
This is explained here with particular emphasis:
namely, the five factors such as the basis (*sthāna*).
Among all types of karma, only immediate retribution (*ānantarya-karma*) possesses these five characteristics.
Because they are easy to see and easy to know, they are explained separately;

other karmas are not so, and therefore they are not mentioned here. Regarding the five factors beginning with "place" (*sthāna*), the *Nyāyānusāra* (Treatise on the Correct Principle), fascicle 43, explains as follows:

The *Vibhāṣā* states that these five causes and conditions— namely, the place, the destiny, the birth, the fruit, and the person— are easy to see and easy to know, and are thus designated as karmic obstructions (*karmāvaraṇa*).
"Abode" (sthāna) refers to the fact that these five destinies take mothers and so forth as their place of origin.
"Destination" (gati) refers to the fact that these five destinies have the hells as their destination.
"Birth" (upapatti) refers to the fact that these five destinies produce their respective karmic maturations (vipāka) immediately [upon death].
"Result" (phala) refers to the fact that these five definitely bring about undesirable results.
"Person" (pudgala) refers to the fact that these five heinous crimes (*ānantarya*) rely upon grave afflictions;

it is universally recognized by persons that such an individual is capable of harming their mother and so forth. Other karmas are not so, and thus they are not established as obstructions. Furthermore, in the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 115:
Among these five, "place" is not mentioned; instead,
"intrinsic nature" is added.
Therefore, that treatise states:
"By way of intrinsic nature" means that these five types of nature are determinate and extremely grave evil karmas.
The remaining four are discussed in the same manner as this treatise.
Regarding the statement that "the establishment or rejection of other obstacles should be understood accordingly":
the other afflictive obstacles (*kleśāvaraṇa*) and the obstacle of maturation (*vipākāvaraṇa*) are established or rejected according to their respective meanings.
It should be understood as follows: first, the afflictive obstruction (*kleśāvaraṇa*) is established on the basis of a single principle, namely, those afflictions that are habitually active;
others that are not habitually active are not established as obstructions. Furthermore, the ripening obstruction (*vipākāvaraṇa*) is established on the basis of a single principle.
This means that if one is born in such a place, they will certainly not enter the state of a noble one (*ārya*);
as for other places where this is not certain, they are not established as obstacles.
Furthermore, the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 115, states:
Question: On other continents as well, there are those for whom karmic maturation acts as an obstacle, such as those who are *śaṇḍha*, *paṇḍaka*, sexless, or hermaphrodites.
Why are these not mentioned here?
The answer is that this should have been explained here;
however, the fact that it was not stated should be understood as an incomplete exposition.
For this reason, it was previously stated that within this context, all three obstructions are presented as incomplete expositions.
Furthermore, there are those who say:
"In this context, only that which is definitely an obstacle is mentioned;
that [other factor] is not definite."
Depending on the specific karmic maturation (vipāka) of those sentient beings,
it may either act as an obstacle or not act as an obstacle.
For this reason, it is not explained by saying that eunuchs (paṇḍaka) have pulled out the [seeds of] all oxen.

Since those such as eunuchs can manifest the male organ (puruṣendriya) and are also able to enter the state of a noble one (ārya), it is said that [the timing of liberation] is not fixed. Furthermore, this explains the establishment and exclusion of the other two obstacles.
This should be understood as appropriate within the context of five causal conditions.
Among these five types, the obstacle of afflictions (*kleśāvaraṇa*) is established by way of two meanings:
the locus and the person (*pudgala*).
"Location" refers to the locus where the active defilements arise;
"person" refers to the individual who gives rise to those defilements.

One who practices what is unloved is so because they are agitated regarding both the defiled and purified categories.
One who dwells in purity is not a transgressor of the precepts.
Because those who have violated the precepts lack authority in their speech;
for this reason, it is known that the schism of the Saṃgha occurs first, followed by the severing of the roots of goodness.
It is required that one possess *śīla* because it implies a majestic and solemn demeanor;
furthermore, if one severs the roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*), one abandons the precepts.
Thus, the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 116, states:
Question: What kind of person (*pudgala*) destroys the wheel of the Dharma?
Answer: There are two kinds of persons:
first, those who act out of craving (*tṛṣṇā-carita*).
Second, those who act out of views.
It is those who act out of views who fracture the Saṃgha of the Wheel of Dharma,
not those who act out of affection.
Because the intentions of those who practice through vision are firm and intense,
they possess certainty regarding what is to be done in the categories of affliction and purification and never regress;
those who practice through craving do not possess such qualities.
Therefore, it cannot be destroyed. Furthermore, only men can destroy the Saṃgha by causing a schism in the Wheel of Dharma;
neither women, nor *śaṇḍhas*, nor *paṇḍakas*, and so forth, can do so.

Why is this? Because when the Wheel of Dharma is destroyed, it is the natural law that one establishes oneself as the Great Teacher; however, women are not superior vessels, and thus [the status of] a Great Teacher is not their lot.
Therefore, they are unable to cause a schism.

Nevertheless, they are capable of extensively employing the means for causing a schism in the Saṃgha, just like the bhikṣuṇī Audārikī and others. All *śaṇḍhas*, *pandakas*, those without sexual organs, and those with both sets of organs are characterized by passionate conduct.
The intentions of those who act out of craving are neither firm nor intense;
they are indeterminate regarding both the defiled and the purified categories.
Therefore, such individuals cannot cause a schism in the Saṃgha;
it must be in a separate location, for once the schism reaches the point of confrontation, no one has the power [to prevent it].
This explains "in a separate location."
"Another location" refers to Mount Kajaśīrṣa, which in this language is called Elephant-Head Mountain (Gajatārāga).
It is so named because the summit of the mountain resembles the head of an elephant.
To the north of Vulture Peak Mountain, at a distance of three or four *li* within the same boundary,
Devadatta resided there and caused a schism in the Saṃgha; therefore, it was not in the presence of the Great Master.
The old transcription "Mount Gayā" is erroneous.
Because the sounds of *Kaṭaśa* and *Gayā* are similar,
it was thus mistakenly transmitted.
However, there is another Gayā Mountain in the western region,
located more than one hundred and fifty *li* from Vulture Peak Mountain;
they do not belong to the same realm.
This is not a case of schism in the Saṃgha;
it refers only to the breaking [of the Saṃgha] by ordinary beings (pṛthagjana), which is why the term "foolish person" (bāla) is used.
This explains the "foolish person."

The term "foolish person" (*bāla*) is used here to encompass both meanings previously mentioned: that of one who has not yet attained the name of a noble one (*ārya*), and that of one who has not yet attained forbearance (*kṣānti*).
As for the requirement that the schismatic saṃgha must exist at such a time: it refers to the period when the saṃgha is actually in a state of division.

To clarify the time when the Saṃgha is broken, it is said that there must be a remaining noble path;

"The Śramaṇa Gautama is not [right].

When, precisely, is it said that the Wheel of Dharma and the Saṃgha are split?
The *Prakaraṇapāda-śāstra* states:

At this point, it should be said that the Wheel of Dharma and the Saṃgha are destroyed.
Furthermore, there are those who say that once the formal declaration has been made,
the speaker departs from the place where the teaching was heard.
Furthermore, there are those who say it is apart from the object seen;
others say it is apart from the sphere of seeing and hearing.
When one speaks in this way, if by intention one pledges to follow another teacher, [one abandons the precepts].
It refers to that group of foolish bhikṣus who,
out of a fixed intention, give rise to such a thought and utter such words:
"Devadatta is our great teacher."
It is not the Buddha, the World-Honored One.
Up to this point, it should be said that the Wheel of Dharma and the Saṃgha have been destroyed. Regarding the "five dharmas," the *Nyāyānusāra* states:
Regarding what is called the "false path":
Devadatta falsely proclaimed five matters to be the path to liberation.
The first is that one should not consume milk and other such things.
Second, abstaining from meat;
third, abstaining from salt;
fourth, one should wear uncut garments.
Fifth, one should reside in a monastery on the outskirts of a village. The commentary explains that "milk and so forth" includes curd, fresh butter, clarified butter, and ghee.
These five are designated as "named flavors."
The rest of the text may be understood. Furthermore, the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 116, states:
"What are the five dharmas?
First, wearing rag-robes (*pāṃsukūla*) for as long as one lives."
Second, to beg for food for the rest of one's life;
third, to eat while seated in a single posture for the rest of one's life;
fourth, to dwell constantly in the open air for the rest of one's life.
Fifth, for as long as one lives, one must abstain from all fish, meat, blood, salt, clarified butter, milk, and so forth—these five items according to the *Vibhāṣā*.
This differs from the *Nyāya* (Correct Principle).

Regarding the statement, "This night must be spent in harmony so as not to cause a schism in the Saṃgha," the Master Paramārtha explains that this means one should not spend the night apart [from the community].
The Master Paramārtha says: [text continues].
The schism occurred when the sun was about to set;
by the third watch of the night, they had returned to harmony once more.
Therefore it is said that they must reconcile this very night and shall not remain divided for even a single night.
This is called the schism of the Wheel-turning Sangha (cakrabheda).
Because it obstructs the wheel of the Noble Path and destroys the harmony of the Sangha,
the failure of the Noble Path to turn is termed the "schism of the Wheel."
To destroy the harmony of the Saṃgha is called "schism.
Thus, the *Nyāyānusāra* states:
"When the assembly endorses what he has said, it is termed 'breaking the Wheel of Dharma' (*cakrabheda*)."
It is also called "schism of the Saṃgha.
Regarding the question of how many people from which continent [can cause it] and how many from which continent [are required]:
this section below, the fourth, clarifies the distinction between the two types of schisms.
The questions concern both the subject matter and the persons involved:
first, the question regarding the Wheel of Dharma;

The verse states: "Reaching the three continents, eight [types], etc.
The first two lines answer the initial question;
the latter two lines answer the subsequent question.
The Commentary states: "Reaching beyond this limitlessly" explains the two preceding lines,
clarifying the breaking of the Wheel of Dharma (*cakrabheda*).
This can be understood from the text as it stands.
Furthermore, the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* states:
"Question: At the time of the schism of the Saṃgha, was the Buddha present within the assembly?"
Answer: When the Buddha was in that realm, he was not among the assembly.
How is this known? It has been heard as follows:
When Devadatta sought to cause a schism in the Saṃgha,
the Buddha, out of compassion, rebuked and restrained him,
saying: "Devadatta, do not cause a schism in the Saṃgha."
"Do not give rise to extremely heavy, evil, and unwholesome states;
do not proceed toward the state of great suffering that is undesirable.
Although the Buddha thus earnestly rebuked and restrained them,
Yet he had no intention at all of ceasing [his actions].
At that time, the World-Honored One gave rise to right knowledge and vision and examined the past:
"In former times, I caused the dissolution of others' retinues."
He immediately perceived for himself:
"In the past, during immeasurable and incalculable eons, I once destroyed the retinue of another rishi.
The ripening of that karma is now manifest before me."
Having perceived this, he knew that the Saṃgha would certainly be split;
he then entered his private chamber and sat in silent meditation.
Devadatta then proceeded to cause a schism in the Saṃgha.
Thus, one should know that the World-Honored One was within the boundary but not among the assembly;
"only the breaking of the *karmavācanā* applies" refers to the reason for this, and the word "etc.
(*ādi*) explains the two subsequent phrases. Regarding "pervading the three continents":
Because there is the sacred teaching (āgama) and because there is the community of ordained disciples (pravrajita-śrāvaka-saṃgha).
The rest of the text may be understood accordingly. The *Nyāyānusāra* states:

At what time can there be a schism of the Saṃgha and a schism of the Saṃgha regarding formal acts? From the time after the establishment of the boundary until now, and even until the Dharma has not yet ceased, there may be a schism of the Wheel of Dharma.
Excluding the six time-periods. Furthermore, the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 116, states:
Question: Regarding the schism of the Saṃgha by means of formal acts (*karmabhedaka*) and the schism of the Saṃgha by means of the Wheel of Dharma (*dharmacakrabhedaka*).
What is the distinction?
The answer is: "One who breaks the *karmavācanā* (formal act) refers to a case where there are two assemblies of monks within a single boundary (*sīmā*)."
To perform the *poṣadha* ceremony and recite the precepts while dwelling separately is what constitutes "breaking the wheel of the Dharma"; that is to say,
establishing a different teacher and a different path.
Just as Devadatta said, "I am the Great Teacher,
not the śramaṇa Gautama;
these five dharmas are the path."
When the Noble Eightfold Path taught by Gautama is not present,
at that time the Wheel of Dharma cannot be split;
this is the fifth occasion when the Wheel of Dharma cannot be split.
The treatise states: "Up to the point where there is no one who destroys the Wheel of Dharma. A "pustule" refers to a boil or ulcer.

Wrong precepts and wrong views are called the two pustules. Wrong precepts refer to asserting that the five factors constitute the Path; wrong views refer to repudiating the Buddha’s Eightfold Noble Path as not being the Path.
The remainder of the text may be understood. Furthermore, the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 116, states:
"It is neither the beginning nor the end," because at these two times, the community of bhikṣus [is particularly vast].
"In the holy teaching, they are unified in a single flavor and indestructible" means that within the holy teaching, the two types of "cysts"—namely, those of precepts and views—have not yet arisen;
it does not mean that they have not yet been unified by collectively establishing a boundary (*sīmā*).
Because it is only when there are two monastic communities within a single boundary (*sīmā*),
dwelling separately and holding divergent views, that it is termed "schism" (*saṃghabheda*);
this does not apply before the first pair [of disciples] has been established.
This means that as long as the first pair [of disciples] has not yet been established,
there is certainly no one capable of breaking the Wheel of Dharma within the Sangha;
for it is the natural law of all Buddhas that they always have a pair of noble disciples who are their foremost companions.
If there should be a monastic community that has split the Wheel of Dharma,
before even a day and night have passed,
this first pair shall cause them to be reconciled once more.
"Not after the Great Teacher has entered parinirvāṇa" means that if,
after the Great Teacher has passed into parinirvāṇa,
one were to say, "I am the Great Teacher, not the Tathāgata."
They all reproached him together, saying:
"When the Great Master was in the world, why did you not say, 'I am the Great Master'?
Only now, after his parinirvāṇa, do you speak these words."
Therefore, it is certain that during these six periods the Wheel of Dharma cannot be destroyed, whereas during other times the Wheel of Dharma may be destroyed.
It is not the case that the destruction of the Wheel of Dharma occurs only when these specific conditions exist.
This demonstrates that the breaking of the Wheel of Dharma results from past karma;
as previously stated, he once destroyed the retinue of another rishi. Furthermore, the *Nyāyānusāra* states:
Regarding this, during the time of Kāśyapa Buddha in this Bhadrakalpa,
Śākyamuni once defeated the assemblies of others; thus,
both the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* and the *Nyāyānusāra* each cite this as an instance.
This is why they differ.
Let us set aside this digression for now and proceed to the point that it harms those who are no longer in training (*aśaikṣa*).
This constitutes the third [section], clarifying the establishment of adverse conditions (*pratyaya*).
