Furthermore, because it is capable of destroying the superior qualities that can arise in others, it constitutes a heinous offense (*ānantarya*) by destroying the physical body that serves as the basis for those superior qualities. Moreover, the *Nyāya* states:
"If there is a father or mother, at the time their child is first born..."
He was abandoned on a path frequented by jackals and wolves for the purpose of killing him;
or else, while still in the womb, he was sought to be killed by various means,
yet due to the power of his fixed karma (*niyata-karma*), the son did not die.
What kindness did he have that one would abandon him and commit such a transgression?
It must certainly be due to the fear of being unable to survive;
driven by an urgent concern for his own livelihood, he suddenly gave rise to the intent to kill his son.
However, when abandoning them, one must certainly harbor compassion;
for one's mind is repeatedly entangled by affection for one's children.
If one abandons this kindness, one incurs the grave offense of patricide or matricide.
This is to show that there are inferior, middling, and superior degrees of the heinous crimes (ānantarya).
Thus it is said that all forms of abandoning kindness constitute a heinous crime;
or rather, it is because the field (kṣetra) of the mother and others is naturally such by its very nature.
If one were to take the life of someone who has done no kindness to them,
that person would certainly be reborn in the Avīci Hell;
this is what all wise people say.
The World-Honored One, having thoroughly realized the root source of the Dharma, spoke these words: "One should simply have deep faith.
Regarding the question, "If one kills by transforming the physical form of one's father or mother, does this constitute a parricidal offense?"—this explains the second phrase.
This is the question. Regarding the statement that the crime of immediate retribution is also established even when the father changes gender,
this is the answer.
The crime of immediate retribution (ānantarya) is also established,
because the body upon which it depends is one and the same both before and after.
For this reason, the *Vibhāṣā* poses the following question:
Is there a case where one causes a male to lose his life-force, yet he is neither his father nor an Arhat, and nevertheless incurs the offense of an immediate retribution?
The answer is: Yes.
That is to say, the mother has undergone a change of gender and become male.
Question: Is there any case where one causes a woman to lose her life-force, yet she is neither one's mother nor an Arhat?
"And would one incur the offense of immediate retribution (ānantarya)?
He replied: "Yes;
that is to say, when a father changes his gender and becomes a woman."
"If there were a woman who committed the crime of matricide,
which is an immediate transgression," this explains the third phrase; it is a question.
Regarding the phrase "because that blood serves as the cause for its growth and development," the answer is:
it is because the body is formed by means of those drops of blood.
This is because she is the biological mother, and by killing her one incurs the immediate transgression (*ānantarya-karma*), as she is the source from whom one was born.
The second woman is merely the foster mother;
regarding all matters such as coming and going, one should consult the latter mother.
Because that stepmother was able to suckle, nourish, and bring him to maturity,
the *Nyāyānusāra* states:
"That which is born from her blood."
Because consciousness increases only when it has a basis,
the second woman is merely like a foster mother;
although all actions should be consulted with and decided upon her, [she is not the primary cause].
However, the harm merely constitutes an "immediate" (ānantarya) offense of a similar class.
If one kills one's parents while intending [to kill] someone else,
this will be explained below as being without [the specific gravity of] error and so forth.
This correctly clarifies that there is no *ānantarya* offense for killing by mistake;
this may be understood from the text itself.
Therefore, the *Vibhāṣā* states:
One incurs the offense of immediate retribution through two causal conditions:
first, the initiation of the preparatory effort;
second, the completion of the result.
Although one initiates the preparatory effort (*prayoga*) but the result is not finalized,
one does not incur the offense of immediate retribution (*ānantarya-karma*). Likewise,
although the result is finalized, if one did not initiate the preparatory effort, [one does not incur such an offense].
Nor does one incur the offense of immediate retribution (*ānantarya*).
If it is argued that a single application [of karma] culminates in the formation of an atom (*paramāṇu*),
this is precisely what is subsumed within the "equal" category, according to the intended meaning of the former master.
First, regarding the predominance of the manifest action (*vijñapti*): if both are equally predominant,
as in the case where a single preparatory effort results in the killing of both father and mother, two types of manifest and non-manifest actions (*vijñapti-avijñapti*) arise for each, totaling four.
If both are inferior, as in the case of harming one who is not a relative,

there likewise arise two types of manifest action (vijñapti) and two types of non-manifest action (avijñapti). The intention of the latter master is that in all such cases, both manifest and non-manifest actions arise.
Manifest and non-manifest [karma] differ from one another.
It is because of manifest karma that one is able to take the life of another;
if manifest karma were absent, how could the life of another be taken?
Therefore, the *Mahāvibhāṣā* states that the Venerable Ghoṣaka said:
"All informative karmas (*vijñapti-karman*) are composed of atoms (*paramāṇu*).
The atoms involved in killing one's mother and those involved in other [informative karmas] are each distinct."
Therefore, there are cases where a manifest offense (*vijñapti*) is acquired in relation to two persons.
Furthermore, when receiving the five precepts according to the *Saṃghabhedavastu*, one simultaneously acquires five manifest acts and five non-manifest acts (*avijñapti*).
Thus, it is known that manifest and non-manifest karma can arise in multiple instances at once.
If one were to harm an Arhat, it would also constitute a heinous crime;
this interpretation may be understood as being held by some.
If it is argued that [the offense] ranges from harming one's father up to [harming] those who rely on [the Buddha],
this should also be understood as being included by the word "equal" (*sama*).
If so, as for the illustrative statement regarding the killing of an Arhat...
Citing a sutra as an objection:
If that is so, how should one reconcile the *Dṛṣṭāntaparyāya-sūtra*?
The Buddha told Śikhaṇḍin: [text follows].
"You have already committed two heinous crimes, namely: killing your father and murdering an Arhat.
Long ago, when the Buddha was in the world, there was a king in a kingdom in South India who entrusted the realm to his crown prince, Śikhaṇḍin."
He went to Śrāvastī, took refuge in the Buddha, left the household life, and attained the fruit of arhatship.
The crown prince was unrighteous, persisting exclusively in illegal acts and bringing turmoil to the common people.
An elderly former minister went to the father king and reported these matters in detail.
"Please return to your kingdom and instruct the crown prince.
The father-king granted his consent, and the request was fulfilled as he returned to his own country.
The treacherous ministers of the crown prince feared they would be executed.
The sycophant said to the crown prince, "The father king intends to come and seize your position; I request that you dispatch a messenger to kill him on the road.
Having accepted these sycophantic words, the crown prince subsequently dispatched a messenger to carry out the murder.
The father king, knowing that the karmic conditions required his son to kill him, accepted death with a willing heart.
The Buddha, aware of this matter, sent a disciple to go and tell Prince Śikhaṇḍin: "Your father has said..."
"You have already committed two heinous crimes:

namely, harming your father and killing an Arhat. [The text] begins with "Holding this Uṣṇīṣa" (or "Uṣṇīṣa-śikhin"), which indicates one heinous crime, up until the point where he rebukes him for his transgression.
Answer: This refers generally to the statement in that sūtra.

That sūtra clarifies that a single immediate transgression (*ānantarya*) is constituted by two conditions: the father and an arhat. It states that one commits two immediate transgressions, or uses the two categories of the field of gratitude (*upakāra-kṣetra*) and the field of virtue (*guṇa-kṣetra*) to rebuke those who have begun to fail in maintaining their precepts. Regarding the question concerning the simultaneous occurrence of the first three [immediate transgressions], it says "as in the case of being born under another."
When anger, killing, and stealing occur simultaneously—
since they too rely upon a single basis—
there are three courses of action that proceed at the same time.
The cases of killing one's father and killing an Arhat who is one's preceptor are likewise the same.

What prevents these from both constituting two distinct immediate transgressions (*ānantarya*)? The explanation says: because the karmas of malice, killing, and stealing are distinct, they are separately established as paths of action (*karmapatha*).
Since taking life constitutes one [of the five heinous crimes], two *ānantarya* offenses are not established together.
As for the question of whether one incurs an *ānantarya* offense against the Buddha,
this explains the fifth and sixth phrases.
Because the character "no" (無) below applies to both instances,
this is the question: "If one must have a murderous intent to reach the Avīci Hell, then [the offense] would not exist [in other cases]."
Answer: It must be with the intent to kill that one sheds the blood of a Buddha for it to constitute a heinous crime (ānantarya-karma).
Shedding blood through the intent to strike does not.
Because the offense is light, there is no immediate retribution (*ānantarya*).
As for the question of whether one incurs the crime of immediate retribution (*ānantarya-karma*) at the time of the preliminary effort (*prayoga*) of killing,
this explains the sixth phrase.
This is the question. Regarding the statement,
"Because there is no preparatory effort for killing within the body of one beyond training (aśaikṣa)," the answer may be understood.
If it is argued that [the path of action] is established as immediate because it is definitively contrary [to liberation],
this is the fourth point clarifying the certainty of the preparatory stage (*prayoga*).
If the immediate preparatory stage is necessarily accomplished, [it constitutes an immediate transgression].
In the interim, there is absolutely no abandoning of defilements or attaining of the fruit;
for that karma is so powerful that its retribution must necessarily be experienced in the very next life.
This refers to the path of abandoning defilements and the path of attaining the fruit.

Because one cannot prevent those courses of action from arising, it is certain that there is no attainment of the fruit through the abandonment of defilements. It should be understood that there are two types of preparatory application (*prayoga*) for the immediate [offense]: first, that which is reversible;
[the second is that which is irreversible].
Second, it is irreversible.
Here, the question is posed based on that which is irreversible;
thus, the *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya-ṭīkā* (Xianzong lun), fascicle 23, states:
However, according to our own school, uninterrupted preparatory application (*anantarya-prayoga*) is generally said to be of two kinds:
first, the proximate;
second, the remote.
That which is proximate cannot be altered;
that which is remote possesses the sense of being alterable. The commentary explains: when various treatises state that something "can be altered," they speak from the perspective of the remote;
when various treatises state that something "cannot be altered," they speak from the perspective of the proximate.
As explained in detail in the *Nyāyānusāra* and the *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya*:

except for the karma of immediate retribution (*ānantarya-karma*), if one performs the preparatory stage (*prayoga*) or the intermediate stage (*madhya*) of any other unwholesome path of action (*akuśala-karmapatha*).
If the Noble Path arises and the paths of action do not occur,
one transitions to the body that serves as the basis for the state of a Noble One;
this is because such a body is necessarily incompatible with those unwholesome paths of action.
Because the power of that path of noble realization is superior while the power of those karmic paths is weak,
it prevents these karmas from manifesting; thus, one is able to enter the state of a noble one (ārya).
The path of detachment is inferior and cannot prevent those evil karmas from arising; furthermore, this interpretation does not claim that detachment is omitted or left unmentioned.
Regarding those among all evil actions that yield great fruits even within the worldly wholesome.
This constitutes the fifth [point], clarifying the gravity of the offense and its great fruit.
The first two phrases clarify the gravity of the offense;
the latter two phrases clarify the great fruit.
The Commentary states: "Because [the Buddha's] supreme kindness and so forth are slight" explains the two preceding phrases.
Although Devadatta understood that the Eightfold Path is the true Dharma, [he did not practice it].
The fifth is an unrighteous act:
to utter false speech with the intent to cause a schism in the Saṃgha.
To erroneously demonstrate that the five dharmas are the true Dharma and that the eightfold noble path is not the Dharma constitutes the greatest offense among those of immediate retribution.
Because this wounds and destroys the body of the Buddha-Dharma,
it obstructs the worldly path to the heavenly realms as well as the path to nirvāṇa; that is to say,
the Saṅgha has not yet attained harmony.
All those in the world who ought to enter the noble state,
who ought to attain the fruits, who ought to be free from defilement, and who ought to exhaust their outflows,
are all thereby obstructed.
The cultivation of various meditative concentrations, the recitation of scriptures, and activities such as hearing and reflecting are all brought to a halt;
because the wheel of Dharma does not turn and both body and mind are in disorder,
one incurs the retribution of an intermediate kalpa in the Avīci Hell.
Among the five acts of immediate retribution (*ānantarya*), this schism of the Saṅgha is the gravest offense;
the other four acts of immediate retribution follow in sequence,
with the fifth being the shedding of the Buddha’s blood.
The third is killing an arhat;
the first is killing one’s mother.
These three, in their respective order, become progressively lighter.
The second, killing one's father, is the lightest,
because the debt of gratitude is relatively small.
"Relatively" (等) means including [the father's] virtues.

Between the two fields of gratitude and virtue, the field of virtue is superior to the field of gratitude, because that field of virtue can uproot sentient beings from the suffering of birth and death.
Therefore, an offense against the field of virtue is more serious than one against the field of gratitude. Regarding the three types within the field of virtue:
Schisming the Sangha is the most grave offense because it harms the Dharma-body;
for that which all Buddhas take as their teacher is the Dharma.
Next, the offense of drawing blood from the Buddha's body is most grave;
this is because the Buddha’s merit surpasses that of an Arhat and because he is the Teacher.
Next, killing an Arhat is lighter because it is a field of merit (*guṇakṣetra*) where the subsequent qualities are few; therefore, the offense is light.
In the former case, the qualities were many, and thus the offense was heavy.
Within these two types of fields of gratitude,
the father’s debt is less than the mother’s;
for the mother carries him in her womb and nurtures him, and thus her compassionate kindness is greater.
The mother is heavy and the father is light.
If that is so, why is it said that reaching the peak of wrong view is the greatest? This is a difficult objection.
If the karma of false speech constitutes the most grave offense,
why did the Buddha state among the three types of punitive karma— of body,
speech, and mind— that mental punitive karma is the greatest sin?
"Punishment" refers to the disciplinary retribution for those who commit evil deeds;
because such punishment leads one into hell, karma is termed "punishment.
Furthermore, the Sūtras state that among all offenses, false view is the greatest.
Regarding the statement that, among the five immediate transgressions (*ānantarya*), they are explained as being heavy in successive order:
the answer is that within each respective category of dharmas, one [transgression] is considered the most serious.
If one refers to the five deeds of immediate retribution (*ānantarya-karma*), the schism of the Sangha is said to be the most grave;
if one considers the three types of punitive karma, the offense of mental punishment is said to be the greatest;
and among the five false views, wrong view is said to be the heaviest.
Alternatively, the gravity of the offense of schism (*saṃghabheda*) is explained on the basis of its great fruit,
because one must undergo it in the Avīci hell for one eon (*kalpa*).
The gravity of the mental karma is explained on the basis of its harming many sentient beings.
Because the sages’ minds were incensed by the harm done to many sentient beings,
it is said— based on the meaning of severing the roots of virtue— that the sin of wrong view is particularly grave;
therefore, it is stated that they are grave respectively.
Regarding the phrase "feeling the first existence" up to "speaking words of worldly goodness," the following two lines are explained:
wholesome volition at the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*) brings about the greatest fruit.
This statement is made with reference to the fruit of maturation (*vipākaphala*).

However, among the five fruits, if one considers the fruit of disjunction (*visamyogaphala*), then the volition associated with the diamond-like concentration (*vajropamasamādhi*) is able to attain a great fruit.
Therefore, because the permanent severance of all fetters is the fruit of this volition,
although the volitions of all untainted uninterrupted paths (*ānantarya-mārga*) achieve disconnection from bondage,
they do not do so in this specific manner.
The term "worldly wholesome" is stated in order to exclude this untainted volition (*anāsrava-cetanā*).
Is it only those who commit the immediate transgressions (*ānantarya-karma*) who are certain to be reborn in hell?
Below this, the sixth section clarifies the "congruent types" (*sabhāga*) of the immediate transgressions.
This is the question:
"Regarding those [factors] that are of the same class as immediate [causes], how can they arise without being immediate?
The answer is:
Those who commit the various deeds of immediate retribution (ānantarya-karma) and those who perform acts similar to them are likewise certain to be born in hell.
Other masters say that although those who perform deeds similar to the immediate retributions are indeed certain to be born in hell,
it is not necessarily the case that they are born there immediately.
Because they are permeated by subsequent [moments] and because they are indeterminate,
the *Nyāyānusāra* states:
"All [factors] that are immediate and of the same kind also necessarily produce those [subsequent factors]."
It does not necessarily arise immediately after [the preceding moment],
because it is not an uninterrupted karma (*ānantarya-karman*). What is its "homogeneous" [cause]?
Question:

The verse says, "Reaching this, those who are of the same class as the five heinous crimes. To say they are "of the same class" means they are similar. This refers to one who [commits an offense] against his mother, who is an arhat-nun.
Or, to commit an act of extreme defilement against one's mother or an arhatī,
namely unchaste conduct (abrahmacarya);
this is called the karma of the same category as killing one's mother.

Because it is a karmic action committed against one who is the same as one's mother, it is called "homogeneous karma" (*sabhāga-karma*). Alternatively, there may be the killing of a Bodhisattva established in the certainty [of enlightenment] who has remained so for a hundred great eons;
this is the essential nature of homogeneous karma equivalent to harming one's father.
Because the Bodhisattva’s kindness is profound, like that of a father,
committing an act against him is termed "homogeneous karma" (*sabhāga-karma*). Alternatively,
killing a trainee (*śaikṣa*) or an Ārya constitutes the essence of homogeneous karma for the killing of an Arhat.
Because those in training (*śaikṣa*) and those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) are equally fields of merit for the noble ones (*ārya-kṣetra*),
karma performed toward them is called "homogeneous karma" (*sabhāga-karma*). The conditions for the harmony of the Saṃgha refer to requisites and the like.
If there is one who seizes away the conditions for the harmony of the Saṃgha and causes the Saṃgha to be divided,
this is called the substantial essence of an action similar to schism (*saṃghabheda-sabhāga-karma*).
The conditions that support harmony are equivalent in meaning to the Saṃgha itself.
The karma performed therein is called "karma of the same category. For instance, there may be one who destroys a stūpa of the Buddha;
this is termed the "substantial nature of karma of the same category as shedding the blood of a Buddha.
Because the multitude honors this stūpa as being similar to the Buddha [himself].
The karma created therein is called "karma of the same class" (sabhāga-karma); these are what are termed the five types of karma similar to the immediate transgressions (*ānantarya*).
Regarding the maturation-producing karma that reaches two [levels], it is as previously illustrated.
This corresponds to the fifth major section of the text, which clarifies the obstacles of the three times.
Within indeterminate karma (*aniyata-karma*) as well, a small portion should be excluded;
because half acts as an obstacle while the other half does not, it is not mentioned.
Thus, the *Nyāyānusāra* (Treatise on the Principles of Correct Reasoning), fascicle 43, states:
However, within this context, one must exclude those actions whose results are to be experienced in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharmavedanīya*), those whose results are not fixed (*aniyatavedanīya*),
and among those with fixed maturation (*niyatavipāka*), those whose maturation does not occur in another location.

By this one may infer that among karmas to be experienced in the next life (*upapadyavedanīya*), in subsequent lives (*aparaparyāyavedanīya*), and those of indefinite timing (*aniyatavedanīya*), all those whose maturation is fixed and whose maturation occurs in a specific location are capable of acting as obstacles; the rest of the text is clear.
From what was stated above up to "is called concentration," this concludes the sixth major section, which clarifies the characteristics of a bodhisattva.
Within this:
First, clarifying the stage of abiding;
second, clarifying the cultivation of the characteristics of karma;
third, clarifying the making of offerings to the Buddha.
The fourth clarifies the perfection of the six pāramitās.

This is the first clarification: the stage of abiding in certainty (*niyata-pada*). Regarding what was stated above—by virtue of which stage does a bodhisattva who abides in certainty receive the name "abiding in certainty"?

This question concerns the stage of a bodhisattva; furthermore, it asks at what point one is said to be "established in meditative concentration" (*samādhi*). This is a question regarding the name of that concentration.
The verse says: "Upon reaching the state of being fully endowed with manhood, mindfulness, and firmness."
The first two lines answer the initial question;
the latter two lines answer the subsequent question.
Here, "certainty" (*niyama*) refers to the fact that one is certain to be reborn in the happy realms (*sugati*) and so forth; this is what is termed "certainty."
This is not the attainment of meditative concentration (*samādhi*). A bodhisattva who dwells in this is said to be "dwelling in concentration.
The Commentary states: "As for 'reaching' and 'noble families,' etc."
This brief commentary on the verses may be understood according to the text itself.
The thirty-two marks are explained in detail in the *Vibhāṣā* (Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra), fascicle 177.
"Those born in the happy realms" up to "those who are forever without retreat or dejection" constitute the separate explanation of the second half of the verse.
First, the happy realms are explained.
Second, being born into a noble family: either born into a brāhmaṇa family,
or born into a kṣatriya family,
or born into the family of a wealthy householder.
Or he may be born into a great Brahmin family—"Brahmin" (婆羅) here being translated as "noble clan" (豪族).
Alternatively, "great Brahmin" (大婆羅) may encompass all three aforementioned places; the third [alternative] is the complete [etymology], while the fourth is the masculine [derivation].
Fifth is the explanation of mindfulness;
sixth is the explanation of firmness—
namely, that which is without retreat or dejection is called firmness.
This means that regarding the capacity to shoulder all benefits and happiness, there is no separate explanation for lack of retreat or discouragement. *Dhava* here means "slave";
because it was not purchased with money, it is called "priceless."
This means that those bodhisattvas accept being driven into service for the benefit of sentient beings,
much like purchasing a slave without using money. Regarding "unconditioned great compassion," it refers to the great compassion that those bodhisattvas give rise to.
It does not arise only because sentient beings have rendered a favor to the bodhisattva;
rather, it arises even in the absence of such a favor, and is therefore called "unconditioned great compassion" (*nirālamba-mahākaruṇā*).
Because it spontaneously and at all times remains bound to others, it is free from pride.

To embrace all beings as identical to oneself is the matter of resemblance; to grant one's eyes and other organs whenever they are required is the matter of what is difficult to seek; and to be able to undergo various sufferings on behalf of sentient beings is the matter of toil and oppression.
This demonstrates the absence of despondency; the remainder of the text may be understood accordingly. Furthermore, the *Nyāyānusāra* states:
"For what reason must one be in the stage of cultivating the karma for the marks of excellence before a bodhisattva is designated as being in the 'fixed' (*niyata*) state?"
At that time, humans and devas were for the first time able to know it together;
previously, it had been known only by the devas.
Or, at that time, he entered the meditative concentration of perfect enlightenment.

First, the state of Equal Enlightenment (samyak-saṃbodhi) alone is certain and nothing else. The commentary explains: when cultivating the karma of characteristics and when proceeding toward Bodhi, one is certainly first fixed upon Bodhi; it is certain that one does not arrive at anything else.
Regarding "cultivating the karma for the marks of excellence until each is adorned with a hundred merits," this is the second section clarifying the cultivation of the karma for the marks.
The treatise states: "up to those not of the class of hearing or cultivation."
The first two lines are explained:
first, an explanation of Jambudvīpa;
second, an explanation of "male."
Third, the explanation of the response to the Buddha;
fourth, the explanation of the Buddha’s reflection;
fifth, the explanation of that which is accomplished through reflection.
Therefore, the *Nyāyānusāra* states:
"It is produced solely by reflection (*cintāmaya*) and not by cultivation (*bhāvanāmaya*),
because it does not pertain to a fixed realm (*aniyata-dhātu*)."
Because the maturation (vipāka) that is experienced is bound to this [realm], it is not produced through hearing (śruta-maya), for that is weak and inferior;
nor is it acquired at birth (upapatti-labdha), because it arises from preparatory effort (prayoga). Furthermore, the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* (Vasubhāṣya), fascicle 177, states:
Question: What constitutes the intrinsic nature of karma that results in marks?
Is it bodily action (kāyakarman) or vocal action (vākkarman)?
Is it mental action?
Answer: Its intrinsic nature consists of the three types of action, yet mental action is predominant.
Some say that it has only mental action (manas-karman) as its intrinsic nature, and not bodily or vocal action. Why is this?
Because this [mental] action is sharp and intense, whereas bodily and vocal actions are dull.
Question: Is karma that has its maturation as a mark (nimitta-vipāka) located in the mental ground (manobhūmi), or in the five groups of sensory consciousness (pañcavijñānakāya)?
Answer: It is located in the mental ground, not in the five groups of sensory consciousness.
Why is this? Because the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) possesses discrimination and functions only after having performed observation;
the five [sensory] consciousnesses lack discrimination and arise by the power of their respective objects.
Question: Is karma that has the marks as its maturation acquired through preparatory effort (*prayoga*), acquired through the abandonment of defilements (*vairāgya*),
or acquired through birth (*upapatti*)?
Answer: It is acquired solely through application (prayoga), not through the abandonment of defilements (vairāgya), nor is it innate (upapatti-pratilambhika). Why is this so?
This karma must necessarily be attained after having cultivated the various *pāramitās* throughout three incalculable eons (*asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*),
through the mental application (*manasikāra*) of preparatory effort within the perfected body.
Some say that this karma is obtained through application (*prayoga*) and also obtained by birth (*upapatti-labdha*), but it is not obtained through the separation from defilements (*vairāgya*).
Question: Is karma whose maturation is a characteristic (*lakṣaṇa-vipāka*) produced by hearing (*śruta-maya*), reflection (*cintā-maya*), or cultivation (*bhāvanā-maya*)?
Answer: It is produced solely by reflection;
it is not produced by hearing, nor by cultivation.
Why is this? Because this karma is preeminent, it is not produced by hearing;
because it is bound to the desire realm, it is not produced by cultivation.
Some say that this karma pertains to what is accomplished through hearing (*śruta-maya*) and reflection (*cintā-maya*),
but not to what is accomplished through cultivation (*bhāvanā-maya*); although the *Mahāvibhāṣā* lacks an explicit evaluation by its own school,
since all the treatises agree with the former masters [on this point].
As for where this arises— taking the former master’s view as correct—
it arises among humans of the desire realm,
specifically in Jambudvīpa and no other continent.
Regarding the body upon which it arises:
it arises based on a male body, not a female body or others.
Regarding the time at which it arises: it arises when a Buddha has appeared in the world.
It is not that there is no Buddha in the world.
As for the object upon which it arises:
one gives rise to superior thoughts and vows by taking the present Buddha as the focal object.
It does not take other objects as its conditions.
Question: Are the thirty-two marks of a Great Man produced by a single volition, or by many volitions?
The commentators say:
According to this explanation,
thirty-two volitions induce the thirty-two marks of a Great Man.
Each [mark] is further perfected by many karmas.
Question: Among the thirty-two marks produced by a bodhisattva’s volitions (*cetanā*), which mark is first induced?
Answer: Some say that the mark of the soles of the feet being level, full, and well-settled is induced first.
Later, the remaining marks are cited;
because one first establishes the feet and subsequently [the others].
Some say that the mark of the deep blue eyes is cited first.
Because one first observes the world with eyes of loving-kindness,
such a statement is not definitive; rather,
according to the convergence of conditions for these characteristics, those very characteristics are induced.
"Only the remaining hundred kalpas down to ninety-one kalpas" explains the third phrase; that is to say,
outside of the three incalculable kalpas, there remain only one hundred kalpas for the cultivation of practice, rather than many.
Such is the natural law regarding the causal stage of all Buddhas:
they all cultivate the karma of maturation for the marks [of a Great Man] throughout one hundred great eons.
From the words "Only the Bhagavat" onwards, the distinctions are specified. Village Headman.
This refers to the lord of a city and the lord of a village;
the rest of the text may be understood accordingly.

According to the Sarvāstivāda school, only after one has emerged from the cultivation of the karma for the marks of excellence throughout three incalculable eons (*asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*) does one finally abandon the four faults and attain the two merits.
Regarding the statement that "the former masters say one attains two qualities," this records a divergent view.
It refers to the explanation of the ancient masters within the Sautrāntika school.
Since the Bodhisattva has emerged from the first incalculable eon,
he has immediately abandoned four faults and attained two virtues. As for abandoning the four faults,
this refers to being free from the evil destinies.
One leaves behind a poor household,
leaves behind impaired limbs,
and leaves behind female bodies and the like; thus one attains two merits.
This refers to attaining the recollection of past lives,
achieving non-retrogression, and—
as previously explained— reaching the stage of being adorned with a hundred merits.
This explains the fourth phrase.

As previously analyzed, each of the thirty-two marks is individually adorned with a hundred merits. What are these "hundred merits"? Answer: In this context, one hundred volitions (*cetanā*) are termed the "hundred merits."
Therefore, the *Mahāvibhāṣā* (177) states:
Question: As it is said in the Sūtra that each and every mark of the Buddha is adorned by a hundred merits (*puṇya*), what is meant by "a hundred merits"?
Answer: In this context, one hundred thoughts are called "one hundred merits.
What are these one hundred thoughts?
They refer to when a bodhisattva performs and cultivates the karma that brings about the mark of the well-placed feet.
First, fifty volitions arise to cultivate and purify the vessel of the body, making it supple and pliant.
Next, one volition arises to correctly draw forth that [result].
Finally, another fifty volitions arise to bring it to completion.
It is like a farmer who first prepares the furrows and ridges,
next sows the seeds,
and finally covers and irrigates them with manure and water.
It is the same for him: as the karma for the mark of well-placed feet is adorned by such a hundredfold intentionality,
so too is it for the karma for the mark of the *uṣṇīṣa* on the crown of the head.

For this reason, it is said that each of the Buddha’s marks is adorned by a hundred merits (*śata-puṇya*). Question: What are these fifty volitions (*cetanā*)? Answer: There are five volitions for each of the ten paths of action (*daśa-karmapatha*).
This refers to the five volitions based on abstaining from the path of action of killing:
first, the volition of abstaining from killing;
second, the volition of assisting and guiding [others to abstain].
Third, the volition of praise;
fourth, the volition of sympathetic joy;
fifth, the volition of dedication.
This applies likewise up to right view;
these are called the fifty volitions (*cetanā*).
Some say that based on each of the ten paths of action, five grades of wholesome volition arise: inferior, middling, superior, most superior, and extremely superior.
As with the mixed cultivation of dhyāna,
some say that based on each of the ten paths of action, five volitions arise:
first, the purification of the preliminary application (*prayoga*).
Second, purity of the root;
third, purity of the subsequent action;
fourth, being unharmed by obstacles.

Regarding the inclusion by means of the five recollections (*pañca-anusmṛti*), some say that fifty moments (*kṣaṇa*) arise in succession, focusing on each individual mark (*lakṣaṇa*) of the Buddha, as a continuous flow of previously uncultivated reflection. Furthermore, the *Nyāyānusāra* states:
Furthermore, there are masters who say that each individual mark is produced by its own karma acting as a condition;
having never been cultivated through contemplation, all one hundred manifest simultaneously to serve as adornments.
What is called the measure of each individual merit? Regarding the question of the measure of each individual merit,
some say that it can only be known by reaching the state of a Buddha.
Those who draw near to Buddhas and Bodhisattvas are individuals who have cultivated meritorious deeds for a hundred kalpas;
therefore, they must eliminate [these obstacles].
The three explanations herein can be understood from the text as it stands.
Furthermore, we shall take the later masters as authoritative. Thus, the *Vibhāṣā* (177) states:
"The commentators say: 'That which has been thus explained...'"
All of these are merely praises of the magnitude of a bodhisattva’s merit through the skillful means of pure intention;
however, none of them have yet attained its actual reality.
As for the meaning according to reality:
The measure of each individual merit generated by a bodhisattva is immeasurable and boundless;
for having accumulated and perfected all the pāramitās throughout three incalculable eons, the bodhisattva has reached fulfillment.
Because the volitions and aspirations thus induced are exceedingly vast, only a Buddha can know them; they are not to be fathomed by others.
As for my current Great Teacher, he is the seventh thousandth Buddha.
Below this, the third section clarifies the number of Buddhas.
Within it, the first part clarifies the number of Buddhas to whom offerings are made.
Second, the clarification of encountering the names of the Buddhas: this is the first [section] clarifying the number of Buddhas.
Because the later stages within the three *kalpas* are progressively superior, the number of Buddhas he makes offerings to is greater.
Because the preceding stages are inferior to the subsequent ones, the offerings to the Buddhas are fewer.

The rest of the text may be understood accordingly. Regarding the phrase "the three incalculable eons [are] one by one the same as those," this is the second section clarifying the names of the Buddhas encountered.
This can be understood from the text itself. According to the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, the True Dharma lasts for five hundred years;
according to this text, it lasts for one thousand years.
Is this not contradictory? The explanation says: because the nuns were ordained according to the *Sudarsana-vinaya*, five hundred years were reduced;
however, because they practiced the Eight Respectful Rules (*gurudharma*), those five hundred years were recovered.
That treatise refers to the period of the initial decline and thus states five hundred years;
this treatise, based on the later period, speaks of one thousand. Furthermore, Paramārtha states:
"From the time of the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa until now, one thousand two hundred and sixty-five years have elapsed."
Regarding "I, the Śākya Bodhisattva, having reached the stage of practicing the perfections to completion in due order":
this refers to the fourth [section], which clarifies the perfection of the six pāramitās.
The first verse consists of four lines, each revealing a single stage.
The subsequent verse pairs the six with the four.
The Commentary states, "up to the perfection of cultivation," which explains the first stage.
This demonstrates the excellence of birth resulting from the complete cultivation of the single practice of generosity,
namely, birth as a human or a celestial being.
The remainder of the text is self-evident.
"When the bodhisattva reaches the perfection of cultivation" explains the second stage.
This reveals the perfection of the two cultivations of ethical discipline (*śīla*) and patience (*kṣānti*).
By not retaliating even when the body is struck, the perfection of pure ethical discipline is achieved;
because the mind is free from anger, the perfection of patience is achieved.
Therefore, the *Nyāyānusāra* states:
"One whose patience is perfected has no anger in their mind toward those sentient beings;
one whose ethical discipline is perfected does not initiate physical or verbal actions that harm others."
Because there is no anger,
body and speech are free from evil;
when there is no anger, morality and patience are perfected.
When the Bodhisattva reaches the perfection of cultivation,
this explains the third stage,
revealing the single perfection of cultivation of diligence. Tiṣya is translated here as "Perfection."
This is the name of a star;
it is named after the star.
The *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 177, states:
Question: Through how much time must these marks of maturation be cultivated until they are perfected?
Answer: For the most part, it takes one hundred great eons, with the sole exception of the Bodhisattva Śākyamuni.
Because the Bodhisattva Śākyamuni was of such supreme diligence, he bypassed nine great eons;
thus, by practicing for only ninety-one eons until his cultivation was perfected, he attained unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
What is this matter?
As it is said in the Sūtra: "In the past, there was a Buddha named Tiṣya, or alternatively, Puṣya."
That Buddha had two bodhisattva disciples who diligently practiced the holy life (*brahmacarya*):
the first was named Śākyamuni, which means "Able to Pacify," because he pacifies all evils;
the second was named Maitreya, which means "Loving-kindness."
"Li" (儷) is translated here as "clan" (氏).
The Bodhisattva was born into the Maitreya clan;
because his name was established according to his clan, he is called Maitreya (慈氏).
The old translation "Maitreya" is an error. At that time, that Buddha observed which of his two disciples had first reached maturity in their faculties;
he knew it as it truly was:
Maitreya had matured first.
Śāntamati’s faculties ripened later.
Furthermore, he observed which of the two individuals had faculties that would ripen first among those beings to be converted.
Moreover, he knew with perfect accuracy that among those to be converted by Śākya, [Śāntamati’s] faculties were the ones that should ripen first.
Having understood this, he immediately thought:
"How can I now cause those who possess the karmic potential to meet and encounter one another?
However, it is easier to bring a single person to swift maturity."
He did not wish to involve many people.
Having formed this thought, he addressed the Śākyas:
"I intend to travel to the mountains; you may accompany me."
At that time, the Buddha took his sitting mat and proceeded ahead along the road.
Upon reaching the mountain, he entered a cave of vaidūrya,
spread out his sitting mat, sat down cross-legged, and entered the fire-element samādhi for seven days and nights.
Experiencing sublime joy and with his majestic radiance blazing forth,
Śākyamuni also went to the mountain in an instant;
he searched for the Buddha everywhere, like a calf seeking its mother.
Passing along by turns, he arrived before that grotto chamber.
Suddenly, he beheld the Buddha’s majestic demeanor, solemn and upright, with radiance shining brilliantly;
with single-minded sincerity and earnest devotion, he gave rise to joy and admiration.
Unable to walk for even a moment without forgetting to set down his foot, he gazed upon the Blessed One’s countenance without averting his eyes for seven days and nights.
With a single verse, he praised that Buddha, saying: "O Heaven, O Earth, this world, and the Abode of the Learned!"
"In the celestial abodes and the palaces of the departed, throughout the ten directions, there is no one equal to this Great Śramaṇa, the Bull among Men.
Searching the earth, the mountains, and the forests, none can be found as his peer. Having praised him thus, he immediately transcended nine *kalpas*.

One attains unsurpassed enlightenment in the presence of Maitreya; it is asked that a bodhisattva who is close to the stage of Buddhahood must necessarily attain a hitherto unobtained skillful mastery over the collections of names, phrases, and phonemes.
One should praise the Buddha using distinct verses and various methods;

why, then, did he praise the Buddha with only a single verse for seven days and nights? Answer: At that time, because the Bodhisattva’s intention and aspiration were so supreme, he did not repeat the phrasing or the verses.
If one alters the phrasing of the verses, one's contemplation and aspiration will not be pure.
Furthermore, at that time, the bodhisattva fears distraction,
for as the distinctions in the verses differ, so too do the states of mind.
How does one attain the continuous flow of a single mind?

Furthermore, a bodhisattva manifests their own mind as being free from weariness, because they are able to newly and repeatedly generate sublime thoughts and vows regarding even a single verse. Question: For what reason did the Bodhisattva Maitreya first ripen his own faculties and only later ripen those of the beings he was to convert?
Is it not the case that Śākyamuni Bodhisattva was the opposite of this? Answer: Maitreya Bodhisattva primarily benefited himself and only slightly benefited others;
Śākyamuni Bodhisattva primarily benefited others.
Because they provide little benefit to themselves, they do not stand on equal footing with those being transformed. As the commentary on the verses explains:
"Heaven and earth are taken together."
"Among the heavens and on the earth" refers to this realm;
"this three-thousandfold great thousandfold world system" refers to the Hall of Much Learning;
"the abode of Vaiśravaṇa" refers to the palace of the deva Vaiśravaṇa.
Because this deity’s reverent faith and fame spread throughout the ten directions, he is called "Much-Hearing" (Bahuśruta).
His "abode of the departed" refers to the palace of Brahmā; for that Brahmā King reckons it to be eternal.
The Buddha named it "Abode of the Departed" (*śivagati*) as an antidote to that conception of permanence;
"departed" (*śiva*) carries the meaning of impermanence.
Furthermore, another interpretation holds that the "Abode of the Departed" refers to the "Abode of Humans."
Because the human realm quickly returns to destruction, it is called the "realm of the departed" (*gati*). Regarding the celestial abodes:
this refers to all other celestial realms excluding the Hall of the Learned (*śubhakṛtsna*) and the realm of the departed. They do not exist in the ten directions.
It means that not only is there none in this trichiliocosm, but there is also none in the worlds of the other ten directions; having searched everywhere for one who is peerless, he says:
"O Great Śramaṇa, Bull among Men! I have now searched the earth, searched the mountains, and searched the forests."
"Throughout [the world], there is none equal to me, O Blessed One"—this further explains the "Hall of Great Learning.
Among the heavens of the desire realm, by citing one from among the first group of heavens, the other three are implied; likewise, this implies the five higher heavens.
These are the six heavens of the desire realm (*ṣaḍ-kāmadhātu-deva*). Regarding "the abodes of the departed" (*gati-pura*):

among the heavens of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), the first heaven is cited to represent the remaining two, as well as to indicate all the heavens above them. Regarding "the celestial abodes" (*devasthāna*).
This refers to the celestial abodes of the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*); the remaining explanations are the same as before.
When the bodhisattva reaches the stage of perfected cultivation, this explains the fourth level.
This reveals the perfection of the two cultivations of concentration and wisdom;
that which follows the knowledge of exhaustion (kṣayajñāna) is called unsurpassed enlightenment (anuttara-bodhi).
Prior to this unsurpassed enlightenment...
This is the diamond-like concentration (*vajropama-samādhi*).
At this time, the cultivation of concentration and wisdom is perfected.
This refers to the six perfections as taught within the causal stage of a bodhisattva’s practice.

This does not refer to the stage of fruition (*phala-avasthā*). If one speaks of the six perfections in relation to the stage of fruition, it is at the time of attaining the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣaya-jñāna*) that they are so designated.
Therefore, the *Vibhāṣā* (178) states that there are three explanations in total. Regarding the third,
the Master of the Final Evaluation (*pūrvapakṣa*) says:
Regarding such statements:
all that has been said is taught as being complete based on a single moment and a single aspect.
As for the true meaning:

When the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) is attained, these four *pāramitās* are fully perfected. The commentary explains that because ethical discipline (*śīla*) subsumes patience (*kṣānti*) and wisdom (*prajñā*) subsumes meditative concentration (*samādhi*), only four are mentioned.
This treatise agrees with the second master’s explanation.
Furthermore, the *Nyāyānusāra* states:
"By principle, at this stage, it should be immediately followed by a square."
Because it is only at the moment of attaining the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) that this [perfection] is fulfilled;
thus, one is able to reach the *pāramitā* (perfection) to which one has been proceeding.
This explains the fifth phrase regarding the six *pāramitās*.
"Pāramitā" is here translated as "the other shore" (pāra) and "arrival" (mita).
This is because the Bodhisattva is able to reach the state on the other shore of perfected merit, which is the destination of their own vehicle.
Therefore, these six types are called *pāramitās*.
As the Sūtras state, there are distinctions in their culmination similar to those found in the paths of action (*karmapatha*).
Hereafter, in the seventh major section, the topics of giving (*dāna*), ethical discipline (*śīla*), and cultivation (*bhāvanā*) are elucidated.
Among these, the first briefly explains giving, morality, and cultivation;
the second extensively explains giving, morality, and cultivation. This is the brief explanation of giving, morality, and cultivation.
The Commentary states: "Up to 'neither karma nor action'":
this is a brief explanation of the verse.
It is called "merit" (*puṇya*) because it is wholesome.
That which is performed is called "karma" (action);
this consists of body, speech, and mental volition (*cetanā*).
That upon which volition relies is called the "basis" (*vastu*).
"Category" (*jāti*) refers to a class of nature (*prakṛti*). Thus, the *Mahāvibhāṣā* (vol. 126) states:
"The natures of giving, morality, and cultivation... From this, it is known that while the names for category and nature differ, their meaning is the same.
Generosity, morality, and cultivation— these three categories are all merit because they are wholesome.
Within these three categories,
some are karma.
Alternatively, regarding the matter,
it should be understood as appropriate according to what was explained in the section on the paths of action;
that is, as it was analyzed in the exposition of the ten paths of action.
There are courses of action that are also karma,
namely the first seven types.
There are courses of action that are not karma.
This refers to the latter three [types of action].
The name "path" (mārga) applies generally to all ten;

however, "action" (karman) applies only to the first seven. One should know that within this context, the application of the terms "merit" (puṇya), "action," and "basis" (vastu) is likewise both general and specific.
Merit is itself supernormal power (*abhijñā*).
Since karma and its objects are not fixed,
they collectively form four categories.
Furthermore, regarding those among the categories of giving that receive only the name "merit":
hereafter, merit, action, and the basis will be clarified by way of giving, morality, and cultivation.
This [section] clarifies them by way of the category of giving.
Furthermore, among the types of giving, the two actions of body and speech possess the threefold designation of "merit" (puṇya), "action" (karma), and "basis" (vastu).
They are called "merit" because they are wholesome;
they are called "action" because they are performed.
That which is the basis upon which volition relies is called "the object" (*vastu*).
Thus, the *Nyāyānusāra* states:
"Within the category of giving, the two types of action—bodily and vocal—possess the threefold designation of 'merit' (*puṇya*), 'action' (*karma*), and 'object' (*vastu*)."
It is called "merit" (*puṇya*) because it is wholesome; it is also called "action" (*karman*) because it is something performed.

It is also called a "basis" (*vastu*) because it serves as the gateway through which the volition (*cetanā*) that initiates bodily and vocal actions operates. Regarding the aforementioned treatise, the volition that is the causal motivation (*hetu-samutthāna*) is termed solely "meritorious action."
It is called "merit" (puṇya) because it is wholesome;
it is called "action" (karman) because it is performed.
Volition (cetanā) is not called a "substantial entity" (vastu), as it does not depend upon itself.
The factors coexistent with volition (cetanā) receive only the designation "merit" (puṇya).
They are called "merit" because they are wholesome;
they are not called "karma" because they are not [volitional] actions.
Because volition does not directly rely upon them, they are not termed "entities" (vastu).
Since volition directly relies upon the body and speech to arise,
the co-existent factors (sahabhū-dharma) are likewise not termed "entities."
Since the category of precepts (śīla) is designated solely by the term "meritorious action-base" (puṇyakriyāvastu),
this is explained with reference to that category of precepts;
for the category of precepts consists exclusively of the nature of bodily and vocal actions.
Therefore, they all possess the names "merit" (puṇya), "action" (karman), and "matter" (vastu).
It is called merit because it is wholesome;
it is called action because it is performed.
It is called a "matter" (*vastu*) because it serves as a basis for volition (*cetanā*).
Regarding the statement that within the category of cultivation (*bhāvanāmayī*), from loving-kindness (*maitrī*) up to [the stage where] one receives only merit (*puṇya*),
this is explained by way of the category of cultivation.
Among the types of cultivation, loving-kindness has non-hatred as its intrinsic nature;
it is called a "meritorious action" solely because it is wholesome, and thus is termed "merit."
It is called a "matter" (vastu) because it is that upon which volition relies;
the reason compassion is called a matter is that it is the matter of karma, for the karma of volition associated with compassion is produced by taking compassion as its gateway.
Therefore, loving-kindness (*maitrī*) is called a "thing" (*vastu*).

Because it is not something produced [by volition], it is not called "karma. The volition (*cetanā*) that accompanies loving-kindness and the morality (*śīla*) that accompanies loving-kindness are called only "meritorious karma" (*puṇya-karman*).
They are called "merit" (*puṇya*) because they are wholesome (*kuśala*).
It is called "action" (karma) because it is performed;
volition (*cetanā*) is not itself designated as a "matter" (*vastu*) because it does not depend on anything external.
Volition associated with loving-kindness (*maitrī-sahagata-cetanā*) and ethical discipline (*śīla*) are not designated as "matters" because they arise by depending directly upon volition.
Because it arises by correctly entrusting thought to the gateway of loving-kindness (*maitrī*), only loving-kindness is designated as the "matter" (*vastu*). Question:

Why is it that within the category of morality (*śīla*), morality itself is called the "matter," whereas within the category of cultivation (*bhāvanā*), morality is not so called? Explanation: Within the category of morality, morality refers specifically to the *prātimokṣa* vows.
Because this volition (cetanā) relies upon and depends on [the object], it receives the designation of "action" (karma).
Among the types of cultivation, ethical discipline (śīla) is the discipline that follows the movement of the mind;

because it does not arise by directly relying on volition, it is not called "action. Other co-existent factors (sahabhū-dharma) that accompany loving-kindness (maitrī) receive only the designation of "merit" (puṇya).
It is called "merit" (puṇya) because it is wholesome;
it is not called "action" (karma) because it is not an actual performance;
and it is not called a "transaction" (vastu) because it does not arise as a direct entrustment of volition (cetanā).
Alternatively, the term "meritorious action" (puṇyakarman) is so named because it reaches the preparatory application (prayoga) for generating merit;
this is the second interpretation.
Alternatively, the term "meritorious action" is used to manifest the meaning of performing merit.
This means that meritorious application refers to the preliminary application preceding generosity, ethical discipline, and cultivation.
Application itself is called "merit," hence the term "meritorious application.
It is called merit because this application is virtuous.
"Performing" refers to karma, or the preliminary application (*prayoga*) of merit.
Merit consists of giving, ethical discipline, and cultivation.

Because karma is the preliminary application preceding merit, it is called the "preliminary application of merit. "Basis" indicates that which is relied upon; that is to say, giving, ethical discipline, and cultivation are the bases for those meritorious actions.
This is for the sake of accomplishing those three matters of giving, ethical discipline, and cultivation.
Therefore, one first initiates the preparatory application of merit. Alternatively, it is explained that the term "meritorious action" (*puṇyakarman*) reveals the sense of performing merit.
This means that "merit" refers to the preparatory application (*prayoga*), which indicates the dependent;

"matter" (*vastu*) indicates the basis, namely giving, morality, and cultivation. Because the dependent and the basis are spoken of together, they are called "bases of meritorious action" (*puṇyakriyāvastu*).
As for those who say that it is "only volition" because it proceeds as a meritorious action,
this is the third interpretation;
or perhaps it is the view of certain Sautrāntikas.
Only volition is true meritorious action.
It is called "merit" because it is wholesome;
it is called "action" because it is something performed.
It is not called "matter" (vastu) because it is not a matter of being entrusted;
rather, the matter of meritorious action refers to giving, morality, and cultivation,
for it is by means of these three as supporting doors that meritorious action proceeds.
Because these three are that which is entrusted, they are called "bases" (*vastu*);
because they are not true meritorious karma, they are not called "meritorious karma. Alternatively, [the term] "true meritorious karma" refers to volition (*cetanā*);
this reveals the basis upon which it depends.
The "bases of meritorious action" refer to giving, ethical discipline, and cultivation;
these indicate the basis.
Because the basis and that which depends upon it are spoken of in combination, they are termed "bases of meritorious action."
The *Nyāyānusāra* (Treatise on the Principles) also provides three explanations, which are the same as those in this treatise.
Regarding what dharma is called "giving" (*dāna*) and what fruit such giving brings about:
Below this is the second section, which extensively explains generosity (*dāna*), ethical discipline (*śīla*), and cultivation (*bhāvanā*). Within this,
the first part explains generosity.
Second, the explanation of morality and cultivation;
third, the explanation of the gift of Dharma. Regarding the first [section], the explanation of giving, there is first the explanation of the essence of giving and its fruit.
Second, the distinctions in the benefits of giving;
third, the distinct causes for the fruits of giving;
fourth, the preeminence of the merit of giving.
Five, it clarifies that the fruits of giving are immeasurable;
six, it clarifies the characteristics of the gravity of karma;
seven, it clarifies the performance and accumulation [of karma].
8. Explaining the merit of giving to a *caitya*.
9. Explaining that the fruit [of giving] arises from the internal mind. This is the first [section], explaining the essence of giving and its fruit.
First, it asks: what dharma is called "giving"?
Second, the question regarding what fruit is summoned by giving.
The verse says: "Up to this point, it summons the fruit of great wealth.
The first three lines answer the initial question.
The following sentence answers the subsequent question.
The *Śāstra* states: "That which reaches this true essence of giving" (*tattva-dāna-svabhāva*) explains the first phrase.
Although the material objects that are relinquished also receive the designation "giving," within the nature of this giving, it is the instrument for relinquishing the material object— namely,
these actions of body and speech— that is designated as "giving."
Furthermore, because the relinquishing of the object is accomplished through that which initiates it;
[this refers to] the body and speech by which the object is relinquished,
as well as that which initiates them.
This is the essence of giving (*dāna*). "Abandoning" (*tyāga*) means relinquishing.
"Possessing" (*samanvāgata*) has the sense of being equipped with [the causes]. Alternatively, one is called a "giver" (*dātṛ*) because they have reached this state of equipment out of fear.
This explains the second phrase.
Alternatively, among the eight kinds of giving, there is giving out of fear and giving out of longing;
"giving out of longing" refers specifically to giving in order to seek a reward.
"Either hoping for a heavenly reward" means hoping for the gift of heaven;
"seeking" means seeking a karmic retribution for the gift. It is called "greed" because of this craving. The word "etc. (ādi) includes other factors not yet mentioned.

Excluding only the eighth [type of gift], which consists of taking up the previous seven types of giving—wherein the act of relinquishing material objects in those seven cases would also constitute giving, though it is not what is intended here—the term "offering" (*pūjā*) is used to distinguish them from those seven gifts;
that is to say, it refers to that which is performed out of respect and veneration for another.
To give while benefiting those who are impoverished—this giving is called "complete. This refers to the eighth of the eight kinds of giving.
What is meant by "complete"?
The following explains the third phrase.
This is the question: namely, bodily and vocal actions, as well as that which originates them.
Answer: What is that which can produce it? This is the inquiry.
Regarding the statement that non-attachment, when conjoined with [other factors], is collectively designated by the name "giving" (dāna):
the answer is that it is because non-attachment, at the same time, is able to initiate these bodily and vocal actions.

The collection of mind and mental factors is called "that which initiates. Alternatively, it is explained as the mind and mental factors occurring simultaneously with non-attachment, which are capable of giving rise to this collection of bodily and vocal karma.
That which is capable of arising is called "capable of producing. The former interpretation is superior. To demonstrate this intent, a verse is cited:
the five aggregates of a single moment of virtue are collectively designated by the name "giving" (*dāna*).
The term "moment" (*kṣaṇa*) here does not refer to a single *tatkṣaṇa*, but is based on a *tatkṣaṇa* [in its conventional sense].

The grasping of the motivating cause—the mind and mental factors that constitute the four aggregates—as well as the body and speech that are produced [by them], which constitute the aggregate of form;
these five aggregates, both preceding and succeeding, are collectively termed "momentary. Furthermore, this verse is explained according to momentary motivation (*kṣaṇasamutthāna*).

Therefore, it is said that these five wholesome aggregates of that single moment are collectively designated by the name "giving" (*dāna*). Question: As explained in the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* (Vibhāṣā), fascicle 29, regarding the essence of material offering (*āmiṣa-pūjā*), the critique states:
"It should be stated as follows."
It consists of the material object that is relinquished,
the two types of action— bodily and vocal— of the one who relinquishes,
and the mind and mental factors that give rise to that [act of relinquishment].

If the recipient, having received [the gift], experiences the growth of the sense faculties (*indriya*), the primary elements (*mahābhūta*), and the derived matter (*upādāyarūpa*), all of which constitute its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*);

thus, material offering (*āmiṣa-pūjā*) has, in general, the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) as its intrinsic nature. According to the *Vibhāṣā*, the material object that is relinquished is also taken as the essence of giving (*dāna*).

Why does this treatise not include material wealth? The explanation states: because the *Vibhāṣā* masters who provide the definitive assessment (*viniścaya*) maintain that the essence of giving consists of both the relinquishing of material wealth and the [relinquishing of] the sense faculties and so forth; therefore, it includes both.
This treatise specifically relies upon the essential nature of true giving;
therefore, it states that the act of relinquishing the requisite factors is called "giving.
One should understand that this applies even to cases such as giving grass or a shelter.
The fourth phrase is explained as follows:

It should be understood that such meritorious actions consisting of giving (*dāna-maya-puṇya-kriyā-vastu*) are able to bring about the fruit of great wealth in both the future and the present. Regarding the term "meritorious actions consisting of giving": [it refers to...]
The term "category" (*jāti*) refers to essence (*svabhāva*).
This indicates that merit has giving as its essential meaning; it is like the category of "leaf," for in the West, lotus leaves and the like are used as vessels.
To manifest the meaning of a vessel having leaves as its substance is like the case of a house made of grass;

to manifest the meaning of a house having grass as its substance is [the same]. The term "and so forth" (ādi) refers to other examples not yet mentioned. The two categories of ethical discipline (śīla) and cultivation (bhāvanā) should be explained accordingly.
Regarding the phrase "giving that is not for the sake of any benefit nor for the sake of duality," this is the second [section] clarifying the distinctions in the benefits of giving.
The treatise says: "up to honoring and repaying kindness."
Because they transcend the stage of the fruit.
This means that noble ones who have abandoned desire transcend the stage of the ripening fruit of the desire realm; the rest of the text is understandable.
It has already been explained in general that there are distinctions regarding the attainment of the fruit.
Below this, thirdly, is the clarification of the specific causes for the fruits of giving.
Within this section,
first, there is a general explanation of the differences between the primary [donor] and others.
Second, the specific explanation of the donor, the object, and the field. This constitutes the first [section], the general explanation of the differences among the donor and so forth.
It concludes the preceding discussion and raises a question:
it has already been generally explained that giving invites great wealth.
Now, we shall examine the distinct causes for the fruits of giving,
or the distinct causes belonging to the category of the fruits of giving;
alternatively, the term "distinct" (bīja) may apply to both the fruit and the cause.

The remainder of the text may be understood. Now, regarding the statement that "the fruit of a donor cannot be taken away once it has reached its proper time," the following section is the second part, which specifically clarifies the [distinctions of] the donor, the gift, and the field.
Within this:
First, the difference in the master;
second, the difference in the wealth;
third, the difference in the field. This is the first [point], clarifying the difference in the master.
The Commentary states: "As for the difference between the giver and the fruit," this explains the first phrase.
It is because the donor has accomplished the distinguished merit of the seven kinds of noble wealth, such as faith, ethical discipline, and learning.
Therefore, it is called a difference in the donor.
Because the donors differ, the causes of giving become distinct.
Because the causes of giving are distinct, [the results differ].
Therefore, there is a difference between the cause of giving and its fruit. Here, the word "etc.
refers to including wisdom (*prajñā*), equanimity (*upekṣā*), shame (*hrī*), and dread of blame (*apatrāpya*). As for the "seven noble riches" (*saptāryadhanāni*):
First is faith, which refers to profound faith;
second is precept, which refers to pure precepts;
third is learning, which refers to extensive learning.
The fourth is wisdom (*prajñā*), meaning discernment;
the fifth is relinquishment (*tyāga*), meaning generosity;
the sixth is shame (*hrī*).
Seven types of shame (*hrī*).
The two kinds, *hrī* (self-respect) and *apatrāpya* (dread of blame), have already been explained as before.
Therefore, the *Saṃgītiparyāya-śāstra*, chapter sixteen, states:
The seven riches are:
first, the richness of faith;
second, the richness of ethical discipline.
Third is the wealth of shame (*hrī*).
Fourth is the wealth of dread of blame (*apatrāpya*).
Fifth is the wealth of learning (*śruta*).
Sixth is the wealth of relinquishment;
seventh is the wealth of wisdom.
These are explained in detail as in that [text].
Furthermore, the lower fascicle of the *Ratnavyuha-sūtra* states:
"The seven riches are faith, generosity, ethical discipline, learning, wisdom, shame, and dread of blame. Generosity (*dāna*) and relinquishment (*tyāga*) differ in name but are identical in meaning.
Although the various treatises differ in their sequence, the seven names are identical in all of them.
Regarding those donors who encounter destruction by fire and so forth,
the following three phrases provide the explanation.
When donors possess such meritorious qualities as faith and so forth,
they are able to practice the four types of giving— veneration and the rest— in accordance with the Dharma; accordingly,
they shall obtain the four corresponding fruits, beginning with being honored.
The causes are to be correlated with the results as can be understood from the text. Regarding "giving without causing harm":
this means that when practicing giving, one does not cause injury or distress to others, and thus the act of giving is successfully accomplished.
Regarding the fact that the material objects bestowed upon the field of merit all possess distinctions:
this is the second point clarifying the differences in the material gifts.
This is because the material objects bestowed may either lack or possess color, fragrance, flavor, and tangibility.
Accordingly, one obtains the fruits of exquisite physical form and so forth, either deficient or complete;
this is the general explanation.
That is to say, regarding the material wealth offered, such as that which reaches the level of a "jewel-like woman" (strī-ratna) and so on.
A [karmic] release may possess color, fragrance, taste, and tangibility;
accordingly, one obtains results that likewise possess excellent color and so forth. If there is a reduction in the results, it is due to a deficiency in the causes.
If one is deficient in form, fragrance, flavor, or tangibility,
one will accordingly obtain results that are likewise deficient in form and so forth;
it should be understood that both types [of causes] are present herein.
Alternatively, "endowed" refers to possessing all excellent color, fragrance, taste, and texture;
or it may also be called "endowed" when possessing three, two, or even just one of these qualities.
There are likewise two types of deficiency.

Either all [of the objects]—exquisite color, fragrance, flavor, and tangibility—are entirely absent, or they are missing three, two, or even one; these are also termed "deficient. There are also those that possess occasional tangibility.
In the cold there is the sensation of warmth;
in the heat there is the sensation of coolness.
Thus it is said that [the fruit] accords with the time. Likewise, regarding the experience of karmic results, there may be both completeness and deficiency.
Not only can it be produced by those [actions of] body and speech,
but it is also called "diversity of wealth" because it is endowed with color, fragrance, taste, and so forth.

Because the material objects differ, there are distinctions in both the essence of true giving and the fruits it induces. Question: As stated in the first chapter of the *Saṃgītiparyāya*, what is meant by "material offering"?
He replied by giving pleasing forms, sounds, smells, tastes, tangibles, clothing, food and drink, bedding, medicine, and other requisites.
To be able to bestow, to give, to relinquish, to renounce, and to completely abandon [possessions] for the sake of other sentient beings—this is called material offering (*āmiṣa-pūjā*).
Why does that treatise differ from this? The explanation is: this treatise does not mention sound, because it is not constantly present.
Objects such as clothing and so forth are subsumed under "color" and the like;
therefore, they are not mentioned separately.
This is because there are distinctions among the fields of generosity based on the degree of their kindness and virtue.
This is the third clarification regarding the differences among fields (*kṣetra*).
The treatise states: "Up to the point where there are distinctions in the fruits of giving"—this is the general explanation.
There are four general types of fields for giving: first, the realm of existence (*gati*);
second, suffering (*duḥkha*).
The three types of benefactors and the four virtues each have their own distinctions; therefore, they are called "different fields.
Because of these differences in the field, the substance of the gift and its fruit are rendered distinct.
Regarding the phrase "from the distinction of destinies up to receiving a thousandfold fruit," this is the detailed explanation below;
this constitutes the first explanation of the distinction of destinies.
The distinctions in the fruits of giving according to the differences in the realms of rebirth can be understood from the text.
Regarding the distinctions based on suffering, up to the point where it cannot be measured:
This is the second explanation of the distinctions among sufferings:
because the sufferings differ, there are distinctions in the fruits bestowed;
for by means of these seven kinds [of giving], one relieves the suffering of others.
Because these seven kinds of merit increase based upon them, they are called "with support" (*sopadhi*).
The three types of meritorious actions have already been explained as before. Regarding the "seven kinds," the first is giving to travelers.
The first refers to those who are travelers in a foreign land;
the second refers to those who practice giving while on the road.
Third, giving to the sick,
which refers to those afflicted by illness.
Fourth, giving to those who attend to the sick.
That is to say, the caregiver.
Fifth, the gift of groves and gardens,
which refers to giving groves and gardens to various monasteries and the like.
Sixth is the gift of regular food.
This refers to when a donor gives money, property, fields, or other such assets,
and addresses the community of monks, saying:
From this day forward, provide a vegetarian feast for seven monks for me every day; this is called "regular food.

This practice currently exists in the various monasteries of the Western Regions. Furthermore, it is explained that according to the customs of the Western countries, there are many faithful and meritorious people who [sponsor such meals].
On long journeys through remote regions where villages were scarce, fearing that his traveling companions might suffer from hunger and thirst along the way,
he built dwellings by the roadside near groves and orchards, deposited his wealth there, and stored up abundant food and drink.
One gives whatever is required to all who come and go;
or one gives universally to all practitioners;
or one specifies only those who have gone forth.
Because one constantly gives food, it is called "constant eating" (*nityabhojana*).
Seventh is giving at the appropriate time (*kāladāna*),
which refers to when there is cold, wind, or heat.
Giving them food, drink, clothing, and so forth at the appropriate times according to their needs is collectively termed the seventh type:
giving at the proper time (*kāladāna*). The Sūtra further states:
"If there are men or women endowed with pure faith who fulfill these seven bases of reliance (*saptāśrayadāna*)."
The merit thus obtained cannot be measured.
Regarding the distinction by way of gratitude, this extends to all those who have been kind;
this is the third explanation of the distinction by way of gratitude.

If one falls into an evil rebirth due to a single unwholesome deed,
at the time of its preliminary application it is called "committed" (kṛta) but not "accumulated" (upacita);
if it reaches completion, it is called both "committed" and "accumulated."

It is not by the power of the field that there is a reversal of the fruit produced from a seed;

Thus, although a donor plants the seeds of various gifts in an unwholesome field with the intention of benefiting others,
