Therefore, the preceding text states: "The doctrine of having perception,
the doctrine of having no perception,
and the doctrine of neither having perception nor having no perception."

This is precisely the view of eternalism. Furthermore, it is asked: why is it that within the doctrine of non-perception (*asaṃjñika*) and the doctrine of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñika*), the eight propositions such as "I possess perception" and so forth are not mentioned? The answer is: if they were also mentioned, [it would be redundant].
All of these should be termed "theories of having perception" (*saṃjñivāda*),
because those who possess perception and feeling are not without perception,
and so forth; for all such theories of having perception and so on speak of the state after death.
All of these are subsumed under the speculative views concerning the future limit. Regarding the seven theories of annihilationism:
first, one forms this thought: "This self possesses form; it is composed of the coarse four great elements as its nature."
After death, there is annihilation.
He thinks: "When I was first conceived in the womb, I came into being from what previously did not exist."
If, upon reaching the stage of death, that which existed previously ceases to exist, this is called "wholesome annihilation.
These two [types of persons] think:
"This self of mine will be annihilated after death in the heavens of the desire realm."
He formed this thought:
"Since I was not born through the birth canal, I have come into being from what was originally non-existent."
That which exists and then returns to non-existence,
such as a comet and the like,
is called "wholesome eradication."
Third, they think:
"This self, a deva of the form realm, is annihilated after death. They think thus.
I was not born from a birth canal; I existed where there was originally nothing.

Through the power of meditative attainment (*samāpatti*), that which had come into being returns to non-existence—this is called "wholesome eradication" (*samyak-prahāṇa*), as explained at length in the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*.
Fourth, they form this thought:
"This self, as a deity of the Sphere of Infinite Space, is annihilated after death.
They thus cling to the sphere of space as the pinnacle of birth and death, asserting that it is annihilated after death.
The fifth thinks thus: "This consciousness of mine in the heaven of Infinite Consciousness will be annihilated after death.
They hold the sphere of consciousness to be the pinnacle of birth and death.
"Annihilation after death.
Sixth, they think:
"This heaven of the sphere of nothingness is annihilated after death."
They hold that the sphere of nothingness is the pinnacle of saṃsāra,
and that after death there is annihilation.
Seven [of them] think thus.
"This god of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception perishes after death.
They hold that the Peak of Existence (bhavāgra) is the summit of birth and death,
and that it perishes after death.
Thus, these seven types are all said to be comprised within the speculative views regarding the future after death.
These seven all have the nature of the view of annihilationism;
therefore, the preceding text states:
That doctrine of annihilationism is precisely this view of nihilism. As for those who advocate for nirvana in the present life, there is one who,
while experiencing the pleasures of the five sensory desires,
first forms this thought:
This is my pure liberation and deliverance from all calamities and misfortunes;
that is to say, the present enjoyment of the exquisite pleasures of the five senses.
At that time, it is called attaining *nirvāṇa* in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharmanirvāṇa*).
Abiding in the first dhyāna,
the second [stage] is able to perceive the faults of all sensual desires;
he then reflects as follows:
The pleasure born of desire is accompanied by manifold sufferings and beset by many harms;
the pleasure born of meditative concentration is subtle, serene, free from accompanying sufferings, and devoid of all harms.
Again, he thinks:
"This self is pure, liberated, and has emerged from all calamities and misfortunes;
that is to say, it currently abides in the first dhyāna."
At that time, it is called attaining nirvāṇa in the present life.
Abiding in the second dhyāna,
one is then able to perceive the faults inherent in all desires, applied thought, and sustained thought.
He forms this thought:
"This is my purity, liberation, and deliverance from all calamities and misfortunes," namely,
that he currently dwells in the second dhyāna.
At that time, it is called attaining nirvana in the present life.
Abiding in the third dhyāna,
one is able to perceive the faults of sensual desires, applied and sustained thought, and joy in the fourth [dhyāna].
He forms this thought:
"This is my purity, liberation, and deliverance from all calamities and misfortunes," namely,
that he currently dwells in the third dhyāna.
At that time, it is called "attaining nirvāṇa in the present life.
Abiding in the fourth dhyāna, one is able to see the fifth [object]: all desires, vitarka and vicāra, joy, and inhalation and exhalation.
All [of these] possess faults.
He forms this thought:
"This is my pure liberation, the departure from all calamities and misfortunes."
That is to say, when one currently abides in the fourth dhyāna, at that time it is called attaining *nirvāṇa* in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharmanirvāṇa*). Question:

Why are these five theories of *nirvāṇa* in the present life subsumed under the speculative views concerning the future limit (*aparāntakalpakavādāḥ*)? Answer: Although these five take the present as their object, they are designated as "future" because they depend upon the past.
Therefore, this is called "discrimination regarding the future limit" (*aparānta-vikalpa*), as explained in detail in the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*. Regarding the explanation of the term:
if one experiences peace and happiness in the present, it is called "attaining nirvāṇa. Regarding the explanation of its essential nature (*svabhāva*):
Since it has the grasping at views as its essence,
the preceding text states:
"The doctrine of nirvana in the present life is precisely this grasping at views."
Regarding the statement "the Vaibhāṣikas [hold that one] reaches [the state of] Devadatta":
the intention of the Vaibhāṣikas is that an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) is able to sever the afflictions of both seeing (*darśana*) and cultivation (*bhāvanā*) within the lower eight stages.
The commentary on that sutra states:
"One who has already abandoned the defilement of desire but gives rise to views will temporarily regress at the moment those views arise."
As in the case of Devadatta.
Thus, the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 85, states:
"As in the case of Devadatta."

Having first attained meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), he used his supernormal power of the base of psychic power (*ṛddhividhi-jñāna*) to transform himself into a small child wearing golden necklaces and a five-flower topknot,
and placed himself upon the lap of Prince Ajātaśatru.
As he played about, he allowed the Crown Prince to know that this was the Venerable Devadatta;
then Ajātaśatru took him up with compassion, fondled him, cooed over him, and finally placed saliva in his mouth.
Because Devadatta craved gain, he swallowed his saliva; therefore,
the Buddha rebuked him, saying,
"You are a corpse."
Regarding "those who eat human saliva":

when they swallow their saliva, they immediately fall away from meditative absorption (dhyāna), yet they quickly regain it, causing their transformed body to remain as before on the crown prince’s knee while playing; this concludes the preceding treatise. Question: As stated in the section on the schism of the Saṃgha, Devadatta was one whose temperament was dominated by views (dṛṣṭicarita). Why is this so?
If one is a practitioner of views (*dṛṣṭicarita*), they are of sharp faculties (*tīkṣṇendriya*);

how then can it be said that such a person may fall away? The explanation is: it is not necessarily the case that all practitioners of views are of sharp faculties, nor is it necessarily the case that all practitioners of craving (*tṛṣṇācarita*) are of dull faculties (*mṛdvindriya*).
Just as a bodhisattva, though characterized by craving, possesses sharp faculties,
one may infer from this that those characterized by views likewise possess dull faculties.
Although Devadatta was sharp among those who act through views,
one cannot establish that he possessed sharp faculties based solely on his acting through views;
in general terms, this is so.
Regarding the two types of practice—craving and views—both are common to those of dull and sharp faculties. Question: How can it be said that Devadatta, despite having sharp faculties, regressed?
And how is it that a Bodhisattva, despite having sharp faculties, first attains the eight meditative absorptions?

"Later, beneath the Bodhi tree, did he give rise to the three evil thoughts? The explanation says: "During the stage of an ordinary being (*pṛthagjana*), one's spiritual lineage (*gotra*) is not yet fixed;
thus, although there are six kinds [of thoughts], they are semblances and not real."
Because it is not truly real,
even those of sharp faculties may still undergo regression; however,
once one reaches the stage of a noble being (ārya), their spiritual lineage (gotra) becomes fixed.
This is the true [nature], not the semblance;
therefore, among the six types of spiritual lineages (*gotra*),
the first five are subject to regression.
Sixth, Non-retrogression. Furthermore, another explanation is that retrogression is briefly of three kinds.
First, retrogression due to place;
for example, when a person of sharp faculties who is a worldling (*pṛthagjana*) resides among human beings.
Second, falling away by way of lineage,
as in the case of a noble one of dull faculties.
Third, falling away by way of stage.
Just as there are three types of non-retrogression for ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) who have not yet attained *kṣānti*,
the first is non-retrogression by way of place (*sthāna*).
This refers, for example, to an ordinary being of dull faculties (*mṛdv-indriya*) who dwells among the gods.
Second, non-retrogression by way of lineage,
such as those noble ones with sharp faculties;
third, non-retrogression by way of stage.
Just as those ordinary beings who have already attained forbearance,
one should know that Devadatta Bodhisattva,
though belonging to a lineage of sharp faculties, is nonetheless subject to regression.
Because they exist among humans and have not yet attained *kṣānti* (receptivity), there is retrogression. Question:

If it is said that Bodhisattvas also undergo retrogression, why does the seventh fascicle of the *Abhidharmamahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* state that the roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*) in both the stages of liberation (*vimukti*) and decisive selection (*viniścaya*) all possess the six lineages (*ṣaḍgotra*)?
"One is certainly not subject to regression from the bodhisattva lineage. The commentary explains: "Certainly not regressing" means one does not regress from the lineage of one's own vehicle;

it does not mean that one is definitively incapable of regressing by giving rise to afflictions. Furthermore, it is asked: if, during the stage of an ordinary being (*pṛthagjana*), regression from the sixth lineage were possible...
For what reason does the *Pūrvakarmavarga* state that one who is firm in a stage free from passion (*vītarāgabhūmi*) does not create karma that leads to rebirth? Furthermore,
the prose commentary (*śarīra*) states:
One whose name is "Non-retrogression" is called "Firm.
By this standard, even ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) of sharp faculties cannot fall back.
How then can it be said that although the Bodhisattva Devadatta possessed sharp faculties...

On this basis, can it be said that ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) may fall back? The explanation states: it is merely said that ordinary beings who do not fall back do not create karma for rebirth while in a stage free from defilement;
it does not mean that all six types of spiritual lineage (*gotra*) are necessarily fixed in non-retrogression.
Alternatively, it is said that they do not regress because they abide within the celestial realms.
Regarding the statement that "due to differences in practice, one arrives at these five views as their own essence":
this marks the third section below, which specifically clarifies the essential nature of the five views.
Among these, the first correctly clarifies the essence of the five views,

and the second provides a detailed explanation of the grasping at precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*). This is the first [section], which correctly clarifies the essence of the five views.
This cites the name [of the treatise] to inquire about its essential nature and provides the response in verse.
The *Śāstra* says: "Up to this point, it is the view of a transitory collection (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*)."
The commentary explains "self" and "what belongs to self" as clarifying the view of a personal body (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*);
it holds that the grasping at "self" and "what belongs to self" is the view of a personal body.
Regarding the statement, "It is called *sat* because it perishes, and one subsequently clings to it as a self," the Sautrāntika masters explain:
it is called *sat* because it perishes.
"Aggregate" (skandha) refers to *kāya*.
*Kāya* means "body. "Destruction" (*bhaṅga*) signifies the meaning of impermanence.
"Aggregate" (*caya*) has the meaning of "accumulation" or "conglomeration.
"Body" (*kāya*) combined with "self" (*sat*) forms *satkāya*;
this is a *karmadhāraya* (appositional) compound.
This *satkāya* refers to the five aggregates of clinging (*pañcopādānaskandha*).
The term *sat* is established to negate the notion of permanence,
while the term *kāya* is established to negate the notion of unity.
This is because one first conceives of this as being permanent and unitary,
and only thereafter grasps it as a self;
thus, the view of a personal identity (*satkāya*) is called the *satkāyadṛṣṭi*.
This is an *adhikaraṇa-samāsa* (dependent determinative compound).
Regarding the phrase "the *Vibhāṣā* teachers [state] up to 'arising from the five aggregates of grasping,'" this is the explanation of the second *Vibhāṣā* master.
Because it exists, it is called "sa";
the meaning of "kāya" (body) is as explained previously.
Thus, the *Nyāyānusāra* states:
Because it exists, it is called "sat" (being);
"kāya" refers to an aggregate,
meaning a collection formed by a combination of elements.
*Kāya* (body) and *sat* (existence) combined form *satkāya*.
This means that which is substantially real and not unitary. [As stated] above in the treatise: "Do not be without an object of perception while conceiving of 'self' and 'what belongs to self'."
Unlike the Sautrāntikas, who maintain that there is a mind that takes non-arising as its object,
this view is said to take the existing body (*satkāya*) as its object and not a non-existent thing;
it arises by taking the *satkāya* as its basis.
It is named according to its object;
therefore, this view is designated as *satkāya*.
Since "body" (*kāya*) is equivalent to "existence" (*sat*), it is called the "body of existence" (*satkāya*).
This is a *karmadhāraya* (appositional) compound.
The view of a self-identity is called "view of a self-identity" (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*);
this is a *tatpuruṣa* (dependent) compound. All views that take only contaminated phenomena as their object [are included herein].

All [of these] should be designated by the name "satkāya" (the transitory collection), because they all arise conditioned by the body; yet the Buddha applied this name specifically to the grasping at "I" and "mine."
One should cause them to know that this view arises conditioned by the existence of a body,
and is neither "I" nor "mine," because "I" and "mine" are ultimately non-existent.
As it is said in the Sūtra:
Regarding all those who cling to a self,
the Buddha and others observe them as follows:
their [notion of] "self" arises entirely with respect to the five aggregates of clinging (*pañca-upādāna-skandha*).
It is not directed toward other phenomena.
For this reason, it is known that one takes only the body as the object, and not as "I" or "mine. Furthermore, this explains those who cling to a self in various states of existence.
He personally observes and sees that all those who grasp at a self also grasp at "mine";
the Buddha observes and sees that all those who grasp at a self also grasp at "mine."
He personally observes this for himself and further understands that names and so forth serve as universal objects;
this distinct arising is called "conformity" (anuvicāra). Initially, the investigation of names is termed "observation" (vitarka).

The term "view" (*dṛṣṭi*) is defined as that which is subsequently determined. This means that one gives rise to a view by contemplating any of the aggregates (*skandha*) in such a manner. Furthermore, it is explained that "equal" (*sam-*) refers to being equally directed toward those phenomena;
prior to the arising of this view, one must first engage in observation.
"Now, the arising of the view of a self-identity (satkāyadṛṣṭi) following this contemplation is called 'contemplation-following-view.

As for the phrase 'because it pertains to the extremes of annihilation and permanence regarding that which is grasped,' this explains that [the view of a self-identity] constitutes the view of clinging to extremes (antagrāhadṛṣṭi), clarifying the extremes of annihilation and permanence."
Regarding the objects grasped as "self" and "mine," one either clings to them as being annihilated or clings to them as being eternal.
To deviate from the Middle Way is to contradict the principle that there is neither annihilation nor permanence.
Because one falsely clings to the extremes of annihilation and permanence, it is called the "view of clinging to extremes" (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*); it arises as a clinging directed toward these extremes.
Because it is an adherence to extremes, it is called "extreme-adherence" (*antagrāhika*);
this is an *ṣaṣṭhī-tatpuruṣa* (genitive determinative) compound. Extreme-adherence itself is a view; thus, it is named "extreme-adherence view" (*antagrāhika-dṛṣṭi*).
This is a *karmadhāraya* compound.
Regarding the phrase "because it denies a truly existent entity up to other superimpositions," this explains that the term "denial" (*apavāda*) refers to wrong view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*).

To give rise to views that deny the four noble truths of suffering, origin, cessation, and the path—which possess real substantiality—is called wrong view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*). Furthermore, the *Abhidharmamahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle nine, states:
Question: For what reason do wrong views not take space (*ākāśa*) and non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) as their objects?

Answer: Because those phenomena which are the aggregates (*skandha*), the cause of the aggregates, the cessation of the aggregates, and the antidote to the aggregates—[wrong views do not take these as objects].
Wrong view takes [the self] as its object;
however, because space and non-analytical cessation are not among the aggregates and so forth, they do not take them as objects.
This is explained in detail in that [text]. Furthermore, it says:
Question: Regarding those who deny the existence of space and non-analytical cessation (apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha), what phenomena do they take as their object?
Answer: They take the very names "space" and "non-analytical cessation" as their objects.
Why is this? Because those who deny its existence lack a profound and respectful mind,
just as they would when slandering the phenomena of affliction and purification.
Question: What kind of knowledge is this?

Answer: This is the knowledge of the aspect of non-obscured neutral wrong conduct among those things to be abandoned through cultivation in the desire realm. Furthermore, according to the treatise above, all five views are erroneous in their operation and should all be termed "wrong."

As for the designation "wrong view" (*mithyādṛṣṭi*) applied specifically to the denial [of existence], it is established as such exclusively because its fault is particularly grave. It is like saying "stinking ghee":

while all ghee might be stinking, that which is the most extreme among the stinking is called "stinking ghee. Likewise, all *caṇḍālas* are said to "grasp what is evil," yet those who are the most extreme among them are specifically designated as such.
Among these, those who commit extremely grave evil are called "those with evil attachments" and so forth;
this indicates that the categories of phenomena have not been fully exhausted,
because such wrong views consist solely of deprecation.
The remaining four views involve superimposition (*samāropa*);
that is to say, the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), the grasping at views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*), the grasping at precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*),
and the eternalist portion of the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*) involve only superimposition.
Furthermore, because it involves augmentation,
although the view of annihilationism is also a form of diminution,
it is not the only one; for that [annihilationism] is itself a [wrong] view.
This is called "wrong view" (*mithyādṛṣṭi*),
which is a *karmadhāraya* compound.
Regarding that which is inferior as being superior, this is designated simply as "view-grasping" (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*).
To explain "inferior" as meaning "superior" refers to the grasping at views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*).
All contaminated phenomena (*sāsravadharma*) are termed "inferior."
Because it is abandoned by the Noble Ones,
the grasping at these inferior phenomena as supreme is collectively termed "adherence to views" (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*).
In principle, one does not only cling to views as supreme dharmas,
but also clings to non-views as supreme dharmas; therefore,
in accordance with reality, the designation "view and so forth" (dṛṣṭyādi) should be established.
The word "etc. is omitted so that it is simply called "view-grasping" (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*).
Furthermore, the *Nyāyānusāra* states:
"Alternatively, because the view is predominant, only the name 'view' is mentioned."
Because one takes other dharmas with "view" as the primary [object], the above treatise states: "Regarding 'adherence to views' (dṛṣṭiparāmarśa):
because one gives rise to adherence by taking views as the object, it is called 'adherence to views.'"
This is an *adhikaraṇasamāsa* (dependent determinative compound).
Regarding the phrase "that which is not a cause or a path, yet is merely termed 'clinging to precepts and observances' (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*)," this explains the third line:
the false assertion regarding what is not a cause or a path.
This clarifies the clinging to precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*): to falsely claim that what is neither a cause nor a path is, in fact, a cause and a path.
This view of all things is collectively termed the "clinging to rules and observances" (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*).
For example, various non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) may reckon Maheśvara as the cause,
or reckon Prajāpati as the cause— Prajāpati being the Lord of Beings.
He is none other than Brahmā,
who is able to give birth to all worlds and is the lord of the world.
Some take the Lord as the cause;
others, such as the non-Buddhists, conceive of time, space, and so forth as the cause.
Such conceptions as these are false attachments to causes that are not the actual causes of the world.

Or there are various non-Buddhists who engage in various wrong practices, such as throwing themselves into water or fire; they falsely give rise to attachments regarding causes that are not for rebirth in heaven, yet they merely observe precepts and prohibitions.
"Precepts" refers here to the precepts of the inner path, namely the five precepts and so forth.
"Vows" (vrata) refers to the vows of non-Buddhists (tīrthika), such as the vows concerning dogs, oxen, and so forth.
Alternatively, these precepts and vows apply to both Buddhists and non-Buddhists. The non-Buddhist Nirgranthas constantly reckon the enumeration of various phenomena as the path to liberation.
Knowledge that accords with calculation is called "knowledge corresponding to calculation," and so forth.
This refers to other non-Buddhists and the like; what they grasp is not the path to true liberation.
To falsely give rise to an attachment to the true path is all termed the grasping at rules and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*).
This grasping at rules and observances does not merely consist in clinging to rules and observances as the cause or the path.

Furthermore, one clings to what is not a precept or observance as being the cause and the path; although it would logically be appropriate to establish the name "clinging to precepts and observances, etc.," the word "etc.
has been omitted, and it is simply called "clinging to precepts and observances" (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*).
Furthermore, the *Nyāya* states:

"Alternatively, because ascetic observances (*śīla-vrata*) are superior, they alone are established under the name 'clinging to ascetic observances' (*śīla-vrata-parāmarśa*). This concludes the passage from the treatise. Regarding the term "clinging to ascetic observances":
Grasping arises conditioned by precepts and observances (śīlavrataparāmarśa).
"Grasping at precepts and observances" is a *tatpuruṣa* compound (dependent determinative) in which the term "precepts and observances" is the subordinate member.
"This is what is called the intrinsic nature of the five views that should be known" explains the fourth phrase;
this constitutes the conclusion.
Regarding why three among the five views are established as "views" (dṛṣṭi) while two are established as "grasping" (parāmarśa),
the *Vibhāṣā* states:
Question: For what reason are these two views designated only as "grasping" (*upādāna*)?
Answer: Because these two views function by way of grasping characteristics, they are designated only as "grasping.
That is to say, the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) clings to "self" and "what belongs to self" (*ātman* and *ātmīya*).
The view of extremes clings to annihilationism or eternalism;
false views cling to non-existence.
Because one grasps these various views as being supreme, it is called the "clinging to views" (dṛṣṭiparāmarśa).

Because one grasps various prohibitions and observances [thinking] they can bring about purification, it is called "clinging to rules and observances" (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*). Furthermore, because the three preceding views involve the estimation of their objects with such intense and sharp force, they are termed "views."
The latter two views are called "grasping" (*upādāna*) because they grasp at the object of cognition with such intense and sharp functional activity.
Regarding those [views] that are not causes and are abandoned by the path of seeing the origin (*samudaya-darśana-heya*), this concludes the first section;
next follows the second part, which provides a specific explanation of the grasping to precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*).
If one gives rise to the view that what is not a cause is a cause,

why is this view not said to be abandoned through the vision of the origin (*samudaya-darśana-prahātavya*), but rather said to be abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*)?
The verse says: "Because it has been reached, it is abandoned only by seeing suffering.
This is the answer in the verse.
The commentary says: "The clinging to causes is also abandoned. This is the explanation in the treatise.
Various non-Buddhists maintain that Maheśvara, Brahmā, Prajāpati, or others such as Time (kāla) and so forth,
act as the cause of the world, producing the world.
Regarding the meaning of the coarse fruit of suffering, such as that of Īśvara and others,
one must first conceptualize their essence as permanent;
"permanent" refers to the views of permanence, unity, self, and agency.

Regarding the view of self (*ātmadṛṣṭi*): by this same principle, the two views of the body (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*) are abandoned only through the vision of suffering (*duḥkhadarśana-prahātavya*).
Having first conceived of a self and permanence, one subsequently gives rise to the attachment to a worldly cause regarding that self and permanence. This is "attachment to a cause" (*hetugrāha*).

This refers to the clinging to precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*). At the very moment one perceives the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkhasatya*), the eternalistic grasping at a self (*ātman*) regarding [entities such as] Īśvara and so forth is severed without remainder.

Consequently, the causal clinging to precepts and observances—which arises from that [grasping at a self as] permanent—is also severed. This demonstrates the misapprehension of what is not a cause as being a cause (*ahetutve hetudṛṣṭi*).
The observance of precepts and ascetic practices arises from the notions of permanence and self;

because they originate from coarse fruits and bases, they are abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*). It is not that one falsely conceives of the cause of origination (*samudaya-hetu*) as being a self or permanent, and only then gives rise to attachment; therefore, this is not the "clinging to what is not a cause as a cause" (*ahetutve hetu-grāha*).

It is not abandoned by the vision of the origin (*samudaya-darśana-prahātavya*). If that were so, there would be those who maintain that it is abandoned by the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*);
thus the author of the treatise raises an objection.
If that were so, there would be those who hold that various wrong practices, such as throwing oneself into water or fire, are the cause for rebirth in heaven;
or those who hold that one attains purification, liberation, and nirvāṇa merely by observing vows and prohibitions.
Since this [view] of throwing oneself into water or fire does not arise from that [notion of] permanence and self,
it should not be abandoned through the vision of suffering.
However, the root treatise states that this is abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*). Thus, that treatise says:
"There are certain non-Buddhists who, by observing the cow-vow (*go-vrata*) and other such practices, believe they will attain purity, liberation, and nirvāṇa."
Departing from birth and death, one forever transcends all worldly suffering and pleasure,
reaching the state that transcends all worldly suffering and pleasure;
this state is precisely nirvana.

All such types of clinging to what is not a cause as being a cause should be understood as the view of adherence to precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*), which is abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkhadarśana-prahātavya*).
This is as explained at length in that original treatise.
One should know that these do not arise from the inversion of permanence or self.
For what reason, then, are they abandoned through the vision of suffering?
It is because they are delusions regarding the Truth of Suffering.
The Vaibhāṣika masters reply:
Although it does not arise from that [view of self] as permanent or as a self,
because it is deluded regarding the truth of suffering, it is abandoned through the vision of suffering.
One should understand that the verse provisionally bases itself on the view of eternalism and the view of a self as being abandoned through the vision of suffering;
however, in reality, there are also [views] that do not arise from eternalism and the view of a self.
The *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 199,
states: "All instances of the grasping at rules and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) mentioned previously are abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkhadarśana-prahātavya*)."
The inversion of "self" arises constantly because it functions with respect to the locus of the fruit; thus,
although it is not a cause, one conceives of it as a cause.
It is said that [this view] is abandoned through the vision of suffering;
that is to say, the clinging to precepts and observances (śīlavrataparāmarśa) consists generally of two types:
first, regarding what is not a cause as being a cause.
Second, regarding what is not the path, one regards it as the path;
regarding what is not the cause, one regards it as the cause. This further has two categories:
first, that which arises from deluded attachment to a self and permanent phenomena.
The second [type of delusion] arises from ascetic practices and the like based on past actions;
it also operates with respect to the fruit, as it is based on the inversions of self and permanence.
The two [types of] inverted views are abandoned through the vision of suffering;
the latter operates only with respect to the fruit,
because the characteristics of the fruit are coarse and manifest, making them easy to perceive.
Because the estimation of suffering’s cause as a cause is not entirely erroneous,
it is abandoned through the vision of suffering since it is deluded regarding the characteristics of the fruit.
The estimation of what is not the path as the path likewise has two categories.
First, there is the adherence to impure precepts and the like as the path;
because this arises from delusion regarding the coarse and manifest characteristics of the fruit,
it is permanently severed upon the realization of the Truth of Suffering.
The second consists of the false views that grasp at what is not the Truth of the Path as being the Path;
these directly contradict the Path because they involve a deluded attachment that fails to distinguish between cause and effect.
They can only be permanently severed at the time of seeing the Path (*darśanamārga*).
When one slanders the truths of origination and cessation, one negates both the phenomena to be abandoned and those to be realized.
If one then clings to [a mere conceptualization] as the Path, it becomes useless;
for the Path is established precisely by depending upon that which is to be abandoned and that which is to be realized.
Furthermore, that which they negate is distinct from the path;
there is certainly no one who, having previously perceived it as not the path, would subsequently perceive it as the path.
If at a later time they were to perceive it as the path, [it would follow that their previous cognition was erroneous].
One forms an attachment to the path with respect to the state of fruition;
since this view is abandoned upon seeing the truth of suffering (*duḥkhasatya*),
there is no grasping at precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) that is to be abandoned by seeing the truths of origin (*samudaya*) or cessation (*nirodha*).
Regarding the phrase "because there would be the fault of over-extension, leading all to be deluded by suffering," the following section presents the Master of the Treatise’s fourfold critique.
The first is the critique of the fault of over-extension.
2. The objection regarding the absence of distinct characteristics;
3. The objection regarding the adherence to views and doubt;
4. The objection regarding wrong views concerning origination and cessation. This constitutes the first objection of excessive fault.
If it were the case that [afflictions] are abandoned through seeing suffering simply because they are deluded regarding the truth of suffering, there would be the fault of over-extension;
for all afflictions with outflow (sāsrava) that are abandoned by the five categories are deluded regarding suffering.
"All [of these] should be abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*). The *Nyāya-samarthana* (The Rational Defense) states:
"Because they take such things as the 'cow-vow' (*go-vrata*) as their object, and because they merely conceive of coarse results as being the cause of those [results]."
By this, the objection raised by the Master of the Sūtras (Sūtrāntavādin) has already been refuted:

that there would be the fault of over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) because all afflictions (*kleśa*) conditioned by outflows (*sāsrava*) are deluded regarding the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkhasatya*). This is because they are all indeed deluded regarding suffering.
Since not all defilements (*āsrava*) that have outflows take the suffering of their own fruit as their object,
how could there be the fault of over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*)? The Vaibhāṣika masters refute this, saying:
The lower [afflictions] of suffering and the precepts have outflows as their object;
they arise specifically with respect to the fruit.
Other afflicted states with outflows likewise have outflows as their object.
"Is it not rather that [the view] arises regarding what is not the fruit?
Furthermore, what characteristic leads to delusion regarding the Truth of Suffering?
This is the second objection concerning the absence of a distinct characteristic.
In your school, the grasping at rules and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) is abandoned through the path of suffering (*duḥkhamārga*).
Furthermore, what specific characteristic of the grasping at rules and observances could be said to be abandoned by the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*),
such that it would give rise to various [afflictions] conditioned by dharmas abandoned by the path of seeing?
That [view] should also be called delusion regarding the truth of suffering;
therefore, it ought to be abandoned through the vision of suffering.
The *Nyāya* (Principles) defends this by saying:
However, regarding that which is not the path, one conceives it to be the path;

if one opposes this view by means of the "strong path," then it is abandoned through the vision of the path (*darśana-mārga-prahātavya*). To explain: the intent of that treatise is to state that the adherence to precepts and observances (*śīla-vrata-parāmarśa*) consists in conceiving what is not the path to be the path.
Because there are two types:
those that arise in the state of being a fruit are abandoned by seeing suffering;
those that arise not in the state of being a fruit, which take as their object the direct delusion regarding the Path, are abandoned by seeing the Path.
If the misapprehension of views is stronger, it is abandoned by the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*). The masters of the *Abhidharmakośa* refute this, saying:
"Both types of *śīlavrataparāmarśa* take the contaminated (*sāsrava*) as their object and both falsely reckon what is not the path to be the path;
why then does one arise with respect to the fruit?"
First, it does not arise from a non-resultant state.
Since the principle is equal in both cases, they should both arise as results.
If they both arise as results, their characteristics would still have no distinction.
To speak merely in words while contravening the Way,
and furthermore to claim that even the ultimate principle of the Truth of the Path (mārgasatya) cannot be established—
this is the third difficulty, namely the attachment to views and doubt.
Furthermore, there are wrong views and doubt that take the Truth of the Path as their object:
either the denial that the path to liberation exists,
or the doubt that the path to liberation does not exist.
How could they possibly maintain that this wrong view and doubt can lead to eternal purification?
If they deny the true path to liberation taught by the Tathāgata,
they falsely cling to other causes for purification, such as the so-called "attainment of non-perception" (asaṃjñi-samāpatti).
This would mean that one clings to other states such as the attainment of non-conceptualization (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*) as being able to bring about purification,
rather than clinging to wrong views and the like; thus,
the principle that this clinging to rules and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) has as its object what is abandoned through the path of seeing (*darśanamārga-prahātavya*) is likewise untenable.
The *Nyāyānusārin* replies:
It is not that the essence of this adherence to precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) is non-existent;

for one who holds the false view that denies the Path (*mārga-prativedha-mithyādṛṣṭi*) yet clings to it as the means capable of realizing eternal purification [is indeed characterized by such adherence].
This is because they consider it to be a correct understanding;
that is to say, having first retained another path of liberation within their minds,
they subsequently grasp at the false view that slanders the true path as being a correct realization.
Regarding the term "in accordance with reality" (*yoniśas*):
it refers to the fact that they deny the path of true liberation as being non-erroneous;
because it accords with reality, they cling to it as the cause of purification.
By this, the essential nature of the grasping at rules and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) is established.
That mental aggregate is not abandoned by the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), but rather by the remaining paths of liberation (*vimuktimārga*).
This is because the object of focus for the grasping at rules and observances consists solely of dharmas belonging to its own category.

There are many types of paths, which is not a fault from the perspective of principle. The commentary explains that these refer to other paths of liberation, namely the attainment of non-perception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*) and so forth.
The intention of the *Nyāyānusāra* in its defense is as follows:
Having already rejected the doubt regarding the path and truth propounded by others,
they further cling to this rejection of doubt as being "awakening according to reality";
thus, they immediately grasp that very [rejection] as the cause of purification.
Because time passes so rapidly, [the view] arises in a place where it is not the result of causes and conditions;
thus, it is not abandoned by the vision of suffering and its origin, but is abandoned by the path of vision.
Furthermore, they falsely reckon that the remaining aggregates of mental factors, such as the state of non-perception (*asaṃjñika*), constitute the path of liberation.
Because it arises in the stage of the fruit, it is abandoned by the vision of suffering;
one should know that there are many types [of afflictions],
some of which are abandoned by the path of vision.
Alternatively, what logical fault is there in [asserting that] some [of these views] are abandoned through the vision of suffering? The masters of the *Abhidharmakośa* refute this, saying:
"There are also certain precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*)—namely, those which grasp at them as causes of purification—which are abandoned through the vision of suffering."
This too would then be what kind of grasping that is not abandoned by the path of seeing?
If it were not grasping itself, but rather grasping something else as a cause of purity,
then it would follow that it could not be abandoned by the path of seeing.
Furthermore, if there are those who take as their object that which is not to be abandoned by seeing,
this constitutes the fourth difficulty regarding the false view of accumulation and cessation.
Moreover, if there are those who take as the cause of purification false views and other such attachments that are to be abandoned by seeing the truths of accumulation and cessation.
What are the causes and conditions for this adherence to rules and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*)?
Is it not because one does not see their origin, cessation, and abandonment?
The *Nyāya* [school] offers this defense:
If one reckons that the false view which denies the origin [of suffering] can bring about purification,
would this view not lack the function of abandoning the origin?
If one reckons that the false view which denies cessation can bring about purification...

Is it not the case that this view lacks the function of realizing cessation? To explain: the intent of that treatise is to say that if one denies the existence of origination (*samudaya*), there would be nothing to be abandoned;
thus, one would reckon the Path (*mārga*) to be useless.
If one were to deny cessation, there would be nothing to be realized.
The Master of the *Abhidharmakośa* refutes the claim that the Path is useless by stating:
"Just as if one were to deny the Path, there would be no one capable of realizing it."
Even if one negates the Path while reckoning another path as capable of realization,
what prevents one from likewise negating Origination and Cessation while reckoning other forms of origination and cessation as that which is to be abandoned and that which is to be realized?

Therefore, regarding the point that "the meaning thus grasped should be further examined," the Master of the Treatise, having finished his refutation, again exhorts that it should be examined; the examination according to correct principle (nyāya) should be understood as before.
The further refutation in the *Abhidharmakośa* is also as previously stated.
Regarding what was previously stated up to "the two kinds of inversion," the following fourth section clarifies the four inversions. Question:
As previously stated, the clinging to precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) arises from the inversions of permanence and self.
If it is asked whether there are only these two kinds of inversion,
and how one should understand that inversions extend to the inversion of grasping at a self, the answer is as follows:
In total there are four.
Regarding these four inversions, what is their essential nature?
This is the question.
Since the names are thus, what is their nature?
The verse says: "Reaching perception, the mind follows the power of views."
The first two lines set forth the nature of the inversion;
the third line establishes its refutation;
and the fourth line harmonizes with the sūtras.
The Commentary states: "Regarding 'up to [the point where] it is taken as the inversion of self,' this explains the first two lines.
In total, there are two interpretations."
This is the first master’s position.
Among the five views, he establishes the essence of the four perversions based on three views;
that is, from among the extreme views (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*), he takes only the eternalist view (*śāśvatadṛṣṭi*) as the perversion of permanence.
One does not adopt the view of nihilism (*ucchedadṛṣṭi*).
Among all forms of grasping at views, only that which conceives of what is inferior in suffering as being pleasant or pure constitutes the perversions of pleasure and purity;
it is not any other form of grasping at views.

Among the contaminated phenomena (*sāsrava-dharma*), that which is not true happiness is falsely conceived as happiness and purity; therefore, it is said to be the "conception of the non-superior as superior.
Within the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), only the conception of a self is taken as the inversion of self, and not the conception of "mine" (*ātmīya*).

It should be understood that the four inversions arise only with respect to the coarse fruits within the contaminated (*sāsrava*) realm and are abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*).
Although the view of grasping at views (*dṛṣṭi-parāmarśa*) also extends to the other three truths,
it is not established as an inversion because it is not predominant therein.
Therefore, the *Vibhāṣā* (104) states:
Some say that among the four perversions (*viparyāsa*),
three views each take one portion [of the five views] as their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).

That is to say, among the views of a self-existent body (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), the view of a self (*ātmadṛṣṭi*) is the intrinsic nature of the inversion of "self," whereas the view of "mine" (*ātmīyadṛṣṭi*) is not.
Among the views of extreme adherence (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*), the view of permanence (*śāśvatadṛṣṭi*) is the intrinsic nature of the inversion of "permanence."

It is not the view of nihilism (*ucchedadṛṣṭi*). Among the views of grasping at views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*), the attachment to pleasure and purity that is abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkhadarśana-prahātavya*) is the intrinsic nature of the perversions of pleasure and purity;

it is not other views of grasping at views. Furthermore, the *Nyāyānusāra* (Treatise on Following Reasoning), chapter 47, states the same as the first master mentioned at the beginning of this treatise.
Since this treatise, the *Abhidharmamahāvibhāṣā*,
and the *Nyāyānusāra* all define their essential natures based on the five views, they state that three views each constitute one part [of the self-view].
Some say that the inversion of self (*ātma-viparyāsa*) subsumes the entirety of the view of a self-identity (*satkāya-dṛṣṭi*).
This is the second explanation.
The inversions of permanence, bliss, and purity are explained as before;
however, because the inversion of self is explained differently, it is recounted separately.
Thus, the *Vibhāṣā* (104) states: Question:
Among the five views, how many views constitute its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*)?
Answer: This has two and a half views abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*) as its intrinsic nature.
That is to say: the view of a self-identity (satkāyadṛṣṭi), the entirety of the grasping at views (dṛṣṭiparāmarśa),
and the eternalist view within the view of extremes (antagrāhadṛṣṭi).
Two and a half views do not have a perverted nature as their intrinsic essence;
namely, wrong view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*) and the entirety of the grasping at precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*).
Furthermore, among the views of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*), there is the view of annihilation (*ucchedadṛṣṭi*).
Moreover, the *Nyāyānusāra* (Treatise on Reasoning), fascicle 47, states:
"However, the definitive meaning of the *Vibhāṣā* is as follows..."
In the analysis of the twelve views, only two and a half views constitute the essence of inversion: namely, the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*),
the entirety of the clinging to views regarding suffering (*duḥkhadṛṣṭiparāmarśa*), and the portion of the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*) that clings to permanence.
The modes of activity (*ākāra*) of the two views of annihilationism and eternalism are mutually contradictory;

therefore, it can be said that their two natures are distinct. This treatise, the *Abhidharmamahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, and the *Nyāyānusāra* all define their essential nature (*svabhāva*) by way of the five categories (*pañca-varga*) and twelve views (*dvādaśa-dṛṣṭi*).

Therefore, it is said that [the view of self] consists of the entirety of the view of a self (satkāyadṛṣṭi), the entirety of the clinging to views (dṛṣṭiparāmarśa), and one portion of the view of extremes (antagrāhadṛṣṭi).
Although this treatise contains no evaluative commentary on these two positions,
the intention of the *Abhidharmamahāvibhāṣā* and the *Nyāyānusāra* is that the latter master’s view in this treatise is correct.
The *Abhidharmamahāvibhāṣā* does not state that there is such an opinion;
furthermore, the *Nyāyānusāra* states that it is because [the view of self] has a definitive meaning.
How, then, can the inversion of self be subsumed under the view of "mine"?
This is the question itself.
As for how they are not included,
some say it is a counter-accusation.
Regarding the passage from "Because of the sūtra on the inversions" up to "that which is seen as 'mine'," the answer is:
it is because this was stated based on the sūtra on the four inversions.

Those who conceive of a self and hold that they possess sovereign power over those objects perceive them as "mine. Since "what belongs to the self" (*ātmīya*) is explained as distinct from the "self" (*ātman*), it is clear that "what belongs to the self" is not subsumed under the inversion of the self.
Furthermore, this passage explains that some cite a sūtra to prove that "what belongs to the self" is indeed subsumed [under the inversion].
Regarding the sense of mastery over those phenomena,
this is what I have perceived;
there is no separate entity.
Regarding the statement, "This very view of 'mine' should also be distinguished from the view of 'self,'" some explain the sutra as follows:
this view of "mine" is itself the view of "self."
It is explained separately because it functions through the two gateways of "I" and "mine.
"This is I" is the first case (nominative) expressing the view of self; "belonging to me" [expresses possession].
"This is what I have seen" is the sixth case (genitive).
"By me"—meaning "by me in this way"—is the third case (instrumental). "For me."
The statement "it is for me thus" constitutes the fourth case-ending (*caturthī-vibhakti*).
Among the eight case-endings, if the first and sixth are considered distinct from the third and fourth, [then this is the fourth].
The views should also be distinct;
since the third and fourth views are not different,
how could there be any difference between the first and sixth views?
"Why are the other afflictions not the essence of inversion?
This explains the third phrase; it is a question.
Regarding the response that one must possess three causes to reach the state of non-inversion:
it is said that only when these three superior causes are fully present does inversion arise.
As for what these three causes are:
Because it is a one-sided perversion,
because its nature is that of speculative inference,
and because it falsely superimposes [what does not exist].
Furthermore, the *Nyāyānusāra* states:

"The addition of the word 'also' (*api*) indicates that its essence is superior. This concludes the treatise. Among the five views, the view of adherence to precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*), although it possesses the nature of speculative investigation and involves false superimposition, [is nonetheless distinct].
It is not exclusively erroneous,
because one attains purification by taking only a portion of phenomena as an object;
it is like the grasping at precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*), which calculates that the path of outflows leads to pure nirvāṇa.

Although this does not constitute the ultimate severance of afflictions or the realization of cessation, it is able to temporarily distance one from the defilements of the lower eight stages and realize their cessation; thus, the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* (Vibhāṣā), fascicle 14, states:
"The grasping at precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*), though of a nature of speculative investigation and false superimposition..."
It is not, however, exclusively inverted,
because it also operates upon a small portion of what is real;
that is to say, the path of the form realm can purify the existence of the desire realm.
The formless path can purify existence in the form realm;
paths of higher stages can purify lower stages.
Through the untainted path, one abandons defilements and realizes cessation.
Because their meanings are similar. Furthermore, the *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya* states:

"The adherence to precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) is not exclusively erroneous, because that which is adhered to may potentially be free from the defilement of desire (*kāmarāga*), and so forth."

Because they attain purification for a small portion and for a brief time. Question: Just as the adherence to views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*) conceives pleasant feeling (*sukhavedanā*) to be pleasure and conceives wholesome phenomena (*kuśaladharma*) to be pure, these too function with respect to a small portion of reality.
Why are these considered inversions? The explanation states: they cling to the out-flowing (sāsrava) as being identical to the bliss of nirvāṇa and identical to the purity of nirvāṇa.

Since there is not even the slightest bliss or purity within the out-flowing, to equate it with that nirvāṇa—which is exclusively [the opposite]—is an inversion; therefore, they are called inversions.
The clinging to precepts and observances (śīlavrataparāmarśa) consists in regarding what is not the path as the path;
however, because it shares a portion with the uncontaminated noble path and its realization of the purity of nirvāṇa, it does not constitute a perversion.
Although the view of annihilation (ucchedadṛṣṭi) and false views (mithyādṛṣṭi) are exclusively perversions and possess the nature of speculative investigation, [they do not share this portion].
It is not a false superimposition,
because it does not function through a gateway;
therefore, it is not an inversion.
The remaining [afflictions], such as greed, hatred, pride, and doubt,
although they are entirely inverted and involve false superimposition,
are incapable of such deliberative estimation.
Because it does not perceive a self-nature, it is not an inversion.
An inversion is established by one who possesses three causes.
Therefore, other afflictions are not of the nature of inversion.
The views of holding as supreme (*agrāhadrṣṭi*) directed toward the truths of origination, cessation, and the path should likewise be distinguished separately,
but they are omitted here for brevity.
Therefore, the *Nyāyānusāra* states:

"Because the view of grasping at views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*) of other schools is not predominant," as cited above in the treatise. As for the view of "mine" (*mamakāradṛṣṭi*), since its various attachments differ, it is not separately distinguished.
If one follows the first master,
my view is not erroneous;
one should say that although my view involves speculative reasoning and false conceptualization, it is nonetheless not inverted.
It is not an absolute perversion,
because it also operates with respect to a small portion of what is real,
such as when one conceives of real dharmas as being "mine."
It is not because they lack intrinsic nature that they are not inverted; rather,
it is according to the second master’s view.
This view of "mine" is itself the view of "self.
Although explained through two distinct modes,
it is subsumed within the view of self.
It also possesses three causes;
therefore, it is an inversion.
If that is so, why is it that [the notion] "it is not-self" is likewise [an inversion]?
The following explains the difficulty regarding the fourth phrase:
If only "view" were designated as "perversion," why does the Sūtra state that there are twelve perversions in total?
It is also said that this refers to perception and mind.
To the question, "In principle, one should know that this is because they share the same characteristics up to the stage of application," the answer is as follows:
In principle, only views are perversions;
however, perception and thought are also designated as "perversion" because they follow along with the view.
Because its mode of activity is identical to that of views with which it is associated,
it is described as an inversion by way of its characteristics; however, its essential nature is not that of inferential cognition.
It is not subsumed under the four inversions.
If that is so, why is it not said that feeling and the other [aggregates] are also [inversions]?
This is the objection.

If that were the case, then feeling (*vedanā*) and the other [aggregates] would also have to be called "inversions of feeling" and so forth, since they too reach the world. To this, the answer is given: the Sūtra does not mention them because...
Because [the existence of] feeling and so forth is not universally established in the world.
That is to say, the inversion of thought and perception is universally established in the world;
as when one says, "This matter vexes my thought and perception."
However, it is not stated that they "afflict my feeling" and so forth;
therefore, the Sūtra does not mention them.
Thus, these various inversions are abandoned by the path of seeing (*darśana-prahātavya*).
This demonstrates that [these perversions] are abandoned solely through seeing. Thus, these various perversions have already been abandoned by a stream-enterer (srotāpanna),
because the views and their associated factors— such as perception (saṃjñā) and mind (citta)— are abandoned through seeing (darśana-prahātavya).
The statement by other schools, "How could one who has attained [the dhyānas] give rise to sensual desire?
is a citation of a divergent view;
this is based on the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* and the *Nyāyānusāra*.
According to this Vibhajyavādin,
among the twelve [factors], eight are abandoned solely by vision;
the [notions of] permanence and self are each threefold.
Namely: perception, mind,
and view.
The [perceptions of] pleasure and purity each have one [type],
namely the inversion of view (*dṛṣṭi-viparyāsa*).
These four are abandoned through both seeing (*darśana*) and cultivation (*bhāvanā*).
Pleasure and purity each have two aspects:
namely, perception and mind.
If one were to say this is not so,
how could a noble one who has not yet abandoned desire give rise to sensual greed when their mind is free from the perception of pleasure and purity?
For this reason, it is known that the perceptions of pleasure and purity also extend to the abandonment through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*).
As for the Vaibhāṣika masters who cite the case of the painted yakṣa as an instance of delusion:
The Vaibhāṣika masters do not accept this view;
they maintain that if the perceptions of pleasure and purity were to manifest in the mind,
one would have to concede that noble ones (āryas) possess the distortions of pleasure and purity.
If an Noble One (ārya) were also to give rise to the perception and thought of a sentient being,
then one must likewise admit that he possesses the inversion of the view of a self (ātma-dṛṣṭi-viparyāsa).
This would apply not only to women and the like, but also to his own person.
Because the mind still gives rise to desire and greed for the notion of a sentient being,
once the notion of a sentient being has arisen in the mind,
the perversion of the view of self (ātma-dṛṣṭi) should also arise.
Furthermore, he cites a sūtra as proof that [the path] does not apply to the abandonment through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*).
The sūtra states: "The noble ones perceive the Noble Truth of Suffering as it truly is during the path of immediate succession (*ānantarya-mārga*)."
One knows the path of liberation as it truly is.
In this way, one sees and knows the noble truths of origin, cessation, and the path as they truly are; the correct principle is fully supported by the scriptural texts.
Because this treatise briefly cites the scriptural text, it says "up to" (*yāvat*).
It skips over the other three truths and takes up the subsequent scriptural passage:
"At that time, that noble disciple [erroneously] conceives the impermanent as permanent."
The perversions of perception, mind, and view regarding [the notion of] pleasure, purity, and self have all been permanently severed.
This is explained at length for the three aspects of suffering, impurity, and non-self;
that is, the perversions of perception, mind, and view that reckon [what is suffering] as pleasure, [what is impure] as pure, and [what is non-self] as self, have all been permanently severed.
Therefore, one should know that these perceptions and cognitions are inverted perceptions and inverted cognitions arising solely through the power of association with the view of inversion;
they are not other perceptions and cognitions.
In truth, the four inversions are abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*).

As for the statement in this sutra that "at the time of seeing and knowing the truths of origination and so forth as they truly are, [the afflictions] are all already permanently abandoned," this refers to those who have attained the vision of the noble truths (āryasatyadarśana),
because it is said that they have already permanently abandoned them.
Although the noble ones perceive objects as suffering and impure,
because they are at times momentarily deluded and oppressed by craving,
a perception of pleasure and purity may suddenly arise toward an object; however, once their minds have become aware of this, it immediately ceases.
Because it is not a result of inferential deliberation (*tarka*), it does not constitute a cognitive distortion (*viparyāsa*). This is like the case of a whirling firebrand:
although it is not actually a wheel, due to delusion one suddenly sees it and perceives it as a wheel.
One gives rise to the thought of a wheel;
once awakened, it is immediately gone,
just as one perceives a painted yakṣa due to delusion.
It was not an actual yakṣa, yet upon suddenly seeing it,
he took it to be so; the thought arose in his mind and fear was born,
but once he awoke, it was gone.
Since this is not an inversion,
the same applies to the Noble Ones. If that is so, why does it not contradict that sūtra?
Regarding the difficult point concerning the Vaibhāṣika masters: Ānanda—
whose Sanskrit name is Ānanda, meaning "Joy" or "Pleasure"—
is one who has attained the first fruit [of the path].

If one considers that the inversion of perception (*saṃjñā-viparyāsa*) is abandoned only through the path of vision (*darśana-heya*) and does not extend to the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*), why did Ānanda tell Vijaya-kīrti:
"Because of the inversion of your perception, your mind is burning with fever"?
Subsequently, having attained the fruit of arhatship and being far removed from those perceptions, craving ceases and the mind becomes pure. In the stage of training (śaikṣa), however,
one still gives rise to both the inversion of perception and the inversion of mind.
Therefore, it is known that the perversions of perception and mind also pertain to those abandoned through cultivation. Furthermore, other masters of the Sautrāntika school state:
"The eight perversions of perception and mind are not yet fully abandoned by one in training."
The intention of that school is as follows:
because *dṛṣṭi* (views) are exclusively deluded regarding principles (*tattva*), they are abandoned only through seeing (*darśana-prahātavya*).

Because *saṃjñā* (perception) and *citta* (mind) arise through delusion regarding both principles and phenomena (*vastu*), they are abandoned through both seeing and cultivation (*bhāvanā-prahātavya*).
Furthermore, this connects back to the preceding sutra.

Regarding what was stated in that sutra— that the misconceptions, mental distortions, and views concerning the four noble truths are all permanently severed through seeing and knowing them as they truly are—
this present sutra does not speak of only those [defilements] abandoned by seeing.

They are also to be abandoned through cultivation. Thus, these eight types are ultimately severed forever during the stage of cultivation only by means of seeing and knowing the Noble Truths as they truly are;
for apart from this contemplation of the truths, there is no other means for the permanent abandonment of these eight types.
These eight types taught by the Sautrāntika school also pertain to those abandoned through cultivation;
this does not contradict the aforementioned sutra.
The master’s intention aligns with the Sautrāntika position.
Therefore, in this context, the twelve inversions are refuted;
according to the Vaibhāṣika masters, they are abandoned only through the vision of suffering (duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya), because coarse fruits arise [only] from that.

Among the various defiled perceptions and minds in the stage of training (śaikṣa), as well as the neutral perceptions and minds in the stage of no-more-training (aśaikṣa), those that possess delusion may indeed be said to be "inverted" (viparyāsa);
however, they do not constitute the four inversions.
Possessing these three meanings, they are designated as "perversions" (viparyāsa) based on their predominance, as previously explained.
According to other schools, however, these eight are exclusively abandoned through insight (darśana-heya).
The fourfold cultivation of insight should be understood as previously explained.
According to the masters of other Sūtra schools:
Four are abandoned by insight alone;
eight are abandoned by both insight and cultivation,
as previously explained.
Regarding the question of whether it is only the latent tendency of views (*dṛṣṭy-anuśaya*) that exists, or if others also exist:
hereafter, the fifth section clarifies the seven and nine types of pride (*māna*).
Within this:
I. A direct explanation of the seven and nine types of pride.
II. An explanation of why they do not arise when not yet abandoned. Regarding the first [section], a direct explanation of the seven and nine types of pride:
Question—Is it only the latent tendencies of views (*dṛṣṭy-anuśaya*) that have many different distinctions based on their differing modes of activity?
Question: Are there also distinctions among the other latent dispositions (*anuśaya*), and is there also [a distinction] for pride (*māna*)?
Answer: Yes.
What is this? It is an inquiry.
The verse says: "Up to those who have abandoned through cultivation but do not practice."
The first line provides the direct answer;
the second line clarifies what is abandoned through seeing and cultivation;
the final two lines demonstrate that what has not yet been abandoned does not manifest.
The commentary states: "As for the phrase 'divided into seven types because they reach [the object],' this below explains the seven kinds of pride (*māna*).
This constitutes the general explanation."
Regarding the general explanation of pride (*māna*) with respect to those who are inferior or equal,
the following section provides a detailed analysis of the seven types of pride;
the text itself consists of seven parts.
This explains the first type of pride:
regarding oneself as superior when one is inferior,
and regarding oneself as equal when one is equal.
That which causes the mind to become uplifted is, in general, termed pride (*māna*). How is it [applied] to equals?
For example, there may be two persons whose mental faculties are equal.
First, one who has already mastered the recitation of the Āgama sūtras,
and later, another who masters the recitation,
the mind of the former then becomes uplifted and conceited.
Therefore, the *Nyāyabindu* (or *Prayoga*) 47 states:

"To consider oneself superior or equal in terms of lineage, intelligence, and so forth, when one is actually inferior or equal to others, is called pride (*māna*). But would it not be the case that these two [types of pride] do not constitute pride, since they operate toward their objects in accordance with reality?"
To speak of oneself as superior when one is inferior,
or to speak of oneself as equal when one is equal—

knowing this through comparison, what fault constitutes pride (*māna*)? When the mind develops attachment toward an agreeable object and proceeds in accordance with reality, how does this constitute greed (*lobha*)?
Since this involves the pursuit of agreeable objects without inversion,
it should not be an affliction; yet,
because it arises from this [pursuit] and is able to defile and distress the mind, it is admitted to constitute greed (*lobha*).
This is the nature of affliction (*kleśa*).
Thus, although it arises in superior or inferior states,
it causes the mind to become uplifted and defiled.
This is called the affliction of pride (*māna*).
What fault is there in this principle? The explanation says:
"Lineage."
This refers to lineage and clarity;
"clarity" means intelligence.
The word "etc.
indicates [attributes such as] complexion, strength, wealth, and so forth.
When one regards oneself as equal to or superior to those who are actually equal or superior, this is collectively termed *abhimāna* (overweening pride).
This explains the second type of conceit:
regarding those who are equal, one considers oneself superior; regarding those who are superior, one considers oneself equal.
This is collectively termed *atimāna* (excessive pride).
Because pride is excessive, one falsely advances one rank,
or exceeds the aforementioned types of pride.
Alternatively, because pride is excessive and precedes [the object],
it is called "excessive pride" (*abhimāna*).
The *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra* states:
To consider oneself superior or equal to others who are actually equal or superior—
in terms of lineage, knowledge, and so forth— is called *abhimāna* (conceit).
Regarding the superior, to claim superiority is called *mānātimāna* (conceit exceeding pride).
This explains the third type of conceit: regarding one who is superior, to claim superiority—where "superior" means surpassing oneself.
It is called "conceit beyond conceit" (*mānātimāna*) because it exceeds other forms of conceit;
alternatively, "conceit" refers to loftiness,
and because it is loftier than that [other] conceit, it is named "conceit beyond conceit."
The *Nyāyabindu* states:
"Regarding the superior lineage, knowledge,
and so forth of others..."
To consider oneself superior to another is called *mānātimāna* (conceit beyond conceit).
Regarding the statement "applying [this] to the five aggregates of clinging is called *asmimāna* (the conceit 'I am')":
this explains the fourth type of conceit.
To grasp at the five aggregates of clinging as "I" and "mine" is the view of self (satkāyadṛṣṭi); or it is conceit arising with reference to a self,
or conceit based on relying upon a self.
Alternatively, because pride arises from the notion of "I," it is called "pride of self" (*asmimāna*).
To claim that one has attained what has not yet been realized is called "overweening pride" (*abhimāna*).
This explains the fifth pride:
regarding superior qualities that one has not yet realized,
one claims to have realized them.
This is called "overweening pride" (*adhimāna*).
The *Nyāyānusāra* states:
"Other masters say..."
To claim for oneself that one has realized many virtues when one has realized only a few,
and thus for the mind to become puffed up, is called *adhimāna* (overweening pride).
To consider oneself inferior to those who are superior by a great margin is called *ūnamāna* (inferiority pride).
The sixth type of pride is explained.
The *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra* states:
"There are those who dwell in the household."
Alternatively, when a renunciant perceives themselves as slightly inferior to others who possess a great abundance of qualities such as craftsmanship or ethical discipline (*śīla*),
yet gives rise to a mind of haughtiness, this is called "inferior pride" (*ūnamāna*).
In this context, one who is haughty regarding their own mind considers themselves superior to others and deems themselves inferior;
because they increase [the estimation] of themselves, it is also called "haughtiness" (māna).
Regarding the statement, "To attain [the notion of superiority] amidst the absence of virtue is called false pride," this explains the seventh type of pride.
It refers to [the conceit] regarding various unwholesome actions and qualities that lack virtue.
To claim for oneself virtues that one does not possess is called *mithyāmāna* (false pride).
Thus, the *Nyāyānusāra* states:
"To claim for oneself virtues that one lacks is called *mithyāmāna*."
That which is called "lack of virtue" refers to all unwholesome actions.
It is designated by the name "lack of virtue" because it is contrary to merit,
just as [the term] "unwholesome" (akuśala) is used.
In the midst of possessing such unvirtuous qualities, one claims for oneself these superior merits;
because one relies on this evil and becomes haughty, it is called "wrong pride" (*mithyāmāna*). If one were to say that "lack of merit" is a negation of "possessing merit," [it would not be so].
To claim that one possesses qualities when, in reality, one lacks them is called false pride (*mithyāmāna*).
In the analysis of the distinctions between overweening pride (*adhimāna*) and false pride, it is stated that that which is without seeds is called overweening pride,
while that which has seeds is called false pride.

Otherwise, the distinction between overestimating one's qualities to the full extent being called "overweening pride" (*adhimāna*), and overestimating them only to a small degree being called "false pride" (*mithyāmāna*),
would logically fail to be established.
Therefore, one should know that what was stated previously is superior.
As for the statement in the root treatise regarding those who emerge from among the three,
the following explains how the nine arise from the three.
This explains the root treatise (*mūla-śāstra*).
However, the *Jñānaprasthāna* root treatise states that there are nine types of pride (*māna*): "I am superior," and so forth.
"I am superior to him" means "I am equal to him.
"I am equal to him" means "I am inferior to him.
"I am inferior to him" means "there is someone superior to me."
That is to say: there is another who is superior to the self, while the self is equal;
there is another who is equal to the self, while the self is inferior;
there is another who is inferior to the self, while there is no one superior to the self.
This means: "There is no one superior to me; I am equal to those who are my equals.
"There is no one equal to me" means: "There is no one who is my equal, yet I am superior to them. "There is no one inferior to me."
That is to say: "There is no other who is inferior," "I am inferior," and "I dwell in inferiority. These nine [conceptions] arise from three among the previous seven.
From which three? Question: [What are they?]
Regarding the statement "from pride (māna) up to excessive pride (adhimāna) and inferiority pride (ūnamāna)":
the answer is that these refer to the first through the seventh types of pride.
The second is overweening pride (*adhimāna*);
the sixth is inferiority pride (*ūnamāna*).
These three types of pride, if they arise and function based upon the view of self (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), [are to be abandoned by insight].
There is a distinction in their sequence,
which forms three groups of three, totaling nine types of conceit (*māna*).
Among these nine, the first three follow their respective order as follows:
The type of pride called "pride of superiority" (*abhimāna*) consists of thinking, "I am superior to them.
To think one is superior when one is actually equal is "excessive pride" (*atimāna*).
The type of pride called "pride of equality" (*mānamāna*) consists of thinking, "I am equal to them."
Regarding those who are equal, to consider oneself equal is pride (*māna*).
Regarding those who are inferior, to consider oneself superior is the type of pride of superiority (*atimāna*).
Regarding those who are superior, to consider oneself inferior is the pride of inferiority (*ūnamāna*). Among these nine types, the three middle ones follow their respective order.
There is the class of *māna* (pride) called "pride of superiority," which consists of thinking, "I am superior to those who are superior to me.
Thinking oneself inferior to those who are superior is *ūnamāna* (inferiority pride).
There is the class of *māna* called "pride of equality," which consists of thinking, "I am equal to those who are equal to me."
Regarding equals, to consider oneself equal is pride (*māna*).
Regarding those who are inferior, to consider oneself superior is the class of pride regarding the inferior (*ūnamāna*).
Regarding equals, to consider oneself superior is over-pride (*atimāna*). Among these nine types, the last three follow their respective order.
The class of "unconquerable" (*atimāna*) conceit refers to thinking, "I am not surpassed by others.
Regarding those who are equal, to think "I have already surpassed them" is *adhimāna* (excessive conceit).
The class of "not inferior" (*anavamāna*) conceit refers to thinking, "I am not inferior to others."
To consider oneself inferior when one is superior is the pride of inferiority (*ūnamāna*).
