What is that which reaches the highest point when one is superior by a great margin?
[This is] the question.
Just as one might develop the conceit of inferiority (*ūnamāna*) regarding the many superior qualities of others,
thinking oneself to be slightly inferior or lowly,
because there is a sense of being on a higher level.
Regarding those types of inferior *asmimāna* (the conceit "I am") that arise from a high position, from what do they arise?
It refers to one who, having reached such a state, regards themselves with self-importance. The answer is as follows:
Although the "inferiority-inflation" (*ūnamāna*) lacks a sense of loftiness,
when one regards oneself in comparison to a group of beings whom one loves as superior,
one perceives oneself as being extremely inferior.
Because one respects oneself, one is able to give rise to that "inferiority-free" *asmimāna*.
This concludes the explanation according to the *Jñānaprasthāna-śāstra*.
These nine types of pride (*māna*) are explained for now according to the *Jñānaprasthāna-śāstra*.

Regarding the statement that they are distinguished "according to the categories of the *Prakaraṇapāda* based on the differences in their objects and degrees," this further explains the types of pride according to the *Prakaraṇapāda*.
Furthermore, the category of "conceit of superiority" (*abhimāna*) arises from three types of conceit.
If one regards an inferior object as superior to oneself, it is subsumed under "conceit" (*māna*).
If one regards an equal object as superior to oneself, it is "excessive conceit" (*atimāna*).
If one contemplates a superior object and considers oneself superior, this is pride beyond pride (*mānātimāna*).
The remaining eight types of pride should be explained accordingly according to reason.
As for these seven types of pride, by what are they abandoned?
The second phrase is explained.
This is the question:
"Are all [afflictions] abandoned through both seeing and cultivation?"
Answer: Thus, all seven types of pride are common to both the path of seeing and the path of cultivation, according to their respective applications.
If they take as their object that which is abandoned by the path of seeing, they are abandoned by the path of seeing.
If one practices abandonment by taking objects as conditions,
it should be understood that all seven types of pride pervade the three realms;
thus, the *Abhidharmamahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 43, states:
The commentary states: It should be explained in this way.
Inferiority-complex (*ūnamāna*) and the like do not arise by means of inferring the superiority or inferiority of others;
rather, they arise through the power of repeated practice since beginningless time.
Although they also manifest even in the higher realms,
all three realms are thus endowed with the seven types of pride.
These are among those abandoned through cultivation that are capable of manifesting.
Question:
When a noble one (*ārya*) has not yet abandoned the conceit (*māna*) to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*), is it possible for it to manifest?
This is not determined until [the point] where it is exclusively abandoned by cultivation.
Answer: This is not certain.
Among the seven types of pride, some may be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*), and it is possible for them to manifest in noble ones (*ārya*) while they have not yet been abandoned.
That is to say, excluding the category of pride and the pride of "I am," among the remaining types of pride, some are to be abandoned through cultivation;
while they have not yet been abandoned, the noble ones certainly do not manifest them.
This refers to the class of pride known as *asmimāna* (the conceit "I am").
The reasons why this does not function will be explained immediately hereafter by means of an illustrative analogy.
Just as the fetter of killing is abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*),
yet it never manifests in any noble being (*ārya*);
the "fetter of killing" indicates that one initiates intentional thought (*saṃcetanā*) by means of this affliction to take the life of a living being.
The verse uses the word “etc. to indicate the fetters of stealing, sexual misconduct, and deception.
Craving for non-existence (*vibhavatṛṣṇā*) does not arise at all;

craving for existence (*bhavatṛṣṇā*) does not arise in one part. Question: What phenomenon is designated as “non-existence”? Answer: It refers to the cessation of the impermanent nature of the three realms; this is what is called non-existence.
Craving for non-existence (*vibhava-tṛṣṇā*) refers to the intense longing for this very impermanence.

If one speaks generally of the impermanence of the three realms, all craving for non-existence is abandoned through both the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*) and the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*). However, the intention here is to speak specifically regarding the three realms.
The characteristic of impermanent cessation within the homogeneous class of beings (*nikāya-sabhāga*) is called "non-existence" (*vibhava*). The craving for the thought,
"May I be annihilated and cease to exist after death," directed toward this non-existence,
is called "craving for non-existence" (*vibhavatṛṣṇā*).
Because such craving does not arise at all for the Noble Ones, and because it is abandoned solely through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*),
it is designated as "craving for non-existence" (*vibhava-tṛṣṇā*) when it refers specifically to the craving for the impermanence of the homogeneous class (*nikāya-sabhāga*).
Therefore, the *Vibhāṣā* (vol. 27) states:
"Non-existence" refers to the impermanence of the homogeneous class (*nikāyasabhāga*).
Craving that takes this as its object is called "craving for non-existence" (*vibhavatṛṣṇā*).
Therefore, this craving is abandoned only through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*),
because the homogeneous character (*nikāya-sabhāga*) is abandoned only through cultivation.
Furthermore, the *Nyāyānusāra* (Treatise on the Correct Principles), fascicle 47, states:
Do you not see that among those things abandoned by insight, there are also impermanence and the absence of craving?
For what reason are they said to be abandoned only through cultivation? In reality, they are also abandoned by insight;
however, for the time being, I follow the statement of the Sūtra.
It refers to what is taught in the sūtras regarding the three types of craving:
craving for sensory desire (*kāmatṛṣṇā*), craving for existence (*bhavatṛṣṇā*), and craving for non-existence (*vibhavatṛṣṇā*).
In this particular sūtra, it is craving for non-existence that is being discussed.
Regarding those who take as their object the impermanence of the homogeneous class (*nikāya-sabhāga*) conditioned by grasping:
because the continuity of the maturation (*vipāka*) of craving is severed, it is as stated in the Sūtra:
"A certain class of beings, oppressed by suffering, reflects thus:"
"May I, after death, be severed and destroyed; there is no such thing as the bliss of being free from illness.

For now, based on this statement, it refers only to what is abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*), not to what is abandoned through insight (*darśana-heya*). This concludes the preceding portion of the treatise. Furthermore, [the text] explains that the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) of the three realms possess the characteristic of impermanence and cessation.
The craving for this [non-existence] is called "craving for non-existence" (*vibhavatṛṣṇā*).
This is a general designation for all forms of craving for non-existence;
however, it specifically refers here to the craving for the impermanence of the homogeneous class of beings (*nikāyasabhāga*).
Because such craving does not arise at all in the Noble Ones,
and because it is abandoned solely through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*), the *Mahāvibhāṣā* states:

This treatise clarifies that while it was previously established in accordance with the meaning of the sūtras that craving for non-existence (*vibhava-tṛṣṇā*) is abandoned solely through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*),
it now reveals, in accordance with the actual reality, that craving for non-existence is abandoned by both [paths].

Because the three realms are impermanent and are subject to both types of abandonment, one knows by this that "the three realms are impermanent" is a general statement regarding all craving for existence (*bhava-tṛṣṇā*). It is called "craving for existence" because it arises with regard to a future body. As for the phrase "a portion": [Note: The provided text fragment ends here; the translation reflects the content available.]
This means that while still an ordinary being (*pṛthagjana*), one makes a vow to become the great nāga king Elāpattra and others.
The *Nyāyānusāra* states:
"The word 'etcetera' (*ādi*) is used to indicate the asura kings."
Uttarakuru; the Heaven of Non-conception, and so forth—this concludes the preceding treatise.
Airāvaṇa is the name of a water [serpent].
The "water-dwelling nāga-elephant" is named after its aquatic origin;
it is the king of nāga-elephants ridden by Śakra.
Thus, the *Nyāyapraveśa* (Treatise on Right Reasoning), fascicle 75, states:
The great elephant king Airāvaṇa is the sovereign elephant ridden by the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa heaven;
this concludes the treatise. Although noble beings may give rise to attachment toward a body within the happy realms, [they do not cling to it].
Regarding the "one portion of craving for existence" (*bhavarāga*) that has not been abandoned in the case of the nāga kings and others in the miserable destinies (*apāya*):
it does not arise because noble ones do not crave the bodies of those miserable destinies;
therefore, it is called "one portion of craving for existence."
These fetters of killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, and deception;
these various forms of craving for existence and craving for non-existence.
Because all [of these] take only those dharmas abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) as their objects, they are abandoned through cultivation alone.
Although dharmas abandoned through seeing (*darśana-heya*) can also take dharmas abandoned through cultivation as their objects,
they are not abandoned through cultivation alone because they do not take [these] exclusively as their objects.
The fetters of killing, stealing,
and sexual misconduct arise conditioned by bodily karma that is abandoned through cultivation.
The fetter of deceit arises conditioned by verbal karma that is abandoned through cultivation.
There is no arising of impermanent phenomena within the homogeneous class (*nikāya-sabhāga*) abandoned through cultivation, conditioned by craving for non-existence (*vibhava-tṛṣṇā*).
A portion of craving for existence (*bhava-tṛṣṇā*), however, arises conditioned by the body that is to exist in the future, which is itself abandoned through cultivation.
As for the statement, "Because the types of pride (*māna-vidha*) and so forth increase due to [the presence of] views (*dṛṣṭi*) and doubt (*vicikitsā*)," it has already been explained.
This is the second explanation regarding "non-arising despite not having been abandoned.
The treatise states, "up to 'all are certainly not produced,'" where the word "etc.
(*ādi*) is intended to reveal the various envelopments (*paryavasthāna*) of killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, and deceit.
The entirety of craving for non-existence (*vibhavatṛṣṇā*) and one portion of craving for existence (*bhavatṛṣṇā*), as well as these types of pride (*māna*) and so forth, namely,
the pride of "I am" (*asmimāna*).
Evil regret is closely increased by views and doubt. "Closely increased" means that it is directly led, induced, and continuously manifested by them.
Although it is abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*), because its opposition to [right] view and doubt has already been broken, it is so designated.
Although the Noble Ones have not yet severed them,
these [defilements] certainly cannot arise;
for views and doubt possess the power to support conceit and the others.
It is severed like a broken back;
though it exists, it does not function—
namely, the nine types of conceit and the "I-conceit" (asmimāna) among the seven types of conceit.
The view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) is augmented by the arising of a self;
one should know that there are nine types of pride (*māna*).
According to the *Jñānaprasthāna*, these arise from pride (*māna*), excessive pride (*atimāna*), and inferiority pride (*ūnamāna*).
That is to say, one portion of these three types of pride does not function.
Furthermore, if categorized by their specific varieties, there are also pride (*māna*) and excessive pride (*atimāna*);
thus, one portion of four types of pride does not function.
The fetters of killing, stealing, sexual misconduct,
and deception are increased by wrong view;
it is due to wrong view that one commits acts such as killing.
Among the four types of verbal transgressions, false speech is mentioned separately because it is that which is abandoned by the precept of non-false speech within the five precepts.
Furthermore, all forms of craving for non-existence are increased by the view of annihilationism; such craving arises by taking as its object the cessation of future existence.
One portion of craving is increased by the view of eternalism (*śāśvatadṛṣṭi*),
because through greed one may expect to dwell for a long time in the bodies of great nāgas and the like.
Among the types of regret (*kaukṛtya*), unwholesome regret is increased by doubt (*vicikitsā*).

Because regret (*kaukṛtya*) and doubt (*vicikitsā*) are similar in certain respects, even though they have not been abandoned within the continuum of an Arya, they certainly do not arise because they have been "broken by turning away" (*parāmarśana*).
Question: Are greed (*rāga*) and the other [afflictions] to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) also taken as universal causes (*sarvatraga-hetu*) by means of view and doubt?
How do the noble abandonments of wrong view and doubt arise? The explanation states: one should know that those abandoned through cultivation arise due to multiple causes;
some must be induced to arise by means of a direct cause.
As with the types of pride and so forth,
some may arise even through remote causes,
such as greed, hatred, and the like.
There are two kinds of causes:
first, the cause that has not yet been abandoned;
second, the cause that has already been abandoned.
Just as with the types of pride and so forth,
which can only arise when their causes have not been abandoned,
other afflictions such as greed and hatred can also be induced even when their causes have already been abandoned.

Regarding the statement, "Among the ninety-eight underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*), up to those that are also included as universal (*sarvatraga*)," this marks the second major section: the analysis by way of various categories. Within this:
1. Universal and non-universal;
2. With outflow and without-outflow objects;
3. Two kinds of increase.
4. The discrimination of the two natures;
5. Clarifying faculties and non-faculties;
6. Clarifying the afflictions that bind.
7. Explaining how the afflictions increase;
8. Explaining their sequential arising. This clarifies the universal and non-universal [afflictions].
The treatise says, up to the point where the name "universal" is established:
Explaining the first verse:

Only the eleven underlying tendencies (anuśaya) that are abandoned through the path of suffering and its origin can function as universal (sarvatraga) with respect to the five categories within their own realm and level.
Therefore, these eleven [defilements] all receive the name "pervasive" (sarvatraga).
Apart from these eleven, the remaining afflictions of the five categories lack the power to pervade all five categories within their own realm and stage.
Therefore, none of them are established as "universal" (sarvatraga).
Thus, these eleven [defilements] universally take as their object all phenomena belonging to the five categories within their own realm and stage.
Because they take all five categories as their objective domain,
they are "universal" (sarvatraga); because they increase as latent tendencies (anuśaya) across all five categories, they are "pervasive" (sarvatragānuśaya).
Taking these three as causes,
they universally produce defiled dharmas of all five categories.
Based on these three meanings, the name "pervasive latent proclivity" (sarvatraga-anuśaya) is established.
Aside from these eleven [universal mental factors], the other five classes of afflictions and their associated and co-existent dharmas lack all three characteristics.
The eleven universal factors and their associated dharmas [possess them].
There are cases where the first and last meanings are present but the middle meaning is missing;
there are eleven universal concomitants (sarvatraga) among all co-existent dharmas where the last meaning is present but the first two meanings are missing.
Therefore, universal latent dispositions (*sarvatraga-anuśaya*) are not established in all cases.
Regarding what is here called "reaching" (*prāpti*) or "worldly cause" (*laukika-hetu*),
a question is asked:
Regarding what is here called "universally taking the five categories as objects":
does this occur gradually or simultaneously? If it occurs through gradual succession:
Other afflictions such as greed should also be called "universal" (sarvatraga),
because afflictions like greed take the five categories [of phenomena] as their objects. If they were to take them all at once,
who then would not universally [take as objects] all contaminated phenomena within the entire realm of desire?
One suddenly reckons this to be supreme and gives rise to the grasping of views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*),
believing it can attain the purity of nirvāṇa;
or one gives rise to the grasping of precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*), taking it to be the cause for rebirth in the heavens within the mundane world.
Regarding the statement that it does not say "simultaneously taking as its object" up to "can simultaneously take as its object the five categories," the answer is:
it does not say that it simultaneously takes as its object all contaminated phenomena within its own realm and level.
All are most excellent,
capable of attaining purity,
or serving as causes for the mundane world.
However, it is said that those [causes] which have the power to simultaneously take as their objects even a small portion of each of the five categories are called "pervasive" (sarvatraga).
Nevertheless, the Sautrāntika school objects: "If that is so, then the pervasive [cause] would also be a cause that acts upon everything."
Nevertheless, the universal [defilements] do not consist of only these eleven underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*).
According to reason, wherever the view of a self (*ātmadṛṣṭi*) operates, [the universal defilements are present].
In this regard, self-love and self-conceit must necessarily arise;
or, if one is able to attain purification therein,
there may be the practice of the view of attachment to precepts and observances.
To regard what is not superior as superior is the activity of the view of holding to views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*).
In such a case, there must necessarily arise craving for that object and the conceit of self-exaltation (*abhimāna*);
thus, craving and conceit would also have to be considered universal (*sarvatraga*).
If that is so, to what extent are [the afflictions] abandoned when they arise by taking [objects] simultaneously?
The Vaibhāṣikas thus challenge the Sautrāntikas:
"If you say that craving and pride arise by taking simultaneously those [afflictions] to be abandoned through seeing and through cultivation."
One should say: "What is abandoned by craving and pride? One should say:
"They are abandoned through cultivation (bhāvanā-heya), because they are drawn forth by the power of [wrong] views.
This is the Sautrāntika response.
It should be said that they are abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*), because their objects of focus are mixed;
whereas craving and pride abandoned through vision (*darśana-heya*) have distinct and specific objects of focus.
Alternatively, they should be abandoned by insight (*darśana-prahātavya*),
because they are induced by the power of insight. According to the intention of the Sautrāntikas, both craving (*tṛṣṇā*) and pride (*māna*) are also universal (*sarvatraga*),
because they are able to take all five categories of phenomena as their objects.
Regarding the statement that "the Vaibhāṣikas [hold that] it is established even without being explicitly stated," this describes their own school's position; the Vaibhāṣikas speak as follows.
These two—craving and pride—are afflictions of specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa-kleśa*), not of general characteristics (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa-kleśa*).

Because they lack the power to simultaneously take [all objects] as their objective support, they are not universal (*sarvatraga*); therefore, the universal [afflictions] consist of only these eleven.
Other afflictions such as hatred and so forth are not universal.
By this principle, it is established as a matter of course that craving and pride are also not [universal].
Among the eleven [types of latent dispositions], those that reach their objects in lower realms are the underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*).
The following explains the fifth and sixth phrases.
Because it does not increase in accordance with superior objects, there is no fault in taking them as objects;
because it increases in accordance with inferior objects, there is the fault of not taking them as objects.
Therefore, the *Vibhāṣā* says:

Question: Why is it that the afflictions (*kleśa*) of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) are able to take the form and formless realms as their objects, whereas the afflictions of those two realms cannot take the desire realm as their object?
There is another explanation which says:
Furthermore, if the afflictions of the form and formless realms were to take the desire realm as their object, they would necessarily increase accordingly.
If they were to increase accordingly, the realms would become intermingled and confused.

Therefore, those afflictions do not take the desire realm as their object. Question: Just as the afflictions of the desire realm, though taking the higher realms as objects, do not increase in accordance with them, why is it that the afflictions of the higher realms are not likewise?
Answer: The aggregates of the upper realms are superior;
although afflictions of the desire realm arise taking them as objects, they do not increase therein.
The aggregates of the desire realm are inferior.
If the afflictions of the higher realms take this as their object, they immediately increase accordingly;
just as an inferior person, though able to see a superior being directly before them, does not cause them harm.
Just as one who is superior and powerful can inflict harm upon an inferior person,
so it is in this case as well.
Regarding these nine [factors], although they can lead [to rebirth], one should reflect upon them according to their respective realms.
Although these nine [cognitions] can generally take both their own and higher levels as objects,
it is logically impossible for them to take both their own and higher levels simultaneously.
Regarding the taking of higher levels as objects, this is explained here primarily in terms of the realms (*dhātu*).
Alternatively, it may take only one realm as its object, or it may take two realms combined as its object;

the supporting evidence for this can be understood from the scriptures. One should reflect upon the distinctions according to the stages (*bhūmi*) in accordance with the principles applied to the realms.
Furthermore, the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 19, states:
Question: Why do [the afflictions] not simultaneously take as their object the suffering or the origin of the three realms in a single moment?
Answer: Because those [afflictions] also increase in accordance with their objects within the desire realm.
Because they do not increase in accordance [with the defilements] when taking the form and formless realms as their objects.
Question: Why is it that while they increase in accordance when taking the desire realm as their object, they do not increase in accordance when taking the form and formless realms as their objects?
There is another explanation which says:
Furthermore, in the desire realm, there exist those results of outflow and results of maturation.
In the form and formless realms, there is no such outflow [result],
because it is a ripened fruit (*vipākaphala*).
Furthermore, another explanation for why [the mind] does not perceive [objects] instantaneously is as follows:
If that which takes the desire realm as its object were to increase accordingly [in that realm],
and the same were true for the form and formless realms,
then the realms would become intermingled.
If it were the case that, just as [afflictions] do not increase in the formless realm with respect to their objects,
they likewise do not increase with respect to objects of the desire realm,
this would be unreasonable.
Regarding those [defilements] that lack afflictions as their object and take dharmas of their own realm as objects,
yet possess both types of increase— namely,
through the object and through association— it is as follows:
Factors belonging to their own level necessarily possess an object of cognition (*ālambana*),
because they are bound by association (*samprayoga*).
If, in a single moment, one were to simultaneously take the suffering of the three realms as an object...
If they are accumulated,
among the objects of focus, there are those that increase [afflictions] and those that do not increase them.
Furthermore, there would likewise be [factors] that increase in accordance with associated dharmas and those that do not increase in accordance with them;
this would contradict the principle of this cause and also undermine the nature of associated dharmas.
Do not fall into this error.

Therefore, the principle that [the universal proclivities] take as their objects those belonging to their own realm and other realms at different times is well established, as explained extensively in that [text]. Furthermore, the *Abhidharmamahāvibhāṣā* asks:

"For what reason can the universal proclivities increase in relation to factors of another category (*pakṣa*), but not in relation to other realms or stages? It answers: "The universal proclivities have outflowing fruits (*niṣyanda-phala*) with respect to factors of another category."
Or it is a ripened fruit (vipākaphala);
thus, it is able to increase accordingly.
In other realms or stages, there are neither outflowing fruits (niṣyandaphala) nor ripened fruits.

Therefore, they do not increase [in accordance with them]. Furthermore, within one's own realm, different categories can increase [in accordance] because they are similar in terms of being coarse or subtle;
however, because the stages of the higher realms are subtle, they cannot increase [in accordance].
Regarding the phrase "born in the desire realm up to not taking the higher realms as an object":
the intent of the question can be understood.
Regarding the phrase "not grasping those [realms] as a self because the view of a self (satkāyadṛṣṭi) does not arise": [the meaning is as follows].
Answer:
One born in a lower realm will certainly not grasp those dharmas of a higher realm as "self" or "mine."
Since extreme views necessarily arise from the view of a self,
when the view of a self does not arise,
extreme views likewise do not arise. Furthermore, the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 18, states:
Question: Why do these two not take other realms as their objects?
Answer: Because they possess only such power regarding their objects;
furthermore, because these two views operate only with respect to coarse resultant phenomena.

This means that these two views perceive only the coarse manifestations of the aggregates and thereby grasp at them as "self" and "mine," or conceive of them in terms of annihilationism and eternalism.
If one is born in the desire realm, because one cannot directly perceive the subtle aggregates of the form and formless realms, one does not grasp them as self, mine, and so forth.

Question: If that is so, why do those born in the form realm (rūpadhātu) not grasp as "self" or "mine" the coarse and manifest aggregates (skandha) of the desire realm (kāmadhātu) that they clearly perceive?
Answer: Because they have already become detached from passion (vītarāga).
This refers to those born in the form realm (rūpadhātu).
Because they have already attained detachment from the aggregates (skandha) of the desire realm (kāmadhātu),
although they perceive them directly, they do not grasp them as "I" or "mine," and so forth.
Furthermore, because the afflictions of the higher stages do not take the lower stages as their objects.
A question arises from this discussion:
for what reason do the afflictions of the higher stages not take the lower stages as their objects?
The answer is: because one has already become detached from those defilements.
That is to say, only one who has already become detached from the defilements of a lower stage can give rise to the manifestation of afflictions belonging to a higher stage.
Since one has already become detached from the dharmas of the lower stages, how could the afflictions of the higher stages still take them as objects?
Question: How is it known that one must first become detached from the defilements of the lower stages?
The afflictions of the higher stages only then become manifest.
The answer is as stated in the *Prajñapti-śāstra*:
there are six types of non-restraint (*asaṃvara*).
That is to say, each of the three realms has two types:
first, associated;
second, dissociated.
When a non-restraint associated with the desire realm is present,
six non-restraints are accomplished and four non-restraints are also present.
This refers to two [types] in the desire realm;
in the form and formless realms, they do not correspond to one another.
In the form realm, when non-restraint (a-saṃvara) is present, it does not correspond [to restraint].
Four do not possess non-restraint;
three do not possess non-restraint and are also not manifest,
namely the two [types] of the form realm.
It is not dissociated from the formless realm.
When non-restraint associated with the formless realm is manifested,
both the possession of non-restraint and its manifestation occur.
That is to say, there are two [types] in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).
Among these, defiled phenomena (*kliṣṭadharma*) are termed "non-restraint" (*asaṃvara*). By this, it is known.
One must depart from the defilements of the lower stage;

only then do the afflictions of the higher stage manifest, as explained at length in that [text]. If this is so, one might ask: to which view is the conception of "reaching" (prāpti) subsumed? This is a difficult objection.
If that is so, when one conceives of the Brahmā kings of the higher realms as either sentient beings or as eternal,
what kind of view does this fall under?
Regarding the statement that "the Abhidharmikas say this is subsumed under false knowledge," the answer is:
the Abhidharmikas say.
The view that this sentient being is eternal and non-physical is the extreme view of permanence;
it is subsumed under wrong knowledge (*mithyājñāna*). What is meant by "wrong knowledge" here is wrong knowledge associated with ignorance (*avidyā*).
Within the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), one first gives rise to two views that grasp at a self.
Grasping at permanence,
immediately thereafter, independent ignorance arises,
taking that Great Brahmā as its object and conceiving him to be "I" and "permanent."
Because its mode of activity (*ākāra*) is obscure and it cannot be definitively apprehended,
it is not a view (*dṛṣṭi*).
Therefore, the *Nyāyānusāra* states:
If one born within the desire realm gives rise to the view of a sentient being or the view of permanence with reference to Mahābrahmā,
by which [category of] view should these be subsumed?
In truth, it should be said that these two are not views.
This body is a false cognition induced by extreme views (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*).

Having perceived a self and permanence within the manifest aggregates, one then infers that which is not manifest to be likewise. Furthermore, cognition associated with the resolution of doubt is also considered false cognition.
That is to say, following upon the body and its periphery, one further gives rise to doubt regarding that Great Brahmā:
"Is he permanent or impermanent?
Is he the self or not the self?"

Because it is not a definitive adherence, it is also not a view (*dṛṣṭi*). Furthermore, after the view of self-existence (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*), it gives rise to the non-obscured, neutral (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*) [state] of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
It is simply with reference to the desire realm that the name "Brahmā King" is spoken.
That is to say, the notions of "self" and "permanence" are termed false knowledge (*mithyājñāna*) because they do not take that [ultimate] essence as their object.
This is because the unobscured-neutral [state] does not take what is above it as its object;
just as taking space or non-analytical cessation as an object is termed not taking that [ultimate] essence as an object.
It is called "erroneous" (mithyā) not because it accords with reason, but because it is not afflicted (kliṣṭa).
One should know that this refers to three types of mind among the four neutral (avyākṛta) states: those of deportment (īryāpathika), craftsmanship (śailpasthānika), and maturation (vipākaja).

However, they are not universal fruits, because they take only form as their object. Furthermore, some explain that they are only the two types of postures and crafts, and not the other two; although there are these two interpretations, the former is superior.
Regarding the question, "For what reason are the remaining *prāptis* (possessions) not views?
this is an objection. For what reason are the remaining two types of grasping (*parāmarśa*) and false view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*), when they take those [objects] as their conditions, considered views?
Is this false wisdom also an object-condition for that [object] without being a view?
Since the statement was made on the basis of the tenet as the authority,
the Vaibhāṣika masters reply:
This statement is made because the treatise (śāstra) is taken as the authority.
It serves to explain the latter two lines of the question regarding whether the nature of the pervasive [defilements] consists solely of latent proclivities (anuśaya).
Is the substance of the universal cause (sarvatraga-hetu) exclusively the latent dispositions (anuśaya)?
If not, the answer is as follows:
"What is it? This is the inquiry.
"Together with the concomitant dharmas, up to what should be analyzed according to principle" refers to the following.
Explanation:
This includes the concomitant dharmas,
namely the eleven underlying tendencies (anuśaya) mentioned above.
Furthermore, those [factors] that accompany and are associated with it, as well as those that coexist with it, are all subsumed under the category of universal causes (*sarvatragahetu*).
However, its acquisition (*prāpti*) is excluded;
for since the acquisition and the acquired factor do not share a single fruit, the acquisition is not a universal cause. For this reason, some have raised the following question:
Are all pervasive latent dispositions (sarvatraga-anuśaya) pervasive causes (sarvatraga-hetu)? The answer is: regarding this, one should formulate four alternatives (catuṣkoṭi).
The first alternative refers to the pervasive latent dispositions of the future period.
Because it is subsumed under the eleven [categories], it is a pervasive latent disposition (*sarvatraga-anuśaya*);
because there is no sequence [of prior and posterior], it is not a pervasive cause (*sarvatraga-hetu*). As for the second phrase:
This refers to those co-existent dharmas of the past and present;
because they possess temporal priority and posteriority, they constitute the pervasive cause (*sarvatraga-hetu*).
However, because they do not comprise all eleven [categories], they are not pervasive latent dispositions (*sarvatraga-anuśaya*).
The third phrase refers to the pervasive latent dispositions (*sarvatraga-anuśaya*) of the past and present;
because they are subsumed within the eleven [categories], they are pervasive latent dispositions.
Because there is a sequence of before and after, it is a universal cause (*sarvatraga-hetu*).
As for the fourth phrase, it refers to that which is excluded from the aforementioned characteristics.
Therefore, it should be explained according to the principle.
Regarding the phrase "among the ninety-eight latent tendencies (anuśaya), because of their being [characterized by] tranquility, purity,
and excellence," this refers to the general explanation in the first verse concerning those with outflows (sāsrava) and those without outflows (anāsrava).
The second verse provides a detailed explanation, while the third verse distinguishes the dharmas.
The treatise states: "Up to 'it is established by this analogy.'"
This explains the first verse.

[The afflictions] associated with Cessation and the Path pertain to the lower six [realms]. Excluding these six types, the remaining afflictions of the five categories all take the contaminated (*sāsrava*) as their object.
Based on this, the verse is established as a matter of course and is not explained separately.
Regarding the phrase "among these six, up to the analytical cessation of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra-pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*)," this explains the fifth and sixth lines.
Among these six, those that take cessation as their object each take the cessation of the various formations of their own level and those of higher levels as their objects.

Because the analytical cessations (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) of the various levels do not stand in a cause-and-effect relationship with one another, they do not take other levels as objects. This is because wholesome wisdom that realizes the object can universally take multiple levels as its objects, unlike defiled phenomena.
Therefore, the *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya* states:
"However, regarding the objects realized by various wholesome cognitions,
it is logically possible for them to simultaneously take as their object the cessation (*nirodha*) of multiple stages."
Various wrong views arise from delusion regarding their objects;

because they are obstructed by stubborn adherence, they are unable to take multiple objects as a whole. Question: The afflictions directed toward the nine higher realms are likewise deluded regarding their objects.
How, then, can they take the suffering and origin of multiple stages as their objects? Answer: Although they arise from delusion regarding their objects, [they do so]...

The various stages (*bhūmi*) of suffering and its origin (*samudaya*) may take multiple stages as their objects, because they serve as the efficient cause (*kāraṇa-hetu*) and the dominant fruit (*adhipati-phala*) in relation to one another.
Furthermore, the *Nyāyānusāra* asks:
"Does the false view that denies cessation constitute a view regarding cessation?"
Do you not see cessation?
If you do see cessation,
how can you see cessation and yet slanderously claim that there is no cessation?
If it is not perceived as ceasing,
how can it have the untainted as its object?
And furthermore, how can one say that this thing does not exist?
One should say that it is the view of cessation (*nirodha-dṛṣṭi*). However, by merely following the teaching and seeing [it as such], one slanders this aforementioned cessation as being non-existent.
Is it not the case that this view directly takes cessation as its object?
How can one then negate this cessation as being non-existent?
It is like a person with sight who, seeing someone standing at a distance in a place full of tree stumps, negates that it is a person.
Although one may personally associate with such people, it does not mean they do not slander [the Dharma].
Thus, there are those who, upon seeing cessation (nirodha), deny its existence;
yet this is not the case for all who possess wisdom regarding the denial of cessation and the path (mārga).
All these are views abandoned through the vision of cessation and the vision of the path;
that is to say, if there is wisdom that arises without analytical investigation, one will immediately give rise to slander upon hearing the teachings on cessation and the path.

Because they take only names as their object, they are not abandoned by insight (*darśana-prahātavya*). If wisdom arises through the definitive determination produced by investigating, deliberating, and inferring regarding an object, and then negates what has been taught—namely, cessation and the path—only then are they abandoned by insight. [This is the conclusion of the preceding treatise. Regarding the passage from "those that take the truth of the path as their object" up to "because they are similar in kind": [The text continues: Those [afflictions] that take the truth of the path as their object are abandoned by insight, because they are of the same category [as those previously discussed]. Why? Because they are associated with the view of negation (*apavāda-dṛṣṭi*) and the view of attachment to views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa-dṛṣṭi*). Furthermore, the afflictions that take the truths of suffering and origination as their objects are abandoned by insight; those that take the truth of cessation as their object are abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-prahātavya*); and those that take the truth of the path as their object are abandoned by insight. Why? Because they are associated with the view of negation and the view of attachment to views. Among these, the view of negation is the denial of the noble truths of suffering and origination, and the denial of the noble truths of cessation and the path. The view of attachment to views refers to the estimation of inferior things as superior, such as the five aggregates of clinging (*pañcopādānaskandha*), and the estimation of what is not the supreme as supreme, such as the various heterodox paths.
