Explaining the seventh phrase:
it refers to the false views, doubt, and ignorance bound to the desire realm,
which take as their object only the path belonging to the category of dharma-knowledge across the six stages.
It does not take as its object the path belonging to the category of subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*).

If it counteracts the desire realm—meaning that the path belonging to the category of dharma-knowledge (*dharma-jñāna*) within the *anāgamya* concentration can counteract desire—if it is able to counteract anything else [it takes that as its object].
This refers to the categories of dharma-knowledge regarding cessation and the path within the six stages;
during the stage of cultivation, these are able to counteract the remaining [defilements] of the form and formless realms, all of which take that wrong view, doubt, and ignorance as their objects.

Because the categories of dharma-knowledge (*dharmajñāna*) are identical, if there are three latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) in each of the upper eight stages, each one can only take as its object the path belonging to the category of subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*) across all nine stages, but cannot take the path belonging to the category of dharma-knowledge as its object; this is because they counteract [the afflictions] of their own respective stage.
That is to say, among the nine stages, the path belonging to the category of subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*) that can counteract its own stage;

or if it can counteract others—namely, the path belonging to the category of subsequent knowledge among the nine stages that can counteract the other seven stages—all these are the objects of focus for those wrong views, doubt, and ignorance.
Because these are of the same category as the knowledge of categories (*anvaya-jñāna*),
why is it that the objects of cessation extend to six [categories] and nine [categories] for those of the same class?
This explains the eighth phrase.
This is the question. The answer is:
"Because the paths of the various stages reach the three objects that are not of the desire realm."
This is because, within the various stages (bhūmi),
the paths belonging to the category of dharma-knowledge and the paths belonging to the category of subsequent knowledge (anvaya-jñāna) each serve as homogeneous causes (sabhāga-hetu) for one another.
Because they are causes by way of their characteristics:
if it takes dharma-knowledge as its object, it takes the six stages as its object;
if it takes subsequent knowledge (anvaya-jñāna) as its object, it takes the nine stages as its object.
Although the category of dharma-knowledge and the category of subsequent knowledge (anvaya-jñāna) also serve as similar causes for one another when viewed reciprocally,
the category of subsequent knowledge does not govern the desire realm.
Because they have distinct antidotes,
the path belonging to the category of subsequent knowledge (anvaya-jñāna-pakṣa) does not take the three types [of objects] of the desire realm as its focal objects.
As for the path belonging to the category of dharma-knowledge (dharma-jñāna-pakṣa), it is able to reach each of the three focal objects.
Question:
It is difficult [to understand] how the dharma-knowledges of cessation and the path during the stage of cultivation in the desire realm can treat the higher realms of form and formlessness.
It should be understood that for each of those eight [fetters], there are three respective objects;
it is not the case that all [objects] can serve as the antidotes for all [fetters]. This is the general principle.
It is not the case that all these knowledges of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*) can serve as antidotes for the realms of form and formlessness;
for the category of the knowledges of phenomena regarding suffering and origin is not the path of antidote for those higher realms.
The suffering and origin of the nine stages are coarse in the lower and subtle in the upper.
Because that which takes coarse objects as its condition cannot abandon what is subtle,
the dharma-knowledge (dharmajñāna) regarding the suffering and origin of the desire realm cannot serve as an antidote for the eight higher stages.
Alternatively, because the coarse can be abandoned by taking the subtle as its object,

the dharma-knowledges of cessation and the path regarding the desire realm are able to counteract the afflictions of the higher realms. [This refers to] the dharma-knowledges of cessation and the path.
Nor does it have the power to remedy both the form and formless realms;
it merely abandons the afflictions to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) but cannot remedy those to be abandoned through insight (*darśana-heya*).
Therefore, its function as an antidote is determined specifically with respect to the afflictions abandoned through insight.
Furthermore, because it is swift and rapid during the stage of seeing (*darśana-mārga*),

the category of the dharma-knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-dharmajñāna*) and the path (*mārga-dharmajñāna*) within the path of seeing cannot serve as the antidote for the afflictions of the higher realms (*ūrdhvadhātu*) that are abandoned through seeing.
Because they serve as antidotes for the abandonment of afflictions through cultivation and are not fixed [in their timing],
and because there is still some leeway during the stage of cultivation,
the dharma-knowledges of cessation and the path within the path of cultivation [are included].
And it is able to counteract the afflictions of the higher realms cultivated through meditation. Question:

One who has previously abandoned the defilements of desire and subsequently enters the path of seeing—since there is nothing further to be abandoned during the dharma-knowledges of suffering and the path within the stage of seeing, one should be somewhat at leisure.

Why is it that one does not treat the afflictions of the higher realms? The explanation states: it is not necessary to give rise to the dharma-knowledge (dharmajñāna) of the desire realm in order to sever these afflictions.
Rather, this dharma-knowledge arises for the purpose of contemplating the principle of the Truths (satya).
Furthermore, subsequently, one must necessarily give rise to the path belonging to the category of subsequent knowledge (anvayajñāna) to sever the afflictions of the higher realms.

Therefore, the dharma-knowledge (dharma-jñāna) of desire cannot counteract the afflictions of the higher realms. Within the category of dharma-knowledge, the four truths are differentiated; it lacks the first [truths] of suffering and origin.
When differentiated by way of seeing and cultivation, it lacks the beginning of the path of seeing. Thus it is said that "the two beginnings are absent."
It is not the object of the three delusions of that eighth stage.
Furthermore, it is explained by analogy:
for this very reason, the previous [knowledge] takes only cessation as its object, while the six and nine [knowledges] take the path as their object due to various causes and conditions.

This demonstrates that among the universal afflictions (*sarvatraga-kleśa*), there are those that take suffering (*duḥkha*) and origin (*samudaya*) as their objects across the nine stages, because these objects are not mutually obstructed and serve as reciprocal conditions for one another;
or they take two combined as their object,
and so on, up to taking eight combined as their object.

The various types of cessation are not related to one another as conditions or causes, because they are the cessation of the Truth of Cessation (*nirodha-satya*). Regarding the term "condition-cause" (*pratyaya-hetu*),
it refers to a remote condition-cause, thereby distinguishing it from the immediate causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*).
That is the efficient cause (*kāraṇa-hetu*).

Alternatively, the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*) is termed the "condition-cause. Another interpretation holds that the "condition" refers either to the dominant condition or to the immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*).
It may be an object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*),
it may be both of the former two,
or it may generally encompass all three causes.
This refers to the efficient cause (*kāraṇa-hetu*); it is not an outflow-free (*anāsrava*) antidote.
It takes one stage as its object, rather than six or nine stages, unlike the Truth of the Path (*mārga-satya*), which, when taking the path as its object, takes six or nine stages as its object.
"For what reason do greed, hatred, and pride not take the untainted as their object?
This introduces the explanation of the final verse;
it constitutes the question.
Regarding the statement "from the latent tendency of greed up to not taking the untainted as an object," the answer explains greed, hatred, and pride.
As well as the two types of grasping (*dvaya-grāha*),
they do not take the untainted (*anāsrava*) as their object;
this may be understood from the text.
Regarding the statement, "Among the ninety-eight latent dispositions (*anuśaya*),
those that increase by way of association," this constitutes the third section clarifying the two types of increase.
The preceding six phrases clarify increase by way of the object (*ālambana*).

The latter two lines clarify concomitant increase (*anuvṛddhi*); among the first six lines, the initial four lines correctly clarify increase through the object (*ālambana-anuśaya*), while the latter two lines distinguish their specific differences.
The Commentary states: "Because it serves as the object-condition (*ālambana*).
This explains the first verse;
it may be understood according to the text.
The *Nyāyānusāra* states: "As for the term 'increasing in accordance' (*anuśerate*),
it means that the various latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) abide within and increase in accordance with these phenomena."
This means that [ignorance] increases the sense of being bound and the state of mental dullness and stagnation.
The phrase "this is stated in general up to 'because it is contradictory'" explains the fifth and sixth lines below.
This statement regarding the increase [of defilements] with respect to their objects is made by way of general description.
If one were to distinguish them specifically, there are the six types of non-outflow (anāsrava) object-defilements under the Truths of Cessation and the Path,
as well as the nine types of higher-object (ūrdhvālambana) defilements under the Truths of Suffering and Origination.
There is no sense of increase (anuśaya) with respect to their objects.
Why is this? Because the objects of cessation (nirodha), the path (mārga), the untainted (anāsrava), and those of higher stages [are not subject to such increase].
First, because it is not grasped by either views or craving;
second, because it is diametrically opposed to the afflictions that take it as their object.
This constitutes the formal statement of the heading.
This refers to those dharmas that do not increase by way of being an object of focus (*ālambana*).
This explains the first chapter.
That is to say, those dharmas which constitute the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) within this stage.
Furthermore, regarding the appropriation [of objects] as one's own through craving,
it is logical that the latent dispositions (anuśaya) existing within the stage of craving can increase by taking this view of self (satkāyadṛṣṭi) as their objective support (ālambana).
Just as dust settles upon a moist garment:

the garment is a metaphor for the Dharma; the moisture is a metaphor for the body, views, and craving; and the settling of the dust is a metaphor for the increase of delusions. It is not the case that the various untainted dharmas (*anāsrava-dharma*) are grasped as "mine" by the view of a self-identity (*satkāya-dṛṣṭi*) or by craving.

The dharmas of the higher stages are not grasped as "mine" by the views and craving of the lower stages; therefore, there are no untainted (anāsrava) objects for those afflictions, nor are there afflictions directed toward the lower stages that take those higher stages as their objects.
It does not increase by way of its object (*ālambana*).
Regarding the statement that "abiding in a mind of a lower stage" does not mean it is a latent tendency (*anuśaya*),
this universally addresses the objection.
The intent of the anticipated objection is as follows:
"If greed for a higher stage is precisely this same greed for a lower stage that can take the higher stage as its object," it is in order to resolve this objection that these words were spoken.
Abiding in a mind of a lower stage while seeking a higher stage and so forth is the desire for wholesome dharmas;
it is not what is meant by latent tendencies (*anuśaya*).
"Regarding the noble path and nirvana being sufficient and not abiding therein":
this explains the subsequent section.
If it refers to the noble truth of the path, [it is as follows].
The truth of cessation, which is nirvana,
is incompatible with the afflictions that take it as their object;
likewise, dharmas of a higher stage are incompatible with the lower-stage afflictions that take them as their objects.
Those [defilements] that have the untainted as their object, and those nine that have the higher realms as their object—
these two types likewise lack the principle of increasing through the objects of perception.
Just as one's feet do not remain upon a heated stone: the heated stone is a metaphor for the object,
and the feet not remaining upon it is a metaphor for the afflictions that take that object as their cognitive support.
The statement that "the latent dispositions (anuśaya) persist even where they do not increase" records a divergent opinion;
this is explained in terms of "conformity" (anuloma) as the meaning of "increasing" (anuśayana).
Some say that *anuśaya* has the meaning of "conforming.
Since uncontaminated objects do not conform to the various *anuśayas*,

and since objects of a higher stage do not conform to the various *anuśayas* of lower stages, there is no principle for them to increase [in strength] despite being objects of perception (*ālambana*).
It is like a patient suffering from wind disorders who takes dry and astringent medicine;
the patient does not accord with the medicine, nor does the medicine increase in accordance with him,
and the medicine possesses no efficacy over the patient.
It does not increase [the afflictions]. The sick person is a metaphor for the object;
the medicine is a metaphor for the affliction that takes it as its cognitive object (*ālambaka*). Here, specifically, the sick person suffering from wind-disease is taken as the metaphor.

It is not that the wind disorder is grasped; rather, if one regards the wind disorder as being concordant with drying and astringent medicines, there will be a corresponding increase due to such conformity.
Thus, having considered the object-condition (*ālambana*), it increases in accordance with that.
The last two phrases are explained as follows:
this refers to whichever [cognition] takes as its object— whether pervasive or non-pervasive, whether with outflows (*sāsrava*) or without outflows (*anāsrava*),
or whether belonging to one's own realm (*svadhātu*) or another realm (*paradhātu*).
All latent dispositions (anuśaya) increase with respect to their own associated dharmas by virtue of association.
Regarding those who state that "increase" applies until they have been abandoned, [it refers to] the point at which they are designated as such.
Regarding all that has been stated above concerning "that which increases along with" (anuśaya),
this refers to the fact that these latent dispositions (anuśaya) persist until they have been abandoned;
therefore, the first verse at the beginning specifies the term "not yet abandoned."
"Is there any latent disposition (anuśaya) that reaches [an object] without being its objective condition (ālambana)?
The intent of this question is clear.
There are indeed latent dispositions that reach [an object].
Answer: It is said that they exist; this refers to the universal underlying tendencies (*sarvatraga-anuśaya*) of the higher stages.
For example, the universal underlying tendencies of the first *dhyāna* take the three higher stages as their objects.
Furthermore, just as the pervasive latent dispositions (*sarvatraga-anuśaya*) in the sphere of infinite space take the three higher stages as their objects,
yet do not increase (*anuśerate*) by taking the higher realms as their objects—
occurring only through association (*samprayoga*) and not through the object (*ālambana*).
Regarding the statement, "Among the ninety-eight latent dispositions (*anuśaya*), up to this point all others are unwholesome":
this constitutes the fourth classification by way of the two natures.
The treatise says: "Because [the wholesome] is definitely non-existent therein."
This explains the first phrase.
The various afflictions (*kleśa*) of the higher realms are exclusively indeterminate (*avyākṛta*).

This is because, among defiled phenomena (*kliṣṭadharma*), if they were unwholesome (*akuśala*), they would have the fruit of ripening as suffering (*duḥkhavipāka*); however, such [unwholesome states] do not exist in the two upper realms.
Because the causes for its affliction are definitively non-existent, it is said that it has no fruit;
this also demonstrates that its cause is likewise non-existent. Furthermore, the *Nyāya* states:
"All latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) of the form and formless realms..."
Because they are suppressed by the four-fold and five-fold meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*), they lack the power to bring about ripened results (*vipākaphala*);
therefore, they are all subsumed under the category of the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*). Furthermore, the *Vibhāṣā* states:
If a phenomenon has the intrinsic nature of lack of shame and lack of dread, is associated with lack of shame and lack of dread,
and is the result of origination or outflow from lack of shame and lack of dread.
These are unwholesome.
The afflictions of the form and formless realms are not thus, and are therefore indeterminate (*avyākṛta*), as explained at length therein.
Regarding the two views—view of self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*)—as they extend to other sentient beings:
The second and third phrases are explained:
the body-view (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), extreme-views (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*),
and the delusion (*moha*) associated with them.
It is also of an indeterminate nature (*avyākṛta*). Why is this? That which is contrary to the wholesome is called unwholesome;
however, this view of self and permanence is not contrary to [acts such as] giving and so forth.
Those who grasp at a self as permanent fear that this permanent self will suffer in the future;
for this reason, they hold that this permanent self will enjoy the pleasures of humans and devas in future lives.
Now, by diligently practicing generosity, ethical discipline, meditative concentration, and so forth, one abandons the extreme view of nihilism as it accords with nirvāṇa;
because it is capable of bringing about cessation,
the Blessed One has said that among all the various views of the non-Buddhists, this nihilistic view is the most excellent path.
That is to say, one seeks [liberation] by thinking: "I do not exist;
what belongs to me (*mamakāra*) does not exist either.
Grasping at 'I' and 'mine' has already ceased to be in the present."
Because one seeks for it within the body and does not find it, one considers it already severed, thinking: "I shall not exist;
what belongs to me shall not exist."

One clings to the notions of "self" and "what belongs to self," thinking that they will only cease after death; alternatively, one interprets the first two lines as meaning that the clinging to "self" and "what belongs to self" is severed simultaneously with the death of the present body.
The latter two phrases refer to the grasping at a self and what belongs to a self as never arising again in future lives;
because they accord with nirvāṇa, they are not unwholesome.
Furthermore, the two views of identity and extremes are delusions regarding one's own basis.
Because it does not intend to oppress or harm other sentient beings, its fault is slight; therefore, it is neutral (*avyākṛta*).
If that is so, one might raise the objection: "In what case would even covetousness (*abhidhyā*) be likewise [neutral]?"
If that is so, then the pursuit of heavenly pleasures and the arising of pride are likewise not contradictory to generosity and the other perfections.

The two types, greed and pride, should also be indeterminate; for one may crave celestial pleasures and likewise give rise to the conceit of "I am," both of which involve delusion regarding one's own affairs.
It does not harm sentient beings and should therefore be termed indeterminate (*avyākṛta*); or, it may involve the cultivation of generosity and so forth while seeking the pleasures of the heavens,
as well as the arising of the conceit of "I am" (*asmimāna*).
Because it is deluded regarding its own object and does not intend to harm others, it should be classified as indeterminate (*avyākṛta*).
As for the fact that the former masters consider this to be of an unwholesome nature (*akuśala*): [it is because...]
To describe alternative views:
the masters of former generations among the Sautrāntika school have stated that the innate view of a self (*sahaja-satkāyadṛṣṭi*) is of an indeterminate nature (*avyākṛta*).
The view of a self (satkāyadṛṣṭi) that manifests in animals and the like is called "innate" (sahaja) because it arises simultaneously with the body;
it is abandoned through the path of cultivation (bhāvanāmārga). If it arises from conceptual discrimination (vikalpa) or is based on [misunderstanding] the teachings, this is unwholesome (akuśala).
Regarding the view-eliminated [afflictions], the establishment of the two types of *satkāyadṛṣṭi* (view of a self-identity) accords with the explanations in Mahāyāna sūtras.

If one follows the Sarvāstivāda school, the view of a self-identity is exclusively conceptual (*parikalpita*), being eliminated solely by the path of seeing (*darśana-heya*) and lacking any innate (*sahaja*) form; however, the notions held by birds, beasts, and so forth should be understood as being eliminated only by the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*).
"Unstained neutral [states] subsumed under false wisdom;
the rest, bound to the desire realm, are all of an unwholesome nature" explains the fourth phrase.
Within the three realms, all other latent dispositions (anuśaya) bound to the desire realm— excluding those previously mentioned—
are entirely of an unwholesome nature, being the opposite of what was stated above regarding those [dispositions] up to greed, hatred, and unwholesome delusion.
Below this, the fifth section clarifies the faculties (*indriya*) and non-faculties.
Within this, the first part clarifies the unwholesome roots (*akuśalamūla*).
Second, the explanation of the indeterminate roots (*avyākṛta-mūla*). This is the first [section], the explanation of the unwholesome roots (*akuśala-mūla*).

The treatise states: "Up to the point where it says 'therefore not mentioned in the verse,' this refers exclusively to all greed (*rāga*) and hatred (*dveṣa*) belonging to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) across all five categories (*pañca-nikāya*)."
And unwholesome delusion is subsumed under the unwholesome roots;
this can be understood from the cited scriptural evidence. As for what are called "unwholesome roots":
Only those afflictions that are exclusively unwholesome are established as unwholesome roots (*akuśalamūla*). Others are not so; therefore, only these three are mentioned.
The fact that the remaining afflictions do not constitute unwholesome roots is already established by implication, and thus they are not mentioned in the verse.
The *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 112, regarding the establishment and rejection [of categories],
states: "Furthermore, these three types possess five meanings,
namely, that they pervade the five divisions."
It pervades the six consciousnesses;
it is of the nature of latent tendencies (anuśaya) and is capable of giving rise to coarse and evil bodily and vocal actions.

Because it constitutes a firm and powerful preparatory application for severing the roots of virtue, it is established alone as an unwholesome root (*akuśalamūla*). That which pervades the five categories excludes the five views and doubt;
that which pervades the six consciousnesses excludes the various forms of pride (*māna*).
The nature of latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) excludes the fetters (*paryavasthāna*), defilements (*mala*), and so forth;

it refers to that which can give rise to coarse and evil bodily and vocal actions, and which performs the firm and powerful application of cutting off the roots of goodness—this demonstrates the meaning of "faculty" (*indriya*). Furthermore, these five meanings exclude all other phenomena and establish the sense of being a faculty.
That is to say, non-defiled phenomena possess all six characteristics across the six consciousnesses,
whereas defiled form-aggregates entirely lack five of these characteristics;
the same applies to defiled feeling-aggregates and perception-aggregates.
Furthermore, the remaining associated defiled formations within the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*), which are bound by other afflictions and impurities,
although they pertain to all five categories and pervade all six consciousnesses,
do not possess the nature of latent dispositions (*anuśaya*).
Although it can give rise to coarse and evil actions of both body and speech, it is not the abandonment of the roots of goodness;
rather, it is a strong, preparatory application (*prayoga*) that is defiled and dissociated from the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*).
While it pertains to all five categories (*pañca-varga*), it lacks the other four [defining] characteristics.
Within the defiled aggregate of consciousness, the five consciousnesses—eye-consciousness and so forth—are entirely devoid of these five characteristics.
Although mental consciousness pertains to all five categories, it is also capable of initiating coarse and evil bodily and verbal actions.
And there are no other three meanings.
Among the ten afflictions,
these are the five views and doubt.
The nature of latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) lacks the other four meanings.
Pride (*māna*) pervades all five categories;
it is of the nature of a latent disposition.
It is capable of giving rise to coarse and evil bodily and verbal actions;
it has no other two meanings.
Among the ten fetters (*paryavasthāna*), it consists of torpor (*styāna*), restlessness (*auddhatya*), lack of shame (*āhrīkya*), and lack of dread (*anapatrāpya*).
Although it pervades the five aggregates and all six consciousnesses,
it is not of the nature of a latent tendency (*anuśaya*).
Although it gives rise to coarse and evil bodily and vocal actions, [it is still not a latent tendency].
However, it is not the firm preparatory application that severs the roots of goodness;
as for sleep, although it belongs to all five categories, it lacks the other four characteristics.
The remaining five envelopments (paryavasthāna),
although they give rise to coarse and evil bodily and vocal karma, lack the other four meanings [of affliction].
As for the six defilements (kleśamala):
Although there are also times when one can give rise to coarse and evil actions of both body and speech,
these lack the other four meanings;
only greed, hatred, and delusion possess all five meanings in their entirety.
It is not any other dharma;
therefore, it is established independently as an unwholesome root (*akuśalamūla*).
According to this passage from the *Abhidharmamahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, defiled sleep does not give rise to bodily or vocal karma.
According to this principle, wholesome sleep does not initiate karma;
regarding obscured-unwholesome (nivṛtāvyākṛta) sleep,
the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* and the *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra* each present two different views.
One [school] asserts that it initiates karma; another asserts that it does not initiate karma.

The ten underlying fetters (*paryavasthāna*) below shall be cited and explained in full. Furthermore, according to this text, regret (*kaukṛtya*) initiates bodily and vocal karma. Question: Regret is a dharma associated with the faculty of sorrow (*daurmanasyendriya*); how can it be abandoned through the relinquishing of desire?

If one has attained the Prātimokṣa vows, could these vows ever be abandoned through the separation from desire? The explanation says: *kaukṛtya* (remorse) and the faculty of mental distress (*daurmanasyendriya*) can only give rise to intermediate wholesome or unwholesome bodily and vocal karma.
Since one cannot generate the Pratimokṣa vows [in that state],
there is no contradiction;
it is merely a case of remorse (*kaukṛtya*) for past events.
The faculty of grief (*daurmanasyendriya*) has its own distinct objects of concern;
for this characteristic is absent at the moment one formally undertakes the precepts.
Furthermore, according to this text, the six stains (*ṣaḍkaṣāya*) give rise to karma.
Regarding the statement above that "up to the third dhyāna, all are delusion," this section below is secondly explained as the exposition of the indeterminate roots (*avyākṛta-mūla*).
Within it, one part specifically clarifies the indeterminate roots.
The second section, "The Treatise on Causes Clarifying the Four Indeterminates," is the first part that correctly clarifies the roots of indeterminacy (*avyākṛtamūla*).
The first three phrases describe this country [India],
while the latter three phrases describe other regions [the northern lands].
The Commentary states: "As for 'even non-greed is subsumed under the roots of the indeterminate,' this explains the first two phrases.
This is the teaching of the masters of this land."
The indeterminate roots are also of three kinds.
The term "indeterminate" applies to both the obscured and the unobscured;
that is, the obscured types of craving and delusion.
Furthermore, all obscured and unobscured wisdoms—
within the category of the unobscured, down to those born of maturation (*vipākaja*)—
are also subsumed under the neutral roots (*avyākṛta-mūla*).
Therefore, the *Vibhāṣā*, fascicle 156, states:
"The Vaibhāṣika masters of Kaśmīr say that there are three roots of the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*)."

This refers to indeterminate craving, wisdom, and ignorance. Regarding "indeterminate craving," it refers to the craving belonging to the five categories within the form and formless realms. Regarding "indeterminate wisdom": [it refers to the wisdom associated with those same realms].
That is to say: obscured-unspecified wisdom,
unobscured-unspecified wisdom,
and obscured-unspecified wisdom.
This refers to the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and the view of extreme adherence (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*) in the desire realm,
as well as the five categories of afflicted wisdom and non-obscured neutral wisdom in the form and formless realms.
The wisdom co-arising with the minds of deportment, craftsmanship, maturation, and transformation is indeterminate.
"Indeterminate ignorance" refers to the ignorance associated with the view of a self-identity and the view of extremes within the desire realm.

And the five categories of ignorance pertaining to the form and formless realms. Question: Among the indeterminate factors, why are these three specifically established as faculties (*indriya*)? Explanation: "Faculty" has the meaning of "cause."
These three are established as faculties because they are preeminent in producing all phenomena as causes.
Craving is the foothold for all afflictions,
and delusion is universally associated with all delusions.
Wisdom (*prajñā*) is able to discern and serve as the leader for the multitude.
For what reason are doubt (*vicikitsā*) and pride (*māna*) not considered roots of the indeterminate (*avyākṛta-mūla*)?
This explains the third statement. Question: Among the ten underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*), it is beyond words to state why hatred (*pratigha*) is not indeterminate.
For what reason are doubt (*vicikitsā*) and pride (*māna*) not considered roots of the indeterminate (*avyākṛta-mūla*)?
Regarding the statement that "because doubt wavers between two courses, it is not a root," the answer is as follows:
The meaning can be understood from the text. The others are not *anuśayas*, or they lack superior function;
therefore, they are not established as faculties (*indriya*).
Regarding the phrase "the masters of foreign regions [proceed] as far as the negation of good and evil":
this explains the fourth and fifth phrases.
"Foreign regions" refers specifically to the masters of the West.
There are four types of neutral roots (*avyākṛta-mūla*) in total:
namely, the four kinds of obscured-neutral (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*) craving, views, pride, and ignorance.
In the verse, the term "neutral" (*avyākṛta*) is used as a shorthand for "obscured-neutral."
Because it obstructs both the wholesome and the unwholesome,
this [state] is exclusively obscured (nivṛta) and does not extend to the unobscured (anivṛta).
Therefore, the *Vibhāṣā* says:
The masters of the West state that there are four roots of the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*):
namely, indeterminate craving (*tṛṣṇā*), views (*dṛṣṭi*), pride (*māna*), and ignorance (*avidyā*).
As for indeterminate craving:
This refers to the fivefold craving of the form and formless realms.
As for neutral views,
these refer to the view of a self-identity and the view of extreme attachment within the desire realm.
Furthermore, regarding the five views of the form and formless realms,
as well as the indeterminate conceit:
this refers to the indeterminate ignorance associated with the five categories of conceit within the form and formless realms.
This refers to the ignorance associated with the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and the view of extreme attachment (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*) within the desire realm,
as well as the five categories of ignorance within the form and formless realms.
For what reason are these four established as neutral roots (*avyākṛtamūla*)?
This explains the sixth phrase;
it constitutes the question.
From "Because all foolish commoners... up to "...are the roots of the indeterminate."
Answer: Because those foolish persons who cultivate higher meditative absorptions do not go beyond relying upon the three— craving, views, and conceit.
That is to say: one who craves higher meditative absorptions,
one who views higher meditative absorptions with attachment, and one who is conceited regarding higher meditative absorptions.
Some arise through the power of craving;
some through the power of views;
and some through the power of conceit.
Since these three all function through the activation of ignorance and possess this superior efficacy,
these four are established as the indeterminate roots (*avyākṛtamūla*).
The others are not established as faculties because they lack preeminence. Question:
Why is it that this country and foreign lands differ in this regard?
Regarding which of these two explanations is correct, the commentary states: "Since the meanings they rely upon are distinct, the explanations differ.
Between the two, the former explanation is correct.
Thus, the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* says:
Question: For what reason do the masters of the West establish pride (*māna*) as an indeterminate root (*avyākṛtamūla*)?
Answer: They state that the meaning of "root" is the sense of being firm and powerful.
Because the power of pride is firm and strong, it is established as a root.
This means that the reason a practitioner of yoga falls away from hundreds of thousands of wholesome qualities is entirely due to the power of conceit (*māna*).
Question: For what reason do the masters of this country not establish it as a faculty (*indriya*)?
Answer: This explains that the meaning of "root" (indriya) is "inferiority.
Pride causes the mind to be uplifted;
because it does not accord with inferiority, it is not established as a root.
Question: For what reason do the masters of this country establish non-obscured neutral wisdom (*anivṛtāvyākṛta-prajñā*) as a root of the neutral?
Answer: This teaching takes the sense of being a supporting cause (*niśraya-hetu*) to be the meaning of "root" (*mūla*).
Because non-obscured neutral wisdom is preeminent as a supporting cause, it is established as a root.
Question: For what reason do the masters of the West not establish [this] as a faculty (*indriya*)?
Answer: They state that the meaning of "faculty" is the sense of having firm and powerful strength.
Since the power of wisdom (*prajñā*) that is unobscured-neutral (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*) is weak and inferior, it is not established as a faculty.
Question: For what reason does that Master of the Nation (Rāṣṭrapāla) not establish doubt as an indeterminate root (*avyākṛtamūla*)?
Answer: Both [the Abhidharma masters and the Master] state that the meaning of "root" is the sense of being firmly established;
doubt is not firmly established.
Because they undergo transformation through two gates,
they are not established as faculties (*indriya*).
According to this explanation, both wholesome and unwholesome roots each possess three types.
The same should apply to neutral [pride].
Furthermore, just as unwholesome pride is not established as an unwholesome root,
neutral pride should likewise not be so established.
Therefore, it is correct that the indeterminate roots are only three.
Regarding the question in various sūtras as to whether [certain factors] are included within the indeterminate:
this section below is the second part, which clarifies the four types of formal questions (*vyākaraṇa*) based on the treatise.
The various sūtras speak of fourteen indeterminate points (*avyākṛta-vastu*).
Are these also subsumed under the "indeterminate" (*avyākṛta*) within these three natures (*trisvabhāva*)? No, they are not.
Answer: What is it? This is an inquiry.
If it is asked: "In that sutra, why is the name 'indeterminate' (avyākṛta) established solely in reference to [the state of] reaching [the object]?
The answer is:
"In that sutra, there are fourteen [such states]."
Among the four ways of answering questions, the term "avyākṛta" (unanswered) is established specifically with respect to the fourth type—the question to be set aside.
The word "vyākaroti" (to answer) means "to respond.
Thus, it is said that there are four general types of questions and answers.
The Master of the Treatise, in response to this question, generally clarifies four types.
He uses the term "recording" (jì) to mean "answering" (dá);
all subsequent instances are to be understood accordingly.
It is said that there are four general types of the method of question and answer. What are these four?
Question:
The verse says: "Regarding 'reaching my aggregates,' 'identity,' 'difference,' and so forth":
the first two lines provide the direct answer;
the latter two lines explain by citing specific instances.
The Commentary states: "As for 'reaching' refers to answering the four questions," this means that within the prose section,
one Vaibhāṣika master explains the four types of answers.
"The two masters' explanation of the four types of answers," etc.;
the "etc. (ādi) includes the various masters of the Abhidharma and so forth.
Thus, the *Nyāyānusāra* states:
The word "etc. (*ādi*) serves to include [other categories] according to different perspectives;
furthermore, the question regarding the four [categories] is a general enumeration of their number.
The first question should be answered categorically;
the second question should be answered analytically;
the third question should be answered by means of a counter-interrogation.
The fourth question should be answered by setting it aside.
These four types of answers respond to those four questions in their respective order;
this explains the first half of the verse. For example, as there may be an inquirer:
First, he asks about death;
second, he asks about birth;
third, he asks about victory.
The four questions—"Is it one? "Is it different?
and so forth—specifically point to and individually manifest these four matters. The reason there are four records is that they provide answers to these four questions.
This explains the second half of the verse. Regarding the question, "If one asks [about] the nature of white, black, and so forth," the following provides a detailed explanation.
The first three questions have already been answered.
This can be understood from the text. Regarding the fourth question and its answer:
if one were to ask whether the aggregates (skandhas) and the sentient being are identical or distinct.
When this question is posed, one should set it aside as a matter to be left unanswered regarding their identity or difference, merely saying:
"This should not be answered," because those sentient beings do not exist as substantial entities.
Since neither identity nor difference can be established as their intrinsic nature, it is said that such questions should be set aside and not answered.
Furthermore, it is like asking:
"Is the son born of a barren woman white,
black, or of some other nature?"
If one receives such a question, it should likewise be set aside as indeterminate.
A barren woman originally has no child;
how then can one discuss whether that child is white or black? One who does not give birth to a son is called a barren woman.
Therefore, the *Vibhāṣā* (Taishō 1545), fascicle 16,
states: "Just as a female body that is incapable of conceiving is called a 'barren woman' (*vandhyā*) because it is empty and lacks offspring."
How is it that one sets aside [a question] yet establishes the designation of "answering"?
Question:
How is it that one sets aside questions regarding identity or difference and does not answer them, yet still establishes the designation of "answering"?
Regarding the statement that the question is "not to be answered" (avyākṛta) because it was answered as such:

Regarding this first type of categorical response (*ekāṃśavyākaraṇa*), if someone were to ask:

"Are the Four Truths well-established? To all such questions, one should give a categorical answer:

Because it accords with the true meaning.

A counter-question:
Are both types [of questions] answered by means of a counter-question?

Answer: It is as if someone were to request, saying, "Please tell me the way.

Answer: It is not so; the intent of the question is straightforward.

One should further counter-interrogate:
"In dependence upon what subtle self?
If you say it is in dependence upon the other three aggregates," [one should respond as follows].
One should state that [the self] is different from perception (saṃjñā).
If one says it depends on perception,
one should answer that they are one.
Because the coarse self (*ātman*) is definitely distinct from perception (*saṃjñā*),
the treatise specifically mentions it;
whereas the subtle self is not fixed, and thus it is omitted and not discussed.
This question is called one that should be answered by counter-interrogation.

Because non-Buddhists (tīrthikas) cling to this very [self] as being the self, there are the four views such as "the world is eternal," the four views such as "it has an end," and the four views such as "it exists."

Regarding the question of what things sentient beings are bound by:
the following section, the sixth, clarifies that it is the afflictions (*kleśa*) that bind. Within this:
First, the explanation of bondage in terms of the time periods;
second, the explanation of bondage in terms of abandonment. Regarding the explanation of bondage in terms of the time periods:
first, the direct explanation of bondage in terms of the time periods.
Second, clarifying the existence or non-existence across the three times. Below this, the first section correctly explains the bondage (*bandhana*) in relation to the time periods.

It establishes the fundamental tenet and raises the inquiry: "When the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) of sentient beings increase in accordance with a particular object, they are said to be bound to that object."
This marks the thesis: it should be explained which latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) of the three time periods can bind which objects.
This constitutes the inquiry.
The verse says: "Those that reach the present and are currently taking an object can bind."
Answer: The first phrase clarifies the objects that are bound;
the subsequent seven phrases clarify the factors that bind. In the second phrase, it refers to those not yet abandoned.
In the eighth phrase, that which is capable of binding (bandhana) applies accordingly to the intermediate phrases. There are two types of pervasive [factors] (sarvatraga):
first, those that universally bind across the three periods of time.
The two [types of attachment] universally bind their own respective objects.
Among those in the future, if they arise, there are three—greed, hatred, and pride—of the mental consciousness;
among those not arising in the future, there are the greed and hatred of the five sensory consciousnesses.
As for the remaining faults— namely, non-seeing, doubt, and ignorance—
they all possess both types of universality (ubhayatobhāgīya) as appropriate to each case.
Regarding the designation "pervasive" (*sarvatraga*): although the three— greed, hatred, and pride— of past mental consciousness also bind [the mind] across the three periods of time,
they do not pervasively bind their own objects.
Therefore, the universal [factors] are not mentioned separately herein;
they are spoken of in conjunction with the five [categories],
as they currently serve as conditions for common delusions.
Although there are indeed those that possess both types of universal [factors], there are also those that do not;
because they are not fixed, they are not called "universal."
The treatise says: "Reaching the subsequent section" is a brief indication and explanation.
That which arises conditioned by distinct phenomena is called its specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*).
That which arises conditioned by many factors is called a "common characteristic" (sāmānyalakṣaṇa).
Among the delusions regarding specific characteristics (svalakṣaṇa),
the associated ignorance (saṃprayuktāvidyā) is omitted from discussion because it is necessarily present.
Although objects are manifold, they are briefly categorized as fivefold:
first, the object as intrinsic nature;
second, the object as cognitive support.
Third, the objects to which one is bound;
fourth, the causal objects;
fifth, the encompassed objects.
This explains the third category of objects to be bound.
In the second phrase, that which has not yet been abandoned flows accordingly into subsequent sections.
As for the statement, "if within this object it necessarily arises universally":
This explains the first three phrases:
if, regarding this object, greed, hatred, or pride have already arisen in the past and have not yet been abandoned.
Those that have already arisen now bind this object,
because greed, hatred, and pride are afflictions of specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa-kleśa*) that arise by taking individual objects as their conditions.
It is not the case that all sentient beings necessarily give rise to [the thought] regarding all things throughout the three periods of time;
for when the essence is present before one, there is no possibility of its cessation.
Therefore, regarding the present, one does not say it is "not yet severed," whereas for the past, the term "not yet severed" is applied.
If future [defilements], upon arising, were also capable of binding the three times, [the distinction would be untenable].
The next three phrases are explained as follows:
If, in a future life, the three— greed, hatred, and pride— associated with the mental consciousness (manovijñāna) are present,
they universally bind all three time periods.
Although delusion may arise or not arise regarding this object,
as long as it has not been abandoned, it is capable of binding;
this includes future greed and hatred associated with the five consciousnesses.
If it has not yet been abandoned and is capable of arising,
because the object must necessarily coexist [with the mind],
it is bound only to the future.
Therefore, the *Nyāyānusāra* states:
"By this, it has already been demonstrated that the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) associated with the five consciousnesses can arise."
If one reaches the past, one is bound only to the past;
it is the same when reaching the present.
This meaning may be understood by analogy.
If it is associated with the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) can arise.

If they have reached the past, present, or future and have not been abandoned, they may bind one even to phenomena that do not belong to their own time period. Regarding the above-mentioned treatise, [it concerns] greed and hatred associated with the five sensory consciousnesses of the future.
If they have not been abandoned, because there are many types that do not arise [yet], they can also bind the three periods of time;
this is because their objects of perception may exist in the future or flow into the present.
Or it enters the past;
although the object of cognition may be absent and thus not arise,
because it has not been abandoned, its nature remains bound to the three periods of time.
"All the remaining [defilements] that can bind this object" explains the latter two phrases.
This refers to all views, doubts, and ignorance, excluding the three types mentioned previously.
Those belonging to the past and future have not been severed;
they universally bind all phenomena across the three periods of time.
For this reason, these three—view, doubt, and ignorance—are universal afflictions (*sāmānyalakṣaṇakleśa*).
Because all sentient beings are universally bound by those objects of the three times, when one perceives the present, there is doubt and ignorance regarding them;
this occurs precisely when one is taking the objects of the three times as one's cognitive focus.

Regarding the question of whether one should distinguish between the attainment (*prāpti*) and the dissociation (*visamyoga*) of these various entities according to what is appropriate for binding them:
the following section is the second [part], which clarifies the existence or non-existence of the three time periods.
Among these, first is the statement of the thesis,
and second is the formal refutation. Regarding the statement of the thesis:
First, the proof of existence through scripture and reasoning;
second, the statement of the established tenet. Herein follows the proof of existence through scripture and reasoning.
The Sautrāntika asks: one must explain how past and future entities exist.
Only when it can be determined whether this [bond] truly exists or truly does not exist can one speak of "being bound."
If the past and future worlds were substantially existent,
then because all conditioned phenomena would exist at all times,
they should be described as permanent.
If the past and future were truly non-existent,
how could one speak of that which binds, that which is bound, and liberation from bonds?
[This applies] up to the Vaibhāṣikas who maintain the doctrine of Sarvāstivāda (the existence of all).
Answer: The Vaibhāṣika masters definitively establish that the two periods of the past and future exist as real entities;
however, conditioned phenomena (saṃskāra) are impermanent because they are conjoined with the four characteristics.
To this end, the established position that the past and future truly exist is definitively clarified.
One should briefly state the thesis to manifest its underlying principle:
the three time periods truly exist because the Buddha so taught.
Second, because they arise dependently;
because consciousness possesses an object;
and because karma possesses its fruit.

The *Śāstra* states, "As for 'the three time periods truly exist,'" which explains the existence of the three time periods.

Regarding the statement in the sūtra, "By means of diligent effort, one abandons longing," the answer is:
since the sūtra already states that one diligently cultivates revulsion toward and relinquishment of past form (*rūpa*).
Regarding future form, there is diligent effort to abandon it and a longing for its cessation.
This clearly demonstrates that one knows past and future forms to be substantially existent (*dravyasat*).

By contemplating the impermanence of form, one is able to diligently cultivate disenchantment and equanimity toward past form. Furthermore, it is explained that because one contemplates impermanence, this is called "diligently cultivating disenchantment."
Because one does not look back with longing, it is called "diligently cultivating equanimity.
By contemplating the impermanence of form, one can sever the yearning for future form;
this yearning is precisely craving conditioned by future form. Furthermore, another interpretation is that because one contemplates impermanence, it is called "diligently severing yearning."
Because one does not long for desires, it is called "diligently abandoning seeking.
Furthermore, regarding the statement that "possessing two conditions, they reach consciousness; arising from two conditions," this explains the two [conditions].
The Sūtra states that consciousness arises from two conditions;
this clearly demonstrates that the two time periods of the past and the future truly exist. What are these two?
Question:
Regarding the statement that "from the eye and visible forms up to [the case where] two conditions would be lacking," the answer is as follows.
The six sense faculties and the six objects each give rise to their respective consciousnesses;

these are called the two conditions. If the past and future were not substantially existent, then the mental consciousness that takes the past and future as its objects would be deficient in these two conditions.
Since the past does not exist, the supporting conditions (āśraya) and objective conditions (ālambana) would be deficient;
since the past and future do not exist, the objective condition would be deficient.
Furthermore, according to the sacred teaching, once consciousness has already ceased, it too should be non-existent.
This is because consciousness has an object. According to reason,
consciousness can only arise when there is necessarily an object.
The principle that "what does not exist is not produced" is certain. If the past and future were non-existent, there would have to be consciousness without an object of cognition (*ālambana*).
Since the object of cognition would be absent, consciousness itself would also necessarily be non-existent.
Furthermore, regarding those past karmas for which present causes still exist,
they are explained as having results;
moreover, this refers to karmas that have already fallen away into the past.
Because there is a fruit that is to be experienced, this demonstrates the existence of two time periods;
for if the past did not truly exist as a substantial entity, [the fruit could not arise].
The substantial entities of both wholesome and unwholesome karma would not exist;
because karma is absent,
the future fruits that are to arise would likewise not exist.

It is not the case that a present cause exists at the time when a present fruit arises, because a maturation fruit (vipākaphala) does not coexist with its cause. Furthermore, another interpretation holds that it is not the case that a present cause exists at the time when a future fruit arises.

Because the ripening fruit (vipākaphala) does not arise immediately after its cause; furthermore, it is explained that at the time when the present or future fruit arises, there is no present cause existing, because the ripening fruit is neither simultaneous with nor immediately following its cause.
This concludes the demonstration that [the three time periods] exist as real entities in two ways,
based on the two preceding scriptural authorities and the two subsequent logical arguments.
The Vaibhāṣika masters establish the existence of going and coming.
If one considers oneself a follower of the Sarvāstivāda school,
one should explain the following two phrases.

because [the Sarvāstivādins] maintain that all three time periods definitely exist in reality;
therefore, they are accepted as Sarvāstivādins.
This means that if someone belongs to a school other than this one,

Half is correct and half is incorrect;

Regarding the statement in the *Śāstra*, "As for the essence of non-abandonment and non-acquisition," there are four explanations in total.
This refers to the first master,
who can rescue the True Dharma,
or by whom the True Dharma is rescued.
Alternatively, because he saves people through the True Dharma, he is named Dharmatrāta;
some say that the Venerable One is this very person. Dharmatrāta said:
The distinction between the three time periods arises from three different categories;
that is to say, when dharmas proceed through the three times,
they differ due to these three categories, not because there is any difference in their essential nature.
It is like when a golden vessel is broken to be made into other objects;
although the shapes, such as square or round, differ,
the manifest color remains no different.
Furthermore, just as when milk transforms into curd,
it relinquishes the sweet taste and the cold potency of the milk,
