Therefore, they are not established as fetters conducive to the higher realms (*ūrdhvabhāgīya-saṃyojana*).
Furthermore, that which is practiced by those who are "superior" (the *uttara-pudgala*) is called "conducive to the higher.
These superior persons are the noble ones (*ārya*), not ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*).
The fetters abandoned through seeing arise only in ordinary worldlings;
therefore, they are not established as "fetters conducive to the higher realms" (*ūrdhvabhāgīya-saṃyojana*).
Among noble ones, only those fetters arising in non-returners (*anāgāmin*) are established as "conducive to the higher realms. Question: From this discussion, another question arises.
Why are the fetters (saṃyojana) that arise in stream-enterers (srotāpanna) and once-returners (sakṛdāgāmin) not considered "fetters conducive to the higher realms" (ūrdhvabhāgīya)? Answer:

Those termed "conducive to the higher realms" are so called because they lead to rebirth in the upper [realms]. However, the fetters arising in stream-enterers and once-returners also cause rebirth in the lower [realms].
Therefore, it is not established as one of the fetters leading to the higher realms (*ūrdhvabhāgīya-saṃyojana*), as explained at length in that [text].
Having already distinguished the fetters up to "all delusion" (*moha*), this now clarifies the second [section]: the three bonds (*bandhana*).
They are designated as "bonds" (bandhana) because they are capable of binding.
There are three distinct types of bonds.
For what reason are only these three described as bonds?
Question:
Among all the afflictions, for what reason are only these three designated as "bonds" (*bandhana*)?
Is it because they follow the three types of feeling (*vedanā*) that this definitive statement was made?

Answer: It is said that there are three types of bonds because they are induced by the power of the three feelings. Regarding one's own pleasant feeling, greed increases predominantly, because it increases both through the object of perception (*ālambana*) and through association (*samprayoga*).
Hatred increases predominantly with respect to one's own painful feeling,
because it increases both through its object and through association.
Ignorance increases predominantly with respect to one's own neutral feeling.
Because they increase together through both the object of perception (*ālambana*) and association (*samprayoga*),
it is said that aversion arises toward painful feeling (*duḥkhā vedanā*) and delusion arises toward neutral feeling (*upekṣā*).
It should be understood that the same applies here:
although attachment and aversion also exist toward one's own equanimity,
both increase in regard to their respective objects and through association.
It is not because it is like delusion (*moha*).
This point should also be understood by implication within this passage;
for although delusion is said to exist even in relation to one's own pleasure.
Both the object-condition (*ālambana*) and association (*samprayoga*) increase [the defilement];
this is because it is not like craving (*rāga*).
Although delusion (*moha*) is also said to exist even toward one's own suffering, [it is still classified as an affliction].
Both the object and the associated factors increase [the defilement];
it is not like the case of hatred. Furthermore, it should also be clarified that although greed is said to exist even toward one's own suffering.
It increases through both its object and its association,
unlike hatred; for although hatred is said to exist even toward one's own pleasure, [it does not increase in that way].
The object of focus increases [affliction] because it is not like craving;
this is with respect to the three feelings— pleasure and so forth— within one's own continuum.
Speaking in terms of the majority, it is said that these are the objects of bondage:
attachment increases in dependence upon pleasure,
and aversion increases in dependence upon suffering.
Delusion increases by taking equanimity as its object.
If one considers the three feelings— pleasure and so forth— within the bodies of other continuums as the objects of bondage,
this is indeterminate.
Because all three feelings can serve as objects of perception to give rise to the three fetters:
just as hatred increases when one perceives the pleasure of an enemy,
so too does craving increase when one perceives the suffering of an enemy.
Ignorance (*moha*) also increases accordingly with respect to suffering, pleasure, and that which is neither-pleasure-nor-suffering, whether they are related to enemies or friends, as appropriate.
Therefore, the *Nyāyānusāra* (Treatise on the Principles), fascicle 54, states: "Other masters say..."
Based on the influence drawn forth by the three types of sensation (*vedanā*), it is said that there are three bonds (*bandhana*).

That is to say, for the most part, craving (*rāga*) increases in two ways— by way of its object (*ālambana*) and its association (*samprayoga*)— with respect to one's own pleasant sensation (*sukha-vedanā*).
To a small extent, one also [experiences] neither-pain-nor-pleasure;
regarding the suffering of oneself and others,
one takes up the pleasure of others and abandons [one's own].
There is only one type of object that increases [the defilement];
furthermore, hatred for the most part increases in two ways—
by way of the object and by way of association— with respect to its own painful feeling.
To a small extent, they also [direct their minds] toward the neither-painful-nor-pleasant [feeling],
toward one's own and others' happiness,
as well as toward the suffering and equanimity of others.
Only one type of object-condition (ālambana) increases [the defilements];
furthermore, delusion (moha) for the most part increases through both the object-condition and the association-condition (samprayoga) with its own neutral feeling (upekṣā).
To a small extent, they also increase by way of being objects (*ālambana*) with respect to pleasant and painful feelings; with respect to all other feelings, they increase solely as objects.
Therefore, the Blessed One spoke according to the principle of the majority.
It is said that the three bonds (bandhana) are established in accordance with the three feelings (vedanā).
As for the phrase "having already analyzed the bonds as previously explained," this constitutes the third clarification regarding the latent dispositions (anuśaya).
This refers back to what was previously stated.

Since the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) have already been explained as being subsumed under the defilements (*kleśa-mala*), this now clarifies the fourth category: the secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*).
Brief explanation of the verse: "Aggregates" (skandha) excludes the unconditioned;
"formations" (saṃskāra) excludes the four aggregates beginning with form; and "mental factors" (caitta).
From within the formations dissociated from mind (*viprayukta-saṃskāra*), it excludes [those that are] defiled;

from among the mental factors (*caitta*), it excludes those that are wholesome or indeterminate; and from within the defiled [factors], it further excludes the primary afflictions (*mūlakleśa*), meaning these primary afflictions and their remaining secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*).
Regarding the headings:
before explaining the secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*), one first explains the root afflictions (*mūlakleśa*).
These various root afflictions are also called secondary afflictions.
Because they all function as afflictions that disturb the mind,
there are furthermore these remaining root afflictions,
which are distinct from the other primary afflictions and are included within the aggregate of mental factors (*caitta*) that defile the mind.
Because they arise following the primary afflictions (*kleśa*), they are also called secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*).
They are not called "afflictions" because they are not fundamental.
[The text] sets forth in detail the characteristics of those secondary afflictions.

As stated in the ninth fascicle of the *Dharmaskandha-pāda-śāstra*, in the section on Miscellaneous Matters (*Saṃkīrṇa-vastu*): "Furthermore, regarding the brief discussion of what is subsumed under the ten envelopments (*paryavasthāna*), six are subsumed under the defilements of affliction (*kleśamala*)."
Furthermore, one should first distinguish those [afflictions] that lead to regret, arising from doubt, concealment, and contention;
this constitutes the fifth clarification of the *paryavasthānas* (envelopments).
The first verse clarifies these *paryavasthānas*.
The final one and a half verses clarify the outflowing fruit (*niṣyanda-phala*) of the fundamental afflictions (*mūlakleśa*).
The treatise states: "Up to what is called 'concealment' (*mrakṣa*)," which explains the first verse.
Before explaining the various envelopments (*paryavasthāna*), one first resolves the fundamental afflictions (*mūlakleśa*).
The root afflictions are also termed "envelopments," as the Sūtra states that the envelopment of sensual desire (*kāmarāga-paryavasthāna*) serves as a condition. However, the *Prakaraṇapāda*...

It is taught that there are eight *paryavasthānas*, excluding *krodha* (anger) and *mrakṣa* (concealment). According to the Vaibhāṣika school, there are ten *paryavasthānas*. They are called *paryavasthānas* because they bind sentient beings and place them within the prison of birth and death (*saṃsāra*). Among these, *middha* (drowsiness/sleep) is taken here only in its defiled form.
Generally speaking, there are four types of sleep:
wholesome, unwholesome, obscured-neutral, and unobscured-neutral. The wholesome type is exclusively innate (*upapattilābhika*) and does not extend to the acquired (*prāyogika*).
Therefore, the *Nyāyānusāra* states:
"However, during the preparatory stages (*prayoga*), wholesome minds consisting of hearing and reflection do not manifest while one is asleep,
because their intrinsic natures (*svabhāva*) are mutually contradictory."
Because these [afflictions] are counteracted by the mind produced through the cultivation of application (*prayoga-bhāvanāmayi-citta*), they do not manifest therein;
only a certain class of innate wholesome minds (*upapatti-lābhika-kuśala-citta*) can manifest while one is asleep.

Because their nature is weak and inferior, the unwholesome (*akuśala*) and the obscured (*nivṛta*) are both admitted to manifest; however, there are differing opinions regarding the unobscured-neutral (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*).
Thus, the *Nyāyānusāra* (Treatise on Correct Reasoning), fascicle 54, states:
The unobscured-neutral [mind] arises solely as a result of maturation (*vipākaja*),
because the arising of minds such as those of craftsmanship would destroy the state of sleep.
Other masters say that within the state of sleep, minds of deportment (*airyāpathika*) and craftsmanship (*śailpasthānika*) may also arise.
However, it cannot be practiced at the initial stage;
it can only be practiced later within the dream state.
Furthermore, the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 37, states:

The non-obscured and neutral [states] refer to those born of deportment (*airyāpathika*), those belonging to the arts and crafts (*śailpasthānika*), and those born of maturation (*vipākaja*), excluding the fruits of supernormal powers (*abhijñā-phala*).
Regarding "those born of deportment":
this refers, for example, to when one in sleep or a dream thinks to oneself that one is walking and so forth.
Regarding the sphere of craftsmanship (*śailpasthānika*):
it is, for example, as when one thinks in a dream that one is painting and so forth. Regarding that which is born of maturation (*vipākaja*): [it is as follows].
In the state of sleep, apart from what was previously mentioned, there is no other transformation of the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*).
Other masters say that it is exclusively that which is born of maturation (*vipākaja*),
being the unobscured-indeterminate (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*) within sleep.
Because the mind is dull and obscured,

it does not initiate bodily or vocal activity; therefore, there is no deportment (*airyāpathika*) or craftsmanship (*śailpasthānika*), according to the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* and the *Nyāyānusāra*.
Furthermore, the commentator provides no brief explanation for *middha* (torpor).

The remaining nine [defilements] are as stated in the text. Question: Why are the other secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*) not classified as *paryavasthāna* (envelopments)? Answer: It is explained that, according to their respective gravity, those with heavy faults are established separately as such, while those with light faults are not.

Among the great afflictions (*mahākleśa*), lethargy (*styāna*) is established as a separate entanglement (*paryavasthāna*) because it particularly obstructs wisdom (*prajñā*), and restlessness (*auddhatya*) is so established because it particularly obstructs meditative concentration (*samādhi*).

The three types— lack of faith (*āśraddhya*), laziness (*kausīdya*), and heedlessness (*pramāda*)— are not established as entangements because they do not particularly obstruct either concentration or wisdom.
Therefore, the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* states:
"The three [defilements] beginning with lack of faith (*āśraddhya*) are not established as latent dispositions (*anuśaya*), envelopments (*paryavasthāna*), or stains (*mala*),
because their faults are slight."

"Because they are easily eliminated," as stated in the treatise above; since ignorance (*avidyā*) is a fundamental affliction (*mūlakleśa*), it is not established as an entanglement (*paryavasthāna*).
Lack of shame (*āhrīkya*) and lack of dread (*anapatrāpya*) are established as entanglements because they are exclusively unwholesome (*akuśala*) and their transgressions are particularly grave.

Among the secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*), envy (*īrṣyā*), avarice (*mātsarya*), anger (*krodha*), and concealment (*mrakṣa*) are established as *paryavasthāna* (outbursts) because they are particularly heavy;
the remaining six are established as *upakleśa* (secondary stains) because they are relatively light.
Furthermore, among the factors belonging to other stages, sleep (*middha*) is preeminent in its obstruction of wisdom (*prajñā*).
Because remorse (*kaukṛtya*) is a more powerful obstacle to meditative concentration (*samādhi*), it is established separately as an entanglement (*paryavasthāna*);
whereas vitarka and vicāra are not obstacles [to concentration],
vitarka is established as a factor of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*).
This is conducive to wisdom (*prajñā*).
Vitarka and vicāra are established as factors of dhyāna;
this is conducive to concentration (*samādhi*).
Therefore, the *paryavasthānas* (envelopments) are not established.
Greed, hatred, pride, and doubt are all fundamental delusions;
thus, they are also not established as *paryavasthānas*.
Regarding the phrase "as explained here, up to their respective order," this explains the final one and a half verses. As for the term "outflow" (*niṣyanda*),
it refers to the immediate outflow fruit (*niṣyandaphala*) of those fundamental afflictions (*mūlakleśa*).
If it is someone who knows [the truth], this concealment is a derivative of greed (*lobha*),
because they conceal it out of attachment to fame and profit.
If it is someone who does not know [the truth], this concealment is a derivative of ignorance (*avidyā*).
Because they do not understand due to ignorance and conceal it, respectively:
furthermore, understanding with knowledge is the first teacher;
lacking knowledge is the second teacher.
The third teacher maintains that "having knowledge" and "not having knowledge" [are the causes].
Therefore, it is said that according to their respective order, the former interpretation is superior.

The rest of the text may be understood accordingly. Thus, the *Nyāyānusāra* states: "Lack of shame (*āhrīkya*), stinginess (*mātsarya*), and restlessness (*auddhatya*) are the outflows (*niṣyanda*) of greed."
Because greed must serve as the proximate cause for them to arise;
lack of shame (*āhrīkya*), torpor (*middha*), and lethargy (*styāna*) are outflows (*niṣyanda*) of ignorance (*avidyā*),
for they are extremely closely related in character to ignorance.
Envy and resentment are outflows of hatred,
because they share the same nature as hatred.
Regret is an outflow of doubt.
Because it arises from doubt,
some say that concealment (*mrakṣa*) is a derivative of greed (*lobha*),
while others say it is a derivative of ignorance (*avidyā*).
Some say they are both outflows:
for those with knowledge, they arise from craving;
for those without knowledge, they arise from delusion.
Regarding the statement, "The remaining afflictions and stains up to deceit arise from the various views":
this constitutes the second major section, which elucidates the six stains of the afflictions.
The first two lines specifically clarify these six stains.
The final four phrases clarify that these are the immediate outflow fruits (*niṣyanda-phala*) of the fundamental afflictions.
The Commentary states: "Reaching what are called the 'defilements' (*kleśa-mala*)," which explains the first two phrases. [These are] *śāṭhya* (deceit).
It is defined as having the nature of causing the mind to be crooked.
Because of this, one is unable to manifest oneself as one truly is;
rather, for the sake of deceiving another person, or through hypocrisy, one denies or slanders that person's enemies in order to cause them to rejoice.

Because one deceives others or employs various expedient means and displays signs that cause their understanding to be unclear, it is called *śāṭhya* (deceit). The rest of the text may be understood accordingly.
Regarding these six types, as for the name "secondary afflictions" (*upakleśa*): [the remainder follows].
Explanation of the final four phrases: Regarding the term "outflow" (*niṣyanda*), it refers to the immediate outflow fruit (*niṣyanda-phala*) of those fundamental afflictions (*mūlakleśa*).
Deceit (*śāṭhya*) is the outflow of the five views (*pañcadṛṣṭi*). As it is asked:
"What dharma is crooked?
He replied: "It refers to all wrong views;
wrong views are called 'crooked'."
Because it is similar to *śāṭhya* (deceit),
*śāṭhya* is certainly an outflow (*niṣyanda*) of the various views (*dṛṣṭi*).
Therefore, the first chapter of the *Abhidharmāvatāra-śāstra* states:
Deceit (*māyā*) and arrogance (*mada*) are both outflows of greed (*lobha*), as they belong to the category of greed.
Harmfulness (*vihiṃsā*) and resentment (*upanāha*) are both outflows of hatred (*dveṣa*), as they belong to the category of hatred.
The stain of vexation (*pradāsa-kleśa*) is specifically an outflow of the view of grasping at extremes (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*).
Because those who cling to their own views as superior cause affliction for both themselves and others,
the stain of guile is the outflow of various views;
for when views increase, crookedness and guile generally abound.
As it is said, "crookedness" refers to various wrong views.

Regarding these defilements (*mala*) and envelopments (*paryavasthāna*), up to their being designated as "arising independently," this concludes the second major section: the detailed classification by way of various categories.
Among these, first is the classification according to the three types of abandonment,
and second is the classification according to the three natures.
Third, the classification by way of the three realms;
fourth, association with the six consciousnesses;
fifth, association with the five feelings—this is the classification by way of the three types of abandonment.

Furthermore, among the ten envelopments (*paryavasthāna*), five types—lack of shame (*āhrīkya*), lack of dread (*anapatrāpya*), sleep (*middha*), lethargy (*styāna*), and restlessness (*auddhatya*)—are common to both those abandoned by vision (*darśana-heya*) and those abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*).
This is because they arise in association with the two categories of afflictions abandoned by vision and cultivation respectively.
Therefore, it pertains to both types of abandonment.
Within the category of abandonment through seeing, whichever [affliction] is associated with what is abandoned by seeing a particular truth is designated as "abandoned by seeing that truth."

Those abandoned through seeing (*darśana-heya*) are explained individually because they pertain to all four categories (*nikāya*); those abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) are not explained separately because they belong to only one category.
The remaining [defilements]—envy (*īrṣyā*), avarice (*mātsarya*), regret (*kaukṛtya*), anger (*krodha*), concealment (*mrakṣa*), as well as the six stains (*mala*)—[are likewise].
Because it arises autonomously, it is abandoned only through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*).
It is called "autonomous arising" because it is associated exclusively with the other-power ignorance (*paratantra-avidyā*) that is abandoned through cultivation.
Therefore, they are abandoned only through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*). Thus, the *Nyāyānusāra* states:
"They are associated with spontaneously arising (*svatantra*) envelopments (*paryavasthāna*) and impurities (*mala*)."
Since all ignorance is abandoned solely through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*),
when these secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*) are subsumed under the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) nature,
this constitutes the analysis according to the three natures (*tri-svabhāva-vibhāga*).
The three [defilements] bound to the desire realm— namely, sloth (*styāna*), torpor (*middha*),
and restlessness (*auddhatya*)— are unwholesome when associated with greed and so forth;
they are neutral (*avyākṛta*) when associated with the view of self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) or the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*).
All remaining seven envelopments (paryavasthāna) and six stains (mala) are exclusively unwholesome (akuśala).
In the two higher realms, all instances of lethargy, restlessness,
as well as guile, deceit, and pride,
are exclusively comprised within the category of the indeterminate (avyākṛta).

Regarding these secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*) that pertain exclusively to the Desire Realm (*kāmadhātu*), this constitutes the third classification of the three realms. Concealing one's own true state of mind is termed *śāṭhya* (dissimulation); manifesting signs to deceive others is termed *māyā* (deceit). Furthermore, it is said that *śāṭhya* and *māyā* are correctly understood [as follows]: [the former is] dissimulation; [the latter is] deceit.

It is traditionally said that this arises only in ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*) and is not something that can be manifested by the noble ones (*ārya*). The rest of the text may be understood accordingly.
Thus has been explained [the section] from "the latent dispositions" up to "because they are all capable of arising."
This is the fourth [category] associated with the six consciousnesses; it should be understood as being explained in brief:

all [defilements] of the three realms abandoned through seeing the truths (*darśana-heya*) and abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*), as well as all forms of pride (*māna*) and torpor (*middha*) among the secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*).
Those that arise independently are the fetters of envy, avarice, anger, concealment, and regret,
as well as the six stains.

All of these depend exclusively on the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), because there is no possibility for them to arise in dependence upon the five groups of sensory consciousness (*pañcavijñānakāya*). All remaining [afflictions] depend on all six consciousnesses;
namely, greed, hatred, and ignorance that are to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*).
And those associated secondary afflictions (upakleśa),

namely the four entanglements (paryavasthāna) of shamelessness (āhrīkya), lack of dread (anapatrāpya), torpor (styāna), and restlessness (auddhatya), as well as the secondary afflictions subsumed under the great ground of affliction (mahākleśabhūmika).
These are precisely heedlessness (*pramāda*), laziness (*kausīdya*), and lack of faith (*āśraddhya*),
because they can all arise in dependence upon the six groups of consciousness (*ṣaḍ-vijñāna-kāya*).
This is as previously established regarding how [these factors] extend to all sensations within their respective consciousnesses.
Below this is the fifth section, on association with the five feelings (*pañca-vedanā*).
Within this, the first part clarifies association with the fundamental afflictions (*mūla-kleśa*).

Second, the explanation of association with secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*). This is the first [section], explaining association with primary afflictions (*mūlakleśa*). Within the introduction of the inquiry, there is:
(1) a general question;
and (2) specific questions followed by a response in verse.
This can be understood.
The *Śāstra* states, "up to 'because it belongs solely to the mental level'":
this refers to craving among the afflictions of the desire realm.
Because it proceeds as a mode of joy (*prīti*) associated with pleasure (*sukha*),
and because it is not associated with sorrow (*daurmanasya*) or suffering (*duḥkha*) nor is it a mode of dejection (*arati*),
it is associated with joy and pleasure throughout the six consciousnesses.
If it is associated with the faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*) in the five sensory consciousnesses,
or if it is in the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*),

it is associated with the faculty of joy (*saumanasyendriya*). It is associated with aversion (*dveṣa*), sorrow (*daurmanasya*), and pain (*duḥkha*), because it proceeds with a mode of activity characterized by dejection.

Because it is not associated with joy or pleasure and does not function as a state of gladness, it is associated with sorrow and suffering throughout the six consciousnesses; if it occurs within the five sensory consciousnesses, it is associated with the faculty of suffering.

If it is associated with the faculty of grief (*daurmanasyendriya*) within the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), ignorance is universally associated with the four aforementioned feelings (*vedanā*): joy, pleasure, grief, and suffering.
Because it functions through a mode of elation, it is associated with joy and pleasure.
Because it functions through dejected conduct, it is associated with sorrow (*daurmanasya*).
Because it pervades the six consciousnesses, it is associated with the four feelings (*vedanā*).
If it occurs within the five sensory consciousnesses, it is associated with the faculties of suffering (*duḥkhendriya*) and pleasure (*sukhendriya*).
If [wrong view] is associated with joy or sorrow in the mental consciousness, it is generally associated with both sorrow and joy.
Because it proceeds with a mode of elation, it is associated with the faculty of joy;
because it proceeds with a mode of dejection, it is associated with the faculty of sorrow.
Because it belongs solely to the mental level (*manobhūmi*), it is associated with sorrow and joy;
because it is not part of the five sensory consciousnesses, it is not associated with suffering or pleasure.
For what reason do wrong views proceed through both modes of elation and dejection?
Question:
Regarding the statement that it is because one has previously created sinful or meritorious karma in succession, the answer is as follows.
If one first creates sinful karma and subsequently gives rise to wrong views, it proceeds with joy,
because although one has created sinful karma, there is no bitter fruit.
If one first creates meritorious karma and subsequently gives rise to wrong views, it proceeds with distress.
Because labor expended in vain yields no fruit of merit.
As for "associated with doubt and sorrow, up to necessarily abiding in equanimity":
it is because that which is associated with doubt and sorrow proceeds as a mode of dejection.
Because it is not associated with joy (*prīti*) and does not function as a state of gladness,

it is associated only with the faculty of sorrow (*daurmanasyendriya*), since it belongs exclusively to the mental level (*manobhūmi*). Because it does not belong to the five sensory consciousnesses (*pañcavijñāna*), it is not associated with suffering (*duḥkha*).
Because the pursuit of a definitive knowledge involves mental distress and sorrow, it proceeds through a mode of displeasure (*daurmanasya*). As for the other four views and pride,
they proceed through a mode of pleasure (*saumanasya*), as they are associated with joy (*prīti*).

Because they are not associated with sorrow (*daurmanasya*) and do not consist of dejected activity (*asātā-saṃprayukta*), they are associated only with the faculty of joy (*saumanasyendriya*), as they belong exclusively to the mental level (*manobhūmika*).

Because they do not belong to the five sensory consciousnesses (*pañcavijñāna*), they are not associated with the faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*). Thus, the association of the various afflictions (*kleśa*) with the feelings (*vedanā*) has been explained according to their specific characteristics.
Speaking in terms of general characteristics regarding those associated with feeling (*vedanā-samprayukta*):
all afflictions (*kleśa*) are associated with the feeling of equanimity (*upekṣā-vedanā*).
This is because at the stage when the continuity of the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) is severed, their power having subsided, they necessarily abide in the feeling of equanimity.
Because the state of equanimity (upekṣā) does not conflict with either joy or grief when situated in the middle,
it is universally associated.
If the case in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) is thus, what is it like in the higher realms?
The following explains the latter two phrases.
This constitutes the question.
As for the statement, "Because they all proceed according to what is appropriate, they are not explained separately":
Answer: Because there is sorrow and suffering in the realm of desire, the various afflictions proceed with a mode of activity characterized by dejection;
in the higher realms, there is no sorrow or suffering.
Furthermore, because they are moistened by meditative concentration (*samādhi*), the various afflictions (*kleśa*) proceed without any state of distress;
this applies to whatever afflictions belong to the consciousness of any given stage (*bhūmi*).
Each is associated with all feelings within its own respective consciousness. If the first dhyāna possesses all four consciousnesses,
then the afflictions arising from each of those individual consciousnesses are respectively associated with all feelings within their own respective consciousnesses.
If [the afflictions] exist in the three consciousnesses, they are associated with equanimity (*upekṣā*).
If they exist in the mental ground (*manobhūmi*), they are associated with joy (*prīti*) or equanimity. From the second dhyāna upward, there is only mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).
The afflictions arising from the mental consciousness in these two dhyānas [are as follows].
The afflictions arising from the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) of the third dhyāna are universally associated with pleasure (*sukha*) and equanimity (*upekṣā*).
The afflictions arising from the mental consciousness of the fourth dhyāna and above are universally associated with equanimity (*upekṣā*).
It is universally associated with the feeling of equanimity (*upekṣā*) in the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).

Regarding the quantity of consciousness and feeling in the higher stages, they have already been analyzed as before and thus are not explained separately here. Furthermore, the *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya* (Cheng weishi lun), fascicle 27, states:
For what reason are both types of doubt equally indeterminate?
While the higher [doubts] can be associated with joy and pleasure, doubt in the desire realm does not arise together with the sensation of joy.
This is because all afflictions exist in stages that are free from desire.
Although it is not certain, one does not feel sorrow or distress;
although entangled by doubt, one does not abandon a joyful disposition.
It is like being in the human world where, having found what one loves, despite much toil and fatigue, a sense of pleasure arises.
Although one may harbor doubts regarding the realm of form (rūpadhātu),
because within those doubts one forms the conception that they belong to the wholesome side (kuśalapakṣa),
it is therefore able to be associated with joy (prīti) and bliss (sukha).
Having already distinguished the afflictions that correspond with the other four universal [factors], this second section clarifies the correspondence with the secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*).
The treatise states: "Because they pertain exclusively to the mental ground (*manobhūmi*)."
The first three phrases are explained as follows:
among the secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*), the six types— envy (*īrṣyā*), regret (*kaukṛtya*), anger (*krodha*), resentment (*upanāha*), malice (*vihimsā*), and enmity (*pradāśa*)—
are all associated with the faculty of mental grief (*daurmanasyendriya*).
Because it functions as a state of dejection,
it is not associated with joy (*prīti*) and does not function as a state of gladness;
because it belongs exclusively to the mental level (*manobhūmi*), it is associated with the faculty of sorrow (*daurmanasyendriya*).
Because it is not among the five consciousnesses, it is not associated with suffering. Furthermore, the *Nyāyānusāra* states:
"Other masters say that it is associated with joy (*saumanasya*), because the outflow of the view of grasping at views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*) should be of a joyful nature."
"Because stinginess is associated with joy and reaches an extreme similarity" explains the fourth phrase; it means that stinginess,
being associated with joy, functions as a mode of mental elation (*prīti*).
Because it is neither associated with sorrow nor characterized by dejection,

it is associated with the faculty of joy (*saumanasyendriya*) alone, as it belongs exclusively to the mental level (*manobhūmi*). Because it does not belong to the five sensory consciousnesses, it is not associated with the faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*).
"Flattery, deception, torpor, and concealment, up to mental states associated with grief":
this explains the fifth and sixth phrases— namely, flattery (*māyā*),
deception (*śāṭhya*), torpor (*middha*), and concealment (*mrakṣa*).
Because they proceed as modes of joy and grief associated with sorrow and gladness:
if they proceed as modes of joy, they are associated with the faculty of gladness (*saumanasyendriya*);
if they proceed as modes of grief, they are associated with the faculty of sorrow (*daurmanasyendriya*).
Because it belongs solely to the mental level (*manobhūmi*), it is associated with sorrow and joy;
because it is not part of the five sensory consciousnesses, it is not associated with suffering or pleasure.
Furthermore, the *Nyāyānusāra* states:
Other masters say: Since it has been stated that deception (*māyā*) is an outflow (*niṣyanda*) of greed (*lobha*), it should be associated exclusively with the faculty of joy (*saumanasyendriya*);
it should not be said to be associated with the faculty of grief (*daurmanasyendriya*).
Because this [deceit] is a natural outflow (*niṣyanda*) of joy, it should not be associated with dejection.
Furthermore, because one should not feel dejected at the very moment of deceiving,
or else one should state that deceit is a natural outflow of delusion (*moha*).
The *Nyāyānusāra* explains:
"In principle, one should explain that cause and effect are distinct;
for example, although lack of shame (*āhrīkya*) and restlessness (*auddhatya*) are outflows of greed (*lobha*), they are distinct from it."
Furthermore, it possesses the sense of being associated with sorrow and suffering.
Therefore, one should know that what has been stated regarding association with feeling (*vedanā*) does not refer solely to a common cause;
rather, it is based on a distinction in their characteristics that the existence of grief and lamentation is admitted.
One who acts with deception has a mind filled with anxiety because of that deceptive conduct.
Regarding "associated with joy," "delight," and "pleasure"— that is, being associated with joy—
this explains the first three characters of the seventh phrase.
Because it proceeds with a mode of activity that is joyful, associated with rapture and pleasure,
it is not associated with sorrow nor does it have a dejected mode of activity;
because it belongs solely to the mental level, it is associated with rapture and pleasure— this refers to the three dhyānas.
Because it is not the five consciousnesses, it is not associated with that pleasure.
The phrase "as explained above, up to being universally associated" explains the last two characters of the seventh clause.
Among the twelve types mentioned above,
the *mada* (conceit) associated with the path exists only from the fourth dhyāna upward, as it belongs exclusively to the stage of equanimity (*upekṣā-bhūmi*).
By the same principle, *styāna* (sloth) and *auddhatya* (restlessness) also logically belong only to the stage of equanimity.
Because they will be explained separately later on, they are not discussed here.
The rest of the text can be understood accordingly.
As for the remaining *āhrīkya* (lack of shame) and *anapatrāpya* (lack of dread), they are included within the category of universal mental factors (*mahābhūmika*).
[The author] explains the final phrase.

Question: Since the other great afflictions (*mahākleśa*) are already clarified within the context of the association with the six consciousnesses (*ṣadvijñāna-saṃprayukta*), why are they not likewise clarified here? Answer: Because the preceding text has already explained their association with the six consciousnesses.
Since it is already evident that [the afflictions] are associated with those various feelings,
they are not mentioned here.
As for the statement that there are only five afflictions because they reach the aggregate of obstacles (*āvaraṇa-skandha*):
This is the third major section, clarifying the five hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*). It consists of five parts: first, the designation of names and enumeration;
second, [the explanation that they] exist only in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*);
third, the classification; fourth, the two subsequent lines clarifying the combination of the hindrances; and finally, the single line concerning their establishment and exclusion.
The Commentary states: "Regarding the five hindrances of doubt (*vicikitsā-āvaraṇa*)," this explains the five hindrances.
The *Abhidharmāvatāra-śāstra* says:
The fivefold greed of the desire realm is called the first hindrance;
the fivefold hatred is called the second hindrance;
and the torpor and unwholesome sleep of the desire realm are called the third hindrance.
The restlessness of the desire realm and unwholesome remorse are called the fourth hindrance;
the doubt of the four categories of the desire realm is called the fifth hindrance.
Regarding the question of whether what is explained here extends throughout all three realms:
This explanation applies only to the desire realm;
this is the question.
It should be understood that these three extend up to the formless and formless realms.
Answer: The Sūtra states that because they are unwholesome, they exist only in the desire realm.
Furthermore, the *Nyāyānusāra* says:
To demonstrate that the two types, lethargy and restlessness,
are established as hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*) only within the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*),
they are established in conjunction with sleep and regret.
Because sleep (*middha*) and regret (*kaukṛtya*) are exclusively bound to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*),

they are established in conjunction with lethargy (*styāna*) and restlessness (*auddhatya) to show that only those instances of sleep and regret that are defiled (*kliṣṭa*) receive the designation of "hindrances" (*nīvaraṇa*).
Because lethargy (*styāna*) and restlessness (*auddhatya*) are exclusively defiled by nature.
As for doubt (*vicikitsā*), it should be understood—following the previous four—to exist only in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
Why are lethargy and sleep (*middha*) combined and established as one?
The following explains the second and third phrases;
this is the question itself.
"Food, remedy, and function are the same up to 'food'; what is the same regarding 'non-food'?"
Answer: It can be known.
What is called the nutriment for the hindrance of sloth and torpor?
Question:
Regarding what is called the state of mental dullness and inferiority resulting from five kinds of factors? Answer:
"Food" means that which can provide benefit.

These five [factors] can benefit torpor and drowsiness; therefore, they are their food. Furthermore, it is explained that these five are all subsumed within the minor afflictions (*upakleśa*). As for "mental fogginess" (*styāna*):
The premonitory signs of sleep: "displeasure" means the mind is not joyful;
"yawning" results from the exhaustion of worldly activities.
That which arises from fatigue gives rise to yawning;
it is named after its cause by means of its effect.
"Uneven eating" refers to consuming food and drink in excess of the normal measure.
Alternatively, there may be an increase in certain odors, tastes,
or tactile sensations that cause the body and mind of the eater to become dull and obscured;
this is a result arising from the inequality of food.

"Named after its cause; the nature of the mind being dull and weak" means that by the power of those [afflictions], the mental sovereign (*citta-rāja*) apprehends objects without clarity, which is "dullness" (*mūḍha*);
its grasping power is feeble, which is "weakness" (*hīna*).
It is named according to its function.
What is meant by "that which is not the nutriment for this hindrance"? [This is] the question.
Regarding the sign of light:
the answer is that when one gives rise to the perception of light, the mind immediately awakens.
Because lethargy (*styāna*) and sleep (*middha*) do not arise when they would be beneficial, they are called "non-nutriment" (*an-āhāra*).
Thus, these two types [of factors] lead to the mind becoming sunken and dull;
this explains that the function of lethargy and sleep is the same.
Although restlessness and remorse are two distinct factors, their nutriment and non-nutriment are the same;
this clarifies that the two types— restlessness and remorse— share both the same nutriment and the same non-nutriment.
What are called the "nutriments of the hindrance of restlessness and remorse"?
Question:
It refers to the four kinds of factors, beginning with attending to [the body] and so forth.
Answer: At times one investigates matters concerning relatives;
at times one investigates matters concerning various countries.
Or again, one may reflect, "I shall not die; I will perform such and such activities in the future.
Or at times, one may follow the flow of thought, recollecting various past events experienced in former lives.
By taking relatives and others as objects, through the influence of such distraction, restlessness increases.
There are those who give rise to sorrow and regret because things do not accord with their expectations.
What is called the "nutriment" for this hindrance?
Question:
As for what is called śamatha:
the answer is, śamatha.
This is called concentration (*samādhi*).

Because of this concentration, restlessness (*auddhatya*) and remorse (*kaukṛtya*) cannot arise. Question: Why was it previously stated that the antidote to lethargy (*styāna*) and sleep (*middha*) is the perception of light (*ālokasaṃjñā*)?
It does not mention vipaśyanā. It states that restlessness and regret are not the nourishment for śamatha, but it does not mention "darkness.
The commentary explains that there are many kinds of non-nourishment, each of which is cited according to the context.
Alternatively, these may be indicated through mutual abbreviation.
In this way, regarding these two types of non-quiescence of the mind,
their functional application is explained as being identical.
This concludes the explanation that when two [units] are combined, they constitute one.
Furthermore, the *Nyāyānusāra* states:
For what reason are the hindrances of sensual desire, ill will,
and doubt each established as a distinct hindrance despite being of a single nature,
whereas torpor and drowsiness [are combined]?
Restlessness and remorse:
these two hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*) are each established as a single hindrance by combining their two constituent factors.
Their nutriment (*āhāra*) and their antidote (*pratipakṣa*) are distinct for each.
Therefore, the names of the hindrances (nīvaraṇa) are established individually:
because of torpor (styāna) and drowsiness (middha),
as well as restlessness (auddhatya) and regret (kaukṛtya).
The food consumed, its capacity to counteract [the hindrance], and its function are all identical;
therefore, although their natures differ, they are collectively established as one.
The nutriment of the hindrance of sensual desire (*kāmacchanda-nīvaraṇa-āhāra*) refers to the aspect of being attractive (*priya-lakṣaṇa*).
The antidote to this hindrance is the sign of impurity.
The nutriment of the hindrance of ill-will is the sign of the loathsome;
the antidote to this hindrance is the root of goodness that is loving-kindness.
The nutriment of the hindrance of doubt (*vicikitsā-nīvaraṇa*) refers to the three periods of time. As stated in the Sūtra: "One gives rise to such doubt regarding the past," and so on at length.

The antidote to this hindrance is the ability to observe, as it truly is, the nature of conditions and dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*). The *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra* explains torpor and drowsiness (*styāna-middha*) as follows: [text continues].
Restlessness and remorse (*auddhatya-kaukṛtya*). Regarding food and non-food, the explanation is the same as in this treatise. Furthermore, it says:
"Alternatively, greed (*rāga*), hatred (*dveṣa*), and doubt (*vicikitsā*) are the pervasive afflictions (*paripūrṇa-kleśa*)."
Each [of the two] individually possesses the function of a single "enveloping" (paryavasthāna);
however, torpor-drowsiness (styānamiddha) and restlessness-remorse (auddhatyakaukṛtya) are not full-fledged afflictions;
only when combined do they together possess the function of a single enveloping.
Regarding the statement that "only these five [factors] are taught among all the afflictions and so forth," this explains the subsequent phrase.
This constitutes the question. Etc.
This refers to the inclusion of the secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*).
Why are these alone established as hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*) among the five aggregates? Answer:
Although the afflictions (*kleśa*) and so forth also possess the quality of being hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*),

it is only these [two] that can act as the most significant obstacles to the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*). That is to say, the hindrance of sensual desire (*kāmacchanda-nīvaraṇa*) and the hindrance of ill-will (*vyāpāda-nīvaraṇa*) are the afflictions that destroy ethical discipline (*śīla*).
It can obstruct the aggregate of ethical discipline because lethargy and drowsiness are by nature obscure;
it can obstruct the aggregate of wisdom.
Restlessness and remorse cause mental distraction, thereby obstructing the aggregate of concentration (*samādhi-skandha*).
Due to the absence of concentration and wisdom, one harbors doubt regarding the Four Noble Truths.
Because they remain bound by the fact that doubt has not been severed, they prevent even the two aggregates of liberation and the knowledge and vision of liberation from arising.

Therefore, only these five are established as hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*). Question: If it is on account of being obstacles to excellence that they are established as hindrances, [why are only these five so designated]?

Why is ignorance (*avidyā*) not established as an obscuration (*nīvaraṇa*)? The explanation says: those things that bear an equal burden are established among the obscurations; however, among those borne, ignorance is disproportionately heavy.
For this reason, it is not established [as an obscuration].
If ignorance were established as a single hindrance,
then all the burdensome obstructions of every affliction would collectively fail to equal it.

Therefore, they are not established within the category of the *nīvaraṇas* (hindrances). Question: If that which is not the most predominant is nonetheless established as a *nīvaraṇa*, why are the other primary afflictions (*kleśa*) and secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*) not so established?
Answer: It is explained that the meaning of "hindrance" (*nīvaraṇa*) is that which causes the mind to incline toward the lower [realms].
Because they are chronically elevated, they do not constitute hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*).
The nature of a hindrance is dullness,
whereas the nature of a view (*dṛṣṭi*) is sharp and swift.

Although they do not conform to the definition of an *āvaraṇa* (hindrance), they are nonetheless established as such; among the secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*), torpor (*styāna*) and sleep (*middha*) are preeminent in obstructing wisdom (*prajñā*), while restlessness (*auddhatya*) and regret (*kaukṛtya*) are preeminent in obstructing meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
Therefore, they are established separately as hindrances.
The remaining secondary afflictions, the hindrance to concentration,
and the hindrance to wisdom are not established as *nīvaraṇas* because they are not particularly powerful.
If one were to proceed in this manner until reaching fear, restlessness, and remorse...
The Master of the Treatise refutes the explanation of the Sarvāstivādins:

if one were to interpret the meaning of the sūtra in such a manner, restlessness and remorse ought logically to be mentioned before lethargy and sleep; for wisdom arises only by depending upon meditative concentration.

This indicates that the objects to be obstructed are first concentration (*samādhi*) and subsequently wisdom (*prajñā*); for the obstruction to concentration should likewise be preceded by the obstruction to wisdom.
This indicates the sequential order of the obstructions; it is based on this principle.
The Sautrāntikas say:
Among these five hindrances, torpor and drowsiness obstruct meditative concentration (*samādhi*),
because the nature of torpor and drowsiness is one of sinking and depression.
Concentration cannot arise.
Restlessness and remorse obstruct wisdom;
because restlessness and remorse repeatedly cause distraction, wisdom cannot arise. This is why the sutra states that one who cultivates meditative concentration fears lethargy and sleep.
Thus one knows that they obstruct concentration.
One who cultivates the discernment of dharmas knows this because of the fear of restlessness and remorse.
Regarding the obstruction of wisdom,
there is another distinct explanation that establishes only five causes;
this recounts the Sautrāntika interpretation.
Regarding what that statement means:
it is asked,
"It refers to being in the stage of practice until only these five [aggregates] remain."
The Sautrāntika replies: This refers to the stage of practice, specifically at times such as when begging for alms;
first, among various objects such as forms and so forth.
Because one grasps the two types of signs— those that are attractive and those that are repulsive— one subsequently abides in the state of dwelling; that is,
at times such as when staying in a quiet room and so forth,
one does so by means of the previously grasped two signs of attraction and aversion acting as causes.
Toward agreeable objects, sensual desire arises;
toward disagreeable objects, ill will arises.

These two are able to obstruct the mind that is about to enter meditative absorption—that is, the mind immediately preceding absorption. Consequently, at a later time when one is actually entering the state of absorption, [these obstacles must be removed].
That is, even within a concentrated mind,
because one is unable to properly cultivate serenity (*śamatha*) and insight (*vipaśyanā*),
lethargy and sleep arise from this, thereby obstructing concentration.
Restlessness and remorse obstruct wisdom, preventing it from arising.
Even if one has already entered meditative absorption,
because of these two, [wisdom] will not arise in the state subsequent to emerging from concentration.
This refers to the state of the distracted mind (*vikṣipta-citta*).
When one investigates and discerns phenomena (*dharmas*), doubt again acts as an obstacle. [The question arises: Is it a proof or not?
Now, one must investigate by what cause [doubt] persists until its abandonment.
In the following section of this chapter,
the second major heading explains the extinction of delusions. Within this:
First, the clarification of the four causes for severing delusions;
second, the clarification of the four types of remedies;
third, the clarification of the locus where afflictions are severed.
The fourth clarifies the four types of distant nature;
the fifth clarifies the attainment of cessation through the severance of delusions;
the sixth clarifies the nine kinds of thorough knowledge. Below this, first is the question clarifying the four causes for the severance of delusions.
Now, one should reflect upon and discern the suffering and origin [of suffering] in the desire realm,
as well as those [afflictions] that are universal across other realms.
Furthermore, regarding the cessation and the path within the three realms, there are the afflictions that take outflows as their object and are abandoned through the vision of these truths.
At the stage of their abandonment, one does not know those objects [of the afflictions].

That is to say, when the Dharma-knowledge-acceptance (*dharmajñānakṣānti*) arises taking the two truths of suffering and origin in the desire realm as its object, it abandons the afflictions of those two truths.
At the stage of abandoning those universal [defilements] pertaining to other realms, one does not know their objects,
because they take as their objects only the suffering and its origin within the desire realm.
This refers to the arising of the receptivities to the dharma-knowledge of cessation and the path,
which sever the afflictions of the two truths;
specifically, it refers to the stage when the afflictions conditioned by outflows regarding those cessations and paths are severed.
One does not know that those [afflictions] have outflowing objects as their focal point,
because they take only uncontaminated objects as their focal point; yet when one knows their focal point, those [afflictions] are not severed,
namely, when taking the two truths of suffering and origin belonging to the higher realms as their focal point.
When the patience of subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna-kṣānti*) arises and one knows those objects of universal [defilements] belonging to other realms,
those universal [defilements] of other realms are not yet abandoned.
This refers to the time when the patience regarding the dharma-knowledge of suffering and origination arises,
taking as its object the extinction and the path; at that time,
the afflictions associated with outflows that take extinction and the path as their objects are not yet abandoned.
By what cause are these various afflictions abandoned? Furthermore, why is it that they are not abandoned at the time one understands their objects?
For example, when the patience of the subsequent knowledge of suffering (*duḥkhe ’nvayajñānakṣānti*) knows those objects of the universal [afflictions] belonging to other realms.
Furthermore, those universal [defilements] pertaining to other realms remain unsevered.

Those universal [defilements] pertaining to the suffering of the desire realm that have already been severed are designated as "unsevered" [in this context], while those universal [defilements] pertaining to the origin of the desire realm that have not yet been severed are designated as "unsevered."
Just as when one knows those universal objects of the other realms through the acceptance of the subsequent knowledge of suffering (*duḥkhe 'nvayajñānakṣānti*),

those universal [defilements] of the desire realm belonging to other realms are already abandoned and are termed "not abandoned," so too it is when the acceptance of the dharma-knowledge of suffering and origination (*duḥkha-samudaya-dharmajñānakṣānti*) arises.
When one knows that cessation and the path are the objects of those defilements conditioned by outflows,
yet those defilements conditioned by outflows directed toward cessation and the path are not abandoned—
this state of not being abandoned is called "non-abandonment."
Because the objects of the afflictions that take the contaminated as their object are subsumed under Suffering and Origin.

Furthermore, when one understands the objects of the universal [afflictions] of other realms that are abandoned through the vision of Origin within the Desire Realm, at that time, one realizes the patience of the subsequent knowledge of suffering (*duḥkhe ’nvayajñānakṣānti*).
Furthermore, it distinguishes those universal [defilements] of other realms belonging to the lower [stages] as "not abandoned.
The intended meaning of this explanation is that what has not yet been abandoned is termed "not abandoned."
The remaining explanations are as before.
Regarding the point that it is not necessary to fully comprehend the object of cognition (*ālambana*) for [afflictions] to be abandoned, the answer is as follows:
If that is so, by how many causes in total is the abandonment of afflictions brought about?
Question:
It is by four kinds of causes.
Answer: What are the four? Question:
The verse says: "Because the antidote arises, there is abandonment.
The first three lines clarify the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*);
the final line clarifies the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*).

The Commentary says: Regarding "up to the abandonment of those [afflictions] having uncontaminated objects," first, the abandonment of afflictions abandoned through seeing occurs by means of the first three causes.
First, they are abandoned by means of thoroughly understanding the object (*ālambana*).
This refers to the afflictions of one's own realm that are abandoned through the vision of suffering and its origin,
as well as the afflictions pertaining to the untainted (anāsrava) that are abandoned through the vision of cessation and the path.
Since delusion and awakening are mutually exclusive, such a principle of abandonment is logically necessary.
One should also state that within the two higher realms,
the universal afflictions (sarvatraga-kleśa) that take other realms and levels as their objects are also abandoned by means of thoroughly understanding their objects.
The subsequent-knowledge-forbearance regarding suffering and origination arises;
this is because it can simultaneously contemplate the objects of both realms.
As for the statement in the text that "those [afflictions] which take their own realm as an object are abandoned by the vision of suffering and origination":
Furthermore, according to the explanation that one realm pervades the three realms:

second, "because by abandoning those [defilements], one abandons them accordingly as they reach their respective realms" means that they are abandoned by abandoning those objects which take them as cognitive supports (*ālambana*).
This means that the afflictions of other realms which are to be abandoned through the vision of suffering and the vision of origin are the objects of focus.
This is because the afflictions of one's own realm that take those [afflictions] of other realms as their objects can perceive them;
when those perceiving [afflictions] are abandoned, the afflictions that serve as their objects are also abandoned accordingly.
Although the conditions differ, they are nonetheless capable of acting as causes;
therefore, the conditions of one's own realm possess power relative to those [of another],
and because the afflictions of other realms rely upon this power, they are able to take the higher realms as their objects.
It is like a weak and sick person leaning against a pillar and looking up;
when the pillar breaks, he falls down along with it.
Third, because by severing that [basis], that [which depends upon it] is severed accordingly.
Third, they are abandoned by abandoning their objects;
that is to say, the defilements with outflow (*sāsrava*) that have outflowing objects are abandoned through the vision of cessation and the path,
because the defilements with no outflow (*anāsrava*) can serve as the objects for those defilements with outflow.
When the afflictions that take uncontaminated objects as their focus are abandoned,
the afflictions that take contaminated objects as their focus are also abandoned accordingly;
it is like a weak and sickly person who cannot walk without a staff.
Because when the staff breaks, it also falls down accordingly.
If the afflictions to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) reach the point where they are all severed at once, this clarifies the abandonment of the afflictions of cultivation.
Regarding which afflictions of which category are countered by what:
this is the question.
It refers to those from the highest-of-the-high grade up to what will be explained in detail later.
Answer: The object to be remedied and the remedy.
Each has nine grades, corresponding to the forward and reverse orders;
these shall be explained in detail later. Furthermore, the *Nyāyānusāra* states:
"Is it not the case that when all afflictions abandoned through insight (*darśana-heya*) are severed..."
This also occurs through the arising of the path of antidotes;
for when the path of antidotes for a particular category arises,
all the afflictions within that category are abandoned.
In truth, this is indeed so.
However, within this context, these words are spoken to demonstrate that among the afflictions abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) in the three realms,
there are none that are not definitively abandoned by the antidotes of the nine grades of the path.
Among those [defilements] abandoned through seeing, only the antidote for the defilements of the Peak of Existence (bhavāgra) is fixed,
as has already been explained previously; alternatively, when the various defilements abandoned through seeing are being severed,
they are treated separately because their preparatory means are necessarily threefold.
The means for abandoning the afflictions to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) are not fixed;

therefore, the above treatise speaks of them in general terms. Question: How can the principle of the Four Noble Truths (*catur-ārya-satya*), which takes as its object the truths themselves, abandon the afflictions of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*) that consist of concrete phenomena (*vastu*)? This is called "abandonment by means of the antidote" (*pratipakṣa-prahāṇa*). Answer: It is because the [afflictions of] concrete phenomena are coarse.
The principle is subtle, and the object of focus is subtle; thus, the coarse can be severed.
Therefore, the nine grades of the Path sever the nine grades of afflictions.
Regarding the statement "the remedies consist of abandonment, maintenance, distancing, and revulsion," this clarifies the second point: the four types of remedies.
The treatise states: "...until one develops a profound sense of revulsion."
1. The antidote of abandonment (*prahāṇa-pratipakṣa*), which refers to the path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*);
for this path is precisely capable of abandoning those afflictions. 2. The antidote of maintenance (*ādhāra-pratipakṣa*).
This refers to the path of liberation immediately following that [path of abandonment],
because that path of liberation is able to maintain the acquisition of that abandonment. Third is the counteractive remedy of distance (*dūrabhāga-pratipakṣa*),
which refers to all superior paths (*viśeṣamārga*) subsequent to the path of liberation.

Because that path of superior progress (viśeṣamārga) causes the defilements abandoned by this path of uninterrupted transition (ānantaryamārga) to become further removed, it is called the counteractive of distancing (dūrabhāga-pratipakṣa). Other masters say:
The distant-remedy (*dūrabhāga-pratipakṣa*) is also the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*),
because the path of liberation, like that [path of special progress],
causes the afflictions abandoned by the immediate path to become even more remote. Fourth is the remedy of revulsion (*vidūṣaṇā-pratipakṣa*).
That is to say, if there is a path that perceives the faults of this realm and gives rise to profound wearying revulsion toward it,
it is for the most part called the path of preparation (*prayoga-mārga*).
However, this counteractive path continues until the arising of the path of advancement (*viśeṣa-mārga*).
The Master of the Treatise explains:
However, if one wishes to explain this antidote well,
the logical sequence should actually be as follows.
1. The antidote of revulsion (*vidūṣaṇa-pratipakṣa*), which refers to the path of preparation (*prayoga-mārga*) arising with suffering (*duḥkha*) and origination (*samudaya*) as its objects. 2.

The antidote of abandonment (*prahāṇa-pratipakṣa*), which refers to the uninterrupted path (*ānantarya-mārga*) arising with all four truths (*catuḥ-satya*) as its objects. 3. The sustaining antidote (*ādhāra-pratipakṣa*).
This refers to the path of liberation arising in relation to all four truths; it is the antidote through remoteness.
This refers to the path of excellence arising in relation to all four truths; although its sequence differs from the preceding one.
Explanation of the Four Similarities: The four factors—disenchantment (*nirveda*) and so forth—clarified above each reside in a single path.
This is discussed according to the manifest [function] in terms of severing the specific category [of defilements].
If one were to further explain the four factors of disenchantment and so forth in relation to the four paths, their commonality and exclusivity would be as follows.
First, the antidote of revulsion applies to all four paths;
when the treatise speaks of "preparatory effort," it does so from a general perspective.
Therefore, the *Nyāyabindu-ṭīkā* (or *Tarkaśāstra*), in its explanation of the antidote of revulsion (*vidūṣaṇā-pratipakṣa*), states:
"It should be understood that for the most part [this refers to] the path of preparation (*prayoga-mārga*). It further states:
"The phrase 'for the most part' is used..."

It should be understood that this is stated in order to reveal that within the paths of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*), liberation (*vimukti-mārga*), and special progress (*viśeṣa-mārga*), those which take the truths of suffering and its origin as their objects also function as the antidote of revulsion (*vidūṣaṇa-pratipakṣa*). [The above is the treatise. Second, the antidote of abandonment (*prahāṇa-pratipakṣa*).
Only the path of uninterrupted transition (ānantarya-mārga) does not apply to the other three; it is the antidote that holds [the abandonment].
If one speaks according to the manifest correspondence of the respective categories, it refers only to the path of liberation (vimukti-mārga);
however, if one speaks according to the various categories abandoned prior and subsequent [to it], [it applies to all].
The combined discussion of the hidden and the manifest applies to all four paths,
because they are all capable of maintaining that attainment of abandonment (*prahāṇa-prāpti*). As for the antidote of remoteness (*dūrabhāga-pratipakṣa*),
if one bases it on the manifest aspect, it refers exclusively to the path of special progress (*viśeṣamārga*).
If one considers the various categories of afflictions abandoned throughout the preceding and succeeding stages,
and discusses them by combining those that are obscured and manifest, they likewise pertain to all four paths;
for in each case, they are able to cause the afflictions to be abandoned to become further removed.
If one follows the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, it further explains "the antidote of abandonment" (*prahāṇa-pratipakṣa*):
whichever path among the various realms of existence is capable of abandoning a particular phenomenon,
as appropriate to each case, that is called the antidote of abandonment.
Regarding the question of from what [level] the permanent abandonment of all afflictions (*kleśa*) definitely arises:
this is the third section below, which clarifies the stage for the abandonment of afflictions. It asks:
from what [level] does the ultimate and permanent abandonment of all afflictions definitively occur?
The verse says: "Because they will not arise again.
The answer is:
one should know that this refers to the time when the acquisitions (*prāpti*) of all afflictions (*kleśa*) have been permanently severed to their ultimate extent.
One must not allow them to be separated from their associated states (*saṃprayukta-dharma*).
That is to say, although the increase (*anuśaya*) within the associated states has been severed, the nature of being an associate (*sahāya-bhāva*) is not severed;
therefore, they are still said to be "possessing latent dispositions" (*sānuśaya*).
Because of this proximity, it is not called "permanently severed"; rather,
one can only cause that [defilement] to distance itself from its object,
so that it no longer arises with respect to that object.
This means that regarding the object of focus, because one has severed that which increases in accordance with it, it is not called "possessing an increasing latent tendency" (*anuśaya*).
Because it is remote, it is termed "permanently severed.
This statement of permanent severance refers to [the state] where latent tendencies still exist.
Therefore, the *Mahāvibhāṣā* (Vol. 22) states:

"In this context, it is taught that the various latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) are to be abandoned with respect to their objects (*ālambana*), but not with respect to their associated factors (*saṃprayukta*)."

The statement that "based on the basis, there is the sense of being possessed by latent dispositions" (anuśaya) is spoken with reference to the meaning of the "basis," not with reference to the meaning of "increasing along with" (anuśerate). This is because,
according to the meaning of "increasing along with," both [the defilements and the basis] would be subject to abandonment.
Regarding the question, "To what does the abandonment of future afflictions ultimately lead?"— this is an objection.
It may indeed be logically acceptable that the abandonment of future afflictions occurs in this manner.
It is said that [defilements] are "abandoned" because they are rendered incapable of arising again with respect to their objects.
However, past defilements are phenomena that have already arisen;
since it is impossible to prevent them from having already arisen, how can they be said to be abandoned?
If it is argued that the verse’s mention of "from the object-condition" (ālambana) intends to show that [afflictions] are abandoned because their objects are fully known,
rather than being called "abandoned" because they no longer arise with respect to those objects;
To claim that the mere knowledge of the objects of the various afflictions constitutes their abandonment is also unreasonable,
because it is not definitive;
for one must abandon suffering, its origin, and those [afflictions] that are universal across other realms.
And when [the path] ceases, the afflictions that take outflows as their object are severed.
This is not because they are severed by means of fully knowing the objects of cognition.
Having finished the difficult question, he asks:
Based on this, it should be explained from what the abandonment of afflictions and so forth definitively proceeds.
Regarding the phrase "because they reach ultimate abandonment within one's own continuum," the Master of the Treatise provides another explanation.
Now, the abandonment of tainted phenomena (sāsrava-dharma) consists of two types: first, abandonment by way of intrinsic nature;
second, abandonment by way of the severance of objective fetters.
If the afflictions and so forth within one's own continuum are severed,
then because they have been attained as severed,
the self-substance is no longer established; this is what is called "severance."
This refers to abandonment by way of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
As for the various afflictions within the bodies of other continuities (*saṃtati*),
as well as all material forms (*rūpa*) and all non-defiled phenomena (*akliṣṭadharma*), their abandonment is [to be understood differently].
Because all afflictions within one's own continuum that take those [objects] as their objective support have been ultimately severed up to the ninth grade, it is said to be "severed.
This is based on the severance of the bondage of objective support.
Regarding the question, "How many kinds of remoteness (dūratā) are there?"—this section below is the fourth, which clarifies the four types of remoteness. Question:
As previously stated, there is the remedy for remoteness (dūrabhāga-pratipakṣa).
Generally speaking, how many kinds of remoteness are there in total?
The verse says: "That which is reached is also called remote. Answer:
Because it is separated from the present, the past and future are called "distant.
The rest of the text may be understood accordingly.
With reference to what is it said that they are distant?
The Master of the Treatise asks:
"Regarding those who look toward the present world," the Sarvāstivādins answer.
The two periods of past and future are called "distant" because they are separated from the present;
by implication, one should understand that the present is called "near.
Thus, the *Prakaraṇapāda* (Treatise on Categories), chapter six, states:
What are distant phenomena?
Past and future phenomena. What are proximate phenomena? Present phenomena.
This refers to present phenomena and unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*).
The author of the treatise raises an objection: how can that which has just ceased in the immediate past be called "distant"?
In the past, [dharmas] have already ceased without interval;
in the future, they are currently in the state of arising.
How can they be called "distant" when they are adjacent to the present?
Regarding the statement that things are designated as "distant" because their temporal natures differ from the present:
the Sarvāstivādins reply that they receive the designation "distant" because past and future [dharmas] differ in their temporal nature from the present.
Only that which has ceased not long ago or will arise not long hence receives the designation "distant."
If that is so, and the present is designated as "distant" [from the past], then the Master further objects:
the nature of the present relative to the past and future is also distinct; it too should be called "distant.
If you claim that past and future phenomena lack functional activity (*kāritra*), [then the same applies to the present].
If that which is called "distant" is so because it lacks functional activity,
then since all unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*) likewise lack functional activity,
how can they be called "near"?
If it is claimed that one can attain these [cessations] by means of the present time,

then it would follow that the unconditioned state of cessation through deliberation (pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha) would exist universally upon all contaminated phenomena (sāsrava-dharma), and the unconditioned state of non-deliberative cessation (apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha) would exist universally upon all conditioned phenomena (saṃskṛta-dharma).
Therefore, it is said that the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta) is called "near.
The same principle should apply to the two periods of the past and the future;
for one also gives rise to the acquisition (prāpti) in the present moment and thereby acquires those dharmas of the past and the future.
The two periods of past and future should also be called "near.
The two types of cessation (nirodha) can be called "near" because they are currently attainable;
however, since unconditioned space lacks any attainment, it cannot be so designated.
How are they called "near"? According to the Sarvāstivāda school,
all three unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛtadharma*) are called "near," because the two types of cessation (*nirodha*) possess acquisition (*prāpti*).
Since space is unattainable,
this objection is raised.
Thus, the *Nyāyānusāra* states:
Furthermore, because the essence of space pervades all places and its characteristics are unimpeded, it is said to be "near.
The essence of non-analytical cessation does not depend on effort.
Because it can be attained with respect to all entities, in all places, and at all times,
it is called "proximate. This refers to the unconditioned state of analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
When those who possess diligence and practice correctly sever all afflictions, they do so without distinction across all entities because of their swift realization;
therefore, it is called "proximate. The explanation is that whatever phenomena occupy space are termed "proximate."
Non-analytical cessation is called "near" because it is easily attained;
analytical cessation is called "near" because it is swiftly attained. If one were to claim that the past and the future are mutually near to one another...
Because it is separated by the present, it is called "distant";
however, in relation to the two periods of the past and the future, both are extremely proximate as there is no interval between them.
Furthermore, because the three unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*) likewise lack any interval, they are all considered "near."
Thus, the past and future should be called "near" because they are adjacent to the present world;
yet they are called "far" because there is a separation between them.
Therefore, they possess both names.
"One should not categorically state that it is called 'distant' [only].

If, according to correct reasoning, it reaches the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of the dharmas of correct reasoning," here the Master of the Treatise (*śāstrakāra*) sets forth the Sautrāntika explanation of the characteristics of distance.
The past and future, being without intrinsic substance (*svabhāva*), are called "distant.
By this, it is understood that the present, possessing intrinsic substance, is called "near.
The word "etc. (*ādi*) is used to indicate that the examples cited are not exhaustive.
Regarding the explanation of the word "and so forth" (ādi) in the verse:
although the primary elements (mahābhūta) are mentioned among the distant characteristics,
the derived matter (upādāyarūpa) and so on have not yet been discussed.
Regarding distance in terms of practice, although observing the precepts and violating the precepts,
as well as the wholesome and unwholesome, have been mentioned, they have not yet been fully explained.
Regarding distance in terms of location, although the eastern sea and the western sea have been mentioned...
Because the Southern and Northern oceans and so forth have not yet been mentioned, the word "etc.
(*ādi*) is used to indicate that although one type of distant time has been fully cited,
it is stated as such by way of representing the majority of cases.
Regarding the preliminary statement on the six periods from the severance of delusions up to the refinement of the faculties (*indriya-parāvṛtti*):
