The explanation says: "By this very reason, it is proven that one does not practice. Furthermore, another explanation states: "One who attains the 'Supreme Mundane Dharma' (laukikāgradharma) will certainly not be a woman."
Therefore, one does not cultivate the female [nature].
Regarding the first three [faculties], there is the possibility of them having the sense of being male or female;
even non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) would likewise mutually cultivate them.
Furthermore, the *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra*, fascicle 61, states:
"These four roots of goodness depend exclusively upon males and females.
Of these four, the first three are both obtained by males and females."
The female body also attains two kinds [of roots].
This is so that one does not later attain the male body and fail to achieve *ūṣmagata* and the other stages.
Based on the male body, one attains only the wholesome roots of the male body.
Because a noble one does not become a woman again in subsequent lives,
it is possible for those in the stages of Heat, Summits, and Patience to undergo a change of gender;
therefore, these two bases serve as successive causes for the roots of goodness.
The Supreme Mundane Dharmas (*laukikāgradharma*) based on a female body can serve as two causes,
because once a woman has attained the state of an Arya, there is the possibility that she may subsequently undergo a transformation to obtain a male body.
Those based on a male body serve as only one cause.
Because one has already attained the non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) of the female body; furthermore, the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle seven, states:
"Question: Upon what kind of body do these stages of Heat (*uṣmagata*), Summits (*mūrdhan*), Patience (*kṣānti*), and the Supreme Mundane Dharmas (*laukikāgradharma*) arise?"
Answer: It depends on whether one possesses a male or female body.
Question: Based on a female body, one attains the "heat" (*uṣmagata*) arising from a female body;
does one also attain the "heat" arising from a male body?
Answer: Yes, it is attained.
As with the attainment of *ūṣmagata* (Heat), so it is for *mūrdhan* (Summit) and *kṣānti* (Patience).
Question: Is the *ūṣmagata* that arises from a male body attained by depending on a male body?
Is it also attained by one who has taken birth in a female body?
Answer: It is attained.
Just as it is attained in the stage of Heat (ūṣmagata), so too is it attained in the stages of Peak (mūrdhan) and Patience (kṣānti).
The warmth that arises in a female body with respect to a female body is also obtained;
it is both present in the body and accomplished,
and it is also manifested.
The heat produced in relation to a male body is attained,
yet it does not abide in the body;
it is accomplished [therein].
It does not manifest before one.
As it is said for "Heat" (ūṣmagata), so it is for "Summit" (mūrdhan) and "Patience" (kṣānti).
One may also attain Heat arising within a male body from the perspective of a male body.
It exists in the body, it is accomplished,
and it is present before one;
it is the attainment of "heat" (ūṣmagata) arising in relation to a female body.
Yet they are not accomplished within the body,
nor do they manifest before one.
As it is said regarding "Heat" (uṣmagata) and "Summit" (mūrdhan), so it is for "Patience" (kṣānti) as well.
The heat produced by a female body serves as the cause for the heat produced by a female body;
it also serves as the cause for the heat produced by a male body.
As it is said regarding heat, so it is for patience (*kṣānti*).
The heat generated by a male body serves as the cause for the heat generated by a male body;
it does not serve as the cause for the heat generated by a female body. Why is this so?
The superior is not the cause of the inferior, because that [inferior] is inferior.

As it is said regarding "Heat" (ūṣmagata) and "Summits" (mūrdhan), so it is for "Patience" (kṣānti). The commentary explains: according to the *Abhidharmakośa*, the first three [levels] are acquired mutually by both men and women.
Regarding the fourth root of goodness, two types are attained based on a female body,
while only one is attained based on a male body;
it is not said to be a cause.
The *Nyāyānusāra* states that the phrasing is the same as in the *Abhidharmakośa*.
Among the four types, the first three—males and females—are mutually causes for one another;
the fourth, the female, serves as two kinds of causes.
A male is not the cause of a female.
According to the first three sections of the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, males and females mutually obtain [the cause].
A female is the cause of a male.
A male is not the cause of a female;
it is not said that the fourth [condition] is obtained as a causal characteristic.
The *Purāṇa-vibhāṣā* states:
The statement that "a man does not obtain the wholesome roots such as the warmth (*uṣmagata*) of a woman" is merely an error of the translators;
the *Abhidharmakośa* does not state that [the gender] acts as a cause.
The *Mahāvibhāṣā* does not state that the fourth root of goodness is obtained through the characteristic of being the cause;
it omits this because it follows the interpretation of other treatises. Question: Since the *Nyāyānusāra* and the *Mahāvibhāṣā* state different views on this matter...

Regarding the interpretation: it is explained that the *Nyāyānusāra* and the *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* differ in their underlying intent. The *Nyāyānusāra* relies on the principle of a single path (*ekamārga*).
According to this, although the three roots of goodness depend upon the physical body, they remain the same regardless of whether one is male or female.
Some may change from male to female,
while others may change from female to male; however,
regarding the stages such as "heat" (*uṣmagata*) and so forth, they are distinguished as male or female solely based on the difference of the physical body upon which they depend.
Just as a single body of precepts, during the stage of changing gender,
may pertain to both a bhikṣu and a bhikṣuṇī;
because their physical forms differ, these are spoken of as two distinct sets of precepts.
It may be said that both bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs obtain two types of precepts;

one should know that the same applies to the first three wholesome roots. Regarding their being causes: the first three wholesome roots serve as homogeneous causes (*sabhāga-hetu*) for one another among males and females.
The fourth root of goodness can become male;
therefore, the female obtains two [roots] and serves as the cause for those two.
A man does not [attain it] for the sake of a woman; thus, a man attains it only when alone as the cause.

According to the *Vibhāṣā*, this is based on the meaning of "many paths," meaning that there are many types of *uṣmagata* (heat) and so forth that depend on distinct bodies. Regarding "attainment," the first three [stages] are attained by both men and women, who each attain two types.
One [root] is both acquired, present in the body, accomplished, and active;
one is acquired but not present in the body, accomplished, and inactive—therefore, they are known to be distinct.
Regarding the fourth root of goodness, because a woman may become a man, she acquires the male [roots].
Because a male cannot become a female, a male does not obtain a female [as a cause].
Regarding the statement that [the female body] acts as a cause: it serves as the cause for two [results] because the roots of goodness within the female body are inferior;

it serves as the cause for only one [result] because the roots of goodness within the male body are superior. Although the preceding discussion has treated both the single path and the multiple paths.

Many paths represent the position of the *Vibhāṣā* commentators (*vibhāṣā-vādin*), while one path represents what is not the correct meaning of the *Vibhāṣā*. Furthermore, it is explained that both the *Nyāyānusāra* and the *Vibhāṣā* rely upon the meaning of many paths.
The *Abhidharmamahāvibhāṣā* explains the superiority or inferiority of the path based on the superiority or inferiority of its support (*āśraya*).

As for why it is superior rather than inferior, this is the intention of the *Nyāyānusāra*: although the supports of males and females differ in superiority or inferiority, [the path remains superior].
Furthermore, the paths that depend [upon them] can serve as causes for one another in succession.
For example, although there are distinctions of superiority and inferiority among the bases— the noble paths of the nine stages—
those paths which depend upon them can still serve as causes for one another in succession.
Whether following the *Abhidharmakośa*,
the *Nyāyānusāra*, or the *Mahāvibhāṣā*,
there is no contradiction in any case. Furthermore, [the text] explains the four kinds of roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*).
Males and females are distinct bodies, yet they both cultivate [the roots] in mutual relation and serve as causes for one another.
When the various treatises state that only the first three wholesome roots are obtained mutually by males and females,
it is because once these first three have been obtained, one may subsequently become either male or female.
This is why it is stated separately.
Because one who attains the "supreme mundane dharma" (laukikāgradharma) will certainly not be female, it is said that they do not [attain it as a woman].
However, speaking according to the actual principle:
Although the female body of the future has attained non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*),
it can still serve as the basis for the cultivation of that first [root of goodness].
The *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* states that the three preceding roots of goodness serve as causes for two [subsequent ones] in women.
This is the sole cause for a male.
This has been explained based on a single characteristic;
however, to speak according to reality:
The male also serves as a cause for the female,
because there are distinctions of inferior, middling, and superior grades;
otherwise, how could it be that the warmth and other factors of a male body are of an inferior grade?
The superior grade [of wholesome roots] on a woman's body does not serve as the cause for a man;
however, the fourth wholesome root serves as a mutual cause for both men and women.

The explanation for why this is so is as previously stated in the *Prāpti* [chapter]. Furthermore, another interpretation holds that the *Nyāya* (Correct Principle) refers to those who currently manifest a change of gender when it speaks of "men" and "women."
The *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* bases its explanation on the distinction between male and female within a single lifetime;
therefore, there is a difference [in their attainment].
As for the noble ones, from this stage upward, even ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) do not undergo retrogression.
This explains the seventh, eighth, and ninth phrases.
There are three general types of relinquishing all roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*):
first, relinquishment through loss of the stage (*bhūmi*).
Second, they are abandoned at the end of life;
third, they are abandoned through regression.
The noble ones attain these roots of goodness by relying on this stage.
When one loses this stage, the roots of goodness are then relinquished.
The term "losing the stage" indicates that at the end of life in a lower stage, one transmigrates and is reborn in a higher stage.
This applies whether an ordinary person (pṛthagjana) has lost the stage or not.
However, at the time of death, when one loses the homogeneous class (*nikāyasabhāga*), these roots of goodness must necessarily be relinquished;
therefore, the *Nyāyānusāra* states:
"Because the body of an Noble One is sustained by the power of the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*)."
These four roots of goodness are not abandoned through death.
How is it known that abandonment through death applies only to ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) and not to noble ones (*ārya*)?
Because the *Mūlaśāstra* states that an ordinary being within an egg or a womb possesses only the body (*kāya*), but does not possess bodily action (*kāyakarman*).

Is it not the case that ordinary beings, having previously relied on a lower stage to give rise to the "heat" (ūṣmagata) and other factors, must necessarily abandon those roots of goodness such as "heat" when later born into a higher stage?
There is no such fault.
Because that ordinary person at that time abandons the roots of goodness due to the abandonment of their homogeneous class (*nikāyasabhāga*). That is to say,
while abiding in the state of death-existence (*cyuty-bhava*), lacking the support of the Noble Path, they abandon all roots of goodness.
It is not by means of the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) of a higher realm.
If noble ones (*ārya*), while abiding in the intermediate state at death, sustain themselves through the Noble Path and do not abandon "heat" (*uṣman*) and the other factors,
they nevertheless abandon the roots of goodness of the lower realms solely by means of the arising of the intermediate state of a higher realm.
Although the timing of their abandonment is the same, the causes differ.
Therefore, ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) do not abandon [the roots] by losing their stage (*bhūmi*).

Noble ones (*ārya*), however, certainly never abandon them by the end of their life. Thus, according to the first two sections of the treatise, the two wholesome roots are abandoned not only by losing the stage or at the end of life, but also by falling away (*parihāṇi*).
Abandonment through death or falling away occurs only for ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*), not for noble ones (*ārya*).
Abandonment through losing a stage occurs only for noble ones, not for ordinary persons.
Furthermore, there is no falling away from the level of acceptance (*kṣānti*) or the highest worldly dharma (*laukikāgradharma*), even for ordinary persons.
"Because at the end of life, one loses the stage and must relinquish it accordingly" explains the tenth phrase.
"Because it relies on the fundamental stage and reaches the utmost intensity" explains the [eleventh] phrase.
Based on the four roots of goodness, such as "heat" (*uṣmagata*) and so forth, one must complete three lifetimes;
in that [third] lifetime, one will certainly attain the vision of the truths (*satyadarśana*),
because the mind of revulsion toward birth and death is extremely intense.
If one relies on the *anāgamya* (preliminary) or the *dhyānāntara* (intermediate), the aversion is not intense;
thus, one may either enter [the attainment] or not enter it.
Furthermore, the *Abhidharmamahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle six, states:
Regarding those who give rise to the stages of Heat (*uṣmagata*) and so forth based on the fundamental stage (*maulabhūmi*):
they will necessarily enter the state of rightness and departure from birth (*samyaktva-niyāma*) in their present body. Why is this?
Because they are induced by the Noble Path,
those who give rise to "Heat" and the other stages based on the *anāgamya* concentration or the intermediate dhyāna do so through the guidance of that path.
This, however, is not fixed.

Why is this so? Because they are led to the Noble Path by means of "Heat" (*uṣmagata*) and the other stages, it is explained that the Noble Path—which is the fundamental path of bliss—is easily aroused.
Because it can induce "heat" (*uṣmagata*) and the other stages, one currently enters the state of a noble one (*ārya*).
The preliminary (*anāgamya*) and intermediate (*dhyānāntara*) concentrations are difficult paths for the arising of the noble path,
because they are induced by "heat" and the others.
One does not enter [the path] based on those stages or persons.
Furthermore, the *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra*, fascicle 61, states:
"The roots of goodness such as *ūṣmagata* arise based on the fundamental stages (*maulabhūmi*)."
In this life, such a person will certainly attain the vision of the truths (satyadarśana),
because their faculties are sharp and their revulsion toward existence is profound.

However, those who give rise to "Heat" (ūṣmagata) and the other stages based on the *anāgamya* or the *dhyānāntara* concentrations need not necessarily enter the vision of the truths in this very life.
Other masters say:
"For one who gives rise to the stages of Heat (uṣmagata) and so forth based on the fundamental dhyānas,
this birth will certainly lead to the attainment of nirvāṇa."
Because their weariness with existence is profound, the masters of the *Abhidharmakośa* raise this objection:
"Just as there are six types of spiritual lineage (gotra) for those who have attained 'Heat' (*uṣmagata*) and so forth,
it is further stated that 'Heat' and the other stages are accessible across all six levels."
Furthermore, the subsequent text states:
"Based on the separation from defilement, the one who follows by faith (śraddhānusārin) constitutes seventy-three types of persons.
Moreover, among the four paths of practice (pratipad), both those of dull and sharp faculties are common to both the painful and pleasant [paths].
From this, it is known that even those of dull faculties enter the path of vision (darśanamārga) by relying on the fundamental dhyānas.
How can the correct principle state that one necessarily enters the noble state (ārya) by relying on the fundamental dhyānas only because of being of sharp faculties?
This statement contains an error.
If one were to offer a defense by saying that those with sharp faculties are so called because their mind of revulsion is intense and keen, [that would be incorrect].
It is not that being immovable constitutes having sharp faculties;
if one were to offer such a defense, it would be the fallacy of confusing names and characteristics.
Furthermore, the *Nyāyānusāra* states:
If one relies on skipping stages because of being of sharp faculties, the attainment through the refinement of faculties (*indriya-saṃcāra*) is excluded.
For this reason, it is known that the intention of the *Nyāyānusāra* is to state that [the practitioner] relies on the fundamental stage (*maulabhūmi*) and is of sharp faculties.
If one has previously abandoned [the roots] and then returns to cultivate them from the beginning,
this explains the eleventh phrase:
when the roots of goodness such as *uṣmagata* (heat) and so forth are obtained again after having been previously abandoned, that which is thus obtained...
It is certainly not something previously abandoned;
it is like when a person, having first abandoned the prātimokṣa,
later reacquires the precepts and thereby obtains them once again.
It certainly cannot be that which was previously abandoned;
for wholesome states such as "heat" (*uṣmagata*) have never been cultivated since beginningless time,
but must be accomplished through vast and extensive effort.
Because one conceives reverence for what has not yet been attained, one attains what was previously unattained;
because one does not take delight in what has already been attained, one does not cling to what was previously attained;
and because one proceeds toward the Noble Path in pursuit of further advancement.
If one attains another meditative concentration because it was previously cultivated with familiarity—and not by means of great effort—one subsequently reacquires what was previously abandoned.
This occurs when roots of goodness such as *uṣmagata* (heat), which were previously attained and fully cultivated, are lost due to the passage of a lifetime.
When, in a subsequent life, one encounters a Dharma teacher who has attained the stage of penetration and possesses the knowledge of past lives (*pūrvanivāsajñāna*),
and recognizes that one had previously cultivated the "Heat" (*uṣmagata*) and other stages,
the teacher then explains the "Summits" (*mūrdhan*) and so forth to them, whereby they subsequently give rise to the "Summits" and the rest.
If one does not encounter [the conditions for it], one must again cultivate it from the root stage of *ūṣmagata* and so forth,
or cultivate it from the root stage of mindfulness of breathing (*ānāpānasmṛti*) and so forth.
Therefore, the *Vibhāṣā* states:
Question: If one gives rise to the "Summit" (*mūrdhan*) within another lifetime, from what kind of attention (*manasikāra*) does it arise immediately after?
Answer: It is like the attention present at the time of giving rise to "Heat" (*uṣmagata*).

As it is said that from *ūṣmagata* one arises in *mūrdhan*, so too does one arise in *kṣānti* from *mūrdhan*. Question: If this is so, why is it said that *mūrdhan* arises immediately after *ūṣmagata*, and *kṣānti* arises immediately after *mūrdhan*? Answer: Such a statement is made with reference to their arising as a continuous succession within a single continuum (*saṃtāna*).
"However, it is not the case for all [faculties].
Regarding the statement that 'the two types of relinquishment— loss and regression— do not necessarily lead to loss,' this explains the final phrase."
The two types of abandonment—loss (*hāni*) and regression (*parihāṇi*)—have non-possession (*aprāpti*) as their essence, because they consist in the relinquishing of what has been attained.
Regression necessarily involves the arising of faults, because it entails falling away due to the arousal of afflictions; however, loss does not necessarily do so.
"Loss" refers to the end of life or the transition to another stage;
it does not necessarily involve the arising of transgressions.
Because the mind at the time of death can pertain to all three natures,
the *Nyāyānusāra* states:
"Relinquishment through falling away necessarily occurs by reason of giving rise to faults."
Regarding "losing and abandoning," it may occur through advancement in stages;
"losing" refers to transcending a level or simply passing away.
In the case of noble ones, their name and status increase as they progress through the stages;
for ordinary beings, this is not so.
Therefore, it is said with the word "or" that those who attain these roots of goodness reach the first entry into the state of being free from birth.
This is the third clarification of the excellence of the roots of goodness.
The treatise states, "Because one will certainly reach nirvāṇa," which explains the first phrase.
Among the four roots of goodness, if one attains the stage of "Heat" (ūṣmagata),
although there are four faults, there is also one virtue;
this may be understood from the text.
If that is so, how does it differ from the factors conducive to liberation (*mokṣabhāgīya*)?
Question:
If there is no obstruction, since they are identical in reaching the stage of practice (*pratipatti*).

The "first fruit" refers to the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpatti-phala*). Because this is necessarily the first attained among all four fruits of the śramaṇa, it is called the "first fruit.
If, while still in the stage of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*), one has already abandoned six, seven, or eight grades of defilement of the desire realm;
Upon reaching this stage of the path of seeing, it is called the second "candidate for a fruit" (*pratipannaka*),
because one is proceeding toward the second fruit.
The second fruit refers to the fruit of once-returning (*sakṛdāgāmiphala*).
If based on the "leap-over" (vyutkrāntaka) attainment, this is also the first time it is acquired;

however, in the present case, based on the sequential attainment, it is the second [fruit] among those fruits that are fully attained. This applies to one who, while still at the level of an ordinary person (pṛthagjana), has already abandoned the ninth grade of defilement of the desire realm.
Alternatively, having already abandoned one grade of the first dhyāna,
up to being fully detached from the ninth grade of defilement of the sphere of nothingness,
one is designated as the third candidate upon reaching this stage of seeing (*darśana-mārga*).
Because one is proceeding toward the third fruit.
The third fruit refers to the fruit of non-returning (*anāgāmiphala*).
The enumeration follows the same pattern as the preceding explanation of the fruit of once-returning (*sakṛdāgāmiphala*).
If based on the "leap-over" (vyutkrāntaka) attainment, this is also the first time it is acquired;
however, here we base ourselves on the sequential attainment, as this is the third fruit among those obtained in succession.
In total, there are seventy-three for each of the two types of persons who rely on faith (śraddhānusārin) and those who follow the Dharma (dharmānusārin).
Therefore, the *Nyāyānusāra* (Treatise on Right Reasoning), fascicle 64, states:
"In this way, for those who follow by faith (*śraddhānusārin*) and those who follow by dharma (*dharmānusārin*),
there are distinctions based on whether they were previously bound by all fetters (*sakalabandhana*) or had already abandoned some defilements (*kleśa*)."
These categories are each divided into seventy-three types.
That is to say, beginning with those who are fully bound in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) as the first,
up to those who have abandoned the nine grades [of afflictions] as the tenth.
In this manner, up to the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*),

there are nine for each stage, totaling seventy-three. Those who remain bound by all fetters in the subsequent stages are precisely those who have previously abandoned the nine [categories of afflictions].
Therefore, in the subsequent seven stages, there is no distinct state of being bound by all fetters;
according to this treatise and others, those of dull faculties are likewise able to realize the fruit of transcendence.
Next, regarding the reliance on the path of cultivation, it is also distinguished by the difference between dull and sharp faculties.
This is the second [point], established based on the sixteenth moment of mind.
Within this, first is the establishment of the distinctions among fruits.
Second, the explanation that one who abides in the fruit is not a candidate [for further attainment]. This constitutes the first establishment of the distinctions among the fruits.
The treatise states: "Because one has reached the separation from the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*).
This explains the two preceding lines.

The preceding faith-follower (*śraddhānusārin*) and dharma-follower (*dharmānusārin*) up to the stage of the subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārgānvayajñāna*) are called "fruits" (*phala*), not "candidates" (*pratipannaka*).
Accordingly, of the seventy-three types of persons previously mentioned, those in the three stages of candidacy now abide in the three fruits.
That is to say, the six types of persons previously in the candidate stage for stream-entry (*srotāpatti-pratipannaka*) now abide in the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpanna-phala*).
The first three individuals, who were previously candidates for the fruit of once-returning (*sakṛdāgāmipratipannaka*), now abide in the fruit of once-returning (*sakṛdāgāmiphala*).

The previous sixty-four individuals, who were candidates for the fruit of non-returning (*anāgāmipratipannaka*), now abide in the fruit of non-returning (*anāgāmiphala*). Regarding the fruit of arhatship (*arhattvaphala*), it is necessarily never attained for the first time among these four fruits.
Why is this? Because the path of seeing (darśanamārga) does not admit of the abandonment of the afflictions to be abandoned by cultivation (bhāvanā-heya).
Furthermore, while formerly in the stage of an ordinary person (pṛthagjana), the mundane path (laukikamārga) did not admit of the transcendence of the Peak of Existence (bhavāgra).
Therefore, the fourth [fruit] is necessarily not first attained.
Regarding the distinction between the names "one who abides in the fruit" (*phalastha*) and "one who has attained vision" (*dṛṣṭiprāpta*),
this explains the two subsequent phrases.

Upon reaching the stage of abiding in the fruit, one abandons the two names "faith-follower" (*śraddhānusārin*) and "dharma-follower" (*dharmānusārin*), and acquires the two names "faith-understanding" (*śraddhādhimukta*) and "vision-attainer" (*dṛṣṭiprāpta*).
Regarding these, "faith" (*śraddhā*) refers to pure faith; "understanding" (*adhimukti*) refers to resolute conviction (*adhimokṣa*).
Because it is manifested through the predominance of faith and the excellence of resolute conviction (adhimukti), it is called "faith-understanding" (śraddhādhimukta).
Thus, the *Nyāyānusāra* states:
Because their resolute conviction (*adhimokṣa*) is manifested through the predominant power of faith, they are called "attained through vision" (*dṛṣṭiprāpta*).
Because their right view (*samyagdṛṣṭi*) is manifested through the predominant power of wisdom (*prajñā*), they are named "attained through vision.
Thus, the *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya* (Treatise on Correct Principles) states:
Because right view is manifested through the predominant power of wisdom, it is so called. As for the term "attainment" (prāpta):
because one has previously directed oneself toward vision and thereby attained the vision of the fruit, it is called "vision-attainment" (dṛṣṭiprāpta).
Therefore, the *Vibhāṣā* (53) states:

"That is to say, based on the faith subsumed under the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), one attains the faith and resolve (*adhimukti*) subsumed under the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*). It further states:
"Attaining the fruit by relying on inclination and faith is called 'resolute through faith' (śraddhādhimukta).
Furthermore, it is said that because the mind is liberated from the three fetters preceded by faith, it is named 'resolute through faith.
This refers to the vision comprised within the path of seeing."
One attains the vision subsumed under the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*). Furthermore, it is said:

based on the vision subsumed under the path of approach (*prayogamārga*), one attains the vision subsumed under the path of fruition (*phalamārga*). It is also said: [one attains the vision subsumed under the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*)].
Because one’s mind is liberated from the three fetters preceded by [the attainment of] vision, one is called "attained through vision" (*dṛṣṭiprāpta*).
For what reason is one who has previously abandoned [the defilements] called "abiding in the fruit" rather than "heading toward it"?
This is the second [section], clarifying that one abides in the fruit and does not head toward it. [The section on] the five [types of noble persons], etc.
The phrase "and so forth" includes the abandonment of the six categories [of afflictions] and so on, up to the ninth category of the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*).
The term "fruit and so forth" includes the fruits of the once-returner (*sakṛdāgāmin*) and the non-returner (*anāgāmin*).
Question: For what reason, when one in the stage of an ordinary person has previously abandoned from one up to five categories of the afflictions of the desire realm to be abandoned by cultivation,
and reaches the sixteenth moment of mind— the *mārgānvayajñāna*—
is it said that one abides in the first three fruits but not in the [first] three paths?
This constitutes the question and the response in verse.

The treatise states: "Up until one is not yet designated as 'progressing toward the subsequent [fruit]'" refers to the time when, upon reaching the Knowledge of the Path of Similarity (*mārgānvaya-jñāna*), one attains the three fruits.
Since one has certainly not yet attained the path of superior fruit,
those who abide in the three fruits but have not yet given rise to the superior path are merely designated as "abiding in the three fruits."
They are not designated as the three subsequent candidates (*pratipannaka*).
Thus, the *Nyāyānusāra* states:
"The eight noble ones (*ārya*) are established based on the attainment of the Noble Path."
As previously stated,
at the time one attains a fruit, one has necessarily not yet attained the path of the superior fruit;
for the mind that attains the fruit is not an antidote to the afflictions that are to be countered by the path of the superior fruit.
It is not the case that when the antidote to those [defilements] is present, one attains the path that serves as their antidote,
as has already been stated previously.
Furthermore, it is not at the very moment of attaining the fruit that the acquisition of dissociation from the defilements abandoned by the superior path arises.
Because the patience regarding the subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārgānvayakṣānti*) cannot sever the acquisition of those fetters (*bandhana-prāpti*).
If the power of the path is able to sever that acquisition of fetters,
then this path brings about the arising of the acquisition of disjunction (*visamyoga-prāpti*) from them.
It can be said that this path is able to realize that cessation;
for when one has attained a prior fruit, one has not yet attained the path to a superior fruit.
Therefore, as long as one who abides in a fruit has not yet given rise to the path to a superior fruit, [they remain in that state].
Although one has previously abandoned the first grade or other grades of those afflictions to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*),
such a person is called one who "abides in the fruit" and not one who "proceeds toward the subsequent [fruit].
At what later time does one obtain the untainted acquisition (*anāsrava-prāpti*) of disconnection (*visamyoga*) from those previously abandoned afflictions of cultivation?

This concludes the preceding scholastic treatise regarding the manifestation of the path of superior fruit. Now, concerning those who have previously abandoned [defilements] up to the point where they achieve the faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*) through meditative concentration:
this refers to those who have previously abandoned from one to five levels of the afflictions to be abandoned through cultivation in the desire realm.
Upon reaching the time of attaining the fruit, one will certainly give rise to the path of superior fruit (*viśeṣamārga*) in this very life before passing away;
there is absolutely no case of passing away without having first given rise to it.
To provide scriptural proof for this, he says:
Therefore, for those in the stage of an ordinary person who have previously abandoned the defilements of the lower three dhyānas and subsequently enter the path of seeing based on a lower level,
once they have attained the fruit, they will necessarily be able to induce the subsequent path of superior fruits within that very same lifetime.
If it were otherwise, then for noble ones born in the fourth dhyāna or in the stages above it,
it would be impossible to say that they necessarily possess the faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*);
yet the fundamental treatise states in all cases that noble ones born in the higher stages necessarily possess the faculty of pleasure.
Therefore, one knows that this body is certainly capable of giving rise to the subsequent path of superior fruition.
The "path of superior fruition" refers to the path directed toward the subsequent fruition;
it is called the "path of superior fruition" because it is superior to the preceding fruition.
Alternatively, the subsequent fruit is called "superior.
Because this path leads toward that [fruit], it is called the "path to the superior fruit" (*viśeṣa-phala-mārga*).
Question: Does the arising of the subsequent path to the superior fruit occur instantaneously or gradually? Answer: It arises gradually, not instantaneously.
Therefore, the *Vibhāṣā* (171) states:
"Is it possible to attain the four untainted (*anāsrava*) dhyānas gradually?
Answer: Yes."
Because the noble ones have abandoned the defilements of the lower stages, and because they attain [the higher stages] gradually when the path of superior fruit arises. Furthermore, it is asked:
"Is it possible for the three formless [attainments] to be attained gradually in a manner that is untainted (*anāsrava*)?"
Answer: Yes. This is because they are acquired gradually when one becomes detached from the defilements of the lower stages and when the path of superior fruition arises.
Thus, having already categorized [the paths] into three each— lower, middle, and upper—
this second section concerns the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) and the path of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣamārga*). Within this:
First, the enumeration of the virtues of clarity;
second, the detailed explanation of the stages. This refers to the enumeration of the virtues of clarity.
The Treatise says: "Up to the ninth grade, it is likewise."
The first phrase has been explained.
As for how the faults and virtues are each divided into nine grades,
the following explains the second phrase.
This is the question.
Regarding the statement in the Fundamental Chapter that even a small lamp can extinguish [a fire],
this is the answer.
The nine faults and virtues, corresponding respectively to the forward and reverse orders, can be understood through their analogies.
Having already analyzed the faults and virtues up to the stage of "not yet having severed them at all," the following section is the second part,
which provides a detailed explanation by traversing the stages.
Among these, the first clarifies the seven births of a stream-enterer (*srotāpanna*);
the second clarifies the stages of the candidate for and the fruit of once-returning (*sakṛdāgāmin*).
The three knowledges (vidyā) refer to the stage of the non-returner’s path and fruit;
the four knowledges refer to the stage of the arhat’s path and fruit. This clarifies the seven births of the stream-enterer (srotāpanna).
There are four [verses] preceding this.
First, the preceding section concludes:
namely, the nine grades of distinctions regarding the faults and defects have already been analyzed.
Second, the following section is introduced in general.
That is to say, next, one shall establish the distinctions among noble beings based on the cultivation of that path of no-more-learning.
Third, the distinct arising of the path of cultivation:
this refers, first of all, to the stage of the path of cultivation for those who are still in training (*śaikṣa*).
Collectively, these are also termed "those liberated through faith" (śraddhādhimukta) and "those who have attained vision" (dṛṣṭiprāpta);
they are of many types according to their respective stages.
[The following] four verses are composed separately.
This refers to first establishing those who have not yet abandoned [the defilements] at all.
The verse says: "The meaning of 'up to seven rebirths' can be understood."
From the various untainted paths up to the point where one is designated as a "stream-enterer" (srotāpanna),
this explains the meaning of the term "stream-enterer.
In general, all untainted paths are termed "streams" (srotas).
Because one flows toward Nirvana with these untainted states as the cause,
the term "entering" (srotāpanna) is used to signify the sense of first attaining [the fruit].
Since one has entered the stream of untainted dharmas, one is called a Stream-enterer (srotāpanna).
This name "stream-enterer" (srotāpanna) is applied to one who has reached the state of being a stream-enterer.
Question:
To what meaning does this name "stream-enterer" refer?
If one who first attains the noble path is called a stream-enterer (*srotāpanna*),
then that very name "stream-enterer" should also apply to the eighth person;
for the "eighth person" refers to one who is still in the stage of approaching the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpattipratipannaka*).
Regarding the four paths and four fruits, counting from the last back to the first, the first path corresponds to the eighth fruit.
Thus, the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* (vol. 46) states:
"The eighth noble one refers to those who follow by faith (*śraddhānusārin*) and those who follow by dharma (*dharmānusārin*)."

It is because it is the eighth when counted from the superior [stages]; alternatively, it is because when counting backward from the end among the eight patiences (*kṣānti*), the Dharma-patience regarding suffering (*duḥkha-dharmakṣānti*) is the eighth.
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states that the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) is called the stage of the eight persons (*aṣṭamaka-bhūmi*).
If one who has first attained the fruit is called a Stream-enterer (srotāpanna),
then those who have either partially or entirely abandoned desire attain the fruit of Once-returner (sakṛdāgāmin) upon reaching the subsequent knowledge of the path (mārgānvayajñāna).
If one who attains the fruit of non-returner (anāgāmiphala) also attains it for the first time, they should likewise be called a stream-enterer (srotāpanna).
Regarding this name "stream-enterer," why is it called "stream-enterer"? The answer is: [it is so called] because they have entered [the stream].
This designation "stream-enterer" (srotāpanna) refers to the initial attainment of the fruit and does not refer to the eighth [birth].
However, this name is established based on the first fruit attained by one who will eventually attain all four fruits.
The once-returner and non-returner stages are not necessarily attained for the first time;
although there is the sense of initial attainment for those who skip stages,
for those who proceed through them in regular succession, it is not an initial attainment.
Since this [attainment] is definitely acquired for the first time when it is obtained, it is called "Stream-enterer" (*srotāpanna*).
For what reason does this name not refer to the eighth [stage]?
Question.
For what reason is this stream-enterer not designated by the eighth [moment]?
The eighth is explained as before.
It is because one must reach the attainment [of the fruit] that one is not designated by the eighth.
Answer: Because,
upon reaching the moment of attaining the subsequent knowledge of the path (mārgānvaya-jñāna),
one simultaneously acquires the entire set of the untainted paths of both the stage of approach (pratipannaka) and the fruit (phala).
Second, because they have fully attained both the path of vision and the untainted path of cultivation;
third, because they have attained the sixteen aspects throughout the four truths within the stream of clear observation (*abhisamaya*).
One who possesses these three meanings is called a "stream-enterer" (*srotāpanna*).
The eighth [stage] is not so;
because it does not possess the three meanings,
the name "stream-enterer" (srotāpanna) does not refer to the eighth stage.
"From that point onward, up to what was said as 'thus'" refers here to the specific explanation of the seven births.
This means that after one has attained the fruit of the noble ones (*āryaphala*) from this body...
Apart from humans, there are at most seven intermediate existences (*antarābhava*) and seven births (*upapattibhava*);
the same applies to gods.
Thus, four sets of seven amount to twenty-eight births in total.
One should say there are twenty-eight;

because each consists of seven [factors], they are called "at most seven rebirths," just as in the case of the "skillfulness in the seven bases" (*saptasthānakauśalya*), where each of the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*) has seven [aspects].
Regarding the five sets of seven, there should be thirty-five;
however, they are called "skillful in the seven bases" because the seven are identical in each case, and thus only the number seven is mentioned.
The "skillfulness in the seven points" is as previously explained. It is like the *saptaparṇa* tree:
in the West there is a tree where upon every branch there are seven leaves;
yet in reality, the leaves are immeasurable.

Regarding the term "seven-leaf tree" (*saptaparṇa*), it is so called because of the similarity of the number seven; such is the explanation given by the Vaibhāṣika masters. "Fetter" (*saṃyojana*) signifies the sense of binding together and non-interruption;
alternatively, "fetter" refers to the afflictions (*kleśa*).
Because one undergoes seven [existences] through the fetters (*saṃyojana*). If that is so, why is it said that there is a sense of reaching the eighth existence?
This is the objection.
Alternatively, this may be an objection from the Mahīśāsaka school.
They maintain that humans and devas together undergo seven births;
if it were the case that they each undergo seven births separately, [the objection would stand].
For what reason does the Sūtra state:
"It is impossible and there is no occasion to see one who has attained perfection [still] having the sense of undergoing an eighth existence"?
Regarding the point that the intention of this sutra implies that there should be no intermediate state (*antarābhava*), the Sarvāstivādins reply:
"The intention of this sutra is stated with reference to a single realm of rebirth (*gati*); it says 'one does not undergo an eighth [birth]' in this sense."
If one adheres to the literal statement that the eighth birth is not received,

then the intermediate state (antarābhava) should not exist. If that were so, then for those who ascend to the higher realms and do not undergo an eighth birth, [the intermediate state would likewise be non-existent].
This is difficult.
If one says that there is no eighth birth for those of a single destiny (*ekayānika*),
yet those who ascend through all stages (*ūrdhvasrotas*) reach even the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*).
One might argue that there should likewise be no eighth birth for those in a single destination (*ekāyana*),
since [the sūtra] speaks in reference to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and thus there is no fault. To this,
the answer is:
The statement that there is no eighth [consciousness] is made with reference to the desire realm (kāmadhātu), and thus there is no fault.
What is the proof for this? [It is because] it does not include the seven [consciousnesses] associated with feeling (vedanā). This is the inquiry.
What serves as the proof for this?
Is it based on scripture,
or is it based on reasoning?

Within the scriptural teachings and the logical principles, by what means is it proven that one undergoes seven births separately among humans and devas, rather than receiving those seven births collectively?
This is because the Sūtra states that one should not adhere dogmatically to [the literal phrasing].
The Sarvāstivādins reply:
Since the sūtra speaks of "the seven [classes of] devas and humans," and employs the word "and" (*ca*), [it follows that they are distinct].
It is clearly known that each [of the two] consists of seven;
the scriptures of the Kāśyapīya school likewise accept seven for each.
Therefore, one should not insist here that humans and gods together constitute seven.
If one passes from the human realm back to the celestial realm,
it clarifies that there are seven births remaining.
This refers to one who has attained the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpanna*) within the human realm.
He is reborn seven times in the heavenly realms and seven times among human beings;
upon reaching his seventh birth, he returns to the human realm and attains parinirvāṇa.
This applies if he has attained the fruit of a stream-enterer while in the heavenly realm.
Those who are born seven times among humans and seven times in the heavens—
reaching the seventh birth, they return to the celestial realm and attain parinirvāṇa.
From this, it is known.
Excluding the body of one who has attained the Path;
if one were to include the body of one who has attained the Path, there would then be twenty-nine.
For what reason does that [attainer] not undergo an eighth existence?
Question:
For what reason does that person undergo only seven births and not an eighth?
Why is the continuity [of rebirth] limited to this, like a malarial fever that recurs every fourth day?
Answer: It means that within this continuum of existence, spanning up to these seven births,
all noble paths (āryamārga) will necessarily be accomplished.
This demonstrates that due to the power of karma, one undergoes seven births;
the category of the Noble Path persists until the seventh birth,
and it is the natural law that it should thus be able to exhaust all afflictions.
This demonstrates the power of the Path, such that one does not reach the eighth [stage],
like the seven-step snake; thus,
the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* says:
Furthermore, the power of that karma is capable of undergoing seven existences;
however, by the power of the Noble Path, one does not reach an eighth.
It is like being bitten by a venomous snake that can only travel seven paces.
By the power of the great elements (*mahābhūta*), he was able to walk seven steps;
by the force of the poison, he did not reach the eighth.
This is also like a quartan fever.
Those suffering from various types of malaria have different patterns of onset;
some do not manifest for half a day and then manifest for half a day,
while others do not manifest for one full day and then manifest for one full day.
There are also those that manifest very late; they do not manifest on the first day or the second day, nor on the third day, but necessarily manifest on the fourth day.
This is called the quartan fever.
By the fourth day, it is natural that this malarial fever will inevitably break out.
The Noble Path is likewise;
it certainly does not exceed seven days.
Upon reaching the seventh birth, by the very nature of things (*dharmatā*), one will necessarily exhaust all remaining afflictions and attain parinirvāṇa.
This "seventh" is used as a metaphor for the ultimate limit of the slowest possible duration of this natural process.
It is not a numerical analogy.
Furthermore, there are others who possess up to five of the higher fetters;
this is the second interpretation.
Furthermore, because he still possesses seven remaining fetters, he undergoes seven more births;
namely, the two lower fetters: sensual desire and ill will.

The five higher fetters (*pañcordhvabhāgīya-saṃyojana*) are craving for the realm of form (*rūparāga*), craving for the formless realm (*ārūpyarāga*), restlessness (*auddhatya*), pride (*māna*), and ignorance (*avidyā*).
The *Nyāyānusāra* refutes this, stating:
"This [argument] likewise lacks the capacity to prove that there are only seven [existences]."
Only the fetters of greed and hatred lead to seven existences.
Furthermore, no sutra states that a non-returner undergoes up to seven existences;
nor does any sutra state that the five higher fetters lead to rebirth in the desire realm.
Therefore, what they have stated lacks the power of proof;

it is simply due to the nature of things (*dharmatā*) that one undergoes at most seven births, and within this context, one should not insistently propound further logical arguments. The Vaibhāṣika masters offer this defense:
Although the fetters of the upper realms do not themselves project birth in the desire realm, because one has established them,
the two lower fetters possess the power to project birth in the desire realm.
What harm is there in this? Question: How many births can one who abides in the fruit of stream-entry (srotāpanna-phala) undergo? Master Tai explains:
One who abides in the fruit of stream-entry does not undergo even a single birth.
Even among those proceeding toward the stage of once-returner, there is no one who must undergo a single birth.
If there were karma for a single birth that could not be transformed,
then all other [karma] that could be transformed would be rendered incapable of being avoided.
That person first abandons six grades of afflictions before receiving one more birth.
If they have already abandoned six grades of afflictions,
this person is then a Once-returner (sakṛdāgāmin).
Regarding the subsequent experience of one more birth,
this refers specifically to experiencing one more birth within the stage of the Once-returner (sakṛdāgāmin),
and not to experiencing it within the stage of the candidate for that fruit (pratipannaka).
As the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states:
"There are two kinds of srotāpannas:
first, those of sharp faculties."
The second is those of dull faculties.
Such persons of dull faculties return among humans and devas seven times.
Furthermore, these persons of dull faculties are of five types.
There may be six, five, four, three, or two types.
Those of sharp faculties may attain the fruit of a stream-enterer up to the fruit of an arhat in their present body.
If there is such a thing as being "born once more," why is it not mentioned?
Furthermore, the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra* states:
"The person who is a *srotāpanna*..."
If one undergoes two births up to seven births,
or even a single birth,
why is this not mentioned?
Furthermore, the *Abhidharmamahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 46, states:
"Regarding the statement that one is born seven times in the heavens and seven times among humans,
this is said with reference to a perfected stream-enterer (*srotāpanna*)."
The Elder Tiṇṭha and others likewise received seven more births; however,
there is a distinction between those who have attained the stage of Stream-enterer (srotāpanna) and those born as devas.
That is to say: seven [rebirths] among devas and six among humans;
or seven among humans and six among devas; or six among devas and five among humans;
or six among humans and five among devas; or five among devas and four among humans.
Either five for humans and four for devas; or four for devas and three for humans.
Or four for humans and three for devas; or three for devas and two for humans.
Or three for humans and two for devas; or two for devas and one for humans.

"Or seven times among humans, once among devas"—this is stated here because it refers to those who take the maximum number of births; thus, it says that stream-enterers (srotāpanna) undergo seven births each among humans and devas.
In the *Abhidharmamahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, within the discussion of the maximum, it likewise states that humans and devas each undergo seven births.
In the "Extremely Small" [category], it does not mention "one person" or "one birth.
Therefore, we know that one who abides in the fruit of stream-entry (srotāpanna) does not undergo another birth. This is explained at greater length and so forth;
I cannot describe it in full detail. My current interpretation, however, is not thus.
One who dwells in the fruit of stream-entry may undergo up to seven births, or even as few as one birth;
since the treatise uses the term "at most" (*parama*), it implies this limit.
This is to show that while rebirths are most numerous [in this case],
not all stream-enterers (srotāpanna) undergo exactly seven returns;
it is for this reason that we know [this].
It does not exclude the possibility that even the very few may receive only one birth.

When the *Abhidharmamahāvibhāṣā* does not state that humans and devas each receive one birth, it is merely based on the preceding discussion of their alternating numbers; it does not mean they each receive exactly one.
Speaking in terms of reality, it is also possible that each receives but one birth.
If one were to claim that something does not exist simply because it was not mentioned,
then [the sūtra] would likewise not have mentioned the six classes of devas, the six classes of humans, and so forth.
It should be understood that humans and devas each have six births and so forth;
therefore, we know that these are omitted for brevity,
or that they are indicated through mutual implication by way of ellipsis.
What reasoning allows for two gods and one human,
or two humans and one god, and so forth,
yet does not allow that each receives a single birth?
Furthermore, as for citing the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* and the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra* as proofs,
these do not belong to the same school;
how, then, can they serve as proof?
The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states that all possess Buddha-nature,
while the *Tattvasiddhi Śāstra* speaks of the existence of various seeds;
how could these possibly be the same?
This cannot serve as proof.
There are further arguments of this sort,
which I am unable to refute in detail.
Although there may be those among them who do not realize parinirvāṇa during that interval—
meaning that although the Noble Path manifests within those seven births,
they do not realize parinirvāṇa due to the sustaining power of residual karma— the term for "parinirvāṇa" in Sanskrit is *parinirvāṇa*.
"Pān" means "round," and "Nirvāṇa" means "quiescence.
As for those who reach the seventh existence or go forth into homelessness in other realms:
Regarding the physical characteristics of one who completes seven births during a period when the Buddha-dharma does not exist,
the former master’s view is that upon encountering such a time and attaining arhatship, one will certainly not remain in the household life.
It is the natural law that one spontaneously assumes the physical appearance of a bhikṣu—shaving the hair and donning the dyed robes—but it is not said that the precepts are thereby obtained.
Among the ten ways of obtaining the precepts, it is not stated that they are obtained at the moment one becomes an arhat; this is the intended meaning of the latter master.
He went among other non-Buddhist renunciants and assumed the appearance of a non-Buddhist.
Between these two explanations, the former is correct;
thus, the *Nyāyānusāra* (Treatise on Correct Reasoning), fascicle 64, states:
Since the distinct discipline of individual liberation exists only by virtue of a Buddha’s appearance in the world,
it follows that if one in that seventh [state] does not encounter the Buddha-dharma,
they may attain the fruit of arhatship while remaining a householder.
Having attained the fruit, he will certainly not remain at home;
the bhikṣu’s majestic deportment will be naturally perfected,
even though he has not encountered what was previously taught by former Buddhas.
He developed an intense sense of revulsion toward his remaining life and entered parinirvāṇa before long;
some say that he went forth as a renunciant in another realm.

This is logically untenable, because those who go to other realms do so through the transformation of wrong karma driven by the power of false views. Furthermore, the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 46, states:
"Question: If seven existences are completed [before encountering a Buddha], yet no Buddha appears in the world..."
Does he attain the fruit of arhatship while remaining at home?
Some say he does not;
he must necessarily go forth and receive the saffron robes before attaining arhatship.
Some say that once a layperson has attained arhatship,
they will necessarily leave the household life and receive the robes of another dharma;
those who speak thus maintain that it is the natural law (dharmatā) for such a person to become a disciple of the Buddha.
Until they attain the ultimate fruit,
as in the case of the five hundred rishis who practiced the Way on Mount Isigili.
Originally, these were śrāvakas who had emerged during a world without a Buddha;
the monkey manifested himself as a disciple of the Buddha,
and they all followed his example to realize the fruit of pratyekabuddhahood.
Because those beyond training (aśaikṣa) do not accept the characteristics of non-Buddhist paths (tīrthika),
how is it that they are called "those whose nature is not subject to falling away" (avinipātadharman)?
Question:
If a stream-enterer can also give rise to unwholesome afflictions of cultivation,
why does the sutra state that such a stream-enterer is called one who possesses the quality of not falling back into the evil destinies?
It is because they do not grow [in those afflictions], up to and including being able to float upon them.
Answer: First, because one does not produce karma leading to decline or downfall;
second, because one acts contrary to that karma which would produce such results.
Third, because powerful roots of virtue suppress his body;
fourth, because both his physical and verbal applications as well as his intentions are pure;
fifth, because even those karmas that would certainly cause him to fall into the evil destinies do not arise in him until he attains patience (*kṣānti*).
How much more so for one who has attained the stage of stream-entry?
Using the inferior to illustrate the superior,
there is a verse that says:
Even if a fool commits only a minor transgression,
he will fall into the evil realms because he lacks shame and dread of blame.
Wisdom is of great importance regarding transgressions;
it can also bring liberation from the bitter fruits of the evil realms because of the presence of shame and remorse.
The analogy is clear enough to understand.
The intent of this verse is that ordinary, deluded persons are said to possess the nature of falling back,
whereas noble ones who possess wisdom are said to be without such falling back.
Although ordinary persons may also not fall into the evil destinies, because this occurs only rarely and is not certain, they are not said to possess the quality of being non-retrogressive.

Question: Since noble ones also give rise to afflictions, why do they not fall into retrogression? Answer: Although they give rise to afflictions of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*), because these lack the assistance of afflictions of the path of seeing (*darśana-heya*), they are unable to induce rebirth in the three evil destinies.
Therefore, the *Vibhāṣā* (125) states:
"The fetters of the two categories bind sentient beings and cause them to fall into the evil destinies;
namely, the fetters abandoned through seeing (*darśana-heya*) and those abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*)."
Although those who have attained the fruit of stream-entry (srotāpanna) have not yet permanently severed the fetters to be abandoned through cultivation (bhāvanā-heya),
they have already permanently severed the fetters to be abandoned through seeing (darśana-heya).
Lacking but a single portion of the requisite provisions (sambhāra), they do not fall into the miserable destinies (apāya).
Just as a chariot has two wheels for transport and a bird has two wings to fly through the sky,
if either one is missing, it cannot function.
This is also the case here.
Therefore, a stream-enterer does not fall into the evil destinies.
However, there are those who say:
The fool falls into the evil destinies;
the wise person does not.
Since all stream-enterers (*srotāpanna*) are wise persons, it is explained at length as in that [text].
Regarding the scriptural statement that the stream-enterer reaches the limit of suffering,
a question is raised based on that scripture:
"Based on this very birth, one reaches what is called nirvāṇa."
Answer: There are two interpretations here.
According to the first interpretation, the "limit of suffering" (duḥkhānta) refers to the point where suffering is exhausted.
The subsequent explanation is based on the fact that emerging from the locus of suffering is termed the "limit of suffering" (*duḥkha-paryanta*).
Thus, the *Mahāvibhāṣā* states:
"To bring about the limit of suffering means to realize the limit of suffering."
Question: Does this limit of suffering exist within suffering, or does it exist outside of suffering?
If it were within suffering, it could not be the limit.
If one asks how worldly analogies manifest outside of suffering, how would you explain them?
For example, just as a golden tally in the world is gold from its beginning, middle, and end,
so too the limits of suffering must also be suffering.
There are those who say that the limit of suffering exists within suffering itself; thus,
although the substance of the final aggregates of an Arhat is indeed suffering,
they are not the cause of future suffering.
Not giving rise to future suffering,
such that future suffering does not continue—
this is called the "limit of suffering."
Other masters say that the "limit of suffering" (duḥkha-anta) refers to that which lies outside of suffering;
that is, nirvāṇa, because it is the eternal emergence from suffering, and is thus called the limit of suffering.
As for worldly metaphors, they need not necessarily be explained through logical consistency.
This is because it is not included within the Tripiṭaka and thus does not require an explanation;
furthermore, the principles of mundane phenomena and noble phenomena are distinct.
How, then, could Nirvāṇa be something that is produced?
The question concerns the subsequent explanation.
Regarding the passage from "removing those obstacles" up to "destroying the terraces and pavilions," the answer is as follows:
Because it removes the obstacles to attaining that nirvāṇa.
This attainment prevents the arising of other afflictions; if those afflictive obstacles are severed, this attainment arises, whereby the essence of nirvāṇa is manifested.

Therefore, it is said that nirvāṇa is called "that which is to be accomplished. Furthermore, by eliminating those delusions and attaining the arising of freedom from obstacles, nirvāṇa becomes manifest;
thus, the term "to be accomplished" is used.
To speak of "making empty" means to demolish a terrace or pavilion;
since emptiness manifests the aspect of meaning, "emptiness" is termed that which is produced.
Nirvana is also like this;
as for the statement that it is not mentioned because other states also reach this [state], these refer to other states of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*).
Although there are indeed those who attain parinirvāṇa after being reborn at most seven times,
this is not certain; for some may even exceed that number.
Therefore, it is not mentioned;
the supreme limit of the noble ones is only seven,
and for this reason it is stated separately.
Therefore, the *Nyāyānusāra* (Treatise on Right Reasoning), fascicle 64,
states: "If one attains the fruit of a Stream-enterer within the human realm,
it should be understood that seven full days [of rebirth] apply to the human realm."
Even those who are not noble possess the limit of seven returns;
through the accomplishment of their continuity, they attain the state of nirvana,
yet this is not certain.
Therefore, it is not explained here.

*Abhidharmakośabhāṣya-ṭīkā* (Kusharon-ki), Fascicle 23. On the twenty-second day of the second month in the fourth year of Jōshō (829 A.D.), at the hour of the horse (mid-morning), at Ōdōji in Tahanri, Yamashiro Province, I completed the intensive recitation and textual analysis together with my third younger brother. The Junior Sōjū Kakujū is suffering from an illness that increases day by day, and his aged eyesight is also failing; what can be done for him?
(Postscript) On the seventeenth day of the sixth month of the second year of Ten'yō, I read this through once at the Betsumaru-bō.
Recorded by the śramaṇa Śākyamuni Kō, *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya-ṭīkā*, Fascicle 24.
The sixth chapter, "Discrimination of the Noble Ones," part three:
Having already explained those who abide in the fruits and those who are candidates for the fruit of once-returning,
the following second section clarifies the candidate for and the fruit of once-returning.
In this passage: first, the preceding section is concluded;
second, the subsequent section is introduced in general.
Third, a separate verse is presented.
The verse says: "Up to the abandonment of six [defilements], one attains the fruit of a Once-returner.
This is the response in verse.
Among these, the first three phrases clarify the orientation (*mukha*),
and the final phrase clarifies the fruition (*phala*). Regarding the orientation:
The first two lines clarify the "family-to-family" (kulaṃkula) practitioner;
the third line correctly clarifies the "candidate" (pratipannaka).
The treatise states: "Upon reaching [the stage where] the name changes to 'family-to-family'..."
The following explains the two preceding lines; this constitutes the general heading.
If the three conditions are fully present, it is termed "one who goes from family to family" (kulaṃkula);
if any one is lacking, it is not so termed.
Regarding "first, by means of abandoning afflictions up to the third or fourth category":
first, by means of abandoning afflictions,
it refers to abandoning the third or fourth categories of the afflictions to be abandoned through cultivation in the desire realm.
This means that they are either abandoned during the previous stage of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*),
or abandoned now during the stage of advancing toward stream-entry (*srotāpanna*).
By specifying "three or four grades," it excludes the abandonment of one grade, two grades, or five grades.
Although there may be those who have severed one grade, two grades, or five grades,
some may emerge from contemplation,
while others may regress.
There must be no one who undergoes death and rebirth in the interval;
therefore, there are none who are called "family-to-family" (kulaṃkula) by having abandoned only one, two, or five categories [of afflictions].
The reason we know there is no death and rebirth is as follows:
Therefore, the *Abhidharmamahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 53, states:
"Furthermore, as for those who have attained the stage of stream-entry (*srotāpanna*),
if they sever one or two categories of fetters (*saṃyojana*) of the desire realm..."
Because there is no meaning of birth and death [in that state], it is not mentioned;
this is like the severing of the five grades.
That is to say, once a practitioner of yoga has attained the first fruit.
One initiates great application of effort in order to sever the fetters of the desire realm that are to be abandoned through cultivation;
for it is impossible to die and be reborn without having severed at least one category of these fetters,
just as when one severs five categories.
It is certain that there is no possibility of death and rebirth for one who has not yet severed the sixth grade of fetters;

this is because the three types of practitioners, such as those who go from family to family (*kulaṃkula*), do undergo death and rebirth, and it is with reference to them specifically that this is stated here.

According to that treatise, one knows that for those who have abandoned one, two, or five categories [of defilements], there is absolutely no possibility of death or rebirth in the intermediate state (*antarābhava*). Question: According to the *Vibhāṣā*, it neither mentions emerging from meditative absorption nor does it mention falling away (*parihāṇi*).
How is it known that one has emerged from meditative absorption (*vyutthāna*) or has regressed? Answer: As stated in the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* (Vibhāṣā), fascicle 32:

"When a stream-enterer (*srotāpanna*) proceeds toward the fruit of a once-returner (*sakṛdāgāmin*), at the time of the preparatory path (*prayoga-mārga*) for those who do not enter meditative absorption, they attain the non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) regarding the six classes of rebirth in the desire realm."

When one emerges from meditative absorption, at the time of the sixth uninterrupted path (*ānantarya-mārga*), one attains the non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) regarding the six births in the desire realm.
This also applies when a once-returner (*sakṛdāgāmin*) proceeds toward the fruit of a non-returner (*anāgāmiphala*).

For one who does not enter meditative absorption, the non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) of a single birth in the desire realm is attained during the stage of the preparatory path (*prayoga-mārga*).
For one who does enter meditative absorption, it must wait until the ninth uninterrupted path (*ānantarya-mārga*).
One attains the non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyānirodha*) of one birth in the desire realm.
Since the *Mahāvibhāṣā* neither states that one attains the non-analytical cessation of six births in the desire realm through the fifth path of immediate succession (*ānantarya-mārga*),
nor states that one attains the non-analytical cessation of two births through the first path of immediate succession, [the former interpretation is untenable].
In the second uninterrupted path (*ānantarya-mārga*), one attains the three types of non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*);
this clearly shows that one may emerge from meditative absorption in each and every stage,
and that one may likewise fall away from them.
The treatise states that "by abandoning the fifth, one necessarily abandons the sixth" based on those who are non-regressive,
because for them there is no death or rebirth in the intermediate state (antarābhava).
One must necessarily sever the sixth [consciousness] within this very lifetime.
Second, "because one perfects the faculties up to the faculty of non-decline" refers to the second condition.
This means that by attaining the untainted faculties (*anāsrava-indriya*) capable of counteracting those three or four categories,
one first abandons three or four categories while still in the stage of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*),
and subsequently abides in the first fruit (*phala-prathama*) without yet having generated the path to a superior fruit.
Although there are initial and subsequent conditions, they have not yet established those untainted faculties (*anāsrava-indriya*);
thus, regarding the phrase "because one undergoes birth up to three times and two births," this refers to the third condition.
This means that by virtue of being born [in the form realm], one undergoes three more births in the desire realm due to two remaining births.
If one abandons three categories [of afflictions], one undergoes three more births;
if one abandons four categories, one undergoes two more births.
Because there is no death or rebirth in the interim after abandoning one, two, or five grades [of defilements],
there are no "five-birth," "four-birth," "one-birth," or "half-birth" *kulaṃkula* [families].
Question: Do noble ones (ārya) create projecting karma (*ākṣepaka-karma*)? Answer: According to the *Nyāyānusāra*, fascicle 64, it says:
"These three [types of karma] are produced in two lifetimes;
they are performed and accumulated during the stage of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*)."
Third, regarding the karma of two births:
no noble ones (ārya) within their state of nobility can further create new karma that draws them toward future existence.
Because they turn their backs on saṃsāra and face toward nirvāṇa, this sūtra states:
"The noble ones only experience karma already incurred; they do not incur new karma."
Furthermore, in the *Abhidharmamahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 53, in the explanation of the "family-to-family" (*kulaṃkula*) and "one-interval" (*ekavicika*) [practitioners], it says:
"Question: Does a noble one (*ārya*) create karma that projects a commonality of group (*nikāyasabhāga*) in the desire realm? Some say he does not."
Why is this? Because the desire realm abounds in manifold faults and afflictions,
and is rife with manifold calamities and misfortunes.
Therefore, noble beings do not perform karma that projects a homogeneous class (*nikāya-sabhāga*) in the desire realm;
they only perform karma that completes a homogeneous class in the desire realm.
Some say, however, that noble beings also perform karma that projects a homogeneous class in the desire realm.
Although there are these two views, there is no commentary evaluating them.

Furthermore, the *Nyāyānusāra* agrees with the former explanation. Question: If it is said that noble ones (āryas) do not create projecting karma (*ākṣepaka-karman*), how can they be born in those five Pure Abodes (*śuddhāvāsa*)? Answer: It is explained that the statement "they do not create" refers to the realm of desire (*kāmadhātu*).

It should be understood that the same applies to karma because it is merely feeling (*vedanā*). Question: Since even the roots of goodness conducive to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya-kuśalamūla*) do not create projecting karma (*ākṣepaka-karma*), why does one now create projecting karma upon reaching the stage of the Noble Ones (*ārya*)? Answer: It is explained that the roots of goodness conducive to penetration involve a state of aversion toward and turning away from existence (*bhava*). However, [the Noble Ones] have already transcended such aversion. Therefore, they create projecting karma for a future birth within the realm of existence (*bhavagati*). Furthermore, because they have abandoned the afflictions (*kleśa*) that obstruct the attainment of nirvāṇa, they do not create projecting karma for rebirth in the miserable destinies (*durgati*). Consequently, they create projecting karma only for rebirth as a human or a god. Thus, although they create projecting karma, they do not create completing karma (*paripūraka-karma*) that leads to the various specific conditions of those states. This is because they possess the wisdom that thoroughly discerns the nature of all phenomena. Moreover, since they have attained mastery over their mind, they are able to transform their physical body at will; therefore, they do not create projecting karma for rebirth in the formless realms (*ārūpyadhātu*). For these reasons, it is said that while they create projecting karma, they do not create completing karma. Furthermore, because they have severed the continuity of the afflictions, they do not create projecting karma for rebirth in the hells or the animal realm. They create projecting karma only for rebirth among humans or gods. Even when creating projecting karma for rebirth as a human, they do not create projecting karma for rebirth in the borderlands (*pratyantajanapada*) or as a person with defective faculties. They create projecting karma only for rebirth in the central lands (*madhyadeśa*) and as a person with complete faculties. Even when creating projecting karma for rebirth as a god, they do not create projecting karma for rebirth in the heavens of the non-percipient beings (*asaṃjñisattva*) or the heaven of the long-lived gods (*dīrghāyuṣka-deva*). They create projecting karma only for rebirth in the heavens of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) or the form realm (*rūpadhātu*). Even when creating projecting karma for rebirth in the heavens of the desire realm, they do not create projecting karma for rebirth as a malevolent deity (*asura*) or as a hungry ghost (*preta*). They create projecting karma only for rebirth as a god or a human. Even when creating projecting karma for rebirth as a human, they do not create projecting karma for rebirth in the three evil destinies (*durgati*). They create projecting karma only for rebirth in the two happy destinies (*sugati*). Even when creating projecting karma for rebirth in the central lands, they do not create projecting karma for rebirth as a woman, a eunuch, or a hermaphrodite. They create projecting karma only for rebirth as a male. Even when creating projecting karma for rebirth as a male, they do not create projecting karma for rebirth as a person incapable of spiritual practice. They create projecting karma only for rebirth
Because they are directed toward the path of seeing and are conducive to the path of seeing,
they perform only completing karma (*pūrṇakarma*) and do not perform projecting karma (*ākṣepakarma*).
The state of a noble one (*ārya*) is not thus;
it is possible for them to create projecting karma (*ākṣepaka-karman*).
Furthermore, the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 64, states:
Question: Why is it that noble ones (ārya) pass away having separated from defilements, whereas ordinary beings (pṛthagjana) do not?
Answer: Because noble ones possess untainted meditative concentration (anāsrava-samādhi).
It sustains the continuity [of the mind] and renders it extremely firm.
Ordinary beings possess only mundane concentrations;
these sustain the continuity but do not render it extremely firm.
This is explained in detail as in that commentary.

As for the statement in the verse that [the second condition] is not fully explained because it merely says "reaching," this explains the reason why the second condition is not mentioned in the verse.
