Regarding the fact that among the three conditions, the verse mentions only the first and the last:
after the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpatti-phala*), it is stated that one further proceeds to abandon three or four grades of afflictions;

since the meaning that the various untainted faculties (*anāsrava-indriya*) which serve as their antidotes are thereby established is already implicitly understood by analogy, they are not mentioned in full detail.
"However, one should further explain that it reaches or even exceeds this," is a response to an anticipated objection.
The intent of the objection is as follows:
The verse should likewise not mention the subsequent conditions;
however, since the meaning of abandoning three or four grades [of defilements] can be understood by analogy as involving the experience of three or two births,
these words were spoken to resolve such an anticipated objection.
Furthermore, one should explain the three types of those born twice. Regarding "those born twice," this refers to those who,
through progressive advancement,
are born into a state of existence at the time they abandon the afflictions.
Or they may have three or two births remaining;
or none of the three or two births;
or they may exceed these three or two births.
Experiencing one birth or half a birth is called "fewer" or "less";
attaining parinirvāṇa in the present life within the desire realm is called "none";
and as for those who go upstream and experience four births or more, it is called "exceeding this."
Therefore, the verse treats the arising [of the faculties] separately,
unlike the second case where the untainted faculties (*anāsrava-indriya*) are established.
For what reason is it that these [faculties] are not interrupted by the five grades?
Question:
Regarding the statement, "Because one has abandoned the fifth [category] up until not yet having transcended the realm," the answer is as follows.
Because one who has severed the fifth [fetter] will, if they do not fall back, necessarily sever the sixth within this very life;
there is no intermediate death and rebirth.
If one does not fall back, one will necessarily sever the sixth.
The single grade of afflictions of the sixth [dhyāna] is not able to obstruct the attainment of the fruit of once-returner,
just as there is still one interval remaining.
Having abandoned the eighth category but not yet abandoned the ninth, one possesses only a single seed.
This is because by abandoning the ninth category, one transcends the desire realm;
thus, that ninth category constitutes an extreme obstacle.
Although one who has abandoned the eighth category and abides in the ninth [path] undergoes rebirth,
one who has abandoned the fifth category or is about to abandon the sixth does not,
because they have not yet transcended the realm.
This sixth category is not an extreme obstruction;
therefore, by abandoning the fifth, one does not undergo further rebirths.
One must abandon the sixth to attain the fruit of a Once-returner (*sakṛdāgāmin*). An ancient master said:
If one were to abandon the fifth [defilement] and not emerge from meditative absorption, while abandoning the sixth as a remainder— this interpretation is incorrect,
as it contradicts the *Vibhāṣā*,
as has been fully cited previously.
One should know that there are generally two or three [types]. To explain the *kulaṃkula* (family-to-family) practitioner specifically:
one should know that there are generally two types of *kulaṃkula*.
One who attains parinirvāṇa after three or two births within a single heavenly realm; that is, one born in the desire realm heavens who attains parinirvāṇa after three or two lifetimes,
or one who undergoes three or two births within a single celestial abode.
Alternatively, one may undergo two or three births among the devas;
or one may undergo three births among the devas. Regarding the "family-to-family" (kulaṃkula) person:
this refers to one who attains parinirvāṇa after being born into two or three families within the human realm.
Alternatively, one may undergo three or two births within a single continent;
or undergo three or two births within two continents;
or undergo three births within three continents. Now, let us examine this treatise.
It is permitted that one may undergo two or three births within a single celestial realm or a single continent.
Furthermore, according to the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* (Vibhāṣā), fascicle 53,
it is likewise permitted for one to remain in a single celestial abode.
A single celestial abode may undergo three or two births;
therefore, that treatise states:
"Or, a single celestial abode."
Or they are born into two celestial families,
or three celestial families,
receiving two or three births. It is also said:
Either one household, or two households,
or three households.
Receiving two or three births. Question: Regarding those who attain the state of *kulaṃkula* (family-to-family) after three or two births, do humans and devas each receive three or two births?
Explanation: If one is a *deva-kulaṃkula* (family-to-family among devas), they receive three births.
Three [births] among devas and two among humans; or,
if one is a *kulaṅkula* (one who goes from family to family) among devas,
there are two among devas and one among humans.
If a person is a "family-to-family" (kulaṃkula) being among humans, it should be understood that this is the reverse.
Thus, the *Nyāyānusāra* (Treatise on Right Reasoning), fascicle 64, states:
"If a 'heavenly family-to-family' being undergoes three births..."
Humans receive two [births] and those in the heavens receive three.
Regarding those who receive two births: humans constitute one and heavens constitute two.

This should be explained by analogy for the "family-to-family" (kulaṃkula) type among humans. Question: For what reason do those who abide in the fruit [of stream-entry] have seven births each when alternating between humans and gods?
"Is it not the case that those in the 'house-to-house' (kulaṃkula) stage do not undergo even one more birth? The commentary explains: Those abiding in the fruit may each undergo seven births;
those in the preparatory stage (pratipannaka), being constrained by time, undergo two or three births before their number is fulfilled and they enter parinirvāṇa.
Therefore, they do not undergo even one more minor birth. Furthermore, regarding the various conditions for the "family-to-family" (kulaṃkula) practitioners:
if they belong to the celestial family-to-family type, there are three births among the gods and two among humans;
if they belong to the human family-to-family type, there are three births among humans and two among the gods.
Having fulfilled the conditions for three or two births, one ceases [further rebirth];
thus, one does not undergo even one more minor birth.
It should be understood that those who belong to the "family-to-family" (kulaṃkula) class attain the Way among human beings.
Regarding "family-to-family" (kulaṃkula): it refers to one who attains the Path among the devas;

alternatively, it is explained as one who attains the Path among the devas and subsequently enters parinirvāṇa within the realm of the devas—meaning that after first attaining the Path among the devas.
Passing away from that place, they are reborn again among the devas;
because they take birth in the heavens with joy,
they are reborn in a celestial realm immediately upon their first conception.
The body first attained upon reaching the Path is not comprised within the "family-to-family" (kulaṃkula) state of two or three births;
therefore, being born in the heavenly realms is not termed "rebirth.
Only subsequently does one undergo alternating births between the human and heavenly realms.
This principle should be applied to explain every household case.

Although there are two interpretations, the former is superior. Question: Do the *Abhidharmakośa* and the *Mahāvibhāṣā* agree with the *Nyāyānusāra*? Answer: Since there are no explicit statements in the *Abhidharmakośa* or the *Mahāvibhāṣā* that they agree with the *Nyāyānusāra*, [they do not].
Alternatively, the *Nyāyānusāra* is based on the minimum number of "families" (*kula*) for those who go from family to family (*kulād-kulaga*),
whereas this treatise and the *Mahāvibhāṣā* are based on the maximum number of families. Or else,
the intended meaning of each treatise is distinct.
If one adopts this interpretation,
then according to the *Abhidharmakośa* and the *Mahāvibhāṣā*, humans and devas each undergo two or three births.
Furthermore, the *Nyāyānusāra* states:
If there are those with seven births, it does not necessarily mean they complete all seven.
They do not attain parinirvāṇa during the intermediate stage of the "family-to-family" (kulaṃkula) state;
what category do such individuals belong to within the classification of those with seven births?
The term "at most" (*parama*) in the seventh [category] indicates the maximum limit;
by this, it is already shown that those who attain parinirvāṇa before their lifespan is complete are also included therein.
Those with the most dull faculties may undergo up to seven births;

however, those with sharp faculties do not necessarily complete all seven births. Question: Is one who attains parinirvāṇa before completing the seven births still included within the category of "seven births"?

Question: Are those who attain parinirvāṇa within two or three births included among the *kulaṅkula* (those who go from family to family)? Answer: It is explained that although they do not complete seven births because the conditions are not fully met, they are nonetheless included therein.

Regarding the "house-to-house" (kulaṃkula) practitioner, in terms of the requisite conditions, they must necessarily have completed [the required births] before being included therein. Question: If one attains parinirvāṇa after only two or three births, they do not qualify as a kulaṃkula.
How then can they be so designated?
To what category does this belong? The explanation says: it is included within the stage of "one who is heading toward the fruit of once-returner" (sakṛdāgāmipratipannaka).
This is because the category of "heading toward" (pratipannaka) is broad, whereas the meaning of "family-to-family" (kulaṃkula) is narrow.
Therefore, they are not included therein.
As for the phrase "from the moment one becomes a stream-enterer until [the subsiding of] greed, hatred,
and delusion," this explains the two subsequent lines.
That is, one who has entered the stream proceeds to abandon from one grade up to five grades of the afflictions to be abandoned through cultivation within the desire realm.

It should be understood that the transformation [of the sixth affliction] is designated as the fruit of Once-returner (sakṛdāgāmin) and the candidate for that fruit (pratipannaka). The sixth uninterrupted path (*ānantarya-mārga*) should likewise be a candidate;
however, it is not mentioned in the verse because the sixth category is not entirely a candidate stage.
Half [of this] is comprised within the fruit.
When the path of liberation that abandons the sixth category [of afflictions] manifests, one becomes a Once-returner (*sakṛdāgāmin*).
Excluding the attainment of the body of the path, such a person goes once to the heavens and returns once to the human realm.
And parinirvāṇa is termed the fruit of once-returning because after this there is no further birth;
since one who returns must necessarily depart, it is called "once-returning."
Regarding the statement "there is going but no coming," it does not mean that there is only a single departure.
This passage is based on those who attain the Way among human beings;
therefore, it says that they go to the heavens and return once more to the human realm.
If one attains the Way while in the heavens,
it should likewise be said that such a person goes among humans and returns once more to the heavens;
this is the fruit of "once-returner" (sakṛdāgāmin).
Alternatively, they are also called those who have attenuated greed,
hatred, and delusion; among the nine grades [of defilements], they have already abandoned the six superior and middle grades which are heavy and thick,
leaving only the three inferior grades of attenuated greed, hatred, and delusion.
It should be understood that if a noble one who has taken birth in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) gives rise to the noble path (*āryamārga*) and is able to further sever the afflictions (*kleśa*),
they will necessarily attain the fruit of arhatship (*aśaikṣaphala*) in this very life.
However, since the path that severs [defilements] arises only through arduous and strenuous effort,
who would be willing to take birth again?
For they have already experienced birth and are utterly weary of suffering.
If a noble one in the stage of seven births who has already undergone births is able to further abandon the afflictions,
they will certainly no longer become a "family-to-family" (kulaṃkula) practitioner or similar.
If a noble one in the stage of "family-to-family" (*kulaṃkula*) who has undergone rebirth is able to further abandon the afflictions (*kleśa*),
they will certainly not again become a "once-returner" (*sakṛdāgāmin*) or similar.
If a noble one in the stage of a Once-returner (sakṛdāgāmin) who has undergone rebirth is able to further abandon the afflictions,

they will certainly not again become a person of "one interval" (ekavicika). Now, following the discussion on the meanings of "family-to-family" (kulaṃkula) and "once-returner," I shall briefly clarify the increase and decrease of rebirths resulting from the nine grades of afflictions in the desire realm.
According to various sūtras and śāstras, there are differing explanations regarding the seven births.
Some state that the seven births encompass both humans and devas collectively, combining the intermediate birth (antarābhava) with the subsequent birth (upapattibhava).
In some expositions of the fourteen births, humans and devas are discussed separately, yet their births are treated together.
In other expositions of the twenty-eight births, humans and devas are discussed separately, yet their births are treated individually.
The distinction lies in their opening and closing,
with increases and decreases applied accordingly.
For now, these increases and decreases shall be clarified by way of the seven births.
In brief, the nine grades of afflictions increase or decrease across seven births.
Those not yet severed are called "increased," while those already severed are called "decreased."
If one distinguishes them individually, the three superior grades of afflictions increase or decrease four births;
the three middle grades of afflictions increase or decrease two births;
and the three lower grades of afflictions increase or decrease one birth.

The strengths and weaknesses differ, each successive stage being double that of the preceding one. Question: How is this known? Answer: It is explained that within the nine grades [of afflictions], if three grades are severed, there remain three more births.
It is clearly known that when the upper three grades of afflictions increase or decrease, four births remain;
furthermore, when the middle three grades of afflictions are severed, one birth remains.
It is clearly known that when the middle three grades of afflictions increase or decrease, two births remain.
The lower three grades of afflictions increase or decrease one birth;
if subdivided further, the nine grades of afflictions increase or decrease seven births;
and the upper three grades of afflictions—the uppermost grade—increase or decrease two births.
The superior, middle, and inferior grades of afflictions each increase or decrease one birth;
among the three middle grades of afflictions, the middle-superior grade increases or decreases one birth,
while the middle-middle and middle-inferior grades each increase or decrease half a birth.
If it concerns the three lower grades of afflictions:
the lower-upper grade affliction increases or decreases by half a birth;
the lower-middle and lower-lower grade afflictions together increase or decrease by half a birth. Question: Regarding these three sets of three grades of afflictions...

How is it known that there is distinct increase and decrease? The commentary explains: "The three grades of lower defilements and the three grades of middle defilements are said to involve distinct increase and decrease;
this can be understood from the treatise (*śāstra*).
Although there is no separate explanation in the treatise regarding the three grades of upper defilements," [it is so understood].
The increase and decrease for the middle three grades may be understood by analogy with the lower three grades.
As for the specific increase and decrease of the middle three grades:
among the nine grades, if one has abandoned three grades, there remain three births.
If one has abandoned four grades [of afflictions], there remain two more births;
thus we know that the middle and superior grades [of abandonment] reduce the number of births by one.
If one has abandoned the fourth grade, there remain two more births.
If one severs the sixth [grade of defilement], there remains only one more birth;
thus we know that the medium-medium and medium-low [grades] together increase or decrease one birth.
If one were to speak of them separately, the medium-medium and medium-low [grades] each increase or decrease half a birth.
Although there is no separate textual passage providing an explicit explanation, it must be so by way of reasoning;
otherwise, there would be the fault of excessive addition or subtraction.
If the medium-medium grade [defilement] alone increases or decreases by one unit,
then the medium-inferior grade defilements undergo no increase or decrease.
If it is said that the medium-medium grade increases or decreases by half a birth, then the medium-inferior grades can only increase or decrease the existence at birth (*upapatti-bhava*).
There are intermediate and inferior [beings], but not superior and excellent ones.
Furthermore, the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) and the state of birth (*upapattibhava*) are called "half-births.
However, the karma that draws one's existence (*ākṣepaka-karma*) must be identical and cannot be divided.
Thus, one should know that for the middle-middle and middle-low [levels], the increase and decrease are each half [of a birth]. For example,
while the three middle grades collectively involve an increase or decrease of two births,
when stated individually, the middle-high grade involves an increase or decrease of one birth.
The middle-middle and middle-low [levels of defilement] each increase or decrease by half a birth.
It should be understood that the same applies to the three superior grades of defilement.
In summary, there are four births [resulting from] such increases and decreases.
Setting aside the specific case of the two births involving superior-superior increase and decrease,
there are two cases each for superior-middle and superior-inferior involving both increase and decrease.
If one were to explain these further in detail:
In the cases of the medium-upper and the upper-lower grades, there is an increase or decrease of one [unit] each;
however, if the medium-upper grade alone increases or decreases by two,
then the upper-lower grade afflictions undergo neither increase nor decrease.
If one says that the upper and middle [stages] increase or decrease by one and a half lifetimes,
while the lower and upper [stages] increase or decrease by half a lifetime,
then there would be the fault that the lower and upper are not equal to the middle and upper.
This should be understood as before.
Furthermore, regarding the three lower grades of afflictions:
if six grades have been abandoned, there remains one more birth.
If one has abandoned seven grades and has half a birth remaining, one knows that for the lower-upper and upper-middle grades, there is an increase or decrease of half a birth;
for the middle-lower and lower-lower grades, there is likewise an increase or decrease of half a birth. Question: How is it known that they [all] increase or decrease by one [birth]?
Therefore, the *Mahāvibhāṣā* states:
Question: Since there are two remaining types of fetters (*saṃyojana*), why is it said that there is only one type of "single-seeded" (*ekabījika*)?
Answer: One is not designated as "single-seeded" on account of the presence of two types of fetters.
"Because there exists the seed of karma for one more existence, it is called 'one-seeded' (*ekabījika*)," as stated in the treatise. Question:

If, even when the eighth [birth] is severed, one still undergoes half [a birth], how can it be said that two categories together increase or decrease by half a life? Answer: In reality, there is indeed a ninth category of one grade that increases or decreases by half a life.
Because it is extremely capable of acting as an obstacle,
and because this statement is made with reference to the fact that the eighth category has not yet been abandoned,
it is said that two categories together increase or decrease by half a lifetime.
Among these, there is that which is born called "half-birth.
Since the projecting karma is necessarily the same,
it is impossible to distinguish within it any increase or decrease.
Therefore, they increase and decrease together.

Furthermore, since one undergoes the intermediate existence (*antarābhava*) for the sake of the birth-existence (*upapattibhava*), it is impossible to sever the eighth category [of afflictions] while in the intermediate existence. Thus, one must diminish [the afflictions] within the intermediate existence.
Since they only undergo rebirth,
there is no further separate increase or decrease.
As stated below, the three lower grades collectively describe an increase or decrease of one lifetime.
To speak specifically, the lower and upper grades [of afflictions] each increase or decrease by one small birth (*kalpa*).
The middle-lower and lower-lower grades together increase or decrease by one small birth.
It should be understood that the same applies to the three upper grades of afflictions.
In general, this explains the increase and decrease of the four modes of birth (*yoni*);

specifically, it explains the increase and decrease of two modes of birth through the "superior-superior" (*uttarottara*) [classification], as well as the "superior-middle" (*uttaramadhya*) and "superior-inferior" (*uttarādhamā*) [classifications], which together explain the increase and decrease of two modes of birth.

If one were to further explain the upper, middle, and lower grades by separately increasing or decreasing one birth for each, all other explanations would incur the fault of being either excessive or deficient, as previously stated.
Question: For what reason, among the nine grades, do the second, third, and fourth grades of afflictions each increase or decrease one birth?
The fifth, sixth, and seventh grades of defilements each increase or decrease by half a birth;
their strength is similar. The commentary explains: regarding the nine grades, there is an increase or decrease relative to seven births.
The three upper [stages] increase or decrease by four;
the three middle [stages] increase or decrease by two;
and the three lower [stages] increase or decrease by one.
This is explained by way of resemblance and mutual comparison;
within these three categories, they further compare their own characteristics,
because the first is equal to the latter two.
Furthermore, one cannot use the fourth category before the third and second categories,
nor the seventh category before the sixth and fifth categories; moreover,
if one were to further distinguish between their quantities therein, [it would be as follows].
This would entail the faults of excess or deficiency. Furthermore, it is explained that there are two births involving increase and decrease for the "superior-superior" [grade];
two births involving increase and decrease for the "superior-middle" and "superior-inferior" [grades] combined; and one birth involving increase and decrease for the "middle-superior" [grade].
The middle-middle and middle-low [levels] together increase or decrease one lifetime;
the low-high increases or decreases half a lifetime;
and the low-middle and low-low together increase or decrease half a lifetime.
However, although the eighth grade [of afflictions] may sometimes be severed,
the ninth grade of affliction alone is capable of increasing or decreasing half a lifetime.
Because it is extremely capable of acting as an obstacle, it possesses the power of a distinct condition (*pratyaya*);
it cannot be compared to the sixth or third categories, as they lack such a distinct condition.
Furthermore, another explanation is given:
An increase or decrease of one degree in the highest-of-the-high [grade] affects two lifetimes;
an increase or decrease of one degree in the highest-of-the-low [grade] affects two lifetimes;
an increase or decrease of one degree in the middle-of-the-high [grade] can only provide mutual assistance.
It is not a case of correct increase or decrease,
because its nature is indeterminate as it exists in between,
just like a eunuch.
As in the eighth category, whether there is abandonment or non-abandonment,
the ninth category increases or decreases by half a lifetime,
which is equal to the seventh category.
Each increases or decreases by half a lifetime;
by this standard, it should be known that one grade at the upper or lower limit is equal to the highest-of-the-high grade.
If it is of the middle three grades,
the middle-upper grade increases or decreases one birth,
and the middle-lower grade increases or decreases one birth.
The middle-of-the-middle grade can only assist one another; it does not constitute actual increase or decrease, as previously explained in the general commentary.
As for the three lower grades:
The uppermost grade of the lower level increases or decreases by half a lifetime;
the lowest grade of the lower level increases or decreases by half a lifetime.
The single grade of the middle level of the lower stage can only provide auxiliary assistance and does not constitute a primary increase or decrease.
This is also explained as before.
If the former proponent challenges me as to how the first and third powers, etc.,
are equal to the fourth and sixth powers, etc.
Regarding the seventh and ninth powers and so forth,
I shall also challenge you:
how can the second power be equal to the fourth power?
The fifth and seventh powers are equal; furthermore, it is explained that as long as the nine grades [of afflictions] have not been severed,
one is able to increase or decrease seven births.
However, among them, strength and weakness were unequal;
it was just as when nine people of differing sizes and strengths, some strong and some weak,
together lift a seven-stone rock.
If one has severed one grade [of defilement], the remaining eight grades of affliction will increase or decrease five births;
this is like eight people lifting a five-stone weight together.
Other cases should be understood by analogy.
Thus far, this has been explained by way of seven births;
if one considers fourteen births or twenty-eight births, the same principle applies.
This can be understood by applying the same principles of interpretation.
Having already distinguished the Once-returner up to the abandonment of the ninth [affliction] as the Non-returner fruit,
this now constitutes the third section, clarifying the path and fruit of the Non-returner.
Among these, first,
the path of approach and the fruit of the non-returner are clarified;
second, the distinctions among non-returners are clarified.
This is the first [section], clarifying the candidate for and the fruit of the Non-returner (*anāgāmin*).
It connects the preceding [context] and introduces the following.
Within the response provided in verse, the first three lines clarify the candidate.
The following phrase clarifies the fruit.
Within that, the first two phrases clarify the "one-interval" (ekāvakrāntika) stage,
while the third phrase correctly clarifies the "approach" (pratipannaka).
The Commentary states: "As for the phrase 'the meaning of the limit is as explained before,' this below explains the two preceding lines;
that is, the once-returner proceeds to abandon the remaining afflictions."
If these three conditions are fully met, one is designated as an "ekāyana" (one-interval practitioner);
if any one is lacking, one is not so designated. The first [condition] is due to the abandonment of afflictions.
This is because one has abandoned seven or eight categories of afflictions belonging to the desire realm that are to be abandoned through cultivation;
secondly, it is because one has acquired the untainted faculties (anāsrava-indriya) of the immediate and liberation paths which serve as their antidotes.
Third, by way of rebirth:
because one takes yet another birth among the gods of the desire realm or among humans.
In the verse, only the first and last two conditions are mentioned, and not the attainment of the faculties (*indriya*).
The meaning should be understood as explained previously in the section on the *kulāntara-gāmin* (one who goes to another family).
How is it that a single grade of afflictions (*kleśa*) constitutes an obstruction to attaining the fruit of a non-returner (*anāgāmi*)?
Question:
How does the ninth grade of affliction obstruct the attainment of the fruit of non-returning?
Regarding the statement, "Because by their abandonment one reaches the stage of maturation (*vipāka-bhūmi*)," the answer is:
because by their abandonment, one transcends the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
It was previously stated that karma from the three times constitutes an extreme obstruction;
one should know that afflictions are likewise identical to karma in this regard.
If the ninth [affliction] is severed, [the path is attained].
Because it transcends the stage of the outflow-result of the afflictions bound to that desire realm as well as the stage of the maturation-result,
it constitutes an extreme obstacle.
"Interval" (antara) refers to a separation; one who has reached such a state is called "one-interval" (ekāntarika).
This explains the etymology of the term "one-interval. The preceding [explanation] was based on maturation (vipāka).
Subsequently, the name "ekavīcika" (one-intervener) is explained in terms of the afflictions (*kleśa*).
It is said that one who possesses this single interval is called an ekavīcika.
Furthermore, the *Nyāyānusāra* states:
What is called an "interval" (antara) is another name for a gap;
that is to say, within that state,
by virtue of having a single gap, one obtains a single birth.
"Therefore, one has not yet attained nirvāṇa" refers to the third phrase:
"one immediately abandons the afflictions to be abandoned through cultivation until reaching the untainted faculties."

It should be understood that one who has abandoned seven or eight categories of the afflictions to be abandoned through cultivation is likewise called a candidate for the fruit of non-returner (*anāgāmiphalapratipannaka*).
This is established based on the presence of a single interval (*ekavicika*) and its requisite conditions.
Previously, the distinction between the two was based solely on the abandonment of afflictions;
this refers to the stage of an ordinary person.
Those who first sever three or four grades of afflictions,
or seven or eight grades of afflictions, and then enter the vision of the truths,
subsequently attain the fruit of stream-entry (srotāpanna).
Or at the time of the fruit of once-returning,
until one has yet to cultivate the superior path of the third, fourth, seventh, or eighth category.

Nevertheless, they are not yet designated as "those who go from family to family" (kulaṃkula) or "those with one interval" (ekavicika), because although they possess both conditions, they have not yet established the untainted faculties (anāsrava-indriya) required to counteract those three or four grades of afflictions, or seven or eight grades of afflictions.
Since ancient times, all masters have said that when one was formerly an ordinary person, one severed the five grades of afflictions of the realm of cultivation;
subsequently, at the stage of the fruit of once-returner, one attains the realization of liberation.
Not so. Therefore, the *Vibhāṣā* (158) states: Question:
Suppose one has previously abandoned the five grades of defilement of the desire realm.
Subsequently, one enters the state of right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*).
At the moment the dharma-knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-jñāna*) arises, regarding the five categories of phenomena previously abandoned through the vision of suffering:
Furthermore, regarding the four categories of phenomena abandoned through the vision of suffering that are abandoned at this present time,
one attains the untainted acquisition of dissociation (*anāsrava-visaṃyoga-prāpti*) until the moment the dharma-knowledge of the path (*mārga-dharmajñāna*) arises.
Regarding the five categories of phenomena previously abandoned through the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) and the four categories of phenomena now being abandoned through the path of seeing,

one attains the untainted acquisition of dissociation (*anāsrava-visaṃyoga-prāpti*). As for those five categories of phenomena previously abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), [one likewise attains their dissociation].
"When is the untainted acquisition of dissociation obtained? The Venerable Saṃghavasu stated: "At the time of the subsequent knowledge of the path (mārgānvayajñāna)."
Because at that time, it is called both the fruit of stream-entry and the path of the once-returner;
therefore, their statement is incorrect. Why is this so?
Since at that time one has attained the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpanna*),
and until the path leading to the fruit of once-returner (*sakṛdāgāmin*)— or even a single moment of it— has arisen and become manifest,
how can one be said to be "one who is proceeding toward the fruit of once-returner" (*sakṛdāgāmipratipannaka*)?
Some say that when one undertakes the path of preparation for the fruit of once-returner,
it is because this is subsumed under the stage of being a candidate for once-returner.
Other masters say that it is attained at the time of attaining the fruit of once-returner,
because this occurs while abiding in the sixth uninterrupted path (*ānantarya-mārga*).

It is able to induce the arising of the untainted acquisition of disjunction (*anāsrava-visaṃyoga-prāpti*) regarding the dharmas abandoned through seeing (*darśana-heya*) within the three realms, as well as the first six categories of dharmas abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) in the desire realm,
because one thereby attains the fruit of the Once-returner (*sakṛdāgāmin*).
According to this explanation,
one definitely gives rise to the path of superior progress from the fruit of stream-entry;
it is attained at the time that [the path] manifests.
When one proceeds from a lower fruit toward a higher fruit by means of the path of superior progress,
one must necessarily cultivate the paths that serve as the antidotes for the various fetters of the higher stages previously abandoned. This is because,
when the ninth [category of fetter] is abandoned, it constitutes the collective abandonment of all [fetters].
Explaining the fourth phrase:
if one abandons the ninth [defilement], one achieves the fruit of non-returning (*anāgāmiphala*).
Because one will certainly not return to be born in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), it is called the fruit of non-returning.
This fruit of non-returning is also called the "severance of the five lower fetters," particularly for one who transcends [the realms] by leaping.
First, one abandons the two fetters of greed and hatred;
subsequently, one abandons the three fetters of the view of a self-identity, attachment to precepts and rituals, and doubt—
for those who follow the gradual path.
First, one abandons the three fetters of satkāyadṛṣṭi, śīlavrataparāmarśa, and vicikitsā;
subsequently, one abandons the two fetters of rāga and pratigha.
Although one must first abandon either [the former] or the latter two.
Or there are three;
however, because they are abandoned collectively at this time,
it is called the abandonment of the five lower fetters (*pañcāvarabhāgīya-saṃyojana*).
Based on the stage of the non-returner (anāgāmin) up to those who attain parinirvāṇa while dwelling here;
this is the second section concerning the distinctions among non-returners. Within this:
First, the seven types of non-returners are explained;
second, the nine types of non-returners are explained;
third, the seven virtuous non-returners are explained.
Fourth, it clarifies that [beings] are not born in the higher realms;
fifth, it clarifies the mixed cultivation of dhyāna;
sixth, it clarifies that there are only five Pure Abodes.
7. Explaining the Body-Witness Non-Returner: This is the first [section], explaining the seven types of non-returners.
It is presented according to the arising of the Sūtra and is distinguished by citing the verse.
The Commentary states: Regarding those who are called "Upstreamers" (ūrdhvasrotas), these Non-returners (anāgāmin) are generally said to be of seven types when categorized across the three realms.
For now, however, we shall discuss five types based on their specific practices within the form realm (rūpadhātu).
Their names may be known from the list.
Among these five, the first four attain parinirvāṇa definitively within this very body.
This is why they are designated by the specific term "parinirvāṇa.
Among those who ascend to higher realms (*ūrdhvasrotas*), some may undergo many births before finally attaining parinirvāṇa;
it is not the case that all who ascend necessarily attain nirvāṇa.
Because it is not fixed, one does not say "parinirvāṇa. As for the explanation of the term:
because one attains parinirvāṇa in the interval between the two realms of existence, it is called "intermediate parinirvāṇa" (antarā-parinirvāṇa).
It should be understood in this way: once this has arisen,
it proceeds by means of the path that exists.
Because they attain parinirvāṇa through the path of non-application,
these three types of persons— namely, those who attain parinirvāṇa upon rebirth and so forth— are so designated.
Because these two types of beings, having been born, flow upward toward higher realms, they are called "Upstreamers" (ūrdhvasrotas).
Regarding the term "one who attains parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state" (antarāparinirvāyin),
this is explained separately below.

Regarding those who attain parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state (*antarāparinirvāyin*): this refers to one who, having passed away from the desire realm and proceeding toward the form realm, while abiding in the state of the intermediate existence (*antarābhava*),
gives rise to the noble path that should manifest in their place of rebirth.

Having severed the remaining afflictions and attained arhatship, one immediately enters parinirvāṇa without remainder; therefore, this is called "parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state" (antarā-parinirvāyin).
Thus, the *Abhidharmamahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 174, states:
Having passed away from that state, one arises as an intermediate existence (*antarābhava*) in the form realm;
while abiding in that intermediate existence, one attains a type of untainted path (*anāsravamārga*) such that,
by means of this path, one proceeds to abandon the remaining fetters (*saṃyojana*).
One who attains parinirvāṇa within the realm of nirvana without remainder is called one who attains parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state (*antarāparinirvāyin*).

According to the *Abhidharmamahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, "intermediate" (*antara*) is explained in reference to the realm of nirvana without remainder. Furthermore, another interpretation states: [text continues].
It also extends to *parinirvāṇa* with remainder;
the *Abhidharmamahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* does not mention it because its characteristics are not manifest and thus it is omitted.
How could one who has already severed the afflictions enter the remainderless [nirvāṇa] in the very second moment?

Therefore, it is known that this also applies to the state with remainder. Question: From which stage does the noble path arise? Answer: It arises from the fundamental path of the stage to which one is destined to be born.
Because this pleasant path arises easily, it does not arise in the *anāgamya*,
the intermediate state (*dhyānāntara*), or the formless realm (*ārūpya*);
because this painful path arises with great difficulty.
Even after attaining the state of one beyond training (aśaikṣa), they are likewise unable to give rise [to it];

as explained in detail in the *Vibhāṣā* (175). Regarding the statement "one who attains parinirvāṇa upon rebirth" up to "one who has a remainder of the substrate of existence" (sopadhiśeṣa): [this refers to those who attain nirvāṇa in the intermediate state, at the time of birth, or after having been born.]
Regarding those who attain parinirvāṇa upon birth (upapadyaparinirvāyin):
this refers to those who, having passed away from the desire realm and gone to the form realm,
are able to give rise to the noble path not long after being born there.
Having severed the remaining afflictions, he becomes an Arhat and attains parinirvāṇa,
owing to his possession of both the path of diligent cultivation and the path of swift progress.
Therefore, having been born, they attain parinirvāṇa before long.

By specifying "having been born," they are distinguished from those who attain parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state (*antarāparinirvāyin*). Because they possess both paths, they are distinguished from those who attain parinirvāṇa through exertion (*sābhisaṃskāraparinirvāyin*) or without exertion (*anabhisaṃskāraparinirvāyin*).
Regarding the parinirvāṇa spoken of as occurring "in this very life," this refers to the state with remainder;
only when one's lifespan later comes to an end does one enter the state without remainder.

Therefore, the explanation of "attaining parinirvāṇa upon rebirth" (upapadyaparinirvāyin) is based on the state with remainder (sopadhiśeṣa) and does not rely on the state without remainder (nirupadhiśeṇa).
As for why nirvāṇa is not separately explained within the category of "attaining parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state" (antarāparinirvāyin),
it is because its characteristics are not manifest there.
The subsequent [categories], such as those with practice (*śaikṣa*), etc., can be understood by analogy;
therefore, they are not explained here.
Other masters state that there is also the "without remainder" (*anupadhiśeṣa*).
Other masters say that birth-attainment (upapadya-parinirvāyin) applies not only to those with a remainder of substrate (sopadhiśeṣa),
but also according to those without a remainder (nirupadhiśeṣa).
Because one enters the remainderless [nirvāṇa] immediately after having abandoned the afflictions, it encompasses both types.
This master’s intention is that this is identical to the case of one who attains parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state (*antarāparinirvāyin*);
for such a person, having exhausted all remaining afflictions and attained parinirvāṇa with a remainder, [then enters the remainderless state].
As for the argument that "one who is without delusion moistens birth but does not seek existence in birth,

thus attaining parinirvāṇa without remainder; by analogy, one who attains parinirvāṇa upon rebirth (*upapadya-parinirvāyin*) likewise lacks a basis for remainder (*anupadhiśeṣa*)," this is unreasonable because it would lead to a lack of mastery.
The author of the treatise refutes this,
stating: "This is not reasonable,
because within that realm of form (rūpadhātu), one lacks mastery over voluntarily relinquishing life and entering nirvāṇa."
One who, at the very moment of birth, exhausts all remaining afflictions is called "one who attains parinirvāṇa upon birth" (upapadya-parinirvāyin).
Since they attain parinirvāṇa without remainder only after their lifespan has later come to an end,
the explanation of "attaining parinirvāṇa upon birth" does not refer to the state of being without remainder (anupadhiśeṣa).
Therefore, the *Nyāyānusāra* states: "One is said to be 'attaining parinirvāṇa upon birth' (*upapadya-parinirvāyin*) with reference to the state of having a remainder of support (*sopadhiśeṣa*);
it does not mean that one attains parinirvāṇa without remainder (*nirupadhiśeṣa*) immediately upon being born."
Because he lacks mastery over the relinquishing of his life-span;
as for the one who attains parinirvāṇa through exertion (sābhisaṃskāra-parinirvāyin) because he has not reached the path of rapid progress—
this refers to the one who attains parinirvāṇa through exertion.
That is to say, one who passes away from the desire realm and is reborn in the form realm,
having practiced with application for a long time after birth,
attains parinirvāṇa with a remainder only through great effort.
Because this involves only diligent cultivation, it is called "with application" (*sābhisamskāra*); because there is no rapid progress, it is called "without swift advancement" (*anabhisamskāra*).

The term "having been born" (*upapanna*) distinguishes it from the one who attains parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state (*antarāparinirvāyin*); "for a long time" (*cirakāla*) distinguishes it from the one who attains parinirvāṇa upon birth (*upapadyaparinirvāyin*).
Regarding the statement that "there is diligent cultivation,

distinguished from the absence of practice" and that "the one who attains parinirvāṇa without practice [does so] because they reach the path of swift progress": as for the one who attains parinirvāṇa without practice...
This refers to one who passes away from the desire realm and is reborn in the form realm;
having been born there for a long time, they become indolent in their application and,
without much effort, enter parinirvāṇa with a remainder.
Because it lacks both the path of diligent cultivation and the path of rapid progress, it is called "without application" (*anabhisamskāra*).
The term "having been born" distinguishes it from one who attains parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state; "after a long time" distinguishes it from one who attains parinirvāṇa upon being reborn.
"Omitting diligent cultivation and distinguishing it from 'having practice'":
some say that these two lead to the attainment of nirvāṇa;
this is a citation of a divergent view.
Those who attain nirvana by severing afflictions through a conditioned noble path are said to be "with practice" (sābhoga).
Those who attain nirvana by severing afflictions through an unconditioned noble path are said to be "without practice" (anabhoga).

Regarding the statement that "this explanation is unreasonable because it entails the fault of over-extension," the Master of the Treatise refutes it by showing that those who attain parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state (*antarāparinirvāyin*),
upon being born (*upapadyaparinirvāyin*), and so forth, also eliminate afflictions by taking both conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) phenomena as their objects.
They should also be called "with effort" (*sābhisaṃskāra*) and "without effort" (*anabhisaṃskāra*).
However, regarding those who attain parinirvāṇa upon arrival,
this describes the Sautrāntika interpretation.
However, in the sūtras, the state of attaining parinirvāṇa without exertion is taught first,
followed by the state of attaining parinirvāṇa with exertion;
this sequence is consistent with reason.
The Master’s intention accords with the Sautrāntika school,
for they maintain that there is a path of swift progress through practice without exertion,
whereby even those who do not engage in formal cultivation achieve realization.
There is no path of rapid progress for one who practices with diligence;
this is because a person who possesses practice achieves accomplishment,
or because one who lacks practice yet possesses [the potential for] practice is able to achieve the fruit of arhatship.
A person of non-practice gives rise to the path of swift progress and attains parinirvāṇa without effort;
a person of practice gives rise to diligent cultivation and must attain parinirvāṇa through effort. Based on this principle, one further explains "attaining parinirvāṇa upon rebirth."

Because they have attained the most superior path and their latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) are the most feeble, they attain parinirvāṇa shortly after birth; thus they are called "attaining parinirvāṇa upon birth" (*upapadya-parinirvāyin*).
As for those called "those who go upstream" (*ūrdhva-srotas*), they attain parinirvāṇa only upon reaching [the highest realm].
This refers to those born in the form realm who, after two births or more, attain parinirvāṇa;
they are collectively termed "Upstreamers" (*ūrdhva-srotas*).
Because they proceed only upward and do not flow downward, they are called "Upstreamers."
Although ordinary beings (pṛthagjana) may also be "those who go upstream" (ūrdhvasrotas),
they are not designated as such because they also flow downward;
it is only those who reach the ultimate limit who are called "those who go upstream."
This clarifies the distinctions regarding those who proceed upward (ūrdhvasrotas). To provide a brief explanation of this section:
it refers to those who attain parinirvāṇa while still within the dhyānas.
A separate explanation of the "Mixed Cultivation" (miśra-bhāvanā) and the "Upstreamer" (ūrdhva-srotas). Within this, there are three types:
first, the "Total Leaper" (pluta), who is born first among the Brahmakāyika gods and subsequently born in Akaniṣṭha.
To leap directly over the fourteen intermediate celestial realms is called "complete leaping" (*skanda*). Second is "half-leaping":
within the sixteen celestial realms of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), one gradually and sequentially descends from those Brahmakāyika heavens down to the lower Pure Abodes (*śuddhāvāsa*).
One may leap over thirteen bases or twelve bases,
or even in the interim,
leap over a single base.
One is born in Akaniṣṭha;
because one transcends [the intermediate heavens] but not entirely, it is called "half-leaping.
A noble one (ārya) will certainly never be born in the realm of Mahābrahmā.
Because it is the locus for the arising of heterodox views regarding precepts and prohibitions,
and because they claim to be teachers of the ultimate singular path,
one is not reborn there.
Because the principle of non-arising and non-conceptualization lies beyond the reach of words, it is not separately distinguished;
alternatively, it may be understood as implicitly revealing that this "half-surpassing human" [attainment] requires at least three births within the sixteen heavens.
First, one is born among the Brahmakāyika gods;
next, one is born in one of the fourteen heavens;
finally, one is born in Akaniṣṭha. At most, one undergoes fifteen births.
Regarding the sixteen heavens, according to their respective circumstances, they skip one in the middle and are born in the remaining fifteen. Third is "universal destruction":
from that Brahmakāyika heaven, they are gradually born into the subsequent fourteen celestial abodes.
They take birth everywhere;
only at the very end are they able to be born in Akaniṣṭha.
Because they die in every location, it is called "universal dissolution" (sarvacyuta).
"All places" refers to the sixteen places.
There is no non-returner who undergoes a second birth in a place where they have already been born,
because such a person may seek further progress within that birth and thus ascend to a higher realm.
Because he does not seek equality, he is not reborn in a higher state;
because he does not seek inferiority, he is not reborn in a lower state.
It is precisely for this reason that the meaning of "Non-returner" (anāgāmin) is fulfilled.
Because they are no longer reborn in the places where they were previously born, they do not even take birth in their original place, much less in a lower one.
It is precisely by this principle that it is shown that when a noble one is about to be born [in the form realm], they are not designated as "Non-returners" (anāgāmin).
However, there is the sense of "rebirth" in a single location;
thus, the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 174, states:
"Furthermore, an noble one (*ārya*) born in the desire realm is not called a non-returner (*anāgāmin*)."
They are thus designated as "those who return seven times at most" (saptakṛtparama) and so forth.
Therefore, even when reborn in higher or lower realms, they may be reborn again in the same place.
A noble one (ārya) who is born into a higher realm is called an "Non-returner" (anāgāmin).
Therefore, one is born only in the higher realms and is not born again [in the lower ones].
By this principle, the meaning of "Non-returner" (Anāgāmin) is fulfilled;
for if one is not even born in one's own original realm, how much less could one be born in the lower realms? This concludes the preceding section of the treatise. Furthermore, the summary states:

It should be understood that among the two types of *ūrdhvasrotas*, this refers to those who attain parinirvāṇa in Akaniṣṭha due to the cause of having practiced the meditative absorptions with intermingling (*vyavakīrṇa-dhyāna*);
others attain parinirvāṇa only upon reaching [the respective levels] within the form realm.
To provide a separate explanation for those who do not practice mixed meditation (*miśrabhāvanā*) among the "Upstreamers" (*ūrdhvasrotas*):
there are other types of Upstreamers who have not practiced mixed meditation within the dhyānas.
They are able to go as far as the Peak of Existence (bhavāgra) before attaining parinirvāṇa;
that is to say, they previously lacked the practice of mixed dhyāna,
because their craving for the flavors of the four dhyānas served as the condition for rebirth there.
Passing away from here, they are reborn throughout the eleven abodes of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*),
except that they cannot go to the five Pure Abodes (*śuddhāvāsa*).
Furthermore, they pass away from the Bṛhatphala heaven of the form realm.
Having successively been reborn in the three lower formless realms,
one is finally reborn in the Peak of Existence (bhavāgra) and there attains parinirvāṇa;
this should be understood as the "one who flows upward through the blissful concentrations" (sukhavihāry-ūrdhvaja).
In fifteen locations,
one undergoes two births by leaping entirely;
in the case of partial leaping, there are at least three births.
At most there are fourteen births;
including the universal dissolution, there are fifteen births.
Thus, the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 174, states:
Furthermore, there are three types of those who ascend in succession (*ūrdhvasrotas*):
first, the one who leaps entirely (*pluta*); second, the one who leaps halfway (*ardhapluta*).
Regarding those who pass away from all stages and leap entirely:

this refers to one who passes away from the desire realm and is reborn in the Heaven of the Brahma-multitude (Brahmapārisadya), and passing away from the Heaven of the Brahma-multitude, is reborn in the Akaniṣṭha heaven.
Or one is born in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception and attains parinirvāṇa. As for the "half-leaper":
this refers to one who passes away from the desire realm and is born in the Heaven of the Brahma-multitude;
having passed away from the Heaven of the Brahma-multitude, they are born in any of the higher celestial realms, or are born again in a single location.
Sometimes two, three, four, or five;
or even skipping over only one stage, they are born everywhere else before finally being born in Akaniṣṭha.

Or one is born in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception and attains parinirvāṇa. As for "passing away from all places," this refers to passing away from the desire realm and being born in the Heaven of the Brahma-multitude;
or passing away from the Heaven of the Brahma-multitude and being born in the Heaven of the Ministers of Brahma.
In this manner, they are born successively in the higher realms up to the Bṛhatphala heaven.
Beyond this, there are two distinct paths.
There are two types of entry: first, entry into the Śuddhāvāsa heavens; second, entry into the formless realms (*ārūpya*). Regarding entry into the Śuddhāvāsa heavens:

one passes away from the Bṛhatphala heaven and is reborn in the Avṛha heaven, proceeding in succession until being reborn in the Akaniṣṭha heaven, where one attains parinirvāṇa. Regarding entry into the formless realms: one passes away from the Bṛhatphala heaven and is reborn in the Sphere of Infinite Space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*).

Proceeding in succession up to being born in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana) and there attaining parinirvāṇa—just as there are no two distinct paths in all the stages, one should know that it is the same for the "complete leaper" (sakalābhisambhinna) and the "half-leaper" (ardhapluta).
To explain the term "Brahmapurohita heaven": [it refers to those who have previously practiced the Brahma-conduct].
The Brahma King wishes to go out and takes his place in the vanguard;
or he is in the vanguard. Furthermore, the *Abhidharmamahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* states:

Question: It is said that one who falls from the first dhyāna and is reborn among the Brahmakāyika devas may become a "full-leaper," a "half-leaper," or one who "vanishes everywhere" and proceeds upstream.
If such a person were to fall from the second dhyāna and be reborn among the Parīttābha devas, [would they likewise attain those states?]
If one falls back from the third dhyāna and is reborn among the Śuddhāvāsa deities,
or falls back from the fourth dhyāna and is reborn among the Anabhraka deities and so forth,
can such a person also achieve the "complete leap" (skandha-pratāpana), the "half-leap" (ardhapluta), or the "falling away everywhere" (sarvasthānacyuta) types of *ūrdhvasrotas*?
Some say this is not possible,
because for one born in the Brahma-world, there is no further deficiency regarding the places where they ought to be reborn in the higher realms;
it is based on that [possibility of deficiency] that the categories of "complete leaper," "half-leaper," and "one who dies in all places" are established.
Because one who falls back and is reborn in a higher stage lacks [the full sequence],
the "Complete Leaper" (kūṭastha) and other such attainments are not established based on that case.
Some say that such a person may also be called a "Half-Leaper" (ardhapluta).
Because they transcend a small portion of the intermediate state,
some say they also obtain the designation "complete" in three ways;
they further state that from the time of death in the desire realm, wherever one is reborn, [one obtains these].

Furthermore, it can also be established that within those very places where they are to be reborn, there are those who leap entirely (sakalābhisārin), those who leap halfway (ardhapluta), and those who vanish from all locations (sarvasthānacyuta).
Question: If a non-returner (anāgāmin) passes away in the desire realm (kāmadhātu) and is reborn in the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu), [how is this categorized]?
Can one also achieve the "complete leap-over" (*sakalābhisamkrama*) and so forth? Some say it cannot;
others say that it may also be termed a "half-leap-over" (*ardhābhisamkrama*).
Some say that these are also fully possessed [of the three types]; the reasons for this are all as explained previously.
Regarding the phrase "among the two types of *ūrdhvasrotas*, those who go to the form realm (*rūpadhātu*)":
this clarifies the differences between the two types of *ūrdhvasrotas*.
Regarding the two types of *ūrdhvasrotas* (those who ascend),
there is a distinction between those who prioritize insight first and then tranquility, and those who prioritize meditative absorption first and then wisdom.
Regarding the two types of *ūrdhvasrotas* (those who stream upwards), it is not contrary to reason that they attain parinirvāṇa in the lower stages after having been reborn there twice or more;
yet, it is said that their ultimate destination is the Akaniṣṭha heaven or the Bhavāgra heaven.
Because there is no further place of rebirth beyond this limit,
just as for a stream-enterer who is subject to at most seven more births,
among which there may also be one or two births and so forth.
Furthermore, to summarize:
these five are called those who proceed to the form realm (*rūpadhātu-gāmin*).
Although those who delight in meditative concentration (*samādhi-rata*) and ascend to the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*), they are included herein.
Because they have previously been born in the form realm, they are also called "those who proceed to the form realm" (*rūpaga*).
These are included among the five types of non-returners (*anāgāmin*) who are "up-streamers" (*ūrdhvasrotas*).
As for those who proceed to the formless realm (*ārūpyaga*), when they are completed, they constitute the six types of non-returners.
The preceding section explained the first six phrases;
this explains the seventh phrase,
clarifying the four types of non-returners in the formless realm.
There are four distinctions regarding those who practice the formless [attainments]:
namely, those who, while residing in the desire realm, pass away from there and are reborn not in the form realm, but by leaping over it, are born in the formless realm.
Within this, there are only four distinct types,
due to the distinctions such as "attaining parinirvāṇa upon rebirth" (upapadyaparinirvāyin) and so forth;
among the five previously mentioned, only the "attaining parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state" (antarāparinirvāyin) is excluded.
These four together are called "formless non-returners.
This single formless [non-returner],
along with the five preceding types, constitutes the six non-returners.
Furthermore, there are those who do not proceed [to the higher realms], which, together with the previous six, constitute seven;
this explains the eighth phrase. This clarifies the one who attains parinirvāṇa in the present life (dṛṣṭadharma-parinirvāyin).
Furthermore, there are those who do not proceed to the realm of form or the formless realm,
but instead attain the fruit of non-returning while remaining within this very birth in the desire realm.
Having attained that fruit, they...
One who is able to attain parinirvāṇa in this very life is called one who attains parinirvāṇa in the present life (dṛṣṭadharma-parinirvāyin).

This includes those such as the family-to-family (kulaṃkula), once-returner (sakṛdāgāmin), and one-interval (ekavicika) practitioners, even if they have already undergone seven births within the desire realm.
In this stage, they are also called those who attain parinirvāṇa upon manifestation (dṛṣṭadharma-parinirvāyin).
This single type of manifest-attainer,
together with the six preceding types, constitutes the seven kinds of non-returners (anāgāmin).

Regarding the statement that "nine distinct types are established based on reaching the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) during their course," this is the second section clarifying the nine non-returners (*anāgāmin*).
The treatise states: "Based on reaching [the form realm], nine types are established."
This is the general heading. "What are the three?
is the question.
Regarding the statement that there is a distinction among those who are reborn in the intermediate state and those who ascend to the higher realms:
the answer is,
"How is it that each of the three types is further divided into three?"
He asked again about the nine types.
Regarding the one who attains parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state up to the one who is without confusion or loss,
he replied:
The intermediate parinirvāṇa is divided into three types:
first, the swift;
second, the non-swift.
Three [types of beings] attain parinirvāṇa after a long time.
The three similes of the sparks should be understood as before.
Therefore, the *Nyāyānusāra* states:
From the first arising up to those who attain parinirvāṇa in the distant, near, or at the place of rebirth—there are also three types of those who attain parinirvāṇa upon rebirth:
first, those who attain it with effort; second, those who attain it with exertion.
Because there are three types of parinirvāṇa without exertion, there are likewise three types of those who go upstream (*ūrdhvasrotas*):
first, the one who transcends entirely (*pluta*); second, the one who transcends halfway (*ardhapluta*).
Because there is no distinction among the three [turns], and because each of the three is not a single [type] but consists of three kinds, these three sets are collectively called the "nine types.
Furthermore, all nine types are divided into nine based on whether they attain parinirvāṇa quickly, not quickly, or after a long duration.
They gaze at one another without confusion or error.
The three [realms] in the middle are swift;
the three births are not swift.
Regarding the three sūtras on the "Upstreamer" (Urdhvasrotas),
each of these three categories is further divided into three types:
first, the "swift" (kṣipra).
Second, it is not swift;
third, it takes a long time.
Thus, these three types differ in that they take a long time to reach [their goal].
This is the general heading for the separate explanation of the three types and nine types of non-returners (*anāgāmin*). As for the phrase "first,
they are generally established as three because of the distinctions in their faculties (*indriya*)," it means:
This specifically clarifies the three types of non-returners (*anāgāmin*). Briefly stated,
they are established as three because,
by performing and accumulating karma conducive to rebirth, they are termed "those who attain parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state" (*antarāparinirvāyin*).
Among these, there is that called "arising" (*utpāda*),
so named because it arises momentarily facing toward what is to be born,
as has already been explained previously.
Because they perform and accumulate karma conducive to rebirth in the next life, they are called "attaining parinirvāṇa upon rebirth" (upapadyaparinirvāyin).
Because they perform and accumulate karma conducive to a subsequent life, they are called "those who go upstream" (ūrdhvasrotas).
These three types are thus explained and assigned according to their respective order.
Alternatively, according to their respective order, those who attain parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state are of inferior grade;
those who attain parinirvāṇa upon rebirth are of middling grade;
and those who go upstream are of superior grade.
They are divided into three types due to differences in the manifestation of their afflictions:
those who attain parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state (antarāparinirvāyin) possess superior faculties; those who attain parinirvāṇa upon rebirth (upapadyaparinirvāyin) possess middling faculties.
Because there are distinctions between those who ascend and those with dull faculties, they are divided into three types.
Each of these three further branches into nine distinct categories, resulting in a total of twenty-seven.
This specifically clarifies the nine types of non-returners (*anāgāmin*):
the three— intermediate (*antarāparinirvāyin*), one who is reborn [in the higher realms] (*upapadyaparinirvāyin*),
and one who proceeds upward (*ūrdhvasrotas*)— each, as appropriate, possesses distinctions based on karma, afflictions (*kleśa*), and faculties (*indriya*).
Because each of these three has three distinct varieties, they constitute nine types.
These three are not all necessarily due to karma, afflictions, and faculties;
rather, it is said "according to what is appropriate."
The general categories are largely the same;
within them, a detailed explanation reveals that there are indeed distinctions— namely, the first two and the third,
which refers to the first two and the third among the three sets of three.
That is to say, among these, there are three births;
however, they each constitute three types solely due to differences in afflictions and faculties,
not due to differences in karma.
The three types of those who attain parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state (antarāparinirvāyin) equally experience the karma that initiates existence, as there is no distinction between them.
The three types of those who attain parinirvāṇa upon being born (upapadyaparinirvāyin) equally experience the karma of birth.
Because there is no distinction [among them],
the latter three types of *ūrdhvasrotas* (those who flow upwards) are divided into three kinds not only due to differences in their afflictions and faculties,
but also because of differences in their *aparaparyāya-vedanīya-karma* (karma to be experienced in subsequent lives).

Regarding the "Upstreamer" (ūrdhvasrotas), three types are distinguished based on the differences in their karma: those who leap entirely (pluta), those who leap halfway (ardhapluta), and those who die everywhere (sarvasthānacyuta). As for what is called "karma to be experienced in a subsequent life" (aparaparyāya-vedanīya-karman), it does not refer solely to the determinate karma to be experienced in a subsequent life among the four types of karma.
Since noble ones (*ārya*) also create indeterminate karma (*aniyata-karma*),

the term "karma to be experienced in a subsequent life" (*aparaparyāya-vedanīya-karma*) is stated in contrast to [karma] to be experienced in the intermediate [life] (*antara-bhava*) or the [present] birth (*upapadya*). Furthermore, another interpretation holds that, in actual fact, noble ones also create indeterminate karma.

This passage speaks, for the time being, of karma to be experienced in a subsequent life (*aparaparyāya-vedanīya-karma*). Question: For example, one who is born in the Form Realm (*rūpadhātu*) as an "upward-streamer" (*ūrdhva-srotas*) possessing both bliss and wisdom may be reborn in all five Pure Abodes (*śuddhāvāsa*).
Should he not be designated as "reborn" (*jāti*) at the very beginning?
The second [category], "already gone," is called "subsequent" (*paścāt*).

How is this passage designated as "conducive to the subsequent" (*paścātpādaka*) in its entirety? The explanation says: when one is in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), one creates the projecting karma (*ākṣepaka-karman*) for the five Pure Abodes (*śuddhāvāsa*).
If it were not so, how could it be called "subsequent"? Furthermore, another explanation says that one also creates [karma] conducive to the next birth (*upapadyavedanīya*).
As for the latter statement, it is said from the perspective of the majority.

If this interpretation is adopted, then in the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) one also creates the projecting karma (*ākṣepaka-karman*) for the Pure Abodes (*śuddhāvāsa*). Furthermore, according to another interpretation, one also creates the karma conducive to rebirth (*upapadyavedanīya*).
Regarding the phrase "conforming to what follows":
it is called "following" because it is spoken in contrast to the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) and the state of birth (*upapatti*). The summary can be understood accordingly.
If that is so, why is it said, "because one goes toward existence but does not return"?
This is the third clarification concerning the seven destinations of the noble beings (*saptasatpuruṣagati*).
If there are nine types of non-returners (*anāgāmin*) who proceed to the form realm (*rūpadhātu*),
why does the Buddha state in the sūtras that there are only seven destinations of the noble beings?
Regarding the question and the response in verse,
the *Śāstra* states: "Up to 'and established as one,' this explains the two preceding lines."
The intermediate state and those born [in the form realm] each consist of two types, which are further divided into three;
the "Upstreamer" (ūrdhvasrotas) constitutes one.
Based on this, the Sūtra establishes the seven destinies of the noble person (satpuruṣagati).
This means that because those who go upstream (ūrdhvaṃsrotas) possess the dharma of going upstream, they are called "those who go upstream.
For this reason, although there are three types [of such persons], they are established as one due to their shared characteristics.
Furthermore, the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 175, states:
Question: Just as there are three types each for those who are born [in the intermediate state] and those who are not born [there], the same applies to those who go upstream (*ūrdhvasrotas*):
namely, those who leap entirely (*pluta*), those who leap halfway (*ardhapluta*), and those who pass away in every place (*sarvasthānacyuta*).
Why is it said to be one? Answer:
Birth and non-birth each constitute a single continuity of existence (*bhava-saṃtati*).
Within this, the distinctions between its various states are difficult to discern.
In order that [the distinctions] may be understood, three types are each explained;
the number of births for the three types of *ūrdhvasrotas* is distinguished by itself so that their differences are easily known.
Therefore, following the principle that the superior meaning takes precedence, these are explained as a single type.
Furthermore, since the duration of both arising and non-arising is brief, there is only so much that can be established regarding their distinct characteristics.
Therefore, they are divided into three.

As for the "Upstreamer" (ūrdhvasrotas), because there are many distinctions regarding the duration of their time and it is difficult to discern their specific limits, they are combined and established as one. Furthermore, there is also the sense of "arising" and "not arising" being equal.
The upward-streaming [attainment] also has a distinct meaning.

Because one wishes to clarify these two passages through their mutual illumination, this statement was made. Furthermore, the characteristics of the destination of the noble beings (satpuruṣagati) regarding birth and non-birth are easily understood when they manifest before one.
Because they each quickly attain parinirvāṇa, they are each divided into three types.
As for those who proceed to the upper realms (ūrdhvasrotas), the characteristics of their path as noble beings (satpuruṣagati) are subtle, hidden, and difficult to discern.

Because they still undergo many births and deaths, it is appropriate to speak of them collectively as one. One interpretation states: "those who are born" refers to the existence of birth (*upapatti-bhava*), while "those who are not born" refers to the intermediate state (*antarābhava*).
Why rely solely on this [distinction] until there is no difference?
The following two lines pose a question:
Why is it that the "destination of the noble person" (satpuruṣagati) is established based on these [two] alone,
and not based on the remaining noble learners (śaikṣa), such as stream-enterers (srotāpanna) and once-returners (sakṛdāgāmin)?
"Going" (gati) has the meaning of "proceeding.
As for the remaining learners—the stream-enterers and once-returners—they proceed by means of wholesome karma no differently than the non-returners;
therefore, it is only these seven types who are established as "noble beings' destinies" (satpuruṣagati).
Answer: Only these seven types all practice wholesome karma and do not perform unwholesome karma;
others, such as stream-enterers (*srotāpanna*) and so forth, are not like this.
Because although they practice wholesome deeds, they also practice unwholesome ones;
furthermore, only those who practice the seven types of conduct proceed to the higher realms and no longer return to take birth in the desire realm.
Because others, such as stream-enterers and so forth, are not like this—
since they do not ascend to the higher realms but are born only in the desire realm—
it is based solely on this that the "destination of the virtuous person" (satpuruṣagati) is established.
"If that is so, for what reason [is it said] 'up to and including the full explanation'?
This is an objection. "If that is so, why does the Sūtra state:"
What is a virtuous person?
It refers to one who has accomplished the right view of a trainee (*śaikṣa*),
and so forth, as explained at length.
Being fully endowed with the eightfold noble path,
those in training are all called "noble persons" (satpuruṣa).
For what reason, then, is it said that others do not belong to the destiny of a noble person?
Regarding "all other learners (śaikṣa) who go up to the higher realms":
this refers generally to all other learners, such as stream-enterers (srotāpanna) and so forth.
If one considers it from another perspective, those who have accomplished the eightfold path may also be said to possess the nature of a true person (*satpuruṣa*),
because all those in training (*śaikṣa*) accomplish the eightfold path.
Because they have attained the ultimate restraint of non-action regarding the five types of unwholesome deeds— killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, false speech, and drinking intoxicants—
and because the unwholesome afflictions have for the most part been abandoned.
They should be called "virtuous persons.
The seven courses of virtuous persons now established do not rely on different perspectives.
Because they practice only what is wholesome and do not engage in what is unwholesome,
and because they rely solely on superior causes to ascend to the higher realms, they are established as the "destinies of noble beings" (satpuruṣagati).
Furthermore, the *Abhidharmamahāvibhāṣā* states:
It is asked, there are five matters in which a non-returner who proceeds to the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) excels over a non-returner who proceeds to the form realm (*rūpadhātu*).
Namely: excellence of realm, excellence of stage, excellence of abandonment of afflictions, excellence of attenuation of the aggregates, and excellence of meditative attainments (*samāpatti*).
Why is it not established as a destination for noble beings (*satpuruṣagati*)?
Some say: "If something is coarse, manifest, and easy to understand, it is established as a destination for noble beings;
since this [state] is neither manifest nor clearly understood, it is not so described."
It is as explained at length there. Furthermore, it says:
Question: Why is the Arhat not considered a "destination of the virtuous" (*satpuruṣagati*)?
Answer: Moreover, those who proceed toward higher rebirths are established as the "destinations of the virtuous."
The Arhat is without further birth;
therefore, he is not established [as such]. Furthermore, those who proceed toward a higher fruit are established as "noble beings" (satpuruṣa-gati);
the Arhat is precisely that higher fruit.
There is no further fruit to be attained;
therefore, it is not established,
as explained at length in that [text].
All those who abide in the noble stages, up to those who have not yet refined their faculties (*indriya*) and those who have fallen away—
this constitutes the fourth [point], clarifying that they do not take birth in the higher realms.
The preceding two lines clarify that they do not take birth in the upper [realms].
The final two lines clarify that there is no falling away from the refinement of faculties (*indriya-saṃcāra*).
The Treatise says: "Reaching the ultimate Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*)" means that one intends to be reborn in the desire realm.
If one can exert effort to give rise to the Noble Path and sever all afflictions,
one will certainly not be reborn in the higher realms;
for one comes to loathe birth in the desire realm because it is fraught with much suffering and distress.
Fearing that birth in the higher realms would entail suffering for a long duration—
since those realms are similar to the desire realm—
