and those in the subsequent stages of both the non-learner (aśaikṣa) and the learner (śaikṣa).

Through the practice of training the faculties (*indriya-saṃskāra*) by means of the three types of cultivation beginning with that of reflection (*cintāmayī*), one may attain the three levels of protection (*ārakṣya*) and so forth, all of which admit of the possibility of regressing from their lineage (*gotra*).
Furthermore, when one transitions to a higher level of protection and so forth and attains the fruit of a learner (*śaikṣaphala*), there is likewise the possibility of regressing from that fruit.
Therefore, the *Nyāyānusāra* (Treatise on Correct Reasoning), fascicle 68, states:
"They cultivate the practice of refining the faculties (*indriya-saṃskāra*) through reflection and so forth;
they subsequently attain the state of being protected (*ārakṣya*) and so on, yet they remain only capable of falling away from their lineage (*gotra*)."
Even for one who has transformed their lineage and attained the fruit of training (*śaikṣa-phala*), there is still the possibility of falling away.
This is because such a lineage is not firmly established by both paths.
Furthermore, there is no case where one falls away from the stage of the "worthy one" (*arhat*) that would constitute a fall rather than progress.
Regarding the four fruits, the meaning of "retrogression from the fruit" is clarified therein.
Although all five spiritual lineages may retrogress from a fruit,
there is likewise no retrogression from a fruit previously attained.
Among the four fruits, those who first attain them are necessarily non-retrogressive.
If one attains the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpanna*), it is necessarily attained first.
Those who realize the fruits of once-returner (*sakṛdāgāmin*) and non-returner (*anāgāmin*) by means of leaping over stages likewise attain them first.
Regarding the fruits attained subsequently, there is the possibility of falling away from them.
If one takes the first fruit as the preceding stage,
then the second, third, and fourth fruits constitute the subsequent stages.
If one takes the second fruit as the prior,
then one takes the third and fourth fruits as the subsequent.
If one takes the third fruit as the prior...
Thus, the fourth fruit is taken as the final one; therefore,
there is certainly no falling back from the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpanna*),
because the fruit of stream-entry must necessarily have been attained first.
In this context, the once-returner and non-returner are not mentioned separately because they are not fixed [in their destiny]. Therefore,
they are not specifically cited.
It should be understood that the stream-enterer (srotāpanna) occurs only first and not later;
the arhat occurs only later and not first;
whereas the once-returner (sakṛdāgāmin) and the non-returner (anāgāmin) both apply to both first and later.
Consequently, there is no sense of falling back from a fruit previously attained,
nor a sense of falling back from a subsequent fruit;
thus, for those who are subject to falling away (parihāṇadharman), there are three types of Arhats.
First, those who advance their faculties;
second, those who regress and remain in the stage of training;
third, those who attain parinirvāṇa while abiding in their own station.
It is stated only that one regresses and remains in the stage of training (*śaikṣa*),
and not that one regresses and remains as an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*).
By this, it is clearly known.
One does not fall back from the first fruit.
There are four types of those who practice through reflection (*cintāmayī*); three are as previously explained.
Furthermore, there is one type of regression characterized by remaining in a state of regression from the lineage;
the other three follow in sequence.
There are five types of those who protect the Dharma.
The four are as previously explained;
adding one more type, those who abide in the lineage of reflection (cintāmayagotra),
there are six who abide securely in the Dharma.
The five are as previously explained;
adding one more type— the lineage of those who abide in the protection of the Dharma—
there are seven types of those capable of attaining the state of a *prativedhanādharman*.
The six are as previously explained;
to these is added one more type: the lineage of abiding in retreat (*pratyāgamana-sthiti-gotra*).
This refers to the time when those in the four stages of training, such as the practitioner of reflection (*cintaka*), abide in the state of retreat.
They return to abide in their original lineage of falling away (*parihāṇadharman*), and not in any of the other four types of thought and so forth.
If it were otherwise, then at the time of the previous stage of training (*śaikṣa*), one would have been of the lineage of falling away.
Now, as for those who have regressed and abide in the four castes such as the Śaikṣa and so forth,
because they have attained a superior lineage,
this should be an advancement rather than a regression.
"For what reason is it certain that there is no falling away from a previously attained fruit?
This section below clarifies the disputes among various schools regarding whether one may fall away from the four fruits.
According to the Sarvāstivāda school:
The first fruit is not subject to regression;
the latter three fruits may be subject to regression,
as has been explained in detail previously.
Question: For what reason is it certain that there is no falling back from a previously attained fruit?
The Sarvāstivādins answer: Because for those [defilements] abandoned through seeing (*darśana-heya*), there is the principle that they can never again fall back.
Because that which is abandoned by insight (*darśana-heya*) has no objective basis (*anālambana*), there is necessarily no possibility of falling back from it.
If this is so, one must then say that these afflictions take non-existence as their object. [This] is the objection.
Since there is no entity of a self, it should be said that the object-conditions are non-existent.
It is not the case that these non-existent object-conditions reach [the mind] without being perceived as they truly are; this applies universally.
This view of self does not take non-existent phenomena as its object,
because it takes the truths as its objective domain;
however, it does not apprehend those objects of the truths in accordance with reality.
"Among all afflictions, which ones are not like this? This is the interrogation.
Although they are all like this, [the distinction applies] up to those afflictions that depend on a real object (*savastuka*).
The explanation of the distinction between that which possesses activity and that which does not is as follows:
"The agent" refers to that which is capable of creating the world;
"the experiencer" refers to that which is capable of utilizing the world.
Because one attains mastery over this process of performing actions and experiencing their results,
one gives rise to greedy attachment toward agreeable objects and to hatred and aversion toward disagreeable objects.
One gives rise to the inflation of pride (*māna*) toward inferior, equal, or superior objects.
One gives rise to ignorance (*avidyā*) because of a lack of understanding regarding the facts.
The remainder of the text is clear.
Furthermore, regarding the afflictions abandoned through seeing (*darśana-heya*) up to those based on existing entities (*savastuka-kleśa*):
there is also an interpretation that distinguishes between those with and without a basis (*sāśraya-vastu*).
Moreover, the afflictions abandoned through seeing [operate] within the context of the principles of the truths (*satya-tattva*).
The view of a self-body clings to "I" and "mine";
the view of extremes clings to annihilationism or eternalism;
and false views cling to non-existence.
The term "and so forth" includes the view of holding to views, the view of holding to precepts and observances, ignorance, and doubt.
These seven all arise from delusion regarding the principle of the truths;
there is not even the slightest entity such as a "self" within the truths.
Among those [afflictions] to be abandoned by insight (*darśana-heya*), the three—greed, hatred, and pride—arise in relation to seven [objects].
Therefore, they are all termed "afflictions based on non-existent objects" (*avastuka-kleśa*).
The associated ignorance (*saṃprayukta-avidyā*) is explained in the same manner as greed and the others.
The afflictions to be abandoned through cultivation consist of the notions of beauty, ugliness, and so forth, regarding form and other objects.
It is not that there is no slight distinction between beauty, ugliness, and the like;
therefore, they may be termed "afflictions based on existing entities."

Furthermore, it is observed that among those who have abandoned the afflictions to be severed through seeing (*darśana-heya*), there are some who fall away due to the loss of mindfulness. Moreover, it is explained that one does not fall back from having abandoned the afflictions that obscure the principles (*tattva-mūḍha*),
whereas one may fall back from having abandoned the afflictions that obscure phenomena (*vastu-mūḍha*).

Alternatively, regarding those who have abandoned the afflictions through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) and attained the state where there is no possibility of falling back from meditative absorption: another interpretation holds that afflictions abandoned through cultivation arise without deliberate reflection (*avicāra*), and thus the Noble Ones may fall back from them;

however, because afflictions abandoned through seeing (*darśana-heya*) arise from deliberate reflection, the Noble Ones do not fall back from them. The above explains the Sarvāstivāda position clarifying the meaning of non-retrogression upon first attaining the fruit of the path.
Regarding the statement, "The Sautrāntika masters say that their explanation is logical":
hereafter, the Sautrāntikas clarify the falling away from and non-falling away from the four fruits.
Since the master of the treatise (Vasubandhu) sides with the Sautrāntikas, he states, "their explanation is logical."
The Sautrāntika position states that for the stream-enterer (*srotāpanna*) and the arhat, there is never any falling away from what has been abandoned by noble wisdom (*āryaprajñā*); however,
for the once-returner (*sakṛdāgāmin*) and the non-returner (*anāgāmin*), there may still be falling away from what is attained through the mundane path (*laukikamārga*).
The abandonment through the untainted path (*anāsrava-mārga*) is likewise non-retrogressive.
Therefore, the *Nyāyānusāra*, fascicle 68, states:
"However, the intention of the Sūtra’s author is as follows:"
The fruit of arhatship is likewise without any falling away.
As for the once-returner and non-returner fruits attained via the mundane path, there is room for the possibility of falling away.
Citing scripture as proof, it is said that when afflictions are severed by noble wisdom, this is called "actual severance."
First, regarding the two fruits at the beginning and the end,
because they are realized by severing afflictions through noble wisdom alone, there is no possibility of falling away from them. How is this known to be so?
Question:
"By means of scripture and reasoning.
The Sautrāntika replies.
How is this established by scripture?
It is asked:
The Sūtra states, "O Bhikṣus, [this applies] up to those who are not Arhats."
Answer: The Sūtra states that the elimination of afflictions by means of untainted noble wisdom is called "actual abandonment.
The fruit of Arhatship is abandoned solely by means of noble wisdom.
Since it is stated that there is actual abandonment,
it is clearly known that one does not regress.
The sūtra warns those in training that they should be diligent and not negligent.
Because there is fear of falling back from training,
it is not said that an Arhat should practice heedfulness;
it is clearly known that he does not fall back.

Although there is a sūtra passage stating that one attains "abiding in happiness in the present life," the Sautrāntikas interpret the text as follows: although there is a sūtra passage where the Buddha told Ānanda,
"I say that gain and so forth are also obstacles for an arhat."
Although this statement exists,
it does not say that there is falling away from the untainted dharmas of the fruit of arhatship; rather,
it speaks only of falling away from the tainted meditative absorptions of abiding in happiness in the present life.
Regarding the scriptural statement, "Because it does not move until one falls back from this," the Sautrāntika school cites this as proof.
Furthermore, the sūtra says that it is not moved by afflictions (*kleśa*).
Because one has realized the cessation [of suffering] within a body whose mind is liberated from defilements,
I definitively declare that there is no cause or condition for falling back from this state;
thus, the immovable [state] is itself the fruit of arhatship.
Therefore, it is known that there is no falling back.
If one were to argue that because there is falling back to the [lower] realms, it is not called "craving," the Sautrāntika school cites this objection and provides a comprehensive explanation.
If it is claimed that there is falling away because the Sūtra states that there is "liberation through love" (*sneha-vimukti*), I also admit that there is falling away;
however, one must examine what it is that falls away:
is it the fruit of Arhatship, which is of an untainted nature (*anāsrava-svabhāva*)?
Are these the mundane (*sāsrava*) dhyānas and so forth?
In our own school, it is said that one may fall back from mundane concentration;
this liberation is explained here with reference to mundane concentration.
Furthermore, regarding the explanation of the names:
since those who possess dull faculties must maintain a superior moment for the four fundamental dhyānas and the formless attainments (*ārūpya-samāpatti*) to manifest before them.
Liberation from the hindrances to concentration is called "liberation by occasion" (samayavimukti).

Because he possesses a wholesome desire for the Dharma that repeatedly aspires for its manifestation in order to attain the blissful abiding in the present life (dṛṣṭadharmasukhavihāra), it is termed "craving" (tṛṣṇā).
Some say: because this contaminated meditative absorption is the object of relish for that craving, it is called "craving."
The "liberation at all times" (*asamayavimukti*) should be understood as previously explained.
Since the Arhats whose nature is the fruit of the outflow-free state are liberated from afflictions and are constantly followed by that liberation at all times, it should not be called "timely."
Since it constantly follows along, it is "fulfilled";
because one no longer seeks it with longing, it is not called "craving" (*tṛṣṇā*).
If it pertains to the nature of the fruit of arhatship (*arhattvaphala*), it should be understood according to the principle that applies.
The Sautrāntika school raises an objection:
If it is said that the nature of the fruit of arhatship is untainted (anāsrava),
then even those of dull faculties (mṛdvindriya) could still be subject to falling away from it.

Why does the Blessed One speak only of the contaminated meditative attainments realized as dwelling in happiness in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharmasukhavihāra*) as being subject to the possibility of falling away,
and not of those that are uncontaminated?
From this it is proven that the nature of the fruit of arhatship must be immovable;
"immovable" means it is definitively free from falling back or wavering.
Nevertheless, due to the fault of being disturbed by gain, honor, and so forth—
There are those who, because they have not attained mastery over the blissful abiding in the present life that they have acquired, undergo a decline;
this decline of mastery refers to those of dull faculties.
As for those of sharp faculties, there is no decline from the bliss of the present life.
Therefore, because there is regression regarding the attained dwelling in happiness in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharmasukhavihāra*),
it is called the first, the "quality of regression" (*parihāṇadharman*);
because there is no regression, it is called the sixth, the "quality of non-regression" (*aparihāṇadharman*).
In this manner, the four types of spiritual lineages (gotra), beginning with the "thought-possessor" (cetanādharmā), should be considered according to reason.
Because there is falling away, the first is called the "thought-possessor";
because there is no falling away, the sixth is called the "non-falling-away dharma" (anirākaraṇadharmā).
Thus, because there is still the possibility of falling back, it is called the "dharma of being capable of reaching" (*kāmada-dharma*);
because there is no falling back, it is called the sixth, the "dharma of non-retrogression.
This sixth is also termed "immovable" (*akopya*).
The Sautrāntika school explains the distinctions among the six lineages solely in terms of the boundaries of contaminated meditative concentration (*sāsrava-samādhi*). However,
from the perspective of the nature of the uncontaminated fruit (*anāsrava-phala*),
there is only the "unshakable" (*akopya*) lineage, and no sixfold distinction exists.

Furthermore, there is no falling back. Moreover, it is explained that "having falling back" is termed the first, the *parihāṇadharman* (one liable to fall away), while "not having falling back" is termed the sixth, the *aparihāṇadharman* (one not liable to fall away).
The four types beginning with the *cetana-dharman* (one intent on volition) should be considered accordingly.
However, all of them may regress from the dwelling in happiness in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharmasukhavihāra*).
One who possesses volition is called "one of the nature of reflection" (*cetanā-dharman*),
while one who lacks volition is called "one of the nature of non-reflection" (*aceta-nā-dharman*), which is the sixth.
Thus, up to the point where "capable of penetration" (prativedhanā-dharman) is named as the fifth, "capable of penetration";
"incapable of penetration" (akopya-dharman) is named as the sixth, "incapable of penetration.
What is the distinction between "non-retrogressive," "abiding securely," and "immovable"?
Question:

Regarding the sixth stage of non-retrogression, which is also called "immovable," and the fourth stage of "abiding," since their three characteristics are similar, what is the difference between them?
Is it not the case that the distinction among these three types is attained through the refinement of the faculties (*indriya*)?
The Sautrāntika school replies:
Non-retrogression is obtained by way of one's original nature,
not through the refinement of the faculties.
If one refines their faculties and attains the name "Unshakable" (akopya),
the supramundane qualities arising from these two states— the superior meditative attainments— do not regress even when encountering conditions; as for abiding,
it merely means being able to remain without loss within the various mundane, superior virtues already attained.
It cannot further induce the arising of other superior contaminated virtues;
even if it were later to induce them, one could subsequently fall away from them—
these are the three distinctions.
However, regarding the case of Godhika attaining the fruit of arhatship,
the Sautrāntikas further interpret this sūtra;
the reason they must interpret this scriptural passage is as follows:
According to the intention of the Sarvāstivādins,
there was an Arhat named Godhika who,
due to his dull faculties, fell away from the state of Arhatship six times.
Regarding the seventh case, when one attains the fruit of arhatship through regression,
fearing further loss of that attainment, one may take one's own life with a blade;
therefore, it is now stated generally.
As for the six times that Kautika regressed,
it was because in his former stage as a learner (*śaikṣa*), he intensely relished the tainted concentration of temporary liberation (*samayavimukta*), and furthermore,
because his faculties were dull (*mṛdvindriya*).
Having fallen back and lost [the state] six times,
he deeply reproached himself and took up a blade to end his own life,
as he felt no attachment or regret for his body or life.
Upon reaching his seventh and final rebirth at the time of death,
he attained arhatship and entered parinirvāṇa;
thus it was with Ghoṭika.
However, one may fall away from impure meditative attainments while still in the stage of training (śaikṣa), yet one does not fall away from the fruit of arhatship. Kautika was of the cowherd caste.
Furthermore, Paramārtha says:
Kauṭika— here translated as "potter"—
was originally a non-Buddhist ascetic who always carried a clay vessel with him.

The name remains as it was originally. The *Daśottara-sūtra* (the Sūtra on Increasing by Ten) is so named because it increases from one dharma-gate up to ten kinds.
Furthermore, the *Daśottara-sūtra* within the Āgamas speaks as follows:
"One dharma should be cultivated."
This refers to the liberation through a mind imbued with attachment during a state of contaminated meditative concentration (*sāsrava-samādhi*).
One dharma should be realized: the unshakable liberation through a mind free from outflows (*anāsrava-akopya-ceto-vimukti*).
This is according to the scriptural rebuke.
This can be understood from the text.
Therefore, *samayavimukta* is exclusively *sāsrava* (with outflows) and is not of the nature of the fruit of arhatship;
it is thus termed "liberation by occasion" (*samayavimukta*).
It is sometimes called "liberation through love at the proper time" (*kāla-prema-vimukti*), and sometimes called "liberation of mind through love at the proper time" (*kāla-prema-citta-vimukti*);
the difference lies only in the breadth or brevity of the expression, while the meaning is essentially the same.
One who awaits the proper time and whose mind is liberated from the hindrances of meditative concentration with a rarefied aspiration is called "liberated by love for time" (*samayavimukta*).
"Liberated at any time" (*asamayavimukta*) should be understood accordingly.
If one speaks of "unshakable liberation of the mind" (*akopya-cetovimukti*), [it refers to the latter].
The untainted fruit of arhatship (anāsrava-ārhattva-phala) is free from any regression or mental liberation through affliction (kleśa).
If this is so, why is it said that there is an "arhat liberated by time" (samaya-vimukta)?
This is the objection raised by the Sarvāstivādins.

If the state of one liberated by occasion (*samayavimukta*) were not the essence of the fruit of arhatship (*arhattvaphala*), why would it be said that there are fruits of arhatship called "liberated by occasion"?
[It is because] there are indeed fruits of arhatship that reach the designation of being "not liberated by occasion" (*asamayavimukta*).
The Sautrāntika replies:
Those who possess the faculty-nature of an Arhat (*arhat-phala*) and must wait for the proper time because their faculties are dull,
such that their various contaminated meditative attainments (*sāsrava-samādhi*) only manifest at that time, are called "those liberated by time" (*samaya-vimukta*).
It is not that "timely liberation" (samayavimukta) is the nature of the fruit of arhatship (arhattvaphala);
rather, that which is contrary to it is called "untimely liberation" (asamayavimukta) arhatship.
This may be understood by analogy with the preceding explanation.

Regarding the statement, "The Abhidharma is authoritative in this matter because it is based on scripture," the Sautrāntikas further cite scriptural authority to prove that those beyond training (aśaikṣa) do not fall away from their fruit.
The treatise states that an affliction can only arise when three causes are present.
Since an Arhat who has attained the fruit does not possess these three causes when an affliction arises,
it is clear that he does not fall back.
If it is argued that this is said according to the production of afflictions when all three causes are complete, then what other afflicted phenomena could arise when their causes are incomplete?

If it is further argued that for one who has fallen away from the state of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*), the causes for producing afflictions are incomplete because those afflictions have already been abandoned, [then we reply: ...
"How can it arise?"—this is a critical inquiry based on principle. It must possess the causes.
Furthermore, another interpretation holds that this refers to the teaching that [arising] occurs by means of possessing three causes.
Furthermore, what other phenomena arise without their causes being complete?
For example, defiled minds and mental factors necessarily arise with five causes; there is no case where they arise without these five being complete.
One should know that the three causes for the arising of delusion are likewise so;
this is the application of the same principle by way of reproof. This is what is meant by "by means of scripture."
Regarding "how by way of principle":
the question is,
if one becomes an arhat, this is called "by way of principle."
The Sautrāntika replies:
If an Arhat possesses the untainted path of antidote that has already arisen, which causes the afflictions to never arise again, then there is indeed a real abandonment.
In that case, one should not regress by giving rise to afflictions;
for if the path of remedy has not yet arisen in an Arhat,
they have not yet been able to permanently uproot the seeds of the afflictions.
It would follow that he has not exhausted the outflows (āsrava-kṣaya). If the outflows have not been exhausted, how can he be said to be one who has attained the fruit of arhatship (arhattva-phala)?
Thus he is interrogated from both sides.
An Arhat necessarily never regresses;
this is known by reason.
If that is so, one should explain the meaning of "having attained the state of an Arhat."
The Sarvāstivādins further cite a sutra as a challenge:
"If it is asserted that those who have attained the fruit of arhatship are necessarily non-retrogressive,
then one must explain the passage in the Charcoal Simile Sūtra."
Since this sutra states that even the noble disciples (ārya-śrāvaka) may at times lose mindfulness and give rise to unwholesome thoughts,
it is clear that even those who have attained the fruit of arhatship (arhattva-phala) can undergo regression. How, then, is it known that they are indeed arhats?
Because this sutra speaks exclusively of arhats.
Furthermore, by what textual passage is the fruit of arhatship (āgāmiphala) proven?
It is by means of the charcoal simile in the *Aṅgārakṛtya-sūtra*.
Regarding the statement that "the mind of that noble disciple has,
for a long night, conformed to seclusion and so forth," since it is said to have "conformed to seclusion":
It is clearly known that this is the fruit of arhatship.
Furthermore, how is it known?
It is because one conforms to and dwells in detachment that one is an arhat.
In other sūtras, these very factors conducive to seclusion and so forth are described as the powers of the fruit of arhatship (*arhat-phala*).
Furthermore, the *Aṅgāra-upama-sūtra* states that those noble disciples have already been able to permanently vomit up all that is conducive to the outflows (*āsrava*).
It reveals the permanent severance of all outflows (āsrava) and the attainment of coolness;
it reveals that one has already attained the coolness of nirvāṇa.
From this, it is known with certainty that the *Aṅgārakṛtyaupama-sūtra* refers to an Arhat.
As for the statement that there is no fault because what was said later is "ultimate" (*prāpta*), [it is explained as follows].
The Sautrāntikas explain that this is actually what is taught later, or as stated in the latter portion of the *Aṅgāra-upama-sūtra* (Charcoal Simile Sūtra):
"One who has already been able to spit out [the defilements] forever and has attained coolness is an Arhat."
However, regarding the analogy of the charcoal cited there, it is possible that for those noble disciples previously mentioned,
while they were walking or standing and had not yet fully mastered the principle of the Four Noble Truths,
there might occasionally be a lapse of mindfulness and the arising of unwholesome thoughts.
This refers to those in training who are once-returners and non-returners.
Having attained those two fruits by means of the mundane path,
they may still give rise to afflictions during the course of their conduct and dwelling due to a lapse in mindfulness.
Subsequently, by means of noble wisdom, one abandons the remaining afflictions to be abandoned through cultivation and realizes the fruit of arhatship (*aśaikṣa*).
Once one has thoroughly mastered the principle of the Truths, there is no possibility of [the defilements] arising again.
Thus, the scriptural passage cited previously—which was spoken with reference to those in the stage of training (*śaikṣa*)—is not subject to contradiction regarding the possibility of falling away.
In the *Aṅgārakalpa-sūtra*, after the preceding passage had extensively debated the point that even the Vaibhāṣikas admit the possibility of falling away (*parihāṇi*),
[the discussion concludes].
To conclude by returning to our own school:
according to the *Saṃayabhedoparacanacakra*,
those of the Mahāsāṃghika and other schools maintain that there is the possibility of falling away for a stream-enterer (*srotāpanna*).
An Arhat has no possibility of falling away.
Regarding the statement that "only an Arhat who has not yet cultivated the faculties (*indriya*)":
this clarifies the fourth point concerning the lineages (*gotra*) of those in training (*śaikṣa*) and ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*).
Question:
Is it only for Arhats that there are six lineages (gotra),
or do the other learners (śaikṣa) and ordinary worldlings (pṛthagjana) also possess these six types of lineage?
If so, are all [those in training] able to cultivate and refine their faculties?
The verse says: "As for those in the stage of no-more-learning.
Answer: [They are].
Because there were six types in the prior stage of an ordinary person (pṛthagjana), there are six types of those in training (śaikṣa).
Because there were six types of those in training previously, there are six types of those who have attained the fruit (arhat).
In the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), there is no arising of preparatory effort (*prayoga*);
in other stages, such effort can arise, and one is able to cultivate the refinement of the faculties (*indriyasaṃcara*).

However, the cultivation of the refinement of the faculties occurs only during the stage of a faith-follower (*śraddhādhimukta*) who is still an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*), just as it does in the stage of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*).
The *Vibhāṣā* (Treatise on the Great Abhidharma), fascicle seven, states:
"The factors conducive to liberation (*mokṣabhāgīya*) are also of six kinds, namely:
those of the regressive lineage (*parihāṇadharman*) up to those of the immovable lineage (*akopyadharman*)."
One transforms the *parihāṇadharman* lineage’s stage of the aids to liberation (*mokṣabhāgīya*) into the *cetanādharman* lineage’s stage of the aids to liberation, and so on,
up to transforming the *prativedhanādharman* into the *akopyadharman*.
One may turn from the śrāvaka [lineage] to arise as a pratyekabuddha or a buddha;
one may turn from the pratyekabuddha [lineage] to arise as a śrāvaka or a buddha.
Once the factors conducive to liberation (mokṣabhāgīya) have arisen within the buddha-gotra, [they cannot be lost].
It cannot be diverted because it is extremely intense.

Furthermore, it is said that the levels conducive to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*) also possess six natures. Question: If you say that even at the stage of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*), the levels conducive to liberation (*mokṣabhāgīya*) also have six types of lineage (*gotra*).
For what reason does the *Mahāvibhāṣā* (68) state that there are six lineages (*gotra*) only in the stage of the "decisive distinction" (*nirvedhabhāgīya*), and not in the preceding stages?
Therefore, that treatise says:
"Just as there are six types of lineage in the stage of the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*)."
The stage of corresponding practice (*saṃprayukta-caryā-bhūmi*) also possesses these six lineages (*gotra*):
namely, the lineage of the dharma of falling away (*parihāṇa-dharman*) among those of corresponding practice,
up to the lineage of the immovable dharma (*akopya-dharman*) among those of corresponding practice.
Regarding the six types of lineages within this stage:
they are the levels of Heat (uṣmagata), Summits (mūrdhan), Patience (kṣānti), and the Supreme Mundane Dharmas (laukikāgradharma).
These constitute the proximate preparatory practices for the Noble Path.

Because they practice the noble path in accordance with the truths (*satya*) and because they rely on the same body and meditative absorption (*samādhi*) as those who have entered the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), while those in the preceding stages do not;
therefore, the six spiritual lineages (*gotra*) are not established [for them]. The commentary explains: the subsequent text provisionally relies upon a single characteristic.
The preceding section has already explained the stage of training (*śaikṣa*).
The paths of application for the transformation of the faculties (*indriya-saṃcāra*) and so forth will be explained later.
As the Sūtra says regarding those who fall back from the "abiding in happiness in the present life" (*dṛṣṭadharmasukhavihāra*):
This is the fifth [section], clarifying the differences among the three types of falling back.
It raises a question based on a sutra,
as stated in the *Sūtra*:
I say that based on this, one realizes the four kinds of fundamental dhyānas which are predominant mental factors;
when any one of these abidings in the joy of the present dharma manifests,
the others are said to be subject to regression.
Since it is said that one who has attained the immovable state does not regress,
how can one of immovable dharma regress from the blissful dwelling in the present life?
This "mind" refers to meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
Alternatively, it is a mental factor of resolute belief (*adhimokṣa*).
Thus, the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 81, states:
"As it is said in the Sūtra..."
There are four kinds of higher mental states (*adhicitta*) that constitute dwelling in happiness in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharmasukhavihāra*).
Question: Why are they called "higher mental states"?
Answer: These mental states are precisely meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
Because there is no samādhi that possesses such great power, such great efficacy,
and the capacity to accomplish great tasks as the fundamental four dhyānas,
this alone is designated as the "higher training in mind" (adhicitta).
Furthermore, there are four types of the four dhyānas;
they possess immeasurable kinds of preeminent mental qualities (adhicitta),
such as the [four] immeasurables (apramāṇa) and so forth.
This is explained in detail as in that commentary.
The verse says: "In the sharp and medium [faculties], there are three, including the final dull [faculty].
The first two lines enumerate the three types of regression.
The latter two phrases clarify this in terms of persons.
The *Śāstra* states, "As for 'not appearing before one,'" this explains the preceding two phrases.
This may be understood from the text as it stands.
The *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra* states:
"Among these three, the first two have non-acquisition (*aprāpti*) as their essence."
"Regarding the third, only that [defilement] does not manifest;
as for the phrase 'because one has attained the virtues within these three,'" this explains the latter two lines.
Among the three types of decline,
the Blessed One possesses only the last one, which is the decline regarding enjoyment (*parihāṇi-vihāra*),
because it is impossible for all his manifold virtues to manifest simultaneously.
The non-manifestation of one [attainment] while another is manifest is termed "retrogression from enjoyment.
Among the three types of retrogression, those Arhats who possess other benefits and are immovable, as well as Pratyekabuddhas, possess only the latter— retrogression from enjoyment.
Furthermore, there is no falling back from what has not yet been attained; nor has one yet attained the supreme qualities of the unique Buddha-dharmas that surpass oneself.
This concludes the explanation of the middle section.
Because those who have already attained merit will certainly not fall away from it, there is no "falling away from what has been attained" for them.
As for the other five spiritual lineages (*gotra*), they may possess all three types of falling away because their faculties are dull;
thus, they are also susceptible to losing the merit they have already attained. This explains the three types of falling away for those of dull faculties.
Regarding the point that there is no contradiction from the perspective of falling away from enjoyment (*bhoga-vihāni*) up to the point of signlessness (*animitta*):
this directly addresses the previous objection.
As for the statement in the Sūtra concerning "falling away":
Among the three types of falling away, with respect to the falling away from enjoyment (*parihāṇi*),
it is said that those of immovable dharma (*akopyadharman*) all fall away from the dwelling in happiness in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharmasukhavihāra*); thus,
there is no fault of contradiction.
Regarding the passage from "The proponents of non-retrogression" up to "it should not be difficult [to refute]," this describes the Sautrāntika school.
The proponents of non-retrogression speak as follows:
All untainted liberations within the body of one beyond training (aśaikṣa) are termed "unshakable" (āneñjya),
because they are free from falling back or fluctuation.
An objection is raised as follows:
If all the untainted dharmas within the body of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) are free from regression or fluctuation,
then all six spiritual lineages (*gotra*) should be designated as "immovable" (*akopya*).
Why, then, is a sixth type, the "immovable-dharma" (*akopyadharman*), established separately?
To resolve this anticipated objection, he speaks as follows: "However,
among the six lineages (*ṣaḍ-gotra*), the sixth, the immovable lineage (*akopyadharman*),

is established separately with reference to the six types of lineages as they pertain to abiding in happiness in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharmasukhavihāra*) through impure meditative concentration (*sāsrava-samādhi*)."
The first five [attainments] are subject to regression;
the sixth is non-regressive and is thus called "immovable.
This is not based on the untainted (anāsrava) state, as explained previously in the general interpretation.
One should not raise this objection.
Regarding the statement that "all Arhats, when reaching the point of falling away, do not [perform] it," the following section,
the sixth, clarifies the characteristics of the time of falling away from the fruit.
The question arises as before.
If it is not so, he replies.
Regarding the phrase "For what reason": this is an inquiry.
The verse states: "Because shame has increased to the point of reaching [the limit], one does not act."
The verse provides the answer.
The commentary states, "As for 'reaching a place where one may rely with full confidence,'" this explains the two preceding lines.
This clarifies that one who has fallen away from the fruit (*phala*) certainly does not die.

This may be understood from the text as it stands. Question: If one who falls away from the fruit does not die, why is it that one who falls away from the stage of "approaching" (*pratipannaka*) does indeed die? Answer: As stated in the *Abhidharmamahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* (Vibhāṣā), fascicle 61: [text follows].
Furthermore, the fundamental stage of fruition possesses five causal conditions:
first, the relinquishing of previously attained paths;
second, the attainment of paths never before attained.
Third, the realization of the severance of fetters through the attainment of a single flavor;
fourth, the simultaneous acquisition of the eight knowledges;
fifth, the simultaneous cultivation of the sixteen aspects of contemplation.
Therefore, when one falls back from the fruit,
there is no principle of death before the [lost] attainment is regained;
this is not the case for those mentioned above.
Therefore, at that time of retrogression,
although they have not yet returned [to the higher realms], there is the sense of passing away;
this is explained in detail as in that commentary.
Furthermore, regarding the phrase "abiding in the stage of fruition such that one may stumble but not fall," this explains the latter two lines;
it may be understood according to the text.
Furthermore, the *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra* (Treatise on Following Right Reasoning),
fascicle 70, states: "Moreover,
who undergoes regression, and who does not?"
Those who enter the noble path by practicing the contemplation of impurity may experience regression;
those who enter the noble path by practicing mindfulness of breathing will certainly not regress.
By honoring calm abiding and insight, greed and delusion increase.
It should be understood that there is falling away and non-falling away respectively,
as stated above regarding the attainment of the path of fruition alone.
This constitutes the seventh [section], clarifying the differences in the refinement of the faculties (*indriya*).
The first three phrases answer the first question;
"untainted" (*anāsrava*) answers the second question; and "based on the three lower [stages] of persons" answers the third question.
The Commentary states: "Reaching each stage, there is one for each" explains the first three phrases.
This refers to the transformation of the faculties (*indriya-parāvṛtti*) of those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), whereby each lineage (*gotra*) is transmuted into another.
There are nine paths of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*) and nine paths of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*) for each [fruit].

This is just as one who attains the fruit of arhatship (*arhattva-phala*) eliminates the afflictions of the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra) through nine paths of uninterrupted transition and nine paths of liberation;
for those of dull faculties have long practiced the path of training (*śaikṣa-mārga*), and what is accomplished by the path of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa-mārga*) is therefore firm.
For those in training who transform their faculties,
each lineage requires one path of uninterrupted transition and one path of liberation;
this is just as when one attains the first fruit of stream-entry through a single path of uninterrupted transition.
The path of liberation (vimukti-mārga) alone abandons the afflictions of the higher realms to be abandoned through seeing (darśana-heya),
because these [afflictions] are not long-practiced and are thus easily transformed.
Therefore, the *Nyāyānusāra* states:

However, regarding the number of paths cultivated when one in the stage of no-more-learning (aśaikṣa) cultivates the faculties (indriya), it is as in the case of abandoning the Peak of Existence (bhavāgra).
As for the number of paths cultivated when one in the stage of learning (śaikṣa) cultivates the faculties:

As with the abandonment of what is to be abandoned by the path of seeing in the higher realms—because those [paths] are similar to the paths at the time of attaining the neighboring fruits—so it is according to the aforementioned treatise. Those [paths] belong to the stage of the path of preparation, the stage of training, and the stage beyond training.
For each individual lineage, there is one preparatory effort (*prayoga*).
In the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*),
there is one preparatory effort, nine uninterrupted paths (*ānantarya-mārga*), and nine paths of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*).

If one in the stage of training (śaikṣa) has one path of preparation (prayoga-mārga), one path of uninterrupted transition (ānantarya-mārga), and one path of liberation (vimukti-mārga)—this is asked because the paths of the dull-facultied trainee and the adept (aśaikṣa) are established as firm.
The "nine times nine" refers to the nine uninterrupted paths (*ānantarya-mārga*) and the nine paths of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*).

Since the dull-facultied learner (*śaikṣa*) also establishes firmness through both mundane and supramundane paths, they too should employ these nine. The commentary explains that the refinement of faculties (*indriya-saṃcāra*) for those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) occurs entirely within the state of the fruit of arhatship (*arhattva-phala*).
The refinement of faculties for those in training occurs entirely within the first fruit;
furthermore, it is accomplished by the two noble ones among those beyond training.

It cannot be taken as a precedent that a learner (śaikṣa) who is still an ordinary person (pṛthagjana) may do so. Question: Both paths accomplished [by these practitioners] are capable of further advancement.

"Are both types of paths accomplished through cultivation subject to regression? The explanation says: "When the mind seeks excellence with vigor, both types of maintenance (the path of cultivation) may shift;

when the mind inclines toward inferiority with laxity, both accomplishments do not regress. Question: Regarding the preparatory, uninterrupted, and liberation paths for refining the faculties (*indriya*) at the stage of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*), how are they? Answer: As stated in the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* (Vibhāṣā), fascicle 68: [text follows].
The commentary states: Regarding those who transform their faculties (indriya-parāvṛtti) at the stage of practice through application (prayoga-mārga),
although they do not abandon inferior [faculties] to obtain superior ones,
because the lineage (gotra) of the inferior type does not manifest at the time of obtaining the superior, it is also termed "abandoning."
Therefore, when one transforms from the *parihāṇadharman* lineage and so forth to give rise to the *cetanādharman* lineage and so forth,
it does not contradict reason that one employs increased application to induce a single path of immediate succession (*ānantarya-mārga*) and a single path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*),
thereby attaining the transformation of the faculties (*indriya-saṃcāra*).
Because the cultivation of the "heat" stage (*uṣmagata*) and so forth does not take a long time,
and because the contaminated preparatory practices (*sāsrava-prayoga*) are difficult to accomplish;
if one were to turn toward another vehicle, there would be no [attainment of] the uninterrupted path (*ānantarya-mārga*) or the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*).

Because it is accomplished only after a long period of time has passed, the commentary explains that "the stage of application" (*prayoga-bhūmi*) refers to the four roots of goodness (*kuśala-mūla*), namely *uṣmagata* and so forth. Furthermore, the *Nyāyānusāra* (Treatise on the Principles), fascicle 70, states:
"All the great masters from whom I have received instruction say:"

The refinement of the faculties in all cases serves to eliminate the manifestation of non-obscured, neutral ignorance that is induced by the power of the afflictions to be abandoned through seeing and meditation;
therefore, those in the stage of training (śaikṣa) refine their faculties.
The former is specifically for the purpose of eliminating that which is produced by the afflictions of view;
the latter is specifically for the purpose of eliminating that which is produced by the afflictions of cultivation for those in the stage of no-more-learning who are training their faculties.
Just as there are various numbers of uninterrupted (*ānantarya*) and liberated (*vimukti*) paths arising when one abandons those afflictions that give rise [to ignorance],
so too are the numbers of paths of present conduct that abandon the ignorance produced by them.
Therefore, when one beyond training (aśaikṣa) cultivates the faculties (indriya),
nine paths of uninterrupted transition (ānantarya-mārga) and nine paths of liberation (vimukti-mārga) are employed;
for one in training (śaikṣa), two paths are used for each of the two types of cultivation of the faculties.
However, the ignorance produced by the afflictions of the path of seeing and the path of cultivation has many categories according to the specific differences in what they obstruct; therefore,
when [the practitioner] transforms and regresses from [the state of] intention and so forth, [it becomes] volition and so forth.
The various paths manifesting before one each have their respective [afflictions] to be abandoned.

For this reason, there is no such thing as "leaping over" to attain a superior lineage (*gotra*). The commentary on the above treatise states: although those in training (*śaikṣa*) who refine their faculties (*indriya-saṃcāra*) are also able to abandon what is produced by the afflictions to be cultivated (*bhāvanā-heya*), [the leaping over of lineages does not apply here].
This is precisely for the purpose of eliminating what is produced by the afflictions of the views;
therefore, there is one path of uninterrupted transition and one path of liberation.

Although the refinement of the faculties in the state of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*) is also capable of eliminating what is produced by the afflictions of the views, [the former case is specifically addressed here].
This is precisely for the purpose of eliminating the afflictions produced by cultivation;
thus, there are nine paths of uninterrupted transition and nine paths of liberation.
As for the statement that such uninterrupted paths do not extend to the stage of non-increase (*anāgāmin*):

The commentary on the verse explains that "untainted" (anāsrava) refers here to the uninterrupted path (*ānantarya-mārga*) and the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*), which are exclusively untainted. However,
if one relies on the preparatory path (*prayoga-mārga*), they may be either tainted (*sāsrava*) or untainted.
Therefore, the *Vibhāṣā* (68) states:
"That path of preparation may be either contaminated (*sāsrava*) or uncontaminated (*anāsrava*). The *Nyāyānusāra* also says:
All preparatory applications (*prayoga*) pertain to both types.

Regarding the phrase "the basis refers to the body and the stages, up to relying on only six stages," this explains the three verses concerning the persons who rely [on these stages] and the final verse.
It is only in the three continents that there is fear of falling back;
therefore, one cultivates the refinement of the faculties (*indriya*).
This is because the Noble Path does not exist in Uttarakuru or in the miserable destinies (*apāya*).
Although the noble path exists within the other heavenly realms,
because there is no falling away from it, they do not cultivate the refinement of the faculties.
Those beyond training (aśaikṣas) rely upon nine [faculties].
Those in training rely on six [faculties].
If one who abides in a fruit transforms their faculties,
they immediately relinquish the former fruit and attain the latter fruit.
If one who abides in the path of the superior fruit transforms their faculties,
they relinquish both the fruit and the path of approach;
what is acquired is exclusively the fruit.
Because this is not fixed, the term "possible" (kṣama) is used.
Since the mind aspires solely for the fruit,
that which is attained is exclusively the fruit.
The mind generally abandons that which is inferior;
therefore, it relinquishes the supernormal powers (*abhijñā-phala*) and turns toward [the higher].
Furthermore, the *Nyāyānusāra* (Treatise on Correct Reasoning), fascicle 70, states:
Furthermore, when the various noble ones cultivate the faculties (*indriya*) during the stages of training,
their basis may be either the same as or different from that of the stage where they originally attained the fruit.
That is to say, for the first and second fruits, the basis must necessarily be the same.
Because both rely on the stage of *anāgamya*,
the stages upon which the Non-returner (*anāgāmin*) and the Arhat (*arhat*) rely are not fixed;
they may rely on their own original stage.
Regarding the distinction between those who progress upward and those who regress downward:
if those who are non-returners (anāgāmin) rely on a lower stage to refine their faculties, they cannot attain a higher fruit.

The Arhat is not like this, because he attains the fruit as originally acquired. Question: According to the *Nyāyānusāra*, if it is said that those who have attained the fruit of Non-returner (*anāgāmiphala*) cannot attain a higher fruit by refining their faculties (*indriya-saṃcāra*) while relying on a lower stage, why does the *Vibhāṣā* (67), in the opinion of the *viniścaya-vādins* (*pūrvapakṣa*), state: [text follows]?
It should be stated as follows:
if one has already attained mastery over a higher stage,
yet relies upon a lower stage to train in the transformation of the faculties and so forth.
One may also attain the untainted fruit-path of the higher stages;

however, at the time of the transformation of the faculties (*indriya-saṃcāra*), one does not attain the formless realm (*ārūpya*), because that realm certainly lacks the fruit of a non-returner (*anāgāmin*). The *Nyāyānusāra* explains: this is based solely on those who lack mastery within the higher stages.
The *Mahāvibhāṣā* generally refers to those who have attained mastery within the higher stages;

each [explanation] is based on a specific meaning, and thus they do not contradict one another. Question: Regarding all those who rely on the higher stages to attain the fruit of non-returner (*anāgāmiphala*)...
Regarding those who later cultivate the transformation of faculties (*indriya-parāvṛtti*) based on a lower stage, they should possess mastery over all those higher stages.

How then can it be said that the *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra* states that because one lacks such mastery, one does not cultivate the higher stages? The explanation is: this does not refer to one who has attained the fruit (*phala*) by relying on a higher stage.
Regarding those higher stages, one attains mastery over them; however,
because one must exert effort to suppress [lower states] in order to attain the fruit— and thus does not do so with ease—
there are cases where one transforms the faculties based on a lower stage and fails to attain the higher.
Regarding the nine distinctions up to the stage of those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*):
this is the eighth [section], clarifying the nine types of those beyond training.
There are two types of the immovable (*akopyadharman*).
It is subsequently attained through the refinement of the faculties; that which was previously obtained remains as it was.
The rest of the text may be understood accordingly.
Regarding the phrase "because there are two for each of the three paths within the stages of training and beyond training":
this marks the second major section below, which clarifies the seven types of noble beings (*ārya*). Within this, [the following is explained].
First, the establishment of the seven types of persons;
second, the explanation of liberation through wisdom and liberation through both [wisdom and concentration]. This is the first section: the establishment of the seven types of persons.
Based on those seven names, two questions are posed.
The first two lines answer the initial question;
the latter two lines answer the subsequent question.
The *Śāstra* states: "Up to the point of establishing those liberated through both [paths]."
This explains the first two phrases:
the meditative attainment of cessation is called liberation;
it is the eighth liberation among the eight liberations.
Based on the fact that non-afflicted ignorance constitutes the essential nature of the obstruction, it is called the "obstruction to liberation" because it hinders the liberation of others.

When one attains the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*), one is able to abandon this obstruction to liberation; therefore, it is called "abandoning the obstruction to liberation."

Therefore, it is said that those who attain the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*) based on both [the dhyānas and the formless attainments] and are free from the obstacles to liberation are established as "liberated in both ways" (*ubhayatobhāga-vimukta*).

The remainder of the text is clear. Regarding the statement, "Although these names are seven, they should be reflected upon according to reason": *Note: This passage refers to the classification of noble individuals (ārya-pudgala) based on their faculties, attainments, and the nature of their liberation.*
The two subsequent phrases are explained as follows:

among the seven [types of noble persons], the "body-witness" (*kāyasākṣin*) is subsumed within the two types—those resolved through faith (*śraddhādhimukta*) and those who have attained vision (*dṛṣṭiprāpta*)—among the six; it exists nominally but lacks a distinct substantial entity. Among the seven, [the body-witness] possesses both wisdom (*prajñā*) and meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
All are subsumed within the six [types of] timely and untimely [attainments].
Those with full fetters constitute one; those who have abandoned the defilements of the eight stages constitute eighty-nine, which multiplied by nine equals seven hundred and twenty-two.
Together, these total seventy-three [categories], including the gods of the desire realm.
This refers to the six classes of desire-realm devas, those who practice in accordance with the Dharma (dharmanusārin), and so forth;
"and so forth" includes the other four types of persons.
The remainder of the text may be understood accordingly.
What is meant by "liberation through the simultaneous attainment"?
This refers to the second type, liberation through wisdom (*prajñā-vimukti*).
Since this was not previously explained, it is now clarified separately.
Those Arhats who have attained the meditative absorption of cessation (nirodha-samāpatti) are called "liberated in both ways" (ubhayatobhāga-vimukta).
This means that by the power of wisdom (prajñā), they are liberated from the hindrance of afflictions (kleśāvaraṇa);
and by the power of the absorption of cessation, they are liberated from the hindrance to that very liberation, which is therefore called the "hindrance to liberation" (vimokṣāvaraṇa).
Those remaining Arhats who have not yet attained the meditative absorption of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti) are called "liberated by wisdom" (prajñāvimukta),
because they have attained liberation from the hindrance of afflictions (kleśāvaraṇa) solely through the power of wisdom.
These very afflictions that are able to obstruct the arising of wisdom are termed the "hindrance of afflictions."
Furthermore, the *Nyāyānusāra* (Treatise on the Principles of Correct Reasoning), fascicle 70, states: "What is the essence of the obstacle to liberation?
It is that although the minds of all Arhats are already liberated..."
Yet they further seek liberation;
in order to liberate them from those obstacles,
it refers to the inferior ignorance regarding the various forms of liberation that are obstructed.
The nature of the unobscured-neutral (anivṛtāvyākṛta) that can obstruct liberation is the essence of the obstacle to liberation.
When one attains detachment from various realms,
although [the obstacle] has already been abandoned without remainder, liberation is only designated when it arises and [the obstacle] no longer functions.
Furthermore, other masters say that this obstacle to liberation has as its essence the lack of mastery over the various meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*).
Other masters say:
This hindrance to liberation has as its essence the failure to attain the various meditative concentrations (*samādhi*).
Other masters say that it consists in not diligently seeking them during their preparatory practice (*prayoga*).
Because they have not heard [the teaching] and have not practiced it repeatedly,
liberation does not arise.
This is precisely what is called the essence of the obstacle to liberation;
the first explanation is the correct one. Why is this so?
There must be some slight power of dharma capable of acting as an obstacle,
causing him to lack mastery over meditative concentration. If it were not so,
[he would have attained it].
What is the cause by which he lacks mastery over the various meditative concentrations?
One who fails to attain concentration must have a specific reason;
it cannot be said that the very failure to attain it constitutes the cause.
The self-substance (*svabhāva*) cannot be the cause of itself;

otherwise, the obstacle of afflictions (*kleśāvaraṇa*) would also have to be described as having the non-attainment of the fruit of arhatship (*arhattvaphala-aprāpti*) as its nature. But since that is not the case, [the same must apply here].
Why is this so? Even in the case of the fruit of arhatship, because one does not diligently seek it through preparatory application (*prayoga*) and so forth, its essence cannot arise;
yet, does this mean that there is no distinct entity of the afflictive obstruction (*kleśāvaraṇa*)?
Therefore, the latter three explanations should not be accepted; among the four explanations, the first one is logical.
Why is this so? There must exist a non-afflicted ignorance (*akliṣṭājñāna*) whose weak power is capable of acting as an obstruction, causing that person to lack mastery over meditative concentration.
If it were not so, what would be the cause for their lack of mastery over the various meditative absorptions? This refutes the second teacher.
"How could those who have not attained meditative absorption reach this state? This refutes the third teacher.
The fourth teacher’s position is refuted by the fact that the fruit of arhatship is [the culmination].
Therefore, the latter three explanations are all unreasonable.
As the Blessed One said, it is only when one reaches the state of being "alone" that one is called "complete."
Below this, the third major section explains the fulfillment of the stages of training and beyond-training (*śaikṣa-asaikṣa*).
Question:
As the Blessed One has said:
The permanent abandonment of the five lower-tier fetters constitutes the fruit of non-returning (*anāgāmin*).
One can no longer be led away by the afflictions and karma of the desire realm;
thus, although one may undergo rebirth in the desire realm with fully developed faculties and fruits, [one does not remain there].
Because they have not yet attained the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*), they are not yet called "perfected learners" (*paripūrṇaśaikṣa*).
Based on this sūtra, a question is raised:
by how many causes does each of the stages of the learner (*śaikṣa*) and the non-learner (*aśaikṣa*) arise?
Among those in the stage of training (*śaikṣa*) and those in the stage beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), he alone is designated as "perfected.
The verse says: "He reaches [perfection] solely by means of faculties and meditative concentration.
This refers to the response.
The first two lines clarify the fulfillment of training (*śaikṣa*), while the latter two lines clarify the fulfillment of no-more-training (*aśaikṣa*).
The treatise states: "Even [the stage] up to that point receives the name 'fulfillment'."
The first two lines are explained as clarifying the fulfillment of those in training (śaikṣa).
"Faculties" refers to the sharp faculties (tīkṣṇendriya).
Because they surpass those of dull faculties;
"fruit" refers to the non-returner (anāgāmin),
because they surpass the previous two.
"Concentration" refers to the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*), because it is utterly tranquil;
alternatively, it is so called because it excels the preceding seven liberations (*vimokṣa*) among the eight.
In the stage of training (śaikṣa), if one possesses all three causes, one alone receives the designation "complete" (pūrṇa);
if any one of these three is lacking, although one is called "partially complete," one is not called "alone."
The intent of the *Nyāyānusāra* is that only when all three causes are present is something designated as "complete";
if any one is lacking, it is not called complete.
The *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya-vibhāṣā-ṭīkā* states: "This is not to be relied upon.
How could one who is still in training [possess] all the superior qualities of those in training?"
The Abhidharmakośa master offers this defense: although they have not yet fully realized [the fruit], they are permitted to be called "complete.
There are two kinds of completeness: first, completeness by way of possession (*paripūrṇatva*); [and second, completeness by way of realization].
That is to say, it is designated as "complete" only when all three causes are present.

Second, there is "partial completeness," which refers to obtaining two or one of the three causes; it is called "complete" in terms of its partial fulfillment, and this does not contradict the underlying meaning.
The *Nyāya* does not state that the meaning is diminished by the opposite;
rather, it explains the final two phrases with reference to those who are beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) and have attained the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*).

This clarifies the perfection of the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*). Within the stage of no-more-learning, if one possesses both the faculties (*indriya*) and meditative absorption (*samādhi*), one alone receives the name "perfected.
If there is a deficiency in either of these two, one does not.
Although the name and portion are complete, it is not called "solitary.
Because there are three fruits within the stage of training (śaikṣa), one may say that the fruit is complete;
in the stage of no-more-learning (aśaikṣa), there is only one, so it is not discussed in terms of "fruit."
The intent of the *Nyāyānusāra* is that one must possess both causes to be designated as "complete";
if either is lacking, it is not called complete.
The *Nyāyānusāra* refutes this with an intention that should be understood according to what was stated previously;
the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya*’s defense likewise follows the previous explanation.
The detailed exposition of the various paths up to the point where it says "the remaining three paths" is as follows.
Below this, the third major section explains the distinctions among the various paths. Within it:
first, the distinctions among the four paths;
second, the four types of practice.
Third, it elucidates the factors of enlightenment (bodhipakṣadharma).
Fourth, it elucidates the four kinds of verified confidence (avetyaprasāda).
Fifth, it elucidates right knowledge and liberation (samyagjñānavimukti).
Sixth, the clarification of the pervasiveness and limitation of wearying detachment (*nirveda*). This constitutes the first [section], clarifying the distinctions between the four paths.
It may be understood by citing the extensive question and providing a concise explanation.
What is the meaning of "path" (*mārga*)?
Question:
Regarding the statement, "It is called the path to nirvana because it leads to the fruit of nirvana," the answer is as follows.
It refers to the path to nirvāṇa;

because the noble assemblies of the three vehicles ride upon this and are thereby able to proceed to the city of nirvāṇa, it is called the "path" (*mārga*). Alternatively, the "path" is that which serves as the basis for seeking [liberation].
Because one relies on this to seek the fruit of nirvana, it is called the "path.
As for how liberation (*vimukti*) and higher progress (*viśeṣagamana*) are termed the "path": [it is because they lead toward it].
Question:
Preparatory application (*prayoga*) and the immediate path (*ānantarya-mārga*) involve the pursuit of nirvāṇa and may thus be called "the path.
However, since the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*) and the path of excellence (*viśeṣa-mārga*) do not involve such pursuit, how can they be considered the path?
How is it called the "Path"?
It is so named because it is similar in nature to the Path and leads to the attainment of Nirvana without remainder.
This refers to liberation, superior progress, preparatory application, and the immediate [attainment].

It is called the "path" (*mārga*) because its nature is identical [to that of liberation]. Furthermore, it is called the path because, as one understands liberation and progresses toward higher advancement, one gradually turns toward subsequent superior grades;

thus, it serves as the path for what follows. Moreover, it is called the path because the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*) is of the same class as the path of preparation (*prayoga-mārga*) and the uninterrupted path (*ānantarya-mārga*).
It is called the "path" (mārga) because it proceeds as a superior path of advancement (viśeṣamārga) in its highest degree;
or alternatively, it is called the "path" because, through the power of successive liberation and advancement, it leads accordingly to each subsequent stage of the path.
Alternatively, because both of these two types can lead to entry into the nirvana without remainder (*anupadhiśeṣa*), they are also called the "path" (*mārga*).
Regarding the question of upon what basis the path is established elsewhere:
hereafter follows the second section, which clarifies the inquiry concerning the four paths of practice (*pratipad*).

The Path is established under the name "supernormal power" (abhijñā) in other contexts. "Supernormal power" (abhijñā) means thorough penetration (abhijñāna); "power" (jñā) refers to penetrating through, while "path" (mārga) refers to the track (gati).
That which can correctly penetrate is called "supernormal power," and that which proceeds toward Nirvāṇa is called "path. How many kinds of this are there?
On what basis is this established?
The verse says: "From the slowest to the swift, those with dull and sharp faculties.
The first line answers the initial question.
The final three phrases answer the second question.
The Treatise states: "That which is extremely swift is the opposite of this" refers to the manifestation of suffering and pleasure according to their respective stages (*bhūmi*).
Depending on the faculties or the individual, one clarifies the speed [of progress];
depending on the fundamental dhyānas, there is an equilibrium of śamatha and vipaśyanā when all noble paths arise.
Spontaneity is called the "pleasant path of practice";
it is not, however, the feeling of pleasure.
This occurs when one relies on the meditative equipoise (śamatha) and insight (vipaśyanā) being balanced in other stages.
Whenever the noble paths arise, that which is characterized by hardship is called the "difficult practice" (*duḥkhā pratipad*).
This does not refer to the sensation of suffering (*duḥkhavedanā*). As for the "limbs," they refer to the limbs of dhyāna; the rest of the text may be understood accordingly.
Furthermore, the *Nyāyānusāra* (Treatise on the Principles of Correct Reasoning), fascicle 71, states:
"This practice has the five aggregates as its nature, or the four aggregates as its nature,
depending on the distinction between the meditative absorptions of the form realm (*rūpadhyāna*) and the formless realm (*ārūpyadhyāna*)."
As for the designation "Path of Seeing," it is because wisdom is predominant; just as in the stage of the Path of Seeing,
although all five aggregates are present, [it is named after its dominant factor].
Because wisdom is preeminent, it is specifically designated by the name "view.
As for the Path being called the factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipākṣika-dharma*),
this constitutes the third [section], clarifying the factors conducive to enlightenment.
Within this, first is a general explanation of several points together;
second is the formal presentation of the essential nature.
The third [section] clarifies the three knowledges (*vidyā*), mindfulness, and so forth; the fourth clarifies the increase of the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa*);
the fifth clarifies the outflows (*āsrava*) and the outflow-free (*anāsrava*).
Sixth, the classification according to the stages (*bhūmi*). This is the first [section], providing a general explanation by enumerating the categories.

Because ignorance (*avidyā*) and torpor (*middha*) have been forever abandoned, and because one has known the objects of the Four Noble Truths as they truly are, what was to be done has already been accomplished.
This is the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*), because one no longer acts [toward defilements];
this is the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*).
These two are called awakening (*bodhi*); in the language of Brahmā, it is *bodhi*.
This is translated as "awakening" (jue).
The remaining text may be understood accordingly.
These thirty-seven [factors] up to the other nine are the same as those mentioned previously.
This is the second [section], the correct determination of their essential nature.
Although there are thirty-seven names,
in actual substance there are only ten.
The Vaibhāṣika masters say there are eleven,
because the two types of action— bodily and vocal— are not intermingled, and thus ethical discipline (*śīla*) is divided into two.
Right livelihood is identical to right speech; because it is an action (*karman*), it is not mentioned separately.
The remaining nine factors are the same as before.
In the *Vibhāṣā*, fascicle 95, there are three explanations.
Both of these views agree with this treatise.
Furthermore, there is another view:
that right livelihood exists apart from right speech and right action.
If one speaks of three categories, there are twelve [precepts];
however, there is no commentator who has provided a formal evaluation. Although they differ in their expansion or condensation, all take the precepts as their essence.
In brief, although there are thirty-seven names, their actual substance consists of only ten:

namely, wisdom (*prajñā*), diligence (*vīrya*), concentration (*samādhi*), faith (*śraddhā*), mindfulness (*smṛti*), joy (*prīti*), equanimity (*upekṣā*), pliancy (*praśrabdhi*), ethical discipline (*śīla*), and applied thought (*vitarka*). Question: Why is it that among the seventy-five dharmas...
Question: Why are these ten dharmas established as factors of enlightenment (bodhipakṣa), while others are not?
Answer: It is explained that those which accord with purity and are particularly predominant are established as factors of enlightenment.
The others are not established because they do not accord with purity (*viśuddhi*). As the *Vibhāṣā* states:
"Question: For what reason, among all phenomena such as form (*rūpa*) and so forth..."
Is it only non-informative matter (avijñapti-rūpa) that is established as a factor of enlightenment (bodhipakṣa), and not other dharmas?
Answer: Right speech, right action, and right livelihood are in conformity with the Noble Path.
Because their functional power increases predominantly [in this stage], they are established as factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*);
others do not do so, and therefore they are not so established. Furthermore, it is explained that ethical discipline (*śīla*) can serve as the hub, whereas other material qualities cannot.
Furthermore, the *Nyāyānusāra* states:
"For what reason is informative action (*vijñapti-karman*) not established as a factor of enlightenment (*bodhipākṣika-dharma*)?
The factors of enlightenment are exclusively wholesome dharmas that are conducive to meditative concentration (*samādhi*)."
The unmanifest (avijñapti) coexistent with the mind possesses a superior capacity for conformity and efficacy;
manifest action (vijñapti-karman) is not so. Therefore, it is not established [as such].
The *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 96, states:
Question: Why is the mind (*citta*) not established as a factor of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*)?
Answer: Because the mind lacks the characteristics of a factor of enlightenment.
Furthermore, the mind possesses equal functional capacity regarding both the categories of affliction and purification;

whereas the factors conducive to enlightenment possess a disproportionately greater functional capacity within the category of purification. For this reason, they are not established [as being of the same nature as the mind].
Furthermore, the factors of enlightenment (bodhipākṣika-dharma) assist toward awakening;
the mind-king (citta-rāja), however, should not be assisted by them,
for it would be like a king who lacks the principle of having assisting ministers.
The details are as explained in that [commentary]. Question:
Among the forty-six mental factors (*caitasika-dharma*), why are only mindfulness, concentration, wisdom, feeling, faith, diligence, equanimity, pliancy, and applied thought established?
Regarding the non-establishment of other dharmas: as stated in the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, it asks:

"Among the great earth-dharmas (*mahābhūmika*), why are only mindfulness (*smṛti*), concentration (*samādhi*), wisdom (*prajñā*), and feeling (*vedanā*) established as factors of enlightenment (*bodhipākṣika-dharma*)?"
Answer: Among the three factors conducive to purification—mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom—their functional power is predominant.
The factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa-dharma*) are likewise;
therefore, these three are subsumed [within them].
Because they possess superior power and function within both the categories of defilement and purification,
they are also established as factors of enlightenment (bodhipakṣadharma). Other masters say:
Although the power and function of the defiled factors they receive are superior,
they perform beneficial work for the purified factors;
this is like the Caṇḍāla caste, which, though lowly and inferior, [performs essential services].
Furthermore, because they perform beneficial acts for noble families,
these— namely perception (*saṃjñā*), volition (*cetanā*), contact (*sparśa*), and desire (*chanda*)— are likewise established as factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*).
Because its force and function are predominantly increased within the category of affliction (*saṃkleśapakṣa*),
it is not established as a factor of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*).
In the case of conceptual meditation (*parikalpita-bhāvanā*), resolute conviction (*adhimukti*) is predominantly increased.
The factors conducive to enlightenment (bodhipākṣika-dharma) accord with the contemplation of reality;
therefore, resolute belief (adhimukti) is not included among them.
Other masters say:
The factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*) predominate during the stage of training (*śaikṣa*);
however, it is only upon reaching the stage of no-more-training (*aśaikṣa*) that resolute conviction (*adhimukti*) becomes truly superior.
Therefore, [resolute conviction] is not established as a factor conducive to enlightenment.
Mental attention (*manasikāra*) causes the mind to perceive its object and makes it easy for the mind to become distracted and unsettled;
since this is inconsistent with the meaning [of the factors of enlightenment],
which cause the mind to abide upon its object, other masters do not establish it as one of them.
At the initial moment of apprehending an object, the power of attention (*manasikāra*) is predominant;
as the continuity of the object persists, that power gradually diminishes.
The factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*) only arise after the object has been apprehended for a considerable duration.
It is also not established because it is inconsistent with the meaning.
