Question: Why are all three feelings (*vedanā*) common to the untainted (*anāsrava*), yet only joy (*prīti*) is established as a factor of enlightenment (*bodhipākṣika-dharma*)?
Answer: Because the two feelings of pleasure (*sukha*) and equanimity (*upekṣā*) lack those characteristics.
Furthermore, because the aspects (*ākāra*) of the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*) are sharp and intense,
while pleasure (*sukha*) and equanimity (*upekṣā*) are dull, neither of them is established [as a factor].
Furthermore, because untainted pleasant feeling (*anāsrava-sukha-vedanā*) is obscured and impaired by the pleasure of pliancy (*praśrabdhi-sukha*).
Equanimity is not established as a factor of enlightenment because it is obscured and impaired by the equanimity of practice, and thus its characteristic is not clearly manifest.

Question: Within the great wholesome mental factors (*mahābhūmika-dharma*), why are only these four—faith, diligence, pliancy, and equanimity—established as factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*)?
Answer: Because these four are particularly favorable to enlightenment.
Therefore, it is established separately as a factor of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*).
That is to say, faith is the foremost in the pursuit of enlightenment;
when about to initiate various practices, faith serves as the primary foundation.
Therefore, faith is established as a factor of enlightenment (bodhipakṣadharma).
Diligence universally exerts itself toward the practice leading to enlightenment,
causing one to swiftly advance toward the enlightenment of the three vehicles.
Therefore, these are also established as factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*).
Pliancy (*praśrabdhi*) and adaptability counteract lethargy (*styāna*), excelling in the category of insight (*vipaśyanā-pakṣa*);
equanimity (*upekṣā*) and evenness counteract restlessness (*auddhatya*), excelling in the category of tranquility (*śamatha-pakṣa*).
Among the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*), calm abiding (*śamatha*) and insight (*vipaśyanā*) are predominant;
therefore, they are both established as factors of enlightenment.

Although the six virtues of the wholesome class (*kuśalapakṣa*), such as shame (*hrī*) and dread of blame (*apatrāpya*), possess superior power and function within that category, [they are not so designated].
However, because their power and efficacy within the category of wholesome concentration (*samādhi-kuśala*) are weak and inferior,
they are not established as factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*);
for the factors of enlightenment are comprised within wholesome concentration.
Other masters say that among the great wholesome dharmas,
those whose counteractive factors are strong and whose intrinsic nature is superior are established as factors of enlightenment (bodhipakṣa).
The others are not so. That which is strong in terms of what it counteracts refers to that which is associated with all defiled minds.
That which is superior by nature refers to the root of all conditioned phenomena.
The arousal of various practices assists the excellence of tranquility (śamatha) and insight (vipaśyanā).
Faith, diligence, pliancy, and equanimity all possess both meanings [of tranquility and insight].
Among the six qualities such as shame (hrī) and dread of blame (apatrāpya), none possess both.
That is to say, in the case of the five [factors] beginning with shame (*hrī*), both meanings are absent;
in the case of heedfulness (*apramāda*) alone, only its own specific nature (*svabhāva*) is lacking.
Therefore, they are not established as factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*).
Question: Why are *prāmodya* (rejoicing) and *vidveṣa* (aversion), which are also by nature wholesome, not established as factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*)?
Answer: Because these two dharmas cannot take all objects universally, and they cannot arise simultaneously within a single mental state (*citta-kalāpa*).
Because the aids to enlightenment (*bodhipākṣika*) are not superior [to the factors themselves], they are not established as such.
Question: Why is it that while both *vitarka* (applied thought) and *vicāra* (sustained thought) are common to the untainted (*anāsrava*), only *vitarka* is established as a factor of enlightenment?
Answer: Vicāra is not established because it lacks those characteristics.

Furthermore, the modes of activity (*ākāra*) of the factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*) are sharp and intense, whereas the function of vicāra is subtle and weak; therefore, it is not established [as such].
Furthermore, because vicāra (sustained application) is obscured and impaired by vitarka (initial application), the function of vitarka predominates in directing right view;
therefore, vicāra is not established as a factor of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*). [End of citation from the *Mahāvibhāṣā*].
The intention of the *Nyāyānusāra* is also the same as that of the *Mahāvibhāṣā*: two among the other great unwholesome mental factors (*akuśala-mahābhūmika*),
six among the great afflictive mental factors (*kleśa-mahābhūmika*),
and ten among the minor afflictive mental factors (*parīttakleśabhūmika*).
Furthermore, greed, hatred, pride, and doubt within the indeterminate stages (*aniyata-bhūmi*) are all not established [as independent factors],
because they are concordant with defilement (*saṃkleśa*).
Although sleep (*middha*) and regret (*kaukṛtya*) also extend to the wholesome, they are exclusively acquired by birth (*upapatti-labdha*).

The factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*) are the wholesome states of preparatory application (*prayoga-kuśala*). Furthermore, the *Nyāyānusāra* (Treatise on the Principles of Correct Reasoning), fascicle 71, asks:
"For what reason are the dissociated formations (*viprayukta-saṃskāra*) not established as factors of enlightenment?"
They possess no distinct or superior capacity for assisting awakening because they are dissociated [from it],
unlike the unmanifest (avijñapti), which, despite being dissociated, does possess such a capacity.
However, because they serve as the hub for the wheel of the path (mārga-cakra),
they are not established separately among the factors of enlightenment (bodhipakṣadharma).
Other masters say that the two mindless attainments (acittaka-samāpatti) are contrary to enlightenment because they can extinguish the mind.
The four characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) and their acquisition (*prāpti*), in relation to that which is characterized (*lakṣya*), constitute existence, transition, and function.
These function equally with respect to both defilement (*saṃkleśa*) and purification (*vyavadāna*).

Because the factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*) increase in their function toward purification, they are not established separately. It is explained that the remaining seven [characteristics] are indeterminate (*avyākṛta*); the reasoning for this lies beyond words.

Therefore, those other masters do not provide a separate explanation for them. Question: Why are the three unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*) not established [as faculties]? Answer: It is explained that that which accords with enlightenment must necessarily give rise to activity.
Since the unconditioned is devoid of activity, it is therefore not established [as such].
Because of these reasons for exclusion and inclusion, only ten types are established as factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*);
all others are not so established.
Furthermore, the *Nyāya* states:
For what reason is faith not established as a factor of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*) or a path-factor (*mārgāṅga*)?
Because it is predominant at the time of first setting out on the path;
once one has entered the stage of the noble ones (*ārya*), it is established as a factor of enlightenment and a path-factor.
At that time, faith is weak in its power and function;
therefore, it is not established among the factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*) or the path factors (*mārgāṅga*).
For what reason, however, are joy (*prīti*), tranquility (*praśrabdhi*), and equanimity (*upekṣā*) established among the factors of enlightenment?
Nor is it established that they are included among the factors of the path,
because they accord specifically with awakening (*bodhi*) rather than with the path (*mārga*).
In what way do they accord with awakening?
Furthermore, within the path of cultivation, one cultivates nine grades of supreme awakening in each stage, repeatedly awakening to the suchness of the truths;
as this occurs, a corresponding degree of supreme joy arises.
Because he gives rise to supreme joy, he further delights in contemplating the truths;
just as a person digging the earth feels joy upon finding treasure,
because that joy has arisen, he further delights in digging more deeply.
Therefore, joy increases through the power of conformity to awakening;
this requires the pacification of all activities through lightness and ease,
as well as the equalizing of the mind through the power of equanimity.
Only when one is able to examine the object with precise discernment can equanimity (*upekṣā*) be established within the factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*).
Why are these three not conducive to the Path?
To proceed with rapid momentum is the meaning of the Noble Path (*āryamārga*).
This is slightly inconsistent with the rapid movement [of the mind],
for both are able to cause the mind to abide in tranquility.
For what reason are vitarka and śīla established as factors of the path?
They are not likewise established among the factors of enlightenment (bodhyaṅga),
because those [factors] conform specifically to the path and do not conform to enlightenment.
In what way do they conform to the path?
Furthermore, within the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*),
investigation (*vitarka*) urges the right view (*samyagdṛṣṭi*) to swiftly observe the objects of the eight truths, both superior and inferior;
morality (*śīla*) serves as the hub that completes the wheel of the path of seeing.
It causes one to turn swiftly toward the Truths;
therefore, both investigation (*vitarka*) and ethical discipline (*śīla*) are established as branches of the Path.
How, then, would these not be conducive to awakening?
Furthermore, while seeking the truths, one proceeds without tranquility because one is still characterized by the search for the nature of the Noble Truths;
once awakened, one proceeds with tranquility through having seen the truths.
Therefore, upon investigation, there is some slight contradiction with enlightenment (*bodhi*).
Enlightenment is associated (*samprayukta*), possesses an object of cognition (*ālambana*), and has a basis and a mode of activity (*ākāra*);
morality (*śīla*) is the opposite of this.
Therefore, those [factors] are not established among the factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*).
The term "path" (*mārga*) refers to that which functions universally; thus, it cannot be used as a precedent [for this case].

As for the three—mindfulness, effort, and concentration—reaching the state of wisdom (*prajñā*): they are the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), right effort (*samyak-vyāyāma*), and right concentration (*samyak-samādhi*).

Below this, the third section clarifies three questions concerning the foundations of mindfulness (smṛtyupasthāna), the bases of psychic power (ṛddhipāda), and the right efforts (samyakprahāṇa). Among these three categories of names, there is nothing further that specifically corresponds to them individually.
Why are the foundations of mindfulness (smṛtyupasthāna) described as exclusively wisdom (prajñā)?
Why are the right efforts (samyakprahāṇa) described as exclusively diligence (vīrya)?
Why are the bases of psychic power (ṛddhipāda) described as exclusively concentration (samādhi)?
The verse says: "Reaching and concentration.
The answer is:
the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right endeavors, and the three categories of the bases of supernormal power (*ṛddhipāda*) constitute the roots of goodness.
If its essential nature were defined according to associated and co-existent factors (*sahabhū-dharma*),
it would actually encompass all preparatory wholesome states;
however, its essential nature is defined here according to the predominant wholesome roots of its own category.
They should be explained in their respective order:
the foundations of mindfulness consist of wisdom,
and the right efforts consist of diligence.
The bases of psychic power constitute meditative concentration.
Why, then, is the name "foundation of mindfulness" established for wisdom?
This is the question.
Regarding the statement that the Vaibhāṣika masters [hold that mindfulness] "reaches, maintains, and causes to abide," the answer is:
wisdom is called the foundation of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*).
"It is so called because of its cause" means that,
in reality, it is established through wisdom;
this is the Master’s correct explanation.
Wisdom is called "application of mindfulness" (smṛtyupasthāna) by way of its fruit;
this refers to the same meaning as previously stated.
Why, then, is diligence (vīrya) called "right abandonment" (samyakprahāṇa)?
Question:
Regarding the phrase "because one has reached this most excellent state through correct cultivation," what is the answer?
In the stage of diligently abandoning the two evils and diligently cultivating the two virtues during correct cultivation, this power of diligence is able to sever laziness;
therefore, these four are collectively termed "right abandonments" (*samyakprahāṇa*). As for what is meant by "four kinds":
First, one employs skillful means to abandon unwholesome states that have already arisen;
second, one employs skillful means to prevent unwholesome states that have not yet arisen from arising;
third, one employs skillful means to give rise to wholesome states that have not yet arisen.
Fourth, one cultivates already arisen wholesome dharmas so that they increase and expand.
Thus, the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* states:
"The essence of right effort has four functions."
Just as a lamp simultaneously performs four functions, so too the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 141, states:
Regarding the four right efforts (*catvāri samyakprahāṇāni*):
first, for the sake of abandoning evil and unwholesome states that have already arisen, one generates desire, exerts effort, applies the mind, and sustains the mind.
Second, for the purpose of preventing unarisen evil and unwholesome states from arising;
the rest is as previously explained.
Third, for the purpose of causing unarisen wholesome states to arise.
The rest is as explained previously.
Fourth, for the sake of causing already arisen wholesome dharmas to remain stable, not be forgotten, and to be practiced further so that they increase and expand;
the rest is as explained previously. Question: For what reason are these four called "right abandonments" (*samyakprahāṇa*)?
Answer: Because these four are able to correctly abandon [the afflictions]. Question: While the first two may be so, how are the latter two?
Answer: They are designated by the name of the first.
Therefore, there is no error.
Alternatively, all four of these possess the meaning of "abandonment";
that is to say, the first two abandon the afflictive obstructions (*kleśāvaraṇa*).
The latter two abandon the cognitive obstacles (*jñeyāvaraṇa*), because ignorance is abandoned when cultivating wholesome dharmas;
furthermore, both temporary abandonment and permanent abandonment are termed "abandonment. Moreover, the *Saṃyuktābhidharmahṛdaya*, chapter eight, states:
Although Arhats possess no unwholesome dharmas and have already abandoned their antidotes,
they are still said to possess the four right efforts because they maintain the antidote of destruction, the antidote of maintenance, and the antidote of distancing.

The same applies to the form and formless realms; this concludes the treatise. The section beginning with "Alternatively named" below provides an explanation of alternative names, which may be understood from the text itself.
For what reason is the name "basis of spiritual power" (*ṛddhipāda*) established for meditative concentration?
It is asked:
because it is that upon which all sublime and wondrous virtues depend.
Answer: They are called "divine" (*deva*) because they possess the supreme and wondrous merits of various spirits;
they are called "feet" (*pāda*) because they are the basis upon which those deities rely.
Because they are the feet of the divine, they are called "divine feet" (ṛddhipāda).
As for the statement by other masters that "the feet refer to desire and so forth," this records the explanation of those other masters.
The divine power (*ṛddhi*) is concentration (*samādhi*), because it functions through the divine power.
"Sufficiency" (*pāda*) refers to the four kinds: desire, effort, mind, and investigation.

Regarding the statement that "the factors of enlightenment (bodhipakṣa) reach meditative concentration (samādhi) and are thus called 'limbs' (aṅga)," the master of the treatise refutes other teachers by stating:
"If one says that the limbs refer to desire (chanda) and so forth."
For him, there should be thirteen factors of enlightenment;
by adding desire and the mind to the eleven factors previously mentioned by the Vaibhāṣikas, there are thirteen.
Because the two types [of mindfulness] already exist within the eleven [factors], diligence and discernment are not said to increase.
Because desire is not present in the mind, it is mentioned separately as "increased.
The virtuous masters of old have said that the mind is concentration.
This interpretation is incorrect.
If the mind were already in a state of concentration,
it would only need to increase its desire.
Because concentration exists first,
one now increases desire and the mind; thus,
one knows that the mind is not concentration.
If the self were identical to meditative concentration,
it would further contradict the scriptural teachings.
For the sūtras state that the "self" refers to the enjoyment of various supernormal powers, such as dividing one into many and so forth.
Therefore, one should know that "divine" (*divya*) refers to the wondrous virtue of spiritual power (*śakti*).
It is appropriate to call the four *samādhis*—such as the desireless (*anabhisaṃskāra*) and others—"feet" (*pāda*).
Thus, one should know that the meditative concentration (*samādhi*) which serves as the basis for this divine power is designated by the name "foot."
The Master of the Treatise explains the sūtra as follows:
herein, the Buddha refers to the fruit of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) by the name "supernormal power" (*ṛddhi*);
the meditative absorptions (*samāpatti*) produced by the four causes, such as desire and so forth, are termed "bases" (*pāda*).
Therefore, one should know that this supernormal power (ṛddhi) is not identical to meditative concentration (samādhi).
In terms of ultimate reality, meditative concentration constitutes its essential nature;
yet it is called the "four bases of supernormal power" (catvāra ṛddhipādāḥ).
The four [elements] are spoken of from the perspective of their causes; when considered from the perspective of their effects,
they are called "spirits" (ātman).
Thus, it is said that this is sufficient.
Therefore, the *Vibhāṣā* states:
"A single samādhi arises from four causes."
Therefore, the four designations are established based on their respective causes. Question:
Are these produced from the four causes according to simultaneity or according to temporal sequence? Explanation: These names are established based on simultaneity.
Although many factors coexist simultaneously with meditative concentration (*samādhi*),
these four are superior in their ability to nourish it;
"desire" (*chanda*) refers to aspiration.
"Diligence" refers to exertion;
"mind" refers to the basis;
and "contemplation" refers to investigation.
Therefore, it is named after its four simultaneous causes.
Thus, the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* states:
"That is to say, among the co-existent and associated dharmas..."

Because these four are superior to the *sāmantaka* (preparatory stage) of *samādhi*, they are called "accessories" (*upakāra*); this is the conclusion of the treatise. Furthermore, it is explained that these names are established based on their preparatory application (*prayoga*).
"Desire" (*chanda*) refers to the wish to give rise to this meditative absorption.
This means that in the stage of preparatory application (*prayoga*), concentration is induced and arises through the power of desire;
"diligent" refers to one who diligently cultivates this concentration,
meaning that in the stage of preparatory application, concentration is induced and arises through the power of diligence.
The mind (citta) is the basis for mental factors (caitta);
that is to say, in the stage of preparatory application (prayoga), meditative concentration (samādhi) is induced by the power of the mind.
Contemplation (vipaśyanā) is the observation of objects through wisdom (prajñā).
This means that in the stage of preparation (*prayoga*), meditative concentration (*samādhi*) is induced through the power of contemplation.
Although there are many factors within the stage of preparation, these four are preeminent as provisions; thus, they are designated by way of these four.
Therefore, the *Vibhāṣā* states:
"That is to say, in the stage of preparatory application (*prayoga*), one may either through the power of desire induce meditative concentration (*samādhi*) to manifest;
this is explained at length, and so forth."
Alternatively, as stated in the aforementioned treatise regarding the four [bases of psychic power] that are induced to manifest through the power of contemplation:
first, the basis of psychic power of desire;
second, the basis of psychic power of exertion.
Third is the basis of psychic power of faith;
fourth is the basis of psychic power of investigation.
For what reason are faith and the others designated as "powers" (bala) only after they have reached their culmination?
Question:
For what reason are the five dharmas, beginning with faith, both faculties and powers by nature,
yet are first designated as faculties?
The subsequent statement that "these are called powers because by means of these five dharmas one reaches a state of being invincible" is the answer.
Based on these five factors, the faculties (*indriya*) are explained first in their weak form,
while the powers (*bala*) are explained later in their strong form.
Furthermore, they are designated as "faculties" when they are susceptible to being overcome.
"Power" is defined as being incapable of being overcome.
Regarding the question: "For what reason do faith and the others follow this specific sequence?"—this is the inquiry.
Regarding the statement, "As for [the sequence] of cause and effect reaching such a succession," the answer is that it may be understood from the text as it stands.
Regarding the question of at which stage one should say that the factors of enlightenment increase in successive order:
this is the fourth [section], clarifying the increase of the factors of enlightenment,
consisting of the question and the verse response.
The Commentary states: "Regarding the phrase 'up to what has been explained as such':
in the stage of the beginner, one is able to clearly and minutely discern the specific and general characteristics of the four objects, beginning with the body."
Because the function of wisdom (*prajñā*) is predominant, it is said that the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) increase [in this stage]. Within the stage of "Heat" (*uṣmagata*),

because one is able to realize the superior qualities of the wholesome factors of the "levels of penetration" (*nirvedhabhāgīya*) which are of a distinct category, it is said that the right efforts (*samyakprahāṇa*) increase.

In the stage of the Dharma of the Summit (*mūrdha-dharma*), because one is able to maintain superior wholesome states and has reached a stage of patience from which there is no regression, it is said that the bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*) increase. In the stage of Patience (*kṣānti-dharma*),

because one will certainly not retreat and will certainly not fall into the evil realms, and because the roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*) have become firm and attained the sense of supremacy, it is said that the faculties (*indriya*) increase.
In the first stage,
they are said to possess increased power because they cannot be overcome by any defiled phenomena or other worldly dharmas.
In the stage of the path of cultivation (bhāvanāmārga)...
Because they assist awakening as one approaches the stage of enlightenment, they are said to increase as factors of awakening (bodhyaṅga).
Within the stage of the path of seeing (darśanamārga),
fifteen moments proceed with rapid transition.
Because they are superior in terms of their function, the path factors (*mārgāṅga*) are said to increase;
however, in the sūtras, they are taught in order of their numerical increase—first seven and then eight—and not according to the sequence of cultivation.
If one were to rely on the actual sequence of cultivation:
First eight, then seven; within the [first] eight, the subsequent meanings are already explained by implication.
Such is the teaching of the Vaibhāṣika masters.
Others, however, state that this [fifth category] is the fifth.
To describe the explanation of other masters: regarding the "four matters," it means diligently abandoning the two evils and diligently cultivating the two virtues;
their names are listed as before.
Power (*bala*) has the meaning of being invincible.
It is able to correctly subdue and eliminate the afflictions that are its opposites,
preventing them from manifesting and causing the noble dharmas to arise.
For this reason, it is called the fifth power.
The rest of the text is understandable.
Regarding the phrase "because one reaches the four noble truths at the stage of the path of seeing":
The seven factors of enlightenment (bodhyaṅga) are established at the stage of the path of seeing (darśanamārga),
because one realizes the four noble truths (catvāry āryasatyāni) as they truly are.
They pertain to both stages [of seeing and cultivation] because they lead to the city of nirvāṇa.
The eight factors of the noble path are established as being common to both the stages of seeing (*darśana*) and cultivation (*bhāvanā*),
because they all lead directly to the city of nirvana without remainder (*anupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*).
Alternatively, this nirvana may also include that with remainder (*sopadhiśeṣa*).

As stated in the Sūtra regarding "attaining and also cultivating perfection," other masters cite this scripture as proof that the eight branches of the noble path also pertain to the stage of cultivation.
Since the scriptural text explicitly states that one cultivates these eight branches of the path to perfection, [they must apply to that stage].
Since the seven factors of enlightenment are also cultivated to perfection,

one should know that the eightfold path likewise pertains to the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*). If it is said that the seven factors of enlightenment belong to the path of cultivation, [it follows that the eightfold path does as well].
The eight [factors] exist in the path of vision;
how could one not cultivate them? At that time, even the seven are perfected.
By this it is clearly known.
When one cultivates the eight [limbs] at the stage of the path of cultivation (bhāvanāmārga) until they are complete, it is called "cultivation to fulfillment.

Furthermore, regarding the sūtra statement "reaching the eight branches of the noble path," this again cites scripture to prove that the eightfold path is cultivated throughout. Thus speaks the one who proclaims words of reality.
This is analogous to the Buddha, the World-Honored One, teaching the Four Noble Truths;
this reveals the Path of Seeing (darśanamārga),
for by means of the Four Noble Truths being exactly as they are, it causes those who rely on the original path to proceed swiftly toward liberation.
This metaphor instructs one to cultivate the eight branches of the noble path;
this reveals the path of cultivation (bhāvanāmārga),
because these eight branches of the path were the original route traversed by the Buddhas of the past.
As it is said in a sutra: there was a caravan of merchants who boarded a ship and entered the ocean until they reached an island of sea-monsters (*sāgara-dvīpa*).
There, rākṣasīs manifested lovely forms to entice the merchants.
Gradually entering their own city, they each took a wife.
After many days had passed,
a celestial deity in the sky addressed the caravan merchants, saying:
"The inhabitants within this city are not human beings;
they are all rākṣasas who have brought about this delusion. Therefore, before long, they will all be devoured.
I shall now proclaim words that accord with reality."
Thereupon, everyone within the city suffers; this is a metaphor for the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkhasatya*).
You must not harbor greedy attachment.
This metaphor illustrates the truth of the origin of suffering (*samudaya-satya*). The sudden desire to escape from the city illustrates the truth of cessation (*nirodha-satya*).
One must urgently seek an exit;
this is a metaphor for the Truth of the Path (mārgasatya).
Therefore, one proclaims words that accord with reality.
This metaphor illustrates the Four Noble Truths,
revealing the Path of Seeing.
A deity in the sky further addressed the merchants:
"One may depart quickly by way of the original path.
This "original path" is a metaphor for the cultivation of the eight branches of the noble path, which illustrates the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*).
All Buddhas of the past have relied upon this fundamental path of cultivation to transcend birth and death.
If you wish to seek deliverance from the ocean of birth and death,
you may rely upon the fundamental path of the Buddhas of the past and proceed swiftly to emerge from it.
Those who seek swift deliverance should diligently cultivate the eight branches of the noble path;
by this it is known that [this teaching] also applies to the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*). Another interpretation states:
The statement in this treatise applies generally to both the paths of seeing (*darśana-mārga*) and cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*).
If one interprets it in this way, it is proven that the eightfold path (*āryāṣṭāṅgamārga*) pertains to both seeing and cultivation.
Thus, we know that the eight factors of the path are taught as applying to both stages.
Having concluded the citation of the two proofs,
the other masters summarize:
"The statement 'up to the contaminated and the uncontaminated' refers to the stage of increase."
This is the fifth [section], clarifying the contaminated (*sāsrava*) and the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*).
It may be understood from the text as it stands.
Furthermore, the *Nyāyānusāra* states:
This means that at the stage of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), the seven factors of enlightenment (*saptabodhyaṅga*) increase as they draw near to awakening (*bodhi*).
Because they counteract the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*), the essence of these factors of enlightenment is exclusively untainted (*anāsrava*).
All factors of enlightenment assist toward awakening.
The reason these alone are specifically designated by the name "factors of enlightenment" (bodhyaṅga) is that they are most proximate to the fruit of bodhi;
it is by this principle that the seven factors of enlightenment are established.
It should be understood that this is stated solely with reference to the antidote to the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*).
As the foremost among those that serve as antidotes for the lower stages,
it is only within the untainted (*anāsrava*) state that the name "limb of enlightenment" (*bodhyaṅga*) is established.
If this is not accepted,
how could it not be common to both? Or rather,
among all the factors conducive to enlightenment (bodhipakṣa), [it is so].
The designation "factors of enlightenment" (*bodhyaṅga*) is established based on proximity to enlightenment.
Within the path, at the stage of the cultivation of the path, that which is proximate to the nature of enlightenment— proximity to enlightenment being exclusively untainted (*anāsrava*)—
is therefore only the untainted path of cultivation that receives the name "factors of enlightenment."
In the stage of the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), the eight factors of the path (*mārgāṅga*) are predominant;
therefore, these are exclusively subsumed under the nature of the untainted (*anāsrava*).
As for the statement that "these thirty-seven [factors] reach up to the untainted": [it means they exist therein].
This is the sixth classification according to the stages (*bhūmi*):
because one still exerts effort to transform [the mind] and because doubt still persists.
Therefore, there is no joy.
The rest of the text may be understood accordingly; this passage provides a general explanation based on all the stages (*bhūmi*).
If, however, one considers them according to their actual manifestation (*samudācāra*), one takes only a single type from among the four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*).
The others may arise together.
Thus, the *Abhidharmamahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 96, states:
"Question: In which stage (*bhūmi*) do how many factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*) manifest simultaneously?"
Answer: Within the preparatory concentration (anāgamya-samādhi), there are thirty-six factors conducive to enlightenment (bodhipākṣika-dharma);
however, only thirty-three manifest simultaneously, excluding the three applications of mindfulness (smṛtyupasthāna).
Why is this so? Because the objects of the four foundations of mindfulness are each distinct;
there is not even the possibility for two to exist simultaneously.
How much more so for the third and fourth dhyānas?
Within the first dhyāna there are thirty-seven [factors],
yet only twenty-four manifest simultaneously.
Excluding the three applications of mindfulness,
there are thirty-five [factors] each in the intermediate dhyāna and in the third and fourth dhyānas;
however, only thirty-two manifest simultaneously.
Excluding the three applications of mindfulness,
in the second dhyāna there are thirty-six [factors], of which only thirty-three manifest simultaneously.
Excluding the three applications of mindfulness, in the first three formless attainments there are thirty-two.
Only twenty-nine [factors] manifest simultaneously,
excluding the three applications of mindfulness.
In the desire realm and the Peak of Existence, there are twenty-two.
Only nineteen [factors] manifest simultaneously;
excluding the three applications of mindfulness,
the others are explained according to their respective meanings.
It does not require a separate entity.
Regarding the statement that when the factors of enlightenment (bodhipakṣa) transform, all four [foundations] become exclusively untainted (*anāsrava*):
this constitutes the fourth major section, which clarifies the four kinds of verified confidence (*avetyaprasāda*).
There are four questions in total.
The first two lines answer the first question;
the subsequent four lines answer the second question.
The seventh phrase answers the third question;
the eighth phrase answers the fourth question. The Treatise says:
"Regarding the clear confidence in the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīla-prasāda*)."
The first two phrases are explained as follows:
because one realizes the principle of the Truths (satya), one gives rise to faith toward the Buddha; this is called "purity of conviction regarding the Buddha" (buddha-prasāda).
The same applies to the Dharma and the Saṅgha.
Because it is that which the Noble Ones cherish and revere, it is called "Noble Precepts" (ārya-śīla).
Since its essential nature is pure and it arises based on realization, it is also called "Purity through Realization" (avetyaprasāda).
The first three are expressed in words because they are objects of faith;
the fourth lacks words because it relies on direct realization.

Regarding the "Chapter on Discriminative Knowledge":
it is called "knowledge" (*jñāna*) because it involves decisive discernment and profound understanding.
This chapter is called "Discrimination" because it explains [the subject] in detail.
The reason the "Wisdom" chapter follows is that the preceding chapter explained the fruit.
This chapter clarifies the cause (*hetu*).
Since the cause is proximate to the fruit (*phala*), knowledge (*jñāna*) is explained next.
At the beginning of the preceding chapter, it was asked: "Does not the knowledge of arrival (*anvaya-jñāna*) constitute vision (*darśana*)?"
Within this chapter,
there are two main sections: first,
the elucidation of the distinctions among the various types of knowledge.
Second, the qualities accomplished through clear knowledge (*vidyā*). Within the distinctions of clear knowledge, there are two parts:
first, clarifying the differences between patience (*kṣānti*), knowledge (*jñāna*), and vision (*darśana*);
second, clarifying the specific characteristics of the ten knowledges (*daśajñāna*).
The aspects of the three knowledges (*vidyā*) and the ten knowledges (*jñāna*).

Fourth, the classification of knowledge by way of various gates. This is the first [section], which distinguishes between acceptance (*kṣānti*), knowledge (*jñāna*), and vision (*darśana*), restating the preceding inquiry.
In the initial section on the "Former Sages" (*Pūrvārya*), within the stage of the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*), the eight patiences (*kṣānti*) and the eight knowledges (*jñāna*) were explained.
Subsequently, in that same chapter, within the context of the Eightfold Noble Path (*āryāṣṭāṅgamārga*), Right View (*samyagdṛṣṭi*) was further explained.
Among the ten qualities of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), right knowledge (*samyagjñāna*) is further mentioned.
Is there any patience (*kṣānti*) that is not knowledge?
Or is there any knowledge that is not vision (*dṛṣṭi*)?
The verse says: "Reaching all, wisdom, the six, and the nature of views.
Within this response in verse form, there are the first two lines and the remaining two.
The first part is explained in terms of the untainted (*anāsrava*); the tainted wisdom (*sāsrava-prajñā*) and the subsequent final phrase are distinguished in terms of the tainted.
Patience (*kṣānti*) applies to both ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) and noble ones (*ārya*).
The words of the Sage distinguish it from the mundane;
although this patience is wisdom,
it is not yet knowledge.
Generally speaking, there are briefly four kinds of patience (*kṣānti*).
If patience is defined as forbearance, then non-aversion (*avyāpāda*) is called patience. If patience is defined as the endurance of suffering (*duḥkhādhivāsana-kṣānti*), then...
Vigor itself is called patience; if one grants [the truth] through patience, it is called patience.
Faith itself is called patience; if one observes the Dharma with patience, it is called patience.
Wisdom itself is called patience; herein, it is termed patience.
Taking wisdom as its intrinsic nature, views in general are briefly of two kinds. First,
that which involves inferential deliberation is called "view."
It has wisdom as its intrinsic nature.
The two acts of illuminating are called "vision" (*darśana*);
these consist of the eye faculty and the ten types of knowledge (*jñāna*).
Because their nature all possesses the function of illuminating the objects before them,
the term "view" (*dṛṣṭi*) here refers to that which involves conceptual deliberation;
therefore, the terms "exhaustion" (*kṣaya*) and "non-arising" (*anutpāda*) are not called "views."
The remainder is as in the prose [commentary].
The treatise states, "up to the nature of deliberation," which explains the first phrase.
In brief, there are two kinds of wisdom: first,
that which is with outflows (sāsrava).
The second is the untainted (anāsrava).
Only untainted wisdom is designated by the name "noble" (ārya);
it is called noble because it is able to correctly contemplate the Four Truths in accordance with reality.
Although the wisdom associated with outflows (*sāsrava-prajñā*) also contemplates the truths,
it is not called "noble" (*ārya*) because it is not clear and distinct. Furthermore,
among the noble wisdoms, the eight patiences (*aṣṭau kṣāntayaḥ*) do not possess the nature of knowledge (*jñāna*).
Decisive judgment is termed "knowledge" (*jñāna*).
Doubt is its opposite in terms of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), being characterized by hesitation.
When the eight patiences (*kṣānti*) arise, they are simultaneously accompanied by the acquisition (*prāpti*) of the doubt that they themselves sever.
At that time, because the opposing and contradictory factors have not yet been abandoned, they are not definitively severed;
because they are not definitively severed, it is not called "knowledge" (jñāna).
Because the nature of inferential cognition (tarkatva) is subsumed within the nature of being visible (dṛśyatva).
Although one has already abandoned self-doubt during the stage of the four dharmakṣāntis when previously detached from desire,
this doubt is associated with the kṣāntis because it belongs to the same category as those kṣāntis.
Therefore, it is also not wisdom.
Although the various uninterrupted paths (*ānantarya-mārga*) that sever the afflictions of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) are accompanied by doubt, they are not true antidotes.
Because it is not ultimately contradictory— since there is the possibility of later regression—
it can still be designated as "knowledge" (*jñāna*).
Thus, the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 44, states:
Furthermore, because patience (kṣānti) arises simultaneously with the acquisition of the doubt to be abandoned, it is not subsumed under knowledge (jñāna);
even if it were not simultaneous, it would still belong to that same category.
Because the path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*) associated with outflows (*sāsrava*) is not a true antidote;
thus, although it coexists with doubt, it is nonetheless a form of knowledge (*jñāna*). This concludes the preceding treatise. Question: Doubt obstructs decisive resolution.
If *kṣānti* (receptivity) were to coexist with doubt (*vicikitsā*), then *kṣānti* would not be designated as "knowledge" (*jñāna*).

Since ignorance (*avidyā*) obstructs inferential deliberation, if *kṣānti* were to coexist with delusion (*moha*), then *kṣānti* should likewise not be designated as "view" (*dṛṣṭi*). The commentary explains: there exists an associated ignorance that coexists with doubt.
When assisted by doubt, ignorance gains the power to oppose patience (*kṣānti*);
whereas independent ignorance lacks the assistance of other afflictions.
Thus, both patience and that [ignorance] when conjoined with it may be designated as "view" (*dṛṣṭi*).
If it is said that there is also ignorance associated [with wisdom],
what is now called "aid" refers to a distinct moment. Furthermore, another interpretation is that repeated observation is termed "wisdom."
The statement "not yet abandoned" indicates that [the object] has not been known repeatedly.
Thus, the *Vibhāṣā* says: "Question:
For what reason are the various untainted patiences (*anāsrava-kṣānti*) not considered knowledges (*jñāna*)?"
Answer: Because one has not yet repeatedly contemplated the objects of various views;
that is to say, since beginningless time, one has not yet perceived the Four Noble Truths with untainted, true wisdom.
Although it is seen for the first time now, it is not yet called "wisdom" (*jñāna*) because it has not been repeatedly observed;
for it is only when a similar type of discernment (*prajñā*) repeatedly observes an object that it becomes wisdom.
Furthermore, the *Abhidharmamahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 196, states:

"It is shown that the various types of patience (*kṣānti*) arise simultaneously with the acquisition of doubt (*vicikitsā*) which they themselves sever; because they have not yet reached a state of repeated and definitive discernment, they do not receive the name of 'knowledge' (*jñāna*)."
"Exhaustion and non-arising, up to not being subject to deliberation" explains the second phrase.
Within noble wisdom (*āryaprajñā*), both exhaustion (*kṣaya*) and non-arising (*anutpāda*) are two kinds of knowledge (*jñāna*).
Because it is of a decisive nature,
or because it is a repeated cognition,
it is not of the nature of vision (*darśana*).
"Because the mind of seeking has already ceased and there is no further deliberation;
the remaining [factors] all pertain to the nature of deliberation" explains the other two [factors] within the third phrase.

Excluding the eight preceding patiences (*kṣānti*) and the knowledges of exhaustion (*kṣaya-jñāna*) and non-arising (*anutpāda-jñāna*), all remaining untainted wisdoms (*anāsrava-prajñā*) each possess both the nature of knowledge (*jñāna*) and the nature of vision (*darśana*).
This is because they have already severed their own doubt and possess the nature of decisive resolution.
Alternatively, it is called "knowledge" (jñāna) because it cognizes with weightiness,
and it is called "view" (dṛṣṭi) because its nature is that of deliberative investigation.
All forms of contaminated wisdom (sāsravaprajñā), up to and including worldly right view (laukikasamyagdṛṣṭi), constitute these six.
Regarding the explanation of tainted wisdom (*sāsravaprajñā*) and the subsequent phrase:

because all tainted wisdom possesses the nature of decisive discernment (*pariccheda*), it is entirely subsumed within the nature of knowledge (*jñāna*). Among these, it is clarified that six types also possess the nature of vision (*dṛṣṭi*).
Because it has the nature of speculative investigation (*tarka*). This refers to the six [types of view]:

the five defiled views, such as the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), and worldly right view (*laukikī samyagdṛṣṭi*) associated with the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*). Question: Since patience (*kṣānti*) and doubt (*vicikitsā*) can coexist, why is patience not designated as knowledge (*jñāna*)?

It would follow that wisdom arising together with doubt should likewise not be called knowledge (*jñāna*). The explanation says: wisdom arising together with doubt is concordant with it and shares the same object;
yet, because it exercises decisive judgment regarding its object, it is also termed knowledge.
Therefore, the *Vibhāṣā* (106) states: Question:
For what reason is it called "knowledge" (*jñāna*)?
What is the meaning of "knowledge"?
Answer: The meaning of "decisive determination" is the meaning of "wisdom.
Question: If that is so, then the discernment associated with doubt should not be called wisdom, because it is not determinate regarding its object of focus.
The answer is that this too is wisdom (*jñāna*),
because it is also determinate with respect to its object for the duration of a single moment.
However, within this collection [of mental factors], the functional force of doubt (*vicikitsā*) is predominant.
When the mind wavers and fails to reach a decision regarding its object over many moments, this is called the "mass of doubt" (vicikitsā-skandha).
This is contrasted with samādhi, which remains constantly upon its object within a single moment.

Sometimes, if it is associated with restlessness (*auddhatya*), causing the mind to shift toward objects for many moments, it is called "distraction" (*vikṣepa*). Furthermore, all contaminated wisdom (*prajñā sāsravā*) is subsumed under the nature of knowledge (*jñāna*) because it involves repeated cognition.
The interpretation is as explained previously.
Thus, the *Abhidharmamahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 44, states:
"There is not a single sentient being who [possesses knowledge] regarding all objects."
Because it has not been repeatedly observed by impure wisdom (*sāsrava-prajñā*) since beginningless time, all impure wisdom is subsumed under knowledge (*jñāna*).
[End of treatise. Question: The wisdom associated with the five consciousnesses (*pañca-vijñāna-kāya-samprayukta-prajñā*) perceives its respective objects moment by moment.

If it does not involve repeated cognition, it should not be called "wisdom" (jñāna). The commentary explains: although the wisdom associated with the five consciousnesses does not involve repeated apprehension, it is described as involving repeated apprehension with respect to its own kind.
The contaminated mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) has necessarily previously taken those five objects as its objects.
When the wisdom (*prajñā*) concomitant with the five sensory consciousnesses takes them as objects again at this time, it is termed "re-cognition" (*punarjñāna*);
therefore, it is also called "knowledge" (*jñāna*). Thus, all that has been described is subsumed under the nature of wisdom.

Thus, both noble wisdom (*āryaprajñā*) and contaminated wisdom (*sāsravaprajñā*) are subsumed under the nature of wisdom (*prajñāsvabhāva*), as both are capable of discerning their respective objects.
As for the types of knowledge (*jñāna*): how many kinds are there that take the truths (*satya*), such as suffering (*duḥkha*), as their objects?
Below this, the second section clarifies the distinct characteristics of the various knowledges (*jñāna*). Within it,
the first part clarifies their gradual increase up to ten.
Second, it clarifies the distinction between the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya*) and non-arising (*anutpāda*). Third, it clarifies the establishment [of the stages] as ten.

Fourth, it clarifies that the Dharma-knowledge (*dharmajñāna*) and subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*) together constitute the antidotes. Regarding the first point, which clarifies the gradual increase up to ten:
One clear illumination, two knowledges, three knowledges;
two clear illuminations, three increased to nine;
three clear illuminations, nine increased to ten—this constitutes the first [section]: one clear illumination, two knowledges, three knowledges, and ten knowledges, answering the initial question.
The answer to the second question: Alternatively, within this verse, "wisdom" (*jñāna*) is tenfold, which collectively indicates the names and number;
the subsequent text specifically clarifies two wisdoms and three wisdoms.
The Commentary states: "Regarding the phrase 'taking the Four Truths as the object,' the meaning of this passage in the treatise is for the most part clear.
Furthermore, the *Nyāyabindu* (or *Prakaraṇapāda*), fascicle 73, says:
The preceding impure knowledge is collectively termed "conventional" (*saṃvṛti*).
Since the nature of objects such as jars and garments is subject to destruction,
this reveals the conventional perspective.
Therefore, it is called "conventional" (saṃvṛti),
because this wisdom mostly takes conventional objects as its domain and mostly functions in accordance with worldly, conventional matters.
The designation "conventional knowledge" (saṃvṛti-jñāna) is established primarily based on its multiplicity;
it does not function by apprehending the ultimate (paramārtha), nor does it operate in accordance with things that conform to the ultimate.
Nevertheless, it is an object of craving.
Because it lacks the superior capacity to pacify the various internal afflictions,
it is not untainted (*anāsrava*).
Alternatively, because it conceals the supramundane and induces the mundane, it receives the designation "worldly" (*laukika*).
Its essence is precisely non-wisdom (*ajñāna*).
Wisdom receives its respective name according to that to which it is subordinate;
this indicates that the term refers to contaminated wisdom (*sāsrava-jñāna*), as explained at length therein.
Regarding those who have reached this point where they first possess only the categories of suffering and its origin (*duḥkha-samudaya-nirvedhabhāgīya*):
this is the second [section], clarifying the increase from three up to nine.
The Treatise says: "Up to the four knowledges of cessation and the path (*nirodha-mārga-jñāna*)."
This explains the first two phrases:
among the aforementioned three types of knowledge, the objects of the knowledge of phenomena (*dharma-jñāna*) and the subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*) are distinct.
It is further divided into four types.
The *Nyāyānusāra* (Treatise on the Principles of Correct Reasoning), fascicle 73, asks:
"For what reason does conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*) also take suffering and the other truths as its objects while forming the aspects (*ākāra*) of suffering and so forth?"
It is not, however, the knowledge of suffering and so forth;
for since one has previously contemplated suffering and so forth through the aspects of suffering and so forth,
it would subsequently be possible to contemplate those same objects of suffering and so forth as being pleasant and so forth.
Furthermore, having attained such conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*),
because doubt regarding the truths may subsequently manifest as an object of cognition,
these six knowledges thus come to have [the truths] as their objective domain.
The two following lines are explained as follows: Such dharmas, anvaya-jñāna, and the four truths—

when they are comprised within the state of no-more-learning (aśaikṣa) and are not of the nature of vision— are termed the knowledge of exhaustion (kṣaya-jñāna) and the knowledge of non-arising (anutpāda-jñāna).
This is the knowledge of exhaustion and the knowledge of non-arising.
If, at a later time, they take all four truths as their object, they function through fourteen aspects;
however, when these two knowledges first arise, they consist only of the categories of suffering and its origin.
Because one contemplates the aggregates of the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*) as the object by means of the six modes of activity associated with the truths of Suffering and Origin. Question:
For what reason does the first stage take only the Suffering and Origin of the Peak of Existence as its object? Answer: Because the Suffering and Origin of the Peak of Existence—
Having been unable to sever [these afflictions] since beginningless time, they are now severed for the first time;

therefore, one first takes them as an object and gives rise to joy and consolation. Question: Why does one not employ the mental aspects (*ākāra*) of emptiness (*śūnyatā*) and non-self (*anātman*)? Explanation: Because these two types of wisdom involve the conventional (*saṃvṛti*).
This means that after emerging from contemplation, one forms the understanding that "I am born" and so forth;
whereas during the preceding internal contemplation, one did not practice [the views of] emptiness or non-self.
This is thus a case where the cause involves the fruit.
Previously, while in meditative observation, he perceived the internal as empty and not-self;
subsequently, upon emerging from meditation,
his mind likewise cannot form the conception that "I am born" and so forth.
Regarding the question, "Is the objective sphere (*ālambana*) of the diamond-like concentration (*vajropama-samādhi*) the same as this?
[it is asked:

"While the concentrations taking suffering (*duḥkha*) and its origin (*samudaya*) as their objects are the same, why are those taking cessation (*nirodha*) and the path (*mārga*) as their objects different?"
Answer: The diamond-like concentration (*vajropama-samādhi*).
If it takes the suffering and origin of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception as its object, it is the same.
If one takes the cessation or the path of the nine stages as an object, the case is different;
for taking the cessation or the path of the three realms as an object enables the abandonment of those afflictions.
Regarding what was previously stated concerning "all" up to the second or third moment:
This is the third [section], clarifying the increase from nine to ten.
The *Śāstra* states: "When it reaches others, it is not so," which explains the two preceding lines.
Among the nine types of knowledge previously mentioned, the knowledge of phenomena (dharma-jñāna),
subsequent knowledge (anvaya-jñāna), path-knowledge (mārga-jñāna), and conventional knowledge (saṃvṛti-jñāna) constitute the knowledge of others' minds.
This applies when one knows the untainted (anāsrava) mind of another.
One knows [the minds of others] through the knowledge of dharma, subsequent knowledge, path-knowledge, or the knowledge of others' minds.
If one knows another's mind that is with outflows (sāsrava),
one knows it through conventional knowledge or the knowledge of others' minds.
The other five are not so.
Because the untainted knowledge of others' minds does not know tainted minds, it is not the knowledge of suffering or the knowledge of the origin.
Because cessation is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), it is not the knowledge of cessation.

Because the knowledge of others' minds has the nature of vision (*darśana*), while the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣaya-jñāna*) and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpāda-jñāna*) do not have the nature of vision, they are not [included in] the knowledge of others' minds.
"This wisdom reaches its object through the stages, faculties,
and positions" explains the third and fourth lines;
this constitutes the opening of the chapter.
Regarding the phrase "the wisdom of a lower stage does not know the mind of a higher stage," this is a specific explanation.
Since the wisdom of a lower stage does not know the mind of a higher stage...
By logical inference, it is established that [a mind] knows its own level and lower levels;
however, no cognition of a lower level knows the mind of a higher level.
If one were to know both its own and lower levels, there would necessarily be a distinction [between them].
Therefore, the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* (Vol. 99) states:
"There are fifteen kinds of previously acquired contaminated minds and mental factors that constitute the objects to be apprehended by the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*)."
This refers to the desire realm and the four dhyānas,
each of which possesses three grades of mind and mental factors— inferior, medium, and superior.
When considering the previously acquired knowledge of others' minds with outflows (sāsrava), there are twelve types.
This means that each of the four dhyānas possesses three grades—lower, middle, and superior—of the knowledge of others' minds (paracittajñāna) with outflows (sāsrava).
Among these, there is the case where one has previously attained the lower grade of the knowledge of others' minds with outflows belonging to the first dhyāna.
One is able to know the three grades of the desire realm,
as well as the inferior-grade previously acquired contaminated mental states and mental factors of the first dhyāna;
one who possesses the middle grade is able to know the three grades of the desire realm.
Furthermore, regarding the first dhyāna, there are two grades— the lower and the middle—
of previously attained contaminated minds and mental factors;
the superior grade is able to know the desire realm.
And in each of the first dhyānas, there are three grades of previously acquired contaminated minds and mental factors;
thus, proceeding in this manner up to the fourth dhyāna, there is the previously acquired superior-grade contaminated knowledge of others' minds.
One is able to know the desire realm and the three grades of each of the four dhyānas as they were previously attained— namely, the contaminated minds and mental factors—
as in the case of the twelve types of previously attained knowledge of others' minds that are contaminated.
One knows fifteen types of previously acquired tainted minds and mental factors;
one knows twelve types of previously unacquired tainted knowledge of others' minds.
It is the same for knowing fifteen types of previously unacquired tainted minds and mental factors.
There are twelve types of untainted mind and mental factors that constitute the objects to be apprehended by the knowledge of others' minds;
the untainted knowledge of others' minds itself also consists of twelve types.
That is to say, each of the four dhyānas has three grades.
Among these, the inferior grade of untainted knowledge of others' minds in the second dhyāna can know [the minds of those in] the first dhyāna.
Furthermore, in the second dhyāna, there are only the inferior grades of untainted mind and mental factors;
those of the middling grade can know the untainted mind and mental factors of both the inferior and middling grades of the first dhyāna and the second dhyāna.
One of superior grade can know the three grades of untainted minds and mental factors of the first dhyāna and the second dhyāna; in this manner,
proceeding successively up to the superior grade of untainted knowledge of others' minds in the fourth dhyāna.
One is able to know the three grades of untainted minds and mental factors of each of the four dhyānas.
Question: Why is it that the knowledge of others' minds regarding the tainted [minds] of higher stages, lower stages, and middle grades [is not so]?
Both [types of knowledge] are able to know the three grades of contaminated minds and mental factors of a lower stage,
as well as the lower and middle grades of uncontaminated knowledge of others' minds belonging to a higher or lower stage;
however, they do not know the middle and upper grades of uncontaminated minds and mental factors of a lower stage.
Answer: The establishment of contaminated (*sāsrava*) and uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) minds and mental factors (*caitta-dharma*) differs.
That is to say, contaminated minds and mental factors are established based on the continuum (*saṃtati*).
Within a single continuum of existence, there are three grades of contaminated minds and mental factors;
uncontaminated minds and mental factors are established according to the category of their respective faculties.
Within the continuum of a single body, one cannot achieve two categories of untainted mind and mental factors;
how much less could there be those who achieve three?
Since their establishments are distinct.
Thus, we know there is a distinction. Furthermore, the *Nyāyānusāra* (Treatise on the Correct Principles), fascicle 73, asks:
"How can it be said that a single *pudgala* accomplishes the nine grades of the path in order to abandon the nine grades of afflictions?"
These distinctions in the path do not arise from differences in the faculties;
rather, as the cause gradually increases, the subsequent path becomes progressively more exalted,
thereby enabling the successive abandonment of various categories of afflictions.
Alternatively, each of the various lineages (gotra) may possess nine grades;
since one who has attained the first grade of a particular lineage necessarily does not attain the others,
there is no fault of contradiction between the preceding and subsequent statements.
Furthermore, the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* states:

Question: Regarding the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*) in the first dhyāna, how many types of minds and mental factors within the desire realm and the four dhyānas—specifically those that are the fruits of supernormal powers (*abhijñā-phala*)—can it cognize?
Some say that one can know four kinds. Why is this so?
Because all [of these] are subsumed under the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
Furthermore, there are those who say that [the knowledge of others' minds] can only know the supernormal powers resulting from meditative attainment (*abhijñā-phala*) of the first dhyāna.
One does not know the other three.
Why is this? It is because one does not know the cause.
Because the fruit is also thus.
Furthermore, the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* says:
"Question: Regarding the mind and mental factors of the intermediate dhyāna..."
By the wisdom of which stage can it be known?
Some say that it can be known by the superior wisdom of the first dhyāna.
Furthermore, there are those who say that the lower grade of wisdom in the second dhyāna can know it;
the critique states that one should speak as follows.
The three categories of knowledge of the first dhyāna can all be known. Why is this?
Because they are subsumed within a single stage.
The commentary explains that this refers, for the time being, to the first dhyāna.
In reality, the two meditative attainments (*samāpatti*) and others can also know; furthermore, the *Vibhāṣā* states:
"The Tathāgata once possessed tainted (*sāsrava*) minds and mental factors (*citta-caitta-dharma*).
If the Buddha wishes to make others know them, he knows them immediately."
It is as explained extensively in that [text].
Regarding the faculties, it refers to those whose faith and understanding have reached a superior stage;
such individuals are unable to know the higher faculties or higher stages.
By implication, this wisdom knows its own faculty and lower faculties,
as well as its own stage and lower stages;
it does not know that which reaches up to the level of the object of cognition.
Within the three periods of time, one knows only the present functions of another's mind and so forth;
because they have no function in the past and future, they cannot be known.
Furthermore, regarding the statement that "the categories of dharmas and anvaya-jñāna reach [them] as their objects":
This explains the fifth phrase:
because dharma-knowledge takes as its object the antidotes for the entirety of the desire realm,
and because subsequent knowledge takes as its object the antidotes for the entirety of the higher realms.
Therefore, the Dharma-knowledge and Subsequent Knowledge (anvaya-jñāna) do not take one another as objects.
Although the Dharma-knowledge of Cessation and the Path can also counteract the defilements to be abandoned through cultivation in the higher realms,
they do not counteract them entirely.
The dharma-knowledge of suffering and its origin,
and the dharma-knowledge of the path of seeing,
do not govern the higher stages.
Regarding the phrase "this knowledge of others' minds reaches the objects of this knowledge":
the following explains the latter three phrases.
This knowledge of others' minds knows the specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) of others; it is a path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) that proceeds with deliberation.
It does not exist within the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*),

because it observes the principles of the truths (*satyārtha*) in their totality and proceeds with extreme rapidity; thus, although the two types of cultivation— cultivation by practice (*niṣevaṇabhāvanā*) and cultivation by attainment (*pratilambhabhāvanā*)— are absent there.
Nevertheless, all [of these] may serve as the objects of this wisdom;
because it contemplates the principles of the truths in their totality, there is no cultivation by application (*ābhisamskārika-bhāvanā*);
and because it proceeds with extreme rapidity, there is no cultivation by acquisition (*pratilambha-bhāvanā*).
If there are sentient beings who have not yet reached the path of knowledge and vision,
the śrāvakas may do so either through superior application or through middling application.
Upon reaching the completion of the preparatory stage (prayoga), one is able to know and see the first two moments of the path of seeing (darśanamārga).
For the time being, this is explained based on the initial [moments], and thus it is said that there are only "two moments";
the subsequent thirteen moments are likewise included.
All of these may also serve as objects of the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*). Question:

Having already known the first two moments of mind, why does one not immediately know the third moment—the mind belonging to the category of subsequent cognition (*anvayajñāna*) and so forth? Answer: It is because the categories of Dharma-knowledge (*dharmajñāna*) and Subsequent-knowledge (*anvayajñāna*) are distinct.
Because the objects of focus differ,
they cannot be known [as such]. If,
however, one wishes to further know the categories of mind, [one should proceed as follows].
He practices a distinct preparatory application (*prayoga*).
After thirteen moments of thought, the preparatory application reaches completion.
He has already transcended and reached the sixteenth moment of mind.
Although one knows this mind,
it is not the Path of Vision;
as for the "Rhinoceros-like" [Pratyekabuddha] who attains the Dharma-part at the fifteenth moment of mind:
A Pratyekabuddha can know and see the three moments of mind of the path of seeing.
Having known the first two moments, he further cultivates the preparatory application (*prayoga*) with five moments of mind and knows the eighth moment;
this is because he does so solely by means of inferior preparatory application.
Furthermore, based on knowing these three moments of mind, it is possible for the remaining twelve moments of mind to also serve as objects of another’s cognition. Question:

Having already known the eighth moment of mind, why does one not further take five moments of mind as an object of added knowledge to know the fourteenth moment of mind? Answer: It is explained that one may indeed know them if one so desires.
However, those who do not understand see that the mind at the stage of the path (*mārga*) consists generally of two parts:
first, the dharma-part.
Regarding the two types of classification:
one knows that the first two moments are the classification of phenomena (dharmapakṣa),
and one knows that the eighth moment is the classification of types (anvayapakṣa).
Since one has already fully understood that the two [aspects] of the mind have completely ceased, there is no further knowing. Furthermore, even if one wishes to know, it cannot be obtained.
When first practicing the preparatory application (*prayoga*), one knows the first two moments.
Secondly, one again employs five moments of mind as the preparatory application (*prayoga*) to know the eighth moment of mind.

When reaching the third [application], if one further cultivates the preparatory application with its power being weak—employing only five or six moments of mind—it cannot be accomplished. Another interpretation holds that the preceding moments of mind were somewhat inferior.
One can know [the object] through five moments of preparatory application (*prayoga*).
Subsequent moments become progressively superior;
however, one cannot know it through five or six moments as the preparatory application. Furthermore, another interpretation holds that one knows it after the first two moments have already passed.
If one intends to know that third *duḥkhe ’nvaya-jñāna-kṣānti* mind, one proceeds through five minds of preparatory application until the completion of the application,
whereby one attains knowledge of the eighth *samudaye ’nvaya-jñāna* mind;
this is because the objects of focus for that third and eighth [minds] are identical.
The meanings of cause and effect are divided between suffering and its origin;
when one understands this, it becomes easy.
Although one may not understand the third [truth], [the first two are sufficient].
One is able to know the eighth;
having known the eighth,
one further desires to know that ninth mind of the patience regarding the dharma of cessation.
One employs five moments of mind as the preparatory application (prayoga),
yet one does not know the fourteenth moment of mind, which is the dharma-knowledge (dharma-jñāna) of the path,
because the objects of those two moments of mind are distinct.
One has conditioned phenomena as its object;
one has unconditioned phenomena as its object.
They are not a single entity.
Because knowing the proper time is itself difficult, one cannot know it;
even if one employs six moments of mind as the preparatory application (*prayoga*),
one still cannot know the fifteenth moment of mind.
Some say that the Pratyekabuddha knows the first two moments,
and by adding twelve more moments as an act of supernormal knowledge (*abhijñā*), he knows the fifteenth moment of mind.
Furthermore, the *Nyāyānusāra* (Treatise on Reasoning), fascicle 73, states this.
There are four explanations regarding the Pratyekabuddhas.
The first two explanations are the same as this treatise.
Regarding the latter two explanations, some say that the Rishyashringa-type Pratyekabuddha knows [the four truths] in four moments.
This refers to the first two moments of mind, the eighth, and the fourteenth;
this statement is logical. Why is that?
Having permitted the knowledge of the first two moments of mind,
one knows the eighth mind by skipping over five moments;
if one further cultivates the preparatory application (*prayoga*) of the dharma-portion (*dharmāṃśa*), [one may know even more].
The preparatory application should be accomplished within the duration of five moments of attention;
why then do you not allow that the fourteenth moment is known?
Others have also said this.
It is known that there are four moments:

namely, the first two moments and the eleventh and twelfth, because they accord with the *Nyāya* (Principles); this contradicts this treatise (*Abhidharmakośa*), which adopts the third [position]. Furthermore, the *Mahāvibhāṣā* (99) states:
There are also four theories that accord with correct reasoning; however, there is no adjudicating commentary [from the Master].
The Blessed One desired to know everything and attained the capacity to know all things.
World-Honored One, if you wish to know:
by means of application, one fully knows the fifteen moments of mind of the path of seeing;
from the knowledge of exhaustion up to the knowledge of non-arising, one is designated as a "knower of non-arising."
This is the second [section], clarifying the distinction between the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣaya-jñāna*) and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpāda-jñāna*).
It cites the root treatise to demonstrate the distinction between these two types of knowledge.
"Knowledge" (*jñāna*) here refers to decisive discernment.
Some say it is "repeated cognition";
others say it is "investigation" (vitarka), meaning seeking;
still others say it is "present illumination."
"Clarification" (ming) means illuminating;
"awakening" (jue) means being enlightened;
"understanding" (jie) means penetrating comprehension.
"Insight" (prajñā) refers to discernment;
"light" refers to the light of insight;
"contemplation" (vipaśyanā) refers to observation.
The eight types beginning with "knowledge" (*jñāna*) are all synonyms for wisdom (*prajñā*).
The *Nyāyānusāra* (Treatise on the Principles of Correct Reasoning), fascicle 73, asks:
"For what reason does the treatise state this further within the context of the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*)?"
"I have already known suffering, etc."—
in principle, one should only say this and not "I know it again," because two modes of activity cannot occur simultaneously.
If it were to proceed sequentially,
it would not differ from the knowledge of exhaustion (kṣayajñāna) in its preceding stage;
therefore, it should not be stated again.
It should be understood that the intent of this statement is to dispel doubt,
for there may be those who fear that one liberated by occasion (samayavimukta) might first give rise to the knowledge of exhaustion (kṣayajñāna).

Subsequently, one attains the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*). Thus, one must admit that for one liberated at any time (*asamayavimukta*), the knowledge of non-arising arises first, followed by the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*).
This is to demonstrate that for all [Arhats], the knowledge of exhaustion arises first.
Therefore, he again first states the words "already known" and so forth;
or alternatively, he first simply says "I have already known," etc.,
to show that for one liberated by time (samayavimukta), there is only the knowledge of exhaustion (kṣayajñāna).
The subsequent repetition of the statement, "I have already known," etc.,
demonstrates that for one who is not liberated at any time (*asamayavimukta*), the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) arises last,
followed by the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*). Therefore, although it is repeated, there is no fault.
Regarding the "knowledge of non-arising":
what is meant by "non-arising"?
The Master of Right Reasoning (Nyāyācārya) says:
This refers to cessation through non-analytical discernment (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*). Because there is the non-arising [of phenomena], this knowledge arises.
Since this knowledge relies upon non-arising, it is termed "knowledge of non-arising" (*anutpāda-jñāna*).
Although cessation is ever-present, it does not constitute "attainment.
It is only when that cessation is attained that this wisdom arises.
It is only through the arising of attainment that one can be said to possess cessation.
This wisdom arises precisely at the stage when existence ceases;
alternatively, the term "non-arising" refers to the acquisition of that cessation,
just as the acquisition of nirvana is also called "nirvana."
Because the Sūtra states that one places nirvāṇa within the mind,
this wisdom only arises when one attains that state.
Since this wisdom relies upon non-arising, it is called the "knowledge of non-arising" (anutpādajñāna).

Others raise this objection: "If that which relies upon non-arising is called the 'knowledge of non-arising,' then the knowledge of non-arising would have as its object a phenomenon that is not a Truth (satya)."
This would contradict your own tenet,
which holds that the arising of untainted wisdom takes only the four truths as its object.
They have raised this objection without careful consideration.
I have already stated above that such conceptualizing cognition arises only after one has emerged from meditative absorption. Alternatively,
this "seventh" [case] refers to the genitive case (*saptamī*) based on the word "sound" (*śabda*), and not to the genitive case based on the "object" (*viṣaya*).
Just as in the case of the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*), it may be granted that this knowledge takes non-arising (*anutpāda*) as its object;
it is subsumed under the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkhasatya*).
"Because it is not the case that [the truths] are not truths. [End of the treatise. Question: How can untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*) produce such a cognition?
How is it that untainted wisdom can function in this way?
"I have already understood the [four] noble truths such as suffering.
Regarding the distinction between the two knowledges from Kaśmīra, the answer is as follows:
According to the correct tenets of the Sarvāstivāda school,
from within the contaminated wisdom (*sāsrava-jñāna*) that arises subsequent to the two knowledges of exhaustion (*kṣaya-jñāna*) and non-arising (*anutpāda-jñāna*),
one forms the cognition: "I have already known suffering," and so forth.
It is not through untainted contemplation (*anāsrava-vipaśyanā*) that such knowledge is produced;
therefore, there is no fault.
This is because the two types of subsequently attained knowledge (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*) have distinct fruits.
This table distinguishes between the two types of causes for the two knowledges mentioned in the preceding contemplation.
Since these two knowledges are induced by two causes, they are their *puruṣakāra-phala* (fruits of human effort).
This, therefore, distinguishes the causes by means of their fruits.
If there were no intervening mind,
then immediately after the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*), there would arise the realization that "I have already known suffering," and so forth;
and immediately after the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*), there would arise the realization that "there is nothing further to be known," and so forth.
