However, because it is interrupted by the right view of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) and other factors, it arises only later.
Some say that untainted knowledge (*anāsrava-jñāna*) also functions in this way;
this is the tenet of the Western Śramaṇas, such as the Sautrāntikas.
It is taught that untainted wisdom does not perform the sixteen aspects;
rather, it also functions by knowing:
"I have already known suffering," and so forth.
However, the statement that even "seeing" (dṛṣṭi) is itself seeing is consistent with the main body of the treatise;
yet, speaking in terms of ultimate reality:
Exhaustion-knowledge (*kṣaya-jñāna*) and non-arising-knowledge (*anutpāda-jñāna*) are the cessation of seeking and the absence of [wrong] views.
In the *Mūla-śāstra*, these ten knowledges are explained,
with each one being described as possessing eight qualities, such as knowledge (*jñāna*), vision (*darśana*), and so forth.
Even though [the knowledge of] exhaustion and non-arising has reached its ultimate limit, it is still called "vision.
This is for the sake of following the conventional usage of the term. Furthermore, regarding the interpretation of the knowledge of exhaustion and non-arising:
if one examines it according to the cessation of seeking, it is not termed "vision."
Because it functions as a direct illumination of the principles of the truths (*satya*), it is also called "view" (*dṛṣṭi*).
For this reason, the fundamental treatise also states:
"Furthermore, all forms of knowledge (*jñāna*) are also views."
Regarding how these ten knowledges are mutually subsumed:
as for the question,
"From conventional knowledge up to six [knowledges] comprise a small portion," it is as follows.
Answer: It comprises one entire category of conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*) and a small portion of one category of knowledge of others' minds (*para-citta-jñāna*).
Dharma-knowledge and subsequent knowledge each encompass one entire category [of their respective types], as well as a small portion of seven others:
the knowledges of suffering, origin, cessation, the path, exhaustion, non-arising, and the minds of others.
The knowledges of suffering, origin, and cessation each include their own respective single category in its entirety,
as well as a small portion of the four categories of dharma, subsequent, exhaustion, and non-arising knowledge.
The knowledge of the path includes its own single category in its entirety.
Five partial portions— namely, the dharma-knowledge, subsequent-knowledge, knowledge of exhaustion, knowledge of non-arising, and knowledge of others' minds—

are subsumed [by the knowledge of others' minds]. The knowledge of others' minds itself comprises one full portion and four partial portions— namely, the dharma-knowledge, subsequent-knowledge, path-knowledge, and conventional-knowledge.

The knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*) each encompass their own single totality and a small portion of six [knowledges]: suffering, origin, cessation, path, dharma, and subsequent knowledge.
For what reason are these two knowledges established as ten?
Below this, the third section explains the establishment of the ten knowledges (*jñāna*). Question:
For what reason are the two knowledges—impure (*sāsrava*) and pure (*anāsrava*)—established as ten?
The verse says: "Because they arise with [the former] as their cause."
Answer: Two are established as ten by virtue of seven conditions.
First, conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*) is established by way of its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
Its essence is with outflows (*sāsrava*),
because it is a conventional phenomenon (*saṃvṛti-dharma*). This conventional knowledge does not have untainted ultimate knowledge (*anāsrava-paramārtha-jñāna*) as its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
If one relies on the preceding text, the name is also established based on the object;
therefore, the preceding text states:
"The prior contaminated wisdom is collectively termed conventional (*saṃvṛti*)."
Because they take many conventional objects such as vases and so forth, two types of knowledge are established as antidotes: dharma-knowledge and subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*).
Dharma-knowledge is fully capable of counteracting the desire realm, while subsequent knowledge is fully capable of counteracting the higher realms.
Although the dharma-knowledges of cessation and the path can also counteract the afflictions to be abandoned through cultivation in the higher realms, they do not do so completely;
therefore, the knowledges of suffering and origin are established by way of their three aspects.
This is because there is no difference in the essential nature of the objects of these two knowledges.

It is solely due to the difference in the aspects (*ākāra*) of the cognitive objects that knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-jñāna*) is established by means of the four aspects of impermanence (*anitya*) and so forth,

while knowledge of origination (*samudaya-jñāna*) is established by means of the four aspects of cause (*hetu*), origination (*samudaya*), and so forth. Furthermore, it is explained that these aspects reside within the object.

Although the essential nature of the objects of these two types of knowledge is not distinct, they are differentiated as suffering and origin based on the difference in their modes of activity (*ākāra*). Furthermore, it is explained that the mode of activity (*ākāra*) and the characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) are present both in the subjective cognition (*ālambaka*) and in the objective referent (*ālambana*).
Because there are eight modes of activity, such as impermanence and so forth, upon that object,
the cognizing consciousness is said to be "the cognizer" by virtue of appearing as those eight modes.
Although the essential natures of these two— the object and the cognition— are not distinct, [they are so designated].
Regarding the classification by way of aspect, there are two: knowledge of cessation and knowledge of the path are established because they have four aspects and objects respectively.
Since these two sets of aspects differ, [the former] functions as the four aspects beginning with cessation.
Alternatively, it is said that there are four types of aspects (*ākāra*), such as the aspect of the Path (*mārga*).
Regarding these three interpretations of the aspects, they should be understood according to the previous [explanation].
This is because there is a distinction between the objects (*ālambana*) of these two.
One has the unconditioned as its object;
one has the conditioned as its object.
Based on the difference in their modes of activity and the distinction in their objects, the knowledge of cessation and the knowledge of the path are established.
The knowledge of others' minds is established because of its preparatory application (*prayoga*);
it derives its name from that application.
Since the mind is primary, at the outset one knows only the mind. The knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) is established because the task is accomplished.
It is called the "knowledge of non-arising" (anutpādajñāna) because it arises for the first time within the body of an Arhat who has accomplished his task;
it is established as such because seven causes are perfected, and it comprises all noble paths of both seeing (darśana-mārga), cultivation (bhāvanā-mārga), and no-more-learning (aśaikṣa).
It is called "perfection of causes" because it arises by way of being a homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*).
Although the initial arising of the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣaya-jñāna*) takes the noble paths of seeing and cultivation as its causes,
it has not yet taken the noble path of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa-mārga*) as its cause.
It is not called "perfection of causes.
Although the subsequent stage of continuity also takes the path of an adept (aśaikṣa-mārga) as its cause, it should nevertheless be called "perfection of causes."
According to the first explanation,
or because that knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) does not arise with the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*) as its cause,
it is not termed "perfected in causes" (*hetu-saṃpanna*).
Regarding what was stated above concerning "the supreme desire for ultimate governance," this constitutes the fourth [section],
which clarifies the categories of both phenomena (*dharma*) and types (*jāti*),
and restates the preceding inquiry to initiate the discussion.
As stated above, dharma-knowledge is fully capable of counteracting the phenomena of the desire realm,
while subsequent knowledge is fully capable of counteracting the phenomena of the higher realms.
Is there any portion of dharma-knowledge that remedies the higher realms?
Or is there any portion of type-knowledge that remedies the desire realm?
The verse says: "Up to the point where none can remedy the desire [realm]."
Answer: The knowledge of the dharma regarding cessation and the path (nirodha-mārga-dharma-jñāna), which is subsumed under the path of cultivation (bhāvanā-mārga),
is also capable of serving as the antidote for the afflictions of the higher realms to be abandoned through cultivation.
The cessation and path of the desire realm are superior to the suffering and origin of the higher realms;
therefore, that which is inferior in the lower [realms] can serve as an antidote for that which is superior in the higher [realms].
The suffering and origin of the desire realm are coarse.
The upper [realms] have subtle suffering and origination;
because coarse conditions cannot remedy the subtle,
there is thus the dharma-knowledge of suffering and origination.
It does not treat the higher afflictions;
furthermore, having already eliminated the enemies of its own realm,
it is able to simultaneously counteract the enemies of other realms.
Because this subsequent knowledge (anvaya-jñāna) lacks the capacity to counteract the desire realm,
the Nyāyānusāra states: "Only when what is to be accomplished within one's own realm has been fully completed [can it counteract the higher realms]."
Only then can it simultaneously perform its functions for other realms;
it is not the case that when the task for one's own category is accomplished,
the tasks for others remain unaccomplished.
There is a sense in which assistance is required;

therefore, there is no subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*) that remedies the dharmas of the desire realm—this is the aforementioned treatise. Furthermore, the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 158, states:
"Question: If one employs the dharma-knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-dharma-jñāna*) or the dharma-knowledge of the path (*mārga-dharma-jñāna*..."
When one abandons the defilements to be abandoned through cultivation belonging to the form and formless realms,
the untainted acquisition of dissociation from those dharmas to be abandoned through cultivation in the form and formless realms is subsumed under the category of dharma-knowledge (*dharmajñāna*).
Is it subsumed under the category of subsequent knowledge (anvaya-jñāna)?
If it were subsumed under the category of dharma-knowledge (dharma-jñāna), this would not be logical.
Because those dharmas and their abandonment are known by subsequent knowledge (anvaya-jñāna),
they are subsumed under the category of subsequent knowledge.
This is also illogical,
because that abandonment and attainment are realized through the knowledge of phenomena (dharmajñāna).
Some say that the acquisition of dissociation (visamyoga-prāpti) therein is subsumed under the category of subsequent knowledge (anvaya-jñāna).
Question: Is it not the case that both the abandonment [of defilements] and the acquisition [of dissociation] therein are realized by dharma-knowledge (dharma-jñāna)?
Answer: Although it is realized by dharma-knowledge, it is also known by subsequent knowledge (anvaya-jñāna);
thus, other masters say this.
That untainted acquisition of dissociation is subsumed under the category of dharma-knowledge.
Question: Is it not the case that those dharmas and their abandonments [are also included]?
Is it that which is known by subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*)?
Answer: Although it is known by subsequent knowledge, it is subsumed under dharma-knowledge (*dharma-jñāna*) because it is realized by dharma-knowledge.
The commentary states:

Among these, the first explanation is superior, because the category of subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*) is its specific and definitive antidote. Within these ten knowledges, "up to" refers to that which is devoid of emptiness and non-self.
This is the third section, clarifying the aspects (*ākāra*) of the ten knowledges (*daśajñāna*). Within this,
the first part clarifies the aspects of the ten knowledges.
Second, the thorough purification through the inclusion of practice;
third, the actual entity as subject and object—this clarifies the aspects (*ākāra*) of the ten knowledges (*jñāna*).
The treatise says: "Up to the four kinds of aspects."

Explanation of the first verse: "Etc. refers to including conceptualization (*parikalpa*) and so forth. The rest of the text is self-evident. Regarding the phrase "within the knowledge of others' minds, up to not taking conceptualization as an object":
[it means that while knowing the mental states of others, one does not take their conceptual constructions as the primary object].
Explaining the second verse:
although untainted knowledge of others' minds takes a common characteristic as its object,
it is nevertheless an act of mental application characterized by joy.
One is able to discern [them] individually;

the rest of the text may be understood. Question: While one knows another’s untainted mind (*anāsrava-citta*) by means of the four lower aspects of the Path (*mārga*), why does one not know another’s tainted mind (*sāsrava-citta*) by means of the eight aspects of Suffering (*duḥkha*) and Origin (*samudaya*)? Explanation: This is stated as a prelude to answering this question.
This will be briefly analyzed through three sections:
first, an account of ancient interpretations;
second, the exposure of errors and fallacies.
Third, stating the correct meaning and recounting the ancient interpretations: First, Master Yuan said,
"It is the knowledge of another's untainted mind (*anāsrava-citta*)."
Because the knowledge of the path (mārgajñāna) functions as the preparatory application (prayoga), it takes the four aspects of the path as its object;
it knows the contaminated minds of others,
but does not take the knowledge of suffering (duḥkhajñāna) or the knowledge of origination (samudayajñāna) as its preparatory application.
Therefore, one does not cultivate the eight aspects of suffering and origin. Regarding this, the second Wei master, Dhyāna-dhara, said:
"If one knows another's untainted mind, one cultivates the four lower aspects of the path."
One then knows that the application of knowing another's mind is exhausted; if one knows another's tainted mind,
one does not employ the eight aspects such as suffering and so forth.
Thus, his knowledge of the minds of others is not exhaustive;
he may know suffering but not its origin,
or he may know its origin but not suffering.

Regarding why [the path] does not employ the eight aspects of suffering and origin: the third master, Dharma Master Song of Pengcheng, stated that the subjective faculty (ālambaka) and the objective referent (ālambana) must be equal in terms of both principle and phenomenon.
Since the object of focus here is an untainted mind, it is necessarily a contemplation of principle.
The knowledge of others' minds that takes them as objects must still be understood through rational contemplation (*yukti-vipaśyanā*);
thus, when knowing another's untainted mind (*anāsrava-citta*),
it functions with the four aspects (*ākāra*) of the Path.
Since the mind with outflows (*sāsrava*) that serves as the object is itself a contemplation of phenomena (*vastubhāvanā*),
the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*) that takes it as its subject must likewise know it through a contemplation of phenomena;
thus, one knows another's mind with outflows.

Regarding the second point concerning the refutation of errors: First, Master Yuàn (Yuán Fǎshī) states that since the *Mūla-śāstra* says that the eight knowledges (*jñāna*) of those in training (*śaikṣa*),
when viewed in relation to one another, are all capable of serving as equal-and-immediate conditions (*samanantara-pratyaya*).

Furthermore, to speak of the preparatory stages (*prayoga*) for the knowledge of the path (*mārgajñāna*) and the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*), does this not constitute a contradiction? Second, [the author] refutes the Wei-period Master Nian, saying:
"The four aspects (*ākāra*) also exist upon the untainted mind (*anāsravacitta*)."
Knowing one [aspect] while not knowing the others, one still does not know them exhaustively;
therefore, one should not form the mental aspect of practicing the path at a lower level. Regarding this, Master Seng of Song stated:
"Since the mundane *uṣmagata* (heat) and other stages constitute contemplation of principle (*li-guan*)."
The knowledge that takes another's mind as its object should also be considered a contemplation of principle (*yuktinirūpaṇā*).
If one were to say it is not a contemplation of true principle, then it would be a semblance-contemplation of principle (*tadyuktyābhāsa-nirūpaṇā*).

Furthermore, one should know through the knowledge of others' minds by means of an analogical contemplation (*yathābhūta-nyāya-vipaśyanā*), not through a factual contemplation (*vastu-vipaśyanā*). Third, regarding the statement of the correct meaning:
one interpretation states that the untainted mind (*anāsrava-citta*) is superior.
Because it is difficult to know,
the knowledge of others' minds that is subject to outflows (*sāsrava*) cannot know it;
one must give rise to the untainted (*anāsrava*) [knowledge] in order to be able to know it.
Thus, one knows another's untainted mind by means of the four aspects of the lower path;
for a tainted mind is inferior and therefore easy to discern.
Because the outflow-tainted knowledge of others' minds is capable of knowing that [other mind],
it does not arise as an outflow-free knowledge of others' minds to know it.
Why is this? Because the outflow-tainted knowledge of others' minds has been cultivated repeatedly since beginningless time.
It is easy to arouse at the time [of its arising].
However, the untainted knowledge of others' minds has not been extensively cultivated since beginningless time.
It is difficult [to know] when it arises,
because it is easy for outflowing (sāsrava) minds to arise;
thus, one knows another's outflowing mind.
One again gives rise to the knowledge of others' minds that is associated with outflows (*sāsrava*),
because it is difficult for the untainted (*anāsrava*) to arise;
thus, one knows the tainted mind of another.
One does not perform the eightfold contemplation of suffering and its origin;
it is easy to arouse and easy to know.
Who, moreover, would abandon what is easy to follow what is difficult? [Question: Should one only employ the knowledge of others' minds (paracittajñāna) within the first dhyāna?
The knowledge of the minds of others regarding the desire realm is easy to produce; therefore,
the knowledge of others' minds applies from the two meditative absorptions upward.
One should not be able to know the minds of others in the desire realm, because it is difficult for them to arise.
Who, moreover, would abandon what is easy and follow what is difficult? The explanation says: [this refers to] one who wishes to know the minds of the desire realm.
One certainly does not intentionally arise in the second dhyāna or above to know the minds of others;
rather, one enters the second dhyāna and so forth for other purposes,
and by virtue of entering that meditative absorption, the knowledge of others' minds subsequently arises.
[The opponent] knows the mind of the desire realm. An objection is raised:

one might also, for some other reason, give rise to an outflow-free (anāsrava) mind, and then, by means of that outflow-free knowledge of others' minds (paracittajñāna), know another's outflow-tainted (sāsrava) mind. [The proponent] explains: it is easy to give rise to an outflow-tainted knowledge of others' minds from an outflow-free mind.

The difficulty regarding the arising of the untainted knowledge of others' minds (*anāsrava-paracittajñāna*) is easy to understand as being difficult to arise; therefore, it is not raised as a point of contention.
Question: When one enters the two meditative absorptions (*samāpatti*) and so forth and knows a mind belonging to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), [how does this occur]?

Why does a Non-returner not give rise to the knowledge of others' minds belonging to the first dhyāna to know a mind of the desire realm, but instead gives rise to [the knowledge of others' minds] belonging to the second dhyāna and so forth to know a mind of the desire realm?
The explanation says: because it is easier to give rise to [knowledge] belonging to one's own level, one gives rise to that which belongs to one's own level.
Regarding the objection that [the knowledge of others' minds] does not arise when one is in a different stage (*bhūmi*) or when not having entered the first dhyāna, the second explanation states:
Since the contemplation of joy (*abhirati*) can be known separately,
one knows the uncontaminated mind (*anāsrava-citta*) of another.
When practicing the four aspects of the path below,
one must necessarily abandon them all through the contemplation of revulsion;
thus, we know that these are other types of tainted consciousness.
Because one does not perform the eightfold contemplation of suffering and its origin,
the *Nyāyānusāra* (Treatise on Reasoning), fascicle 73,
states: "The uncontaminated mind and mental factors of another's body are subtle."
Because it is superior,
it is not an object of the knowledge of others' minds that pertains to one's own outflows;
this principle is reasonable.
For what reason is it that one’s own uncontaminated knowledge of others' minds cannot know another's contaminated mind and mental factors?
[Because] uncontaminated knowledge arises with respect to contaminated objects.
Because its mode of activity (*ākāra*) and object (*ālambana*) differ from this knowledge;
that is to say, when untainted knowledge (*anāsrava-jñāna*) takes tainted phenomena as its object,
it necessarily takes them in a collective manner with a mode of activity characterized by revulsion.
Therefore, it is certain that one cannot produce a knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*) by taking other minds and mental factors as distinct objects.
This is because when the various noble knowledges take contaminated phenomena (*sāsrava*) as their objects,
they necessarily give rise to a profound sense of revulsion toward those objects.
One delights in relinquishing them as a whole rather than observing them individually,
because joy arises when taking the untainted (*anāsrava*) as an object; yet,
once they have been observed as a whole, one also delights in observing them individually.
If one encounters or hears of unpleasant matters,
one abandons them by taking them as a collective object of focus, rather than delighting in focusing on them individually.
It is not so with that which is beloved;
having seen and heard them collectively, one also delights in individual conditions.
Therefore, [this applies] to the other tainted minds and so forth.

It is certainly not the case that noble wisdom observes each [object] individually to constitute an uncontaminated knowledge of others' minds (paracittajñāna) that takes contaminated states as its object;
for such knowledge of others' minds is determinate.
Because one knows the minds and mental factors of others individually,
would it not also be the case that the patience and knowledge regarding suffering and its origin are subsumed under the three applications of mindfulness?
Although they exist, they do not take only a single dharma as their object.
"Because it has multiple entities," as stated in the treatise above.
If that is so, why [is it said] "regarding the mind possessed of greed" and so forth?
This is the objection.
If the knowledge of others' minds takes each mind and mental factor as a distinct object,
why does the Buddha say that he knows with exactitude minds such as those possessed by greed?
According to this scriptural passage:
Greed and the other [afflictions] apprehend simultaneously with the mind.
Regarding the statement that they do not apprehend simultaneously up to the point of being "stains," the answer is as follows:
Just as one might take up a garment but not its stains,
or take up the stains but not the garment,
so too does one apprehend the mind associated with greed and other afflictions by distinguishing between their preceding and succeeding moments.
It is not that they are apprehended simultaneously.

Regarding the passage from "one who has a mind possessed by craving" up to "bound only by craving," this is for the purpose of explaining the sūtra’s mention of "a mind possessed by craving" and so forth.
This generally clarifies the eleven pairs of mental states.
Below this, first is the explanation of the mind with attachment and the mind free from attachment.
To explain the mind with attachment in general:
There are two senses in which a mind is "possessed of greed": first, a mind associated with greed is called "possessed of greed";
second, a mind bound by greed is called "possessed of greed."
A mind associated with greed possesses both meanings [of being "associated" and "bound"].
Other impure minds are bound by greed alone.
Some say that the Sūtra states this until it reaches the point where they are designated as "having become free from greed."
Regarding the interpretation of the Sūtra on the Knowledge of Others' Minds concerning "minds with attachment" and so forth by the various masters below,
one master of the Sarvāstivāda school says:
"In this Sūtra, the phrase 'a mind with attachment' refers to..."
Regarding the first two types, only the first— the mind associated with greed— is mentioned;
as for the mind free from greed,
it refers to the mind that counteracts greed.
This refers to wholesome minds, both with outflows (*sāsrava*) and without outflows (*anāsrava*).
Only those that can counteract greed are called "minds free from greed" (*vītarāga-citta*).
If there were other teachers who, contrary to my teaching, claimed that a mind dissociated from greed is what is meant by "free from greed," [that would be incorrect].
Other afflictions such as hatred that are associated with it should also receive the designation "free from greed."
However, it cannot be said that this is called a "mind free from greed," because it is defiled. If that were so,
there would be a mind that reaches the state of being free from greed and so forth.
The author of the treatise raises an objection:
If that were so, there would be states of mind that are not antidotes to greed and are non-defiled by nature—
namely, a portion of the unobscured-neutral and the wholesome mind.
One should admit that this mind is not called "possessing greed" because it is dissociated from greed,
nor is it called "free from greed" because it does not counteract greed;
nevertheless, it is indeed a mind possessing greed.
Because it is bound by greed.
The term "and so forth" includes states such as a mind possessed of hatred.
If these were not included:
There are thus eleven pairs that do not fully encompass the concentrated mind;
for this reason, one must admit that the term "mind with attachment" (*sarāga-citta*) applies even to such states.
Having finished his objection, the master of the treatise further says:
Therefore, one should accept the explanation of the other masters of the Sarvāstivāda school:
a mind bound by greed is called "a mind with greed," while a mind that is the antidote to greed is called "a mind free from greed."
Their detachment from the mind of greed is the same as that of the first master;
therefore, it is not explained separately.
Thus, the *Vibhāṣā* says:
It is well said thus: that which is bound by craving is called a "mind with craving," while that which is the antidote to craving is called a "mind free from craving.
Furthermore, another interpretation holds that since the latter master has already stated that being bound by craving constitutes a "mind with craving," [the former master’s position is redundant].
Because it is known to be the antidote to greed, it is called the "mind free from greed.
If one understands this as referring exclusively to the untainted (*anāsrava*), then all such minds can be subsumed.
The Master [Vasubandhu], in this passage, provisionally challenges the first master's position and establishes the second master's view.
This is also refuted in the second section of the subsequent text.
As for the statement "even so for one who possesses delusion and one who is free from delusion," this is an analogical explanation.
The second pair consists of those with aversion and those free from aversion;
the third pair consists of those with delusion and those free from delusion—
it should be understood that it is likewise so.
Regarding the statement that "the Vaibhāṣika masters [hold this] because it must be understood through correspondence":
the fourth pair concerns the concentrated mind (*samkṣipta-citta*) and the distracted mind (*vikṣipta-citta*).
"Distracted" (*vikṣepa*) is a synonym for "distractedness" (*vikṣepa*).
The essence is concentration itself.
The designation "distraction" is established based on the state of the continuum, because it enumerates the moments of distraction.
Question: Can concentration remove distraction?
The essence of distraction is meditative concentration (*samādhi*);
wisdom (*prajñā*) dispels ignorance (*avidyā*).
The essence of ignorance is wisdom. The commentary explains: this refers to concentration and distraction as they pertain to the state of the mental continuum (*saṃtati*).
If one considers it in terms of moments, concentration is also not dispersed;
ignorance is not like this,
for there is no wisdom in every moment of its continuity.
Therefore, its essence is not wisdom (*prajñā*).
The rest of the text may be understood accordingly.
The *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* states that a concentrated mind is a "contracted mind" (*saṃkṣipta-citta*).
The names differ but the meaning is the same.
When it says "the masters of the West" regarding the term *vikṣipta* (distracted),
these "masters of the West" refers specifically to the masters of the country of Gandhāra.
The *Abhidharmamahāvibhāṣā* states that the masters of foreign lands [hold this view],
but it is not logical for one who has reached the knowledge of the path;
thus, the Vaibhāṣika masters refute it.
This is not reasonable;
for if defiled minds were associated with torpor,
they would necessarily involve both concentrated and distracted states.
Because it is characterized by sleep, it is called "aggregation" (caya); because it is characterized by defilement, it is called "dispersion" (vikṣepa).
Furthermore, this would contradict what is stated in the *Jñānaprasthāna-śāstra*.
To know the concentrated mind as it truly is is to possess four types of knowledge:
namely, dharma-knowledge, subsequent knowledge, conventional knowledge, and path knowledge.
Furthermore, the *Vibhāṣā* (190) states: "To know a contracted mind as it truly is—that is, 'this is a contracted mind'—consists of four types of knowledge:
dharma-knowledge (*dharmajñāna*), subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*), conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*), and path-knowledge (*mārgajñāna*)."
One knows a distracted mind as it truly is: "this is a distracted mind.
This is one type of knowledge, namely conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*). This follows what is appropriate, as previously [stated].
The *Vibhāṣā* in its preceding fascicle explains:
Question: Why is the knowledge of others' minds (paracittajñāna) not mentioned here?
Answer: The knowledge of others' minds cognizes the minds and mental factors (citta-caitta-dharma) within the mental continuum of another;
whereas the knowledge of reality as it is (yathābhūtajñāna) herein cognizes the minds and mental factors within one's own mental continuum.
Therefore, it is not mentioned.
Furthermore, the knowledge of others' minds knows present minds and mental factors;
herein, the knowledge of things as they truly are knows past minds and mental factors.
It is explained at length in that commentary. Furthermore, it says:
"Question: For what reason are the knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-jñāna*) and the knowledge of origin (*samudaya-jñāna*) not mentioned here?
Some say that although the knowledge of suffering and origin should also be mentioned here, their omission indicates that the meaning [of the teaching] is incomplete (*sāvaśeṣa*)."
Some say that the knowledge of suffering and the knowledge of the origin are knowledges with the aspect of revulsion, whereas in this context,
the knowledge of reality as it is is a knowledge with the aspect of aspiration.
Therefore, it is not so stated.
Some say that the knowledge of suffering and the knowledge of the origin take as their object things that are to be loathed.
In this context, the knowledge of reality as it is takes the desired object as its focal point, as explained at length in that [text]. Furthermore, it says:
"The knowledge of exhaustion and non-arising is not mentioned."
This refers to the aggregate of views (*dṛṣṭiskandha*), which speaks only of the nature of knowledge that consists of various views;
it does not speak of that knowledge whose nature is [the knowledge of] views. Therefore, the *Abhidharmamahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* does not exclude the knowledge of cessation (*nirodhajñāna*).
Because the mind is not known,
this lies beyond words.
If one speaks of sleep, it is called the "concentrated mind."
According to the text of the *Vibhāṣā*,
it should simply state that it is known by conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*);
how then can it be said that it is known by four knowledges?

The *Vibhāṣā* masters who provide the critical evaluation likewise refute this treatise [on the basis that] "the sunken mind reaches up to the arising of associated [states]. This refers to the fifth pair:
the sunken mind (*līnacitta*) and the exerted mind (*pragṛhītacitta*).
The *Vibhāṣā* states that "lowering the mind" and "elevating the mind" differ in name but are identical in meaning.
"A mind of little" refers to one who has attained only a small measure of greatness.
The sixth pair concerns the limited mind and the vast mind.
The "limited mind" refers to the defiled mind,
because it is that which people who possess few pure qualities habitually cultivate.
The "great mind" refers to the wholesome mind,
because it is that which is favored and practiced by those with many pure qualities;
therefore, the defiled is called "small."
"Good" is termed "great" either by way of the smallness or greatness of the three roots,
or by way of the smallness or greatness of its value.
Either due to the smallness or greatness of its retinue;
or due to the smallness or greatness of its concomitants;
or due to the smallness or greatness of its functional power.
Therefore, they are called "small" and "great.
A defiled mind has few roots;
if it arises together with independent ignorance (*mūla-moha*), [it has more].
That is, it is associated with one faculty.
If it arises together with greed or hatred,
it is associated with two faculties.
Because greed and hatred necessarily arise with their corresponding ignorance (*avidyā*),
it is said that they are "extremely associated with two.
Logically, even when defiled, these are not termed "cultivation" (*bhāvanā*).
Present wholesome dharmas are also termed "cultivation" (*bhāvanā*).
Furthermore, with respect to the future, they clarify their retinue;
for [in that state], defiled minds follow along only rarely.
This is because it consists only of the three aggregates of feeling, perception, and formations.
Wholesome minds are frequently accompanied by these;
although distracted minds are also accompanied by the three aggregates of feeling, perception, and formations, [they do so less often].
If it is within a concentrated mind,
it functions in conjunction with the four aggregates of form, feeling, perception, and formations;
the rest of the text may be understood accordingly.
Regarding the phrase "the distracted mind up to that which can counteract it":
this constitutes the seventh pair, the distracted mind and the undistracted mind.
That which can counteract the former is precisely the concentrated mind (*samāhita-citta*).
Therefore, the *Vibhāṣā* states:
"One whose mind is not agitated is one whose wholesome mind is associated with *śamatha*."
Alternatively, that which is able to remedy those [distractions] is precisely the practice of equanimity (*upekṣā*).
Thus, the *Mahāvibhāṣā* states:
"One whose mind is not agitated..."
This means that because the wholesome mind functions in association with equanimity (*upekṣā*), it should be understood that the same applies to the non-quiescent and quiescent minds.
This refers to the eighth pair: the non-quiescent mind and the quiescent mind.
This is explained according to the commentary on "agitation" and "non-agitation.
Furthermore, the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* states:
"One whose mind is not tranquil..."
This refers to the defiled mind;
because it is associated with non-quiescence,
all afflictions are by nature non-quiescent.
A "calmed mind" refers to a wholesome mind,
because it is associated with tranquility;
all wholesome phenomena possess the nature of tranquility.
Regarding the phrase "the undetermined mind [is so called] because it reaches the point of being able to counteract that":
this refers to the ninth pair, the undetermined and the determined mind;
that is to say, the determined mind is able to counteract that distracted and wavering mind.
This is precisely the concentrated mind.
Thus, the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* says:
"As for the unconcentrated mind..."
This refers to the defiled mind,
because it is associated with distraction.
As for the concentrated mind:
This refers to the virtuous mind (*kuśalacitta*).

Because it is associated with meditative concentration (*samādhi*), it is not a "cultivated mind" (*bhāvitacitta*); as for the statement that there may be two types of cultivation, this is because [the cultivated mind] can extend up to that point.
The tenth pair concerns the non-cultivation and cultivation of the mind.
As for the non-cultivated mind,
it refers to the defiled mind.
Because it is not included in either the cultivation of acquisition (*pratilambha-bhāvanā*) or the cultivation of practice (*niṣevaṇa-bhāvanā*).
"Cultivation of the mind" refers to wholesome states of mind (*kuśala-citta*).
There may be "attainment" (pratilambha), because of the cultivation of two kinds of practice.
That which was never previously attained but is newly attained at this time is called "cultivation by attainment" (pratilambhabhāvanā).
This applies to both the simultaneous attainment with the dharma and the attainment prior to the dharma.
When the essence manifests before one, it is called cultivation through practice (*abhyāsa-bhāvanā*).
This applies to both the beginning and the end, and is termed cultivation through practice within all wholesome dharmas.
There may be cultivation through acquisition that is not cultivation through practice,
such as when wholesome states of the future are first cultivated at the present moment;
or there may be cultivation through practice that is not cultivation through acquisition.
For example, when previously cultivated wholesome states manifest in the present,
there is both acquisition and cultivation through practice. Or,
for example, when wholesome states previously cultivated in the future now first manifest in the present.
There may be cases where there is non-acquisition (*aprāpti*) that is a cultivation (*bhāvanā*) but not a cultivation by practice (*abhyāsa-bhāvanā*).
This is because, apart from the three aforementioned characteristics, they do not all necessarily coexist; therefore, the term "possible" (*sambhavati*) is employed.
Therefore, the *Vibhāṣā* states:
"Cultivation of the mind" refers to cultivation by acquisition (*pratilambha-bhāvanā*) and cultivation by practice (*niṣevaṇa-bhāvanā*).
Regarding the statement "cultivating the mind either individually or simultaneously,
until the non-liberated mind becomes capable of liberation":
this refers to the eleventh pair, concerning the non-liberated and liberated minds.
The "unliberated mind" refers to the defiled mind;
it is so called because its very essence is defiled.
It is not liberated by its own nature because it arises within a body possessed of delusion; therefore,
it is called "unliberated in its continuity."
Therefore, the *Vibhāṣā* states:
"That which is not liberated from the mind" refers to being unliberated from both liberation by nature (*svabhāva-vimukti*) and liberation through the continuity [of the path] (*saṃtati-vimukti*).
A liberated mind refers to a wholesome mind,
which by its very nature is capable of liberation.
The continuum may be liberated.
Briefly stated, all wholesome minds are of two kinds:
first, those with outflows (*sāsrava*).
The second is the untainted (anāsrava). If it is untainted,
it is called liberation by intrinsic nature (svabhāva-vimukti).
Because its essence is free from bondage,
it pertains to both those in training (śaikṣa) and those beyond training (aśaikṣa).
Since not all wholesome mental factors are termed "liberation," the word "possible" (or "may be") is employed.
The body upon which a wholesome mind relies is briefly of two kinds:
first, a body with afflictions;
second, a body without afflictions.
If one relies on the body free from affliction, it is called the "body of liberation through the continuity [of the stream].
This refers to the "body of liberation" by virtue of having emerged from obstacles;
however, since not all bodies of reliance are termed "liberation," the word "potentially" (or "may be") is employed.
That is to say, within a wholesome mind, if it is liberated by its own nature (*svabhāva-vimukta*), it is called a "liberated mind.
If it is liberated through the continuity of the stream (*saṃtati-vimukti-kāya*), it is also called a "liberated mind.
One should formulate four permutations (*catuṣkoṭi*): there may be a wholesome mind that is liberated by its own nature but not liberated through the continuity of the stream.

That is to say, for a learner (*śaikṣa*), there may be an untainted (*anāsrava*) mind, or a wholesome (*kuśala*) mind that is liberated by continuity (*prabandha-vimukta*) but not liberated by nature (*svabhāva-vimukta*).
For one beyond learning (*aśaikṣa*), there may be a tainted wholesome mind, or a wholesome mind that is both liberated by nature and liberated by continuity.

This refers to the untainted mind of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), or to wholesome minds that are neither liberated by nature (*svabhāva-vimukta*) nor liberated through continuity (*prabandha-vimukta*).

These refer to the tainted minds of those in training (*śaikṣa*) and the wholesome minds of ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*). Among these four categories, the first three are called "liberated minds."
Therefore, the *Vibhāṣā* states:
"The liberated mind refers to liberation by its own nature (*svabhāva-vimukti*) and liberation through the continuity of the stream (*saṃtati-vimukti*)."
Whether it be one or both types of liberated minds—
such is the explanation regarding the specific meanings of the various phrases.
Here, the Sautrāntika masters ask:
This interpretation is flawed in two respects: first, it does not conform to the sūtras;
second, it fails to distinguish the specific meanings of the individual phrases.
How is it that this interpretation does not conform to the sūtras?
The Vaibhāṣika asks: How is it that my interpretation does not accord with the sūtra?
For the sūtra says: "This mind reaches to insight (vipaśyanā) but lacks tranquility (śamatha)."
The Sautrāntika master replies:
The Sūtra asks, "How is this mind inwardly withdrawn?
It means that if the mind functions in association with dullness (*styāna*).
It is accompanied by sleep; or,
internally associated, it consists of calm abiding (śamatha) without insight (vipaśyanā),
namely, the formless attainments (ārūpyasamāpatti).
As for what is called "internal," this refers to the internal mind; it does not necessarily require meditative concentration (*samādhi*),
because according to the Sautrāntika school, concentration and wisdom do not arise simultaneously.
Therefore, it is said that there is "stopping" (śamatha) without "insight" (vipaśyanā).
Such categories as these are all termed "internal gathering.
What is "external distraction"?
This refers to the mind wandering through and flowing along with the five objects, such as visible forms,
and being either accompanied by insight (vipaśyanā) without tranquility (śamatha),
namely in the preliminary (anāgamya) and intermediate (dhyānāntara) stages.
As for what is called "internal," it refers to the internal mind; it does not necessarily require meditative concentration (*samādhi*),
because according to the Sautrāntika school, concentration and wisdom do not arise simultaneously.
Therefore, it is said that there is observation (*vipaśyanā*) but no cessation (*śamatha*).
Such categories as these are all termed external distraction (*bahirdhā-vikṣepa*).
Was it not previously stated that one who reaches the state of pervasive gathering and scattering commits a transgression?
The Vaibhāṣika masters object:

"Did we not previously raise this objection against the Western masters? That if a defiled mind were associated with sleep, it would entail the error of a single moment of mind being both concentrated (*samkṣipta*) and distracted (*vikṣipta*).
Even though you claim that [sleep] is illogical because it belongs to a distracted state of mind, [the fault remains]."
Although the explanation of the Sautrāntika masters is unreasonable,
our own school does not admit that defiled minds associated with sleep are distracted minds.
Because the defiled mind associated with sleep is exclusively a concentrated mind,
there is no fault of a single moment of mind being both concentrated and dispersed.
"Is it not also said that this contradicts the *Mūla-śāstra*?
The Vaibhāṣikas raise the objection:
"Is it not also said [in the *Mūla-śāstra*] that a concentrated mind (*samāhita-citta*) possesses four knowledges (*jñāna*)?"
Regarding the statement, "It is better to contradict the treatise than to contradict the scriptural teaching," the Sautrāntika master asks:
"How can you fail to distinguish the specific meanings of these various phrases?"
The Vaibhāṣika asks:
"Regarding the statement that this explanation extends up to the eight distinct characteristics," the Sautrāntika replies:
Among the eleven pairs, it may reasonably be granted that the first three pairs— greed and so forth— are not concurrent,
as they are clearly explained separately; however,
one cannot discern the distinct characteristics of the eight pairs concerning the scattered (*vikṣipta*) and the collected (*saṃkṣipta*), and so on.
That is to say, a single moment of a defiled mind consists of the eight [states] such as distraction;
a single moment of a wholesome mind consists of the eight [states] such as concentration.
Regarding my own explanation up to the point where eight distinct names are established,
the Vaibhāṣika masters offer this defense:
"According to my own explanation, it is not that I am unable to distinguish the specific meanings of these eight phrases within this sūtra."
This means that although distraction and the other states are equally defiled minds,
eight distinct names are established based on eight different meanings in order to manifest their specific differences in fault.
It is intended to cause sentient beings to develop weary detachment;
furthermore, although states such as accumulation are equally wholesome mental states,
it is for the purpose of manifesting the distinctions among their respective merits.
Therefore, eight distinct names are established based on these eight meanings in order to inspire joy and aspiration in sentient beings.
Since it cannot lead to universal penetration, it is termed "cultivation at an improper time."
The Sautrāntika masters refute this,
stating that since he cannot resolve the contradiction with the sūtra teachings,
his exposition of the eight points is untenable.
Because it does not accord with the sūtras, the principle is also untenable.
Furthermore, if a mind associated with lethargy were identical to a mind associated with agitation,
the sūtra should not have stated [them as distinct].
If at that time the mind is sunken,
and one cultivates the three factors of enlightenment— tranquility, concentration, and equanimity— out of fear of further sinking, this is called untimely cultivation.
Cultivating investigation, energy, and joy is called timely cultivation.
If at that time the mind is agitated,
and one cultivates investigation, energy, and joy out of fear of agitation, this is called untimely cultivation.
To cultivate tranquility, concentration, and equanimity is called timely cultivation.
The meaning of this sutra is that when the mind is sunken, it must be roused;
when the mind is agitated, it must be suppressed.
Since the *Sūtra on the Sinking Mind and the Agitated Mind* explains them separately,
it is clear that sinking and agitation do not arise simultaneously. How,
then, can one say that the sinking mind is itself the agitated mind?
"Is there not a principle that the factors of enlightenment (bodhyaṅga) can be practiced separately?
The Vaibhāṣika masters raise this objection:
"The seven factors of enlightenment must necessarily be present as constituent parts within meditative concentration."
How could there be a distinct principle for cultivating the factors of enlightenment within a distracted state of mind? Why, then,
speak of distinctions between the appropriate and inappropriate times?
Regarding the statement, "There is no fault because this refers to the point when attention has reached [the object]," the Sautrāntika masters explain:
This refers to the cultivation of the factors of enlightenment (bodhyaṅga) at the time when one is about to enter meditative absorption; it is called "cultivation" [in that sense].
There is no fault, because one is not currently cultivating the untainted factors of enlightenment (*anāsrava-bodhyaṅga*).
Would you not say that what I have called "reaching" and what I have called "the essence" are one and the same?
The Vaibhāṣika masters explain the sūtra by stating that they separately mention *laya* (sinking) and *auddhatya* (restlessness) based on their respective predominance.
If one considers that restlessness and lethargy correspond [to their respective opposites],
I say that the essence of the defiled mind is one.
As for the statement "speaking according to one's own intent," it does not apply to the mind in this way.
The Sautrāntika masters are incorrect.
Regarding the previous statement that all states of reaching [an object] constitute a mind possessed of desire (*sarāga-citta*),
the Master [Vasubandhu], having previously raised an objection, provisionally accepts the second master’s explanation.
Now, this is refuted in turn.

Regarding the previous statement that "all minds bound by craving are called 'minds with craving' (sarāga-citta)," what is the meaning of "being bound by craving" (rāga-saṃyukta)? This restates the position and poses the inquiry: if it is because the acquisition (prāpti) of craving follows [the mind] that it is called "bound by craving," [then...]
The untainted mind of one in training (*śaikṣa*) should be called "a mind possessed of greed" (*sarāga*),
because it follows the acquisition of greed. If it were called "bound by greed" (*sarāga*) because greed takes it as its object,
then the tainted mind of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) should also be called "a mind possessed of greed."
Furthermore, it is because [the mind] serves as an object for the greed of others.
If one does not admit that the contaminated mind of an Arhat can be an object for greed,
how could that mind be considered contaminated?

If you should further argue that the outflow-tainted mind (*sāsrava-citta*) of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) is called "outflow-tainted" because it is an object-condition (*ālambana*) for common delusions such as views (*dṛṣṭi*), etc.;
Because it does not take the specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) of afflictions such as greed as its object,
it is not called a "mind possessed of greed" (*sarāga-citta*); nor can it be said that [the mind] is not possessed of greed simply because it does not take greed as its object.
Since it is conditioned by ignorance as a common delusion,
it should be called "possessing delusion," because it is the object of delusion.
Furthermore, this is refuted by reasoning:
the knowledge of others' minds does not take the acquisition of greed as its object,
nor can it be said that it takes the greed which is directed toward that [object] or toward the mind itself as its object.
Since one cannot apprehend [the other's mind] as an object,
how could one know that another's mind possesses greed and so forth? Therefore,
it is not the case that a mind bound by greed is called "a mind with greed."
Since that [previous] interpretation of the sūtra also fails to capture its intended meaning,
the Master of the Treatise now restates the objection and refutes it.
If this is so, how [should it be understood]?
The second master previously raised a question;
now, as the meaning of the sutra reaches the point where it says "named detachment from greed" and so forth,
the author of the treatise provides the third and correct explanation.
Now, examining the intent of the sutra:
it is called a "mind with greed" because it is associated with greed;
it is called a "mind free from greed" because it is dissociated from greed.
This refers to all virtuous minds and all non-obscured [neutral] minds;
the term "and so forth" includes those with anger and the like,
which may be understood according to the explanation.
"If that is so, why is it said that one who has reached the stage of a non-returner (anāgāmin) still falls into the three realms of existence?
This is the objection raised by the second master.
He asks: "If you say that the mind free from greed, hatred, and delusion can also be associated with outflows (sāsrava), [then how can it be said that a non-returner does not fall back]?"
For what reason does the Sūtra state that a mind free from greed, hatred, and delusion does not return to fall into the three realms of existence?
Since it is stated that it does not fall into the three realms of existence,
it is clearly understood that a mind free from greed and the others is exclusively untainted (*anāsrava*).
Regarding the claim that there is no fault because it is spoken in reference to attainment through detachment,
the Master of the Treatise (the author) explains the sūtra by stating that it is spoken in reference to attainment through detachment from the afflictions of the three realms.

To say that they do not fall back into rebirth within the three realms of existence (*tridhātu*) means that it is not merely because their untainted essence (*anāsrava-svabhāva*) does not pertain to those three realms; rather,
it refers to being called "detached from craving" (*vītarāga*) based on the fact that they have attained liberation and thus do not fall back into the three realms.
I maintain that they are called "detached from greed" and so forth based on their non-association with greed;
since each is established according to a specific sense, there is no fault.
Is it not the case that, as previously stated, this is because of non-association?
The second master’s position is refuted in the same manner as the first.
Has this not already been refuted by the first master? [For it was argued:
"If a mind dissociated from greed were called 'a mind free from greed,' [then what of a mind associated with hatred]?"
Those associated with other afflictions should also receive the designation "free from greed," since they too are dissociated from greed. How, then,
can you establish the meaning of that which is to be refuted?

Regarding the statement, "If one follows this intention, because there is delusion and so forth," the Master of the Treatise defends his position by asserting that he takes reason as the standard of correctness.
How could it be that what was previously refuted is itself non-existent?
If this is the intended meaning,
then even if other afflictions associated with it are called "free from greed," there would be no contradiction in accepting this.
However, it is not described as a mind free from greed because it is associated with anger, delusion, and so forth.
By this principle, it should be understood.
Contaminated (*sāsrava*), uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) wholesome minds, and non-obscured (*anivṛta*) minds are all termed "minds free from greed.
Generally, a mind is called "possessing greed" for two reasons:
first, it is associated with greed (*lobha-samprayukta*).
It is bound by two types of craving.
Generally, the mind is said to be "detached from craving" based on two meanings:
first, it is dissociated from craving.
The second is the antidote to greed.
Altogether, there have been three explanations above.
According to the first master, it is called a "mind possessed of greed" (sarāga-citta) because it is associated with greed.
It is called "a mind free from greed" because it is the antidote to greed.
According to the second master, it is called "a mind with greed" because it is bound by greed;
it is called "a mind free from greed" because it is the antidote to greed.
Third, the author of the treatise [states] that because it is associated with greed, it is called a "mind with greed";
because it is dissociated from greed, it is called a "mind free from greed. Question: According to the *Abhidharmamahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 190...
There are also these three explanations.
The first and last explanations are refuted, and this second one is taken as correct. [An objection:
How can the Master of the Treatise adopt an incorrect doctrine from the *Vibhāṣā*? [Response: It is explained that the Master takes reason (*yukti*) as the standard of correctness.
It is not by taking the *Vibhāṣā* commentators as the authoritative standard [that this is determined].
The first master’s explanation of the sūtra does not fully encompass the collected mind;
the second master’s statement fails to grasp the intended meaning of the sūtra.
Therefore, the Master of the Treatise now takes this as correct.
As for the phrase "ceasing the collateral discussion and arriving at the aspect of the cognitive object," it means ceasing the dispute to state the established tenet.
Question:
Since this aforementioned knowledge of others' minds (paracittajñāna) knows the minds of others,
is it also able to apprehend the objects of those minds, such as form (rūpa) and so forth?
And does one also grasp the aspect of the object of cognition belonging to another's mind?
For example, when another person takes that other's mind as their object,
the mind of this other person is called the "aspect of the object of cognition belonging to another's mind."
Regarding the point that neither can apprehend [the other], up to the point where it would result in the fault of [a cognition] taking itself as its object:
the answer is that neither can apprehend [the other].
When knowing that mind, one does not observe the object of that mind,
nor does one observe the mode of apprehension (ākāra) by which that mind’s basis acts as the subject;
that is to say, the knowledge of others' minds merely knows whether that mind is defiled or otherwise.
One does not know the colors and so forth that color the mind of another,
nor does one know the mental aspects (ākāra) by which that mind takes its object.
If one were to know the objects perceived by another's mind, [one would likewise know those aspects].

In that case, there would be the fault that the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*) would also take form and other [objects] as its objects, being termed "knowledge of others' forms" (*pararūpajñāna*).

Furthermore, if one holds that the mode of apprehension (*ākāra*) within the knowledge of others' minds can itself take [that knowledge] as an object, then there would also be the error of it taking itself as an object.
Because the knowledge of others' minds (paracittajñāna) possesses the aspect (ākāra) that takes the mental states of others as its object;

for this school does not admit that a mind can take itself as its own object. Furthermore, it is explained that when the knowledge of others' minds arises, it is the aspect of taking others' minds as its object that constitutes what is perceived by that knowledge of others' minds.
Furthermore, if the mental state that takes another's mind as its object has as its aspect (ākāra) the very act of cognizing that [other] mind,
then if the knowledge of others' minds were to know both the object and the cognitive aspect of that other mind,
it would also follow that it possesses the fault of being able to cognize itself.
It is not the knowledge of others' minds;
this constitutes a double refutation.
Therefore, the *Abhidharmamahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 99, states:
The knowledge of others' minds takes only the other's mind as its object, not the mental factors associated with that mind nor their modes of activity (*ākāra*).
If it were to take those mental factors or modes of activity as its objects,
it would be taking one's own mind as its object and would therefore not be the knowledge of others' minds.
Because one's own mind is both the objective referent (*ālambana*) and the subjective aspect (*ākāra*) of that [cognition].
All the masters state:
"The subjective aspect" refers to...
This refers precisely to the cognitive aspect (*ākāra*) that is capable of apprehending the other's mind.
One merely knows the substance of the other's mind,
but does not know the cognitive aspect that is capable of apprehending it upon the other's mind.
Not so; for the *Abhidharmamahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* is extremely clear on this point.
Regarding the various forms of knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*), it should be understood that they exist as far as is appropriate.
This describes his own school’s position. Furthermore, this interpretation also answers the preceding question:
it clarifies that the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*) does not know the objects or the subjective aspects (*ālambana* and *ākāra*) of another's mind.
All forms of knowledge of others' minds possess a determinate character.
This means that it can only apprehend those things bound to the desire realm and the form realm,
as well as those not so bound; the mention of the "desire realm and so forth" serves to distinguish these from the formless realm.
Because one does not know what is above, it is "another's continuum" (parasantāna),
which excludes one's own body.
Because one does not know oneself, it is "present."
Excluding the past and the future, because those [factors] lack functional activity. Regarding "homogeneous" (*sabhāga*):
it means knowing a factor-part as a factor-part, a category-part as a category-part, the contaminated (*sāsrava*) as contaminated, and the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) as uncontaminated.
"Knowing the untainted (*anāsrava*), etc."—
this distinguishes it from other categories.
"Mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta-dharma*)" distinguish them from matter (*rūpa*) and so forth.
Because it cannot cognize objects such as form (*rūpa*) and so forth, it distinguishes the one from the two;

that is, it cognizes only the one and not the two. It distinguishes the real from the provisional, because the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*) does not cognize the provisional. [It cognizes] the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*).
This excludes the universal characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*), because the universal characteristic is not known [by it].
This is just as consciousness (*vijñāna*) is defined by its own characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), namely, "discernment" (*vijñapti*).
Although uncontaminated knowledge of others' minds takes a common characteristic as its object,
because it observes a single phenomenon individually rather than multiple phenomena,
it is also termed a "specific characteristic" (svalakṣaṇa).
Because one takes these phenomena as objects of focus and cultivates the four modes of practice on the path,
this is associated with the wishless samādhi (*apraṇihita-samādhi*),
and no other mental aspects are produced.
It is not associated with the samādhis of emptiness or signlessness;
it is not subsumed under the knowledges of exhaustion or non-arising;
and the knowledge of others' minds is of the nature of vision (*darśana*).
This is because it is the cessation of seeking, not the seeing of the nature [of reality].
The knowledges of suffering, origin, and cessation have already been distinguished as before;
however, they are distinguished again here because the knowledges of exhaustion and non-arising also apply to the truth of the path.
It does not exist in the path of seeing,
because of its rapidity and because there is no room for deliberation.
It does not exist in the path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*), because it severs hindrances and because there is no room for deliberation.
This is because they may appropriately exist within the remaining paths of cultivation— namely, the path of preparation (*prayoga-mārga*),
the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*), and the path of advancement (*viśeṣa-mārga*).
As for the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣaya-jñāna*) and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpāda-jñāna*) up to the point of no further rebirth:
The last two phrases are explained as follows:

when the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*) first arise, they take only the suffering and origin of the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*) as their objects through six aspects;
if they occur at a later time, they pervasively take all four truths as their objects.
Among the sixteen aspects, excluding emptiness (śūnyatā) and non-self (anātman),
each possesses the remaining fourteen aspects.
The reason they do not constitute the aspects of emptiness and non-self is as follows:
Although these two types of knowledge are subsumed under the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*),
they involve conventional expressions such as "my births have been exhausted" and so forth;
therefore, within contemplation, they are distinct from emptiness and non-self.
This refers to the preceding cause impinging upon the subsequent effect;
that is to say, by virtue of the power of contemplating internal exhaustion and non-arising,
one speaks thus within the subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*) at the time of emerging from meditative equipoise.
Because of [the realization] "my births are exhausted," and so forth,
one remains within contemplation, detached from emptiness and non-self;
for emptiness and non-self are contrary to the notion of a self.
Therefore, the *Vibhāṣā* (29) states:
"My births are exhausted" refers to the four aspects of the origin of suffering (*samudaya*). "The holy life has been established" refers to...
"The path has been cultivated" refers to the four aspects of the path;
"what was to be done has been accomplished" refers to the four aspects of cessation;
"there will be no further existence" refers to the two aspects of suffering.
That is to say, [they are] suffering and impermanent.
Furthermore, the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 102, states:
"As it is said in the Sūtra..."

The various Arhats, knowing for themselves in accordance with reality: "Birth has been exhausted for me; the holy life has been established; what was to be done has been accomplished; there is no further existence.
Regarding this, "birth has been exhausted" means:
However, the term "birth" (*jāti*) manifests various meanings;
that is to say, some instances of the term "birth" manifest entry into the mother's womb,
while others manifest emergence from the mother's womb.
Some births are named to manifest the five aggregates in their specific states;
some births are named to manifest a portion of the dissociated formations (*viprayukta-saṃskāra-skandha*);

and some births are named to manifest the four aggregates of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*). Regarding these four types of birth, as explained in the *Mahāvibhāṣā*, I am unable to cite them in full.
There are those whose birth is designated as that which manifests the four aggregates of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
As it is said here, "My births have been exhausted.
One asks: what kind of birth is this exhaustion of?
Is it the past? Is it the future?
Or is it the present?
If it were the exhaustion of past births,
since past births have already ceased, what need would there be for their exhaustion?
If it were the exhaustion of future births...
What is exhausted when future births have not yet arrived?
If it were the present birth that is exhausted,
then the present birth would not abide.
What need is there to exhaust [the cycle]?
One should answer: "It is the exhaustion of births throughout the three periods of time."
Why is this so? Because here the term "birth" (jāti) clearly indicates the four aggregates of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception;

thus, all practitioners of yoga collectively contemplate the four aggregates of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception across the three periods of time in order to become detached from their defilements.
This causes both birth and its causes and effects to be unestablished,
as explained at length in that commentary.
Regarding the phrase "the holy life has been established":
This refers to the fact that untainted conduct has already been established.
Question: Is it that the brahmacarya of one in training (śaikṣa) has been established, or is it that the brahmacarya of one beyond training (aśaikṣa) has been established?
Answer: It is the brahmacarya of one in training that has been established.
It is not the brahmacarya of one beyond training (aśaikṣa). Why is this?
Because the brahmacarya of one beyond training is only now being established. As for "one who has done what was to be done" (kṛtakṛtya):
Because all afflictions have been completely severed;
because all that was to be done has been fully accomplished;
and because all paths have been blocked.
This is explained in detail according to that commentary. Regarding the phrase "not subject to further existence," the Venerable Ghosaka states:
"Because all Arhats are without further existence."
It is generally explained as "not being subject to further existence.
This is explained in detail as in that [text]. Furthermore, it says:
"Question: From 'my births have been exhausted' up to 'I am not subject to further existence.'"
Regarding each of these, one should ask: "What kind of knowledge is this?

Some say that herein, "my births are exhausted" refers to the knowledge of origination (*samudaya-jñāna*), and "the holy life has been established" refers to the knowledge of the path (*mārga-jñāna*).
"That which has been done is the knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-jñāna*);
'there is no further existence' is the knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-jñāna*)," as explained extensively in that [text].

Regarding the statement, "Because there is a treatise that explains the existence of untainted [attainments] reaching others," this constitutes the second section clarifying that the practice is complete and exhaustive.
The preceding sentence sets forth the main body of the teaching.
The second phrase describes alternative interpretations.
The *Śāstra* states, "As for 'transcending these sixteen,'" this explains the preceding phrase.
The *Nyāyānusāra*, fascicle 73, states:

"Is it not the case that some say the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*) necessarily cognize for themselves: 'My births are exhausted,' and so forth?
This does not contradict [our position], because it has already been explained previously."
This means that as previously stated, after the untainted contemplation (*anāsrava-vipaśyanā*),
one performs this mode of activity within conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*);
this mode of activity does not proceed within untainted knowledge.
The conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*) is induced by the [knowledges of] exhaustion (*kṣaya*) and non-arising (*anutpāda*).
Because its merit is attributed to the fundamental [knowledge], it is said that "it realizes" [them].
Therefore, this knowledge is admitted to be free from emptiness and non-self. Furthermore, it is said:
If that were so, since there exists an untainted knowledge of others' minds (anāsrava-paracittajñāna),
it would follow that there are untainted modes of activity (ākāra) beyond the sixteen;
for all knowledge of others' minds takes the single, real, specific characteristic (svalakṣaṇa) as its object.
The aspects (ākāra) of the [four] paths and so forth all take the collective common characteristic (sāmānyalakṣaṇa) as their object.
Since those [aspects] and these [objects] are distinct,
it is known that there definitely exist uncontaminated (anāsrava) aspects separate from the sixteen [standard ones].
The objection is not valid because it is not definitively asserted;
that is to say, our own tenet does not definitively assert that the aspect of the universal characteristic (sāmānyalakṣaṇa) merely takes a collection as its object.
Because it is admitted that there are two applications of mindfulness— those of sensation and mind—
just as when one contemplates a single entity of sensation as impermanent,
this knowledge arises with a universal characteristic as its mode of activity.
It is universally established that [the knowledge of others' minds] takes the unique particularity (*svalakṣaṇa*) of a single real entity as its object.

Why, then, would you not admit that uncontaminated knowledge of others' minds (*anāsrava-paracittajñāna*) likewise takes the unique particularity of a single real entity as its object by way of a common characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*)?
This refers to knowing that the mind of another is truly the Path and so forth;
that is, taking as its object the single reality of the characteristics of being the Path and so forth.

If it is argued that this should be like the mindfulness of feelings and the mindfulness of mind, which take as their object all feelings and minds throughout the three periods of time in a general manner.
It takes the aspects (ākāra) of the common characteristics (sāmānyalakṣaṇa), such as impermanence;
likewise, untainted knowledge of others' minds (anāsrava-paracittajñāna) also collectively takes as its object the untainted minds and so forth of others across the three periods of time,
taking them as the aspects of the Path (mārga) and so forth.
This would contradict your own school’s tenet that the knowledge of others' minds arises only by taking a single, real, specific characteristic (svalakṣaṇa) of the present as its object;
yet this is not so, because the preparatory application (prayoga) is different.
This preparatory practice for wisdom is intended to discern whether another’s present cognizing mind possesses specific states such as greed;

whereas this preparatory practice for the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) regarding impermanence and so forth is intended for the general revulsion toward all contaminated phenomena (*sāsravadharma*).
Due to the distinctions in the power of the preceding preparatory stages,
at the time of reaching fulfillment, there appears a synthesis of what was previously differentiated;
therefore, there is no fault of violating the logical analogy.
If it is argued that [feeling] is not permanent because its intrinsic nature is not [permanently] experienced,
then when one contemplates feeling as impermanent,
one is not taking a single, real, specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) as the object.
Rather, one might as well cite this as an analogy for the knowledge of others' minds;
in that case, they would have to admit that feeling is not impermanent,
and thus they should not give rise to the contemplation of impermanence regarding feeling.
Just as feeling and mind are distinct in essence,
it is certainly impossible to contemplate feeling as being the mind;
even though one may contemplate feeling itself as impermanent, [it remains feeling].
Yet there is no fault of a single entity having multiple natures, because the experience itself is not a manifold nature that is distinct [from it].
For instance, [qualities] such as impairment or benefit are not separate from the experience; they are merely other modes of manifestation (*ākāra*).
"The other dharmas are likewise" as stated above in the treatise.

Regarding the statement by the foreign masters (bāhyaka-ācārya) that "it extends beyond the sixteen," the following explains the latter phrase; these foreign masters are the śramaṇas of the West (i.e., the Sarvāstivādins).
This records a divergent opinion.
How is this known to be so?
The question from Kaśmīra [states]:
Regarding the statement, "From the perspective of the *Mūla-śāstra*, [the claim] that it is unreasonable to provide an explanation," the masters of the Western Regions (Bahirdeśaka) respond:
"It is from the perspective of the *Mūla-śāstra*."
This refers to the *Vijñānakāya-pāda-śāstra*.
As stated in that treatise:
"Is there an untainted, non-bound mind capable of discerning phenomena bound to the desire realm?"
Answer: It can discern; that is to say, by means of the eight modes of activity such as impermanence and so forth, as well as the principle that "this is possible."
"Abiding" (sthiti) refers to the sense of being consistent with reason and compatible with acceptance;
furthermore, there is "this matter" (vastu),
where "matter" means functional activity.
These ten are all termed "discriminations induced by correct reasoning.
Since the root treatise excludes the eight modes of activity (*ākāra*),
it separately states that there exist "this possibility" (*sthāna*) and "this fact" (*vastu*), which are minds not bound [to the realms].
Therefore, it is known that apart from the sixteen aspects,
there exists a separate untainted mind;
this is your position, O Kaśmīrī.
If it is argued that the aforementioned passage does not demonstrate that, when an unconditioned mind discerns a phenomenon bound to the desire realm,
there exists something other than the eight modes of activity previously explained, which is "possible" (sthāna).
There is this mode of activity; however,
it is merely for the purpose of demonstrating that the unconditioned mind performs eight modes of activity while taking phenomena bound to the desire realm as its object.
"There is such a place; there is such a thing.
The first eight are explained individually.
The latter two [sections] provide a summary,
stating that there is no separate substantial nature;
this interpretation is incorrect.
Because this statement does not appear in other passages of the treatise;
