because they have not yet increased during the stage of cultivation (*bhāvanā-avasthā*), one likewise definitely accomplishes seven knowledges (*jñāna*).
This applies equally to ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) and to the stage of the sixteen moments of mind (*ṣoḍaśa-citta*).
If one has already become free from desire, each [of these knowledges] increases by the knowledge of others' minds;
however, in the state of being free from defilement, the knowledge of others' minds is not established for ordinary beings (pṛthagjana) who are born in the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu).
All others are accomplished.
Therefore, the *Nyāyānusāra* states:
"However, during the stage of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*)."
Furthermore, within the Path of Seeing (darśanamārga),
one can only achieve conventional and knowledge of others' minds; at the time of the subsequent knowledge of the path (mārgānvayajñāna), both types are fully achieved,
because it is then that one first attains the fruit of Non-returner (anāgāmiphala).
Furthermore, one attains the untainted [knowledge] to constitute the essence of the fruit;
in all other stages of cultivation, both types are fully present.
For those born in the formless realm, the conventional [knowledge] is abandoned. This concludes the treatise above. Regarding those liberated by time, they definitely possess nine knowledges.
Furthermore, when the knowledge of exhaustion (kṣayajñāna) is added,
one who is liberated at any time (asamayavimukta) definitely possesses ten knowledges; when the knowledge of non-arising (anutpādajñāna) is further added, [they possess eleven].
Regarding the question of at which stage one suddenly cultivates how many knowledges (*jñāna*),
the following section, sixth, distinguishes the cultivation of knowledge according to the stages. Within this:
First, cultivation is distinguished in relation to the path of seeing;
second, cultivation is distinguished in relation to the path of meditation;
third, cultivation is distinguished in relation to the path of no-more-learning.
Fourth, cultivation is distinguished according to other stages;
fifth, cultivation is distinguished according to the supporting levels (bhūmi);
sixth, the meaning of the four types of cultivation is explained comprehensively. This constitutes the general inquiry.
There are four types of cultivation: attainment (*pratilambha*), practice (*niṣevaṇa*), counteraction (*pratipakṣa*), and elimination (*vinirdhāvana*).
Hereafter, for the time being, these shall be distinguished by way of the two cultivations of attainment and practice.
Furthermore, the *Nyāya* states:
"One should first investigate:
what is meant by 'cultivation' (*bhāvanā*)?"
This refers to the cultivation of wholesome conditioned phenomena so as to bring them to fulfillment and mastery;
it is not defiled or neutral,
because there is no superior fruit of craving.
That which is non-virtuous or unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) does not exist within the continuum, because it is not part of the continuity [of rebirth].
Furthermore, the unconditioned has no fruit.
Moreover, regarding that which is attained solely through application (*prayoga*) up to the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*):
Within the response,
this first section distinguishes cultivation in relation to the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*). Now,
the various types of cultivation will be distinguished.
Briefly, based on the four paths—preparatory (*prayoga*), uninterrupted (*ānantarya*), liberation (*vimukti*), and advancement (*viśeṣa*)—the ten knowledges (*jñāna*) are clarified.

Regarding the cultivation of acquisition (*pratilambha-bhāvanā*) and the cultivation of practice (*niṣevaṇa-bhāvanā*): the knowledges of suffering, origin, cessation, path, dharma, subsequent (*anvaya*), and conventional (*saṃvṛti*) may all be cultivated through both acquisition and practice within the context of the four paths.
Because it is broad and pervasive,
if one is in the preparatory path (*prayoga-mārga*) for the knowledge of others' minds, cultivation (*bhāvanā*) may occur since it does not involve the severing of hindrances; however,
because there is no room for delay, there is no cultivation through practice (*abhyāsa-bhāvanā*).
In the path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*), because it functions to abandon obstructions, there is no acquisition (*prāpti*) or cultivation (*bhāvanā*).
In the paths of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*) and special progress (*viśeṣa-mārga*), because they do not abandon obstructions, acquisition and cultivation are possible;
because they are paths of leisure (*kṣema-mārga*), cultivation through practice (*abhyāsa-bhāvanā*) is possible.
If, among the four paths, the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) is connected with them,

it may be cultivated in all of them; however, because the path of preparation (*prayoga-mārga*) and the path of immediate succession (*ānantarya-mārga*) are of the nature of seeing (*darśana*), they do not constitute cultivation through practice (*bhāvanā*).
Regarding liberation (*vimukti*), because it allows for the cessation of seeking and the cultivation of practice, there is further progress.
As for the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpāda-jñāna*), it is explained as being like the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣaya-jñāna*);
the difference is as follows:
Since there is no room for the arising of cultivation through practice (*abhyāsa-bhāvanā*) within the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*),
one should understand that, based on all four paths in brief, each has its respective two types of cultivation according to what is appropriate;
such is the determination and explanation.
The distinctions therein are as follows in the treatise.
The treatise says: "Reaching the foundations of mindfulness" explains the first two lines.
In the stage of the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), as each of the eight patiences (*kṣānti*) and seven knowledges (*jñāna*) arises,
one cultivates their respective types in the future; specifically, when a patience arises,
one cultivates that very patience itself.
One cultivates wisdom through wisdom itself;
however, one is able to fully cultivate the four aspects of the applications of mindfulness (smṛtyupasthāna) regarding the truths of oneself.
One attains patience (kṣānti) but has not yet attained wisdom (jñāna).
Once wisdom and patience have been attained, they do not cultivate one another;
this is because the patience and wisdom being cultivated both pervade the four aspects of practice and the four foundations of mindfulness,
such that each is cultivated in relation to all four.
For what reason is it that the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) is cultivated only as a homogeneous cultivation?
Question:
Because it is determined that what was previously never attained is now reached simultaneously.
Answer: Because this lineage had never been attained previously,
it is now being attained for the first time.
Because their power has not yet expanded, one cannot cultivate the similar [factors] by way of lateral cultivation.
Furthermore, since the various patiences (kṣānti) and knowledges (jñāna) are determined in terms of their antidotes and determined in terms of their objects,
one can only cultivate the similar [factors] and cannot cultivate them laterally.

Just as the patience regarding suffering (*duḥkha-kṣānti*) and the knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-jñāna*) definitely counteract the afflictions pertaining to the level of suffering and definitely take the truth of suffering (*duḥkha-satya*) as their object,
so it should be understood for the patience regarding the path (*mārga-kṣānti*) and the knowledge of the path (*mārga-jñāna*) as well.
Therefore, the *Vibhāṣā* (107) states: "Furthermore,

because the objects of focus (*ālambana*) and the antidotes (*pratipakṣa*) of the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) are fixed, one cultivates only those [factors] that are of the same category (*sabhāga*)."
The objects of focus for the path of cultivation are not fixed, nor are its antidotes fixed;
therefore, one can cultivate both those that are homogeneous and those that are heterogeneous.
This applies until one is able to cultivate them concurrently regarding suffering, origin, and cessation.
Explaining the third and fourth phrases:
only at the time of the three types of subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*) regarding suffering, origin,
and cessation can one simultaneously cultivate the conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*) pertaining to the limit of clear observation (*abhisamaya-antya*) in the future.
Only at the conclusion of the clear realization (abhisamaya) of each individual truth can this conventional knowledge (saṃvṛtijñāna) be cultivated concurrently; therefore,
it is designated by the name "conventional knowledge at the conclusion of clear realization" (abhisamayāntika-saṃvṛtijñāna).
Because of this name, one cannot practice them concurrently during the remaining stages of the path of vision (*darśanamārga*),
for conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*) has existed from time immemorial.
Having previously known suffering,
abandoned the origin,
and realized cessation, one likewise knows suffering at the conclusion of these three types of clear realization.
The abandoning of origination and the realization of cessation constitute one and the same task.
Furthermore, this conventional wisdom (saṃvṛti-jñāna) has been uninterrupted from beginningless time;
now that non-perception (asaṃjñi) is severed,
the conventional wisdom rejoices, giving rise to sympathetic joy (anumodana) at its attainment.
"Why is this not cultivated at the time of the subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārgānvayajñāna*)? This is the question.
[The answer is:
"At the time of the subsequent knowledge of the path, it is likewise at the limit of clear realization (*abhisamayāntika*)."
"Why do you not cultivate this conventional knowledge (saṃvṛtijñāna)?
[The questioner asks: "Because conventional knowledge has previously been cultivated extensively within the lineage (gotra). [The respondent] answers:

Because conventional wisdom has previously known, abandoned, and realized the three truths through repeated practice, one cultivates conventional wisdom at the conclusion of the clear realizations (*abhisamaya*). However,
because there was no prior clear realization of the path as an objective reality, it is not termed "cultivation" [in that specific context].
Because the Path does not constitute a single object, the subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārgānvayajñāna*) does not cultivate conventional knowledge;
furthermore, there is necessarily no comprehensive realization (*parijñā*) of all objects within the Path,
namely the three [truths] of suffering, origin, and cessation pertaining to the three realms.
Suffering can be fully understood;
the origin can be fully abandoned;
cessation can be fully realized.

Therefore, at the conclusion of the clear realizations (abhisamaya), one is able to cultivate conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*); however, it is absolutely impossible to cultivate [it] universally regarding the Path.
Consequently, at the conclusion of the clear realizations, conventional knowledge is not cultivated.
Although, from the perspective of the truth of origination (*samudaya-satya*), one has not yet severed all origination nor exhausted it entirely,
one has nonetheless completed the severance of origination within the present state of origination;
and although, from the perspective of the truth of cessation (*nirodha-satya*), one has not yet realized all cessation nor exhausted it entirely.
At the stage of cessation, the realization of cessation is already complete;
however, this is not the case for the Path,
because there are many lineages (gotra).
Because one cannot cultivate the path of a different lineage;
although cultivation of one's own faculty and lineage is possible,
not even one part in a hundred thousand arises [from it].
Since suffering must be fully known at the conclusion of the clear observation (*abhisamaya*) of suffering,
it is not explained separately.
Some say that because this [state] is one of arrival (*prāpti*), one cannot cultivate it.
Some say: This conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*) is an attendant of the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*);
since that subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārgānvayajñāna*) is subsumed under the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), it cannot be cultivated [at that time].
Regarding the point that "a principle not universally established should not serve as proof," the author of the treatise raises an objection:
some schools maintain that the sixteenth moment of mind is also subsumed within the path of vision (*darśanamārga*).

The statement that "what is not established by reason should not be used as proof" explains the phrase "non-arising" within the fifth clause, meaning that this conventional knowledge reaches a point where its arising is no longer possible.
Therefore, the *Nyāyānusāra* states:
"This wisdom does not arise based on these bodies," namely,
the bodies of those who follow by faith (*śraddhānusārin*) and those who follow by dharma (*dharmānusārin*).
It is possible for this [body] to serve as the basis for inducing the arising of this wisdom;
however, during the stage of the path of seeing (darśanamārga), it cannot possibly arise.
Therefore, this body remains in a state where the dharma is not produced.

Because it does not arise based on this, it necessarily does not arise. Question: When is non-analytical cessation (apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha) attained? Explanation: It is said that one attains non-analytical cessation at the conclusion of the three types of clear observation (abhisamaya).
Therefore, the *Nyāyānusāra* states:
This means that at that time, although one has attained mastery over it,
its essence does not manifest due to the obstruction of other conditions.
If this is so, why is it called "cultivation"?
The Sautrāntika asks:
When something arises with mastery, it may be called "cultivation" (*bhāvanā*);
since this [unconditioned] does not arise, how can it be called cultivation?
Regarding the statement, "Because it was previously unobtained and is now for the first time obtained," the Sarvāstivādins reply:
"Because it is now for the first time obtained, it is called 'cultivation' (bhāvanā)."
"If it cannot arise, upon what could it depend? This is the objection of the Sautrāntikas;
since that conventional knowledge cannot arise, [upon what could it depend?]
Upon what does the acquisition of an object depend?
Since, according to the Sautrāntika school, acquisition is merely a designation,
it is simply by virtue of this acquisition that one is said to "possess" [the object].
The Sarvāstivādins reply:
It is called "attainment" (prāpti) simply because it arises from the present;
it does not necessarily require actual manifestation.
Regarding the point that "because it is obtained, the attainment of the ultimate principle is not established," the Sautrāntika further challenges: "I ask:
upon what basis does the meaning of 'non-arising' as an attainment depend?"
This should be explained by means of another meaning,
not by means of another [explanation].
Yet now it is said that it is called "attainment" (prāpti) because of attainment.
This is an interpretation based on what has been obtained;
however, such an interpretation has never been heard before.
Therefore, the reasoning you have established does not hold.
Regarding the claim that the meaning of cultivation can be established according to the ancient masters,
after the critique is concluded, the Sautrāntika position will be set forth as explained by the ancient Sautrāntika masters.
The meaning of cultivation can be established.
As for what that [teaching] says: the Sarvāstivādins ask.
Regarding the point that one reaches a state of non-delight in this meaning through the power of the Noble Path,
the Sautrāntika replies:
"Because of observing the internal power of the Noble Path by means of this [insight]."
The seeds of conventional wisdom (*saṃvṛtijñāna*) are perfumed and cultivated until they become predominant;
after emerging from meditative absorption, the conventional wisdom that takes the truths as its object manifests with greater excellence than it did previously.
This is due to the power of the Noble Path while one was still within the state of contemplation.

This is called "attaining this conventional wisdom upon emerging from meditative absorption" because it serves as the basis for the arising of that conventional wisdom upon emergence, and since the basis is itself the seed,
one is said to have attained this conventional wisdom upon emerging from absorption.
This is a case of naming the attainment of the cause as the attainment of the fruit;

it is like naming the attainment of the cause—the gold ore—as the attainment of the fruit—gold. Alternatively, because one attains this conventional wisdom (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*) by means of its arising basis (the body), it is called the attainment of the fruit of this conventional wisdom.
One should say "seed. However,
because the Vaibhāṣika masters do not accept the existence of seeds,
it is said to "rely on the body."
Because those seeds are not separated from the body, or because one attains the noble path that serves as the basis for the arising of this conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*),
it is therefore called the attainment of the fruit of this subsequent conventional knowledge.
Although this was stated,
the Vaibhāṣika masters do not accept this interpretation; rather,
they maintain that it refers to conventional knowledge (saṃvṛtijñāna) up to the seventh stage, depending on whichever level it may belong to.
Regarding the statement "it abandons its own level and lower levels":
although conventional knowledge (*sāṃvṛtijñāna*) takes distinct objects and, being contaminated (*sāsrava*), can cultivate its own level and lower levels,
other contaminated phenomena lack this capacity for distinct objectification.
For the most part, one cultivates [the path] of one's own level.
Furthermore, the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 4, states:
"Question: For what reason is it that, on the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*) within the six stages, one is able to cultivate the lower [stages]?"

Question: One does not cultivate the higher [stages] while in a lower one. Answer: Because the dharmas of the higher stages are superior, when they manifest before one, one is then able to cultivate those of the lower stages.
The dharmas of the lower stages are inferior;
when they manifest, one cannot cultivate those of the higher stages.
It is as when the inferior precedes the superior, it is not the case that the superior precedes the inferior.
This is also like that, as explained in detail in that commentary.
Furthermore, the *Abhidharmamahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 168, states:
The path of seeing (darśanamārga) necessarily does not cultivate higher stages when based on a lower stage,
because it is the first attainment of the Path. However,
the untainted path (anāsravamārga), when based on a higher stage, necessarily cultivates the lower stages.
Because they are sovereign and unbound;
as for the statement that one cultivates up to the foundation of mindfulness of phenomena alone at the limits of suffering and its origin,
this explains the sixth phrase and may be understood accordingly.
"Whichever truth it follows, taking that truth as its object" explains the seventh phrase.
Furthermore, the *Nyāyānusāra* states:
Whichever truth one cultivates at the conclusion of its clear realization,
one takes that very truth as the object by means of those same aspects.
That is to say, if one cultivates at the conclusion of the clear realization of the truth of suffering:

That is to say, regarding the four aspects of the contemplation of suffering: if those bound to the desire realm take the suffering of the desire realm as their object, and those bound to the form realm take the truth of suffering of the higher realms as their object;
or if they are cultivated at the conclusion of the clear realization (*abhisamaya*) of the truth of origination.
One employs the four aspects of the origin of conditions (*samudaya-pratyaya*).
If that which is bound to the desire realm takes the origin of the desire realm as its object,
and that which is bound to the form realm takes the truth of origin (*samudaya-satya*) of the higher realms as its object.
If one practices at the stage of the clear realization of the truth of cessation,
one does so by means of the four aspects that take cessation as their object.
If it pertains to the desire realm and takes the cessation of the desire realm as its object:
Those bound to the form realm take the cessation truth of the higher realms as their object;
because they are obtained through the power of the path of seeing, they are obtained solely through application.
This explains the eighth phrase.
Because it is obtained through the power of the path of seeing,
it is acquired solely through application;
it is neither innate nor obtained through the separation from defilements.
"Because wisdom increases, it constitutes its intrinsic nature" identifies the essence [of this stage].
Within the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*), it is designated by the name "wisdom" because wisdom predominates.
If taken together with their retinues,
they have the four aggregates of the desire realm and the five aggregates of the form realm as their intrinsic nature.
Furthermore, the *Nyāyānusāra* states:
That which is comprised within the desire realm is produced by reflection;
that which is comprised within the form realm is produced by cultivation, not by hearing,
because the latter is weak.
Next, regarding "in the path of cultivation, one cultivates six and eight respectively," this is the second [section] distinguishing cultivation with respect to the path of cultivation.
The treatise says: "Because it is the antidote up to the Peak of Existence."

At the first moment of the path-knowledge of subsequent realization (*mārga-anvaya-jñāna*) during the cultivation of the path, one presently cultivates two knowledges, namely, the knowledge of the path (*mārga-jñāna*) and the subsequent realization (*anvaya-jñāna*).
For one who has not yet abandoned desire, six knowledges are cultivated in the future.
That is to say: the Dharma-knowledge, the subsequent knowledge, and the knowledges of suffering, origin, cessation, and the path.
Seven are cultivated by one free from desire;
that is to say, with the addition of the knowledge of others' minds.
The *Nyāyānusāra* states:
"For one who has previously abandoned desire and entered the Noble Path,
for what reason is the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*) not cultivated during the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*)?"
The knowledge of others' minds is subsumed under the stage of contemplative observation;
it possesses the sense of cultivation only by relying on the path of deliberate application (*savitarka-savicāra*).
Within the stage of the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*), one contemplates the principles of the truths (*satya*).
Because the preparatory application (*prayoga*) is extremely rapid, one cannot cultivate [the antidote];
the same principle applies to the path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*).
Now, at the time of the sixteenth moment, the subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārgānvaya-jñāna*):
[The text] allows for inclusion within the path of cultivation;
thus, having cultivated this knowledge [as stated] in the treatise above, one does not cultivate conventional knowledge,
because the subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārgānvayajñāna*) serves as the antidote to the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*).
Therefore, although the three truths are antidotes for the Peak of Existence,
conventional wisdom is cultivated separately because its objects of focus are distinct.
Because there is no other condition for this, it is not cultivated.
The phrase "having abandoned the cultivation of abandonment regarding desire, one proceeds to suffering, origin, cessation,
and the path" explains the third and fourth lines.
In the nine paths of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*) and the eight paths of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*) for abandoning desire through cultivation,
one currently cultivates conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*), the knowledge of the four truths (*satya-jñāna*), and the knowledge of phenomena (*dharma-jñāna*) as appropriate.
In the various paths of uninterrupted transition for abandoning the [defilements of] the seven higher stages, [the same applies].
The knowledge of the four truths, subsequent knowledge, conventional knowledge, and the dharma-knowledge of cessation and the path are cultivated as appropriate in the present moment.
This constitutes the path of preparation for abandoning the desire realm.
"There is the path of further progress" and "there is the desire to speak":
these indicate that the abandonment of afflictions is not yet complete.
This refers to the aforementioned eight paths of further progress: conventional knowledge, the knowledge of the four truths, dharma-knowledge, and subsequent knowledge.
According to the circumstances,

one should practice the paths of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*), preparation (*prayoga-mārga*), and advancement (*viśeṣa-mārga*). These constitute the paths subsequent to the path of uninterrupted continuity (*ānantarya-mārga*).
From this point upward, in the future, one cultivates all seven knowledges— namely,
conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*), dharma-knowledge (*dharmajñāna*), subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*), and the knowledges of suffering, origin, cessation, and the path.
Because the cultivation in the present moment differs, these were previously mentioned separately.
The reason they are explained together is that their future cultivation is identical.
The phrase "from the abandonment of the stage of the Peak of Existence up to the addition of the knowledge of others' minds" explains the fifth and sixth phrases.
The present cultivation can be understood as it is.
There are likewise seven for the future;
however, among those previously mentioned for future cultivation, one must exclude the mundane [path] that serves as the antidote to the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*).
Because the knowledge of others' minds (paracittajñāna) may include the Path,
[the text] explains the seventh and eighth phrases regarding the abandonment of the Peak of Existence (bhavāgra) up to the knowledge of others' minds concerning the Four Truths.
Regarding the ninth stage of further progress in the cultivation for abandoning desire:

as for why his mind does not currently cultivate [the path], it is because he has only just begun to separate from the defilements of desire and has not yet attained full mastery; therefore, it is not currently cultivated.
Because the superior progress of the higher stages is characterized by leisure,
they are cultivated in the present;
whereas the various paths of preparation (prayoga-mārga) are not characterized by such leisure.
Nor is it that one presently cultivates the knowledge of others' minds.
One does not attain the cultivation of the knowledge of others' minds by means of abandoning obstacles;
the rest of the text may be understood accordingly.
Furthermore, the *Nyāyānusāra* states:
"The four [subsequent] knowledges cannot sever the defilements of the desire realm;
the two dharmas of suffering and origin are not antidotes for the higher realms."
For what reason does that antidote arise?
This wisdom is cultivated in the future; if one were to allow that it is cultivated concurrently with what is not its antidote, [it would follow that there is no distinction].
The objection that one who is detached from the defilements of the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*) and so forth should also concurrently cultivate the conventional (*saṃvṛti*) [path] is unreasonable.
It is solely for the sake of the common antidote,
because it is not admitted that cultivation occurs in the future; rather,
it is admitted that cultivation occurs because there is a relationship [of connection].
Just as one cultivates conventional knowledge within the path of seeing,
or cultivates it through the mutual support of causal forces—
for example, when abandoning desire, one simultaneously cultivates the four types of subsequent knowledge.

In the stage of abandoning the defilements of the higher realms, one cultivates the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*) regarding suffering and its origin. If one abandons the defilements of the desire realm, one does not cultivate subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*).
When abandoning the defilements of the higher realms, one does not cultivate either of these two knowledges—suffering or its origin.
In that case, for one who attains the fruit of non-returner gradually,
there would be no possibility for the subsequent knowledge (anvaya-jñāna) to arise and manifest; likewise,
an arhat would have no occasion for the dharma-knowledge of suffering and its origin (duḥkha-samudaya-dharma-jñāna) to arise.
This is because those previously acquired have all been relinquished,
and those not yet acquired are not objects of cultivation;
this is determined by way of their categories.
If one has previously attained [a wisdom], it acts as the power of a homogeneous cause (sabhāga-hetu) to induce the arising of a subsequent wisdom of similar outflow (niṣyanda);
this wisdom arises because it was induced by that prior wisdom.
Furthermore, this category of knowledge can serve as a cause for that [subsequent knowledge]. Therefore, by the power of the cause from which this knowledge arises, it supports that [knowledge];
thus, although they do not share the same antidote, it is cultivated in the future as well.
Next, regarding the clarification that the same applies from the path of detachment up to the path of advancement:
this constitutes the third [section], which distinguishes cultivation with respect to those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*).
The treatise says: "Because it takes the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*) as its object."
Explaining the first phrase:

"The first moment of no-more-learning" refers to the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) within the category of suffering (*duḥkhajātīya*), which is the ninth liberation (*vimokṣa*) that severs [the afflictions] of the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*).

Alternatively, one may cultivate the knowledge of the exhaustion of categories (*jāti-kṣaya-jñāna*) as appropriate, because it takes the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*) as its object in the present cultivation.
Regarding the nine or ten [moments] of superior progress (*viśeṣa-mārga*), they are cultivated in the present as appropriate.
Explaining the fourth phrase:
following the second moment of thought, the various paths of further progress (*viśeṣamārga*) accordingly cultivate nine knowledges or ten knowledges as they manifest.

Because the present cultivation and the aforementioned path of liberation have the same number of acquisitions (*pratilambha-bhāvanā*), it is said that they are likewise. As for the phrase "the future [cultivation] corresponds accordingly up to the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*"):
it means that the future cultivation follows its respective application until one reaches the knowledge of non-arising.
This explains the second [section].
Regarding the third phrase:
for liberation and superior progress, one should cultivate nine or ten future [attainments] as appropriate.
Next, regarding the statement "the remaining stages are to be understood as appropriate," this constitutes the fourth section,
which distinguishes cultivation according to the remaining stages.
The first verse clarifies cultivation with respect to the refinement of the faculties (*indriya-saṃcāra*).
The second verse clarifies cultivation by way of both the mixed and the general;
the subsequent verse clarifies cultivation by way of the noble and the ordinary.
The Commentary states: "Up to 'not cultivating the knowledge of others' minds.'"
Regarding the first and second phrases, among the six types of training in the stage of learning (*śaikṣa*),
during the five uninterrupted paths (*ānantarya-mārga*) for the transformation of the faculties (*indriya-saṃcāra*) by those of the various spiritual lineages (*gotra*),
four dharma-knowledges (*dharmajñāna*) and four subsequent knowledges (*anvayajñāna*) are respectively cultivated in the present as appropriate.

Because the roots of ignorance that are severed through the training of the faculties are precisely those induced by the delusions of view; thus, they are severed in the same manner as the delusions of view.
The four dharmas and the subsequent knowledge (anvaya-jñāna) are cultivated as they correspondingly manifest;
therefore, when one in training (śaikṣa) refines the faculties, just as those [knowledges] arise in the present, one cultivates six in the future:
the four truths, dharma-knowledge, and subsequent knowledge.
It resembles the eight paths of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*) of the forbearances (*kṣānti*) within the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*),
as it is not separately designated;
or it resembles the four paths of uninterrupted transition for abandoning the stage of the Peak of Existence (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*) within the path of seeing.
The afflictions of seeing (*darśana-heya*) on that stage are not abandoned by the mundane path;

or rather, they are abandoned by what resembles the path of seeing (*darśanamārga-pratirūpaka*), because there is only one uninterrupted path (*ānantarya-mārga*) for abandoning the truth of the path (*mārgasatya*) on the stage of the Peak of Existence (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*).

Because the training of the faculties (*indriya-saṃcāra*) is like attaining the first fruit through a single path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*), although there are three different types of liberation (*vimukti*), none involve the cultivation of conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*).
Furthermore, because the path of uninterrupted transition is capable of severing hindrances, one does not cultivate the knowledge of others' minds (*paracitta-jñāna*).
Because the supernormal knowledge of others' minds (paracittajñāna) obstructs those very [four] right abandonments (samyakprahāṇa), it cannot be cultivated during them.
Regarding the statement that "the various paths of liberation (vimuktimārga) reach [this stage]," adding the supernormal knowledge of others' minds here explains the third phrase below.
Regarding the five lineages (*gotra*) prior to the refinement of the faculties (*indriya-saṃcāra*) during the stage of a trainee (*śaikṣa*):
in all paths of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*), one should practice the four *dharmajñānas* and the four *anvayajñānas* as appropriate.
The explanation for why this is so is as previously understood.
One who has not yet abandoned desire cultivates six in the future:
namely, the knowledges of the four truths, the dharma-knowledge, and the subsequent knowledge.
One who has already abandoned desire cultivates seven in the future.
That is to say, one applies the knowledge of others' minds;
however, one does not cultivate the future knowledge of others' minds for the purpose of severing hindrances,
because the liberation that results from severing hindrances does not admit of delay.
The knowledge of others' minds is not cultivated through direct realization.
Question: Just as in the Path of Seeing, the three paths of liberation at the conclusion of the three types of clear observation also cultivate conventional knowledge?

Regarding the question of why the liberation of those refining their faculties (*indriya-saṃcāra*) does not cultivate [the conventional path], the explanation is as follows: There are seven types of liberation within the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*).
Although three of them cultivate the conventional [path], four cannot.
Because they predominantly resemble [the path of seeing], they do not cultivate the conventional.

Because they are not entirely similar, the treatise does not state that they are "similar to seeing. Furthermore, it is explained that there are eight types of liberation from the afflictions of seeing;
three are mundane conventional wisdoms (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*) acquired through cultivation.
The fifth [reason] is that they cannot be cultivated.

Because they are for the most part similar [to the path], conventional wisdom is not cultivated. Furthermore, another interpretation holds that conventional wisdom is not cultivated during the paths of liberation, just as it is in the sixteenth path of liberation.
Because when one trains the faculties through study, it is like attaining the single liberation of the first fruit;
thus, although there are three different liberations, none involve the cultivation of the conventional [path].
Other masters, however, say that one also cultivates the conventional path upon reaching [the higher stages].
The intention of this master is as follows:

because one cultivates conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*) during the paths of liberation at the conclusion of the three types of clear observation (*abhisamaya*) within the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*),
it is said that conventional knowledge is also cultivated during the liberation resulting from the refinement of the faculties (*indriyasaṃcāra*).
This is not correct, because conventional wisdom cannot sever the afflictions of view pertaining to the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*).
As for those who claim that the preparatory paths (*prayoga-mārga*) extend up to the knowledge of others' minds (*paracitta-jñāna*): [this is also incorrect].
The training of the faculties for those in the stages of realization (*śaikṣa*); the preparatory paths (*prayoga-mārga*) of the first five lineages;
and the four worldly dharmas (*laukika-agra-dharma*) and the subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*).

One practices them in accordance with what is appropriate for the present moment. Since conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*) can also serve as a preparatory application (*prayoga*), it may be practiced in the present;
however, because it does not involve direct engagement [with the object], the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*) cannot be practiced in the present.
Those who have not yet abandoned desire cultivate seven future [knowledges];
those who have already abandoned desire cultivate eight, namely adding the knowledge of others' minds.
One does not cultivate the knowledge of others' minds for the purpose of abandoning hindrances.
Regarding the statement that "the various paths of superior progress (viśeṣamārga) up to the future also consist of eight":
this refers to the five types of spiritual lineages (gotra) who refine their faculties (indriya-saṃvaraṇa) during the stage of training (śaikṣa);
these can be understood according to the text.
Because it is possible to engage in the path,
and not because of the severance of hindrances;
it is possible to practice and attain the cultivation of the knowledge of others' minds.
Regarding the statement "the one beyond training (aśaikṣa) refines their faculties (indriya-saṃcāra) up to the level of the Peak of Existence (bhavāgra)":
this is a re-explanation of the first phrase and the seven [paths] of the one beyond training within the second phrase.
In the refinement of faculties by the one beyond training, there are five types of spiritual lineages (gotra), and nine uninterrupted paths (anantarya-mārga).
4. The subsequent knowledge (anvaya-jñāna), the knowledge of cessation (nirodha-dharmajñāna), and the knowledge of the path (mārga-dharmajñāna) are cultivated as they apply;
for these are abandoned through the refinement of faculties (indriya-saṃcāra) by one beyond training (aśaikṣa).
The ignorance regarding the faculties that serve as obstacles is precisely that which is induced by the afflictions to be abandoned through cultivation at the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*).

Just as when one abandons the afflictions to be abandoned through cultivation at the Peak of Existence, one accordingly cultivates in the present moment the four [knowledges], the subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*), and the two [knowledges] of phenomena (*dharma-jñāna*) as appropriate.
Therefore, when refining the faculties (*indriya*) now, it is like their present manifestation.
In the future, one cultivates seven: the four truths, the dharma-knowledge (*dharmajñāna*), the subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*), and the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*).
Because this is the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) and not a state where seeking has ceased, the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) is not cultivated in the present.
Because of their categorical connection, one cultivates the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) in the future;

one does not cultivate conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*). This is because, just as one does not cultivate conventional knowledge when treating the afflictions of the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*) through the path of cultivation, so it is here.
The same applies to the refinement of the faculties (*indriya-saṃcāra*).

Because they are able to sever hindrances, one does not cultivate the knowledge of others' minds; however, regarding the five [knowledges] and the first eight liberations (*vimokṣa*), when reaching the future, one cultivates ten.
This below explains the fourth phrase.

Among the five lineages, for each of the first five types of those training their faculties (indriya-saṃcāra) who are beyond training (aśaikṣa), they respectively practice the eight prior liberations (vimokṣa),
the four [formless attainments],
and the two knowledges (dharma-jñāna and anvaya-jñāna) as appropriate in the present.
In the future, eight [knowledges] are cultivated:
the four truths, dharma, subsequent, others' minds, and exhaustion.
This is because they are not supernormal powers or liberations.
The knowledge of others' minds is not cultivated through actualization because it does not sever hindrances; however, there is cultivation through attainment regarding the knowledge of others' minds.
The first eight liberations have not yet brought about the cessation of seeking.
Because it is still [a matter of] seeing,
none of these are currently cultivated; rather, one attains the cultivation of the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) because they belong to the same category and are mutually connected.
This explanation should consist of eight parts.
Within the first five lineages,
each of the first four lineages has its own ninth liberation.
One practices the contemplations on suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path as appropriate.
Just as when one attains the ninth liberation that severs the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*),
one first gives rise to the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) at the moment of attaining the fruit of arhatship.
In the future, one cultivates nine [knowledges], excluding the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpāda-jñāna*). This explanation should apply to nine [types of practitioners].
Among the five lineages (*gotra*), this refers to the fifth lineage.
In the ninth and final path of liberation,
one practices the knowledge of suffering, the knowledge of origin, the subsequent knowledge, and the knowledge of cessation, as appropriate to the situation.

In the future, one cultivates ten knowledges, including the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpāda-jñāna*). This explanation applies to all cases. Regarding the statement that "in the preparatory paths (*prayoga-mārga*), up to the future, nine [knowledges] are cultivated": [This refers to the following: In the preparatory path of the desire realm, one cultivates the conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*) and the knowledge of the dharma (*dharma-jñāna*). In the preparatory path of the first dhyāna, one cultivates the conventional knowledge, the knowledge of the dharma, and the subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*). Similarly, in the preparatory paths of the second, third, and fourth dhyānas, as well as the preparatory path of the intermediate dhyāna (*dhyānāntara*), one likewise cultivates these three knowledges. In the preparatory path of the sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*), one cultivates the conventional knowledge, the knowledge of the dharma, the subsequent knowledge, and the knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-jñāna*). In the preparatory path of the sphere of infinite consciousness (*vijñānānantyāyatana*), one cultivates the conventional knowledge, the knowledge of the dharma, the subsequent knowledge, the knowledge of suffering, and the knowledge of origin (*samudaya-jñāna*). In the preparatory path of the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*), one cultivates the conventional knowledge, the knowledge of the dharma, the subsequent knowledge, the knowledge of suffering, the knowledge of origin, and the knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-jñāna*). In the preparatory path of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*), one cultivates the conventional knowledge, the knowledge of the dharma, the subsequent knowledge, the knowledge of suffering, the knowledge of origin, the knowledge of cessation, and the knowledge of the path (*mārga-jñāna*). Thus, up to the preparatory path of the peak of existence (*bhavāgra*), nine knowledges are cultivated. As for the statement "in the future, ten are cultivated," this means that when one enters the fundamental dhyānas (*maula-dhyāna*) and the formless attainments (*ārūpya-samāpatti*), one additionally cultivates the knowledge of non-arising. Therefore, it is said that in the future, ten knowledges are cultivated. This interpretation should apply to all instances.
To re-explain the nine points:

regarding the preparatory paths (*prayoga-mārga*) for the five types of spiritual lineages (*gotra*) who refine their faculties (*indriya-saṃcāra*) while being beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), the current cultivation is the same as that of those still in training (*śaikṣa*).
The mundane, the four [noble] paths, the dharmas, and the subsequent knowledge are cultivated as they correspond to the occasion;
this is because the path of preparation admits no delay.
The knowledge of others' minds is not cultivated as a present realization.
Because seeking has not yet ceased, the knowledge of exhaustion (kṣayajñāna) is not currently cultivated.
Nine [knowledges] are cultivated in the future,
namely, excluding the knowledge of non-arising (anutpādajñāna).
Regarding the statement that "the various paths of superior progress (*viśeṣa-mārga*) up to the future also number ten," this is a re-explanation of what applies to all [paths]: namely,
the various paths of superior progress when an adept (*aśaikṣa*) refines their faculties (*indriya-saṃcāra*).

In the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*), from the second moment onward, all are paths of further progress (*viśeṣamārga*); according to their respective applications, the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*) can be cultivated through actual practice.
Because it is a path of leisure (*praśrabdhamārga*), the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*) may also be cultivated through actual practice.
"From the stage of mixed cultivation up to the future cultivation of seven":

this below explains the second verse regarding mixed cultivation and the supernormal powers; this explanation of mixed cultivation [shows that] immediately following it, one cultivates the seven [limbs] of training.
The various uninterrupted paths (*ānantarya-mārga*) of the mixed cultivation of the stages are both contaminated (*sāsrava*) and uncontaminated (*anāsrava*).
Among these two types of uninterrupted paths, in the first uninterrupted path,
there are four dharmas.
4. Regarding the subsequent cultivation according to the specific case:
in the second uninterrupted path (*ānantarya-mārga*), conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*) is cultivated according to the specific case.
In the future, seven are cultivated;
because they can sever hindrances, the knowledge of others' minds is not cultivated.
In all paths of liberation (vimukti-mārga), up to the future, eight are cultivated.
Explaining the third phrase:
because the various paths of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*) in the stage of training (*śaikṣa*) that involve mixed cultivation are exclusively untainted (*anāsrava*),
one cultivates only four [knowledges]— the knowledge of phenomena (*dharma-jñāna*) and the subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*)— as appropriate for each case.
Because it is untainted (*anāsrava*), conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*) is not cultivated in the present;
because it is not the path of liberation (*vimuktimārga*) for the knowledge of others' minds, the knowledge of others' minds is also not cultivated in the present.
If it is the path of preparation (*prayogamārga*), conventional knowledge is added above the aforementioned six [knowledges] and is cultivated in the present as appropriate.
Because conventional wisdom (*saṃvṛtijñāna*) serves as the preparatory application (*prayoga*),
and because such application does not allow for delay, the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*) is not cultivated in the present moment.
Regarding the various paths of advancement (*viśeṣamārga*), they occur above the preceding seven [stages].
Furthermore, the knowledge of others' minds (*paracitta-jñāna*) is cultivated as appropriate;
during the stage of superior progress (*viśeṣa-mārga*), there is leisure for the present cultivation of the knowledge of others' minds.
In all three paths above this, eight knowledges (*jñāna*) are cultivated in the future.
None of these attain the cultivation of the knowledge of others' minds by means of abandoning hindrances.
Regarding the statement that for those in the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*) who practice mixed meditation, the dull-witted reach eight and the sharp-witted nine:
this explains that immediately following mixed meditation, there should be eight or nine [moments].
In the uninterrupted paths (*ānantarya-mārga*) of the various mixed cultivations of those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), the present cultivation is the same as that of those in training (*śaikṣa*):

the four [knowledges], dharma-knowledge (*dharma-jñāna*), subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*), and conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*). This is because the nature of the uninterrupted path is not one that seeks cessation.
The knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*) are not cultivated through present application.
As for those cultivated in the future, there are eight for those of dull faculties and nine for those of sharp faculties;
in each case, the knowledge of others' minds is excluded because it has already been abandoned.
Regarding those liberation paths that are identical to those for refining the faculties (*indriya-saṃcāra*),
it should be explained that the remaining paths are either nine or all [nine].
This refers to the various liberation paths of the *aśaikṣa* who practices mixed meditation (*vyavakīrṇa-bhāvanā*).

Only four [knowledges]—the knowledge of phenomena (dharma-jñāna) and the subsequent knowledge (anvaya-jñāna)—are cultivated in the present according to their respective applications. Because they are untainted (anāsrava), conventional knowledge (saṃvṛti-jñāna) is not cultivated in the present.
Furthermore, because it is not a path of liberation (vimukti-mārga) for the supernormal power of others' minds (paracitta-abhijñā), the knowledge of others' minds is not cultivated in the present.
Since this path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*) is a path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*) rather than one of cultivation through cessation and seeking,
the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣaya-jñāna*) and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpāda-jñāna*) are not cultivated in the present.
If it is the path of preparation (*prayoga-mārga*), then in addition to the aforementioned six, conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*) is also cultivated in the present as appropriate.
Because it is produced through conventional preparatory application (*prayoga*), it can be cultivated in the present;
because it does not allow for leisurely deliberation, the knowledge of others' minds (*paracitta-jñāna*) cannot be cultivated in the present.
This is because preparatory application consists of insight (*darśana*) and is not characterized by the cessation of seeking.
The knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*) are not cultivated through actualization (*sammukhībhāva*).
Regarding these two paths mentioned above, nine [minds] are cultivated for the dull faculty and ten for the sharp faculty in the future.
All paths of further progress (*viśeṣamārga*) are the same as those for the refinement of the faculties (*indriyasaṃcāra*).
For those of dull faculties, nine knowledges are cultivated in the present as appropriate;
nine are also cultivated in the future.
For those of sharp faculties, ten knowledges are cultivated in the present as appropriate.
The future [attainments] are also ten.
Regarding the statement that "one who trains in the supernormal powers (abhijñā) cultivates seven in the future," this section below clarifies the cultivation of the supernormal powers.

This explains that for one training in the uninterrupted path of the supernormal powers (abhijñā), there are seven [paths]; for one in the stage of training (śaikṣa) who cultivates the supernormal powers, there are five uninterrupted paths.
Because these involve contemplation of phenomena, conventional knowledge (saṃvṛtijñāna) is cultivated in the present moment.
Although the liberation through knowledge of others' minds (paracittavimukti) encompasses both the untainted (anāsrava) and the three applications of mindfulness (smṛtyupasthāna),
the immediate observation of phenomena (anantaryālambana-vipaśyanā) is exclusively tainted (sāsrava) and consists solely of the application of mindfulness to the mind (cittasmṛtyupasthāna).
Regarding the statement "In the future, one cultivates seven [knowledges] because they can sever obstacles, but does not cultivate the knowledge of others' minds;
from the knowledge of past lives to the knowledge of supernormal powers, one cultivates all eight knowledges," this explains the third phrase.

The two paths of liberation—namely, the recollection of past lives (*pūrvanivāsa*) and the supernormal power of the divine eye (*ṛddhividhi*)—are contemplations of phenomena (*vastubhāvanā*); therefore, conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*) is cultivated in the present.
All five paths of preparation (*prayogamārga*) are likewise contemplations of phenomena; thus, conventional knowledge is cultivated in the present.
The five acts of immediate retribution are all conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*);
they cannot be superior uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) preparatory application (*prayoga*),
as they constitute inferior preparatory application.

Therefore, on the path of preparation (*prayoga-mārga*), only conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*) is cultivated in the present. As for the liberation of the knowledge of others' minds (*paracitta-vimukti*), it may be either contaminated (*sāsrava*) or uncontaminated (*anāsrava*).

If it is uncontaminated, then the knowledge of phenomena (*dharma-jñāna*), subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*), knowledge of the path (*mārga-jñāna*), and knowledge of others' minds (*paracitta-jñāna*) are cultivated in the present as appropriate.
If they are with outflows (sāsrava),
then conventional knowledge, knowledge of others' minds, and all the superior paths of the five supernormal powers (abhijñā) are cultivated as appropriate;
these consist of the aforementioned dharma-knowledge, subsequent knowledge, path-knowledge, conventional knowledge, and knowledge of others' minds.
Furthermore, one should practice the [truths of] suffering, origin, and cessation as appropriate.

Since it is permissible for the higher progress of the five supernormal powers (*pañcābhijñā*) to give rise to the knowledge of others' minds, it should be understood by analogy that the higher progress of the five supernormal powers may also give rise to the other four supernormal powers. In all three of these paths, eight knowledges (*jñāna*) are cultivated in the future.
Exhausted and non-arising; because they have not yet been attained.
Regarding the ninth [point], the ninefold mastery of the supernormal powers cultivated by those beyond training (aśaikṣa):

In the case of one who cultivates the supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), there should be eight or nine [paths of immediate succession]. For one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) who cultivates the supernormal powers, during the five paths of immediate succession,
they cultivate only conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*) in the present, just as in the case of one in training (*śaikṣa*).
Regarding those to be cultivated in the future, the dull [faculties] are eight and the sharp are nine;
because they can sever hindrances, the knowledge of others' minds is not cultivated.
Regarding the liberation and preparatory paths for those who train their faculties (indriya) in other ways,
it should be understood that the remaining paths consist of nine or all [nine] paths.
As for the cultivation of the liberation and preparatory paths in the present moment, they may be inferred from what was previously stated regarding the learner (śaikṣa).
Regarding those to be cultivated in the future, the dull [faculties] are nine and the sharp are ten.
All paths of further progress (*viśeṣamārga*) are to be understood as being analogous to the path of refining the faculties (*indriyasaṃcāra*), as previously explained.
The divine eye and the divine ear are not even called "cultivation";
this excludes these two as being non-cultivated.
Among the six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍabhijñā*), the power of the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya*) is not mentioned here.
This refers to what was previously stated regarding the exhaustion of all afflictions;
as for the statement that "the Noble Ones give rise to the remaining [attainments] which are exclusively mundane cultivation," the following explains the third verse.
The following section explains the first line and the two subsequent lines.
This clarifies that when noble beings give rise to other contaminated (*sāsrava*) merits,
they do not separately eliminate obstacles.
Therefore, it is not explained by means of the four paths.
At the moment of entering the meditative attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*), the mind is called the "subtle-subtle mind" (*sūkṣma-sūkṣma-citta*).
This mind is weak and inferior; its manifestation and its object are exclusively conventional (*saṃvṛti*).
Because they do not cultivate the untainted (anāsrava).
Thus, the *Abhidharmamahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 155, states:
"When one gives rise to the extremely subtle mind (*sūkṣma-sūkṣma-citta*)."
When the wisdoms arising from hearing, reflection, and so forth are produced,
one neither abandons nor acquires the untainted faculties (anāsrava-indriya).
It is neither ceasing nor arising.

According to that *Vibhāṣā*, the extremely subtle mind (*sūkṣma-sūkṣma-citta*) as well as the wisdoms of hearing and reflection (*śruta-mayī* and *cintā-mayī prajñā*) do not cultivate the untainted (*anāsrava*).
The rest of the text may be understood accordingly.
If one gives rise to other remaining contaminated states that are similar to those previously mentioned,
this refers to giving rise to other uncontaminated qualities;
here too, there is no distinct removal of hindrances.
Therefore, the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*) are not explained by means of the four paths.

Why, then, is it not stated here that they are cultivated in the present? The explanation is as follows: this passage clarifies the untainted (*anāsrava*) merits of meditative wandering and contemplation (*caryā-vipaśyanā*).
All of these are the vision of the nature (dharmatā).

Since the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*) have ceased seeking and are not [mere] views, they are not mentioned here. Alternatively, it is explained that the knowledge of exhaustion and the knowledge of non-arising have already been discussed previously.

What is clarified here is that the arising of other virtues is fully subsumed within either the four knowledges— dharma-knowledge, subsequent knowledge, and the knowledge of non-arising— or within [the knowledge of] non-arising itself.
The first two interpretations are superior.

Regarding the phrase "an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) who has become free from defilement and practices only the conventional (*saṃvṛti*)," the following explains the second line and the subsequent two lines.
The final two lines apply to both preceding cases.

An ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*), when free from defilement, currently cultivates the conventional [knowledge]. Question: For what reason can a noble one (*ārya*), when advancing through the stages of being free from desire, give rise to the knowledge of others' minds?

Regarding the statement that ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) do not practice [the path] in the stage of superior progress (*viśeṣagamana*): the commentary explains that when a noble one (*ārya*) is in the stage of superior progress toward the abandonment of desire-taints (*rāgasaṃkleśa*), they give rise only to untainted knowledge of others' minds (*anāsrava-paracittajñāna*).
This is because it performs the four modes of activity (*ākāra*) similar to the path of abandonment (*prahāṇamārga*).
Furthermore, the path that accords with abandonment possesses power over the path;
the knowledge of others' minds in ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) is exclusively contaminated (*sāsrava*),
whereas it [the path] possesses the six aspects of the path capable of abandonment.
They are different,
because principle and phenomena are distinct and because they do not accord with one another.

It cannot be cultivated in the present; however, in the stage of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*), when one is free from defilements and progressing toward excellence, it is possible for the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*) to arise.
This text speaks only of conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*), based on the preparatory (*prayoga*), uninterrupted (*ānantarya*), and liberation (*vimukti*) stages.
This is stated from the perspective of the majority; alternatively,
it should also be stated that what is not mentioned here is omitted for brevity and not discussed.
If one abandons the ninth liberation of the desire realm,
as well as the ninth liberation of the first three dhyānas of the form realm,
one attains the fundamental higher knowledge of others' minds.
The first eight have not yet been attained;
furthermore, because one does not cultivate the lower [stages],
they are not separately designated.

Furthermore, regarding the paths of superior progress (*viśeṣa-mārga*) and the paths of application for detachment (*vairāgya-prayoga-mārga*) that arise based on the four fundamental dhyāna concentrations,
one cultivates two knowledges in the future— namely, the aforementioned conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*).
Furthermore, with the addition of the knowledge of others' minds,
all remaining preparatory, uninterrupted, liberation, and special progress [attainments], excluding those previously mentioned,
cultivate only conventional knowledge (saṃvṛtijñāna) in the future.
Regarding the statement that when cultivating the five supernormal powers (pañcābhijñā), they pertain only to the conventional (saṃvṛti) in both the present and the future:
this clarifies that when ordinary beings (pṛthagjana) cultivate the five supernormal powers, at the time of such cultivation, [they are conventional].
In the five paths of preparation (*prayoga-mārga*),

during the two paths of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*) for the knowledge of past lives and the supernormal power of the divine ear, conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*) is cultivated in the present.
In the single path of liberation for the knowledge of others' minds, [the same applies].
In the five paths of superior progress (*viśeṣamārga*), one presently cultivates the conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*) and the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*).
One presently cultivates either the conventional knowledge or the knowledge of others' minds, as appropriate.
From this point upward, in the future, one cultivates both conventional knowledge and the knowledge of others' minds in all cases.
In the five paths of immediate succession,
in the present and future, one cultivates only conventional knowledge.
The two paths of liberation— divine eye and divine ear—
are not termed "cultivation" because they are of an indeterminate nature.
Regarding those that depend on the fundamental dhyānas and are cultivated for the present and future:
This clarifies that when ordinary beings cultivate other meritorious qualities:
if they cultivate those other qualities— such as the four immeasurables— based on the levels of the four fundamental dhyānas,
they all practice conventionally in the present.
In the future, two [knowledges] are cultivated, namely with the addition of the knowledge of others' minds.
However, during the aids to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*), one certainly does not cultivate the knowledge of others' minds,
because these are the immediate attendants of the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*).
Excluding those based on the fundamental dhyānas,

if one cultivates other qualities such as the meditation on impurity (aśubha-bhāvanā) and so forth based on concentrations of other stages, these are all exclusively conventional knowledge (saṃvṛti-jñāna),
cultivated in both the present and the future.
Because the verse text is concise, it mentions only the cultivation of future [dharmas];
because the prose commentary is extensive, it includes the cultivation of present [dharmas] as well.
Regarding the various future cultivations that reach what was previously attained, these are not considered "cultivation" (bhāvanā).
This constitutes the fifth [section], which distinguishes cultivation according to the stages (*bhūmi*).
First, it asks: regarding the future cultivation of various [dharmas], how many stages are cultivated?
Second, it asks: are all acquisitions (*prāpti*) that arise considered cultivation?
The first seven phrases answer the first question;
the final phrase answers the second question.
The Treatise says: "Regarding those with outflows (*sāsrava*) in this stage..."
The first two phrases are explained:
this clarifies the cultivation of the contaminated (*sāsrava*) path.
This refers to both the various contaminated paths and the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) path.
The cultivation of contaminated phenomena (*sāsravadharma*) generally comprises two categories. First,
at the time they arise based on this specific stage (*bhūmi*).
One can cultivate the outflow-tainted dharmas of this stage in the future;
second, at the time of attaining this stage,
one can cultivate the outflow-tainted dharmas of this stage in the future.
Therefore, the *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya* (Xianzong lun), fascicle 36,
states: "When various paths rely upon a particular stage (*bhūmi*) and when they attain that stage,
they are able to cultivate the future contaminated (*sāsrava*) dharmas of that same stage."
This means that when the mundane noble path (*laukika-āryamārga*) of this stage manifests,
one cultivates only the contaminated (*sāsrava*) dharmas of this stage in the future;
for contaminated dharmas are firmly bound to their respective stages, making it difficult to cultivate others.
Whichever stage one relies upon to become detached from the defilements of a lower stage,
when the ninth liberation is present before them,
they also cultivate the future, acquired, mundane merits of the fundamental and preparatory stages of the higher stage.
"Because one must necessarily attain the higher stage upon being freed from the fetters of the lower stage" (Nyāyānusāra, fascicle 74;

the text is identical to the Abhidharmakośabhāṣya). Question: Among the cultivation of contaminated [attainments], why is it not stated that they are for the purpose of becoming free from this specific stage?

Regarding the statement "one cultivates the outflow-tainted [dharmas] of this stage," the commentary explains that this refers to the time when one becomes free from defilement by means of both the outflow-tainted path and the outflow-free path.
It further explains that the cultivation of all outflow-tainted dharmas is not distinct from the basis of this stage, nor does it occur at a time other than the moment of attaining this stage.
While cultivating the contaminated states of this stage,
one gradually detaches from the defilements of the higher stages by relying on the path of the lower stages;
consequently, one is unable to cultivate the contaminated states of the higher stages.

Because they do not differ in their cultivation of the untainted (*anāsrava*), they are not explained separately. Question: Just as the untainted path relies upon this lower stage to become detached from the defilements of that lower stage—consisting of nine paths of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*) and eight paths of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*)—[is there a similar distinction here?]
Is the contaminated path of the preparatory stages (*sāmantaka*) cultivated?
If you say it is cultivated,
why is this not mentioned in this text?
Furthermore, this contradicts seventy-four points of the *Nyāyānusāra*.
As that treatise states:
"Even when the lower [stages of] the Noble Path abandon the afflictions..."
Although there are antidotes in the upper stages that can counteract [the afflictions] equally,
because the bonds of the contaminated (sāsrava) stages are firm,
one cannot cultivate those [antidotes] as long as one has not yet abandoned the lower stage. If one does not cultivate them, this would indeed accord with the literal meaning of this text.
To practice this based on this [view] is directly contrary to the characteristics of the noble ones (ārya) as previously described.
As it is said in that verse:

The prose commentary explains:

When noble ones who are still in training (śaikṣa) employ the contaminated path (sāsrava-mārga) to abandon the defilements of the lower eight stages that are to be abandoned through cultivation (bhāvanā-heya).
It is able to fully induce the acquisition of two types of dissociation (*visamyoga-prāpti*).

The same applies to abandoning those [defilements] by means of the untainted path (*anāsrava-mārga*), because both types of paths perform the same function. One cannot cultivate the contaminated (*sāsrava*) preparatory stages (*sāmantaka*) of the higher levels. Question: If this interpretation is adopted, it accords with the treatise and also conforms to correct reasoning;

however, how should one explain the text in the "Chapter on the Noble Ones" (*Āryapudgala-varga*)? Answer: It is explained that if one abandons the defilements of the lower eight levels by means of the uncontaminated path (*anāsrava-mārga*), [the preparatory stage of the first dhyāna is not cultivated].

Furthermore, regarding the statement that it can also induce the acquisition of two types of dissociation (*visamyoga-prāpti*): this refers to the ninth path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*), when one has exhausted the defilements of the lower realm and only then cultivates the contaminated preparatory stage (*sāmantaka*) of the higher level.
To speak of them individually:
when one is free from the defilements of a lower stage during the nine paths of immediate succession and eight paths of liberation,
one has not yet cultivated the contaminated preparatory stages (*sāmantaka*) of the higher stages.
At that time, there is only a single untainted acquisition (*anāsrava-prāpti*);
therefore, there is no contradiction. Furthermore, another explanation states:
when one becomes free from the defilements of the lower realm by means of the untainted path (*anāsrava-mārga*).

The nine paths of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*) and the eight paths of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*) also cultivate the contaminated preparatory stages (*sāmantaka*) of the higher levels, because they are cultivated as having the same object of counteraction (*pratipakṣa*).
Question: If one interprets it in this way, although it accords with the text of the *Āryavaṃśa* (Chapter on the Noble Lineages),...
Why does this text not state that one cultivates this based on this?
Furthermore, how does the *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra* explain and resolve this? The explanation is: it is stated from the perspective of the majority that one cultivates this based on this.
Therefore, it is explained selectively.
The preparatory stages (*sāmantaka*) of the higher levels may or may not be cultivated.
If the untainted path abandons the defilements of a lower stage, it immediately cultivates [the corresponding meditative attainment].
If other untainted paths arise based on a lower stage,
they do not cultivate the tainted *sāmantaka* (preparatory) stages of the higher stages.
Because it is indeterminate, it is therefore not mentioned.
The *Nyāyānusāra* states that this is merely the opponent's own conception;
since it is not what [the author] accepts, there is no need for further reconciliation.
The *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya* also presents two views, stating:
"Even when the noble path of a lower stage eliminates afflictions,
there are [factors] belonging to the limits of the higher stages that can act as concurrent antidotes."
However, because the bonds of the stages associated with outflows (sāsrava) are firm,
one cannot cultivate those [higher stages] as long as one has not yet abandoned the lower ones;
though some say that one does cultivate them.
Because it arises from the attainment of that abandonment.
The former interpretation is the same as the previous statement in the *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya-ṭīkā* (Xianzong lun);
the latter interpretation is the same as the later master in the *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya-ṭīkā*.
Furthermore, the *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya* (Exposition of the Doctrine), chapter thirty-two,
states: "By this, for one in training (*śaikṣa*) who has abandoned the eight [categories of] afflictions to be eliminated through cultivation, either the mundane or supramundane path manifests."
In each case, one cultivates the mundane and supramundane paths in the future;
this is stated in terms of general characteristics.
This is because when one abandons the first eight categories [of afflictions] of the seven higher stages by means of the untainted path.
Because one has not cultivated the higher mundane paths,
there is only the single acquisition of disjunction (visaṃyoga-prāpti) that is untainted (anāsrava);
it is only upon abandoning the ninth category [of afflictions] that both [types of acquisition] can be fully possessed.
Alternatively, one must admit that the path of disconnection (*visamyoga-mārga*) is cultivated [at that time];
or, at the time of abandoning defilements, one must admit that one relies on a lower stage to cultivate a higher one.
These are the three explanations given in the *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya*.
The former explanation accords with the first master’s view in the *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya-ṭīkā-prakaraṇaśāsana* (Xianzong lun);

the latter explanation accords with the latter two views in that same work. Question: With which explanation does the *Abhidharmakośa* itself accord? Answer: It may accord with the former explanation.
Alternatively, it may be the same as the latter interpretation;

in either case, there is no contradiction. Question: When one gives rise to untainted (anāsrava) dharmas based on a particular stage (bhūmi), does one necessarily cultivate all the tainted (sāsrava) dharmas of that stage? Answer: There are indeed cases where they are not cultivated, as stated in the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 163.
Regarding the fourfold classification of the pure (*śuddha*) and untainted (*anāsrava*) states of the first dhyāna,
it is stated that there is the cultivation of the untainted first dhyāna that is not the pure one:
"The noble one, relying on the first dhyāna, becomes detached from the defilements of the first dhyāna up to the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*)."
At the time of the nine paths of uninterrupted transition and nine paths of liberation [for the cessation of the desire realm],

as well as at the time of the nine paths of uninterrupted transition and eight paths of liberation for becoming free from the defilements of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana).

Since the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* states that one who relies on the first dhyāna to become detached from the defilements of the first dhyāna does not cultivate the pure [meditation] of the first dhyāna.
It is clearly known that when one relies on a particular stage for the untainted (anāsrava), one does not cultivate the tainted (sāsrava) of that same stage.

when one gives rise to the untainted path of liberation (vimukti-mārga) and so forth based on the first dhyāna.

Within the cultivation of the untainted (*anāsrava*), there are generally three categories.
First, when one becomes detached from a particular stage,

When one has not yet become detached from the lower stage, one is unable to cultivate that [higher path].

The Path of Seeing (*darśana-mārga*) is able to abandon the afflictions of seeing (*darśana-heya*) within the three realms.
Depending on whichever stage (*bhūmi*) it relies upon, it cultivates only its own stage and those below;
