The path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) does not necessarily cultivate a higher stage based on a lower one, because it is the first attainment of the path.

The untainted (*anāsrava*) [path] based on a higher stage must necessarily cultivate the lower stages, because it is sovereign and unconditioned. The commentary explains: because the path of seeing is the initial attainment, its power is not yet strong and it lacks sovereignty.
Depending on whichever level one relies upon, one cultivates only that level and those below it; one cannot cultivate the levels above.
Although within the higher levels there exists a common antidote to the afflictions of views during the untainted path of vision (*anāsrava-darśanamārga*), [one does not cultivate them].
Those with inferior power are unable to cultivate the higher [stages].
The untainted path of cultivation is not something newly acquired;
rather, when one's power is strengthened and one becomes free from the defilements of a higher stage in reliance upon any given level, [the path arises].

One is able to cultivate the uncontaminated path of cultivation that serves as the common antidote for the higher stages. Question: If it is the case for the third category that one can, based on this stage, cultivate the uncontaminated [paths] of this stage and those below, but not those above, why is this so?
This directly contradicts the *Vibhāṣā-śāstra*, specifically its section on the "Aggregates" (*skandha*),
which states: "One may undergo the transformation of faculties (*indriya-parāvṛtti*) by relying on a lower stage while free from the defilements of a higher stage."

One is also able to cultivate the higher stages that have already been freed from defilement. The *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* explains that, according to the gradual attainment of stages, one cultivates those of one's own level and the lower levels;
one does not cultivate the higher levels because they have not yet been attained. Alternatively, it may be interpreted as follows:
The *Abhidharmakośa* states that one cultivates [the antidotes] of one’s own level and lower levels;
this is said according to a definitive rule.
Since cultivation of higher levels is not fixed, it is not mentioned separately—or so it may be understood.
The statement in the *Abhidharmakośa* that one does not cultivate the higher [realms] is based on a lack of mastery;
the statement in the *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* that one cultivates the higher [realms] within the *Saṃgītiparyāya* is spoken from the perspective of mastery.
To speak according to reality:
If one has attained mastery over a higher stage, one is able to cultivate that higher stage;
if one lacks mastery over a higher stage, one cannot cultivate it.
Thus, the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 67, states:
One should state it thus:
if one has already attained mastery over a higher stage,
yet relies upon a lower stage to train in the transformation of the faculties and so forth.
One may also attain the untainted fruit-path of the higher stages.
Furthermore, in the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 90, in the explanation of the faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*), it says:
"Question: If one has already become detached from the defilements of the third dhyāna and relies upon the second dhyāna or the three lower stages..."
One who transforms their faculties through the liberation of faith becomes one who has attained vision;
such a person does not die while still in the stage of "further progress" toward that state,
but is reborn in the fourth dhyāna or in higher stages.
What faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*) does he accomplish?

Answer: If he attains mastery over the higher stages, then at the time of refining his faculties (*indriya-saṃcāra*), he is also able to cultivate the untainted (*anāsrava*) faculty of pleasure of the higher stages.
Even if they do not attain mastery over the higher stages,
once they have attained the fruit, they will necessarily give rise to the path of superior fruit;
only after cultivating the untainted states of the higher stages will they pass away.
Therefore, noble ones born in the fourth dhyāna or above definitely possess the untainted faculty of pleasure (*anāsrava-sukhendriya*);
this applies specifically to those from the first *kṣayajñāna* up to the ninth path of liberation.
This explains the fifth, sixth, and seventh phrases.
This demonstrates that when practicing the various contaminated [attainments] through distinct conditions,

This power is able to universally cultivate immeasurable merits— such as the contemplations on impurity consisting of hearing, reflection, and cultivation— which are comprised within the contaminated mental stage of the nine stages. Why is this so?
Because the various afflictions that bind one within the three realms and nine stages have been severed without remainder,
and because the wholesome dharmas that were bound thereby flow freely—
just as when the binding rope is cut, the breath of the bound person flows unimpeded.
Furthermore, having slain the enemies of afflictions with his own mind, he now ascends the throne;
all wholesome dharmas arise and come to court,
just as on the day a great king ascends the throne.
In the customs of the Western Regions, it is the practice to sprinkle water upon the crown of the head;
for this reason, the Sūtra refers to him as the "Anointed Great King.
All territories come to pay tribute, bringing various rare and precious objects according to the local preferences of each region.
However, once born in a higher realm, one certainly does not cultivate the lower realms;
for example, one born in the first dhyāna who attains arhatship does not cultivate the various contaminated wholesome states of the desire realm,
and so on up to one born in the Peak of Existence (bhavāgra) who attains arhatship.
One does not cultivate the various contaminated wholesome states of the lower eight stages,
because when one is born in a higher meditative absorption, it is impossible to produce the contaminated wholesome states of the lower levels. Therefore,
being born in a higher stage, one cannot cultivate those of the lower.
The initial mention of "knowledge of exhaustion" (kṣayajñāna) indicates the ninth path of liberation from the Peak of Existence (bhavāgra),
as well as the ninth path of liberation at the stage of refining the faculties for the first five spiritual lineages.

Because they all abandon their previous paths and newly attain the fruits, they are all able to cultivate the contaminated conventional knowledge (*sāsrava-saṃvṛtijñāna*) of the nine stages. Question: The three types of knowledge at the edge of the subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*) also take specific objects;
can they likewise cultivate the contaminated conventional knowledge of their own stage and the lower stages?
Why is it that only "knowledge of exhaustion" (kṣayajñāna) is mentioned here? Answer: As the *Nyāyānusāra* states:

"In the stage of the path of seeing (darśanamārga), at the conclusion of the three types of subsequent knowledge (anvayajñāna), although one is also able to cultivate conventional knowledge (saṃvṛtijñāna) pertaining to one's own level and lower levels," [it is not so designated].
Since this has already been explained previously, it will not be discussed further here.
Regarding the statement that "the power of cultivation is inferior," this explains the eighth phrase.
Regarding all that is called "cultivation":
only that which was previously unattained and now arises in the present is the agent of cultivation;
that which is now attained in the future is the object of cultivation.
This refers to the detailed explanation below:
first, clarifying what is to be cultivated and what is not to be cultivated;

second, clarifying what is capable of cultivating and what is not capable of cultivating. Question: If it is said that only that which was previously unattained and is now attained constitutes "that which is to be cultivated," [then...]
That which was previously abandoned and then reacquired is not "cultivation" (bhāvanā).
Why is this? The *Abhidharmamahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 150, states:
Question: If one falls back from a higher fruit and abides in a lower fruit...
Is the attainment of a lower fruit termed "attainment" (*prāpti*) or "cultivation" (*bhāvanā*)?

Answer: It is termed "attainment," not "cultivation. Question: When one subsequently advances to attain a fruit from which one had previously fallen, [is it still termed "attainment" or "cultivation"]?
Is that which is attained as a superior fruit called "attainment-cultivation" (pratilambha-bhāvanā)?
Answer: If it is past, it is called attainment, not cultivation;
if it is future, it is called both attainment and cultivation.
Question: Why is it that what is past is called "attained" (*prāpta*) but not "cultivated" (*bhāvita*), while what is future is called both "attained" and "cultivated"?
Answer: If the present path serves as the cause for that [future state], [then it is so designated].
One may say that it is "attained" (prāpta) and "cultivated" (bhāvita).
However, because there is no causal relationship between the present path and the past path,
it is called "attained" rather than "cultivated."
Question: When one falls back from a higher fruit and abides in a lower fruit,
since there is already a present acquisition (*prāpti*) of the cause for the future lower untainted fruit (*anāsrava-phala*),
why is it not called "cultivation" (*bhāvanā*)?
Answer: If a present cause, by means of superior progress, results in the attainment of a future state, that may be called cultivation (*bhāvanā*).

However, when one has regressed and abides in a lower fruit, although the present untainted acquisitions (*anāsrava-prāpti*) are indeed causes for those [future states], [they do not constitute cultivation].
Because it is not a superior advancement, it is not called "cultivation" (*bhāvanā*).
It is not attained through the present, for one cultivates that which is future;
rather, it manifests only through falling away (*parihāṇi*). This is according to the *Vibhāṣā*.
When one falls away from a higher fruit and attains a lower fruit,
that lower fruit is not called "cultivated.
Furthermore, when one returns from a lower fruit to attain a higher fruit, that higher fruit is called "cultivated."
Since this has already been attained, how can it be called "cultivation"?
Would this not contradict the *Abhidharmakośa*? The explanation is that there are two types of what has not yet been attained.
First, that which has never been obtained before;
second, that which was previously obtained but is now superior, termed "never-before-obtained," such as when one regains a higher fruit after having fallen from it.
Although there is that which was previously attained,
because it is attained through a superior stage (*viśeṣa-bhūmi*) as something superior to what was previously attained,
it is also called "previously unattained."
The term "previously acquired" (*pūrvapratilabdha*) cannot be said to encompass both of these meanings;
therefore, it is not subsumed under this specific textual passage. Furthermore, there are three types of "previously acquired":
first, the previously acquired of inferior [attainments].
Just as when one falls from a higher fruit and attains a lower fruit,
both types of attainment— the previously unobtained and the previously obtained—
are acquired; likewise, from the second moment onward, one acquires dharmas of their own kind.
There are three types of "previously acquired" (*pūrvapratilabdha*):
those acquired through regression from a higher fruit and those subsequently reacquired.
This treatise, for the most part, refers to the first two types of previously acquired states.
Therefore, it is said that what was previously attained but is not currently being cultivated is not "cultivation.
However, if one considers even a partial attainment of a superior state as a form of previous attainment, then that too is cultivation;
this is the third explanation according to the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*.

Each [interpretation] relies on a single meaning and they do not contradict one another; furthermore, the intended meanings of the treatise differ in each case, so there is no need for laborious reconciliation.
The rest of the text can be understood accordingly.
Is it only with respect to acquisition (*prāpti*) that one speaks of "cultivation" (*bhāvanā*)?
This concludes the sixth section, which generally clarifies the meaning of the four types of cultivation; this is the question.
If it is not so, [the questioner] asks:
"In what way? [The respondent] answers.
Investigation:
Regarding the four kinds of cultivation up to the four cultivations of removal, this is the explanation.
Regarding the question of upon what dharmas these four types of cultivation are established,
the verse says: "Up to the establishment of the cultivation of remedies and the cultivation of elimination."
Regarding the response in verse:
the first two lines clarify the two cultivations of attainment (*pratilambha*) and practice (*niṣevaṇā*);
the latter two lines clarify the two cultivations of removal (*vidūṣaṇā*) and expulsion (*vibhāvanā*).
The Commentary says: "Reaching the present, one possesses both types of cultivation" explains the two preceding lines.
If it is the present...
If one has not yet produced that dharma, its acquisition is termed "cultivation through attainment" (*pratilambha-bhāvanā*);
this applies only to the first moment and does not extend to subsequent ones.
However, when it reaches the present and its essence manifests before one, it is termed "cultivation through practice" (*niṣevaṇa-bhāvanā*).
Alternatively, it is called "cultivation through practice" (*caryā-bhāvanā*). This applies to both the beginning and the end;
thus, the *Nyāyānusāra* states:
All previously unattained qualities manifest before one,
and one attains the remaining future qualities; because these are newly cultivated and acquired,
they are all termed "cultivation through attainment" (pratilambha-bhāvanā).
"Previously acquired and previously unacquired meritorious qualities manifest;

because they are currently cultivated, they are all termed 'cultivation through practice' (*abhyāsa-bhāvanā*). [End of treatise]. The *Abhidharma-hṛdaya-śāstra*, Chapter on Selection (*Vibhaṅga-varga*), states:

"Cultivation through practice refers to the continuous arising of wholesome dharmas that have been previously acquired. [End of treatise]. That explanation is incorrect; for how could a dharma-body that has never before been acquired, when it first manifests, not be called cultivation through practice?
This must be an error on the part of the translator.
Both of these are established based on conditioned wholesomeness (*saṃskṛta-kuśala*).
The term "conditioned" serves to distinguish them from the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
Wholesome speech is concise, untainted, and indeterminate.
Thus, the *Vibhāṣā* (Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra), fascicle 106, states:
"As it is said in the Sūtra..."
Virtuous conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) are what should be cultivated, and nothing else. Why is this?
Because if wise persons act for the sake of a beloved fruit...
Diligent cultivation that causes [wholesome qualities] to gradually increase is called "cultivation" (*bhāvanā*).
Wholesome conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) are able to obtain desirable fruits;
that is to say, they obtain the desirable results of maturation (*vipāka-phala*) and dominant results (*adhipati-phala*) within the world.
Furthermore, because one also attains the supramundane fruit of dissociation,
those who possess wisdom should practice with diligence,
progressing from the lower to the middle, and from the middle to the superior.
[This causes one] to quickly obtain the desired and beloved fruits.

Because defiled (*kliṣṭa*), neutral (*avyākṛta*) dharmas, as well as wholesome unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) dharmas, do not possess such a function, they are not called "cultivated" (*bhāvita*). [End of preceding treatise. Question: Are matter (*rūpa*) and the dissociated (*viprayukta*) also called "cultivated"? Answer: It is explained that all are indeed called "cultivated."
If that which originates from innate goodness (*upapatti-pratilambhika-kuśala*) is subsumed under innate goodness,
and if that which originates from applied effort (*prāyogika-kuśala*) is subsumed under applied effort,
then since the treatises state that all conditioned wholesome states (*saṃskṛta-kuśala*) are termed "cultivation" (*bhāvanā*), [how is this to be understood]?
What is this cultivation, and how many [factors] are involved?
Therefore, the *Prakaraṇapāda-śāstra*, in the "Chapter on the Fifteen Thousand Questions," regarding the discrimination of the twelve bases (*āyatana*) as cultivated or uncultivated, states:
"As for how many should be cultivated and so forth, eight are not to be cultivated."
The fourth [category] should be analyzed.
That is to say, the sense-base of form (rūpāyatana) is either to be cultivated or not to be cultivated.
How is it to be cultivated?
This refers to the wholesome sphere of form. What is not to be cultivated?
This refers to the unwholesome and indeterminate spheres of form.
The sphere of sound and the sphere of mind are likewise.
As for the sphere of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*), it may be cultivated or not cultivated.
How is it to be cultivated?
This refers to the sphere of wholesome conditioned phenomena. What is not to be cultivated?
This refers to the sphere of unwholesome and indeterminate phenomena.
And because of the [attainment of] analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*),
it is known that form and so forth are definitely categorized as "cultivation" (*bhāvanā*) according to their temporal periods;
in the future, they are merely attained (*prāpti*).
Because it arises through acquisition, there is "cultivation by acquisition" (pratilambha-bhāvanā).
Since its essence has not yet manifested, there is no "cultivation by practice" (niṣevaṇa-bhāvanā).
When it is manifest, both types of cultivation are present; because there is simultaneous acquisition of the dharma, there is "cultivation by acquisition."

Because it manifests before one's eyes, there is cultivation through practice (*abhyāsa-bhāvanā*). Question: Can the two types of wisdom—those of hearing (*śruta-mayī-prajñā*) and reflection (*cintā-mayī-prajñā*)—cultivate the future? Answer: It is explained that they cannot.
Thus, the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 188, states:
Question: Among these three applications of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), which one is cultivated when which is manifested?

Answer: When that which is produced through hearing (*śrutamaya*) is manifested, one cultivates only that which is produced through hearing, and not those produced through reflection (*cintāmaya*) or cultivation (*bhāvanāmaya*).
When that which is accomplished through reflection (cintāmayī) manifests,
one practices only reflection, not hearing (śruta) or cultivation (bhāvanā).
In this context, when the moments of hearing and reflection manifest:
It is called "cultivation" (bhāvanā) because it is practiced through repeated cultivation;
it does not cultivate the future because their power is inferior.
For this reason, one cultivates only that which belongs to oneself and not that which belongs to others.
When the wisdom produced by cultivation (bhāvanāmaya-jñāna) is present before one,
one is able to cultivate three types;
although the power of hearing (śruta) and reflection (cintā) cannot cultivate future [dharmas], [this is not the case for the wisdom of cultivation].

The passage from "and by means of other power there is the sense of future cultivation" onwards is the treatise itself. The phrase "the two cultivations— remedy and removal— rely upon contaminated phenomena (*sāsrava-dharma*)" explains the following two lines,
clarifying the cultivation of remedy (*pratipakṣa-bhāvanā*) and the cultivation of removal (*vinirdhāvana-bhāvanā*).
These two types of cultivation are established based on contaminated phenomena (*sāsrava-dharma*).

Because these contaminated phenomena possess the capacity to counteract when viewed from the perspective of the arising of the path of antidotes (*pratipakṣa-mārga*), they are termed "cultivation as an antidote" (*pratipakṣa-bhāvanā*).
This "antidote" consists of four kinds of antidotes.
Therefore, the *Saṃyuktābhidharmahṛdaya*, in the Chapter on Selection (*Vibhaṅga-varga*), states:
"Cultivation as an antidote (*pratipakṣa-bhāvanā*) refers to the cultivation of the four kinds of antidotes, which is termed 'cultivation as an antidote.'"

This is because it is the antidote to the *sāsrava* (contaminated) dharmas; thus says the treatise (*śāstra*). From the perspective of the meaning of being freed from bondage, the elimination of the bondage of afflictions (*kleśa*) is called "cultivation through elimination" (*prahāṇabhāvanā*).
Therefore, the *Nyāyānusāra* (Treatise on Reasoning), fascicle 74, states:

Because one attains the remedies for phenomena such as the body, those [phenomena] to be remedied— namely the body and so forth— are called "cultivation of the remedy" (*pratipakṣabhāvanā*). Therefore,
when one attains the remedy for the body and so forth, [it is this cultivation].
This is precisely what is meant by "cultivating the body and so forth.
The same principle should apply to other contaminated phenomena (*sāsrava-dharma*),
because the afflictions that take the body and such as their objects are thereby abandoned.
The teaching that phenomena such as the body are to be eliminated is called "cultivation through elimination.
Therefore, when afflictions directed toward the body and so forth are severed,
it is likewise said that one is cultivating the body and so forth.
Other contaminated (*sāsrava*) phenomena should be understood by this same principle.
These two [categories] are established solely based upon contaminated phenomena.
Furthermore, the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 155, states:
Question: How are the faculties such as the eye not cultivated?
And how are they cultivated?
Answer: Up to and including the various faculties such as the eye.
The non-cultivation of the faculties refers to the state in which the path of antidote has not yet arisen;
this is explained in terms of the cultivation of the antidote.
Furthermore, it includes all afflictions that take the eye and so forth as their objects.
When [the defilements] have not yet been abandoned and their names have not yet been known, this refers to the cultivation of the faculties through the practice of elimination.
Once the path of antidote has arisen for the various faculties such as the eye, it is called the cultivation of the faculties.
This is explained in terms of cultivation as an antidote.
Furthermore, when all afflictions associated with the eye and so forth have been abandoned and fully understood,
this is called the cultivation of the faculties (*indriya-bhāvanā*).
This is explained based on the cultivation of elimination (*vibhāvanā-bhāvanā*).
Therefore, regarding the statement that "impure wholesome states extend to both the preceding and succeeding cultivations," this is a comparative analysis of their breadth and narrowness.
Therefore, contaminated wholesome states possess all four types of cultivation (*bhāvanā*).
From the perspective of their wholesome nature, they possess the two cultivations of acquisition (*pratilambha*) and practice (*niṣevaṇa*);
from the perspective of their contaminated nature, they possess the two cultivations of counteraction (*pratipakṣa*) and removal (*vidūṣaṇa*).
Therefore, there are four types [of cultivation].
Uncontaminated conditioned phenomena possess the first two—the cultivation of acquisition (*pratilambha*) and the cultivation of practice (*niṣevanā*).
As for the remaining contaminated, defiled, and neutral phenomena, they possess the latter two.
It possesses subsequent cultivation and involves the dispatching of two kinds of cultivation.
Thus, the *Abhidharmamahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 105, states:
"However, the four kinds of cultivation are analyzed according to the dharmas."
One should formulate four permutations (*catuṣkoṭi*).
There are phenomena that are cultivated by the first two [types of cultivation] but not by the latter two;
namely, uncontaminated conditioned phenomena (*anāsrava-saṃskṛta-dharma*). There are phenomena that are cultivated by the latter two but not by the former two.

That is to say: defiled dharmas and non-obscured neutral conditioned dharmas; there are dharmas that are both the two former cultivations and the two latter cultivations, namely, wholesome contaminated dharmas;
and there are dharmas that are neither the two former cultivations nor the two latter cultivations.
This refers to unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛtadharma*).
The phrase "the masters of foreign lands... up to the detailed exposition" records alternative interpretations.
This treatise refers to the masters of foreign lands (*bāhyaka-ācārya*).
The *Mahāvibhāṣā* calls them the masters of the West (*paścāt-pathika-ācārya*);
because they reside outside of Kaśmīra, they are termed "foreigners."
Because it is to the west of the kingdom of Kaśmīra, it is called the Western [tradition].
It teaches six types of cultivation:
the four previously mentioned, plus the two cultivations of protection (*ārakṣā*) and observation (*vipaśyanā*).
Guarding the sense faculties is called "cultivation through guarding";
observing the body is called "cultivation through observation";
in the *Vibhāṣā*, it is called "cultivation through discernment."
The names differ while the meaning remains the same.
The former sutra establishes the cultivation of protection,
while the latter sutra establishes the cultivation of investigation.
Regarding those who immediately administer punishment and exercise restraint upon arrival in the kingdom of Kaśmīra:
the masters of the treatises in the kingdom of Kaśmīra state that this is the correct principle consistent with the sūtras.
Regarding what are called the two cultivations of guarding and observation,
they should be understood as being subsumed within the two cultivations of antidote and elimination among the aforementioned four cultivations.

Regarding the faculties and the body, if one considers them from the perspective of their capacity to prevent, protect, and investigate, it is called "cultivation as an antidote" (*pratipakṣa-bhāvanā*).

If one considers them from the perspective of their capacity to eliminate the delusions that are to be prevented or investigated, it is called "cultivation of removal" (*vinirdhāvana-bhāvanā*). Thus far, the four types of cultivation have been explained according to their actual practice (*bhāvanā*).
If one considers the distinction between this [category] and the preceding one based on what is to be cultivated (*bhāvanīya*),
the *Nyāyānusāra* (Treatise on Correct Reasoning), fascicle 74, states:
"In this context, there are those who differentiate the various dharmas according to the meaning of what is to be cultivated, determining the number of cultivations they possess."
There are dharmas that possess all four [characteristics] and are termed "to be cultivated";
there are dharmas that possess three;
and there are dharmas that possess two.
There are phenomena that possess one [of these characteristics], and there are phenomena that possess none at all;
namely, when wholesome contaminated phenomena have not yet been permanently abandoned.
That which is obtainable and producible is complete in four aspects.
Because this has not yet been permanently severed, it should be complete in the cultivation of counteracting and dispelling;
because it is obtainable, it should be complete in the cultivation of attainment.
That which is capable of arising should be fully practiced and cultivated;

that which has already been attained and is capable of arising possesses all three [factors], with the exception of attainment (*prāpti*). That which is capable of being attained but will not arise possesses all three, with the exception of practice (*bhāvanā*).
Those already attained that do not arise, as well as those unattainable that have already arisen, possess both [types of cultivation], namely:
cultivation by antidote and cultivation by elimination.
The same applies to defiled and neutral states that have not yet been abandoned.
When wholesome contaminated dharmas have been permanently severed,

there are those that can be acquired and produced, which possess both the acquisition (*prāpti*) and the cultivation (*vāsanā*); and there are those that can be acquired but not produced, which possess only one, namely, acquisition.
That which has already been attained and is capable of arising consists of one [type], namely, cultivation (*bhāvanā*).
It should be understood that the same applies to conditioned uncontaminated (*anāsrava-saṃskṛta*) phenomena.
Apart from what has been mentioned previously, all others are entirely non-existent.
That is to say, regarding untainted dharmas that have already been attained and are non-arising, if one were to claim that even though these non-arising dharmas do not abide within the body,
they are nonetheless called "cultivated" solely by virtue of their attainment,
then one must also admit that analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) is likewise called "cultivation."
Because there is no distinction, this objection is unreasonable;
for those dharmas of the same class abide within the body.
That is to say, although dharmas that do not arise do not abide in the body, [the objection does not apply].
There is no error in calling the abiding in a homogeneous class (*nikāya-sabhāga*) "cultivation" (*bhāvanā*).
Furthermore, this is because it abides as a result of attainment;
that is to say, it refers to wholesome dharmas that do not arise in the future.
Because they have now attained birth, they abide as the fruit of manifestation;
the meaning of the statement "we lack conditions and thus do not arise" is that we are not currently being summoned [to rebirth], not that we are not receiving the inducement [of birth].
Cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) is distinct from this and cannot be used as an analogy.
Furthermore, even future wholesome dharmas that have not yet arisen can be sustained by the power of causes to benefit the present body.
Cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) is not like this, and therefore it lacks the sense of being "cultivated.
Furthermore, because cessation through deliberation is exclusively a fruit,
cultivation is undertaken primarily for the sake of attaining a superior fruit.
Cessation (*nirodha*) should not be cultivated because it is not a fruit;
furthermore, because analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) is without increase or decrease.
That is to say, the dharmas that can be cultivated range from the inferior up to the intermediate.
From the middle [dhyāna] up to the highest,
[the path] is so; cessation through deliberation (pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha) is not, because it is useless for cultivation.
*Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya-ṭīkā*, Fascicle 26. Completed at Ōdōji on the nineteenth day of the seventh month in the first year of the Hōen era.
*Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya-ṭīkā*, Fascicle 27, composed by the śramaṇa Śākya Kō.
The second part of the seventh chapter, "The Analysis of Wisdom" (*Vibhaṅga-jñāna-varga*).
Having thus completed the preceding discussion, that which is now to be demonstrated is as follows:
the second major section of this chapter, which elucidates the virtues accomplished through wisdom (*jñāna-samudāgata-guṇa*).
Among these, first is the summary that connects the preceding [section] to what follows;
second is the specific clarification. This, then, is the summary that connects the preceding to what follows.
Regarding the statement that there are first eighteen types of "attainment" (*samāpatti*) to be distinguished therein,
this is the second section below which explains them individually. Within this:
First, the elucidation of the unique qualities (*āveṇika-dharma*);
second, the elucidation of the shared virtues. Within the elucidation of the unique qualities:
first, the enumeration and designation of their names.
Second, the detailed explanation according to the names. Below this, first, the enumeration and the presentation of the names.
Within this, first, the introduction.
Second is the question;
third is the explanation.
This constitutes the introduction.
"What are the eighteen?"—this is the question. The verse says:
"Because they have been attained, they are called 'unshared' (āveṇika)."
This is the explanation.
Furthermore, as for how the characteristics of the Buddha’s ten powers are distinguished:
from here below is the second section, which provides a detailed interpretation according to their names.
Among these, first is the elucidation of the Buddha’s ten powers (daśabala),
and second is the elucidation of the four fearlessnesses (catvāri vaiśāradyāni).
The third explains the three types of clear knowledge and the three foundations of mindfulness; the fourth explains the Buddha’s great compassion;
and the fifth explains the similarities and differences among Buddhas. These are presented within the context of explaining the Buddha’s ten powers.
First, the power of the Buddha’s mind is clarified;
second, the power of the Buddha’s body is clarified. Below this, the first section clarifies the power of the Buddha’s mind;
this is the question.
The verse says: "Because it is unimpeded with respect to its objects.
Within this response in verse form, the first six lines set forth its essential nature (*svabhāva*).
The next two phrases rely on the stages (*bhūmi*);
the next one phrase relies on the locus and the body;
the final phrase explains the meaning of power (*bala*).
The Commentary states: "Up to having ten knowledges as its nature" explains the first phrase.
"Place" (sthāna) means a locus.
That which accords with reason and is consistent with the meaning of acceptance is called "a possible case" (*sthāna*).
For example, it is said that virtuous causes produce desirable results;
such things certainly constitute a possible case.
That which is not consistent with reason and cannot be logically accommodated is termed "impossible" (*asthāna*).
For example, it is said that it is absolutely impossible for a wholesome cause to produce an undesirable result;
such a thing simply does not occur.
This [power] of the possible and the impossible applies to all phenomena,
because all phenomena possess the meaning of possibility and impossibility.
Because wisdom can know this possibility and impossibility, it is called the "power of knowledge regarding the possible and the impossible."
It has as its nature the ten knowledges (*jñāna*) of the Tathāgata,
because the Buddha’s ten knowledges universally and appropriately know what is possible (*sthāna*) and what is impossible (*asthāna*). Therefore,
the *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya-ṭīkā* (Exposition of the Treasury), chapter thirty-six, states:
To know that the intrinsic functional capacity and principle of all phenomena definitely exist is called the wisdom of the locus (*sthāna-jñāna*).
To know that the intrinsic functional capacity and principle of all phenomena definitely do not exist is [the wisdom of the non-locus].
This is called the knowledge of what is impossible (*asthāna-jñāna*). This knowledge universally takes as its object both sentient and non-sentient realms,
and it is not in contradiction with any form of omniscience (*sarvajña*).

Fearing that [the audience] might find it difficult to realize [the truth] due to the brevity of the explanation and the small amount of effort expended, he has further extracted the remaining nine from within this [text].
Regarding the phrase "the maturation of the two types of karma, up to excluding the Path": this refers to the exclusion of the Path.
Explaining the second phrase:
knowing that this kind of karma produces this specific maturation is called the power of knowledge regarding the maturation of karma.
The verse mentions only "karma," which implies its maturation;
this is the maturation of that karma.
If one speaks from a distant perspective, karma is said to be the cause and maturation (vipāka) is the fruit.
However, if one analyzes in detail:
Moments of the same category, viewed in relation to one another across preceding and succeeding instants,
all possess cause and effect;
these apply equally to both the Truths of Suffering and Origination.
Therefore, among the ten knowledges, it has eight knowledges as its nature,
excluding the knowledge of cessation and the knowledge of the path,
because it does not take suffering, its origin, karma, or its maturation as its object.
Therefore, the *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya* states:

"The unimpeded knowledge that correctly discerns how such types of karma produce such types of various ripened fruits (*vipākaphala*) is called the power of knowledge regarding the ripening of karma."
Or it is called the power of knowledge regarding one's own karma (*svakarmasvakatājñānabala*).
This refers to the skillful discernment that such types of fruits are summoned by the power of the karma created by oneself.
It cannot be given away or taken away by one's wife, children, or others.
Karma of such a nature inevitably brings about its own fruit;
it cannot be bartered for anything else.
Unobstructed wisdom is called the power of knowledge regarding one's own karma (*svakarmajñānabala*).
In the *Abhidharmamahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* (Vol. 30), it is called the power of knowledge regarding the accumulation of karmic phenomena (*karmadharmasamudayajñānabala*). Karma is the cause.
Dharmas are the fruit;
origination (samudaya) encompasses both cause and fruit;
karma is that which accumulates.
The Dharma is that which is accumulated;
it is synonymous with the *Abhidharmakośa* (Treasury of Abhidharma) in meaning despite the difference in name.
Regarding the power of knowledge concerning the meditative attainments (*samāpatti*) up to the third dhyāna:
The following explains the third phrase: meditative absorptions (dhyāna) refers to the four dhyānas;
liberations (vimokṣa) refers to the eight liberations; and meditative concentrations (samādhi).
That is to say, the three samādhis and the attainments (samāpatti).
These refer to the eight attainments; all of these are synonyms for meditative concentration (dhyāna).
Wisdom is that which knows dhyāna and so forth as they truly are.
This is called the power of knowledge regarding dhyāna and so forth.

Regarding the power of knowledge regarding the superior and inferior states of the four faculties: it is the knowledge of the distinctions between superior and inferior states of the faculty of faith and the others.
This is called the power of knowledge regarding the superior and inferior faculties (*indriya*).
Therefore, the *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya* states:
"If one knows, as it truly is, the distinctions among the classes of sentient beings regarding their faculties that enable them to attain superior qualities."
Unimpeded wisdom is called the power of knowing the superior and inferior faculties (*indriya-parāpara-jñānabala*).
Although there are those of middling faculties,
they are not separately manifested because, in relation to the superior and inferior, they are subsumed within the category of the inferior or the superior.
In this context, what phenomena are designated by the term "faculties" (*indriya*)?
They refer to faith and the other [wholesome roots].
Even in the continuum of one who has severed the roots of goodness (*samucchinna-kuśalamūla*), there still exist past and future wholesome dharmas such as faith.

Regarding the power of knowing the various inclinations (*nānādhimukti-jñāna-bala*), it refers to the knowledge of the differences in the various inclinations and underlying dispositions of sentient beings, such as those of the eye, the mind, and so forth.
This is called the power of knowledge regarding the various inclinations (*nānādhimukti-jñāna-bala*).
Inclination (*adhimukti*) is a mental factor (*caitta-dharma*).
Therefore, the *Abhidharmakośa-vyākhyā* states:
If one possesses unimpeded knowledge that knows, as they truly are, the differences in the dispositions and inclinations of sentient beings,
this is called the power of knowing various inclinations (*nānādhimukti-jñāna-bala*).
This is because "disposition" (*āśaya*) and "inclination" (*adhimukti*) are designated as distinct categories.
Regarding the sixth power, the knowledge of the various elements (*nānādhātu-jñāna-bala*):
it is called the power of the knowledge of the various elements because it knows the diverse elemental natures of sentient beings.
Therefore, the *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya* states:
If one knows, as it truly is, the various distinctions among sentient beings— their dispositions formed through repeated practice from beginningless time in the past,
their latent tendencies (*anuśaya*), and the diverse natures (*gotra*) of their dharmas.
Unobstructed wisdom is called the power of knowledge regarding the various elements (*nānādhātu-jñānabala*).
It should be understood that within this context,
"element" (*dhātu*) is a designation for "disposition" (*adhimukti*), "latent tendencies" (*anuśaya*), and "dharma-characteristics" (*dharmasaṃjñā*).
Regarding these four powers up to the power of knowledge that eliminates [defilements]:
as clarified above, the objects of these four powers—concentration, faculties, understanding, and elements—all pertain to and are subsumed within the truths of suffering, origin, and the path.
Therefore, these four powers all have the nature of nine knowledges (*jñāna*);
because they do not take the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) as their object, the knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-jñāna*) is excluded.
As for the power of knowing the paths leading everywhere (*sarvatragāminī-pratipad-jñānabala*), it has the nature of ten knowledges.
Explaining the fourth phrase:
all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*), according to their respective capacities, are able to lead toward their results; thus they are called "paths leading everywhere" (*sarvatragāminī-pratipad*).
The Buddha’s power of knowing the paths leading everywhere as they truly are,
among all paths leading to every destination, is called the *sarvatragāminīpratipajjñānabala*. The previous explanation [of the nine powers] excludes the knowledge of cessation (*nirodhajñāna*).
According to this, the fruit toward which one proceeds is exclusively cessation (*nirodha*).
The latter interpretation holds that the ten knowledges (*daśajñāna*) comprehensively understand both cause and effect;
thus, the *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya* (Xianzong lun) states:
It refers to knowing, as it truly is, the causes and effects of birth and death,
as well as possessing unimpeded knowledge regarding the path to their exhaustion;
this is called the power of knowledge regarding the paths leading everywhere.
Regarding the statement that "the eight knowledges of former abodes up to [the knowledge of] all mundane phenomena are of the nature of conventional knowledge," this explains the fifth phrase:
knowing the past events of former lives.
Therefore, it is called the power of the knowledge of recollecting past lives (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛtijñānabala*).
Because mindfulness (*smṛti*) is particularly strong herein, it is specifically designated;
it is called "recollection" (*anusmṛti*) because it recollects events according to their sequence.
In future lives, dying here and being born there is called "death and birth.
Knowing this as it truly is is the knowledge of death and birth. These two powers are both contemplations of phenomena (*vastu-darśana*).
All are of the nature of conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*). Therefore, the *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya* states:
"That is to say, knowing as it truly is the distinctions regarding the past lives of oneself and others."
The unimpeded knowledge [regarding the cessation of outflows] is called the eighth power.
If one knows, as it truly is, the continuous rebirth of all classes of sentient beings in future existences, this unimpeded knowledge is called the ninth power.
(Above is from the treatise. As for the knowledge of death and rebirth (*cyutyupapāda-jñāna*), if one refers to its fundamental [state]:
This supernormal power of the divine eye (divyacakṣus-abhijñā) takes only the present as its object;
the statement that it "takes the future as its object" is made in reference to the secondary factors (parivāra) induced by this power.
As for the six supernormal knowledges (*ṣaḍabhijñā*), they shall be explained separately below.
Regarding the statement that "the power of the knowledge of the destruction of the outflows (*āsravakṣayajñānabala*) has ten knowledges as its nature," this explains the sixth phrase.
The exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya*) is cessation (*nirodha*). The remainder of the text may be understood accordingly.
Furthermore, the *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya* states:
These latter three powers are identical to the three supernormal knowledges (*abhijñā*).
Because these three among the six supernormal knowledges are particularly distinguished,
they are established as the "three clear knowledges" (*vidyā*) within the stage of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*).
That which exists within the body of a Tathāgata is also called a power (*bala*).
However, the supernormal powers of the psychic realm (*ṛddhi*) and the divine ear (*divya-śrotra*), even when present in the Buddha’s body,
do not constitute powers because they lack great utility.
Furthermore, for example, the divine eye can perceive the distinctions in the maturation (*vipāka*) of sentient beings within the happy and miserable realms;
by means of this, it can induce the arising of superior knowledge,
and one also correctly understands the karma that brings about those results.
It is for this reason that the name "knowledge of death and rebirth" is established;
the supernormal powers of the divine eye (*ṛddhi*) and the divine ear (*divyaśrotra*) do not possess such a great function.
Therefore, they are also not established as powers (*bala*).
However, the power of others' minds is not mentioned separately because its meaning is already subsumed within the powers of the faculties and so forth,
since mind and mental factors exist among the faculties of others.
Having already distinguished the essential nature up to the point of attaining the male Buddha-body,
this explains the seventh, eighth, and ninth phrases.
The eighth is the power of knowledge consisting in the recollection of past abodes (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛtijñānabala*).
The ninth is the power of knowledge regarding death and rebirth;
because it is of the nature of the five supernormal powers (*pañcābhijñā*), it relies upon the four fundamental meditative concentrations (*mauladhyāna*).
The remaining eight [knowledges] generally rely upon eleven stages, because conventional knowledge is broad;
their reliance on specific bodies can be understood accordingly. Furthermore, if one distinguishes them according to the applications of mindfulness (smṛtyupasthāna):
As stated in the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 34:

"The foundations of mindfulness consist of the power of knowledge regarding various inclinations (*nānādhimukti-jñānabala*) and the power of knowledge regarding the recollection of past abodes (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛti-jñānabala*)."

The foundation of mindfulness of phenomena alone constitutes the power of knowledge regarding death and rebirth; the foundation of mindfulness of the body alone constitutes [the power of knowledge regarding the recollection of past lives].

Regarding the power of the knowledge of the destruction of the outflows (*āsravakṣayajñānabala*): if it takes as its object the state of the destruction of the outflows, it is the application of mindfulness to phenomena (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*);
if it relies on the body in which the outflows have been destroyed, it consists of all four applications of mindfulness (*catvāri smṛtyupasthānāni*).
The remaining powers are all the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*). The commentary explains:

because the power of knowledge consisting of resolve (*adhimokṣajñānabala*) takes as its specific object the mental factor of resolve (*adhimokṣa*), it is exclusively the foundation of mindfulness of phenomena (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*). As for the power of knowledge consisting of the recollection of past lives (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛtijñānabala*): [it is likewise].
It takes the five aggregates of the past as its object;
it is also exclusively the application of mindfulness to phenomena (dharmasmṛtyupasthāna). This is the power of knowledge regarding death and rebirth (cyutyupapādajñānabala).

Because it takes material phenomena (rūpadharma) as its object, the power of the knowledge of the destruction of the outflows (āsravakṣayajñānabala) consists solely of the application of mindfulness to the body;
both explanations are as stated in the text. The remaining six powers all consist of the four applications of mindfulness.

Among the six types [of powers], the knowledge of what is possible and impossible (*sthānāsthāna-jñānabala*), the knowledge of the maturation of karma (*karmavipāka-jñānabala*), and the knowledge of the paths leading everywhere (*sarvatragāminīpratipad-jñānabala*)—these three each pertain to four [foundations of mindfulness].
Their characteristics are manifest and thus easily known. As for the power of concentration (*samādhibala*), it pertains to all four.
The term "concentration" (samādhi) subsumes both associated and co-existent factors.
If one knows the form that follows [the mind], this is the foundation of mindfulness of the body (kāyasmṛtyupasthāna).
If one knows feelings and the mind,
this is the application of mindfulness to feelings and the mind; if one knows other phenomena, [this is the application of mindfulness to phenomena].
Regarding "the mindfulness-establishment of phenomena (dharma-smṛtyupasthāna) is called such; the faculties (indriya) and powers (bala) pertain to all four":

the faculties refer to the wholesome faculties such as faith, or the mental faculty (manas-indriya), and thus they pertain to all four mindfulness-establishments. Regarding "the elements (dhātu) and powers pertain to all four": [the same applies].
The "elements" (dhātu) refer to the latent dispositions (anuśaya) of one's fundamental nature and the lineage of all phenomena; therefore, they also pertain to all four [foundations].
Having already explained the basis of the body, why are they called "powers" (bala)?
The latter phrase is the question. "Because [it occurs] in all [beings],
up to the number of births," and so forth, is the answer.
Because wisdom functions without obstruction regarding all objects of knowledge,
it is called a "power" (*bala*). For this reason,
these ten powers depend exclusively upon the body of a Buddha.
Why is this? Because only the Buddha has eliminated all afflictions along with their habitual tendencies regarding all objects.
They are able to know according to their desire.
This is contrary to the case of the other vehicles, which,
despite possessing wisdom, encounter obstructions regarding their objects.
Therefore, it is not called "power.
For example, when Śāriputra abandoned his quest to save others:
long ago, during the time when the Buddha was in the world, there was a certain man.
At the gate of the Jeta Grove, he sought ordination and entry into the homeless life.
Śāriputra and the others perceived through their insight that this man had not planted the roots of merit conducive to liberation for eighty thousand kalpas.
Because he lacked the causal conditions for renunciation, [the Buddha] set him aside and did not ordain him.
The man lamented and felt resentment, seeking ordination without ceasing.
Later, the Buddha came and saw him.
He ordained him, and through the teaching of the Dharma, he attained the fruit of realization.
Śāriputra and the others, finding this strange, questioned him about it.
The Buddha told him:
"In the distant past, in the kingdom of Nāgarahāra, I lived together with the people of this country."
They swept and sprinkled the streets and prepared various ritual implements,
desiring to invite the Tathāgata Dīpaṃkara to offer him worship.
At that time, seeking to attain liberation, he entered the city to sell firewood.
Having learned of this matter, he immediately made a vow: "I shall gather more wood and obtain money to make offerings.
When he reached the mountain, he was bitten by insects.
As he was about to reach the end of his life,
he wished to recite the name of that Buddha,
but he forgot it and could not remember it.
It is therefore said: "The 'namo' (homage) that one desires to encounter within the city is precisely what is called the 'wholesome root conducive to liberation' (*mokṣabhāgīya-kuśalamūla*).
Although this wholesome state was previously aroused,"
Because of the vastness of time, Śāriputra and others were unable to know it. Question: The maximum speed for a śrāvaka is three births;
the minimum duration is sixty kalpas.

Question: Why are the eighty thousand [beings] not included among the noble ones (*ārya*)? Answer: It is explained that the "three births" and "sixty [kalpas]" are based on continuous cultivation (*saṃtati-bhāvanā*).
If there is an interruption, it does not hinder [the process] over many kalpas. Question: Previously, one had never yet produced the factors conducive to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*).

"How can one enter the state of a noble one (*ārya*) in this present life? The explanation says: Because he previously also gave rise to the wholesome roots conducive to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*), he enters the state of a noble one and attains the fruits in this present life.
Furthermore, it is like Śāriputra being unable to perceive the number of births of the pigeon being pursued by the hawk throughout its two temporal limits (*pūrvānta* and *aparānta*).
As stated in the Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra:
"The Buddha was staying at the Jetavana;
in the late afternoon, he was walking in meditation."
At that time, a hawk was pursuing a dove.
The dove flew to the Buddha’s side and stayed there;
as the Buddha walked by, his shadow covered the dove.
The pigeon’s body was at peace;
its fear was immediately dispelled,
and it ceased making any sound.
Afterwards, when Śāriputra’s shadow reached the pigeon,
it immediately cried out and trembled with fear as before.
Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Both the Buddha and my own body are equally free from the three poisons.
For what reason does the pigeon become silent and no longer terrified when covered by the Buddha’s shadow,
yet when covered by my shadow, it immediately makes a sound and trembles with fear as before?"
The Buddha said,
"Because the habitual tendencies of your three poisons are not yet exhausted,
for this reason the fear caused by your shadow's obscuration has not been eliminated."
"Observe this pigeon's karmic conditions from past lives; for how many lifetimes has it been a pigeon?
Śāriputra immediately entered the samādhi of knowledge of past lives (*pūrvanivāsajñāna-samādhi*) and beheld that this pigeon had come from among pigeons.
In this manner, for one, two, three, and up to eighty thousand great kalpas, he constantly took the body of a pigeon.
After this period had passed, he could no longer be seen. Śāriputra arose from his samādhi and addressed the Buddha, saying:
This pigeon has constantly been in the form of a pigeon for eighty thousand great kalpas;
prior to this period, it is impossible to know further.
Thus spoke the Buddha.
If you cannot fully know the past,
try then to observe the future:
when will this pigeon be liberated?
Śāriputra immediately entered the samādhi of the wisdom of vows and observed this pigeon through one,
two, three, and up to eighty thousand great kalpas.
He had not yet been released from his pigeon body;
even beyond this, he could not know what had transpired.
Rising from samādhi, he addressed the Buddha, saying:
I have seen this pigeon from one lifetime, two lifetimes, and so on,
up to eighty thousand great kalpas, yet it has not escaped its pigeon body;
beyond this point, I can know no further.
I do not know the limits of the past or the future;
I cannot discern when this pigeon shall be liberated.
The Buddha told Śāriputra:
"This pigeon is not within the scope of what can be known by śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas.
Even throughout great kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges River..."
He constantly took the form of a pigeon;
once his retribution was exhausted,
he was released from that state and, after cycling through the five realms of existence, attained human birth.
After five hundred lifetimes, he finally attained sharp faculties.
At that time, there was a Buddha who delivered immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* sentient beings and subsequently entered *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*.
While the Bequeathed Dharma remains in the world,
this person becomes a lay follower (upāsaka) who observes the five precepts.
From a bhikṣu, he hears praise of the Buddha’s merits.
Thereupon, he first resolves his mind, wishing to become a Buddha;
thereafter, throughout three asaṃkhyeya kalpas,
he practices the six pāramitās.
Having fully perfected the ten stages and attained Buddhahood,
he delivers immeasurable sentient beings and enters *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*.
At that time, Śāriputra repented before the Buddha.
He addressed the Buddha, saying:
"I am unable to know the beginning and end of even a single pigeon;
how much more so regarding all dharmas, which remain unknown due to the vastness of time?"
Regarding the statement that "thus all Buddhas reach this [state] which has contact as its nature," this clarifies the second [topic]: the power of the Buddha-body.
The Treatise says: "Reaching Nārāyaṇa."
This explains the first phrase: Nārāyaṇa.
This is the name of a deity;
here it is translated as "Human Seed" (Renzhong).
Other masters state that "reaching the power of the mind that is limitless" explains the second phrase;
this records a divergent interpretation.

Regarding the superiority or inferiority of the power of the Greatly Awakened One (Mahābuddha) and the Solitary Realizer (Pratyekabuddha), they are further distinguished by three factors: the connection of their limbs and joints, their vows, and their differences.
As for the connection of the limbs and joints of the Greatly Awakened One, it is like the coiled knots of a dragon.
The joints of the Pratyekabuddha’s limbs are connected like a chain;
the joints of the Wheel-turning King’s limbs are connected like interlocking hooks.
Therefore, when these three are compared, there is a distinction in their relative strength.
According to the *Vibhāṣā* (Treatise on the Great Abhidharma), Volume 30:
those whose limbs and joints are interlocked belong to the copper-wheel-turning kings;
if one follows the case of the gold-wheel-turning kings, their bone joints are linked together like chains.
"What is the measure of the strength of Nārāyaṇa?
This is the question that explains the third phrase.
Regarding the statement that [the strength] increases tenfold up to that of a Nārāyaṇa:
the answer is that it is because the strength of ordinary elephants and so forth increases tenfold at each successive stage.
It is said that each subsequent power increases tenfold over the preceding one.
The first is the ordinary elephant,
referring to the common elephants used for transport in the Western Regions.
Second, the fragrant elephant (*gandhahastin*).
In the Western lands, there is a distinct class of excellent elephants called "fragrant elephants," which are employed for use in battle.
The name of this deity is Mahānagna,
which in this language means "Great Bare-bodied One.
The four Pārṣadyas are likewise names of deities.
*Prala* is translated here as "victorious" (*śreṣṭha*).
*Sakuntī* is translated here as "aggregate" (*skandha*).
*Pañcavālaka* is likewise the name of a deity.
This is translated as "Wondrous Branch.
Ṣaḍānura is also the name of a deity;
this is translated as "Grasping."
The seven Nārāyaṇas are as previously explained;
there are those who say they are to be known.
Among what has been stated, only that which is most consistent with reason should be accepted.
Thus far, there have been three explanations in total.
Regarding the physical power of the Tathāgata,
the Master of the Treatise (Śāstrakāra) adopts the explanation provided by Dharmatrāta.
Therefore, it is said that among the three explanations, only the first is largely consistent with reason.
The *Nyāyānusāra* and the *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya-ṭīkā-tattvārthā* also agree with this view.
Thus, regarding bodily power (*kāyabala*), it exists as something distinct from the seven external [elements].
The fourth phrase is explained as follows;
herein there are two interpretations.
One interpretation holds that force (*bala*) is a specific differentiation of the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) among those that are tangible.
If the primary elements (mahābhūta) are predominant, they are termed "powers" (bala).
They are called "distinctive" because they differ from other primary elements.
Some say that power is a derivative tangible (upādāyarūpa).
To claim that there is a distinct force-contact (*bala-spraṣṭavya*) apart from the seven [types of tangible objects] is not the correct interpretation.
Furthermore, in the *Abhidharmamahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 30, five explanations are presented regarding bodily strength and bodily weakness.
The first explanation states that there is no partial increase among the four great elements;
rather, what is strong and superior is called "bodily strength," while what is weak is called "bodily inferiority.
The second explanation states that the increase of the earth element is called "bodily strength."
The increase of water is called inferiority of body;
this refers to the increase of the primary elements (*mahābhūta*).
The third [increase] is called strength of body due to the increase of heaviness.
The increase of lightness is called inferiority of the body.
The fourth [point] states that there are external derived tangibles distinct from the seven derived tangibles [already mentioned].
Regarding the inferiority of the body of names and the body of power,
the fifth critique states that it should be explained as follows:
namely, the four great elements and the derived tangible objects.
Both are of the nature of bodily strength and bodily weakness;
that is to say, if they are in harmony, both are termed bodily strength,
and if they are not in harmony, both are termed bodily weakness.
The intention of the *Nyāyānusāra* is the same as that of the *Mahāvibhāṣā*.
Its first exposition corresponds to the first exposition of the *Mahāvibhāṣā*,
and its second exposition corresponds to the fourth exposition of the *Mahāvibhāṣā*.

Since the Abhidharmakośa contains no *viniścaya* (authoritative adjudication), one takes the *viniścaya* of the fifth [section] of the Mahāvibhāṣā as authoritative; furthermore, it is explained that the Abhidharmakośa does not take the *viniścaya* of the Mahāvibhāṣā as its standard of measure.

If one adopts this interpretation, the first master’s view is taken as correct. Furthermore, the explanation that "power" (*bala*) refers to a specific differentiation among the great elements (*mahābhūta*) within the tangible is the position of the Sautrāntikas.
In that school’s tenet, the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) within the sense-field of tangibility (*spraṣṭavya*) are real,
while all others are merely nominal (*prajñapti*),
because they are established based upon the primary elements.
Now, it is explained that power (*bala*) is a differentiation of the primary elements (*mahābhūta*).
Since the master’s intention aligns with the Sautrāntika school,
this interpretation, which follows their tenet, appears superior.
"From the Buddha’s four fearlessnesses up to the first twelve of the seven powers":
this is the second section clarifying the four fearlessnesses.
The treatise says: "Up to such as the seventh power."
The Buddha’s four fearlessnesses are explained at length in the sūtras.
The first is: "Regarding all phenomena, I have attained perfect awakening;
if an outsider were to challenge me, saying that I have not attained perfect awakening..."
Because one explains according to reality without fear, its nature consists of the ten knowledges,
as in the first case previously mentioned regarding the power of the possible and the impossible.
Second, "I have attained the permanent exhaustion of all outflows."
If an external objection states that the outflows are not yet eternally exhausted,
one should provide a reasoned explanation for the absence of fear;
alternatively, it may have the six knowledges as its intrinsic nature.
Alternatively, it has the ten knowledges as its nature,
as explained previously in the tenth power, the power of the destruction of the outflows (*āsravakṣaya-bala*).
Third, for my disciples, I have taught that those factors which are obstructive will necessarily constitute an obstruction to defilement.
If an external objection states that defilement (*kleśa*) is not an obstacle,
it should be explained according to reason that there is no fear because its nature consists of the eight knowledges (*jñāna*),
just as previously [stated] regarding the second power of the maturation of karma (*karmavipāka*).
Fourth, when I have taught my disciples that the path leading out [of suffering], if cultivated, will certainly lead to the transcendence of suffering,
if an outsider challenges me by claiming that the path does not lead to the transcendence of suffering,
I am able to explain it according to reason without fear.
It has either nine knowledges as its nature,
or ten knowledges as its nature,
just like the seventh power previously mentioned, the power of the practice leading everywhere.
Therefore, the *Vibhāṣā* (31) states: "First is the fearlessness of the Perfectly Enlightened One (*samyaksaṃbuddha-vaiśāradya*),
as explained in the Sūtra."
I am the one who has attained perfect and complete enlightenment regarding all phenomena.
Should there be any śramaṇas, brahmins, celestial Māras, or Brahmās in the world who, relying on the Dharma,
should raise an objection against me.
Or, to cause one to recollect that such a teaching was not perfectly awakened by the Fully Enlightened One—that is impossible;
were it ever to be so, I would have no grounds for right view regarding that matter.
Therefore, having attained security, being without fear or dread, he proclaims for himself:
"I occupy the exalted position of the Great Sage;
amidst the great assembly, I roar the true lion's roar and turn the Great Brahma Wheel."
It cannot be overturned by any śramaṇas, brahmins, celestial Māras, or Brahmās in the entire world.
He possesses the fearlessness of the eternal exhaustion of the two outflows,
as stated in the sūtra.
I have attained the permanent exhaustion of all taints (*āsrava*).
If there were any recluses, brahmins, celestial Māras, or Brahmās in the world who, relying on the Dharma,
were to raise an objection or cause me to recall that such taints remain inexhausted, it would be impossible for that to be so.
"Suppose there were [any such thing]," and so forth, as explained at length.
This is the third declaration of fearlessness regarding the obstructing dharmas, as stated in the Sūtra.
I have taught my disciples that obstructive dharmas are necessarily obstructions when they defile.
Should any worldly śramaṇas, brahmins, celestial Māras, or Brahmās raise objections based on the Dharma, [they will find no ground].
Or, if one were to cause them to recollect that these obstructing dharmas, though defiled, do not constitute an obstruction—such a thing is impossible;
even if it were so, [it would be as stated] at length.
Fourth is the fearlessness regarding the path leading out of suffering.
As it is said in the Sūtra:
"I have taught my disciples the path that leads out;
by practicing it, one will certainly emerge from suffering."
If there should be any recluses, brahmins, celestial Māras, or Brahmās in the world who, relying on the Dharma, raise an objection—
claiming that it is impossible for one who practices such a path to remember [the teachings] and yet fail to emerge from suffering— that is not possible.
If such a thing were to exist, I would have no basis for right view regarding it;
therefore, I have attained peace, being without fear or dread.
Thus, I declare myself to abide in the exalted position of a Great Sage.
In the midst of the great assembly, he rightly roars the lion’s roar and turns the Great Brahma-wheel,
which no śramaṇa, brahmin, celestial Māra, or Brahmā in any world can turn.
Furthermore, the *Abhidharmamahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 31,
states: "Regarding these ten powers and four fearlessnesses as thus described,
each individual power subsumes the four fearlessnesses."
Since each of the four fearlessnesses subsumes the ten powers,
there are forty powers and forty fearlessnesses. Nevertheless,
it was previously stated that the first fearlessness is identical to the first power.
The second fearlessness is the tenth power;
the third fearlessness is the second power;
and the fourth fearlessness is the seventh power.
This is explained by way of its characteristics.
In reality, the Blessed One possesses forty powers (*bala*) and forty fearlessnesses (*vaiśāradya*);
however, based on the fundamental [classification], it is simply said that he possesses ten powers and four forms of fearlessness.
Regarding how the name "fearlessness" is established for wisdom:
the question asks,
does this name "fearlessness" refer to the essential nature of the various types of wisdom?
The meaning of the response can be understood from the text.
In reality, fearlessness culminates in the very essence of wisdom;
this is the Master’s interpretation.
In reality, fearlessness is accomplished by means of wisdom;
wisdom is the cause,
and fearlessness is the result.
One should not say that the essence is itself wisdom.
Therefore, the *Nyāyānusāra* (Treatise on Correct Reasoning), fascicle 75, asks:
"How can it be said that fearlessness is itself wisdom?"
One should say that fearlessness is accomplished by wisdom;
this is indeed logically correct.
However, it is stated thus merely to demonstrate that wisdom is the immediate cause of fearlessness.
Therefore, fearlessness is realized through wisdom. Now,
as for fearlessness, it means the absence of timidity or dread.
Because one possesses wisdom, one does not feel fear toward others;

therefore, wisdom serves as the causal nature of fearlessness (*vaiśāradya*). Furthermore, it is explained that the Master [Vasubandhu], recounting the Sautrāntika interpretation, maintains that the essential nature of fearlessness exists separately from wisdom.
If the *Nyāya* [school] asks: "Apart from cognition (*jñāna*), what is its distinct substantial entity?"—[the answer is:
"The Buddha’s three foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) which extend to objects that are favorable, unfavorable, or both.
This is the third section, clarifying the three foundations of mindfulness.
Regarding the question and the response in verse,
the treatise states: "As for reaching the third application of mindfulness," this explains the three applications of mindfulness mentioned in the preceding line and the subsequent line.
First, the general indication as stated in the Sūtra;
second, the specific explanation in three parts:
first, when encountering favorable objects, one does not give rise to joy, but dwells in right mindfulness and clear comprehension.
Second, when encountering adverse objects, one does not give rise to sorrow, but dwells in right mindfulness and clear comprehension.
Third, when encountering favorable or adverse objects, one does not give rise to joy or sorrow, but dwells in right mindfulness and clear comprehension.
The *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra* states:
As four were previously explained, three are now further explained.
One may say in total that there are seven applications of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*),
because these three are subsumed within the previous four.
This means they are comprised within the mindfulness-establishment (smṛtyupasthāna) that takes external phenomena as its object.
Furthermore, the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* (Vibhāṣā), fascicle 30, states:
"These three types of uncommon mindfulness-establishments..."
One should know that these are also subsumed within the power of knowing what is possible and what is impossible (*sthānāsthāna-jñānabala*).
The detailed analysis of their meaning should be contemplated according to reason.
As for the statement that these three all have mindfulness and wisdom as their essence:
The preceding phrase, "mindfulness and wisdom," establishes the essential nature [of this practice].
Regarding the passage from "all great śrāvakas" up to "unshared Buddha-dharmas":
Question:
These three applications of mindfulness can also be fully possessed by Śrāvakas;
why, then, are they called the unique qualities (āveṇika-dharma) of the Buddha alone?
Regarding the statement that "only the Buddha attains here the name of the 'Unshared'":
the answer is that it is only the Buddha who, amidst the joy and sorrow of his disciples, [remains unshaken].
Not only are the afflictions eliminated, but their habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) are also severed;
therefore, it is called "unshared.
This is because the śrāvakas still possess the habitual tendencies of joy and sorrow. Alternatively, it refers to all disciples who have gone forth from the household life.
All of them are subject to the Buddha, being either compliant, non-compliant,
or both compliant and non-compliant.
One should feel profound joy and sorrow;
that the Buddha can remain unmoved is truly marvelous.
This is not because the Śrāvakas lack such joy and sorrow, for their inability to do so is not extraordinary.
Although the śrāvakas and others have disciples,
these merely dwell in dependence upon them and do not truly belong to them;
those who truly belong [to him] belong only to the Great Teacher, the Buddha.
Therefore, the name "unshared" (āveṇika) applies exclusively to the Buddha.
Regarding the statement that the great compassion of the Buddhas surpasses all other forms of compassion due to eight causes:
this is the fourth [section], clarifying the great compassion of the Buddha.
The Commentary says: "As for those who possess shared compassion," this explains the first phrase.
The Great Compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) of the Tathāgata has conventional wisdom (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*) as its nature.
If one were other than such a conventional knower,
one would be unable to take all sentient beings as an object,
nor would one be able to form the mental aspect of the three types of suffering.
Just as ordinary compassion has non-hatred as its nature and takes sentient beings of the desire realm as its object, perceiving them through the aspect of the suffering of suffering—
on what basis is the name "great compassion" established?
The second and third phrases of the verse are now explained;
this constitutes the question.
Regarding the phrase "because it relies upon five meanings... up to because it can equal this": [the explanation follows].
The meaning of the response can be understood from the text.
Regarding the phrase "the difference between this [compassion] and pity (karuṇā), up to the difference between [compassion] and compassion with concern (anukampā)," this explains the fourth line.
This clarifies that great compassion (mahākaruṇā) differs from ordinary compassion (karuṇā). Great compassion has non-delusion as its essential nature,
whereas compassion has non-hatred as its essential nature.
The aspect of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) is the practice of the three sufferings; the aspect of compassion (*karuṇā*) is the practice of the suffering of suffering.
Great compassion takes sentient beings of the three realms as its object.
Compassion takes sentient beings of the desire realm as its object;
great compassion relies upon the fourth dhyāna,
while ordinary compassion may rely upon any of the other dhyānas.
Great compassion relies exclusively upon the Buddha-body;
ordinary compassion extends to relying upon other bodies as well.
Great compassion is realized by departing from the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*).
Compassion is realized through detachment from the desire realm;
great compassion accomplishes the welfare of others;
ordinary compassion is merely an aspiration.

Great compassion equally uproots suffering for all sentient beings, whereas ordinary compassion is unequal, as it uproots suffering only for those sentient beings in the desire realm. Question: By what power is this great compassion subsumed? Answer: It is subsumed by the power of knowledge regarding the possible and the impossible (*sthānāsthāna-jñānabala*).
Because most of the Buddha-Bhagavān’s unique qualities (*āveṇika-guṇa*) are subsumed within the power of knowing what is possible and impossible (*sthānāsthāna-jñānabala*),
the distinction among the qualities of the Buddhas has already been established. As for the differences that exist among the various Buddhas:
This is the fifth [section], clarifying the similarities and differences among Buddhas.
It concludes with the summary verse and its response.
The Treatise says: "Because they have reached the ultimate equality," and so forth.
This explains the first two lines.
It is due to three equalities.
First, because the two types of provisions—merit and wisdom—have been equally perfected over three incalculable eons (*asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*).
Second, because it is accomplished through the fivefold dharma-body and so forth;
third, because the sentient beings to be converted for the benefit of others have reached their ultimate fulfillment.
Regarding the phrase "from lifespan and lineage to the distinctions of capacity": [it refers to these factors].
The following two lines explain the distinctions among Buddhas;
for there are some Buddhas whose lifespan is one hundred years.
There may be Buddhas whose lifespans are twenty thousand years and so forth. "Species" (*gotra*) refers to their general category;
this is stated according to the general sense.
"Lineage" (*jāti*) refers to the specific lineages within those categories.
One should know that within each of the lineages there are many clans.
Gautama is one clan among the Kṣatriyas;
those born of the Gautama [lineage] are called Gautamas.
The old term "Gautama" is a corruption.
I have heard that in the past, a member of the Kṣatriya caste was usurped by bandits;
when his father died, his son fled.
There was a rishi who compassionately took in his son and raised him,
thinking to himself that the lineage should not be severed for want of descendants.
Later, the boy gradually grew up.
An astrologer informed the hostile king that the Kṣatriya still possessed the "star-jewel.
The hostile king then issued a reward to recruit people to capture him.
The immortal departed.
Later, he was captured and brought before King Vairaṇya.
The resentful king pursued him, intending to punish his person for his transgression;
the seer returned to his dwelling,
but the young child was not to be seen.
Observing where he was located, [the deity] went to that place;
knowing that he could not be revived,
[the deity] urged the child from afar to rise according to worldly sentiments.
He hoped to leave behind his physical remains;
