however, the young child was so afflicted by suffering that he would not comply with this intention.
The immortal then transformed into a cloud of honey to shield and conceal him.
As a fine rain sprinkled down, his suffering hunger was momentarily stilled.
A woman appeared to stir his thoughts;
because of this, the boy discharged semen onto the ground.
The rishi wrapped it in cow dung and returned;
he brought it to his sugarcane grove,
where, upon contact with the sunlight, the dung ball opened and was cut.
A son was born, whose physical form was exceptionally sublime;
later, he grew up to become a king.
For this reason, it was traditionally transmitted as the "Cow-Feces Lineage," or called the "Earth Lineage," or the "Sun Lineage"— Kāśyapa.
This is translated as "Drinking Light" (Kāśyapa), which is one of the clans among the Brahmins. Some Buddhas have bodies one zhang and six chi tall;
others have bodies even taller than this.
There are some Buddhas whose Dharma remains for a thousand years after their parinirvāṇa;
there are some Buddhas whose Dharma remains for as little as seven days after their parinirvāṇa.
The rest of the text may be understood accordingly.

For those wise ones who have developed deep affection and reverence, the following section briefly elucidates the Buddha’s virtues based on the preceding context, exhorting people to practice and study; it does so by stating the titles and enumerating the categories.
What are these three? [The text] asks:
"First, the perfection of causes, up to third, the perfection of benefits."
Answer: To list the names of the three virtues:
first, from the virtue of the perfection of causes up to the cultivation of non-arrogance.
The following is a detailed explanation.
This explanation of the perfection of causes further consists of four kinds,
as can be understood from the text.
Next, regarding the phrase "the perfection of the fruit reaching beyond a hundred thousand days," this explains the second perfection of the fruit, which also has four aspects.
The first is wisdom (*jñāna*).
Second, abandonment;
third, majestic power;
fourth, the form body. Furthermore, regarding the perfection of wisdom, there are four kinds of virtues.
First, the wisdom of self-mastery,
because it is realized through one's own awakening; second, omniscience.
The first is the knowledge of the essence of all phenomena; the third is the knowledge of all modes,
which knows the distinct functions of all phenomena.
Alternatively, the knowledge of all things (*sarvajñā*) cognizes the specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) of all phenomena,
while the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñā*) cognizes their common characteristics (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*).
Alternatively, the knowledge of all things realizes ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*).
The perfection of omniscience regarding conventional phenomena consists of the four types of effortless wisdom (*anābhoga-jñāna*),
because they arise spontaneously without the need for applied effort (*prayoga*). Second, the perfection of abandonment also has four kinds.
1. The attainment of analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) through the abandonment of all afflictive hindrances (*kleśāvaraṇa*).
2. The attainment of non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) through the abandonment of all meditative hindrances and non-afflicted ignorance (*akliṣṭājñāna*).
3. The state of ultimate abandonment, which consists in not falling back from the abandonment of the aforementioned two hindrances.
This distinguishes [the practitioner] from those of dull faculties.
Fourth, they not only sever the afflictions but also sever their habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*),
which distinguishes them from those of the Two Vehicles.
The habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of delusion have no separate essence;
it is simply that when these tendencies are absent, they are termed "severed.
This severance, too, has no separate essence.
Within this context, one should also separately explain the obstacles to the abandonment of the faculties (*indriya*) and so forth;
the mention of the obstacles to meditative concentration (*samādhi-āvaraṇa*) serves as an illustration that can be understood by analogy, as they are of the same category.
Alternatively, it may not have been stated in brief.
Furthermore, according to what is clarified herein,
the attainment of abandonment applies to both types of cessation.
Alternatively, the virtue of abandonment (*prahāṇa-guṇa*) consists solely of analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*);
however, if stated inclusively, it also extends to non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
This passage concerning the virtue of abandonment refers to both the primary and the inclusive sense.
Therefore, it encompasses both types of cessation.
The preceding explanation of the virtue of abandonment (prahāṇa-guṇa) was based on the primary [meaning], and thus referred exclusively to analytical cessation (pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha).
The third, the perfection of majestic power (*prabhāva*), also has four aspects.
First, regarding external objects that previously did not exist,
they may suddenly be manifested as existing now.
At times, that which previously existed undergoes transformation, departing from its original state;
through the sovereign power of miraculous transformation, it remains sustained and maintained.
Second, regarding the lifespan, they may shorten it to eighty years or extend it for three months; third,
they possess sovereign power over space, obstructions, and extreme distances, being able to travel swiftly through them all.
Some lie prostrate in mid-air; some can cross over even the most extreme obstructions;
some travel with great speed to the furthest reaches;
and some cause tiny mustard seeds and the vast Mount Sumeru to enter into one another.
Through sovereign power,
wherever the four Buddhas go, they cause the various natures of worldly flowers, fruits,
and other things to undergo a natural transformation that is far more excellent than before.

Regarding the marvelous majesty, there are furthermore four kinds of majesty and perfect qualities, which may be understood from the text. Fourthly, the perfect qualities of the form-body (*rūpakāya*) also consist of four kinds.
First, he is endowed with the thirty-two marks of a great man;
second, he is endowed with the eighty secondary characteristics;
third, he is endowed with great power.
The power is as previously explained;
the fourth [power] may be understood accordingly.
Regarding the final quality of perfected benefit, it leads those of the three vehicles to the happy realms.
Among the three preceding [categories], the virtue of perfecting the subsequent benefit also has four kinds:
namely, causing permanent liberation from the three evil destinies constitutes three;
and causing permanent liberation from birth and death within the good destinies constitutes one.
Therefore, they are called "four": either because one can establish [beings] in the happy realms as the first, and further establish them in the three vehicles as the [remaining] three;
thus, they are called "four."
The general exposition of the Tathāgata being like a great mountain of jewels is as stated above;
a detailed exposition would be inexhaustible.
This reveals the mountain of jewels consisting of the Buddha’s three virtues;
that there are foolish people who cannot even believe in or revere it is a lament for the ignorance and lack of faith of such fools.
Regarding those wise ones who will surely attain cessation in the future:
they praise wisdom and obtain merit,
because by relying on the Buddha, they bring forth five kinds of fruits.
First, one attains the fruit of non-futility,
because when one sees the Buddha, one necessarily obtains the fruit.
Second, one attains the fruit of what is desirable.
Third, because one attains the fruit of excellence;
fourth, because one attains the fruit of swiftness;
fifth, because one attains the fruit of ultimate nirvāṇa.
The cited verse makes this clear.
The *Nyāyānusāra* and the *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya-ṭīkā-tattvārthā* explain the three aspects of the Buddha: his causes, his results, and his beneficent qualities.
Furthermore, they agree with this present treatise.
Having already explained [the qualities] up to this point regarding the Tathāgata, that which is now to be distinguished is as follows:
the second major section below clarifies the common qualities (*sādhāraṇa-guṇa*). Within this:
First, the general designation of the names; second, the detailed explanation. This constitutes the general designation that concludes the preceding section and introduces the following.
The verse says: "Reaching [the goal] and also sharing with ordinary beings" clarifies the Buddha’s shared virtues.

That is to say: the absence of conflict (*araṇā*), the knowledge resulting from aspiration (*praṇidhijñāna*), the four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*), the six supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), the four dhyānas, the four formless attainments (*ārūpyasamāpatti*), the eight meditative absorptions (*samāpatti*), the three samādhis, the four immeasurables (*apramāṇa*), the eight liberations (*vimokṣa*), the eight spheres of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*), and the ten spheres of totality (*kṛtsnāyatana*).
According to what is appropriate:
that is to say, the first three gates are shared only with the two vehicles,
while the supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*), and so forth, are also shared with ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*).
The *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra* states:
"Although all the aspects of merit within the Buddha’s body are pure, sublime, and sovereign—
and thus differ from the merits of the śrāvakas and others— "
Nevertheless, they are called "common" because they are similar by category.
Regarding those afflictions with objective referents (*savastuka-kleśa*) that exist within the desire realm among the first three categories,
this is the second section, which provides a detailed explanation.
Among these, first is the clarification of virtues shared with the sages,
and second is the clarification of virtues shared with ordinary beings. Within the clarification of virtues shared with the sages:
First, the elucidation of the practice of non-contention;
second, the elucidation of the cultivation of the knowledge of vows;
third, the elucidation of the unhindered analytical knowledges.
"Attaining the concentration of the limit of the four reliances; this is the first [section] clarifying the practice of non-contention (*araṇā*).
Regarding the statement in the treatise, "having conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*) as its nature," this explains the first phrase.
The *Śāstranāmavyākhyāna* (Explanation of Terms) sets forth the essential nature [of the dispute].
Thus, the *Nyāyabindu* states: "However, all disputes are comprised of three types in total."
Because there are distinctions between the aggregates (*skandha*), disputes (*vāda*), and afflictions (*kleśa*):
"aggregate-dispute" refers to death;
"dispute" refers to strife.
The "contention of afflictions" refers to the one hundred and eight afflictions.
It is because of this power of conventional knowledge that one is able to cease the contention of afflictions.
"Attaining the name 'Non-contention' (araṇā)" refers to the fourth dhyāna. "Reaching the afflictions of another's body" explains the second phrase.
The fourth dhyāna serves as its basis,
because it is the most excellent among the four modes of practice characterized by ease (*sukha-pratipad*).
The term "immovable" (*akopya*) distinguishes it from the previous five spiritual lineages (*gotra*).

The term "fruit of arhatship" (arhattvaphala) excludes those still in training (śaikṣa). Among the fruits of arhatship, only those of the sixth lineage—the immovable (akopyadharman)—are able to give rise to it;
neither the other five lineages nor those still in training can do so.
Others are not even able to prevent the arising of delusions within themselves,
much less be able to cease the afflictions of others' bodies.
This is because it relies solely upon [the stage of] "arrival" to take the universal object as its sphere.
The following two lines are explained:
this [attainment] relies exclusively upon the human bodies of the three continents, because their faculties are sharp; it does not rely on other places.
This refers to the defilements to be abandoned through cultivation that take the future objects of the desire realm as their conditions;
it is not because other defilements take already-arisen things as their conditions.
This applies to all defilements abandoned through insight that lack a [corresponding] objective basis.
It cannot be prevented; it arises from delusion regarding the principles of truth,
because internally it arises by taking its objects as a whole according to its specific mode.
Regarding the phrase "having already distinguished the absence of contention, it takes that as its object":
this is the second [section], which clarifies the Knowledge of Aspiration (*praṇidhijñāna*).
Its definition can be understood from the name itself.
The intrinsic nature of this knowledge resulting from aspiration is conventional knowledge;
its stage is the fourth dhyāna;
its lineage is the unshakable.
The physical basis is the human body of the three continents,
which is the same as for the *araṇā* [the state free from conflict]; the only difference is the object of focus.
Because it is able to universally take as its object all phenomena of the three realms and the three times.
Regarding the statement that "the Vaibhāṣikas are like farmers," some Vaibhāṣikas have said this: [text continues].
The knowledge of aspiration cannot directly realize the formless realm; however,
by observing the specific characteristics of the causal conduct that leads one to enter the formless realm— namely, its state of tranquility—
one is then able to infer the fruit of the formless realm.
When observing that initial mind emerging from the formless realm,
because its specific outflow fruit (niṣyanda-phala) is still tranquil,
it is called an "outflow" (niṣyanda) because it resembles that formless realm mind.
One is then able to infer the prior absence of the cause for formlessness,
just as a farmer infers the seed upon seeing the sprout,
or infers the sprout upon seeing the seed.
This is not correct reasoning.
One should state it thus:
that formlessness is realized through direct knowledge.
Therefore, the *Vibhāṣā* (179) states: Question:
How does the knowledge resulting from aspiration (*praṇidhijñāna*) know the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*)?
Some say it is by means of observing the outflow (*niṣyanda*) and the distinctions in activity (*carita*).
It is like a person traveling along a road who knows the destination they are heading toward.
Some say that if this were so, the knowledge resulting from aspiration (praṇidhijñāna) would be inferential cognition (anumānajñāna) rather than direct perception (pratyakṣajñāna).
To this, one should reply as follows:
This knowledge of aspiration does not observe the cause to know the effect, nor does it observe the effect to know the cause;
therefore, this knowledge is direct perception (*pratyakṣa-jñāna*) and not inference (*anumāna-jñāna*). Furthermore, the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* states:
Question: What is the difference between the knowledge of recollecting past lives (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛtijñāna*) and the knowledge resulting from aspiration that takes the past as its object?
Furthermore, regarding the knowledge of recollecting past lives:
One knows the five aggregates with outflows (*sāsrava*).
This knowledge of aspiration (*praṇidhijñāna*) knows all aggregates, both with and without outflows.
Furthermore, there is the knowledge of recollecting past abodes (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛtijñāna*).
One knows the five aggregates of the desire realm and the form realm.
Through this knowledge of aspiration (*praṇidhijñāna*), one knows the aggregates of the three realms as well as those that are unconditioned (*apratisaṃyukta*). Furthermore:
The knowledge of recollecting past lives (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛtijñāna*) knows the common characteristics (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*) of the aggregates (*skandha*).
This knowledge resulting from prayer (*praṇidhijñāna*) knows both the specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) and the common characteristics of the aggregates. Furthermore, it is said:
Question: What is the difference between the knowledge of others' minds and the knowledge of vows that takes the present as its object?
Furthermore, the knowledge of others' minds takes a single entity as its objective sphere.
This knowledge resulting from aspiration takes either a single object or multiple objects as its objective field.
Furthermore, the knowledge of others' minds takes the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) as its objective field.
This knowledge resulting from aspiration takes as its objects both specific and general characteristics.
Furthermore, the knowledge of others' minds takes the mental continuum of another as its object.
This knowledge resulting from aspiration takes as its object the mental continua of both oneself and others. Furthermore,
the knowledge of others' minds takes as its objects the mind and mental factors.
This knowledge resulting from prayer (*praṇidhijñāna*) takes the five aggregates as its object. Furthermore, it is said:
"Question: How can the knowledge resulting from prayer know the future?
Some say it is known by means of inference based on the past and the present."
Just as a farmer, having sown seeds, knows by inference that such a fruit will arise,
so it is with this case as well. Some say:
If that were so, the knowledge resulting from aspiration (*praṇidhijñāna*) would be an inference (*anumāna*) rather than a direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
It should be stated thus:
this knowledge resulting from aspiration knows the effect without depending on the observation of its cause.
Therefore, this wisdom is direct perception (*pratyakṣa-jñāna*) and not inferential cognition (*anumāna-jñāna*).
For those who wish to give rise to [the knowledge] that reaches all things as they truly are,
this clarifies the preparatory application (*prayoga*).
Intending to arouse the knowledge resulting from aspiration (*praṇidhijñāna*), one first makes a sincere vow to seek knowledge of that object.
One then enters and emerges from the eight meditative attainments of the mind with their forward and reverse sequences.
Finally, at a later time, one enters the ultimate fourth dhyāna as the preparatory application (*prayoga*).
Immediately following this concentration, according to the superior or inferior strength of the power of the previously entered "limitless concentration" (prāntakoṭika-samādhi),
right knowledge arises as led by the force of one's prior vow;
this is called "vow-knowledge" (praṇidhijñāna).
One knows all sought-after objects exactly as they are.
Having already explained the knowledge resulting from aspiration (*praṇidhijñāna*), the remainder is as described for the absence of conflict (*araṇā*).
This constitutes the third [section], clarifying the four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*).
The Commentary states: "As for 'further revealing the objects of cognition,' this explains the first verse.
Unimpeded comprehension and decisive discernment regarding an object is termed 'unimpeded analytical knowledge' (*pratisaṃvid*)."
Because these possess sharp faculties, they are called those with "knowledge of non-retrogression.

That is to say, the knowledge of non-retrogression takes as its object the designations of the dharmas—namely, the collections of names (*nāma-kāya*), phrases (*pada-kāya*), and phonemes (*vyañjana-kāya*)—and establishes this as the first [of the knowledges].
The *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra*, fascicle 76, states:
That which indicates the referent object is called a "name" (*nāman*);
that is to say, it is what expresses the meaning of the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of a phenomenon.
That which distinguishes the referent object is called a "phrase" (*pada*).
This refers to the meaning of the differentiation of dharmas.
That which does not depend on the sound of the meaning but is able to serve as the basis for the arising of cognition by itself is called "vyañjana" (phoneme/letter);
these are [the phonemes] ka, ca, ṭa, ta, pa, and so forth.
Logically, there must be an awareness that does not depend on the sound of the meaning;
this awareness cannot be without an object of cognition (*ālambana*).
This object of cognition is what is called the "syllable" (*vyañjana*).
"Phrases" (vyañjana) refers to that which cannot directly perceive the meaning;
rather, they serve as the basis for names (nāman) and phrases (pada) to express that meaning.
These three [names, phrases, and phrases] are able to sustain all the meanings they express.
Furthermore, because it gives rise to understanding through its mode of operation (*vṛtti*), it is called "Dharma" (*dharma*).
These three self-natures (*trisvabhāva*) are taught as the "body" (*kāya*),
for "self-nature" (*svabhāva*), "entity" (*tattva*), and "body" (*kāya*) are synonymous terms.
Third, because sound and its meaning are extremely closely intertwined,
when they arise as objects to produce cognition,
their distinct characteristics are difficult to discern.

Therefore, the statement regarding the "body" (kāya) is taught to reveal that it possesses a distinct substance; this concludes the treatise. Excluding names, phrases, and phonemes, one establishes the second analytical knowledge of meaning (*arthapratisaṃvid*) by taking as its object the referents expressed [by those linguistic units]. One takes as objects the various expressions used in all regions.

The third analytical knowledge (pratisaṃvid) is established as the analytical knowledge of eloquence (*pratibhāna-pratisaṃvid*). It takes as its object unimpeded speech that accords with correct reasoning;
this unimpeded speech is termed "eloquence" (*pratibhāna*).
Furthermore, it takes as its objects the two paths of concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*), which manifest spontaneously through mastery.
Because of the existence of the Path, one possesses the capacity to respond skillfully to sentient beings with unimpeded eloquence;
since the Path is the cause of discernment (*pratibhāna*), it is itself called discernment.
This is established as the fourth analytical knowledge, the analytical knowledge of eloquence (*pratibhāna-pratisaṃvid*).
Therefore, the *Nyāyānusāra* states:
"If there were no regression of knowledge, one could speak of it as being in accordance with correct principle (*nyāya*) without obstruction;
furthermore, by taking the concentration of mastery (*vaśitā-samādhi*) and the two paths of wisdom (*prajñā-mārga*) as the object, it is established as the fourth [knowledge]."
The ability to correctly proclaim both the words and their meaning with unimpeded speech is called *pratibhāna*.
Furthermore, the sovereign capacity by which all attained qualities manifest spontaneously without the need for further application (*prayoga*) is also called *pratibhāna*.
This is that which is capable of giving rise to and establishing analysis by means of analysis;
the knowledge that discerns and analyzes [phenomena] along with their causes is called the unimpeded analytical knowledge (*pratisaṃvid*).
This is explained at length as in that commentary.
This is a general statement regarding the essence of the analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*),
which also reveals their objects of focus.
Among these, the [analytical knowledge of] phenomena and [the analytical knowledge of] language extend up to the stage where vitarka and vicāra are absent.
Explanation of the fifth and sixth phrases:
Among the four [unhindered knowledges], the two—dharma-pratisaṃvid and nirukti-pratisaṃvid—are subsumed under conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*) alone.
They are not untainted knowledge (*anāsrava-jñāna*), because they take as their objective domain the bases of name-groups (*nāmakāya*) and so forth, as well as worldly terminology and phenomena.
This constitutes the definition of its essential nature. Regarding the statement "it relies on the stages":
the analytical knowledge of phenomena (dharma-pratisaṃvid) relies universally upon five stages;
that is, it relies upon the desire realm and the four fundamental dhyānas.
Because names and so forth do not exist in the higher stages,
and because those [beings] do not separately take the names and so forth of the lower stages as objects;
furthermore, the *Vibhāṣā* (180) states:
The "ground" refers to the analytical knowledge of phenomena (dharma-pratisaṃvid).
Some say it exists on two grounds:
namely, the desire realm and the first dhyāna.
Some say it exists in five stages,
namely the desire realm and the four dhyānas;
others say it exists in seven stages.
This refers to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), the threshold concentration (*anāgamya*), the intermediate dhyāna (*dhyānāntara*), and the four dhyānas; however, there is no commentary on this.
The explanation states that the initial mention is based on the name, as it follows the linguistic convention of the connection [to the realms].
The unimpeded analytical knowledge of dharma (dharmapratisaṃvid) relies solely on two stages;
as for the latter two [analytical knowledges], they are designated according to the name and bound to the body.
The unimpeded analytical knowledge of dharma, however, extends throughout the higher stages.
Regarding the difficulty of [the object] being a dharma that serves as a condition, it must necessarily depend on its own level and take dharmas of its own level as objects;
this treatise, the *Nyāyānusāra*, and the *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya-ṭīkā-tattvārthā* all agree with the second explanation in the *Mahāvibhāṣā*, which takes the five levels as correct.
The analytical knowledge of unimpeded eloquence (*nirukti-pratisaṃvid*) relies exclusively upon two stages:
namely, the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and the first fundamental dhyāna (*mauladhyāna*).
This is because, in the higher stages, there is an absence of applied and sustained thought (*vitarka-vicāra*), and thus speech necessarily does not exist there.
"Because the difficulty regarding the object consists in [the knowledge] being restricted to its own level,
whereas the analytical knowledge of meaning arises in all cases" explains the seventh and eighth phrases.
The analytical knowledge of meaning (arthapratisaṃvid) is comprised by either ten knowledges or six knowledges;
that is to say, if all phenomena are designated as "meaning" (artha).
The analytical knowledge of meaning (arthapratisaṃvid) is comprised of ten knowledges.

According to some explanations in the *Abhidharmamahāvibhāṣā*, it has eight knowledges as its nature, excluding the knowledge of exhaustion (kṣayajñāna) and the knowledge of non-arising (anutpādajñāna),
because this analytical knowledge is of the nature of vision (darśana).
If only nirvāṇa is designated as "meaning," then the analytical knowledge of meaning (arthapratisaṃvid) is comprised of six knowledges:
namely, conventional, dharma, subsequent, cessation, exhaustion, and non-arising.
The *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* states that [the analytical knowledges] have four knowledges as their nature, excluding the knowledge of exhaustion and the knowledge of non-arising,
because the analytical knowledges are of the nature of vision (*darśana*).
It is established that the analytical knowledges are subsumed within nine knowledges.
This means that, with the exception of the knowledge of cessation,
it takes verbal expression, concentration, wisdom, and the path as its objects. Regarding this,
some in the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* state that there are seven knowledges.
Exhausted and non-arising; because this unimpeded analytical knowledge (pratisaṃvid) is the very nature of seeing.
This constitutes its essential substance. As for the phrase "relying on the stages" (bhūmi):
These two [supernormal powers] arise based on all stages,
namely from the desire realm up to the Peak of Existence; however,
verbal expression occurs only within the desire realm and the first dhyāna.
Regarding how the analytical knowledge of eloquence (pratibhāna-pratisaṃvid) applies to all nine [categories]:
it is because it is accepted that the analytical knowledge of eloquence can arise in relation to either the teaching or the path, depending on the specific conditions.
Therefore, it pervades the nine stages.
Regarding the *Prakaraṇapāda-śāstra* reaching four types of sequence,
this describes the *Prakaraṇapāda*.
To explain these four terms:
the non-retrogressive knowledge that takes names, phrases, and phonemes as its object is established as the analytical knowledge of phenomena (*dharmapratisaṃvid*).
The non-retrogressive knowledge that takes the various meanings expressed by those names and so forth as its object is established as the analytical knowledge of meaning (*arthapratisaṃvid*).

The term "condition" (pratyaya) refers precisely to this meaning, distinguished by whether it is expressed as a singular, dual, or plural, or by whether it is in the masculine, feminine, or neuter gender.
Non-retrogressive wisdom is established as the analytical knowledge of language (*nirukti-pratisaṃvid*),
because one speaks without impediment regarding these verbal expressions.
Furthermore, regarding the exposition of the bases— the two paths of meditative concentration and wisdom—
it is because one is able to teach by means of these paths that the non-retrogressive knowledge is established as the analytical knowledge of eloquence (*pratibhāna-pratisaṃvid*).
First, that which expresses arises; subsequently, one apprehends the meaning.
Once the meaning has been apprehended, speech then occurs without obstruction.
It is by virtue of this sequence of priority and posteriority that the fourfold order is revealed.
The statement by other masters that [the power] extends to where there is no obstruction describes a divergent view;
since the terms *vāc* (speech) and *pratibhāna* (eloquence) are synonymous, they are explained here in relation to one another.
Regarding the statement, "Because of the distinction between phenomena (*dharma*) and meaning (*artha*),
they are not manifested as opposites," and the traditional teaching that "these four reach the analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*)," this clarifies the preparatory application (*prayoga*).
According to a tradition of the Vaibhāṣika masters,
these four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*) arise in the following order:

the preliminary practice for the analytical knowledge of phenomena (*dharmapratisaṃvid*) consists of the repeated cultivation of calculation regarding the bodies of names (*nāma*), phrases (*pada*), and phonemes (*vyañjana*).
Thoroughly practicing the Buddha’s words to understand the meanings of all phenomena is the preparatory application for the analytical knowledge of meaning (*arthapratisaṃvid*).
Thoroughly practicing the treatises on grammar and linguistics regarding verbal expression is the preparatory application for the analytical knowledge of language (*niruktipratisaṃvid*).

Thoroughly practicing the principles of establishing and refuting through the study of logic (*hetuvidyā*), including the reasons (*hetu*) and examples (*dṛṣṭānta*), serves as the preparatory application for the analytical knowledge of eloquence (*pratibhānapratisaṃvid*).
If one has not attained skillfulness in these four areas, [one cannot achieve it].
This is because one would necessarily be unable to produce the unimpeded analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*).
This is not the correct principle; in reality, all [attainments] are capable of serving as preparatory applications (*prayoga*).
The Master of the Treatise states the correct principle:
In reality, all unhindered knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*) arise;
however, only by training in the Buddha’s words can one perform the preparatory application (*prayoga*).
Because the Buddha’s words fully elucidate the four aspects of dharma, meaning, phrasing, and eloquence.
Therefore, the *Vibhāṣā* (180), in the section of the *pūrvapakṣa*, states: "Thus it is said."
The four analytical knowledges (pratisaṃvid) all take the practice of the Buddha’s words as their preliminary application (prayoga).
For example, within a single verse, one should speak thus: "That name is to be spoken; such is the name. This is called "practice" (abhyāsa).
This is the preparatory application for the analytical knowledge of phenomena (*dharmapratisaṃvid*).
One should understand its meaning in this way; practicing such an understanding of the meaning is the preparatory application for the analytical knowledge of meaning (*arthapratisaṃvid*).
One should train in these words and practice training in these words;
this is the application for the analytical knowledge of language (*nirukti-pratisaṃvid*).
One should speak without impediment in this manner.
Practicing such unimpeded exposition is the preparatory application (*prayoga*) for the analytical knowledge of eloquence (*pratibhāna-pratisaṃvid*). Therefore,
all four types of analytical knowledge take the practice of the Buddha’s word as their preparatory application.
"These four kinds can be called 'attainment' (prāpti).
This explains the ninth phrase,
demonstrating that attainment must necessarily be possessed.
Because at the time of attaining the fourth limit-attainment concentration (*prāntakoṭika-samādhi*),
the four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*) arise with mastery,
they are said to be "fully possessed."
Therefore, the text below states:
"Although the analytical knowledge of language (nirukti-pratisaṃvid) is attained based upon that [concentration],
its essence is not subsumed under those dhyānas."
Furthermore, the Nyāyānusāra states:
Other masters say that there is the acquisition of non-possession.
One may obtain [the first] without effort,
but one must certainly cause the other four to be obtained.
These four objects of focus are as explained in the *araṇā* (non-contention) discourse.
This explains the tenth phrase.

It reveals the similarities and differences among these four unhindered knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*) in terms of three aspects: their objects (*ālambana*), their intrinsic natures (*svabhāva*), and their levels (*bhūmi*).
The distinction from the aforementioned *araṇā* (non-contention) is as follows.
Regarding the lineage (*gotra*) and the physical basis (*āśraya-deha*), it is as explained in the case of *araṇā*:
namely, one of the immovable lineage (*akopya-gotra*) who relies on a human body from any of the three continents.
Furthermore, the *Abhidharmamahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 180, states:
"All 'worlds' (adhvan) fall within the three times.
The two analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*) of phenomena (*dharma*) and meaning (*artha*) take the three times as their objects."
The unimpeded analytical knowledge of language (nirukti-pratisaṃvid) takes the past as its object when directed toward the past,
the present as its object when directed toward the present,
and the future as its object when it arises in the future.
The unborn does not take the three periods of time as its object.
Some say that "dharma" is identical to "word";
others say that "dharma," "word," and "eloquence" refer to the three analytical knowledges (pratisaṃvid).
The past and present [analytical knowledges] take the past as their object; the future [analytical knowledge] takes the three periods of time as its object.
Regarding the analytical knowledge of meaning (*arthapratisaṃvid*), some maintain that it takes only that which is beyond the three periods of time as its object.
Some maintain that [these] take the three times and that which is beyond time as their objects;
however, there is no master who has provided a formal evaluation of this. Such is what has been stated regarding [the qualities] up to those attained by the Buddha through subsequent application.
This is the fourth [point], clarifying that attainment is achieved by relying on the meditative absorption of the limit (*prāntakoṭika-samādhi*).
The treatise states: "Regarding 'attainment through reaching the meditative absorption of the limit,' this explains the first phrase."
This clarifies that six types are obtained by means of the limit (*prāntakoṭika*),
because they are induced by the power of the limit.
These are the meditative absorptions of the limit (*prāntakoṭika-dhyāna*) which are subsumed under the category of "extreme absorption" (*dhyānāntara*).
Regarding the second phrase, "the six limits":
in summary, the essential nature of the limit-dhyānas consists of six types.
Among the aforementioned six, the analytical knowledge of language (*nirukti-pratisaṃvid*) is excluded because it exists only in the desire realm and the first dhyāna; thus,
five [analytical knowledges] are taken in part.
Because the five existences (*bhava*) are pervasive yet not ultimate,
one takes a small portion of them and adds other limits, namely,
those of extension and contraction, and so forth.
Therefore, the Nyāyānusāra states:
"The essential nature of the ultimate dhyāna consists of six types;
from the preceding six, the 'vocal' [dhyāna] is excluded."
The remaining five [dhyānas] in part, as well as other superior dhyānas acquired through preparatory application (prayoga) outside of these,
are called the "limit-dhyāna" (prāntakoṭika-dhyāna).
Thus, there are six types.

The above is from the treatise. Although the analytical knowledge of language (*nirukti-pratisaṃvid*) relies upon the fourth dhyāna of the ultimate limit (*prāntakoṭika*), it is said to be "attained" because it arises with mastery.

Just as it was said at the time of the Buddha’s attainment of the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) that he had attained the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*), based on his mastery in its arising;
so too, the preceding text states that the four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*) were attained simultaneously.
However, the analytical knowledge of unimpeded eloquence is bound to the first dhyāna;
yet when it is attained at the limit of its development,
its essence is not subsumed under those dhyānas.
Furthermore, according to the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* (Vibhāṣā), fascicle 180, it is stated therein:

"In this context, the knowledge resulting from prayer (*praṇidhi-jñāna*) subsumes the knowledge resulting from prayer, the ultimate knowledge (*prāntakoṭika-jñāna*), the knowledge of non-contention (*araṇa-jñāna*), and the four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*)."

It should be understood that this is the same as the knowledge of aspirations (praṇidhijñāna). The same applies to the analytical knowledge of meaning (arthapratisaṃvid). The knowledge of the ultimate limit (prāntakoṭikajñāna) does not include the analytical knowledge of language (niruktipratisaṃvid).
The rest is as explained regarding the knowledge of aspiration (*praṇidhijñāna*).

The knowledge of non-contention (*araṇājñāna*) subsumes the knowledge of non-contention, the knowledge of aspiration, the knowledge of the ultimate limit (*prāntakoṭikajñāna*), and the analytical knowledge of meaning (*arthapratisaṃvid*).
It does not subsume the three analytical knowledges of phenomena (*dharma*), expression (*nirukti*), and eloquence (*pratibhāna*).
As it is with the absence of contention (*araṇā*),
so it should be understood for the three analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*) of phenomena, expression,
and eloquence; each is described according to its respective inclusion.
Excluding the knowledge of non-contention and the analytical knowledge of language,
and also not including the knowledge of the ultimate limit (*prāntakoṭika-jñāna*),
these seven types are all attained based on the meditative concentration of the ultimate limit (*prāntakoṭika-samādhi*).
Because it is induced by the power of the ultimate concentration (*prāntakoṭika-samādhi*),
the essence of the ultimate dhyāna consists of six types;
that is to say, the seven [limbs] excluding speech.
Because the fourth dhyāna is designated as "limit" (*prāntakoṭika*) when it is of the highest degree; the commentary explains that if one relies on its excellence or its initial arising,
the knowledge resulting from prayer (*praṇidhijñāna*) depends solely upon the fourth dhyāna.
If based on what is not superior,
and based on what arises subsequently,
it also extends to the lower stages down to the desire realm.
Regarding the statement in various treatises that the "knowledge resulting from prayer" (*praṇidhijñāna*) relies upon the fourth dhyāna,

this is based on its preeminence and its initial occurrence. The *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, however, takes a comprehensive view, including cases where it is not preeminent and occurs subsequently.
Therefore, it is said that the analytical knowledge of eloquence (*nirukti-pratisaṃvid*) is subsumed under the knowledge of aspiration (*praṇidhijñāna*).
Furthermore, because it concerns the general names and meanings of all phenomena,
the analytical knowledge of meaning (*artha-pratisaṃvid*) is explained in the same manner as the knowledge of aspiration.
Furthermore, the knowledge of the ultimate limit (prāntakoṭika-jñāna) exists only in the fourth dhyāna; therefore, it does not include the knowledge of language (nirukti-jñāna).
Moreover, the knowledge of non-contention (araṇa-jñāna) takes as its object afflictions that have not yet arisen.
The [unretained] factors, eloquence, and analytical knowledge— these three—
are distinct because the objects of focus for the factors, eloquence, and analytical knowledge each differ; furthermore,
they do not take as their object afflictions that have not yet arisen.
It does not include the knowledge of non-contention (*araṇā*).
Furthermore, because the unimpeded knowledge of language (*nirukti-pratisaṃvid*) exists only in the desire realm and the first dhyāna,
it does not include the knowledge of the ultimate limit (*prāntakoṭika-jñāna*).
Although these seven differ in their respective levels of attachment (*bhūmi*), they are all induced and attained by relying on the power of the *prāntakoṭika* concentration.
As for why the term "limit" (*prānta*) applies only to the fourth dhyāna: [it is because it is the ultimate limit of the form realm].
The explanation of "subsequent attainment" concludes this section. The phrase "this [attainment] reaches the limit of all stages" explains the third line.
This comprises three chapters in total:
first, because this [practice] is universally accordant with all stages;
second, because it increases until reaching the ultimate.
Regarding the third attainment of the name "limit" (*prāntakoṭika*):
what does it mean for this name to be "conducive to reaching the universal"?
This explains the first chapter.
The questions and answers may be understood as before.
As for the phrase "how this is called reaching the ultimate," this explains the second chapter.
The questions and answers may also be understood accordingly.
Thus, the statement regarding "meditative concentration" (*dhyāna*) up to and including "the limit of reality" (*bhūtakoṭi*) explains the third chapter.
Thus, this meditative absorption (dhyāna) receives the name "limit" (prāntakoṭika).
Here, the term "limit" signifies the sense of being unsurpassed;
because no superior state surpasses this concentration, this concentration is called the "limit."
The term "limit" (*koṭi*) is used here to signify the sense of "category," because within this meditative absorption there are many similar types of categories.
This is as when one speaks of the "four limits."
This refers to the demarcation of the four lines within a single verse,
or like the demarcation of the four oceans within a single realm;
all of these signify the meaning of similarity in category.
Alternatively, it reveals the ultimate meaning,
as when it is said that the vajra is the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi),
or as when it is said that the limit of reality of all phenomena is what is called nirvāṇa.
"All are ultimate meanings" refers to the fourth phrase:
"because, with the exception of the Buddha, all others reach the state of sovereign mastery."

With the exception of the Buddha, the six types taught by all other noble ones are acquired solely through application (*prayoga-prāpta*) and not through the abandonment of defilements (*vairāgya-prāpta*),
because they are not attained by everyone.
If one practices the meditative concentration of the ultimate limit (*prāntakoṭika-samādhi*), one attains it;
if one does not practice it, one does not attain it.
Only the Buddha attains these six kinds of qualities through detachment from defilements (*vairāgya-prāpti*).

Subsequently, it manifests spontaneously without depending on preparatory effort (*prayoga*). However, in the *Mahāvibhāṣā*, regarding both the knowledge resulting from aspiration (*praṇidhijñāna*) and the knowledge of non-contention (*araṇājñāna*), it is stated:
"According to this explanation, if it is determinately obtainable, it is acquired through the abandonment of defilements (*vairāgyalābhika*)."
Because it is attained at the moment of the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*),
the subsequent preparatory effort (*prayoga*) manifests; however,
for a Buddha, no preparatory effort is required.
The preparatory application (*prayoga*) of the Pratyekabuddha is inferior;
that of the Śrāvaka is either middling or superior.
Furthermore, there exists the knowledge resulting from aspiration (*praṇidhijñāna*) and the absence of contention (*araṇā*).
It is attained through the preparatory application (*prayoga*) of the *prāntakoṭika* concentration;

it manifests through that same application. The commentary explains: because the *Mahāvibhāṣā* generally refers to a limited portion [of the path], it states that the two vehicles also attain it through the removal of defilements (*vairāgya-lābhika*).
In the *Abhidharmakośa*, because the two vehicles attain [the supernormal powers] through detachment from defilement in an indeterminate manner,
it is stated that they are acquired through preparatory effort (*prayoga*).
Having already explained the first three, we shall now proceed to explain those that are common to all.
Below this, secondly, the shared virtues with ordinary beings are clarified;
that is, the six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍabhijñā*) are explained. Within this:
First, a direct explanation of the six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍabhijñā*);
second, a differentiation of the three kinds of clarity (*vidyā*); third, an explanation of the three demonstrations (*prātihārya*).
4. A detailed explanation of the supernormal power of the divine realm (*ṛddhiviṣaya*). 5. A detailed explanation of the [divine] eye and ear.
6. An explanation of the types of supernormal powers. This is the first [section], the formal explanation of the six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍabhijñā*).
Connecting the preceding section to the subsequent one, the verse says: "Up to the other four [higher knowledges], they are exclusively wholesome.
Regarding this within the verse:
First, the enumeration of names;
second, the definition of its essence;
third, the wisdoms.
Fourth, the stages; fifth, the objects of the supernormal powers;
sixth, the two types of attainment.
The seven applications of mindfulness and the eight [factors] of the three natures.
The treatise says: "Up to 'also shared with ordinary beings'."
The first three phrases explain the enumeration of the names of the six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍabhijñā*).
"Spiritual power" (*ṛddhi*) refers to meditative concentration (*samādhi*); "object" (*viṣaya*) refers to that which is performed.
When wisdom realizes its object without obstruction, it is called "penetration" (*abhijñā*).

It is so named because it arises from meditative concentration, its object, and the capacity for realization; thus, it is termed the "supernormal power of the penetration of knowledge regarding the objective field" (*ṛddhiviṣayajñānasākṣātkriyābhijñā*).
Although other supernormal powers also rely on meditative concentration,
these particular powers have such distinct characteristics that they are specifically designated by the term "supernatural power" (*ṛddhi*).
The divine eye and divine ear are the sense faculties upon which they depend.
Knowledge (*jñāna*) is the wisdom (*prajñā*) associated with these two consciousnesses.
Because it perceives its two objects without obstruction, it is called "supernormal knowledge" (*abhijñā*).
It is designated by way of its faculty (*indriya*) and its capacity for realization.
These are called the supernormal power of the realization of knowledge of the divine eye, the supernormal power of the realization of knowledge of the divine ear,
and the supernormal power of the realization of knowledge of others' minds; they are named after their preparatory application and the knowledge that realizes them.
It is named "the supernormal knowledge of the realization of the recollection of past lives" based on its object, its association, and the realizing wisdom.
If it is Nirvana, it is named "the exhaustion of the outflows."

It is named "the supernormal knowledge of the realization of the destruction of the outflows" (āsravakṣayajñānasākṣātkriyābhijñā) based on both that which is realized and the realizing wisdom. If the body in which the outflows are destroyed is called "one whose outflows are destroyed" (kṣīṇāsrava), [then this is the case].
It is named "the supernormal knowledge of the realization of the destruction of the outflows" (āsravakṣayajñānasākṣātkriyābhijñā) based on its support and the realizing wisdom that constitutes it.
Among the six supernormal knowledges, this sixth one belongs exclusively to the noble ones (ārya).
The first five supernormal powers (abhijñā) belong to ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*); for the most part, speaking in general terms, they are shared with worldlings.
Thus, these six supernormal powers extend to the meaning of manifesting beyond obstructions.
Explaining the fourth phrase:
the term "liberation" (vimukti) is used here to indicate the initial emergence from obstructions.
In reality, it is also possible for the path of superior progress (*viśeṣamārga*) to arise.
Therefore, the *Nyāyānusāra* (Treatise on Right Reasoning), fascicle 76, states:
"The term 'path of liberation' (*vimuktimārga*) signifies the sense of emerging from obstacles."
Since it is also possible for [these powers] to exist within the path of superior progress (*viśeṣamārga*),
the phrase "the four [powers], such as the supernormal power of the basis (*ṛddhiviṣaya*),
reach all objects" explains the fifth and sixth lines.
The four supernormal powers (abhijñā)— the power of the divine realm, the divine eye, the divine ear, and the recollection of past lives—
are comprised solely of conventional knowledge (saṃvṛtijñāna), because they take objective phenomena as their domain.
The power of knowing others' minds is comprised of five types of knowledge.

The name is as in the text; the supernormal power of the destruction of the outflows (*āsravakṣaya-abhijñā*) is as previously explained under the power of knowledge of the destruction of the outflows (*āsravakṣaya-jñānabala*).
If it takes the destruction of the outflows as its object, it is comprised within six knowledges.
If it arises based on the body of one whose outflows are exhausted,
it is comprised within the ten knowledges; because it is comprised within the ten knowledges.

By this, it has already been shown that the supernormal knowledge of the destruction of the outflows (āsravakṣaya-jñāna-abhijñā) relies upon all stages (bhūmi) and takes all objects (ālambana) as its domain;
since it is subsumed under the wisdom of causes,
it thereby clarifies the stages and the objects upon which the destruction of the outflows depends.
The statement that "the first five supernormal powers (abhijñā) rely upon the four dhyānas" explains the seventh phrase;
this clarifies the basis (bhūmi).

Among the six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍabhijñā*), the first five rely upon the four dhyānas, but not upon the formless attainments (*ārūpyasamāpatti*), the access concentrations (*sāmantaka*), or the intermediate dhyāna (*dhyānāntara*). As for the power of the destruction of the outflows (*āsravakṣayābhijñā*), its basis and its objects of focus [are as follows]:
[the basis] relies on all stages, and [the objects] take all things as their domain.
This has already been clarified above,
so it will not be discussed again here.
For what reason do these five [meditative attainments] not rely upon the formless realm?
Question:
Regarding the inability of the first three [faculties] to individually reach their objects,
the general answer is as follows.
The first three— supernormal power (*ṛddhi-vidhi*), the divine eye (*divya-cakṣus*), and the divine ear (*divya-śrotra*)—
each take form as their respective objects. One cultivates the supernormal power of knowing the minds of others (*paracitta-jñāna*).
Because one must first take the observation of physical forms as the gateway for entry,
one cultivates the supernormal power of recollecting past lives by gradually recalling the successive characteristics of form from stage to stage.
Because it is only through the distinct differentiation of eleven stages— the five stages from birth until emergence from the womb,
the five stages within the womb, and the stage of the intermediate state— that [the self] is established; at the time of its establishment,
it is able to cognize that it previously existed in a certain place, possessed a certain lineage, and so forth.
It should be understood that this refers only to gradual recollection by way of successive stages,
not by way of moments (*kṣaṇa*). If one were to recollect gradually back through moments,
one would die as soon as one had recollected the events of half a lifetime.
How could one possibly cultivate until the preparatory application reaches fulfillment?
There is no such capacity based on the formless realms (ārūpyadhātu). For those who wish to cultivate until they are able to know things as they truly are:
Below this, the preparatory practices (*prayoga*) for the five supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) are explained in detail.
This specifically clarifies the preparatory practice for the supernormal power of knowing the minds of others (*paracittajñāna-abhijñā*).
It may be understood according to the text.
For those who wish to cultivate [the supernormal power] that arises within their own continuum,

there is a specific explanation of the preparatory practice for cultivating the supernormal power of recollecting past lives. For all those who wish to cultivate the supernormal power of recollecting past lives:
First, one examines the mind that has just ceased; then,
one gradually and in reverse order contemplates the ten temporal stages of this life, observing their successive distinctions,
until reaching the mind of rebirth-linking (*pratisandhi-citta*).
When one is able to gradually recollect and know the final moment of consciousness at death from the preceding life within the intermediate state (*antarābhava*),
it is said that the preparatory application for the recollection of one's own past lives has been perfected.
The *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 100, states:
It should be stated thus:
when one gradually and carefully recollects up to the penultimate moment of mind prior to this intermediate state (*antarābhava*),
it is called the completion of the preparatory application (*prayoga*).

Because that is the final consciousness of the previous life, it is able to recollect and know [the object] as being "well-perfected. The *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya* (Vibhāṣā) explains this based on the arising of the path of immediate succession (*ānantarya-mārga*), stating that the preparatory stage (*prayoga*) is perfected [at that point].

The *Abhidharmakośa* states that [the path] is called "perfected" (*niṣpanna*) based on its preparatory application (*prayoga*) having ceased; alternatively, the term "perfected" indicates that it has already been perfected.
The texts of the *Nyāyānusāra* and the *Abhidharmasamuccaya-vyākhyā* are identical to the *Abhidharmakośa*. Alternatively, it may be interpreted as follows:
The intent of the treatise is distinct in each case.
In its established state, it is called the path of immediate succession (*ānantarya-mārga*);
it takes as its object the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) at the moment of death of the preceding life.
As stated in the *Vibhāṣā*: the path of immediate succession (*ānantarya-mārga*) regarding the recollection of past lives is the application of mindfulness to phenomena (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*),
because it is produced by two aggregates and one karma from the intermediate state and the birth state.
Therefore, it is understood that even the first moment of consciousness in the intermediate state (antarābhava) is still subsumed under this very birth.
From the point when one has not yet attained the name "knowledge of past lives" up until the knowledge of the state of mind at the time of death in a previous existence,

it is designated as the path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*). The second moment of consciousness is designated as the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*), at which point the supernormal power of recollecting past lives (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛti-abhijñā*) is perfected.
Since the application of cultivation for oneself is thus,
the application for recollecting others is likewise.
This [knowledge] first arises in those of the two vehicles and in ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*).
One knows past births sequentially; once this has become habitual through repeated practice,
one is also able to recollect past births by skipping over them.
All things remembered must have been previously experienced in the past before they can be recollected.
As for the supernormal power of recollecting past lives (pūrvanivāsānusmṛti-jñāna),
it is able to recall even the gods of the Śuddhāvāsa heavens.
Although one is not born there [in that realm],
because one heard it explained in the past, one is able to remember it at the present time.
Thus, the *Abhidharmamahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* (Vibhāṣā), fascicle 100, states:
Question: Regarding this knowledge of recollecting past lives (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛtijñāna*),
does it only recall and know events previously experienced,
or does it also recall and know events never before experienced?
Answer: This [knowledge] merely recollects and cognizes things previously experienced.
Question: If that were so, this knowledge should not recollect or cognize the matters of the five Śuddhāvāsa heavens, because since beginningless time one has never been born there.
Answer: There are briefly two kinds of previously experienced matters:
first, those previously seen;
second, those previously heard.
Although one has never personally seen the five Pure Abodes,
because one has heard of them, one is still able to recollect and know them;
they are far more remote and sublime than the other realms of the desire and form worlds.

All matters difficult to understand should be understood according to this; the above is the treatise. If that person, having passed away from the formless realm, is reborn in the desire or form realms, they rely upon their own continuum to complete the cultivation of the preparatory application (*prayoga*).
This supernormal power first arises based on the mental continuum of another.
If one dies from the remaining realms of desire or form and is reborn again in the realms of desire or form, it likewise first arises based on one’s own mental continuum.
Furthermore, if one gives rise to the supernormal power of recollecting past lives based on a lower stage, [it likewise first arises based on one's own continuum].
Those who pass away from a higher stage and are reborn in a lower one should be understood in this same way.
This applies to those who cultivate the supernormal powers (*ṛddhi*) and meditative attainments (*samāpatti*), but do not rely on the formless realms (*ārūpyadhātu*).
Next, the preparatory practices for cultivating the remaining three supernormal powers are explained.
When cultivating the first three supernormal powers, such as the power of miraculous movement (*ṛddhi-vidhi*),
one takes the contemplation of lightness as the preparatory practice.
One takes the light of the divine eye as the preliminary application and the sound of the divine ear as the preliminary application;
once these are accomplished, one acts with mastery according to what is appropriate.
Because this form does not exist within the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu),
these five supernormal powers (abhijñā) do not rely upon it.
Furthermore, as for the various formless states, they have already been excluded by this [preceding argument].
The second interpretation:
furthermore, in all formless realms, insight decreases while tranquility increases.
The five supernormal powers necessarily rely upon the contemplation of the "even stage" (samabhūmi).
By this, the "not-yet-attained" (anāgamya) and the "intermediate" (dhyānāntara) stages are already excluded, as they involve an increase in contemplation.
Because it ceases and diminishes.
Furthermore, the *Nyāyānusāra* asks:
"If that is so, for what reason is there the supernormal power of the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya-abhijñā*)?"
Because one can exhaust all outflows (*āsrava*) through pleasure, pain, slowness, speed, and the stages (*bhūmi*),
these five are the distinct cultivation of extraordinary qualities (*viśeṣaguṇa*).
Such extraordinary qualities can only be generated within an extraordinary stage.
Regarding these five supernormal powers reaching incalculable worlds:
this explains the eighth, ninth, and tenth phrases.
First, it clarifies the breadth and narrowness by way of the vertical dimension.
The object consists only of its own level and lower levels;
it does not extend to higher levels because their power is inferior.
Second, this is explained in terms of the horizontal [perspective] to reveal the breadth or narrowness of their functional activity.
This can be understood from the text as it stands.
Thus, the passage from "the five supernormal powers" up to "without relying on effort" explains the eleventh and twelfth phrases.
This clarifies the two types of attainment.
Thus, regarding these five supernormal powers (*pañcābhijñā*),
if they possess an especially superior power and sharp intensity, [they are called "attainments"].
That which has never been attained before is acquired through preparatory effort (*prayoga*).
If it was previously practiced in the past but lacks superior efficacy,
or if it belongs to a category lacking such superior efficacy in the future, [it cannot be attained].
It is acquired through the abandonment of defilements by those of the two vehicles and ordinary beings,
as appropriate to each.
Whether it is acquired through preparatory effort (*prayoga*), acquired through the removal of defilements (*vairāgya*),
or brought into manifestation, all occur by means of preparatory effort.
The Buddha has attained freedom from all defilements;
these manifest according to his will without the need for preparatory effort (*prayoga*).
Furthermore, the *Nyāya* states:
The noble ones of the three vehicles and subsequent ordinary beings (pṛthagjana) may acquire both previously acquired and previously unacquired [attainments];
other ordinary beings acquire only those previously acquired.
Regarding the first three among the six that reach as far as the divine ear for the purpose of perceiving sounds:
this below explains the thirteenth and fourteenth lines, which are the analysis of the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*).
Among the six supernormal powers (abhijñā), the first three are exclusively the application of mindfulness to the body (kāyasmṛtyupasthāna),
because they take only form (rūpa) as their object.
"If that is so, for what reason does it extend to various unwholesome actions, etc.?
This is the question:
If the supernormal power of the divine eye takes only the sense-base of form (rūpāyatana) as its object, for what reason [does the Sūtra state this]?
He explains the knowledge of death and rebirth:
he knows that among the classes of sentient beings, those who have committed various evil deeds of body, speech, and mind in their present existence will be born in the miserable realms.
The intent of the objection here is as follows:
the knowledge of death and rebirth is the supernormal power of the divine eye (*divyacakṣurabhijñā*). Since it is indeed the supernormal power of the divine eye, [it must be so].
One may only know the physical body;
how can one know speech and mind?
It is not that those who possess the supernormal power of the divine eye (divyacakṣus-abhijñā) up to the knowledge of death and rebirth (cyutyupapādajñāna) are excluded from this name.
Answer: The supernormal power of the divine eye cannot know speech or mind,
because the divine eye perceives only the sphere of form (rūpāyatana).
There is a distinct, superior wisdom that is an attendant of the supernormal powers (*abhijñā*).
Arising based on the body of an Ārya, it is able to know in this way;
for this attendant wisdom is induced by the power of the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*).
Therefore, it is established together with the supernormal power (*abhijñā*) as the "knowledge of death and rebirth" (*cyutyupapādajñāna*). Question:

Why is the knowledge of death and rebirth a retinue (*parivāra*) induced by the supernormal power of the divine eye (*divyacakṣur-abhijñā*)? Explanation: It is said that the supernormal power of the divine eye, in the present life...
One perceives sentient beings as dying here and being born there;
furthermore, with the knowledge of death and rebirth,
one knows that sentient beings die here and are born there.
Because it is of a similar class and is induced by that [divine eye],
it is called the supernormal power of the divine eye (*divyacakṣur-abhijñā*) as its retinue;
just as the mind of transformation (*nirmāṇa-citta*) is subsumed under the supernormal power of the realization of the knowledge of supernatural feats (*ṛddhi-vidhi-jñāna-sākṣāt-kriyā-abhijñā*).
That supernormal power (abhijñā) is capable of performing functions such as transporting the body;
that mind of transformation (nirmāṇa-citta) is capable of transforming things.
Because they belong to the same category and are similar in nature, they are subsumed under it.
If one speaks of the supernormal power of the divine eye as the "knowledge of death and rebirth," it is named after its result.
If one speaks of the knowledge of death and rebirth as the "supernormal power of the divine eye," [it is named after its cause].

Precisely because of the name. Question: If it is said that the knowledge of death and rebirth (*cyutyupapādajñāna*) is called the supernormal power of the divine eye (*divyacakṣurabhijñā*), why does the *Abhidharmamahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* (vol. 76) state:
"The knowledge of death and rebirth contemplates future events"? Explanation: That [statement] refers to its retinue (*parivāra*).
Regarding the recollection of past lives, it is said that one contemplates the future. Furthermore, if it is asked:

"If the knowledge of death and rebirth (*cyutyupapādajñāna*) can take the future as its object, why does the *Abhidharmamahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* (Vibhāṣā), fascicle 30, state that the power of the knowledge of death and rebirth takes the past as its object?"
The present takes the present as its object.
Future dharmas that are destined to arise take the future as their object;

those not destined to arise take the three periods of time as their objects. The commentary explains: that statement refers to the fundamental [conditioning] and does not mention taking the future as an object.
Alternatively, it may be based on its retinue.
There are two types of retinue:
first, that which relates to the future.
The second takes the present as its object.

This is based on taking the present as an object. Furthermore, it is asked: if the supernormal knowledge of death and rebirth can take the three types of karma as its objects, why does the *Abhidharmamahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 30, state:

The power of knowledge regarding death and rebirth takes the sense-sphere of form (*rūpāyatana*) as its object. The commentary explains that this refers to the fundamental [power] when it says "takes the sense-sphere of form as its object.
However, if one considers its associated factors (*parivāra*), it universally takes the three types of karma as its objects; or, it may be according to the associated factors.
There are two types of retinues:
first, those that take the sphere of form as their object; second, those that take the three types of action as their object.

That [statement] is based on the explanation regarding the sense-sphere of form (*rūpāyatana*). Furthermore, it was asked: "If the knowledge of death and rebirth (*cyutyupapādajñāna*) were the supernormal power of the divine eye (*divyacakṣurabhijñā*), it should be indeterminate (*avyākṛta*).
Why, then, does the *Abhidharmamahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 30, state: [text follows]?
"The ten powers are exclusively wholesome. The commentary explains: that statement is made with respect to their retinues.
The power of knowledge regarding death and rebirth is exclusively of a wholesome nature when considered according to its fundamental [nature].
If one considers it according to its root...
The supernormal power of the divine eye is said to be exclusively indeterminate (*avyākṛta*). However,
if one considers the breadth or narrowness of the objects it perceives when it is actually manifest,
one should know that the supernormal power of the divine eye is narrow.
The knowledge of death and rebirth takes only the present sphere of form as its object;
the knowledge of the breadth [of the world] takes all five aggregates as its object.
It may take the present as its object,
or it may take the future as its object;
this is because the supernormal power of the knowledge of others' minds reaches all objects.

The supernormal power of knowing others' minds is subsumed under three applications of mindfulness; the supernormal power of recollecting past lives is subsumed under all four applications of mindfulness,
because it takes all five aggregates as its object.
The supernormal power of the destruction of the outflows (āsravakṣaya-abhijñā) is subsumed under the four foundations of mindfulness (smṛtyupasthāna), because it takes everything as its object.
The *Nyāyānusāra* refutes this, saying:

Regarding the recollection of past lives (*pūrvanivāsa*) and the destruction of the outflows (*āsravakṣaya*), the Master of the Sūtras intends for each of these to be subsumed under all four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*),
because they universally take as their object the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*) and all phenomena.
In reality, however, it is subsumed under the application of mindfulness to phenomena (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*).
Although the sūtras state that one recollects past experiences of suffering, pleasure, and so forth,
this refers to the recollection of the various objects (*upakaraṇa*) experienced by feelings of suffering, pleasure, and so on in previous lives.
This is precisely the mixed object;
it is subsumed under the mindfulness-establishment of phenomena (dharmasmṛtyupasthāna) and is like the power of the destruction of the outflows (āsravakṣayabala).

Whether it be a single dharma or four, one should not definitively state that they are subsumed within the four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*). The masters of the *Abhidharmakośa* offer this defense:
"We maintain that because the recollection of past lives (*pūrvanivāsa*) also possesses distinct conditions, it is common to all four foundations of mindfulness."

Regarding the statement that the supernormal power of the destruction of the outflows (āsravakṣaya-abhijñā) consists of the four foundations of mindfulness (smṛtyupasthāna), this is explained according to the ten knowledges (jñāna). Among these, six knowledges are exclusively the knowledge of phenomena (dharmajñāna).
The implication can be understood by analogy;

therefore, it is not stated separately. Question: If it is said that the supernormal power of recollecting past lives (pūrvanivāsābhijñā) pertains to all four foundations of mindfulness (smṛtyupasthāna), this contradicts the position of the *Vibhāṣā* masters.
As stated in the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 100:
"The foundations of mindfulness (smṛtyupasthāna) consist exclusively of the foundation of mindfulness of dharmas with mixed objects."
The Venerable Ghosaka spoke thus: [the application of mindfulness] pervades all four foundations of mindfulness,
as stated in the Sūtra.
I recollect the suffering and pleasure experienced in the past;
having known that pleasure and suffering,
this is the application of mindfulness to feelings (vedanā-smṛtyupasthāna).
The critique states: One should speak thus.
To recollect the various experiences of pleasure and pain in past lives is what is meant by "feeling pleasure and pain.
It is not the case that these are merely objects of feeling; therefore, they do not serve as proof [for the existence of a self].
However, the knowledge of recollecting past lives (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛtijñāna*) observes, in its entirety, the various distinctions of states in previous births;
it is comprised solely within the category of mindfulness of phenomena (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*) that takes mixed objects as its domain. My explanation is based on reasoning as the correct standard.
One should not take the *Vibhāṣā* commentators as the sole authority;
although they agree with Ghoṣaka, there is no fault in this,
for since the sūtra is explicit, one should not provide a divergent interpretation.
Regarding the phrase "among these six supernormal powers, because they reach the wisdom associated with them":
the following section explains the latter two lines through a classification according to the three natures (*trisvabhāva*).
The two supernormal powers of the eye and ear are of an indeterminate nature (*avyākṛta*),
because they are admitted to be wisdom (*prajñā*) associated with the two [visual and auditory] consciousnesses; thus,
it is said that they are not wholesome (*kuśala*).
The five consciousnesses are innate wholesome states (*upapattilābhika-kuśala*),
because they cannot arise in a different stage (*bhūmi*).
Alternatively, the innate wholesome states of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) cannot produce a meditative state of mind (*samāhita-citta*).
Since those two supernormal powers (abhijñā) arise solely from the characteristics of meditative concentration—Question:

Since they are neutral (avyākṛta), among the four types of neutral states, which one are they? Answer: They are the neutral state that is the fruit of supernormal power (abhijñā-phala-avyākṛta). Question: Since the wisdom associated with the divine eye and divine ear is called "supernormal power," [how is it that the powers themselves are neutral?]
How is it called "result" (*phala*)? The commentary explains: because it is a result in a general sense, it is called a "general result" (*anuloma-phala*).
It is called "general" (*anuloma*) because it is unobstructed; it is called a "result" (*phala*) because it arises from meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
If that is so, why say they rely on the four dhyānas?
Question: If that is so, why say they rely on the four dhyānas?
For the two consciousnesses are merely distracted minds of the first dhyāna.

Regarding the statement, "Because it does not rely on meditative concentration; because it is taught according to the faculties; and because it extends to reliance upon the four stages," the answer is as follows:
The faculties that serve as the basis for the supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) are subsumed within the four dhyānas;
because they are described according to those faculties, it is said that they "rely on the four.
Alternatively, this refers to the uninterrupted path (*ānantarya-mārga*) of the supernormal powers.

Because the uninterrupted paths (*ānantarya-mārga*) of the [supernormal knowledges] rely upon four stages (*bhūmi*), it is said that they rely upon four [stages] in accordance with those uninterrupted paths. The *Nyāyānusāra* refutes this, saying:
"This interpretation is not correct."
All six supernormal knowledges (*ṣaḍabhijñā*) are subsumed within the path of liberation (*vimuktimārga*).
However, it is logically untenable for the two consciousnesses of eye and ear to be the path of liberation.
It should be stated as follows:

within the four dhyānas, there exists a superior indeterminate wisdom associated with meditative concentration that is capable of inducing the fruit of superior primary elements (mahābhūta) belonging to its own level.
When this wisdom manifests, it immediately induces the divine eye and divine ear of its own level to appear before one.
This is because these serve as the bases for the arising of the visual and auditory consciousnesses.
The wisdom associated with the two consciousnesses—visual and auditory—is not a supernormal power (*abhijñā*).

It may simply be said that these are induced by the supernormal powers (*abhijñā*). The *Nyāyānusāra* explains that the intention of the *Abhidharmakośa-śāstra* is that all six supernormal powers and liberations (*vimokṣa*) belong to the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*);
the visual and auditory consciousnesses are subsumed under the five sensory consciousnesses and are not the path of liberation.
One should state it thus:
within the four dhyānas, there exists a superior indeterminate wisdom that arises from pure meditative concentration.
To enter and emerge from a state adjacent to pure concentration (śuddha-samādhi) is called "concentration-concomitant" (samādhi-saṃprayukta).
Pure concentration serves as the path of uninterrupted transition (ānantarya-mārga),
while the superior neutral wisdom (avyākṛta-prajñā) of the mental level (manobhūmi) serves as the path of liberation (vimukti-mārga).
This refers to the intrinsic nature of the two supernormal knowledges (*abhijñā*).
They are capable of producing the superior great elements (*mahābhūta*) of their own level as a result, which fashion the divine eye and ear;
these serve as the bases for the sense organs that give rise to the visual and auditory consciousnesses.
Therefore, the wisdom associated with the two consciousnesses of the eye and ear is not supernormal power;
it can only be said to be induced by supernormal power.
As for the superior indeterminate wisdom on the mental level:
Their essence is not the physical sense organs of the ear;
rather, they can induce the divine eye and divine ear.
Because they are designated by the name of their fruit, they are called the supernormal powers of the divine eye and divine ear.
The wisdom associated with the two consciousnesses of the eye and ear is not,
in its essential nature, a supernormal power (*abhijñā*). Nevertheless, it is called a "power" because it is induced by that [supernormal power].
It is named according to its cause.
Regarding the term "supernormal power" (abhijñā):
if the wisdom associated with the two consciousnesses of the divine eye and divine ear, that is the result [of meditation] but not a supernormal power itself.
Regarding the term "result of supernormal power" (*abhijñā-phala*): it is called by the name of its cause because it is the result of supernormal power;
this is an *ṣaṣṭhī-tatpuruṣa* (genitive determinative) compound.
If it is a superior indeterminate wisdom of the mental level,
