You cite two sūtras as proof that the two higher realms lack edible food (*kavaḍīkārāhāra*);
I cite three sūtras as proof that there is no matter in the formless realm: the Discourse states that within that formless realm, there is an escape from matter.
If there were still form within that realm, how could it be called "renunciation"?
Furthermore, a sutra states: "The four formless liberations are the most peaceful, for they transcend all forms."

Since it is said that they "transcend all forms," it is clearly known that those [realms] are formless. Furthermore, a sutra states that sentient beings in the formless realm have "completely transcended all perceptions of form."
The severance of craving for form is called "transcending the perception of form.
Alternatively, since one has already transcended the perception of form in the four fundamental dhyānas and the upper three stages, it is clear that there is no form present.
If, as you maintain, there were actually form in the formless realm, [it would contradict this].
It must necessarily be the case that the specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) of those forms are cognizable;
how then can it be said that "one transcends the perception of form" (*rūpasaṃjñā*)?
The phrase "and so forth" (*ādi*) includes the two preceding sūtras.
If it is argued that one contemplates down to the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*),
this again restates the refutation of the defense:
if it is argued that the formless realm contemplates the coarse forms of the lower desire and form realms (*kāmadhātu* and *rūpadhātu*).
If it is said that one transcends the perception of form and so forth, then one should likewise admit this regarding edible food as well;
namely, that one transcends the coarse edible food of lower levels to attain the subtle edible food [of higher levels]. Furthermore, the four dhyānas transcend the coarse forms of lower levels.
One should also be able to speak of "transcending form.
In that case, the four dhyānas would also have to be called "formless" (ārūpya). Furthermore, one should also speak of transcending feeling and so forth within the formless realm.
Since he also transcends the coarse sensations and so forth of the lower realms,
and because the Sūtra does not mention the phrase "transcending sensations and so forth" regarding the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu),
we know that within the formless realm one universally transcends the category of form, but does not transcend sensations and so forth.
From this, it is known with certainty that that realm is formless;
however, as for the statement in the Sūtra that "one has not yet emerged from it permanently," [it refers to the fact that one has not yet attained final liberation].
The Sarvāstivādins respond to the challenges posed by the Mahāsāṃghikas and other schools.
The intent of these challenges is as follows:
since the sūtras state that there is "non-existence within existence," [how can you maintain that all things exist?]
It is clearly known that the formless existence (*ārūpyabhava*) cannot transcend the existence of form (*rūpabhava*).
If it were able to transcend it, one would have to say that there is an existence that transcends existence.
To resolve this anticipated objection, this sūtra is explained: "However, the sūtra states that the three existences cannot transcend the three existences."
Because they are bound by the afflictions of their own level,
it is said that they are unable to transcend their own level. This refers only to transcending the eight levels,
not to transcending the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*).
Therefore, it is said that they do not emerge universally;
because ordinary persons, after severing their afflictions, may still fall back,
it is said that they do not emerge eternally.
Therefore, the Sūtra says that "existence does not transcend existence";
it does not say that the formless existence (*ārūpya-bhava*) cannot transcend the form existence (*rūpa-bhava*).
Furthermore, for the Blessed One (*bhagavat*), there is no fault of non-attainment up to [the attainment of] the formless.
Furthermore, he cites scriptural evidence to prove that there is no form in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*),
as can be understood from the text.
Having completed the refutation, he concludes by stating:
Therefore, since all the reasons established are formless (*arūpa*),
they are designated as "formless"; thus,
there is no fault of non-establishment (*asiddha*).
Regarding the phrase, "In those many eons, from what does form arise?
this explains the sixth line.
Question:
In those formless realms, the continuity of form is severed for many eons.
When one subsequently passes away and is reborn in the lower desire realm or the form realm,
from what does that form arise?
Regarding the passage from "this arises from the mind" to "it arises from that mind," the Master of the Treatise answers according to the Sautrāntika doctrine.
This correctly explains the verse's statement: "After form has arisen from the mind, this form arises from the mind."
It does not arise from form; rather,
it is the maturation now of a functional capacity within the mind, which was previously cultivated by the causes that produced the fruit of form.
Therefore, at this time, the form of the desire and form realms arises from the seeds of form within that mind of the formless realm.
Upon what does that body and mind of the formless realm depend for their operation?
The Mahāsāṃghikas and others ask:
"Why does [consciousness] not arise apart from the body?
The Sarvāstivādins respond with a counter-interrogation.
Regarding the phrase "because it has never been seen in the lower [realms]," the Mahāsāṃghika and other schools reply:
"The lower realms refer to the desire realm and the form realm."
For it has never been observed that the mind undergoes transformation apart from the physical body.
As for the statement that in the form realm there is no material food (*kavaḍīkārāhāra*) serving as the basis for the transformation of the mind:
The Sarvāstivādins raise an objection:
"In the form realm there is no food consisting of mouthfuls;
upon what, then, does the body depend for its continued existence?"
Furthermore, within the lower desire realm (*kāmadhātu*),
one does not see the physical body (*rūpakāya*) functioning apart from material food (*kavaḍīkārāhāra*).
Moreover, as stated in the "Chapter on Previous Lives" (*pūrvajanmaparivarta*):
It is said that the basis for the transition of the formless mind is the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) and the homogeneous character of the group (*nikāyasabhāga*).
Having explained the general name, is the specific name "acquisition" (*prāpti*) now to be explained?
This explains the latter four lines,
concluding the preceding inquiry.
Otherwise, it would not be so.
Answer: What is it? This is an inquiry.
Regarding the establishment of the names for the three lower formless attainments (*ārūpya*):
this explains that the names of the first three formless attainments are established based on their preparatory stages (*prayoga*).
Thus, the *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra* (77) states:
If one contemplates infinite space through resolute conviction (*adhimokṣa*),
that which is accomplished by such preparatory application (*prayoga*) is called the sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*).
That is to say, even if there are phenomena that coexist with form (*rūpa*), [they are transcended].
Yet its own essence does not depend upon or belong to form; for those who seek liberation from form,
they must first contemplate that phenomenon—
namely, that although the essence of space coexists with form, [it is distinct].
Furthermore, form cannot be clearly discerned without depending on [other factors].
Since external phenomena encompass infinite characteristics,
when one contemplates them, it is easy to become detached from form.
Therefore, when one contemplates space during the stage of preparatory application (*prayoga*),
one may also take other phenomena as objects as appropriate;
however, this name is established solely based on that preparatory application.
If one contemplates infinite consciousness through resolute conviction (*adhimokṣa*),
it is called the sphere of infinite consciousness (*vijñānānantyāyatana*) by virtue of its preparatory application;
that is, within the discernment of the sixfold body of pure consciousness.
Having correctly grasped the signs, one dwells in resolute conviction;
by the power of mental construction,
one contemplates and examines the sign of infinite consciousness.
This is accomplished by taking preparatory effort as its precursor;
accordingly, it may also take other phenomena as its object.
However, this name is established solely on the basis of that preparatory effort.
If, through resolute conviction, one relinquishes all that exists as a result of application,
it is called the sphere of nothingness.
This means that one perceives the infinite aspects as coarse and agitated, and gives rise to this preparatory application (*prayoga*) out of a desire to weary of and abandon them.
Therefore, this stage is called "supreme equanimity" (*upekṣā*),
because within it one no longer takes pleasure in performing the infinite aspects.

"Because the mind dwells in tranquility, having relinquished all that it possessed regarding its objects of focus"—the above is from the treatise. Regarding the establishment of the fourth name, this is the primary reason for establishing the name;
it explains the subsequent formless [attainments].
The fourth name is established because perception (*saṃjñā*) is dull and inferior;
that is to say, because there is no clear or superior perception as in the seven lower stages,
it receives the name "Non-perception" (*asaṃjñin*).
Because there is a dull and inferior perception, it is not the same as the two mindless states and is thus called "neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
Although this thought was also formed during the preparatory stage—
that in the preceding seven dhyānas, all perceptions are like a disease, like an arrow, or like an abscess— or that in the first and second dhyānas, the perception of joy is like a disease.
The perception of bliss in the three dhyānas is like an arrow;

the perception of equanimity in the fourth, fifth, sixth, and seventh stages is like an abscess. If these perceptions were entirely absent, it would be like the two mindless states, which are equivalent to dull ignorance and darkness.
It is similar in that there is no conscious awareness;
it is merely a state within the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception that is peaceful and sublime, being the opposite of the aforementioned [lower states].
In its preparatory practice, one feels aversion toward perception and aversion toward non-perception.
It should be named "neither-perception-nor-non-perception," yet this name is not established on the basis of its preparatory application (*prayoga*).
For if one were to question why the preparatory application involves such a mental orientation, [the answer would be as follows].
One must necessarily answer that it is because the perception (*saṃjñā*) in the fundamental stage of that Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*) is dull and weak;
therefore, the preparatory application (*prayoga*) conforms to that fundamental stage and forms such a thought.
Because the fundamental perception (*saṃjñā*) therein is dull and feeble,
this is the correct reason for establishing the name "Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception" (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*). Therefore,
the name is established based on its fundamental state.
The name is not established based on preparatory application (*prayoga*).
Furthermore, the *Nyāyānusāra* states:
"Regarding these four formless [realms], all are called 'bases' (*āyatana*)."
Because these are the places where all beings are born and grow.

Having already distinguished the formless attainments up to the untainted as being supramundane, hereafter, thirdly, the eight meditative attainments (*samāpatti*) will be explained. Within this section:
First, a general explanation of the eight meditative attainments (*samāpatti*);
second, a detailed explanation of the eight meditative attainments. This is the general explanation of the eight meditative attainments, concluding with a question and answering it in verse.
The Commentary states: "Up to 'because there is no absence of the untainted' (*anāsrava*)";
this explains the first verse and may be understood accordingly.
Regarding the statement that "the initial tasting attainment (āsvādana-samāpatti) receives the name 'tasting' upon reaching this [state]," this explains the fifth phrase.
The "initial tasting attainment" refers to...
This refers to its association with craving (*tṛṣṇā*).
Because craving can relish and become attached to pure meditative concentration (*śuddha-samādhi*), it is termed "attachment" (*āsvāda*);
since the meditative attainment (*samāpatti*) is associated with that craving, it is likewise so named.
These attainments (samāpatti) are given the name "tasting" (āsvādana).
Furthermore, the *Abhidharmamahāvibhāṣā* states:
Question: For what reason is it said that they are associated only with craving (*tṛṣṇā*)?
It is not other afflictions.
Some say that what is described here as "resembling" refers to craving resembling meditative concentration.
It is not other afflictions.
Why is this? Because it flows and continues uninterruptedly toward its object of focus.
Attachment is also like this,
as explained at length there.
Regarding the term "pure attainment" (*śuddha-samāpatti*), it is called "attainment" (*samāpatti*) and is termed "entry" (*praveśa*).
The sixth and seventh phrases explain the term "pure attainment" (*śuddha-samāpatti*), which refers to all mundane,
contaminated wholesome concentrations (*sāsrava-kuśala-dhyāna*).
Because it arises in association with various pure and white dharmas that are intrinsically wholesome, such as non-attachment,
this attainment is given the name "pure.
It is precisely the first object of relish associated with flavor (*āsvādanasamprayukta*).
Immediately after this pure meditative absorption has ceased,
that relishing absorption arises;
it takes the past pure absorption as its object and gives rise to a profound attachment to it.
It does not take the present as its object,
because it necessarily does not contemplate intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) and so forth.
It does not take the future as its object.
Because it has not been experienced before,
whereas the past has been experienced, the past is specifically mentioned. At that time,
although it is called "emerging from the meditative absorption of the tasted object," [it is so designated].
One is said to "enter" (praveśa) into a meditative absorption that can be tasted;
as for the untainted absorption (anāsrava-samādhi), it reaches the point where it is not an object of attachment.
This explains the final phrase.
This may be understood from the text.
It should be known that the three types—the savored (*sāsvāda*), the pure (*śuddha*), and the untainted (*anāsrava*)—are termed "entry" and "exit.
Among the five types of entry and exit, these constitute entry and exit by means of a mind of a different category.
Therefore, the *Vibhāṣā* (161) states:
"Regarding 'entering' and 'exiting' herein,
there are five kinds of entering and exiting."
First, the stage;
second, the aspect;
third, the object of focus.
Fourth, the mind of a different category;
fifth, the moments of entering and exiting the stages and elements.
This means that when the second dhyāna manifests immediately after the first dhyāna,
it is called "entering the second dhyāna" and "emerging from the first dhyāna."
...up to the sphere of nothingness and so forth;
immediately thereafter,
when the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception manifests before one.
It is called entering the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception and emerging from the sphere of nothingness.
Just as one enters and emerges in direct order,
so too does one enter and emerge in reverse order.
The same applies to entering and emerging through the direct and reverse orders and by skipping stages.
Regarding entry and emergence by way of aspect (*ākāra*):
this refers to the uninterrupted [succession] of the aspect of impermanence (*anityatā*).
When the aspect of suffering manifests before one,
it is called entering the aspect of suffering and emerging from the aspect of impermanence;
the same applies to the other aspects as well.
Regarding the entry into and emergence from objects of focus:
this refers to when, immediately following a concentration focused on form,
a concentration focused on feeling manifests in the present.
This is called entering a concentration conditioned by feeling and emerging from a concentration conditioned by form;
it is the same for concentrations conditioned by other objects.
As for entering and emerging with minds of a different category:
This refers to when, immediately following a mind of the desire realm,
a mind of the form realm or an unconditioned (unbound) mind manifests;
this is called entering a mind of the form realm or an unconditioned mind and emerging from a mind of the desire realm.
The same explanation applies to the minds of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) and so forth.
Just as it is with the minds of the desire realm and so forth,
the same holds true for the minds of those in training (*śaikṣa*) and so forth.
The same applies accordingly to other wholesome states of mind and so forth.
Regarding "entering and exiting moment by moment," this refers to the immediate succession of the first moment and so on.
When the second moment manifests,
it is called "entering the second moment" and "exiting the first moment.
The same applies to all subsequent moments.

Regarding what has been stated thus, up to "not for any of the formless [attainments]," this section below is the second part, which specifically explains the eight attainments (*samāpatti*). Within this,
the first part specifically explains the dhyānas.
Second, the explanation of the three types of meditative attainments (*samāpatti*). Within the first section, the detailed explanation of the dhyānas, there are two parts:
first, the explanation of the factors of dhyāna (*dhyānāṅga*);
second, the explanation of the essential nature of the factors of dhyāna.
The third vidyā concerns defilement and its absence;
the fourth is called "immovable";
the fifth concerns differences in birth and experience.
Sixth, explaining the arising of the lower mind.
This is the first explanation of the factors of dhyāna;
therefore, the thesis is stated first: "Among the eight attainments thus described, dhyāna subsumes the factors such as calm abiding (śamatha) and insight (vipaśyanā)."
In the formless attainments, there is no increase in calm abiding and decrease in insight;
for this reason, the preparatory stage (*anāgamya*) and the intermediate dhyāna (*dhyānāntara*) are also not established as having factors (*aṅga*).
Regarding the increase of insight (*vipaśyanā*) and the decrease of tranquility (*śamatha*):
how many branches (*aṅga*) are there in each of the four dhyānas?
This is the question.
The verse says: "One who attains meditative absorption within equanimity and mindfulness.
This is the answer provided by the verse. Within this verse:
This will be briefly analyzed through two sections:
first, clarifying the commonality and specific application of the various stages;
second, clarifying the inequality in the number of factors. Regarding the commonality and specific application of the various stages:
The branches of the four dhyānas total eighteen.
Generally, there are three categories:
first, the meditative absorption which serves as the basis.
This consists of four kinds, which are the essential natures of the four dhyānas;
for these serve as the basis for their respective factors (aṅga).
Therefore, this applies across all stages without the need for further inquiry or response. The factors that ought to exist in the second dhyāna are sixfold;
namely: initial inquiry (*vitarka*), sustained investigation (*vicāra*), and joy (*prīti*) from the first dhyāna.
The joy of the second dhyāna;
the bliss of the third dhyāna;
and the neutral feeling of the fourth dhyāna.
These six kinds of earth-dharmas ought to exist;
therefore, they may be present or absent in various stages.
Without the need for further inquiry or response, there are three distinct establishments of conditions.
These are of eight kinds, namely:
the bliss of the first dhyāna.
In the second dhyāna, there is internal purity and bliss;
in the third dhyāna, equanimity, mindfulness, and wisdom;
and in the fourth dhyāna, equanimity and mindfulness. This is briefly distinguished based on the third question and answer.
The *Abhidharmamahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 80, states in its "Exegesis of Intention":
Question: Since both pliancy (*praśrabdhi*) and equanimity (*upekṣā*) exist in all stages, why are pliancy established [as a distinct factor] in the first two dhyānas, but not equanimity?
3. Regarding the establishment of equanimity (*upekṣā*) as not being pliancy (*praśrabdhi*):
furthermore, in the first and second [dhyānas], the function of pliancy is predominant;
its nature is to counteract lethargy (*styāna*).
3. Equanimity is superior in its function across four stages.
It pacifies restlessness.
Furthermore, it serves to remedy the physical heaviness (dauṣṭhulya) induced by the five sensory consciousnesses.
In the first dhyāna, pliancy is established in order to counteract the heaviness of the three consciousnesses and the body induced by them;
in the second dhyāna, pliancy is likewise established.

2. Because in the second and third dhyānas, there is no coarse body of consciousness (*vijñānakāya*) nor the bodily heaviness (*dausthulya*) induced by it that serves as their counteragent; therefore, pliancy (*praśrabdhi*) is not established as a factor in these two.
3. [Consequently,] lightness (*laghutva*) is also not established as a factor in the third and fourth [dhyānas].
Since there is no pliancy [in those stages], equanimity as an application (*prahāṇopekṣā*) is established.
Furthermore, because the third dhyāna abandons extreme joy and the fourth dhyāna abandons extreme bliss,
equanimity as an application is established.
In the first and second dhyānas, equanimity of application (*praśrabdhi-ūpekṣā*) is not established;

therefore, pliancy (*praśrabdhi*) is established [as a factor]. Question: Since faith (*śraddhā*) is present in all stages, why is it established as a factor only in these two dhyānas? The *Mahāvibhāṣā* states:
Furthermore, in the first dhyāna, vitarka and vicāra are like fire,
and the body-consciousness is like mud;
they cause the mental continuum to become feverish, afflicted, turbid, and disordered.
Faith is not clear and pure;
it is like a reflection on a hot mire that does not appear.
In the two meditative attainments (nirodha-samāpatti), such a thing does not occur.
The faculty of faith is clear and pure,
like a reflection appearing on the surface of clear, cool water.
In the third dhyāna, there is the sensation of extreme bliss.
In the fourth dhyāna, there is a superior equanimous feeling (*upekṣā-vedanā*),
which obscures the continuity of the mind so that the signs of faith do not appear.
Furthermore, the various practitioners of yoga...
Upon attaining the first arising of superior faith in the second dhyāna,
one is already able to separate from both the realms and the stages;
eventually, one will certainly be separated even from the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*).
In the first dhyāna, settled confidence has not yet arisen;
it arises in the latter two, but not in the first.
Furthermore, the arising of superior confidence necessarily depends upon great sympathetic joy.

Because those who possess joy and faith will have firm conviction, and because the second dhyāna possesses an exceptionally superior joy, it is only this [dhyāna] that establishes the factor of internal serenity (*adhyātmasaṃprasāda*). Question: Wisdom (*prajñā*) is present throughout all stages.
Why is it established only in the third dhyāna? The *Vibhāṣā* states:
because it is conducive to the three dhyānas.
Furthermore, in the third dhyāna there is the sensation of extreme pliancy (*praśrabdhi*).
Because of being addicted to this pleasure,
one does not delight in the superior dharmas of the higher stages,
which can act as obstacles to one's own stage.
To counteract this, the factor of right wisdom is established;
therefore, the Blessed One said:
"One should clearly comprehend this pleasure with right wisdom."
Within the higher and lower stages, there is no obstacle to the supreme bliss of one's own stage as great as that which exists in this stage.
Furthermore, the first dhyāna possesses coarse vitarka and vicāra;
the second dhyāna possesses extreme joy and elation.
In the four dhyānas there is a superior equanimous feeling;
because it is superior,
this equanimous feeling is ignorance.
Right wisdom is clarity (*vidyā*).
Clarity and ignorance (*avidyā*) are mutually contradictory and destructive;
for right wisdom is obscured and obstructed by vitarka, vicāra, and so forth.
It is not established in those [lower stages].
Within the third dhyāna, there is no factor that obscures right wisdom as there is in those [lower stages]. Question:
Since mindfulness (smṛti) pervades all stages, why are factors established only in the third and fourth [dhyānas]? According to the intention of the *Vibhāṣā*:
Mindfulness conforms to the latter two.
Furthermore, the third dhyāna is overwhelmed by the intense joy of the second dhyāna,
while the fourth dhyāna is obstructed by the intense bliss of the third dhyāna.
Because they are obstructed by the lower stages,
they are unable to emerge from the defilements of their own stage;
therefore, the Blessed One exhorted them to abide in right mindfulness.
Furthermore, the first dhyāna possesses coarse vitarka and vicāra,
which are like a violent wind;
the second dhyāna possesses extreme joy and elation.
Like waves upon water, they obscure and obstruct right mindfulness.
The latter two [factors] do not have this fault. Second, regarding the inequality in the number of factors: Question: Why are the first, third, and so forth fivefold?
2. Four [factors] each equal to four. The *Vibhāṣā* explains:
Furthermore, because the various evils of the desire realm are difficult to sever, difficult to shatter, and difficult to transcend, the first dhyāna is established with five factors (*pañcāṅga*).
As a firm antidote, the second dhyāna possesses a profound ground of intense joy that is difficult to sever,
difficult to shatter, and difficult to transcend.
The third dhyāna is established as having five factors in order to provide a firm and powerful antidote;
this is because both the first and the third [dhyānas] lack such a factor.
2. Four are only four.
Furthermore, in order to counteract the greed for the five predominant objects of desire in the desire realm, the first five are established as the antidotes.
In the second dhyāna, there are five categories because of the presence of the ground of heaviness and the sensation of joy;
in the third dhyāna, there are five as well. In the first and third [dhyānas], these two matters are both absent.
In the second and fourth [dhyānas], there are four each.
Furthermore, it is for the purpose of conforming to the dharma of transcending meditative absorptions (*samāpatti*).
That is to say, one transcends from a five-limbed absorption and enters a five-limbed absorption;
again, one transcends from a four-limbed absorption and enters a four-limbed absorption.

Regarding the phrase "because the factors, etc., are easily transcended": If one were to leap from the third dhyāna into the sphere of infinite space, and again leap from the fourth dhyāna into the sphere of infinite consciousness.
How do those that lack both [internal and external] factors accord with [the path]? Answer: External and internal things are difficult to produce at the outset;
once they have been accomplished, they do not require further conditioning.
To take external things as an example:
For example, when Caṇaka and his minister Bhinnamāsa studied the art of gold-making for twelve years,
as soon as they had first produced a single grain the size of a barley kernel,
he let out a lion’s roar.
"We are now able to create a mountain of gold.
As for what is called "internal phenomena," it is like a practitioner of yoga cultivating the supernormal power of psychic travel (ṛddhividhi-jñāna).
At first, the beginner rises from the ground as high as half a mustard seed;
later, he rises as high as one mustard seed.
In this manner, he gradually rises to half a barley grain, one barley grain, and even up to one fathom, until finally he achieves perfection.
According to his will, he can travel to the Akaniṣṭha heaven;
he is able to go there with mastery,
and the same applies to transcending meditative absorptions.

Because it was difficult at the beginning, the factors were provisionally made equal; because it was easy later on, even if the factors were not established, one could still leap into the higher stages—this is the meaning of the preceding treatise. Regarding the statement in the treatise, "The meaning of 'reaching' is as explained before": [The commentary continues: As for the phrase "the meaning of reaching is as explained before," this refers to the previous explanation of the term *prāpti* (reaching/attainment). Just as the attainment of the path is explained in detail in the section on the "Path of Seeing" (*darśanamārga*), so too should the attainment of the fruit be understood according to that same principle. Furthermore, regarding the phrase "even if the factors are not established," this indicates that while the formal meditative factors may not be fully present, the practitioner is nonetheless capable of transcending to the higher stages through the power of mastery over the mind. This concludes the explanation of the relevant passage from the treatise.
The first two lines are explained as follows:
herein, "samādhi" (equipoise) is stated in the verse as "dhyāna" (meditative concentration).
Samādhi and dhyāna differ in name but are identical in substance.
Therefore, the sūtra says:
"Concentration of mind (*citta-samādhi*) and equanimity of concentration (*samatā-samādhi*) are called right concentration (*samyak-samādhi*).
Since the sūtra thus explains right concentration by means of *samādhi*, [it follows that they are synonymous].
It should be understood that although the names "samādhi" (equipoise) and "dhyāna" (meditative concentration) differ, their substance is identical.
This samādhi is also termed "one-pointedness of mind" (*cittaikāgratā*),
the meaning of which has been explained as before.
Regarding the tradition that concentration alone extends up to the non-meditative states (*asamāpatti*),
the Vaibhāṣikas maintain that only concentration is both meditative absorption (*dhyāna*) and a constituent of meditative absorption (*dhyānāṅga*).
The remaining four factors are factors of meditative absorption (dhyāna-aṅga) but are not themselves meditative absorption.
According to the true meaning, they are like the four divisions of an army;
this is the Sautrāntika position as stated by the Master of the Treatise.
According to the true meaning, elephants, horses, chariots, and infantry constitute the fourfold army;
individually they are the "limbs" (aṅga),
and collectively they are the "army" (senā).
By synthesizing the particulars, a whole is formed;
thus, an army is a mere designation.
So too are the five factors of dhyāna.
It should be understood that the same applies here: the particulars are the factors (*aṅga*), while dhyāna is the whole;
the whole is constituted by the particulars.
"Dhyāna is conventional;
one should know that the remaining dhyāna factors are likewise" means that each of the other three dhyānas is explained in two ways.
It should be understood that it is likewise so.
Regarding the phrase "the second dhyāna up to the fourfold samādhi," this explains the latter six phrases.
This can be understood from the text.
Furthermore, the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 81, states:
"Question: Do the lower stages also possess untainted equanimity (*upekṣā*) and mindfulness (*smṛti*)?"
Why is it said that only in the fourth dhyāna are equanimity (*upekṣā*) and mindfulness (*smṛti*) pure?
Answer: Because in the fourth dhyāna, both equanimity and mindfulness are free from the eight disturbances;
therefore, they are called "pure."
Suffering, pleasure, grief, joy, inhalation, exhalation, vitarka, and vicāra are called the eight disturbances.
Among these, none is exclusively termed "pure."
It is as explained extensively therein.
Regarding how many types there are in total for the names of the factors of meditative concentration (*dhyānāṅga*),
this second section clarifies the essential nature of those factors.
The preceding question is restated.
The verse says: "That which reaches joy is the feeling of joy.
This is the response provided within the verse.
The first phrase generally reveals the essence and number [of the factors];
the following three phrases distinguish them from non-Buddhist schools.
The Treatise says: "Adding these to the previous ones makes eleven."
Explaining the first phrase:
the actual entities of these factors are only eleven, namely, the first five factors: vitarka, vicāra, prīti, sukha, and samādhi.
That is, there are five actual entities:
the three factors of the second dhyāna— joy, bliss, and meditative concentration—
as well as the previously mentioned addition of the factor of internal clarity.
The first two factors remain as before;
the third dhyāna samādhi adds four further factors—
equanimity, mindfulness, wisdom, and bliss— to those previously mentioned.
Adding the preceding [three] makes ten.
In the fourth dhyāna, the three factors of equanimity, mindfulness, and concentration— as before— plus the factor of neither-pain-nor-pleasure are added, making eleven.
Within this, joy (*prīti*), bliss (*sukha*), and equanimity (*upekṣā*) are explained separately;
therefore, it is said there are eleven.
However, if one considers them according to their categories:
There are only nine types,
because joy (*prīti*), bliss (*sukha*), and equanimity (*upekṣā*) are all of the nature of feeling (*vedanā*).
As for what is called "nine":

That is to say: mindfulness, concentration, wisdom, feeling, faith, pliancy, equanimity, applied thought, and sustained thought. Within this context, I shall now briefly provide a twofold classification.
I. Abolition and Establishment;

II. Question and Answer. Regarding "abolition and establishment": it is asked why, among the seventy-five dharmas, only nine are established as factors of meditative absorption (*dhyānāṅga*), while the others are not.
The explanation says: if a dharma accords with purity, is predominant, and shares the same object as the meditative concentration (*samādhi*), it is established as a factor of meditative absorption.
If it were not so, they would not be established.
Regarding why the first category of material phenomena (*rūpadharma*)—the eleven [factors]—is not established as branches:
they are not established as branches because they do not share the same object of focus (*ālambana*) as the meditative absorption (*samādhi*).
Although the unmanifest (avijñapti) is necessarily co-existent [with the manifest],
it is not established as a factor [of the path] because it does not necessarily share the same object of cognition;
thus, the Nyāyānusāra states:
For what reason is non-informative matter (*avijñapti*) not a factor of meditative concentration (*dhyānāṅga*)?
Because the factors of meditative concentration assist the mind in abiding upon its object, whereas non-informative matter does not take an object; therefore, it is not established as a factor.
Regarding why the second [category], the mental factors (*caitasika-dharma*), are not established as constituent members (*aṅga*):
the *Abhidharmamahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 80, states that the mind conforms to the process of transmigration (*pravṛtti*).
Since concentration (samādhi) necessarily leads toward cessation,
the mind is not established as a constituent of dhyāna.
Furthermore, the mind is preeminent, like a king.
All mental factors (*caitasika-dharma*) are like ministers and assistants;
because concentration (*samādhi*) is itself a mental factor, it is not established as a constituent of dhyāna (*dhyānāṅga*).
This is just as various kings do not serve their own ministers and assistants.
Regarding the third [point], among the forty-six mental factors (*caitasika-dharma*),
only nine are established as branches while the others are not;
these include two from the great unwholesome ground (*akuśala-mahābhūmika*).
The six universal mental factors of great affliction,
the ten universal mental factors of minor affliction,
and greed, hatred, pride, and doubt among the indeterminate mental factors.
Since their nature is entirely defiled and they do not accord with meditative concentration, they are not established as factors [of the path].
Although among the ten universal mental factors (*mahābhūmika-dharma*) some are also wholesome,
only four are established as factors and the others are not.
Mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom—
these three are established as factors because they are preeminent in accordance with purification;
feeling, however, pertains to both the defiled and purified portions.
Because both its power and its function are superior, it is established as such in both cases;
for this reason, it is established as the member of "feeling" (*vedanā*) within the forward progression of dependent origination,
and likewise established as the member of "feeling" within the backward cessation and purification.
It is established as a limb based on its conformity to and purity of the [noble] side.
Furthermore, the *Nyāyānusāra* (Treatise on Right Reasoning), fascicle 71, states: "Other masters say..."
Although sensation is predominant in defilement,
it also possesses the capacity to perform beneficial functions for the side of purity; just as, for example,
although the nature of a caṇḍāla is base and inferior, [it can still serve a purpose].
It is able to perform beneficial deeds for noble families;
therefore, it performs a beneficial function within meditative concentration (*dhyāna*).

Among the factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipākṣika-dharma*), it is designated by the name "factor of enlightenment" (*bodhyaṅga*). Question: Why are there only three among the five feelings (*vedanā*) and not two? Answer: It is explained that because they share the same object as the meditative absorption (*samādhi*), they are established as factors of meditative concentration (*dhyānāṅga*).
Regarding why *vitarka*, *vicāra*, *daurmanasya*, and *duḥkha* are [factors] unique to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and thus do not exist in the other two realms:
the *Mahāvibhāṣā* states: "Regarding why *saṃjñā*, *cetanā*, *sparśa*, *chanda*, *manasikāra*, and *adhimokṣa* are not established as [distinct] factors (*aṅga*):
the *Vibhāṣā* says..."
Perception (*saṃjñā*), volition (*cetanā*), contact (*sparśa*), and desire (*chanda*) all have functions that predominantly favor the process of saṃsāric flow;
because they do not accord with the cessation of suffering, they are not established as factors of meditative absorption (*dhyānāṅga*).
Attention (*manasikāra*) functions preeminently only in the realm of desire (*kāmadhātu*) and in the state of distraction (*vikṣepa*) when confronting objects.
Because they do not belong to the levels of meditative concentration (*samāpatti-bhūmi*), they are also not established as factors of dhyāna (*dhyānāṅga*).
Resolute confidence (*adhimukti*) is preeminent only in the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*),
whereas dhyāna is preeminent throughout all stages.
Therefore, those [factors] are not established as limbs of dhyāna.
Although all ten great wholesome mental factors (mahābhūmika-dharma) are indeed wholesome,
only three are established as limbs.

As for the others that are not established [as factors]: faith (*śraddhā*), equanimity (*upekṣā*), and pliancy (*praśrabdhi*) are established as factors because they are particularly predominant in accordance with purity.
Faith is the primary foundation for all spiritual practices.
Alternatively, like a water-clearing gem,
it is established as a factor because it places the mind within the category of mental states and causes the mind to become limpid and pure;
for since beginningless time, a mind that is dull or agitated has been unable to attain concentration.
Pliancy counteracts lethargy,
and equanimity counteracts restlessness;
through these, one attains meditative concentration.
Alternatively, restlessness is an obstacle to concentration,
which is remedied by equanimity;
torpor is an obstacle to wisdom.
Lightness-and-pliancy (praśrabdhi) can counteract these two; since these two are able to counteract the heavy hindrances to concentration and wisdom,
they are established separately.
Although the other seven factors are wholesome, compliant, and pure, they are not specifically predominant.
The *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* states:
"Question: For what reason is diligence (*vīrya*) not a factor of meditative concentration (*dhyānāṅga*)?"
Answer: Among the factors of the dhyānas, those that accord with their own stage are superior;
diligence is superior in its accordance with other stages.
That is to say, the diligence of the first dhyāna [is superior].
It is conducive to the second dhyāna as superior,
continuing thus up to the exertion of the sphere of nothingness;
it is conducive to the perception of compassion as superior, rather than the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
Therefore, it is not established as a limb of dhyāna.
Furthermore, diligence is detrimental to the cause of samādhi;
the cause of samādhi is precisely sublime bliss.
As the sūtra says: "Because of pleasure, the mind becomes concentrated;
for one who exerts diligent effort, there is much suffering in body and mind."
In the cultivation of samādhi, body and mind experience much pleasure;
therefore, diligence is not a factor of meditative concentration (*dhyānāṅga*). Furthermore, it is asked:

for what reason are shame (*hrī*), embarrassment (*apatrāpya*), non-attachment (*alobha*), non-hatred (*adveṣa*), heedfulness (*apramāda*), and non-harming (*avihiṃsā*) [not factors of meditative concentration]?
Are they not factors of dhyāna?
Answer: No, because they do not conform extremely well to the various dhyānas.
These are all wholesome dharmas.
It serves as a proximate antidote primarily for the unwholesome dharmas of the distracted stage within the desire realm;
its power is thus enhanced,
whereas it is not so in the meditative stages.

Therefore, they are not established as factors of meditative concentration (*dhyānāṅga*). Question: Why are *prīti* (joy) and *daurmanasya* (dejection) not established separately? Answer: It is explained that even the seven factors such as *vīrya* (diligence) and so forth, which are always concomitant with the mind, are still not established separately.
How much less could joy and aversion— which certainly do not arise simultaneously— be established as factors [of absorption]? Furthermore,

among the mental factors of the non-concentrated stage (*asamāhita-bhūmika*), although vitarka, vicāra, regret (*kaukṛtya*), and sleep (*middha*) are all equally associated with the wholesome, [they cannot be factors of absorption].
Regarding the two that are established and the two that are not:
the two factors of vitarka (applied thought) and vicāra (sustained thought) are particularly strong in accordance with purification.
Because it assists meditative concentration (*samādhi*) in restraining and exerting the mind,
causing it to abandon both coarse and subtle [distractions] and counteracting sensual desires and evil, it is established as a factor (*aṅga*).
Regret and sleep are not established as factors because these factors exist only in the preparatory stage and only in the dhyāna realms,
whereas these two arise through birth and exist only in the desire realm.
Therefore, the forty-fourth [point] is that the non-associated formations (*viprayukta-saṃskāra*) are not established as factors of meditative absorption (*dhyānāṅga*).
Because they assist concentration by sharing the same object of focus, they are established as factors of meditative absorption;

however, since these [non-associated formations] are not associated [with the mind], they are not established as such factors. Fifth, the three unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*) are not established as factors of meditative absorption.
Now, for the factors of meditative concentration (*dhyānāṅga*) to be established, they must functionally arise and share the same object as the meditative absorption itself.
Since these [factors] do not functionally arise, they are not established as factors. Regarding the "question and answer," the *Abhidharmamahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* states:
Question: For what reason are vicāra, pleasant feeling (sukha-vedanā), and equanimity (upekṣā-vedanā) not established as factors of enlightenment (bodhipakṣadharma)?
Answer: Because they are obscured and impaired.
That is to say, investigation (*vicāra*) is eclipsed and impaired by right reflection (*samyak-saṃkalpa*);
pleasant feeling (*sukha-vedanā*) is eclipsed and impaired by the bliss of pliancy (*praśrabdhi-sukha*);

and equanimity feeling (*upekṣā-vedanā*) is eclipsed and impaired by the equanimity of formations (*saṃskāra-upekṣā*). Therefore, they are not established as factors of enlightenment (*bodhipākṣika-dharma*).
Question: If that is so, for what reason are the factors of dhyāna established?

Answer: Among the factors conducive to enlightenment (bodhipakṣa), right intention (samyaksaṃkalpa) is established as a factor conducive to enlightenment in order to stimulate right view (samyagdṛṣṭi).
The mode of activity of vicāra is subtle;
because it is obscured and impaired by vitarka during the exertion of right view,
the factors of dhyāna are established.
To exclude the mutual suppression and impairment found among the unwholesome and evil states of the lower stages,
[it is said that] within the factors of enlightenment, pliancy (*praśrabdhi*) and pleasant feeling (*sukha-vedanā*) exist in the same moment without mutual suppression or impairment.
Within the factors of meditative concentration (*dhyānāṅga*), the distinction between levels is established by way of non-obscured impairment;

however, within the factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipākṣika-dharma*), equanimity (*upekṣā*) and the feeling of equanimity (*upekṣā-vedanā*) coexist in a single moment, characterized by mutual obscuration and impairment.

Among the factors of meditative concentration (*dhyānāṅga*), the factors of counteraction (*pratipakṣa*) and the factors of benefit (*anuśaṃsa*) function separately and do not obstruct one another. Diligence (*vīrya*) is not a factor of meditative concentration.

The question and answer are as before. Question: Why are right speech (*samyagvāc*), right action (*samyakkarmānta*), and right livelihood (*samyagājīva*) not factors of meditative concentration? Answer: As for the factors of meditative concentration...
That is to say, when one dwells in association with dhyāna,
there must necessarily be a basis (*āśraya*), an object (*ālambana*), and a mode of activity (*ākāra*);
it is only when there is also alertness that it is termed "associated."
Right speech, right action, and right livelihood do not possess such characteristics;
therefore, they are not established as factors of meditative concentration (*dhyānāṅga*).
This is because of these four characteristics, as well as the various dissociated factors (*viprayuktadharma*) such as acquisitions (*prāpti*).

None of these should be established as factors of dhyāna (*dhyānāṅga*), because they do not assist meditative concentration (*samādhi*) in proceeding toward a single object; this concludes the treatise. Question: For what reason are the four [factors] beginning with diligence (*vīrya*) considered branches of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣya*)? Answer: Enlightenment (*bodhi*) is wisdom (*prajñā*), and its nature is that of energetic exertion (*utsāha*).
Vigor is also characterized by diligence and courage; it follows and urges on the horse of vigor toward enlightenment.
Right speech, action, and livelihood have ethical discipline as their essence, for the purpose of forming the hub of the eightfold wheel of the Dharma.
These four are all conducive to awakening and are powerful;
therefore, they are all established as factors of awakening (*bodhipakṣadharma*).
For this reason, it is said that one should reflect upon them in accordance with reality.
The four propositions for comparing the first with the second can be understood;
the same applies to comparing the first with the third and fourth.
By pairing two with three and four, and three with four,
one may understand this through reflection.
Therefore, it is said that the remaining factors should be considered in relation to one another according to reason.
Why is it that the third [member] speaks of the increase of pleasant feeling?
This explains the second phrase.
This is the question.
Regarding the statement that "the first two [meditative] joys are subsumed under pliancy (*praśrabdhi*)," this is the response of the Sarvāstivādins.
Because the bliss of the first and second dhyānas is comprised within pliancy (*praśrabdhi*),
the third dhyāna is said to have an increase in the sensation of bliss.
What reasoning serves as proof that this [bliss] is pliancy?
Question:
Regarding the statement that "in the first two dhyānas, [the factors] reach up to and include four branches," the Sarvāstivādins respond as follows.
Although the first dhyāna possesses the pleasure of the three consciousnesses,
because the faculty of pleasure (sukhendriya) is absent while one is actually in meditative absorption,
it is not the case that the first and second dhyānas possess the pleasure of bodily sensation (kāyikasukha).
Because the five consciousnesses are absent while one is in meditative concentration,
there is also no mental experience of pleasure;
this is because it is said that there is joy (*prīti*).
Joy is the feeling of joy (*saumanasya*).
Since there is no simultaneous occurrence of both the feelings of joy and pleasure within a single moment of mind, there is no feeling of pleasure (*sukha*).
Furthermore, the feelings of joy and pleasure cannot manifest alternately [within that same moment].
This is because it is taught that the first dhyāna possesses five factors (*pañcāṅga*),
while the second dhyāna possesses four factors (*caturaṅga*).
Some say that there is no faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*) included within the attainment (*samāpatti*).
Explaining the Sautrāntika interpretation:
some say that there is no mental faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*).
As for the mention of the factor of pleasure (*sukha-aṅga*) within the first three dhyānas:
All of these are the faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*) subsumed under bodily sensation (*kāyikī vedanā*);
this is the statement of the thesis.
If so, why is it said that "bodily and mental pleasant sensations" [are meant]?
The Sarvāstivādins raise an objection:
since the Sūtra speaks of the mind,
it is clearly understood that there is also a mental faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*).
Regarding those who ask what merit there is in this,
the Sautrāntika masters respond;
others refer to the Sarvāstivāda masters.
In this sutra, the word "mind" (*citta*) is added,
whereas in the sūtras of other schools, only the "body" (*kāya*) is mentioned.
Furthermore, regarding the factor of bliss (*sukha-aṅga*) established in the third dhyāna:
The sūtra itself states that it is "pleasure experienced by the body.
You, a teacher of the Sarvāstivāda school,
might claim that in this sūtra the term "body" refers to the mind.
What merit is there in designating it as the "body of mind" (manas-kāya)?
Furthermore, why is it said that the fourth dhyāna is superior to the previous two?
The Sautrāntikas further object:
Moreover, since pliancy (*praśrabdhi*) increases even more in the fourth dhyāna than it does in the first and second dhyānas,
yet it is not said that the latter possesses the factor of pleasure (*sukha*).
If you claim that the pliancy (*praśrabdhi*) in the first and second dhyānas must be called "pleasure" only when it accords with a pleasant feeling (*sukha-vedanā*),
then it follows that the "joy" (*prīti*) mentioned in the context of the three feelings in the first and second dhyānas is designated as a pleasant feeling.
The refutation states: Since the pliancy (*praśrabdhi*) of the third dhyāna accords with pleasant feeling (*sukha-vedanā*), it ought to be a factor of pleasure (*sukhāṅga*).
If you claim that the pliancy of those [third and fourth dhyānas]— [...is not a factor of pleasure... (as the original text implies).

Alternatively, it might be argued that because the pliancy (*praśrabdhi*) of those three concentrations is impaired by equanimity (*upekṣā*), equanimity is established [as a separate factor] rather than pliancy.
This is refuted as being not so.
The practice of equanimity is likewise a wholesome dharma because it increases pliancy;
it does not diminish pliancy.
Furthermore, those three and four [factors] constitute pliancy.

Alternatively, why are the pliancy (*praśrabdhi*) of those [higher] three concentrations not established as factors (*aṅga*), given that their pliancy is superior to that of the first and second concentrations?
Furthermore, the Sūtra states that [the third concentration] reaches [a state] that is not merely pliancy.
The Sautrāntika school further cites a sūtra to prove that the two initial types of pleasure are not *praśrabdhi* (serenity).
Furthermore, a sūtra states:
"At that time, if the noble disciples..."
Within a body that has arisen from the detachment of desire and is filled with joy,
he realizes this concentration, fully accomplishes it, and dwells in that concentration.
At that time, he has already abandoned the five lower fetters (*pañca avarabhāgīyāni saṃyojanāni*).
Alternatively, having already abandoned the five hindrances,
one cultivates the five dharmas,
attaining their full perfection and ultimate consummation.
The full explanation, including the questions and answers,
may be understood from the sūtra itself. Because this sūtra distinguishes between pliancy (*praśrabdhi*) and bliss (*sukha*),
the bliss of the first and second dhyānas is not identical to pliancy.
If it is argued that there is no fault in admitting the arising [of consciousness] within meditative concentration,
the Sautrāntika again restates the refutation of the Sarvāstivāda:
"If you say that how could there be body-consciousness within meditative concentration that gives rise to bodily pleasure?"
The opponent objects: "There is no fault in saying it exists.
We, the Sautrāntikas, maintain that within the meditative absorption there is a wind of pliancy (*praśrabdhi*) which is touched;
it arises from the superior concentration.
The pleasant sensation associated with the body-consciousness that arises in accordance [with its conditions] pervades the body-faculty; therefore,
if you claim that the arising of body-consciousness is external, [you are mistaken].
As for the objection that "because it is dispersed, it should be lost and destroyed," the refutation states: there is no such loss.
This wind of pliancy arises from superior meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
Because it draws forth the pleasant feeling associated with internal consciousness and is further able to give rise to the samādhi associated with mental consciousness,
it does not lose or destroy its concentration.
If you claim that the arising of body-consciousness should be called "emerging from meditative absorption," we refute this by stating: this objection is not valid,
for the reasons previously stated.
The aforementioned cause is precisely this wind of pliancy (*praśrabdhi*).
Arising from superior meditative concentration (*samādhi*), it induces internal physical bliss and is further able to facilitate the arising of samādhi.
It is not called "emerging from meditative absorption.

Alternatively, it may be because [the mind] follows the preceding signs that it is not called emerging from absorption. If you claim that it relies upon the body-faculty (*kāyendriya*) of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), [that too is incorrect].

One should not be able to produce a tactile object (*spraṣṭavya*) or a tactile consciousness (*vijñāna*) belonging to the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), because that body and that tactile object belong to its own level (*svabhūmi*). [Objection:
If [it arises] from a distracted mind (*vikṣiptacitta*) based on the body-faculty (*kāyendriya*) of the desire realm...
One does not give rise to body-consciousness taking the tangibles of the form realm as its object;
if it arises in accordance with meditative absorption, it is admitted that it relies upon a body belonging to the desire realm.
There is no fault, because within that meditative absorption there arises a body-consciousness that takes the pliancy of the body as its object.
If it is argued that this would entail the error of contradicting reason while one is actually in the state of attainment (*samāpatti*), [the response is as follows:]
The Sarvāstivādins raise an objection: If that were so,
then while one is actually in an untainted meditative absorption (*anāsrava-samādhi*),
there would be the touch of the wind of pliancy (*praśrabdhi*) and the tactile consciousness (*kāya-vijñāna*).
It would follow that it is untainted (*anāsrava*).
Otherwise, it would be the case that a portion of the established factor of pliancy— the wind-contact of pliancy— is tainted (*sāsrava*),
while a portion of the mental factor associated with the mental consciousness— pliancy itself— is untainted.
This would result in the fallacy of contradicting reason;
otherwise, it would follow that a small portion of the established factor— the wind of pliancy (*praśrabdhi*)— is contaminated (*sāsrava*),
while a small portion associated with the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) is uncontaminated (*anāsrava*).
This would result in the fallacy of contradicting reason.
Alternatively, let it not be the case that a portion of the pliancy-wind-contact and body-consciousness-pleasure established here is contaminated (*sāsrava*),
while a portion associated with mental consciousness (*manovijñāna-samprayukta*) is uncontaminated (*anāsrava*).
This would result in the fault of contradicting reason.
To avoid this fault of contradicting reason,
the Sautrāntika replies:
Why is this? Because the Sarvāstivādins argue that [the term] "physical pliancy" (kāya-praśrabdhi) is spoken of with a hidden intention (abhiprāya).
The Sautrāntika replied:
"The Sarvāstivādins also agree that the sūtras state that bodily pliancy (*kāyapraśrabdhi*) is included within the factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*);
why, then, do you challenge me?"
Although it is intended that the mental factor of pliancy associated with body-consciousness is meant,
because the term "bodily pliancy" is identical to that used in the Sūtra,
you might argue that bodily pliancy is not actually a factor of enlightenment (bodhyaṅga).
Those factors of enlightenment that are conducive to enlightenment are called "factors of enlightenment.
It should likewise be admitted that untainted [states] are so designated because contact and body-consciousness are conducive to the untainted;
thus, there is no fault of partial states being tainted and partial states being untainted. Furthermore, the Sautrāntika master explains:
Our school maintains that the tactile sensation of physical pliancy (*kāya-praśrabdhi*) is included within the factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*), because it is taught as such.
If you argue that physical pliancy is not actually a factor of enlightenment,
but is called a factor of enlightenment only because it is conducive to them, [we reply as follows].
One should also admit that the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) is likewise [designated] as such; in reality, it is not uncontaminated.
Because it is conducive to the uncontaminated, it is called "uncontaminated.
What contradiction to reason is there in this?
If you claim that it is admitted that contact and body-consciousness are untainted (anāsrava),
this would contradict the sūtra;
for the intention of this sūtra is to state that all fifteen elements (dhātu) are entirely tainted (sāsrava).
The general consensus is that this does not contradict the established scriptural tradition.
The intent of this sutra concerns the contact (*sparśa*) of other distracted states,
as well as the underlying intention regarding the body-consciousness (*kāyavijñāna*) of other distracted states.
It is stated that all fifteen elements (dhātus) are entirely with-outflows (sāsrava).
This is not said in reference to their specific states; because it does not exhaustively explain the principle, it is said to have an underlying intention (abhiprāya).
Regarding how the untainted [meditative absorption] can have as few as four factors,
the Sarvāstivādins raise an objection:
"How can the untainted dhyāna manifest?"

Contact, body-consciousness, and a small portion of the factors associated with outflows (sāsrava); and consciousness-associated with the mental consciousness (manovijñāna) and a small portion of the factors free from outflows (anāsrava)—
this is difficult [to reconcile] in terms of their essential nature.
Regarding the phrase "because they do not arise simultaneously and thus cannot be said to have faults," the Sautrāntika replies:
"In their prior and subsequent stages, they do not arise simultaneously; therefore, they may be described as having outflows (*sāsrava*)."
Or, if it is said that [the feeling] is untainted (anāsrava), what fault is there?
If you argue that mental joy (saumanasya) and bodily pleasure (sukha) do not arise simultaneously, [that is incorrect].
As for the argument that "the first dhyāna would lack the principle of having five factors" and "the second dhyāna would lack the principle of having four factors," this too is without fault.
Regarding the first dhyāna stage, it may be argued that there could be mention of the factors of joy and bliss as occurring sequentially;
just as vitarka and vicāra, though belonging to the same stage, do not arise simultaneously,
you might claim that vitarka and vicāra are nevertheless admitted to arise together.
In that case, the example of phenomena that do not arise simultaneously with joy and pleasure is unestablished.
The Sautrāntika offers this defense:
This is not unestablished;
because the grossness and subtlety of the mind are mutually contradictory,
they should not arise simultaneously.
Furthermore, regarding the fact that vitarka and vicāra do not arise simultaneously,
since you, the Sarvāstivādins, are unable to offer a refutation, and being unable to provide such a refutation, [the position remains unestablished].
The analogy is thus established.

As for the statement, "By this, it can be said that [the Sautrāntika] reaches [the conclusion], though they do not explicitly state 'perception' (*saṃjñā*) and so forth," this is the Sautrāntika’s own interpretation based on their own tenets.
From this it can be said:
based on the reduction of the first five factors, the second dhyāna is established by the elimination of vitarka and vicāra;
the third dhyāna is established by the elimination of vitarka, vicāra, and prīti.
The fourth dhyāna is established by the elimination of vitarka, vicāra, prīti, and sukha.
It is precisely by this principle that the first dhyāna is said to possess five factors (pañcāṅga),
because the subsequent dhyānas are established through the gradual abandonment of the preceding factors.
Because there is no gradual diminution [of the factors], the ideations (*saṃjñā*) and so forth are not stated to be branches.
Alternatively, one might ask: why is it said that [the factors] reach the excellence of *vitarka* and *vicāra*?
The Sautrāntika further objects:
One should explain why only five factors are established at the beginning.
If you claim that these five are established as factors because they are superior in supporting the initial dhyāna, [then...]
This is not reasonable.
Since mindfulness and wisdom can support the excellence of initial application and sustained application in the first dhyāna,
mindfulness and wisdom should be established as factors (aṅga).
Regarding the phrase "although there is a certain class [of teachers] because it is commonly established," the Sautrāntika masters say:
"Although there is a certain class of Vaibhāṣika masters..."
Thus they explain the factors of the first dhyāna and so forth;
however, this is not because it was established by the ancient masters of the Sautrāntika school. Furthermore, the masters of the Sarvāstivāda school state:
Although a certain class of Sautrāntikas asserts such things as the factors of the first dhyāna and so forth,
this is not because they were collectively established by the ancient masters of the Sarvāstivāda school.
"One should carefully examine and discern [the state] up to what is called 'internal serenity'" explains the third phrase;
this constitutes the question.
Regarding the statement that "this concentration is far removed from [disturbance], like a river without waves," the Sautrāntika master replies:
"This second dhyāna is able to remain far removed from the agitation caused by vitarka and vicāra."
When the essence of concentration flows in a continuous stream that is pure and tranquil,
it is called internal serenity (*adhyātmasamprasāda*).
If there is agitation caused by vitarka and vicāra, [it is not so].
This concentration is a continuous stream that is not purified;
it proceeds without tranquility, like a river with waves,
and is therefore not called "internal serenity."
"If that were so, this [factor] should be designated as 'inner serenity' (adhyātmasamprasāda).
This is the objection raised by the Sarvāstivādins based on their own tenets:
if the very essence of this meditative absorption, being free from applied and sustained thought (vitarka-vicāra), is what is called "inner serenity," then...
In this case, internal serenity (*adhyātmasamprasāda*) would have no distinct substance;
how then can it be admitted that there are eleven real entities (*dravya*)?
Having concluded the objection, he states his own position.
Therefore, it should be said that this internal serenity is precisely the faculty of faith;
that is to say, when one realizes the second dhyāna,
one is also able to become detached from the defilements of the meditative stages.
The arising of deep faith is called "internal serenity.
When one attains the first dhyāna,
although faith arises again upon being freed from the defilements of the distracted stage (vikkhambhana-bhūmi), [it is distinguished by its depth].
Because faith has not yet arisen while one is still detached from the defilements of the dhyāna stages,
the factor of faith is not established as a limb of concentration within the first dhyāna;
however, once one is subsequently detached from the defilements of the first dhyāna, faith arises again within the dhyāna stages.
Therefore, the factor of faith (śraddhā) is established as a constituent of these two meditative attainments.
Because faith has the characteristic of purity (viśuddhi), it is designated by the name "purity.
Because it is free from external agitation and flows evenly within the concentration, it is called "internal evenness" (adhyātmasamprasāda).
Because it is pure internally and equal,
it is established with the name "internal serenity" (*adhyātmasaṃprasāda*).
Other masters say that up to this point there is no distinct entity.
Other masters of the Sautrāntika school say:
"This internal serenity, meditative concentration (*samādhi*), applied thought (*vitarka*), and sustained thought (*vicāra*) have no distinct entities.
If they have no distinct entities, then mental factors (*caitta*) would fail to be established."
The Sarvāstivādins raise an objection:
"If mental states that differ in their specific conditions may also be called 'mental factors' (caitta),
the Sautrāntikas respond."
Because they are provisionally established based on specific states of the mind,
they are also called mental factors (*caitta*).
Although this principle exists, it is not the doctrine I uphold.
The Sarvāstivādins say:
"O Sautrāntika master, although you possess this principle,
it is not our own tenet."
Regarding the statement "as mentioned above, up to 'knowing for certain that it is so,'" this explains the fourth phrase.
An external opponent raises an objection:
As stated in the verse above, "joy" (*prīti*) is the feeling of joy (*saumanasya-vedanā*).
What serves as proof that this is definitely so?
Would you, members of the Sarvāstivāda, claim that joy is not the feeling of joy? Thus [the author] rebukes them.
"If I accept what other schools accept," the opponent replies,
"how do those other schools accept that there is no feeling of joy?"
The Sarvāstivādins raise an objection, stating that joy (*prīti*) exists separately and its essence is distinct [from pleasure].
The opponent cites the response of another school; "another school" refers here to the Mahīśāsaka school.
This means that there is a distinct joy (*prīti*) which is a mental factor (*caitasika-dharma*) and not the feeling of joy (*prīti-vedanā*).
The bliss (*sukha*) of the first three dhyānas is entirely the feeling of joy.
Therefore, joy (*prīti*) and the sensation of joy (*prītivedanā*) differ in their essential natures.
As for the claim that the bliss (*sukha*) of the [first] three dhyānas is not actually joy but rather pleasure (*sukha*),
this is refuted by the Sarvāstivādins.
It is not the case that the bliss of the first three dhyānas can all be termed the sensation of joy (*saumanasya*).
This is because two Āgamas provide clear proof. *Āgama* is translated here as "transmission" (*chuan*).
This means it was transmitted by all Buddhas of the three periods of time;
the older term "Āgama" is a corruption. The first sūtra states:
"Gradually and without remainder, one extinguishes the five faculties, such as sorrow."
In the first dhyāna, sorrow is extinguished without remainder;
in the second dhyāna, suffering is extinguished without remainder;
in the third dhyāna, joy is extinguished without remainder.
In the fourth dhyāna, pleasure (*sukha*) is extinguished without remainder;
since joy (*prīti*) and pleasure are known to be extinguished separately,
it is clear that the pleasure of the third dhyāna is not the feeling of joy (*saumanasya*).
The *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 81, explains:
"As stated in the Sūtra, the faculty of grief (*daurmanasyendriya*) ceases in the first dhyāna,
and the faculty of suffering (*duḥkhendriya*) ceases in the second dhyāna."
Question: When one becomes free from the defilement of desire, sorrow (*daurmanasya*) and suffering (*duḥkha*) are abandoned.
Why does the Sūtra make this statement? Answer:
It is made with reference to the abandonment of their respective antidotes (*pratipakṣa*).
This means that although the faculty of suffering (*duḥkhendriya*) is abandoned during the stage of detachment from desire,
it is not yet termed "having transcended the remedy for suffering.
This occurs at the time one attains detachment from the first dhyāna.
It is called the cessation of suffering because it is the antidote to past suffering.
The antidote to suffering refers to the first dhyāna. Furthermore, this statement is made based on the transcendence of one's lineage and the basis of suffering.
This means that although the faculty of suffering (*duḥkhendriya*) is abandoned during the stage of detachment from desire,
one has not yet transcended the basis of suffering or the lineage of suffering; therefore, when one attains detachment from the first dhyāna,
it is said that "suffering ceases," because one has then transcended both the basis of suffering and the lineage of suffering.
The basis and lineage refer to the various groups of consciousness. Question:
Although the faculty of grief (*daurmanasyendriya*) is abandoned at the stage of detachment from desire, [why is it not included?]
Furthermore, since it has not yet transcended its antidote, its basis, and its lineage, one should not say that sorrow is extinguished in the first dhyāna.
Answer: The antidote, the basis, and the lineage of the faculty of sorrow all reside in the mental consciousness.
Since it shares the same basis as the faculty of grief within the mental consciousness,
its cessation is stated at the very moment of right abandonment.
This refers to the basis of the faculty of pain and the category of suffering.
Because it does not coexist with its antidote within a single consciousness,
the cessation of suffering is said to occur only after one has transcended the antidote, its basis, and its lineage.
Some have stated this as follows:
Regarding the cessation of the faculty of suffering (*duḥkhendriya*) in the second dhyāna:
this refers to the cessation of applied thought (*vitarka*) and sustained thought (*vicāra*), for the noble ones (*ārya*) conceive of suffering within applied and sustained thought.
Those who have transcended the stage of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) and become weary of the suffering of hell are able to conceive the perception of suffering [even toward that state];
therefore, it is called the faculty of suffering (*duḥkhendriya*). This is from the aforementioned treatise. The second sūtra states:
"In the fourth dhyāna, pleasure (*sukha*) is abandoned and suffering (*duḥkha*) is abandoned."
When one first becomes detached from the defilements of the second dhyāna, joy (prīti) ceases;
when one first becomes detached from the defilements of the desire realm, sorrow (daurmanasya) ceases.
Since this sutra states that after pleasure (sukha) has been abandoned, joy ceases first.
Therefore, one knows that in the third dhyāna there is necessarily no faculty of joy (saumanasyendriya),
but only pleasure (sukha).
This is proven by these two sūtras.
The feeling of joy (*saumanasya*) is joy (*prīti*), not pleasure (*sukha*).
The *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 81, in its commentary on the second sutra, states:
"The abandonment of pleasure..."
Question: When one attains the fourth dhyāna, one is entirely detached from all contaminated phenomena (*sāsrava-dharma*) of the third dhyāna;
why, then, is it said that one only abandons pleasure (*sukha*)?

The answer is that pleasure (*sukha*) is designated as the primary factor because it represents the complete departure from all contaminated phenomena (*sāsrava-dharma*) of the third dhyāna; therefore,
pleasure alone is specifically mentioned.
Furthermore, pleasure is taught specifically because it is difficult to sever, difficult to shatter,
and difficult to transcend.
Moreover, pleasure is characterized by many afflictions that are both intense and firmly entrenched.
Therefore, it is explained selectively.
Furthermore, when one seeks to abandon the defilements of the third dhyāna through the joy [of the fourth],
that [joy] acts as an extreme obstacle, a bond, and a hindrance, like a violent jailer.
Therefore, it is explained selectively.
Furthermore, the various yoga practitioners cultivate the fourth dhyāna specifically as an antidote to pleasure.
Therefore, it is explained selectively.
Furthermore, because the various practitioners of yoga loathe and detest pleasure, they abandon the third dhyāna in its entirety.
Therefore, it is explained selectively.
Furthermore, while the higher stages lack pleasure (*sukha*), other factors may still be present; thus, pleasure alone is mentioned.
For these and various other reasons, it is said that one merely abandons pleasure and abandons suffering.
Question: At the time of becoming free from the defilement of desire, the practitioner who cultivates insight has already abandoned the faculty of suffering (*duḥkhendriya*).
Why is it that the abandonment of suffering is only mentioned at the time of becoming free from the defilements of the third dhyāna?
Answer: This is spoken of as "abandoned" with reference to what has already been abandoned;
that is, the term for the distant is used here to denote the near.
As with those who have already come, one also says they are coming now.
For example, when it is asked, "Great King, from where have you come?

Furthermore, based on the exhaustion of the paired phenomena (*yuganaddha-dharma*), the sound of "abandonment" (*prahāṇa*) is spoken of simultaneously. Regarding what are called the "paired phenomena":
That is to say, regarding suffering and pleasure:
although suffering has already been exhausted at the time of becoming free from the defilements of desire, pleasure has not yet been exhausted.
Now, one becomes free from the defilements of the third dhyāna.
Since suffering and pleasure have both ceased, it is described as the sound of abandonment.
Furthermore, the abandonment of pleasure refers to the abandonment of the faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*) in the third dhyāna.
The abandonment of suffering refers to the abandonment of the mind and mental factors associated with it.
Furthermore, the abandonment of pleasure refers to...
This refers to the abandonment of the faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*) in the third dhyāna.
As for the abandonment of suffering (*duḥkha*),
it refers to the abandonment of inhalation and exhalation (*āśvāsa-praśvāsa*) in the third dhyāna.
That is to say, noble ones conceive the perception of suffering regarding inhalation and exhalation;
this surpasses the perception of suffering that ordinary worldlings conceive regarding the Avīci Hell.
Furthermore, it is the abandonment of pleasure.
This means that the faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*) of the third dhyāna is abandoned;
as for the abandonment of suffering (*duḥkha*),
it refers precisely to the abandonment of that same faculty of pleasure.
As it is said that because of impermanence there is suffering:
regarding the prior disappearance of joy and sorrow,
at the time of becoming free from the defilement of desire, the faculty of sorrow has already disappeared.
When one becomes detached from the defilements of the second dhyāna, the faculty of joy (*saumanasyendriya*) has already ceased;
therefore, it is said here that joy and sorrow cease first.
Regarding this statement, is it the case that not all [faculties] are present?
Below this, the third section clarifies that the defiled [dhyānas] have no branches.
It introduces the following by restating the previous question:
"Regarding the eighteen types of branches of the aforementioned pure and untainted dhyānas..."
Are all [factors] present within the defiled dhyānas?
No; the answer is as follows.
What is this? It is an inquiry.
The verse says: "As for the others, it is said that there is no serenity or equanimity."
The verse provides the answer.
The commentary states: "Up to 'not all possess them,' which is the general heading."
Regarding the aforementioned pure and untainted factors of dhyāna,
they are not all present within defiled dhyānas.
Furthermore, there is one class [of beings] who attain birth therein by reaching it.
There are two masters’ explanations.
Here below, the first master’s interpretation is presented.
