This clarifies that in the first dhyāna, there are no factors of joy or bliss, but there are the factors of applied thought (*vitarka*), sustained thought (*vicāra*), and concentration (*samādhi*).
Therefore, the *Nyāyānusāra* (Treatise on the Principles of Correct Reasoning),
fascicle 78, states: "Furthermore, there is a certain class [of teachers] who, according to their own characteristics,
claim that the joy and bliss born of seclusion (*vivekaja-prītisukha*) do not exist within the first dhyāna when it is defiled."
Because it does not arise apart from the afflictions;
although this defiled concentration is associated with joy,
it is not included among the factors [of dhyāna] because it does not arise from detachment.
This does not merely refer to the arising of joy through detachment from desire;
it also refers to the arising [of joy] due to detachment from the defilements of one's own level,
for the Sūtra first states as follows:
Having already become detached from all sensual desires and unwholesome states,
it further says, "born of detachment, joy and bliss. In this context,
the term "born of detachment" is stated again for emphasis.
To show that there is also joy which arises from being free from the afflictions of its own level,
and to show that the factor of joy is exclusively wholesome in nature,
the Blessed One spoke of it in conjunction with pleasure.
Because that which is associated with pliancy (praśrabdhi) is necessarily wholesome in nature,
defiled meditative absorption (samādhi) must necessarily lack the factor of joy (prīti).
Therefore, as stated in the treatise, the first dhyāna in its defiled form possesses only three factors.
Regarding the phrase "in the second defiled [dhyāna], it reaches a state of being disturbed and turbid":
this clarifies that the defilement of the two dhyānas lacks internal purity (*adhyātmasaṃprasāda*).
Since their bliss (*sukha*) is the same as that of the first dhyāna, they are not distinguished separately.
Because there are two factors— joy (*prīti*) and concentration (*samādhi*)— the *Nyāyānusāra* states:
"Within the second defiled [dhyāna], there is no internal clarity (*adhyātmasaṃprasāda*)."
Because he is disturbed and turbid by afflictions,
although worldly people speak of "defiled faith," it is not established as a factor because it is not encompassed by [true] faith.
Joy (*prīti*) is pliancy (*praśrabdhi*) and is comprised solely within the category of the wholesome (*kuśala*);
as it is analogous to the first dhyāna, it is not explicitly excluded here.
Therefore, these defiled factors consist of only two types.
It is accepted that the second defiled dhyāna possesses the factor of joy (*prīti*),
whereas it is absent in the first defiled dhyāna.
What serves as the proof for this?
The joy of the first dhyāna is said to arise from seclusion because the phrase "arising from seclusion" is absent in the second [dhyāna].
Regarding the third [dhyāna], it is because one reaches a state of delusion within its defiled aspect.
This clarifies that in the three dhyānas, there is no mindfulness (*smṛti*) or wisdom (*prajñā*) when they are defiled;
as for equanimity (*upekṣā*), it is logically impossible.
Because they are excluded in the same manner as the fourth [dhyāna], they are not mentioned separately.
Since there is only pleasure and concentration,
the *Nyāyānusāra* states:
"In the third [dhyāna] when it is defiled, there is no right mindfulness or wisdom."
Because he is deluded by defiled pleasure, although mindfulness and wisdom exist within that defiled concentration,
they are termed "loss of mindfulness" and "incorrect wisdom. Therefore,
these two factors do not exist within the defiled state.
The factor of equanimity (*upekṣā*) is comprised solely of wholesome factors;
as this case is analogous to the fourth [member], it is not excluded here.
Therefore, these defiled members consist of only two types.
Regarding the phrase "in the fourth defiled [dhyāna], because it reaches that which is defiled":
this clarifies that the fourth defiled dhyāna lacks both equanimity (upekṣā) and mindfulness (smṛti),
while it possesses feeling (vedanā) and concentration (samādhi).
Therefore, the *Nyāyānusāra* states:
"In the fourth defiled [dhyāna], there is no equanimity or purity of mindfulness,
because it is defiled by the afflictions."
"Because of this, in the fourth [dhyāna], the defiled state consists of only two branches.
As for the statement, "because it is included within the great wholesome," this is the interpretation of the second master.
Other masters say that within the first two defiled [dhyānas], there is simply no *praśrabdhi* (pliancy). Thus,
the first defiled dhyāna has four factors.
The second defiled [dhyāna] has three factors;
in the latter two defiled [dhyānas], there is only the absence of equanimity of formation (*saṃskāra-upekṣā*).
The third defiled [dhyāna] has four factors.
The fourth defiled [jhāna] consists of three factors.
Since pliancy (praśrabdhi) and equanimity (upekṣā) are subsumed under the great wholesome mental states,
internal clarity (adhyātmasaṃprasāda) is faith (śraddhā).
Faith may be either defiled or undefiled;
therefore, it is said that the second [member] has three branches when it is defiled.
The *Nyāyānusāra* states:
Other masters say that in the first two defiled concentrations there is simply no pliancy (*praśrabdhi*),
while in the latter two defiled states there is simply no equanimity of formation (*saṃskāropekṣā*).
Because they are subsumed by "great wholesomeness" (*mahākuśala*).

That [text] states that joy (*prīti*), faith (*śraddhā*), mindfulness (*smṛti*), and wisdom (*prajñā*) within the defiled [states] are all included as factors (*aṅga*), because they are common to both the defiled and the wholesome.
The *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* (Vibhāṣā), fascicle 160, also contains this discussion with these two interpretations.
Furthermore, it is said:
regarding this, some maintain that none of the defiled dhyānas are established as having constituent factors (aṅga).
As for the statement that there is only the absence of joy and bliss,
this is spoken according to the definitive meaning (*nītārtha*);
it refers to the joy and bliss born of seclusion in the first dhyāna.
Because there is the expression "detachment from birth," and because there is the expression "purity" regarding internal serenity (*adhyātmasaṃprasāda*) in the second dhyāna.
In the third dhyāna, there is right mindfulness and right awareness because of the presence of right speech.
In the fourth dhyāna, there is purity of equanimity and mindfulness.
Because there are statements regarding purity,
these [factors] are said to be "non-existent" in the defiled state because they are clearly contradictory to it;
yet in reality, none of the members [of dependent origination] exist within the defiled state.
Some say that [the factors] are designated according to what is predominant.
That is to say, in the first dhyāna, which emerges from the heavy suffering of the desire realm,
the factors of benefit are predominant.
In the three higher dhyānas, the factors of counteraction are superior with respect to the excellence of detachment from passion; therefore,
it is said that they are absent in the dhyānas associated with passion, according to their respective degrees of excellence.

However, the other factors are not established as such even in the defiled dhyānas; this is the conclusion of the treatise. Question: Why are they called "joy and bliss born of seclusion," and so forth? Answer: Because one is secluded from sensual desires and from unwholesome, evil states.
Because it gives rise to joy and bliss, it is called "joy and bliss born of seclusion.
Because it is free from applied and sustained thought, faith is called "purity.
Because it is free from joy, mindfulness and wisdom are called "right."
Because it is free from the eight calamities, its equanimity and mindfulness are called "pure.
Therefore, they are specifically designated according to the characteristics manifest in each of the four stages.
As for the statement in the Sūtra that one reaches the fourth stage regarding inhalation and exhalation:
This is the fourth explanation of the immovability (*āniñjya*) taught in the Sūtra.
Based on the Sūtra’s questions and answers, the Treatise states: "Up to the calamities, there are eight."
The first two lines explain what those eight are;
the latter two lines provide their explanation.
This is the question. Regarding the statement that vitarka,
vicāra, and the four sensations culminate in being called "unshakable" (āneñja),
the answer may be understood [as follows].
However, when the sūtras speak of those "moved by joy and pleasure," this is an interpretation based on the sūtra.
Furthermore, in the *Madhuvāsiṣṭha-sūtra*, it is stated as follows:
The fourth dhyāna is not disturbed by vitarka, vicāra, prīti, or sukha;

however, this is stated only with respect to its constituent factors (aṅga) and does not imply that it lacks non-constituent factors. Furthermore, this interpretation of the sūtra does not fully capture its intended meaning.
This is explained exhaustively according to the correct principle (*nyāya*). Thus, the *Nyāyānusāra* states:
"However, the Sūtra speaks only of the fourth dhyāna."
That which is not moved by vitarka, vicāra, prīti, or sukha is what the Sūtra teaches with intentional meaning (saṃdhāya-bhāṣita);
the Śāstra relies on the characteristics of phenomena (dharma-lakṣaṇa).
For the Bhagavat has stated in some places: "With the abandoning of pleasure and the abandoning of pain,
and with the prior disappearance of joy and grief..."
He dwells fully established in the fourth dhyāna.
Furthermore, it is said that in that concentration, the bodily formations (kāya-saṃskāra) cease together;
inhalation and exhalation are what are called bodily formations.
Therefore, it should be known that this concentration does not merely avoid the four calamities of movement—vitarka, vicāra, prīti, and sukha.
Other masters say that it is "without movement" up to the stage of āloka (illumination).
Other masters say that the fourth dhyāna is called "unshakable" (āneñjya) because it is like the light of a lamp in a honey-cell, being without movement;
for this is stated in the *Dṛṣṭānta-sūtra*.
If it is asked whether the meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*) of the concentration realm are the same as those pertaining to rebirth,
this is the fifth [point] clarifying the differences in the experience of rebirth.
Question:
Just as there are various feelings in the meditative absorptions (dhyāna):
in the first and second, there is joy (prīti);
in the third, there is bliss (sukha).
There is equanimity in the fourth dhyāna.
Is it also thus in the dhyānas of rebirth? It is not so.
Answer: "What is it? is an inquiry.
The verse states: "Regarding the distinction up to feeling":
this explains that in the second dhyāna there is no feeling of pleasure (*sukha-vedanā*), because the other three consciousnesses are absent.
Because the mind’s delight is coarse,
it is called only "joy" (prīti) and not "bliss" (sukha).
The rest of the text is self-evident.
Regarding the three higher dhyānas up to and including the arising of informative action (*vijñapti-karman*):
this is the sixth clarification concerning the arising of a lower mind.
Question:
In the three higher meditative attainments (*dhyāna*), the three groups of consciousness (*vijñānakāya*) are absent,
as are vitarka and vicāra. How, then, can those born there see, hear, touch,
and initiate manifest action (*vijñapti-karman*)?
Regarding the statement "not born in that stage up to not being bound by it," the answer is:
one is not born in that stage because the three consciousnesses, as well as vitarka and vicāra, do not exist there.
However, it is not bound by that.
Why is this? This is the inquiry.
The verse says: "Because one has reached what is inferior. The commentary explains:
One born in the three higher stages gives rise to the three lower consciousnesses.
And as for the manifestation of the mind,
all are bound to the first dhyāna; when born in a higher realm, one may give rise to [a mind] belonging to a lower realm.
Just as when one gives rise to a transformative mind (*nirmāṇa-citta*) of a lower stage, one is thus able to see, hear, touch,
and manifest [karmic] expression.
These four are all unobscured-neutral (anivṛtāvyākṛta).
They do not give rise to the defilements of a lower level because one has already become free from those defilements;
nor do they give rise to the wholesome states of a lower level because those are inferior.
Although the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) is inferior, it is not a state of true revulsion;

because it is neutral, it arises [in such a manner]. Question: When one born in a higher realm gives rise to a lower realm, among the four types of indeterminate states, which one is this? Master Tai’s explanation:
It is said that although the visual, auditory, and tactile consciousnesses are not themselves the neutral mind of transformation (*nirmāṇa-citta*),
they belong to the category of the transformative mind because they are necessarily bound to another [realm].
This is collectively termed the "mind of the fruit of dhyāna.
Therefore, the *Samyukta-abhidharma-hṛdaya-śāstra*, in its Chapter on Concentration (*Samādhi-varga*), states:
"That which does not arise in the desire realm is not the fruit of dhyāna."
However, the mind of transformation is also called a fruit of dhyāna;
therefore, in the *Vibhaṅga-paṭala* of the *Saṃyuktābhidharmahṛdaya*,
it is explained that there are four types of minds in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).
It is said that there is no mind of transformation (*nirmāṇa-citta*) and no mind of deportment (*airyāpathika-citta*).

Apart from the fruits of dhyāna, the four remaining types of deportment exist in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*). This text serves as proof for the arising of the three bodies of consciousness (*vijñānakāya*).
Because this is of the same category as the mind of transformation (*nirmāṇa-citta*), it is subsumed under the neutral (*avyākṛta*) fruits of dhyāna.
If one initiates verbal action, it is solely by means of the mind of transformation;
therefore, the preceding treatise states:
Whether it be the creator or the created person,
if they are in a state above the third dhyāna, they speak with a mind belonging to the first dhyāna;
for in the realm of form (rūpadhātu), there is no mind of craftsmanship (śailpasthānika-citta).
One should not speak with a mind of craftiness,
for sound has no characteristics of walking, standing, sitting, or reclining;
one should not speak with a mind of formal deportment.
As the previous treatise states that the four consciousnesses take postures as their object,
by inferring from this principle,
one born in the third dhyāna speaks only with the mind of transformation (*nirmāṇa-citta*).
If one gives rise to bodily manifest karma (kāya-vijñapti), it is either of deportment (airyāpathika) or transformation (nairmāṇika). Question: How is this known?
That a mind of transformation gives rise to bodily and vocal manifest karma? Answer: As stated in the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 139: [text follows].
If one is born in the first dhyāna, one accomplishes one [mental application] of the desire realm,
namely the mental application of equanimity regarding phenomena (dharmopavicāra), which is associated with the mind of supernormal power (abhijñā-citta).
Because they arise by taking the aggregate of form and so forth as their object,
some say that one accomplishes three: namely,
the mental applications of equanimity regarding forms, sounds, and mental phenomena (*dharmas*).
It is concomitant with the mind of fruition (vipākaja-citta).
If this mind takes as its object the bodily intimation (kāya-vijñapti) that has arisen,
there is then the mental application of equanimity (upekṣā-manopavicāra) taking form (rūpa) as its object.
If this mind takes as its object the vocal intimation that has arisen,
it then possesses the mental application of equanimity taking sound as its object;
if this mind takes as its object a manifested phenomenon, it does so by way of a collective apprehension.
That is to say, there are mental applications (*manopavicāra*) that abandon their objects;
these are associated with the mind of supernormal power (*abhijñā-citta*). This mind is capable of taking both general and specific objects. Now, [the following] is the explanation.

Not so. When one is born in the upper three meditative absorptions (dhyāna), the various consciousnesses of the lower levels arise. If the body-consciousness (kāyavijñāna) of the lower level arises, [it must be accompanied by a mental consciousness].
It is either the mind of deportment itself,
or the mind that takes deportment as its object,
or a mind resembling deportment.
If an inferior eye-consciousness arises,
that which is acquired through cultivation is subsumed under the supernormal powers;
that which arises casually is a mind of deportment.
Or it may be conditioned by a mind of deportment,
or a mind resembling a mind of deportment;
if a lower-level ear-consciousness arises.
That which is acquired through cultivation is subsumed under the result-of-attainment [mind].
That which arises casually is merely a mind resembling deportment.
If a mind that initiates karma belonging to a lower level arises, [it is likewise so].
If one initiates physical or vocal karma in a general manner, this is the mind of deportment (*airyāpathika-citta*).

Since the mind of deportment can even take all twelve bases (*dvādaśāyatana*) as its object, it stands to reason that it should likewise be able to initiate vocal karma. Furthermore, in Master Kōng’s *Commentary on the Chapter on the Five Aggregates*, regarding the aggregate of deportment, he states:
The aggregate of matter consists of five, namely the five sense objects (*pañca-viṣaya*).
Question: If it is said that the deportment (*īryāpatha*) possesses all five sense objects, why is this so in the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* and the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya*?
It further states that there are only four types of sensory objects (*dhātu*), excluding sound.
The commentary explains that walking, standing, sitting, and reclining are termed "modes of deportment" (*īryāpatha*).
Sound is not the essential substance of these modes of deportment.

Therefore, while the two treatises state that [such action] does not exist, it is said here that it exists based on the principle that sound is produced by the mind of deportment (*airyāpathika-citta*). This has already been explained above.
Furthermore, if a person created by a higher stage (*ūrdhvabhūmi-nirmāṇa-puruṣa*) produces [action] that is neither bodily nor vocal karma...
It arises immediately from the mind of the fruit of penetration belonging to a lower stage;
it is not a mind of transformation (nirmāṇacitta).
Thus says Master Tai.

If one considers the two consciousnesses of the divine eye and divine ear attained through cultivation, it is reasonable that they belong to the category of transformation-minds (*nirmāṇa-citta*) and are thus termed "fruits of supernormal power" (*abhijñā-phala*).
However, if one were to broadly designate any arising of visual, auditory, or tactile consciousness as "minds of supernormal power," [that would not be correct].
This is not correct.
According to the various treatises,
among the twenty types of consciousness, the mind of fruition (vipākaja-citta) arises only from a concentrated mind (samāhita-citta).
How could it be that one enters meditative absorption while all three lower consciousnesses arise indifferently?
The *Abhidharmahṛdaya* states:
"Because [consciousness] does not arise in the desire realm, it is not the fruit of dhyāna."
Now, let us further examine in detail the section on the *samādhi* of the mixed mind (*miśracitta*).
When one is born in a higher stage and gives rise to the three consciousnesses of the first dhyāna, they do not arise within the desire realm;
this is because they are neither of the desire realm nor the fruit of cultivation (*bhāvanāphala*).
It does not speak of the fruit of dhyāna;
this is therefore a mistaken citation as proof.
As for what is called the "fruit of cultivation":
Because they are bound to the stages of meditative concentration (samāhitabhūmi), they are collectively termed the fruits of cultivation (bhāvanāphala).
If one were to say that the fruit of cultivation is identical to the fruit of dhyāna, [it would be incorrect].
Because they are bound to the stages of meditative concentration (*samāhitabhūmi*), they are collectively termed "fruits of dhyāna.
This differs from the transformation-mind (*nirmāṇacitta*), which is subsumed under the "fruition-mind" (*phalacitta*).
Furthermore, [the author] cites the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* as proof that the transformation-mind initiates bodily and vocal karma.
Alternatively, it may be that the *abhijñā-phala-citta* (result-of-supernormal-power mind) is broad while the *nirmāṇa-citta* (transformation mind) is narrow;
that is to say, all *abhijñā-phala*-minds are transformation minds.
In various passages of the text, such divergent interpretations have been made;
these were already refuted previously, yet the same arguments recur. Furthermore, Master Kung (Kong) said:
To claim that one born in the three higher meditative absorptions gives rise to the deportment-minds and the three types of sensory consciousnesses of the first dhyāna,
as well as the minds that initiate karma through deportment,
is likewise not exhaustive of the truth.
If it is based on that which arises in a general sense,
there is no contradiction; however,

if it is based on the two types of supernormal powers (abhijñā) and the karma-initiating actions of a magically created person (nirmāṇapuruṣa), these are all termed "dignified deportment" (īryāpatha).
This is not the case; it should be refuted according to the previous [analysis].
Thus, having provided this separate explanation, one asks: "How is it that [the fruit] is first obtained?"
Below this, secondly, the three types of meditative attainments (*samāpatti*) are explained.
Within this section,
first, the initial attainment of these meditative states is explained.
1. Explaining the arising of the meditative attainments (*samāpatti*). 2. Explaining the sequential [attainment] (*anuloma*) and the fourfold division of concentration (*dhyāna*). 3.
Explaining the cultivation of the leaping attainment (*vyutkrāntaka-samāpatti*).
Five explain the basis of meditative attainment (samāpatti) as the body;
six explain the objects of meditative attainment;
and seven explain the abandonment of afflictions through meditative attainment.
8. Explaining the distinctions of the preparatory stages (*sāmantaka*).
9. Explaining the differences among the intermediate concentrations (*dhyānāntara*). This is the first [section], explaining the initial attainment of meditative equipoise (*samāpatti*);
it concludes the preceding discussion and introduces the inquiry.
The verse says: "Reaching defilement occurs through birth and through falling away.
This is the answer in verse.
The commentary says: "Reaching the undefiled occurs because of birth."
To explain the two preceding lines:
regarding the eight fundamental attainments (*mauladhyāna-samāpatti*), as appropriate to each case,
if one attains them without having previously cultivated them at all, [it is called "attainment through effort"].
The various pure attainments (śuddhaka-samāpatti) arise from two causes and conditions:
first, through the abandonment of defilement (vairāgya);
second, through rebirth (upapatti). Regarding the phrase "through the abandonment of defilement":
This means that when one in a lower stage becomes free from the defilements of that lower stage, one attains the pure [attainment] of the higher stage.
As for the term "rebirth," it refers to the attainment of the pure [attainment] of one's own stage when one is born from a higher stage back into one's own stage.
Among the eight attainments (*samāpatti*), the same applies to the lower seven;
however, the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*) is not so.
Therein, the attainment of detachment occurs solely through the process of becoming detached from defilements.
Because there is no descent from a higher stage to a lower stage,
there is no acquisition through rebirth (*upapatti-pratilambhika*). The *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra* states:
In this context, only the fundamental attainments (*mauladhyāna*) are mentioned because,
regarding the preparatory stages (*sāmantaka*), as long as one has not yet abandoned defilement,
they may be entirely unaccomplished and are obtained solely through application (*prayoga*).
Regarding the reason for stating the phrase "not at all established":
it is a question [intended] to exclude what is already established, up to the point where one should reflect according to principle.

Answer: It is to preclude the notion that what has already been attained can be further acquired in part, such as the aids to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*) obtained through application (*prayoga*), and so forth.
"And so forth" means including the aids to advancement (*viśeṣabhāgīya*).
The reason why one does not abide in the stage of decline (hānabhāgīya) is because it has already been previously attained; that is to say,
one has already previously attained both the stage of decline and the stage of stability (sthityaṃśika).
Subsequently, through preparatory application, one may attain the stage of distinguished progress or the stage of penetration;
this is not termed "attainment" [in the strict sense].
Because these four parts are equally pure in meditative concentration,
and because one attains the part conducive to decline at the time of falling away from or departing from one's own defilements,
having previously attained the part conducive to stability and the part conducive to progress.
Or, regarding the stage of "decisive distinction" (nirvedhabhāgīya), although one may now further attain the "stage of decline" (hānabhāgīya),
it is not reckoned as an attainment.
Because these four categories are identical in being pure concentration (*śuddha-samādhi*),
the *Vibhāṣā-śāstra* poses this question based on that very principle:
"Is there any pure concentration that is obtained through the abandonment of defilements (*vairāgya-lābhika*)?"
It is abandoned through detachment from passion;
it is acquired through falling away;
and it is lost through falling away.
It is acquired through birth and relinquished through birth;
the same applies to the questions.
Answer: There is; it refers to the stage conducive to decline (*hāna-bhāgīya*).
Specifically, that which is subsumed under the stage conducive to decline within the first dhyāna is attained at the time of becoming free from the defilements of the desire realm.
It is abandoned when one becomes detached from the defilements of its own level;
it is acquired when one falls away from detachment from the defilements of its own level.
It is abandoned when one falls away from detachment from the defilements of the desire realm.
It is acquired when one is born from a higher level into the first dhyāna;
it is relinquished when one descends from that same level into the desire realm.
The acquisition and relinquishment of those comprised by other levels should be understood accordingly.
"Regarding the statement that the untainted [attainments] are obtained solely through reaching [the state of] being in accordance with reality,
this explains the third phrase:
the untainted are obtained solely by means of detachment from defilement."
This refers to when a noble one, having become detached from the defilements of a lower stage, attains the untainted [attainment] of a higher stage.
This also refers exclusively to the fundamental dhyānas;
it concerns those who have not previously accomplished them at all and now acquire them for the first time.
If it has already been established previously,
it is also attained at other times; that is,
at the stage of the knowledge of exhaustion (kṣayajñāna), one further attains the path of no-more-learning (aśaikṣamārga).
At the time of refining the faculties, one further attains the paths of training and no-more-training;
or, through application, one cultivates and attains the superior untainted dharmas of that stage;
or, through falling away, one attains the untainted dharmas of that stage.
All these should be reflected upon in accordance with reason.
Such phenomena as these have not been non-existent previously and newly attained at this present time.
Therefore, it is not mentioned here;
for in this context, which refers to the fundamental stage (*maulabhūmi*),
"acquisition" (*prāpti*) is defined as the initial attainment of what was previously entirely unestablished.
Even if one now further attains what was previously attained in part,
it is not called "attainment.
Is it not because one has entered into the untainted meditative attainments (*anāsrava-samāpatti*)?
Question:
Is it not also by entering the state of right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*) that one first attains untainted meditative attainment (*anāsrava-samāpatti*)?
Why is it said that the untainted [attainments] are acquired through the abandonment of defilements alone,
and not that they are acquired at the time of entering the state of rightness and departure from birth?
This is because they are not necessarily acquired until one reaches the state of certainty.
Answer: Entering the path of seeing does not necessarily entail obtaining this;
for although there are persons who enter the path of seeing by relying on the fundamental dhyāna stages through the method of leaping over (vyutkrāntaka).
One also attains the fundamental uncontaminated meditative attainments (*anāsrava-samāpatti*). However,
for one who enters the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*) by way of gradual progression (*ānupūrvika*),
this is not necessarily the case at that time, because they have not yet attained the fundamental dhyānas.
In this context, we are discussing only those who definitely attain it;
therefore, the *Nyāyānusāra* states:
"Because a noble one who is free from the defilements of a lower stage will necessarily obtain the fundamental untainted concentration (*anāsrava-samādhi*) of a higher stage."
"Defilement is acquired through birth and by attaining this stage" explains the fourth phrase.
Defilement is acquired through birth, as well as through falling away.
This refers to obtaining defilement of a lower stage when dying from a higher stage and being reborn in a lower stage,
as well as obtaining defilement of that same stage when falling away from detachment from it.
It certainly cannot be obtained through the abandonment of defilements (*vairāgya*) or through application (*prayoga*).
Therefore, the *Nyāyānusāra* states:
"There is no means by which it can be obtained through the abandonment of defilements or through application."
Because one is able to abandon defilement during these two periods.
What is it that, following an attainment (*samāpatti*), gives rise to a defiled state belonging to its own level or a lower level?
This is the second [section], clarifying the arising of attainments.
Regarding the question and the response in verse,
the treatise states: "Up to 'and both [factors] of its own stage,'" which explains the first two lines [of the verse].
The untainted attainments arise in succession from their own level, from higher levels,
and from lower levels;
the term "wholesome" fully includes both the pure (*śuddhaka*) and the untainted (*anāsrava*).
Because they are utterly contradictory,
defilement will certainly not arise;
however, in both the higher and lower realms, one may reach up to the third stage.
Because it is remote, one is unable to leap over to the fourth [dhyāna].
Therefore, among the seven attainments consisting of the four untainted (anāsrava) dhyānas and the three formless (ārūpya) attainments:
From the first dhyāna, six [minds] arise immediately thereafter:
namely, the pure and uncontaminated [minds] of its own level, and those of the second and third levels,
each being both pure and uncontaminated.
Immediately following the sphere of nothingness, seven [minds] arise:
namely, two from its own level and four from the lower levels, totaling six.
The higher stages consist exclusively of the pure [attainments], totaling seven types.
From the second dhyāna, eight [attainments] arise immediately:
namely, two from its own stage.
There are six states that include the four of the higher stages;
together with the two of the lower stage, there are eight in total.
From the Sphere of Infinite Consciousness, nine states arise in immediate succession.
That is to say, there are two of its own level,
four of the lower levels— making six in total—
and three of the higher levels.
That is to say, there are two [realms] of nothingness and one of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, totaling nine.
These are the third dhyāna, the fourth dhyāna, and the sphere of infinite space.
Each arises immediately after ten:
namely, four from the higher stages and four from the lower stages, totaling eight.
Together with the two [knowledges] of its own level,
there are ten in total.
As for the statement that "subsequent knowledge (anvaya-jñāna) immediately follows [the path] because it takes the lower levels as its object and support":
To distinguish the differences:
within the dhyānas, subsequent knowledge (anvaya-jñāna) can immediately give rise to the formless realm (ārūpya),
whereas dharma-knowledge (dharma-jñāna) cannot.
Because it relies on a body belonging to the lower desire realm and because it takes objects of the lower desire realm as its cognitive domain,
there are two types of transcendence.
The first is transcending meditative absorption;
the second is transcending objects.
Both of these types of transcendence reach the third [dhyāna].
It does not reach the fourth [dhyāna],
because the knowledge of phenomena (dharmajñāna) takes the objects of the desire realm as its domain,
whereas the formless attainments take the objects of the formless realm as their domain.
Because one cannot suddenly leap over the four stages of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*),
and because the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) does not arise immediately after the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*), the *Vibhāṣā* (165) states:

Question: How does a practitioner of meditation transcend their object of focus? Answer: By means of non-recollection and mental attention (*amanasikāra*), they take each of the nine stages individually as an object through the first dhyāna;
therein, they are able to transcend and focus upon only a single stage.
That is to say, immediately following the desire realm as its object,
one is able to ascend and take the first dhyāna or the second dhyāna as an object, but not any other.
Immediately following the first dhyāna,
one is able to take the desire realm as an object below and the second dhyāna as an object above.
Or, it may be the third dhyāna and not others;
immediately following the second dhyāna,
it is able to look downward upon the desire realm or the first dhyāna.
It takes the third dhyāna or the fourth dhyāna as its object, and not others.
Immediately following the third dhyāna,
it is able to take the first dhyāna as its lower object.
Or, in the second dhyāna,
it takes the fourth dhyāna as its superior object; or,
in the sphere of infinite space, it does so and not otherwise.
In this manner, even up to the immediate [consciousness] conditioned by the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception,
it is able to take the sphere of infinite consciousness or the sphere of nothingness as its lower object, and not anything else.
Just as it is in dependence on the first dhyāna, so it is in dependence on the other dhyānas;
in each case as appropriate, the object-condition (ālambana-pratyaya) should be explained in detail.
Just as one cannot transcend the objects of focus of two stages,
so it is with transcending meditative absorption;
therefore, one does not enter the fourth stage.
Question: If that is so, why is it said that after the pure liberation (śubha-vimokṣa), five moments of mind arise?
The pure liberation-mind takes as its object the pervasive latent tendencies (sarvatraga-anuśaya) of the fourth dhyāna within the desire realm (kāmadhātu).
It can take as its objects [realms] from its own level up to the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*).
Is it not the case, then, that it transcends the objects of two levels?
Answer: It is said that an undefiled mind cannot transcend two levels.
Since that mind is defiled, there is no contradiction.

Question: Just as the Dharma-knowledge of suffering (duḥkha-dharma-jñāna), taking the desire realm as its object, arises immediately followed by the subsequent patience regarding suffering (duḥkha-anvaya-kṣānti), and so on up to the Peak of Existence (bhavāgra).
Question: Why is it said that an undefiled mind cannot transcend the two? Answer:
That [mind] merely takes a general object and is therefore not called "transcending.
Furthermore, because it also takes other stages as its objects, this is not a valid objection. Explanation: The "five minds" refer to the minds of the five categories (pañca-varga).
"From the pure meditative attainments (*śuddha-samāpatti*), eleven [attainments] arise; from others, eleven likewise.
This explains the third and fourth lines.
From the pure meditative attainments, those that are produced are also the same.
Furthermore, each [meditative attainment] also gives rise to the defiled states of its own level;
this is because the pure and other [neutral] states extend upward to the untainted (anāsrava),
while those below connect to the defiled.
Immediately following the pure [attainment] of the Peak of Existence (bhavāgra), six [minds] arise:

namely, its own two—the pure and the defiled—and four from below: the pure and the untainted [minds] of the Sphere of Nothingness (ākiṃcanyāyatana) and the Sphere of Infinite Consciousness (vijñānānantyāyatana).
From the first dhyāna, seven [minds] arise immediately:
namely, three of its own level and four of the higher levels; and eight from the sphere of nothingness:
namely, three of its own level, one of the higher level, and four of the lower levels.
In the second dhyāna there are nine:
namely, three of its own level, four of the higher levels, and two of the lower level.
In the sphere of infinite consciousness (*vijñānānantyāyatana*), there are ten.
This refers to three from its own level, three from the higher levels, and four from the lower levels.
In the remaining cases— the third dhyāna, the fourth dhyāna, and the sphere of infinite space— all eleven arise.
This refers to the three [types] of one’s own level, with four types each for the higher and lower levels.
The phrase "from a defiled attainment to a pure state born immediately below" explains the fifth and sixth lines.
This may be understood from the text.
The *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra* states:
"Because they are utterly contradictory, the untainted [state] does not arise."
Regarding the passage from defilement to purity, and how one arises from defilement to attain purity—
the intent of the question is clear.
As for the statement that through the power of prior vows one is able to awaken— this refers to the capacity to realize awakening by virtue of previous aspirational force.
The answer may also be understood.

Regarding the distinction between the untainted (*anāsrava*) and the defiled (*kliṣṭa*) as they reach the three realms of existence (*tridhātu*): this serves to distinguish their specific differences.
The untainted and the defiled do not necessarily produce one another because they are utterly opposed;
the pure and the defiled, however, produce one another because they exist in between them. Thus, there is a distinction among the three.
The statement "as thus explained, up to 'because one has not yet abandoned the lower [realms]" explains the latter two phrases,
as previously described.
"Purity" and "defilement" give rise to defilement;
this is stated solely with reference to the pure and defiled states within meditative concentration.
When one is born in those stages, they are designated as "born of purity" and "born of defilement."
"Pure birth" refers to innate wholesome states;
"defiled birth" refers to the dispersed afflictions of that stage.
If pure birth or defiled birth can produce defilement, [then it follows that they are themselves defiled].
That reasoning is incorrect;
for at the time of death, from each and every pure wholesome state acquired at birth,
there is immediate succession.
Defilements arising from one's own stage, as well as those of all higher and lower stages,
arise; if they arise from defilements of their respective stages,
each immediately gives rise to all defilements of its own stage and all lower stages.
Those who do not give rise to a higher [state] have not yet abandoned the lower one.
As for the question, "Can one arise from the pure [attainments] into all [others]?
this refers to the third section, which clarifies the meditative absorptions that accord with the four categories.
The preceding question is restated to raise an objection.
To this, he replies: "It is not so."
What does this mean?
It is an inquiry.
The verse says: "Up to two, three, two, three, and one births."
The verse provides the answer.
The treatise states: "Regarding that which is subsumed under the stage of excellence and progress (*viśeṣabhāgīya*)," this explains the first verse.
Listing the numbers and names:
each of the first seven stages has four parts;
the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*) has only three.
This is because the stage of supreme progress (*viśeṣabhāga*) and the unsurpassed stage (*anuttarabhūmi*) are excluded.
The *Abhidharmamahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* (vol. 11) states the same as this treatise:
the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*) possesses only three parts.
Excluding the *viśeṣabhāga* (part of further advancement). Question:

If that is so, why does the *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya*, in its *Karmavarga*, state that the stage of the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*) has four parts? Explanation: This treatise and the *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle eleven, [address this].
Because there is no higher stage above the Peak of Existence (bhavāgra) toward which one could aspire,
it is said that in that stage there is no "part conducive to progress" (viśeṣabhāgīya).
(*Abhidharmamahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, Karma-skandha).
Because there exists within that [state] a further superior excellence toward which one may aspire,
it is said that "there is further progress. Thus,
the *Nyāyānusāra* (Treatise on Reasoning), fascicle 78, states:
Regarding the factors of superior progress, there are generally two types:
first, the distinguished qualities of one's own stage;
second, the distinguished qualities of higher stages.

"If one is able to draw forth that [attainment], it is called the 'part conducive to supreme progress' (*viśeṣabhāgīya*)," as stated in the aforementioned treatise. Therefore, it is said that the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*) may either exist or not exist; each statement is based on a specific sense.

Regarding these four [types of attainment], from "up to" "arising only from this": [Note: This passage explains the nuances of the *bhavāgra* (the highest realm of existence) and its relationship to the stages of meditative attainment (*samāpatti*), specifically addressing the conditions under which it may be present or absent, and how it serves as a basis for further spiritual advancement.]
The explanation of the fifth and sixth phrases may be understood from the text as it stands. Furthermore,
according to the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 165, regarding the "arising of the pure [state] which is outflow-free" (*anāsrava-śuddha-janman*), it says:
This [attainment] arises only from the aids to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*);
some say it also arises from the aids to progress (*viśeṣabhāgīya*).
Although the commentator did not judge the former explanation to be correct, [the latter view is accepted].
Therefore, the *Nyāyānusāra* (Treatise on Correct Reasoning), fascicle 78,
states: "It should be understood that the meaning of 'certainty' (*niyata*) herein refers to the fact that the various noble paths necessarily arise immediately after this."
It is not the case that immediately following this [the worldly supreme dharma], one must necessarily be able to produce the Noble Path.

If it were otherwise, then it would have to be stated that only the Worldly Supreme Dharma is called the "factor conducive to penetration" (*nirvedhabhāgīya*). This is the text of the treatise. Furthermore, all treatises state that the factors conducive to penetration can produce the Noble Path. Question: Regarding the untainted [path], how many factors can it further produce? Answer: It produces the latter two factors.
Therefore, the *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra* (Treatise on the Correct Principle), fascicle 78, states:
"Regarding the immediate succession of the untainted (*anāsrava*), which [type of] part manifests?
Some say it is common to all three, excluding the part conducive to decline (*parihāṇa-bhāgīya*)."
In reality, there are only two, namely the latter two kinds.
Furthermore, in the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 165, regarding the statement that "the untainted [attainment] gives rise to the pure," it says: "Thus it is said."
When entering [the stages] gradually, it also serves as the immediate antecedent (*samanantara-pratyaya*) for the stage of excellence (*viśeṣa-bhāgīya*).

When entering by means of leaping over (*vyutkrāntaka*), it serves as the immediate antecedent only for the stage conducive to penetration (*nirvedha-bhāgīya*). Question: For what reason, when entering by leaping over, [does it serve as the immediate antecedent only for the stage conducive to penetration]?
Only the factors conducive to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*) and the untainted path (*anāsravamārga*) serve as immediate conditions (*samanantarapratyaya*) for one another;
at other times, this is not the case.
The answer is: at the time of transcendence (*vyutkrānti*), there exist only intense and firm roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*).
The factors that induce the aids to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*) are intense and firm; the other factors are not so.

Question: If the factor conducive to decline (*hānabhāgīya*) conduces to the afflictions (*kleśa*), as when one who has already become detached from the defilements of a particular stage regresses and gives rise to the defilements of that stage, [how does this occur]?

Once the stage conducive to decline (*hāna-bhāgīya*) has been abandoned, from what does the arising of afflictions (*kleśa*) proceed? The explanation states that it arises from the stage of stability (*sthiti-bhāgīya*).
Thus, the *Nyāyānusāra* (Treatise on the Principles of Correct Reasoning), fascicle 78, says:
"That which accords with affliction is called the stage conducive to decline."
How could there be any possibility of regression for the Arhats?
For they no longer possess the meditative absorption conducive to falling away (*parihāṇabhāgīya-samādhi*) that could be brought into manifestation,
as they have abandoned it through detachment from passion.
Although this objection is raised,
there is in fact no contradiction;
for even that which is conducive to abiding (*sthity-anuloma*) may be established as being "conducive to decline" (*hāna-bhāgīya*) when it possesses the quality of leading toward decline.
There is falling away from that, as has already been stated previously. Furthermore, the *Abhidharmamahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* (165) states:
"When afflictions manifest immediately after pure meditative concentration (*śuddha-samādhi*), etc."
One should know that this arises from either the stage conducive to decline (*hāna-bhāgīya*) or the stage conducive to stability (*sthiti-bhāgīya*).

This is because there is a distinction in the arising of afflictions of one's own level, depending on whether one has already abandoned or not yet abandoned the defilements of that level. By means of this textual evidence, it is known [that this is so].
There are also those that give rise to afflictions from the state of abiding.
Regarding these four, they are mutually related such that each is itself and not the others;
this explains the final two lines.
Regarding the mutual production of these four in relation to one another:
the first can produce two,
namely the stage conducive to decline (*hāna-bhāgīya*) and the stage conducive to maintenance (*sthiti-bhāgīya*).
The latter two do not arise [from them] because they are separated by a great distance;
all treatises agree on this.
From the second [dhyāna], three arise, excluding the *nirvedhabhāgīya*.
Because they are also separated by distance,
all treatises agree on this.
The third [dhyāna] gives rise to three types of minds, excluding the *anuloma-prativedha-bhāga* (the stage conducive to falling away).
Because they are separated by a great distance.
The *Vibhāṣā* (vol. 11), the *Nyāyānusāra*, and the *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya-ṭīkā-tattvārthā* all agree with this treatise.
However, according to the *Vibhāṣā* (vol. 165), there is a different explanation.
Therefore, that treatise states:
"Regarding the factors conducive to progress (*pratipakṣa-bhāgīya*) and the factors conducive to decline (*parihāṇi-bhāgīya*), some say..."
It is merely an object and a dominant condition,
because the stage immediately conducive to progress does not manifest when one is in the stage immediately conducive to decline. Thus it is said.
It also manifests in the present.
Therefore, it constitutes three conditions for the factors conducive to decline;
the causal condition is excluded because that [condition] is inferior.
The same applies to the stage conducive to abiding (*anuloma-sthiti-bhāgīya*).

Regarding the two explanations in the *Vibhāṣā*, the latter is the position of the *Vibhāṣā* masters (the *viniścaya-vādin*), while the former is considered incorrect by the *Abhidharmakośa* and other treatises;
[according to them], only three types arise.
The critics give rise to four [interpretations].
Since there are already these critical commentaries, they take the later master as correct; or else, the intent of the treatises differs for each.
The *Abhidharmakośa* takes reason as its standard of correctness;
it does not take the *Vibhāṣā* commentators as its authority.
Now, the characteristic of purity (*śubha-nimitta*) and the characteristic of production (*utpāda-nimitta*) ought to be adjacent to one another.
How could there be any skipping?
The fourth birth produces only one [result], namely itself and nothing else;
for, delighting in the untainted (anāsrava), it does not give rise to anything else.

Question: Since the stages of abiding (*sthiti*) and progress (*viśeṣa*) can arise sequentially, why is it determined that the stage of penetration (*nirvedha*) does not arise as a stage of progress immediately preceding it? Answer: It is explained that penetration aspires toward the outflow-free (*anāsrava*) state and does not arise as a stage of progress immediately preceding it.
Abiding and superior progress do not involve delighting in the untainted; they may occur prior to the arising of the subsequent [state],
for their nature is not one of cessation, as they involve the seeking of higher dharmas through the aspect of superior progress.
The nirvedhabhāgīya does not give rise to the viśeṣabhāgīya;
there is cessation of both the sthitibhāgīya and the hānabhāgīya natures.
It is possible for the sthitibhāgīya to arise from the viśeṣabhāgīya, and for the hānabhāgīya to arise from the sthitibhāgīya.
Both the *Nyāyānusāra* and the *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya-ṭīkā-tattvārthā* present two views.
One view is the same as that in this treatise;
another view states:
Some say that it also produces the factors conducive to advancement (*viśeṣabhāgīya*),
yet there is no formal evaluation by the Master [Vasubandhu].
The intention of the latter school is as follows:
Just as with abiding, superior progress can produce the preceding one;
likewise, the aids to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*) also produce the preceding one.
According to the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* (vol. 11), this is so.
According to the later masters of the *Nyāyānusāra*,
if one relies on the *Mahāvibhāṣā* (vol. 165), it states that the aids to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*) and the aids to abiding (*sthityanukūla*) [are distinct].
Some say that they serve only as objects of perception (*ālambana*) and dominant conditions (*adhipati*),
because the stage conducive to maintenance (*anurakṣaṇā-bhāgīya*) does not manifest immediately after the stage conducive to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*).
When it is said in this way,
it also manifests before one; therefore,
it serves as three conditions for that [object], excluding the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*).
The same applies to the stage conducive to progress (*prativedhanā-bhāgīya*).
As previously stated, according to the latter master who accords with correct reasoning,
[the stage conducive to penetration] is able to produce both parts.
Later, the school of Righteous Meaning (Zhengyi-jia) was able to produce three parts.

Question: For what reason did only one [part] arise after the *Vibhāṣā*, whereas previously there were those who "leaped over one"? Answer: It is explained that because it gave rise to superior [insights] and difficult [arguments], only one arose.

Regarding the arising from inferior [realms] and the ease of transcending one [level]: A question is raised as to which among the various treatises is correct. The explanation states: Since the *Vibhāṣā* contains the "Evaluating School" (*pūrvapakṣa* and *siddhānta*), the view that three births are required is correct.

The remaining treatises all describe the views of other masters; alternatively, their intent may differ. The *Abhidharmakośa* takes reason as its standard, rather than taking the *Mahāvibhāṣā* commentators as its authority. Question:

Among the four parts of the pure meditative absorption (*śuddha-samādhi*) that arises from the attachment to flavor (*āsvādana*), into which part does it arise? Answer: If the attachment to flavor gives rise to its own corresponding pure absorption, [it arises from that very part].
The *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* states:
Some say that immediately after the meditative attainments associated with relish (*āsvādana-samāpatti*), [the attainment of cessation arises].
Only the factors conducive to decline (*hāna-bhāgīya*) arise and manifest before one;
some say that the factors conducive to maintenance (*sthiti-bhāgīya*) also arise.
However, there is no commentator [on this].
Regarding the arising of inferior purity from taste,
the *Vibhāṣā* states:
Some say that it arises as the stage conducive to stability because it is easy to arise. Others say:
It gives rise to the factors conducive to superior progress (*viśeṣabhāgīya*), because it protects against the higher stages; however, there is no formal commentary on this point.
As stated above, this applies to those who have reached the state of a non-learner (*aśaikṣa*) and possess keen faculties within the three continents.
This is the fourth [section], clarifying the cultivation of the "leap-over" attainments (*vyutkrāntakasamāpatti*).
It consists of a formal question followed by a verse answer.
The treatise says: "Reaching and transcending—these are called 'leaping'."
The first two phrases can be understood as they stand.
The statement, "That is to say, when the practitioner reaches and transcends into the fourth [dhyāna]," explains the third phrase.
In total there are six types:
the first five are preparatory practices (*prayoga*),
and the last one is the transcendental accomplishment (*atikrānta-siddhi*).
This can be understood according to the text.
Regarding the phrase "practicing the leap-attainment (vyutkrāntaka-samāpatti) and reaching the practice of the leap-attainment," this explains the fourth line.
The *Nyāyānusāra* states:
"The cultivation of the leap-attainments (*vyutkrāntakasamāpatti*) occurs only in the three continents,
excluding Uttarakuru."
However, this applies to both men and women.

Among the Arhats who are liberated at any time (asamayavimukta), only those who have attained the "limitless concentration" (prāntakoṭika-samādhi)— such as the "conflict-free" (araṇā), the "wondrous knowledge of vows" (praṇidhijñāna), and so forth— are able to transcend [the obstacles], and no others.
Because of mastery over meditative concentration and because they are free from afflictions; furthermore, it is said that through the mental application of resolute conviction (adhimukti-manasikāra),
one cannot practice the leap-over attainments (vyutkrāntaka-samāpatti) without interruption.
Because their power is inferior.
Regarding these attainments (*samāpatti*), when they reach the arising of the lower [levels] to exhaust the remaining afflictions (*kleśa*),
this is the fifth [section], clarifying the basis of the body for these attainments.

The commentary states, "up to 'because it is loathsome and contemptible,'" which explains the first two lines of the verse. This consists of a formal restatement of the question followed by a response in verse.
The arising of the various meditative attainments (*samāpatti*) depends upon one's own body or a body of a lower stage;
it is impossible for them to arise based on a body of a higher stage.
This is because there is no purpose in a being of a higher stage giving rise to a lower attainment.
Second, because the higher stages possess their own superior meditative absorptions;
third, because the power of the lower stages is inferior.
These three aforementioned types apply to both the pure (*śuddha*) and untainted (*anāsrava*) attainments (*samāpatti*).
Fourth, because they have already been abandoned;
fifth, because they are objects of revulsion and disparagement.
The latter two are exclusively pure attainments (*śuddha-samāpatti*).
Because untainted concentration (*anāsrava-samādhi*) is not something to be abandoned as being loathsome or contemptible;
although this is the general principle, the phrase "until all remaining afflictions are exhausted" explains the two subsequent lines.
Although this is a general summary distinguishing the differences,
if explained in detail:
when a noble being is born in the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*), they arise from their own pure meditative absorption (*śuddhaka-samādhi*).
One must necessarily give rise to the untainted sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*) in order to exhaust the remaining afflictions of one's own level;
for within one's own level there is no noble path, and because one takes delight in arising in a lower stage.
Because among those [attainments] arising from the lower stages, only the state of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*) is most proximate;
by bringing that into manifestation, one exhausts the remaining afflictions.
Therefore, the *Nyāyānusāra* states:
Apart from the untainted path,
there is certainly no other way to sever those remaining afflictions and become an Arhat; therefore,
[the path must be cultivated] at the Peak of Existence.
The untainted (anāsrava) sphere of nothingness (ākiṃcanyāyatana) relies on the bodies of nine stages;
the tainted (sāsrava) sphere of nothingness relies on the bodies of eight stages;
and the tainted and untainted sphere of infinite consciousness (vijñānānantyāyatana) relies on the bodies of seven stages.
The sphere of infinite space relies on the bodies of six stages,
down to the first dhyāna, which relies on the bodies of two stages— namely, its own stage and that of the desire realm.
Regarding these attainments (*samāpatti*), they do not take lower-level contaminated phenomena as objects.
This is the sixth [section], clarifying the objects of the meditative attainments (*samāpatti*).
It restates the question and answers it with a verse.
The treatise says: "Because [the attainment] must be established as wholesome (*kuśala*)."
This explains the first phrase:
the meditative absorption of taste (āsvādanasamādhi) takes its own level as its object; it does not take lower levels, higher levels, or untainted (anāsrava) phenomena as its objects.
"Pure and untainted [dharmas] do not have non-untainted objects" explains the second phrase.
Neutral and unconditioned (asaṃskṛta) dharmas are not objects of the non-untainted.
Because it is not included within the Truths (*satya*).

The rest of the text may be understood accordingly. Regarding the phrase "because that which is included in the fundamental stage (*maulabhūmi*) necessarily takes what is below as its object": [it means that when one has attained the fundamental dhyāna, one can take the lower stages as objects].
The following two phrases are explained:
the wholesome formless attainments subsumed under the fundamental stages do not take the contaminated phenomena of lower stages as their objects.
Because [the practitioner] has already become weary and detached,
and because their concentration is narrow and inferior; this should be understood according to the underlying principle.
According to what is appropriate,
taking lower pure (anāsrava) dharmas, as well as all impure (sāsrava) and pure dharmas of its own level and higher levels, as objects— there is nothing it cannot take as an object.
Although it can also take lower-level pure dharmas as objects, [the specific conditions apply as follows].
Because the path belonging to the category of subsequent knowledge (anvaya-jñāna) does not take the category of dharma-knowledge (dharma-jñāna) as its object,
the Nyāyānusāra states:
This is because it can only take its own specific category as an object and counteract it entirely;
however, as previously stated, the Dharma-category path does not counteract [the afflictions] entirely.
Furthermore, although the path of the Dharma-category can counteract [afflictions] in the formless realm, [it does so only partially].

Since these are adventitious and not the primary [cognitions], they cannot take the contaminated phenomena of the lower stages as their object, nor can they take the analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) or non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) of the contaminated phenomena of the lower stages as their object. Question: If they take the path belonging to the category of "knowledge of categories" (*anvaya-jñāna-pakṣya-mārga*) of the lower stages as their object...

"Does it also take as its object the non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) of that path? The commentary explains: "It also takes as its object the non-analytical cessation of the higher [stages] belonging to the category of *jñāna* (knowledge) of the lower stages.
Therefore, the *Vibhāṣā*, in the tenth fascicle, within the explanation of the aspect of non-self (*anātman*), states:
The four formless stages also possess these modes of activity (*ākāra*),
yet they cannot take all phenomena as their objects;
that is to say, the mode of activity of "non-self" (*anātman*) in the sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*).
It has as its object the four formless [attainments], their causes, and their cessation;
it consists of all paths belonging to the category of subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*), as well as the non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) of the four formless [attainments].
The non-analytical cessation (apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha) of all paths belonging to the category of subsequent knowledge (anvaya-jñāna),
as well as all unconditioned phenomena (asaṃskṛta-dharma) such as space (ākāśa),
may be intended by some to constitute a single entity.
Or, one may wish to cause these many objects to be fully perceived through their respective modes of activity (*ākāra*);
thus it continues up to the mode of non-self (*anātman-ākāra*) regarding the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*).
The object-condition for the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception consists of its cause, its cessation,
all paths belonging to the category of subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*),
and the non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
The non-analytical cessation (apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha) of all paths belonging to the category of subsequent knowledge (anvaya-jñāna),
as well as all unconditioned phenomena (asaṃskṛta-dharma) such as space (ākāśa),
may be intended by some to be a single entity.
Alternatively, it may be intended that these many objects are all capable of being taken as objects by this mode of activity (*ākāra*);
this represents the position of the *Vibhāṣā* commentators.

By this analogy, it should be understood that the four formless attainments (*ārūpya-samāpatti*) also take as their object the non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) of the higher [realms] belonging to the category of subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*) of the lower stages.
The preparatory stages (*sāmantaka*) of the formless realms likewise take the lower stages as their objects.
Because that path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*) necessarily takes the lower stage as its object.
Regarding the statement that the "tasting" (*āsvādana*), "pure" (*śuddha*), and "untainted" (*anāsrava*) attainments sever all afflictions:
this is the seventh [section], clarifying how the meditative attainments (*samāpatti*) sever delusions.
This is the question. The verse states:
"Even when attained, it cannot sever [the afflictions].

This means that while all untainted meditative concentrations (*anāsrava-samādhi*) are capable of severing delusions, if even the fundamental purity (*prakṛti-viśuddhi*) lacks such power, how much less could the defiled states sever them?
This is by way of comparing the superior with the inferior:
that is to say, the fundamental pure concentration (*maulānāsrava-samādhi*) cannot abandon the lower stages, because one has already become free from defilement (*vītarāga*) regarding them.
One cannot sever the afflictions of one's own level because one is bound by those very afflictions;
nor can one sever the afflictions of higher levels.
Because they are superior to their own level.
If the pure preparatory stages (*sāmantaka*) can also abandon the afflictions,
it is because they are all capable of abandoning the afflictions of the immediately lower stage.
Furthermore, the *Abhidharmamahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 162, states:
Question: For what reason is the contaminated path unable to sever [defilements] of its own stage or of higher stages?
"Can the untainted path (*anāsrava-mārga*) then sever [defilements]?
Answer: "Because the untainted path is a factor that is non-bound (*apratisaṃyukta*), it is in every way superior to tainted factors (*sāsrava-dharma*)."
Therefore, it is able to abandon [defilements].
Furthermore, the path with outflows (sāsrava-mārga) performs six aspects of mental application;
because it feels aversion toward the lower stages while taking delight in its own stage, it abandons only those of the lower stages.
The untainted path (anāsrava-mārga) performs the sixteen aspects (ākāra);
because it turns away from all stages (bhūmi), it is able to completely sever [the afflictions].
Question: Does the tainted path (sāsrava-mārga) also perform the sixteen aspects?
Why is it that they cannot completely sever [the afflictions]?
Answer: Although they train in the aspects of the noble path, because their practice is not clear and distinct, they do not sever the afflictions.

As stated in the treatise above: "Like a lion cub that has not yet been able to kill wild beasts," even if the intermediate [attainment] is pure, it cannot effect abandonment, as explained in the *Mūla*.
How many proximate [attainments] are there? Up to the first, they are either noble or threefold.
This constitutes the eighth clarification concerning the distinctions of the preparatory stages (*sāmantaka*).
First, it asks how many preparatory stages there are;
second, it asks with which sensations (*vedanā*) they are associated.
The three questions concern whether the three [factors], such as taste, are all fully present.
The response in verse may be understood accordingly.
The Commentary states: "Because it serves as the gateway."
The eight preparatory stages (*sāmantaka*) can be understood [as explained above].

As for the statement, "All are exclusively [so] because one has not yet abandoned the fear of the lower [realm]": [This means that] until one has abandoned the fear of falling back into the lower realm, all [meditative attainments] are characterized by this state.
Regarding the explanation of equanimity (*upekṣā*): all access concentrations (*sāmantaka*) are associated exclusively with the feeling of equanimity.
When these access concentrations arise, [they are thus characterized].
Because it functions through arduous effort and because one has not yet abandoned the defilements of the lower realms, the mind harbors fear; therefore,
it is not associated with joy or pleasure.
Regarding the statement that "these eight access concentrations (sāmantaka) possess three types," this explains the term "pure" (śuddha) and the subsequent phrase.
These eight access concentrations are all subsumed under pure concentration (śuddhaka-samādhi).
Only the initial preparatory stage (sāmantaka) also includes the untainted (anāsrava),
because those who have not yet abandoned desire give rise to the Noble Path (āryamārga) by relying on the preparatory concentration.
Therefore, the *Nyāyānusāra* states:
The seven upper preparatory stages (*sāmantaka*) lack the untainted (*anāsrava*) state because they do not feel revulsion toward the phenomena of their own level;
only the first preparatory stage is permeated by the untainted state.
Because one can feel revulsion toward the phenomena of one's own level;

because this level is extremely close to a realm of many calamities; and because, as stated in the treatise, there is no "taste" (āsvāda) in any of these, as they constitute the path of detachment from defilement.
Because it arises from hardship,
craving does not arise;
for that meditative absorption on flavor is produced by a path that is not free from defilement.
This is because it allows the path of arising to proceed with ease;
although there is also a path within the preparatory stages (*sāmantaka*) that does not constitute the actual separation from defilement,
it nevertheless assists in that separation.
Because it is of a nature free from defilement and because there is no room for indulgence,
craving does not arise.
Although the preparatory mind (sāmantaka-citta) possesses the defilement of rebirth-linking (paṭisandhi),
because it is associated with the feeling of equanimity (upekkhā-vedanā) at the moments of conception and death,
one must necessarily give rise to the preparatory stage.
However, because it is intended to exclude those that are definitely defiled, this statement was made:
the near-attainments (sāmantaka) lack flavor;
they exist only in the fundamental [dhyānas].
Some say that the *anāgamya* concentration is also associated with attachment (*sāsvāda*),
because even before the fundamental concentration has arisen, one may still crave this preparatory state.
For this reason, the *anāgamya* possesses all three types [of association].
Regarding the seven lower preparatory stages (*sāmantaka*), because the fundamental [dhyānas] below them have already been attained,
one does not give rise to craving for those preparatory stages; therefore,
they are not said to exist [as distinct entities].
This summarizes divergent views.
Regarding the intermediate dhyānas, there are also differences.
Below this, the ninth section clarifies the distinctions among the intermediate concentrations.

This is the question. Regarding the point that there are distinctions in meaning up to the state where all three [faculties] are exclusively associated with the sensation of equanimity (*upekṣā-vedanā*),
this is the answer.
Their meanings also differ:

it is said that the preparatory stages (*sāmantaka*) serve as the primary cause for entering [the dhyānas] by means of abandoning the defilements of the lower realms, whereas this is not the case for the intermediate dhyāna (*dhyānāntara*).
It is not that one is free from the defilements of the lower realms, nor is it the primary cause for entering [the path], because it is the first fruit.
Furthermore, there is another meaning.
The Commentary states, "Up to 'because it does not exist in this way,'" which explains the first phrase:
the fundamental stage of the first dhyāna and its preparatory stage (*sāmantaka*).
Vitarka and vicāra are associated [with the first dhyāna].
Within the seven higher meditative absorptions (dhyānas),
both the fundamental and the preparatory stages are devoid of vitarka and vicāra.
Only the intermediate dhyāna possesses vicāra but lacks vitarka; thus, it differs from the preparatory stage (*sāmantaka*).
Because it is without vitarka, it excels the first dhyāna;
because it still possesses vicāra, it has not yet reached the level of the second dhyāna.
It is based on this meaning that the name "intermediate" (dhyānāntara) is established.
Consequently, the higher stages lack an intermediate dhyāna,
because there is no such ascent or descent between single stages as there is here.
Regarding the phrase "because this concentration possesses a most desirable savor," this explains its possession of the three [characteristics].
This intermediate concentration possesses all three types of association, such as savoring (*āsvādana*) and so forth.
Because the Great Brahmā possesses supreme qualities that are desirable and savorable,
it is associated with relishing (*sāsvāda*).
That which is included within the "difficult path of practice" (*duḥkhā pratipad*) shared with the various preparatory stages (*sāmantaka*) is likewise so categorized.
This explains the feeling of equanimity (*upekṣā*).
This intermediate dhyāna is similar to the preparatory stages (*sāmantaka*);
it is associated only with equanimity and not with joy (*prīti*).
Because it proceeds through the effort of self-exertion,
it is said to be comprised within the path of difficult practice (*duḥkhā pratipad*).
Furthermore, there is no pleasure therein, because the three consciousnesses are absent.
Therefore, the *Nyāyānusāra* states:

"Because the three bodies of consciousness do not exist, there is no pleasant feeling (*sukha-vedanā*). According to the text of the *Nyāyānusāra*, the intermediate dhyāna (*dhyānāntara*) lacks the three bodies of consciousness.
Question: Why is it that they do not exist?
Explanation: It is said that the five consciousnesses are necessarily associated with vitarka and vicāra; since those [consciousnesses] lack vitarka, [the latter two are absent].
Regarding the statement, "This meditative absorption can bring about rebirth as a Great Brahmā":
this specifically clarifies that the intermediate dhyāna can bring about a superior fruit;
if one practices it extensively, one becomes a Great Brahmā King.
By not practicing extensively, one becomes a Brahmā-purohita;
this is because they occupy the same level.
Having already explained the meditative attainments (*samāpatti*), what then is meditative concentration (*samādhi*)?
Below this, the fourth section clarifies the various meditative concentrations (*samādhi*).
Within it, the first part clarifies the three factors beginning with applied thought (*vitarka*) and sustained thought (*vicāra*).
2. Explaining the three types beginning with "single emptiness" (śūnyatā).
3. Explaining the three types beginning with "repeated emptiness. 4.

Explaining the cultivation of the four meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*). Below this, first, the explanation of the three types beginning with "investigation" (*vitarka*) and "analysis" (*vicāra*).
Regarding the preceding verses, there are two parts:
first, the general;
second, the specific.
This summarizes the preceding inquiry.
As for the statement in the Sūtra, "What are the characteristics of meditative concentration (samādhi)?
this specifically raises the question based on the Sūtra.
The verse says: "Up to and including the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
The answer can be understood from the text.
It is called *samādhi* (equipoise) because it holds the mind equally toward its object.
The sutra further states that one reaches the three untainted gates of liberation (*anāsrava-trimukha*).
This is the second section, which clarifies the three—emptiness and so forth—taken individually.
Based on this sutra, a question is raised.
Regarding the verse and its response:
the *Śāstra* states, "As for 'attaining the meditative concentration associated with [the factors],' this explains the first phrase."
Because this emptiness serves as the antidote to the view of a self-existent body (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*),
the *Abhidharmamahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 14, states:
"Regarding 'as an antidote'..."
This means that the concentration on emptiness (*śūnyatā-samādhi*) is the direct antidote to the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*).
Question: The concentration on emptiness possesses two aspects (*ākāra*): emptiness and non-self.
The view of a self-identity possesses two aspects: "I" and "mine."
In this context, by what kind of aspect is which kind of aspect counteracted?
Answer: The aspect of non-self is used to counteract the aspect of self.

The counteractive application of the aspect of emptiness to the aspect of "mine" is explained at length as in that [previous] commentary. Regarding the phrase "the signless samādhi reaches the signs of the three conditioned existences," this explains the second line.
Because it abides in a manner indistinguishable from the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), "abiding" is not mentioned;
the rest of the text is self-evident.
The phrase "because the wishless samādhi (*apraṇihita-samādhi*) is similar to its own characteristic" explains the third and fourth lines.
The wishless samādhi refers to the meditative concentration associated with ten aspects of the remaining truths of suffering, origin, and the path. These ten aspects are:
impermanence and suffering [regarding the truth of suffering], and [the remaining eight] regarding the truths of origin and the path.
Cause, origin, arising, condition;
path, suchness, practice, emergence.
Impermanence and suffering—this is the Truth of Suffering.
Among the four aspects of suffering, two are [correct] and two are not;
therefore, they are designated separately to reveal the truth of origination (*samudaya-satya*).
This refers to cause (*hetu*), origin (*samudaya*), arising (*jāti*), and condition (*pratyaya*).
Alternatively, by mentioning the first [term], the subsequent ones are implied;
for both the truths of suffering (*duḥkha*) and its origin (*samudaya*) are tainted (*sāsrava*) and thus objects of revulsion.
Although the Path is untainted, during the stage of preparatory application one forms this thought:
"The Path is like a boat or a raft; it must necessarily be abandoned."
The meditative attainments that take these as their objects can be designated as "wishless" (apraṇihita),
because they are all intended to transcend the present objects of focus—
the spheres of suffering, origination, and the path— which are to be loathed and abandoned.
Emptiness is not characterized by self, nor is it something to be loathed,
nor is it something to be abandoned,
because it resembles nirvāṇa.
Therefore, these two aspects cannot be designated as "wishless" (*apraṇihita*).
