then one should not say that visual consciousness cognizes the self;
for this self is not an object-condition for visual consciousness.
Because it is like the sense-sphere of sound and so forth;
the self you postulate is not an object-condition for visual consciousness,
because it is not a sense-sphere of form.
As with the sense-base of sound and so forth; that is to say,
if one were to defend [the position] by claiming that there is a certain class of consciousness which arises by taking this blue object and so forth as its general object.
Taking these objects, such as blue and so forth, as the objective condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*), [the opponent] refutes [this] by saying:
"The person (*pudgala*) is not an object-condition for visual consciousness."

How can it be that what was previously stated as being the object-condition (*ālambana*) of visual consciousness is, by this very fact, certainly not cognized (*vijñāta*) by visual consciousness? Alternatively, the above constitutes a restatement of the opponent's defense:
"If visual consciousness arises..."
If one were to conceive of a self solely by depending on this [body], or by depending on both form and the self,
it would contradict the Sūtra’s teaching that consciousness arises dependent on two conditions.
If it were to take only the self as its object, it would lack the condition of form;
if it were to take form as its object, the self would have to arise by way of three conditions,
since the sutra states that [consciousness] arises by way of only two conditions.
Furthermore, regarding the statement in the sutra that [consciousness] reaches the eye and visible forms,
the Master of the Treatise cites a third sutra to prove that consciousness arises from two conditions.
"It does not arise from a self.
Furthermore, regarding the point that "if this were so, it would contradict one's own tenets," the Master of the Treatise again cites the fourth sūtra to refute it.
Furthermore, if this self were the condition for visual consciousness and could produce visual consciousness,
then the self would have to be impermanent.
The Sūtra states that all things which arise from causes and conditions as consciousness are impermanent;
yet the Vātsīputrīyas do not admit that the self (ātman) is impermanent. If they then offer a rebuttal, claiming that the self is not a condition for consciousness, [the response is as follows:]
The refutation says:
It should not be an object of cognition;
if it is not an object of cognition, it should not be an object of knowledge.
If it were not an object of knowledge, how could there be a self?
If one does not establish the existence of a self, one’s own tenet system is undermined.
Within our own tenet system, the self is established as being subsumed within the fifth category of the inexpressible (avaktavya) among the categories of the Dharma-treasury.
Furthermore, if it were granted that there is a contradiction with one's own tenets [in asserting that [contact] reaches [the object]),
the author of the treatise further cites the fifth sutra to refute it,
thereby demonstrating the contradiction with the scriptures.
First, one establishes the formal argument (prayoga):
"The self is distinct from the six objects.
Furthermore, if one were to concede that the self is cognized by the six consciousnesses, [it would follow that it is an object].
The self you maintain must be distinct from sound,
because it is cognized by visual consciousness,
just like visible form.
The self you maintain must be distinct from form and the other [sensory objects],
because it is cognized by auditory consciousness, just as sound is.
Each of the objects cognized by the other consciousnesses may be challenged by means of inference based on this same principle.
This would then challenge the claim that the self is distinct from the six objects;
how, then, can you say that the self and the six objects are neither definitely identical nor different?
Furthermore, having established that this self is cognized by the six consciousnesses,
one contradicts the scriptural teachings.
The Sūtra says: "O Brahmin, the five faculties have distinct domains and distinct objects;
each experiences only its own respective domain."
And its own objective sphere. Alternatively,
the former is explained in terms of place (*sthāna*),
while the latter is distinguished in terms of realm (*dhātu*).
It is not that there are distinct colors or faculties;
yet, it is also able to experience the spheres of activity and the objects of other faculties.
The mental faculty (manas) further encompasses the experience of the spheres of activity of the five physical faculties.
And as for their objects,
since those five consciousnesses also rely upon the mind,
the mental faculty (*manas*) alone is truly able to experience thirteen realms.

Furthermore, it is capable of experiencing the spheres of activity of the five faculties as well as their respective objects. Moreover, it is understood that because that mental consciousness relies upon the mind-faculty (*manas*),
the mind-faculty and the dependent consciousness take all phenomena as their common object.
It correctly takes thirteen [factors] as its object,
and it also takes the five faculties, their spheres of activity, and the objects of the five faculties as its objects.
The previous interpretation is superior. According to your view, a single mind apprehends the six consciousnesses simultaneously;
if this were so, then the five sense organs would also be able to concurrently apprehend the objects and domains of other sense organs.
Furthermore, this sutra states that the spheres of activity and the objects of the five faculties are each distinct.
Does this not contradict the sutra?
Since it contradicts the sutra, one should certainly not maintain that the "self" is the object of the five faculties.
If it is not the object of the five sense faculties,
then it is not cognized by the five consciousnesses. If it is not cognized by the five consciousnesses, [it is not a sensory object].
Although this does not contradict the sūtras, it nevertheless incurs the fault of contradicting your own tenet,
because your school asserts that the self is cognized by the five consciousnesses.
"If that is so, then the mental faculty (manas) must reach its own object.
This is the objection raised by the Vātsīputrīyas:
"If it is not admitted that the five faculties apprehend a self when they apprehend their respective distinct objects..."
The objects of the sixth faculty, the mind, should likewise be distinct.
As stated in the *Ṣaḍāyatanavibhaṅga-sūtra*:
"In this way, the spheres of activity and the objects of these six faculties each have their own distinctions."
"Up to their own respective spheres.
Here, the intended meaning is that,
as stated in the *Ṣaḍāyatanopama-sūtra*, the domains and spheres of the six sense faculties are each distinct.
In reality, the mental faculty (manas) is also capable of experiencing the domains and objects of the five physical faculties.
What contradiction is there, then, in the previous sutra stating that the domains and objects of the five faculties are each distinct?
Yet it is capable of simultaneously apprehending the objects of different sense faculties.
When the Sūtra states that the five sense faculties each apprehend their own distinct objects,
this is not a statement that fully captures the ultimate truth.
Regarding what is called the *Ṣaḍjātakopama-sūtra*:
that sūtra describes how a bird, a snake, a pig, a crocodile, a jackal, and a monkey are bound with ropes so that they cannot act according to their own will.
The bird flying in the sky is a metaphor for the visual faculty seeing at a distance;
the snake dwelling mostly in its burrow is a metaphor for the auditory faculty being within a deep cavity;
and the pig receiving filth and foul-smelling things is a metaphor for the olfactory faculty.
This is like the nose clinging to fragrance.
The crocodile delighting in the water is a metaphor for the tongue clinging to flavor;
for flavor must necessarily be conveyed by the saliva before the tongue can perceive it.
The jackal delighting in dwelling in a grass hut in the mountain forest is a metaphor for the body being touched by sensations;
the monkey’s nature of restless agitation that never ceases is a metaphor for the mind having many objects of thought and reflection;
and the six types of sentient beings are used as metaphors for those six sense faculties.
It is titled the *Ṣaḍāyatanopama-sūtra*.
This does not mean that what is taught here contradicts what was stated previously;
rather, the Master of the Treatise provides this explanation in order to reconcile it with the *Ṣaḍāyatanopama-sūtra*.
This does not refer to the six sense organs, such as the eye, mentioned here;
rather, the intention of this sutra is to speak of the sixth consciousness. Why is this so?
The five faculties, such as the eye, and the five consciousnesses produced from them lack the capacity for the desire to see and so forth; therefore,
the Sūtra speaks of "seeking with pleasure."
Therefore, one should know that this does not rely on that [other] teaching;
rather, it simply states that the mental consciousness, induced by the predominant power of the five faculties such as the eye,
takes objects such as visible forms as its domain.
Based on their causes, they are designated as the "eye" and other faculties;
the mental faculty (*manas*), acting as the predominant influence for those that function independently,
induces a mental consciousness that takes the thirteen realms as its objects.
It is also named "mind-faculty" (manas-indriya) based on its cause;
since those [faculties] such as the eye are not led by it,
they cannot themselves seek out and delight in the objects led by the five faculties, such as the eye.
Therefore, the meaning of the *Ṣaḍāyatanopama-sūtra* does not contradict the faultless explanation given previously regarding the *Brāhmaṇa-sūtra*.
The former *Brāhmaṇa-sūtra* was based on the essential nature (*bhāva*) of the six sense faculties.
Therefore, it is said that the spheres of the five faculties, such as the eye, are each distinct.
If the mental faculty is induced by the eye and the others,
it is also capable of taking as its objects both the domains of activity and the spheres of those five faculties.
The *Ṣaḍāyatanopama-sūtra* refers to the mental consciousness induced by the predominant power of the six sense-faculties as being "the six faculties";
it follows that each faculty induces its own respective engagement with an object.
Because that mental consciousness is designated as six according to its respective sense faculties,
the six faculties are said to be "those that seek pleasure. Thus,
the meanings clarified in the two preceding sutras are distinct from one another.

Therefore, there is no contradiction with the preceding sūtra. Furthermore, regarding the Blessed One’s statement that "that which reaches its object must necessarily be identical [to it]," the Master [Vasubandhu] cites a sixth sūtra to refute [this view].

"That which is reached" refers to the path of non-interval (ānantarya-mārga); "that which is known" refers to the path of liberation (vimukti-mārga). Alternatively, "that which is reached" refers to the wisdom that reaches [its object].
"Objects of knowledge" (jñeya) refers to that which is known by wisdom; these are all the phenomena reached and known by wisdom.
"Eye" is a synonym for this.
Since this sutra speaks of the phenomena reached and known [by wisdom], it refers to these.
There is only that much;
there is no self-entity.
Therefore, one knows that the self-entity is likewise not an object of cognition.
Although realization and wisdom are prajñā and not vijñāna,
this is because the objects of prajñā and vijñāna must necessarily be identical; therefore,
the self is not an object of cognition.
Regarding those who claim that the statement "the eye sees what it reaches" should not be interpreted otherwise,
the Master of the Treatise further cites the seventh sutra to refute them,
first setting forth their erroneous conception.
Later, citing a sūtra, [the opponent] is refuted.
The Vātsīputrīyas claim that the eye sees the self;
this is refuted as follows:
One should know that the eye-faculty sees all visible forms;
yet, regarding what is not-self in the act of seeing, one falsely claims to see a self.
Consequently, one falls headlong into the deep pit of evil views.
Therefore, the Buddha himself resolved this meaning within the sūtras,
stating that the designation "self" is applied only to the aggregates (*skandha*).
As it says in the *Pudgala-sūtra*:
With the eye and forms as conditions, eye-consciousness arises.
From the conjunction of these three, contact occurs, and simultaneously with it, feeling, perception, and volition arise.
Among these, the latter four—namely, eye-consciousness, feeling, perception, and volition—are [the factors].

Because contact (sparśa) is comprised of the three [factors] and lacks a separate essence,
it is not counted separately.
The Master of the Treatise refutes this using the Sautrāntika position.
Unlike the Sarvāstivādins, who maintain that contact has a distinct substantial entity,
[the Sautrāntikas hold that] the initial eye and visible form are designated as the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*).
It is solely by means of the measure of the five aggregates that one is conventionally designated as a "person.
It is precisely within this conventionally designated person that the sūtra [speaks].
Based on the distinctions of meaning, provisional names and characteristics are established;
for instance, one may refer to them as "sentient beings" because they possess consciousness.

He is called "Mind-born" because he is born from the mind;
he is called "Māṇava" because he is a virtuous youth.
Some call it the nourisher;
some call it the nourished;

or it is called a *pudgala*,
because it repeatedly takes up various realms of existence (*gati*).
One also says of oneself, "I see forms with my eye.

There are names such as Devadatta;
there are castes such as Brahmin; and there are lineages such as Kāśyapa.

this sūtra is of definitive meaning and should not be interpreted otherwise.
Furthermore, regarding the Blessed One’s statement that [the Tathāgata] is "inexpressible," the Master of the Treatise again cites the eighth sūtra to refute it.
Moreover, the Blessed One addressed a brahmin, saying:
I declare that all that exists is entirely subsumed within the twelve bases (āyatana);
outside of the twelve bases, there is no further phenomenon.
If the person (pudgala) were not included among these bases, [it would not exist].
The principle that it lacks intrinsic nature is established.

Regarding the claim that this [person] possesses a substantial entity according to the recensions of that school,
the Master of Treatises further cites the ninth sūtra to refute it;
the sūtra recited by that Vātsīputrīya school also states:
Whatever eyes there are,
whatever forms there are—
expounded at length, and so forth.

all phenomena whatsoever, and so forth,
as explained at length, up to...

herein, there is no self.
"How can it be said that I have a substantial entity?

out of affection for their child, his parents gave him this name. Regarding the sixteen statements therein:

The sūtra states:
"There are five faults in clinging to a self."
First, the arising of the view of a self;
second, the view of sentient beings;

"This is utterly unreasonable."

"It is not so. Why is it unreasonable?
The Vātsīputrīya asks:
