To this, the Vātsīputrīya replies:
The conceptualization of a self constitutes a perversion;
it refers to falsely imagining what is non-self to be a self, rather than conceptualizing a self within a [previously established] self.
Why then trouble oneself with reconciling this?
"What is it that is not the self?
The Master of the Treatise asks:
"It refers to the aggregates (skandhas), bases (āyatanas), and elements (dhātus)."
The Vātsīputrīya replies:
"This contradicts the previous statement that [the person] is neither identical nor different," thus the Master points out the error.
This would contradict the previous statement that the self and the aggregates, such as form, are neither identical nor different.
If it is said that the essence of the aggregates, bases, and elements is not the self,
how can one say that the self is not different from the aggregates?
Furthermore, regarding other sūtras that state one reaches the point of falsely conceptualizing [the aggregates] as a self,
the Master also points out a fault:
the sūtra says that the conception of a self arises with respect to the appropriated aggregates (upādānaskandha).
Since it does not speak of "I," there is no basis for giving rise to the view of self based upon me; rather,
it is merely through the false discrimination of what is not-self as being self.
How can it be said that [the Buddha] did not speak of "self"?
Furthermore, regarding the statement in other sūtras that [the teaching] extends to the *pudgala*,
the Master of the Treatise again points out the error.
The Sūtra states that [the view of self] arises only with respect to the five aggregates of clinging;
it does not state that it arises with respect to a self.
Therefore, there is certainly no self.
"If that is so, for what reason does one arrive at such form and so forth?
This concludes the third section of the main text, which addresses these objections.
The Vātsīputrīya raises the following objection:
If it is said that there is no self,
for what reason does this sutra further state:
"In a past life, I..."?
"There are such things as form and so forth"—
this sūtra is intended to clarify that [the aggregates] reach the state of being like a collection or like a stream;
thus the Master of the Treatise resolves the objection.
This sutra is intended to reveal that within a single continuum of a body capable of recollecting past lives, the conventional designation "self" is used for various phenomena.
If one were to perceive a real self, it would follow that such a self possessed form and other qualities in past lives.
How is it that this does not incur the fault of falling into the view of a self-existent body (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*)?
Yet, the noble ones know that the past is not [the object of] the view of a self-existent body; thus you raise this objection.
You should perhaps deny it by saying that this sūtra does not exist.
Therefore, this sutra speaks of "possessing form" and so forth with reference to the conventional self (*pudgala*) as a continuity of the five aggregates in general:
like a heap, it is a conventionality established through conditions;
like a stream, it is a conventionality established through conditions.
The continuity [of phenomena] is provisional;
it has no separate substance and is merely established as a name by way of designation.
If that were so, the Vātsīputrīyas would object: "The Blessed One is capable of knowing everything;
if there were no self, [how could he know it]?"
The Blessed One would not be omniscient;
for there is no mind or mental factor capable of knowing all phenomena.
... [and so forth] ...
The contemplation of non-self also does not know the intrinsic nature, the associated factors, or the coexistent factors,
because they arise and perish differently at every moment, being distinct in their preceding and succeeding moments.
If one were to admit that the self exists and is not subject to momentary destruction,
it would be possible for it to persist over time and thus be fully known;
otherwise, the person (pudgala) could not be fully known except instantaneously.
The Master of the Treatise resolves the objection.
Before resolving that objection,
he first refutes it as follows:
I must be permanent,
because it is admitted that when the mind ceases, I do not cease;
and if I do not cease, [I am permanent].
In this way, you would be transgressing your own accepted tenet because the self would be permanent.
Furthermore, he correctly explains:
"We do not say that the Buddha [is so] in all respects."
Because he can know all things instantaneously and simultaneously within a single moment,
he is called the "Omniscient One" (sarvajña). However,
this is said only in reference to his capacity over a long duration through the continuity of preceding and succeeding moments.
This refers to attaining the name "Buddha," whereby the continuum of the aggregates achieves such extraordinary capacity and the virtue of omniscience that,
at the mere moment of forming a mental intention, [all things are known].
The non-erroneous arising of knowledge regarding the objects one wishes to know is called "omniscience" (sarvajñatā).
It is not that one can suddenly and instantaneously know all things in a single moment of thought;

therefore, regarding the continuity [of consciousness], there is this verse: "By virtue of the capacity existing within the preceding and succeeding moments of continuity, it is like fire which gradually burns various objects rather than doing so in a single instant. Likewise, omniscience consists in a continuous process of universal knowledge; it is not a matter of instantaneous, simultaneous knowledge in a single moment. If one relies on the *Siddhāntabheda* (Treatise on the Different Tenets):
The Mahāsāṃghikas and other schools maintain that the prajñā associated with a single moment of mind knows all phenomena.
"How is it known that [the Buddha] is an omniscient one who has reached the realization of non-self?
The Vātsīputrīyas ask:
"How is it known that the statement 'he knows all phenomena' is spoken with reference to knowledge within a continuum (*saṃtāna*)?"

Regarding the claim that "it is not my universal knowledge [to know all things], because the Buddha, the World-Honored One, is said to exist in the three periods of time," the Master of the Treatise replies:
Because it is taught that the Buddha, the World-Honored One, possesses the three time periods, it is clearly understood that the knowledge of all phenomena is spoken of in reference to a continuum;
it is not that "I" possess universal knowledge. For they [the opponents] reckon that the World-Honored One has the self (*ātman*) as his essence.
This is subsumed within the fifth, the Dharma-treasury of the ineffable;
it is not a Dharma-treasury of the three periods of time.
Therefore, the author of the treatise replies.
It is said that the Buddha, the World-Honored One, is the treasury of the dharmas of the three periods of time;
he possesses universal knowledge through the continuity of his wisdom,
whereas I do not possess such universal knowledge.
Regarding where this was taught:
the Vātsīputrīyas ask,
"In what place did the Buddha, the World-Honored One, state that there are three time periods?"
Regarding the statement, "As a verse says, because it has reached [this point], it must necessarily be so," this is accepted as the Master’s response,
just as a verse in the Sūtra says:
The Buddhas of the three times extinguish the sorrows of sentient beings; therefore, with respect to the continuity [of the aggregates], they are called "omniscient Buddhas.
In your own school, you maintain that only the aggregates exist across the three times, and not a *pudgala*.
Because the person (*pudgala*) is included within the fifth category of the inexpressible (*avaktavya*) dharma-treasury, it must necessarily be so.
That is to say, it must certainly be explained in terms of dharmas of the three time periods; it is accepted that [the person] is spoken of in terms of the continuity (*saṃtāna*).
The Buddhas of the three periods of time,
by means of the continuity of their wisdom, universally know all things;
they do not [know them] as discrete, individual persons.
If the person (pudgala) were the very essence of the Blessed One,
he would be the one who thoroughly knows all things.
One should not say that the Buddha exists throughout the three periods of time.

[This concludes] the second volume of the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya-ki*. Recorded on the twenty-eighth day of the seventh month in the first year of the Jōhō era (768 CE). Completed at the former residence of the late Great Minister of State who entered the Way, while staying in Kyoto. It was noted that there were some characters in the "Refutation of the Self" (*Pudgala-pratiṣedha*) chapter that were unclear.
Record of the Awakening Tree by the Junior Sōjū Kwan;
Commentary on the Abhidharmakośa-śāstra, Scroll Thirty,
composed by the Śramaṇa Shi Guang.
The Ninth Chapter: Refuting the Attachment to a Self, Part Two.
If it were only the five aggregates of clinging that carry the burden, the teacher of the Vātsīputrīya school again cites a sūtra to raise an objection.
If the proponent of this treatise says that the "self" is merely a conventional designation for the five aggregates of clinging (*pañca-upādāna-skandha*),
why did the Buddha say: "I shall now explain to you the heavy burden, the taking up of the burden,
and the laying down of the burden"?
If there were no self, who would cast off the previous heavy burden and now shoulder a new heavy burden?
In this sūtra, the Blessed One should not have spoken in such a manner regarding "bearing the burden" and so forth.
For what reason should the Buddha not have spoken thus in this context?
The author of the treatise counters by questioning:
"For what reason should the Buddha not have spoken of this?
Because one has never before seen [a case of] carrying a heavy burden."
The Vātsīputrīyas reply: It is not the case that the very substance of the five aggregates of clinging (*pañcopādānaskandha*), which constitute the heavy burden,
is itself designated as the bearer of that burden.
Why is this so? Because it has never been seen that the burden itself is called the bearer;
therefore, we know that there must be a self which is called the bearer.
The aggregates are the objects [of grasping];
the two modes of taking up and discarding are omitted here for brevity and not discussed.
Regarding the point that "the ineffable matter pertains to the *pudgala*," the master of the treatise provides an explanation.
Within this explanation, he first raises an objection.
The subsequent explanation addresses the objection:
"According to your own school, the fifth category— the dharma-treasury of the ineffable—
should likewise not be spoken of."
Why is this? Because it has never been seen before. Furthermore, it is difficult to explain by means of analogy.
The objection states that the one who takes up the burden (bhārahāra) should not be included within the aggregates (skandha),
because it has never been observed that a burden takes itself up.
This is the intent of the objection.
"I, who am the bearer, am not subsumed under the aggregates;
grasping is the grasper, and thus it too should not be subsumed under the aggregates. The illustrative commentary states:
However, since the Sūtra describes craving as the cause and grasping (*upādāna*) as the result— the heavy burden—
craving is that which grasps.
Since it is already subsumed within the aggregates (*skandha*), that which bears the aggregates must likewise be subsumed within the aggregates.
The term "person" (pudgala) is merely a conventional designation established upon the aggregates;
however, the Buddha feared that the Vātsīputrīyas might claim this essence of a self to be a fifth category of inexpressible dharma-treasury, permanent and substantially existent.
Therefore, at the end of this sūtra, the Buddha himself explains:
"It is merely according to worldly convention that we say this venerable one has such a name," and so forth, as extensively stated;
the numerous names are as cited above from the passages of the sūtra.

In order to bring about the understanding that this "self" is a mere designation for the five aggregates, it may be said that they are impermanent and lack a real intrinsic nature. Furthermore, because these five aggregates of clinging, by their very own characteristics, oppress and harm, they receive the name "burden."
Because each preceding moment induces each succeeding one,
it is called "the bearer.
This means that the preceding cause is able to bear the subsequent effect.
Therefore, the *pudgala* is not substantially existent.
Regarding the statement that "the *pudgala* is subsumed under wrong views," the Vātsīputrīyas again cite a sūtra to raise an objection.
This demonstrates that the self truly exists; the self certainly exists in reality.
For the Sūtras state that the wrong view which denies the existence of spontaneously born beings (*upapāduka-sattva*) is subsumed under [the denial of the self].
Spontaneously born beings are precisely the real self.
To deny [the self] is a false view;
it is clear that a real self exists.
Who says there is no [self], given that it persists until it is abandoned through cultivation?
The Master of the Treatise resolves the objection:
Who says that there are no beings born by transformation?
As the Buddha has said:
I teach that there is an intermediate state (*antarābhava*) for those born by transformation (*upapāduka*),
meaning that the continuity of the aggregates (*skandhasantati*) proceeds to a future life;
those who do not arise from a womb, egg, or moisture are called sentient beings born by transformation.
Because this [view] negates the existence of the intermediate state (*antarābhava*), it is subsumed under wrong view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*).
Since the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*) of those born by transformation (*upapāduka*) do indeed exist in reality, the argument is further challenged:
furthermore, if one admits that this wrong view slanders the person (*pudgala*), by what [path] is it abandoned?
The claim that [the self] is abandoned through seeing and cultivation is logically untenable. According to your own tenet,
since the substantially existent self is not subsumed under the Four Noble Truths, it cannot be abandoned through the vision of the truths.
Furthermore, this false view should not be said to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*).
If it is argued that the Sūtra states that there is "reaching" (*prāpti*) which gives rise to the world,
the Master [Vasubandhu] restates that position and refutes it.
If it is argued that the Sūtra states, "There is one person (pudgala) born in the world, namely 'I' or 'the aggregates' (skandha)," this is refuted as being likewise unreasonable.
The Sūtra speaks of "a single self" because it metaphorically designates a single self with respect to the aggregate as a whole;
it is like the common worldly expression of "many atoms."
That which consists of a single sesame seed or a single grain of rice is called "one";
a collection of many grains, such as barley and wheat, is called "a cluster";
and many moments of sound are called "a word. Alternatively, you must admit that the self (ātman) is subsumed within the conditioned (saṃskṛta).
This is because the sūtras speak of "arising in the world.
However, our school does not accept that it is included within the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*).
This statement regarding "arising" is not like the arising of the aggregates (*skandha*) following their cessation.
The Vātsīputrīyas offer this defense:
"This self is not born in the manner that the aggregates newly arise.
In what sense, then, is it said that it is 'born in the world'?"
The author of the treatise raises an objection:
"Because it relies on this present time to reach a distinct state of appropriation.
The Vātsīputrīya school replies.
As for the statement "I am born," this refers to my present relinquishing of a previous collection of distinct aggregates and taking up a subsequent collection of distinct aggregates;
it does not mean that a new self is born.
As it is said in the world, one who has mastered the practice of sacrificial rites and attained accomplishment is called a "born sacrificer" (*yājñika*).
The *Vyākaraṇa* treatise is termed the "Science of Exegesis" (*vyākhyāna-śāstra*).
This refers to the science of grammar (*śabdavidyā*).
One who has mastered the study of the grammatical treatises is called a "grammarian" (*vaiyākaraṇa*).
One is said to be "born" because one takes up these two types of *vidyā-śāstra*.
The treatises studied by that person are called *vidyā-śāstra*. Furthermore, as it is commonly said in the world, when one first leaves the household life, one is said to be "born" as a *bhikṣu*.
When one first enters among the non-Buddhists, it is called "birth as a non-Buddhist.
Because one adopts their own deportment and their own rules through these two types [of birth], they are called "born.
Alternatively, it is like the worldly expression that one with white hair and wrinkled face is called "born old."
The disharmony of the four great elements is called "birth" (*jāti*).
Because these two types [of birth] distinguish specific states, they are termed "birth. What was stated above regarding "birth" refers to the acquisition of distinct dharmas;
it does not refer to initial birth.
My birth is also like this. It is based on the appropriation of distinct aggregates; it is not that a self arises mixed with new [aggregates], for the Buddha has already refuted this.
As for "the Buddha has already refuted it": [it refers to his refutation of such a view].
Below this, the master of the treatise refutes [the opponent's position].
This specifically cites a sūtra to refute it;
the sūtra states that there is karma and there is its maturation (vipāka).
Because a real author cannot be found—
namely, one who could relinquish these preceding aggregates and continue with subsequent other aggregates.
Except for the conventional designation of "self" applied to the continuity of the five aggregates,
the Buddha has already refuted a real self external to the aggregates.
Thus, when Pūraṇa spoke of "taking up and discarding the aggregates," he was referring to this.
The Master of the Treatise further refutes this by citing scripture:
it does not state that there exists a real grasper;
therefore, there is no real self that can grasp or abandon the aggregates.
Furthermore, regarding your citation that "the destination is also like the mind and so forth," the Master of the Treatise again refutes it by means of an analogy.
Moreover, regarding your citation of those such as the sacrificers who are born [in heaven].
What is its nature that it can serve as an analogy for the self? If you maintain that the sacrificer is the self,
then the analogy is not established.
Since I do not admit the existence of a real self-entity, if one maintains that the sacrificer is the mind and mental factors,
they perish moment by moment because they are newly produced.
If [the self] were permitted to be the sacrificial victim, it would be a physical body,
just like the mind and so forth;
that [body] perishes moment by moment.
Because they arise anew at every moment,
appropriation and relinquishment are not established.
Furthermore, the example of light and so forth reaching its destination is likewise unestablished.
The Master of the Treatise further refutes [the opponent's position] by means of an analogy:
"Just as the Vedas and so forth are distinct from the bodies of the officiating priests,
the aggregates (skandhas) should likewise be distinct from the self."
How can it be said that they are not different?
The body of old age and the body of illness each differ from the body in its previous state;

likewise, the aggregates (skandhas) and the person (pudgala) should also be different. If you say that the small body or the beautiful body transforms into [another] body, [then the same logic applies].
This would then be identical to the Sāṃkhya doctrine of transformation (*pariṇāma*).
Since the Sāṃkhya theory of transformation has already been refuted above,
the examples cited by them— such as the birth of a sacrificer— are unestablished.
Furthermore, regarding the admission that the arising of the aggregates is distinct from the existence of the aggregates,
the Master of the Treatise refutes this again:
he maintains that it is the newly arisen aggregates, and not the *pudgala*, [that arise].
If that is so, you must certainly admit that the self is distinct from the aggregates and is permanent;
how then can your own school claim that it is not distinct from the aggregates and is not permanent? Furthermore, the self is a single entity, whereas the nature of the aggregates consists of five.
"Why do you not say that the self is different from the aggregates?
From 'the primary elements are four' up to 'not different from the primary elements,' the Vātsīputrīya school counters with this reprimand."
The proponent of the treatise [asserts]: "The self is one;
the aggregates are five;
the life-principle is distinct from the aggregates; and the great elements are four."
Since derived matter is a single entity,
how can it be said that derived matter is not different from the primary elements?
This is a fault in their own school's tenet.
The author of the treatise replies:
"This is a fault of that school's own tenets;
it does not concern my position."
What is meant by "those of that school"?
The Vātsīputrīyas newly ask:
those who maintain that the person (pudgala) is derived from the conditioned elements (bhautika-rūpa).
The Master of the Treatise replies:

The various deities such as Devaśarman maintain that the derived matter (*upādāyarūpa*) is identical to the primary elements (*mahābhūta*). If one were to follow their view, one should raise this objection:
"Just as the derived matter is identical to the four great elements, so too should the person (*pudgala*) be established as being identical to the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*)."
How can it be said that "I" am not identical to the aggregates?
[The Vātsīputrīya school] objects: if the *pudgala* is identical to the living being (*jīva*), it must be identical to the body (*śarīra*).
Regarding the observation that the questioner is either identical to or different from the self,
the Master of the Treatise answers:
This is because the questioner is an *āśraya* (basis) of the world.
The questioner maintains that there is a single internal self-substance called the "vital principle" (jīva),
and based on this, he asks the Buddha whether it is identical to or different from the body.
Since such a self does not exist at all, [the Buddha remains silent].
First, identity and difference are not established.
How can one predicate identity or difference between [the self] and the body?
It is like being unable to say that a tortoise's hair is soft or hard.

Since the hair of a tortoise fundamentally does not exist, how can one discuss whether it is hard or soft? The masters of antiquity have already explained this difficult point regarding the entanglement [of these concepts]. From "In the past...
onwards, the matters referred to are clear; as for the *āmra* tree:
He was born outside the western city walls,
not within a royal palace.
Why did the Buddha not say that the "life-principle" (jīva) does not exist at all?
The Vātsīputrīyas ask: "Is it not also the case that the Buddha did not answer whether [the person] exists or does not exist, because he considered the disposition of the questioner?
The author of the treatise replies:
Furthermore, it is because one observes the disposition of the questioner.
The questioner may, with respect to the continuity of the aggregates,
conventionally designate a "life-principle."
Based on this, he poses a question.
If the Buddha were to answer that it does not exist,
he would fall into a false view.
Therefore, the Buddha did not speak [of a self], nor did he explain the conventional designation of a "life-principle" (jīva).
This is because they have not yet realized the profound principle of dependent origination (pratītyasamutpāda) regarding all phenomena,
and are thus not vessels capable of receiving the true Dharma.
It is logically necessary that the Buddha did not teach that there is a "person" (jīva) as a mere conventional designation,
for it was so stated by the World-Honored One. Vatsa— here translated as "Calf"—
was a non-Buddhist who questioned the World-Honored One.
Whether I exist in the world or do not exist,
the Buddha does not provide a definitive answer.
If he were to declare that I exist, it would contradict the true nature of reality.
If one says that [the self] does not increase, that would further delude the ignorant;
they would then think, "I existed before, but now I am annihilated," and thus give rise to the view of annihilationism.
Compared to the delusion that clings to existence,
that nihilistic view is even more extreme; because this delusion is so heavy,
it means that by clinging to a self, one falls into the extreme of eternalism.
If one clings to the non-existence of a self, one falls into the extreme of nihilism;
clinging to existence is a minor fault,
whereas clinging to non-existence is a grave fault.
As explained at length in the sūtras:
it would be better to give rise to a view of self as large as Mount Sumeru than to give rise to a view of annihilationism even as small as a mustard seed.
Because one who gives rise to the view of self is able to cultivate various virtues, this [view] is lighter than that;
because one who gives rise to the view of annihilationism is able to commit manifold evils, this [view] is heavier than that.
Therefore, the Buddha did not teach "no-self" for their sake. It is based on such meanings that are inexpressible.
In the Sautrāntika school, Kumāralāta has these verses:
the first verse provides a general statement, while the subsequent verse offers a detailed explanation: "One who contemplates is wounded by views."
He does not speak of existence, lest he destroy all wholesome karma;
nor does he speak of non-existence, for this reason the Buddha teaches the True Dharma.
Neither too hurried nor too slow, it is like a tigress carrying her cub in her mouth.
One must find the proper balance between urgency and relaxation;
if too urgent, one is harmed, and if too relaxed, one falls. If the Buddha were to say that there is a self...
One who clings to the existence of a true self is wounded by views;
for views are like sharp fangs capable of harming a person.
This explains the first line. If the Buddha were to say that there is no self...
He negates the conventional self as being non-existent, thereby destroying the "seed of karma.
Just as a son is called a "son of good karma" when he performs virtuous deeds, this explains the second line.
Based on this principle, the Master of the Treatise now speaks another verse to restate the preceding meaning.
Within these four verses,
the first two lines correspond to the preceding [section] on how the life-principle (*jīva*) is neither identical to nor different from the body.
The subsequent six lines correspond to the preceding [section] on why the Buddha did not state that the life-principle is entirely non-existent.
As for the statement that "the Buddha does not speak because they fall into false views," this refers to the six statements;
the first two lines constitute a general summary verse.

The final four lines provide a specific explanation: fearing that the questioner might deny the conventional self (*prajñapti-ātman*), the Buddha likewise did not say that the life-principle (*jīva*) is entirely non-existent;
rather, he meant that within the continuum of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*).
There is karma and there is its fruit, which are conventionally designated as a "living being.
If the Buddha were to say that no living being exists,
he fears that the questioner might negate even this conventional designation of a living being.

Furthermore, because it would be non-existent, one does not say that it is utterly non-existent. In the third verse, since they were previously unable to comprehend the principle of dependent origination, they were not vessels for receiving the true Dharma;
therefore, the provisional existence [of phenomena] was not taught to them.

The Blessed One did not state that there is a provisional life-principle within the aggregates because he perceived that the questioner lacked the capacity to understand the principle of dependent origination and empty reality.

Therefore, he did not explain it to him. The fourth verse explains that the Buddha, observing the differences in the inclinations of Vatsa as described in the preceding *Vatsasūtra*, was asked by him whether the self exists or does not exist.
The Buddha did not answer them regarding the existence of a self or the non-existence of a self.
For what reason did he not provide a definitive teaching (avyākṛta) on whether the world is eternal and so forth?
Thus asks the Vātsīputrīya school.
For what reason did the World-Honored One not provide a definitive answer regarding the four propositions concerning whether the world is eternal and so forth?
This was because he considered the questioner’s disposition and determined that he was not a fit recipient for such a definitive teaching;
the Master of the Treatise likewise considered that the questioner was a heterodox person (āśaya).
If the questioner conceives of a self as the world and asks the Blessed One,
"Is the world eternal, or is it non-eternal?"

"Is it both eternal and non-eternal? Is it neither eternal nor non-eternal? Since the questioner [presupposes] a real self and a world, and yet the essence of a self does not exist at all, none of these four answers are reasonable.

Therefore, the Buddha did not answer. Furthermore, if one were to insist that the five aggregates of birth and death are all termed "the world," the Buddha’s answers in the four sūtras would likewise be irrational;
thus, he also did not answer. This is because if the world were eternal, it could not be brought to an end.
One would not attain nirvāṇa;

for if it were impermanent, it would simply cease of its own accord, rather than being realized through the attainment of nirvāṇa by means of the diligent cultivation of the path through effort. If one answers that it is both permanent and impermanent, [the fault remains].
If one answers that within the cycle of birth and death, it must be certain that one portion of sentient beings will not attain nirvana,
while another portion of sentient beings will personally realize parinirvāṇa, yet [the Tathāgata] is neither eternal nor non-eternal— then [this is the case].
This world, too, would consequently not attain nirvāṇa, yet it is not that it does not attain nirvāṇa.
Furthermore, since it is explained that [the world] is not impermanent, it would follow that it does not attain nirvāṇa.

If it were not eternal, then it would follow that one could not fail to attain nirvāṇa; yet "neither eternal nor non-eternal" is a definitive contradiction and thus becomes mere frivolous proliferation (*prapañca*).
How, then, could this constitute an answer to the question? Nevertheless, by relying on the Noble Path, one may indeed attain parinirvāṇa.

Therefore, all four types of categorical answers are unreasonable. For example, when the non-Buddhist Nirgrantha Jñātiputra held a sparrow in his hand and asked the Buddha whether it was dead or alive, the Buddha knew that his mind was not fixed [on a definitive answer].
If he answers, "Dead," they will release him alive;
if he answers, "Alive," [they will kill him].
He then desisted from killing;
therefore, the Buddha did not answer.
This case is likewise.
Regarding the statement "because all four positions, such as having a limit, would entail fallacies," the Master of the Treatise provides an analogical explanation:
if one were to ask whether the world has a limit and so forth, according to these four propositions.
The Buddha likewise did not provide a prediction [of their attainment],
because all [theories] such as permanence and so forth share the same fault.
How do we know that these four meanings are identical to permanence and the rest?
The Vātsīputrīyas ask:
Since there are non-Buddhists whose views on this matter are identical to those previously mentioned,
the Master replies:
There was a non-Buddhist named Uttika—
meaning "The Able Speaker" in this language—
who first asked about the four propositions regarding whether the world has an end and so forth.
The World-Honored One did not answer.
Later, employing a skillful means, he artfully questioned the World-Honored One:
"Are all things such as the permanence of the world able to bring about liberation through the Noble Path?"
"Is it only one part that attains deliverance, while another part does not? Venerable Ānanda was standing by the Buddha's side;
the Buddha then said to him, "You have already asked the World-Honored One about this matter."
Regarding the four views concerning whether the world is finite or infinite and so forth, for what reason are these now rephrased as the four views concerning permanence, impermanence, and so forth?

He asked the World-Honored One again: "Is having limits impermanent? Is being limitless permanent? Is both having limits and being limitless both permanent and impermanent? Or is it neither having limits nor being limitless?"
"Neither eternal nor non-eternal"; thus it is known that the latter four meanings are the same as the former.
Furthermore, for what reason are there the four [views] beginning with "existence" (*bhava*)?
This is the question posed by the Vātsīputrīya school.
Furthermore, for what reason did the World-Honored One not declare that after the Tathāgata’s death he exists,
does not exist, both exists and does not exist, or neither exists nor does not exist?
"Is it not the four propositions, such as 'neither existent nor non-existent'?
This is the Master of the Treatise’s response, given because he observes that the question arises based on the specific intent of the interlocutor.
Furthermore, it is because he observes the disposition of the questioner;
for the questioner, having falsely imagined that the self which is already liberated is what is called the Tathāgata,
has posed this question.
Because there is no real self, the Buddha did not provide an answer.
Now, one should interrogate [the opponent] regarding whether [the self] also exists after death.
The Master of the Treatise (śāstrakāra) counters with this inquiry.
Now, one should interrogate the teacher of the Vātsīputrīya school who maintains that there is a self:
for what reason did the Buddha declare that there is a present self?
Regarding the statement that the Tathāgata did not declare whether a self exists after death because he feared falling into the error of eternalism,
the Vātsīputrīyas respond as follows:
Fearing the error of falling into [the view of] permanence, the Buddha did not provide a prediction.
If that is so, for what reason did he go as far as saying [he was] "not omniscient"? Thus the Master of the Treatise raises an objection.
If that is so, for what reason did the Buddha predict the future lives of Maitreya Bodhisattva and his disciples?
Would this not entail the fault of falling into the extreme of eternalism?
Furthermore, if you say that the Buddha previously saw me,
but no longer sees me after he has entered parinirvāṇa,
and thus does not declare my existence because he does not know it— this is refuted by the fact that it denies the Great Teacher’s possession of all-encompassing wisdom (*sarvajñatā*).

Because [the Buddha] cannot know or understand a self that is liberated, you should perhaps admit that he did not provide a definitive answer because the substance of a self is entirely non-existent; yet, if you claim that the Buddha did perceive a liberated self, [you are mistaken].
As for the reason it is not so stated: [the opponent] objects that this would entail the fault of being separate from the aggregates;
for one might then conceive that while the aggregates are extinguished upon entering nirvāṇa, the self does not cease.
Furthermore, there is the fault of [the self] being permanent. How can you say that the self is neither different from nor identical to the five aggregates?

If you say that the self which has already attained liberation is such that the Buddha’s seeing it or not seeing it cannot be described, we refute this by saying: one should then pose the following inquiry.
It cannot be said that the Buddha is omniscient;
nor can it be said that the Buddha is not omniscient. Alternatively, one should pose the challenge: "Is the Buddha omniscient?"
Because they do not see me,
it cannot be said that the Buddha is not omniscient;
because they see me, [it can be so said].
If it is argued that [the self] truly exists because it is clearly stated [in scripture],
the Master of the Treatise again restates that position to refute it:
"If you claim that there is a self because the Sūtra says, 'dwelling with thorough discernment'..."
Regarding the statement, "Those who dogmatically cling to non-self fall into the position of wrong views," the refutation says:
This does not constitute a valid proof.
That sutra also states that those who dogmatically cling to the existence of a self fall into the realm of wrong views;
therefore, one should not conceive of a self. Thus he spoke to the Dharma Master.

The Master of the Treatise maintains that the clinging to the existence or non-existence of a self is subsumed under the two extreme views: if one clings to the existence of a self, one falls into the extreme of eternalism;
if one clings to the non-existence of a self, one falls into the extreme of nihilism.
The teaching of that master is profoundly reasonable,
for it avoids the extremes of eternalism and nihilism by not clinging to existence or non-existence;
this is because it is clearly stated in the earlier Bāhitika Sūtra.
An introductory citation is presented to establish the proof.
The Vātsīputrīyas raise an objection: "If it is certain that there is no reaching [of the object] by the *pudgala*..."
Citing scriptural authority to establish the point: If there were definitively no self,
it could be asked, "Who is it that transmigrates through birth and death?"
Because it would not be subject to transmigration.
The Sūtra states that sentient beings are shrouded by ignorance and bound by craving.
"Because there is a flowing through birth and death, there must certainly be a self.
[The opponent asks: "Furthermore, how does this [self] transmigrate through birth and death?
Thus the Master of the Treatise questions.
"How, then, does this self transmigrate through birth and death by abandoning the preceding aggregates and taking up subsequent aggregates?
Thus the Vātsīputrīya replies.
Because I abandon the preceding aggregates and take up subsequent aggregates,
it is said that "I" transmigrate through birth and death.
Such is the tenet of this doctrine regarding the transmigration through birth and death.
The master of the treatise points out that this is refuted by the same arguments as before,
and then restates the correct position:
just as a fire consuming a vast plain, though it perishes moment by moment, [continues its progression].
However, because there is an uninterrupted continuity from the preceding to the succeeding,
one speaks of a "transmigration" proceeding from here to there.
Thus, this collection of aggregates is conventionally designated as a "sentient being."
With craving and grasping as conditions,
the resultant fruit arises and continues in an uninterrupted succession;
this is called the circulation of birth and death.
If it is held that there are only the aggregates (skandhas) up to the point of being called "one with excellent eyes," the Vātsīputrīyas raise an objection:
if there are only the aggregates and no self (ātman), [how can there be such a designation]?
Why is it that the Buddha says, "In the past, I was the Teacher of the World"?
Since he has spoken these words— that in the past he was the Teacher—
it is clearly known that there is a self.
Regarding the question, "What fault is there in this statement? the Master of the Treatise (śāstrakāra) counters with a reprimand:
"Because the aggregates (skandha) are each distinct."
The Vātsīputrīyas reply:
The aggregates of the present and the aggregates of the past are each distinct from one another in their prior and subsequent states.
If there were no self,
how could it be said, "I, who am now, was the Teacher of the World in the past"?
If that is so, what then is this thing?
The Master of the Treatise asks:
"If that is so, then what is this thing [that you say]: 'In the past, I was the Teacher of the World'?"
Regarding the term "person" (pudgala),
the Vātsīputrīyas reply:
"The 'I' of the past is the very same as the 'I' of the present who previously performed that act of burning."
The Master of the Treatise objects:
If the self of the past were identical to the self of the present,
its essence would have to be eternally abiding.
How can it be said that the self is not eternal?
To resolve this objection and accord with the sutras, it is therefore stated: "The self of the present was the teacher in the past."

To clarify that the past and the present constitute a single continuous succession (*saṃtāna*) by way of designation: it is like saying, "This fire once burned that object," which also clarifies that the fire of the past and the fire of the present time are one and the same fire within a single continuous succession.
Therefore, it is said that this fire once burned that object.
If it is claimed that [the self] is definitively far removed from liberation,
the Master of the Treatise again restates that position and refutes it.
Having set forth the calculation,
the correct refutation is established by citing scriptural authority. If this is so:
This constitutes slandering the Buddha,
being bound by afflictions,
and remaining far removed from liberation.
If it is argued that these words addressed to me are meaningless,
the Master again restates the refutation:
"If you claim that in my case, although the view of self arises together with self-love, there is no bondage of love."
The refutation says:
These words are meaningless. Why is that?
The Vātsīputrīya raises an objection:
"Regarding the statement that one develops the 'sore of views' within the context of non-self," the Master replies:
If you maintain that one might give rise to self-love by erroneously imputing a self within what is not-self, rather than within a real self, we refute this:
such a statement lacks any rational proof.
Therefore, that Vātsīputrīya,
within the Buddha’s teaching, lacks any causal basis;
he has suddenly and arbitrarily given rise to the pustule of the view of self.
"In this way, there is a class [of views] that leads to the fault of never attaining liberation.
By concluding his refutation of the Vātsīputrīyas, the Master [Vasubandhu] incidentally demonstrates that other [views] are likewise incorrect.
In this way, one class of the Vātsīputrīyas maintains that there exists an inexpressible *pudgala*. Furthermore,
there is another class of outsiders who hold the view of emptiness (*śūnyatādṛṣṭi*).
To categorically deny that all phenomena possess any intrinsic nature is one extreme;
meanwhile, non-Buddhist schools such as the Sāṃkhyas and Vaiśeṣikas cling to the existence of a distinct, true self-nature. All such views are irrational.
None can avoid the fault of having no liberation.
As for how all categories [of beings] could possibly possess recollective knowledge,
the Vātsīputrīya school asks.
If the self-entity were entirely non-existent in every respect,
then a mind that perishes moment by moment would [be unable to] [cognize] objects previously experienced or those that are distant yet similar.
How can one recollect?
How can one cognize through memory?
An object from the past that resembles the present is called a "similar object."
Regarding the statement that "thus one recollects and knows the arising of distinctions in the mind," the Master of the Treatise replies:
"One recollects in this way."
Thus it is known through such a record:
from within one's own continuum,
there exists a seed perfumed by the mental representation of an object of memory, which is termed the "aspect-class of the object of memory."
This type of seed, which is a specific functional capacity within the mind, is called a "differentiation of the mind.
Subsequent recollection and cognition arise from this seed— which consists of the mental image (*saṃjñā*) of the object—
produced by a specific functional capacity within the mind.
The Sautrāntika school maintains that recollection and cognition do not possess a separate substantial entity;
rather, they arise from seeds of the category of objects of thought produced within the continuum of the body.
Furthermore, they explain such recollective cognition as arising from seeds of the category of objects of thought within the internal continuum of the body.
The object (ālambana) pertains to both locations.
This text should have spoken only of the category of "recollection" (smṛti);
as for its mention of "perception" (saṃjñā), [it is because]...
The conceptualization (saṃjñā) is separately designated because it is predominant. As for why it does not mention the categories of objects known,
it is because cognition is induced by mindfulness (smṛti), and thus it is not mentioned separately.
Therefore, the subsequent treatise states:

"By the power of this recollection, there arises subsequent cognition (*pūrvānubhūta-jñāna*). Furthermore, it is explained that recollection arises from the category of the object remembered, while subsequent cognition arises from the category of the object of conceptualization (*saṃjñā*).
Because the Sautrāntika school knows that there is no separate entity [for the seeds],
these seeds of conceptualization are perfumed within the mind;
this specific functional capacity is termed "differentiation of the mind."
Regarding the manifestation of recollection:
one knows from the seed that it arises from that [seed].
Furthermore, as for the initial recollection up until its immediate production:
The Vātsīputrīyas ask: regarding the two types, recollection (*smṛti*) and recognition (*pratyabhijñā*), first,
from what kind of mental seed-differentiation does recollection arise?
The preceding moment ceases without interval,
and the succeeding moment arises without interval;
according to the Sautrāntika school, cause and effect exist at distinct times, one preceding the other.
Therefore, because a subsequent recollection arises from the seeds of a preceding thought, this question is posed.
As for the phrase "because there is a capacity [to reach] that which has an object-condition," this is the Master’s response.
First is the arising through recollection;
second is arising by way of conditions;
third is arising by way of causes.
First, regarding arising through conditions:
mindfulness arises conditioned by the power of attention directed toward that past object which serves as its condition.
The past object and the object of mindfulness are called "similar" because they are equal;
by the power of that similar object acting as a condition, mindfulness arises.
Alternatively, one may see the present object as being similar to the past.
Because it is able to give rise to a recollection that takes a former object as its condition, it is said to be "similar.
Alternatively, because the preceding moment of consciousness resembles the subsequent one, it serves as the condition for its arising.
As for the phrase "the mental state is continuous": [it refers to this].
This refers to the conditions such as attention belonging to one's own continuum,
thereby distinguishing it from those of other continua;
or, it refers to the arising of mindfulness through the causal relationship of mutual dependence.
Regarding the phrase "perception and so forth," the term "and so forth" includes craving and other factors.
First, recollection arises due to the power of conditions such as the mental attention directed toward that [object] which exists as its objective support. Second, it arises from causes.
Because the body that serves as the basis is not impaired by conditions such as grief, sorrow, or distraction,
the power of the cause for the differentiation of the mind gives rise to the first recollection.
Although such conditions as mental attention (manasikāra) exist for the arising of recollection,
if there were no cause consisting of a specific differentiation of the mind (citta-viśeṣa),
one would lack the capacity to cultivate this recollection.
Although there exist such causes for the differentiation of the mind,
if conditions such as mental attention (manasikāra) are absent,
there is likewise no possibility of cultivating mindfulness.
One must possess the two types of power— causes and conditions—
in order to be able to cultivate;
thus, various recollections arise.
However, because it arises through the power of these causes and conditions,
one does not perceive any other real self apart from these two types of causes and conditions that possesses the capacity for recollection.
"How can there be a principle of recollection based on a different mind?
This is the objection raised by the Vātsīputrīyas: "If there is no self..."
How could it be that an object seen by one mind at a previous time can be remembered by a different mind at a later time?
It is not the case that Devadatta’s mind can remember an object previously seen by another mind.
Later, when Śāriputra was performing the ritual of offering, he had a recollection based on reason.
Devadatta—whose name in Sanskrit is *Devadatta*—is so called because he was given by the gods (*deva*).
He begged from them, and thus they gave him [the name] "God-given."
He was named after the place from which he was requested;
thus he is called Devadatta.
Yajñadatta is the Sanskrit term for "Sicou" (祠授).
Because he obtained a son by praying to the heavens during a sacrificial rite,
he is called "Cishou" (Sacrificial Bestowal).
This is an Indian name.
Devadatta, Yajñadatta, and others of their kind are indeed numerous; therefore,
they are cited specifically.
Regarding the objection that "this difficulty is irrational because one knows [the arising] through a subsequent cognition," the Master replies:
"This objection is irrational."
Because they are not related to one another.
That is to say, the two minds of Devadatta and Yajñadatta, when viewed in relation to each other, lack the nature of cause and effect,
because they are mutually unrelated.
An object previously perceived by the mind of Devadatta cannot be recollected by the mind of Yajñadatta;
this is not like the nature of cause and effect within the single continuum of one person's body.
Because they are connected in succession:
the preceding mind has previously seen,
and the succeeding mind is able to remember.
We do not say that a different mind perceives an object and a different mind is able to remember it;
rather, because the preceding and succeeding moments in the continuum belong to the same category,
the preceding mind of the same class is able to remember.
Thereafter, the past mind that took that object as its condition perfumes it,
forming a seed; from this seed,
the consciousness capable of recollection is induced at the present time.
That is to say, as previously stated:
first, the continuity;
second, the transformation.
Due to the power of the threefold differentiation,
the recollection arises;
by virtue of this power of the previously accumulated seeds of recollection.
There arises a subsequent thought that remembers and cognizes [the former].
Since the self (*ātman*) does not exist, who is it that is able to remember?
Thus asks the Vātsīputrīya school.
Since the self-entity does not exist,
who is it that can remember?
What is the meaning of "can remember"?
The author of the treatise asks in return:
"Is it by means of mindfulness that the object is apprehended?
The Vātsīputrīyas answer.
"Is this grasping of an object not different from the thought? Thus the Master of the Treatise further rebukes [the opponent], saying:
"Although it is not different from the thought, it is nevertheless due to the agent."
The Vātsīputrīyas reply:
Although the apprehension of that object is not distinct from the cognition itself,
it is only through the power of the person (*pudgala*) that the cognition is able to apprehend the object.
The "agent" is precisely what is referred to as the one capable of recollection;
the Master of the Treatise states his own position to provide a thorough explanation,
identifying this agent with the previously mentioned cause of memory.
This is not a real self; rather,
it refers to the specific seeds within the continuum of mind that belong to the category of memory,
which enable subsequent results to recollect and apprehend objects.
The preceding thought, acting as the cause, is designated as the "agent.
However, it is commonly said in the world that "Caitra remembers."
This Caitra is not a real self;
the name "Caitra" is conventionally established upon the continuum of the aggregates as a provisional self.
With the seeds perfumed by the previously perceived mind serving as the cause,
the subsequent fruit of recollection arises.
Regarding the arising of this fruit of recollection:
The name *Citra* is established upon the fruit of recollection;
therefore, it is said that based on this principle, he is called "the one capable of recollecting.
*Citra* is the name of a star.
It appears in the first month;
the first month is named after this star because it is born in this month.
It is named after this star.
If one who clings to a self is born under this moon,
they are said to have a real self named Caitra.
Therefore, we now provide a comprehensive explanation.
[The opponent asks: "If the self-substance does not exist, whose is this cognition?
This is the question posed by the Vātsīputrīya school.
If there were a self-entity,
it could be recollected as "this belongs to me," thereby becoming the object of the sixth grammatical case.
If the self-essence does not exist,
whose is this mindfulness?
For what purpose is the sixth case used here?
The master of the treatise asks in return:
"This sixth sound belongs to the category of that which is dependent upon or subordinate to something else.
The Vātsīputrīya school answers.
Regarding the question of how an object belongs to a particular owner,
the Master of the Treatise further inquires:
"This is like a cow or other such property belonging to Caitra."
The Vātsīputrīyas reply:
This is like the case where objects such as cattle belong to a person named Caitra;
how then is he the owner of the cattle?
The master of the treatise asks again:
"Regarding those who have attained mastery based on that [attainment]," the Vātsīputrīyas reply.
This means that because Citra possesses mastery over various matters such as riding, milking, and employing [the animals], he is called the "owner of the oxen.
Where, then, should one seek the "master of mindfulness" (smṛtimān)?
The Master of the Treatise asks again:
"In what place do you wish to employ mindfulness as a servant,
such that you diligently apply skillful means to seek a 'self' who is the master of mindfulness?"
Regarding the statement that "one directs mindfulness toward the object of contemplation," the Vātsīputrīyas ask:
for what purpose is mindfulness employed?
The master of the treatise asks again:
"Is it for the sake of causing mindfulness to arise?
The Vātsīputrīyas reply.
"How marvelous! The Sovereign has gone so far as to cause practitioners to harbor such thoughts.
The Master of the Treatise further rebukes him:
"How marvelous! The Sovereign utters words devoid of reason."
"Rather, let me be born for the sake of this [mind] and employ this thought," or alternatively, "rather, let me be for the sake of this thought.
Furthermore, he establishes two further points of inquiry to determine:
"Moreover, how shall I employ this thought?"
It is for the sake of causing mindfulness to arise and for the sake of causing mindfulness to proceed;
since mindfulness has no [independent] proceeding, it should simply be caused to arise.
The Vātsīputrīya replies:
"If it is because the name 'master' reaches [the person], yet that [name] is not separate from the cause.
The Master of the Treatise (the author of the *Abhidharmakośa*) demonstrates the correct principle.
If that which causes mindfulness to arise is called the "master of mindfulness," then the cause of mindfulness is the "master" to which it belongs,
and the result of mindfulness is the "possessor" to which it belongs.
Because the power of mindfulness as the cause is predominant,
it causes the fruit of mindfulness to arise;
therefore, the cause is called the "master."
Since the fruit exists at the time of its arising by virtue of being possessed by the cause, it is "belonging to" that cause;
thus, the arising itself is sufficient to serve as the master of memory.
Why then trouble oneself to establish a self (*ātman*) as the master of memory? It is simply the collection of the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*) of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*).
This is the conventional designation of dependent origination;
the continuity of a single category before and after is the conventional designation of connection.
In the world, it is conventionally designated that this is the ox Caitra;
the name "Caitra" is established as the owner of the ox.
This very owner of the ox is the continuum of the ox.
Because he moves from here to there, being born in different locations,
and because he is the cause of transformation and birth, he is called "the owner of the ox" (Gopi-pati).
In this context, there is no single, substantial self who is the "owner of the ox" Gopi.
Furthermore, there is no real self that is the "cow";
it is merely a conventional designation.
Therefore, it is said that the owner of the cow is likewise not separate from its causes.
The ox that is driven and employed is called the "fruit";
the owner of the ox who is able to drive and employ it is called the "cause.
This is the same as the previous case where the master of mindfulness is not separate from the cause of mindfulness.
"Recollection means that one should know as it truly is when recollecting"—
this is an illustrative explanation clarifying the initial stage of recollection.
Since this is the meaning [of the former], it should be understood that the meaning of the subsequent *anusmṛti* (recollection) and *vijñapti* (informative cognition) is likewise;
both are to be understood according to the principles of recollection and informative cognition.
Who is it that can fully comprehend this?
The consciousnesses of others should likewise be explained by this same analogy.
While the general categories are largely the same, they are not without distinction. Furthermore, as for the causes and conditions of consciousness, they differ from those previously mentioned.
This refers to the six sense faculties, the six objects, and so forth;
one should understand this accordingly. Alternatively, the seeds of consciousness are called the cause, while the faculties and so forth are called the conditions.
Recollection and recognition occur only on the mental level; therefore, they are distinguished from discernment (*vijñāna*).
As for those who say that [recollection] extends up to "the ability to comprehend" and so forth:
Below this, within the section on specific refutations, is the second major heading: the refutation of the Sāṃkhya teachers.
Within that:
First, the exposition of the school's tenets;
second, the formal refutation;
third, the resolution of objections. This is the first: the exposition of the school's tenets.
The Sāṃkhyas say:
"The self certainly exists,
because the performance of an action necessarily depends upon an agent."
This refers to various functional activities.
That which depends on functional activity is,
for example, like the functional activity performed by Devadatta.
"I must certainly wait for Heaven to bestow this upon me;
I shall employ these practices because Heaven has bestowed this name upon me."
If it is argued that all functions such as the discernment performed by consciousness and so forth must depend upon a real self-substance as their basis for that discernment and so on,
one should now challenge them: "In that case, the same would apply to consciousness itself being able to discern."
This is the second correct refutation.
The author of the treatise refutes [the opponent] by saying:
"Now, one should interrogate them."
What is this "Devadatta"?
If it were a real self (*ātman*), it has already been refuted as before.
If it is a conventional person (*pudgala*) established upon the five aggregates (*skandha*), it is not a single entity.
Because this name "Devadatta" is conventionally established upon the continuity of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*),
just as one speaks of Devadatta as a "goer" by way of such a convention,
so too should it be understood that consciousness (*vijñāna*) performs the act of discerning.
It is merely with respect to a conventional designation of a "self" that we speak of one who "understands";
there is no separate, real self.
By what reasoning can it be said that Devadatta is the one who walks?
The following is the third section,
which addresses the Sāṃkhya objection:
"If there is no real self..."

The author of the treatise answers the question: "On what principle is it said that Devadatta can walk, such that this same expression is also applied to his reaching [a destination] in a single moment?"
That is to say, conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*), which arise and perish moment by moment,
are conventionally established through conditions and are not distinct from their continuity.
This is a conceptual construct of continuity.
The name "Devadatta" is established upon these two types of constructs;
therein, the deluded person clings to it as a single, substantial self-entity.
This conventional self serves as the cause for the arising of a body within its own continuum in a different location;
the arising in a different place at a subsequent moment is called "volitional formation" (*saṃskāra*),
and the preceding moment which acts as the cause is likewise termed a "volitional formation."
Based on this principle, it is said that Devadatta can walk,
just as one speaks of a lamp-flame walking or of a sound being transmitted to call a person.
From this point to that other point, there is a continuity through different locations;

it is with reference to this that the world says that "flame" and "sound" can travel. Thus, the body of Devadatta in a preceding moment can serve as the cause for the consciousness of a subsequent moment.
The world also says that Devadatta can cognize; however, the noble ones also speak in this way—
saying "Devadatta can cognize"— in order to conform to worldly conventions of speech.
Regarding the statement in the Sūtra that "the various consciousnesses reach [their objects] to perform their functions," the Sāṃkhya asks:
"The Sūtra states that the various consciousnesses are able to cognize their respective objects."
"What function does consciousness perform with respect to its object?
It performs no action at all, yet it is called 'the cognizer of the object.
Thus the author of the treatise answers.
Consciousness performs no action whatsoever upon its object;
it is merely said to "cognize" the object because it arises resembling it,
just as a barley sprout and so forth are said to "repay" the barley seed and so forth.
Although there is nothing produced,
it arises as if from a cause and is thus called "repaying the cause.
In this same way, although the arising of consciousness involves no productive action, [it is said to arise].
Because it resembles the object, it is called "cognizing the object.
How does it resemble the object?
The Sāṃkhya asks.
Regarding the statement, "The same applies to the consciousness which, bearing that aspect, reaches [the object] and is able to cognize it," the Master of the Treatise replies:
It means that upon the consciousness which acts as the subject (ālambaka), there appears the aspect (ākāra) of the objective sphere (ālambana) being perceived.
Just as when taking blue color as an object, it appears bearing the aspect of blue upon the consciousness that takes it as its object; because the consciousness resembles the object,
it is said that the consciousness can take it as its object.
Just as a mirror reflects an object and produces an image that resembles the original object and is capable of illuminating it,
so too do the various consciousnesses arise in dependence upon the sense faculties.
Because consciousness lacks the characteristics of a faculty and does not resemble a faculty,
it is not called a "cognizing faculty," but is merely called a "cognizer of objects. Alternatively, when consciousness arises in a continuous succession with respect to an object...
When a subsequent consciousness arises with a preceding consciousness as its cause,
it is said that the preceding causal consciousness is "that which cognizes";
this is likewise without fault.
Because in the world one speaks of an agent with respect to a cause;
for example, as it is said in the world that "the bell or drum can sound.
Since they are able to produce the effect of sounding, the capacity to sound is attributed to the cause.
Just as a lamp can illuminate without there being a separate illuminator,
so too consciousness can cognize without there being a separate cognizer.
Based on what principle does the author of the *Śāstra* state that the question regarding the number of lamps should likewise apply to the continuity of flames?
The author of the treatise answers:
The designation "lamp" is applied metaphorically to a continuum of fire;
when this lamp arises in succession from one location to another, it moves from here to there.
It is called the "lamp-like progression," yet there is no separate agent of progression.
In this same way, the name "consciousness" is conventionally established upon the continuum of the mind.
When it arises with respect to diverse objects such as blue or yellow,
it is said to be "capable of cognizing.
This is because, according to the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra*, a single momentary consciousness lacks the capacity to cognize.
One must understand that when the continuity [of consciousness] arises with respect to a distinct object in a subsequent moment,
this continuity is conventionally designated as "consciousness" and is said to be "capable of cognizing."
Alternatively, just as in the case of form, there is the arising of form after the existence of form,
and the abiding of form; and herein, there is no separate entity called "existence" or "abider"—
so too should the principle that consciousness is capable of cognizing be understood.
Regarding the absence of a distinct cognizer:
if a subsequent consciousness arises in the manner of a sprout, stem, leaf, and so forth,
this is the Sāṃkhya objection.
The meaning of the objection here is as follows:
because there is a self (*ātman*),
and "self" carries the sense of being autonomous (*svatantra*).
If one wishes to obtain this dharma, that dharma must first arise;
this dharma arises later.
For this reason, it does not always remain identical.
Regarding the lack of fixed sequence: if a subsequent consciousness arises, it arises from the preceding consciousness and not from a self.
Briefly stated, there are two difficulties.
First, for what reason does a subsequent consciousness not always resemble its preceding [consciousness], such as wholesome or defiled consciousness?
Second, since both arise from consciousness,
for what reason do they not necessarily arise in a fixed sequence, like a sprout first, then a stem, then a leaf, arising in succession?
Regarding the statement that "all conditioned phenomena possess distinctions up to external conditions for the body," the Master of the Treatise answers:

Regarding the establishment of "alteration" (*anyathātva*) as distinct [from other characteristics]: it is simply another name for "alteration.

Because what follows must differ from what precedes it, they are not similar.

Furthermore, the continuity of all mental states also possesses a fixed sequence.
If that subsequent mind is to arise immediately after this mind,
then that mind will necessarily arise following this mind,
as explained in the section on the mutual arising of the twenty types of minds.
Furthermore, within the continuity of the mind,
only those moments whose characteristics and aspects are even slightly similar in their preceding and succeeding phases are able to produce one another,
because they do not give rise to other types of mental seeds.
Just as in the case of a woman’s mind,
there may arise, without interruption, either a mind of physical and mental adornment or a defiled mind.
When thoughts of that husband arise,

from these various minds...

subsequently, a female mind arises again.
Such is the female mind.
Subsequently, the defilements and purities that arise possess the capacity for production;
apart from these, all else lacks the capacity for production.
Because of the distinction of lineage (*gotra*),
it is possible for many minds to arise in immediate succession within the female mind;
however, among those many minds—
Alternatively, that which has previously arisen frequently, or that which arises clearly and proximately, arises first and not others.
Furthermore, another interpretation states: "Alternatively, that which has previously arisen frequently..."
Either that which was previously understood, or that which previously arose nearby; it arises first and not others.
There is an interpretation that if something has previously arisen repeatedly, it arises first.
Regarding the arising from within the arising of numbers, it arises with clarity;
regarding the arising from within clarity, it arises as immediate.
For this reason, it arises first and not otherwise, because the power of cultivation of such a mind is so strong.
Except when, at the moment of arising,
the body is damaged by external conditions such that the specific distinction cannot arise; another interpretation holds that this refers only to the body at the moment of arising.
When encountering external conditions, there is a distinction between good and evil.
Upon meeting such superior conditions, that which has arisen becomes indeterminate.
For all those whose power of cultivation reaches the point of producing its own fruit, [the result follows].

There are those who are inferior or superior.

Because this mind possesses the characteristics of duration and change,
it subsequently becomes gradually inferior to what preceded it;
such is the characteristic of duration and change.
Within the continuous arising of the distinct classes of fruits cultivated in superior, middling, and inferior degrees,
because [the superior fruit] is most conducive [to its own production], it does not constantly produce its own superior fruit.
There are those who produce inferior fruits;
regarding the various categories of mind that are easily understood,
the author of the treatise modestly defers to the World-Honored One.

Based on this principle, there is a verse in the Sautrāntika school which says: Within a single eye of a peacock’s feather, whether blue, yellow, red, white, or otherwise, there exists the causal characteristic of all varieties.

Knowing these characteristics is not within the domain of other forms of knowledge; it is known only by the Omniscient One. This is an illustration of the difficult by means of the easy.
It is already difficult to understand the causes for the differentiation of colors in a single peacock’s eye;
how much more so would it be easy to understand the distinctions among the causes and conditions of the formless phenomena of the mind and mental factors?
Regarding the passage from "A certain class of non-Buddhists... all [arise] from me":
the following section constitutes the third major heading of the detailed refutations, wherein the Vaiśeṣika teacher is refuted.

When various minds arise,
they all proceed from me,

this section below is the second part, the actual refutation.

these two difficulties are most pressing for the Vaiśeṣika. [The first is: "If all minds arise from the self..."

for what reason does the subsequent consciousness not always resemble the preceding one,
and why do they arise in an indefinite sequence, such as sprout, stem, and leaf?

Only then would a distinct consciousness arise,
and its sequence would be indeterminate.
[The author] refutes this, saying:
This principle is certainly not so, because the conjunction of a self with form and mind is not established as a proven fact;
for the tenets of the Buddha-dharma do not admit the existence of a self that conjoins with form and mind. Furthermore, it is refuted by logical reasoning.
Now, when two things combine, there must necessarily be a limit to that combination;
it is not the case that there is no such limit.
This refers to the Vaibhāṣika masters of the Vaiśeṣika school, who explain the characteristic of conjunction (*saṃyoga*) within their own system as follows:
"Non-attainment is prior, and its subsequent attainment is called 'conjunction'. Refuting this:
"If the self were to conjoin with the mind, then because the mind has spatial limitations, the self would also have spatial limitations."
According to the Vaiśeṣika school, the self (*ātman*) is all-pervasive throughout the dharma-realm and lacks spatial limitation;
furthermore, because the self conjoins with the mind (*manas*),
and because the mind moves, the self should likewise move.
Alternatively, if the self were to conjoin with and unite with the mind, the self should likewise undergo destruction along with the mind;
yet, according to that school's tenet, both the self and the mind are eternal. Furthermore, if you claim that the essence of the self is all-pervading, [then...]
It cannot be universally conjoined.
Regarding the claim that form and mind both conjoin with a partial self, the refutation states:
"In principle, this is certainly not so."
The self-entity is one;
since there are no distinct parts within this single self-entity,
how can it be said that it unites with only one part?
It does not combine with other parts; even if one were to hypothetically grant that there is such combination,
since the essence of the self is eternal, [it could not combine].
The mind has no distinction;
it is simply one and constant.

How could there be the production of distinct cognitions when they are conjoined? Furthermore, if you attempt to defend your position by saying that distinct cognitions arise only because the self depends upon the specific discerning wisdom within the category of "qualities" (guṇa), we refute this as follows:
"To be difficult" has the same meaning as "to await.
Since the self is all-pervasive and without distinction,

"Does a distinct consciousness arise? Furthermore, if you say that a distinct consciousness arises because the mind waits for the specific activity (*carita*) within the category of qualities (*guṇa-pada*) before it can combine with the mental factors (*caitta*), then we refute this by saying:
in that case, the mind alone, by waiting for the distinctions among activities, should be able to produce the distinct consciousnesses."
"What use am I? Furthermore, [this is] a total negation:

This is like a quack physician who, when a medicine has successfully cured a chronic illness, falsely and deceitfully utters the words "Svāhā! Svāhā! as if he himself had performed the rite.

this is merely words;
there is no logical proof to establish that they exist because of a self. Moreover, if you claim that these two—mind and formations—...

there would be the fault of mutual obstruction between the self and mental formations, because they would be identical in nature to material phenomena (*rūpa-dharma*).
If it were as in that analogy,
there would also be the occasional loss of distinct residence,
because the fruit of the painted color and its support— the wall or vessel— are occasionally separate.

there is no fault of obstruction when compared to that mind or mental formations.

"It is not like a wall or a vessel being the support for that mind's formations.
